Structural basis of ligand-mediated transition to higher-order rubisco assemblies
papers.abstract: Proteins often assemble as higher order complexes, underlying a diversity of molecular structures and biological functions. The emergence of protein-protein interactions between binding partners is generally considered to be the primary driver of oligomerization. However, ligand binding has also been demonstrated to affect higher-order assembly, though this phenomenon is not widely considered as a primary driver of oligomerization. Here, we describe the mechanism by which different rubisco oligomeric states are induced via ligand binding. By expanding the phylogenetic sampling of a unique clade of rubisco, we discover a range of oligomeric responses to ligand binding across the phylogeny and identify the structural features responsible for shifts in the oligomeric state that ultimately provide a path to evolving new quaternary structures. Here, we identify a ligand-dependent mechanism giving rise to new protein assemblies, in contrast with the typical process of evolving new protein-protein interfaces directly. Our findings describe a means by which binding and entrenchment of a ligand enables an increase in structural complexity. Proteins often assemble into complexes, and while binding partners typically drive this, ligand binding can too. Here the authors show ligand binding drives distinct rubisco assemblies, revealing an evolutionary path to greater structural complexity.

papers.title: Autapse-inspired neuromorphic hardware with synapse–neuron integration for bidirectional feedback control
papers.abstract: Establishing autonomous and energy-efficient feedback control at the hardware level remains challenging because conventional systems rely on centralized processing and continuous external computation, increasing energy consumption and system complexity. Here we show a neuromorphic autapse-inspired system that enables localized and bidirectional feedback control, using thermoregulation as a representative application. An autapse is a self-synaptic connection in which a neuron feeds its output back to its own synaptic input, enabling intrinsic feedback modulation. The system integrates a solid electrolyte-based synaptic transistor capable of multiplexing multiple inputs and a bidirectional leaky integrate-and-fire artificial neuron. By feeding the neuronal output back to an additional synaptic gate, excitatory and inhibitory feedback loops are realized within a compact architecture. Using an artificial thermoregulation platform, temperature-dependent inputs bidirectionally modulate neuronal firing frequency, demonstrating biologically inspired feedback control with a compact set of neuromorphic devices for autonomous and energy-efficient systems. Inspired by autapses in the nervous system, researchers integrated artificial synapses and neurons to enhance or suppress signals through self-feedback, opening a new path toward autonomous, self-regulating hardware.

papers.title: Phylogeographic and functional assembly of population-level bacterial immunity
papers.abstract: Bacterial pangenomes provide a shared reservoir of antiphage defenses, yet the ecological and functional constraints shaping this reservoir remain unclear. Here, we combine comparative genomics of 206 Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae (Xoo) genomes with cross-infection assays of 50 strains against 36 phages and heterologous expression of 24 defense systems in a phage-sensitive Xoo chassis. The Xoo pan-defensome comprises a conserved core of 9 subtypes and a variable layer of 35 accessory and cloud subtypes structured by host phylogeography. Phages are more infectious on sympatric than allopatric hosts, consistent with local adaptation. Variable systems show stronger apparent activity than core systems, whereas resistance breadth is not predicted by defense system number. Co-expression of representative co-occurring and mutually exclusive system pairs reveals synergistic and antagonistic interactions underlying non-random repertoire assembly. Together, these findings extend the pan-immunity framework by showing that population-level immune reservoirs are shaped by both ecological structure and functional compatibility. In this study, the authors use comparative genomics and cross-infection assays to show a spatially and evolutionarily structured bacterial immune reservoir in which interactions among defense systems can reinforce or undermine phage resistance, refining the pan-immunity framework.

papers.title: SIP-enabled multi-omics reveals soil microbiome responses to drought and rehydration
papers.abstract: Soil microbial activity, and the balance of anabolic (carbon assimilating) and catabolic (CO2-releasing) processes, control the magnitude and direction of soil carbon fluxes. Soil hydration controls this activity, and with hydroclimate volatility increasing across many regions, microbial responses to drought-rewetting cycles urgently require quantification. We conducted rainfall exclusion experiments at two Mediterranean-type field sites, coupling isotope labeling with multi-omics, to link microbial growth, greenhouse gas fluxes, and the carbon sources driving both. Rehydration shortened apparent cell generation times from years to days within minutes. High-intensity drought lengthened the lag before growth resumed, yet metagenomic inference indicated post-drought enrichment of rapid-growth phenotypes. Drought and rehydration shifted the soil metabolome, implicating specific osmolytes in the microbial response and suggesting metabolite diversity modulates microbial function. These results constrain soil microbial activity rates and mechanisms underlying drought-rewetting responses and motivate further study of carbon cycling under increasingly volatile hydroclimates. This study demonstrates that soil microbial growth rates are extremely slow under dry conditions, with rehydration causing a rapid increase in anabolic activity within days. These findings refine our understanding of microbial contributions to soil carbon cycling with a warming climate.

papers.title: Thin-film lithium niobate waveguide-integrated p-i-n Tungsten selenide photodiodes with 10Gbit/s data reception
papers.abstract: Thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) is a promising photonic platform in next-generation integrated optoelectronics and on-chip/chip-chip interconnection due to its attractive optical property and versatility. However, integration of conventional-material-based photodetectors on TFLN platforms still faces multiple challenges. Herein, a high-bandwidth TFLN-based waveguide-integrated lateral WSe2 p-i-n photodetector is presented. The localized self-aligned doping process eliminates slow carrier diffusion and defect trapping in doped regions which further boosts modulation bandwidth. Secondly, n-type and p-type Ohmic contacts, along with a high-quality p-n junction, are achieved through Se vacancy defect engineering and high-work function molybdenum oxide buffer layer, respectively. Furthermore, combined with the high dielectric constant of lithium niobate suppressing ionized impurity scattering, carrier mobilities exceeding 350 cm2/V·s are achieved for both electrons and holes, significantly accelerating carrier drift. The device features a measured bandwidth of 1.12 GHz and a data rate up to 10 Gbit/s in visible light. Separately, the device achieves a responsivity of ~492 mA·W−1 and a near-unity external quantum efficiency of 95.6% at 638 nm. This combination of two-dimensional homostructure and TFLN nano-waveguides provides a basis for high-speed photodetectors and visible-light interconnections in future TFLN integrated optoelectronics and optical input/output applications. Thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) is a promising photonic platform, but its integration with 2D materials remains challenging. Here, the authors report the realization of TFLN-based waveguide-integrated WSe2 photodetectors, showing a 3-dB bandwidth up to 1.12 GHz, up to 10 Gbit/s data rates and responsivity up to 492 mA/W in the visible range.

papers.title: Latitude modulates climate-driven maize yield gains across the central U.S. “warming hole”
papers.abstract: Maize yield responses to climate change differ seasonally and regionally, with both positive and negative impacts shaped by local climate trends and management decisions. Here, using a phenology-aligned moving crop-season framework and the Hybrid-Maize model (1991–2024) across five U.S. Corn Belt states, we quantify climate-driven yield contributions and show that they transition from southern declines to northern gains, reflecting the persistent influence of the central U.S. summer warming hole characterized by cooling maximum temperatures and increasing rainfall. A systematic thermal mismatch between environmental heat availability and hybrid growing degree day requirements is observed, particularly south of 42°N, where thermal matching declined despite favorable thermal conditions. Contrasting trends in thermal matching and reproductive duration help explain the latitude-dependent structure of climate-driven yield contributions. Our findings highlight how hybrid selection modulates the impacts of temperature, precipitation, vapor pressure deficit, and radiation trends on maize yield gains across the U.S. Corn Belt. Climate change affects crop yield variation across regions and seasons. This study suggests that climate impacts on maize yields shift from losses in the southern U.S. Corn Belt to gains in the north, driven by climate trends, thermal matching, and hybrid selection.

papers.title: Epigenetic gatekeeping enables genome-scale horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotic cells
papers.abstract: Horizontal gene transfer drives rapid evolutionary innovation, yet well-substantiated cases are largely confined to prokaryotes. Eukaryote-to-eukaryote transfer remains exceptionally rare, and direct genome-scale demonstrations are absent. Here, inspired by endosymbiotic genome acquisition, we show that mammalian cells can initiate genome-scale horizontal gene transfer through phagocytic uptake of intact algal cells, albeit at a much lower frequency than cell fusion. Live-cell imaging captures the early nuclear appearance of transferred algal DNA after fusion, while genome sequencing and cytogenetic analyses reveal stable retention of chromosome-scale algal DNA in mammalian cells. Hybrid cells maintain more than 16 Mb of algal DNA, including intact chromosomes, as telomere-linked structures that persist for 95 generations without selection. Transferred algal DNA shows a progressive increase in DNA methylation together with enrichment of repressive histone modifications, forming heterochromatic domains that physically associate with host chromosomes. Notably, mammalian cells deficient in a de novo DNA methyltransferase show reduced stable establishment and retention of transferred algal DNA, supporting a gatekeeping role for DNA methylation in the stable accommodation of foreign genomes. Our findings reveal an epigenetic mechanism that contributes to the stable accommodation of large-scale foreign DNA between distantly related eukaryotes. Aoki et al. show that mammalian cells can acquire and retain chromosome-scale DNA from algae. The study reveals that host DNA methylation helps establish and maintain foreign DNA, offering insight into gene transfer between distant species.

papers.title: Extinction risks in deep-sea populations revealed by genomic data and ecological niche modeling
papers.abstract: As the global biodiversity crisis accelerates across terrestrial and shallow marine systems, the extent of this collapse remains unknown within the deep sea. Despite encompassing most of the ocean, deep-sea ecosystems remain the planet’s final frontier. Within this vast realm, the mesopelagic zone represents a critical yet poorly understood habitat, particularly in terms of its conservation status. Here, we integrate genomic data with ecological niche modeling to assess and forecast the conservation status of five mesopelagic species in the Gulf of Mexico. Samples were collected from 2011 to 2023, representing one of the longest time-series datasets for mesopelagic fauna in oceanographic history. All species exhibit current effective population sizes below the minimum thresholds for long-term viability. Genomic diversity declined over a decade in some species at rates comparable to or exceeding those reported for threatened and endangered species. Demographic modeling indicates historical population declines across all species. Ecological niche models predict declining Gulf habitat suitability for most species under future climate change scenarios. Together, our results identify indicators associated with elevated extinction risk in Gulf mesopelagic species and raise the possibility of a broader, unnoticed crisis, challenging assumptions of stability and resilience in mesopelagic ecosystems. Here authors use genomic data to reveal indicators of elevated extinction risk in Gulf of Mexico mesopelagic species. Together with projected declines in habitat suitability, these findings raise the possibility of a broader, unnoticed crisis.

papers.title: Cobalt based anode for highly stable alkaline water electrolysis under operation conditions beyond industrial requirements
papers.abstract: Alkaline water electrolysis is the most established route to electrochemical hydrogen production, but the limited lifetime of anode catalysts makes long-term equipment investment costly and hinders miniaturization. Here we show that, unlike the extensively investigated nickel- and nickel–iron-based hydroxides, the long-neglected cobalt–nickel hydroxides are promising anode catalysts whose stability exceeds current industrial requirements. A cobalt–nickel layered double hydroxide anode enables stable alkaline water electrolysis for more than 8,000 hours at 1 A cm–2 in 6 M sodium hydroxide at 80 °C. This stability arises from the strengthened metal–oxygen bonding of the in-situ-formed cobalt–nickel oxyhydroxide, which raises the energy barrier for lattice-oxygen loss during the oxygen evolution reaction. In a practical electrolyzer, the anode achieves an energy consumption of ~4.2 kWh per normal cubic metre of hydrogen at 1 A cm–2 and operates stably for thousands of hours. The design of high-current-density alkaline electrolyzers should therefore prioritize robust anode stability under industrial conditions in addition to activity optimization. Hydrogen production by alkaline water electrolysis is limited by anode durability under industrial conditions. Here, the authors demonstrate a cobalt–nickel layered double hydroxide anode that sustains operation for over 8,000 h at 1 A cm⁻² in 6 M NaOH at 80 °C, enabling durable hydrogen production.

papers.title: Scaling medical imaging report generation with multimodal reinforcement learning
papers.abstract: In medical imaging report generation, supervised fine-tuning can overfit to superficial patterns and generalize poorly across institutions. We introduce Universal Report Generation (UNIRG), which adopts reinforcement learning to directly optimize clinically meaningful quality criteria. With this framework, we developed UNIRG-CXR, an 8-billion-parameter vision–language model trained on four public datasets (MIMIC-CXR, CheXpert Plus, ReXGradient-160k and IU-Xray) by supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning (group-relative policy optimization) against a composite lexical, semantic and clinical-error reward. We evaluated held-out test sets and an external proprietary dataset, with RadCliQ as primary metric and expert radiologist validation. Here we show that our method improves report quality and generalization: UNIRG-CXR surpasses prior models on the ReXrank benchmark across four datasets and two generation settings, exceeding the previous best score by over 50% on two test sets, and produces fewer clinically significant errors while maintaining performance on unseen data sources and across demographic subgroups. Researchers developed UniRG, a reinforcement learning framework that optimizes clinically aligned composite rewards for medical imaging report generation. UniRG outperforms prior models and demonstrates strong generalization across unseen hospitals and datasets

Effect of two common GVHD prophylaxis regimens on the gut microbiome in a randomized phase 3 trial
authors: Marcel R. M. van den Brink
papers.abstract: Allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation can cure certain hematological disorders but has many complications. In retrospective studies, low gut microbiome diversity is associated with adverse clinical outcomes. In 2023, the Blood and Marrow Transplant Clinical Trials Network 1703 randomized phase 3 trial demonstrated the superiority of post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy) and mycophenolate mofetil to tacrolimus and methotrexate (Tac/MTX) for graft-versus-host disease prophylaxis in participants with hematological malignancies undergoing allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation. Here we report on the microbiome-focused companion study to 1703, Blood and Marrow Transplant Clinical Trials Network 1801, which coenrolled participants and shared trial registration. The primary endpoint was association between microbiome diversity at neutrophil engraftment and non-relapse mortality after 1 year; secondary endpoints included associations with other clinical outcomes and with baseline microbiome diversity. Based on 2575 longitudinally collected stool samples from 304 participants (Tac/MTX n = 147, PTCy n = 157), no association between engraftment microbiome diversity and non-relapse mortality was observed (P = 0.314), not meeting the primary endpoint. Lower baseline microbiome diversity was associated with shorter overall survival (P = 0.007). Safety data were reported in the original 1703 publication. In exploratory analyses, microbiome diversity and absolute microbial load were lower in PTCy compared to Tac/MTX on days 14–28 following HCT, independent of non-prophylaxis antibiotics exposure. Microbial domination events, when a single species exceeds 30% relative abundance, did not differ significantly between study arms and reflected both pathogen blooms and less severe disruptions of the microbial community. Clostridium scindens and secondary bile-acid metabolism pathways were less prevalent in PTCy than in Tac/MTX following HCT. In summary, we find prophylaxis regimens likely exert independent effects on both the microbiome and immune compartments and can also impact their interaction. Understanding whether and how microbiome-targeted interventions might improve transplant outcomes will therefore require careful disentangling of these effects within each specific treatment context. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03959241 . In a prespecified companion study (BMT CTN 1801) of the randomized phase 3 BMT CTN 1703 trial comparing two common GVHD prophylaxis regimens, microbiome diversity at engraftment did not associate with non-relapse mortality, but secondary analyses found baseline microbiome diversity was associated with clinical outcomes.

papers.title: PANGEA: an integrated cell atlas across diverse biological contexts enables systematic profiling of multicellular responses in human diseases
papers.abstract: Diseases affect multiple cell types within tissues, but the overall landscape of the multicellular responses in human diseases remains largely unexplored. Here we categorize the multicellular responses of human diseases based on a remapped atlas of human cells, PANGEA, incorporating 12.6 million cells acquired from a pipeline that automatically processes raw sequence files from public repositories. We constructed a hierarchical cell classification framework comprising 32 major cell types and 165 cellular subtypes. On the basis of this annotation framework, we explored an extensive atlas of human cells containing 46.5 million cells from 160 diseases across 48 organs and revealed core archetypes of human diseases repeatedly found across organs. We show that this cell atlas could also serve as a reference for unbiased analysis in spatial transcriptomics, revealing spatial features associated with immunotherapy responses. Collectively, our study provides foundational resources for cell ontologies, enabling cross-tissue comparisons of cellular features in human diseases. PANGEA is a comprehensive single-cell transcriptomic atlas of 160 human diseases across 48 organs.

Mapping mammalian placental formation and implantation transitions with single-cell transcriptomics and live imaging
papers.abstract: Implantation remains the most inaccessible stage of mammalian development. Consequently, we know remarkably little about how the embryo coordinates the cellular transitions that establish the body plan and initiate placental formation, despite this being the period when most pregnancies are lost. Here we combine single-cell transcriptomics, live imaging and functional experiments to define these transitions at cellular resolution. Our results identify an intermediate state bridging naive and primed pluripotency in the embryonic lineage, trace anterior–posterior axis specification origins in the extraembryonic endoderm, and reveal trophectoderm bifurcation into distinct placental progenitors. Strikingly, we find that the placenta arises from two sources: the classically recognized polar trophectoderm and a previously unrecognized population of mural trophectoderm that migrates from the polar–mural border. Human mural trophectoderm shows similar region-specific behaviour and may include invasive-trophoblast-biased progenitors. These findings open new directions for improving stem-cell-derived embryo models and uncovering the early determinants of pregnancy success. Chen, Hu et al. perform single-cell transcriptomics on peri-implantation mouse embryos and film embryo implantation. They find that mural trophectoderm population is an essential component of the placenta.

papers.title: The optogenetic tool ASAP acutely inhibits autophagy
papers.abstract: Autophagy, a conserved recycling process, manages intracellular quality control to mitigate stress. To determine the rapid effects of autophagy perturbation, we developed an optogenetic tool to rapidly inhibit autophagy, termed ASAP. Our approach leverages light-induced proteolytic cleavage to selectively inhibit autophagy within 5 min of light exposure, providing a precise and dynamic approach to study autophagy regulation. Proteomic profiling with ASAP revealed the most tightly regulated autophagy substrates along with previously unidentified substrates, including nuclear pore complex proteins. Of note, autophagy regulates quality control of cytoplasmic complexes of nucleoporins via specific LC3-interacting regions, sparing nuclear pore complex proteins embedded in the nuclear envelope. Upon rapid autophagy inhibition, incomplete nucleoporin complexes accumulate and instead of undergoing autophagic degradation, cytoplasmic nucleoporin complexes aggregate in processing bodies (P bodies). Using ASAP, we demonstrate rapid and specific inhibition of autophagy, revealing that nuclear pore complex proteins are tightly regulated autophagy substrates. Mondal et al. present an optogenetic tool to rapidly inhibit autophagy, named ASAP. Proteomic profiling with ASAP shows the most tightly regulated autophagy substrates, including nuclear pore complex proteins.

papers.title: TMEM192 is a calcineurin-regulated membrane receptor for ubiquitin-independent lysophagy
papers.abstract: Lysophagy is a selective form of autophagy responsible for clearing damaged lysosomes. Although existing models predominantly highlight ubiquitin-dependent mechanisms, here we identify the lysosomal membrane protein TMEM192 as a key ubiquitin-independent receptor for lysophagy. We demonstrate that lysophagy persists in cells even when protein ubiquitination is inhibited or autophagy adaptors are deleted. Following lysosomal damage, the efflux of calcium from lysosomes activates calcineurin, leading to the dephosphorylation of TMEM192 at Ser229. This exposes a latent LC3-interacting region and enables direct recruitment of autophagosomes. Depletion of TMEM192 or blockade of its dephosphorylation severely impairs lysophagy, resulting in the accumulation of damaged lysosomes. In a mouse model of acute hyperuricemic nephropathy, deficiency in TMEM192 exacerbates renal tubular injury. Our findings establish a ubiquitin-independent lysophagy pathway, which holds important implications for understanding and intervening lysosomal-related diseases. Liu et al. show that TMEM192 is a ubiquitin-independent lysophagy receptor. Lysosomal calcium activates calcineurin, which dephosphorylates TMEM192 to expose an LC3-binding site, initiating autophagy without ubiquitination and adaptor proteins.

A single-cell lung cancer atlas reveals cellular and molecular drivers of metastasis and clinical outcome
papers.abstract: Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality, characterized by extensive cellular and molecular heterogeneity. Here, to capture this complexity, we present LuCaS+, a multicenter single-cell RNA sequencing atlas comprising over 2.5 million nuclei from 454 clinically annotated patients with NSCLC with long-term follow-up. LuCaS+ consists of a discovery dataset (Berlin and Cologne, 364 patients) and an independent validation dataset (Munich, 90 patients). Leveraging this dataset, we identified tumor subpopulations with high metastatic potential associated with oncogenic signaling, immune evasion and epithelial–mesenchymal transition. In early-stage adenocarcinoma (lung adenocarcinoma), these cells showed strong prognostic value. Integrating tumor and microenvironmental cell profiles improved survival prediction across all stages, identifying distinct tumor–immune–stromal interaction patterns. These included monocyte- and fibroblast-driven inflammation (lung adenocarcinoma), VEGF–TGFβ-mediated angiogenic feedback loops (lung squamous cell carcinoma) and immune-permissive niches promoting antitumor immunity. LuCaS+ offers a clinically anchored single-cell resource to enable personalized, biology-driven therapies in NSCLC. Jurmeister et al. present a multicenter single-nucleus RNA sequencing atlas of lung cancer combined with spatial transcriptomics and clinical outcomes, delineating cancer–host cell interactions and uncovering tumor subtypes associated with metastatic relapse.

papers.title: Toward a complete diploid chicken genome
papers.abstract: A near-complete diploid chicken genome reveals that previously inaccessible regions contain extensive hidden genetic variation. These findings substantially advance understanding of avian genome complexity and provide a key resource for studies of vertebrate evolution, mutation, and genome function.

papers.title: ZnuB as a targetable vulnerability to combat colistin resistance
papers.abstract: Plasmid-mediated mcr genes compromise colistin efficacy. Cai et al. show that znuB deletion enhances bacterial susceptibility to colistin by relieving H-NS-dependent repression of leuO and disrupting diacylglycerol homeostasis. These findings support zinc uptake as a targetable pathway for restoring colistin activity against resistant infections.

papers.title: Discovery and development of antimicrobial polymers
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is among the most pressing healthcare challenges of our time. Multidrug-resistant ‘superbugs’ continue to emerge at an alarming rate, while antibiotic development has stalled in recent decades. Antimicrobial peptides have attracted interest for their potent bactericidal activity and lower propensity to spur resistance; however, translation into clinical practice has been hampered by poor bioavailability, challenging syntheses and limited stability. By contrast, synthetic copolymers mimicking antimicrobial peptides have received attention for their efficacy and synthetic tractability. Here we highlight recent advances in antimicrobial polymer development and discuss future directions for their design and implementation. We also outline future research directions, including the use of machine learning to guide polymer design and the development of scalable production methods that ensure the worldwide accessibility of these materials. Antimicrobial polymers offer an attractive tool for combating the crisis of antimicrobial resistance. This Review highlights recent advances in antimicrobial polymer development and discusses future directions, including the use of machine learning to guide polymer design and the development of scalable production methods to ensure global accessibility of these materials.

papers.title: Memristors
papers.abstract: Memristors are electronic memory devices whose conductance depends on the evolution of internal physical states. Although they are widely associated with resistive random-access memory (RRAM), memristors exhibit a broad range of dynamic behaviours beyond static RRAM, arising from processes such as ionic migration, electrochemical reactions and phase evolution. These dynamics underpin applications spanning non-volatile memory, in-memory computing and neuromorphic computing systems. This Primer presents a methodological framework for studying memristors as dynamic devices. Experimental approaches for elucidating the physical processes governing memristive switching behaviour are discussed, together with how device dynamics shape performance and determine suitability for different applications. Focus is given to the development of a broader research ecosystem, including the need for standardized data reporting, benchmarking practices and reproducibility across studies. In addition, current challenges and future directions for the field are highlighted, providing an outlook on how advances in materials, characterization and system integration may shape the next generation of memristor technologies. Memristors are electronic devices whose resistance changes in response to the history of electrical current flowing through them, enabling a memory of past electrical activity. In this Primer, Xu et al. outline the study of memristors as dynamic devices.

papers.title: Memristors
An expanded structural and biochemical map of GLI-SUFU recognition identifies binding-defective disease variants
papers.abstract: The tumor suppressor SUFU is a key negative regulator of oncogenic GLI transcription factors. SUFU mutations predispose to medulloblastoma and can cause Gorlin and Joubert syndromes. Limited structural information is available on the GLI-SUFU complex, contributing to the fact that the vast majority of SUFU missense variants sequenced from affected patients are of unknown clinical significance. Using AlphaFold3 and complementary computational analysis, we predicted structures of the three human GLI-SUFU complexes and the orthologous Drosophila Ci-Sufu complex, revealing previously unrecognized contact interfaces. By site-directed mutagenesis and GLI-SUFU binding assays, we validated the importance of key interface residues, many of which are mutated in familial medulloblastoma and Gorlin syndrome. These findings provide new structure-function insights into a signaling complex mutated in cancer and rare congenital diseases, and offer an expanded framework for interpreting clinically observed SUFU variants and mechanisms that tune SUFU repression.
affiliations: University of California, Irvine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Photoswitchable optoGPCRs for reversible control of Gs signalling and arrestin recruitment
papers.abstract: OptoGPCRs are light-activatable G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) used to optogenetically control physiological processes. Most existing optoGPCRs are based on monostable opsins, which are limited by photobleaching and irreversibility. The bistable jumping spider rhodopsin 1 (JSR1) carrying the single point mutant S199F introduces a ~150 nm spectral separation between the active and inactive states, enabling bidirectional control with distinct wavelengths of light. Here, we show that JSR1-S199F robustly and reversibly recruits arrestin and modulates Gq/i protein activity. We then engineered JSR1-S199F-based optoGPCRs with Gs protein activity, guided by AlphaFold-predicted receptor-miniGs complexes, to expand the limited repertoire of bistable Gs-coupled optoGPCRs. Specifically, we present optoDRD1, a chimeric optoGPCR that redirects the native Gq/i protein activity of JSR1 towards the Gs pathway of the dopamine D1 receptor (DRD1). Through systematic screening of intracellular domain combinations, we identified a chimeric configuration with the highest absolute cAMP output comprising ICL2, ICL3, helix 8, and the C-terminus from DRD1. The resulting optoGPCR is activated by violet light ({lambda}max = 397 nm) and deactivated by green light ({lambda}max = 531 nm) at physiologically relevant light intensities. A single violet light pulse drives sustained Gs signalling for several hours, while green light rapidly deactivates the receptor at any chosen time point, enabling repeatable switching between active and inactive states over multiple cycles. OptoDRD1 closely mimics wild-type DRD1 in both cAMP signalling kinetics and G protein selectivity, with a signal amplitude comparable to native Gs-coupled receptors, including JellyOp. We further demonstrate optoDRD1's utility for optogenetic control of Gs-regulated processes in vitro, including insulin secretion in human {beta}-cells and signalling modulation in a neuronal cell line. The biochemical stability and known structure of JSR1 make it a robust scaffold for this rational engineering and for future biophysical characterization. Together, optoDRD1 and JSR1-S199F expand the optoGPCR toolkit and open new opportunities for dissecting dopaminergic signalling, Gs-mediated physiology, and GPCR signalling pharmacology.

papers.title: Apoptotic caspases cleave DRP1 to promote mitochondrial fusion and anti-viral immune responses
papers.abstract: Apoptosis has been recognized as a suicidal host-defense programmed cell death pathway against invading pathogens. However, recent evidences showed that viruses can employ caspases to cleave and inactivate immune signaling molecules to facilitate infection. Whether caspases can instead promote anti-viral immune responses is currently unknown. Here, we demonstrated that the NSs protein of RVFV triggers activation of apoptotic caspases, which cleave the mitochondrial fission factor DRP1 resulting in mitochondrial elongation. Elongated mitochondria promote MAVS aggregation leading to enhanced anti-viral immunity. Apoptotic caspases, including caspase-3, -6, -7 and -8, cleave DRP1 at the motifs of D500FAD503 and/or AEAD556, suggesting that this cleavage event may occur during infection of different viruses. Indeed, infection of H1N1, SeV and HSV-1 all triggered apoptotic caspases activation to cleave DRP1 promoting anti-viral immune responses. Compared with wild-type DRP1, introduction of caspase-resistant DRP1 strongly attenuated immune responses triggered by virus infection. These results revealed a mechanism through which apoptotic caspases promote anti-viral immunity by regulating mitochondrial morphodynamics.
affiliations: Wuhan Institute of Virology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Ksp37 is a rapidly mobilized NK cell secretory protein that engages FGF2
papers.abstract: A key feature of natural killer (NK) cells is their preloaded arsenal of effector molecules, allowing them to rapidly respond upon activation. In this study, we characterized a previously unexplored secretory protein, termed killer-specific secretory protein of 37 kDa (Ksp37), which is highly abundant in differentiated CD56dim NK cells. Ksp37 is rapidly secreted in a dose-dependent and JAK-1 dependent manner upon low levels of cytokine stimulation, making it a sensitive readout for NK cell activation. Following secretion, intracellular levels were rapidly replenished, preserving responsiveness to subsequent cytokine stimulation. We found that Ksp37 is stored in polarized intracellular compartments distinct from those containing canonical cytotoxic effector molecules, including granzyme B and perforin, which require stronger stimulation for release. Lastly, we identified Ksp37 as a novel binding partner of fibroblast growth factor 2 (FGF2). This opens new avenues of exploration for the role of NK cells in remodeling their extracellular environment by modulating the FGF2-FGFR1 axis, which plays a key role in tumor growth, angiogenesis and tissue repair.
affiliations: Karolinska Institutet (corresponding author)

papers.title: Reverse Transcription Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification Combined with Lateral Flow Assay (RT-LAMP-LFA) for Rapid Detection of the 2026 Bundibugyo Virus (BDBV) Outbreak Strain
papers.abstract: Making accurate diagnosis is a critical first step in patient management and control for emerging and re-emerging disease outbreaks. Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) is a filovirus that causes Ebola disease, and the 2026 outbreak highlights the need for rapid diagnostic approaches that can be deployed in settings with limited laboratory infrastructure. Here, we developed a reverse transcription loop-mediated isothermal amplification-lateral flow assay (RT-LAMP-LFA) for rapid detection of the 2026 BDBV outbreak strain. LAMP primers were designed based on the genome sequence of the 2026 outbreak strain, and the conservation of the primer binding sites among all available 2026 outbreak genomes was confirmed in silico. LAMP primers were evaluated for analytical specificity and sensitivity using in vitro-transcribed RNA (ivtRNA) from BDBV and other filoviruses, as well as RNA derived from arboviruses and mammalian cells. Amplification products were detected using a Chromatography-Printed Array Strip (C-PAS) lateral flow platform. The newly designed primers specifically detected the presence of BDBV RNA without nonspecific amplification of the other viral or cellular RNA samples tested. Consistent amplification was observed down to 103 copies per reaction. In addition, BDBV viral RNA was successfully amplified, and the amplification products were detected using C-PAS, with the total workflow being completed within 25 min. These findings demonstrate the analytical specificity and sensitivity of the developed RT-LAMP-LFA assay and its compatibility with rapid visual lateral flow detection, supporting its potential application as a point-of-care approach for BDBV detection.
affiliations: Nagasaki Daigaku (corresponding author)

papers.title: Divergent methane production and microbial community responses to carbon enrichment in freshwater wetland sediments
papers.abstract: Methane (CH4) accumulation in wetland sediments reflects interactions among organic matter, sediment chemistry, and microbial communities. We combined depth-resolved field characterization across four wetland habitats in northern Israel with complementary incubations to examine methane accumulation and responses to labile-carbon enrichment. Sediment cores were characterized using Rock-Eval analysis, porewater chemistry, oxygen profiling at three sites, and mcrA amplicon sequencing. High CH4 concentrations occurred under contrasting conditions: Ein Nimfit (EN) contained approximately 12% total organic carbon and reached 2.1 mM CH4, whereas Ein Afek site EA2 contained approximately 5% carbon and accumulated 0.7-1.7 mM CH4. Both showed sulfate depletion, but EN exhibited pronounced sulfide accumulation, whereas EA2 showed greater dissolved iron and nutrient enrichment. Their classified methanogenic assemblages also differed. EA1 remained methane poor despite increasing carbon content with depth, while EA3 combined low carbon content and CH4 accumulation with detectable methanogens and lower methanogenic diversity. In a 36-day bottle experiments using sediments from two of the four wetland habitats, sucrose-amended EA3 exhibited a transient maximum of 18.8 mmol collected CH4 kg-1 wet sediment during Days 22-29, whereas EN reached its highest collected amount during Days 29-36. Methane proportions increased before the large output increase in EA3 but remained comparatively stable and high in EN. Soluble chemical oxygen demand trajectories and microbial community changes also differed. These findings identify distinct biogeochemical settings supporting methane accumulation and demonstrate methanogenic potential in low-CH4 sediment, emphasizing the complementary information provided by field profiles, microbial characterization, and exploratory enrichment experiments.
affiliations: University of Haifa (corresponding author)

papers.title: The absence of microbiome in germ-free mice exacerbates the pathogenicity of mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 MA10
papers.abstract: Germ-free mice, which are devoid of microbiota, provide a powerful system to define the contribution of the microbiome to host responses during infection. Severe COVID-19 outcomes are associated with multiple comorbidities that are themselves characterized by microbiome dysbiosis; however, the causal role of the microbiota in SARS-CoV-2 pathogenesis remains poorly understood. Here, we use germ-free mouse models to evaluate the impact of the microbiome on disease severity following infection with mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 MA10. Comparison with conventionally housed mice revealed that the absence of the microbiome markedly exacerbates SARS-CoV-2-induced disease in both C57BL/6 and Swiss Webster backgrounds. Germ-free mice exhibited greater weight loss, impaired lung function, worsened pulmonary pathology, and pronounced alterations in circulating cytokine and chemokine profiles compared with conventional controls. These findings show that resident microbiota limit SARS-CoV-2 pathogenicity and establish germ-free COVID-19 models as a powerful platform to identify protective microbial taxa and microbiota-based interventions to reduce severe disease.
affiliations: Tufts University Cummings School of Veterinary Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Endogenous expression of mutant RagC in mice results in early-onset dilated cardiomyopathy with features of the Long-Olsen-Distelmaier syndrome
papers.abstract: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a severe heart condition often linked to arrhythmias, clots, and heart failure, for which treatments are not yet curative. Recently, de novo mutations in genes encoding components of the Rag GTPase nutrient signaling pathway, particularly in RRAGC, have been found in unrelated patients with a severe, early-onset DCM syndrome called Long-Olsen-Distelmaier. Cancer cell lines, hiPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and zebrafish have been used to study this Ragopathy, but a mammalian model to investigate this syndrome has not been generated. Here, we show that mice engineered to endogenously express mutations in Serine 74 (orthologous to the Serine 75 mutated in patients), exhibit early-onset features of DCM with decreased heart size, fibrosis, diastolic dysfunction and aortic insufficiency, characteristics reminiscent of the human syndrome. Moreover, Rragc-mutant hearts display decreased left ventricular mass and interventricular septum. Endogenous heterozygous expression of Rragc mutant variants result in a milder, sublethal defective physiological cardiac growth with increased systolic and diastolic blood pressure. Mechanistically, active RagC does not cause abnormal increase in cardiomyocyte size, but leads to suppressed transcriptional activity of Tfeb and alterations in cardiomyocyte metabolism. Transcriptional profiling of neonatal mutant hearts reveals multiple signatures of impaired mitochondrial activity. Ex vivo and in vitro analyses of murine cardiomyocyte mitochondria from Rragc-mutant mice show suppressed mitochondrial respiration, disturbed complex IV multimerization and super-complex organization. These data point to abnormal early postnatal heart metabolism by deregulated nutrient - Rag GTPase signaling with a potential molecular explanation to the early onset of DCM in patients with de novo missense mutations in RRAGC, and suggests the relevance of early metabolic interventions in conditions with altered nutrient signaling
affiliations: CNIO (corresponding author)

papers.title: Pangenome Discoveries from Clinical Long-Read Genomes in Underrepresented Populations with Neurodevelopmental Disorders
papers.abstract: Genetic diagnoses remain elusive for many individuals with neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), and the gap is wider in populations poorly represented in genomic reference resources. To demonstrate the equitable advantage of long-read whole genome sequencing (LR-WGS) and pangenomes in terms of clinical utility, we analyzed 211 NDD cases and 107 unaffected relatives from 24 populations, integrating their assemblies, resulting in a total of 1204 haplotypes with the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium Release 2 (HPRC_r2) and the Arab Pangenome Reference (APR) datasets. Clinical interpretation of small variants and structural variants (SVs) revealed pathogenic or likely pathogenic findings in 38.9% of the cases (82/211), and our workflow further detected pathogenic repeat expansions in 3.8% of the cases and runs of homozygosity (ROHs) exceeding 300 Mb in 4.7% of the cases, revealing substantial autozygosity suggestive of strong inbreeding. Beyond these clinical assessments, pangenome analysis revealed 3.9 million population-level novel small variants, 39,782 SVs and an average of 2.17 Mb of novel sequence per individual absent from linear references and global pangenomes. We identified 85.9 kb of case-unique nonreference sequences in exonic segments overlapping with curated NDD gene sets. Graph-based tertiary analysis further identified rare exonic complex homozygous rearrangements in the NDD associated genes for 2.4% of the cases. Together, these findings emphasize how diverse genome assemblies extend variant discovery beyond established linear reference-based clinical interpretation.

papers.title: Structure of human hephaestin reveals a homodimer anchored to the cell membrane
papers.abstract: Hephaestin (Heph) is a membrane-bound ferroxidase that oxidizes ferrous ion (Fe2+) exported by ferroportin (Fpn) to ferric ion (Fe3+), enabling iron loading onto transferrin for systemic delivery. Loss-of-function mutations in Heph cause iron accumulation in intestinal enterocytes and systemic iron deficiency in animal models, underscoring its role in iron export. Heph has a large extracellular domain anchored to the cell membrane by a single transmembrane helix. However, full-length Heph has not previously been purified, and our understanding of its structure and function remains incomplete. Here, we report the expression and purification of functional fulllength human Heph and determination of its structure by cryo-electron microscopy at an overall resolution of approximately 2.3 [A]. The structure reveals a stable homodimer with well-resolved extracellular domains. Although the transmembrane helices are less well resolved, their positions can be defined. The substrate-binding site is connected to an electronegative funnel that may facilitate Fe2+ capture. These findings establish the structural organization of full-length human Heph and provide structural constraints for understanding its interaction with Fpn.
affiliations: Baylor College of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Volumetric Cross-Amplitude Modulation (VxAM) for Transcranial Gas Vesicle Imaging
papers.abstract: Cross-amplitude modulation (xAM) is a commonly used pulse sequence for non-destructive, quasi-artifact-free detection of gas-vesicle (GV) contrast agents, but it has so far been limited to two-dimensional cross-sections acquired with one-dimensional linear arrays. We present the first implementation of xAM on a fully sampled two-dimensional matrix array, extending the half-aperture split of conventional xAM to a family of 2D sub-aperture partitions on a 32x32-element Vermon probe (7.81 MHz, 300 m element pitch). Angular spectrum simulations compared three primary bisections (X-axis, Y-axis, and diagonal (D1,D2)), and the selected Y-split was tested experimentally in GV-loaded tissue-mimicking phantoms. We also simulated an electronic asymmetric-angle sweep as an alternative to the robotic translation used in the experiments, and measured contrast through an ex vivo mouse skull. The non-emissive regions between the elevation panels of the Vermon probe accounted for most of the simulated differences among partitions, through both the continuity of the aperture parallel to the bisector plane and the side-lobe structure. At a 6 degree steering angle, the Y-split gave a contrast-to-tissue ratio (CTR) of ~29 dB for single frames and ~49 dB with 100-frame averaging without the skull, and a contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) of ~8 dB for single frames and ~12 dB with 100-frame averaging through the skull, where the inclusion remained resolvable. These results give design rules for xAM on matrix arrays. The through-skull result comes from a single ex vivo specimen, and in vivo work is the next step toward non-invasive, longitudinal, three-dimensional monitoring of GV-labeled glioblastoma and other targets of nonlinear contrast agents.
affiliations: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (corresponding author)

papers.title: DeePEn - A Depth sensitive benchmark for Protein Engineering
papers.abstract: Recent progress in modeling techniques and high-throughput screening has significantly enhanced the accessibility of protein engineering. Nevertheless, further progress gets hindered by the lack of robust benchmarks that capture the practical challenges for real-world protein engineering. Here, we introduced DeePEn, a Depth-sensitive benchmark for Protein Engineering that quantifies model generalization to held-out variants at increasing mutational distance from the wild type. We defined distance as the number of simultaneous point mutations, i.e., single amino acid variants (SAVs), moving from wild-type to mutant (edit distance in computer science jargon). DeePEn retrospectively evaluates prediction and prioritization using experimentally labelled variants from deep mutational scanning (DMS) datasets; it does not benchmark prospective sequence generation or goal-directed optimization. Specifically selecting four DMS datasets with sufficient multi-mutation data points from ProteinGym, we assessed recent predictive models, including general and biophysics-informed protein Language Models (pLMs), and a non-transformer neural network. Our results highlight how the performance of all models deteriorates with increasing mutational distance and that no single metric sufficiently captures the diverse requirements of protein engineering. To overcome these shortcomings, DeePEn provides a readily available resource for multi-metric benchmarking that focuses on variant-effect prediction of variants distant from the wild type.
affiliations: Technical University of Munich (corresponding author)

papers.title: AntiSite: Unified paratope prediction for antibodies and nanobodies with or without structure
papers.abstract: Accurate paratope prediction provides insights into antibody--antigen recognition while supporting antibody discovery and engineering. Existing predictors are fixed to a single input setting: sequence-based methods cannot use an antibody structure, structure-based methods require coordinates, and methods covering both combine separately trained predictors. We present AntiSite, an antigen-agnostic predictor whose sequence encoder, fusion block and prediction head are shared across both settings; structure-aware inference adds molecular-surface features from our previously developed ParaSurf model, used here as a frozen, separately trained structural encoder. Structural-modality dropout enables both inference settings without retraining. Across five antibody--antigen benchmarks, structure-aware AntiSite achieved the highest mean PR-AUC among all evaluated methods, while sequence-only PR AUC was generally lower than that of the strongest dedicated antigen-agnostic sequence baseline. AntiSite also demonstrated zero-shot generalization to nanobodies without additional training. We further evaluated structures from recent antibody-specific and general protein folding methods, including Ibex, Protenix-v1, Boltz-2 and Chai-1, in antibody-only or antigen-aware co-folding settings. Their benefit was associated with structural accuracy, with the most accurate inputs yielding performance close to that obtained with experimental structures. AntiSite thus provides a shared predictor for antibody and nanobody binding sites, usable from sequence alone and refined when reliable structural information is available. Code and trained checkpoints are openly available.
affiliations: Information Technologies Institute, Centre for Research and Technology Hellas, Thessaloniki, Greece (corresponding author)

papers.title: DemuxHMM: Large-Scale Single-Cell Embryo Profiling via Recombination Barcoding
papers.abstract: High-resolution developmental time-courses with single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) increasingly target trajectory inference and other analyses in the study of development and disease. Researchers can efficiently generate these datasets by pooling individuals and inferring cell-to-individual mappings after sequencing, in a process called demultiplexing. Existing demultiplexing methods face limitations in the number of timepoints they can support, due to either the need for individual-by-individual processing or reduced accuracy at large numbers of individuals. To address these limitations, we introduce a computational framework for demultiplexing large-scale, individual-resolved datasets. Our framework includes a recombination-aware demultiplexing method, DemuxHMM, which uses a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) to explicitly model contiguous SNP patterns that arise from simple breeding schemes. We demonstrate substantial performance and scalability gains from this recombination-aware approach on both a real Diversity Outbred (DO) mouse data and a simulated Drosophila dataset. This performance demonstrates the value of the method when used for common applications on model organisms such as time series, crossover position inference, and eQTLS, among others.
affiliations: The University of British Columbia (corresponding author)

papers.title: Panmap: Scalable phylogeny-guided alignment, genotyping, and placement on pangenomes
papers.abstract: Pangenomes capture population-level variation but remain computationally challenging at scale. We present Panmap, a tool that leverages evolutionary structure to place, align, and genotype sequencing reads against mutation-annotated pangenomes containing up to millions of genomes. Panmap introduces a phylogenetically compressed k-mer index that stores only sequence differences along branches, enabling efficient comparison of reads to both sampled genomes and inferred ancestors. This approach reduces index size by up to 600-fold and construction time by over three orders of magnitude relative to existing tools. Panmap places a 100x coverage SARS-CoV-2 sample onto 20,000 genomes in 0.4 seconds and onto 8 million genomes in under two minutes. Furthermore, it enables accurate haplotype identification and abundance estimation in metagenomic samples and sensitive placement of ancient environmental DNA without prior alignment. Our approach makes large-scale pangenomes directly amenable to read mapping, genome assembly, alignment-free phylogenetic placement, and metagenomic analysis.
affiliations: University of California, Santa Cruz (corresponding author)

papers.title: Macroscopic Vibronic Coherence and Non-Dispersive Soliton Propagation Across a Protein-Solvent Interface
papers.abstract: A foundational tenet of modern biophysics dictates that protein-solvent interactions and charge-transport dynamics operate strictly within microscopic, sub-nanometer boundaries where long-range coordination is natively suppressed by rapid room-temperature thermal dephasing. Here, we report an unexpected phenomenon that fundamentally challenges this paradigm: the long-distance, quantum-coherent communication between isolated protein samples in aqueous solution across macroscopic spatial separations. By mapping the distance-dependence of a weak, protein-emitted electromagnetic field on the response dynamics of an adjacent complex, we demonstrate that this inter-protein communication establishes a stable, intermolecular vibronic coupling operating across millimeter-scale distances up to at least 40 mm. This field interference induces a robust quantum coherence that lowers the local potential energy surface, transforming the coupled protein-solvent network into an un-attenuated, low-barrier energy transfer conduit. This stabilized pathway launches a topologically protected, non-dispersive soliton that exhibits exceptional phase stability against room-temperature thermal dephasing. These findings provide definitive empirical evidence of a sophisticated, field-driven quantum infrastructure embedded within a biological macromolecule. More explicitly, they reveal that a protein can possess an inherent capacity to preserve coherent wave propagation over macroscopic scales previously deemed impossible in room-temperature aqueous environments.
affiliations: TUM (corresponding author)

papers.title: Comparative cryo-EM structures of CGMMV and ToMMV reveal divergent coat protein packing and electrostatics indicating Tobamovirus host specificity
papers.abstract: Tobamoviruses are a group of economically important plant viruses exhibiting extreme stability and persistence. Despite high morphological similarity, they show extensive host-family specificity, induce a wide range of symptoms, and inflict significant global yield losses in fruit and vegetable crops. Composed of a rod-shaped helical assembly of identical coat proteins encasing a single-stranded RNA, tobamoviruses have long served as fundamental models for understanding helical assemblies. Here we report the cryo-EM structures of two viruses from this genus, cucumber green mottle mosaic virus (CGMMV) and tomato mottle mosaic virus (ToMMV), at 2.86 [A] and 2.71 [A] resolution, respectively, revealing divergent packing strategies within the virion assembly. Whereas the solanaceous-infecting ToMMV closely mirrors genetically-similar canonical tobacco mosaic virus (TMV), CGMMV employs a specialized hydrophobic packing strategy based at the solvent-exposed inner loop lining the solvent-exposed central canal. Comparative biophysical and molecular dynamics analyses from the reconstructed structures reveal more stable and compact protein packing for CGMMV at both the subunit and assembly levels. Furthermore, we identify a conserved electrostatic pentapeptide motif (residues 113 to117) on the lower radial alpha helix that serves as an additional RNA-stabilizing region, harbouring a clade-defining Lys113 synapomorphy in cucurbit-infecting tobamoviruses. Together, our findings elucidate how subtle electrostatic tuning and divergent hydrophobic packing strategies drive differential virion stability and host-family adaptation within a strictly conserved helical scaffold.
affiliations: Indian Institute of Science Education And Research Kolkata (corresponding author)

papers.title: Digital molecular kinetics enabled by large-scale nanopore arrays for multidimensional biophysical profiling
papers.abstract: While widely used, traditional technologies like surface plasmon resonance (SPR) are limited by narrow temporal windows (transient capture and baseline drift), dynamic heterogeneity, and poor physiological temperature performance. Meanwhile, early nanopore approaches are often constrained by limited throughput and heavy reliance on customized modification schemes. Here, we present a digital molecular kinetics (DMK) platform based on large-scale nanopore arrays. By introducing a universal coupling and probe reporting system, DMK achieves broad versatility across diverse molecular pairs, including proteins, peptides, small molecules, DNA, and polymerase complexes. In addition to accurately recovering classical SPR association and dissociation rate constants, by harnessing massive single-molecule event analysis, DMK breaks traditional performance boundaries: it facilitates robust thermodynamic-kinetic profiling across a wide temperature range, resolves distinct conformations in heterogeneous samples, enables ultra-low dissociation rate quantification via maximum likelihood estimation, and reveals energy wells via voltage gradients for binding analysis against environmental perturbations. Furthermore, DMK enables the capture of rapid binding events missed by SPR, offering a new perspective on molecular interaction complexity. This platform offers an effective alternative and upgrade to SPR, opening a digital paradigm for complex molecular analysis and drug discovery.
affiliations: Geneus Technologies (Chengdu) Co., Ltd. (corresponding author)

papers.title: HERC1-mediated orphan subunit quality control maintains proteasome homeostasis and is disrupted in HERC1-associated neurodevelopmental disease
papers.abstract: Biallelic hypomorphic variants in the E3 ubiquitin ligase HERC1 cause a neurological disorder clinically characterized by macrocephaly, dysmorphic facies, and psychomotor delay. Identifying the substrates of HERC1 is essential for understanding its biological functions and the mechanisms underlying disease-associated variants. To address this, we performed a quantitative proteomic analysis using biotinylated ubiquitin to identify HERC1 targets and examine their regulation in cells expressing HERC1 with or without ubiquitin ligase activity. This approach revealed a broad set of HERC1-dependent ubiquitylation substrates, including proteins from major multiprotein complexes such as the proteasome, the translation initiation machinery, and pathways involved in cell metabolism. Focusing on the proteasome, the most prominently represented complex, we identified several regulatory particle subunits, including PSMC6, PSME1, and PSME2. Specifically, within the 19S regulatory particle, we demonstrated that ubiquitylation of the PSMC6 subunit involves the formation of K48-linked polyubiquitin chains and depends on HERC1 activity. Other 19S subunits, such as PSMC2, PSMC4, and PSMC5, undergo a similar modification. Mechanistically, we show that HERC1 selectively recognizes unassembled subunits, promotes their ubiquitylation, and targets them for proteasomal degradation. Notably, in HERC1-deficient cells, disruption of this mechanism impaired proteasomal activity. At the disease level, quantitative proteomic analysis of the pathogenic HERC1 variant c.1448G>A (p.Gly483Glu) likewise identified altered ubiquitylation of proteasome subunits and components of the translation initiation machinery. Biochemical analyses further revealed impaired ubiquitylation of PSMC6 by the mutant HERC1 protein, associated with a loss of interaction between HERC1 and PSMC6. Together, these findings establish a link between HERC1-associated neurological disorders and defective ubiquitylation pathways. They elucidate the molecular mechanisms by which HERC1 regulates proteostasis and demonstrate how disruption of these processes contributes to disease pathogenesis, thereby highlighting potential avenues for therapeutic intervention.
affiliations: University of Barcelona (corresponding author)

papers.title: Expansion of human hematopoietic stem cells by inhibiting translation
papers.abstract: Hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) transplantation using umbilical cord blood (UCB) is a potentially life-saving treatment for leukemia and bone marrow failure but is limited by the low number of HSCs in UCB. The loss of HSCs after ex vivo manipulation is also a major obstacle to gene editing for inherited blood disorders. HSCs require a low rate of translation to maintain their capacity for self-renewal, but hematopoietic cytokines used to expand HSCs stimulate protein synthesis and impair long-term self-renewal. We previously described cytokine-free conditions that maintain but do not expand human and mouse HSCs ex vivo. Here we performed a high-throughput screen and identified translation inhibitors that allow ex vivo expansion of human HSCs while minimizing cytokine exposure. Transplantation assays show a ~4.3-fold expansion of long-term HSCs from UCB after one week of culture in low cytokine conditions that include the translation initiation inhibitor 4E1RCat. Single cell transcriptomic analysis demonstrates maintenance of the HSC/MPP transcriptional signature and reduced expression of stress markers under culture conditions that maintain or expand functional long-term HSCs. Addition of 4E1RCat induces a dose-dependent increase in autophagic vacuoles and reduces expression of oxidative phosphorylation and cell cycle gene expression programs. These culture conditions maintain adult HSCs after CRISPR/Cas9 editing of the BCL11A+58 enhancer, overcoming a major obstacle to ex vivo gene correction for human hemoglobinopathies.
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania (corresponding author)

papers.title: Co-aggregation of pre-conditioned cell populations drives controlled lineage bias and formation of gut tube-like structures in human stem cell-based embryo models
papers.abstract: Human stem cell-based embryo models (hSCBEMs) provide a powerful platform for investigating post-implantation human embryo development but are frequently hindered by variability in growth and morphogenesis as well as incomplete lineage representations. Here, we present a modular hSCBEM aggregation approach based on co-aggregation of differentially pre-conditioned, human pluripotent stem cell derived cells pools. Using this strategy, we generated hSCBEM with consistent morphotypes that targets robust morphogenesis of gut tube-like structures in combination with mesodermal lineages. Our findings demonstrate that co-aggregating defined cellular heterogeneity represents a versatile approach to specifically guide self-organization in hSCBEMs while improving reproducibility and developmental fidelity. The approach provides a robust platform for supervised morphogenesis in hSCBEMs.
affiliations: University of Oslo (corresponding author)

papers.title: Neural regulation of hatching in amphibians
papers.abstract: Many animal embryos hatch in response to threats or opportunities, yet how cue sensing activates hatching is unknown. We screened red-eyed treefrog (Agalychnis callidryas) eggs in the field with small molecules to discover that the neurotransmitter acetylcholine is a key mediator of hatching enzyme release. Using behavioral pharmacology, microscopy, and transcriptional profiling we identify direct cholinergic input on hatching gland cells that triggers enzyme release for egg rupture, and serotonergic transduction of embryonic hypoxia sensing. Independent hypoxia-sensing and mechanosensory predation-detection pathways converge on a hatching decision that elicits acetylcholine-dependent enzyme release and coordinated hatching-specific behavior. Cholinergic regulation of hatching enzyme release is conserved in a distantly related frog and salamander, suggesting a shared ancestral hatching mechanism. These results provide a neural basis for hatching plasticity which may have contributed to the evolution of diverse hatching modes in amphibians.
affiliations: Boston University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Towards Understanding the Microenvironmental Control of Reindeer Antler Regeneration
papers.abstract: Deer antlers are the only mammalian appendages capable of complete periodic regeneration and therefore provide a natural model for investigating mechanisms of skeletal regeneration. However, current knowledge of the structural and molecular characteristics of the regenerative antler microenvironment remains incomplete. Here, we compared antler tip and antler base tissues from Rangifer tarandus (reindeer) with mature metacarpal cortical bone using structural, compositional, histological, and proteomic analyses. Antler tissues exhibited smaller and less crystalline apatite structures, elevated carbonate substitution, and higher organic matrix content compared with metacarpal bone, indicating an immature mineral phase. Antlers also exhibited lower bone mineral density, greater porosity, reduced bone volume fraction, and greater trabecular separation, particularly in central regions, consistent with a dynamic remodeling microenvironment. Histological examination revealed abundant active osteons and extensive osteoid seams in antler tissues, whereas metacarpal bone predominantly comprised mature lamellar bone with limited remodeling activity. Proteomic profiling identified distinct extracellular matrix signatures between antler and metacarpal tissues. Metacarpal bone was enriched in proteins associated with skeletal homeostasis, mechanotransduction, and bone remodeling, whereas antler tissues were enriched in proteins involved in extracellular matrix reorganization, metabolic adaptation, and regeneration. Collectively, these findings indicate that reindeer antlers possess a specialized regenerative skeletal microenvironment characterized by immature mineral organization, active remodeling, and distinct molecular signatures associated with rapid tissue growth. These results provide new insights into the biological basis of mammalian appendage regeneration and may facilitate the development of regenerative strategies for bone repair and skeletal tissue engineering.
affiliations: University of Turku (corresponding author)

papers.title: S-adenosylmethionine supply controls DNA methylation turnover in synovial sarcoma
papers.abstract: Background: Methionine is the nutrient source of the metabolite S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) used to methylate chromatin for regulation of gene expression. Disruptions to this metabolic supply, including nutritional deficiency of certain B vitamins, alter chromatin methylation and have been implicated in tumor growth. Objective: To define how cellular SAM supply controls DNA methylation dynamics and the disruption of oncogenic gene expression in synovial sarcoma. Methods: Cell line models of synovial sarcoma were treated with the DNA methyltransferase inhibitor azacitidine or the small-molecule MAT2A inhibitor AG-270, which blocks SAM synthesis from methionine. Intracellular SAM concentrations were quantified by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. Global DNA methylation rates were measured by stable isotope tracing with [2H3-methyl]-methionine. Genomic sites of altered DNA methylation were identified by EM-seq and the associated transcriptional changes measured by RNA-seq. Results: Inhibition of SAM synthesis reduced intracellular SAM concentration from 94 uM to 5.6 uM (p value < 0.0001) at 24 hours. This was associated with a 19% decrease (p value < 0.0001) in the global 5-methyldeoxycytosine turnover rate, while total DNA methylation levels were maintained. In contrast to the global DNA hypomethylation induced by azacitidine, SAM depletion resulted in a redistribution of DNA methylation with loss at 252 and gain at 206 genomic sites, and the transcriptional response to SAM depletion was not associated with changes in promoter methylation at the altered genes. Both azacitidine and SAM depletion activated mesenchymal genes, while suppressing cell cycle progression. Conclusions: Metabolic supply of SAM is a major regulator of DNA methylation turnover providing a mechanism by which nutritional or genetic disruptions to SAM metabolism can alter chromatin methylation and gene expression.
affiliations: Rutgers University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Engineering a High-Fidelity CRISPR-Cas13d System for Targeted RNA Depletion in Plasmodium falciparum
papers.abstract: Functional genomics in Plasmodium falciparum is severely constrained by the evolutionary absence of an endogenous RNA interference pathway and the requirement for time-consuming direct target locus modification by conventional conditional genetic engineering systems. To overcome these limitations, we established a programmable post-transcriptional gene silencing system in P. falciparum using High-Fidelity RfxCas13d (HF-RfxCas13d), an RNA-guided RNA nuclease that has been previously tested in several eukaryotic hosts. Using CRISPR-SpyCas9 we integrated a HF-RfxCas13d expression cassette at the dispensable pfs47 locus and generated a stable marker-free transgenic line capable of constitutive HF-RfxCas13d cytosolic expression without impairing intraerythrocytic asexual growth. Episomal delivery of single or dual guide RNAs (gRNAs) achieved significant target mRNA depletion (41%-76%) across three endogenous loci atp4, ap2-exp, ap2-g genes. Applying this system to the master transcriptional regulator of gametocytogenesis (ap2-g) resulted in transcript depletion that functionally impaired sexual differentiation in committed parasites, reducing significantly the Sexual Conversion Rate a 70%. Overall, our novel HF-Cas13d line provides a flexible, scalable, and non-locus-modifying addition to the P. falciparum genetic toolbox to accelerate functional genomics and malaria drug target identification.
affiliations: Instituto de Parasitologia y Biomedicina Lopez Neyra, Granada, Spain (corresponding author)

papers.title: Tet2-Clonal Hematopoiesis Promotes Whereas Dnmt3a-CH Inhibits Breast Cancer Progression During Aging
papers.abstract: Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) driven by somatic mutations in blood cells increases with age and is associated with adverse outcomes in cancer patients. How CHIP mutations influence solid tumor progression remains unclear. Using inducible murine models of Dnmt3a- or Tet2-mutant CHIP combined with orthotopic syngeneic breast cancer models, we demonstrate that upon aging Dnmt3a-mutant CHIP prevents whereas Tet2-mutant CHIP drives breast cancer progression. Dnmt3a-mutant immune infiltrates established interferon-mediated MHCIIhigh tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) that supported cytotoxic CD8+ T cell-mediated tumor rejection. In contrast, Tet2-mutant TAMs exhibited an inflammatory, immunosuppressive phenotype characterized by increased IL-1 and CXCL2 production, reduced MHCII expression, and impaired T cell recruitment and activation. Therapeutic blockade of IL-1R1 or CXCR2 reduced tumor progression in aged Tet2-mutant CHIP mice and partially restored anti-tumor immunity. These findings establish that the effects of CHIP on cancer are mutation- and age-dependent and identify IL-1/CXCL2-driven inflammation as a therapeutic vulnerability of tumor-promoting Tet2-mutant CHIP.
affiliations: Department of Medical Oncology and Hematology, University Hospital Zurich and University of Zurich, Switzerland and Comprehensive Cancer Center Zurich (CCCZ), Z (corresponding author)

papers.title: Peptide-level assay of protein interaction using combinatorial native and denatured proteolysis
papers.abstract: Protein protein interactions underlie many extracellular defense and protease regulatory processes, yet identifying their structural interfaces directly in complex biological samples remains challenging. Limited proteolysis coupled with mass spectrometry provides peptide level readouts of local protease accessibility, but linking condition dependent peptide recovery to structural regions in endogenous proteomes requires complementary analysis. Here, we report peptide level assay of protein interaction (PLAPI) using combinatorial native and denatured proteolysis. A single human serum specimen was analyzed in three paired technical preparations using brief trypsin digestion under native conditions and extended digestion after denaturation, followed by isotopic diethyl labeling and LCMS/MS. Applying a 2 of 3 detection rule yielded 920 denatured only peptides and 124 peptides detected under both conditions, with no native only peptides. Mapping to the reference structures placed 13 denatured only C3b peptides at the Factor B binding interface and identified multiple denatured only A2M intersubunit contact regions. Within the A2M bait region, adjacent peptides exhibited different detection patterns; two were detected under both conditions, whereas one was detected only after denaturation. STRING association and enrichment analyses linked the candidate proteins to extracellular defense and protease regulation. These results indicate that PLAPI can provide peptide level evidence for prioritizing structural regions in complex serum samples and guide focused follow up analyses.
affiliations: Tongji University (corresponding author)

papers.title: The relevance of GGCC methylation for cyanobacterial gene expression regulation
papers.abstract: Compared to eukaryotic organisms, the regulatory significance of epigenetic DNA modifications is much less well understood in bacteria. In the cyanobacterium Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803, the DNA-specific methyltransferase M.Ssp6803II modifies the first cytosine in GGCC, forming N4-methylcytosine (GGm4CC). This motif occurs 38,512 times in the Synechocystis 6803 chromosome alone. Previous analyses showed that deletion of the gene encoding M.Ssp6803II ({triangleup}sll0729), caused a bluish phenotype due to the aberrant expression of the hemJ gene encoding protoporphyrinogen IX oxidase, HemJ. This effect was caused by the lacking GGCC methylation in the discriminator sequence of the hemJ promoter in the sll0729 deletion mutant. In the present study, we analyzed the impact of GGm4CC methylation on the overall gene expression. Bioinformatic analyses of multiple, independently obtained DNA microarray datasets revealed reproducible methylation-dependent changes in the expression of more than 300 genes. We selected 26 genes that had the GGCC methylation motif in different locations of their promoter sequences and verified their differential expression through qPCR analyses. Classification of the promoters according to the relative position of GGCC motifs suggested context-specific effects on gene expression. These findings imply that GGm4CC methylation via DNA methyltransferase M.Ssp6803II has an important impact on proper gene expression in Synechocystis 6803, and likely other bacteria.
affiliations: Genetics and Experimental Bioinformatics, Faculty of Biology, Institute of Biology III, University of Freiburg (corresponding author)

papers.title: Multi-target biocontrol by avocado fungal endophytes and their metabolites
papers.abstract: Background: Endophytic fungi can contribute to host defense against pests and pathogens through insecticidal and/or antifungal activity. Here, we evaluated the multi-target biocontrol potential of 11 avocado endophytic fungal strains against three plant pathogens (Colletotrichum gloeosporioides, Fusarium solani and Phytophthora cinnamomi) and two insect pests (Sitophilus zeamais and Xyleborus bispinatus) and analyzed the metabolomic profile of the two fungal strains with strongest bioactivity. Results: Trichoderma species exhibited the strongest pathogen inhibition in dual-culture and diffusible compound assays. Purpureocillium and Pochonia strains combined pathogen inhibition through diffusible metabolites with strong insecticidal activity, supporting their multi-target potential.
