Ethyl acetate (EtOAc) extracts from strain Trichoderma 3 inhibited all phytopathogens, whilst strain Purpureocillium extracts were most active against P. cinnamomi. Compounds tentatively identified as macrocyclic trichothecenes (Trichoderma 3) and cyclosporine-like cyclic peptides (Purpureocillium) were potentially responsible for the displayed bioactivity. Conclusion: Avocado endophytic fungi and their crude extracts show promising potential for multi-target biocontrol, whilst their metabolomic profiles provide candidate compounds for further chemical isolation and bioactivity evaluation.
affiliations: Instituto de Ecologia, A.C. (corresponding author)

papers.title: PKR inhibition prevents maladaptive responses to endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress in early-onset dystonia DYT-PRKRA.
papers.abstract: DYT-PRKRA is a rare, childhood-onset dystonia caused by mutations in the PRKRA gene, which encodes the protein PACT. PACT activates protein kinase R (PKR) in response to endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress. In DYT-PRKRA patient cells, the PACT-PKR interaction is enhanced, increasing sensitivity to ER stress-induced apoptosis. The canonical protein kinase activated by ER stress is PKR-like endoplasmic reticulum kinase (PERK), which phosphorylates the subunit of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2 (eIF2) to initiate the integrated stress response (ISR) and restore cellular homeostasis via the transcription factor ATF4. However, under persistent stress, ATF4 induces CHOP, shifting the adaptive response toward apoptosis. PKR, also activated by ER stress, phosphorylates eIF2, but its contribution to cellular homeostasis remains understudied. This work shows, for the first time, that PKR activation is essential for CHOP induction during ISR, directly linking enhanced apoptosis in DYT-PRKRA cells to prolonged PKR activation and heightened CHOP induction. Strikingly, a small-molecule PKR inhibitor effectively blocks CHOP expression and significantly decreases apoptosis in DYT-PRKRA cells, suggesting PKR inhibition as an effective therapeutic strategy for DYT-PRKRA.
affiliations: University of South Carolina (corresponding author)

papers.title: Lipid-Mediated Control of ER Function During Apoptosis
papers.abstract: Lipid-derived metabolites act as potent regulators of cell fate by disrupting organelle homeostasis, yet the mechanisms by which they trigger apoptosis remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigate how the sphingolipid-derived aldehyde trans-2-hexadecenal (t-2-hex) promotes apoptotic signaling through coordinated effects on endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and mitochondrial function in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. We show that t-2-hex induces ER stress and activates the unfolded protein response via the canonical Ire1-Hac1 pathway, while simultaneously impairing mitochondrial protein import. Mechanistically, we identify the ER chaperone Kar2/BiP as a direct target of covalent lipidation by t-2-hex at a conserved cysteine residue, resulting in defective protein folding and proteostasis collapse. We further define the ER-associated short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase Fmp52 as a critical protective factor that, together with the mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase Hfd1, counteracts lipid-induced stress. Notably, the human ortholog Tip30 functionally substitutes for Fmp52, highlighting evolutionary conservation. Our findings uncover a lipid-mediated mechanism that coordinately disrupts ER and mitochondrial proteostasis to drive apoptosis, and identify Fmp52/Tip30 as a conserved safeguard against lipid-induced cytotoxicity.
affiliations: Instituto de Biomedicina de Valencia IBV-CSIC (corresponding author)

papers.title: Intercellular trafficking of latent TGF-β1 converts integrin expressing cells into signaling relays
papers.abstract: TGF-{beta}1 is secreted as a latent complex tethered to the cell surface by milieu molecules such as GARP, and its activation requires direct engagement by integrin-expressing cells. How this interaction converts the latent complex into signaling-competent growth factor (GF) remains unclear. Here we show that contact between GARP/TGF-{beta}1-presenting cells and cells expressing integrin V{beta}6 or V{beta}8 triggers rapid trogocytosis of the latent complex, both in transfected cells and two cancer cell lines that natively express these integrins. Independent labeling of the prodomain, GF, and GARP shows that all three components are co-transferred to the integrin-expressing cell, and a TGF-{beta}1 mutant (RGE) that cannot bind integrins shows little transfer. Using a reporter system that tracks pathway activation in presenting, integrin-expressing, and bystander cells, we find that GF-neutralizing antibodies block downstream signaling more effectively in bystander cells than in the first two cell types that participate in trogocytosis. Blocking cleavage between the prodomain and the GF blocks signaling in bystander cells while still permitting signaling in trogocytosing cell types. Finally, we integrin-expressing cells that have taken up latent TGF-{beta}1 by trogocytosis can activate it and signal to bystander cells after the TGF-{beta}1 cells are removed, indicating that trogocytosis converts integrin-expressing cells into TGF-{beta} signaling relays. These findings identify a role for trogocytosis in regulating the specificity of TGF-{beta}1 activation and signaling, and reveal a novel function of integrins in controlling protein localization.
affiliations: Boston Children's Hospital (corresponding author)

papers.title: Single-cell Transcriptome-Proteome-PTMome(x8)-Metabolome (scTPPM) co-profiling decodes multimodal regulation during mouse oocyte meiosis
papers.abstract: Single-cell multi-omics technology is crucial for comprehensive characterization of cellular molecular features. Despite recent advances in single-cell multi-omics approaches, co-profiling of nucleic acids, proteins, metabolites, and post-translational modifications (PTMs) within the same cell individuals remains major challenges. Here, we developed a single-cell transcriptome, proteome, PTMome, and metabolome (scTPPM) profiling approach, enabling simultaneous analysis of transcriptomes, proteomes, eight types of PTMs (e.g., phosphorylation, methylation, ubiquitination, O_GlcNAc, acetylation, crotonylation, lactylation, and succinylation), and metabolomes in individual cells. We demonstrated the scTPPM's performance in tumor cell lines and oocyte samples, reaching total identification and quantification of 27,668 genes, 4,847 proteins, 1,508 PTM sites, and 680 metabolites in single mouse oocytes. We profiled previously-uncharacterized dynamic crosstalk among the entire metabolic pathways from metabolic enzyme expression and regulation to metabolite-mediated post-translational modifications during oocyte maturation. In summary, scTPPM provided an effective workflow for multi-omics co-profiling in single cells, enabling multi-layered insights into complex regulatory network.
affiliations: Institute of Microanalytical Systems in Department of Chemistry, Zhejiang University (corresponding author)

papers.title: A dynamic phosphoproteome reveals stage-specific regulation of cytokinesis in Leishmania
papers.abstract: Leishmania parasites undergo extensive morphological and metabolic remodelling during their transition from motile insect promastigotes to non-motile intracellular amastigotes, yet how dynamic protein kinase signalling drives this process remains poorly understood. Here, we present a high-resolution temporal phosphoproteome of L. mexicana promastigote to axenic amastigote differentiation, profiling 16,495 phosphosites on 3,101 proteins across seven developmental time points and identifying 5,795 dynamically regulated sites. This temporal map reveals stage-specific signalling programs, including regulated sites in MPK2 and non-regulated sites in MRK1, protein kinases known to be essential for amastigote differentiation. Using analogue-sensitive (AS) chemical genetics, we show that acute inhibition of either kinase in axenic amastigotes disrupts the spatial coordination of cleavage furrow ingression with nuclear and kinetoplast segregation, revealing essential cytokinesis roles obscured in constitutive gene deletions. Despite generating similar cytokinesis phenotypes, genetic over-expression and cellular localisation analyses demonstrate that MPK2 and MRK1 act through spatially segregated signalling pathways. Time-resolved phosphoproteomics upon MPK2 inhibition places its activity upstream of cytoskeletal remodelling networks. Importantly, we show that the stage-specific requirement for MPK2 is defined by the parasite's morphology: while motile promastigotes tolerate MPK2 inhibition, genetic ablation of flagellar motility sensitises them to loss of MPK2 activity. Thus, flagellar motility acts as a mechanical buffer during promastigote division, explaining why non-motile amastigotes are vulnerable to MPK2 inhibition. Together, our findings provide a systems level framework for Leishmania signalling and demonstrate that cellular architecture and biomechanics dictate protein kinase dependency across developmental stages of the parasite.
affiliations: University of York (corresponding author)

papers.title: SUMOylation Regulates IRF2BP2 Nuclear Localization and Stability
papers.abstract: Interferon Regulatory Factor-2 Binding Protein 2 (IRF2BP2) is a transcriptional cofactor implicated in diverse biological processes. Although it functions primarily as a repressor, it can also activate gene expression. However, the mechanisms governing IRF2BP2 regulation remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that IRF2BP2 interacts with UBE2I, the SUMO E2 ligase, and undergoes multi-SUMOylation, which enhances its nuclear localization. We further show that IRF2BP2 nuclear import is importin-{beta}-dependent and requires the functional nuclear localization signal (NLS). IRF2BP2 preferentially accumulates in transcriptionally active euchromatin in both resting and S-phase cells, consistent with its role in transcriptional control. We further reveal that SUMOylation contributes to IRF2BP2 stability. Moreover, IRF2BP2 is also ubiquitinated, predominantly through K6-linked ubiquitin chains, a non-proteolytic modification that aligns with our observation that IRF2BP2 is not degraded by the proteasome. Together, these findings identify SUMOylation and non-proteolytic ubiquitination as key mechanisms regulating IRF2BP2, highlighting a novel SUMO1-NLS-importin-{beta}-dependent pathway that governs its localization.
affiliations: Program of Immunology and Tumor Biology, Brazilian National Cancer Institute (INCA), Rio de Janeiro, 20231-050, RJ, Brazil. (corresponding author)

papers.title: NMR assignment and functional characterization of biotechnologically modified xanthan
papers.abstract: Xanthan gum is one of the most important industrial microbial polysaccharides, yet comprehensive molecular-level structural characterization remains limited because of its high molecular weight, conformational rigidity, and severe spectral overlap in nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy. Here, we present a near-complete 1H/13C NMR chemical shift assignment of the xanthan repeating unit by combining multidimensional NMR spectroscopy with targeted glycosyltransferase knockout strains and controlled enzymatic depolymerization. Comparative analysis of xanthan from the wild-type strain and the{Delta} gumI and{Delta} gumK variants enabled unambiguous assignment of {beta}-mannose and glucuronic acid resonances and, by extension, the remaining sugars, supporting future structural studies of engineered xanthan variants. In addition, we investigated how side-chain composition affects xanthan properties by analyzing genetically modified variants lacking specific acetyl, pyruvyl, or sugar residues. Temperature-dependent 1H NMR determined order-disorder transition temperatures and revealed that removing pyruvate or negatively charged side-chain components increased thermal stability, whereas losing the terminal {beta}-mannose destabilized the ordered conformation. Together, these results establish a robust NMR assignment for xanthan and provide new insights into how individual side-chain substituents influence the structural stability of this polysaccharide, facilitating the rational characterization of engineered xanthan variants and structurally closely related polysaccharides.
affiliations: Norwegian University of Science and Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Aging Remodels the Female Skeletal Muscle Proteome Toward Matrix, Chromatin and Lysosomal Programs that Track Loss of Physical Function
papers.abstract: Loss of skeletal muscle strength and mobility is among the most consequential features of human aging, yet the molecular programs that accompany this decline in women remain poorly understood. Here, we performed deep comprehensive data-independent acquisition (DIA) proteomic profiling of vastus lateralis biopsies from 10 younger (24-30 years) and 10 older (70-84 years) healthy women enrolled through the NIH Common Fund Cellular Senescence Network (SenNet), with matched measurements of grip strength and gait speed. Of 2,391 quantified protein groups, 163 were significantly altered with age, and partial least squares-discriminant analysis completely separated the age groups (cross-validated AUC = 1.00). Older muscle showed increased extracellular matrix and vascular remodeling proteins (TIMP3, COL8A1, ELN, FBN1), nuclear, chromatin and RNA-binding proteins (HMGB1, HMGB2, histone H1.0, MATR3, NCL), and lysosomal and senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP)-associated proteins (CTSZ, CTSD, PSAP), together with reduced glycolytic and energetic proteins (GAPDH, ENO3, PHKA1, CYCS). Age effects were robust to adjust for body mass index (BMI). Integrating differential abundance, multivariate importance and participant-level consistency, we defined a 24-protein skeletal muscle aging signature whose score separated all younger from all elderly women. Combining grip strength and gait speed into a combined function score, we found that 23 of the 24 signature proteins correlated with physical function (FDR < 0.05), and the signature score correlated strongly with function (r = -0.79). The senescence-associated alarmins HMGB1 and HMGB2 emerged as lead proteins: HMGB1 showed the strongest association with function (r = -0.86), and both remained associated after adjustment for age group. Together, these data define a senotype proteomic program in aging female skeletal muscle and a molecular signature of muscle function that, after validation, may serve as a readout for interventions that aim to preserve physical performance in elderly women.
affiliations: Buck Institute for Research on Aging, Novato, CA, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Selected for the surface: adaptive laboratory evolution for accelerated cathodic biofilm development in Cupriavidus necator
papers.abstract: Cupriavidus necator is a metabolically versatile facultative chemolithoautotroph and a promising chassis for sustainable bioproduction from CO2. Efficient coupling of its metabolism to renewable electricity through microbial electrosynthesis (MES) requires the organism to form stable, electroactive biofilms on cathodes. This step is hindered under oxic conditions (oxic MES, oMES) by electrochemically generated reactive oxygen species (ROS), mass-transfer limitations and poor biofilm stability. Systematic strategies to improve C. necator biofilm formation on cathodes have been lacking. Here we used adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) to address this gap. The progenitor strain colonised graphite cathodes only after an initial heterotrophic phase and formed spatially uneven biofilms whose distribution mirrored the local flow field, as resolved by micro-particle tracking velocimetry. Populations were then selected over five passages under controlled, oxygen-limited cathodic conditions. Resequencing revealed that the recovered population was genetically heterogeneous, and its dominant isolate, strain 890, was characterised in a microfluidic oMES platform. Strain 890 reached the target electrode coverage in about one day instead of six and maintained a robust biofilm at the progenitor's steady-state biovolume, whereas the multi-strain pool peaked higher but proved unstable. Relative to the progenitor, the accelerated biofilm phenotype of strain 890 is driven by a single novel mutation in a bifunctional diguanylate cyclase/phosphodiesterase locus, which likely encodes a central regulator of the planktonic-to-biofilm transition. The steady-state biovolume itself remained bounded, most probably due to a mass-transfer ceiling set by the counter-directional supply of H2 and O2. This work shows that ALE renders the initial-attachment barrier of cathodic biofilm formation genetically tractable, providing strain 890 as a robust chassis and a well-defined starting point for oMES-based CO2 valorisation.
affiliations: Hamburg University of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: DECODE: DEcomposition of COupled and DEcoupled Brain States: Separating Structure-Coupled and Structure-Decoupled Functional Organization in Alzheimers Disease
papers.abstract: Brain functional activity emerges within an underlying structural scaffold. While structural network connectivity provides a relatively stable anatomical backbone for large-scale communication, functional interactions are high-dimensional and temporally dynamic, forming recurrent patterns that can be represented in a latent space of transient functional states. Yet, how these transient functional states are organized and the extent to which they remain constrained by structural network connectivity or become relatively decoupled from structural organization over time remain poorly understood. To address this gap, we introduce DECODE (DEcomposition of COupled and DEcoupled Brain States), a data-driven latent-space framework that uses independent component analysis (ICA) and multimodal data to decompose resting-state dynamic functional network connectivity into a lower-dimensional representation of transient functional states. These states capture temporally varying structure-coupled and structure-decoupled patterns using diffusion MRI-derived structural network connectivity priors. Structure-coupled states reflect functional configurations more strongly anchored to major structural motifs, whereas structure-decoupled states represent configurations less constrained by the identified structural organization, while potentially remaining within structurally defined dynamical bounds. DECODE identifies reproducible structure-coupled and structure-decoupled states, with mean squared error reconstruction of dynamic information < 0.1 and adjusted R-squared = 0.4. Applied to Alzheimers disease (AD), DECODE revealed stronger group differences (FDR-corrected p-value 0.05) in both connectivity organization and temporal dynamics for decoupled states. These findings suggest that functional states less constrained by identified structural organization may be more vulnerable to AD-related disruption, whereas structure-coupled states may be relatively preserved. More broadly, DECODE provides a reproducible and generalizable framework for quantifying how functional dynamics are shaped by, or diverge from, structural organization by incorporating a latent representation of the structural connectome as an informative prior. Our findings established structural and functional alignment variation by distinguishing dynamic functional patterns closely coupled with structure from those that deviate from it.
affiliations: Tri-Institutional Center for Translational Research in Neuroimaging and Data Science (Georgia State University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Emory Universit (corresponding author)

papers.title: REZCUE: Rescuing 3D spatial omics from archived FFPE tissue
papers.abstract: Archived formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue represents a vast clinical resource, yet three-dimensional imaging and omics-wide molecular profiling remain largely incompatible because current antigen retrieval and clearing can degrade nucleic acids. We developed REZCUE, a depth-invariant antigen retrieval chemistry that enables 3D multiplexed immunofluorescence imaging of intact FFPE tissue while quantitatively preserving DNA, RNA, and protein for multi-omics analyses. REZCUE restores antigenicity in tissue archived for up to 30 years, supports 160 commercial whole-IgG antibodies across tissue types, and enables imaging to 6 mm depth. Imaging before destructive molecular profiling establishes a 3D spatial reference for registering molecular assays to intact tissue architecture. REZCUE enabled multi-modal mapping of spatial niches of the mouse brain and identified a human breast tumor compartment not distinguishable by conventional section-based spatial-omics, revealed after integrating 3D image-guided segmentation with spatial transcriptomics, mass spectrometry, miRNA sequencing, and whole-genome sequencing. In short, REZCUE transforms archived FFPE specimens into spatially registered, molecularly resolved, 3D substrates for sequential spatial multi-omic interrogation.
affiliations: Stanford University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Single Nucleus Profiling Reveals Rewired Tumor-Immune-Stromal Cell Communication in Plasmacytoid Urothelial Carcinoma
papers.abstract: Plasmacytoid urothelial carcinoma (PUC) is an aggressive histologic subtype of bladder cancer associated with worse patient outcomes and therapeutic response compared to conventional urothelial carcinoma (CUC). While recent work has demonstrated metastatic lymph nodes from PUC tumors have an inflamed phenotype, how the tumor microenvironment (TME) and crosstalk between tumor, stromal, and immune cells in primary PUC bladder tumors differs from those in CUC remains poorly understood. The impact of these differences on response to immunotherapy is also unknown. To understand TME differences between CUC and PUC and their impact on cell signaling, we performed single nucleus RNA sequencing on PUC and CUC tumors, as well as Xenium spatial transcriptomics on a mixed CUC / PUC tumor. We identified increased signaling between PUC-enriched, CDH1-low urothelial cells, immunosuppressive lipid-associated macrophages, and SFRP2+/CTHRC1+ fibroblasts in PUC tumors compared to CUC. Spatial transcriptomics identified increased macrophage infiltration in PUC histology and colocalization of PUC tumor cells, immunosuppressive macrophages, and SFRP2+ fibroblasts. Taken together, this study delineates PUC architecture and demonstrates interplay CDH1-low tumor cells, EMT, and immunosuppressive macrophages, identifying possible therapeutic vulnerabilities in PUC.
affiliations: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (corresponding author)

papers.title: An anaerobic cell-free protein synthesis formulation for the in vitro study of oxygen sensitive proteins
papers.abstract: Anaerobic microbes harbor unique enzymes and metabolic pathways with potential biotechnological applications, yet these microbes remain difficult to study and engineer. Research is limited by the labor-intensive workflows required to maintain anoxic environments and the lack of genetic tools available for non-model anaerobes. Here, we present an anaerobic cell-free protein synthesis (CFPS) platform for the in vitro study of oxygen-sensitive enzymes. This study establishes two methods for conducting anaerobic CFPS, achieving an anoxic environment by (1) sparging with inert gas or (2) lyophilizing to remove oxygenated water. We show the functionality of our anaerobic CFPS formulation by producing oxygen-independent fluorescent protein reporters and a [4Fe-4S] cluster pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase (PFOR) with a specific activity of 5.2 {+/-} 0.3 x 10-4 U/{micro}L cell-free extract. This highly modular platform will allow study of diverse oxygen-sensitive proteins and requires only minor modifications to commonly used CFPS workflows.
affiliations: University of California Santa Barbara (corresponding author)

papers.title: Associative Learning and Memory Erasure in a Synthetic Multicellular System
papers.abstract: Learning is a basic form of adaptation that organisms display from neural systems to single cells. In associative learning, the pairing of two stimuli lets one of them evoke the response to the other. Engineering this behavior in a living cell is difficult, because coincidence detection, memory, and conditional readout must be wired into a single regulatory network. Here we build a consortium of five E. coli strains that distributes the operations of associative learning and communicates through one diffusible quorum-sensing signal. The same signal acts as the memory trace. One strain detects the coincidence of the two inputs, a second maintains the memory through positive feedback in the shared medium, a third reads it out on the conditioned stimulus, a fourth reports the unconditioned response, and a fifth erases the memory on command. We show experimentally that the assembled consortium learns the association, since a stimulus that is silent before training evokes a strong response after pairing. Memory is retained through a medium exchange in which both stimuli are removed, and then the conditioned stimulus alone evokes the response. The reporter is not produced without its input. An erase command returns the response to the background. A population model of the consortium accounts for the sequence of responses and gives design rules for writing, retention, and erasure, and a trade-off in storing memory in a shared extracellular signal. Distributing the operations over strains makes each of them separately tunable and testable and provides a route to microbial communities that learn from their history.
affiliations: European Molecular Biology Laboratory (EMBL-Barcelona) (corresponding author)

papers.title: Self-organized criticality in a mammalian RNA-interference circuit
papers.abstract: Living systems have been argued to operate near critical points, but their relevance at the cellular level is poorly understood. Critical states allow for a high sensitivity to external inputs and maximal information transfer and display fluctuations at all scales. Critical points are very special, and require the fine tuning of a control parameter, which is hard to reconcile with the robustness of living cells. Self-organized criticality (SOC) proposes that feedback, rather than tuning, brings a system to its critical point. Here we show that RNA interference, in which messenger RNAs compete for shared silencing machinery and so queue for service, together with negative feedback gives rise to SOC in mammalian cells. In a synthetic circuit, a protein repressor whose mRNA competes with the mRNA of a fluorescent reporter that it represses senses the congestion of the queue, closing the feedback loop. Theory and stochastic simulations show that the loop holds the queue near its critical point despite changes in its parameters, and that expression becomes intermittent, with scale-free bursts. Measurements in human cell lines show the predicted power-law distributions of single-cell fluorescence. RNA interference could thus support engineered SOC in animal cells and may also contribute to SOC in natural systems.
affiliations: European Molecular Biology Laboratory (EMBL-Barcelona) (corresponding author)

papers.title: Coarse-tuning to improve a protein foundation model for a domain of proteins: the example of outer membrane beta barrels
papers.abstract: Foundation models for proteins have shown great potential in addressing a wide range of challenges in computational molecular biology. State-of-the-art models are trained on large and diverse corpora of protein sequences, enabled by self-supervised training. The models are then used in transfer learning and the embeddings they calculate are used in supervised downstream tasks. We propose a novel focusing mechanism for foundation models, which we call 'coarse-tuning'. In coarse-tuning, we further update the model, using a defined yet unlabeled, dataset to enhance its performance in a specific domain. We demonstrate this approach using Outer Membrane Beta Barrels (OMBBs) - proteins that are found in the distinct biophysical environment of the outer membrane. Our results show that coarse-tuned models outperform the original foundation model when applied to various transfer learning tasks. Additionally, we study the embeddings generated by the coarse-tuned models and compare them to those from the original foundation model, including an investigation of the learned attention matrices via contact map predictions. Our work suggests that a medium-sized dataset (fewer than 100,000 protein sequences) is sufficient to effectively specialize a foundation model to a specific domain, enhancing its utility for domain-specific applications.
affiliations: University of Haifa (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cortical ER-PM contact sites promote nuclear ER membrane integrity and mitotic nuclear segregation
papers.abstract: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) extends from the nuclear envelope through the cytoplasm to the cell cortex, where it contacts the plasma membrane (PM) at ER-PM membrane contact sites (MCSs). We hypothesized that as contiguous extensions of nuclear ER these cortical ER (cER) attachments to the PM might dampen shearing stresses on the nuclear envelope and help orchestrate nuclear ER dynamics. Although individual cER-PM tether proteins promote cER inheritance during mitosis, our findings reveal that removing all cER-PM tethers collectively disrupts nuclear envelope membrane integrity. In yeast {triangleup}-super-tether ({triangleup}-s-tether) cells lacking seven cER-PM tethers, cER detachment causes membrane blisters and nuclear envelope ruptures; however, individual tether deletions or ER stress do not disrupt nuclear containment. Despite the extensive nuclear envelope lesions in {triangleup}-s-tether cells, ESCRT-III (Endosomal Sorting Complex Required for Transport-III)-mediated membrane repair sustains cell viability. The loss of nuclear integrity, however, appears to disrupt genomic repair and promotes spontaneous mutation; separately, nuclear inheritance is also disrupted. Without cER-PM MCSs, cortical actin depolarization and defects in nucleopodia impair mitotic nuclear dynamics and segregation, which triggers a Spindle Position Checkpoint (SPOC) cell-cycle delay. That cER-PM MCSs serve as dual-function hubs for the preservation of nuclear envelope integrity is indicated by two independent mechanisms capable of rescuing the observed nuclear membrane defects: the restoration of phospholipid metabolism or the re-establishment of nonspecific cER-PM contact.
affiliations: Simon Fraser University (corresponding author)

papers.title: The performance of genetic-constraint metrics varies significantly across the human noncoding genome
papers.abstract: A longstanding goal in human genetics is to prioritize noncoding loci that, when disrupted, lead to developmental disorders and other Mendelian traits. In pursuit of this goal, multiple metrics have been developed to distinguish neutrally evolving sequences from those subjected to purifying selection. These metrics are commonly evaluated genome-wide, e.g., by computing a precision-recall curve on windows tiling the entire noncoding genome. Here, we identify parts of the noncoding genome where these metrics are distorted due to "bias" in the underlying models of neutral genetic variation and underperform due to a low "signal-to-noise ratio" in the genetic data. The most extreme effects are found for Gnocchi (Chen et al. 2024), the performance of which declines as GC content increases. We trace the source of the bias in Gnocchi to a mismatch between the training set of de novo mutations (DNMs) used to adjust expected SNP counts and the genomic windows on which those expected counts are computed. Resolving that mismatch produces a more calibrated version of Gnocchi, significantly improving its interpretability in applications. Looking forward, we suggest annotating constraint scores of noncoding genomic intervals with robust measures of the bias of the corresponding model, allowing users to gauge confidence in those scores.
affiliations: University of Utah (corresponding author)

papers.title: Deconstructing evolutionary histories of complex genomic rearrangements in lung malignancies
papers.abstract: Complex genomic rearrangements (CGRs) are hallmarks of tumor genomes, yet their architectures and origins remain poorly understood. We utilized optical mapping to profile the genomic landscapes of lung tissues across various stages - from normal and benign lesions to advanced carcinomas - to characterize genome disorganization during carcinogenesis. We developed omcplR to resolve the CGR architectures and predict their genesis using the genome-graph framework. Our findings reveal that many CGRs arise from hierarchical combinations of localized structural variations that are unlikely due to break-fusion-bridge, chromothripsis, or chromoplexy. We termed this process chromodiadochi: a cascade of nested rearrangements accumulating over multiple generations during carcinogenesis. Early intra-chromosomal junctions in CGRs typically localized within specific chromatin domains, while late junctions in advanced tumors occurred in more heterogeneous contexts and showed signs of positive selection. A composite signature of genomic alterations, including the CGRs, captures the trajectory of progressive genomic structural disorganization and instability from benign tissue to malignancy.
affiliations: Rutgers University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Shared Molecular Signatures and Pathways in Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder, Schizophrenia, and Bipolar Disorder: An Integrative Transcriptomic and Machine-Learning Study
papers.abstract: Abstract Objective: Psychiatric disorders such as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), schizophrenia, and bipolar disorder (BD) are complex conditions with overlapping molecular features that remain poorly understood. This study aimed to identify shared molecular abnormalities and potential therapeutic targets associated with these disorders. Methods: RStudio (version 4.4.1) was used to process and analyze gene expression datasets from the NCBI database to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs). FunRich, DAVID, STRING, and NetworkAnalyst were used for gene ontology and pathway enrichment, protein-protein interaction analysis, transcription factor and microRNA regulatory network analysis, and protein-chemical interaction analysis. The discriminatory ability of prioritized hub genes and transcription factors was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Four machine-learning algorithms (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, SVM-RBF, and Gradient Boosting) were compared using leave-one-out cross-validation on the GSE403628 dataset, comprising 14 controls and 14 cases. Results: Among 32 common genes, several candidate hub proteins were identified, including HLA-DRA, HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-DOB, and BRD2. The analysis also identified transcription factors (FOXC1, NFYA, RELA, GATA2, FOXL1, SRF, and NFIC), miRNAs (hsa-mir-129-2-3p, hsa-mir-148b-3p, hsa-mir-196a-5p, hsa-mir-26a-5p, hsa-mir-27a-3p, hsa-mir-23b-3p, hsa-mir-500a-3p, hsa-mir-423-5p, hsa-miR-142-5p, and hsa-miR-671-5p), and chemicals, including estradiol, antirheumatic agents, and valproic acid. ROC analysis showed the highest AUC for HLA-DRA (0.760) among hub genes and FOXC1 (0.658) among transcription factors. The hub-gene set consistently outperformed the transcription-factor set across all four machine-learning algorithms, with Logistic Regression achieving the highest AUC (0.800). Random Forest and SVM-RBF achieved the highest accuracy (0.679) under leave-one-out cross-validation. Conclusion: This computational approach identified potential biomarkers linking PTSD, schizophrenia, and BD to immune-related and infectious disease pathways. ROC and machine-learning analyses highlighted HLA-DRA as a promising discriminator between disease and control samples, providing candidate molecular targets for further investigation.
affiliations: Khwaja Yunus Ali University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Substrate binding and activation mechanism of the essential bacterial septal cell wall synthase FtsW
papers.abstract: Septal peptidoglycan (sPG) synthesis in most bacteria is driven by the essential, highly conserved FtsWIQLB synthase complex, comprising the SEDS (Shape, Elongation, Division, and Sporulation) glycosyltransferase FtsW, the monofunctional transpeptidase FtsI, and the scaffolding and regulatory subcomplex FtsQLB. Although apo structures of FtsWIQLB are known, no substrate-bound structures exist, likely due to the intrinsic flexibility of lipid II (L2) substrates. Here, we combined all-atom molecular dynamics simulations of E. coli FtsWIQLB with cysteine-based mutagenesis and cell-based assays to investigate donor and acceptor L2 binding sites in FtsW and to elucidate the complex's activation mechanism. We show that conserved arginine residues adjacent to membrane-accessible cavities in FtsW coordinate donor and acceptor L2 pyrophosphate groups, stabilizing substrate binding. The FtsWIQLB complex appears to adopt a self-inhibitory architecture in which gating elements and a periplasmic loop prevent the donor and acceptor from approaching FtsW's catalytic residue D297. Activation by FtsN or a superfission FtsW variant relieves these constraints, stabilizes acceptor-site binding, and reorients both substrates into a catalytically primed state. Long donor glycan chains further stabilize this activated conformation at the acceptor site, possibly promoting processive sPG polymerization. Comparative modeling of ESKAPE pathogen homologs reveals both conserved and divergent features of binding-site engagement and activation. We corroborate these computational findings with cysteine-based mutagenesis and crosslinking experiments. These results establish a mechanistic framework for FtsW substrate recognition and functional activation, highlighting tractable sites for structure- and mechanism-based antibiotic discovery targeting SEDS-class cell wall synthases.
affiliations: Department of Biophysics and Biophysical Chemistry, Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, Baltimore, MD 21205, United States (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Sequential Assembly Mechanism for Stable Cdc13 Dimerization on Telomeric DNA
papers.abstract: The telomere-binding protein Cdc13 specifically binds to single-stranded telomeric DNA, playing a critical role in telomere protection and length regulation. While extensive biochemical, molecular biological, and genetic studies have shown that Cdc13 can form dimers or oligomers in solution and bind telomeric DNA with high specificity, the dynamic mechanism of its loading onto telomeres is less well characterized. Combining two single-molecule methods, single-molecule fluorescence resonance energy transfer (smFRET) and colocalization single-molecule spectroscopy (CoSMoS), we demonstrate a kinetically favored sequential assembly pathway on a 12-nucleotide telomeric DNA segment involving an initial Cdc13 binding event followed by recruitment of a second Cdc13 molecule. While genetic studies suggest that monomeric Cdc13 binding alone is insufficient to maintain telomere length, our findings underscore the Cdc13 monomer regulatory importance in coordinating telomere synthesis and protection. This monomer-to-dimer transition provides a mechanistic basis for understanding the multifunctional roles of Cdc13 in telomere replication and protection.
affiliations: National Taiwan University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Nanocellulose hydrogels as bio-interface analogs for studying nanomaterial transport and accumulation
papers.abstract: Nanoparticles have been proposed as drug delivery vehicles to enhance targeting and efficiency of traditional and novel therapeutics. Previous studies have identified size, surface charge, and volume exclusion as factors that influence nanoparticle diffusion and retention. However, there is little accepted or successful quantification of how these parameters influence nanoparticle penetration relative to biological adaptation and biological response. Part of the challenge is the response of living biological interfaces to many of these nanoparticle delivery vehicles and nanosized drugs. This study aimed to emulate key physicochemical barriers to diffusion found in living biomaterials by developing a tunable, synthetic hydrogel. Through the controlled exposure of 150 kDa and 2 MDa nanodextrans with neutral and negative surface charge, we evaluated the system's ability to emulate three core physicochemical features often implicated in biofilm-associated transport resistance: size exclusion, charge interactions, and volume exclusion. We demonstrated a 30% statistically significant decrease in partition coefficients for 2 MDa nanodextran from 150 kDa nanodextran, confirming the ability of the nanocellulose-based microcaps to size based exclusion of hydrated biomaterial matrices. We combined our results with bioaccumulation data from the literature and found only the interaction of size and charge had a statistically significant effect (p-value < 0.05, F-statistic = 4.8). This controllable system can be coupled with in silico modeling to understand interfacial transport phenomena for nanomaterial-biomaterial interactions.
affiliations: Duke University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cell death and growth dynamics shape DNA-replication-based estimates of microbial growth
papers.abstract: A widely used approach for estimating bacterial growth rates is the origin-to-terminus ratio, or peak-to-trough ratio (PTR), which estimates DNA replication activity from origin and terminus copy numbers. Although PTR is theoretically related to bacterial growth rate, it is often compared with, or used to reason about, changes in population size, which reflect the balance between cell division and loss. These quantities may therefore diverge when cell death is appreciable. Here, we used stochastic, cell-based modelling and controlled laboratory experiments to examine how cell death affects the relationship between PTR and changes in population size. We show that transient stress-induced mortality and heterogeneous survival can cause PTR to fail to reflect changes in population size but still reflect bacterial growth rate. We experimentally validated these predictions by exposing \textit{Escherichia coli} to osmotic shock or antibiotics, and measuring change in population size and DNA replication activity. We further show that initial physiological state, lag before replication resumes, and abrupt growth arrest can alter the relationship between PTR and change in population size. In the presence of mortality, lag can make PTR more reflective of changes in population size whereas it decreases its correspondence with bacterial growth rate. Together, these results demonstrate how cell death and changes in replication dynamics can bias the interpretation of PTR-based estimates of population change under controlled laboratory conditions.
affiliations: University of British Columbia (corresponding author)

papers.title: Genetics and genomics of enteroarthroconidial development in Coccidioides
papers.abstract: Regulated cell death is a cornerstone of plant and animal development. Distant orthologs of some cell death genes are also found in microbes, with roles that remain incompletely understood. The human fungal pathogen Coccidioides causes the disease Valley fever when infectious spores called enteroarthroconidia are inhaled from soil. These spores develop via an unusual checkerboard-style differentiation in which alternating segments of hyphae (cellular filaments) die and disarticulate, releasing mature spores on either side. The molecular mechanisms are unknown. We first adapted single-cell transcriptomics for filamentous fungi, cataloguing expression across the specialized cells of a developing Coccidioides colony. With the resulting profiles, and cell-biological validation via protein tagging, we characterized high expression of the pyroptosis-like cell death pathway in hyphal segments destined to die. Next, we tested the function of pyroptosis-like pathway genes directly by genetic knockout; strains lacking these factors exhibited a phenotype of developmental arrest at a late stage in the colony, preserving hyphal growth but abrogating cell death and spore production. Together, these findings reveal the pyroptosis-like pathway as a requirement for enteroarthroconidial development, and thus infectivity, in Coccidioides. We propose that regulated cell death may prove to mediate events in development in many fungi with multicellular life cycles.
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley (corresponding author)

papers.title: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase organization is crucial for mammalian brain development
papers.abstract: Central nervous system development relies on spatially regulated protein synthesis, which includes the aminoacylation of tRNAs. Developmental brain disorders, such as leukodystrophies, can be caused by the exclusion of Arginyl-tRNA synthetase (RARS1) from the multi-tRNA synthetase complex, which does not affect its enzymatic function. To understand the purpose of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase complex formation, we engineered a mouse line where RARS1 is untethered from the complex in forebrains. We observed profound behavioral phenotypes and anatomical changes originating from a severe reduction in oligodendrocytes and subsequent myelination defects. On the molecular level, disruption of the multi-tRNA synthetase complex caused RARS1 mis-trafficking, which resulted in lost colocalization with ribosomes, leading to the concomitant activation of integrated stress response. Proteomics analysis of newly synthesized proteins suggested that mRNA translation in cellular projections was specifically reduced, affecting myelin structural proteins. In summary, exclusion of RARS1 from the multisynthetase complex led to its altered subcellular localization and decreased protein synthesis in oligodendrocyte projections, directly linking molecular effects to white matter pathologies. Altogether, our results reveal the necessity of aminoacylation organization for mammalian neurodevelopment.
affiliations: University of Toronto (corresponding author)

papers.title: Extending intravitreal retention of CNTF via fusion to the HA-binding protein VG1
papers.abstract: Glaucoma is the leading cause of permanent blindness worldwide. Vision loss in glaucoma stems from the loss of retinal ganglion cells (RGC). Ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF) has been shown to protect RGCs in pre-clinical models of glaucoma. However, CNTF has a short ocular retention time following intraocular injections due to rapid diffusion. To address this, we developed a fusion protein between CNTF and the hyaluronic acid- (HA) binding G1 domain of endogenous extracellular matrix (ECM) protein, versican (VG1; CNTF-VG1). We hypothesize that a CNTF-VG1 protein will have an extended ocular retention time compared to CNTF due to HA-binding with endogenous vitreous-HA. We demonstrate that CNTF-VG1 non-covalently binds HA with high affinity and is bioactive. We show that the vitreous and thermal stability of CNTF-VG1 can be significantly increased through co-formulation with HA. In an in vivo pharmacodynamic study, we show that VG1 significantly increases the window of neuroprotective JAK/STAT3 pathway activation in un-injured mice (C57BL/6J, female) retina. Finally, we close our work by showing that CNTF is neuroprotective of primary mouse cortical neurons in an acute H2O2 cytotoxicity model. Taken together, our work demonstrates the potential of HA-binding domain VG1 to improve the ocular retention of neuroprotective CNTF following intraocular injection.
affiliations: Pharmaceutical Development, Drug Delivery, Genentech, 1 DNA Way, South San Francisco, California 94080, US (corresponding author)

papers.title: Distinct effects of Atg3 and Atg10 on Autophagosome Formation in Yeast
papers.abstract: Autophagosome formation involves two E2 enzymes: Atg3, which conjugates Atg8 to the lipid phosphatidylethanolamine, and Atg10, which conjugates Atg12 to Atg5. Although both are required for autophagy, it is unclear exactly what roles these pathways play in the process of autophagosome formation. We used baker's yeast expressing mutant versions of both Atg3 and Atg10 that reduce, but do not eliminate, their activity to better understand their effects on Atg8 lipidation, autophagic flux, and the size and number of autophagosomes formed during nitrogen starvation. We found that while Atg3 primarily affects Atg8 lipidation and autophagosome size, Atg10 has less of an effect on Atg8 lipidation and primarily controls autophagosome number. This demonstrates that these two enzymes have distinct mechanistic roles in autophagosome formation, and implies an as-of-yet undiscovered function for the Atg12-Atg5 conjugate.
affiliations: Eastern Michigan University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Chemical crosslinking enables profiling of endogenous cell surface galectin-3 interactions
papers.abstract: Galectin-3 is a {beta}-galactoside-binding lectin that organizes glycoproteins into cell surface lattices (multivalent interaction networks) that regulate biology spanning immune function, fibrosis, heart disease, and cancer progression. Galectin-3 engages promiscuous but low-affinity glycan ligands, posing technical challenges for faithfully mapping the cell surface galectin-3 interactome. Here, we introduce Crosslinking-assisted Galectin Lattice Affinity Purification Mass Spectrometry (xGL-APMS), a facile and stringent proteome-scale approach that captures galectin-3 interactions natively at the cell surface, without the need for exogenous galectin-3, and is extendable to XL-MS. We identified 125 N-glycan branching-dependent surface galectin-3 interactors on Jurkat cells, validated interactions with six orthogonal approaches, and compared low and high-dose galectin-3 interactomes, revealing differences in both distribution and interactome composition. Finally, without exogenous or modified bait, we performed immediate crosslinking of endogenous galectin-3 to identify 69 galectin-3-associated proteins on primary mouse thymocytes. Together, these approaches provide a readily adoptable framework for measuring endogenous surface galectin-3 and profiling its interacting partners.
affiliations: University of California, Irvine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Inhibiting the interaction between the mitochondrial receptor Tom70 and SARS CoV 2 Orf9b with small molecules
papers.abstract: The SARS CoV 2 accessory protein Orf9b is in a complex monomer-dimer equilibrium that influences its interactions with the host mitochondrial receptor Tom70. This interaction is critical for viral suppression of a Type-1 interferon response during infection. Modulating this equilibrium with a small molecule, either by stabilizing the Orf9b dimer or blocking its interaction with Tom70, represents a promising strategy for restoring interferon signaling and the antiviral response. To build tool molecules that could test this concept, we performed two screens: a crystallographic fragment screen against the Orf9b homodimer and a high-throughput fluorescence polarization screen for competitors of an Orf9b-derived peptide binding to Tom70. Fragment screening revealed two binding sites with potential to be developed into an inhibitor: one located at the peripheral dimer interface and the other just outside the lipid-binding channel that defines the central dimer interface. Functionalization of the fragments outside of the lipid-binding channel with hydrophobic moieties stabilized the Orf9b dimer thereby indirectly inhibiting association with Tom70. In parallel, the high throughput screen for competitive inhibitors of the Tom70:Orf9b interaction discovered a separate series of molecules. These molecules display dynamic structure activity relationship (SAR) and could be improved in the future to modulate the interaction between Tom70 and potentially a wide range of substrates. Collectively, these results demonstrate the feasibility of two distinct strategies to manipulate the Orf9b-Tom70 equilibrium, which is critical to the host response to SARS CoV 2 infection.
affiliations: University of California, San Francisco (corresponding author)

papers.title: Kinase-phosphatase cycles drive self-sustained oscillations of protein condensates
papers.abstract: Phase-separated protein condensates organize biochemical processes in cells. ATP-driven enzymatic reactions can change the physical properties and even trigger the dissolution of such condensates. Here we use molecular simulations to show how ATP-driven kinase and phosphatase reactions modulate the organization of TDP-43 low complexity domain (LCD) condensates. TDP-43 phosphorylation is enhanced by condensation, as CK1{delta} preferentially binds to and acts in TDP-43 LCD condensates, whereas dephosphorylation by the phosphatase calcineurin occurs predominantly in the dilute phase. This differential recruitment of kinases and phosphatases, together with the slow redistribution of kinases into newly formed condensates, triggers oscillatory appearance and disappearance of TDP-43 LCD condensates. The oscillations are self-sustained, persisting at constant chemical driving, showing that an antagonistic kinase-phosphatase pair can endow a condensate with autonomous dynamics rather than only setting its structure.
affiliations: Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (corresponding author)

papers.title: Tumor vascularization and the nonlinear dynamics of metastatic cancer treated by oncolytic viral therapy
papers.abstract: Oncolytic viral therapy (OVT) is an emerging cancer treatment where therapeutic viruses are injected into a patient. Models have been developed which describe the interactions of the virus, tumor and immune system through systems of nonlinear ordinary differential equations (ODEs). Some suggest that an initial phase of treatment with immunosuppressants could improve the efficacy of OVT by preventing the immune system from attacking the oncolytic viruses before they can infect many tumor cells. However, all such models have focused on a single, localized tumor. Here, we model a primary tumor and its continuous metastatic seeding of a secondary organ under simplifying assumptions about tumor vascularization. Bifurcation analysis and simulations reveal regions in parameter space for which immune modulation encourages distant metastasis, leading to the dangerous scenario where the elimination of a primary tumor creates the false impression of a good prognosis. We also suggest that vascular disrupting agents may be useful for treating small tumors while they may promote OVT resistance in larger tumors.
affiliations: Northwestern University (corresponding author)

A plant RNA-binding protein senses 2′,3′-cNMP produced by insect effectors
papers.abstract: RNA-derived 2′,3′-cyclophosphate-terminated nucleotides act as immune signalling molecules in prokaryotes and eukaryotes1–3, but how plants perceive them remains unknown. Sucking insects inject digestive enzymes including RNases into the host plant to acquire nutrients. Here we demonstrate that NIB1, a glycine-rich RNA-binding protein in rice, senses 2′,3′-cyclic nucleotide monophosphates (2′,3′-cNMPs; 2′,3′-cAMP and 2′,3′-cGMP) and adenylyl-(3′→5′)-guanosine 2′,3′-cyclic phosphate (ApG>p) produced by a salivary T2 ribonuclease of green stink bug during feeding. Binding of the RNase products promotes formation of nuclear condensates containing NIB1, which recruit the core immune regulator Enhanced Disease Susceptibility 1 (EDS1) and activate defence, potentially contributing to the immune signalling of Toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) proteins that also produce the nuclease products. Exogenous application of 2′,3′-cAMP, 2′,3′-cGMP or ApG>p elicits NIB1 and EDS1-mediated immune responses. Our findings unveil a conserved pathway in plants, in which glycine-rich RNA-binding proteins perceive the nuclease-generated second messengers to launch defence and point to a potential link between plant TIR nuclease activity and EDS1 signalling. The rice RNA-binding protein NIB1 detects 2′,3′-cyclic nucleotide products from insect saliva RNase, forming nuclear condensates that recruit EDS1 to activate defence, revealing a conserved messenger-based immune pathway in plants.

papers.title: Domain-alteration chimeras rewire oncogenic complexes in prostate cancer
papers.abstract: Transcriptional addiction to the androgen receptor (AR) underlies metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer1, in which AR maintains oncogenic programs through domain-specific interactions with the acetyltransferases p300 and CBP (collectively p300/CBP)2. Here we describe a novel therapeutic modality, domain-alteration chimeras (DALTACs), that rewire endogenous protein complexes by enforcing non-native domain–domain interactions. Our first-in-class AR–p300/CBP DALTAC-1 induces synthetic proximity between the ligand-binding domain of AR and the bromodomain of p300/CBP, misconfiguring their native interface and locking the complex in a non-productive state. DALTAC-1 triggers a ‘super-inhibitory’ effect, suppressing AR-driven transcription and proliferation more potently than combined AR and p300/CBP inhibition. Mechanistically, DALTAC-1 reprograms p300/CBP substrate engagement, abolishing the histone mark H2B N-terminal acetylation and inducing neomorphic acetylation of AR and coactivators, ultimately collapsing the AR neo-enhanceosome. Chromatin profiling revealed redistribution of AR and p300/CBP towards palindromic androgen response elements, accompanied by disruption of cofactor and transcriptional machinery recruitment at oncogenic AR and ERG neo-enhancers. DALTAC-1 exhibits exquisite lineage selectivity, displaying potent activity in AR–p300/CBP dual-dependent cells and sparing AR-negative cells. In multiple in vivo models, DALTAC-1 induces deep and durable tumour regressions. Together, these findings establish DALTACs as a broadly applicable strategy to rewire disease-defining complexes through domain-topology alteration, expanding induced-proximity therapies, and the precise lineage selectivity of DALTAC-1 supports its translational potential in AR-driven prostate cancer. A novel therapeutic modality enforces non-native androgen receptor (AR)–p300/CBP interactions to collapse AR transcriptional programs, producing super-inhibitory, lineage-selective suppression of metastatic prostate cancer and establishing domain-alteration chimeras as a broadly applicable therapeutic strategy leveraging induced proximity.

papers.title: DeepMind's ultra-powerful AI for genome mapping wows scientists
Independent interferometric observable confirms black hole shadow in M87*
papers.abstract: A new epoch for direct visualization of accretion dynamics near the event horizon of a black hole began when the Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration synthesized an Earth-sized aperture with millimetre radio interferometry and published the first reconstructed image1–4 of a black hole shadow at the core of radio galaxy Messier 87 (M87). The image appeared as a ring-like structure, representing the gravitationally lensed and redshifted emission around the central supermassive black hole, M87*, located at the galactic nucleus. However, application of various data analysis and imaging heuristics resulted in divergent representations of M87* fine-scale features3,5–7, with some external analyses even challenging the fundamental ring-like morphology of the source8,9. Such difficulties arise as a consequence of the inherent sparsity of the very long baseline interferometry measurements, making interferometric image reconstruction an inadequately constrained problem. Moreover, the solution is sensitive to instrument calibration, post-processing algorithms and imaging hyperparameters. Here we apply an independent imaging algorithm that we have developed to the M87* dataset that is free from prescriptive morphological priors and founded on observables immune to instrument calibration errors. We reconstruct the black hole shadow image and unequivocally reproduce a ring-like morphology, with an angular diameter of 42.2 ± 1.5 μas corresponding to a black hole mass of 6.5 ± 0.5 billion solar masses assuming nominal scaling parameters, observed at an inclination angle of approximately 20° from the approaching jet. An imaging algorithm using closure-invariant formalism and diffusion-based reconstruction applied to supermassive black hole very long baseline radio interferometry datasets enables independent recovery of the ring-like shadow and mass that is free from the usual calibration and imaging assumptions.

papers.title: Suppression of epithelial proliferation and tumorigenesis by IgA
papers.abstract: Immunoglobulin A (IgA) is the most abundant antibody isotype produced by mammals, and has a specialized role in mucosal homeostasis1. IgA is constantly secreted into the intestinal lumen and binds to commensal microorganisms to regulate their colonization and function2,3, with unclear implications for health. IgA deficiency is common in humans, but difficult to study, because of its complex aetiology and comorbidities4–8. Here we use genetically and environmentally controlled mice to show that various models of IgA deficiency result in increased susceptibility to several models of endogenous colorectal cancer. Cellular and molecular analyses revealed that, in the absence of IgA, colonic epithelial cells induce antibacterial factors and accelerate cell cycling in response to the microbiota. Oral treatment with IgA was sufficient to reduce steady-state proliferation and protect mice from tumours; however, this function was due to the structure of the antibody rather than to binding specificity. In a reductionist culture system, IgA directly suppressed epithelial growth. Co-immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry and targeted CRISPR screening identified DMBT1 as an IgA-binding epithelial surface protein that is required for IgA-mediated suppression of proliferation. Together, IgA and DMBT1 tune the normal cycling of absorptive colonocyte progenitors. In IgA-knockout mice, deleting the transmembrane and cytoplasmic signalling portions of DMBT1 was sufficient to reverse both the increased epithelial cell proliferation and the increased tumour susceptibility seen in these mice. These experiments establish a homeostatic function for IgA in tempering physiological epithelial responses to the microbiota to maintain mucosal health. Experiments in mouse models show that immunoglobulin A in the gut lumen has a role in regulating the turnover of colon epithelial cells and reduces the susceptibility of mice to colorectal cancer.

papers.title: Glycosylation and importins liquefy the FG barrier in live nuclear pores
papers.abstract: The nuclear pore complex (NPC) regulates molecular traffic between nucleus and cytoplasm1,2. Its permeability barrier is formed by intrinsically disordered phenylalanine-glycine-rich nucleoporins (FG-NUPs), whose physical state has long been debated3–13. Deciphering how FG-NUPs behave inside living cells is crucial for understanding how NPCs achieve both selective and rapid transport. By combining site-specific labelling with time-resolved fluorescence anisotropy, here we show that FG domains exhibit nanosecond-scale, liquid-like segmental motion in live cells, whereas reconstituted FG condensates undergo a liquid-to-solid transition in vitro. Experiments and molecular-dynamics simulations further show that importin-β, a principal nuclear transport receptor, and O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine, a key post-translational modification of FG-NUPs, together stabilize the dynamic FG network. Finely balanced FG–FG and FG–importin-β interactions maintain FG-NUP liquidity and generate a radial organization in which importin-β is enriched near the NPC periphery and extended FG domains remain in the central channel, forming the transport barrier. This organization explains recent MINFLUX observations14 of rim-biased transport trajectories and is supported here by direct MINFLUX imaging of importin-β in mammalian cells. Together, our results reconcile conflicting models of FG-NUP organization4,5,7,9,15 and establish a framework for understanding how cellular context tunes intrinsically disordered proteins in health and disease. Nuclear pore proteins maintain a fluid, spatially organized barrier through coordinated molecular interactions, explaining how cells achieve selective transport and reconciling competing models of pore structure.

papers.title: Bureaucratic incentives shaped effectiveness of the one-child policy in China
papers.abstract: Empirical research so far largely suggests that population policies around the world do not explain a majority of the global fertility decline1–10. Notably, even China’s total fertility rate declined little after implementation of the one-child policy in 1979 and 1980, but fertility then fell sharply by more than one-third during the early 1990s. Here we show that strengthening bureaucratic incentives under China’s one vote veto policy, which strictly prohibited career advancement for adherence failure, was instrumental in more effective implementation of the one-child policy, and in its delayed impact on fertility. Using provincial variation in implementation timing, we find that the one vote veto explains nearly half of China’s total fertility rate decline during the 1990s, driving fertility below the replacement rate. Increases in use of intrauterine devices (the most prevalent form of modern contraception in China) that were recommended by local officials were particularly salient. Overall, our findings suggest that population policy, when more strictly enforced due to stronger bureaucratic incentives, made a greater contribution to low fertility in China than suggested by past research. Stronger bureaucratic incentives under China’s one vote veto policy intensified enforcement of the one-child policy, accounting for nearly half of China’s fertility decline during the 1990s.

papers.title: Evolutionary dynamics in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia
papers.abstract: Somatic evolution in ageing tissues underlies many cancers1,2. However, our quantitative understanding of the rules governing this pre-cancerous evolution remains incomplete. Here we exploit a unique collection of serial blood samples3, collected annually for up to a decade and beginning as early as 15 years before diagnosis of acute myeloid leukaemia, to provide a quantitative description of pre-cancerous evolutionary dynamics. Using deep duplex sequencing and evolutionary theory, we quantify the acquisition ages and fitness effects of the key driver events in acute myeloid leukaemia development. The first driver mutations are typically acquired in the first few decades of life, when the blood remains highly polyclonal. These early slow-growing clones subsequently acquire multiple further driver mutations that confer selective advantages up to 100-fold larger than the early drivers. These faster-growing clones harbouring multiple driver mutations can cause complete somatic sweeps of the blood decades before diagnosis, a feature strongly associated with future acute myeloid leukaemia. Our data show that the clonal dynamics of blood are consistent with a set of remarkably simple evolutionary rules that strike a balance between chance and determinism. The somatic evolutionary histories of haematopoietic cells in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia diagnosis show that the clonal dynamics of blood comply with a set of simple evolutionary rules.

papers.title: Epigenetic heterogeneity in breast tumours informs diagnosis and prognosis
papers.abstract: Breast cancer, the most diagnosed cancer among women, is stratified by gene expression patterns into luminal and basal-like subtypes, and the latter is associated with worse prognosis1–3. Recent advances in single-cell technologies have underscored the presence of intratumour heterogeneity, which poses substantial challenges in cancer treatment and achieving long-term disease-free survival4–7. Here we extensively profile epigenetic heterogeneity in a cohort of treatment-naive human luminal tumours, which were obtained directly after surgical resection. By applying a single-cell epigenetic approach based on cytometry by time-of-flight, we identify a recurrent subpopulation of basal-like cells in luminal tumours with a conserved epigenetic signature across patients. These basal-like cells, also identified by deconvolution of whole-genome DNA methylation patterns, are characterized by high expression of aggressive oncogenic traits and downregulation of hormone receptor signalling. Direct comparison of single-cell proteomic and genomic profiling of monomethylation and trimethylation of histone 3 on lysine 4 revealed that these marks are key features associated with loss of luminal identity. Finally, we highlight the potential of concomitant single-molecule profiling of histone modifications on cell-free nucleosomes in blood as an epigenetic liquid biopsy approach for early diagnosis of breast cancer. Moreover, the epigenetic basal signature measured in blood is linked to prognosis, which enables the identification of patients at increased risk for disease relapse. Single-cell epigenetic analyses reveal a conserved epigenetic signature across patients that may help identify those at increased risk for disease relapse in breast cancer.

papers.title: NRF2 is a mechanosensitive checkpoint for NLRP3 inflammasome activation
papers.abstract: Disconnects between in vitro and in vivo results in experimental biology have long been recognized as potential hurdles to understanding health and disease. A prototypical example of such a disconnect is the NLRP3 inflammasome, which mediates inflammation in diverse settings of disease and protective immunity1,2. Activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in vitro requires two signals: (1) priming by pathogen-associated molecular patterns such as bacterial lipopolysaccharides and (2) activation by molecules that disrupt cellular homeostasis1,3. By contrast, the NLRP3 inflammasome in vivo is activated by lipopolysaccharide alone. The mechanisms that underlie the difference between in vitro and in vivo activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome are undefined. Here we report that extracellular matrix (ECM) stiffness is a determinant of NLRP3 activities and that in vitro systems using physiological ECM stiffness enable one-signal in vivo-like NLRP3 activities to occur in human and mouse phagocytes. Physiological ECM stiffness induced expression of the transcription factor NRF2, which was found to be necessary for one-signal NLRP3 activation. Mechanistically, we identify Panx1 as an NRF2-regulated gene that promotes NLRP3 activity. Macrophages derived from the stiff matrix of the bone—osteoclasts—had reduced NRF2 levels and impaired NLRP3 activity. Moreover, alveolar macrophages from patients with pulmonary fibrosis displayed reduced NRF2 activity. Finally, NRF2 was required for antitumour immunity induced by cancer vaccines consisting of NLRP3 agonistic adjuvants. These findings indicate that NRF2 may be a transcriptional checkpoint that controls NLRP3 inflammasome activity. The stiffness of the extracellular matrix is identified as a pivotal factor that influences activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in vitro and in vivo.

papers.title: Bistable regulation of adipocyte heterogeneity governs thermogenesis
papers.abstract: Brown adipocytes (BAs) are thermogenic cells that regulate energy homeostasis, and age-related declines in thermogenesis contribute to cold sensitivity1–5. We previously identified a BA subpopulation with low UCP1 expression (hereafter, BA-L cells) that coexists with the classical, high-UCP1-expressing BAs (hereafter, BA-H cells)6. Here we show that IL-1β secreted by neutrophils and macrophages stabilizes nearby BAs in the BA-L state. Specifically, IL-1β stabilizes hexose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (H6PD) protein from degradation to ensure the generation of active glucocorticoids, which activate the glucocorticoid receptor (GR, encoded by Nr3c1) and increase the expression of its target gene, regulator of G-protein signalling 2 (Rgs2), thereby suppressing UCP1 expression. Cold exposure reduces IL-1β levels, depending on sympathetic innervation, leading to H6PD degradation and the conversion of BA-L cells to BA-H cells, thereby enhancing UCP1-dependent thermogenesis. Rising environmental temperatures trigger the opposite events. BA-specific inducible deletion of Nr3c1 during cold exposure locks these cells in the BA-H state, leading to persistent thermogenesis and increased energy expenditure days after the mice return to room temperature. Notably, IL-1β is elevated in aged brown adipose tissue, resulting in a locked low BA-H/BA-L ratio and cold intolerance. Suppressing GR in aged mice restores the BA-H/BA-L ratio, resumes thermogenesis and increases energy expenditure. Our findings reveal a spatiotemporal neuronal–immune regulation of BA heterogeneity that governs thermogenesis and offers a fundamental understanding of the mechanisms underlying increased cold sensitivity in older individuals. IL-1β from neutrophils and macrophages stabilizes nearby brown adipocytes in a low-UCP1 state; cold temperature reduces IL-1β via sympathetic nerves, leading to transition to a high-UCP1 state and increased thermogenesis, while higher temperatures have the opposite effect.

papers.title: Severe drought and warming increase the extinction risk of cacti
papers.abstract: Extreme climatic events are increasing in frequency and intensity with climate change1. Their effects on species’ distributions and extinction risk remain poorly understood2–9. Most species distribution models rely on long-term mean climate, overlooking potentially important nonlinear effects of extremes. Here we integrate new spatial data on severe drought10, including compounding effects of warmer temperatures, with a comprehensive curated dataset of cactus occurrences (648,316 records) and species distribution models to assess how severe drought alters projected suitable climatic area for 993 species of Cactaceae, a highly threatened family11 that is commonly considered drought tolerant. In 91% of cases, models including severe drought were better supported than mean-climate models. Across emissions scenarios (Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) SSP1-2.6 to SSP5-8.5) with 100-km dispersal, including severe drought increased the share of species losing suitable climatic area from 58–61% to 69–72%. The proportion of species projected to lose over a quarter of suitable area increased from 26–43% to 55–58%, and the proportion projected to lose over four-fifths increased from 1–15% to 25–35%. With severe drought, restricting dispersal from 100 to 0 km increased the share losing suitable area from 69–72% to 84–85% across SSPs. These declines reduced regional richness, with five bioregions potentially losing over 25% of species. These findings demonstrate that accounting for climatic extremes can alter assessments of biodiversity vulnerability under climate change. Integrating climatic extremes into ecological forecasting will be critical for assessing biodiversity loss and designing effective conservation strategies across taxa and ecosystems. Severe drought and warming will substantially increase the loss of suitable climatic area for cactus species.

papers.title: Non-halogen aqueous electrolytes for four-electron iodine conversion
papers.abstract: Accessing reversible four-electron iodine redox chemistry in aqueous metal–iodine batteries offers a promising route towards high-energy aqueous energy storage, but has conventionally relied on highly concentrated, corrosive halogen-containing electrolytes to stabilize reactive hypervalent iodine cations through interhalogen complexation1–9. Here we show a kosmotropic anion–polar anion–nucleophilic species (Nuc) electrolyte framework that harnesses anionic chemistry to coordinate the interfacial microenvironment and molecular interactions, enabling reversible four-electron iodine conversion in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes. Polar anions establish a water-deficient, anion-enriched interfacial microenvironment, whereas kosmotropic anions regulate water–Nuc interactions to increase the availability of Nuc for stabilizing hypervalent iodine cations through Nuc–I+–Nuc halogen bonds. This electrolyte framework is validated across diverse Nuc and in both aqueous Zn–I2 and Al–I2 batteries. Moving beyond conventional interhalogen stabilization, these findings establish a distinct electrolyte chemistry framework and represent a mechanistic shift for reversible multi-electron iodine chemistry in aqueous environments. An electrolyte framework that harnesses anionic chemistry to coordinate the interfacial microenvironment and molecular interactions enables reversible four-electron iodine conversion in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes, and is validated in metal–iodine batteries.

papers.title: Hadean mantle depletion and 3.95-Gyr subduction implied by North China rocks
papers.abstract: The scarcity of terrestrial rocks older than 3.9 billion years (Gyr) has hindered our understanding of Earth’s early evolution, fuelling persistent debates on how and when the first continental crust formed and plate tectonics started. At present, the only unequivocally documented >3.9-Gyr-old rocks are from the Acasta Gneiss Complex, Canada1–3. Here we report a 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss from eastern Hebei, North China Craton, in which primary magmatic zircon records elevated δ18O values (average +6.77 ± 0.23‰) and positive εHf(t) values (weighted mean +1.45 ± 0.27). This suggests a low-temperature altered basaltic source that originated from a mantle depleted in the Hadean. In contrast to the low-pressure origin inferred for the roughly 4.0-Gyr-old Idiwhaa unit in Acasta2, the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss reported here exhibits geochemical signatures attributed to a high-pressure origin4. Thermodynamic and trace element modelling demonstrate that its parental magma formed by means of low-degree (8–16%) melting of basaltic crust at >1.6 GPa and 740–820 °C, suggesting rapid burial of (near-)surface-altered oceanic crust to mantle depths along a cool thermal gradient. We propose that this rapid burial was most likely achieved through a transient subduction event. Analysis of a 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss from eastern Hebei, China, reveals a composition suggesting a low-temperature altered basaltic source, that originated from a mantle depleted in the Hadean, was most likely transported to mantle depths through a transient subduction event and partially melted to produce the trondhjemite.
