papers.title: Dynamic plasmonic imaging of electromechanically driven nano-oscillators for charge-resolved multiplex biosensing
papers.abstract: Multiplexed profiling of diverse biomarkers is essential for precision diagnostics, but remains challenging for label-free sensors because signals typically scale with analyte mass. Here, we present a dynamic plasmonic imaging platform based on electromechanically driven nano-oscillators for multiplexed, label-free quantification of nucleic acids, proteins, and small molecules within a unified sensing architecture. Size-encoded nanoparticles tethered to a plasmonic surface are electrically actuated to oscillate vertically within the evanescent field and tracked by distance-resolved surface plasmon resonance imaging. Molecular binding alters the effective surface charge of each nano-oscillator, modulating the electrostatic-driven forces and changing oscillation amplitude. This charge-to-motion transduction mechanism reduces dependence on molecular mass and enhances sensitivity for low–molecular weight analytes. This platform simultaneously detects microRNAs, proteins, and small molecules spanning a ∼300-fold molecular weight range within a single field of view. We further demonstrate multiplexed profiling of tumor-associated microRNAs in pretreated supernatants from patient-derived breast cancer cells across 24 clinical samples. Dynamic plasmonic nano-oscillators provide a scalable architecture for multiplex molecular diagnostics.

papers.title: Neuromelanin-inspired metal-selenomelanin nanonetworks restore neuronal excitability in radiation-induced brain injury
papers.abstract: Radiation-induced brain injury (RIBI) affects up to 30% of patients receiving cranial radiotherapy, representing an irreversible complication lacking effective therapies. Research advances are limited by poor blood-brain barrier drug penetration and overreliance on ex vivo pathology, which cannot resolve dynamic neuronal dysfunction. Inspired by neuromelanin, we fabricated metal-selenomelanin nanonetworks (MSMNs), combined with in vivo electrophysiology to investigate and mitigate radiation-triggered neural dysfunction. In 6-gray whole body–irradiated mice, MSMN normalized neuronal excitability and restored medium spiny neuron firing and striatal circuit activity, improving locomotor and anxiety-related behaviors. Besides central functional recovery, MSMN provides systemic radioprotection, ensuring full 30-day survival, protecting radiosensitive organs and facilitating hematopoietic recovery. This work identifies neuronal excitability as an underexplored therapeutic target for RIBI, establishing neuromelanin-mimetic selenomelanin nanonetworks as a bioinspired platform linking molecular radioprotection to circuit-level restoration for radiation-induced neurological injury.

papers.title: Controllable fabrication of visible-spectrum 3D photonic crystals
papers.abstract: The fabrication of visible-spectrum three-dimensional (3D) photonic crystals (PhCs) remains highly challenging, because existing manufacturing techniques cannot simultaneously achieve high processing precision and sufficient geometric freedom. Here, we propose a suspended pyrolysis-assisted two-photon polymerization (SP-TPP) printing strategy, achieving the controllable fabrication of visible-spectrum 3D PhCs. The resulting 3D diamond PhCs exhibit a remarkable lattice-period standard deviation of only 5.75 nm, approximately 1/45 of that achieved without suspended pyrolysis. Microscopic reflection spectra confirm these PhCs possess uniform optical responses across all spatial positions. By tuning the lattice period and structural duty cycle, the PhCs operating at diverse wavelengths are systematically realized. Moreover, through the demonstration of PhC prototype structures and in situ arrayed fabrication, the SP-TPP printing strategy paves the way for applications in photonic microcavities, 3D optical waveguides, optical splitters, and integrated micro-optical systems.

papers.title: Boosting stability and charge transfer of conducting polymer poly(benzodifurandione) (PBFDO) through complementary topology
papers.abstract: Poly(benzodifurandione) (PBFDO) is a benchmark n-type conjugated polymer known for its record-high electrical conductivity. Nevertheless, its thermal robustness and charge/ion transport characteristics remain insufficient. To address this issue, we report a hierarchical complementary topology strategy via doping PBFDO with choline chloride (ChCl). At the molecular scale, the cations Ch + selectively intercalate along the out-of-plane direction while simultaneously densifying the in-plane π-π stacking, accompanied by partial removal of H + . At the submicrometer scale, this induces distinct phase separation into high- and low-density stacking domains. As a result, the product PBFDO-ChCl exhibited a synergistic performance boost, with a 2.8-fold enhancement in high-temperature resilience, a 1.6-fold increase in sheet conductance, and a 15.9-fold reduction in ion diffusion resistance. Then, organic electrochemical transistors (OECTs) using PBFDO-ChCl as channel material further confirm these performance enhancements. As a whole, this work closes the performance gap between n-type PBFDO and state-of-the-art p-type conjugated polymers, potentially advancing its applications from energy storage to bioelectronics and neuromorphic computing.

papers.title: Weak adsorption, strong consequences: How trace gases control ice growth and quasi-liquid-layer structure
papers.abstract: Gases in the atmosphere are often treated as passive background species in cold environments, yet their molecular roles at icy interfaces remain poorly understood. Here, we show how hydrophobic and hydrophilic trace gases can actively reorganize the ice interface and regulate freezing through interfacial stabilization. We find these gases can actively modulate both the kinetics and thermodynamics of the water-ice interface. Using molecular simulations, we find that all gases examined retard ice-front propagation relative to pure water to different extents. This slowing arises from weak but preferential adsorption at the water-ice interface, where gases occupy water-dense interfacial layers and locally suppress ice-like ordering. After freezing is complete, gases do not distribute uniformly across the frozen surface, but partition selectively among multiple adsorption regions across the ice–quasi-liquid-layer (QLL)–air interfacial landscape. Relatively hydrophobic gases exhibit a three-region adsorption pattern, whereas relatively hydrophilic gases occupy only two dominant adsorption regions. Despite these differences, both classes preferentially accumulate near the QLL-air boundary and its immediate outer region rather than the ice-QLL interface. There, gases pair with and compensate for dangling surface bonds (through a surface-passivating effect reminiscent of ligand stabilization), reducing the thermodynamic driving force for premelting and thereby thinning the QLL. These results establish a unified molecular picture in which atmospheric gases are active interfacial modulators of both ice growth and ice structure, with implications for freezing, ice-cloud microphysics, and heterogeneous atmospheric chemistry.

papers.title: Arbitrarily cuttable and ultrathin MXene structural colors for customizable and wearable multispectral information management
papers.abstract: Structural colors based on natural and artificial microstructures show promising light manipulation. As atomically thick building blocks, Ti 3 C 2 T x sheets have been successfully assembled into the ultrathin, flexible, arbitrarily cuttable, large-size structural colors by the simple and low-cost spray methods based on the lossy thin-film interference. By ordered stacking atomically thick Ti 3 C 2 T x layer by layer at well-organized low–surface tension semidry assemble state, rich colors from yellow to gray with the thickness from ∼22 to ∼154 nanometers of uniform Ti 3 C 2 T x colors are obtained, having the thinnest framework among solution-processed flexible structural colors with similar optical performance. Low-infrared emissivity from room to 300°C temperature and region-selective patterns make highly information-fused and complex visible-infrared (VIS-IR) Ti 3 C 2 T x colors camouflage. Without conventional dielectric layer between Ti 3 C 2 T x and substrate, automated spraying system can produce meter-scale films that can be cut and sewn into VIS-IR concealment “camouflage cloaks” easily, promising ultrathin multifunctional information systems and beyond.

papers.title: Single-cell profiling of the duodenum during chronic human norovirus infection
papers.abstract: Human noroviruses are a major cause of diarrheal disease, yet their pathogenesis remains poorly defined. We performed single-cell RNA sequencing of duodenal biopsies and matched stem cell–derived enteroids from immunodeficient individuals with chronic norovirus infection. Norovirus RNA was detected primarily in enterocytes, enteroendocrine cells, and macrophages, with the highest proportion of viral RNA-positive cells observed among M2 macrophages, followed by late enterocytes. Despite this distribution, late enterocytes produced higher viral yields than differentiated M2 macrophages in vitro. Norovirus infection was associated with the up-regulation of MHC class I-related genes and IL15 in duodenal macrophages and late enterocytes, together with increased IFNG expression by CD8 T cells. Macrophages and late enterocytes up-regulated CXCL9 and CXCL10/11 , respectively, consistent with CD8 and CD4 T cell recruitment to the duodenum. These findings show that noroviruses infect and persist across multiple permissive cell types during chronic infection, resulting in marked dysregulation of innate and adaptive immune responses that may drive pathogenesis.

papers.title: Incomplete synaptic vesicle priming functionally disconnects CA1 pyramidal cells
papers.abstract: The hippocampal CA1 area is perceived as a nonrecurrent neuronal network, i.e., CA1 pyramidal cells (CA1PCs) within the CA1 area innervate mainly γ-aminobutyric acid–releasing interneurons but not each other. Here, we performed an unbiased examination of the functional properties of local CA1PC output synapses using in vitro two-photon glutamate imaging. Fluorescent transients measured with iGluSnFR3 in individual boutons displayed extraordinary heterogeneity in their amplitudes and short-term plasticity patterns upon a complex train of presynaptic action potential firing. Post hoc electron microscopy of the imaged boutons demonstrated that distinct postsynaptic structure-innervating boutons display different functional properties. Approximately 25% of the boutons innervate CA1PC spines, which either release glutamate with very low release probability or completely fail to release. Phorbol 12,13-dibutyrate and elevated calcium (2+) concentration, manipulations that enhance synaptic vesicle priming and fusion, convert these silent into properly functioning synapses. Our results provide evidence that CA1PCs are interconnected with structurally and molecularly intact glutamatergic synapses, but incomplete synaptic vesicle (SV) priming precludes SV release.

papers.title: A LiDAR-based reconstruction reveals increasing Arctic phytoplankton production during low-light winter-shoulder period
papers.abstract: Arctic marine productivity is traditionally considered concentrated in the sunlit season, yet low-light winter-shoulder periods remain poorly constrained because passive ocean color observations require sufficient solar illumination. Here, we use 2.39 million spaceborne LiDAR profiles from CALIOP (2006–2023) to reconstruct Arctic net primary production (NPP) and evaluate how active-sensor observations reduce this seasonal blind spot. The bio-optical retrieval model was trained using MODIS-constrained observations under illuminated conditions; accordingly, low-light estimates represent physically constrained extrapolations beyond the primary MODIS-observable training domain rather than direct NPP measurements. Within this framework, LiDAR increases winter half-year observational coverage from ∼20 to 30% to ∼70 to 75% and reveals widespread low-light winter-shoulder production across marginal seas and seasonal ice-edge regions. Pan-Arctic NPP integrated over this period increased at an estimated rate of 0.75 Tg C year −1 during 2007–2023, whereas the corresponding passive-sensor signal was negligible. Accounting for this component raises annual Arctic NPP estimates by ∼13.3% indicating that passive sensor-based assessments may underrepresent the magnitude and seasonal structure of Arctic productivity. Associations with declining sea ice and surface warming suggest this underrepresented production is consistent with ongoing seasonal reorganization of Arctic carbon fixation. Uncertainties from model parameterization, low-light extrapolation, and limited in situ validation are largest in the lowest-light and highest-latitude regimes. These findings do not imply photosynthesis during absolute polar night, but show that active LiDAR observations with explicit light constraints and transparent extrapolation limits can test how unresolved low-light winter-shoulder production may alter Arctic NPP seasonality under continuing sea-ice loss.

papers.title: Structural insights into light harvesting and photosystem II evolution in the basal streptophyte Mesostigma viride
papers.abstract: The basal streptophyte Mesostigma viride represents a critical evolutionary transition toward land plants, yet the molecular basis of its ancestral light-harvesting strategy remains elusive. Here, we present a 2.25-angstrom resolution cryo-EM structure of the M. viride PSII-LHCII-LHCP supercomplex, revealing a unique C 2 S 2 M p2 L p2 -type architecture. Our structure reveals a nearly complete set of conserved PSII core subunits, indicating that much of the PSII structural framework found in terrestrial plants was established early in the streptophyte lineage. At the periphery, the complex features a specialized antenna module in which two ancestral LHCP monomers flank CP29. These ancestral antenna proteins bind an unusually high number of carotenoids, with seven carotenoids per subunit, and extensively incorporate marine-type keto carotenoids, siphonaxanthin, and siphonein, throughout the complex, thereby broadening absorption in the blue-green region. The canonical LHCII trimer exhibits a distinctive chlorophyll b macrocluster and a 96-femtosecond ultrafast energy transfer component. Together, these findings provide a high-resolution molecular framework for an evolutionary intermediate that combines high-capacity aquatic light harvesting with structural features potentially relevant to photoprotection during the transition toward terrestrial life.

papers.title: Piezoelectrically actuated magnetic dipole twisting resonators enable miniaturized low-frequency antennas
papers.abstract: Miniaturized low-frequency antennas are essential for underwater, underground, and biomedical communications, yet their performance is constrained by the fundamental size-efficiency trade-off, a long-standing physical bottleneck. Here, we introduce a radiation mechanism that circumvents this constraint by replacing the time-varying currents in conventional antennas with the mechanical twisting oscillation of a magnetic dipole. Using piezoelectrically actuated, biomimetic twisting resonators with ultrahigh mechanical quality factors, we demonstrate that low-frequency antennas operating at 15.4 and 668 hertz can be miniaturized to centimeter- and millimeter-scale, respectively, with radiation efficiencies exceeding those of size-matched loop antennas by factors of 49,000 and 5000, respectively. This electromechanical-magnetic transduction enables underwater cross-medium communication over 115 meters with only milliwatt-level power consumption, using 99.9% less power than loop antennas. It also supports implantable wireless devices that achieve a fourfold increase in communication range at identical power consumption, opening a route to long-range, low-power wireless systems capable of operating in some of the most demanding environments.

papers.title: Evolutionarily reinforced GC-rich motif enables non-AUG translation in mammals under eIF1/5MP-mediated fidelity control
papers.abstract: Non-AUG translation contributes to proteome diversity, but its regulatory principles remain unclear. Here, we show that a GCC-rich upstream extension, termed the NAT1 motif, acts as a potent enhancer of near-cognate initiation in mammals. Cell-free and reporter assays revealed that eIF1 and 5MP act as conserved inhibitors of non-AUG initiation across mammals and plants, while the NAT1 motif enables enhanced initiation within this fidelity framework. Mutational analysis identified −6 and −7 positions within the GCC repeat as key determinants of motif activity. Genome-wide analyses uncovered evolutionary depletion of NAT1 -type non-AUG codons in human 5′UTRs, suggesting purifying selection against excessive initiation. Nevertheless, more than a hundred retained sites are associated with genes involved in cell proliferation and migration, suggesting that regulated non-AUG initiation may contribute to disease-relevant translational programs. The motif’s enrichment within GCC repeats further suggests a mechanistic link to repeat-associated non-AUG translation.

papers.title: STAT3 controls IL-6–induced epigenomic remodeling and restrains a latent STAT1-associated interferon program in human macrophages
papers.abstract: Interleukin-6 (IL-6) is a pleiotropic cytokine that drives macrophage functions ranging from tissue homeostasis to inflammation, yet how STAT3 specifies these divergent outcomes remains unclear. By integrating transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling with selective STAT3 degradation, we show that STAT3 controls IL-6–induced epigenomic remodeling and restrains a latent STAT1-associated interferon program in human macrophages. Graded STAT3 chromatin recruitment scales with locus-specific H3K27ac deposition and transcriptional output across homeostatic and inflammatory programs. STAT3 degradation permits STAT1 recruitment at a subset of regulatory regions and engages a delayed amplification loop that is partially dependent on STING and type I IFN signaling. In severe COVID-19, monocytes exhibit exaggerated STAT3-associated inflammatory signatures together with attenuated STAT1-associated interferon responses, consistent with a skewed STAT3-STAT1 balance. These findings define a framework in which STAT3 calibrates IL-6–induced chromatin output while maintaining pathway fidelity by limiting STAT1 cross-talk.

papers.title: Integrating biomass production platform and identification approach for stereochemical assignment of super-carbon-chain compounds
papers.abstract: Super-carbon-chain compounds (SCCCs), marine long-carbon-chain polyketides featuring numerous carbon stereocenters, fall into untapped chemical space in between drug-like small molecules and biopolymers. Due to mass-material unavailability and flexible-structure complexity, the reliable stereochemical assignment of SCCCs has long remained stagnant. In this work, a modern microalgal biomass production-platform is created for pilot-scale cultivation of marine dinoflagellates to produce over 100 milligrams of minor SCCCs. The modular fragment-based identification (MFBI) approach is successfully employed to establish the relative and absolute configurations of SCCCs. As an example, 157.7 mg of a minor SCCC, named amphidiketol A, featuring a highly-flexible C 76 -linear carbon backbone and thirty-three carbon stereocenters, is obtained from Amphidinium sp. in our platform. Its hybrid architecture contains eleven‌ distinct modular fragments. Its relative and absolute configurations are successfully established by the MFBI approach. Collectively, an undescribed paradigm for stereochemical assignment of SCCCs is presented. Nine senescence-associated protein targets of amphidiketol A in lung cancer A549 cells are identified.

papers.title: Frequency of pharmacogenomic variation and medication exposures among participants in the All of Us Research Program
authors: All of Us Research Program Investigators
papers.abstract: Pharmacogenomics promises improved outcomes through individualized prescribing. However, the lack of diversity in pharmacogenomics studies impedes clinical translation and the application of precision medicine across populations. We evaluated the frequencies of variants in 16 pharmacogenes ( ABCG2 , CACNA1S , CYP2D6 , CYP2C Cluster , CYP2C19 , CYP2C9 , CYP3A5 , CYP4F2 , DPYD , G6PD , NUDT15 , RYR1 , SLCO1B1 , TPMT , UGT1A1 , and VKORC1 ) and predicted phenotypes and medication exposures using whole-genome sequencing and electronic health record data from nearly 100,000 All of Us Research Program participants. We report that 100% of participants carried at least one pharmacogenomic variant and nearly all (99.5%) had a predicted phenotype with prescribing recommendations. Clinical impact was high with 24.4% of participants having both an actionable phenotype for these pharmacogenes and a prior exposure to an impacted medication with pharmacogenomic prescribing guidance. Importantly, we report thousands of previously unrecognized pharmacogene variants and hundreds of alleles and predicted phenotypes that deviate from known frequencies across populations or were previously unreported, especially in the Americas and African ancestry groups.

papers.title: Human antibody combinations determined by epitope mapping of orthopoxvirus A33/A35 confer therapeutic protection in mice
papers.abstract: Human infections with mpox virus (MPXV) since 2022 have resulted in more than 188,000 cases reported globally as of June 2026, highlighting the urgent need for effective therapeutics. Here, we recruited smallpox vaccinees and donors with incidental vaccinia virus (VACV) exposure and isolated a panel of human anti-A33/A35 monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) from the latter using recombinant MPXV A35 as a cross-reactive bait. These mAbs recognized four distinct nonoverlapping epitopes (epitopes 1 to 4) and one composite epitope (epitope 3 + 4) on MPXV A35 and exhibited cross-reactivity against multiple orthopoxviruses (OPXVs). Cryo–electron microscopy structural analysis revealed that the high-affinity epitope 3 + 4 mAb HD15 engages an epitope at the A35 dimer interface that is conserved across OPXVs. Combinations of mAbs targeting nonoverlapping epitopes mediated synergistic, Fc-dependent neutralization in vitro; conferred therapeutic protection against lethal VACV challenge; and reduced viral burden and disease severity after MPXV challenge in mice. Together, these findings establish a single-antigen, multiepitope strategy for the development of broadly protective therapeutics against OPXVs.

papers.title: Sleep-like slow waves during wakefulness are associated with hallucinations and poorer cognition in Parkinson’s disease
papers.abstract: Slow waves during sleep are fundamental for neural homeostasis, metabolic regulation, and waste clearance and are known to be altered in neurodegenerative diseases. Sleep-like slow waves (SLSWs) have been observed in awake, healthy individuals, where they are linked to fluctuations in vigilance and mind-wandering. Whether SLSWs are altered in Parkinson’s disease (PD), and whether such alterations contribute to psychiatric or cognitive complications, remains unknown. In a cohort of 84 nondemented patients with PD and 30 healthy older adults, we found that SLSWs occurred more frequently in patients with PD. Hallucinatory traits in patients with PD were associated with higher SLSW amplitude, especially over frontocentral regions. Moreover, more prominent SLSWs were associated with poorer cognitive functions. We conclude that, whereas slow waves during sleep have positive physiological functions, exacerbated diurnal SLSWs may reflect responses related to PD neuropathology, at the cost of hallucinations and reduced cognitive function.

papers.title: Dual inhibition of TNF-α and IL-1β signaling through BIG2 ameliorates osteoarthritis in mouse and primate models
papers.abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA), a leading cause of disability, is characterized by chronic low-grade inflammation and metabolic dysregulation in chondrocytes. TNF-α and IL-1β are key inflammatory drivers in OA pathogenesis, but clinical trials targeting them individually have been unsuccessful, highlighting the potential need for dual-targeting strategies. By screening a US Food and Drug Administration–approved drug library, we identified dabigatran, a thrombin inhibitor, as a potent dual suppressor of TNF-α and IL-1β signaling that restored chondrocyte metabolism. In preclinical OA models, including both mice and cynomolgus macaques, dabigatran attenuated cartilage degeneration, alleviated pain, and improved joint function. To elucidate the molecular mechanisms, we performed biochemical copurification coupled with mass spectrometry, identifying brefeldin A–inhibited guanine nucleotide–exchange protein 2 (BIG2) as a previously unknown dabigatran-binding target. Mechanistically, dabigatran binds to BIG2, promoting BIG2-dependent TNFR1 release to dampen TNF-α signaling while enhancing BIG2-mediated IL-1R1 degradation through the autophagy-lysosome pathway to limit IL-1β effects. These findings establish BIG2-mediated receptor trafficking and membrane dynamics as a regulatory node that concurrently inhibits TNF-α and IL-1β signaling, suggesting this pathway as a potential therapeutic strategy for OA.

papers.title: Albumin-bound paclitaxel–induced stromal reprogramming drives resistance to neoadjuvant chemotherapy in patients with pancreatic cancer
papers.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a highly lethal malignancy for which neoadjuvant chemotherapy with albumin-bound paclitaxel combined with gemcitabine (AG) is a standard first-line approach for borderline resectable and locally advanced disease. However, secondary resistance to this regimen is common, and its underlying mechanisms remain poorly defined. In this study, we investigated how neoadjuvant AG therapy shapes the tumor stroma in PDAC. Single-cell transcriptomics of patient tumors revealed that AG treatment induces a phenotypic switch of cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) from myofibroblastic (myCAF) to inflammatory (iCAF) states and identified a previously unrecognized TMEM100 + CAF subset enriched in nonresponders. Mechanistic studies showed that albumin-bound paclitaxel activates IL-2–STAT5 signaling to drive TMEM100 expression and that TMEM100 + CAFs promote chemoresistance through paracrine secretion of amphiregulin (AREG) and activation of tumor EGFR signaling. Genetic ablation of TMEM100 + CAFs in mouse models reversed CAF switching and enhanced the antitumor efficacy of AG therapy. These findings map chemotherapy-induced CAF plasticity, reveal a TMEM100-AREG axis of resistance, and highlight TMEM100 + CAFs as a promising target to sensitize PDAC to neoadjuvant treatment.

papers.title: Osimertinib, platinum, and etoposide for patients with metastatic EGFR / TP53 / RB1 -mutant lung cancers at risk for histological transformation
papers.abstract: Although EGFR inhibitors are highly effective for treating EGFR- mutant lung adenocarcinomas ( EGFR + LUADs), resistance inevitably emerges, with histologic transformation to small cell lung cancer (SCLC) representing a particularly aggressive mechanism. Our prospective trial enrolled patients with EGFR + LUAD at high risk of transformation ( TP53 / RB1 -deficient) and treated them with first-line osimertinib combined with platinum and etoposide. Despite the addition of SCLC-directed chemotherapy, nearly half of patients (5 of 11) underwent SCLC transformation, with median progression-free survival of 11 months and overall survival of 33 months. Genomic and single-cell transcriptomic profiling of patient samples revealed clinical and subclinical plasticity associated with TP53 / RB1 comutations, including histological transformation to SCLC, as well as mesenchymal and squamous histologies. These changes in plasticity were linked to progressive disruption of the RB pathway, leading to altered chromatin accessibility and induction of neuronal differentiation and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition transcriptional programs, further intensified by osimertinib treatment. These findings provide insights into the role of plasticity in mediating drug tolerance.

papers.title: Erratum for the Research Article “Preclinical and clinical evaluation of systemic danegaptide for the treatment of nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy”
The blood-brain barrier imports diverse neuroprotective proteins through pathways impaired early in Alzheimer’s disease models
papers.abstract: Bioorthogonal proteomics reveals that the blood-brain barrier (BBB) imports diverse plasma proteins to specific brain cell types through receptor-mediated transport, a process dysregulated early in an Alzheimer’s model. Restoring one diminished protein, liver-derived apolipoprotein A1, rescues Alzheimer’s glial and neuronal dysfunction, recasting the BBB as an interface recruiting peripheral signals for brain health.

papers.title: A sequence-encoded promoter-proximal super pause stabilizes an offline RNA polymerase II state
papers.abstract: Vazquez Nunez et al. develop GATO-seq, a cell-free genomics method to directly measure RNA polymerase II elongation dynamics. They identify a “super pause” DNA sequence near gene start sites that alone potently pauses RNA polymerase II, trapping it in a yet undescribed “sidetracked” conformation, showing how DNA sequence itself controls pausing.

papers.title: Extracellular vesicle-mediated CD47 transfer rewires integrin-IGF1R signaling and tumor immune remodeling to propagate cetuximab resistance
papers.abstract: Sakaguchi et al. demonstrate that ALIX-dependent sorting of CD47 into extracellular vesicles propagates cetuximab resistance by promoting integrin-IGF1R signaling. Disrupting EV release remodels the tumor immune microenvironment and restores cetuximab sensitivity.

papers.title: The fungal phosphate starvation regulator CtPHO4 couples nutrient adaptation to host colonization through the effector NFC1
papers.abstract: Newfeld et al. identified a fungal effector NFC1 that is necessary for root colonization and host circadian clock perturbation by the conditional plant pathogen C. tofieldiae. NFC1 is tightly suppressed under phosphate deficiency by the fungal transcription factor CtPHO4, showcasing the crucial role of CtPHO4 in balancing virulence with growth.

papers.title: Multi-ancestry genetic analysis of lung function identifies candidate causal variants and improves polygenic prediction
papers.abstract: Most genetic studies of lung function rely on European-ancestry cohorts. Jiang et al. conduct a multi-ancestry analysis that expands East Asian representation, pinpoints novel candidate causal variants and genes, and delivers polygenic scores with improved prediction accuracy in East Asian populations.

papers.title: Retraction Notice to: A 20-amino-acid Cardiovirus protein exhibits cytokine-mimicry activity to regulate viral replication
Uncoupling hypersensitive cell death response and disease resistance activated by effector-triggered immunity
papers.abstract: Chhillar et al. show that hypersensitive cell death and disease resistance are genetically separable outputs of effector-triggered immunity. Loss of CBP60g and SARD1 enhances cell death despite compromising pathogen resistance. These transcription factors coordinate defense-promoting and cell-death-limiting programs, with NUDT7 contributing to the restraint of excessive cell death.

papers.title: Programming intestinal immune tolerance: The pivotal role of gut microbial metabolites
papers.abstract: Intestinal immune tolerance enables coexistence with commensals while preserving defense against pathogens. Wang et al. synthesize how gut microbial metabolites program this balance by reinforcing epithelial barriers and shaping regulatory immune cells. The review highlights metabolites as promising biomarkers and therapeutic targets in disorders of impaired immune tolerance.

papers.title: Longitudinal dynamics of gut microbiota maturation and its modulators from infancy through childhood
papers.abstract: Peng et al. map gut microbiota maturation in 695 COPSAC2010 children from 1 week to 6 years, revealing rapid early development, late-childhood stabilization, exposure-linked maturation patterns, and modest non-random prediction of later maturity from 1-year microbiota and bacterial co-abundance modules.

papers.title: A SIRT6-OVOL2 axis governs excitatory neuron resilience to chronic stress
papers.abstract: SIRT6 overexpression in excitatory neurons enhances resilience to chronic stress. Zhou et al. identify a SIRT6-OVOL2-NRG1 signaling axis that maintains hippocampal plasticity and show that pharmacological activation of SIRT6 alleviates stress-induced depression-like behaviors.

papers.title: FBXO45-mediated K63 ubiquitination of HYOU1 sustains UPR signaling and promotes chemoresistance in gastric cancer
papers.abstract: Pan et al. show that FBXO45-mediated K63-linked ubiquitination of the ER chaperone HYOU1 recruits PPM1B to inhibit dephosphorylation of PERK and IRE1α, sustaining unfolded protein response activation and acquired chemoresistance. Targeting this axis restores drug sensitivity, revealing a potential therapeutic strategy for gastric cancer.

papers.title: Retrosplenial cortex exhibits parallel directional codes and contributes to medial entorhinal spatial coding in 3D curved-surface navigation
papers.abstract: Zhang et al. find parallel directional representations in the mouse retrosplenial cortex during navigation across curved surfaces and show that retrosplenial activity contributes to stable medial entorhinal positional coding when visual cues are limited. The findings provide insight into how directional and positional representations are organized across complex environmental surfaces.

papers.title: Impressions in biomolecular condensates
GPCR-MAPS: high-resolution functional and allosteric mapping of G-protein-coupled receptor activation functions and bias
papers.abstract: G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are important drug targets. Approaches targeting allosteric modulation and biased signaling, as opposed to the orthosteric pocket, can improve safety profiles of therapeutics. However, rational design of precision therapies is limited by the lack of high-resolution quantitative functional annotation of GPCR structures. Here we present GPCR-MAPS—a fast and general approach to build complete, high-resolution, multimodal functional and allosteric maps of GPCRs. GCPR-MAPS quantifies direct recruitment of proteins and deconvolves the substantial effects of amino acid substitutions on receptor expression. We applied GPCR-MAPS to the β2 adrenergic receptor to generate >7,500 dose–response curves and reveal a modular receptor architecture, with a core activation network surrounded by residues controlling quantitative parameters and bias. We used this information to identify multiple allosteric surface pockets. The application of this approach across the superfamily of GPCRs could unlock deep understanding of these receptors and enable rational design of precision GPCR therapeutics. Mighell and Lehner present GPCR-MAPS, which enables scalable functional mapping of G-protein-coupled receptors. They obtained measurements across multiple phenotypes of the β2 adrenergic receptor to reveal a modular activation architecture and determinants of signaling bias, prioritizing undrugged allosteric sites.

papers.title: TF-MAPS: fast high-resolution functional and allosteric mapping of DNA-binding proteins
papers.abstract: Transcription factors (TFs) bind specific DNA sequences to control gene expression. Modulating TF activity is of considerable therapeutic interest but very few TFs have been drugged successfully. TF DNA-binding interfaces are large and most TFs have no known allosteric ligands or allosteric sites. Here we introduce TF-MAPs, a scalable and general platform to chart complete functional maps of sequence-specific DNA-binding proteins. We apply TF-MAPS to three human disease TFs: HNF1A, FOXG1 and FOXP1. Allostery in all three proteins is distance-dependent, anisotropic and couples the DNA-binding interface to the protein surface. The allosteric surfaces of FOXG1 and FOXP1 are quite diverged, revealing a potential for protein-specific regulation in protein families. All three TFs have potentially druggable small pockets where mutations affect DNA binding, either within the binding interface or distant from it. Application of TF-MAPS will potentially lead to charting functional and allosteric maps for hundreds of human TFs and other DNA-binding proteins to understand DNA recognition and TF regulation, to interpret clinical variants mechanistically and to guide the development of TF-modulating therapeutics. Li and Lehner present TF-MAPS, a scalable platform to chart functional maps of sequence-specific DNA-binding proteins. The authors map allostery in three transcription factors implicated in human disease and reveal potentially druggable small pockets.

Distinct T cell subsets associated with responses to different neoadjuvant treatments in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma
papers.abstract: Song et al. find that neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy maintains immunoresponsive CXCL13+ CD8+ T cells, with responders showing a shift toward a less exhausted, progenitor-like phenotype, whereas chemoradiotherapy reduces this compartment and enriches PD-1- effector CD8+ T cells. Their findings provide a cellular rationale for optimizing the sequencing of immunotherapy and radiotherapy.

papers.title: Temporal control of CAR expression by a tumor-targeting albumin adapter and logic gating enhances CAR-T cell therapy for solid tumors
papers.abstract: Chen et al. develop MANAGE CAR-T cells that employ an artificial-antigen-sensing synNotch receptor to gate CAR expression and an albumin-based tumor-targeting adapter bearing the artificial antigen for priming. Adjusting the adapter dosing schedule enables tumor-restricted and intermittent CAR expression. These temporally tuned CAR-T cells exhibit reduced exhaustion and improved efficacy against solid tumors.

papers.title: The expansion of kinase drug discovery: new targets, platforms and indications
papers.abstract: In the past 25 years, kinase drug discovery has grown into one of the most thriving areas in pharmaceutical research and development. What began as a field dominated by ATP-competitive small molecules has diversified into a broad therapeutic landscape that includes allosteric and covalent inhibitors, activators, proximity-induced modulators, targeted protein degraders and antibody-based therapies, with more than 150 regulatory approvals so far worldwide. In this Review, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the current kinase therapeutic landscape, including more than 2,100 kinase-targeting agents that have entered clinical development in more than 23,000 clinical trials. We cover drug platforms, new targeting approaches, the expanding target spectrum, approvals and clinical trends. Nearly half of the canonical human protein kinases have at least one clinical-stage agent, placing kinases among the most intensively explored drug target classes. Nevertheless, development remains highly concentrated around a small set of blockbuster kinase targets, such as EGFR. We also examine the features associated with successful kinase-targeting agents and causes of agent discontinuations and regulatory withdrawal. Over the past 25 years, kinase drug discovery has been one of the most active areas in pharmaceutical research and development. This article provides a comprehensive analysis of the kinase therapeutic landscape, covering drug platforms, new targeting approaches, the expanding target spectrum, approvals and clinical trends.

papers.title: l-carnitine links red meat consumption to inflammation
Genotype-Informed Drosophila Kinome Screening Prioritizes PRKX as a Candidate Vulnerability in Bladder Cancer
papers.abstract: Muscle-invasive bladder cancer is molecularly heterogeneous, and the basal/squamous subtype frequently exhibits elevated EGFR expression and TP53 and RB1 alterations. Functional vulnerabilities associated with these alterations remain incompletely defined, while large-scale in vivo screening in mammalian models is experimentally demanding. Therefore, we developed a genotype-defined Drosophila melanogaster model combining Egfr overexpression, mutant p53, and Rbf suppression in Malpighian tubules. The resulting 3-hit model showed increased Malpighian tubule volume and reduced adult eclosion rate. A dominant modifier screen targeting 216 kinase genes identified 72 genes whose perturbation significantly increased the eclosion rate, and a complementary RNA interference screen identified eight kinases whose knockdown increased the eclosion rate. Among these hits, Pka-C3, which is a Drosophila ortholog of human PRKX, emerged as one of the strongest suppressors of the 3-hit phenotype. PRKX was prioritized for further study because public transcriptomic datasets showed higher PRKX expression in bladder tumors than in normal bladder tissue. PRKX knockdown reduced spheroid volume in four human bladder cancer cell lines with distinct EGFR, TP53, and RB1 profiles. Both small interfering RNAs produced significant reductions in two cell lines, whereas only one siRNA reached significance in the other two. These findings nominate PRKX as a candidate vulnerability in bladder cancer and highlight a cross-species approach that combines genotype-informed Drosophila screening with functional testing in human cancer cells to prioritize targets for further investigation.

papers.title: Mechanical and chemical macrophage activation differ by arm, not by amplitude
papers.abstract: Mechanical cues are widely reported to polarize macrophages toward an M1-like state, but the claim rests on nuclear factor kappa B/activator protein 1 (NF-{kappa}B/AP-1) effector markers read without a common scale, and the literature does not agree on the sign of the stiffness effect. We asked a quantitative question instead: by what fraction of the chemical M1 response does mechanical perturbation move the interferon-stimulated gene factor 3 (ISGF3)-dependent interferon-stimulated gene module? Scoring ten independent studies of substrate stiffness and applied force against lipopolysaccharide (LPS) + interferon-gamma (IFN-{gamma}) anchors, processed through an identical pipeline, we find a pooled shift of -0.9% of the chemical response (95% confidence interval -6.2% to +4.5%), equivalent to zero at a {+/-}10% margin (p = 0.0019) with a minimum detectable effect of 8.8%. The result is unchanged across three independent ISG definitions. Nor is it a sensitivity failure: the most transcriptionally responsive mechanical contrast rewires thousands of genes while leaving the module inside a size-matched random distribution. Extending to ten further mechanical modalities shows mechanics is not inert toward these genes; shifts run in both directions, but no contrast supported by within-study inference exceeds 15% of the chemical anchor. Rescoring the same contrasts against an NF-{kappa}B effector module anchored on human LPS kinetics separates the two arms: across 21 modality contrasts the effector arm sits 17.7 percentage points above the interferon arm (paired p = 0.032), and in the four designs whose permutation space can reach p < 0.05 the separation is 34 points. Compression moves the effector arm +36% of the LPS anchor (p = 0.002) and the interferon arm -9% (p = 0.004). The separation is absent under static stiffness, where neither arm moves, and its sign is not fixed. A three-arm in-vivo magnetomechanical dataset assigns the effect to the rotating field rather than the internalized particle, raising the effector arm while lowering the interferon arm. Mechanically induced "M1-like" states are not the chemical M1 program rescaled. Where mechanical loading registers at all, it moves the effector arm and not the interferon arm: interferon-stimulated genes are the wrong readout for mechanical perturbation of macrophages.

papers.title: Longitudinal CCR2 PET Imaging Tracks Early Inflammatory Monocyte and Macrophage Infiltration in Experimental Arthritis
papers.abstract: Objective. Recruitment of C-C motif chemokine receptor 2 (CCR2+) inflammatory monocytes and macrophages represent an early event in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) pathogenesis that cannot be tracked noninvasively with existing imaging modalities. We evaluated longitudinal Ga-DOTA-ECL1i positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) to track and quantify CCR2 cell recruitment in experimental inflammatory arthritis. Methods. Longitudinal Ga-DOTA-ECL1i PET/CT imaging was performed in K/BXN serum transfer arthritis (STA) mice. Imaging findings were validated using biodistribution, autoradiography, histopathology, immunofluorescence, microCT, cytokine profiling, clinical assessment, and pain-related behavioral testing. Results. Joint Ga-DOTA-ECL1i uptake increased during the acute arthritis and declined with disease resolution. Increased tracer signal localized to inflamed joints, coinciding with CCR2 monocyte and macrophage infiltration, synovial inflammation, cartilage damage, local CCL2 elevation, and mechanical allodynia. PET uptake correlated with ankle swelling, clinical disease severity, pain, and paw CCL2 levels, with peak tracer signal preceding progressive structural bone remodeling. Conclusion. Longitudinal Ga-DOTA-ECL1i PET/CT enables noninvasive visualization and quantification of early CCR2 monocyte and macrophage recruitment, establishing CCR2 PET imaging as a mechanism-based molecular platform for early detection, risk stratification, and therapeutic monitoring in inflammatory arthritis.

papers.title: A proteomics screen of HIV-1 ASP interactors reveals multifaceted effects on host cell homeostasis
papers.abstract: Nearly four decades after the identification of the HIV-1 antisense gene asp, the function of its protein product remains unclear. Evidence of ASP expression in vivo and the high degree of conservation of the asp gene among pandemic HIV-1 strains suggest a beneficial role for the virus. Using a mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics screen for ASP interactors, we identified nuclear, cytosolic, and mitochondrial host factors, congruent with variable sub-cellular ASP localization. A majority of the host factors identified in the MS screen are involved in pathways essential for host cell homeostasis, including DNA damage repair, intracellular protein transport, mitochondrial function and protein translation. Validating the biological relevance of these findings, we demonstrate that ASP shuttles to the nucleus to promote DNA damage repair and cell viability in response to genotoxic stress. We also finds that ASP promotes translation of mitochondrially encoded host proteins involved in cellular respiration and contributes to maintain mitochondrial membrane potential. Together, these studies identify ASP as a modulator of two major pathways of cellular homeostasis in infected cells, which has direct implications for HIV-1 persistence, spread, and the long-term survival of the viral reservoir.

papers.title: Structural signatures of salinity adaptation in Microviricetes capsids
papers.abstract: Phages, like their bacterial hosts, have evolved to proliferate across the full range of environments on Earth, but the specific amino acid residues that underlie their environmental adaptations remain elusive. Here, we developed a computational framework that uses structure-based multiple sequence alignments, a random forest classifier, and a phylogeny-aware regression model to find amino acid residues linked to specific environments. Applying this framework to public metagenomic data, we analyzed 1,110 Microviricetes major capsid proteins (MCPs) from the lake and ocean biomes, and found that ocean virus capsids were highly enriched in negatively charged residues on internal and external surfaces. This adaptation likely helps maintain solubility at high salt concentrations and stabilizes ssDNA-capsid interactions by sequestering positively charged ions inside the capsid. At intersubunit interfaces, ocean capsids showed enrichment of cation-{pi} and {pi}-{pi} interactions, which are more resistant to solvation than salt bridges and hydrogen bonds. Amino acid residues in lake capsids were more often substituted by biochemically dissimilar amino acids in ocean capsids than the reverse. Together, these results show that microvirus capsids adapt to high-salt environments through changes in surface charge and substitutions affecting intersubunit interactions. Further, we describe a general approach for studying the adaptation and stability of any protein family under complementary environmental or phenotypic conditions.

papers.title: Within-host evolution of an avirulent Salmonella vaccine strain reveals regulatory tuning of virulence functionality without loss of function
papers.abstract: Non-typhoidal Salmonella (NTS) relies on a costly epithelial invasion program encoded in Salmonella pathogenicity island 1 (SPI-1) to overcome microbiota-mediated colonization resistance. Because SPI-1 expression is a cooperative trait in which a minority of invasive SPI-1ON cells benefits the wider bacterial population, inflammatory infection models readily select for permanently avirulent "cheater" mutants defective in SPI-1 function. However, while frequently observed during acute infection, isolates from persistent human NTS infection rarely exhibit obvious SPI-1 loss-of-function mutations, raising the question of whether SPI-1 contributes to bacterial fitness beyond induction of acute intestinal inflammation and tissue persistence. Here, we addressed this question using a metabolically attenuated yet epithelial-invasive auxotrophic Salmonella serovar Typhimurium (STm) vaccine strain (STmAux) that persistently colonizes the murine intestine without causing overt inflammatory pathology or tissue infection while retaining SPI-1-dependent host interaction and immunogenicity. Following within-host evolution for up to five years, STmAux populations did not accumulate classical hilD or other obvious SPI-1 loss-of-function cheater mutants. Instead, parallel evolution repeatedly targeted the BarA/SirA two-component regulatory system, closely mirroring previous observations in persistent human NTS infections. Functional analyses demonstrated that evolved barA and sirA alleles tune rather than abolish SPI-1 function by sharply reducing the proportion of SPI-1ON cells while preserving their individual epithelial invasion competence. Reconstructed in a prototrophic strain background, early evolved isolates retained full intestinal and systemic virulence in vivo despite exhibiting strongly reduced SPI-1ON frequencies in vitro. Remarkably, identical sirA mutant alleles also emerged in a hilD-deficient strain background, indicating that selection for these adaptive variants is not contingent on canonical HilD-dependent SPI-1 activation. During prolonged evolution, additional mutations accumulated that were associated with loss of systemic virulence despite preservation of epithelial invasiveness, suggesting subsequent adaptation affecting host-interaction pathways beyond SPI-1-mediated virulence. Together, these findings identify regulatory tuning of the BarA/SirA control network as a conserved evolutionary trajectory during prolonged NTS persistence. Rather than favoring classical cheater-driven loss of virulence functions, long-term adaptation preserves substantial SPI-1-dependent host interaction while reducing the proportion of phenotypically virulent SPI-1ON cells.

papers.title: De novo design of ligases for programmable site-specific protein ubiquitylation
papers.abstract: Protein ubiquitylation regulates numerous cellular processes, but difficulties in generating site-specifically ubiquitylated proteins limit our understanding of individual modification events. In cells, ubiquitylation is mediated by an E1-E2-E3 enzyme cascade, with substrate recognition largely determined by more than 600 human E3 ligases, making it challenging to redirect ubiquitin transfer to a chosen lysine. Here we use RFdiffusion3 to design ubiquitin ligases from scratch that use a cysteine-based catalytic triad to conjugate an activated ubiquitin donor to a selected lysine in a chosen target substrate. Of 48 tested designs, 35 ubiquitylated a model peptide, with the most active ligases achieving near-quantitative ubiquitin transfer. We next challenged the approach with the homotrimeric sliding clamp proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA), whose ubiquitylation at lysine (K) 164 governs DNA damage tolerance while displaying 45 off-target lysines for ubiquitination. Screening of 48 designs delivered a site-selective ligase. Incorporation of a single activity-increasing substitution and coupling to E1-dependent donor activation resulted in 90% conversion from unactivated ubiquitin, delivering higher rates and superior selectivity compared to a natural promiscuous E2. Using this cascade, we transferred di-, tri- and tetraubiquitin chains of defined length to PCNA K164 through a native isopeptide bond. These results establish de novo enzyme design as a route towards programmable, site-specific protein ubiquitylation. That a single de novo designed protein can bind both an activated ubiquitin donor and a globular target, and use a proficient catalytic machinery to selectively transfer ubiquitin to one lysine among 45, illustrates the level of functional complexity now within reach of de novo enzyme design.

papers.title: Population-level emulation enables fast Bayesian calibration of cardiac digital twins
papers.abstract: Purpose: Patient-specific cardiac digital twins have the potential to guide individualized therapy, but generating these in a routine clinical workflow remains challenging. This is especially true when the twins must carry quantified uncertainty: Bayesian calibration requires thousands of simulations per patient, and the emulators that reduce this cost are typically trained one patient at a time. We aimed to train a single emulator across a patient cohort, so that a new patient can be calibrated in minutes without new simulations. Methods: We trained a population-level Gaussian process emulator whose inputs included a 12-dimensional latent encoding of the clinical features of each patient, so that a single emulator represents the whole cohort. We compared spending simulation budgets on resampling the real cohort with augmenting the cohort with digital chimeras, synthetic patients interpolated between real patients. Seven parameters of a closed-loop heart and circulation model were calibrated by Markov chain Monte Carlo to ten clinical biomarkers in 26 patients with left bundle branch block, each using an emulator trained without that patient, and the calibrated posteriors were compared against the full simulator. Results: A single emulator, trained without the held-out patient, calibrated the digital twin of each patient in 59.7-63.0 s per patient, versus 15 h with the simulator. Resampling the real cohort was the more efficient training strategy, bringing every output to R2 greater than or equal to 0.9, which augmentation did not achieve for the same simulation budget. For held-out patients, both strategies performed comparably (median leave-one-out normalized root-mean-square error 11.0% vs. 10.7%; p = 0.745), and error rose with distance from the cohort centroid (Spearman rho = +0.406). The calibrated models showed no cohort-wide bias (median standardized residual -0.12 against the clinical targets), and 95% predictive intervals contained 78.5% of targets, with the largest misfit in systolic blood pressure. Conclusion: Removing the need for new simulations for every new patient is a meaningful step toward uncertainty-aware cardiac digital twins that fit within a routine clinical workflow. Because the simulator, surrogate and sampler are interchangeable, the approach used here can be applied to other (cardiac) models and cohorts.

papers.title: Multi-omics profiling links epigenetic and lncRNA changes to early human endochondral ossification priming
papers.abstract: Differentiation programs remain incompletely understood across stem cell types, including for human bone marrow mesenchymal stromal/stem (BM-MSCs) cells, a heterogenous population orchestrating bone formation and establishing a functional hematopoietic niche in the bone marrow. BM-MSCs form and repair bone through the evolutionarily conserved process of endochondral ossification (EO), initiated by deposition of a transient cartilage template subsequently remodeled into bone and bone marrow tissues. Despite their considerable potential for skeletal regeneration, the early molecular and cellular events underlying BM-MSCs commitment to EO remain elusive. To overcome donor dependent variability in chondrogenic potential that limits mechanistic studies, we here exploit OssiGel as a potent chondro-inductive extracellular matrix offering robust recapitulation of EO by BMMSCs. Through multi-omics profiling of OssiGel-primed BM-MSCs, we identify rapid chromatin remodeling at chondrogenic loci as concomitant for lineage commitment. The emergence of a chondro-progenitor population is detected as early as 3 days in vivo and correlates with successful EO recapitulation. Mechanistically, we identify LINC02511 as novel enhancer-associated element involved in the onset of EO. We confirm presence of LINC02511 in human skeletal atlases, and its CRISPR-mediated silencing significantly impaired EO. By integrating human tissue engineering strategies with single cell multi-omics profiling, our study provides a framework for deciphering BM-MSCs fate decisions, highlighting the role of enhancer and non-coding elements as key determinants of early lineage specification. These findings advance our understanding of BM-MSCs biology and will prompt their translational exploitation in regenerative medicine.

papers.title: CheckAMG: Accurate Identification of Auxiliary Viral Genes with Genome Language Models
papers.abstract: Viruses shape microbial metabolism through auxiliary viral genes (AVGs) that reprogram host metabolism, physiology, and gene regulation during infection. Identifying AVGs is complicated by ambiguous viral versus cellular assignment, inconsistent curation, and reliance on sequence homology that misses divergent functions. Here we present CheckAMG, which pairs annotation-based AVG prediction, curated with a per-gene viral scoring system and ontological mapping of metabolic function, with a finetuned genome-language model for annotation-independent discovery. Benchmarked against DRAM-V and VIBRANT across three ecosystems, CheckAMG produced more strongly supported auxiliary metabolic gene (AMG) calls, and uniquely among AMG tools reports auxiliary physiological (APGs) and regulatory (AReGs) genes. Applied to 1,005,980 fragmented or complete soil and human-gut viral genomes, CheckAMG identified 541,199 AVGs tracking biome-specific protein clusters and functions, including 109,107 with no detectable sequence similarity to any reference database. CheckAMG thus provides a reproducible, scalable framework for identifying the genes through which viruses reprogram host biology.
affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison (corresponding author)

papers.title: An interactive web application for exploring human plasma and fibroblast metabolomics data from patients with inborn errors of metabolism
papers.abstract: Metabolomic profiling is instrumental in understanding the systemic and cellular impact of inborn errors of metabolism (IEMs), monogenic disorders caused by pathogenic genomic variants in genes involved in metabolism. This study encompasses metabolomics analysis of plasma from 474 individuals and fibroblasts from 67 subjects, incorporating healthy controls, patients with 65 different monogenic diseases, and numerous undiagnosed cases. We introduce a web application designed for the in-depth exploration of this extensive metabolomics database. The application offers a user-friendly interface for data review, download, and detailed analysis of metabolic deviations linked to IEMs at the level of individual patients or groups of patients with the same diagnosis. It also provides interactive tools for investigating metabolic relationships and offers comparative analyses of plasma and fibroblast profiles. This tool emphasizes the metabolic interplay within and across biological matrices, enriching our understanding of metabolic regulation in health and disease. As a resource, the application provides broad utility in research, offering novel insights into metabolic pathways and their alterations in various disorders.

papers.title: Serum extracellular vesicle proteomics reveals treatment-associated biomarkers in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
papers.abstract: Background Longitudinal biomarkers of treatment response in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) are needed. Extracellular vesicle (EV)-enriched serum proteomics may provide a minimally invasive approach for monitoring systemic and tumor-associated responses to therapy. Methods Paired pre-treatment and post-treatment serum samples were analyzed from 51 patients with pancreatic cancer, including 25 treated with FOLFIRINOX and 20 treated with gemcitabine-based therapy. EVs were enriched using the Mag-Net method and profiled by data independent acquisition mass spectrometry. After batch correction and filtering, 941 proteins were retained for differential and pathway analyses. Paired linear models and gene set enrichment analyses were used to assess treatment-associated changes. Baseline protein abundance and longitudinal changes were evaluated in relation to overall survival (OS) using Cox models. Results A total of 2,089 EV-associated proteins were identified, with an average of 1,186 proteins quantified per sample. Across the cohort, 26 proteins differed between post- and pretreatment samples. Proteins that increased after treatment were primarily related to extracellular matrix organization and cell adhesion, whereas proteins that decreased after treatment were associated with actin cytoskeletal organization, coagulation, and hemostasis. Treatment-associated changes were more pronounced in the FOLFIRINOX group, in which 32 proteins were differentially expressed. FOLFIRINOX was characterized by coordinated reductions in platelet- and coagulation-associated proteins, including PF4, PF4V1, PPBP, GP5, ITGA2B, and ITGB3, accompanied by enrichment of platelet activation, coagulation, and hemostasis pathways among down-regulated processes. No individual proteins met the same significance threshold in the gemcitabine group. A composite seven-protein platelet score decreased significantly after FOLFIRINOX but not for gemcitabine, and the between-regimen difference in score change was significant. Higher pretreatment ITGB1 abundance was associated with longer OS after multiple-testing correction (HR, 0.112; BH-FDR = 0.0063). In multivariable analysis, greater treatment-associated platelet-score depletion was independently associated with shorter OS (HR per unit increase in {Delta}score, 0.56; P = 0.030). Conclusions Longitudinal serum EV-enriched proteomics identified treatment-associated biological changes in PDAC, including a coordinated platelet-related response predominantly observed after FOLFIRINOX. Baseline ITGB1 abundance and longitudinal platelet-score changes represent potentially complementary prognostic and pharmacodynamic markers. These findings are exploratory and require validation in larger, independent cohorts incorporating platelet counts, coagulation measurements, and targeted proteomic assays.

papers.title: Genome-wide diversity across 130 years reveals drastic post-bottleneck genetic erosion in a recovering population of golden eagles (Aquila chrysaetos)
papers.abstract: Many wild populations have experienced severe human-induced declines, but the genetic consequences of such bottlenecks are often poorly understood. In Finland, as well as in many other countries, golden eagles were heavily persecuted during the 19th-20th centuries, disappearing from southern regions and reaching their lowest population size in the 1950-1960s. Although conservation efforts facilitated demographic recovery, the long-term genomic consequences of the bottleneck remained unknown. Here, we used whole-genome sequencing data spanning 136 years to evaluate patterns of genetic diversity in 26 Finnish golden eagles before, during, and after the mid-20th century bottleneck. We found substantial loss of genetic variation, including an 82% reduction in genome-wide heterozygosity, a 42% decline in nucleotide diversity, a 67% reduction in Watterson's theta, and a substantial loss of variable sites. Analyses of the site frequency spectrum and Tajima's D confirmed historical population contraction, and runs of homozygosity analysis indicated elevated post-bottleneck inbreeding. These results indicate strong genetic erosion in Finnish golden eagles despite the census size recovery. Therefore, incorporating genomic indicators in conservation monitoring and performing regional assessments are necessary to guide management and preserve biodiversity in line with the Global Biodiversity Framework's goal of maintaining genetic variation.
affiliations: University of Oulu (corresponding author)

papers.title: Affordable 96-parallel SPPS: hardware and software add-on for automated liquid handling platforms
papers.abstract: ParSynt-P is a hardware and software add-on that converts a liquid-handling robot already available in a proteomics laboratory (Tecan Freedom EVO) into a parallel plate-format peptide synthesizer for generating libraries of candidate peptide standards for targeted blood plasma proteomics. The manifold is milled from polytetrafluoroethylene and has ports for an inert gas and a vacuum line; a standard commercially available 96-well filtration plate is secured to it with an airtight seal. The software layer generates robot worklists from a table of peptide sequences and controls switching of the N?/vacuum lines, including pulsed gas mixing. The system performs up to 96 syntheses per run, and coupling of one residue takes 94 min. Workability of this 96-well format was verified on three fully loaded plates. The uniformity of synthesis conversion across the plate was measured quantitatively using a characterized NAT/SIL standard pair. The add-on cost $351, while the synthesis cost is $0.23 per coupling and $1.14 per milligram of crude product, an order of magnitude below the market price of custom synthesis.
