papers.title: Boosting Single-Cell Methods Significantly Enhances Cell-type Classification
papers.abstract: Single-cell sequencing drives biological discovery by revealing key cellular processes, cell types, and cell states. Recent technological advances have accelerated atlas-scale data generation across laboratories. With the increasing amount of single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) data, new challenges emerge, including effective batch correction, cell-type annotation, rare cell-type and cell-state detection, as well as biological pathway discovery. Inspired by methods for boosting weak learners such as AdaBoost, here we present a novel paradigm, scBoost, that combines single-cell analysis methods using stacked ensembles to boost task performance beyond that of individual methods. We show that scBoost pretrained on Tabula Sapiens 2.0 dataset performs significantly better than existing methods in cell-type classification on the real-world Human Fetal Heart Map and Plaque Atlas. We also demonstrate that scBoost substantially improves the performance of cell-type classification and ranks at the top of the leaderboard on the OpenProblems benchmark, a standard-in-the-field. scBoost is modular and is adaptive to new single-cell methods, which will enable it to continue to serve as a resource to the community in the future.
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Binding mechanisms of therapeutic antibodies to human claudin-18.2
papers.abstract: Claudin-18.2 (CLDN18.2) is a tight junction component with highly restricted expression in the paracellular space of nonmalignant gastric epithelial cells. It becomes accessible on tumor cell surface during malignant transformation, making CLDN18.2 an attractive target for targeted therapies against gastric cancer. Recently, zolbetuximab has become the first FDA-approved monoclonal antibody that targets CLDN18.2 in advanced gastric cancer, and others like osemitamab have entered phase 3 clinical trials. However, the high-resolution structure of CLDN18.2 is lacking, and how CLDN18.2 is recognized by therapeutic antibodies remains undefined. Here, we report cryo-EM structures of human claudin-18.2 (hCLDN18.2) in complex with the Fab fragments of zolbetuximab and osemitamab, revealing the structure of hCLDN18.2 and its binding mechanism to the therapeutic antibodies. Further analyses reveal that three residues in the first extracellular loop of hCLDN18.2 that are different from human claudin-18.1 (hCLDN18.1) play a critical role in antibody binding. Our data elucidate the structural basis for selective binding of therapeutic antibodies to hCLDN18.2, which should aid rational design of next-generation immunotherapies targeting hCLDN18.2.
affiliations: Sichuan University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Where the magnet sits sets the sign of the scaling law: membrane-anchored versus intracellular magnetic actuation of cells
papers.abstract: Magnetic nanoparticles apply mechanical force to cells in two incompatible geometries: anchored to the plasma membrane, where a rotating field twists a surface-bound cap, and internalized into lysosomes, where an assembled rod stirs the organelle lumen. They are treated as interchangeable, and the choice is made on synthetic convenience. They obey opposite design rules. Treated analytically at matched single-cell magnetic moment, the step-out frequency of an intracellular rod falls with assembly size while that of a membrane cap rises linearly; the scaling exponents have opposite sign and the curves cross at 184 particles and 4.04 Hz, inside the window in which published experiments operate. The cap tension resultant reduces to an identity in which cell radius cancels, leaving magnetic texture as the decisive design variable: a field-oriented cap reaches 2.69 mN m-1, the same particles with random easy axes reach 0.0033 mN m-1, and a superparamagnetic cap transmits no torque at all. The model reproduces four published measurements with no fitted parameters. One disagrees: our intralysosomal wall shear stress is 33 to 81 times below the published value while reproducing every structural feature of it. The model yields two zero-predictions that one experiment would falsify.
affiliations: Stony Brook University (corresponding author)

papers.title: TREM2-stimulated, PDGF-dependent macrophage-fibroblast crosstalk induces beneficial plaque remodeling in clonal hematopoiesis
papers.abstract: Background: In Jak2V617F clonal hematopoiesis, inflammatory signaling suppresses macrophage TREM2 and promotes features of plaque instability, while therapeutic TREM2 agonism reverses plaque instability by increasing fibroblasts and fibrous cap formation. We tested whether macrophage-derived PDGFB and stromal cell PDGFR? signaling mediate this response. Methods: Low allele burden (LAB) Jak2V617F atherosclerosis models were combined with inducible Pdgfb deletion in CX3CR1-lineage monocytes/macrophages or Pdgfra deletion in Col1a2-lineage fibroblast-enriched stromal cells. Mice were treated with the TREM2 agonist 4D9. Plaque composition, macrophage-fibroblast interactions, and aortic stromal cell populations were analyzed. Human WT and JAK2V617F iPSC-derived macrophages were used for validation. Results: TREM2 activation with 4D9 increased macrophage PDGFB production and promoted fibrous cap formation in LAB Jak2V617F atherosclerosis. Deletion of Pdgfb in CX3CR1-lineage cells markedly attenuated the 4D9-mediated increase in fibrous cap area and lesional PDGFR?+ cells, establishing macrophage-derived PDGFB as a key signal for the stromal response. Consistently, Col1a2-lineage Pdgfra deletion abolished the 4D9-induced fibrous cap response without significantly altering lesion or necrotic core area. Single cell RNA-seq identified increased Fmod+ and CD26/Dpp4+ fibroblast populations associated with 4D9 treatment. Fmod+ fibroblasts represented an abundant matrix-associated population, whereas CD26+ fibroblasts showed greatest enrichment, prominent extracellular matrix, collagen organization, and matrix-remodeling programs that were enhanced by 4D9 and attenuated by Pdgfra deletion. The stromal response was also associated with reduced macrophage migration-related programs and predicted chemokine communication from CD26+ fibroblasts to macrophages which was verified by macrophage migration studies. Moreover, stromal Pdgfra deletion increased lesional CCR2+ and CCR5+ macrophages. Conclusions: In a CH model of inflammatory atherosclerosis, TREM2 activation promotes a macrophage PDGFB-stromal PDGFR? pathway that expands Fmod+ and CD26+ fibroblast populations and increases fibrous cap matrix formation. CD26+ fibroblasts impair macrophage chemotaxis in a DPP4-dependent manner, suggesting reciprocal macrophage-fibroblast communication that coordinates matrix remodeling and inflammatory cell trafficking in the plaque.
affiliations: New York-Presbyterian/Columbia University Irving Medical Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Rab27a modulation reverses hemorrhage-induced neutrophil dysfunction in response to secondary respiratory challenge
papers.abstract: Patients recovering from hemorrhage are susceptible to secondary respiratory infections, owing to dysregulated innate immune responses. Using a two-hit mouse model of hemorrhage followed by a secondary respiratory challenge with Staphylococcus aureus or lipopolysaccharide (LPS), we investigated the role of Rab27a in the neutrophil response to pulmonary inflammation and host defense. Hemorrhage followed by S. aureus infection increased surface CD63 expression on pulmonary neutrophils, indicating azurophilic granule release, and was accompanied by reduced neutrophil entry into the airspaces of the lung. Using HoxB8-conditional neutrophil progenitor (NP) transplantation to neutrophil chimeric mice, we observe that Rab27a-deficient neutrophils have enhanced recruitment into the extravascular pulmonary compartment compared with wild-type (WT) neutrophils. Furthermore, pharmacological intervention with Nexinhib20, a small-molecule inhibitor of Rab27a-JFC1 interactions, attenuated systemic and pulmonary inflammatory responses in the two-hit model, including a reduction in circulating myeloperoxidase (MPO) levels. Nexinhib20 also enhanced neutrophil-mediated S. aureus killing that was accompanied by increased intracellular MPO levels in neutrophils. Collectively, these findings implicate Rab27a-associated functions in the regulation of neutrophil trafficking and inflammatory responses following hemorrhage and secondary respiratory challenge, highlighting the potential of pharmacological targeting of Rab27a to attenuate inflammation without compromising antimicrobial host defense.
affiliations: Division of Surgical Research, Department of Surgery, Rhode Island Hospital and Brown University Health, 593 Eddy Street, Providence, RI 02903, United States (corresponding author)

papers.title: Evolutionarily distinct dengue virus type 2 with a unique type-specific neutralization determinant
papers.abstract: Dengue viruses 1-4 (DENV1-4) mostly circulate in endemic cycles involving humans and Aedes mosquitoes. However, rare dengue outbreaks originate from non-human primates. These spillovers are caused by sylvatic virus genotypes that are closely related to endemic strains of the same serotype, but some are caused by strains that fall between the four canonical serotypes on phylogenetic trees. It is not clear whether these genotypic differences are reflected in corresponding antigenic differences. Here, we characterized the antigenic features of QML-22, a divergent strain most closely related to DENV2. On an antigenic map, QML-22 clustered with other globally representative DENV2 strains. QML-22 was not as well neutralized by antisera raised against endemic DENV2 and was better neutralized by antisera from DENV1, 3, and 4 infections than other strains of DENV2. QML-22 had a cluster of distinct amino acid residues in domain I of the envelope (E) protein, with only scattered point mutations elsewhere in the envelope. A potently neutralizing anti-DENV2 antibody that targets this site in domain I of the E protein, 3F9, had >1000-fold lower neutralization of QML-22 than other endemic DENV2 strains, whereas other cross-reactive and DENV2-specific antibodies neutralized QML-22 and endemic strains to similar titers. When antisera from non-human primates infected with QML-22 or DENV2 reference strain S16803 were depleted with the heterologous virions, homologous neutralization was unaffected but heterologous neutralization was reduced, suggesting homologous neutralization was due to distinct epitopes. Evolutionary analyses showed the 3F9 epitope was under relaxed selection pressure compared to other neutralizing epitopes and that QML-22 had unique amino acids in this epitope relative to the likely common ancestor of all DENV2. These findings provide insight into the antigenic diversification of DENV and the possible evolution of new serotypes.
affiliations: Viral Epidemiology and Immunity Unit, Laboratory of Infectious Diseases, National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, National Institutes of Health, B (corresponding author)

papers.title: Sphingolipid Hydroxylation Governs Fungal Pathogenicity and Drug Susceptibility: Scs7 as a Druggable Target in Candida albicans
papers.abstract: Sphingolipids are essential structural components of the fungal plasma membrane and key signaling hubs that orchestrate pathogenicity. While both fungi and mammals perform sphingolipid hydroxylation, they rely on evolutionarily divergent enzymatic systems, establishing a biochemical divergence exploitable for selective targeting. Here, through a screening of sphingolipid metabolic genes, we identify the sphingolipid -hydroxylase Scs7 as a central regulator of membrane homeostasis, virulence, and caspofungin susceptibility in Candida albicans. Genetic ablation of SCS7 depletes hydroxylated sphingolipids, disrupts memberane organization, and compromises cell wall integrity, which collectively impair hyphal morphogenesis, biofilm formation, and stress tolerance through blockade of the cAMP-PKA signaling axis. In a murine cutaneous infection model, SCS7 deletion markedly attenuates fungal burden, hyperinflammation, and epidermal barrier disruption, underscoring its non-redundant role in host-pathogen interaction. Leveraging the fungus-specific architecture of Scs7, we performed virtual screening and identified resveratrol as a natural Scs7 inhibitor. Resveratrol recapitulates the lipidomic and phenotypic defects of SCS7 deletion and synergizes with caspofungin to enhance fungal killing. Our study establishes sphingolipid -hydroxylation as a master determinant of fungal membrane fitness and validates Scs7 as a promising, fungus-specific antifungal target with dual anti-virulence and chemosensitizing activities.
affiliations: Nanchang University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Hyperactivation of Mincle in exacerbated apical periodontitis in an autoinflammatory mouse model for cherubism
papers.abstract: Aims: To examine the role of Mincle, a C-type lectin (Clec) pathogen recognition receptor (PRR), in exacerbated apical periodontitis (AP) in an autoinflammatory mouse model for cherubism (CBM). Methodology: Patients with immune system dysfunction have higher prevalence of AP but the mechanism remains largely unknown. We studied a knock-in (KI) mouse model carrying a Sh3bp2 mutation for CBM. We performed pulp exposure in one lower 1st molar of 5- to 6-week-old mice to introduce pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMP)-induced endodontic infection. We determined the expression levels of Clec subfamily genes by qPCR. To suppress Mincle, we generated Sh3bp2+/+Mincle+/+, Sh3bp2+/KIMincle+/+, and Sh3bp2+/KIMincleKO/KO mice or injected Sh3bp2+/KI mice with a Mincle-binding DNA aptamer (AptMincle). Mice were analyzed 42 days after pulp exposure by micro-CT (mCT), qPCR and immunoblotting. Statistical analysis was performed by one-way ANOVA followed by post-hoc analysis with Tukeys test or two-way ANOVA followed by Sidak correction. p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results: Expression of Clec4e (Mincle) was significantly increased in Sh3bp2 mutant mice after pulp exposure compared to WT littermates (p<0.0001). Sh3bp2+/KIMincle+/+ and Sh3bp2+/KIMincleKO/KO mice had a comparable response to pulp exposure, including the degree of bone loss and induction of inducible NOS (iNOS), IL-1b, and TNF-a. Sh3bp2+/KI mice injected with AptMincle after pulp exposure for 21 days showed significant amelioration of bone loss compared to mice with vehicle injection (p<0.0001). Conclusions: These seemingly conflicting data of suppressing Mincle by crossing with Mincle KO mice and AptMincle injection suggest that Mincle has dual functions upon PAMPs stimulation, consistent with a previous study showing that Mincle enhances tissue destruction during the inflammatory stage and is subsequently needed for inflammation resolution. Fine-tuned suppression of Mincle significantly reduces the severity of AP in Sh3bp2+/KI mice. This study suggests that patients with CBM may benefit from more frequent dental examinations and early intervention to reduce or prevent severe progressive bone loss in periapical tissues.
affiliations: University of Connecticut School of Dental Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Surface adhesion-dependent DNA extraction bias points to an 'anvil effect' during mechanical lysis
papers.abstract: DNA extraction bias is usually treated as an intrinsic property of a cell's envelope, size, or physiology rather than a feature of its physical location. Most soil bacteria live attached to surfaces, and attached cells should lyse preferentially during bead-beating if a bead striking a particle crushes the cell against it, as on an anvil, whereas a free cell must be caught between colliding beads. We tested this 'anvil effect' in sterile synthetic soil microcosms using isogenic strain pairs that differ in adhesion in two bacteria with different modes of attachment. Agrobacterium tumefaciens anchors with a unipolar polysaccharide and aggregates in an exopolysaccharide matrix, whereas Caulobacter vibrioides attaches individually by a polar holdfast. Within each strain we calculated the ratio of DNA yield from mechanical to chemical lysis, then compared adherent with non-adherent strains. In support of the anvil effect, mechanical lysis favored adherent cells in A. tumefaciens (2.0-fold) and C. vibrioides (2.6-fold). The route by which soil was transferred to the lysis tube altered the extent of bias observed, further indicating the importance of considering physical context during DNA extraction. Our synthetic soil was standardized and aggregate-free, leaving cells exposed on particle surfaces, making these results a direct test of the anvil effect. In natural soils, the aggregation, texture, and moisture may offset or amplify this effect. Surface attachment therefore biases soil DNA extraction, complicating corrections that treat extraction efficiency as a fixed, strain-specific coefficient.
affiliations: Purdue University (corresponding author)

papers.title: A chromosome-level genome assembly of the endangered northern dragonhead sap beetle, Thymogethes norvegicus (Easton, 1959)
papers.abstract: The northern dragonhead sap beetle (Thymogethes norvegicus) is believed to be endemic to Norway and is classified as endangered. Its life cycle is closely tied to the host plant northern dragonhead (Dracocephalum ruyschiana), itself classified as vulnerable in Norway. Here, we present a chromosome-level genome assembly of a male T. norvegicus. The assembly comprises two pseudo-haplotypes, hap1 and hap2, of 1,142 and 1,109 Mb, with 96.3% and 96.8% scaffolded into chromosomes, respectively. Hap1 contains 8 autosomes and the X chromosome, while hap2 contains 8 autosomes. Assembly quality was high, with conserved single-copy ortholog completeness scores of 96.6% and 90.7% and combined k-mer completeness of 98.1%. A total of 13,484 and 12,550 protein-coding genes were annotated in hap1 and hap2, respectively. This assembly provides a valuable genomic resource for the conservation of this endangered endemic species totally dependent on the vulnerable plant, the northern dragonhead.
affiliations: Department of Biosciences, University of Oslo, Oslo, Norway (corresponding author)

papers.title: Long-read analysis of complete human 5S rDNA arrays reveals a zoned organization with two-state unit methylation linked to chromatin architecture
papers.abstract: Despite the fundamental importance of the 5S ribosomal DNA (rDNA) to all cellular life, the landscape of its units by position along its array has remained poorly understood. Here, recent telomere-to-telomere long-read sequencing is used to resolve 5S rDNA arrays from flank to flank and to follow the state of each unit along single molecules. The array is zoned at both the sequence and the epigenetic level. Notably, methylation is bimodal at the level of the unit, and the combination of low-methylation and high-methylation units gives rise to the overall methylation pattern of the array. Moreover, the average number of low-methylation units remains relatively constant regardless of array length. Chromatin fiber sequencing (Fiber-seq) data further show that low-methylation units are more accessible, have lower nucleosome occupancy and are more frequently footprinted at the TFIIIB-binding site, consistent with analyses of ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq data from cell lines. Across species, this pattern is shared among apes, whereas other species show diverse patterns. These results provide a unit-resolved view of the human 5S rDNA array and reveal a zone-specific organization of unit methylation that is associated with chromatin architecture.
affiliations: Seoul National University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Comprehensive Characterization of Somatic Mutations and Gene Expression on TP53/PTEN DKO Murine Glioblastoma Cell Lines: Insights from Whole-Exome and RNA-seq Analysis
papers.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is an aggressive brain tumor characterized by genomic instability and transcriptional plasticity. To investigate the somatic evolution of GBM, we performed an integrated analysis using Whole-Exome Sequencing (WES) and RNA-seq on a murine glioblastoma model representing two stages: early-stage transformed neural stem cells (tNSC) and late-stage malignant GBM (mGB). The comparative analysis of mutational signatures provides evidence of a two-phase evolutionary path for tNSC and mGB. Variant calling in tNSCs revealed mutations in Pfdn2, Oip5, Trmt10a, Nabp2, Man2b1 with mGBs acquiring additional putative progression-associated genes such as Cdk4, Ubap2, Ccdc11, Errfil, and Tead2 associated with malignancy and Temozolomide (TMZ) resistance. Samples in tNSCs exhibited signatures associated with stress-(SBS4) and development-associated (SBS40) processes. In contrast, mGB samples exhibited an increase inmutation signatures, specifically associated with replication- (SBS5) and mismatch repair (MMR) processes (SBS26). Notably, SBS26 consistently ranked in the top five mutational signatures across all samples, indicating that there may have been an early, and sustained, loss of MMR. Ti/Tv ratio also revealed elevated transversions in tNSCs supporting early instability post TP53/PTEN knockout, while mGB demonstrated normal transition-to-transversion ratio. Gene ontology reveals activities in neurodevelopmental pathways in tNSCs such as neurogenesis, axon guidance, and synapse regulation while in mGB it shifts to cellular transformation and invasion, and epidermal development. Moreover, differential expression analysis showed extreme downregulation against control neural stem cells (ctrlNSCs) indicating genomic instability and then the partial restoration of expression in mGB, resembling ctrlNSCs but with a bias toward malignant upregulations. Together this suggests, early genomic instability disrupting developmental programs and blocking differentiation, and later on replication-driven mutations and cytoskeletal remodeling reprograms the tumor into a proliferative, invasive, and therapy-resistant state.
affiliations: Department of Computer Sciences, University of Agriculture, Faisalabad (corresponding author)

papers.title: Scientific Figure Library connects visual examples with reusable plotting code
papers.abstract: Code-generating assistants can adapt plotting scripts, while researchers select visual examples and assess their relevance. Reusing those examples requires the image, implementation, and input context to remain connected. Scientific Figure Library (SFL) organizes visual examples, plotting code, input descriptions, and provenance as reusable figure assets. A user-selected local library retains working revisions and published releases, while a common provider interface makes local and externally maintained collections available through the same discovery workflow. Researchers browse candidate figures, inspect an exact preview, confirm a selection, and materialize the corresponding assets into a project for adaptation and execution. Local clients and external agents access a shared service, connecting visual selection with code-based analysis across research environments. An accompanying open resource, ScientificFigureLibrary-personal, supplies modular examples through the Open Figure Modules provider. Its organization combines previews, reusable scripts, example inputs, and licensing information, making it a concrete resource for learning and adapting scientific visualization patterns. We describe the asset model, retrieval and confirmation workflow, execution handoff, and resource organization, supported by implementation inspection and automated software checks. In a public lung single-cell case study, we reused a cell-composition template for 32 idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and 28 control donors and verified the donor-level inputs and plotted proportions. SFL provides a practical connection between finding a figure and obtaining the materials needed to work with it, while preserving the identity and provenance of the selected example.
affiliations: National Key Laboratory of Plant Molecular Genetics (NKLPMG), CAS Center for Excellence in Molecular Plant Sciences (CEMPS), Institute of Plant Physiology and E (corresponding author)

papers.title: Towards a best-in-class IgE disruptor for food allergy with Claude-enabled antibody design
papers.abstract: Food allergy affects an estimated 220-250 million people worldwide, for whom the constant risk of a severe reaction weighs heavily on quality of life. Allergic reactions are triggered by the cross-linking of allergen-specific IgE bound to its high-affinity receptor, Fc{epsilon}RI, on mast cells and basophils, causing degranulation, inflammation and, in severe cases, anaphylaxis. Omalizumab (Xolair), the sole FDA-approved biologic for food allergy, neutralizes circulating IgE; however, it does not effectively remove IgE from Fc{epsilon}RI, where it can persist for weeks and where even a small residual amount can sustain sensitivity. Here we describe an agentic computational design campaign with Claude toward a disruptive inhibitor antibody that physically removes bound IgE from Fc{epsilon}RI. Guided by our research team, Claude pursued a biparatopic molecule that pairs a disruptor arm, which displaces IgE from Fc{epsilon}RI, with a non-competing anchor arm that holds the molecule on receptor-bound IgE. Of 91 experimentally characterized disruptor designs, 20 showed activity against receptor-bound IgE by competitive bio-layer interferometry, and in a dose-titration assay three variants removed more IgE than omalizumab at therapeutically relevant concentrations (25-400 nM). De novo designs for the anchor arm bound IgE at diverse epitopes with apparent affinities of 3.4-235 nM. These subcomponents provide the starting point for further characterization toward a best-in-class IgE disruptor.
affiliations: Divergence Labs (corresponding author)

papers.title: DE-Rigor-Agent: An Agentic Workflow for Assumption-Aware Differential Expression Analysis of Bulk RNA-seq Data
papers.abstract: Differential expression (DE) methods for bulk RNA-seq differ in their statistical assumptions, input data requirements, and supported study designs. Large language model (LLM) agents can automate DE analysis, but they may default to popular methods without checking whether these methods are appropriate for the data. We introduce DE-Rigor-Agent, an assumption-aware agent that organizes DE analysis into three stages: input standardization, method filtering, and method execution. Before executing any DE method, the agent uses expert-curated criteria and dataset-specific diagnostics to evaluate six commonly used methods, documents the reasons for retaining or excluding each method, and executes all retained methods. We evaluated DE-Rigor-Agent on 140 simulated datasets spanning 14 challenging scenarios involving small sample sizes, zero inflation, expression outliers, pre-normalized inputs, and confounded batch effects. Benchmarks showed that method-dataset incompatibilities could lead to inflated false discovery rates (FDRs) or reduced statistical power. Two general-purpose LLM agent baselines, including one explicitly prompted to consider statistical assumptions, selected DESeq2 or edgeR for nearly all datasets. In contrast, DE-Rigor-Agent's filtering decisions closely matched the incompatibilities introduced in the simulations and remained consistent across random seeds, with little additional computational cost. These results demonstrate that DE-Rigor-Agent provides an automated approach to assessing method suitability, making DE analysis more rigorous and transparent.
affiliations: Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Catalytic domain-lipid interactions negatively regulate RhoA signaling by modulating conformational dynamics
papers.abstract: RhoA belongs to the Ras superfamily of small GTPases, regulates cytoskeletal actin organization and cell motility, and is implicated in cancer metastasis and neurodegenerative diseases. It is predominantly anchored to the cytosolic side of the plasma membrane (PM) via its prenylated C-terminus, but little is known about its PM organization, dynamics, and lipid interactions. In this work, we used extensive atomistic molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and simulations-guided experiments to study the molecular details and functional consequences of RhoA membrane targeting, interactions and dynamics. We found that both GDP- and GTP-bound RhoA adopt a well-defined, stable membrane organization and binding mode irrespective of initial conditions and bilayer lipid composition. RhoA membrane organization is determined by hydrophobic interaction of the prenylated C-terminus with the membrane, and a previously unknown, critical role of electrostatic interactions between cationic residues on the G-domain and N-terminus with anionic lipids in the PM. N-terminal interactions are mediated by a polybasic patch including residues R5, K6, and K7, and substitution of these residues with Ala increased RhoA-mediated F-actin accumulation and effector activation in cells. MD simulations suggest that the triple mutant retains the global membrane organization of wild type RhoA but alters key protein-lipid interactions. Specifically, we observe a loss of cooperative lipid engagement involving the polybasic patch and Switch II residues with amine-bearing lipids, and a rerouting of intra-protein dynamic networks that primes Switch I for effector recognition. These results suggest that the membrane serves not just as a scaffold but also as an allosteric partner of RhoA to fine-tune intra-protein dynamics in a functionally relevant manner.
affiliations: UTHealth Houston (corresponding author)

papers.title: SilencioMA: A single compound that targets both MAPT and APP as a potential disease modifying therapeutic for Alzheimer's Disease
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is the most common age-related neurodegenerative disease and the leading cause of dementia worldwide. AD pathogenesis involves aggregation of amyloid-beta (A{beta}), produced from amyloidogenic proteolytic processing of Amyloid Precursor Protein (APP), and accumulation of misfolded, pathological tau (Microtubule Associated Protein Tau, MAPT). Current efforts focus on developing disease modifying therapeutics (DMTs) against single targets: A{beta} or tau. However, DMTs that concurrently target both tau and A{beta} are likely to have the greatest impact since they target both culprits of AD pathogenesis. Here we describe the development of SilencioMA, a single compound that targets both MAPT and APP messenger RNAs (mRNAs) based on silencing connected interfering oligonucleotides against MAPT and APP. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) administration of SilencioMA reduces A{beta} and tau and pathology after a single intracerebroventricular injection in 5XFAD/PS19 mice, an animal model of severe amyloidosis and tauopathy. SilencioMA does not rely on lipid nanoparticles or lipophilic conjugates for CSF administration. At the same time its modular design permits conjugation of ligands that facilitate transcytosis through the blood brain barrier, allowing systemic administration. Our findings provide proof-of-concept for a strategy that targets the dual A{beta} and tau pathologies of AD, and establishes a compelling foundation for further development of SilencioMA as a next-generation DMT for AD.
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania (corresponding author)

papers.title: Denaturation-sensitive BRET probes enable intracellular thermal shift measurements across diverse protein targets and biomolecular complexes
papers.abstract: Thermal shift assays have revolutionized drug discovery, but can be limited in sensitivity and scalability. Combining the unique attributes of differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) and cellular thermal shift (CETSA), we report the methodological framework for the bioluminescence resonance energy transfer shift assay (BRETSA). BRETSA utilizes denaturation sensitive BRET probes, in combination with luciferase-tagged target proteins, to track and longitudinally record thermal shift in living cells. Denaturation profiles were successfully measured for over 500 globular proteins, spanning 24 target families in diverse cellular compartments. Among these, target engagement was confirmed for over 200 proteins; including validated drug targets as well as understudied members of the kinase subfamily. Leveraging orthosteric, allosteric, and covalent ligands in potency studies, this method offers improved sensitivity and scalability compared to other thermal shift methods. We extend the utility of BRETSA to interrogate target engagement at biomolecular complexes and query cooperative binding for molecular glues and emerging tricomplex drug modalities.
affiliations: Promega Corporation (corresponding author)

papers.title: Biological aging and comorbidities are linked to HIV 1 reservoir size despite suppressive antiretroviral therapy
papers.abstract: Background The HIV reservoir persists in long-living immune cells after antiretroviral therapy initiation. Proviral DNA integrates at preferential host DNA sites, while HIV transcription continues under treatment, with potential biological consequences. Treated people with HIV remain at increased risk for premature aging and non-AIDS comorbidities compared to people without HIV. Whether HIV reservoir size and activity impact health outcomes during treatment remains unclear. Methods We analyzed 1895 people with HIV using antiretroviral therapy from the 2000HIV cohort to study associations between the reservoir and historic and prospective virologic and immunological response markers, comorbidity outcomes and biological aging scores. The reservoir was assessed by quantifying total and intact proviral HIV DNA in circulating CD4+ T cells, along with measures of HIV transcriptional activity, including cell-associated HIV RNA. Results HIV reservoir markers were highly correlating and associated with older aging scores and adverse virologic outcomes, including quantifiable and residual viremia at study entry and during follow-up. Total HIV DNA, unlike the minor fraction of intact HIV DNA, correlated with prevalent cardiovascular disease, subclinical atherosclerotic disease, liver fibrosis and incident malignancies independent of circulating inflammatory markers and lowest CD4 nadir. Total HIV RNA associated with prevalent cardiovascular disease and liver fibrosis. Conclusion The HIV reservoir associated with older aging scores and long-term health outcomes in people with HIV using antiretroviral therapy, independent of inflammation and immune suppression history. Whether reservoir-reducing interventions lower the risk of non-AIDS comorbidities should be studied in people with high reservoir markers. Funding and trial registration ViiV Healthcare; 2000HIV ClinicalTrials.gov number: NTC03994835
affiliations: HIV Cure Research Center, Ghent University, Ghent, Belgium (corresponding author)

papers.title: Heat-killed Latilactobacillus sakei D279 Attenuates Lipopolysaccharide-Induced Intestinal Inflammation and Barrier Disruption
papers.abstract: Intestinal barrier dysfunction and excessive inflammation contribute to the pathogenesis of various metabolic and gastrointestinal diseases. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) induces systemic and intestinal inflammation, disrupts epithelial tight junctions, and impairs intestinal barrier integrity. Although heat-killed Latilactobacillus sakei D279 exhibits antiviral activity, its effects on intestinal barrier function remain unclear. In this study, we examined whether heat-killed D279 preserves intestinal barrier integrity and attenuates LPS-induced inflammatory responses in vivo (LPS-challenged mice), ex vivo (mouse peritoneal macrophages), and in vitro (IEC-6 intestinal epithelial cells). Cytokine and receptor gene expression in macrophages was measured to evaluate inflammatory responses. Furthermore, barrier function was assessed using transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), and the expression of tight junction-related genes was assessed. D279 alleviated LPS-induced intestinal injury in LPS-challenged mice, as indicated by the attenuation of colon shortening and histopathological changes compared to those in the LPS control group. In peritoneal macrophages, D279 pretreatment suppressed LPS-induced expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-, IL-1{beta}, and IL-12{beta}), increased IL-10 expression, and reduced LPS-induced upregulation of MLCK expression. This postbiotic increased basal cell viability in a concentration-dependent manner in IEC-6 cells. Moreover, it enhanced epithelial barrier development (increased TEER) and upregulated tight junction gene expression. These findings demonstrate that heat-killed D279 primarily confers its benefits by attenuating LPS-induced cytokine responses, limiting the upregulation of MLCK expression, and partially preserving goblet cell abundance. This is consistent with its protective postbiotic role in intestinal homeostasis. Thus, this study introduces a candidate postbiotic for the promotion of intestinal resilience under systemic inflammatory stress.
affiliations: Mitsubishi Gas Chemical Co. Inc. (corresponding author)

papers.title: NON-NUCLEOSIDE REVERSE TRANSCRIPTASE INHIBITORS BLOCK THE INCORPORATION OF VIRAL GLYCOPROTEINS INTO HIV-1 VIRIONS
papers.abstract: Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) are a key component of antiretroviral therapy that block reverse transcription in newly infected cells. NNRTIs have also been reported to induce premature activation of the HIV-1 protease in virus-producing cells, an activity that has been optimized in a class of NNRTIs known as targeted activators of cell kill (TACK). In this study, we used the TACK compound Pyr01 to investigate how NNRTI-induced premature protease activation affects virion composition and infectivity. We found that Pyr01 treatment markedly reduces the incorporation of the HIV-1 envelope (Env) glycoprotein into virus particles in an Env cytoplasmic tail-independent manner. Pyr01 treatment also disrupts the virion incorporation of foreign viral glycoproteins and causes a substantial loss of the viral enzymes from virions. Virions produced from NNRTI-treated cells exhibit reduced membrane order. The defect in viral glycoprotein incorporation requires an active protease, implicating premature protease-mediated disruption of the Gag lattice and resulting changes in membrane properties as the primary mechanism underlying these effects. These findings reveal that NNRTI-induced premature protease activation during virus assembly fundamentally changes the protein composition and membrane order of HIV-1 virions to markedly reduce particle infectivity. These results have implications for the use of TACK compounds therapeutically and provide basic insights into the properties of the viral membrane that promote viral glycoprotein incorporation.
affiliations: National Cancer Institute, Frederick, MD (corresponding author)

papers.title: Functional characterisation and identification of a core interactome of Plasmodium regulatory protein Alba4
papers.abstract: Plasmodium spp. parasites have complex lifecycles that rely on strict regulation of gene and protein expression. Current evidence suggests that P. falciparum has a relatively limited repertoire of canonical transcriptional regulators and RNA interference (RNAi)-associated small RNAs compared to model eukaryotes, potentially reflecting a greater reliance on RNA binding protein (RBP)-mediated post-transcriptional regulation (PTR). Among these RBPs, the acetylation lowers binding affinity (Alba) family of DNA/RNA-binding proteins has been implicated in RNA metabolism and regulation of mRNA stability and translation. In Plasmodium spp. parasites, the Alba family has expanded to include up to six members, with sequence divergence and structural modifications beyond the conserved Alba domain leading to diversification of family members, some of which appear restricted to Plasmodium and related parasites. In this study, we were unable to truncate PfAlba4, but successfully generated an endogenously tagged PfAlba4 parasite line, representing the first successful instance of endogenous tagging of a PfAlba family protein. Utilising this transgenic line, we confirm ubiquitous expression throughout blood stage development and its predominantly cytosolic localisation. Conditional loss of PfAlba4 through the knock-sideways approach demonstrated an important role for PfAlba4 in blood stage development and proteomics analysis defined a protein interaction network of 67 significantly enriched proteins, with notable enrichment of proteins potentially involved in RNA processing and regulation. Further characterisation of one of these proteins, the uncharacterised protein PF3D7_0706500, revealed a partially overlapping network of proximal proteins enriched for RNA-regulatory factors, suggesting potentially shared roles in PTR. RNA Immunoprecipitation-Sequencing (RIP-seq) identified 692 PfAlba4 associated transcripts, with an enrichment of a pyrimidine-rich motif in their 3' untranslated regions, suggesting a potential sequence-dependent mechanism of RNA recognition. Integration of proteomic and RIP-Seq datasets in late blood stage parasites revealed a consistent association with RNA processing and regulatory pathways, implicating PfAlba4 in post-transcriptional regulation. Together these findings establish PfAlba4 as an important component of the RNA-regulatory landscape in P. falciparum and highlight the importance of PfAlba proteins for malaria parasite blood stage development.
affiliations: The University of Adelaide (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Xenopus laevis Model for Systemic Fungal Infections
papers.abstract: Xenopus laevis possesses both innate and adaptive immune systems, and we previously demonstrated its utility as an infection model for human bacterial pathogens. In this study, we investigated the utility of X. laevis as a model for fungal infections. The human-pathogenic fungi Candida albicans and Aspergillus fumigatus exhibited greater lethality in X. laevis than the nonpathogenic fungi Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Schizosaccharomyces pombe. In frogs infected with C. albicans, viable fungal cells were detected in the blood and multiple organs early after infection, and gross white lesions and fungal hyphae were observed in the kidneys. C. albicans infection also increased renal expression of the proinflammatory cytokine gene s tnf and il1b, as well as the tissue injury-associated gene clu. Treatment with the antifungal agents amphotericin B and micafungin significantly improved the survival of C. albicans-infected frogs. Furthermore, a homozygous deletion mutant of UME6, a gene associated with C. albicans virulence, exhibited reduced lethality compared with the wild-type strain. These findings establish X. laevis as a vertebrate model of systemic fungal infection that enables the evaluation of fungal virulence, host responses, and the therapeutic efficacy of antifungal agents.
affiliations: Okayama Daigaku (corresponding author)

papers.title: Establishment of split-TurboID in Plasmodium falciparum facilitates identification of a PfAlba2 protein interaction network during late blood stage development
papers.abstract: Malaria parasites of the genus Plasmodium undergo complex multi-host lifecycles that require precise regulation of gene expression. Unlike model eukaryotes, Plasmodium spp. genomically encodes a limited repertoire of canonical transcriptional regulators, but possess a substantial complement of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), highlighting the importance of post-transcriptional regulatory mechanisms in regulating parasite gene expression. Among these RBPs are a family of DNA/RNA-binding proteins termed 'Alba' (acetylation lowers binding affinity) of which six have so far been identified in these parasites. Here, we investigated the localisation, functional importance and molecular associations of P. falciparum Alba protein PfAlba2 using two different endogenously tagged parasite lines. Using a GFP-FKBP tagged line, we demonstrated that PfAlba2 is expressed throughout asexual blood stage development and primarily localised in the cytosol. Conditional mislocalisation experiments indicated that PfAlba2 contributes to normal parasite growth. To overcome challenges in generating a miniTurboID proximity labelling line, we established a custom split-TurboID proximity labelling system for use in P. falciparum to characterise the PfAlba2 proxiome during asexual blood stage development. The split-TurboID system facilitated identification of 101 enriched PfAlba2 proximal proteins in schizont stage development, with significant enrichment for proteins involved in translation initiation, including two additional Alba family members, PfAlba1 and PfAlba4. Complementary RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing (RIP-seq) identified 380 PfAlba2-associated transcripts with significant enrichments including cytosolic ribosomes, rRNA-processing factors, PfAlba1, and egress and invasion-related transcripts (PfRALP1, PfRON4, PfRH1, PfRH5). Together, these findings implicate PfAlba2 in RNA metabolism and translational regulation, suggesting an important regulatory function for this protein during parasite blood stage development.
affiliations: The University of Adelaide (corresponding author)

papers.title: Tracking the conformational dynamics of single molecules in live cells; GTPase cycling in Cdc42 gradients and microclusters
papers.abstract: The Rho family of GTPases play a critical role in many cellular processes by acting as molecular switches relying on conformational changes to transition between active and inactive states. The spatial distribution and kinetics of these conformational changes are complex and vary across the cell. We describe here biosensors based on environment-responsive fluorescent dyes, capable of reporting the conformational changes of individual GTPase molecules as they traffic within living cells (SPARC Cdc42 and SPARC Rac1, 'Single Particle Activation Reporter Constructs'). We use SPARC Cdc42 to determine the rates of different steps in GTPase regulation, activation/inactivation and membrane insertion, that together generate localized gradients of Cdc42 activity driving cell motility. The biosensors also revealed heterogeneously distributed clusters of Cdc42, the mechanisms of their activation, and potential roles in polarized motility.
affiliations: UNC Chapel Hill (corresponding author)

papers.title: Male-specific genome sequences for non-invasive sex identification in Nishikigoi (Cyprinus carpio)
papers.abstract: Nishikigoi, ornamental cultivars of the common carp (Cyprinus carpio), are economically valuable aquaculture teleosts in which mature females command significantly higher market prices due to superior body conformation and coloration. Consequently, early and non-invasive sex identification is highly desirable for commercial breeding. Although sex determination in common carp follows an XX/XY system, sex-chromosome-specific markers and field-applicable diagnostic methods for Nishikigoi have remained limited. In this study, we conducted sequence-based bulked segregant analysis using whole-genome shotgun sequencing of female and male pools in Kohaku, a representative Nishikigoi lineage. We identified male-specific candidate contigs and successfully developed PCR-based male-specific markers. Validation across multiple Nishikigoi varieties and wild common carp demonstrated that primary primer pairs achieved high diagnostic accuracy. Comparative genomic analysis revealed that these candidate contigs mapped to the genomic region on chromosome 25B containing the male-determining gene Pangu, with the primary marker located in immediate physical proximity to the gene. To enable field diagnostics, we combined non-invasive epidermal mucus DNA extraction, loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP), and chromatography-printed array strip (C-PAS) technology, establishing a rapid on-site detection workflow. Overall, this study provides highly reliable PCR markers associated with the sex-determination locus and establishes a non-invasive, field-applicable diagnostic platform to streamline commercial Nishikigoi breeding and sex-selected stock management.
