papers.title: Single-nucleus long-read RNA sequencing reveals isoform usage shifts in mouse acute kidney injury
papers.abstract: Introduction Single-cell and single-nucleus short-read RNA sequencing has elucidated transcriptomic changes across kidney cell types at the gene expression level. However, its limited read length precludes reliable isoform identification, hindering the characterization of individual protein-coding isoforms and non-protein-coding isoforms. We combined long-read sequencing with single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing technologies to investigate isoform regulation in healthy and acutely injured mouse kidneys. Methods Single-cell and single-nucleus long-read RNA sequencing datasets were generated from kidneys of three healthy adult male C57BL/6J mice. An additional three adult male C57BL/6J mice underwent bilateral renal ischemia-reperfusion injury, and kidneys were subjected to single-nucleus long-read RNA sequencing. Results A total of 1.3 billion reads were generated, with a median read length of 757-884 bases across samples. Single-nucleus libraries yielded a smaller proportion of reads assigned to isoforms than single-cell libraries, reflecting their larger proportion of intronic reads. Nevertheless, single-nucleus libraries detected more distinct isoforms and greater isoform expression diversity, partly owing to the near absence of mitochondrial gene-derived transcripts. Single-nucleus analysis of healthy and injured kidneys revealed that ischemia-reperfusion injury downregulated oxidative phosphorylation-associated genes in proximal tubule cells both at the gene expression level and through shifts in isoform composition. Beyond oxidative phosphorylation-associated genes, Fut9 and Prrc2b were identified as genes exhibiting prominent shifts in isoform usage after ischemia-reperfusion injury. Conclusion Single-nucleus long-read RNA sequencing detected injury-induced shifts in isoform usage in mouse kidney, adding a layer of transcriptomic information that is largely inaccessible to conventional gene-level short-read analysis.
affiliations: Division of Nephrology, Department of Medicine, Washington University in St. Louis (corresponding author)

papers.title: The chromosome-scale genome of the drought-adapted Caatinga tree Spondias tuberosa reveals a conserved, unduplicated architecture within Anacardiaceae
papers.abstract: Spondias tuberosa (umbu) is a tree endemic to the semi-arid Caatinga of north-eastern Brazil, adapted to recurrent drought and high temperatures. Although genomes of mango (Mangifera indica), pistachio (Pistacia vera) and cashew (Anacardium occidentale) are available, comparative analyses of genome evolution across Anacardiaceae remain scarce. We aimed to generate a chromosome-scale reference genome for S. tuberosa and use it to examine genome architecture, meiotic recombination and gene family evolution within the family. We assembled the genome of a single individual using PacBio HiFi and Omni-C (Hi-C) data, mapped meiotic crossovers by single-nucleus RNA sequencing of pollen, and compared the genome with those of six other Sapindales species through orthology, synteny, synonymous substitution (Ks) and gene family expansion/contraction analyses within a dated phylogenomic framework. The assembly anchors 288 Mb onto 16 chromosomes (98.8% BUSCO completeness) and contains 24,232 protein-coding genes, 52.01% repetitive DNA and 1.78 million heterozygous SNPs (0.62%). We identified 1,740 crossovers in 153 pollen nuclei (4.01 cM.Mb1), which were depleted in repeat-rich pericentromeric regions. Ks analyses revealed a whole-genome duplication shared by Mangifera and Anacardium that is absent from S. tuberosa, which retains only the ancient {gamma} triplication. The 97 gene families expanded in S. tuberosa, mostly through tandem duplication, include receptor-like kinases, glutathione S-transferases and disease-resistance proteins, consistent with roles in environmental sensing and stress tolerance. Genome structure has remained highly conserved across Sapindales, except in the mango cashew lineage, which underwent extensive rearrangements following a whole-genome duplication. As sister to the remaining Anacardiaceae sampled and with an unduplicated, largely collinear architecture, S. tuberosa provides a reference for comparative mapping and for transferring genomic information to economically important woody relatives.
affiliations: Federal University of Alagoas (corresponding author)

papers.title: Multi-Structure Segmentation of Type B Aortic Dissection from CT Images with U-Net
papers.abstract: Type B aortic dissection (TBAD) is a life-threatening condition in which a tear in the intimal layer separates the aortic wall into a true and a false lumen. Assessment of the lumen, the intimal flap, and false-lumen thrombosis from CT images is important for risk analysis and treatment planning. This work applied U-Net-based deep neural networks to the automatic segmentation of these structures in TBAD. We collected 46 CT scans from 20 patients, with voxel-wise annotations of three structures: the aortic lumen, the intimal flap, and the thrombus. We explored four models: two convolutional networks, nnU-Net 2D and 3D, and two transformer-based architectures, TransUNet 2D and 3D. We observed that (1) for both nnU-Net and TransUNet, the 3D models outperformed their 2D counterparts on all three structures. The difference was small for the aortic lumen but large for the thin flap and the thrombus. The best model, nnU-Net 3D, reached a DSC of 93.05% for the lumen, 50.22% for the flap, and 69.94% for the thrombus. (2) The intimal flap was the most difficult structure for all models. Even the best 3D models showed large thrombus boundary errors in a few scans. These results provide a baseline for developing more advanced models for accurate segmentation of these structures in TBAD.
affiliations: University of Miami (corresponding author)

papers.title: A multi- tissue atlas of age-associated differential transcript usage in mouse reveals predominantly regulatory isoform switching across brain, liver, and adipose
papers.abstract: Alternative splicing is increasingly recognized as dysregulated in the aging process across tissues and affects proteome and other regulatory changes which can be biomarkers of aging. In this study, we aimed to identify differential transcript usage (DTU) and isoforms switch accompanied with functional annotation and structural analysis in mouse brain, liver and adipose tissue during natural aging and Ercc1 knock out mice. Age associated isoform switches affected both coding and non-coding transcript features. Across tissues, 36.5-42.6% of switches altered the predicted coding sequence, 31.2-36.5% involved non-coding alternative arms, and 11-18% involved transcripts encoding an identical protein. We observed overall 3'-UTR lengthening in the brain and shortening in the adipose. A single pan-organ isoform switch event in the gene Ighm, recurs in seven separate tissue samples. BioEMU modeling confirms feasibility for a minority of switches following a seven-fold eligibility cascade; the Cyth1 exemplar shows an intrinsically disordered N-terminal extension that does not change the shared SEC7 and PH domains. Together, these results distinguish age-associated isoform changes as predominantly regulatory in mechanism, with structural consequences restricted to tissue-specific events that form a tractable target for conformational ensemble modeling.
affiliations: University of Minnesota (corresponding author)

papers.title: DiffTernary: a Diffusion Model for Molecular Glue Ternary Complex Docking
papers.abstract: Molecular glues (MGs) modulate protein function by inducing or stabilizing protein interactions. However, accurately modeling MG ternary complexes remains challenging. Here, we present DiffTernary, a diffusion-based docking method for the joint prediction of relative protein arrangement and MG binding pose. We introduce Ternary-PDB, a dataset of 76,702 experimentally determined ternary complexes curated from the Protein Data Bank using structural filters and a release cutoff aligned with AlphaFold 3 (AF3). When trained on this dataset, DiffTernary achieved acceptable protein-protein interaction (PPI) predictions (DockQ > 0.23) for 50.0% of MGBench complexes with a single prediction, compared with 51.1% for AF3. In comparisons with AF3, OpenFold3, ESMFold2, Protenix-v1 and Protenix-v2, DiffTernary ranked second with a best-of-25 PPI prediction success rate of 78.4%, behind ESMFold2 (90.9%) and ahead of AF3 (72.7%). A separate DiffTernary model trained on TernaryDB achieved a mean DockQ of 0.306 on the 94 complexes in the TernaryDB MGD test set with a single prediction, compared with 0.228 for DeepTernary. Confidence-based selection among 40 samples yielded acceptable PPI predictions for 41.5% of complexes, compared with 30.9% for DeepTernary. An E2Former variant increased training and sampling throughput 6.90-fold and 4.37-fold, respectively, under the evaluated configurations. Together, DiffTernary and Ternary-PDB provide an efficient docking approach for MG complex prediction and a valuable structural resource for MG discovery and design.
affiliations: Center for Quantitative Biology, Academy for Advanced Interdisciplinary Studies, Peking University, Beijing 100871, China (corresponding author)

papers.title: SpaAxFormer: Fine-Grained Token Modeling of Spatial Transcriptomics with Axial Transformers
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics combines gene-expression measurements with spatial relationships between cells. We investigate how spatial context can be incorporated into gene-resolved representations while preserving explicit input-gene correspondence. SpaAxFormer is a spatially constrained factorized formulation that maintains contextual cell-gene states throughout the encoder. It first contextualizes genes within each cell and then exchanges corresponding gene states across spatial neighbors, while a separate CLS representation provides a cell-level summary. Contextual gene states support gene-expression reconstruction, while CLS-conditioned reconstruction and contrastive learning provide complementary supervision for the cell-level representation. We evaluate SpaAxFormer on gene-expression imputation and spatial-domain identification across multiple spatial-transcriptomics technologies. Compared with the included baselines, imputation results were most favorable on dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) datasets and more mixed on additional technologies, while post-hoc spatial refinement consistently improved mean ARI on the Visium spatial-domain datasets where it was applied. In a single-slice component-addition analysis, mean clustering ARI increased as CLS-conditioned reconstruction and contrastive supervision were added. Together, these results show that the same gene-resolved formulation can support complementary gene-level prediction and cell-level spatial representation while preserving explicit input-gene correspondence.
affiliations: University of California, Irvine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Fast Pangenome Matching Statistics in Compressed Space with Move Structures
papers.abstract: Matching statistics and supermaximal exact matches (SMEMs) are key inputs for sequence homology search and classification. Methods such as MONI, PHONI, and ropebwt3 compute these statistics using compressed pangenome indexes, but are substantially slower than methods that compute approximations of matching statistics, such as pseudo-matching lengths (PMLs). PMLs can be computed quickly in a single pass, but SMEM computation can require overlapping forward or backward passes over the query. We present ms2, a suite of algorithms that use "move structures" to compute matching statistics and SMEMs efficiently in compressed space. Our four algorithms compose move structures for the LF, {Psi}, {varphi}, and {varphi}-1 permutations with additional longest common prefix (LCP) array summaries and samples. The algorithms offer different tradeoffs among speed, index size, and support for reporting SMEM offsets. They inherit the move structure's fast, constant-time operations and achieve high throughput by leveraging the move structure's locality of reference. Thanks to recent advances, move structures can be constructed in optimal time and compressed space, including the LCP information needed for "match recovery" during SMEM computation. On 100 haplotypes of human chromosome 22, ms2's fastest algorithm computes matching statistics 35 to 48 times as fast as PHONI's online approach, while using an index of similar size. On the 472-haplotype HPRC2 pangenome and human reads, three ms2 modes achieve speedups of at least 22, 19, and 15 times over ropebwt3, whose index is about 15% the size of ms2's fastest mode. When additionally reporting SMEMs and their offsets, ms2 achieves speedups of 25 to 34 times over ropebwt3. Together, these advances enable online computation of matching statistics and SMEMs at a throughput that supports real-time processing of approximately 21 PromethION nanopore flow cells on a single thread. The ms2 software is open source and available at https://github.com/langmead-lab/ms2. It builds on the open-source TeraTools suite (https://github.com/ucfcbb/TeraTools) and Orbit library (https://github.com/drnatebrown/orbit). Experimental scripts and other details are described in: https://github.com/langmead-lab/ms2-experiments.
affiliations: Johns Hopkins University (corresponding author)

papers.title: SubCellSeg: A generalist model for subcellular structure segmentation in 3D fluorescence microscopy
papers.abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) segmentation of subcellular structures from fluorescence microscopy images is the foundation of many analyses in quantitative cell biology. The prevailing approach addresses 3D segmentation one structure at a time, with a separate model trained for each structure type. By developing SubCellSeg, we demonstrate that a single model, trained jointly across a diverse range of structures, substantially and consistently outperforms structure-specific specialist models. SubCellSeg is a 3D segmentation model trained on expert-curated fluorescence images and their computationally generated reference masks, of 13 morphologically distinct subcellular structures in human induced pluripotent stem (hiPS) cell lines from the Allen Cell Collection, spanning compact puncta, planar junctions, reticular networks, and tubular structures. Without any structure-specific input, SubCellSeg achieves a mean Dice score of 0.909 across the 13 structures and outperforms each of the 13 specialist models on the structure it was trained for (specialist mean Dice 0.773). SubCellSeg also achieves zero-shot generalization, segmenting subcellular structures with morphologies not represented in the training data. This generalization extends to images acquired on different microscopes and with different imaging configurations, to cells under drug perturbation, and to a morphologically distinct cell type, hiPS cell-derived cardiomyocytes. Where zero-shot results are insufficient for a specific application, SubCellSeg can be fine-tuned: starting from its pretrained weights, 10% of the labeled images (16 images) gave better results than training a new model from scratch on all of them. SubCellSeg is distributed through the napari plugin allencell-segmenter-ml[1] with pretrained checkpoints, so it can be run on new data without any training; the training and evaluation code is available at https://github.com/AllenCell/SubCellSeg.
affiliations: Allen Institute (corresponding author)

papers.title: The Confessions of a Protein Language Model: Steering, Activations, and What Predicted Confidence Cannot Certify
papers.abstract: Protein generate-and-screen pipelines use interventions and readouts to select candidates, but rarely test whether these track their intended targets. We audit published repetition steering, ESMFold confidence, and an activation readout. Steering preserves confidence at its operating point, but a fitted cliff follows at alpha_50 = 1.240x (sweep's own control: 64.0%). Direction matters at moderate matched-norm push, but not at saturation. Unsteered generator activations predict the confidence gate (ROC-AUC 0.786 +/- 0.004), supporting cost-aware, model-specific triage. We also replicate established length sensitivity, through which shortening can manufacture false nulls. Yet on composition- and length-matched design--scramble pairs, no balanced-accuracy interval excludes chance for experimental stability. Predicting the gate does not establish foldability. We should test what a readout measures before using it to select. Code and data: https://github.com/paninishah/plm-steering-audit
affiliations: Dwarkadas J Sanghvi College of Engineering (corresponding author)

papers.title: REVEAL: RNA Ensemble Validation and Exploration with AI-guided Landscapes
papers.abstract: Capturing the sparsely populated but functionally important, excited states of RNA remains a central challenge for molecular simulation, because the underlying transitions are rare events that unbiased molecular dynamics cannot reach from a single starting structure. Here we introduce REVEAL (RNA Ensemble Validation and Exploration with AI-guided Landscapes), a workflow that couples generative secondary structure sampling, secondary structure conditioned tertiary structure prediction with trRosettaRNA2, unbiased molecular dynamics and Markov state modeling. Using only the sequence of the engineered HIV-1 TAR mutant, in which the excited state ES2 is the dominant conformation, we show that REVEAL captures the reversible ES2 to GS register shift from 6.8 s of aggregate unbiased sampling across 34 seeds, recovering both basins, the intermediate states, and correctly identifies ES2 as the dominant state, consistent with the design of the construct. In contrast, molecular dynamics seeded from the ES2-dominant HIV-1 TAR mutant NMR ensemble remains trapped in ES2 despite substantially longer aggregate simulation time, and sequence-only ensemble predictors (AlphaFold3, Boltz-2, ESMFold2, OpenFold3 and Protenix-v2) place every structure near the ground state and invert the experimentally observed population ordering. The information content of the seed ensemble, rather than the total simulation time, determines whether the transition is sampled. We further introduce ''population-weighted consensus score'' (PWCS) that ranks conformers by how representative they are of the equilibrium ensemble directly from the simulation data, without experimental restraints and independent of the choice of collective variables. PWCS identifies the dominant state even when low-dimensional representations fail to separate the states. Built entirely from open-source tools, REVEAL provides a transparent and extensible route to RNA conformational ensembles beyond the single-structure paradigm.
affiliations: AlloTec (corresponding author)

papers.title: Inferring chromatin looping interactions from microscopy-based measurements: opportunities and pitfalls
papers.abstract: Chromatin looping plays essential roles in several nuclear processes and live-cell microscopy has become a key method for studying how chromatin loops behave in time. Extracting dynamical parameters including looping probability, lifetime, and search time from live-imaging data requires inferring looping events from noisy 3D distance trajectories. By analyzing polymer simulation data with known ground truth, we show that with realistic localization precision, the common method of simple thresholding on 3D distance measurements can result in severe misestimation of looping probability, lifetime, and search time. We use simple statistical considerations to show that inference from simple thresholding becomes infeasible when localization error is comparable to the size of the interaction to be studied. Finally, we demonstrate how noise-aware methods can be used to estimate looping parameters more accurately in these regimes.
affiliations: SISSA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Theory of large-bead AFM compression of pressurized rod-shaped bacteria
papers.abstract: Motivated by our atomic force microscopy (AFM) experiments measuring turgor pressure in living bacteria, we develop a theoretical description of pressurized spherocylindrical cells compressed by spherical probes whose radius greatly exceeds the cell radius. In this global-loading regime, the mechanical response is governed primarily by cell geometry and turgor pressure, while the elastic properties of the cell envelope enter as higher-order corrections. The strong confinement imposed by the probe drives water efflux from the cytoplasm, thereby increasing the turgor pressure. We present a theoretical framework for determining bacterial turgor pressure from AFM force--displacement curves, accounting for cell geometry and probe dimensions. Combining numerical simulations with analytical theory, we show that the mechanical response can be approximated in terms of cylindrical and hemispherical contributions. The leading-order force--displacement dependency is captured by an analytical description derived in the large-aspect-ratio limit, where the mechanics reduce to a tension-dominated cross-sectional problem. Finite cell aspect ratio and probe curvature are incorporated through geometric renormalizations. The resulting framework provides a quantitative basis for extracting bacterial turgor pressure from AFM measurements while simultaneously predicting cell deformation geometry.
affiliations: Duke University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Preferential recruitment of PML isoform II by incoming HPV16 genome transport vesicles facilitates early stage of infection
papers.abstract: The interplay between promyelocytic leukemia nuclear bodies (PML NBs) and viral infections is complex and multifaceted, with viruses often engaging in a delicate balance of exploitation and evasion of host immune responses. It is well-established that incoming human papillomavirus (HPV) virions associate with PML NBs; however, the mechanism by which HPV targets PML NBs to facilitate early transcription and replication remains elusive. We have shown that HPV genomes are delivered to the nucleus inside membrane-bound vesicles during mitosis and that PML proteins are recruited to HPV-harboring nuclear vesicles prior to egress. Herein, we demonstrate that the PML isoform II (PMLII), but not other PML isoforms, is selectively attracted to incoming HPV still residing in transport vesicles. Using individual PML NB isoform and HPV16 minor protein, L2, over-expression experiments in HeLa cells, we conclude that PML II binds to the lipids of the HPV harbouring membrane-bound vesicles rather than L2. This is in line with previous observations that PML II is the only isoform binding to lipid droplets in the nucleus. We observed that the association of PML NBs with the HPV16 viral genome was transient and lost over time. We also found that nuclear Phospholipase C {beta}4 and {gamma}1 colocalize with PML II-L1 complexes in infected cells. Our data support a model in which PML II contributes to the establishment of early HPV16 infection by organizing host lipid regulatory factors at incoming viral transport vesicles.
affiliations: LSU Health Shreveport (corresponding author)

papers.title: HIV broadly neutralizing antibody precursor maturation induced by mRNA vaccination in nonhuman primates
papers.abstract: The induction of broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) is a principal goal of prophylactic HIV vaccines. For many bnAbs, priming ultrarare precursors from the naive B cell repertoire is the first major immunological hurdle. Previous studies have shown that the germline-targeting (GT) priming immunogen N332-GT5 delivered as adjuvanted protein to non-human primates (NHPs) activates bnAb precursor B cells for the human bnAb BG18 targeting the V3-glycan supersite on the HIV envelope (Env) glycoprotein. Here, we engineered N332-GT6 to improve binding affinity to diverse BG18-class precursor naive B cells by 9-fold. mRNA-LNP vaccines expressing N332-GT5 or N332-GT6 as membrane-bound (gp151) trimers were evaluated for their ability to prime BG18-class precursor B cells in NHPs across three related studies. Although N332-GT5 gp151 mRNA-LNP priming induced BG18-class precursor B cells in most animals after two vaccinations, the higher-affinity N332-GT6 gp151 induced responses more consistently after only one immunization. Sequential vaccination with two heterologous mRNA-LNP booster immunizations drove affinity maturation and induced BG18-class memory B cells capable of binding wildtype HIV Env. Together, these findings demonstrate that mRNA immunization can achieve GT priming, boosting, and early maturation of ultrarare bnAb-class B cells in NHPs.
affiliations: The Scripps Research Institute (corresponding author)

papers.title: Herbivore and carnivore microbial signatures indicate diet and health variation in human gut microbiota
papers.abstract: Diet is a key factor shaping gut microbiota in mammals, with herbivores and carnivores harboring distinct microbial communities. However, despite humans being highly omnivorous, it remains unclear whether their gut microbiota more closely resembles that of herbivores or carnivores or how individual-level variations along this spectrum are associated with human health status. We compared gut microbiota profiles of 858 samples from 109 mammalian species and constructed a Herbivore-Carnivore (HC) index based on bacterial groups characteristic of each diet. The HC-index positioned humans between herbivores and carnivores and showed that traditional hunter-gatherers and nonhuman apes retained herbivore-leaning profiles, whereas urbanized humans exhibited a shift toward a carnivore-leaning state. By applying the HC-index to >72,000 participants across multiple cohorts worldwide, we found that elevated HC-index values were associated with plant-based and fiber-rich diets, greater microbial diversity, enhanced potential to degrade plant-derived carbohydrates, favorable clinical measures, and lower prevalence of self-reported disease. We demonstrated that the HC balance of gut microbiota captures a conserved diet-related gradient across mammals and provides an interpretable framework linking human diet, microbial function, and health.
affiliations: Laboratory of Animal Science, Department of Applied Biological Sciences, Faculty of Agriculture, Setsunan University, Osaka 573-0101, Japan (corresponding author)

papers.title: Saturation barcoding of ribosomal DNA resolves the nucleolar organizer regions of the human genome
papers.abstract: The nucleolus is the hub for ribosome biogenesis in eukaryotic cells. It is assembled on nucleolar organizer regions (NORs), tandem arrays of ribosomal DNA (rDNA) units. In humans, each rDNA unit is ~45 kb and encodes the 47S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) precursor. Hundreds of rDNA units are present per germline genome, spread across 10 NORs positioned on the short arms of the five acrocentric chromosomes. However, their precise count and structure are unknown. In fact, twenty-five years after the first draft of the human genome, NORs are the only regions of the human genome that remain incompletely resolved, represented in telomere-to-telomere (T2T) reference genomes as gaps or modeled sequences rather than bona fide assemblies. Here we use prime editing to insert degenerate 6-bp DNA barcodes to 99% of taggable rDNA units in a clonal derivative of the leukemia-derived K562 cell line. Following ultra-long-read sequencing, these barcodes serve as molecular identifiers that guide the end-to-end assembly of all 18 NORs of K562s pseudotriploid genome. The assembly yields: (i) a precise rDNA copy number for each NOR (range 5-43; total 290); (ii) the cis- and trans- architecture of intragenomic variation in rDNA sequence, both structural and fine-scale; and (iii) patterns of divergence and homogenization within and across NORs that may have arisen during cancer evolution and the subsequent passaging of this line. Finally, by reading the same tags from RNA, we define the relationship between DNA methylation and Pol I transcription at the resolution of individual rDNA units. Together, our study demonstrates how the final tangles of the human genome can at last be resolved, and opens the door to more extensive investigations of how genetic, epigenetic and functional rDNA variation contributes to health and disease.
affiliations: School of Life Sciences, Westlake University, Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China; Westlake Center for Genome Editing, Westlake University, Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China; Dep (corresponding author)

papers.title: Rise and Fall of a Superbug: Analyzing the epidemic success of a distinct clone of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium ST117/CT71 in Germany, 2017 - 2024.
papers.abstract: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) is a major cause of healthcare-associated infections, yet outbreak analysis remains challenging, particularly for prevalent lineages. One of the most striking examples is the Sequence Type (ST) 117/Complex Type (CT) 71/vanB lineage, whose rapid expansion across Germany coincided with a sharp rise in VRE prevalence observed around 2019. Defining reliable genomic thresholds remains particularly difficult, as current core-genome Multi-Locus Sequence Typing (cgMLST) cutoffs are based largely on expert consensus or limited case series. Here, we evaluate the discriminatory performance of cgMLST and split k-mer analysis (SKA) for resolving relatedness within ST117/CT71 and investigate whether low core-genome diversity represents a lineage-specific trait or a population-wide property of E. faecium. While cgMLST captures the overall population structure of ST117/CT71, SKA provided higher resolution, distinguishing isolates identical by cgMLST. Analysis of 2,505 genomes showed that ST117/CT71 does not exhibit reduced allelic variability compared with other hospital-adapted lineages, suggesting that limited core-genome diversity is a broader population characteristic. Complementary transposon analyses further identified two temporally distinct ST117/CT71 sublineages carrying different Tn1549-like structures. To assess allelic variation within confirmed transmission events, we analyzed 138 outbreak clusters from 96 hospitals. Outbreak-associated isolates showed sharply compressed allelic differences (median = 1), with 90% of pairwise comparisons falling within [≤]9 alleles. Thus, the commonly applied [≤]20-allele threshold risks overestimating genomic relatedness and grouping unrelated isolates. Based on these data, we propose lowering the cgMLST alert threshold to [≤]9 alleles for initial cluster detection of local outbreaks, followed by confirmatory high-resolution analyses such as SKA.
affiliations: Robert Koch Institut (corresponding author)

papers.title: PAMP: Continuous-to-Discrete Mutation Projection for Enzyme Engineering
papers.abstract: Efficient enzyme engineering requires translating quantitative turnover predictions into specific mutations that im- prove catalytic activity while reducing experimental search. Here we introduce Proximal Adversarial Mutation Projection (PAMP), a gradient-guided framework that maps a differentiable turnover objective directly to single-amino-acid substitutions by combining multi-point gradient averaging with distance-penalized projection in protein embedding space. Using a substrate-conditioned Resid- ual Predictor trained on CataPro-derived data, PAMP achieved a mean first-round predicted gain of 0.1795 log2 units across 2,754 enzyme substrate pairs, with positive changes in 84.64% of cases; among the top five ranked substitutions, 99.49% of records contained at least one positive candidate. Five sequential rounds increased the mean cumulative predicted gain to 0.5631 log2 units, and re-scoring with an independent, non-differentiable predictor left the ordering of the methods intact while attenuating the absolute gain. PAMP provides a computationally efficient strategy for prioritizing experimentally testable enzyme mutations under small candidate budgets.
affiliations: university college london (corresponding author)

papers.title: OligoFragger: spectrum graph-guided analysis of modified RNA oligonucleotides by mass spectrometry
papers.abstract: RNA modifications are widespread modulators of RNA function, but comprehensive identification remains technically challenging. This is especially true for densely modified RNAs such as tRNAs, where multiple modified residues and many possible chemistries occur within short sequence contexts. Tandem mass spectrometry provides direct chemical and positional evidence for modified oligonucleotides, but current database-search strategies struggle when dozens of candidate modifications must be considered simultaneously. Here, we present OligoFragger, a spectrum graph-guided computational tool that uses fragment evidence to constrain modified-oligonucleotide searches before full database scoring, enabling rapid and robust oligonucleotide identification. Using controlled RNA samples and tRNA datasets from E. coli and human cells, we demonstrate that OligoFragger increases identifications under stringent FDR control while recovering known modification patterns and supporting label-free quantification. This strategy enables sensitive, FDR-controlled identification and label-free quantification of modified RNA oligonucleotides in complex epitranscriptomic search spaces.
affiliations: University of Michigan (corresponding author)

papers.title: Differential regulation of myeloid Scavenger Receptor A (CD204) expression in humans versus mice in response to sepsis
papers.abstract: Sepsis is the number one cause of mortality in the critically ill patient. The underlying pathophysiology of sepsis is not fully understood. Scavenger Receptor A (SR-A) is a promiscuous receptor of myeloid cells that binds multiple pathogen associated molecular patterns (PAMPs). We have demonstrated that SR-A promotes mortality in murine sepsis. The present study sought to examine the effect of sepsis on myeloid SR-A expression in septic mice and compare it to sepsis patients. Leukocytes were isolated from mice after cecal ligation and puncture. Blood leukocytes were isolated from sepsis patients. Myeloid cells were isolated from healthy mice or human subjects and were treated with PAMPs. Leukocyte phenotype and SR-A expression were determined by flow cytometry. CLP increased SR-A expression when compared to sham operated animals on both neutrophils and monocytes/macrophages. In contrast, SR-A expression was not changed on either neutrophils or monocytes from sepsis patients when compared to healthy control subjects. Treatment of murine neutrophils and macrophages with Pam3CSK4 and treatment of macrophages with LPS increased SR-A expression. Human neutrophil SR-A expression was not altered by any PAMPs, and only treatment with C. albicans glucan increased SR-A expression on human monocytes. Myeloid SR-A expression is increased in septic mice, and this increase plays a detrimental role in the response to sepsis, while SR-A expression is not changed in leukocytes from septic patients and does not correlate with SOFA II scores. Thus, myeloid SR-A expression does not appear to play significant a role in the pathophysiology of human sepsis.
affiliations: East Tennessee State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Necroptosis is a targetable driver of severe coronavirus pathogenesis
papers.abstract: Human-pathogenic coronaviruses differ dramatically in pathogenicity but the underlying mechanisms are incompletely understood. Here, we demonstrate that highly pathogenic coronaviruses trigger necroptosis in the infected cells and lung tissues, whereas necroptosis is not detected in cells infected by seasonal coronavirus. Mechanistically, highly pathogenic coronaviruses produce Z-RNA, activate ZBP1 and initiates necroptotic cell death signaling, triggering necroinflammation and lung injury. In contrast, seasonal coronaviruses produce little to no Z-RNA, and do not activate necroptosis. Importantly, small-molecule inhibition of necroptosis attenuates inflammatory cytokine expression and markedly ameliorates lung damage in mice infected with all three highly pathogenic coronaviruses, independent of virus clearance. Overall, our study identifies necroptosis as a dominant mediator of coronavirus pathogenesis, and positions necroptosis blockade as a new therapeutic target against severe coronavirus diseases.
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong (corresponding author)

papers.title: A ribosome-dependent small-ORF switch controls flagellar gene expression and virulence
papers.abstract: RNA structures are active regulators of bacterial translation. Here, we identified a naturally occurring translation-enhancing small open reading frame (tesORF) that controls the expression of the flagellar operon fliFGHIJK in Salmonella enterica and other motile Enterobacterales. Nucleotide-resolution ribosome profiling revealed this previously unannotated 54-nucleotide ORF immediately upstream of fliF. Genetic, transcriptomic, and biochemical analyses support a model in which tesORF translation counteracts an inhibitory RNA structure, exposing the fliF ribosome-binding site and promoting translation initiation independently of the encoded peptide sequence. Disruption of tesORF translation reduced expression of the downstream operon and impaired motility and virulence-associated phenotypes in Escherichia coli, Salmonella, and Yersinia. Together, our findings reveal how translation of a conserved small ORF regulates an entire flagellar operon through RNA structural remodelling, with consequences expending to the wider flagellar regulon, linking RNA structural dynamics to bacterial motility and virulence.
affiliations: University of Cambridge (corresponding author)

papers.title: Distinct binding modes shape exploitable asymmetries between echinocandin and triterpenoid resistance landscapes in Fks1
papers.abstract: Echinocandins are the first-line treatment for invasive fungal infections and work by inhibiting the fungal {beta}-1,3-glucan synthase Fks1. Recently, a first-in-class triterpenoid Fks1 inhibitor, ibrexafungerp, was approved for clinical use. The extent to which the difference between these drug classes alters the landscape of resistance mutations in Fks1 is unknown. We used deep mutational scanning (DMS) to quantify the effects of all single-amino-acid variants spanning 159 residues across the three canonical Fks1 resistance hotspots and flanking regions in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Drug selections revealed widespread position-specific cross-resistance and differential resistance, including an ibrexafungerp-specific resistance cluster downstream of hotspot 2 that defines a novel triterpenoid-specific resistance hotspot. We defined this as hotspot 4 and redefined the boundaries of the remaining three canonical echinocandin hotspots, based on the mutational landscape of our DMS analyses. Susceptibility testing of individual FKS1 variants of S. cerevisiae and Candidozyma auris strains confirmed conserved class-specific and cross-resistance patterns. Structure-guided ligand placement, molecular dynamics-based simulated annealing, and DMS-informed pose selection linked drug-specific phenotypes to distinct interaction networks, providing a molecular rationale for the observed differential resistance patterns. These data provide a framework for predicting antifungal resistance, informing treatment strategies and future drug design.
affiliations: Universite Laval (corresponding author)

papers.title: Elevational variation in gut microbial community composition and predicted functional potential across three Himalayan redstart species
papers.abstract: Environmental gradients and seasonal migration may influence host-associated microbial communities, yet their contributions to gut microbiome variation in montane birds remain poorly understood. We investigated gut microbial communities across 1,300 to 4,200 m in three Himalayan redstarts (Phoenicurus fuliginosus, P. leucocephalus, and P. frontalis) exhibiting contrasting seasonal movement strategies. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing of 46 fecal samples, we characterized microbial diversity, community composition, distance decay relationships, co-occurrence networks, and predicted functional potential. Elevation was significantly associated with microbial community composition, explaining approximately 3% of variation, whereas host species showed no significant association after accounting for elevation. P. fuliginosus exhibited significant compositional differences among most sampled elevations, whereas P. leucocephalus showed significant positive distance decay relationships. Alpha diversity showed no consistent elevational trend, while core microbial taxa and co-occurrence networks varied among elevational groups. PICRUSt2 analyses identified 28 predicted KEGG Level 3 pathways differing significantly among elevations, including pathways associated with amino acid, lipid, glycan, carbohydrate, and bile acid metabolism. Together, these findings highlight elevation as a significant correlate of gut microbial community composition and predicted functional potential, with distinct patterns of microbial turnover among closely related Himalayan redstarts.
affiliations: Department of Biological Sciences, Kent State University, Ohio, USA. (corresponding author)

papers.title: Desiccation stress enhances virulence potential of group B Streptococcus
papers.abstract: Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus, GBS) asymptomatically inhabits the gastrointestinal and female reproductive tracts but can also cause invasive diseases in susceptible individuals. Despite its clinical importance, relatively little is known about its ability to survive outside the host and whether environmental persistence contributes to transmission and infection. Here we investigate the GBS survival under nutrient starvation and desiccation, characterizing phenotypic and genomic adaptations associated with environmental persistence. GBS remained viable for 30 days during starvation at room temperature and for more than 80 days under desiccated conditions, with GBS grown to stationary-phase bacteria exhibiting greater survival than actively growing bacteria. Survival under desiccation was conserved among several clinically relevant GBS serotypes. Following rehydration desiccated GBS exhibited enhanced biofilm formation compared to control non-desiccated strains. Whole-genome sequencing identified mutations in genes involved in capsule biosynthesis, cell-envelope homeostasis, nutrient transport, and carbohydrate metabolism, suggesting that multiple adaptive pathways may contribute to environmental persistence. Importantly, desiccated GBS retained the capacity to colonize the vaginal mucosa and displayed increased invasion of reproductive tissues in a murine vaginal colonization model. In a systemic infection model, desiccated GBS exhibited enhanced virulence compared to control non-desiccated GBS, demonstrating that environmental survival does not diminish pathogenic potential. This environmental persistence may represent an underappreciated factor contributing to GBS transmission and the epidemiology of late-onset neonatal disease.
affiliations: University of Tennessee (corresponding author)

papers.title: Hepadnavirus tropism determined by diversified NTCP functionality in Feline species
papers.abstract: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) exhibits a narrow host range, largely determined by sodium taurocholate cotransporting polypeptides (NTCP), a hepatic bile acid transporter acting as the HBV receptor. NTCP among animals appears to have evolved following trade-off mutations to lose its viral receptor activity while preserving its transporter function. Here, through profiling of the NTCP homologs from 23 mammalian species, we uncover unexpected functional heterogeneity of feline NTCPs. NTCPs derived from cat, tiger, and leopard supported viral preS1 binding and HBV infection, whereas lion-NTCP was deficient for preS1 binding and, notably, exhibited markedly reduced bile acid transport. Cat-NTCP was further demonstrated to have viral receptor function by productive infection in primary cat hepatocytes. Experimental mutagenesis identified double substitution at positions 191 and 268 as key determinants: introducing lion-type substitutions into cat-NTCP (G191R and T268A) abolished preS1 binding, whereas reciprocal substitutions in lion-NTCP restored receptor function. Molecular dynamics simulations suggested that lion-NTCP adopts conformation in which a transmembrane helix bending enlarges the whole bile acid tunnel and disrupts preS1 compatibility. Such differences also determined host susceptibility to another feline-infected domestic cat HBV. These findings reveal diversified NTCP functionality with evolutionary plasticity that acquires resistance to hepadnavirus infection at the expense of physiological transporter function.
affiliations: Japan Institute for Health Security (corresponding author)

papers.title: Differential properties of gp120 from HIV-1 group M subtypes A and B
papers.abstract: HIV-1 group M subtypes A and B differ substantially in their gp120 sequence. To determine whether these differences contribute to subtype-specific complications, particularly pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), rats were injected with gp120 from subtype A or B. Pulmonary artery (PA) remodeling was assessed after four weeks using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining and the Vessel Morphometry Analysis tool by Autona (autona.org). Subtype A gp120 potently increased PA wall thickness and right ventricular hypertrophy. The CD4-binding region of subtype A lacks a stretch of 16 amino acids (V1 N-glycosylation site), and experiments showed stronger binding of subtype B to CD4. Subtype B gp120 contains an RGKV sequence, which resembles the RGKR sequence of the rabies virus glycoprotein G that binds to the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR). Subtype A gp120 possesses a KDKK sequence instead. Molecular dynamics simulations indicated that both sites are surface-exposed. Although nAChR is expressed in PA cells and could potentially drive the pronounced effects of subtype A, MD simulations estimated that subtype B gp120 binds more strongly to nAChR. We also noted a single amino acid difference immediately preceding the REKR furin cleavage sequence: glutamate in subtype A versus glutamine in subtype B gp120. Simulations predicted that subtype A gp120 interacts more effectively with furin, and enzyme assays demonstrated that subtype A promotes a positive feedback loop more strongly than subtype B. Thus, HIV-1 gp120 subtype A is more potent in promoting PAH, and the mechanism may involve enhancing furin activity to elevate gp120 levels.
affiliations: Georgetown University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Uncovering Features of ProteinMPNN with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.abstract: Customization and modification of machine learning derived sequences can be achieved by understanding the mechanics behind state-of-the-art protein design models such as ProteinMPNN. Uninterpretability is hypothesized to be due largely to polysemanticity where neural networks store more features than they have dimensions. Here, we introduce sparse autoencoders (SAEs) into ProteinMPNN which expand its latent space and uncovers correlations between the activations in sparse dimensions and the presence of protein features such as secondary structure, residue volume, residue shape, disulfide bridges, and coordination to ligands. Additionally, we show that sparse activations can be manipulated to produce a variant of the short chain variable fragment Brolucizumab that is more thermostable than variants produced by traditional machine learning methods based on high temperature molecular dynamics simulations. Thus, SAEs provide both mechanistic understanding of protein design models and allow customizable manipulation of sequence prediction.
affiliations: Santa Clara University (corresponding author)

papers.title: RawMod: Modification-Agnostic Detection of DNA Base Modifications from Nanopore Signal Pileups
papers.abstract: Summary: Identifying epigenetically modified bases (e.g., methylation) is crucial for many important applications such as discovering mechanisms of cancer development, cell differentiation, and bacterial defense. Nanopore sequencing generates electrical signals that can differentiate canonical bases from modified ones. To detect base modifications from signals, machine learning (ML) methods and statistical approaches are commonly used. These methods can either detect a specific modification type or require an additional unmodified copy of the same DNA as a control group. However, no released model detects modification types beyond those it was trained for, which makes it difficult to detect rare modification types without an unmodified control. Our goal is to accurately identify the presence of modified sites regardless of their modification type, which we define as modification-agnostic detection. To this end, we propose RawMod, a transformer-based modification-agnostic and control-free method for detecting epigenetically modified genomic positions. The key idea of RawMod is to compare the raw signals of many reads at each site with the unmodified reference sequence, using a small model that learns many modification types as a single modified class. Based on our extensive evaluations on the detection of various modification types (5mC, 5hmC, 4mC, 6mA, and 5hmU) using various genomes, RawMod achieves the highest mean AUROC across modifications compared to control-based methods and control-free modification models. A single RawMod model with 0.23M parameters detects five modification types with a mean AUROC of 0.964, against 0.799 for the best released model. When a modification type is withheld from training, RawMod still detects it (AUROC 0.91--0.98), provided another modification of the same base was seen in training. We use RawMod to map 5hmU without a control across a 7.7 Mb contig of the Amphidinium carterae genome, consistent with two published trends. Further, we show that the modification-aware embeddings from RawMod can be used to differentiate read origin (e.g., cell types, tumor/normal origin, and native/PCR-amplified DNA). We discuss how RawMod can enable further work on label-free classification of cell types using these modification-aware embeddings. Availability and Implementation: RawMod is available at https://github.com/STORMgroup/RawMod and at https://huggingface.co/STORMResearch/RawMod. We also provide the scripts to fully reproduce our results on our GitHub page and release our datasets on SquiDBase.
affiliations: University of Maryland, College Park, MD, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Paired-unit activation steering for context-aware protein design
papers.abstract: Activation steering in protein language models enables controllable sequence generation without changing the model weights. However, existing methods typically construct steering vectors from global differences between property-positive and property-negative protein populations, overlooking how property-improving directions vary across different protein sequence backgrounds. To address this, we propose \textit{Paired-Unit local steering of embeddings (PULSE)}, which matches positive- and negative-property proteins by maximizing their representation cosine similarity and constructs steering vectors by aggregating similarity-weighted, unit-normalized differences between matched pairs. Across three protein optimization objectives--solubility, immunogenicity, and toxicity--PULSE consistently outperforms global population-centroid steering in both final predicted property scores and optimization success rates. Further analysis reveals that conventional static steering-vector diagnostics cannot adequately explain optimization performance. To characterize steering reliability during iterative sequence editing, we introduce \textit{Local Directional Support (LDS)}, which measures how well successive representation changes align with property-improving directions from similar protein backgrounds. We show that LDS captures differences in trajectory reliability and enables predictor-free candidate prioritization, enriching successful protein designs without requiring property predictions during candidate selection. Together, these findings demonstrate the importance of context-aware steering and trajectory-level evaluation for controllable protein sequence optimization.
affiliations: Texas A and M University (corresponding author)

papers.title: A High-Efficiency Geranylation Platform Enabled by Rational Tuning of a Single-Residue-Coded Chemo- and Regioselective Switch in Aromatic Prenyltransferases
papers.abstract: Geranylation is an efficient post-modification strategy for enhancing or introducing new properties to molecules; however, achieving both high efficiency and precision remains challenging. Aromatic prenyltransferases (PTs) provide a mild and sustainable approach, yet their practical application is often limited by the trade-off between broad substrate scope and low selectivity, and successfully balancing these properties is rare. Here, using the pharmaceutically relevant cannabigerol framework as a model, we identify a single-residue switch in a prenyltransferase from Aspergillus terreus (AtaPT) that governs both chemo- and regioselectivity. Rational tuning of this switch preserves broad substrate scope while enhancing selectivity, enabling the selective formation of each of the three possible mono-geranylated products in the model reaction. Structural analysis reveals that this residue modulates the selectivity and activity through coupled steric and electrostatic effects. Notably, transplantation of this site into three homologous PTs similarly reprogrammed selectivity, establishing a conserved and generalizable control mechanism. Leveraging these insights, we achieved selective geranylation across 36 aromatic substrates, affording 41 products. Integration with an efficient geranyl donor regeneration system enabled preparative-scale synthesis, reaching titers up to 324 mg/L. This work defines a unifying mechanism for selectivity control in PTs and provides a high-efficiency platform for geranylation.
affiliations: Key Laboratory of Multiple Organ Failure (Zhejiang University), Ministry of Education, Department of General Intensive Care Unit of the Second Affiliated Hospit (corresponding author)

papers.title: Avian reovirus triggered ferroptosis, modulated lipid metabolism, and induced lipid droplet formation in infected cells, which was mediated in part by the p10/FAST protein
papers.abstract: In this study, we evaluated how avian reovirus (ARV) affected lipid metabolism and lipid droplets (LDs) in cell culture. ARV infection of chicken LMH cells significantly increased the size and number of LDs, however, LDs did not co-localize with virus factories, and neither overexpression by treatment with fatty acids (FAs), nor inhibition by treatment with TOFA or DGAT inhibitors significantly affected ARV replication. Lipidomic analysis revealed that following infection, total cellular lipid content increased approximately 25-fold, phosphatidylcholine (PC) content increased from 23.5 to 57.9%, and the polyunsaturated FA:monounsaturated FA ratio (PUFA:MUFA) decreased in membrane phospholipids but increased in triglycerides. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that there was also a reduction in the expression of genes involved in PUFA synthesis. As membrane PUFAs are susceptible to peroxidation, we investigated whether ARV induced ferroptosis. Consistent with this, ARV led to an increase in oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation that was partially iron dependent, and we found evidence that ferroptosis was proviral. Moreover, as ARV is known to form syncytia, we hypothesized that our observations were also the result of plasma membrane remodeling. Consistent with this, cells transfected with the ARV fusogenic p10/FAST protein formed syncytia, had a significantly upregulated number of LDs, and displayed hallmarks of ferroptosis. Taken together, we hypothesize that ARV induces syncytium formation and ferroptosis to facilitate viral spread to neighboring cells, but to prevent premature cell death due to these processes, lipid metabolism is modulated by infection, leading to an increase in LDs.
affiliations: University of Maryland, College Park (corresponding author)

papers.title: POM121 regulates lentiviral nuclear import in a capsid-host factor-dependent manner
papers.abstract: Lentiviruses such as human immunodeficiency virus 1 (HIV-1) access the nuclear lumen through the nuclear pore complex (NPC), a process coordinated by the interactions between the viral capsid and nucleoporins (NUPs). Here, using unbiased proteomic screens, we identified several capsid-associated NUPs, including POM121. Depletion of POM121 impaired HIV-1 infection in multiple cell lines and in primary CD4+ T cells, whereas equine infectious anaemia virus (EIAV) infection was enhanced, indicating that POM121 effect is virus-specific. A cytoplasmic carboxy-terminal fragment of POM121, containing its FG-rich region inhibited HIV-1 and a broader range of lentiviruses. Analysis of HIV-1 capsid mutants showed that physical interaction with POM121 does not predict functional dependence, as capsids retaining POM121 binding remained insensitive to its depletion. Strikingly, loss of cyclophilin A (CypA) completely abolished HIV-1 dependence on POM121, whereas depletion of CPSF6 produced only partial rescue, demonstrating that POM121 sensitivity is dictated by the broader network of capsid-host interactions. Finally, POM121 depletion impaired HIV-1 nuclear accumulation and selectively disrupted the nuclear import of other viral and cellular cargo. Together, these findings identify POM121 as a selective regulator of lentiviral nuclear entry whose functional contribution is determined by capsid and host-factor context.
affiliations: Universidad de Las Palmas de Gran Canaria (corresponding author)

papers.title: Prevalent Integration of both Xenotropic and Ecotropic Murine Leukemia Virus in the Human Genome of Xenografts
papers.abstract: Humanized mouse models are widely used in medical research to represent human conditions (1, 2), but their fidelity could be compromised by mouse-originated infections. However, their susceptibility to mouse pathogens are rarely questioned (3). Here we screened 1,619 publicly available genomic sequencing runs from patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models for the integration of murine leukemia virus (MLV), a rodent retrovirus exists in the mouse genome as an endogenous retrovirus (4), within the human genome. We discovered substantial enrichment of human-MLV chimeric DNA in approximately 25% of them. Analyzing the human-MLV junctions, we found about 90% of them bearing the unmistakable hallmarks of retroviral integration, including the canonical MLV boundaries and the distinctive 4-bp target site duplications (5, 6). It was also assumed that mouse strains without the highly infectious Bxv1 provirus are safe from MLV contamination in xenografts (7, 8). However, we found many PDX models derived from Bxv1- strains, including the widely used NSG strain, are also contaminated by the supposedly rodent-specific ecotropic MLV (E-MLV). We further confirmed a complete E-MLV integrated into the human genome by both HiFi and sanger sequencing. Our discovery raises concerns that mouse-to-human retroviral transmission and integration is more common and less restrictive than previously appreciated. They support examination of MLV integration as a feature of humanized mouse models with implications on the fidelity of these models in recapitulating human cells and tissues. Our discovery also has underscored the importance of comprehensively inactivation of porcine endogenous retroviruses for the clinical application of xenotransplatation (9, 10).
affiliations: Washington University in St. Louis, School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Adult-like thick-filament protein stoichiometry in immature human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes
papers.abstract: Human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CMs) retain immature sarcomeric isoforms, raising questions about their ability to recapitulate the protein stoichiometry of adult human myocardium. We integrated two independent quantitative proteomic datasets of iPSC-CMs with published fetal and region-resolved adult human heart proteomes to compare sarcomeric protein abundance. Although iPSC-CMs clustered with fetal heart based on their global shared proteome and retained fetal troponin I expression, key thick-filament protein ratios closely matched those of adult myocardium. Myosin heavy-to-light chain ratios approached the expected 2:4 stoichiometry, while myosin-binding protein abundance relative to myosin heavy chains was comparable across iPSC-CMs and adult cardiac regions. These findings reveal that developmental immaturity in sarcomeric isoform expression does not entail altered thick-filament protein proportions. Preservation of adult-like myosin-binding protein stoichiometry supports the use of iPSC-CMs to investigate sarcomeric diseases associated with altered protein dosage, particularly MYBPC3-associated hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
affiliations: Gulbenkian Institute for Molecular Medicine; Faculdade de Medicina da Universidade de Lisboa (corresponding author)

papers.title: Filament mechanics and turnover organize dynamic load bearing structures in a cellular-scale model of the actomyosin cortex
papers.abstract: The actomyosin cortex controls cell shape and movement by generating and transmitting contractile forces. Its actin filament (AF) network adopts diverse spatial organizations, while spatially biased contractility drives cortical flow that transports components and reorganizes the network. However, how turnover and spatial redistribution organize and maintain tension-bearing structures in a dynamic steady state, and how localized contractility reorganizes them through flow, remain unclear. We developed a cellular-scale discrete model of the actomyosin cortex representing AFs, cross-linkers, and myosin minifilaments. Local surface stress was reconstructed from discrete-element internal forces based on continuum mechanics. We related cortical tension to component abundance, tensile deformation, AF orientation, turnover, and network connectivity, and compared different AF disassembly, relocation, and myosin-localization mechanisms. Simulations produced a heterogeneous, network-like distribution of local cortical tension. Tensile energy per element correlated more strongly with local tension than component abundance, with the strongest correlation for AFs. Highly stretched AFs preferentially occurred in high-tension regions and aligned with the first-principal-tension orientation, indicating anisotropic load-bearing pathways. Despite continuous component replacement and reorganization of local tension patterns, global AF-network connectivity and cell-scale cortical tension were maintained. The characteristic time of tension-pattern reorganization was closest to the persistence time of myosin, suggesting an association between myosin dynamics and rapid force redistribution. AF relocation to low-density regions replenished spatial gaps, whereas bending-dependent disassembly limited the accumulation of strongly deformed AFs. Direct myosin localization and AF accumulation produced comparable equatorward cortical flows but differed in the spatial organization of the tension-bearing network. Collectively, these results demonstrate that cellular-scale cortical tension is organized not only by component abundance but also by filament-scale mechanical loading, AF orientation, and network connectivity.
affiliations: Institute of Science Tokyo (corresponding author)

papers.title: Using Oyster Genomics to Understand Human Health
papers.abstract: As sessile filter feeders that experience continuous environmental exposure, oysters, particularly Crassostrea virginica, offer a unique opportunity to understand how environmental exposure alters the genome and influence health. Furthermore, oysters must be sorted by size for market value for premium size and taste. However, it requires intensive labor, specialized equipment (tumblers), and is susceptible to environmental risks like pollution. Therefore, it is desirable to produce uniform oysters without machines. However, limitations in the previous reference genome [2] have constrained our understanding of how genes are organized and maintained in oyster populations. To this end, we harvested 240 adult oysters in same location, 120 extremely large size and 120 extremely small, controlled with all confounding factors such as age and water temperature. We perform a genome wise associate study (GWAS) using next generation whole genome sequencing, aiming to discover genomic regions associated with oyster size. Using PacBio HiFi, Illumina, and Hi-C technologies, we generated a 99.7% complete chromosome-level genome assembly for C. virginica (NCBI RefSeq GCF_053477285.1) [75]. We identified a ~13 Mb region on chromosome 1 uniquely expanded in C. virginica and enriched for innate immune and stress-response genes. To evaluate whether these structural features are reflected at the population level, we then conducted a k-mer analysis. This revealed differential sequence patterns by size, including enrichment of bacterial DNA in smaller individuals and host variation at the RNF213 locus within this region. By highlighting genome structure as a mediator of immune resilience, this work supports the use of oysters as sentinels to advance out understanding of how the dynamic reassembly of the genome due to environmental exposures influence health in human populations.
affiliations: Yale University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Comparative functional genomics reveals distributed SERPINE1 like characteristics among Drosophila serpins
papers.abstract: Serpins (serine protease inhibitors) regulate proteolytic activity through a suicide-substrate inhibitory mechanism, whereby the serpin covalently traps and inactivates their target protease. Serpins are broadly conserved across eukaryotes, but the evolutionary and functional relationships between human SERPINE1, and Drosophila Serpins in incompletely defined. To identify candidate Drosophila functional analogs of SERPINE1/PAI-1, a multi-omics framework was applied to thoroughly compare the serpins across species. The multi-level analysis integrated orthology prediction, protein sequence and structural characterization, phylogenetic reconstruction, bulk tissue transcriptomics, single-cell transcriptomics, and aging-associated expression analysis. Candidate serpins (Spn42Da, Spn42Db, Spn42Dc, Spn42Dd, Spn28B, and Spn28F) were evaluated using DIOPT, AlphaFold/ChimeraX structural comparisons, reactive center loop analyses, phylogenetic distances, GTEx, Human Protein Atlas, FlyAtlas2, Fly Cell Atlas, and Aging Fly Cell Atlas datasets. Comparative analyses demonstrated full-length sequence and reactive center loop (RCL) divergence despite preservation of the canonical serpin fold. Tissue, cell-type, and age-associated expression analysis revealed distinct candidate-specific patterns. Spn42Dd comparisons uncovered similarities to human SERPINE1 in sequence/structural and broad expression but did not represent the strongest overall cross-species expression correlations. Spn42Da and Spn42Db received the highest cross species integrated support. Quality check of the ranking confirmed that Spn42Da and Spn42Db were stable top candidates across orthology, sequence alignment, and expression domains. The multi-domain analysis was unable to identify a single definitive Drosophila serpin as the closest counterpart to human SERPINE1, indicating that cross-species similarity is distributed across multiple candidate serpins. This study therefore provides a quantitative method for prioritizing potential evolutionary and functional analogs across highly divergent species.
affiliations: Iowa State University of Science and Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Defining the Antigenic Topology and Prospective Binding Breadth of Vaccination-induced SARS-CoV-2 Neutralizing Antibodies
papers.abstract: Antibodies that neutralize SARS-CoV-2 primarily target the viral spike glycoprotein, yet the breadth of these responses is continually challenged by viral evolution. While extensive structural studies have defined epitopes across the spike protein, how antibodies elicited by the initial mRNA vaccination campaigns perform against subsequently emerging variants remains an important question.Here, we structurally and functionally characterize a panel of early plasmablast-derived human monoclonal antibodies isolated following primary mRNA vaccination, targeting both the receptor-binding domain (RBD) and the N-terminal domain (NTD) of spike. Using cryo-electron microscopy, variant-binding analyses, and viral-fusion inhibition assays, we observe that antibodies directed against immunodominant regions of the RBD and NTD are highly potent but more frequently impacted by variant-associated mutations. In contrast, antibodies engaging a conserved hydrophobic pocket within the NTD exhibit broader reactivity and neutralize through distinct molecular mechanisms. Together, these findings extend prior structural studies of spike-directed antibodies by prospectively assessing the breadth of vaccine-elicited antibodies against later variants and identifying structural features associated with differential escape sensitivity. These results contribute to a growing understanding of how early vaccine-induced antibody repertoires relate to subsequent viral evolution.
affiliations: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai (corresponding author)

papers.title: TriMic: a Triticum aestivum microbial culture collection and synthetic community for dissecting wheat-microbe interactions
papers.abstract: Microbial culture collections and synthetic microbial communities (SynComs) are essential experimental resources for investigating underlying mechanisms of plant-microbe interactions. However, such resources remain scarce for agriculturally relevant crops. Here, we address this gap by developing TriMic, a community resource to investigate plant-microbe interactions in wheat. We employed a host-mediated isolation approach to obtain a bacterial collection from wheat roots and characterized its taxonomic representation and functional potential through whole-genome sequencing. We further evaluated the community dynamics of a consortium derived from this collection across time and wheat genotypes to inform the selection of a simplified community. TriMic includes core and keystone taxa reported in previous wheat microbiomes studies. Moreover, genomic analysis revealed genetic potential for diverse genes associated with plant colonization, nutrient cycling, plant growth promotion, and biosynthetic gene clusters with taxa exhibiting metabolic patterns associated with both generalist and specialist strategies. The proposed 15-member SynCom reflects the taxonomic and functional relevance of the full collection. By integrating publicly accessible bacterial isolates, whole-genome sequences, and an ecologically informed SynCom, TriMic provides a foundation for translating ecological and genomic observations into testable hypotheses, advancing mechanistic investigations of microbial community assembly and plant-microbiome interactions.
affiliations: North Carolina State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: FTO does not function as an m6A eraser in AML: a reassessment using direct RNA nanopore sequencing
papers.abstract: A central concept in epitranscriptomics is that the RNA demethylase FTO acts as a site-selective eraser of N6-methyladenosine (m6A) in specific mRNAs. This is most well-established in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), where demethylation of MYC is thought to promote leukemogenesis. Using nanopore direct RNA sequencing to quantify m6A transcriptome-wide, we find that m6A stoichiometry, including at MYC-specific sites, remains unaffected by FTO knockdown or pharmacologic inhibition in AML. Conversely, levels of N6-2'-O-dimethyladenosine (m6Am) are markedly increased in snRNAs, indicating that m6Am, not m6A, is the major substrate of FTO in AML. We extend these results outside the AML context in FTO knockout brain and HEK293T cells, detecting no selective increases in mRNA m6A but widespread increases in snRNA m6Am levels following FTO depletion. These findings suggest that FTO has minimal ability to erase m6A in mRNA. Instead, the reported biological effects of FTO are likely mediated by demethylation of m6Am.
affiliations: Department of Pharmacology, Weill Cornell Medicine, Cornell University, New York, NY 10065, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: CBKMR: A Copula-based Bayesian Kernel Machine Regression Framework for Optimal Marker Detection in Omics Data
papers.abstract: High-throughput bulk and single-cell omics technologies enable comprehensive molecular profiling, yet identifying compact, biologically interpretable marker sets that distinguish cell types, conditions, or disease states remains challenging. Standard pipelines rely on univariate differential expression tests, which ignore gene--gene dependencies and nonlinear effects, while multivariate machine-learning (ML) methods often lack principled feature selection} and {uncertainty quantification. The Bayesian kernel machine regression (BKMR) framework offers an appealing alternative because it (a) captures nonlinear gene--outcome relationships and higher-order interactions, and (b) enables {automatic relevance determination (ARD)} through sparsity-inducing priors. However, we show that the traditional latent Gaussian process (GP) formulation of BKMR is inadequate for discrete outcomes (e.g., cell-type labels), leading to biased inference and unstable variable selection. We propose a copula-based Bayesian kernel machine regression (CBKMR) model that uses outcome-appropriate discrete marginals while a Gaussian copula captures kernel-induced dependence across observations. To ensure scalability to modern single-cell datasets, we further introduce a nearest-neighbor GP-based variant, NNCBKMR, which reduces computational complexity from O(N3) to nearly linear in N. Simulation studies show that CBKMR more accurately captures nonlinear effects and yields stronger marker-selection performance than BKMR and top ensemble ML methods (e.g., random forests, XGBoost). Applications to multiple scRNA-seq datasets demonstrate that CBKMR identifies concise marker panels that align closely with expert-annotated gene signatures while providing{posterior uncertainty} for principled decision-making.
affiliations: Department of Public Health Sciences, Medical University of South Carolina, Charleston, South Carolina, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: BIG-TB: A benchmark for evaluating prediction and interpretability of sequence-based machine learning using Mycobacterium tuberculosis genomes
papers.abstract: Foundation models aim to learn useful representations of biological sequences, but are hindered by a lack of benchmarks to jointly evaluate predictive performance and variant attribution on diverse tasks. To this end, we present the Benchmark for Interpretable prediction from Genomes of Tuberculosis, BIG-TB. We curate over 17,000 genomes with high-quality sequencing data and experimentally measured antibiotic resistance phenotypes, combined with a curated list of WHO-catalogue of resistance-associated variants, and provide these data in an ML-ready format. BIG-TB defines two tasks: (1) predictive performance of antibiotic resistance phenotypes, and (2) attribution of predictions to known resistance-conferring variants. Using our tasks, we evaluate DNA- and protein-based foundation models, showing that DNA-based foundation models do not yet outperform simple machine learning baselines (mean test AUC = 0.888 vs. 0.865 for best CNN variant vs. best Evo2 variant across drugs). In a lineage-informed evaluation across DNA and protein modalities, predictive signal for well-characterized drugs was largely preserved (mean AUC 0.846-0.963). Across both evaluation settings, models with the highest predictive performance did not necessarily achieve the strongest recovery of resistance variants, underscoring the value of evaluating both predictive accuracy and biological interpretability. Overall, BIG-TB provides a reusable resource for developing sequence representations that are both accurate and mechanistically meaningful.

papers.title: Track Display Jockey (trackDJ): a user-friendly R package for visualization of epigenomic data
papers.abstract: Background Visualization of epigenomic data such as coverage tracks, peak calls, and chromatin interactions is a critical task in genomic data analysis. Although genome browsers such as the Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV) and the UCSC Genome Browser permit user-friendly exploration of genomic tracks, they are not optimized for fully programmatic and reproducible generation of publication-quality figures. In contrast, existing programmatic tools lack a user-friendly interface and require extensive configuration. Results We present trackDJ (Track Display Jockey), an R package for visualization of epigenomic data. trackDJ prioritizes usability by favoring convention over configuration; it provides high-level plotting functions with sensible defaults, aiming to allow users with minimal programming experience to generate clear, publication-quality figures with relatively little coding. Within a unified plotting framework, users can stack and align multiple data types, including coverage tracks, peak annotations, chromatin loops, and gene annotations. trackDJ allows users to select plotted genomic regions by coordinates or by gene name, enabling rapid visualization without knowledge of precise locus boundaries. Conclusions trackDJ complements existing epigenomics toolkits by providing a user-friendly, reproducible alternative to interactive genome browsers for epigenomic visualization. By enabling scripted generation of clean, customizable genomic illustrations, trackDJ readily integrates into R-based analysis workflows to streamline the creation of publication-quality figures.
