papers.title: Combined HDAC and ATM inhibition with radiation in preclinical glioblastoma models
papers.abstract: Background: Brain-penetrant histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi) are promising radiosensitizing agents for glioblastoma (GBM). HDAC inhibitors can impair DNA damage response (DDR) pathways and promote persistent DNA damage. Here, we evaluated whether combined inhibition of HDAC and the DNA repair kinase, ataxia-telangiectasia mutated (ATM), could synergize with radiation (IR) and improve therapeutic efficacy in GBM. Methods: In vitro dose-response assays were performed in patient-derived xenograft (PDX)-derived glioma stem cells (GSCs) with both inhibitors of HDAC (quisinostat, QST) and ATM (AZD1390) with or without IR treatment to assess synergy. Pharmacodynamic responses were evaluated by immunoblotting for histone acetylation, DDR signaling, and DNA damage markers. Transcriptomic analyses were performed to evaluate treatment-associated changes in DNA repair pathways. The combination of QST, AZD1390, and IR was further evaluated in an orthotopic GBM survival study. Results: Combined treatment with QST and AZD1390 produced synergistic radiosensitization in multiple GSC models in vitro. Furthermore, QST combined with IR suppressed transcription of homologous recombination (HR) pathway genes in GSCs, impairing double-strand break repair capacity through an epigenetic mechanism that does not directly inhibit ATM kinase activity. Pharmacodynamic analyses confirmed that QST increased histone acetylation while AZD1390 suppressed ATM signaling, together impairing complementary mechanisms to increase radiosensitivity of GSCs. In an orthotopic GBM model, QST combined with IR significantly prolonged survival compared with IR alone. However, the addition of AZD1390 did not provide a significant survival benefit beyond QST+IR, and AZD1390 combined with IR did not significantly improve survival relative to IR alone. Conclusions: Combined HDAC and ATM inhibition with QST and AZD1390 enhances radiosensitivity in patient-derived GBM cells, mechanistically underpinned by QST-mediated increase in DNA damage and dual disruption of DDR through complementary, non-overlapping mechanisms. However, this in vitro synergy did not confer additional survival benefit beyond QST+IR in an orthotopic GBM model under the dosing conditions tested, suggesting pharmacological limitations with the tumor microenvironment or suboptimal dosing schedules may have constrained in vivo efficacy.

papers.title: A novel vimentin-stabilizing urea compound MXC-017 ameliorates DSS-induced colitis and radiation enteropathy in mice
papers.abstract: Ulcerative colitis (UC) and radiation enteropathy involve intestinal epithelial injury, barrier dysfunction, and inflammation, but effective treatments remain limited. This study evaluated MXC-017, a novel vimentin-targeting urea compound, in mouse models of dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis and radiation-induced enteropathy. Acute colitis was induced in C57BL/6 mice using 3.5% DSS for seven days, followed by regular water for seven days. Radiation enteropathy was induced by 13 Gy total abdominal irradiation. Mice received MXC-017 (150 mg/kg) or vehicle. Disease activity, intestinal permeability, inflammatory and epithelial markers, and histopathology were assessed. MXC-017's effects on cancer stem cell frequency, sphere formation, and migration were also examined in PC-3 and DU-145 prostate cancer cells. MXC-017 reduced DSS-induced colitis severity, accelerated weight recovery, lowered disease activity, partially preserved colon length, and restored barrier function. It also reduced proinflammatory cytokines, macrophage infiltration, epithelial injury, and goblet cell loss while preserving epithelial proliferation and markers of intestinal stem cell function and tight-junction integrity. Following irradiation, MXC-017 improved weight recovery, reduced intestinal permeability, preserved epithelial architecture, and partially mitigated villus shortening. Importantly, MXC-017 did not protect prostate cancer stem cells from radiation. Instead, it reduced stem cell frequency, sphere-forming capacity, and cancer cell migration. These findings support vimentin targeting with MXC-017 as a potential treatment for UC and radiation-induced intestinal toxicity and as an adjunct to radiotherapy for pelvic and abdominal malignancies.

papers.title: GraphHDBSCAN*: Graph-based Hierarchical Clustering on High-dimensional Spaces with Applications to Single-cell RNA Sequencing Data
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is widely used to resolve cellular heterogeneity across thousands to millions of cells. A major challenge is identifying biologically meaningful cell populations while preserving their hierarchical organization, because broad cell types often split into more specialized subtypes. However, state-of-the-art approaches mostly focus on flat partitions and ignore the hierarchical nature of single-cell data. Here we introduce GraphHDBSCAN*, a graph-based extension of HDBSCAN* with an effectively hyperparameter-free hierarchical clustering stage that operates on a graph representation of the data, enabling robust recovery of both hierarchical and non-hierarchical (flat) relationships in very high-dimensional, noisy datasets. We evaluate GraphHDBSCAN* across multiple scRNA-seq datasets and show that it recovers biologically meaningful hierarchies that agree more closely with curated biological references than alternative hierarchical clustering methods, while revealing fine-grained structure, including monocyte subpopulations. In addition, the method yields high-quality flat partitions that outperform widely used community-detection methods.

papers.title: Connecting spatial regions to clinical phenotypes by transferring knowledge from bulk gene expression data
papers.abstract: Spatially resolved transcriptomics (SRT) technology has enabled a new level of knowledge about tumors. Many critical tumor properties, such as invasiveness and growth, depend on both specific transcriptomic changes in tumor cells and the tumor microenvironment. However, computational methods to study clinical phenotypes of spatial regions, such as hazard and drug response, have not yet been developed. Since clinical phenotypes are measured at the patient level and not at the level of spatial regions, such a method would require transferring knowledge from the patient level domain to the spot level domain. To overcome this challenge, we developed SpacePhenotyper. Our approach uses algebraic spectral techniques to transfer the predictive relationship between gene expression and clinical phenotypes from bulk gene expression data to SRT data. Our approach captures a gene expression pattern that is predictive of the phenotype of interest in the form of a vector, the Eigen-Patient, which is then used to quantify the phenotype in spatial spots. After extensively validating SpacePhenotyper on simulated and real data, we utilize it to study how the spatial heterogeneity of breast cancer tumors influences residual cancer burden after treatment. By assigning relative quantities of clinical phenotypes to spatial locations, SpacePhenotyper has proven a powerful tool for the identification and interpretation of transcriptional changes over spatial regions and of spatially-regulated patterns of cellular states.

papers.title: ER-associated control of axonal vesicle trafficking during neuronal development
papers.abstract: Axonal vesicle trafficking is essential for presynaptic assembly, yet the intracellular structures that spatially and temporally regulate vesicle transport during neuronal development remain unclear. Here we identify previously uncharacterized membrane contact sites (MCSs) between the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and both synaptic vesicle precursors (SVPs) and dense-core vesicles (DCVs). Using live confocal and cryo-electron microscopy, we reveal that vesicle transport undergoes a transient developmental slowdown in the axons of rat hippocampal neurons, associated with increased tripartite ER-vesicle-microtubule interfaces. Using proximity biotinylation, we identify the ER protein PRG1 as a developmentally regulated factor that modulates vesicle retention at these sites by interacting with KIF5A. Notably, a disease-associated PRG1 mutant fails to regulate vesicle trafficking. Finally, we demonstrate that PRG1 modulation of vesicle trafficking serves as a developmental checkpoint by delaying synapse formation and preventing network hyperactivity. Together, our findings establish ER-vesicle contact sites as a previously unrecognized layer of control of axonal trafficking and link intracellular organization to the timing of synapse assembly.

papers.title: Aberrant splicing prediction during human organ development
papers.abstract: Developmental disorders constitute a major class of genetic diseases, yet tools to identify splicing-disruptive variants during development are lacking. To address this need we extended the AbSplice framework to incorporate splicing dynamics across developmental stages. Moreover, we introduced several improvements including a continuous representation of splice site usage and integration of the rich set of predictions from the sequence-based model Pangolin. These advances improve the performance of the original model at predicting aberrant splicing events and help outperform purely sequence-based models including AlphaGenome, enabling predictions across embryonic, childhood, and adult tissues. Genome-wide scores for all single-nucleotide variants and a web interface to score indels are available to facilitate the exploration of the predictions. Our genome-wide predictions reveal a class of variants with splicing-disruptive effects confined to early development, particularly abundant in the brain (>18,000 variants). These variants are enriched in loss-of-function intolerant genes and neurodevelopmental disorder genes. Within the rare-disease cohort Solve-RD, high-impact brain-specific predictions are significantly enriched in individuals affected by neurodevelopmental disorders (NDD) in NDD-linked genes. Furthermore, the predicted developmental timing of the splicing disruption correlates with the clinical age of onset. Analysis of genomes of individuals with a suspected Mendelian disorder from Genomics England identified 26 unique variants in disease-linked genes, with stronger predicted effects during development than in adulthood, including a candidate new diagnosis in the gene FGFR1. Altogether, these results improve the accuracy of splice-disruptive variant prediction and provide tissue and developmental context to aid interpretation in rare disease diagnostics.

papers.title: The Reasoning Paradox in Scientific Sandboxes: Why Extended Reasoning Fails in Autonomous Bioinformatics and How to Fix It.
papers.abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) trained with extended reasoning, such as DeepSeek-R1 and OpenAI o1, have established state-of-the-art benchmarks in formal logic, competitive programming, and mathematics. In interactive, empirical scientific sandboxes, however, their efficacy remains counter-intuitive. In the Bioinformatics Benchmark (BixBench), extended reasoning models paradoxically degraded in multi-turn environments, leading benchmark authors to exclude them from primary agentic evaluations. In this paper, we conduct the first systematic forensic audit of the internal cognitive monologue ( ... ) of open-weight reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B) and matched instruction-tuned controls (Qwen2.5-Coder-14B) deployed inside containerized computational biology sandboxes on Nvidia H100 GPUs. Our forensic analysis uncovers two distinct systemic failure modes: (1) The PubMed Prior Trap, in which reasoning models engage in epistemic rationalization within their cognitive stream, falsely convincing themselves that empirical datasets are missing and substituting empirical computation with speculative literature recall (e.g., estimating adjusted p-values based on "typical experimental outcomes"); and (2) Tag Language Nesting Collisions, in which models conflate agent-level XML action tags with Python syntax, producing terminal interpreter syntax errors. To resolve this paradox, we introduce Dual Track Decoupled Reasoning (DTDR), an agent scaffolding architecture that evicts internal cognitive monologues from multi-turn history, injects strict empirical grounding guardrails, and dynamically intercepts runtime tool invocations. On a stratified diagnostic benchmark spanning single-cell RNA-seq, bulk differential expression (DESeq2), and genomic variant prioritization (n=22 per arm), DTDR rescues the 14B reasoning model from 0.0% to 9.09% accuracy (2/22), doubling the performance of the matched non-reasoning coder control (4.55%, 1/22) while slashing code execution errors by 81% (13.6% vs. 72.7%) and reducing average steps to solution by 66% (1.77 vs. 5.18 steps). All replication pipelines, prompts, and trajectory manifests are openly released.

papers.title: An interpretable open platform for sequence-based antibody developability prediction
papers.abstract: Antibody developability is increasingly predictable from sequence, yet software and trained models are rarely made available. We present DELPHI, open software for training developability predictors from labelled antibody assay data, together with ready-to-run, retrainable models. DELPHI compares 25 language-model and classifier combinations under CDR H3-cluster cross-validation that reduces sequence-similarity leakage, measures how performance changes with labelled training-set size, and reports residue-level model attributions. Applied to in-house polyreactivity and size-exclusion (SEC) data, it reaches mean AUC 0.959 and 0.933. Trained on those data alone, it transfers to a 246,293-antibody public library (AUC 0.950 with our deployed model) and ranks polyreactivity at a level similar to the best reported Ginkgo competition point estimate, without training on its data. Any laboratory can screen candidates before running assays, generate residue-level engineering hypotheses, and retrain DELPHI for a new assay.

papers.title: Cross-cohort optimal transport maps macrophage plasticity and routes to inflammation and fibrosis in human atherosclerosis
papers.abstract: Single-cell transcriptomics has revealed extensive macrophage heterogeneity in atherosclerotic plaques, but how disease-associated programs reshape cellular identity remains unclear. Connecting macrophage states to these molecular changes could help identify candidate routes through which macrophages contribute to inflammation and fibrosis. We developed a computational method combining optimal transport, RNA velocity and comparative program analysis across 34,533 monocytes and macrophages from seven human cohorts. Optimal transport quantified all 15 pairwise relationships among six macrophage states, and target-association gradients supported source- and destination-program comparisons across 11 relationships. Expression contrasts were calculated within libraries and source subtypes. Robustness was assessed through resampling, cohort omission and held-out-gene analyses. Paired RNA and protein measurements provided complementary molecular evidence, and patient-label permutation tests evaluated exploratory clinical associations in 18 patients. We also applied the method to an independent human liver dataset. Scavenging and inflammatory macrophages formed the closest transcriptional pair in the full atlas and every cohort-omission analysis. Scavenging macrophages retained selected source features alongside inflammatory programming, whereas fibrotic association coincided with attenuation of the broader scavenging signature. This signature showed a lower change along fibrotic than inflammatory association in all 19 matched libraries. Protein measurements corroborated selected changes and revealed coexisting scavenging and activation features within individual cells. Symptomatic patients had a higher fraction of monocytes with strong inflammatory association than asymptomatic patients (median difference, 13.0 percentage points; unadjusted one-sided permutation $p = 0.0017$). Analysis of 8,536 liver mononuclear phagocytes further resolved contrasting source-marker responses along scar-associated macrophage association. These findings connect macrophage heterogeneity to selective identity remodeling across disease-associated states. Integrating population relationships with RNA, protein and clinical measurements provides a strategy for prioritizing candidate pathogenic routes and their associated molecular programs for functional investigation.

papers.title: Interferon gamma-induced MX1 and IFITM1 inhibit Varicella-Zoster Virus Replication
papers.abstract: Interferon gamma (IFN-{gamma}) is a potent cytokine secreted following primary varicella-zoster virus (VZV) infection. Our previous studies demonstrated that pretreatment with IFN-{gamma} completely inhibited VZV replication in lung fibroblast MRC-5 and retinal epithelial ARPE-19 but not in melanoma MeWo cells, suggesting that IFN-{gamma}-stimulated protein(s) inhibit viral replication. Our microarray analysis revealed that 34 interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) were upregulated by greater than 2.5-fold at 8 h post-treatment in both ARPE-19 and MRC-5 cells compared to those of MeWo cells. The depletion of CTSS, GBP4, MX1, IFIT1, IFITM1 and IRF1 by siRNA in IFN-{gamma}-treated cells significantly increased VZV yields. Ectopic overexpression of interferon-induced myxovirus resistance 1 (MX1) or transmembrane protein 1 (IFITM1) significantly reduced VZV yield both in ARPE-19 and MeWo cells. IFITM1 abrogated viral major immediate-early IE62 protein-mediated trans-activation. IFITM1 reduced the level of VZV immediate-early IE62 protein, but not the IE62 mRNA, suggesting that IFITM1 expression reduces the expression level of IE62 by post-transcriptional regulation. Both human primary epidermal keratinocytes and calcium chloride-differentiated keratinocytes exhibit high levels of endogenous MX1 gene expression. Pharmacologic inhibition of JAK signaling reduced MX1 expression and enhanced VZV replication in calcium chloride-induced differentiated keratinocytes. Collectively, these findings identify MX1 and IFITM1 as key IFN-{gamma}-induced restriction factors that inhibit VZV replication and suggest that suppression of JAK-STAT signaling can promote VZV replication in differentiated keratinocytes.

papers.title: TXNDC15 modulated quality control at the endoplasmic reticulum shapes ciliogenesis
papers.abstract: At the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), membrane protein quality control is tightly regulated to ensure excess subunits are recognized and degraded to protect cellular homeostasis. Using genome wide CRISPR screens, we identified a factor of unknown function, thioredoxin domain containing protein 15 (TXNDC15), and showed that it regulates membrane protein stability by tuning the activity of the E3-ubiquitin ligase MARCHF6. TXNDC15 modulates MARCHF6 in two opposing ways: first, it enhances the binding, ubiquitination, and degradation of membrane protein subunits with soluble cytosolic domains; and second, it prevents the inappropriate recruitment and ubiquitination of subunits with globular lumenal domains. Patient mutations to TXNDC15 that cause the ciliopathy Meckel-Gruber syndrome, disrupted its binding to MARCHF6, allowing degradation of critical ciliary proteins as they transit through the ER leading to defects in ciliogenesis. The regulatory function of TXNDC15 therefore exemplifies how protein quality control maintains the integrity of the proteome to prevent disease.

papers.title: RNAquarium: an archive-scale atlas of zebrafish gene expression coupled with pan-taxonomic profiling reveals diverse viral drivers of transcriptomic states
papers.abstract: Zebrafish RNA-seq studies span diverse developmental, physiological, and disease contexts, yet most analyses remain confined to individual experiments and disregard the non-zebrafish component of the data. We present RNAquarium, a scalable framework for joint transcriptomic and metatranscriptomic analysis of RNA-seq data and apply it to all publicly available zebrafish RNA-seq datasets in the Sequence Read Archive. RNAquarium captures transcriptomic structure across development and tissues, reveals diverse microbial and viral associations, and identifies previously undescribed zebrafish viruses including a close relative of human influenza B virus linked to distinct host transcriptional states. We further demonstrate that archive-scale transcriptomes can support foundation-model training and prediction of infection-associated transcriptomic signatures. RNAquarium provides an open framework and interactive portal for exploring the breadth of zebrafish gene expression patterns and associated taxa profiled across a large research community. Moreover, our framework establishes a generalizable strategy for integrating transcriptomic and metatranscriptomic analyses across the diversity of life represented in public sequencing archives.

OsCPK17- and OsMPK6-mediated dual phosphorylation of OsPUB12 maintains OsPUB2-regulated OsPUB12 homeostasis and balances rice immunity
papers.abstract: Numerous E3 ubiquitin ligases regulate plant immunity through mediating protein homeostasis, yet how homeostasis of E3 ligases is finely regulated per se remains poorly understood. Here, we reveal that the ubiquitin E3 ligase plant U-box 2 (OsPUB2) specifically interacts with OsPUB12 and targets it for ubiquitin-mediated degradation. In contrast to the immunity-suppressing role of OsPUB12, OsPUB2 positively regulates resistance to rice bacterial diseases and contributes to pathogen-associated molecular pattern-induced reactive oxygen burst and defense gene expression. Upon pathogen challenge, the calcium-dependent kinase OsCPK17 and mitogen-activated protein kinase OsMPK6 phosphorylate OsPUB12 at Thr154 and Ser460 in a temporally sequential manner. These two phosphorylation events oppositely regulate OsPUB12’s interaction with OsPUB2 and its subsequent ubiquitination, leading to divergent regulation of OsPUB12 stability and rice immunity. Our findings indicate that distinct phosphorylation of OsPUB12 by immune-related kinases OsCPK17 and OsMPK6 synergistically maintains OsPUB2-mediated OsPUB12 homeostasis, serving as a core mechanism to fine-tune rice immunity. OsPUB2 degrades OsPUB12 to promote rice immunity. Phosphorylation of OsPUB12 by OsCPK17 and OsMPK6 at two sites fine-tunes its stability and the plant’s defense response.

papers.title: Pharmacological chaperone treatment with Cystadane in aspartylglucosaminuria: an open-label, phase Ib/II trial
papers.abstract: This phase Ib/II investigator-initiated, open label trial aims to show the safety and efficacy of Cystadane (betaine) in aspartylglucosaminuria, a lysosomal storage disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline, in Finnish patients homozygous for the Finnish major mutation, aged between 3 and 17 years at study begin (recruited: 25, analyzed: 21). Oral Cystadane efficacy and safety were studied over 48 months. The primary endpoint of the study, reduction of glycoasparagines in the urine, was quantitatively determined using liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry and normalized to urine creatinine. Urine glycoasparagines are significantly reduced upon Cystadane treatment (by 68.6% ±10.8%; p = 0.000), and the study thus meets its primary endpoint. Our data show that Cystadane/betaine efficiently improves the main disease biomarker, and it is safe to use in aspartylglucosaminuria. Further studies should be carried out in a larger patient population over a longer time to demonstrate the effects on disease progression. EudraCT registration number 2017-000645-48. Here, this phase Ib/II interventional clinical trial shows that betaine/Cystadane is safe to use and significantly reduces urinary accumulation of glycoasparagines and increases aspartylglucosaminidase activity in aspartylglucosaminuria.

papers.title: High-pressure synthesis of a polymeric N3H2 solid stabilized by hydrogen bonds
papers.abstract: Polymeric nitrogen represents a long-sought class of high energy density materials, in which single-bonded nitrogen networks release large amounts of energy upon decomposition to molecular N2. However, polymeric nitrogen allotropes require extreme pressures to synthesize and cannot be recovered at ambient conditions due to surface instabilities. Hydrogen has been proposed as a key element to stabilize such frameworks, yet polymeric nitrogen–hydrogen solids have until now remained the realm of theoretical calculations. Here, we report the high-pressure synthesis of polymeric N3H2 at 134(3)–139(1) GPa from N2–H2 mixtures. Synchrotron single-crystal X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy and first-principles calculations reveal a fully single-bonded framework of 1-dimensional chains of N6 rings, each decorated by four H atoms. The chains of N6H4 units are cross-linked through hydrogen bonds. Employing modern synchrotron sources, hydrogen positions are directly resolved from diffraction data at 139(1) GPa. At ambient conditions, N3H2 exhibits an estimated energy of decomposition of 7.98 kJ/g, highlighting hydrogen-stabilized polymeric nitrogen as a promising class of energetic materials. Laser-heating nitrogen–hydrogen mixtures at about 139 GPa produces N3H2, a crystalline polymeric solid with only single N–N bonds. The new material has a high energy density, with a predicted energy release exceeding that of conventional explosives.

papers.title: Toward triggered generation of indistinguishable single photons from MoTe2 quantum emitters
papers.abstract: Single-photon sources operating at telecom wavelengths are fundamental components for long-distance optical quantum communication and information processing. Two-dimensional transition-metal dichalcogenides offer a promising platform for such sources, but their development has been hindered by limited spectral range and poor single-photon indistinguishability. Here, we demonstrate a reproducible approach for generating near-infrared (1090–1200 nm) quantum emitters in bilayer MoTe2 using deterministic strain and defect engineering. These emitters exhibit strong linear polarization, sub-nanosecond lifetimes, high single-photon purity (triggered g(2)(0) as low as ~0.01 under p-shell excitation), and resolution-limited emission. Electrostatic biasing enables spectral tuning, suppresses photon bunching, and shortens radiative lifetimes. Most notably, two-photon interference measurements reveal a Hong-Ou-Mandel visibility of ~7.1%, and up to ~60% with post-selection under p-shell excitation, which represents state-of-the-art performance for quantum emitters in the transition-metal dichalcogenide platform. These results establish MoTe2 as a viable platform for tunable, low-noise, high-purity single-photon sources for quantum photonics. Two-dimensional transition-metal dichalcogenides are promising single-photon platforms but achieving photon indistinguishability remains challenging. Here, the authors realize reproducible near-infrared quantum emitters in bilayer MoTe2 with high purity, electrical tunability, and record indistinguishability.

papers.title: UMIche: a UMI-centric analysis platform for enhancing molecular quantification accuracy in bulk and single-cell sequencing
papers.abstract: Unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) are widely utilised in RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) technologies to eliminate polymerase chain reaction (PCR) duplicates, thereby improving the accuracy of molecular quantification. However, synthesis errors in UMIs during sequencing often compromise the reliability of UMI counting. While various computational methods have been developed for error correction, the lack of a unified benchmarking and validation framework impedes systematic evaluation and optimisation. Here, we present UMIche, an open-source, UMI-centric computational platform designed to enhance UMI-assisted molecular quantification. Its application to collapsing monomer and homotrimer UMIs across multiple bulk and single-cell sequencing protocols demonstrates effective PCR-duplicate removal. Across a broad spectrum of simulated and experimental datasets with ground truth, most UMI collapsing methods integrated into UMIche perform similarly under low-error conditions, whereas set-cover optimisation and majority voting show greater robustness as the UMI error profile becomes more pronounced. Together, these capabilities enable scalable UMI collapsing, systematic benchmarking, and method development to improve molecular quantification. Errors in unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) can distort molecule counts. Here, the authors present UMIche, a platform for benchmarking deduplication methods, and show that set cover and majority voting are more robust as barcode errors increase.

papers.title: Topographical mismatch sustains open microchannels in living soft tissue for non-destructive protein biopsy
papers.abstract: Sustaining open microchannels within living soft tissue has remained a problem of mechanics: implants rigid enough to maintain patent channels inflict inflammation, while implants compliant enough to avoid it are sealed within minutes by viscoelastic recoil. Here, we resolve this conflict through topographical mismatch—a deliberate geometric non-conformity between an ultrathin multi-lobed implant and the surrounding tissue. Engineered to exceed the conformability limit of skin, these conduits sustain patency for over 42 hours of sustained physiological deformation and for at least 7 days in living skin without triggering the mechanotransductive signalling that initiates fibrotic encapsulation, and transmit macromolecules of up to 70 kilodaltons through intact skin—surpassing the molecular weight ceiling of transdermal iontophoresis. In vivo, this access reveals that interstitial fluid concentration of a model protein peaks 4.7-fold higher than serum at 2 hours, inverts at 8 hours and rebounds by 24 hours, uncovering tissue-level pharmacokinetics inaccessible to blood sampling. Topographical mismatch establishes a generalisable design principle for sustained, biocompatible interfaces between soft devices and living tissue. Skin-attached devices can easily inflame or collapse. Here, the authors show a multi-lobed microneedle device that holds micron-scale conduits open for seven days, allowing repeated protein sampling from interstitial fluid

papers.title: Experience modifies the synaptome architecture in the developing and adult mouse brain
papers.abstract: Synaptome architecture describes the spatiotemporal distribution of highly diverse excitatory synapses throughout the brain. Whether and how this architecture is impacted by experience and sensory input is unknown. We found that environmental enrichment and monocular visual deprivation drive large-scale reconfiguration of excitatory synapse populations in more than one hundred regions of the mouse brain. Different experiences modify distinct subsets of synapse types and subtypes, with patterns aligned with protein turnover rates and connectome architecture. Similarity in experience-dependent reconfiguration during development and adulthood indicates shared mechanisms of synaptome adaptation across the lifespan. Our findings support a population-selection model in which experiences drive adaptation by selectively modifying synapse types and subtypes distributed across the brain. Experience-driven reconfiguration of synaptome architecture shares features with the response to aging, sleep deprivation, brain injury and genetic mutations, supporting a unifying principle of brain adaptation. The effect of experiences on brain-wide synapse populations is unknown. Here, the authors show that environment and visual input drive changes in excitatory synapse types and subtypes across the mouse brain during development and adulthood.

papers.title: Functionally divergent RHOA mutations drive peripheral T cell lymphoma development by engaging a common neomorphic pathway
papers.abstract: RHOA, a RAS superfamily member, is frequently mutated in peripheral T-cell lymphoma (PTCL). These mutations are puzzling because variants have opposite effects on conventional RHOA signaling: some (e.g., RHOAG17V) inhibit normal RHOA function, whereas others (e.g., RHOAC16R) are constitutively active. Here we show that all PTCL-associated RHOA mutants acquire a non-canonical VAV1-like activity that activates the transcription factor NFAT. This activity is mediated by complexes between mutant RHOA and the RAP1GDS1607 isoform, is enhanced by T-cell receptor stimulation, and requires components of the T-cell receptor–VAV1 pathway, including PLCγ1 and calcineurin. Unlike canonical RAS superfamily signaling, this neomorphic activity does not require prenylation, the lipid modification anchoring RHOA to membranes. Genetic or pharmacological disruption of this pathway impairs RHOA-mutant PTCL in mouse models and patient-derived cells. These findings explain how mutations with opposing canonical effects converge on a shared oncogenic mechanism and reveal a potential therapeutic vulnerability in RHOA-mutant PTCL. RHOA mutation variants, exerting opposite effects on canonical RHOA signaling, are associated with peripheral T-cell lymphomas (PTCL). Here, the authors show that different RHOA mutants share a neomorphic activity that activates the transcription factor NFAT to drive PTCL.

papers.title: Frequency-tagged fMRI reveals dual mechanisms of attentional enhancement and suppression
papers.abstract: Selective attention biases competition between concurrent visual inputs, yet its computational implementation in the human cortex remains unclear. Using frequency-tagged fMRI (ft-fMRI), we resolve how attention shapes the spatiotemporal dynamics of competing stimulus-driven responses at fine spatial scales. Distinct cortical populations exhibit either in-phase synchronization (target enhancement) or anti-phase synchronization (surround suppression) with attended stimuli. Population receptive field mapping reveals a target–surround organization, with in-phase populations biased toward the attended target and anti-phase populations biased toward the surrounding visual field. Directed attention uniformly amplifies surround suppression across the visual hierarchy, consistent with a distributed suppressive field, whereas modulation of target-related activity increases hierarchically from V1 to hV4. Critically, modulation of surround suppression, but not target enhancement, predicts behavioral performance. These findings dissociate the mechanisms of target enhancement and surround suppression and reveal the computational architecture underlying biased competition in the human cortex, converging with recent primate electrophysiology research. Rafeh et al. use frequency-tagged fMRI to demonstrate that selective attention relies on dual, independent neural mechanisms for target enhancement and surround suppression, elaborating on traditional unitary models of human visual attention.

papers.title: Normalized membrane ratio of TROP2 as a predictor of clinical outcomes with datopotamab deruxtecan in non-small-cell lung cancer
papers.abstract: Datopotamab deruxtecan (Dato-DXd)—a trophoblast cell surface antigen 2 (TROP2)-directed antibody–drug conjugate—has demonstrated efficacy in patients with advanced nonsquamous non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) ± actionable genomic alterations. However, TROP2 expression by pathologist assessment using conventional immunohistochemistry with visual scoring does not predict response to TROP2-directed antibody–drug conjugates in NSCLC. We developed TROP2 quantitative continuous scoring (QCS)—a fully supervised computational pathology approach that quantifies TROP2 expression in individual NSCLC cells and subcellular components from immunohistochemistry-stained slides. Using QCS to determine TROP2 expression at the tumor cell membrane and cytoplasm, normalized membrane ratio (NMR) was developed (ratio of membrane relative to membrane + cytoplasmic TROP2) in the biomarker-evaluable population of patients with advanced NSCLC in the TROPION-PanTumor01 study (n = 115). The TROP2 NMR cut-point was optimized and validated in patients with nonsquamous NSCLC without actionable genomic alterations (primary intended-use population, n = 221) in the biomarker-evaluable population (n = 352) of the TROPION-Lung01 trial. Association with clinical outcomes was assessed. Progression-free survival was longer in Dato-DXd-treated (median 7.2 versus 4.0 months; hazard ratio 0.40, 95% confidence interval 0.25–0.64) but not docetaxel-treated (median 4.1 versus 4.4 months; hazard ratio 0.94, 95% confidence interval 0.59–1.49) patients with TROP2 NMR-positive versus TROP2 NMR-negative samples (treatment by biomarker status interaction P = 0.0098), indicating that TROP2 NMR may be a predictive biomarker for Dato-DXd. This work developed and validated a computational pathology biomarker—the TROP2 normalized membrane ratio—that quantifies subcellular TROP2 localization and predicts improved progression-free and overall survival with datopotamab deruxtecan in patients with nonsquamous non-small-cell lung cancer lacking actionable genomic alterations.

papers.title: Lessons from recent investigator-initiated trials of gene-editing therapies in China
Advancing multimodal tools to decode organoid complexity
papers.abstract: Organoids are complex, miniaturized three-dimensional structures that replicate key biological features and functions of human tissues and organs. These characteristics make them powerful model systems for investigating tissue and organ development, homeostasis and regeneration; understanding disease mechanisms; and advancing drug development and personalized medicine. To fully harness their potential, it is essential to develop advanced tools capable of comprehensively profiling their intricate composition. In particular, cutting-edge technologies are needed to accurately characterize their genotypic and phenotypic profiles, including DNA, RNA, proteins and physiological functions. In this Review, we examine molecular and functional profiling methods for organoids, providing an overview of emerging techniques, recent advancements, future technologies, key knowledge gaps and challenges, and a framework for multimodal integration of methods. Additionally, we examine current barriers to progress and explore opportunities to refine organoid profiling methods with the aim of deepening our understanding of organoid biology. This Review examines the current state-of-the-art for organoid profiling and existing knowledge gaps in this area.

papers.title: PKA signaling controls ILC3 homeostasis and IL-23-mediated inflammation in the gut
papers.abstract: Group 3 innate lymphoid cells (ILC3s) are tissue-protective lymphocytes that are enriched in the healthy gut and depleted in gastrointestinal disorders. Here we created a single-cell atlas to define how ILC3s respond to distinct stimuli, observing that prostaglandin engages protein kinase A (PKA) to upregulate tissue-protective factors. In contrast, the canonical activator interleukin-23 (IL-23) decreased negative regulators of PKA, including PRKAR1A. Lineage-specific Prkar1a deletion reduced ILC3s and increased susceptibility to enteric infection in mice. PRKAR1A was not required in early life but continuously preserved ILC3 homeostasis in adults by restraining PKA activity. Overproduction of IL-23 was sufficient to reduce PRKAR1A in ILC3s and increase PKA signaling that provoked gut inflammation. Finally, ILC3s from the healthy human intestine expressed PRKAR1A, which was downregulated by IL-23 or in inflammatory bowel disease. These results demonstrate that regulated PKA signaling is essential for tissue-protective ILC3s, while IL-23 drives aberrant PKA signaling to elicit intestinal inflammation. Sonnnenberg and colleagues show that prostaglandin engages protein kinase A (PKA) and sustained PKA activation promotes the depletion of ILC3s. IL-23 can drive aberrant PKA signaling resulting in intestinal inflammation.

papers.title: Saturation genome editing of BRCA1 across cell types improves interpretation of variant pathogenicity
papers.abstract: Germline pathogenic BRCA1 variants predispose women to breast and ovarian cancer. Despite accumulation of functional evidence, over half of reported single-nucleotide variants in BRCA1 lack a definitive clinical interpretation. Furthermore, the consistency of variant effects across cell types remains largely unexplored. Here we performed saturation genome editing (SGE) of BRCA1 in HAP1 cells to score 4,113 previously unassayed variants. Additionally, we developed an SGE assay in human mammary epithelial cells (HMECs), allowing comparison of effects across cell lines, drug treatments and genetic backgrounds. We identified 538 variants impacting gene function through distinct mechanisms. HAP1 function scores discriminate between known pathogenic and benign variants with near-perfect accuracy. Intriguingly, however, nearly half of HAP1 loss-of-function variants scored neutrally in HMECs. We show that discordantly scored variants are hypomorphic and confer intermediate cancer risk. Overall, this work demonstrates how performing SGE across cell models improves the functional interpretation of rare variants. Saturation genome editing maps the functional effects of thousands of BRCA1 variants across two complementary cell models. Discordantly scored variants reflect the importance of context and provide insights for improving BRCA1 variant interpretation.

papers.title: Molecular echoes of a hot Earth
Temperature dependence of binding entropy drives evolution in LacI family proteins
papers.abstract: Proteins operate through ligand and solvent interactions governed by thermodynamics, yet the enthalpy–entropy trade-offs that guide functional evolution remain unclear. Although the evolution of ligand specificity has been well studied, the thermodynamic determinants that underlie changes in specificity are not well understood. Here we reveal a shift from entropy-driven binding in the most distant ancestor to the LacI/GalR family (LGF) of transcription factors, to enthalpy-driven binding in the most recent ancestor and extant LacI. The most distant ancestor is characterized by the ability to bind its ligand in an open and dynamic conformation. We propose that entropically driven binding is allowed by the presence of entropic reservoirs. This thermodynamic binding trade-off between the most distant and most recent ancestor is in accordance with the concept that ancient life existed in a hot environment, where higher temperatures enhanced entropically driven binding. This suggests that molecular binding mechanisms evolved not just for ligand specificity but to adapt to environmental pressures such as cooling temperatures where enthalpic binding modes are favored. Transcription factors of the LacI/GalR family have been diverging for over 2 billion years. Ancestral reconstruction, isothermal titration calorimetry and structural analysis have now been used to show that ligand binding switched from entropy-driven, in an ancient repressor that binds ligand in an open and disordered state, to enthalpy-driven and ordered in Escherichia coli LacI.

papers.title: A chemical key to the brain
FlAsH-ID enables live-cell photoproximity labeling with a short peptide tag
papers.abstract: Proximity labeling has emerged as a valuable tool for the interrogation of protein–protein and protein–RNA interactions. Almost all proximity labeling methods are deployed using large fusion proteins, which, while powerful in many contexts, can disrupt native biology or obscure important epitopes on the protein under study. Here we develop a photoproximity labeling method that is localized to a short 6-aa peptide sequence. Termed FlAsH-ID, this method uses the combination of the Tsien tetracysteine tag with the FlAsH dye for localized singlet oxygen generation. We demonstrate that this green-light-based method is nontoxic and can be used to label proteins within several cellular compartments. Lastly, we establish that FlAsH-ID can be deployed in primary CD8+ T cells to assess the interactome of the transcription factor RUNX3. Our results suggest this technique will expand the field of proximity labeling to small, functionally sensitive proteins in primary cells without perturbing their function. Commonly used proximity labeling methods implement large fusions of a protein of interest to a proximity labeling enzyme, which can block key protein interactions and disrupt native biology. Now, a method called FlAsH-ID has been developed that enables photoproximity labeling of a protein of interest using a 6-aa peptide tag to bind a small-molecule photocatalyst.

papers.title: A conformation-sensitive product inhibitor of HDAC1/2 potentiates WNT signaling
papers.abstract: Pharmacological enhancement of WNT/β-catenin signaling holds promises for tissue repair and regeneration. Here, we identify WNA1, an isoxazole-based small molecule, as a potent activator of WNT/β-catenin signaling. WNA1 stimulates β-catenin signaling in WNT-dependent manner and promotes skin hair growth in vivo. Intriguingly, WNA1 increases histone acetylation with minimal activity on uncomplexed recombinant histone deacetylases (HDACs), while conventional HDAC inhibitors exhibit minimal β-catenin-stabilizing activity. We demonstrate that β-catenin signaling is repressed by the HDAC1/2-containing NuRD complex and WNA1 enhances β-catenin signaling by selectively inhibiting HDAC1/2. Structural and biochemical analyses reveal that WNA1 is hydrolyzed by the HDAC1–MTA1 complex and its product is trapped in the foot pocket of HDAC1 in an inositol-hexaphosphate-dependent manner. HDAC1 mutants with reduced foot pocket abrogate WNA1-induced histone acetylation and β-catenin accumulation. These findings establish WNA1 as a conformation-sensitive, foot-pocket-anchored product inhibitor selectively targeting complex-bound HDAC1/2 and reveal a unique mechanism for HDAC1/2 inhibition and WNT potentiation. A small molecule was identified that boosts WNT signaling through selectively blocking complex-bound histone deacetylases 1 and 2 (HDAC1/2) as a product inhibitor, revealing a unique mechanism for HDAC inhibition and WNT potentiation.

Their experimental and clinical findings connect this pathway to coronary disease and highlight its potential relevance for antithrombotic therapy.

papers.title: Alternaria leaf spot-induced phyllosphere microbiota and metabolite interact to combat leaf spot disease
papers.abstract: Zhang et al. reveal a plant defense “relay” mechanism, whereby an induced response triggered by a foliar pathogen orchestrates the assembly of a specific phyllosphere microbiota that in turn triggers induced resistance to jointly combat further pathogen infection. This elucidates the intricacies of plant-pathogen-microbiota interactions and their ramifications for plant health.

papers.title: Conformationally driven negative chemotaxis in synthetic vesicles
papers.abstract: Chemotaxis—directed movement in response to environmental cues—is fundamental to biological systems but remains rare in artificial systems, where it typically relies on complex catalytic pathways or intricate adaptive designs. The molecular mechanisms underlying artificial chemotaxis are still scarce and poorly understood, posing challenges for the rational design of advanced artificial chemotactic systems. Here we present a minimal polymeric system that achieves negative chemotaxis through intrinsic conformational dynamics, enabling mechanical transduction and directional movement without the need for catalysis or external energy input. Our study uncovers a previously unrecognized molecular mechanism in which hydrophobic membrane domains dynamically reconfigure in response to chemical signals, triggering a cascade of events, from conformational rearrangements to interfacial tension alterations that generate self-sustained motile behaviour. By elucidating the interplay between membrane dynamics, interfacial forces and directional transport, our findings advance the molecular understanding of synthetic systems that emulate cytoskeletal remodelling in biological motility and establish a versatile framework for engineering functional artificial protocells with life-like behaviours. Achieving negative chemotaxis without catalytic designs remains challenging in artificial systems. Now it has been shown that intrinsic membrane conformational dynamics generate interfacial tension gradients, driving polymersomes away from a lactic-acid source without requiring external energy input.

papers.title: 16-h fasting optimizes cancer immunotherapy in mice and humans
First factor XIa inhibitor nabs FDA approval for stroke prevention
PARP1 revisited — integrating DNA repair, replication and therapeutics
papers.abstract: Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 1 (PARP1) is a central regulator of genome integrity and a major therapeutic target in cancer. It is a versatile reader of DNA and chromatin architecture, engaging canonical DNA strand breaks as well as replication-associated and non-canonical DNA structures, including unligated Okazaki fragments, stalled or reversed replication forks, G-quadruplexes, and R-loops. However, how PARP1 recognizes these diverse substrates, and whether they elicit distinct ADP-ribosylation outputs, remains unclear. In this Review, we propose that PARP1 does not respond to DNA damage as a uniform sensor but instead interprets lesion geometry, DNA topology and chromatin context, resulting in dynamic control of chromatin accessibility, repair-factor recruitment, replication fork remodelling, transcription–replication conflicts and PARP1 turnover at DNA lesions. This evolving understanding has important therapeutic implications. PARP inhibitor efficacy, toxicity and resistance are not determined solely by catalytic inhibition or by BRCA1 and BRCA2 status but reflect the combined effects of PARP1 retention, replication stress, repair-pathway choice, chromatin remodelling and tumour context. Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 1 (PARP1) is a versatile DNA damage sensor and a major therapeutic target in cancer. This Review discusses emerging insights into how PARP1 recognizes and responds to its varied substates, and the implications of these insights on the use of PARP inhibitors.

papers.title: Hierarchical design strategies for tuning genetic circuits
papers.abstract: Genetic circuit design is central to synthetic biology, yet achieving predictable and programmable circuit performance remains challenging due to diverse circuit- and host-dependent factors. Thus, a systematic perspective is needed to integrate these factors across multiple design layers. In this review, we establish a hierarchical framework for tuning genetic circuits as an engineering process spanning biological part design, DNA synthesis and assembly, carrier selection, host-cell implementation, and cross-host transfer. We further discuss how each layer contributes to circuit behavior and shapes trade-offs among key performance properties. By integrating hierarchical design strategies with iterative troubleshooting, this review provides a practical roadmap for tuning genetic circuits toward more predictable and reliable performance.

papers.title: Repurposing clofarabine against enteric pathogens via metabolic starvation
papers.abstract: Enteropathogenic and enterohaemorrhagic Escherichia coli (EPEC/EHEC) cause severe global diarrhoeal disease, exacerbated by rising antimicrobial resistance. Pathogenesis relies on "attaching and effacing" lesions, where bacteria generate actin pedestals to adhere, replicate, and destroy intestinal microvilli. To identify novel anti-virulence candidates targeting this process, we conducted a high-throughput phenotypic screen quantifying pedestal formation via high-content fluorescence microscopy. We identified the anticancer nucleotide analogue clofarabine as a potent inhibitor of EPEC growth and pathogenesis. Distinct from its oncology mechanism - inducing DNA chain termination and apoptosis - clofarabine competes with bacterial ATP-dependent processes to impede gene transcription, protein synthesis, and Type III Secretion System (T3SS) function. Remarkably, EPEC counteracts this inhibition by cleaving clofarabine, enabling restored protein synthesis and resumed growth. Furthermore, we report for the first time that clofarabine suppresses protein translation in human monocytes, suggesting an uncharacterised translational impact on mammalian cells. These findings reveal host and bacterial translation as interconnected vulnerabilities to purine antimetabolites, offering a novel strategy to disarm enteric pathogens while uncovering a bacterial enzymatic mechanism for neutralizing host-targeted therapeutics.

papers.title: The nucleus spatially partitions mechanoprotection and mechanosensing
papers.abstract: Mechanical forces shape cell behavior, but how the nucleus integrates its roles as genome protector and mechanosensor remains unresolved. Here, we dissect the spatiotemporal control of transcriptional response to forces during epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT). By combining genome-wide approaches, in vivo nuclear micromanipulation, and quantitative live imaging, we uncover two key properties of nuclear mechanosensing. First, mechanically induced changes in chromatin accessibility and transcription are spatially patterned within the nucleus: genes closest to deformations appear protected, revealing a local shielding mechanism associated with chromatin closure. Second, relocating a gene between chromatin environments is sufficient to alter its mechanosensitivity, challenging the concept of inherently force-sensitive genes. These findings demonstrate unexpected spatial partition of nuclear response to forces.

papers.title: Integrating Long-Read Structural Variant Analysis with single-nucleus RNA-seq to Elucidate Gene Expression Effects in Disease
papers.abstract: Structural variants (SVs) are a major source of genetic diversity, yet how they impact cell types in complex brain diseases remains largely unexplored, partially due to limitations of short-read sequencing. Here, we addressed this fundamental question in Parkinson's disease (PD). generating long-read whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data for 100 post-mortem brain samples from a PD cohort, constructing a high-confidence catalog of 74,552 SVs. To resolve their functional impact, we integrated single-nucleus RNA-sequencing data from two brain regions from the same samples and focused functional analyses on SVs proximal to genes previously nominated as cis-regulated, potential causal targets of PD-associated GWAS loci. Using expression quantitative trait locus and allele-specific expression analyses, we uncovered SVs significantly associated with expression in specific cell types as well as effects shared across cell types. This study demonstrates the power of uniting long-read WGS with transcriptomics to uncover SVs underlying complex disease architecture with cell type resolution.

papers.title: Functional Performance of Electrospun Tissue-Engineered Heart Valve Scaffolds Across Geometries Under Aortic Conditions
papers.abstract: Electrospun, bioresorbable polymer scaffolds are a promising platform for tissue-engineered heart valves (TEHVs) owing to their fibrous microstructure, tunable mechanics and capacity to support host-cell infiltration and remodeling. Recent in-vitro parametric studies of bioprosthetic heart valve (BHV) geometry have used silicone cast valves to link design parameters to hemodynamic performance and leaflet strain, but the functional behavior of electrospun whole-valve TEHV scaffolds across distinct leaflet geometries and clinically relevant aortic conditions remains poorly characterized. Here, we present an end-to-end workflow in which polycaprolactone (PCL) is electrospun directly onto parametrized, 3D-printed mandrels derived from two established analytical leaflet geometry models, yielding 21 whole-valve scaffolds across four geometries without cutting and assembling flat fiber sheets or suturing of flat fiber sheets. Fiber diameter, orientation and pore area were assessed by scanning electron microscopy and found to be consistent across scaffolds and geometries. Two scaffolds of each of four geometries were tested in a pulse duplicator under hypotensive, normotensive and hypertensive aortic conditions. All scaffolds opened and closed physiologically under all conditions, with a mean maximum geometric orifice area (GOA) of 44.5% of the valve area and a mean peak transvalvular pressure gradient of 10mmHg. Leaflet geometry had no apparent systematic effect on flow and pressure waveforms or on GOA. The mean regurgitant fraction was 82%, most likely due to leakage through the porous fiber network rather than incomplete leaflet closure. Electrospun whole-valve scaffolds thus achieve favorable leaflet kinematics at clinically relevant aortic conditions and the presented workflow provides a reproducible, parametric framework for their fabrication and translation toward regenerative heart valve replacement.

papers.title: A reformulation of the t-test in single-cell transcriptomics dramatically reduces false positives
papers.abstract: The default differential expression tests in single-cell analysis software provide fast and simple approaches that help practitioners annotate cell populations identified through clustering algorithms. Here, we use theoretical arguments and empirical studies to show that these tests suffer from inflated false positive rates that affect the resulting annotations. We introduce LN's t-test, which tests a novel, asymptotically unbiased log-fold change estimator and avoids these false positives, without compromising speed.

papers.title: Modulating inter-mitochondrial contacts to increase membrane potential for mitigating blue light damage
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) is essential for mitochondrial functions, yet current methods for modulating MMP lack precise spatial and temporal control. Here, we developed an optogenetic mitochondrial tethering system, termed OptoMitoTether, that enables reversible control of inter-mitochondrial proximity with high spatiotemporal precision. Blue light activation induced CRY2PHR oligomerization between adjacent mitochondrial outer membranes, reduced mitochondrial nearest-neighbor distances, and promoted inter-mitochondrial tethering. OptoMitoTether activation was associated with elevated MMP and was associated with lower reactive oxygen species (ROS) and preserved ATP production during prolonged blue light stress. Moreover, OptoMitoTether expression preserved mitochondrial bioenergetic function in human retinal cells and extended lifespan in C. elegans during chronic blue light exposure. These findings establish OptoMitoTether as a tool for manipulating mitochondrial proximity and reveal a link between inter-mitochondrial tethering and mitochondrial bioenergetic state during blue light stress.

papers.title: Time-Resolved Proteomics of a Polyglutamine-Expanded Huntingtin in vitro Cell Model Reveals Early RNA-Regulatory Compensation and Late Respiratory-Chain Remodeling
papers.abstract: Huntington disease (HD) is caused by a polyglutamine-expanded huntingtin protein that exerts progressive cellular toxicity. However, the temporal order of pathogenic events, and in particular which changes arise early and which emerge late, remains incompletely defined, despite their distinct therapeutic implications. To examine this trajectory, we profiled the proteome of a huntingtin-expressing cell model at early (72 h) and late (144 h) stages. Rather than a linear progression, the proteome changed in two distinct stages. At the early stage, cells showed increased abundance of RNA-processing, splicing, and protein-synthesis proteins, which may reflect an adaptive response to preserve gene-expression fidelity under stress. By the late stage, many of these proteins were depleted and mitochondrial energy-metabolism proteins dominated the response. Notably, 85% of proteins altered at both time points reversed direction between stages (95% at a false-discovery rate below 5%), and all reversals were supported by a significant genotype-by-time interaction, indicating that mutant huntingtin reorganizes the proteome rather than amplifying a fixed set of perturbations. Subunit-level analysis of the respiratory chain showed that Complex IV and ATP synthase subunits were reduced at 72 h, whereas at 144 h subunits of all five complexes were broadly increased, most strongly in Complex I and III, with a few distal subunits (COX5B, ATP5F1A, ATP5F1B) remaining reduced. Leveraging this proteomic map, we applied an AI-assisted, direction-aware drug repurposing strategy. Of 1,712 differentially abundant proteins, 498 were druggable, 109 had at least one agent whose mechanism was concordant with the required correction, and 89 of these 109 proteins mapped to at least one agent listed as approved in the source databases (56 to an agent with current regulatory approval). These included the approved Complex I inhibitor metformin, the investigational Complex I inhibitor ME-344, and pathway-level mitochondria-directed agents (elamipretide/SS-31, approved only for Barth syndrome; MitoQ, a dietary supplement), several of which have previously been evaluated in HD models. Collectively, these findings describe a two-stage proteomic response to mutant huntingtin in this cell model and suggest a putative early window for preclinical intervention testing, before late respiratory-chain remodeling is established.
affiliations: Gebze Technical University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Detection of bifidobacterial lipoproteins with anti-viral potential in donor human milk
papers.abstract: Background: Group B coxsackieviruses (CVBs) are involved in triggering type 1 diabetes. Free bifidobacterial lipoproteins (BLps) prevent CVBs cell infection. Our objective is to isolate free BLps potentially released by bifidobacteria in breastmilk and document their bioavailability. Methods: Bifidobacterium breve and B. longum were quantified by qPCR in samples donated to the hospitals biobank (DHM) within two weeks following delivery. BLps were captured onto CV B4, analyzed by SDS-PAGE and competitive ELISA. BLps transport through Caco-2 monolayers was monitored after DHM contact. Titration of anti-CV B IgA was carried out by ELISA. Results: Among the 90 enrolled donors, seven were excluded, 68 donated a unique sample and 15 donated multiple specimens (2 to 12). B. breve and B.longum were detected in 93.0 % and 32.8% unique DHM samples, respectively. The two species showed unstable counts in the multiple donation group. Although at highly variable amounts, BLps were readily detected. Free B.longum Lps were found in absence of B.longum itself. The BLps crossed the cell layer within 4h still binding CV B4. Conclusion: DHM contained BLps able to cross a cell layer mimicking the intestine still retaining their capacity to bind CV B. It suggested a possible newborns systemic protection against CV B4 infection that needs further investigation.
affiliations: University of Lille (corresponding author)

papers.title: Chemotaxis and motility of Achromatium oxaliferum in response to oxygen, sulfide, and nitrate
papers.abstract: Bacteria of the genus Achromatium are known for their large cell sizes and intracellular calcium carbonate deposits. Achromatium cells inhabit freshwater, brackish, and marine sediments where they accumulate to high abundances at the oxic-anoxic interface. These bacteria alter their vertical position in the sediment along with daily fluctuations in oxygen concentrations. Yet, the mechanism behind their migration in the sediment remains unknown. In this study, we used chemotaxis assays and time-lapse microphotography to analyze the motility and chemotactic behavior of Achromatium oxaliferum. Microscopic observations revealed that rolling and gliding were the main forms of locomotion exhibited by Achromatium. In absence of any stimulant, the movement appeared to be mostly random and changes in direction frequently occurred. Chemotaxis assays showed a negative response of Achromatium to oxygen, sulfide, and nitrate, as evidenced by the change from undirected to directed locomotion against the respective chemical gradient. For periods of more than 1 hour, Achromatium cells moved continuously towards regions of low concentration. We further show that the genetic repertoire of Achromatium corresponds to our observations. Based on lab experiments and bioinformatic analyses we propose that Achromatium motility is propelled by type IV pili guided by a plethora of chemo- and photoreceptors. We further suggest that Achromatium uses negative chemo- and phototaxis to confine their distribution in aquatic sediments between opposing oxygen and sulfide gradients. This allows Achromatium to dynamically adjust its position in redox gradients, and thus is likely to have a major contribution to its success in the global colonization of diverse aquatic sediments.
affiliations: Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries (IGB) (corresponding author)

papers.title: WHaloForce enables chemigenetic imaging of molecular tension in living cells and animals
papers.abstract: Piconewton forces borne by individual proteins within complex assemblies underlie cell adhesion, migration, and tissue morphogenesis, yet remain difficult to image in living systems. Here, we introduce WHaloForce, a chemigenetic HaloTag-based tension sensor that converts force-dependent relief of tryptophan-mediated dye quenching into a fluorescence lifetime change. Optical tweezers revealed a switch-like unquenching transition near 5 pN, and cellular measurements demonstrated dynamic responses to actomyosin activity. WHaloForce enabled quantitative tension imaging of diverse force-bearing proteins (vinculin, E-cadherin, -catenin, and laminin) in mammalian cells, mouse tissue, and C. elegans. Bright synthetic dyes made tension measurements possible at endogenous expression levels. In C. elegans, vinculin and laminin showed opposite tension patterns between tissues, highlighting tissue-specific force transmission through adhesions and the extracellular matrix. We also identified ovulation as a source of molecular loading within the spermathecal laminin network. WHaloForce thus offers a modular platform for imaging spatiotemporal tension patterns in living systems.
affiliations: Janelia Research Campus, Howard Hughes Medical Institute (corresponding author)

papers.title: Endogenous Mechanical Reporters Encode the Global Mechanical Landscape of Morphogenesis
papers.abstract: Developmental systems usually comprise multiple genetically programmed morphogenetic events within a mechanically continuous environment, yet how individual processes interact and contribute to the overall mechanical landscape remains unknown. Here, we introduce the concept of mechanical reporter: endogenous tissues function as in situ probes of the embedded mechanical landscape. We exemplified cephalic furrow (CF) migration as a mechanical reporter in gastrulating Drosophila. Using optogenetics and genetics, we revealed that CF displacement reflects the combined effect of both force and tissue mechanical properties. By incorporating condition-specific mechanical landscape into a continuum minimal-response model, we developed a framework to quantitatively predict the reporter dynamics. Using different genetic mutants, we successfully decoded changes in the mechanical landscape from CF dynamics in gastrulating Drosophila. Overall, we established a predictive framework that uses CF dynamics to infer changes in the global mechanical landscape. Beyond this, the concept of mechanical reporter provides a general strategy for systematically understanding and decoding complex mechanical environments in living systems.
affiliations: Westlake University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Replicative and chronological epigenetic age track genome instability in opposite directions across cancers
papers.abstract: Epigenetic clocks are widely applied to tumor tissue, yet clocks trained to predict chronological age and clocks built to count cell divisions measure different quantities, and how either relates to the heterogeneity of methylation change within a tumor remains unclear. Here we compare four mitotic clocks with Horvath pan tissue clock in 506 matched tumor and normal pairs from 13 adult solid cancers and in 1,731 pediatric tumors. We show that mitotic age is higher in the tumor than in matched normal tissue in every adult cancer type, and that this advance is robust to tumor purity and cell type composition. The advance is explained chiefly by global methylation change and cell composition, with tumor proliferation contributing a small component that generalises across cancer types only for stemTOC; beyond proliferation, mitotic clock advance is associated with tumor grade, stage and genome instability, whereas Horvath clock is not, or is inversely so. Horvath clock, by contrast, reads older in renal clear cell and thyroid tumors and younger in endometrial, lung squamous, head and neck and prostate tumors, while in children 98.1% of tumors return a Horvath age above chronological age. Neither clock family is associated, patient by patient, with the heterogeneity of methylation change once its global magnitude and purity are accounted for, and neither changes consistently between primary and relapse. Methylation change is enriched on the X chromosome in female tumors only, independently of X copy number. Our data indicate that replicative epigenetic age is near uniformly advanced in cancer and records tissue remodelling more than current proliferation, whereas chronological clock readings of tumors are specific to cancer type and do not report clonal diversification in bulk tissue.
affiliations: Lund University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Programmable amide bond formation using de novo ligases
papers.abstract: Amide bond formation is of central importance in the chemical industry, underpinning the synthesis of small bioactive molecules, macrocycles, peptides and their conjugates. Conventional methods of amide synthesis rely on stoichiometric coupling agents and costly protecting group manipulations. While biocatalysis can alleviate some of these challenges, enzymes typically operate across a narrow range of substrates and their adaptation to new coupling partners requires extensive engineering. Here we show that de novo amide ligases featuring a cysteine catalytic triad can be programmed computationally to operate across diverse substrate classes with high selectivity. We first designed complementary peptide ligases to selectively functionalise either the N-terminus or a single lysine residue of a polypeptide sequence containing 36 competing lysines. Crystal structures of both ligases show excellent agreement with the designs, with structural modelling suggesting that amidation outcompetes hydrolysis because the catalytically competent geometry forms only upon acceptor binding. We then extended our approach to the synthesis of small bioactive molecules by designing stereoselective ligases that mediate a key amide bonding forming step in the synthesis of the preventative HIV therapeutic lenacapavir. These results establish de novo enzyme design as a programmable platform for achieving selective amide bond formations across a wide range of molecular targets.
affiliations: Howard Hughes Medical Institute, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA. (corresponding author)

papers.title: SIFT: Syncmer-Informed Selection of Haplotypes for T2T Imputation
papers.abstract: Genome patching improves the completeness of fragmented assemblies by filling unresolved gaps with sequences from reference genomes. Pangenome panels provide diverse candidate haplotypes for this task, but identifying suitable references efficiently becomes increasingly challenging as these panels grow. We present SIFT, a compressed indexing method for selecting reference haplotypes for genome patching with ImpuT2T. SIFT combines closed-syncmer parsing, phrase-level indexing, and pseudo-maximal exact match (pseudo-MEM) queries. Closed syncmers provide a context-independent parsing rule with bounded distances between consecutive selected positions, enabling consistent parsing of reference and query sequences. We demonstrate that two closed syncmers determine the distance at which they can occur consecutively in any string, so that equal substrings of two parses represent identical sequences and no gap sequence need be stored. SIFT indexes the reference parse and its reverse using run-length compressed suffix arrays and adapts the Boyer-Moore-Li search procedure to identify pseudo-MEMs between the reference parse and query parse. It then aggregates matching evidence to identify candidate reference haplotypes for downstream patching. This framework connects compressed sequence indexing with haplotype selection and provides a basis for querying large reference panels at the phrase level. SIFT is publicly available under the GNU license at https://github.com/EddieFerro/SIFT.
affiliations: University of Florida (corresponding author)

papers.title: Assessing the Capacity of Genomic Language Models to Generate Informative Embeddings of Viral Genome Fragments
papers.abstract: Genomic language models (gLMs) trained on large volumes of nucleotide sequences are becoming an alternative to classical methods in metagenomic analysis, particularly for studying genomic "dark matter". In this work, we investigate the ability of four gLMs (DNABERT-2, DNABERT-S, ViraLM, and Evo2-7B) to generate taxonomically informative vector representations of short viral genome fragments. We constructed a balanced reference dataset of viruses based on the ICTV Virus Metadata Resource and compared the representations generated by gLMs with conventional k-mer profiles and MinHash sketches using clustering and neighborhood-based metrics (adjusted Rand index (ARI), precision@k, and CROSS precision@k). On the reference dataset, three of the four gLMs outperformed the 4-mer profile in terms of ARI and precision@5 under the same evaluation protocol. The best performance was generally achieved by intermediate model layers. Conventional k-mer profiles consistently outperformed MinHash sketches. We further evaluated the methods on two viral orders (egoviruses and mriyaviruses) absent from the reference dataset, with model layers and k-mer lengths selected exclusively on the reference dataset. DNABERT-S showed the most consistently strong performance across these two orders, ranking first on mriyaviruses and second on egoviruses, while k-mer profiles with Jensen-Shannon distance remained competitive. We also observed the consistency of representations between forward fragments and their reverse complements. Overall, the best-performing gLMs surpassed conventional baselines, although their advantage depended on the dataset and evaluation metric. The consistently strong performance of DNABERT-S suggests a potential benefit of contrastive fine-tuning and indicates that larger models are not necessarily more effective for generating taxonomically informative representations.
affiliations: Federal Research and Clinical Center of Physical-Chemical Medicine of Federal Medical Biological Age (corresponding author)

papers.title: zsasa: a Zig-based engine for high-throughput solvent accessible surface area at proteome scale
papers.abstract: Advances in structural and computational biology now yield structures by the hundreds of thousands, from predicted-structure databases to molecular-dynamics trajectories. Solvent accessible surface area (SASA), a long-established descriptor of protein stability, binding, and interfaces, remains central to their analysis. Established SASA tools are still widely used, but each covers only part of what such data now demand in input formats, outputs, and speed. We present zsasa, a fast, full-featured, open-source SASA engine for single structures, proteome-scale collections, and trajectories, usable from the command line or Python. It uses the same algorithms as established tools and owes its speed to the implementation, which makes full use of multicore processors and SIMD instructions while keeping memory use low. On a single laptop, zsasa reproduced FreeSASA, a widely used SASA library, down to individual atom areas on 4,370 Escherichia coli AlphaFold models. On the 23,586 structures of the human AlphaFold proteome, it was 3.3-fold faster than FreeSASA run in parallel while using a third or less of the peak memory of the other tools tested, and an optional approximate mode was 10-fold faster, with total SASA within 0.7% of the default results on average. On molecular-dynamics trajectories, it was 12- to 52-fold faster than MDTraj. As a demonstration, we computed interface burial for more than 600,000 predicted human protein dimers in under half an hour and found that a large buried area did not imply a confident predicted interface. zsasa is available under the MIT license at https://github.com/N283T/zsasa.
affiliations: Yokohama City University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Enhanced antitumour activity of combined PD-1 blockade and HER2-targeted therapy is associated with reduced epithelial-mesenchymal transition and extracellular matrix-remodelling signatures in gastric cancer
papers.abstract: Background The combination of PD-1 blockade, HER2-targeted therapy and chemotherapy improves outcomes in HER2-positive advanced gastric and gastro-oesophageal junction adenocarcinoma. However, chemotherapy can independently alter the tumour microenvironment, making the biological effects of PD-1 and HER2 targeting difficult to distinguish. We therefore investigated how PD-1 and HER2 blockade, alone and in combination, affect tumour growth and associated transcriptional programmes. Methods Immunodeficient NOG mice received human PBMCs by tail-vein injection. Three days later, NCI-N87 gastric cancer cells were implanted subcutaneously. Mice were randomised to vehicle, pembrolizumab, trastuzumab, or combination treatment. Tumour growth was assessed, and bulk RNA sequencing was used to identify treatment-associated changes in gene expression, pathway enrichment, and tumour, stromal, and immune cell-associated signatures. Results Combined treatment produced greater tumour growth control than either monotherapy. Trastuzumab-treated tumours showed enrichment of immune activation, epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), and TGF{beta}-associated signatures, whereas pembrolizumab alone produced a limited transcriptional effect. Combination treatment was associated with reduced proliferation, EMT, and stromal-remodelling signatures, alongside increased cytotoxic immune-associated signatures. Expression of extracellular matrix-associated genes, including VCAN, SPARC, POSTN, collagen genes, and FAP, was lower in combination-treated tumours. Complement-related transcriptional pathways were also enriched.
