Conclusions In this chemotherapy-free model, combined PD-1 blockade and HER2-targeted therapy was associated with greater tumour growth control, enrichment of cytotoxic immune-associated transcriptional signatures, and reduced EMT and extracellular matrix remodelling signatures. These findings provide hypotheses for further mechanistic validation.
affiliations: Southwest University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Curvature-based schedule ordering is preserved in homogeneous and heterogeneous tumors
papers.abstract: During treatment, dosing protocols with identical total dose may favor one schedule over another depending on how exposure is distributed over time. In homogeneous cell populations, Jensen's inequality has been shown to predict whether continuous or intermittent high-dose followed by low-dose is favored, based on the curvature of the concentration-effect function. Scheduling ordering can be performed based on curvature only: concave functions favor continuous dosing while convex functions favor intermittent dosing schedules with a high time-variance. However, tumors exhibit heterogeneous drug sensitivities, and treatment preferentially eliminates drug-sensitive cells, progressively shifting the surviving population toward greater drug resistance. Whether this treatment-induced selection can reverse curvature-based schedule ordering remains unclear. We develop a mathematical framework in which phenotypes share a common concentration-effect function but differ by fixed, nonnegative sensitivity scales. We prove that the ordering of equal-mean schedules is administrated solely by the scalar cumulative treatment effect, that is, by the curvature of the effect function alone. Consequently, baseline heterogeneity and treatment-induced selection can alter the magnitude of treatment response and the composition of surviving cells, but cannot reverse the ordering of equal-mean schedules predicted by the curvature of the single-cell concentration-effect function. This preservation holds across different temporal dosing profiles and repeated treatment cycles. Our work uncovers a general principle that curvature-based schedule ordering is preserved in heterogeneous tumors despite treatment-induced selection toward resistance.
affiliations: Moffitt Cancer Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: BAF complexes cooperate with lineage-restricted transcription factors to establish cell-state-specific regulatory programs
papers.abstract: BRG1/BRM-associated factor (BAF) complexes are essential regulators of chromatin organization and cell identity. Genes encoding BAF subunits are among the most frequently mutated in human cancer. Yet, how disruption of a single subunit gives rise to distinct tumor states remains poorly understood. Atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumors (ATRTs) provide a compelling model, as they are uniformly driven by bi-allelic loss of the BAF subunit SMARCB1, yet segregate into distinct molecular subtypes. Using integrated multi-omics profiling of patient-derived ATRT organoids and primary tumor tissues, we show that transcriptional and chromatin accessibility changes upon SMARCB1 reconstitution are directed by subtype- and lineage-specific transcription factor (TF) repertoires. Genome-wide binding and transcriptomic analyses reveal that SMARCB1 reconstitution enables the lineage-specific TF RFX4 to engage regulatory elements and activate neuronal differentiation programs, partially reprogramming ATRT-MYC toward an ATRT-SHH-like identity. Together, these findings demonstrate that SMARCB1 loss disrupts TF-dependent chromatin priming, revealing that the lineage-specific regulatory output of BAF complexes is constrained by the underlying TF repertoire.
affiliations: Princess Maxima Center for Pediatric Oncology (corresponding author)

papers.title: SilencioM: silencing connected interfering oligonucleotides against MAPT as a potential disease modifying therapeutic for tauopathies
papers.abstract: Tauopathies are a diverse group of neurodegenerative diseases whose pathogenesis involves brain accumulation of misfolded, pathological tau (Microtubule Associated Protein Tau, MAPT). More than twenty tauopathies have been identified thus far that collectively impact millions of people worldwide, of which the most common is Alzheimer's disease (AD). Despite substantial efforts to develop drugs for tauopathies, no effective treatments currently exist, highlighting the urgent need for therapeutics to combat these prevalent and ruinous neurodegenerative diseases. Strategies that target tau are likely to have the greatest impact since tau is the proximal cause of their pathogenesis. Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) have emerged as a powerful class of precision therapeutics that silence disease-causing genes through RNA interference with favorable safety profiles. Delivery challenges are rapidly being addressed, and siRNA-based approaches are poised to transform the therapeutic landscape of neurological diseases. In this study, we describe SilencioM (Silencing connected interfering oligonucleotides against MAPT) and show its efficacy in markedly reducing tau pathology after a single intracerebroventricular injection in PS19 mice, a mouse model of severe tauopathy. SilencioM targets human, primate, rat and mouse ortholog genes; thus, the same compound can proceed from efficacy studies to Investigational New Drug Application (IND)-enabling studies. SilencioM is simple to manufacture and is administered without encapsulation in lipid nanoparticles and without requirements for lipophilic conjugation, making it a promising candidate for further development as a novel therapeutic for tauopathies, including AD.
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cytotoxic CD4+ exTregs expressing KLRG1 retain immunosuppressive function in cancer
papers.abstract: The role of cytotoxic CD4+ T cells in cancer remains controversial, with both pro- and anti-tumor functionality described. Based on a prior observation that putatively cytotoxic KLRG1+ FoxP3- conventional T cells (Tconv) associated with tumor progression, we deeply investigated the phenotype and function of KLRG1+ Tconv in multiple murine tumor models and in human clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) specimens. We found KLRG1+ Tconv have a conserved, highly activated, terminally differentiated phenotype across species. In murine tumors, KLRG1+ Tconv resemble tumor-infiltrating regulatory T cells (Tregs) at both transcriptional and proteomic levels, upregulating a spectrum of exhaustion-related checkpoint receptors, producing IL-10 and granzyme B (GzmB), and silencing expression of IFN{gamma} and TNF. Functionally, KLRG1+ Tconv exhibited immunosuppressive function in ex vivo assays. Using an in vivo Treg fate mapping approach in tumor-bearing mice, we found a subset of KLRG1+ Tconv are derived from Tregs that have lost FoxP3 protein expression. Ex vivo functional assays demonstrated the exTreg component of the KLRG1+ Tconv compartment is responsible for IL-10 production and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine expression. In treatment studies, we found that KLRG1-targeted antibody-mediated depletion was more efficient than anti-KLRG1 blockade at slowing tumor growth and improving survival, with responses associating with depletion of intratumoral KLRG1+ Tconv and Tregs. In sum, our study discovered a novel conserved pathway of CD4+ T cell plasticity, wherein intratumoral, cytotoxic KLRG1+ CD4+ Tconv cells can be derived from Tregs and maintain immunosuppressive function, despite loss of FoxP3, and that KLRG1-targeted depletion may outperform KLRG1 blockade as an immunotherapeutic strategy in cancer.
affiliations: Mayo Clinic Arizona (corresponding author)

papers.title: Preclinical Development of Enterobacter ludwigii LS57, a Human-Derived Swarming Strain, as a Live Biotherapeutic Product for Inflammatory Bowel Disease
papers.abstract: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) remains an area of major unmet need, and the undefined composition and manufacturing burden of fecal microbiota transplantation have motivated a shift toward single-strain Live Biotherapeutic Products (LBPs). Swarming bacteria are enriched in the stressed gut and limit mucosal damage, but no human-derived swarming strain has been developed as an LBP. We therefore report the complete preclinical development of Enterobacter ludwigii LS57, a swarming strain isolated from human feces. Chemistry, Manufacturing and Controls (CMC) covered a three-tier cell bank, 30 L fed-batch fermentation and a colon-targeted enteric-coated capsule, enabling consistent pilot-scale production. No treatment-related findings emerged in safety pharmacology (Sprague-Dawley rats) or in single-dose and Good Laboratory Practice (GLP)-compliant 1-week repeat-dose toxicity studies (Sprague-Dawley rats and Beagle dogs). LS57 was identified as E. ludwigii by 16S rRNA and whole-genome sequencing and produced metabolites with reported anti-inflammatory activity in culture. In Dextran Sulfate Sodium (DSS)-induced colitis, LS57 reduced weight loss, preserved colon length, lowered colonic pro-inflammatory cytokines and remodeled the gut microbiota. It also attenuated Trinitrobenzene Sulfonic Acid (TNBS)-induced colitis and enhanced the effect of ciclosporin A. In vitro, LS57 was non-hemolytic, non-cytotoxic, and acid-labile, formed no biofilm, and its resistance to aminopenicillins, cephamycins and imipenem was not transferable by conjugation. In vivo, LS57 colonized the inflamed colon without translocation in wild-type and interleukin-10-deficient mice, and experimental bacteremia was treatable with gentamicin or levofloxacin. LS57 combines efficacy across two mechanistically distinct colitis models with a safety package that addresses the principal regulatory concerns for LBPs, and a scalable manufacturing process, compatible with current good manufacturing practice, in which enteric coating overcomes the strain's poor gastric survival. These data support clinical development of LS57 in IBD.
affiliations: Fudan University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Hyaluronic acid dynamics are regulated by neural crest cells and NEDD4 in the developing cardiac outflow tract valves
papers.abstract: The extracellular matrix (ECM) is essential for cardiac valve development, with hyaluronic acid (HA) playing a critical role in cardiac cushion formation. While HA is required for atrioventricular valve development, its role in semilunar valve formation remains poorly understood. The ubiquitin ligase NEDD4 is essential for cardiac outflow tract development, particularly within cardiac neural crest cells, however its role in semilunar valve development has been unexplored. Here, we demonstrate that neural crest-specific deletion of NEDD4 in mice disrupts outflow tract valve development, resulting in abnormal leaflet number and morphology. Analysis of valve ECM revealed a specific reduction in HA within the neural crest-derived valve mesenchyme, while other ECM components such as fibronectin and versican remained unaffected. In contrast, deletion of NEDD4 in endocardium-derived valve mesenchyme did not alter HA abundance. Using NEDD4-deficient neural crest cells, we further demonstrate a cell-autonomous requirement for NEDD4 in regulating HA abundance, with in vitro evidence supporting impaired HA synthesis rather than increased turnover of HA in the ECM. Our findings identify a previously unrecognised role for NEDD4 in regulating HA synthesis in cardiac neural crest cells, revealing a cell-type-specific mechanism governing semilunar valve development and highlighting distinct cellular requirements for ECM regulation across cardiac valve populations.
affiliations: Adelaide University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Impacts of Environmental Nickel and Chromium Exposure on the Blood Proteome of House Sparrows (Passer domesticus) in New Caledonia
papers.abstract: New Caledonia holds some of the world's largest ultramafic mineral deposits, and nickel (Ni) smelting operations have created a gradient of Ni and chromium (Cr) contamination across the archipelago. Molecular impacts of Ni and Cr toxicity on wildlife remain largely unexplored. Here, we used the house sparrow (Passer domesticus) as a sentinel species to characterise the blood proteomic response to Ni and Cr exposure near the Doniambo smelter in Noumea. Blood was collected from 52 free-living sparrows across 18 sites classified by soil metal concentration. Plasma and blood cell pellet fractions were analysed by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). Plasma proteomics identified histidine-rich glycoprotein (HRG) as the most prominent responder, with approximately 2.1-fold elevation in exposed relative to low-exposure birds. HRG contains a conserved histidine-rich region that binds cations including divalent nickel, and paired plasma-liver analysis confirmed hepatic-driven synthesis. Blood cell pellet proteomics revealed that Ni-Cr co-exposure predominantly disrupts the nuclear compartment: histone depletion indicated chromatin collapse, NUP153 dysregulation impaired nuclear pore function, and VRK1/TRIP13 upregulation suggested DNA damage response activation coupled with mitotic checkpoint override. Concurrent RNA processing collapse (DDX17, DHX15, RBMX, ALYREF) and changes in telomere-associated proteins (TERF2IP, hnRNPA1 and VRK1) implicated disrupted genome maintenance. These findings identify HRG as a candidate plasma biomarker of Ni-Cr exposure and reveal a coordinated nuclear toxicity signature linking heavy metal contamination to DNA damage and epigenetic disruption in a free-living vertebrate.
affiliations: Macquarie University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Single-Component Photo-Crosslinked Lipoic Acid Functionalized Mucin Hydrogels: Dynamic Mucus Mimetics for Antiviral Protection
papers.abstract: Native mucus protects epithelial surfaces through viscoelastic networks of disulfide-linked mucins. However, commercially available mucins often fail to reconstitute comparable mechanical and barrier properties, while synthetic and hybrid mucus mimetics require polymeric crosslinkers that may alter mucus-like composition. Inspired by the native architecture, we directly functionalized porcine gastric and bovine submaxillary mucins with -lipoic acid to develop a single-component, photo-crosslinkable hydrogels. Upon UV irradiation (365 nm), the modified mucins rapidly form disulfide-crosslinked networks without added photo-initiator/ polymeric crosslinkers, two orders of magnitude faster as compared with PEG-SH approaches. The resulting mucin-lipoic acid (MUC-LA) hydrogels exhibit mucus-relevant properties, including tunable viscoelasticity, redox responsiveness, self-healing, and size-dependent restrictions on nanoparticle transport. In transwell-based infection models, MUC-LA hydrogels (2-3%) mimicking the healthy airway mucus (G' {approx} 10-20 Pa) suppress epithelial infection by SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A virus. Crosslinked MUC-LA provides greater protection against SARS-CoV-2 than the non-crosslinked, whereas both formulations suppress influenza A infection, suggesting distinct contributions from network formation and mucin-associated interactions. These findings establish a dynamic, mucus-mimetic platform integrating rapid photo-gelation, controllable mechanics, selective transport, and antiviral barrier functionality. MUC-LA hydrogels offer opportunities to investigate mucosal transport and host-pathogen interactions, with potential applications in drug delivery, and as biomaterials.
affiliations: Academia Sinica (corresponding author)

papers.title: Basic-peptide depletion and precursor masking in bottom-up proteomics
papers.abstract: Biomarker proteomics studies report protein identities at the canonical precursor level, yet the underlying mass-spectrometry evidence consists of peptides whose physicochemical properties may diverge from the annotated protein. We reanalyzed peptide-level evidence from public datasets with a proteoform-aware pipeline that maps detected peptides to canonical sequences under a five-level confidence taxonomy, computes sequence-derived physicochemical features for precursors, peptides, and detected regions, and tests class-composition bias against digestion-matched backgrounds. Across ten public studies spanning five result-file formats and 70,020 peptide-evidence rows, detected peptides are depleted in the basic isoelectric-point class relative to their own proteins' theoretical tryptic peptides (fixed-effect odds ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.44-0.46; leave-one-study-out envelope 0.44-0.49). The depletion is absent among fully tryptic peptides (OR 1.06) and concentrates in missed-cleavage peptides (OR 0.62-0.57), is invariant to detected-abundance stratification, and retains its direction under three independent pI-calculator models. Case studies reveal both directions of precursor-centric masking. Two orthogonal validations ground the framework: a digestion-free synthetic-peptide analysis (basic-class odds ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.71-0.76 under standard DDA) and a paired top-down benchmark, in which detected regions recover top-down sequence space (90% of spans overlapped) but do not delimit proteoform boundaries (8% containment). Pipeline, data, and code are public.
affiliations: William Harvey Research Institute, Faculty of Medicine and Dentistry, Queen Mary University of London, Charterhouse Square, London EC1M 6BQ, UK; Barts Health NH (corresponding author)

papers.title: Pocket similarity guided selection of protein targets for systematic protein ligand dataset generation
papers.abstract: The scarcity of large, diverse, and unbiased protein ligand binding datasets limits the performance of machine learning approaches in drug discovery, particularly for understudied proteins. The Target 2035 initiative aims to address this gap by generating open-access binding data for more than 2,000 human proteins, a goal whose value depends on maximizing the diversity of the selected targets. Because proteins with different folds can share chemically analogous binding sites, we reasoned that pocket similarity, rather than sequence or fold similarity, is the appropriate criterion for selecting representative targets that maximize coverage of the human pocketome. Here, we use PocketVec, an alignment-free descriptor of binding sites, to map the human globular pocketome, identifying 51,535 predicted druggable pockets across 15,559 proteins. A two level hierarchical clustering, first within protein families and then across the whole proteome, grouped these pockets into 1,865 clusters of chemically similar binding sites. After discarding 533 clusters containing pockets with known ligands, we selected the 100 most populated of the remaining 1,332 ligand free clusters and chose two high quality representative pockets per cluster, ranked by their resemblance to known ligand-binding sites. Finally, we implemented two complementary prioritization strategies, one favoring structurally unexplored proteins and the other proteins amenable to experimental follow up, and selected 200 pockets from 100 different clusters from each strategy, with 89 clusters in common. Both selections cover over 10,000 pockets in ~5,600 proteins, approximately 36% of the human proteins with annotated druggable pockets, which represents a 2.8- to 4.4-fold increase in the number of covered pockets, domains, and proteins than random selection baselines. This pocket based framework offers a principled strategy to select diverse targets for Target 2035 and other large scale protein ligand data generation efforts in chemical biology.
affiliations: Institute for Research in Biomedicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Detection of Maximal Exact Matches in Terabases of Genome Assemblies in Compressed Space and Sublinear Time
papers.abstract: Detection of long exact matches between a pair of genomes has historically been a fundamental operation in genomics. Similarly, detection of long exact matches between all pairs of haplotypes in a large panel of genotyping array data or whole-genome sequencing variant calls is a fundamental operation in population genetics. Thanks to various recent pangenome efforts, for the first time, large panels of high-quality genome assemblies are being constructed. Therefore, we propose the intersection of these two approaches: detection of long exact matches between all pairs of assemblies in panels of hundreds to thousands of high-quality assemblies. Since these datasets would contain trillions of basepairs, practically detecting all exact matches requires algorithms operating in at most linear time and compressed space. Previous methods such as Mumemto achieve this, but running them on terabase-sized pangenomes still took very large space and long time. Here, we describe more efficient algorithms for outputting all long exact matches between all pairs of assemblies in compressed space and sublinear time given a compressed index of the panel. Given the construction of an O(r) space compressed index--a one-time cost that can be done in compressed space and close to linear time with previous work--we describe three algorithms taking O(r) words of memory: (1) computing all supermaximal exact matches (SMEMs) in O(r) time, (2) computing all supermaximal exact matches and their occurrences in O(r + occ) time, and (3) computing all maximal exact matches (MEMs) in O(r + occ) time, where r is the number of runs in the Burrows-Wheeler transform of the panel of assemblies and occ is the number of occurrences or matches outputted. Our algorithms use 7.5 times less memory than state-of-the-art competitors on a dataset of human centromere assemblies from 625 haplotypes. They are also 20 times faster if index construction time is counted, and 2,500 times faster if index construction is excluded. Finally, we perform an analysis of all-vs-all MEMs in all well-assembled centromeres of the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium Release 2 dataset that reveals multiple novel insights into structural variation in centromeres. For example, we find that the active -satellite higher-order repeat (HOR) array of Chromosome 2 is flanked by a ~200 kbp inversion on one side and a ~200-300 kbp pseudopalindromic sequence on the other. We also detect large segmental duplications in the centromere of every chromosome except Chromosome Y. These segmental duplications range in size from hundreds of kbp to multiple Mbp and occur both in and out of the active -satellite HOR arrays. Our computational results make pairwise MEM analyses possible in pangenomes, while our biological results show they are likely to be useful. Our algorithms are implemented as TeraMEM in the TeraTools suite available at https://github.com/ucfcbb/TeraTools.
affiliations: Dana-Farber Cancer Institute (corresponding author)

papers.title: CellChat Hotspot: A Targeted Approach to Cell Cell Communication Analysis With Spatial transcriptomics Validation.
papers.abstract: Abstract. In recent years, single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA seq) has enabled the investigation of intercellular communication through Cell Cell Communication (CCC) tools such as CellChat. Despite their potential, these approaches remain challenging to interpret, particularly when global analyses generate complex interaction networks that may include biologically irrelevant signals. To address this limitation, we developed a framework termed CellChat Hotspot, designed to improve the biological interpretability of inferred communication networks. This approach integrates gene set enrichment analysis with a context driven filtering strategy, selecting both genes and cells based on their functional relevance prior to communication inference. Applied to stage II colon cancer data, CellChat Hotspot enabled the identification of condition-specific interaction patterns associated with recurrence. Non recurrent patients showed enrichment of immune related processes, whereas recurrent cases were characterized by pathways associated with invasion and metastasis. Notably, a loss of interaction in the HSPG pathway between CALB1+ and stromal cells was observed in recurrent patients, suggesting a potential disruption of cell matrix adhesion mechanisms. To verify the reliability of this finding, we applied the framework to spatial transcriptomics data, which confirmed the presence of the HSPG2 DAG1 interaction in non-recurrent tumors and its near absence in recurrent ones. Overall, this framework provides a biologically guided strategy for studying intercellular communication in complex systems such as the tumor microenvironment.
affiliations: IRCCS "Istituto Tumori Giovanni Paolo II" (corresponding author)

papers.title: Quantifying electro-osmotic flow in mutant MspA nanopores
papers.abstract: Nanopores have emerged as a powerful tool for single-molecule sensing and sequencing. In a typical nanopore experiment, a charged analyte such as DNA is driven through the pore by an electrophoretic force generated by the applied electric field. This can be problematic, however, when analytes such as proteins carry mixed charges. An alternative driving force can be from electro-osmotic flow (EOF), the water flow that arises from an asymmetric migration of cations and anions through the nanopore. However, despite much recent interest, there is no straightforward experimental method to quantify EOF in nanopores. Here, we trap a dipolar peptide in an MspA nanopore, where studying its escape rate versus voltage allows us to extract the work done by the EOF in various MspA mutants and wildtype MspA compared to a M2-MspA reference. For the 30 amino acid model peptide, this yields values of ~5.6-16.7 kBT for the work done by the EOF at 80 mV. Finite-element simulations confirm the trends observed in the experiments. Charged mutations close to the nanopore's constriction site are found to produce the highest EOF. Our novel method provides a quantitative metric of the EOF in nanopores, opening up its study and broad use in future nanopore sequencing and sensing applications.
affiliations: Kavli Institute of Nanoscience Delft (corresponding author)

papers.title: An auditable harness for biomolecular dynamics simulations by AI agents
papers.abstract: AI agents now generate biological hypotheses faster than they can be tested. Hypotheses stated at the atomic level can be examined with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. For new questions without a reference, trust in an agent-run simulation rests on a tool-written process record, not the agent's account. Existing MD agents leave this record to the language model. Here we present MDClaw, a harness whose validating tools and directed acyclic graph (DAG) check stages before execution and record every simulation stage. On MDDataBench, which grades outputs against deposited simulations, four open-weight models with MDClaw passed all three runs on 81-100% of 31 test systems. The DAG complements this outcome check. An ablation without the DAG revealed 11 successful runs that had skipped minimization or equilibration, or simulated a different structure. MDClaw carried questions from human and AI scientists through simulation to trajectories traceable to their inputs and settings.
affiliations: RIKEN Center for Computational Science, Kobe, Japan; Graduate School of Science and Engineering, Saitama University, Saitama, Japan (corresponding author)

papers.title: Design of colipids with controlled lateral distance of head group moieties for targeting strategies in the field of lipid-based nanoparticles
papers.abstract: Lipid nanoparticles and liposomes are nanoparticle drug formulations which are firmly established in clinics. In order to expand their application and improve efficacy, surface modifications can be a key strategy, especially for cell specific targeting. Targeting can be achieved by integrating ligand functionalized lipids or lipidoids on the nanoparticle surface. In this case, not solely the targeting ligand itself, but also the structure of the whole targeting lipid/lipidoid can affect the interaction of the targeting ligand with the binding motive on cells. Especially, distal spacer structures between lipid anchor and ligand unit, often composed of polyethylene glycol chains, provide a certain distance of the ligand from the nanoparticle surface. A concept which is currently neglected is the control of the lateral distance between ligand structures on the nanoparticle. Herein we investigated the possibility to design lipidoids with a lateral spacer composed of polyethylene glycol units. We synthesized and characterized different lipidoids which provide a primary amine in the head group for possible ligand coupling. In our model lipidoids the head groups were functionalized with a paramagnetic probe to apply electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) methods for the characterization of the lipidoid interaction with model nanoparticles, in our case liposomes. Continuous wave EPR was used to study the efficiency of the novel lipidoids to integrate into lipid bilayers of model liposomes, which was shown to depend on lipidoid structure and liposome composition. Furthermore, using double electron-electron resonance (DEER), we observed lipidoid conformational changes occurring upon integration into liposomes.
affiliations: University of Leipzig (corresponding author)

papers.title: Beyond Sequence and Structure: Pretraining PLMs on Continuous Biophysical Fields
papers.abstract: We introduce the Biophysical Transformer, a protein language model that adds continuous biophysical fields as a third pretraining signal beside sequence and structure. A Poisson-Boltzmann solver computes the electrostatic potential around each three-residue token, and the model learns to predict it from sequence alone. A rotationally invariant spherical-harmonic descriptor serves as the loss target, eliminating the need for frame alignment during training and for coordinates at inference. Against a matched, one-flag control on the FLIP Meltome thermostability benchmark, the field objective raises Spearman correlation on every trained head of both human splits.The gain on human survives residualizing dipeptide composition under two architecturally different readouts and survives removing the test proteins that overlap the pretraining corpus. No effect survives on the organism-mixed split. At 1.1M parameters, both the Biophysical Transformer and its sequence-only control exceed FLIP's one-hot CNN and untrained-ESM baselines on every split. All results rest on a single pretraining run per arm,and the current design does not separate field content from generic regularization.
affiliations: Mayo Clinic (corresponding author)

papers.title: B cells dominate the heart immune infiltrate during chronic infectious cardiomyopathy
papers.abstract: Recent advances in single-cell and spatially resolved multi-omics have revolutionised our understanding of the cellular and molecular niches governing cardiac homeostasis and acute injury. However, the immune-stromal networks sustaining long-term, chronic heart pathology remain poorly defined, largely due to a paucity of physiologically relevant experimental models. Here, through a side-by-side multi-omic comparison of Trypanosoma cruzi-infected mouse models displaying contrasting degrees of chronic myocardial pathology and fibrosis, we define the long-term cellular landscape of the inflamed fibrotic heart. We reveal that class-switched, antibody-secreting plasma B cells represent the predominant immune subset infiltrating the fibrotic myocardium. CellChat intercellular communication modelling identifies plasma cell-fibroblast crosstalk as the strongest immune-stromal interaction in the fibrosis-prone heart, driven by predicted matrix anchoring (CD44-collagen/laminin) and molecular survival axes (App-Cd74, C3-Cr2). Supporting these computational predictions, immunofluorescence and spatial profiling confirm close proximity between plasma B cells and fibroblasts, alongside a striking accumulation of B cells embedded within extracellular matrix-rich cardiac scars. This localised B cell response maintains prominent pools of parasite-reactive and heart-autoreactive antibody-secreting cells despite a lack of detectable parasite signal in their immediate micro-vicinity. Together, these findings identify a matrix-associated plasma B cell-fibroblast niche as a central driver of chronic cardiac remodelling, revealing how persistent tissue scarring can become decoupled from direct local pathogen presence.
affiliations: York Biomedical Research Institute and Hull York Medical School, University of York, York, UK (corresponding author)

papers.title: HCMV glycoprotein B, but not the pentameric complex, is a key target of antibody-mediated phagocytosis
papers.abstract: Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is a leading infectious cause of birth defects globally with devastating fetal health outcomes, and there is currently no HCMV vaccine available. Glycoprotein B (gB) and the pentameric complex (PC) are immunodominant HCMV envelope proteins and candidates of interest in vaccine development due to their ability to elicit strong anti-HCMV neutralization responses. Recent evidence implicates non-neutralizing antibody functions in protection from vertical HCMV transmission, but the involvement of gB and PC in these responses remains incompletely understood. We evaluated immune responses against HCMV elicited by a gB protein subunit vaccine with and without PC in a preclinical rabbit study. Despite improved neutralization and inhibition of cell-associated viral spread, the inclusion of PC did not enhance antibody-mediated phagocytosis or Fc{gamma}R activation against HCMV virions or infected cells compared to gB alone. We additionally found a reduction in phagocytosis function by an HCMV hyperimmune globulin when blocked against gB, but not PC, suggesting that gB is a target of phagocytosis-mediating antibodies while PC is not. Given that antibody-mediated phagocytosis but not neutralization has been associated with protection from vertical HCMV transmission, these findings support the continued assessment of gB, but not PC, as a vaccine antigen for the prevention of vertical transmission via non-neutralizing antibodies to reduce the congenital HCMV burden worldwide.
affiliations: Department of Pediatrics, Weill Cornell Medicine, New York, NY (corresponding author)

papers.title: Structural and functional characterization of polyclonal antibody responses reveals shared and distinct antigenic features of RSV and hMPV fusion proteins
papers.abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and human metapneumovirus (hMPV), members of the Pneumoviridae family, circulate widely and are leading causes of hospitalization for acute respiratory infections in infants and older adults. The viral fusion (F) protein in its prefusion (preF) conformation is the primary target of neutralizing antibodies, yet how naturally elicited circulating polyclonal antibodies are distributed across its antigenic landscape remains poorly understood. Here, we combined serological profiling, site-specific antibody competition assays and electron microscopy-based polyclonal epitope mapping (EMPEM) to characterize preF-directed immunity to RSV and hMPV in healthy adults. All donors exhibited detectable preF-binding antibodies that positively correlated with virus neutralization and broadly recognized multiple antigenic sites, consistent with immunodominance patterns predicted by a surface-centric computational model. Despite this overall similarity, the distribution of responses across individual antigenic sites differed between RSV and hMPV. EMPEM analyses revealed consistent targeting of the highly neutralization-sensitive preF apex (site O) in both viruses, alongside less abundant responses against equatorial and upper-middle epitopes (sites II, III, IV and V). We additionally observed antibody-bound destabilized preF, supporting a model in which antibody binding promotes transient opening of the preF trimer and may interfere with the conformational rearrangements required for membrane fusion. Together, these findings highlight apex-directed antibodies as a prominent feature of naturally acquired pneumovirus immunity in adults and reveal both shared and distinct patterns of antigenic recognition that may inform next-generation vaccine design and antibody-based prophylactics.
affiliations: Karolinska Institutet (corresponding author)

papers.title: Tetravalent dengue mRNA vaccination orchestrates balanced four-serotype immunity with durable memory and protection in mice.
papers.abstract: An effective dengue vaccine must establish durable immunity across four dengue virus (DENV) serotypes, evade antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE), and overcome immune imprinting from prior exposure. Here, we developed TetprM-E mRNA-LNP, a tetravalent vaccine comprising LNP-formulated nucleoside-modified mRNAs encoding DENV1-4 precursor membrane-envelope (prM-E) antigens, and evaluated its immunogenicity, durability, protection and breath across serotype-specific immune backgrounds. Three immunization strategies elicited neutralizing titers greater than 1:1500 against each serotype. Passive transfer of immune sera conferred 100% survival and reduced viremia after lethal DENV2 challenge in immunocompromised mice. Vaccination induced DENV envelope (env)-specific CD8+T cells and CD4-dependent germinal-center responses. DENV env-binding antibodies persisted for 34 weeks alongside DENV env-specific memory B cells. Vaccine-elicited sera showed no measurable in vitro ADE. Although monovalent priming initially biased antibody responses, TetprM-E mRNA-LNP vaccination broadened neutralization across DENV1-4 regardless of priming serotype. Together, TetprM-E mRNA-LNP elicits broad, durable, and protective immunity despite serologic constraints from pre-existing immunity.
affiliations: Yale School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: The antagonism of sex chromosomes and sex hormones dictates outcomes in Th17 cell-mediated central nervous system autoimmunity.
papers.abstract: Biological sex traits are shaped by the combined effects of both sex hormones and chromosomes. How these factors interact in sex-related autoimmune diseases, such as multiple sclerosis (MS), has been a subject of intense recent interest. Here, using the Four Core Genotype (FCG) mouse model, in which these two variables can be disentangled, we describe an antagonism between sex hormones and chromosomes that potently influences outcomes in T helper 17 (Th17)-driven progressive central nervous system (CNS) autoimmunity. Male gonadal hormones dampen disease severity, irrespective of sex chromosome complement, by promoting a Wnt/{beta}-catenin signaling program associated with a homeostatic, non-pathogenic Th17 phenotype. By contrast, XY chromosomal complement exacerbates Th17 pathogenicity in a recipient sex-dependent manner; we identify the X-linked molecule SUV39H1 as an inhibitor of inflammatory Th17 cell function. Unexpectedly, we found that hormonally and chromosomally female FCG Th17 cells induced far more severe disease than WT female counterparts despite being genetically identical, pointing to a parental imprinting effect in dictating Th17 cell pathogenicity. These latter investigations uncovered Runx2, a transcription factor previously linked to developmental programs, as a novel negative regulator of the pathogenicity of Th17 cells. Together, our findings establish biological sex as a multilayered regulator of Th17 pathogenicity, revealing distinct and sometimes opposing contributions of hormones, chromosomes, and parental inheritance.
affiliations: axe Neurosciences, Centre de recherche du CHU de Québec-Université Laval, Pavillon CHUL, 2705 boulevard Laurier, Quebec City, QC G1V 4G2, Canada (corresponding author)

papers.title: A G-Quadruplex Containing First Intron Harbors a Functional Polyadenylation Signal in TP53
papers.abstract: First introns of mammalian genes are often longer than other introns and may contain regulatory elements, suggesting that they may have roles in gene regulation. We detected a previously unannotated, low abundance intronic transcript, TP53-INT1, using long-read direct RNA sequencing data. TP53-INT1 has low coding potential and terminates within the first and longest intron of TP53. The transcript structure and 3'-end were validated by independent experimental and in silico evidence. We identified a canonical polyadenylation signal upstream of the transcript termination site and demonstrated its functionality using reporter assays. Furthermore, a potential G-quadruplex (G4)-forming sequence was identified upstream of this polyadenylation signal. The G4-forming potential was confirmed using spectroscopic and thermal stability analyses. Complementing the in vitro characterizations, treatment with Pyridostatin, a G4-stabilizing drug, was associated with decreased TP53 expression. Together, these findings characterize a previously unannotated TP53 intronic transcript and reveal a local genomic context combining accessible chromatin, a functional polyadenylation signal, and a potential G4-forming sequence that may influence full-length transcription.
affiliations: M.E.T.U. (corresponding author)

papers.title: Sequence context and partner availability specify divergent cell fates from a single transcription factor
papers.abstract: Transcription factors drive the gene regulatory networks that control developmental transitions, yet which of their many targets a cell uses remains unresolved. Expressing Cebp, Cebp{beta} or Cebp{delta} identically, alone or with Oct4, Sox2, Klf4 and cMyc, gave four outcomes: adipocyte from fibroblasts and neural stem cells, trophectoderm from embryonic stem cells, and myeloid from B cells. Raising Cebp levels changed how many sites it reached, not which sequence it read: clustered motifs maintained somatic enhancers, while spillover onto low-copy sites created de novo enhancers carrying composites of Cebp and cell-type-restricted partners. In fibroblasts, Cebp also redistributed Oct4, Sox2 and Klf4 from early targets, blocking iPSC formation. Supplying the predicted partners rewrote the output: Spi1 redirected Cebp into parallel adipogenic and myeloid programs, via a transient PpargCD45 state using separate enhancers for each; TFAP2C abolished adipogenic conversion. Motif density and partner composites therefore assemble a factor's instructive output in the receiving cell.
affiliations: University of Illinois Chicago (corresponding author)

papers.title: Deciphering the Dynamics of Leukemogenic Transformation from Clonal Hematopoiesis in Congenital Neutropenia
papers.abstract: Inherited neutropenia syndromes, severe congenital neutropenia (CN) and Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (SDS), confer a high cumulative risk of MDS and AML. It is not yet clear which somatic mutations, in which combination, allele frequency and sequence identify patients at high risk. We analyzed clonal hematopoiesis (CH) in the largest representative cohort of inherited neutropenia patients to date - 658 samples from 309 patients - using error-corrected panel sequencing with longitudinal sampling. This was complemented in selected cases by single-cell DNA sequencing and genotyping of single-cell derived colonies. CH was detected in early childhood, affecting 37.7% of CN and 60% of SDS patients. The somatic mutation burden remained essentially unchanged over decades. In CN, CSF3R mutations were dominant across genetic subtypes, while additional mutations were rare and included ASXL1, TET2, and DNMT3A. ASXL1 mutations most frequently co-occurred with CSF3R mutations. Co-occurring CSF3R and TP53 mutations were only found in SRP54-CN and CLPB-CN patients. In SDS, TP53 was the most frequently mutated gene, followed by low-prevalence somatic mutations in DNMT3A, IDH1, PTPN11, and RUNX1. In CN-MDS/AML, RUNX1 and SETBP1 mutations emerged shortly before progression to MDS/AML, and membrane-proximal CSF3R mutations only at the leukemic stage. In SDS, biallelic TP53-mutant clones expanded prior to transformation, and a variant allele frequency (VAF) of dominant TP53 clone above 0.074 discriminated between patients who progressed and those who did not. Peripheral blood reflected bone marrow genotype for most key drivers. Leukemic transformation in inherited neutropenia is therefore not stochastic, but rather follows a defined mutational sequence, initiated in childhood.
affiliations: Department of Oncology, Hematology, Clinical Immunology, and Rheumatology, University Hospital Tuebingen, Tuebingen, Germany (corresponding author)

papers.title: A genetic screen to identify host factors required for commensal bacterial adherence to the gut epithelia
papers.abstract: Bacterial adherence to gut epithelial cells likely involves host genetic components. We isolated a gut commensal bacterium, Lelliottia jeotgali, that can robustly colonize C. elegans through attachment to intestinal epithelial cells. Here, we developed a novel screen in C. elegans to identify host genes required for microbiome bacterial colonization. Using transgenic L. jeotgali strain expressing tdTomato, we conducted forward genetic screens in C. elegans to select for mutants that completely lost colonization. We identified multiple allelic mutations in five different C. elegans genes, termed knockout of Lelliottia adherence (kola) mutants, with a near complete loss of adherence. Each of kola-1-5 is uncharacterized and predicted to encode for a secreted or membrane-bound protein. We also identified gly-5, a GalNAc transferase that initiates O-linked glycosylation. Overall, we describe the first C. elegans screen to identify host factors that control microbiome bacterial colonization in the gut.
affiliations: San Diego State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: CellVocal Attributes Transcriptional Dynamics to Spatial Signalling
papers.abstract: Understanding how local signalling shapes cell-state transitions requires linking spatial context to transcriptional dynamics. Here we present CellVocal, a framework that integrates spatial RNA velocity with cell-cell communication to decompose cell-state transitions into intrinsic and communication-associated components and further attribute their contributions to signalling modules and neighbouring sender cells. CellVocal recovered complex trajectories and communication perturbations in simulations and reconstructed coherent dynamics and spatially restricted ligand-receptor programmes across the mouse brain, gut and lung. Further analyses linked inferred NCAM1-NCAM1 signalling to lower cell-cycle-associated RNA velocity during embryonic neurogenesis. In melanoma, inferred local MIF-CD74+CD44 signalling corresponded to a predicted decline in the melanocytic programme. Analysis of acute liver failure identified hepatocyte-derived ANGPTL4-SDC1 signalling in association with acetaminophen-related communication enrichment and predicted matrix-remodelling RNA dynamics. By converting static ligand-receptor maps into velocity-constrained networks of signalling influence, CellVocal provides a general strategy for generating spatially resolved hypotheses about how intercellular communication contributes to predicted transcriptional changes.
affiliations: Xi'an Jiaotong University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Zebrafish lack canonical necroptosis despite retaining functional RIPK3
papers.abstract: Organismal development, homeostasis and immunity are facilitated by distinct forms of regulated cell death (RCD). These include conserved apoptosis and necroptosis, a proposed backup antimicrobial defence that requires RIPK3-mediated activation of MLKL and is predicted to be absent in several species lacking MLKL. Zebrafish studies have identified a RIPK3-dependent regulated necrosis that is distinct from necroptosis and is pathogenic in tuberculosis. Here, we experimentally confirm the bioinformatics-based prediction that zebrafish lack canonical necroptosis because they lack MLKL, despite retaining functional RIPK3. We take advantage of the finding that Caspase-8 promotes apoptosis while restraining necroptosis; its deficiency is embryonic lethal in mice unless RIPK3 or MLKL is also inhibited. In contrast, we found that Caspase-8-deficient zebrafish are viable through adulthood without obvious morphological defects. Inhibition of related caspases did not compromise viability, arguing against functional redundancy. Finally, Ripk3 overexpression failed to induce death in Caspase-8-deficient embryos. Our work highlights the zebrafish as a model for exploring RIPK3 and extrinsic apoptosis biology in disease contexts in the natural absence of canonical necroptotic execution.
affiliations: University of Cambridge, Department of Medicine, MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (corresponding author)

papers.title: ACE-engineered human iPSC-derived neutrophils enhance host defense against multidrug-resistant bacterial infections
papers.abstract: Severe neutropenia predisposes patients to life-threatening infections, while donor-dependent granulocyte transfusions are limited by availability and variable cell quality. Here, we engineered human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) to constitutively or inducibly express angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) and differentiated them into functional ACE-engineered neutrophils (ACE-iNeu). ACE expression enhanced granulocytic maturation, reactive oxygen species generation, inflammatory cytokine production, and antimicrobial signaling. ACE-iNeu exhibited enhanced bactericidal activity against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Following adoptive transfer into neutropenic mice, ACE-iNeu significantly reduced circulating and tissue bacterial burdens. Integrated metabolomic and transcriptomic analyses revealed ACE-associated alterations in adenine nucleotide abundance and developmental and inflammatory pathways. Together, these findings establish ACE engineering as a strategy to enhance the production and antimicrobial function of human iPSC-derived neutrophils and support further preclinical development of engineered granulocyte therapies for severe drug-resistant infections.
affiliations: Cedars-Sinai Medical Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Development of a core genome Multilocus Sequence Typing (cgMLST) and Life Identification Number (LIN) code schema for the Burkholderia cepacia complex
papers.abstract: Background The Burkholderia cepacia complex (Bcc) currently comprises over 20 closely related species; however, understanding Bcc population biology is complicated due to the continual advances in taxonomy and diversity driven by extensive horizontal gene transfer (HGT). Whilst there are conventional typing schemes for the Bcc, including Multilocus Sequence Typing (MLST), there remains a gap for fine-scale resolution typing of the species complex. Here, we present a 1,925 loci core genome MLST (cgMLST) and 14-digit Life Identification Number (LIN) barcoding scheme for the Bcc, that is embedded in the PubMLST database (https://PubMLST.org/organisms/burkholderia-cepacia-complex). Methods A dataset of 142 complete Bcc genomes spanning 19 species were downloaded from NCBI to develop the draft cgMLST scheme (Dataset 1). Two pangenome tools (PIRATE and PEPPAN) were then combined to give a consensus core gene list from Dataset 1. The 'core genes' from these outputs were then screened against the PubMLST loci, using a sequence tag scan, to identify their presence and curate new alleles. The core genes were then validated using a larger Bcc dataset (n = 934 genomes; 22 species) on PubMLST, which had been filtered for high-quality ([≤]200 contigs and 100% ribosomal MLST confidence). This refined the core gene list, ensuring a robust and reliable scheme using a threshold of 99% to classify the gene as 'core'. The population structure of the Bcc was subsequently analysed using the validation dataset to identify genetic clusters using ReporTree. Combined with statistical analysis, 14 allelic mismatch thresholds were identified for the LIN codes. Results The Bcc cgMLST scheme consists of 1,925 loci, which have been designated an arbitrary 'BCC' identifier. The cgMLST scheme and 14-threshold LIN code has been implemented in PubMLST and are publicly available for use. The Bcc genomes in the PubMLST database have been assigned cgSTs and LIN codes. Use cases of the LIN codes were validated using three previously published datasets, which spanned both outbreak investigation and phylogenomic lineage structures. Conclusions This stable, hierarchical LIN code nomenclature enhanced the ability to cluster isolates at multiple levels of resolution with examples overlayed on published datasets provided. The LIN code system is also backwards compatible with previous MLST and clonal complex (CC) nomenclature. Overall, the updated typing scheme will facilitate improve global public health through surveillance of the Bcc epidemiology including source tracing and outbreak investigation
affiliations: University of Oxford (corresponding author)

papers.title: Moderately acid-tolerant Nitrospira strains obtained by single-colony isolation on plates
papers.abstract: Nitrospira are difficult to cultivate, and pure cultures are mainly obtained by dilution-to-extinction combined with other methods, a process that usually takes years to over a decade. Here, we isolated three Nitrospira strains from activated sludge and sediment within one year using conventional single-colony isolation. Pure cultures of two strains could grow and reform single colonies within 25-60 days on all three types of plates prepared with agar, agarose, and gellan gum. Phylogenetic and phylogenomic analyses placed them within lineage I and indicated that they represent potential novel species, with the provisional names Nitrospira monocolonialis for strain Z02 and Nitrospira limosa for strains Z47 and Z70. All three strains were moderately acid-tolerant, with a minimum tolerable pH of 5.0; strain Z02 showed the highest acid tolerance, retaining 74% of its activity at pH 5.5. Strain Z02 was also highly adaptable to oxygen concentrations of 1-21%, retaining 78% and 85% of its maximum growth rate at 1% and 21% O2, respectively. Compared with the representative lineage I strain Nitrospira defluvii, all three strains contain superoxide dismutase encoding genes and some unique genes. Comparative transcriptomic analysis suggested that strain Z02 upregulated genes involved in stress responses, cell envelope modification, and putative type IVa pilus systems under acidic condition. Overall, this study provides the first demonstration that Nitrospira can grow on plates prepared with common gelling agents and form single colonies within a short period, and that Nitrospira can also tolerate moderately acid conditions.
affiliations: south china university of technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: An architectural RNA builds a reaction crucible through molecular concentration and activated enzyme selection
papers.abstract: Architectural RNAs (arcRNAs) scaffold membraneless organelles (MLOs), yet how they organize functional proteins remains unclear. Nuclear stress bodies (nSBs), MLOs scaffolded by HSATIII arcRNAs, incorporate SRSFs during stress. During stress recovery, nSBs function as reaction crucibles that recruit the kinase CLK1 to accelerate SRSF rephosphorylation and normalize stress-induced splicing. Here, we identify the ASAP complex as a recruitment factor that recognizes Ser341-phosphorylated, catalytically activated CLK1. HSATIII-bound SRSFs recruit ASAP, assembling a platform for CLK1 recruitment. Biochemical reconstitution reveals that this platform enhances SRSF phosphorylation by concentrating SRSFs and CLK1 while selectively recruiting activated CLK1, establishing nSB reaction crucibles as molecular concentrators and selectors. The SRSF-ASAP-CLK1 interaction network is conserved between humans and mice, suggesting that primate-specific HSATIII arcRNAs co-opted this pre-existing network to establish reaction-crucible function in nSBs. Our findings reveal how arcRNAs organize functional proteins through quantitative enrichment and qualitative selection to build biochemically active MLOs.
affiliations: The University of Osaka (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cxcr2 is required for ductal outgrowth and shapes the stromal microenvironment in postnatal mammary gland development
papers.abstract: Mammary gland development requires coordinated signaling between epithelial and stromal compartments. While CXC chemokine receptor 2 (CXCR2) is known to regulate inflammatory and tissue remodeling processes in disease, including breast cancer, its role in mammary gland morphogenesis is not well understood. Here, we examined postnatal mammary gland development in germline Cxcr2 knockout mice. Loss of Cxcr2 resulted in delayed ductal outgrowth, reduced epithelial area, and altered stromal architecture, including decreased adipocyte size and increased collagen deposition, despite preserved branching organization. These defects occurred in the context of severe systemic immune dysregulation, marked by expansion of granulocytic populations and loss of adaptive immune cells. Together, our findings indicate that CXCR2 indirectly regulates mammary gland development through coordination between the epithelium and stroma, rather than acting through epithelial cell-intrinsic mechanisms. Because the same myeloid expansion, immune suppression, and collagen-rich stromal remodeling that CXCR2 controls during normal development are hallmarks of the pro-tumorigenic breast microenvironment, these findings establish CXCR2 as a regulator of the immune and stromal landscape of the mammary gland and provide a developmental framework for understanding its contributions to the breast tumor microenvironment.
affiliations: University of Notre Dame (corresponding author)

papers.title: Integrated exome-transcriptome analysis of a schizophrenia case with an exceptionally low polygenic risk score
papers.abstract: Schizophrenia liability reflects both common polygenic variation and rarer variants of larger effect. We investigated a post-mortem schizophrenia case (SZ07) with a schizophrenia polygenic risk score below the first percentile among ancestry-matched cases, asking whether individual-level genomic and transcriptomic analyses could help identify potentially novel schizophrenia-relevant variants. We used exome analysis with multiple variant-prediction tools to generate a panel of variants and corresponding candidate genes potentially implicated in the pathological process in SZ07. The prioritised variants were then assessed using RNA sequencing of three cortical regions. Of these, only an IZUMO4 splice-acceptor variant showed direct RNA-level support. Beyond variant-specific analyses, we characterised broader transcriptomic abnormalities in the SZ07 brain. Pathway analysis of gene-level expression deviations implicated innate immune processes, calcium signalling, synaptic biology, and axon remodelling. Notably, compared with conventional single-sample biological pathway analysis, the analysis we used showed only a weak association with neuronal specificity, suggesting their reduced sensitivity to the main axis of variation related to cellular composition in bulk brain tissue gene expression data. Although the candidate genes showed no significant pathway-level convergence, the broader transcriptomic profile revealed coherent biological alterations largely compatible with the documented history of cerebrovascular disease in SZ07. These results demonstrate how the integration of exome and transcriptome data at the individual level enables the formulation and constraint of hypotheses regarding patient-specific genetic features and their molecular consequences, while highlighting important limitations related to tissue composition, comorbidity, and the choice of reference cohort.

papers.title: Non-coding RNA controls long-range enhancer-promoter interactions
papers.abstract: Transcription regulation depends on interactions between enhancers and gene promoters, which often occur over large genomic distances. The molecular drivers of long-range enhancer-promoter interactions remain poorly understood. Enhancers themselves are known to be transcribed into non-coding RNAs, but the function of these transcripts is unclear. Here, we use acute genetic and chemical perturbations of transcription elongation and termination to study the role of non-coding RNA in enhancer-promoter interactions. By integrating high-resolution 3D genome mapping, transcriptomics, proteomics, biochemistry and live-cell super-resolution imaging in these perturbation contexts, we demonstrate that a strong increase in RNA molecules at enhancers disrupts their long-range interactions with gene promoters, whereas decreased RNA levels lead to stabilization of these interactions. Using separation-of-function perturbations, we show that this regulatory function of RNA is independent from the process of transcription and the proteins recruited to initiate transcription. Functionally, we show that RNA-mediated disruption of enhancer-promoter interactions is associated with reduced transcription of target genes, indicating a regulatory feedback mechanism. Together, our results uncover an additional regulatory principle of enhancer-promoter interactions mediated by non-coding RNA.
affiliations: Max Planck Institute of Immunobiology and Epigenetics, Department of Genome Biology, Freiburg, Germany (corresponding author)

papers.title: Investigating the causal and consequential role of the nuclear encoded mitochondrial genome in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), but which mitochondrial pathways are involved, and whether their involvement is a cause or a consequence of disease remains unclear. We investigated whether nuclear-encoded mitochondrial gene (NEMG) pathways are enriched for ALS genetic risk, which are dysregulated in ALS tissue, whether pathway activity defines patient subgroups that differ in survival, and whether co-expression between the nuclear and mitochondrial genomes is altered. We tested MitoCarta3.0 pathways for enrichment of ALS genetic risk using MAGMA and the largest European ALS GWAS to date (27,205 cases and 110,881 controls), using hierarchical testing across pathway tiers, and annotated the direction of gene-level effects using published TWAS and SMR results. In >1,500 bulk RNA-seq samples from post-mortem motor cortex and spinal cord (KCL Brain Bank, NYGC ALS Consortium) and iPSC-derived motor neurones (Answer ALS), we performed cell type adjusted gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), gene set variation analysis (GSVA)-based clustering with exploratory survival analysis, and nuclear-mitochondrial co-expression analysis. Of seven broad mitochondrial categories, only the mitochondrial central dogma was enriched for ALS risk after correction (Padj = 0.044). Hierarchical testing within this pathway localised the signal to translation (Padj = 0.008) and the mitoribosome (Padj = 0.014). Genetically predicted expression pointed in opposite directions for different mitoribosomal genes (lower MRPS33 and higher MRPL28 expression with increased risk), and did not agree in direction with differential expression in ALS tissue more often than expected by chance. A nominal enrichment in ROS and glutathione metabolism was largely attributable to SOD1. In tissue, mitochondrial genes were broadly more highly expressed in ALS motor cortex in both cohorts, largely as a global shift across mitochondrial genes. OXPHOS subunits and the mitoribosome were enriched beyond this shift in ALS Consortium motor cortex (both PFDR = 0.027), as were OXPHOS subunits in iPSC-derived motor neurones (PFDR = 2.4 x 10-), whereas spinal cord showed no genome-wide enrichment. GSVA based clusters were associated with diagnosis in motor cortex, and nominally with survival in lumbar spinal cord (adjusted HR 0.69, Punadj = 0.013), where cluster structure was weakest. No individual pathway was associated with survival after correction in adjusted models. In all four post-mortem tissues, nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes were more negatively co-expressed with mtDNA-encoded genes in ALS than in controls, most strongly in lumbar spinal cord, whereas iPSC-derived motor neurones showed the opposite pattern. In conclusion, inherited ALS risk shows a modest enrichment centred on mitochondrial translation, with gene specific rather than uniform directions of effect. The same pathway, alongside OXPHOS, is more highly expressed in end-stage ALS motor cortex, which may reflect a response to disease, residual differences in cell composition, or both. At the gene level, genetically predicted and observed expression changes did not agree in direction, so whether inherited risk and these tissue changes are linked remains unresolved.

papers.title: RNA Small-Molecule Binding-Site Prediction by Integrating RNA Language Models and Structural Geometry
papers.abstract: RNAs are emerging as promising therapeutic targets, and small-molecule binding can modulate their structure and function, creating opportunities for therapeutic development. Accurate identification of RNA small-molecule binding sites is therefore important for understanding RNA-ligand interactions and facilitating RNA-targeted drug discovery. However, the structural complexity of RNA and the limited availability of experimentally characterized RNA-ligand complexes pose challenges for computational binding-site prediction. In this study, we propose RSMBind, a graph attention-based deep learning framework for nucleotide-level prediction of RNA-small molecule binding sites. The model integrates geometric descriptors of the local three-dimensional environment with pretrained RNA language model embeddings to capture complementary structural and sequence information. We investigate three pretrained RNA language models RNA-BERT, ERNIE-RNA and RNA-FM and assess the contributions of sequence representations and geometric features through feature-level ablation experiments. The model is developed using the TR60 and HARIBOSS datasets and evaluated on four independent benchmark datasets: RB9, TE18, TL12 and JL10. RSMBind achieves the highest MCC among the compared methods on three of the four benchmarks, with relative improvements of 17.1% on RB9, 7.2% on TL12 and 16.0% on JL10 over the best previously reported results, while achieving competitive performance on TE18. Furthermore, RSMBind retains predictive capability when using only pretrained RNA language model embeddings, highlighting their potential utility when explicit tertiary structural features are unavailable. Structural analysis indicates differences in prediction performance across RNA structural regions, with loop-associated binding sites generally being captured more effectively than those embedded within stem regions. Additionally, 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations of selected RNA-ligand complexes provide insights into the relationship between predicted binding probabilities and dynamic ligand proximity, further highlighting the role of conformational dynamics in evaluating structure-based predictions. The source code is available at [ https://github.com/sharma-nandita/RSMBind].

papers.title: scDeepSim: Deep Generative Simulation for Controlled Benchmarking of Single-Cell Methods
papers.abstract: Benchmarking single-cell computational methods requires both realistic data and reliable ground truth. However, annotating real datasets is costly and, even when available, may not fully represent the diverse settings where methods are used. Simulators address this gap by generating synthetic data that has fully specified ground truth and whose structure can be tailored to challenge competing methods. Existing single-cell simulators can broadly be divided into statistical and deep generative classes. Statistical simulators offer interpretable parameters for controlling simulated data, but their modeling assumptions may not accurately represent real data. Deep generative models can learn complex expression patterns, but it remains unclear how to transparently control individual biological or technical factors without introducing unintended effects. We introduce scDeepSim, a simulator that combines a structured variational autoencoder with latent diffusion to generate synthetic single-cell expression profiles. It allows users to intervene on selected biological or technical factors at user-specified strengths, producing realistic datasets with benchmark ground truth. We demonstrate this capability by benchmarking batch correction and trajectory inference methods, showing how batch-effect strength affects batch mixing and cell-type preservation, and how trajectory geometry and noise affect pseudotime recovery. scDeepSim therefore enables researchers to vary selected biological and technical factors in realistic simulated data and assess how these changes affect the performance of single-cell analysis methods, helping understand when such methods may be appropriately applied. Code for the scDeepSim simulator and experiments is available at https://github.com/LangtianM/scDeepSim.
affiliations: University of Wisconsin - Madison (corresponding author)

papers.title: Leveraging state-of-the-art AI structure predictors to generate atomic resolution ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins
papers.abstract: Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) are central to many biological processes, but their function depends on dynamic conformational ensembles rather than a single structure. Despite the impact of artificial intelligence on protein structure prediction, determining these ensembles at atomistic resolution remains challenging. Recently, we introduced bAIes, a framework that leverages the structural information encoded in AlphaFold2 distograms to generate conformational ensembles of IDPs at atomistic resolution. Here, we extend this framework to six state-of-the-art structure prediction tools (AlphaFold2, AlphaFold3, Boltz-1, Boltz-2, ESMFold, and ESMFold2) and systematically compare the structural information encoded in their predicted inter-residue distance distributions. Despite differences between predictors, we show that bAIes generates ensembles with comparable accuracy against experimental NMR and SAXS data, and competitive performance relative to state-of-the-art all-atom simulations and alternative IDP ensemble generation methods. These results demonstrate that bAIes is robust to the choice of structure predictor and that the distance distributions generated by different deep learning architectures contain valuable information about the conformational preferences of disordered proteins. More broadly, our work highlights the potential of combining AI-derived structural information with physics-based modeling to generate atomistic ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins and regions.
affiliations: Institut Pasteur (corresponding author)

papers.title: Structural relationships between the SLC12 cotransporter C-terminal domain, universal stress proteins and adenylating enzymes
papers.abstract: Several SLC12 cotransporters bind ATP in a cytoplasmic C-terminal domain (CTD). We analysed 16,192 CTD-containing SLC12 sequences and compared 42,845 representative structures to examine the relationship between this nucleotide site, universal stress proteins (USPs) and adenylating enzymes. In phosphorylated NKCC1, D891 and D927 lie near the ATP phosphate chain, while R801 and K889 form a basic phosphate-binding clamp. NKCC1 retains this arrangement, whereas KCC paralogs replace or lose several corresponding groups. In structural comparisons with USP and adenylating-enzyme references, both CTD lobes score between universal stress proteins and EC-annotated domains, and the two lobes form separate lineages that include bacterial transporters. Lobe-specific and nucleotide-frame comparisons place ATP in the corresponding structural region used for -phosphate chemistry by catalytic members of this fold. Published work on UspG provides a precedent for protein-bound AMP in a natural USP. In the examined SLC12 structures and USP models, candidate protein hydroxyls lack an in-line geometry for attack at ATP P. Protein adenylation would require a change in protein or nucleotide geometry, or a different acceptor. These results define a structural basis for testing conditional protein adenylation at SLC12 nucleotide sites. The required evidence is a covalent protein-AMP adduct, identification of its acceptor and measurement of the expected pyrophosphate coproduct, with soluble nucleotide analysis to distinguish accompanying ATP reactions.
affiliations: University College London (corresponding author)

papers.title: The Phospholipase A2 Activity of Peroxiredoxin 6 Protects Hepatocarcinoma Cells Against Ferroptosis and Mitophagy Impairment
papers.abstract: Peroxiredoxin 6 (PRDX6) is a moonlighting protein that plays a key role in regulating redox homeostasis and lipid metabolism through its unique dual peroxidase and calcium-independent phospholipase A2 (iPLA2) activities. Here, we generated a stable HepG2 cell line harboring a D140A mutation to selectively ablate iPLA2 activity, and we compared its phenotype with that of wild-type (WT) and PRDX6-knockout (KO) cells. D140A exhibited low ROS leves, similar to WT cells, confirming that oxidative stress is due to peroxidase deficiency. In contrast, D140A cells displayed higher lipid peroxidation than WT cells, though significantly lower than that of KO cells. Furthermore, the D140A mutant mirrored the KO phenotype regarding intracellular ferrous iron accumulation, impaired lipid droplet biogenesis, and the downregulation of the key ferroptosis regulator GPX4. Mechanistically, integrated proteomic, lipidomic, and enzymatic analyses revealed that a deficiency in iPLA2 activity of PRDX6 disrupted the release of key lipid species necessary for cell structure and signaling. Consequently, organelles involved in lipid synthesis and trafficking, such as peroxisomes, endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria and lipid droplet, were affected. Specifically, we found that mitochondria exhibited a reduction in cristae and a diminished capacity for mitophagy and autophagy, which ultimately makes cells much more susceptible to erastin-induced ferroptotic cell death. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that PRDX6 iPLA2 activity uniquely coordinates organelle lipid homeostasis and mitophagy to protect cancer cells from ferroptotic cell death. Consequently, the use of iPLA2 inhibitors such as MJ33, which decreased PRDX6 iPLA2 activity to a level comparable to the mutant D140A, could represent a promising therapeutic strategy for inducing ferroptotic cell death in hepatocellular carcinoma.
affiliations: University of Cordoba (corresponding author)

High-entropy alloy aerogels promote selective glycerol oxidation to tartronate at industrial current densities
papers.abstract: The highly selective electrosynthesis of tartronate (TA) from glycerol oxidation reaction (GOR) at industrial current densities remains a grand challenge, as it necessitates the concurrent oxidation of two primary hydroxyl groups while suppressing C-C cleavage. Herein, we engineer a PtCuCoCeSn high-entropy alloy aerogel electrocatalyst for efficient glycerol-to-TA electrooxidation under industrially relevant conditions. This catalyst delivers a high current density of 461 mA cm−2 at 1.0 VRHE, alongside a TA selectivity of 81.4%. In situ characterization and theoretical calculations reveal that Ce modulates the glycerol adsorption conformation, enhances the adsorption of glycerate intermediates, and promotes its conversion to TA. Meanwhile, Sn facilitates TA desorption and suppresses the C-C cleavage, thereby ensuring high selectivity at elevated current. Furthermore, in a membrane electrode assembly (MEA) electrolyzer configured with Pt1.5CuCoCeSn | | PtCuCoCeSn, the system achieves a stable TA selectivity of 78.9% at a cell voltage of 1.6 V with a TA production rate of 4.9 mmol h−1, and maintains stable operation for over 240 h. This work provides fundamental insights into the design of high-entropy alloys for the sustainable electrosynthesis of value-added chemicals at scale. The production of tartronate from glycerol electrooxidation is limited by low selectivity at industrial-scale current densities. Here, the authors report a PtCuCoCeSn high-entropy alloy aerogel for regulated glycerol adsorption, enabling 81.4% selectivity and stable operation up to 240 hours.

papers.title: Cryo-EM reveals conserved baseplate-architecture and distinct accessory-protein assemblies in mycobacteriophages Claus, Corndog and Mysterious
papers.abstract: Mycobacteriophages, viruses infecting mycobacteria, hold therapeutic promise against antibiotic-resistant mycobacterial infections. Although thousands of mycobacteriophages have been isolated, high-resolution baseplate structures have been reported for only two, highlighting a gap in understanding phage–host interactions. Most mycobacteriophages are siphophages with four structural components: capsid, connector, non-contractile tail, and baseplate. The baseplate plays a critical role in host recognition, adsorption, and genome delivery. Here, we present atomic-resolution cryo-EM baseplate structures of three mycobacteriophages, Claus, Corndog, and Mysterious. These exhibit distinct inverted crown-, barrel-, and cage-like architectures, respectively, yet share a conserved architecture with a 6:6:3 stoichiometry of homohexameric tail tube proteins (TTPs), distal tail proteins (DTPs), and homotrimeric baseplate hub proteins (BHPs). The baseplate core is formed by DTPs and BHPs, with terminal TTPs making direct proximal contacts with DTPs and contributing to overall structure. While the central core is conserved, the exterior domains diverge across the phages. Surrounding the conserved cores are diverse baseplate accessory proteins (BAPs), including upper baseplate proteins (BppUs), central fiber proteins (CFPs), and others, which assemble into distinct peripheral architectures and give rise to two baseplate-opening mechanisms. These structures reveal a conserved baseplate core complex diversified by BAPs, a feature potentially shared across mycobacteriophage siphophage families. Atomic-resolution structures of three mycobacteriophages reveal a conserved baseplate core decorated by diverse accessory proteins, showing how related siphophages build distinct baseplate architectures from a common structural core.
