papers.title: Electric vehicle battery materials supply disruptions can be mitigated with chemistry changes and recycling
papers.abstract: Battery materials supply chains for plug-in electric vehicles face vulnerabilities to disruptions from geopolitical disputes and natural disasters. Through industry interviews, we identify scenarios that could disrupt materials supply by 2030. We estimate the impacts on US automotive production, prices, and consumer costs in an economic equilibrium model of the US automotive industry. We find year-long disruptions can have large impacts: trade restrictions that reduce processed lithium supply from China by 30% and disasters shutting down the three largest cobalt mines increase average new vehicle prices (including conventional vehicles and plug-in electric vehicles) by $1,100-1,600, costing consumers $14-17 billion. However, feasible changes in battery chemistry and materials supply by 2030 mitigate these negative impacts. If 85% of battery electric vehicle models are produced with lithium iron phosphate batteries and at least 100 kilotonnes of planned production of recycled lithium carbonate equivalent is available, disruption costs decrease by more than half. This study shows that disruptions in US battery materials supply could cost tens of billions of dollars. However, feasible changes in battery chemistry and increasing recycled lithium supply largely reduce the consequences of the disruptions.

papers.title: Pico-X: a 24.9 nanowatt microcontroller for long-duration autonomous operation in flexible landing-pad sensor networks
papers.abstract: Flexible landing-pad sensor networks require local intelligence that can remain dormant for long periods yet respond rapidly to sparse mechanical events. General-purpose microcontrollers incur substantial retained-state and control overhead under such workloads, whereas hardwired controllers sacrifice programmability. Here we present Pico-X, a state-minimized eight-bit programmable processor designed for patch-level wake-up, sensing, event classification and reporting. A compact multi-cycle architecture, unified retentive memory and workload-constrained instruction framework reduce retained state and standby leakage. Fabricated in a 28-nanometre fully depleted silicon-on-insulator process, Pico-X consumes 728.2 nanowatts during active operation at 25 kilohertz and 24.9 nanowatts in state-retentive deep sleep without body bias, while preserving deterministic state recovery after wake-up. We further integrate Pico-X into a 4 × 4 flexible landing-pad demonstrator that records 12,842 events and achieves class-wise detection rates (recall) of 96.3% for occupancy, 92.1% for load imbalance, and 94.6% for deformation. Mean event-to-report latency is 38 milliseconds, packet delivery reaches 99.12%, and operation remains stable for more than 72 hours. These results establish a low-overhead programmable architecture for distributed, long-duration sensing. Researchers present Pico-X, a programmable microcontroller designed for sparse event-driven sensing. Operating at nanowatt power levels, it enables long-duration autonomous monitoring and reliable event detection in distributed flexible sensor networks.

papers.title: Deployability of biotechnologies for environmentally resilient agriculture
papers.abstract: Agriculture is both humanity’s largest infrastructure and the leading driver of environmental degradation. Many early-stage biotechnologies could mitigate this impact, but their deployability has not been systematically evaluated. We analyze deployability of 77 biotechnologies across eight domains (crops, soils, livestock, watersheds, aquaculture, health and security, food loss/waste and frontiers) by applying a Balanced Readiness Level assessment spanning technological, market, regulatory, acceptance and organizational dimensions. We find that market viability and social acceptance, not technological readiness, represent the primary constraints. High-readiness technologies tend to be ‘drop-in’, contained, transient and perceived as natural. These characteristics indicate strategies to elevate overall deployability, such as addressing genetically modified organism containment. Assessing the scalability and environmental impacts of biotechnologies for prioritization requires additional quantitative analysis, as shown in a Fermi analysis of microbial fertilizers. We combine our findings into a near- to long-term roadmap for living infrastructure: predictively designed multicomponent biological communities that function as systems at the ecosystem level to enhance food security and environmental resilience. Seventy-seven biotechnologies that could advance agricultural sustainability are analyzed for deployment readiness.

Cellular agriculture for sustainable and programmable foods
papers.abstract: Cellular agriculture promises to reduce the environmental burden and inefficiencies of food systems. The question is no longer whether precision fermentation and cultivated meat production can produce alternative proteins and other food components, but whether they can attain the cost, scale and quality required for broad adoption. We examine cellular agriculture through the interrelated lenses of enabling technologies, food function and manufacturing economics. The field is approaching an inflection point where biological technology development is less important for commercial success than achieving scalable, affordable manufacturing. Key challenges include how products and their functional attributes are designed and how production processes are configured. For precision fermentation, the most compelling opportunities lie in functional approaches to improve taste, nutritional quality, health benefits and formulation rather than in direct imitation of existing foods or ingredients. For cultivated meat production, impact will come first from hybrid and ingredient-based products that capture specific values of cellular ingredients while avoiding the costs of full tissue mimicry. Making protein using cells, not animals and plants, promises sustainability and food quality benefits.

papers.abstract: Lim et al. identify interferon-γ as a regulator of macrophage function during zebrafish heart regeneration. Macrophage interferon-γ signaling supports debris clearance and regenerative extracellular matrix remodeling. TNIP1 acts as an aggrephagy receptor that assembles clearance machinery for protein aggregate removal
papers.abstract: Park et al. demonstrate that TNIP1 acts as a selective autophagy receptor by recruiting aggrephagy receptors and ubiquitinated protein aggregates upon proteotoxic stress. papers.title: RNA-binding protein NOC4L governs early natural killer cell development through dual post-transcriptional mechanisms
papers.abstract: He et al. show that IL-15 upregulates NOC4L in NK progenitors. papers.title: Metabolic reprogramming by caloric restriction enhances acute phase virological control and reduces chronic inflammation during SIV infection
papers.abstract: Caloric restriction (CR) impacts metabolism and immunity in rhesus macaques. Suresh Babu et al. show that CR reduces acute SIV viremia and chronic inflammation following ART. These findings reveal a transient contribution of metabolism to antiviral immunity and highlight diet as a potential modulator of lentiviral disease.

papers.title: Plasmodium falciparum Hsp90 supports DNA replication
papers.abstract: Malaria parasites depend on PfHsp90, but the cellular pathways supported by this essential chaperone remain poorly defined. Ibrasheva et al. identify PfHsp90-dependent proteins enriched in DNA replication, demonstrate that Hsp90 inhibition impairs parasite DNA synthesis, and uncover synergistic interactions between Hsp90 and DNA replication inhibitors.

papers.title: A sliding annular in situ bioprinting strategy for rapid and robust fabrication of small-diameter vascular grafts
papers.abstract: Chen et al. develop a sliding annular in situ bioprinting strategy that combines a detachable annular printhead, PH hydrogel, and sacrificial PVA scaffold for rapid small-diameter vascular repair. In a rabbit carotid artery model, the strategy restores blood flow and supports vascular tissue integration.

papers.title: In-context learning for medical artificial intelligence
papers.abstract: Wong et al. review how in-context learning enables large language models to adapt to medical tasks using examples rather than model parameter updates. They map its applications and limitations and propose a risk-proportionate framework for evaluation, governance, and monitoring to guide responsible clinical translation.

papers.title: Microbiome-antibiotic-immune interactions influence mortality in preterm infant gut microbiota-humanized gnotobiotic mice
papers.abstract: Preterm infants are commonly treated with antibiotics. Schwartz et al. discover associations between antibiotic administration, systemic immune responses, microbiome composition, and death in gnotobiotic mouse pups humanized with stool from preterm infants. These findings can help contextualize the unintended consequences of antibiotic administration for preterm infants.

papers.title: 3D models to capture and perturb tumour heterogeneity in vitro
papers.abstract: Tumour heterogeneity is a defining feature of cancer and a major obstacle to effective therapy as it drives metastasis, resistance and relapse. Experimental tumour models have largely exploited simplified, homogeneous systems that fail to capture the full biological and spatial diversity of real tumours. Recent advances in 3D models have considerably expanded our capacity to model different dimensions of tumour heterogeneity. These platforms also enable controlled perturbations of cancer-cell-intrinsic and microenvironmental features, including genetic programmes, therapy responses and transport, extracellular matrix composition and mechanics, oxygenation, perfusion, stromal and immune interactions, and tissue architecture. Such perturbations could reveal how different aspects of tumour heterogeneity shape disease progression and therapy response dynamics. However, how close we are to generating 3D models that not only recapitulate the dynamic, multiscale nature of human cancers but also enable systematic perturbations for mechanistic insights remains a key question. In this Review, we summarize the current landscape of 3D models and how effectively they capture tumour heterogeneity, what perturbations they enable, and how these capabilities can be matched to specific biological or therapeutic questions. We also discuss outstanding challenges in model fidelity, standardization, scalability, longitudinal analysis and clinical predictability. Tumour heterogeneity drives disease progression yet remains difficult to capture in experimental systems. In this Review, Fomina and McGuigan discuss how emerging 3D tumour models, including organoids, assembloids and microfluidic platforms, recapitulate distinct dimensions of tumour heterogeneity to enable mechanistic studies of cancer biology and drug response. They also outline future directions for improving model fidelity, scalability and translational utility.

papers.title: A practical guide to vascularized microphysiological systems
papers.abstract: Microphysiological systems (MPS) are emerging as human-relevant models for pharmaceutical research, reducing reliance on animal testing. Despite progress in reproducing organ-specific features, integrating functional microvasculature remains challenging. Advances have expanded the number of available options, making it difficult to identify the most suitable one for a specific MPS. Here, we provide a guide to designing vascularized MPS by comparing current vascularization strategies according to key design drivers, including the microfluidic platform, organotypic vascular architecture, matrix properties, and coculture with perivascular cells. We highlight trade-offs between biological fidelity, engineering control, and translational needs, while considering approaches widely adopted in commercial MPS. Finally, we discuss how close the field is to delivering physiologically accurate vascularized MPS and how emerging omics technologies may redefine vascular identity and functionality.

papers.title: EWSR1::ATF1 hyperactivation via TRIM11 depletion triggers lethal metabolic rewiring in clear cell sarcoma
papers.abstract: Clear cell sarcoma (CCS) is an ultra-rare and aggressive soft tissue sarcoma driven by the EWSR1::ATF1 fusion oncoprotein. Currently, no effective and well-tolerated treatment options are available to CCS patients. Direct inhibition of fusion transcription factors is precluded by the absence of defined ligand-binding pockets, whereas their abundance is under the control of the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS), offering an alternative avenue for biology-guided treatment. Here we show the abundance of EWSR1::ATF1 is tightly regulated by the UPS, and that release of this constraint is lethal to CCS cells. A reporter-based CRISPR/Cas9 knockout screen of UPS components identified TRIM11 as an E3 ligase that regulates turnover of EWSR1::ATF1, which it recognises as a neosubstrate without altering wild-type EWSR1 or ATF1. Depletion of TRIM11 increased nuclear fusion protein abundance, amplified the fusion-driven transcriptional programs and reduced viability. Proteomic analysis identified the cataplerotic enzyme phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase 1 (PCK1), a direct EWSR1::ATF1 target, as the key mediator of lethal effects of fusion hyperactivation. Extracellular flux analysis, isotope tracing and quantitative metabolomics revealed excessive cataplerotic carbon withdrawal and impaired oxidative phosphorylation as the underlying mechanism. In patient tumors, high PCK1 expression associated with metastatic transcriptome programs and disease presentation, as well as shorter survival. Taken together, we report that hyperactivation of EWSR1::ATF1 opens a metabolic vulnerability, establishing TRIM11 as an actionable dependency and PCK1 as a candidate prognostic biomarker in CCS.
affiliations: German Cancer Research Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Illuminating the Role of A-to-I Editing in Cancer using EndoVIA 2.0
papers.abstract: Adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing is an essential post-transcriptional modification catalyzed by adenosine deaminases acting on RNA (ADAR) enzymes, and emerging evidence suggests its dysregulation can contribute to cancer. However, technical barriers have hindered spatial analysis of editing activity in formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissues - an abundant but challenging sample type. Here, we introduce EndoVIA 2.0, an optimized immunostaining assay that enables quantification and spatial mapping of edited RNAs in FFPE tissues. Using human Endonuclease V (hEndoV) as a molecular affinity reagent, we developed a calcium-dependent staining workflow compatible with crosslinked tissues. EndoVIA 2.0 was validated in cell lines having altered ADAR1 expression, fresh frozen (FF) tissues, gastric organoids, and FFPE tissue sections. Using quantitative imaging combined with machine-learning segmentation and spatial analysis, EndoVIA 2.0 successfully detected A-to-I editing changes in ADAR1 knockout (KO) and overexpression models, revealing differential editing patterns across tissues. In gastric organoids and FFPE tissues, the assay also spatially resolved editing heterogeneity and distinguished ADAR1-deficient from ADAR1-sufficient cells. Application to long-archived lung and breast cancer FFPE tissues suggest EndoVIA 2.0's broad utility and potential for capturing disease-associated changes in A-to-I editing. Finally, staining across the gastric neoplastic cascade revealed stage-dependent increases in A-to-I editing and changes in subcellular localization, further supporting the possibility that ADAR plays a critical role in the early development of gastric cancer. EndoVIA 2.0 enables robust, spatial detection of A-to-I editing in FFPE tissues - circumventing the limitations of RNA extraction and unlocking access to archived clinical specimens. This platform lays the foundation for mapping RNA editing dynamics in cancer progression and may support future biomarker discovery.
affiliations: Washington University in St. Louis (corresponding author)

papers.title: A distinct chondrogenic progenitor population from human umbilical cord derived mesenchymal stromal cells for osteoarthritis therapy
papers.abstract: Stem cell-based cartilage regeneration remains constrained by functional heterogeneity and phenotypic drift in conventional cell sources, compromising durable structural repair. Human umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stromal cells (UC-MSCs) represent an accessible, off-the-shelf cell source; however, their broad clinical utility is hampered by cellular heterogeneity, leaving the key chondrogenic subpopulation responsible for cartilage repair unresolved. By integrating single-cell transcriptomics with functional assays, we identified and prospectively isolated a distinct, highly expandable subpopulation of skeletal stem cell-like progenitors (U-CPCs) from the human umbilical cord, establishing an extra-skeletal cell source uniquely primed for joint restoration. Single-cell transcriptomics reveal their inherent regulatory landscape, uncovering a distinct transcriptional state uniquely primed for chondrogenesis. In comparison with conventional stem cells and other tissue-derived SSC-like populations (from umbilical cord, bone marrow, adipose tissue, and dental pulp), U-CPCs exhibit a markedly enhanced chondrogenic capacity. In both a mouse cartilage injury model and a rat osteoarthritis model, the administration of U-CPCs effectively mitigates joint degeneration and drives the restoration of a structurally sound, hyaline-like matrix. Mechanistically, U-CPCs secrete extracellular vesicles enriched with microRNA Let-7a-5p, which specifically modulates DUSP7/MAPK/ERK signaling in recipient chondrocytes, thereby restoring extracellular matrix homeostasis and promoting cartilage repair. By characterizing these specialized extra-skeletal progenitors and elucidating both their intrinsic chondrogenic priming and paracrine regulation of host tissue, this study establishes U-CPCs as a robust, lineage-restricted cellular source for osteoarthritis therapy.
affiliations: Institute of Clinical Medicine, Zhanjiang Central Hospital, Guangdong Medical University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Time-resolved single-cell screening reveals the dynamic regulatory architecture of human cardiogenesis
papers.abstract: Congenital heart disease (CHD) originates during early embryogenesis, yet when disease genes act cannot be determined from existing data. Human fetal heart atlases lack critical time points, and perturbation screens that systematically assess gene function currently profile at most a few time points. Here we combined single-cell CRISPR screening of 400 disease-relevant genes in cardioids, sampled daily over seven developmental days (~975,000 cells), with a matched multiome atlas. Perturbation phenotypes were strongly dependent on developmental stage. Perturbations that reshaped cell-fate allocation or gene expression were enriched for CHD-linked genes, and most acted already during progenitor stages. Timing was largely independent of the target gene's own expression, marking instead when a cell state became functionally dependent on it, and some effects persisted after expression declined. Consensus gene regulatory networks integrating perturbation and multiome data recovered stage-specific regulators and nominated HOXB2 and HOXB3 as candidate cardiac regulators. Many perturbations converged on shared downstream programmes, which were reorganised through differentiation. Effects correlated in progenitors were maintained in differentiated cells, split into distinct programmes, converged with other perturbations or disappeared entirely, indicating that gene function is highly context dependent. Beyond advancing our understanding of the developmental regulatory logic underlying CHD, our work provides a resource for developing context-dependent models for in silico prediction of perturbation effects.
affiliations: Department of Genetics, Stanford University School of Medicine, Stanford, CA, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Homogeneous network inference for subtype-stratified master regulator analysis in cancer
papers.abstract: Master-regulator analysis of 34 TCGA tumour cohorts (cancer x molecular subtype; n between 27 and 562 tumours) requires one regulatory network per cohort. Mutual-information (MI) networks inferred with ARACNe3 are the usual choice, but they are not available for the smallest cohorts; filling the gap with correlation networks would mix two methods inside the very comparison between subtypes that the analysis is meant to make. We therefore infer every network with a single procedure, fixed-size Spearman regulons (FSR): rank correlation between regulator and target, a fixed effect-size threshold rho >= 0.2, the per-target data-processing-inequality (DPI) pruning implemented in corto, bootstrap support, and truncation to the 100 best-supported targets per regulator. We quantify what this choice concedes and what it provides, labelling each claim as a standard result, a heuristic, or an empirical result. Rank correlation is more powerful than the MI estimators we simulated for n = 95) they overlap in 0.7 of the top-20 regulators, the same as two filterings of the same ARACNe3 network, although the rank correlation of the full score vector shows a measurable method effect in the tail. Subsampling large real cohorts indicates that networks inferred from fewer than 60 tumours do not reliably reproduce their own cohort's master regulators, that 60-100 is a grey zone, and that a cancer-wide network does not rescue small subtypes. We present FSR as an adequate and uniform choice for multi-cohort analysis, not as a statistically superior one.
affiliations: INMEGEN (corresponding author)

papers.title: LuCEMe: An accessible luciferase-based method to functionally assess cellular metabolism across model systems
papers.abstract: Metabolic profiling approaches such as extracellular flux analysis, metabolomics, stable isotope tracing and cytometry-based assays have transformed our understanding of cellular metabolism in physiological and pathological contexts. However, most techniques require specialized equipment or reagents, and do not allow differential metabolic analysis in intact multicellular systems. Here, we present LuCEMe, a luciferase-based metabolic phenotyping approach that combines acute metabolic perturbations with quantitative ATP measurements to resolve glycolytic and mitochondrial dependencies and capacities under native culture conditions, including in complex coculture and ex vivo systems without prior cell separation. The assay can also be adapted to increase metabolic resolution and distinguish between glycolytic activity, glucose oxidation and fatty acid/amino acid-driven mitochondrial ATP production. We use LuCEMe to reveal profound metabolic differences between leukemia cells cocultured with macrophages, stromal cells or adipocytes, and demonstrate distinct metabolic rewiring during macrophage polarization, osteogenic and adipogenic differentiation, and T cell activation. Ex vivo LuCEMe analysis identified a particular metabolic adaptation associated with chemotherapy response in acute myeloid leukemia that was not evident from conventional analyses. LuCEMe thus provides an accessible, robust and versatile framework for direct functional metabolic phenotyping across in vitro, ex vivo, and multicellular systems that complements existing metabolic profiling technologies.
affiliations: Catholic University of Louvain, Universite Catholique de Louvain (corresponding author)

papers.title: Dissecting human embryonic patterning during organogenesis reveals a rostral midline progenitor population for mesoendoderm induction
papers.abstract: Understanding how human organogenesis is accomplished via intricate spatiotemporal patterning of organ primordia requires spatial atlases at cellular resolution. However, existing human embryo spatial atlases are built using sequencing-based platforms such as Stereo-seq, which have limited spatial resolution and blurred anatomical boundaries, leading to misclassification across adjacent cells. Here, we integrate in situ imaging-based transcriptomics (Xenium) with transcriptome-wide spatial profiling (Visium-HD) of Carnegie stages 9-12 embryos to delineate the patterning of core embryonic tissues at single-cell resolution, including the brain, spinal cord, somites, neural crest, notochord, heart, and gut tube. A new finding enabled by spatial single-cell resolution is the identification of rostral midline progenitors (RMPs), a cell population co-expressing SOX2, TBXT, and OTX2. Transcriptionally, RMPs are distinct from both neuromesodermal progenitors (NMPs) and prechordal mesoderm, and in vivo clonal barcoding in mice indicates that RMPs share a common developmental origin with rostral neural ectoderm. To interrogate their functional significance, we leveraged our spatial transcriptome data to recapitulate RMP-like cells from human pluripotent stem cells and showed that these cells can induce epiblast-like cells to acquire mesendodermal and endodermal fates, while themselves adopting an ectodermal fate consistent with their in vivo counterparts. This work provides a 3D, stage-resolved molecular cell atlas of tissue patterning in human embryo that serves as a reference for in vitro models.
affiliations: Westlake Laboratory of Life Sciences and Biomedicine; Westlake University School of Life Sciences (corresponding author)

papers.title: In situ single-cell CRISPR screens uncover context-dependent rewiring of glioma states and immune recruitment
papers.abstract: In vivo single-cell CRISPR screens can resolve perturbation effects in native tissues, but few combine cell-type-restricted delivery, somatic tumor initiation, and combinatorial perturbation. Here we developed an RCAS-TVA-based single-cell CRISPR screening approach coupling oncogenic transformation with single- or dual-guide perturbation in defined neural progenitors. In glioma, tumor suppressor loss produced distinct genotype-dependent transcriptional states, including an NF1-loss-associated increase in mesenchymal programs. Introducing a fixed Cdkn2a(ARF) perturbation altered malignant-cell state composition, immune-cell abundance, and the effects of additional tumor-suppressor perturbations, including increased representation of Pten- and Rb1-deficient cells, suggestive of the relief of an ARF-dependent genetic barrier. These perturbations converged on transcriptional states resembling pharmacologic p53 activation in human glioblastoma. Across mouse tumors and human glioblastoma models, this response was associated with increased astrocyte-like state representation. These findings establish a framework for single-cell analysis of context-dependent somatic perturbations during tumor initiation in vivo.
affiliations: Columbia University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Structure-based discovery of new GPR119 ligands from on-demand tera-scale chemical space
papers.abstract: The orphan G protein-coupled receptor GPR119 is involved in glucose homeostasis and is considered a promising target for the treatment of diabetes and other metabolic diseases. The recently solved structures of GPR119 in complex with potential endogenous lipid agonists, including oleoylethanolamide (OEA), provide a solid platform for 3D pharmacology analysis and structure-based ligand discovery. Here, we employed the V-SYNTHES2 approach to screen ~3 trillion on-demand compounds from Enamine xREAL chemical space to identify several new chemotypes of GPR119 agonists and antagonists. Structure-guided analog-by-catalog hit expansion of new chemotypes and stereoselective synthesis resulted in a series of full and partial agonists with low-micromolar potencies in functional assays. Cryo-EM structures of active GPR119-Gs complexes bound to three of the hits validated the docking predictions and established further SAR insights into ligand-receptor interactions, enabling the discovery of BRI-17403 and BRI-17409 agonists with EC50 values of 1.6 M and 1.3 M, respectively. These results demonstrate the utility of structure-based screening of tera-scale on-demand chemical spaces in accelerating drug discovery for therapeutically relevant orphan GPCRs.
affiliations: University of Southern California (corresponding author)

papers.title: Multi-material delivery strategies to create deferoxamine-functionalized collagen scaffolds for craniofacial bone repair
papers.abstract: Craniomaxillofacial (CMF) bone injuries are common and can occur secondary to trauma, bone resection, and congenital abnormalities. While the current standard of care remains allograft or autograft, tissue engineering approaches offer the opportunity for alternative regenerative solutions. Biomaterial design has been central in this effort, with a primary consideration being the incorporation of motifs into biomaterials that accelerate osteogenic differentiation of progenitor cells and subsequent mineral synthesis. However, angiogenic potency, and subsequent angiogenic-osteogenic coupling, represent a critical challenge, as poor angiogenic activity can impair regenerative healing. Deferoxamine (DFO) can mimic cellular hypoxia via iron chelation and has been used as an angiogenic factor. However, its size (<1 kDa) severely limits its retention in the wound area. Here, we report a multi-material approach to improve angiogenic coupling in an osteogenic biomaterial. We report methods to retain DFO in mineralized collagen scaffold via its binding to a second polymer, gelatin, that can be incorporated into the scaffold to boost angiogenic potency while maintaining its osteo-regenerative properties. We employed carbodiimide chemistry to attach DFO to a gelatin backbone and retained 79.6% of the drug over a 7-day culture. Using a composite drug-delivery approach that combines freely soluble DFO with gelatin-bound DFO into the mineralized collagen scaffold, drove increased mesenchymal stem cell metabolic activity and enhanced expression of angiogenic genes in culture over 14 days. This work provides a novel approach to advance acellular regenerative biomaterials for osteogenic-angiogenic coupling processes.
affiliations: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (corresponding author)

papers.title: spSheaf: sheaf-theoretic spatial domain inference from raw molecules without cell segmentation
papers.abstract: Spatial-transcriptomics pipelines usually require cell segmentation and discard 20-60% of transcripts. We introduce spSheaf, a segmentation-free spatial domain inference method built on cellular sheaf theory. Within a domain, neighbouring regions have compatible local expression structure; across a transition between programs they remain discordant after alignment of their local subspaces. spSheaf quantifies this alignment-adjusted disagreement and attenuates transitions during clustering. On the MERFISH hypothalamus benchmark it attains mean ARI 0.571 and NMI 0.655, ranks first of twelve on NMI, and leads SSAM, Points2Regions and FICTURE by 0.16 ARI on held-out slices. On three further annotated sections, every method tuned, it leads on one, ties on one and trails SSAM by 0.06 ARI. The sheaf weighting adds +0.102 ARI where domains are distinct programs and is neutral on laminar cortex. One domain above the annotated count, it divides the BST into the territories of two atlas neuronal populations on both adjacent sections.
affiliations: University of Sevilla (corresponding author)

papers.title: LingoCell interprets gene perturbations through natural language and tissue niches
papers.abstract: Single-cell foundation models are general tools for resolving cell identities and disease states, but struggle to interpret changes in expression magnitude in biological language, to transfer to sparse spatial measurements, and to explain cellular niches. We introduce LingoCell, a foundation model connecting single-cell and spatial transcriptomics. It aligns cell representations with language while keeping gene expression editable, supporting cell annotation, cross-batch integration, description generation, and disease-language readouts of single-gene and combinatorial in silico perturbations. Extended to tissues, it annotates cells without single-cell references, learns identity-conditioned niche embeddings, and performs spatial in silico perturbation by replacing and editing neighbor expression. In lung adenocarcinoma, LingoCell revealed synergistic disease responses to jointly weakening alveolar differentiation programs and strengthening malignant programs. In colorectal cancer, it revealed different programs conveyed by the same fibroblast state to T cells, macrophages, and tumor cells. LingoCell provides a unified framework for prioritizing target combinations and stromal intervention programs.
affiliations: Human Genome Center, The Institute of Medical Science, The University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan; Department of Computational Biology and Medical Science, The Unive (corresponding author)

papers.title: FLASH radiotherapy drives intestinal regeneration via macrophage-derived WNT4 signaling and attenuated T-cell inflammation
papers.abstract: Ultra-high dose rate radiotherapy (FLASH-RT) reduces normal-tissue toxicity, yet how elevated dose rate improves tissue repair remains unclear. Here we combined whole-abdominal FLASH-RT and conventional radiotherapy (CONV-RT) in mice with single-cell transcriptomics, trajectory analysis, cell-cell communication inference, and in vivo perturbation experiments to define the intestinal repair ecosystem. Compared with CONV-RT, FLASH preserved Lgr5+ intestinal stem cells and Fabp1+ absorptive epithelial cells. Trajectory analysis showed that FLASH maintained stem-cell differentiation toward mature epithelial states enriched for fatty-acid metabolism. During a day-3 repair window, FLASH was accompanied by enrichment of Mrc1 macrophages, increased WNT4-associated signaling involving Fzd5Lrp5/6-expressing stem cells, and early transient {beta}-catenin activation. In vivo augmentation of Wnt4 signaling promoted crypt regeneration after CONV-RT. FLASH also reduced Tcf7 and Tbx21 CD4 T-cell populations and TNF- levels, consistent with attenuation of the pro-inflammatory CD4 T-cell response during intestinal recovery. Together, these findings indicate that FLASH-associated tissue sparing involves coordinated remodeling of regenerative and inflammatory immune states, suggesting that radiation dose rate influences not only initial tissue injury but also the immune microenvironment of subsequent recovery. Targeting this immune-stem cell crosstalk may provide a strategy to mimic FLASH-like radioprotection.
affiliations: Sino-French Institute of Nuclear Engineering and Technology, Sun Yat-sen University, Zhuhai, 519082, China (corresponding author)

papers.title: Lateral Membrane Heterogeneity Shapes Antimicrobial Association and Convergent Mechanical Responses
papers.abstract: Bacterial membranes are laterally heterogeneous, creating local physicochemical environments that can shape interactions with membrane-active antimicrobials. However, whether this spatial organization only affects local drug association or propagates into collective membrane responses remains unclear. Here we show that lateral membrane heterogeneity shapes antimicrobial association while distinct molecular responses converge on a common loss of membrane mechanical stability. Combining coarse-grained molecular dynamics, giant unilamellar vesicle fluctuation spectroscopy and microfluidic trapping, we follow octenidine, chlorhexidine and polymyxin B from molecular association to vesicle-scale behaviour. All three compounds preferentially associate with domain-associated membrane environments, but differ in how this preference changes with loading and in their effects on lipid mobility. Despite these differences, all three shift the membrane toward a mechanically softer state, while increasing exposure accelerates loss of vesicle stability under flow. These findings identify lateral membrane heterogeneity as an active determinant of antimicrobial response and provide a physical framework for understanding membrane-targeting activity beyond bulk composition and membrane-averaged charge.
affiliations: Wroclaw University of Science and Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Mechanical Fidelity of Fixed-Cell Traction Force Microscopy
papers.abstract: Cellular traction forces contribute to biological processes including cell migration and tissue morphogenesis. Traction force microscopy (TFM) is widely used to quantify these forces in living cells, but it remains unclear how well measurements after fixation reproduce the live-cell state. Here, we systematically evaluated fixation-induced changes by paired comparison of the same cells before and after fixation using different fixation protocols and substrate stiffnesses. Fixation largely preserved the spatial organization and direction of substrate displacements and reconstructed traction fields, whereas displacement, traction, and strain-energy magnitudes showed fixation-dependent changes. Among the protocols tested, glutaraldehyde (GA) provided the closest agreement with live-cell measurements, retaining up to 99% of displacement and traction magnitudes and strain energy. Paraformaldehyde-based protocols caused larger reductions in these quantities while largely preserving their spatial organization. These results show that fixed-cell TFM, particularly with GA fixation under the conditions tested here, can provide measurements close to the live-cell state and offers a practical approach for combining TFM with post-fixation fluorescence imaging in a multi-well workflow.
affiliations: TU Dortmund and LMU Munich (corresponding author)

papers.title: Bacterial-Mimetic Membranes Reveal Hopanoid-Associated Domain-Like Lateral Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Bacterial membranes are increasingly recognized as laterally heterogeneous assemblies whose local organization can regulate transport, stress adaptation, and interactions with membrane-active compounds. However, the physical principles by which bacterial lipid composition generates spatially distinct membrane environments remain poorly understood, partly because experimentally tractable models that reproducibly exhibit lateral segregation and permit quantitative characterization are limited. Here, we show that a multicomponent, hopanoid-containing bacterial-inspired membrane spontaneously self-organizes into laterally distinct physical environments that are consistently resolved in experiments and molecular simulations. Giant unilamellar vesicles prepared from a lipid mixture inspired by lipid classes found in hopanoid-producing bacteria, including Methylorubrum extorquens, exhibit stable micron-scale lateral segregation, which is independently reproduced in compositionally matched coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations. The resulting membrane environments differ in composition, packing, order, mobility, and mechanical properties. Hopanoid-associated domain-like regions are more condensed, more ordered, and less mobile, whereas PE-rich non-domain regions remain more laterally expanded and exhibit faster lipid diffusion. At the global level, the bacterial-inspired membrane displays greater bending rigidity than a fluid phosphatidylcholine reference, while ATR-FTIR measurements independently support increased lipid-chain ordering and denser membrane packing. Together, these findings establish that hopanoid-containing bacterial-inspired membranes can spontaneously generate coexisting physical environments whose distinct local properties collectively determine global membrane behavior. The resulting experimental-computational framework provides a quantitative basis for investigating bacterial-like membrane heterogeneity and how local composition, dynamics, and mechanics govern responses to membrane-targeting perturbations.
affiliations: Wroclaw University of Science and Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Development of a Thyroid Cancer to Lung Metastasis-on-a-Chip Model
papers.abstract: Background: Study of the metastatic cascade in differentiated non-medullary thyroid cancer (NMTC) is hampered by the relative lack of preclinical models that metastasize from primary tumors to other organs. We previously identified regulator of calcineurin 1 isoform 4 (RCAN1.4) as a suppressor of NMTC cell growth, invasion, and metastasis using in vitro systems and tail vein injections in immunocompromised mice. We then reported a microfluidic device mimicking the mouse tail vein injection where cancer cells were allowed to flow directly to lung organoid constructs. We now report the development of a full primary tumor to lung metastasis-on-a-chip (MOC) model for TC. Methods: Resin molds for primary and secondary sites connected by a channel were 3D printed and filled with polydimethylsiloxane to create a molded silicone elastomer. The primary site was seeded with an organoid composed of a hyaluronic acid and collagen-based hydrogel into which FTC236 and HTh74 NMTC cells with and without knockdown of RCAN1.4 were engrafted. The secondary site consisted of a hydrogel organoid into which bronchial epithelial cells and lung fibroblasts were seeded. Culture media was circulated and movement of NMTC cells to the secondary site was assessed. Results: Both cell lines that expressed RCAN 1.4 metastasized to the secondary lung site. RCAN1.4-reduced FTC236 cells had increased metastatic behavior vs controls while HTh74 was less affected by RCAN1.4 loss, similar to prior studies. To determine if the MOC could be used for incorporation of immune components and therapeutic modeling, NK-92 cells were added and were shown to be reduce metastases for both cell lines in the presence or absence of RCAN1.4. Analysis of MOC circulating fluid revealed elevated levels of granzyme B, consistent with NK-92 cell activation. Cytokine profiling identified elevated probable NMTC and NK-92-derived factors. Conclusions: These results indicate that NMTC metastatic behavior can be modeled using a novel MOC system for mechanistic and preclinical therapeutic studies.
affiliations: The Ohio State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Miniaturized Traceless Staudinger Ligation Enables Direct-to-Biology Screening of Potent BRD4 PROTACs
papers.abstract: Direct-to-biology (D2B) approaches accelerate PROTAC discovery by enabling biological screening of crude reaction mixtures without intermediate purification. However, the range of chemical transformations compatible with these workflows remains limited. Herein, we establish a miniaturized, base-free traceless Staudinger ligation platform diversifying linker chemistry for a preexisting library of E3-ligand-linker adducts bearing azide moieties. As a proof-of-concept target, BRD4 was chosen, yielding amide-linked BRD4-targeting PROTACs. By combining phosphine-functionalized JQ1 derivatives with 72 selected azide building blocks, reactions were performed on a 5 L scale in 384-well plates, achieving a mean LC-MS conversion of approximately 65%. Spiking experiments confirmed that the phosphine starting materials had no significant impact on BRD4 degradation, supporting the direct biological evaluation of crude reaction mixtures in the presence of residual starting material. Cellular screening identified 23 hits at 250 nM screening concentration, reducing BRD4 levels below 40%. Two resynthesized and purified PROTACs were subsequently validated, displaying pDC50 values of 8.2 and 7.0 and a Dmax of 90% and 96%, respectively. This work establishes traceless Staudinger ligation as a complementary D2B strategy for the rapid discovery of amide-linked PROTACs.
affiliations: Institute of Pharmaceutical Chemistry, Goethe University Frankfurt (corresponding author)

papers.title: Developing a Multimodal miR-15a Mimic to Overcome Gemcitabine and RAS(ON) Inhibitor Daraxonrasib Resistance in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma
papers.abstract: Gemcitabine remains a mainstay of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) treatment, while the RAS(ON) inhibitor daraxonrasib has recently demonstrated improved survival in previously treated metastatic disease. However, acquired resistance to both therapies remains a major clinical challenge. Here, we developed MTX-5-FU-Gem-miR-15a, a multimodal microRNA (miRNA)-based therapeutic, by chemically modifying tumor-suppressive miR-15a with methotrexate (MTX), 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), and gemcitabine (Gem) to combine sequence-specific gene regulation with disruption of nucleotide metabolism. MTX-5-FU-Gem-miR-15a exhibited low-nanomolar potency across five PDAC cell lines and retained activity in gemcitabine- and daraxonrasib-resistant models under vehicle-free conditions, substantially exceeding that of stoichiometrically matched free antimetabolites. Treatment induced S-phase accumulation, increased DNA damage and apoptosis, and suppressed checkpoint and survival-associated proteins, including WEE1, CHK1, YAP1, and BCL-2. Transcriptomic and proteomic analyses revealed increased DNA replication, replication-stress, and repair-associated programs, together with reduced oncogenic signaling. In gemcitabine-resistant cells, treatment restored the gemcitabine-activating enzyme dCK, reduced ABCC1 and ABCC3 expression, and suppressed resistance-associated signaling programs, indicating partial remodeling of resistance-associated pathways. MTX-5-FU-Gem-miR-15a also synergized with daraxonrasib (mean Bliss synergy score, 22.52) and activated tumor-cell-intrinsic STING-TBK1 signaling, accompanied by increased interferon stimulated gene expression and IFN-{beta} and CXCL10 secretion. Finally, MTX-5-FU-Gem-miR-15a retained low-nanomolar potency in three patient-derived PDAC organoids and significantly suppressed metastatic tumor growth in vivo at 4 mg/kg. Together, these findings support a multimodal miRNA therapeutic strategy that combines replication-associated DNA damage, checkpoint protein suppression, and innate immune activation-associated responses to target therapeutic resistance in PDAC.
affiliations: Stony Brook University (corresponding author)

papers.title: CD8+ T-cells protect against experimental atherosclerosis through antigen specific interactions in the plaque
authors: van de Sluis, B. A. J. A.
papers.abstract: Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease with a significant adaptive immune component. CD8+ T cells accumulate in plaques and display signatures of antigen-specific activation. However, whether this accumulation is driven by local antigen recognition and what functional consequences follow, remains poorly understood. Here we address this gap of knowledge using loss- and gain-of-function experiments. Atherosclerotic Rag-/-Ldlr-/- mice received adoptively transferred wildtype or antigen-restricted CD8+ T cells alongside CD4+ T cells to distinguish antigen-specific from antigen-independent responses. In a complementary model, ApobOVA-TGxLdlr-/- mice, expressing an ovalbumin-tagged variant of the atherosclerosis-associated ApoB100 protein, enabled OT-I CD8+ T cells to function as atherosclerosis-antigen-specific CD8+ T cells. T-cell distribution, activation and phenotype were assessed systemically and within lesions, plaque burden and composition were quantified histologically. Wildtype CD8+ T cells accumulated significantly more in aortic lesions compared to antigen-restricted CD8+ T cells, and exhibited increased activation, exhaustion and cytokine secretion, indicating that plaque-infiltrating T cells are predominantly antigen-specific. Perturbing antigen-specific CD8+ T-cell interactions significantly decreased plaque stability index, suggesting a protective role for antigen-specific CD8+ T cells. In ApobOVA-TGxLdlr-/- mice, OT-I T cells accumulated at high frequency in the liver, consistent with hepatic ApoB100-expression, and were found in circulation and aorta. Histological analysis revealed reduced plaque burden in OT-I recipients, reproducing an atheroprotective effect of antigen-specific CD8+ T-cell responses. Plaque reduction coincided with reduced TUNEL, but similar Caspase 3 staining, suggesting OT-I transfer results in reduced secondary necrosis. In line with this, CD47 expression in OT-I recipient mice was reduced and in vitro, OT-I but not antigen non-specific CD8+ T cells reduced expression of CD47 on OVA-presenting foam cells. CD8+ T-cell accumulation in experimental atherosclerosis is driven primarily by antigen-specific interactions and such responses are associated with plaque stabilization and reduced lesion formation, potentially through induction of apoptosis and prevention of secondary necrosis
affiliations: Leiden University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Preclinical Evaluation of a Novel BOC-Modified Triazoloacridinone (TRA-01AR) in Combination with 5-Fluorouracil in Colorectal Cancer
papers.abstract: 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) remains a cornerstone of colorectal cancer (CRC) therapy, yet its clinical efficacy is limited by resistance, systemic toxicity, and unfavorable pharmacokinetics. Strategies that enhance tumor sensitivity while maintaining tolerability are therefore of considerable interest. Here, we evaluated 5-FU in combination with two triazoloacridinones, C-1305 and a novel BOC-modified derivative, TRA-01AR, using integrated cellular, transcriptomic, bioenergetic, and in vivo approaches. Both compounds induced cytotoxic effects across cancer cell models and produced overlapping but distinct transcriptional responses, primarily affecting DNA replication and cell cycle pathways. Bioenergetic profiling revealed a shift toward oxidative phosphorylation accompanied by reduced glycolysis, indicating modulation of cellular metabolism relevant to chemotherapy response. Interestingly, TRA-01AR exhibited delayed cytotoxicity relative to C-1305, although the underlying mechanism remains to be defined. In vivo, the combination of 5-FU with C-1305 significantly reduced tumor weight in HT-29 xenografts, whereas 5-FU combined with TRA-01AR did not result in a statistically significant reduction compared to 5-FU alone. TRA-01AR was associated with a more favorable systemic profile and increased intratumoral blood flow compared with C-1305. Collectively, these findings indicate that triazoloacridinones modulate transcriptional and metabolic programs relevant to the 5-FU response. While C-1305 demonstrated greater antitumor activity under the tested conditions, TRA-01AR exhibited distinct biological effects, including improved tolerability and vascular modulation. Further studies are required to clarify TRA-01AR's mechanism of action and assess its potential relevance in CRC-specific therapies.
affiliations: Uniwersity of Wroclaw (corresponding author)

papers.title: Deep CyTOF immune profiles of ex vivo granulomatous responses to Mycobacterium tuberculosis differ with European and African geographical origin
papers.abstract: Genetic and environmental factors influence human immunity and modulate responses to infection. Accounting for immune heterogeneity across human populations is critical to the design of novel vaccines and host-directed interventions that would optimally benefit populations experiencing the highest disease burden. Tuberculosis (TB) burden is unevenly distributed across geographical regions and our understanding of the differential immune response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) across human populations remains limited. Here, we sought to evaluate the impact of geographical origin on ex vivo granulomatous responses to Mtbinfection. We found that peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from healthy African donors exhibited greater control of Mtbgrowth ex vivo than those isolated from European individuals. High-dimensional single-cell profiling of the granulomatous responses by cytometry by time-of-flight (CyTOF) revealed divergent profiles based on the specimens' geographical origin. Monocytes from European donors displayed a pro-inflammatory phenotype - correlating with Mtbgrowth -, whereas PBMCs of African individuals were enriched in activated, cytotoxic T cells - correlating with Mtbcontrol. Reduced inflammatory response in African monocytes following various microbial stimulations was confirmed. Taken together, our comprehensive immune profiling indicates that environmental and genetic factors shape a cytotoxic-regulatory response that promotes bacterial control. Against the current "one-treatment-fits-all" approach, our findings support the use of specimens from intervention-relevant settings to inform the targeted design of TB vaccines and host-directed interventions.
affiliations: Swiss TPH; University of Basel (corresponding author)

papers.title: Identification and localization of bone marrow ILC2s using Id2/Cxcr6 dual-reporter mice
papers.abstract: Type 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s) are present in the bone marrow, where their identification and spatial localization remain challenging because of their low abundance and the expression of shared markers by other lymphoid populations. Here, we evaluated the use of Id2YFP/+ Cxcr6GFP/+ dual-reporter mice to identify and visualize bone marrow ILC2s. Using spectral flow cytometry, we showed that both ST2- and ST2 ILC2s expressed high levels of ID2, whereas CXCR6 expression differed between these subsets. However, the ID2 expressing compartments also contained NK cells, NKT cells, conventional T cells and ILC progenitors. Surface marker profiling identified CD25 and ICOS as useful markers for enriching ILC2 populations, with ST2 enabling the segregation of the ST2- and ST2 subsets. Single-cell RNA sequencing further characterized the diversity of Id2 and Cxcr6 expressing lymphoid populations and supported the use of CD5 and NKp46 as exclusion markers. Combining these markers with the dual-reporter system, confocal microscopy revealed YFPGFPCD5-NKp46- cells compatible with an ILC2 phenotype, distributed throughout the bone marrow as isolated cells or within multicellular clusters. Complementary flow cytometric analyses demonstrated that ILC2s accounted for more than 90% of a phenotypically related reporter-positive population after exclusion of major T and NK cell populations, providing additional support for the identification of the cells visualized in situ as putative ILC2s. Together, these findings establish a strategy combining dual-reporter mice, flow cytometry, transcriptomic profiling and confocal imaging to investigate the localization and spatial organization of putative bone marrow ILC2s.
affiliations: Institut Pasteur, Univ Paris Cite (corresponding author)

papers.title: IL13 critically contributes to the antitumor activity of polyfunctional CD4+ T cells driven by constitutively active Stat5
papers.abstract: The presence of polyfunctional T cells capable of concurrently producing multiple cytokines correlates with favorable clinical outcomes in patients with cancer. We previously reported that overexpression of constitutively active Stat5a (CASTAT5) confers polyfunctionality on tumor-specific CD4 T cells, enabling durable antitumor immunity following adoptive cell therapy. However, the mechanisms underlying the enhanced antitumor effects of CASTAT5-modified T cells remain unclear. Here, we identify interleukin-13 (IL13) as a critical effector cytokine contributing to the multifaceted antitumor activity of CASTAT5-conditioned polyfunctional CD4 T cells (C5-CD4). C5-CD4 T cells exhibit a prominent T helper 2 (Th2) cytokine profile, accompanied by extensive epigenomic remodeling at the Th2 cytokine loci, as revealed by Hi-C and histone-modification CUT&Tag assays. Neutralization of IL13 diminished the antitumor efficacy of C5-CD4 T cells. Furthermore, targeted Il13 disruption substantially impaired tumor control and was associated with reduced donor T cell expansion and persistence, diminished systemic cytokine and chemokine responses, and attenuated activation of endogenous tumor-reactive CD8 T cells. Nonetheless, IL13 overexpression alone in donor CD4 T cells failed to fully recapitulate the therapeutic activity of C5-CD4 T cells, indicating that IL13 is a critical contributor but is insufficient to account for the full antitumor activity conferred by CASTAT5. Single-cell RNA sequencing associated donor-derived IL13 with increased representation of tumor-infiltrating myeloid cells and IL13-signaling in monocytes and macrophages exhibiting tissue-repair-associated transcriptional programs. Moreover, Il13 disruption diminished the therapeutic efficacy of CASTAT5-expressing CD19-targeted CAR-T cells in a mouse B-cell lymphoma model. Reanalysis of a human CD19CAR-T infusion-product dataset further revealed an association between IL13 expression and type 2 cytokine signatures linked to prolonged clinical response, suggesting a potential contribution of IL13 to the efficacy of human CD19CAR-T therapy. Together, these findings uncover an unexpected antitumor role for IL13 and establish it as a critical node linking polyfunctional donor T cells with endogenous immune cells to promote sustained tumor immunity.
affiliations: Augusta University (corresponding author)

papers.title: KAT6 and KAT7 actively maintain mitotic chromatin composition and acetylation to preserve developmental competence
papers.abstract: Mitotic bookmarking enables transmission of regulatory information across cell division, yet how active chromatin states are molecularly preserved during mitosis and how they contribute to postmitotic cell fate decisions remain unresolved. Here, we demonstrate that the acetyltransferases KAT6 and KAT7 remain chromatin-bound and catalytically active throughout mitosis in mouse and human pluripotent stem cells. Acute KAT6/7 depletion disrupts mitotic histone acetylation and the retention of multiple chromatin regulators with minimal effects on chromatin accessibility. Mechanistically, KAT6/7 bookmark both self renewal and developmental gene loci, where they are required for post-mitotic transcriptional reactivation and priming of lineage-specific programs. Consistently, genes impaired during postmitotic reactivation also fail to activate during neuronal differentiation upon continuous KAT6/7 perturbation, compromising the establishment of the neuronal program and identity. Altogether, our findings identify KAT6 and KAT7 as a cooperative mitotic chromatin maintenance system that couples active histone acetylation to preservation of chromatin composition, transcriptional memory, and developmental competence across cell division, extending the bookmarking function beyond transcriptional memory. These findings also provide a new framework for understanding KAT6/7 function in neurodevelopmental disorders and cancer.
affiliations: Sanford I. Weill Department of Medicine, Sandra and Edward Meyer Cancer Center, Weill Cornell Medicine, New York, NY, USA. (corresponding author)

papers.title: The co-evolution of adhesion and F-actin gives rise to hierarchical cellular force generation
papers.abstract: Cells --- the basic units of life --- dynamically adhere to their micro-environment, build their F-actin cytoskeleton, and apply molecular-motor generated contractile forces to it in a remarkably broad range of biological processes and physiological functions, in both health and disease. Yet, how these processes are orchestrated over multiple spatiotemporal scales is not fully understood. Using several experimental approaches and a theoretical framework, we show that adhesion assembly, on-adhesion F-actin accumulation and the contractile force itself all follow the same time evolution over tens of minutes, the cellular force timescale, at well-defined adhesion sites. We also show that the F-actin distribution away from the adhesion site features a multiplicative space-time decomposition. Finally, we show that F-actin retrograde flow --- central in the so-called molecular motor-clutch models --- is markedly faster than force generation rates, that it does not slow down over maturing adhesions and that its density drops at adhesion sites. These findings suggest a hierarchical, multi- scale force generation process that is controlled by slow adhesion recruitment, which is accompanied by rapid, bursty linear actin polymerization. The linear F-actin slowly accumulates with adhesion recruitment to form an extended near-adhesion F-actin network to which molecular motors attach and apply elastic-like contraction.
affiliations: Weizmann Institute of Science (corresponding author)

papers.title: Contig-Resolved Genetic Context of Antimicrobial Resistome in Sediments of Two Contrasting Wastewater-Impacted Rivers
papers.abstract: River sediments harbor diverse antimicrobial resistance (AMR) determinants; however, gene abundance alone provides limited insight into their genomic context, mobility potential, and associated bacterial hosts. This study employed an assembly- and read-mapping metagenomic framework to surface-sediment metagenomes (40.78 Gb clean data) from two contrasting wastewater-impacted Indian rivers, Adyar (Chennai) and Musi (Hyderabad), retaining sample-, contig- and open reading frame level provenance. ARG-carrying contigs (ACCs; n = 2,402) were annotated for mobile genetic elements (MGEs), biocide/metal resistance genes (BMRGs), virulence factor genes (VFGs), nitrogen-cycling genes (NCycGs), and putative host taxonomy. The resistomes exhibited substantial diversity (264 ARG subtypes) and spatial heterogeneity, with subtype richness in the Adyar (up to 171 subtypes) than in the Musi, where richness progressively declined downstream. Rank IV determinants dominated ARG abundance (77.82%), whereas Rank I determinants accounted for only 9.89%. MGEs were detected on just 3.12% (75/2,402) of ACCs, predominantly comprising plasmid-like contigs and proximal ARG-MGE associations. Co-occurrence with BMRGs was observed on 386 ACCs, whereas VFGs were uncommon (26 ACCs) and primarily represented dual-annotated efflux and envelope-integrity determinants rather than independent virulence loci. NCyc annotations were sparse (12 ACCs), with no evidence of complete nitrification or denitrification pathways. Taxonomic classification resolved 217 ACCs to the species level, with no matches to curated human pathogenic bacteria. Only two Acinetobacter-assigned ACCs exhibited both genus-level pathogenicity and mobility evidence. These findings highlight the importance of integrating mobility and host-taxonomic information to distinguish baseline environmental resistance from potential priorities for AMR surveillance.
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology Hyderabad (corresponding author)

papers.title: Long-range regulatory sequence models reveal a phylogenetic boundary in vertebrate genome evolution
papers.abstract: Regulatory activity at a locus depends on local sequence and on long-range interactions with sequence further away, but how long each kind of information stays shared between genomes over evolution is unknown. Here we use sequence-to-function models as a comparative assay, training FunFormer, a long-context binary classifier that reads 20 kb, together with an architecture- and parameter-matched control that reads only the central 1 kb, in six vertebrates spanning 435 million years, and measuring what each retains when applied to another genome. Within species, the long-context model outperformed three published 1 kb classifiers by 1.0 to 3.8 percentage points in every genome, a gain that came from context rather than architecture. Across species, its contribution decayed with divergence, was near zero at the amniote split and reversed between 320 and 435 Mya, while local sequence still transferred into fish. Zebrafish and Atlantic salmon, which share their divergence from tetrapods but differ by the salmonid genome duplication, behaved alike, so the reversal is not explained by the salmonid duplication. An in silico flank intervention showed that replacing the flank with GC-matched sequence from the target genome cost 8 percentage points among mammals. When a mammalian model was applied to fish, a flank drawn from the source genome on average performed as well as the target's own flank, so the model drew nothing from the fish flank that an arbitrary source-genome flank did not provide. The long-range information that these models learn therefore stops being shared between vertebrate genomes well before the local information does. The same boundary sets a practical rule for reusing models in species without their own data, where long context helps among close relatives but is a liability across deep splits, and in variant scoring most foreign models matched a native model in data-limited pig but none did in human.
affiliations: Institute of Clinical Medicine, University of Oslo, Oslo, Norway (corresponding author)

papers.title: Gene-level structure of prior knowledge and perturbation responses informs target-level predictability in prior-informed models
papers.abstract: Background: Predictive models of transcriptional responses to unseen genetic perturbations increasingly incorporate biological prior knowledge. However, it remains unclear how well prior knowledge reflects each target's perturbation-response relationships and how closely prior-derived measures track target-level predictive performance. Here, we develop a gene-similarity framework to quantify agreement among eight sources of biological prior knowledge and between prior knowledge and co-function or co-regulation relationships derived from six Perturb-seq datasets. Results: In genome-wide and essential-gene screens, prior agreement accounted for 30-47% of the variance in co-function agreement and 35-43% in co-regulation agreement. Agreement with Perturb-seq responses was higher for essential genes, lower for transcription factor and signaling genes, and varied with gene expression characteristics and cellular context. We compared prior agreement and prior-derived train-test similarity with measures based on the observed test response in tracking target-level predictive performance. Across three prior-informed models, predictions were more accurate for targets whose observed perturbation-response relationships better matched prior knowledge and that were more similar to training perturbations. Notably, prior agreement and prior-derived train-test similarity, calculated without the test response, tracked relative differences in target-level predictive performance. The strength of these associations varied across models and datasets and, for train-test similarity, across prior sources. Conclusion: Our framework reveals gene- and context-level heterogeneity in how biological knowledge aligns with perturbation responses, and provides an a priori basis for assessing relative perturbation predictability before perturbation responses are measured.
affiliations: Yonsei University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Conserved RNA structural elements mediate WDR5 recognition of the long non-coding RNA UMLILO
papers.abstract: The long non-coding RNA (lncRNA), UMLILO (upstream master lncRNA of the inflammatory chemokine locus), regulates the epigenetic programming of innate immune genes. Although its basic mechanism was revealed in cells, the molecular basis by which UMLILO interacts with its partner, WD repeat-containing protein 5 (WDR5), remained unknown. To understand how UMLILO interacts with WDR5, we determined the secondary structure of UMLILO by chemical probing and performed binding assays, uncovering the multivalent nature of their interaction, involving multiple RNA stem-loops. Conservational analysis revealed a stem-loop structurally conserved across mammals. Furthermore, we found that UMLILO engages multiple sites on the surface of WDR5 as revealed by NMR chemical shift perturbation analysis, and that full-length UMLILO increases WDR5 recruitment into in vitro condensates. Our report provides a detailed characterization of the molecular basis of WDR5 recognition by an RNA and establishes a new paradigm for the role of IPLs in enhancing gene expression.
affiliations: New York University (corresponding author)

papers.title: A shared wireless acquisition core for cortical and peripheral recordings in freely moving mice
papers.abstract: Experiments in freely moving mice often require simultaneous recording of cortical, muscle and movement signals, but adding channels and peripheral sensors increases headstage burden and acquisition complexity. We developed an eight-channel wireless headstage that records six cortical channels and two neck-electrode channels, together with synchronized acceleration. Reassigning electrodes enables cardiac recording with the same electronics. The 13*11*3 mm board forms part of an approximately 1.2-g head-mounted assembly, with the battery carried separately on the back. With inputs internally shorted, root-mean-square noise was 0.176V over 0.5-100 Hz. In four mice with chemically induced seizures, recordings resolved distributed cortical activity and animal-level spectral changes. Subject-dependent evaluation of the seizure detector yielded an overlap-based event F1 of 0.893 +/- 0.022. During pseudo-online replay, inference-software processing took 46.394 +/- 0.363 ms per update. In a separate cohort, recordings revealed distinct coherence patterns associated with movement and social behavior, highlighting potential as biomarkers of behavior-related neural activity. Together, these results demonstrate concurrent cortical, muscle, and movement recording through a common acquisition chain, with electrode reassignment extending the same hardware to cardiac recording.
affiliations: Tsinghua University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Decoupled Surface Engineering Enables Cell-Interactive Edible Microcarriers across Food-Grade Polysaccharides
papers.abstract: Edible microcarriers for cultivated meat must support cell expansion while also contributing appropriately to the properties of the final food product. Food-grade polysaccharides exemplify this design challenge: despite their desirable food-related functions, they generally provide limited support for cell adhesion. This limitation calls for a strategy that introduces cell-interactive functionality without constraining bulk material selection. Here, we developed a decoupled surface-engineering strategy in which a poly-L-lysine/tannic acid (PLL/TA) interface is constructed on preformed polysaccharide microcarriers to enable cell-supportive functionality to emerge through interactions with the culture environment. On alginate microcarriers, PLL/TA modification markedly enhanced initial cell attachment, with 83% of modified microcarriers supporting attached cells compared with no detectable attachment on bare alginate. Cell-covered area subsequently reached 63.74% by Day 6, compared with 9.64% on PLL-coated microcarriers and negligible coverage on bare alginate. The PLL/TA interface promoted the recruitment of culture-medium proteins, including fibronectin, supporting an adaptive mechanism in which a cell-supportive interface develops through protein recruitment rather than predefined protein presentation. Importantly, the same surface modification enhanced early cell attachment when extended to pectin and carrageenan microcarriers and to Hanwoo bovine and Handon porcine muscle cells. On carrageenan microcarriers, the proportion of cell-bearing microcarriers increased from 30% to 100% for Hanwoo bovine cells and from 10% to 100% for Handon porcine cells following PLL/TA modification. These findings establish an adaptive and transferable surface-engineering strategy that enables cell-interactive functionality to be engineered separately from bulk material selection, expanding the design space for edible microcarriers in cultivated meat production.
affiliations: Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH) (corresponding author)

papers.title: Broad-spectrum in situ genetic reprogramming of native microbiomes
papers.abstract: Complex microbial communities are found throughout terrestrial, aquatic, and animal-associated ecosystems. Genetic modification of discrete microbial taxa within native communities represents a powerful tool to study and augment microbiome functions. Herein, we develop Synthetic Phage Assisted Reprogrammable and Targetable Addition (SPARTA) as a one-step strategy for packaging, delivering, and integrating large synthetic DNA into a broad range of native microbiomes. SPARTA leverages a broad-spectrum synthetic phage particle for in situ genome engineering within complex soil, freshwater, and mammalian fecal microbiomes, reprogramming 59 native species across 16 families. By modulating SPARTA components, we further demonstrated tunability of SPARTA towards targeted microbiome population. Additionally, we built a novel companion tool to quantitatively identify engineered taxa, named 16S crRNA-guided inference of bacterial engineering sequencing or ScRibe-seq. The SPARTA-ScRibe-seq pipeline delivered and validated functional synthetic gene clusters in diverse native microbiomes while preserving the original microbial community structure. Together, this novel genome engineering framework constitutes an end-to-end programmable platform for rational and customizable reprogramming of native microbiomes.
affiliations: California Institute of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Parallel transcriptome profiling of soybean cyst nematodes (SCN) during a three-way interaction among SCN, soybean aphids, and soybean
papers.abstract: The soybean cyst nematode (SCN), Heterodera glycines (Ichinoe) (Rhabditida: Heteroderidae) is arguably the greatest yield-limiting factor for soybean (Glycine max [L.] Merr.) production in the United States. Previous research found that the impact of SCN infestation on yield is exacerbated during concurrent infestations with soybean aphids (SBA), Aphis glycines (Matsurmura) (Hemiptera: Aphididae). Although recent research has characterized the host root transcriptomic response during these infestations little is known about the corresponding in planta gene expression dynamics of either pest. This study examines the transcriptomic expression of SCN in soybean cultivars' roots under single or combined SBA infestations at two different time points: 5 and 30 days post-infestation (DPI). The SCN transcriptomics for SCN-susceptible (S) PI 518671 (Williams 82) cultivar reacted equivalently to both SCN and SCN + SBA treatments. However, transcriptomics in SCN-resistant (R) MN1806CN (H. glycines HG type 0/race 3 resistant) demonstrated an elevated significant expression pattern under the SCN + SBA combined treatment. During the early infestation period (i.e., sampled at 5 DPI), both S and R cultivars reacted similarly, irrespective of treatment conditions. The functional enrichment analysis of 1829 differentially expressed genes/transcripts showed that during the early co-infestation period (5 DPI), SCN genes were significant and mapped towards resistance breakage, whereas in the late stage (30 DPI), the gene flux oriented towards nematode dormancy. Together, these results suggest that SCN activity is amplified when combined with SBA, offering foundational data for molecular breeding to produce SCN resistant soybean cultivars.
affiliations: Department of Biology & Microbiology, South Dakota State University, Brookings, SD 57007, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Integrating evolutionary and protein language model representations for thermodynamically consistent stability prediction
papers.abstract: At fixed thermodynamic conditions, protein stability changes obey reversal antisymmetry and path independence, but learned predictors need not satisfy these properties. Explicit alignment-derived evolutionary information may also complement single-sequence protein language model representations, motivating their integration under clearly defined physical constraints. Here, we develop a training-free strategy that combines thermodynamic constraints with complementary sequence representations. We first introduce EvoPhi-DDG, a potential-based adaptation of the alignment-conditioned evolutionary predictor MSAesm_ddG. By antisymmetrizing its predictions and setting the hidden biases to zero, we express stability changes as differences of a learned, evolution-informed effective potential conditioned on the mutation site and alignment context. This guarantees exact reversal consistency and exact same-site transitivity under fixed alignment contexts while preserving predictive accuracy. We further extend the adapted predictor to multiple substitutions through a background-aware construction that preserves whole-variant antisymmetry. We then combine EvoPhi-DDG with the previously published JanusDDG using fixed, equal weight averaging to test predictive complementarity without additional training. The ensemble preserves exact antisymmetry and reduces multisite pathway-closure RMSE relative to JanusDDG across all evaluated path lengths. Furthermore, the ensemble outperforms both components on S669 and S96, achieving Pearson correlations of 0.59 and 0.55, respectively, compared with 0.55 and 0.52 for JanusDDG and 0.53 and 0.48 for EvoPhi-DDG. On the multiple-substitution benchmark PTmul-NR, the ensemble achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.66, improving on JanusDDG's 0.61 and matching the EvoPhi-DDG extension at the reported precision. Together, these findings distinguish two benefits: averaging complementary predictions improves accuracy, whereas the potential-based reformulation strengthens physical consistency. They support the integration of alignment-conditioned and single-sequence representations without additional training, while separating predictive improvements from mathematical guarantees.
affiliations: University of Turin (corresponding author)

papers.title: OmniT2I: a unified table-to-image framework for survival prediction and cross-modal inference with incomplete multimodal cancer data
papers.abstract: Molecular profiles and histopathology provide complementary information about cancer prognosis, but these data are often incomplete for individual patients. Here we present OmniT2I, a table-to-image framework for survival prediction and cross-modal inference from incomplete multimodal cancer data. Each molecular profile was converted into a three-channel image representation with correlation-based feature placement. OmniT2I combines available molecular and histopathology embeddings through availability-aware fusion and predicts missing modalities from those observed. Across 10,373 patients with 32 cancer types, the C-index was 0.631 within cancer types and 0.783 with all cancers pooled (0.660 and 0.787 in 5,605 patients with all five modalities). A single model handled all 31 modality combinations and, compared with nine survival methods trained separately for each, achieved higher C-indices in 240 of 279 pooled and 226 of 279 within-cancer comparisons. Adding predictions of withheld modalities to observed inputs improved pooled C-indices in all 180 pairings of observed and withheld modality sets and within-cancer C-indices in 164.
