Adding measured histopathology to RNA produced the largest within-cancer C-index gain among the four additional modalities evaluated, whereas adding copy number variation reduced it. In seven external cohorts, frozen RNA-only C-indices differed from test performance in the corresponding cancer type in TCGA by a median of -0.003 (range, -0.092 to +0.079). OmniT2I enables prognostic modeling with incomplete multimodal data.
affiliations: The Ohio State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Batch, Prefetch, Skip, Orient, Squeeze: Faster, Smaller k-mer dictionaries via the Spectral Burrows-Wheeler transform
papers.abstract: Looking up k-mers in an index is a core operation in genomics, underlying read mapping, metagenomic classification, and many other tasks. Queries are often streaming: the k-mers come from a longer sequence such as a sequencing read, and consecutive k-mers overlap. The fastest index for such queries is currently the hashing-based SSHash; indexes based on the spectral Burrows-Wheeler transform (SBWT) are competitive in space but slower. We show how to make SBWT indexes both faster and smaller. First, we process queries in small batches and prefetch the memory each will need next, hiding the latency of the dependent random accesses that dominate a lookup; together with a new rank structure that reads one cache line per query, this makes k-mer lookups about seven times faster than unbatched SBWT search. Second, we extend batching to streaming search and show that one failed lookup can rule out many k-mers of a read at once, which removes the need for the longest common suffix array. Third, we build an SBWT that stores only one orientation of each k-mer, thereby halving its size, with a modified search that exploits how rarely the orientation changes along a read. Finally, we adapt a compact subset rank structure to batched search. On the collections of the SSHash benchmark, and on two collections up to 15 times larger, our fastest index answers streaming queries for 31-mers faster than SSHash on every read set, by up to 4.9 times, using 12 bits per canonical k-mer against SSHash's 7.4-11.1. We also show that a 6.1-bit index is still faster than SSHash on most read sets, and that our smallest index needs about 4 bits per canonical k-mer. Unlike that of SSHash, the space of our indexes barely varies across collections. Our code is available at https://github.com/anadis504/sbwt-squeeze-rs.
affiliations: University of Helsinki (corresponding author)

papers.title: ProClust provides reliable statistical significance of clusters for single-cell transcriptomic data
papers.abstract: Clustering of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data is widely used to identify cell populations. However, overclustering can partition a single cell population into multiple clusters, potentially leading to spurious identification of cell subpopulations. Assessing the statistical significance of clusters is therefore needed to support their biological interpretation. We propose ProClust, a statistical test for clustering significance in scRNA-seq data. ProClust defines a single cluster as a log-concave distribution and adopts a projection-based approach to quantify clustering uncertainty through p-values. These projections can also provide interpretable visual evidence for individual clusterings. ProClust merges clusters when there is insufficient evidence to reject the single-cluster null hypothesis, refining an initial overclustering without prespecifying the final number of clusters. Across parametric and PBMC-based semi-synthetic simulations, ProClust avoided false subdivisions under single-population null settings while consistently recovering the underlying population structure across different numbers of true populations. In real scRNA-seq datasets from the Human Lung Cell Atlas, Tabula Muris, and Hydra, ProClust produced clustering solutions that showed overall agreement with reference annotations while retaining supported substructure and merging groups with insufficient evidence for separation. Together, these results demonstrate that ProClust provides a statistically principled and interpretable framework for refining an initial overclustering and distinguishing supported cellular heterogeneity. The ProClust R package is available at https://github.com/Anonym027/ProClust.
affiliations: University of Michigan (corresponding author)

papers.title: Automated Continuous LLM-driven Biomedical Literature Mining for a Large-Scale Hepatotoxicity Knowledge Base
papers.abstract: Predicting whether a chemical disturbs liver and mitochondrial function matters for drug safety and environmental risk assessment, but the data available for training such models are small and mostly curated by hand. We describe an automated pipeline that uses a large language model (LLM) to collect hepatotoxicity findings from the biomedical literature. The pipeline runs a PubMed/PMC query, downloads the matching full texts or abstracts, asks the LLM to record each reported effect in a fixed schema (tested chemical, biomarker, direction of change, and related fields) with controlled vocabularies, and writes de-duplicated records to a database that is updated as new papers appear. The current snapshot holds 189,212 findings on 17,002 chemicals from 53,575 articles (1995-2026), covering 235 biomarkers reported for at least 20 chemicals. In a manual check of 217 findings from 35 articles, 208 findings (from 33 articles) were fully correct; the other 9, all from 2 articles, were incorrect. As a use case, we train structure-based QSAR models, both graph neural networks and classic baselines, for each biomarker; at this data scale the classic models remain competitive. The pipeline and the knowledge base will be made publicly available.
affiliations: Old Dominion University (corresponding author)

papers.title: DaliScope: Distilling Biological Insights from Deep Structural Alignments
papers.abstract: Structural similarity searches reveal protein relationships that sequence alignments miss, but treating DALI results as isolated match lists misses deeper connections. We present DaliScope, an interactive Python framework that treats complete DALI target sets as structured populations for systematic analysis of protein structural neighbourhoods. DaliScope combines structural community detection with sequence profiling, Pfam annotation, residue mapping, and 3D visualization, enabling target sets to be subdivided and examined at the residue level. We demonstrate two applications. In a multidomain protein with sparse domain annotation, structural analysis uncovered previously unannotated domains. A structurally anchored HxD...H signature occurred in 697 of 1,093 Pfam-annotated CUPIN domains and in 15 domains lacking Pfam annotation; relaxing the central residue constraint recovered 96% of Pfam-annotated CUPIN domains among the DALI targets. In a second application, a DALI search with transitive closure returned >12,000 hits. Applying an 80% coverage criterion to a conserved structural core reduced this set to 6,708 domain instances, resolved into 23 structural communities. (80% was chosen instead of the default 50% because the GOLD domain has a compact core with short loops.) Many communities were strongly enriched for individual Pfam families while providing structural context for 1,097 targets lacking Pfam assignments. Three-dimensional superimposition revealed structural continuity among related {beta}-sandwich architectures through progressive changes in sheet geometry and auxiliary elements. Together, these examples show how a single DALI query provides a structural anchor for organizing large neighbourhoods, extending interpretation beyond sequence-based annotations, and deriving structurally anchored sequence signatures from defined populations.
affiliations: University of Helsinki (corresponding author)

papers.title: DecoyOpt: A two-stage pipeline for decoy-aware enzyme discrimination and EC number prediction
papers.abstract: Accurate and efficient EC number prediction is essential for elucidating the catalytic roles of enzymes. Although similarity-based and deep learning-based approaches have advanced this task, they often fail to distinguish active enzymes from closely related decoys inactivated by local functional-site mutations, leading to high false-positive rates (FPRs). We propose DecoyOpt, a two-stage pipeline for decoy-aware enzyme discrimination and EC number prediction. Specifically, we generated putatively inactive functional-site decoys using ESM3 and evaluated 16 protein language models across three splits. An MLP trained with classification and ranking losses distinguishes enzymes from unannotated proteins and decoys before a contrastive learning model assigns EC numbers to predicted enzymes. On the most stringent GraphPart 40% split, DecoyOpt achieves an MCC of 0.899 and a D0 decoy FPR of 6.17%, outperforming retrained baselines. Across all splits, it outperforms these baselines in EC number prediction on the full test set while maintaining performance close to CLEAN on the enzyme subset. It also correctly annotates all four wild-type enzymes and rejects all eight inactive or nearly inactive variants. We believe that DecoyOpt has potential for annotating uncharacterized proteins and their variants, with applications in genomics, synthetic biology, and biocatalysis.
affiliations: Faculty of Applied Sciences, Macao Polytechnic University, 999078, Macau SAR, China (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cross-state representation learning enables prospective discovery of dynamic protein allosteric sites
papers.abstract: Allosteric regulation offers multifunctional induction in therapeutic interventions, yet conformational plasticity hinders computational identification of allosteric sites. Machine learning models rely on static holo (ligand-bound) structures, generalizing poorly to apo or substrate-bound states where binding pockets are transient or cryptic. We present AsBench2, a cross-state site-recognition benchmark, and AllositeUltra, a deep learning framework integrating multimodal protein representations (combining structure-aware language models with physical dynamics) and residue-guided candidate supplementation, effectively decoupling site detection from static pocket geometry. AllositeUltra demonstrates superior generalization, achieving Top-3 site recovery rates of 65.2% and 70.6% on apo and substrate-bound structures, respectively, representing relative improvements of 36.4% and approximately 50% over the best-performing baselines. Prospective application to MAGI2 identifies a previously unrecognized interdomain allosteric pocket, validated at atomic resolution through small-molecule screening and X-ray crystallography. Proteome-wide application yields a high-confidence atlas of targetable allosteric sites, bridging the gap between structural representation learning and prospective AI-driven drug discovery.
affiliations: Shanghai Jiaotong University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Unavoidable Disasters: the Hsp70 Chaperone Can Only Prevent Aggregation Over a Limited Time Span
papers.abstract: Cells must attain and maintain proper protein folding and avoid aggregation: this is a pervasive challenge across all domains of life. Molecular chaperones are central to this process, acting through mechanisms shaped by the free-energy landscapes of their client proteins. The impact of chaperones on client-specific kinetic and thermodynamic characteristics, however, remains poorly characterized. Here, we develop the CHAMPION70 computational model to perform kinetic simulations on the E. Coli Hsp70 chaperone system in the presence of client-protein folding and aggregation. Experimentally determined folding/unfolding/aggregation rate constants are taken into account. In the case of weakly aggregation-prone clients, CHAMPION70 predicts that Hsp70 prevents aggregation only over timescales approaching the average human lifespan (79 years). For strongly aggregation-prone clients, however, aggregation inevitably occurs starting from a few minutes, even at higher-than-physiological Hsp70 concentrations. Thus, the Hsp70 chaperone system merely delays, yet surprisingly does not eliminate, the onset of aggregation. Further, CHAMPION70 predicts that Hsp70 most effectively retards the aggregation of slow-folding, thermodynamically stable clients. In contrast, thermodynamically unstable clients remain engaged with Hsp70 for prolonged periods even when aggregation propensity is low, thereby consuming chaperone capacity and reducing the extent of productive folding. This outcome suggests that condensate formation by proteins containing disordered regions may serve to mitigate unnecessary Hsp70 engagement. In all, our results provide a quantitative framework for understanding how client-specific kinetic and thermodynamic properties shape chaperone activity and show that the Hsp70 chaperone system does not altogether prevent aggregation: it merely retards it.

papers.title: Dynamical Fingerprints of Rare-Event Transitions from Transition Corridors
papers.abstract: Rare transitions are central in science, yet their mechanisms are obscured by the high dimensionality of complex dynamics, a challenge particularly pronounced in biomolecules where rare conformational transitions underlie functional processes. A transition-conditioned dynamical fingerprint is introduced for a rare \(A \mathbin{\text{--}} B\) event, in which the transition-relevant subset is targeted rather than a global decomposition and the problem is treated dynamically. Within a selected transition corridor, barrier-crossing motion is extracted and microscopic players are ranked through a corridor-conditioned informativeness measure, after which the highest-ranked players are subjected to intervention tests of their transition leverage using the REST2 scaling scheme, metadynamics, and targeted mutation. Across three benchmark proteins, targeting these players facilitates basin-to-basin transitions while maintaining high fidelity to the prescribed transition corridor, providing handles for mechanistic analysis, enhanced sampling, control, and design.
affiliations: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Ultra-low-dose same-target combinations control drug resistance across stages
papers.abstract: The emergence of drug resistance continues to limit the long term effectiveness of cancer therapies [1], as tumour cells adapt to therapeutic selective pressure through diverse genetic and non-genetic routes [2,3]. Despite advances in more potent and next generation inhibitors and mechanism based combination therapies [4,5], durable disease control remains difficult to achieve. Here we tested an alternative strategy: combining multiple inhibitors directed against the same oncogenic driver, each at ultra low doses with minimal individual activity, to delay resistance emergence. In epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) driven cancer models, such ultra low dose same target combinations (ULDCs) distributed individually weak perturbations across multiple inhibitors directed against the same target and achieved substantial growth inhibition in vitro and antitumour activity in vivo despite weak effects of the corresponding single agents. Under similar levels of growth inhibition (~50%), single-agent EGFR inhibitors generated resistant outgrowth, whereas a five drug ULDC delayed resistance emergence. Increasing the number of inhibitors further delayed resistance emergence, with no detectable resistant outgrowth observed for combinations containing 8 to 14 inhibitors within the experimental timeframe. The five drug ULDC also retained measurable growth inhibitory activity against gefitinib resistant PC-9/GR cells, and resistant cells arising under five drug ULDC treatment exhibited markedly greater reversibility following drug withdrawal than those arising under single agent treatment. Although pharmacological additivity or synergy may contribute to the collective growth inhibitory effects of ULDCs, the divergent long term resistance outcomes observed under similar levels of growth inhibition indicate that resistance behaviour is not determined by inhibitory strength alone. Instead, our findings support a model in which increasing same target inhibitor diversity progressively constrains the adaptive trajectories available during resistance evolution, while therapeutic perturbation architecture may also influence the stability of resistant states that emerge. More broadly, these findings support the concept of same target collective suppression, in which multiple individually weak perturbations directed against the same target can collectively produce substantial antitumour activity and constrain resistance evolution across multiple stages. We propose that increasing same target inhibitor diversity may restrict accessible adaptive trajectories, while therapeutic perturbation architecture may also influence the stability of resistant states.

papers.title: Molecular Mechanisms of Quizartinib Resistance in FLT3 Mutants
papers.abstract: Quizartinib, a type II FLT3 inhibitor approved for FLT3-ITD-positive acute myeloid leukemia (AML), is frequently limited by acquired resistance, which arises in up to 40% of patients with disease progression and is driven largely by the D835Y and F691L kinase-domain mutations. To define the underlying mechanisms, we performed triplicate 200-ns all-atom molecular dynamics simulations of wild-type FLT3, FLT3-D835Y, and FLT3-F691L in complex with Quizartinib, combining conformational analysis, MM-GBSA binding free-energy calculations, and binding-pocket characterization. Both mutations destabilized the inactive DFG-out conformation required for type II inhibitor binding, with mean binding free-energy reductions of 5 kcal/mol for D835Y and 10 kcal/mol for F691L relative to wild-type. D835Y disrupted the activation-loop electrostatic network and reduced Cys694 hydrogen-bond occupancy from 85% to 45%, whereas F691L abolished key van der Waals contacts and opened a 120 cubic Angstrom hydrophobic void at the gatekeeper position. Both mutants sampled a wider range of conformations and lost 14-17% of binding-pocket volume. These predictions were corroborated by CCK-8 viability assays and Western blotting of p-FLT3 (Y591) in Ba/F3 cells, which reproduced the predicted resistance hierarchy (F691L > D835Y > WT) at the cellular level. Together, these results indicate that D835Y and F691L confer resistance through distinct electrostatic and hydrophobic mechanisms that converge on destabilization of the inactive kinase conformation, providing a structural basis for the design of next-generation FLT3 inhibitors.

papers.title: Parsimonious Creatures: Building Gene Regulatory Networks Robust to Somatic Evolution
papers.abstract: For early multicellular life to have formed and maintained cellular organization, preventing loss of controlled cell replication due to somatic evolution was of critical importance, and remains important to this day for control of cancer. We study how gene regulatory networks (GRNs) can be designed to slow the divergence of somatic clonal lineages in the context of early multicellular life. We model the mutation of GRNs within simplified 12-celled organisms we term "parsimonious creatures", who must replicate from a single cell to 12 cells and then prevent replication past 12 cells to maximize fitness. We found two minimal motifs can achieve these goals, but both are prone to breakdown through somatic evolution: The feedforward motif, which is loosely regulating but relatively robust, and the simple step motif, which uses strong interactions and feedback to form memoryless ultrasensitivity, but is fragile. These simple motifs may be duplicated to form redundant networks via one of two structures: averaging redundancy, which averages multiple sources of information, and min redundancy, which adopts the most conservative source. Averaging redundancy uniformly slows somatic evolution, while min redundancy stalls somatic evolution until neutral mutations accumulate. Either may be superior dependent on life history. However, averaging redundancy slowly increases fitness as the network becomes larger, but large min redundancy networks eventually become "paralyzed", increasing the probability of senescence and reducing fitness. These GRN designs are idealized, yet provide imperfect solutions with fundamental tradeoffs, offering insight as to why somatic evolution remains an incompletely solved problem for multicellular life.

papers.title: Dual CD40/CD28 co-stimulation reprograms the solid-tumor microenvironment to unleash CAR-T and endogenous anti-tumor immunity
papers.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has shown limited efficacy against solid tumors, owing to poor T-cell persistence, an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) and cancer immune evasion. Here we describe LACO-Stim (lymphocytes-APC co-stimulator), a chimeric co-stimulatory molecule composed of an agonistic anti-CD40 single-chain variable fragment (scFv) and the CD28 intracellular signaling domain, such that a single molecule activates CD40-expressing antigen-presenting cells while delivering CD28 co-stimulation to the T cell that bears it. Co-expressed with a 4-1BB-based CAR (LACO-CAR-T), it enhanced anti-tumor activity in vitro and achieved durable, complete in most mice, tumor regression rather than transient control in xenograft and immunocompetent models. In immunocompetent hosts, LACO-CAR-T activated dendritic cells, reprogrammed tumor macrophages toward M1-like, antigen-presenting states, and induced epitope spreading with endogenous CD8 T-cell responses against tumor neoantigens. Single-cell transcriptomics and RNA-velocity analysis revealed coordinated immune remodeling: T cells shifted toward a more stem-like, less terminally exhausted state, regulatory T cells declined in frequency and suppressive function, and myeloid cells acquired antigen-presentation programs while excessive inflammatory and suppressive signaling was restrained. LACO-Stim further synergized with anti-PD-1 blockade to control tumor growth. LACO-Stim thus enables CAR-T cells to coordinate intrinsic T-cell reinforcement with extrinsic immune reprogramming, converting an immunosuppressive TME into a de-inflamed (reduced inflammatory signaling), de-suppressed rather than merely armed niche that supports endogenous anti-tumor immunity.

papers.title: Functional Conservation Amid Extreme Divergence in Freshwater SAR11 Hypervariable Region 2
papers.abstract: The Ca. Pelagibacterales order (SAR11) is a ubiquitous bacterioplankton in aquatic ecosystems. The genomes of SAR11 bacteria contain hypervariable region 2 (HVR2), the largest HVR with extreme diversity. Previous studies collectively indicated the enrichment of cell-surface modification genes on HVR2, which have been hypothesized to facilitate phage evasion. However, characterisation of HVR2 has primarily targeted marine clades and been limited for freshwater SAR11 (aka. Fontibacterium). Here, we employed single-cell genomics and recovered 176 Fontibacterium HVR2 sequences from Lake Biwa (Japan) and Lake Zurich (Switzerland), across multiple sampling years for Lake Biwa. Comparative sequence analyses revealed that freshwater HVR2 showed high intra-population diversity and appears to evolve independently of the rest of the genome, mirroring patterns observed in marine counterparts. Nevertheless, highly conserved HVR2 sequence pairs were observed for distinct Fontibacterium species from the two intercontinental habitats, suggesting horizontal transfers of HVR2 with conserved functional configurations across divergent lineages and large spatial scales. Further comparison with 145 marine HVR2 sequences revealed HVR2 sequences displaying synteny between Fontibacterium and marine SAR11, and 209 gene families conserved across habitats, including three near-universally conserved families. All examined freshwater HVR2s contained initiator methionine tRNA genes concentrated near the boundaries of the 5S region, suggesting a tDNA-anchored integration mechanism. These results suggest the functional equivalence of HVR2 across marine and freshwater SAR11 clades, and the existence of a shared pool of HVR2 sequences that evolve reticulately through mutual genetic exchange, independent of the vertical inheritance of the rest of the genome.
affiliations: Kyoto University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Gene-resolved metagenomics reveals partitioned nitrogen transformation potential in a landfill leachate sequencing batch reactor microbiome
papers.abstract: Landfill leachate can contain high concentrations of ammonia and organic nitrogen requiring treatment before discharge. Sequencing batch reactors (SBRs) promote biological nitrogen removal through alternating aerobic and anoxic conditions, but taxonomic profiling alone cannot resolve how nitrogen transformation and competing retention pathways are distributed across microbial communities. This study applied gene-resolved metagenomics to a sludge sample collected from a UK landfill leachate SBR. Nitrogen-metabolism genes were linked to contig-level taxonomic assignments and metagenome-assembled genome bins to examine nitrification, denitrification, dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA), and assimilatory nitrate reduction (ANR). Nitrogen-transformation potential was partitioned across dominant and minor taxa. Nitrospirota and Pseudomonadota were the most abundant classified phyla, whereas Actinomycetota represented only 4% of the community but included Actinomycetes, which showed the highest within-taxon proportion of nitrogen metabolism associated genes. amoABC was assigned only to Nitrosomonas and Nitrososphaerota, whereas denitrification genes were more widely distributed but frequently occurred as partial pathways. nosZ was detected only in the minor phyla Chloroflexota, Acidobacteriota and Myxococcota. DNRA and ANR-associated genes occurred across multiple lineages; nirA in Nitrospira and DNRA-associated nirBD elsewhere within Nitrospirota suggested nitrifier-associated lineages may also encode nitrogen retention potential. Gene-resolved metagenomics identified candidate low-abundance contributors, restricted distributions of genes associated with ammonia oxidation and nitrous oxide reduction, and nitrogen-retention potential not apparent from taxonomic composition alone. Because the study examined DNA-level potential in a single sludge sample, expression, reactor chemistry and longitudinal data are needed to establish pathway activity and operational relevance.
affiliations: Northumbria University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Northern palsa and peat ecosystem microbiomes are potentially supported by hydrogen and carbon monoxide metabolism
papers.abstract: Northern peatland and permafrost ecosystems are facing rapid changes, with increasing temperatures, permafrost thaw and shifts in hydrology. Characterizing microbial communities and metabolic potential from the soils and associated water bodies is crucial to understanding the changes in biogeochemical cycling in these ecosystems. For this, samples were collected and sequenced from subarctic palsa and peat soils, along with samples from associated thaw ponds and streams. Metagenomics was utilized in describing the microbiome and its metabolic potential in these environments. Palsa soils hosted microbial communities that were distinct from the peatland soils, ponds and stream waters. Soils and their adjacent ponds shared taxa, and peat soils and ponds also shared taxa with the streams, unlike palsa soils which were likely more hydrologically isolated. Based on metabolic marker gene ratio for denitrification [(nirS+nirK)/nosZ], palsa soils had the strongest potential to be a source of nitrous oxide (N2O) out of all the sample types. Marker genes for hydrogen gas (H2) and carbon monoxide (CO) utilization were abundant across soil environments and metagenome assembled genomes, suggesting that trace gas oxidation is likely one of the key energy sources for microbiomes. In the palsa ponds and peat soils pmoA, marker gene for methanotrophy, was the most abundant compared to the other sample types.
affiliations: University of Helsinki (corresponding author)

papers.title: Epigenetic Mechanisms Inhibit Smad7 and Contribute to Fibrosis in Crohn's Disease
papers.abstract: Background & Aims: TGF-beta1 is a central regulator of profibrotic gene expression, extracellular matrix deposition, and the development of intestinal fibrosis in patients with fibrostenotic Crohns disease (CD). Unlike the increased expression of Smad7 in mucosal and lamina propria monocytes, where it impairs Treg function, mesenchymal cells from patients with fibrostenotic CD do not exhibit elevated Smad7 expression and instead display sustained TGF-beta1 signaling. We therefore sought to elucidate the mechanisms underlying the unexpected silencing of Smad7 in fibrostenotic CD. Methods: Subepithelial myofibroblasts (SEMFs) and muscularis smooth muscle cells were isolated from paired normal and affected ileal tissues obtained from the same patients with each Montreal phenotype of CD, as well as from non-CD controls. Gene expression, RNA-binding affinity, transcriptional activity, promoter methylation, protein levels, and the mechanisms that regulate Smad7 expression were evaluated in ex vivo tissues and primary cultured cells. MicroRNA-21 (miR-21) localization was assessed by RNAscope. miR-21-mediated suppression of Smad7 was investigated using antagomiR-21. Smad7 silencing through promoter hypermethylation was confirmed using 5-Azacytidine treatment and DNA methyltransferase 1 (DNMT1) knockdown. Smad7 lysine acetylation and Smurf1/2-mediated ubiquitination were examined using selective inhibitors and proximity ligation assays. Results: In SEMFs from patients with fibrostenotic CD, aberrant silencing of Smad7 resulted from DNMT1-dependent promoter hypermethylation and pSmad3-driven, miR-21-mediated degradation of Smad7 mRNA. In addition, Smurf1/2 promoted ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of acetylated Smad7 protein. Inhibition of miR-21 with antagomiR-21 restored Smad7 expression and reduced TGF-beta 1-dependent profibrotic gene expression. Likewise, demethylation with 5-Azacytidine or knockdown of DNMT1 induced Smad7 promoter hypomethylation and restored Smad7 expression. Furthermore, modulation of the balance between p300 acetyltransferase and histone deacetylase 1 (HDAC1) stabilized Smad7 protein by protecting it from degradation. Conclusions: A distinctive pattern of epigenetic silencing and post-translational regulation of Smad7 was identified in patients with fibrostenotic CD. These mechanisms collectively promote unrestrained TGF-beta1 signaling by suppressing Smad7 expression and stability in SEMFs, thereby contributing to the development of intestinal fibrosis.
affiliations: Washington University School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Matrix Gla Protein deficiency reveals a previously unrecognized mucosal calcification in the mouse airways
papers.abstract: Tracheal calcification is a common finding that is considered to have limited clinical significance when detected most often in elderly individuals. Despite its frequent occurrence, the cellular and molecular mechanisms at the origin of tracheal calcification remain largely unexplored. In this context, we aimed to characterize the development of tracheal calcification, and to determine the role of matrix Gla protein (MGP), a major inhibitor of ectopic calcification whose genetic or pharmacologic deficiency is associated with premature tracheal calcification in humans. We found that wild-type mice undergo an unexpected early physiologic calcification of the tracheal cartilage rings beginning around one month after birth. This calcification progresses in a dynamic rostro-caudal sequence through a process involving terminal differentiation of tracheal chondrocytes. These findings challenge the prevailing view that tracheal cartilage is a permanent hyaline cartilage and instead reveals an early and highly organized physiologic calcification process. Furthermore, our findings further identify MGP as a key regulator of calcification within the respiratory tract. Indeed, MGP deficiency not only markedly accelerates tracheal cartilage calcification through a similar pattern and mechanism but also induces a previously unrecognized calcification of the tracheal mucosa, a lesion absent in wild-type mice. These alterations could partly explain the respiratory manifestations observed in MGP-deficient patients having Keutel syndrome, which include dyspnea, cough, stridor, and recurrent infections, symptoms previously being mainly attributed to calcification of the tracheal cartilage rings.
affiliations: IMoPA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Donor-associated variation outweighs PMOS status in patient-derived iPSC transcriptomes: a genotyped, BMI-adjusted study of 14 lines
papers.abstract: Abstract Background: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from patients have been little used to model polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS, formerly polycystic ovary syndrome, PCOS), and differences between unrelated donors can masquerade as disease effects. Earlier comparisons of three or four donors per group reported hundreds to thousands of differentially expressed genes. We asked whether a disease signature is detectable in a larger, genotyped panel, balanced for BMI category and BMI-adjusted, of full-phenotype patients. Methods: We studied 14 clonal, transgene-free iPSC lines reprogrammed by CRISPR activation from endometrial stromal fibroblasts of seven women with PMOS meeting all three Rotterdam criteria, and seven controls frequency-matched for BMI category ( 30 kg/m2). Bulk RNA-seq (16,489 expressed genes) was related to diagnosis, hormones, metabolic traits, age, and X-inactive specific transcript (XIST) status using gene-wise models, exact enumeration of all 3,432 group splits, and permutation-calibrated gene-set tests. Donors were genotyped within a cohort of 140 women and scored with an imputation-based genome-wide PMOS polygenic risk score (PRS). PMOS risk-locus genes were examined against a 202-line iPSC proteome. Results: PMOS donors had higher anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH), testosterone, and free androgen index than controls. No gene was differentially expressed between PMOS and control lines (false discovery rate < 0.1), and the number of nominally associated genes was no greater than for random 7-versus-7 splits of the lines (p = 0.75). This was unchanged with an alternative read quantification and with count-based models. With seven donors per group, the design could detect 1.8-fold differences per gene, compared with roughly 3- to 6-fold for the three- or four-donor designs used previously. Neither diagnosis nor any hormonal or metabolic trait explained more expression variance than chance, and neither PMOS GWAS-locus genes nor Hallmark pathways were enriched. Two control lines showed near-complete loss of XIST, potentially indicative of X-chromosome inactivation (XCI) erosion, and a third was borderline. Endocrine PMOS-locus genes (e.g., FSHR, AMH) were not expressed, whereas DNA-repair and growth genes were. Across 129 genotyped women, the PRS was higher in PMOS (odds ratio 1.81 per SD; AUC 0.65), but PMOS and control iPSC donors overlapped fully in polygenic risk. Conclusions: In this panel of 14 undifferentiated iPSC lines from women with the full PMOS phenotype, no robust PMOS-associated transcriptomic differences were detected. Expression variation was dominated by line-to-line differences, consistent with donor background as their main source, although with one clone per donor a contribution of clonal variation cannot be excluded. Reduced XIST expression in some control lines is potentially indicative of, but does not establish, X-chromosome inactivation erosion. Disease-associated differences in differentiated, hormone-responsive cells cannot be excluded, and differences reported in smaller panels may partly reflect inter-donor variability. Future studies should use adequately sized panels, control for XIST erosion, select donors by polygenic risk, and examine hormone-responsive derivatives. Keywords: polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome; polycystic ovary syndrome; induced pluripotent stem cells; transcriptome; polygenic risk; XIST erosion; disease modelling; experimental design
affiliations: University of Helsinki and Helsinki University Hospital PO Box140, 00029 HUS, Finland (corresponding author)

papers.title: Distinct Roles of ADP and Magnesium in the Structural Remodeling and Higher-Order Assembly of Peroxiredoxin 2
papers.abstract: 2-Cys peroxiredoxins (Prxs) undergo oligomeric transitions linked to peroxidase and chaperone activities, but the contributions of nucleotides and cations to lipid-dependent assembly remain unclear. We examined phosphatidylserine (PS)-induced Prx2 oligomers using biochemical assays and high-speed atomic force microscopy (HS-AFM). Both wild-type (WT) and P44A/S76A mutant (MT) Prx2 formed chaperone-active oligomers, although MT assembled more slowly and exhibited a more compact lateral geometry. Mg disassembled both oligomers, whereas ADP alone predominantly disassembled WT. Under combined Mg-ADP conditions, HS-AFM directly captured oligomer disassembly in both proteins, and separate experiments demonstrated higher-molecular-weight (HMW) assembly. WT HMW assemblies exhibited greater heights and stronger Mant-ADP co-elution than MT. Structural predictions suggested altered local Ser76-mediated contacts without major backbone changes. These results distinguish PS-induced functional switching from Mg- and ADP-dependent remodeling and support, without directly proving, a disassembly-reassembly route to HMW formation.
affiliations: Kanazawa university (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Fibrous Optofluidic Probe for Endovascular Sensing of Blood Oxygenation and Flow Velocity
papers.abstract: Local hemodynamic information including blood oxygenation and flow velocity could guide vascular interventions, yet obtaining these parameters in deep, narrow vessels remains challenging. Here, we report a flexible, submillimeter-scale fibrous optofluidic probe for endovascular sensing of blood oxygenation and flow velocity. The probe integrates a polymer optical fiber for light transmission with a microfluidic tube for dye injection, enabling spectroscopic oximetry and fluorescence dilution-based velocimetry through a single device. Via vascular intervention, we demonstrate local hemodynamic sensing in rabbit arteries and angiography-guided deployment in canine carotid arteries. The probe captures local changes in blood oxygenation and flow velocity during vascular occlusion and reperfusion, revealing hemodynamic disturbances that are not reflected in peripheral monitors. These results illustrate the complementary information provided by local oximetry and velocimetry and establish a compact optofluidic platform for quantitative hemodynamic monitoring during vascular interventions.
affiliations: Tsinghua University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Reticulation-Aware Dissimilarities for Phylogenetic Networks
papers.abstract: Dissimilarity measures play a critical role in phylogenetics. They help quantify the accuracy of inferences when the ground truth is known, allow comparisons of inferences obtained using different methods, and provide a tool for summarizing sets of phylogenies. A wide array of dissimilarity measures has been introduced for phylogenetic trees over the past half-century, and they vary in their mathematical properties, empirical behavior, and computational complexity. When the evolutionary history involves reticulate processes, such as hybridization and horizontal gene transfer, it is represented by phylogenetic networks. Although the study of phylogenetic network dissimilarity is less established than its tree counterpart, the past two decades have seen an increasing number of measures developed for phylogenetic networks. However, while some have established mathematical properties---for example, metricity on certain classes of phylogenetic networks---none properly separates reticulation disagreement from tree-like disagreement. This is the rationale behind the introduction of the hybrid ancestry error (HAE) measure by Dai and Molloy. The HAE measure, however, is too simplistic to distinguish different reticulation scenarios. In this work, we propose a novel family of network dissimilarity measures that explicitly account for reticulation differences while being more informative than HAE. We prove that our measures are pseudometrics on rooted binary phylogenetic networks on a fixed taxon set, with two instantiations yielding metrics on binary level-1 networks. Empirically, the measures remain sensitive to reticulation errors as network size grows and respond to changes in hybrid identity and parental placement. Calibration experiments further characterize the measures' behavior under network edits of various magnitudes. Data Availability: The dissimilarities are implemented in the PhyNetPy library, available at https://github.com/NakhlehLab/PhyNetPy. All the data simulated for the study is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23933421. Funding: This work was supported in part by the NSF grants DMS/NIGMS-2153704 and DBI-2420499. Declaration of AI-assisted technologies: During the preparation of this work, the authors used OpenAI's Codex (GPT-6 Astra) and Anthropic's Claude (Fable 5) to assist with editing manuscript text, developing proofs and analysis code, and preparing figures. The authors reviewed and edited the resulting material, verified the analyses, and take full responsibility for the content of this article.

papers.title: HV-MultiScaleGNN: A Multi-Scale Graph Neural Network Framework for Host-Virus Protein-Protein Interactions Prediction
papers.abstract: Accurate identification of HV-PPIs is essential for understanding viral infection mechanisms and for developing antiviral therapeutic discovery. However, the experimental identification process is often time-consuming and expensive, while many computational approaches depend on incomplete protein sequences, structural and interaction information. Here, we present HV-MultiScaleGNN, a topology-driven multi-scale GNN framework for HV-PPIs prediction that operates exclusively on the topology of a heterogeneous interaction network. The framework formulates HV-PPIs prediction as a heterogeneous link prediction problem by integrating the human interactome with experimentally validated HV-PPIs. HV-MultiScaleGNN systematically investigates three complementary graph representation strategies, viz. Local view, Global view and an integrated Local+Global view. The Local view employs one-hop relation-aware graph attention to model fine-grained neighbourhood interactions. The Global view captures higher-order structural dependencies through propagation-based neighbourhood aggregation. The integrated representation combines both views to jointly encode local connectivity and global topological context within a unified embedding space, enabling relation-specific link prediction without relying on sequence- or structure-derived features. Experiments on large-scale HV-PPIs datasets evaluate all three strategies using discrimination, calibration, and ranking metrics. The Local view achieved the best discriminative performance (AUROC = 0.9444, AUPRC = 0.9422), whereas the Global view exhibited the lowest ECE (0.0379). The integrated Local+Global view provided consistently strong predictive performance (AUROC = 0.9378, AUPRC = 0.9356). Comparative evaluation against representative graph representation learning methods showed competitive predictive performance. Furthermore, interfacial interactions were identified using protein-protein docking and atomistic-level understanding was explored. Moreover, GO and KEGG enrichment provided additional functional insights into the selected host proteins. The proposed framework enables systematic evaluation of complementary graph representation strategies for heterogeneous biological link prediction and helps experimental researchers to delineate novel HV-PPIs.
affiliations: CSIR - North East Institute of Science and Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Women's health outreach using a rapid and fieldable Nanopore-based microbiome profiling workflow.
authors: van den Braak, N. P. W. C. J.
papers.abstract: Background In recent years, scientific interest in the vaginal microbiome has increased due to its impact on women's health. Colonization of the Lactobacillus species in the vagina may contribute to protection against vaginal infectious diseases. In order to create public awareness regarding vaginal health and to provide insights into the vaginal microbiome, a rapid field microbiome analysis using Nanopore sequencing was evaluated at Lowlands, a three-day music festival in the Netherlands. This study aimed not only to evaluate a rapid sequencing workflow, but also to explore citizen science as a tool for health promotion and public engagement in women's health. Methods The workflow at Lowlands contained the following steps; (i) Dialogue concerning vaginal health, with invitation to participate. (ii) Informed consent and questionnaire to investigate knowledge on vaginal health, life-style and contraceptive usage; (iii) self-collection of a vaginal swab; (iv) DNA isolation using QuickExtract DNA extraction solution; (v) Ultrafast amplification of the 16S rRNA gene using NextGenPCR thermal cycling using 16S Barcoding kit 24 V14; (vi) Library preparation and sequencing was performed according to the manufacturers protocol using R10 chemistry; (vii) For data-analysis, MABA16S was used, with slight modifications. This workflow was established within 4 hours and results were communicated with interested participants.
affiliations: Avans University of Applied Science (corresponding author)

papers.title: Multiple adaptive trajectories shape antimalarial resistance evolution in Ethiopian Plasmodium falciparum
papers.abstract: Plasmodium falciparum malaria continues to impose a substantial public health burden across sub-Saharan Africa, with Ethiopia experiencing a recent resurgence in malaria cases. We analysed whole genome data from 120 P. falciparum isolates collected in 2024 across five ecologically and epidemiologically diverse transmission settings in Ethiopia and placed these in the context of 1,220 publicly available genomes. Parasite populations were highly structured within Ethiopia, while Horn of Africa isolates formed a genetically distinct regional cluster relative to East and West African populations. We identified evidence of recent positive selection surrounding the artemisinin resistance associated PfK13 R622I variant and detected co-occurrence with Pfcrt mutations together with recurrent selection signals at genes within the PfK13-associated haemoglobin endocytosis pathway, including Pfmca2, Pfkic7, Pfkic8 and Pfkic9. We further observed the emergence of the PfPX1 D384A-PIN haplotype, with shared identity-by-descent linking Ethiopian and Ugandan carriers, supporting a recent introduction followed by local selection. Widespread Pfhrp2/3 deletions occurred on diverse genetic backgrounds. Together, these findings reveal a complex adaptive landscape shaped by antimalarial and diagnostic selection pressures and suggest that parasite evolution in the Horn of Africa proceeds through multiple adaptive trajectories, rather than through the spread of a single dominant lineage.
affiliations: Department of Infection Biology, Faculty of Infectious and Tropical Diseases, London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, London, UK.; Malaria Centre, Londo (corresponding author)

papers.title: LIGR-Nue for the global mapping of the bacterial sRNA targetome in vivo
papers.abstract: Interactions between regulatory small RNAs (sRNAs) and their target transcripts are central for post-transcriptional regulation in bacteria. Based on RNA-seq analysis, we determined the relative abundance of several sRNAs in the photosynthetic cyanobacterium Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 under photoautotrophic growth conditions and after transfer to darkness. We observed an increase in the abundance of the sRNAs DsiR1 to 58.6% and of CsiR1 to 19% of the sRNA transcriptome after transfer to darkness. We then developed a duplex-directed, transcriptome-wide mapping strategy of RNA-RNA interactions in vivo, called LIGR-Nue, which involves aminomethyltrioxsalen-mediated UV cross-linking, proximity ligation, crosslink reversal, reverse transcription and sequencing. The data were analysed using the RNANUE pipeline for the detection of chimeric reads and mapping, and benchmarked against known targetome data for the sRNAs PsrR1 and NsiR4. Using this methodology, we identified RNA-RNA interactions, such as PsrR1 as a regulator of carbon assimilation, and DsiR1 as a global silencing factor of photosynthesis-associated mRNAs in the dark. This data enables the comprehensive analysis of sRNA functions in post-transcriptional gene regulation. LIGR-Nue is broadly applicable to map RNA-RNA interactions in bacteria.
affiliations: Department of Biotechnology and Bioinformatics, School of Life Sciences, University of Hyderabad, Hyderabad 500 046, India (corresponding author)

papers.title: EMtrace: offline nanopore metagenomics on a laptop for rapid viral diagnostics, genome recovery and 16S profiling
papers.abstract: Nanopore sequencers produce reads within minutes, but metagenomic analysis remains challenging where internet access is limited, data are sensitive or computing resources are modest. EMtrace is an offline pipeline that runs on a laptop during sequencing: it classifies MinKNOW reads, estimates taxon abundance by expectation-maximization (EM) and assembles reference-based consensus genomes. We benchmarked it against five virome and four 16S rRNA tools on simulated, mock-community and clinical data. On field isolates and 16 SARS-CoV-2 clinical samples, EMtrace had the highest species-level F1 score (1.00 and 0.97) and one false-positive species, against 3-7 for the comparators. It recovered divergent viruses as completely as ViMOP, and low-titre field libraries more completely, at [≥]99.7% identity. In replayed runs, it identified the target virus in the first 4,000-read batch (5-13 min). With a shared 16S reference, EMtrace reported two to three times fewer false-positive species than Emu.

papers.title: Formation of perinuclear actin structures is driven by mechanosensitivity of actin polymerization
papers.abstract: Actin filaments are one of the most dynamic components of the cytoskeleton. Their fast polymerization, particularly in regions around the nucleus, allows the cell to react quickly and efficiently to external mechanical stimuli by controling nucleus morphology and position, thereby influencing the chromatin organization and gene transcription. While the biochemical mechanisms of actin polymerization are well known, the question why polymerization happens most prominently in the perinuclear region has so far remained elusive. Here, we develop a computational model for actin network formation whose key ingredients are: (i) a fully resolved orientational distribution of the local filaments, (ii) a strain-dependent depolymerization rate and (iii) active stress generation by actomyosin motors. With only these ingredients and without any ad-hoc assumptions on the spatial distribution of signaling molecules, our physics-based model explains the formation of perinuclear actin structures after mechanical stimulation as observed experimentally. In addition, our model also provides some insight into the role actin plays in positioning the nucleus, as it predicts the occurrence of a re-centering force when the cell nucleus is displaced, in quantitative agreement with experimental observations.

papers.title: Getting a head start: Craniofacial heterochrony in marsupials involves dynamic changes to cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying neural crest migration
papers.abstract: The neural crest is a vertebrate innovation central to craniofacial development and evolution. While the gene regulatory networks guiding neural crest development are well characterized, the mechanisms generating species-specific craniofacial diversity remain poorly understood. Marsupials provide a unique model for studying neural crest plasticity, having evolved accelerated patterns of craniofacial development. This adaptation arises because marsupials are born altricial after a short gestation yet require well-developed mouthparts to attach to a teat and continue development in the pouch. However, how marsupials achieve this heterochronic shift in neural crest development is largely unknown. Here we investigate the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying their distinct heterochrony across three marsupial species, with mouse and chicken as comparators. We reveal that marsupials produce dense pre-migratory aggregates of neural crest cells at the borders of a still-flat, pre-neurulation embryo, which emigrate as cohesive, E-cadherin-positive, vimentin-negative epithelial-like sheets, potentially facilitating rapid establishment of the facial prominences. Re-analysis of published marsupial single-cell data further suggests that the mesenchymal transcriptional programme is deployed after delamination and migration. These cellular behaviours have not been described in other amniotes, instead resembling patterns in anamniotes which similarly exhibit accelerated craniofacial development to support early feeding. Marsupials thus appear to have evolved a similar mechanism of neural crest migration to facilitate their developmental heterochrony. These findings suggest that vertebrate neural crest migration may be shaped by life history as well as phylogeny, providing new perspectives on neural crest plasticity and the developmental mechanisms driving craniofacial diversity.
affiliations: The University of Melbourne (corresponding author)

papers.title: Electrophilic Multi-Kinase Probes Identify Degradation and Aspartate Conjugation of ULK1
papers.abstract: Kinases have proven to be one of the most fertile target classes for new drug approvals, however, classical reversible inhibitors may not be capable of the levels of specificity or target modulation required across a broad spectrum of disease areas. Approaches that chemically modify kinase inhibitors in solvent exposed regions are unveiling a swathe of mechanisms to address kinase function in new ways. For example, by either covalently recruiting nucleophilic residues outside of the ATP-binding pocket to inhibit, or by recruiting secondary effector proteins to degrade. Here, we established a systematic workflow to assess the cellular impact of minimal electrophilic modifications to ATP-site binding scaffolds. Amongst multiple potential starting points for monovalent kinase degradation that were revealed, we identified that one of our scout molecules was able to control the abundance of the master regulator of autophagy, Unc-51-like autophagy activating kinase 1 (ULK1) and that a scaffold-hop could be performed to generate a targeted monovalent ULK1 degrader chemical tool, we named ALP-1. Remarkably, further investigation of how ALP-1 engages ULK1 unveiled an atypical conjugation event between the chloroacetamide warhead of ALP1 and an aspartate residue on the lip of the ULK1 ATP-binding site. These discoveries reveal new understanding of the potential for non-cysteine reactivity of the commonly employed chloroacetamide warhead, as well as new opportunities for the targeting and covalent engagement of kinases.
affiliations: University of Dundee (corresponding author)

papers.title: Phylogenetic detection of protein sites associated with continuous traits
papers.abstract: Comparative genomic data can be used to look for substitutions in coding sequences that are associated with the variation of a particular phenotypic trait. A few statistical methods have been proposed to do so for phenotypes represented by discrete values. For continuous traits, no such statistical approach has been proposed, and researchers have resorted to sensible but uncharacterized criteria. Here, we investigate a phylogenetic model for coding sequences where amino acid preferences at a site are given by a continuous function of a quantitative trait. This function is inferred from the amino acids and the trait values in extant species and requires inferred point estimates of ancestral values of the trait at internal nodes. For detecting sites whose evolution is associated with this trait, we use a significance test against the hypothesis that amino acid preference does not depend on the trait. This procedure is compared to simpler strategies on simulated alignments. It displays an increased recall for low false positive rates, which is of special importance for performing whole-genome scans. This comes however at a much higher computational cost, and we suggest using a simple test to filter promising candidate sites. We then revisit a dataset of alignments for 62 species of mammals, using longevity as a phenotypic trait. We apply our method to three protein families that have previously been proposed to display sites associated with variation in lifespan in mammals. Using a graphical representation extracted from the detailed phylogenetic analysis of candidate sites, we suggest that the evidence for this in the sequence data alone is weak. The proposed method has been added to our Pelican software. It is available at https://gitlab.in2p3.fr/phoogle/pelican and can now be used with both discrete and continuous phenotypes to search for sites associated with phenotypic variation, on data sets with thousands of alignments.
