papers.title: Novel viral diversity and geographic structuring in the New Zealand West Coast blackfly (Austrosimulium ungulatum)
papers.abstract: Background Vector-borne diseases represent a major global public health burden, with climate change, land-use change and increasing human activity altering arthropod vector distributions and creating opportunities for infectious disease emergence. In Aotearoa New Zealand, insects commonly referred to as "sandflies" are blackflies belonging to the family Simuliidae. The West Coast blackfly, Austrosimulium ungulatum, is an endemic, human-biting species abundant throughout the South Island, yet its associated viral diversity remains largely unexplored. Methods Here, we used metatranscriptomic sequencing to characterise the virome of the West Coast blackfly and investigate patterns of viral diversity and community composition across geographical and environmental gradients. A total of 425 blackflies were collected from 19 locations spanning approximately 187 km. Results We identified 94 viral sequences across 16 orders and six phyla, all of which were putatively novel viruses. These included divergent lineages within families containing recognised vertebrate and arthropod pathogens, such as the Rhabdoviridae and Orthomyxoviridae. Viral community composition varied among sampling locations, but no significant associations were detected between land-use categories and viral diversity or community composition. In contrast, we revealed a weak but significant positive correlation between geographical distance and viral community dissimilarity, suggesting some degree of spatial structuring across the sampling range. Conclusions This study provides the first metatranscriptomic characterisation of the virome associated with the endemic West Coast blackfly, revealing substantial previously undescribed viral diversity and providing insights into the geographical distribution of arthropod-associated viral communities.
affiliations: University of Otago (corresponding author)

papers.title: Metabolism of bilirubin to urobilinogen by human gut bacteria occurs by a branched, multi-enzyme pathway
papers.abstract: Bilirubin, the predominant product of heme catabolism in mammals, enters the intestine via the hepatobiliary system and subsequently is metabolized by the gut microbiome into multiple downstream derivatives, such as urobilinogen and stercobilinogen. Variation in levels of bilirubin and its derivatives are associated with inflammatory and metabolic disorders, but the microbial species and enzymes that metabolize bilirubin have remained largely unknown, which has precluded causal and mechanistic studies. Here, we demonstrate that metabolism of bilirubin to urobilinogen requires multiple distinct reactions carried out by separate enzymes. We find that bilirubin reductase (BilR), an enzyme that was recently discovered and proposed to convert bilirubin to urobilinogen, is specific for reducing the methine bridges of bilinoids, converting bilirubin to the previously uncharacterized intermediate divinylurobilinogen and mesobilirubin to urobilinogen. We identify bilinoid vinyl reductase (BilV), a flavin-dependent oxidoreductase of the Old Yellow Enzyme (OYE) superfamily, as the enzyme responsible for reducing the vinyl groups of bilirubin and divinylurobilinogen. Both BilR and BilV are capable of acting on multiple bilinoids, such that the reductions required to convert bilirubin to urobilinogen can proceed in multiple orders through a branched network of intermediates. BilV is widespread in human gut metagenomes and is broadly distributed across gut bacteria in a manner that overlaps with but does not mirror the distribution of BilR. These findings establish the identities of novel factors in bacterial bilirubin metabolism, delineate the branched architecture of the pathway, and enable defined studies to interrogate how such branched metabolism contributes to human health and disease.
affiliations: Harvard Medical School (corresponding author)

papers.title: Characterization of Lactobacillus rhamnosus-Derived Extracellular Vesicles and Their Cellular Cytoprotective Effects Against Trimethylamine-Induced Oxidative Stress in Caco-2 Cells
papers.abstract: Dietary trimethylamine (TMA) underwent gut microbiota-mediated catabolism and subsequent hepatic oxidation to generate trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), a key metabolic factor linked to vascular and colorectal diseases. While the systemic effects of circulating TMAO were heavily investigated, the direct localized cellular interactions of its precursor, TMA, at the intestinal epithelial level required further elucidation. This study characterized extracellular vesicles isolated from Lactobacillus rhamnosus (Lr-EVs) and evaluated their cytoprotective potential in an in vitro human intestinal Caco-2 cell model under TMA-induced stress. Exposure to a high concentration of TMA (20 mM) significantly reduced Caco-2 viability to 78.8%, triggered intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, and compromised tight junction integrity as observed via the disruption of Zonula Occludens-1 (ZO-1) alignment. Co-treatment with Lr-EVs (100-300 g/mL) counteracted this cellular toxicity, enhancing cell survival up to 172%. Quantitative PCR analysis revealed that Lr-EVs suppressed the transcriptional upregulation of the pro-inflammatory gene IL-1{beta}, restored the expression of the metabolic regulator SIRT1, and stabilized transcript levels of key mitochondrial-encoded electron transport chain genes (ND6, CYTB, CO1, and ATP6). Additionally, Lr-EVs exhibited intrinsic radical scavenging activities in cell-free ABTS and DPPH assays. These preliminary in vitro findings demonstrated that Lr-EVs mitigated TMA-induced cellular injury, oxidative stress, and junctional disruption at the transcriptomic level, supporting further investigation of probiotic-derived EVs as prospective cell-free functional ingredients.
affiliations: BioX Biotech (corresponding author)

papers.title: Viral replication and host response in airway epithelial cells predicts coronavirus pathogenicity and identifies HCoV-229E as an atypical seasonal coronavirus
papers.abstract: Human coronaviruses (HCoVs) range from mild seasonal strains to pathogenic viruses that cause severe pneumonia. The virological and host determinants that distinguish pathogenic coronaviruses (MERS-CoV, SARS-CoV-2) from seasonal strains (HCoV-229E, HCoV-NL63 and HCoV-OC43) remain poorly defined. To identify determinants of pathogenicity, we systematically compared replication, cellular tropism, innate responses and cytopathogenicity of pathogenic compared with seasonal HCoVs across nasal, bronchial, small airway and embryonic stem cell derived alveolar type II (AT2) epithelial cell cultures. All HCoVs preferentially infected ciliated cells in the upper airway, but only pathogenic viruses replicated to high titres in AT2 cells. Pathogenic HCoVs reprogrammed AT2 function and suppressed key innate immune signatures, consistent with distal lung epithelial dysfunction. In contrast, seasonal HCoVs were associated with limited alveolar replication and milder disruption of AT2 homeostasis. Strikingly, despite modest replication in all cell types, HCoV-229E induced pronounced epithelial injury, cilia loss and strong interferon stimulated gene expression, as well as induction of cellular stress/death programmes resembling those induced by MERS-CoV. These findings highlight the striking differences in cellular responses throughout the airways and between distinct HCoV strains and emphasizes the importance of assessing distal lung tropism and epithelial host responses to evaluate emergent coronaviruses to inform pandemic preparedness strategies.
affiliations: The University of Melbourne (corresponding author)

papers.title: Chromosome-scale CRISPR screening reveals secretory pathway genes as drivers of aneuploidy-mediated antifungal tolerance
papers.abstract: The gain or loss of chromosomes in eukaryotes often drives aberrant phenotypes by altering the expression levels of hundreds or thousands of genes. In the case of beneficial aneuploidies, the genetic basis of fitness improvement has rarely been pinpointed, and identifying the causal genes remains a major challenge in engineering biology. The leading cause of human fungal infections, Candida albicans, frequently acquires extra copies of chromosome R (ChrR) following exposure to azole antifungal drugs, resulting in heightened antifungal tolerance. Despite this, why this aneuploidy frequently emerges following azole exposure and how it promotes antifungal tolerance remain unknown. Here, we combine RNA-seq with parallel chromosome-wide CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) and CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) screens to systematically profile the ChrR genes contributing to azole tolerance. Using multiplexed CRISPR-dCas12a tools, we further characterize the combinatorial effects of candidate genes and uncover a central role for post-Golgi secretory trafficking in antifungal tolerance. Specifically, we demonstrate that the secretory pathway regulators SEC4 and YPT31 are both necessary and sufficient for ChrR-mediated azole tolerance, and drive increased ergosterol content in the cell membrane. By leveraging a large-scale CRISPRa screen in a fungal pathogen, our work functionally dissects one of the most common aneuploidies observed in C. albicans, provides mechanistic insight into the molecular basis of antifungal tolerance, and establishes a generalizable framework for studying aneuploidy-mediated phenotypes across eukaryotic organisms.
affiliations: Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology, University of Guelph, Guelph, Ontario, Canada. (corresponding author)

papers.title: Nuclear retention and RNA editing safeguard self-tolerance to immunogenic intron lariats
papers.abstract: Introns are excised as lariats and rapidly degraded upon linearization, leaving their post-splicing role unclear. Here, we investigate their immunoregulatory potential by analyzing the intron lariat landscape upon inhibition of the debranching enzyme DBR1. We find that lariats harboring transposable elements (TEs), especially inverted Alu repeats (IRAlus), elicit cell cycle-dependent activation of protein kinase R (PKR), but only in cells harboring a high burden, such as breast cancer. These immunogenic lariats are initially retained in the nucleus, but upon cytosolic release, they drive PKR activation and apoptosis. Exploiting this, we combine DBR1 depletion with anti-mitotic chemotherapy to enhance lariat-PKR interactions and promote cancer cell death in vitro and in vivo. We further show that A-to-I editing of IRAlus-containing lariats weakens their interaction with PKR and suppresses PKR activation. Our findings highlight two parallel molecular mechanisms to sustain self-tolerance to repeat-rich introns, revealing a vulnerability exploitable for anti-tumor therapy.
affiliations: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: LOca-1: A minimal calcium-activated arginyl-specific orthocaspase from the Loki's Castle hydrothermal vent field
papers.abstract: Orthocaspases are prokaryotic homologs of metacaspases within the C14 family of cysteine proteases, yet their biochemical properties and cellular roles remain poorly understood. Here, we report the discovery and comprehensive characterization of LOca-1, a metagenome-derived orthocaspase from the Loki's Castle hydrothermal vent field. LOca-1 consists primarily of a single, conserved p20 catalytic domain and undergoes calcium-dependent activation through cleavage at a conserved arginine residue. Once activated, LOca-1 displays strict arginyl-specific proteolytic activity and strong selectivity for residues surrounding the cleavage site. The enzyme is both thermoactive and thermostable, exhibiting maximal activity at 65 {degrees}C and a melting temperature of approximately 72 {degrees}C. Structural modelling revealed conservation of the catalytic core relative to plant metacaspases despite substantial sequence divergence. To our knowledge, LOca-1 is only the second biochemically characterized orthocaspase and the first reported from a deep-sea hydrothermal vent environment. LOca-1 expands the known biochemical diversity of prokaryotic metacaspase homologs and provides insights into the properties of a minimal p20-domain orthocaspase. Together, our findings establish LOca-1 as a thermostable, calcium-activated arginyl-specific orthocaspase and provide a foundation for future studies of orthocaspase function in prokaryotes.
affiliations: University of Bergamo (corresponding author)

papers.title: A TMEM175 Mutation Disrupts the Lysosomal-Mitochondrial Axis Causing Short QT Syndrome and Sudden Cardiac Death
papers.abstract: Short QT Syndrome (SQTS) is a rare cardiac channelopathy characterized by abnormally short QTc intervals and increased sudden cardiac death (SCD) risk. Only 20-30% of SQTS cases have been linked to genetic mutations, typi-cally in surface membrane ion channels. We identified a novel lysosomal TMEM175 gene mutation (p.Arg377His) in 7 patients in a family with SQTS and SCD. Genetic analyses, including whole exome sequencing in the family and rare-variant burden testing in [~]118,000 UK Biobank participants, sug-gested an association between TMEM175 rare variants and QT interval short-ening. Functional studies in CRISPR-engineered mice and patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CMs) revealed that TMEM175R377H causes shortened QT intervals and hastened repolariza-tion, respectively, as well an increased arrhythmia susceptibility. Isolated TMEM175R377H cardiomyocytes showed action potential duration (APD) abbre-viation, confirmed in whole TMEM175R377H mouse hearts and patient-specific iPSC-CM monolayers. In silico and electron microscopy studies showed that TMEM175R377H disrupts lysosomal-mitochondrial interactions, leading to mito-chondrial dysfunction, as evidenced by the reduced maximal respiration and spare respiratory capacity, with reduced ATP production, IKATP activation, and APD shortening. This mutation represents the first non-sarcolemmal ion chan-nel defect associated with SQTS and high SCD risk, potentially expanding the genetic landscape of the disease.
affiliations: Centro Nacional de Investigaciones Cardiovasculares Carlos III (corresponding author)

papers.title: Deep Vein Thrombosis-primed neutrophils reshape the brain microenvironment to promote brain metastasis
papers.abstract: Brain metastasis (BrM) is a devastating complication of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), yet how host macroenvironmental conditions influence brain metastatic susceptibility remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the impact of deep vein thrombosis (DVT), a common complication in patients with cancer, on TNBC brain metastasis. Analysis of a large clinical cohort identified DVT as an independent risk factor for BrM in patients with metastatic breast cancer. Using two syngeneic TNBC models, we demonstrated that DVT selectively enhanced brain metastasis without significantly affecting primary tumor growth or lung metastasis. Mechanistically, DVT increased neutrophil accumulation in the brain metastatic microenvironment, and neutrophil depletion completely abrogated the metastasis-promoting effect of DVT. Single-cell RNA sequencing of CD45+ cells in peripheral blood revealed that DVT reprogrammed circulating neutrophils toward migratory and inflammatory transcriptomic profiles characterized by neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation. DVT increased CXCR2 expression on circulating neutrophils and enhanced neutrophil recruitment in brain. Moreover, DVT significantly increased circulating NETs. Collectively, our findings identify DVT as a systemic driver of TNBC brain metastasis and reveal that DVT primes circulating neutrophils toward enhanced vascular recruitment and NET formation, providing a mechanistic link between cancer-associated thrombosis and brain metastatic susceptibility.
affiliations: National Cancer Institute (corresponding author)

papers.title: A LOV-domain photoreceptor mediates phototaxis in brown algae
papers.abstract: Phototaxis enables motile cells to navigate light environments and plays a critical role in survival and reproduction across diverse eukaryotic lineages. This ability has evolved independently through distinct photoreceptor systems. Yet, the molecular mechanisms underlying phototaxis remain poorly understood in many major eukaryotic lineages, including stramenopiles. Here, combining functional genetics, cell biology and evolutionary analyses, we identify Helmchrome (HELM), a LOV-domain protein required for phototaxis in the brown alga Ectocarpus. HELM localizes to the posterior flagellum and is responsible for the characteristic flavin-associated fluorescence of brown algal gametes. Loss of HELM abolishes phototactic accumulation and directional orientation without affecting basal motility or fertilization, demonstrating its specific requirement for light-directed movement. Phylogenetic analyses reveal that HELM-like proteins are distributed across diverse stramenopile lineages and that their domain architecture evolved through repeated duplication of an ancestral RGS-LOV module. Our findings identify HELM as a key component of the light-sensing machinery in brown algae, provide a molecular explanation for the long-standing observation of flagellar flavin fluorescence, and reveal a distinct phototaxis system that expands the known diversity of eukaryotic light-sensing mechanisms.
affiliations: Max Planck Institute for Biology Tubingen (corresponding author)

papers.title: Multiplexed Targeted iprm-PASEF Assays for MALDI Mass Spectrometry Imaging of Lipids, NAD+ 2 , and Related Metabolites in CD38 Knockout Mice
papers.abstract: Mass spectrometry imaging (MSI) maps the molecular landscape of tissues; however, confident in situ identification and accurate quantification of analytes by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization (MALDI)-MSI remain challenging. We present a new targeted imaging methodology, imaging parallel reaction monitoring parallel accumulation-serial fragmentation (iprm-PASEF), which utilizes trapped ion mobility spectrometry (TIMS) and MALDI for assessment of metabolites and lipids on the fragment ion level in tissue. We investigated liver tissues from wild-type and CD38 knockout (CD38-/-) mice, as CD38 contributes to age-related nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) decline and direct detection of NAD+ within tissue remains challenging. The iprm-PASEF workflow enabled confident differentiation of lipid isomers, resolving phosphatidylinositols at m/z 857.52 and confirming the presence of PI 36:4(16:0/20:4) and absence of PI 36:4(14:0/22:4) at the fragment ion level. We confirmed a more than 2-fold increase in NAD+ in CD38-/- liver tissues of male and female animals (n = 3 per genotype and sex) and decreased adenosine diphosphate ribose (ADPR) through relative quantification of characteristic fragment ions, confirming alteration of NAD metabolism in these animals. This approach provided confident and specific MS2-based identification and relative quantification of fragment ions in MSI experiments, with consistent fold changes across multiple characteristic fragment ions and biological replicates.
affiliations: Buck Institute for Research on Aging (corresponding author)

papers.title: Replication stress links Geminin depletion to centrosome amplification
papers.abstract: The timing of DNA replication and centrosome duplication is tightly regulated with cell cycle progression to ensure the faithful duplication of the genome during cell division. Both DNA and centrosomes are licensed for replication in late telophase/early G1, replicated in S phase and segregated during mitosis; yet how defects in DNA replication licensing are coupled to centrosome homeostasis remains poorly understood. Here, we show that depletion of the replication licensing inhibitor Geminin in proliferating mouse embryonic fibroblasts induces robust centrosome amplification together with impaired primary cilium assembly. Rather than promoting whole-genome reduplication, knockdown of Geminin triggers a replication stress response, characterized by DNA damage accumulation throughout the cycle, and activation of an ATR-dependent DNA damage response. Mechanistically, Geminin depletion-induced replication stress activates the ATR-Chk1-Wee1 checkpoint axis prolonging G2 and leading to premature centriole disengagement and centrosome amplification. These findings identify replication stress as the signaling module that couples defective DNA replication licensing to centrosome amplification.
affiliations: California Institute of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Kinetochore-microtubule attachments are strengthened by Cnn1 stabilization of Stu2
papers.abstract: Accurate chromosome segregation requires kinetochores to form robust, load-bearing attachments to dynamic spindle microtubules, mediated primarily by the Ndc80 complex. Two receptors, Dsn1 and Cnn1 (CENP-T), recruit multiple copies of Ndc80c to the kinetochore. We previously demonstrated that kinetochore components co-purifying with the yeast Dsn1 protein can maintain persistent load-bearing attachments that track with microtubule tip growth and shortening, but the properties of the Cnn1 receptor have not been explored. Using an optical trapping-based assay, we show here that Cnn1 purifications also sustain dynamic microtubule attachments under load. Mutation of a conserved region within the disordered N-terminal tail of Cnn1 weakened attachment strength in vitro and caused a growth defect when Dsn1 function was impaired. The Cnn1 mutation reduced Stu2 kinetochore levels without altering other kinetochore proteins. Restoring Stu2, either by direct addition in vitro or by tethering it to Ndc80c in vivo, rescued both attachment strength and cellular viability. These findings reveal a biophysical role for Cnn1 in enabling Stu2-dependent stabilization of kinetochore-microtubule attachments.
affiliations: Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: High-content screening identifies FDA-approved activators of mitophagy
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial diseases are highly heterogeneous disorders caused by defects in oxidative phosphorylation, for which only limited therapeutic options are available. The elimination of dysfunctional mitochondria via mitophagy activation is an attractive strategy to treat several mitochondrial diseases, irrespective of the underlying genetic defect. To identify pharmacological activators of this pathway, we performed a high-content screening of 1,971 FDA-approved compounds using cellular reporters of TFEB nuclear translocation and mitophagy. This screening identified 294 compounds that promoted TFEB translocation, nine of which increased the number of mitolysosomes without compromising cell viability or damaging mitochondria. Among the selected compounds, Meptazinol and Ponatinib emerged as the top-ranked mitophagy inducers in fibroblasts from patients with complex I and IV deficiency, respectively, and were prioritised for further characterisation. However, they did not rescue the bioenergetic defect, suggesting that the stimulation of mitophagy per se is not sufficient to ameliorate the OXPHOS defect in mitochondrial diseases. Overall, our findings establish a scalable platform for the identification of pharmacological activators of TFEB and identify candidate compounds for therapeutic modulation of mitophagy.
affiliations: University of Milan (corresponding author)

papers.title: A population-scale isoform atlas enables isoform-based trait association and regulatory analysis in lettuce
papers.abstract: Genomic variation shapes phenotypic diversity, yet how genetic variation contributes to transcript isoform diversity remains poorly understood at the population scale. Here, we integrated transcriptomic data from 240 lettuce accessions with a lettuce pangenome to construct a comprehensive pan isoform atlas comprising 531,657 isoforms from 49,729 transcribed loci. Isoform presence absence variation (iPAV) captured extensive transcript diversification during domestication and horticultural differentiation, providing additional resolution beyond locus-level analyses, particularly within loci shared across the population. To facilitate the systematic analysis of isoform trait associations, we developed ISONET-GWAS, a computational framework that integrates isoform-based association mapping, functional annotation, and network-based candidate prioritization. ISONET-GWAS recovered the known chlorophyll regulator LsGLK, identified 455 metabolite isoform associations across 77 metabolites, and prioritized candidate regulators of chlorophyll metabolism supported by functional validation. Genome-wide splicing quantitative trait locus (sQTL) mapping identified 10,498 sQTL associations, revealing widespread distal genetic associations with alternative splicing and candidate trans-sQTL hotspots. Notably, we identified a trans-sQTL hotspot overlapping LsPPR, which encodes a pentatricopeptide repeat RNA-binding protein. Perturbation of LsPPR resulted in widespread changes in alternative splicing of floweing-related genes, accompanied by delayed bolting and flowering and altered splicing of flowering-related genes. Together, our study establishes a population-scale pan-isoform resource and a broadly applicable analytical strategy for isoform-level trait association, candidate prioritization, and complementary analysis of the genetic regulation of alternative splicing in crops.
affiliations: National Key Laboratory for Germplasm Innovation & Utilization of Horticultural Crops; Hubei Hongshan Laboratory, College of Horticulture and Forestry Sciences, (corresponding author)

papers.title: MitoScope: a comprehensive mitochondrial genome analysis workflow for long-read sequencing data
papers.abstract: The mitochondrial genome (mtDNA), rich in repeats and prone to nuclear mitochondrial DNA segments (NUMTs), is implicated in cancer, metabolic syndromes, and neurodegeneration, yet short-read sequencing yields incomplete catalogs, mapping artifacts, and false heteroplasmies. We introduce MitoScope, a scalable end-to-end long-read mitochondrial analysis workflow that integrates mtDNA-read selection, heteroplasmic variant detection, assembly, copy number estimation, read-level haplotyping, and NUMT profiling. Applied to benchmarking data from the Somatic Mosaicism Across Human Tissues (SMaHT) Network, we reveal high sensitivity and precision compared to existing methods and successfully uncover known mitochondrial biology relevant for variant interpretation, aging, and human disease.
affiliations: University of Washington (corresponding author)

papers.title: Functional genomics reveals mediators of beta cell survival in ER stress and type 2 diabetes risk
papers.abstract: Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress in pancreatic beta cells contributes to impaired function and type 2 diabetes (T2D). In this study we performed genome-wide perturbation screens and genomic profiling in beta cells to identify novel mediators of ER stress responses and diabetes risk. We defined gene regulatory networks in beta cells and identified specific beta cell networks enriched for T2D risk variants with altered expression in ER stress. We performed a loss-of-function CRISPR screen for survival under ER stress in EndoC-bH1 cells, which identified 167 pro-survival and 47 pro-death genes involved in processes related to insulin secretion, mitochondrial transport and protein ubiquitination. Beta cell survival genes collectively had limited genomic change in stress yet showed significant, independent enrichment for T2D risk variants, including novel T2D candidate gene DTNB which we validated protects against beta cell death during stress. Overall, our results revealed mediators of ER stress responses in beta cells and identified novel therapeutic targets to preserve beta cells in diabetes pathogenesis.
affiliations: University of California San Diego (corresponding author)

papers.title: EngA adopts multiple distinct conformational states during ribosome assembly
papers.abstract: Ribosome assembly, a highly coordinated and crucial cellular process, is assisted by various assembly factors, including GTPases. EngA, an essential P-loop GTPase, is involved in late-stage assembly of the 50S ribosomal subunit. The structures of 50S ribosome in complex with EngA-bound GMPPNP, and EngA-bound GDP alone, without 50S subunit, have been reported previously. However, the molecular mechanism of EngA GTP hydrolysis-assisted 50S maturation remains poorly understood, and structures of the 50S ribosome in complex with EngA-bound GDP have yet to be deciphered. We have reported cryo- EM structures of the Mycobacterium smegmatis 50S ribosome in complex with EngA-bound GTP{gamma}S or GDP at 2.8 - 3.5 [A] resolution. Structural analysis revealed that EngA and 50S subunit undergo a coordinated structural rearrangement, and an assembly intermediate is formed in which the stem-loop of H80 makes base-pair interactions with the junction of H89 and H90, forming a unique stem-loop-junction (SLJ) motif. EngA-bound GDP adopts distinctly different conformations in its ribosome-bound and unbound states. In summary, this study proposed a multi-state conformational model for EngA-assisted ribosome assembly.
affiliations: UNECSO-DBT, Regional Centre for Biotechnology, Faridabad (corresponding author)

papers.title: Disentangled generative modeling of single-cell perturbation responses across dynamic cellular states
papers.abstract: Single-cell perturbation studies are increasingly conducted across complex, multi-condition biolog-ical systems, offering a powerful lens into how interventions reshape cell states and molecular pro-grams. However, standard computational models compress single-cell profiles into unified repre-sentations where treatment effects are obscured by cell division, lineage progression, donor varia-tion, and cellular stress. Here, we present Disentangled Variational Inference for Perturbation Re-sponse (PertVI), a deep generative model that separates baseline mitotic phase, cellular state, and batch effects from treatment-induced shifts while isolating aberrant off-manifold responses in or-thogonal anomaly space. This structured design tackles two intertwined tasks: (1) quantifying treatment-induced changes in cell-state composition, and (2) inferring state-gated transcriptional changes in response to treatment. Across simulated benchmarks, PertVI accurately disentangles coupled biological axes and recovers weak treatment signatures. In conditional chemical and genet-ic screens of primary human CD8+ and CD4+ T cells, PertVI separates memory-precursor adju-vants from toxic phenocopies, resolves co-clustered regulators into directional kinetic trajectories and biphasic rebounders obscured by standard workflows, and reveals that treatment-induced phe-notypic shifting is decoupled from broad transcriptional perturbation responses and instead gov-erned by state-specific impulses. Altogether, PertVI brings unique mechanistic granularity to sin-gle-cell perturbation response modeling, serving as a proof of principle for biology-informed, struc-ture-guided variance disentanglement in dynamic cellular systems.
affiliations: UNIVERSITY OF PITTSBURGH (corresponding author)

papers.title: KLONE: An Imbalance-Robust k-NN Ensemble for Cross-Modal Single-Cell Clone Assignment
papers.abstract: Single-cell DNA sequencing (scDNA-seq) and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enable the inference of copy number clones and transcriptional states in tumor studies. However, these two assays usually profile different cells of the same tumor, requiring computational assignment of unpaired scRNA-seq cells to clones identified by scDNA-seq to link clonal genotypes with transcriptional profiles. This task is challenging because the only connection between the two modalities is a weak, gene-dependent dosage effect, and the absence of clone labels for RNA cells precludes supervised learning of this relationship. Moreover, clonal distributions may differ between the two modalities because the cells are profiled independently, while the inherent clonal imbalance of real tumors can leave minority subclones underrepresented, further compromising assignment accuracy. To address these challenges, we present KLONE, a per-clone $k$-nearest-neighbor ($k$-NN) ensemble that assigns RNA cells directly to copy-number clones based on cross-modal Pearson similarity, without the need for a parametric model or clone labels for RNA cells. To ensure a fair assessment of each clone's compatibility with a given RNA cell, KLONE allocates an identical neighborhood budget to every clone, preventing majority clones from dominating the affinity assessment solely through their greater abundance. We compare KLONE with six existing methods on three colorectal cancer patients, using cells profiled in both modalities as ground truth. KLONE is the most accurate method and recalls minority clones at 100\%. Despite discrepancies in clonal distribution between the two modalities, KLONE recovers the clonal distribution of RNA cells almost perfectly ($\rho = 0.99$).
affiliations: Rice University (corresponding author)

papers.title: ASD Neuro Agentic (ANA): An Agentic Framework for Feature Discovery and Cross Site Generalization in Autism fMRI Classification
papers.abstract: Classifiers of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) from resting state functional MRI rarely generalize across sites, and many reported accuracies are inflated by data leakage.We show that an agentic artificial intelligence framework, ASD Neuro Agentic (ANA), whose language model agents propose features from the literature and researcher input while fixed tools perform every calculation, can search auditably for site independent classifiers while controlling the leakage. In 1,028 participants from 17 ABIDE I centers, ANA tested 71 pipelines and selected a ComBat harmonized ensemble of tangent space connectivity models from six parcellations and 98 public connectivity derivatives. In leave one center out testing, the ensemble reached an area under the curve of 0.814 (95% CI, 0.773 to 0.841), outperforming ASD DiagNet and ASD SAENet. Predictive connectivity was mainly reduced in ASD. Agentic AI offers a systematic and efficient approach to exploring, evaluating, and identifying pipelines as model selection grows complex.
affiliations: University of Hawaii at Manoa (corresponding author)

papers.title: Statistical significance testing for spatial domain detection in spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: In spatial transcriptomics, domain-detection methods group platform-specific spatial measurement units--cells, bins or multicellular spots--into spatial domains for comparing molecular programs, cellular composition and interactions among tissue regions. However, the number of candidate domains detected in the same tissue can vary with user-specified parameters or model-selection criteria. Whether candidate domains should be merged can be framed as a test of a single-domain null hypothesis, under which each gene has constant mean expression across all spatial units in the combined region. However, testing candidate domains on the same gene-expression data used to detect them may induce post-selection bias and yield anti-conservative p-values, increasing the risk of oversegmentation. To address these challenges, we introduce SigDoTS (statistical Significance testing for Domain deTection in Spatial transcriptomics), a hypothesis-testing framework for spatial domain detection. SigDoTS uses hierarchical testing to determine which candidate domains to retain or merge, with adjustment for family-wise error control. It accounts for gene-gene covariance and spatial dependence and computes p-values by rerunning the upstream domain-detection pipeline on datasets simulated under the fitted single-domain null. In simulations, SigDoTS controlled the type I error rate at the root node under the single-domain null and improved recovery of the true spatial domains when multiple domains were present. In human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, SigDoTS retained superficial and deep Layer 6 domains but merged Layer 3 candidate domains across different initial numbers of candidate domains. In ovarian and colorectal cancers, SigDoTS retained epithelial domains with different gene-expression programs and local immune environments, together with immune, stromal and vascular domains.
affiliations: Michigan State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: kache-hash: A dynamic, concurrent, and cache-efficient hash table for streaming k-mer operations
papers.abstract: Many computational genomic analyses spend much of their time inserting and looking up k-mers in large hash tables. These operations stream through sequences, and consecutive k-mers share k - 1 characters. General hash tables ignore this locality. Each k-mer costs them a memory access, and in concurrent builds, a synchronization. We present kache-hash, an exact, dynamic, concurrent, and resizable hash table that places k-mers by their minimizers. A run of consecutive k-mers with the same minimizer then shares its buckets, which it fetches and locks only once. Building on Iceberg hashing, kache-hash handles skewed minimizers with secondary buckets. A compact spill filter lets lookups stop early, yet stay exact. The table stores sets or maps, and doubles in place in parallel. Under a cache-residency assumption, we show that a run that stays in its primary bucket brings in at most that bucket's cache lines, however long the run is. We compare kache-hash with six general-purpose and k-mer-specific tables on five genomic datasets. At 56 threads, it builds k-mer sets 3.5--7.0x faster than the fastest baseline, and answers queries 1.5--5.4x faster. On the human genome, its positive and mixed queries fetch 3.1--3.2x fewer cache lines per k-mer than those of the fastest baseline. In PanGenie, kache-hash speeds up end-to-end genotyping 1.96x with identical outputs. In K2Rmini, it speeds up read filtering 10.7--19.4x over a fixed control version of the release, also making the filter exact. kache-hash is implemented in C++20 and is available at https://github.com/jamshed/kache-hash.
affiliations: Northeastern University (corresponding author)

papers.title: DECONVersation: Single Cell Foundation Model-Derived Embeddings for Robust Cell Type Deconvolution of Bulk RNA-seq
papers.abstract: Motivation: Bulk RNA-seq deconvolution uses single-cell references to estimate cell type proportions in bulk tissue. Existing methods face challenges with batch effects, subject-level variation, and marker gene selection. We propose a new approach leveraging general-purpose single-cell foundation models. Results: DECONVersation combines pretrained or fine-tuned single-cell foundation model embeddings with non-negative least squares for deconvolution. The embeddings eliminate the need for explicit marker selection, and reduce batch effects. Compared against MuSiC, DWLS, and BayesPrism, DECONVersation with Geneformer or Cell2Sentence-2B achieved competitive performance across six bulk datasets with ground truth, with performance improvements after reference-specific fine-tuning. Availability and Implementation: DECONVersation is available through the Python Package Index. The source code is available at https://github.com/nygenome/DECONVersation, and the datasets and Apptainer/Singularity images are archived on https://zenodo.org/records/22949405.
affiliations: New York Genome Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: CPDD: Adapting an autoregressive DNA language model for bidirectional phage genome modeling
papers.abstract: Autoregressive DNA language models generate sequences ef[fi]ciently from left to right, but many genome-analysis and sequence-editing problems are naturally conditioned on both [fl]anks. We introduce CreatiPhage, a 144.5M-parameter autoregressive DNA language model for bacteriophages, and its diffusion extension, CreatiPhage Diffusion DNA-LM (CPDD). CPDD is a 147.5M-parameter bidirectional discrete diffusion model initialized from the six-epoch CreatiPhage checkpoint. CPDD retains the pretrained Transformer, block attention residuals, and Engram conditional memory, while introducing non-causal attention, a MASK-aware base-5 Engram, centered depthwise convolution, and position-aligned nucleotide readout. Training combines masked and GIDD-style uniformly substituted bases with nucleotide- and amino-acid-level losses over a 10 kb, 32 kb, and whole-source context curriculum. On a screened panel of 522 phage CDSs, CPDD achieves higher random-mask restoration accuracy than a comparable diffusion model and performs well above codon-level references. In a mixed-corruption test, it restores 42.4% of visible incorrect bases. Frozen CPDD representations also support infA [fi]tness prediction and seven-class phage virion protein subtype classi[fi]cation. Controlled evaluations further characterize how restoration depends on visible context and identify opportunities to improve longer-range sequence recovery. Together, these results support scaffold-conditioned sequence modeling as a step towards modular design of phage genomes.
affiliations: CreatiPhage Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (corresponding author)

papers.title: Expression-System Biases Compromise the Functional Assessment of KCNH2 Variants and Clinical Risk Assessment
papers.abstract: Background: Functional characterization of KCNH2 variants is essential for assessing pathogenicity in long QT syndrome type 2. Because hERG channels assemble as tetramers, the relative expression of wild-type (WT) and variant subunits critically influences channel function and pathogenicity assessment. However, commonly used experimental systems may not reproduce the balanced allelic expression observed in heterozygous patients. Methods: Allele-specific KCNH2 expression was analyzed in two independent RNA-sequencing datasets from human left ventricular tissue. Using the dominant-negative T74R hERG variant as a model, we calibrated the relationship between WT-to-variant expression ratios and hERG current amplitude. Using automated patch-clamp electrophysiology, we compared 3 dual-expression strategies: internal ribosome entry site (IRES), P2A-linked tandem constructs, and dual cytomegalovirus promoter (dCMV) constructs. Co-electroporation of WT and variant plasmids in different ratios was the reference. Results: Allele-specific expression analysis supported balanced KCNH2 expression in human left ventricular tissue. At a 1:1 WT-to-T74R expression ratio, hERG current amplitude was reduced to 31.0% of WT, consistent with a dominant-negative mechanism in which incorporation of 2 or more T74R subunits renders the channel nonfunctional. All 3 dual-expression strategies produced substantial expression imbalances, with the first cassette consistently favored. IRES constructs showed the greatest asymmetry. P2A constructs partially improved expression balance but introduced an additional N-terminal proline in the second cassette altering T74R-associated trafficking and channel biophysics. The dCMV system also failed to achieve balanced expression, including after stable integration. Co-electroporation of separate WT and variant plasmids provided the most reliable means of controlling their relative expression. Conclusions: Commonly used dual-expression constructs do not reliably reproduce balanced WT and variant hERG expression, potentially distorting assessments of dominant-negative effects and variant pathogenicity. Co-electroporation of separate plasmids provides a robust approach for high-throughput functional phenotyping under heterozygous conditions, with implications for the interpretation of KCNH2 variants and potentially other genes encoding multimeric ion channels.
affiliations: Nantes Universite (corresponding author)

papers.title: Relative expression of THY1 and PDGFRA in equine endometrosis in relation to severity, histopathological features and endometrial transcripts
papers.abstract: Equine endometrosis is a degenerative uterine disease characterized by periglandular fibrosis and represents a major cause of subfertility in mares. While stromal cell activation results in pathological tissue remodeling, the involvement of cell-surface integrators (THY1) and growth factor receptors (PDGFRA) was not researched. This study evaluated the relative mRNA expression of THY1 and PDGFRA across Kenney and Doig (KD) endometrosis categories and specific histopathological features. Additionally, transcriptomic correlation profiles between target genes and markers of myofibroblast differentiation (ACTA2), cellular proliferation (MKI67), and steroid hormone receptors (ESR1, PGR) were analyzed. Endometrial samples (n = 47) were quantified using RT-qPCR. Relative mRNA expression of THY1 differed significantly across KD categories (p = 0.014), exhibiting a transient upregulation in category IIA compared with category I (p = 0.009) and category IIB (p = 0.002). Furthermore, THY1 relative mRNA expression was significantly elevated in tissues with glandular basal lamina disruption (p = 0.022). Conversely, PDGFRA relative mRNA expression remained stable across disease categories (p > 0.05). THY1 relative mRNA expression correlated very strongly with ACTA2 ({rho} = 0.875, p < 0.001) and strongly with ESR1 ({rho} = 0.652, p < 0.001). PDGFRA relative mRNA expression exhibited a very strong positive correlation with ESR1 ({rho} = 0.864, p < 0.001) and a strong positive correlation with MKI67 ({rho} = 0.674, p < 0.001). These results indicate that THY1 transcription is transiently induced during early stromal remodeling and basal lamina loss, whereas PDGFRA maintains constitutive transcript stability. Observed co-expression profiles reflect statistical co-variation among stromal remodeling, proliferative, and steroid-responsive cell populations in bulk tissue.
affiliations: Warsaw University of Life Sciences (corresponding author)

papers.title: CRISPR screens of noncanonical coding sequences and integrative multiomics uncover novel retrovirus-derived proteins
papers.abstract: Ribosome profiling has revealed thousands of noncanonical translation events across mammalian genomes, yet functional characterization has overwhelmingly focused on proliferative fitness in cancer cell lines. Here, we present a comprehensive survey of noncanonical translation in the mouse immune system and its functional consequences in macrophages. By performing a meta-analysis of Ribo-seq across 20 public mouse leukocyte and 5 human leukocyte datasets we define a compendium of 22,572 mouse and 18,701 human noncanonical coding sequences (nCDSs), including upstream ORFs (uORFs), downstream ORFs, and ORFs on noncoding RNAs and pseudogenes (ncORFs). Cross species conservation and proteogenomic integration with reanalyzed mass spectrometry data prioritizes a high-confidence subset. To move beyond cataloging, we carried out two orthogonal CRISPR screens in immortalized bone marrow-derived macrophages: a fitness screen identifying nCDSs required for macrophage viability, and a TLR1/TLR2-NF{kappa}B reporter screen uncovering nCDSs that modulate innate immune signaling. These screens suggested dozens of nCDSs for functional follow up including a family of endogenous retroviral envelope-derived proteins translated in adult mouse myeloid cells. Updated single-cell RNA-seq annotations and an interactive UCSC Genome Browser session integrating Ribo-seq, proteomics, and CRISPR screen data are provided as community resources. Together, these findings expand the functional landscape of noncanonical translation in immunity and nominate endogenous retroviral proteins as previously unrecognized regulators of murine macrophage biology.
affiliations: University of California, Santa Cruz (corresponding author)

papers.title: Replication-stress response shapes Leishmania genome plasticity through non-equivalent RAD9 and HUS1 functions.
papers.abstract: Genome plasticity, manifested as gene copy-number variation and mosaic aneuploidy, enables adaptation in Leishmania , yet how genome-surveillance pathways shape this variation remains unclear. Here we show that partial depletion of HUS1 or RAD9, subunits of the conserved 9-1-1 checkpoint clamp, produces opposing replication-stress responses and contrasting patterns of genome remodelling in Leishmania major . During methotrexate selection HUS1 deficiency restricted DHFR-TS amplification and favoured linear amplicons, whereas RAD9 deficiency was associated with extensive circular amplification. This divergence extended to genome-wide scale: HUS1-deficient cells carried fewer but larger candidate rearrangements, whereas RAD9-deficient cells retained a largely wild-type rearrangement burden. These differences were accompanied by distinct HUS1 and RAD9 occupancy profiles around repetitive DNA implicated in gene amplification. Deficiency of either of these factors also resulted in differing effects on aneuploidy. While HUS1-deficient cells showed limited shifts towards chromosome disomy, RAD9-deficient cells exhibited broader chromosome copy-number gains and losses. Together, these findings identify replication-stress surveillance as a determinant of parasite genome plasticity, revealing that perturbing individual subunits of the same checkpoint complex can produce opposing genome-remodelling outcomes and reshape the variation available for adaptation.
affiliations: Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology, Ribeirão Preto Medical School, University of São Paulo, Ribeirão Preto, 14040-900, SP, Brazil (corresponding author)

papers.title: Alveolar and airway progenitors converge on an epigenetically encoded profibrotic state
papers.abstract: During organ regeneration, epithelial transitional states arise from progenitors and instruct the mesenchyme to remodel the extracellular matrix. However, the identity of the progenitors, the mechanisms underlying this transition, and why these states persist in tissue fibrosis often remain elusive. Here, using lineage tracing in mice, we show that the profibrotic KRT5-/KRT17+ state in pulmonary fibrosis arises convergently from alveolar type (AT) 2 and airway secretory cells. AT1 cells generate neither KRT5-/KRT17+ nor AT2 cells. TGF-{beta}/SMAD3 acts through KMT2A and p300 to epigenetically reprogram human AT2 cells into the KRT5-/KRT17+ state. In human pulmonary fibrosis, KRT5-/KRT17+ cells slough off, and transitional cells re-epithelialize the denuded basement membrane. Transcriptionally convergent states arise in injured kidney, skin, and intestine. This work reframes fibrogenesis as the accumulation of a conserved profibrotic transitional state via ongoing turnover, not persistence alone, and nominates the state transition and its epigenetic regulators as therapeutic targets.
affiliations: University of Michigan (corresponding author)

papers.title: Lifestyle-mediated shifts in the gut microbiome and host genetics modulate gene expression in intestinal organoids
papers.abstract: Industrialization-associated shifts in the gut microbiome have been linked to disease, but the mechanisms by which microbial communities influence host gene regulation remain poorly understood. We developed a live microbiome-colonic organoid (colonoid) co-culture system to investigate genotype-dependent host responses to gut microbial community variation. Colonoid 2D monolayers from healthy donors were co-cultured with live gut microbial communities from individuals living urban or rural lifestyles, followed by RNA-sequencing. Urban and rural microbiomes elicited largely shared transcriptional responses, however they induced distinct host genetic effects on gene expression. We identified 511 host genes with microbiome-dependent allele-specific expression (ASE) which were involved in epithelial architecture, cell-matrix interactions and structural integrity. Notably, 149 host genes had distinct allelic effects between Urban and Rural microbiomes (urban-rural condition specific ASE or cASE), revealing genotype-dependent host responses to lifestyle-associated microbiomes. Urban-rural cASE was associated with microbial community composition, predominantly involving Prevotella and Bacteroides species. Targeted Prevotella copri spike-in recapitulated Prevotella-associated allelic effects at specific loci, including one in the IBD-associated autophagy gene, ATG4B. Together, these findings establish an experimental framework to investigate genotype-by-microbiome interactions, and demonstrate that lifestyle-mediated shifts in the microbiome modify host cis-regulatory genetic effects on gene expression.
affiliations: University of Chicago (corresponding author)

papers.title: mRNABench: A curated benchmark for mature mRNA property and function prediction
papers.abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) is central to gene expression, and its half-life, localization, and translation efficiency drive phenotypic diversity in eukaryotic cells. While supervised learning has been used to study the mRNA regulatory code, self-supervised foundation models support a wider range of transfer learning tasks. However, the dearth of standardized benchmarks limits efforts to pinpoint the strengths of various models. Here, we present mRNABench, a benchmarking suite for mature mRNA biology, focused on human transcripts, that evaluates the representational quality of mature mRNA embeddings from self-supervised nucleotide foundation models. We curate 13 datasets and 81 prediction tasks that broadly capture salient properties of mature mRNA, and assess the performance of 29 families of nucleotide foundation models for a total of 750k experiments. Using these experiments, we study parameter scaling, correlations between sequence compressibility and performance, data-splitting strategies, and the effects of self-supervised training objective on mRNA property prediction. mRNABench can be found at: https://github.com/morrislab/mRNABench.
affiliations: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Telotrons: spliceosomal introns composed of telomeric repeats
papers.abstract: Spliceosomal intron numbers vary widely across eukaryotes, but the only established mechanism for large bursts of intron gain is the spread of transposable introner elements. We describe telotrons, spliceosomal introns composed predominantly of telomeric repeats. In a survey of 10,310 eukaryotic genome assemblies, we identified 7,008 introns with >85% telomeric repeat coverage and an additional 44,423 with >50% to [≤]85% coverage, in 25 genomes spanning haptophytes, dinoflagellates, a cryptophyte, stramenopiles, the apicomplexan Eimeria, and the nematode Mesorhabditis. Most telotrons carry GT-AG or GC-AG splice boundaries, and RNA-seq supports their splicing. Their repeat orientations are consistent with telomerase extension of broken DNA ends, and intron absence at corresponding positions in orthologs supports widespread de novo gain. In Eimeria and Mesorhabditis, telotrons instead occupy positions where orthologs carry ordinary introns, suggesting modification of existing introns. Telotrons thus point to telomerase as an endogenous driver of structural innovation through intron creation and remodeling.

papers.title: Genomes2Genes: A Progressive Cactus Gene Analysis Pipeline
papers.abstract: Whole-genome alignments are fundamental resources in comparative genomics, because they place genes and their surrounding sequences in a shared evolutionary context. Progressive Cactus aligns large numbers of genomes without a reference genome and reconstructs ancestral sequences along the input phylogeny. However, its Hierarchical Alignment Format output has mainly been used for visualization, phylogenomics, and pangenome studies, and gene-level analyses of these alignments remain difficult. Here, we present Genomes2Genes, a pipeline that converts Progressive Cactus graph-based alignments into validated coding sequence alignments of extant species and their reconstructed ancestors. The pipeline extracts exon alignment blocks, handles atypical genomic jumps, stitches exons into transcripts, and reports start codons, stop codons, and frameshifting indels across species, with validation steps throughout and a base-by-base audit of the final alignments. It catches both biological and technical artifacts and can be run on any part of the genome. We anticipate that this pipeline will be useful in identifying and removing problematic regions used in the potential reconstruction of species or gene phylogenies. We developed and tested the pipeline on a whole-genome alignment of 21 Brassicaceae species and 2 outgroups and found that, among 45,491 lineage-specific genes, the pipeline supported 22,376 candidate de novo genes, of which 1,811 had complete evidence of enabler mutations. Genomes2Genes is publicly available and extends whole-genome alignments to gene-level questions in comparative genomics and evolutionary biology.

papers.title: A Y-specific translocated gsdf copy is a candidate master sex-determining gene in common dab (Limanda limanda)
papers.abstract: Sex-determining systems in flatfishes are highly diverse, and even closely related species can differ in both sex-determining loci and heterogametic systems. In common dab (Limanda limanda), the genetic basis of sex determination has not yet been established. Here, we investigated sex determination using pooled whole-genome sequencing combined with long-read genome sequencing of females and males from Iceland and Norway. Genome-wide allele-frequency analyses identified sex-associated regions consistent with male heterogamety (XX/XY), with the strongest signal on chromosome 16. Comparison of the existing reference assembly, which represents an X haplotype at this locus, with a haplotype-resolved male PacBio HiFi assembly revealed a [~]21.5 kb Y-specific insertion on chromosome 16. The insertion showed complete coverage in male pools but little or no coverage in female pools from either population. It contained a translocated genomic segment including a copy of gonadal soma-derived factor (gsdf) and a predicted gene of unknown function. Comparative genomic analyses were consistent with this segment originating from an autosomal gsdf-containing region on chromosome 1. Given the recurrent recruitment of gsdf as a sex-determining factor in teleosts, we designate the Y-linked copy gsdfY and identify it as the strongest candidate for the master sex-determining gene in common dab. Additional broad sex-associated differentiation on chromosome 19 was restricted to the Icelandic samples and may reflect population-specific expansion of the sex-linked region, although its structural basis remains unresolved. Together, these findings provide the first genomic characterization of sex determination in common dab and demonstrate how gene duplication and translocation can contribute to the evolution of novel sex-determining systems in flatfishes.

papers.title: Mitochondrial Signaling: Nitric Oxide Synthesis by Cytochrome c Oxidase and Its Oxygen Sensitivity Are Modulated by Adenine Nucleotides
papers.abstract: Nitrite can be reduced to nitric oxide (NO) by several heme- and molybdenum-containing proteins, including mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase (Cco). This activity, designated Cco/NO, has been implicated in hypoxic signaling, but its regulation and quantitative significance relative to other NO-producing systems remain uncertain. We examined its modulation by adenine nucleotides using detergent-solubilized yeast and mouse brain mitochondria supplied with 1 mM nitrite and an ascorbate/TMPD/cytochrome c electron-donor system. ADP and ATP differentially modulated Cco/NO activity, and ADP shifted the apparent oxygen sensitivity of Cco/NO toward lower O2, with significant stimulation at 10 uM O2 and below. Nucleotide regulation was also isoform-dependent: ATP slightly inhibited Va-containing Cco but strongly stimulated Vb-containing Cco under anoxic conditions. Rates normalized to cytochrome aa3 demonstrate multi-turnover nitrite-reductase capacity under these substrate-driven assay conditions. Both the cellular ADP/ATP ratio and subsequently assayed Cco/NO activity increased transiently following a hypoxic shift. These findings establish metabolic and isoform-dependent gating of the catalytic capacity of Cco/NO; they do not establish its fractional contribution to total cellular NO or its operation at physiological nitrite concentrations in intact, coupled mitochondria.
