papers.title: A Conformational Switch in the Catalytic Lysine Governs the Stereochemical Outcome of DERA-Catalyzed Aldol Addition
papers.abstract: 2-Deoxyribose-5-Phosphate Aldolase (DERA) is a key enzyme in the pentose phosphate pathway. Due to its C-C bond formation and stereoselective capabilities, DERA has been widely used for biocatalytic applications including the synthesis of chiral intermediates for antiviral and anticancer drugs. Protein engineering has expanded its substrate-scope, improved yield, and enhanced S-stereoselectivity. Recently, rational mutagenesis of DERA from Geobacillus sp. (DERAGs) resulted in two enantiocomplementary variants, T12I/S185A and S185G. In particular, the single mutation at Ser185 to Gly inverts the natural S-selectivity to R-selectivity. However, the molecular basis of enantioselectivity remains unclear. Here, we determined high-resolution crystal structures of wild-type DERAGs and two enantiocomplementary variants in the apo form. Using a combination of structural biology, biochemistry, biocatalysis and molecular dynamic simulations, we show that the catalytic lysine adopts two conformations, a finding that relates to the enantioselectivity of DERA. We further identified a mechanism of regulating enantioselectivity via a key conserved amino acid. Using DERA from E. coli, we show that these findings are conserved across bacterial species.
affiliations: Tata Institute of Fundamental Research Hyderabad (corresponding author)

papers.title: One high-order ion-coupling mechanism generates multiple SLC1A stoichiometries
papers.abstract: Human excitatory amino acid transporter 2 (hEAAT2) is a glial transporter that clears glutamate and aspartate from the extracellular space to terminate neurotransmission. When this essential role is disrupted, excess extracellular glutamate causes excitotoxicity and neurological disease. hEAAT2 transports amino acids into cells against their concentration gradients by coupling uptake to the co-transport of Na+ and H+, and counter-transport of K+. Substrate transport also activates a thermodynamically uncoupled Cl- conductance, whose significance is unknown. Here, to dissect the molecular mechanisms underlying coupled and uncoupled ion transport by EAATs, we leverage the tractable Drosophila melanogaster homologue dEAAT2, which transports taurine as well as glutamate and aspartate. By functionally characterising dEAAT2, we confirmed it has features of a canonical EAAT transport cycle, including an uncoupled Cl- conductance. However, it functions an ion-independent electroneutral exchanger, in stark contrast to its ion-coupled electrogenic human counterpart. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and computational simulations confirmed the inability of dEAAT2 to transport cations, but just two point mutations conferred Na+, H+, and K+ dependence, reconstituting the complex ion coupling profile of human transporters in the Drosophila exchanger. We also showed that dEAAT2 transports taurine in a complex with Cl-, bestowing a unique Cl--dependence on taurine transport, independent of uncoupled Cl- flux. Our findings show that ancestral exchangers in the EAAT family preserve the machinery to achieve complex ion-coupled transport, revealing the molecular basis of high-order ion coupling in hEAATs.
affiliations: University of Sydney (corresponding author)

papers.title: Elucidation of Sequence Constraints for Protein Folding on the Ribosome
papers.abstract: The pioneering round of protein folding on the ribosome is critical for the proper assembly and function of many proteins. Emerging evidence suggests some proteins sample distinct conformational intermediates during translation, which implies the mechanisms of cotranslational folding may impose specific constraints on protein sequence. To assess how folding on ribosome may shape mutational tolerance, we paired a fluorogenic arrest peptide sensor with deep mutational scanning to survey how 9,480 mutations modulate E. coli dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) folding on the ribosome in live cells. By controlling for differences in variant abundance, we assess how these mutations specifically impact the efficiency of DHFR folding on stalled ribosomes. Mutagenic trends are broadly correlated with computational estimates for the change in the free energy of the native fold, suggesting that the sequence constraints associated with late-stage folding on the ribosome are broadly similar to those of post-translational folding. However, a close inspection of mutagenic trends reveals that folding on the ribosome is vulnerable to perturbations of specific contacts within a central portion of the adenosine binding domain and the C-terminal {beta}-strands of the discontinuous loop domain. Some of these regions are known to retain structure in the context of conformational intermediates that form on and off the ribosome, while others appear to be specific to cotranslational interactions. Together, our findings highlight how the constraints of folding on the ribosome may constrain evolutionary sequence space.
affiliations: Purdue University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Learning from Hi-C reveals nuclear dynamical reorganization in budding yeast across the cell cycle
papers.abstract: Hi-C contact maps provide population-averaged measurements of chromosomal contacts. Converting these measurements, however, into three-dimensional structures and associated dynamics remains an underdetermined problem. Existing approaches broadly fall into two classes. Data-driven reconstruction methods that infer either a consensus structure or an ensemble of conformations, but do not inform on chromosome dynamics. Physics-based models, which generate dynamical trajectories, but require prior assumptions about nuclear geometry, chromatin mechanics, tethering, or molecular interactions. Here, we bridge these approaches using the Full-Inversion Chromatin model, a data-driven whole-genome polymer framework that learns an effective force field directly from Hi-C contact probabilities, integrated with Serpentine, a tool to quantify contact-map discrepancies while accounting for differences in sequencing coverage and sparsity. This generates structural ensembles of chromosomes and effective chromatin dynamics. We apply this method at 5-kb resolution to Saccharomyces cerevisiae in G1, mid-S, S/G2, G2/M, anaphase, and quiescence. Without explicitly imposing the spindle pole body, centromere or telomere tethering, predefined chromatin states, or nuclear-envelope interactions, the inferred ensembles recover these major features of yeast nuclear organization. Importantly, although dynamical information is not used during model training, the resulting polymer trajectories reproduce the subdiffusive scaling and chromosomal variations of independently measured chromatin motion. The model further predicts heterogeneous mobility along chromosomes and a distinctive telomere-dependent dynamical organization. Thus, population-averaged Hi-C contacts contain sufficient information to infer not only three-dimensional genome organization, but also effective, locus-dependent chromatin dynamics.
affiliations: CNRS - Institut Curie (corresponding author)

papers.title: A global post-transcriptional regulator directs Acinetobacter baumannii carbon preference and gut colonization
papers.abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii is a multidrug-resistant pathogen that colonizes the gut, increasing the risk of subsequent infection and transmission. Recent work showed that A. baumannii catabolizes ornithine, a non-preferred carbon source, to colonize the gut. However, the mechanisms of carbon preference were unknown in A. baumannii. Here, experimental evolution identified the conserved RNA-binding protein CsrA as a regulator of carbon preference in A. baumannii, a previously unreported CsrA function. RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing (RIP-Seq) revealed hundreds of CsrA-associated transcripts. A. baumannii CsrA directly bound and repressed expression of the ast arginine/ornithine catabolic operons. The Pseudomonas aeruginosa CsrA homolog RsmA repressed arginine/ornithine catabolic operon expression, suggesting this CsrA function extends to other bacterial taxa. Finally, CsrA was required for competitive fitness during A. baumannii gut colonization. These findings uncover a previously unrecognized role for a global regulator in A. baumannii carbon preference and persistence in the gut, a critical reservoir for multidrug-resistant pathogens.
affiliations: University of Illinois Chicago (corresponding author)

papers.title: Alternative splicing switches human Musashi-2 between cytoplasmic and nuclear regulatory functions
papers.abstract: Musashi-2 (MSI2) is an RNA-binding protein that controls self-renewal and differentiation in the hematopoietic and nervous systems and sustains myeloid leukemia. It both activates and represses translation of its target mRNAs, outcomes usually attributed to cellular context. We find instead that the capacity to activate translation is determined by an alternative 3' splice acceptor in exon 12, which splits full-length MSI2 into isoforms that carry or lack an 18-amino-acid insertion in the C-terminal disordered region. MSI2-328 is cytoplasmic and the insertion-containing MSI2-324 is nuclear. The insertion is necessary and sufficient for nuclear localization. Tethering MSI2-328 to a reporter mRNA promotes translation, whereas tethering MSI2-324 does not, and removing the insertion restores activation. Consistent with their localization, MSI2-328 binds translation factors and 3' UTRs, while MSI2-324 binds splicing factors and introns. Use of the insertion-generating acceptor ranges from 19% in skeletal muscle to 51% in the brain and increases in several tumor types. Altogether, one splicing event toggles MSI2 between the cytoplasm and the nucleus, so localization, rather than cellular context, determines its regulatory function.
affiliations: University of Colorado Denver School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Protecting host mitochondria with vitamin B3 preserves bioenergetics and thermogenesis during antibiotic treatment
papers.abstract: Antibiotics that target bacterial translation can also impair mitochondrial function because mitochondria retain bacterial-like ribosomes. As antibiotic resistance continues to increase and the use of several broad-spectrum antibiotics has been limited by their mitochondrial toxicity, there is a growing need to understand their off-target effects in host physiology, and to identify strategies that can mitigate antibiotic-induced mitochondrial dysfunction. We demonstrate that antibiotic chloramphenicol (CA) induces a dose-dependent reduction in mitochondrial respiration and mitochondrial thermogenesis in Drosophila S2 cells, human HEK293T cells and in developing Drosophila larvae. In vivo, CA exposure triggers female-biased aberrant innate immune activation of hosts carrying naturally occurring mitochondrial rRNA variants. Metabolomic profiling revealed alterations in vitamin B3 metabolism in Drosophila during and following CA exposure. Among the vitamin B3 vitamers examined, nicotinamide (NAM) exhibited the strongest protective effect, mitigating the CA-induced impairments in mitochondrial respiration and thermogenesis, as well as aberrant immune activation. We identify mitochondrial thermogenesis as a previously unrecognized target of antibiotic-induced mitochondrial perturbation and a sensitive marker of mitochondrial stress. Furthermore, we demonstrate that co-supplementation of CA with NAM mitigates antibiotic-induced mitochondrial toxicity through evolutionarily conserved mitochondrial pathways. Finally, we establish Drosophila as a powerful model for investigating antibiotic-induced mitochondrial dysfunction and for developing therapeutic strategies to protect host mitochondria during antibiotic treatment.
affiliations: Tampere University, Tampere, Finland (corresponding author)

papers.title: Reinterpreting Keratoconus Gene Expression in Light of Inherited Stromal Weakness
papers.abstract: Purpose. To reinterpret keratoconus (KC) gene expression in light of inherited stromal weakness, and to define how expression should guide model and target selection. Methods. We combined genetic and chromatin data with expression from eight studies (182 donors). We compared the same KC samples with normal and pathological controls, built references matched to control source and tissue layer and tested them in independent tissues, and indexed published intervention-outcome records. Stimulated cells and genetic analyses assessed repair capacity and inherited risk. Results. Changing only the control reversed expression directions, flipping KC-like classification in 21-27 of 42 models and supplement-or-inhibit direction in 361-385 of 1,090 targets. Our references addressed this, predicting direction more accurately than published methods in independent spatial stroma and two bulk comparisons. Against these references, 41 of 46 target nominations required a different comparison, measurement, or use. A correct direction described only the stromal state: across control types, KC stroma showed lower inflammatory, immediate-early (stress-response), and transforming growth factor-{beta} (TGF-{beta}) programs, which signaled neither lost repair capacity (stimulated KC cells increased matrix production) nor disease cause (no genetic enrichment). Inherited risk converged on the matrix: collagen assembly was the only replicated pathway family, and genetically predicted higher corneal resistance lowered disease odds independently of thickness. Because these expression changes do not drive disease, reversing them does not ensure functional benefit: among 2,769 intervention-outcome records, the two were separate outcomes. Conclusions. Expression direction therefore reflects the choice of control and the stromal state, and does not indicate how to intervene. Because inherited risk lies in matrix structure and resistance to deformation, repair should restore organized, load-bearing matrix rather than reverse expression changes. Models should therefore be judged against matched references, and targets by measured functional outcomes.
affiliations: Department of Ophthalmology, Peking Union Medical College Hospital, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences and Peking Union Medical College, Beijing 100730, China (corresponding author)

papers.title: LIMBER: A Hybrid RNA Foundation Model for Predicting and Understanding RNA Structure and Function
papers.abstract: RNA foundation models offer a promising route to decoding the relationships between RNA sequence, structure and function, yet how model architecture shapes the acquisition and organization of biological information remains poorly understood. Here we introduce Layer-Interleaved Mamba-Bidirectional Encoder for RNA (LIMBER), a hybrid foundation model integrating bidirectional self-attention with selective state-space modeling, pre-trained on 40.5 million non-coding RNA sequences. With task-specific fine-tuning, LIMBER achieves leading performance on secondary-structure prediction and non-coding RNA classification benchmarks, while demonstrating strong transferability to translation-related tasks and RNA--small-molecule interaction prediction. Beyond model development, we establish a unified, task-agnostic framework to systematically evaluate and interpret the biological knowledge intrinsically acquired by RNA foundation models. This framework validates LIMBER's strong capabilities in recovering RNA structures and predicting mutational effects, while uncovering a hierarchical, task-dependent organization of biological information across model layers. In addition, we demonstrate distinct scaling behaviors across structural, evolutionary, and functional capabilities by training and evaluating a broad panel of model variants spanning model capacity, training duration, and dataset size. Taken together, these findings establish LIMBER as a versatile RNA foundation model and provide insight into how architectural design, internal representations and scaling shape the learning of RNA sequence-structure-function relationships.
affiliations: University of Notre Dame (corresponding author)

papers.title: Uncovering Viral Signals Across Cell Populations in Colorectal Cancer
papers.abstract: Viral sequences have been detected in colorectal cancer, but their cellular and anatomical distribution remains poorly resolved. We aimed to establish a cell-type-resolved map of viral reference-associated RNA signals across colorectal cancer, tumour-adjacent normal tissue, and healthy colon. We repurposed human-unmapped reads from single-cell RNA sequencing libraries generated in ten publicly available studies. We retained cell-barcode and unique molecular identifier information, removed duplicate molecules, and aligned reads to a curated human-associated viral reference using three aligners. Viral signals were analysed across cell types, tissue conditions, and colorectal segments. We used participant-grouped repeated cross-validation to evaluate tissue-condition classification and screened an independent paired colorectal cancer proteomics cohort for compatible peptide matches. The study included 547 libraries from 112 participants, including 49 with matched colorectal cancer and tumour-adjacent normal samples, and approximately 415,000 cells spanning ten major cell populations. Viral reference-associated RNA signals differed across epithelial, immune, stromal, and vascular compartments, tissue conditions, and anatomical regions of the colon. Of 318 independent healthy-reference viral-load comparisons, seven involving six virus-cell-type groups remained significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction, including plasma-cell HHV-7 and HHV-6B and mast-cell HCV-2. Cell-type-resolved viral features distinguished colorectal cancer, tumour-adjacent normal tissue, and healthy colon in participant-grouped validation; random forest achieved a macro-AUC of 0.957 (SD 0.028), with HERV-K113 as the leading quantitative feature. An independent proteomic screen identified peptide matches compatible with 20 candidate viral groups. We established a cell-type-resolved map of viral reference-associated RNA signals across colorectal tissue conditions and anatomical regions. By identifying candidate viral signals in epithelial and immune compartments, this map provides a basis for investigating virus-host pathways involved in tumour biology, immune regulation, and antigen-presentation states, and could help prioritise future combination strategies pairing virus-directed or virus-mimetic approaches with standard treatment or immune checkpoint blockade.
affiliations: University of Hawaii John A. Burns School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Nucleobase-Specific Recognition of DNA by Protamine
papers.abstract: Protamines--arginine (Arg)-rich, intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs)--replace histones to compact DNA in the sperm nucleus. While folded domains can bind DNA site-specifically, whether IDPs exhibit DNA-sequence specificity remains open. Here, we used all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to characterize protamine-DNA binding. Eight copies of salmon protamine (33 residues with 21 Arg) rapidly wrap around a 35-bp DNA molecule. In addition to salt bridges with DNA phosphates, Arg hydrogen-bonds with multiple nucleobases on both strands or the same strand. At the major groove, protamine prefers GC over AT by a 2.6-to-1 ratio, with guanine's O6 and N7 atoms as hydrogen-bond acceptors; the preference is especially strong at G-tracts. This selectivity reverses at the minor groove, where AT overtakes GC by a 2.1-to-1 margin. The net effect is a moderate bias for GC over AT in protamine-base interactions. Additional simulations with 20-bp DNA molecules and free-energy calculations reinforce these observations. For experimental validation, we designed DNA sequences with 0-40% GC content. Protamine-DNA mixtures form aggregates, with an increasing propensity at higher GC content and upon shuffling into G-tracts. This work demonstrates that IDPs can bind DNA in a nucleobase-specific manner, with implications for protamine-mediated transcription silencing and remodeling of paternal chromatin.
affiliations: University of Illinois Chicago (corresponding author)

papers.title: Butyrate supplementation reshapes systemic metabolism and attenuates cardiac aging
papers.abstract: Identifying interventions that improve health and cardiac function is important for extending healthspan. We show that supplementation with the SCFA butyrate beginning at 18 months (late life) extends survival in male and female mice and improves systemic metabolic and physical-performance measures. Treatment reduces adiposity and fasting glucose and attenuates age-associated cardiac hypertrophy, fibrosis, and systolic and diastolic dysfunction. Integrated plasma and myocardial metabolomics and lipidomics reveal compartment-dependent metabolic remodeling, while cardiac proteomics and full-length RNA sequencing identify coordinated changes in extracellular-matrix, RNA-processing, lipid-metabolism, and autophagy-associated programs. These molecular responses are accompanied by improved mitochondrial ultrastructural organization and respiratory function. Butyrate supplementation also enhanced cardiac autophagy and mitophagy, and its beneficial effects on LV hypertrophy and diastolic indices required ATG7. These findings demonstrate that butyrate supplementation initiated at an advanced age modifies systemic and cardiac aging phenotypes and implicate metabolic remodeling and mitochondrial quality control pathways as contributing to these benefits.
affiliations: Stanford University (corresponding author)

papers.title: HaloPROTAC-mediated degradation reveals SOX10-dependent gene expression changes in melanoma cells
papers.abstract: The transcription factor SOX10 is required for melanoma cell proliferation. However, SOX10 expression in single cells is heterogeneous, and low SOX10-expressing melanoma cells exhibit a dormant-invasive phenotype associated with drug resistance and metastasis. Despite longstanding interest in SOX10 as a diagnostic marker and potential therapeutic target in melanoma, the function and targets of SOX10 remain incompletely understood. New tools for the study of SOX10 are needed to address these gaps in our knowledge. In this study, we engineered a patient-derived WW165 melanoma cell line for programmable SOX10 targeted proteolysis. We achieved this by replacing the endogenous copies of SOX10 with a SOX10-HaloTag transgene that supports cell growth, but can be rapidly degraded by the ubiquitin-proteasome system upon with a commercially available HaloPROTAC3 degrader molecule. We demonstrate that inducible degradation of SOX10-HaloTag faithfully recapitulates the known SOX10 transcriptional program, while also enabling discovery of NAV2 and NCKAP5 as novel SOX10 target genes. This study demonstrates that new biological insights into the function of SOX10 can be enabled by targeted degradation.
affiliations: Yale University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Overcoming segmentation bottlenecks in brain tissue for spatial proteomic inference at population scale
papers.abstract: In spatial proteomics across large cohorts, downstream estimates from tens of thousands of images depend on accurate cell segmentation. Yet pretrained segmentation models struggle with morphologically complex cell bodies in human brain tissue, and how domain adaptation affects downstream discovery remains unclear. Here, we introduce SPInfer, a workflow for spatial proteomic inference developed using 5,832 manually annotated cell bodies from 120 immunofluorescence images of the human prefrontal cortex. After benchmarking eight segmentation methods spanning classical, convolutional, and foundation models, we adapted Cellpose-SAM, raising cell segmentation F1 from 0.37 to 0.84 and recovering cell compositions concordant with matched single-nucleus RNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics. Across 14,765 images from 69 postmortem donors, identical Alzheimer's disease pathology models found no significant associations after false discovery rate correction using zero-shot masks, versus four using fine-tuned masks; three linked higher OLIG2-positive fractions to greater neurofibrillary tangle and plaque burden. Using the fine-tuned masks, a graph attention network over nuclear neighborhoods classified four cell types without marker information, and differential expression analysis linked cell morphology to gene expression. This provides a pipeline for fine-tuning foundation models to segment complex tissues, enabling biological discovery in spatial proteomics at the population scale.
affiliations: University of Pittsburgh (corresponding author)

papers.title: Evaluation design shapes estimates of cross-donor generalization in single-cell classification of cell-type
papers.abstract: Motivation: Single-cell cell-type classifiers are often evaluated using random cell-level splits, although cells from the same donor are not independent. We asked how evaluation design affects estimates of cross-donor generalization. Results: Across PBMC and lung datasets, random cell-level splitting consistently yielded higher macro F1 than donor-held-out evaluation across multiple expression representations. This gap persisted after batch covariate adjustment and donor-level mixed-effects modeling. In contrast, evaluation gaps were generally minimal in highly separable, trivially easy kidney, pancreas, and blood classification settings and in a randomized-label setting with no meaningful predictive signal. These results show that evaluation bias depends on the underlying classification difficulty and that donor-held-out evaluation is necessary when claims concern generalization to unseen individuals. Availability and Implementation: Code and analyses are available on GitHub at https://github.com/danielchen05/scRNA-cross-donor-generalization/. Processed data are archived at Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19717558. Contact: ajbattle@jhu.edu
affiliations: Johns Hopkins University (corresponding author)

papers.title: He spent a year on ‘Mars’: NASA science officer emerges from mock mission
How to make failure your friend and teacher in science
Resistance exercise to attenuate lean mass loss during tirzepatide therapy for obesity: a randomized controlled trial
papers.abstract: Incretin mimetics as obesity therapy induce substantial weight and fat loss but also decrease lean soft tissue mass, possibly impairing skeletal muscle function. Here, in this two-arm randomized controlled trial of adding resistance exercise (REx) to tirzepatide (T), 120 adults with overweight or obesity were treated with tirzepatide and randomized to thrice-weekly resistance exercise training or usual activities for 40 weeks. Tirzepatide was safe, and most participants tolerated up-titration to 15 mg weekly. Adherence to resistance exercise was 91%. Weight loss achieved was similar (T = −22.61 kg, T+REx = −22.28 kg, P = 0.694). For primary outcomes, loss of total fat mass was similar (T = −17.19 kg, T+REx = −17.98 kg, P = 0.700; between-group difference = −0.77 kg, 95% confidence interval (CI): −2.14 kg to 0.60 kg), but resistance exercise reduced loss of total lean soft tissue mass (T = −4.67 kg, T+REx = −3.57 kg, P < 0.001; between-group difference = 1.09 kg, 95% CI: 0.43−1.75 kg). For related endpoints, resistance exercise reduced loss of appendicular lean soft tissue mass (T = −3.55 kg, T+REx = −2.92 kg, P < 0.001). Upper and lower body muscle strength decreased with tirzepatide (bench press −4.09 kg, lat pulldown −4.42 kg, knee extension −4.42 kg) but increased with T+REx (+4.68 kg, +8.58 kg, +5.88 kg, respectively, all P < 0.001 versus tirzepatide). In conclusion, resistance exercise training attenuated loss of total lean soft tissue mass, representing an effective adjunct to tirzepatide anti-obesity therapy. Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry identifier: ACTRN12623001236684 . Participants undergoing resistance exercise while receiving tirzepatide lost less lean mass than participants receiving tirzepatide alone.

papers.title: Improving CAR T cells
Clusters amplify gene expression
NAD+-responsive circuit for muscle health
Reconstructing developmental and disease progression with sample-level embeddings
papers.abstract: An scRNA-seq framework that embeds each sample by the density distribution of its cells across cellular states is used to resolve continuous variation in infection, neurodegeneration, embryonic development, and whole-organism perturbation that discrete sample labels obscure.

papers.title: Decoding neutrophil spatial heterogeneity and clinical implications in breast cancer
papers.abstract: Xu et al. investigate neutrophil spatial heterogeneity by integrating AI-powered computational pathology and single-cell spatial omics in comprehensive breast cancer cohorts. They identify clinically relevant neutrophil spatial patterns and provide mechanistic insights into the underlying biology. Combining neutrophil spatial patterns with established biomarkers further refines patient stratification.

papers.title: A stroma-sensing TGF-β blockade reprograms CAF-myeloid niches to induce durable tumor immunity
papers.abstract: Kang et al. show that anchoring a soluble TGF-β trap (FEBP-sTβRII) to FN-EDB-rich matrix overcomes fibrotic immune exclusion. This localized blockade drives IFN-γ-dependent CAF-myeloid reprogramming, enhances T cell infiltration, and establishes durable, cross-protective antitumor immunity.

papers.title: Neutrophils are known by their neighbors in breast cancer
Dot1 triggers a conserved ribophagy signal to govern ribosome quality and longevity by methylating Rpl12
papers.abstract: Chen et al. show Dot1-mediated Rpl12 methylation as a conserved autophagic “eat-me” signal that directs selective ribosome degradation. By coupling nutrient sensing to ribosome quality control, this mechanism promotes cellular adaptation to stress, maintains tissue homeostasis, and supports organismal longevity.

papers.title: Hierarchical buffering of cellular RNA polymerase II pools maintains transcriptional homeostasis
papers.abstract: Gillis et al. integrate quantitative single-cell imaging with genomic techniques to examine transcriptional homeostasis following acute perturbation of RNA polymerase II abundance. This work demonstrates that total mRNA production is buffered against altered polymerase abundance by the transcription cycle and further shows evidence for robustness in RNA polymerase holoenzyme assembly.

papers.title: Promoter-proximal pausing enables transcriptional buffering of RNA polymerase II availability
papers.abstract: Through titration of cellular RPB1 levels, Olthof et al. show that transcription is surprisingly sensitive to RNAPII dosage, but that genes vary widely in their sensitivity. Genes involved in transcriptional maintenance are typically dosage insensitive. Expression of these genes is buffered through decreased promoter-proximal pausing and increased mRNA stability.

papers.title: Lineage-specific metabolic transcription across environmental gradients in geothermal microbial communities
papers.abstract: Chen et al. combine metagenomics and metatranscriptomics to examine microbial metabolism across geothermal springs. They reveal contrasting transcriptional profiles in acidic and non-acidic habitats, with distinct microbial contributions to carbon, sulfur, and nitrogen metabolism, and identify co-expression modules linking microbial lineages to specific metabolic functions.

papers.title: Mouse APOE Christchurch protects against Aβ-induced tau and α-synuclein aggregation
papers.abstract: Soto-Faguas et al. demonstrate that the murine Apolipoprotein E Christchurch mutation (APOE-R128S) reduces α-synuclein Lewy pathology and glial neuroinflammation in multiple Lewy body disease mouse models, potentially by binding α-synuclein more strongly than the wildtype form. APOE Christchurch also reduces amyloid-β-induced tau pathology in an Alzheimer’s disease mouse model.

papers.title: ECHS1 K115 succinylation inhibits fatty acid β-oxidation in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
papers.abstract: Duan et al. demonstrate that widespread succinylation modifications map to the metabolic enzymes, and the differential succinylation sites in PDAC are specially related to FAO metabolism, among which ECHS1 K115 succinylation is significantly decreased in PDAC. Blocking ECHS1 K115 succinylation inhibits FAO metabolism and tumor development.

papers.title: Identification of RNA-binding proteins that regulate circRNAs
Author Correction: A photogenerated triplet aura-nitrene for gold-mediated nitrene transfer
The calcium signaling links to fungal pathogenicity by a dual-action regulator
papers.abstract: Wang et al. characterize Cas5 as a fungus-specific regulator linking calcium-stress responses and pathogenicity in Candida albicans. By orchestrating distinct calcium-response and virulence pathways, Cas5 enables this fungal pathogen to integrate environmental adaptation with infective potential.

papers.title: Tumor-colonizing Bifidobacterium dentium promotes tumor progression and chemotherapy resistance via MMP3 and GABA-FOXA2-P-gp axis
papers.abstract: Pan et al. report that tumor-colonizing B. dentium promotes tumor progression and chemotherapy resistance. Their findings link B. dentium to MMP3 induction and GABA-mediated FOXA2-dependent P-gp upregulation, supporting a role for intratumoral host-microbe interactions in tumor progression and chemotherapy response.

papers.title: The CD39/CD73 adenosinergic pathway is increased by proinflammatory states and modified by chemo-radiation in human non-small cell lung cancer
papers.abstract: Ashley et al. report local expression of adenosine-producing enzymes CD39 and CD73 as an inducible and inflammation-driven immunosuppressive pathway present in >85% of NSCLCs. This pathway displays preferential expression in lung adenocarcinomas with elevated TILs and PD-L1 or in tumors lacking STK11/KEAP1 mutations and is suppressed by radio-chemotherapy.
