papers.title: Engineering regenerative cell therapy products through biofabrication
papers.abstract: Regenerative cell therapies delivered as cell suspensions often face limited survival, retention, and tissue integration. Biofabrication produces structured living products with controlled cellular organization and material environments. Here, we present a product-oriented framework linking fabrication-derived attributes to therapeutic function, delivery compatibility, manufacturing reproducibility, quality control, and safety and regulatory evidence. We distinguish biomaterial-free and biomaterial-based products based on whether exogenous biomaterials are retained as structural or functional components of the administered construct, and examine hybridization as an integration strategy. Comparisons across formats assess whether engineered features provide therapeutic value sufficient to justify added manufacturing and translational burdens. This framework guides product design toward the minimum complexity needed to achieve clinically meaningful function with reproducible manufacture and delivery.

papers.title: Biocatalytic Asymmetric Radical Dearomatization of Electrophilic Heterocyclic and Non-Heterocyclic Arenes
papers.abstract: Catalytic asymmetric dearomatization provides a powerful strategy for converting readily available aromatic feedstocks into valuable three-dimensional molecular scaffolds. Despite substantial advances over the past several decades, general methods for catalytic asymmetric dearomatization of electrophilic arenes, particularly non-heterocyclic substrates with high aromatic stabilization energies, remain a challenging task. Here, we report the use of a hydrogen atom transfer mechanism for biocatalytic radical dearomatization of electron-deficient arenes. Repurposing and directed evolution of our previously developed P450 halogen atom transferases furnished hydrogen atom transfer dearomatases that catalyze the stereoselective dearomatization of a range of electrophilic arenes, including electron-deficient indoles, pyrroles, and simple benzene derivatives. These evolved biocatalysts facilitated both diastereodivergent and enantiodivergent radical dearomatization, providing access to fused and spirocyclic chiral scaffolds bearing challenging quaternary and/or contiguous stereocenters. Computational and experimental studies revealed that a strategically positioned active-site lysine residue enables enzyme-controlled proton transfer against the intrinsic thermodynamic stereopreference, allowing catalyst-controlled reversal of diastereoselectivity from a common radical intermediate. Importantly, the evolved dearomatases efficiently transformed challenging arene substrates that proved recalcitrant under previously optimized Fe, Mn and Co-based metal-hydride hydrogen atom transfer conditions. Collectively, these results establish new-to-nature metalloredox biocatalysis as a powerful strategy for overcoming longstanding challenges in asymmetric radical catalysis.
affiliations: University of California Santa Barbara (corresponding author)

papers.title: Ok-k-mer: Selecting k-mer length ensembles for calculating genomic distance
papers.abstract: Current methods for computing sequence similarity across large groups of genome sequences tend to do so at the level of k-mers since this is far more efficient than base-by-base alignment. While these methods use default k-mer lengths, recent work shows that the particular choice of k-mer length greatly affects accuracy, and that using multiple values of k can boost accuracy relative to the best single choice of k, particularly when the goal is to estimate genomic distances that reflect true phylogenetic relationships. Here, we introduce Ok-k-mer, a tool to systematically select weighted k-mer length ensembles for pairwise genomic distance estimation, thereby increasing the accuracy of those estimates. Given a phylogenetic tree, Ok-k-mer ranks genome pairs by Jaccard distance across a range of k and uses a progressive search to maximize the Spearman correlation, {rho}, between weighted-average k-mer ranks and branch distances. Across eight Genome Taxonomy Database datasets, Ok-k-mer ensembles improved correlation over standard default k-mer lengths. In the Chlamydiales taxonomy, a three-length ensemble k=(9,17,22) achieved a 23.9% relative improvement over the best single length (k=20) and a 36.7% improvement over a commonly used default of 31-mers. We demonstrate that Ok-k-mer k-mer length ensembles remain stable (i.e. lengths and weights change only moderately) under genome subsampling within a taxonomy but vary across datasets. Ok-k-mer can annotate all subtrees of a phylogeny, which reveals distinct patterns of ensembles reflecting potential differences in genome evolution. Ok-k-mer provides a framework for moving beyond a "one-k-fits-all" k-mer analysis, improving genomic distance estimation in the era of massive-scale genomics.
affiliations: Johns Hopkins University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Glycine-Proline driven flexibility and interface-dependent conservation of six-residue {Omega}-loops in protein complexes
papers.abstract: {Omega}-loops are six- to sixteen-residue, non-regular structural motifs that occur in protein structures, connecting regular regions and forming a well-defined, ordered structural segment. They are functionally important because of their strategic location on the protein surface, where they are often associated with molecular recognition, ligand binding, and catalytic activity. Their non-regular nature enables them to adopt different conformations, which makes them important in protein dynamics and allosteric communication. In this work, we have curated six-residue {Omega}-loops from diverse protein-protein complexes of varying stability and found them to be abundant across all. We identified 1205 hydrogen-bonded and 6518 non-hydrogen-bonded {Omega}-loops, leading to an average of ~1.7 {Omega}-loops per structure. Glycine and proline were the most enriched residues in the loop, with proline preferentially positioned at the fourth position and glycine distributed across multiple positions, supporting their roles in chain reversal and conformational flexibility. Using ProteinMPNN-based sequence-design modelling and Rate4Site evolutionary-rate analysis, we show that {Omega}-loops occupy a relatively constrained sequence space, with interface loops in obligate homodimers and heterodimers more conserved than non-interface loops; the opposite trend was observed in transient and crystal dimers. Mapping known pathogenic and benign mutations onto the {Omega}-loop present in human proteins, together with a case study of the TEM1 {beta}-lactamase {Omega}-loop, further illustrates how small sequence changes within these loops can produce crucial structural and functional consequences, leading to altered enzyme activity and antibiotic resistance. Altogether, we report that {Omega}-loops are not merely connectors of secondary structure but are structurally constrained, evolutionarily significant elements that contribute to protein folding, stability and function.
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology Jodhpur (corresponding author)

papers.title: Amino acid clustering and epistasis guide sequence-based prediction of phenotype modulation
papers.abstract: Protein sequences encode the molecular information necessary for their biological function. As functional adaptation often emerges from combined effects of multiple positions, understanding how sequence variation gives rise to functional differences remains a central challenge. Here, we developed an improved strategy to identify phenotype modulating positions and use them to predict phenotypes, by relating amino acid identity to experimentally measured quantitative properties across families. Using family-specific sequence-phenotype datasets, our results show that epistasis plays a crucial role in phenotype modulation. Position specific amino acid clustering further improved performance indicating that key functional information is often captured by broad physicochemical amino acid classes, with hydrophobicity playing a crucial role in phenotype modulation. Our identified phenotype modulating positions involve both proximal and distal sites relative to functional sites. While the former is captured by individual positions, the latter is captured when epistasis is taken into account. Comparison with experimentally identified positions showed partial recovery of known functionally relevant residues, while at the same time revealing candidate positions that may contribute to phenotypic variation. Taken together, these results suggest that quantitative phenotypes are often governed by a network of interacting amino acid residues and may be engineered by a limited amount of sequence modifications. This finding highlights the potential of our framework to deepen our understanding of protein function, evolution, and adaptation, providing new targets for the rational modulation and engineering of protein phenotypes.
affiliations: Universidad de Buenos Aires, Facultad de Ciencias Exactas y Naturales, Consejo Nacional de Investigaciones Cientificas y Tecnicas. Instituto de Quimica Biologic (corresponding author)

papers.title: MELD: Mutation Effect Learning through Differential embeddings
papers.abstract: We introduce MELD (Mutation Effect Learning through Differential Embeddings), a compact model for predicting the functional consequences of single nucleotide variants (SNVs) by training directly on the wild-type (WT) versus mutant differential. Interpreting SNVs is central to clinical genomics, yet experimental characterization cannot scale to millions of observed variants. Leading sequence-to-function models (Enformer, Borzoi, AlphaGenome) are trained on absolute genomic tracks and score variants post hoc through in-silico mutagenesis (ISM), so the WT-mutant difference never enters the training loss. MELD instead places the logit difference {Delta}z = zmut - zwt inside the supervised objective. It combines a shared CNN-Transformer encoder, a mutant-specific mutation-mask boost, multiscale mutation-centered pooling, and a learned adaptive amplification factor . On ClinVar (1.57M variants), MELD (1.9M parameters) reached an AUROC of 0.986 versus 0.800 for a same-data, same-backbone ISM baseline, with ablations confirming the contribution of each component. On a shared benchmark, it outperformed frozen foundation models with 3-1,300x more parameters (AUROC 0.967 vs. 0.924 for AlphaGenome and 0.936 for Nucleotide Transformer). With only 50, 000 training variants, it exceeded the ISM baseline trained on all 1.48M (AUROC 0.903 vs. 0.796) variants. On BRCA1 saturation genome editing, frozen MELD achieved a Spearman {rho} of 0.42, above Borzoi (0.40), and ClinVar transfer raised it to 0.45. These results demonstrate that direct differential supervision is a compact, data-efficient alternative to post-hoc ISM scoring with substantially larger pretrained models.
affiliations: Qatar Computing Research Institute (corresponding author)

papers.title: Realism and resolution: How AI-predicted protein structures differ from experimental structures
papers.abstract: Protein structure predictors can recover protein folds with remarkable accuracy, and their models are increasingly used as if they were experimental structures. Yet even for a confidently predicted fold, it remains difficult to judge how faithfully the model reproduces protein geometry. We introduce WhatRes, which assesses a structure from its coordinates on two complementary axes. Apparent resolution estimates the experimental resolution its local geometry most closely resembles. Realism measures how closely that geometry matches experimental structures at the same apparent resolution. Predicted models can score well on apparent resolution while showing systematically less variation in bond lengths and angles than is observed in high-resolution crystal structures. WhatRes reveals this over-idealisation even in high-confidence models.
affiliations: KU Leuven (corresponding author)

papers.title: mFrag: Integrating External DNA Methylation References Improves Lung Cancer Early Detection by Fragmentomics
papers.abstract: Fragmentomics analyzes features of circulating cell-free DNA fragments (e.g., fragment length or end motifs) derived from whole-genome sequencing of liquid biopsy samples (blood or other body fluids), enabling non-invasive early cancer detection. Here we present mFrag, a framework that integrates external methylation reference atlases with fragmentomic features for lung cancer detection. mFrag comprises two complementary methods: mFrag-Weight, which uses DNA methylation information to weight fragmentomic features, and mFrag-Net, which integrates fragmentomic features and external DNA methylation data through neural networks. We average the output probabilities of the two methods to obtain a final prediction score. The mFrag model was trained using 287 individuals at risk for lung cancer. In an independent case-control testing set comprising 385 non-cancer controls and 46 cancers (28 stage I, 12 stage II, and 6 stage III or IV), mFrag outperforms a DELFI-style fragmentomic approach, improving PR-AUC from 0.455 to 0.720 and sensitivity at 99% specificity from 0.043 to 0.478, with ROC-AUC from 0.871 to 0.908. For stage I lung cancer, mFrag raises PR-AUC from 0.314 to 0.558 and ROC-AUC from 0.855 to 0.894. Applied to end 4-mer motif features, mFrag likewise improved over an unweighted baseline, with gains contributed by both mFrag-Weight and mFrag-Net. In summary, mFrag improves the accuracy of fragmentomics-based lung cancer detection through integrating external DNA methylation data and the complementarity of its two component models, without incurring any additional data-generating cost.
affiliations: Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: THiRST: Computer Vision Empowered Three-dimensional High-Resolution Spatial Transcriptomics Analytics
papers.abstract: High-resolution spatial transcriptomics (ST) preserves gene expression within tissue architecture but remains limited to individual two-dimensional (2D) sections, restricting analysis of continuous three-dimensional (3D) structures and cross-section consistency. We present THiRST, a computational framework for reconstructing multi-resolution 3D spatial transcriptomic representations from serial sections. THiRST combines coarse-to-fine morphology-guided registration, spatial matching of ST units, cross-section association of segmented structures, and integration of Visium V2 and high-definition ST. In serial kidney sections, patch-level refinement increased the same-cluster proportions of matched units at adjacent offsets from 63.8% and 65.6% to 70.7% and 70.0%, respectively, while improving expression concordance. The reconstructed correspondences enabled 3D glomerular and object-level expression analysis, with 54.1% of differential genes detected only in 3D. Cross-platform integration further aligned V2 and high-definition measurements in a shared expression space. THiRST demonstrates the feasibility of object-level 3D ST analysis from serial 2D sections and underscores the importance of accurate local registration.
affiliations: Vanderbilt University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Dual-reporter assay for selective small molecule inhibition of expanded toxic huntingtin
papers.abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by an expansion of CAG repeats in exon 1 of the human huntingtin gene (HTT). The resultant pathogenic allele (mHTT) produces a mutant huntingtin protein (mHtt) containing an expanded polyglutamine tract. Because mHtt drives neurodegeneration while wildtype huntingtin (Htt) remains critical for regulation of gene transcription and cell survival, an ideal therapeutic would specifically downregulate mHtt expression while preserving Htt. Small molecules are attractive candidates for HD given their ability to penetrate the blood-brain barrier and amenability to oral dosing, but there remains no high-throughput platform that reports both efficacy and allele selectivity. Here, we present a bacterial assay in which exon 1 of HTT and mHTT, each fused to spectrally distinct fluorescent proteins, are co-expressed in the same cell, allowing simultaneous quantification of their expression in the presence of small molecules. This high-throughput assay isolates the effect of small molecules on huntingtin expression without confounding factors present in mammalian cells, such as endogenous Htt or human RNA-binding proteins. To validate this assay, we evaluated two previously reported CAG repeat binding compounds and used circular dichroism spectroscopy and cell-free protein synthesis to investigate their underlying mechanisms. Furamidine exhibited reproducible, sequence-dependent effects, altering the structural stability of HTT RNA and selectively decreasing the wildtype Htt expression (a selectivity profile opposite to what is therapeutically required). In contrast, myricetin did not affect HTT RNA stability and its decreased signal in the dual-expression assay was due to fluorophore artifacts. This highlights the importance of complementary workflows in distinguishing genuine modulators from reporter-specific artifacts. Collectively, these findings establish the dual-expression assay as a screening platform for CAG repeat-targeting small molecules and demonstrate the importance of determining which allele reported compounds preferentially affect.
affiliations: University of Southern California (corresponding author)

papers.title: Dehydration-Responsive Left-Handed G-Quadruplexes Expandthe Sequence Repertoire
papers.abstract: G-quadruplexes (G4s) are widely studied noncanonical nucleic-acid structures that carry important biological functions. Typically, G4s form from G-rich sequences containing at least four tracts of more than two consecutive guanines, yet a plethora of unconventional G4-forming sequences have been identified, including sequences that fold into G4s only under specific conditions. These G4 states remain poorly resolved. Here we identify dehydration-responsive left-handed G4s (drLHG4s), a class of left-handed G4 (LHG4) structures accessible under dehydrating conditions. Using d(GT)n repeats, we show that left-handed folding depends on repeat length, salt condition and solvent conditions. Systematic mutational analysis reveals a broader but register-constrained sequence space, while high-resolution crystal structures of d-GTGGTGTGTGGTG, a sequence that folded robustly under dehydrating conditions, establish a bulged LHG4 architecture and reveal a distinctive hydration sphere. We further show that selected peptides and a cationic zinc phthalocyanine derivative, ZnTEGQPyrPc, containing four triethylene glycol methyl ether tails can induce LHG4 states. Together, our findings reveal a dehydration-responsive G4 landscape and expand the experimentally accessible sequence space of LHG4 folding.
affiliations: Inserm / Ecole Polytechnique (corresponding author)

papers.title: TMEM11-Dependent Cristae Architecture Restrains Imiquimod-Induced NLRP3 Inflammasome Activation via Mitochondrial ROS
papers.abstract: Imiquimod (IMQ) is a clinically approved drug widely used to treat skin malignancies; however, its application frequently provokes severe inflammation through NLRP3 inflammasome activation. The mechanism underlying IMQ-induced activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome is not completely defined. While IMQ-induced inhibition of mitochondrial electron transport chain complex I is necessary for activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, it is not sufficient; suggesting presence of additional targets/triggers. The role of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) as the additional trigger to activate the inflammasome remains contentious based on conflicting reports. Using a unique genetic model lacking expression of mitochondrial membrane protein TMEM11 we reaffirm the role of mtROS in IMQ-induced NLRP3 inflammasome activation. Macrophages deficient in Tmem11, a mitochondrial contact site and cristae organizing system (MICOS)-associated membrane-protein, exhibit ultrastructural defects in cristae morphology without altering mitochondrial mass or mtDNA copy number. Loss of TMEM11 influences cristae length and density, reducing mitochondrial oxygen consumption. Tmem11-deficient macrophages exhibit normal NLRP3 inflammasome activation in response to canonical agonists (e.g., ATP, nigericin) but show caspase-1 hyperactivation and exaggerated IL-1{beta} and IL-18 secretion upon IMQ treatment. This exaggerated response is rescued by antioxidant treatment, confirming the role for mtROS. These findings demonstrate that cristae architecture restrains drug-induced mtROS to limit NLRP3 activation and that mtROS is a primary driver of IMQ-mediated NLRP3 inflammasome activation.
affiliations: UCLA (corresponding author)

papers.title: IL4Ra Controls The Medullary Dwell Time Of Mature Thymocytes By Scheduling Their Release From The Thymus
papers.abstract: Following their generation, newly produced single positive (SP) thymocytes must remain in the thymus to undergo post-selection maturation, a process supported by the thymic medulla. This ensures that SP thymocytes are equipped with functional competence prior to S1PR1-mediated thymic emigration. Despite this importance, the intrathymic mechanisms that control the balance between retention and release of SP thymocytes is unclear. Here, we describe a cell autonomous requirement for IL4Ra-signalling in SP thymocytes, that determines the duration of their medullary occupancy. We show that the period of this occupancy is prolonged in the absence of IL4R expression by SP thymocytes, which occurs as a result of impaired interactions with medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTEC). Importantly, extending the duration of medullary occupancy enhances the maturational status and functional capabilities of SP thymocytes, including improved TNF and IL2 production. Collectively, we show that IL4Ra regulates the medullary occupancy of mature thymocytes, which in turn determines the functional properties of thymic output.
affiliations: University of Birmingham (corresponding author)

papers.title: The Src family kinases Lck and Fyn promote transendothelial migration of T cells
papers.abstract: The ability of T cells to cross endothelial barriers and migrate into and within peripheral tissue is crucial for adaptive immunity. Integrins such as LFA-1 play an essential role in this process by acting as adhesion molecules and initiating signaling events that drive the cytoskeletal changes needed for cell migration, however, many of the specific signaling events that promote T cell migration are still unknown. Here, we found that the Src family kinases Lck and Fyn are needed for efficient T cell migration. Primary T cells lacking Lck, Fyn, or both kinases exhibited defects in random migration on ICAM-1 coated surfaces for parameters such as speed and mean squared displacement. Analysis of signaling revealed that Lck was required for PI3K signaling downstream of LFA-1, while Fyn was not. Mechanistically, we found that the absence of Lck disrupted the normal interaction of the PI3K regulatory subunit p85 with tyrosine-phosphorylated binding partners, suggesting that Lck may regulate PI3K activity by controlling p85 protein-protein interactions. Importantly, both Lck and Fyn were required for efficient T cell transmigration across an inflamed endothelial barrier, a critical event for tissue infiltration. Lastly, a small-molecule Lck kinase inhibitor also decreased PI3K signaling and T cell transmigration, indicating the kinase activity of Lck is needed. Together, these data identify a new role for Lck and Fyn in promoting T cell transmigration.
affiliations: SUNY Upstate Medical University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Impaired Fermentation in the Absence of Gut Microbiota Promotes Inulin-Induced Intestinal Inflammation
papers.abstract: Background and aims: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) are characterized by altered gut microbiota composition and impaired dietary fiber fermentation, which can complicate symptom management. Although inulin is a well-established prebiotic fiber, it can exacerbate gut inflammation under certain conditions. We hypothesized that impaired microbial fermentation leaves intact inulin in the gut to activate epithelial immune receptors and promote inflammation, whereas effective fermentation reduces this pro-inflammatory signaling. Methods: We used germ-free (GF) and conventional (CONV) interleukin-10 knockout (Il10-/-) and wild-type (WT) C57BL/6J mice to assess the role of microbial fermentation and host genetic susceptibility in IBD. GF Il10-/- mice were colonized with fecal microbiota from ulcerative colitis (UC) patients or healthy individuals with fiber intolerance (FI). Mice were fed inulin or structurally distinct, physicochemically matched fiber analogs. Colonic inflammatory and barrier-related gene expression and protein levels were assessed by qPCR and ELISA. Results: In GF Il10-/- mice, inulin, but not cellulose, induced weight loss, diarrhea, and rectal prolapse. Increased colonic toll-like receptor expression (TLR2, TLR4) as well as elevated serum amyloid A (SAA) and lipocalin-2 levels indicated immune activation by unfermented inulin in GF mice. Colonization with dysbiotic microbiota attenuated these effects. {beta}-fructan fibers including fructooligosaccharides and chicory-derived inulin elicited marked inflammatory responses, whereas agave-derived inulin did not, highlighting the influence of fiber composition in inflammation associated with IBD. Conclusions: Effective microbial fermentation is essential for host tolerance to fermentable fibers. These findings underscore the need of personalized nutrition when recommending fiber supplementation in immune-compromised individuals or those with gut dysbiosis.
affiliations: Purdue University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Diverse bacteria exhibit superadditive growth on mixed classes of carbon sources
papers.abstract: Heterotrophic bacteria in nature encounter complex mixtures of functionally-distinct carbon sources, yet whether such diversity enhances growth yield across diverse taxa remains unknown. We grew dozens of strains from four phyla on defined mixtures representing five classes of carbon sources. Remarkably, many but not all strains exhibited superadditive growth on a dilute mixture of all 64 compounds--that is, yield exceeding the weighted sum of yields on more concentrated subsets of functionally-similar compounds. Using exometabolomics, pooled genetic screens, and proteomics, we find that superadditive growth is associated with enhanced carbon consumption in the mixed-class medium, combined with reduced dependence on amino acid and nucleotide biosynthesis. Moreover, superadditive growth was predictable from genomes within the tested strain panel and correlated with genomically encoded sugar-over-acid preference. These findings reveal a previously underrecognized axis of physiological variation among heterotrophs and open the door to understanding the biochemical and evolutionary basis of this divergence.
affiliations: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (corresponding author)

papers.title: Integrated Transcriptomic and Translatomic Profiling Reveals Noncanonical RNA Junctions and Hidden Coding Potential in Porcine Epidemic Diarrhea Virus
papers.abstract: Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV) poses a major threat to the global swine industry. Although coronavirus discontinuous transcription is well characterized, the classical model cannot fully explain the diversity of viral RNA junctions, while conventional genome annotations may underestimate viral protein-coding capacity. To address these gaps, we integrated time-resolved RNA sequencing (RNA-seq), cycloheximide (CHX)- and harringtonine (HAR)-treated ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq), comparative genomics, and peptide mass spectrometry to investigate PEDV RNA expression and hidden coding potential. RNA-seq revealed that, at 3 hours post-infection (hpi), the 3 genomic region exhibited strong relative coverage enrichment, whereas the relative contribution of the 5 replicase-coding region increased rapidly between 3 and 5 hpi, suggesting a possible transition from sgRNA-dominated RNA accumulation toward enhanced genomic RNA replication. Genome-wide junction analysis identified 43,635 distinct noncanonical RNA junctions, although canonical sgRNA junctions accounted for 95.5% of all junction-supporting reads. Several abundant noncanonical sgRNAs were predicted to generate novel coding products, including N-x4, N-x2, M-x3, and M-x2, short peptides encoded within the 3 untranslated region (UTR), and two distinct N-terminally truncated S proteins, thereby expanding the potential coding repertoire of PEDV. Genome-wide reading-frame analysis uncovered a pronounced asymmetry in hidden coding potential, identifying 68 overlapping open reading frames (ORFs) longer than 40 amino acids in the +1 reading frame, compared with only three in the +2 frame. Ribo-seq further revealed a progressive redistribution of viral ribosome occupancy toward structural protein-coding regions during the later stages of infection. By integrating HAR-associated translation initiation-site enrichment with CHX-based ORF-level translation analysis, we identified several noncanonical ORFs with strong translation-associated evidence, including N-x1, N-x2, S-x1, and ORF1b-x13. Moreover, peptide mass spectrometry detected a characteristic peptide corresponding to N-x1 in infected samples, providing independent proteomic evidence for the expression of this previously unannotated viral protein. Together, these findings uncover extensive noncanonical RNA synthesis and hidden protein-coding capacity in PEDV, establishing a foundation for understanding novel viral gene expression strategies and their potential evolutionary and pathogenic significance.
affiliations: Northwest Agriculture University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Inter-domain flexibility in F-Box proteins revealed by integrative modeling
papers.abstract: F-box proteins, the substrate-recognition modules of the SCF (Skp1-Cul1-F-box) ubiquitin ligase complex, play a central role in targeted protein degradation by enabling the selective recruitment of diverse substrates. F-box proteins share a common architecture with a conserved anchor domain linked to the substrate-binding domain. Despite extensive structural characterization of F-box proteins, their potential conformational dynamics remain poorly understood. Here, we employ an integrative modeling approach combining cryo-EM structures, cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS), and deep learning-based conformational ensemble prediction to profile the accessible conformations of F-box proteins. Our analyses reveal a significant inter-domain flexibility in FBXL2 and FBXL17 that enables sampling of a broad range of conformations within assembled SCF and CSN-SCF complexes. By contrast, other F-box proteins, including FBXL1 and FBXO22, exhibit intrinsic flexibility but are restricted to a considerably narrower conformational landscape. Together, our work highlights inter-domain plasticity as a tunable architectural feature of F-box proteins, which may shape their functional versatility within SCF complexes.
affiliations: The Hebrew University of Jerusalem (corresponding author)

papers.title: phyB photobodies display molecular memory, regulating light signaling transcriptional states through phase separation.
papers.abstract: Phytochrome B is a crucial red and far-red light sensor, which controls plant development and environmental responses to light and temperature. In the nucleus, phyB forms phase separated condensates, also called photobodies, consisting of various transcriptional regulators and transcription factors. phyB photobodies can form or disperse depending on the amount of light, the light quality, or ambient temperature. However, the biological relevance for forming photobodies is still unclear. In recent years the study of condensates has given rise to the idea that condensates can act as molecular memory, either due to long equilibration timescales arising from strong interactions that can kinetically trap a mixture in a phase-separated state beyond the equilibrium coexistence line, or from phase-separation dependent modification processes or transcriptional regulation. Here, we hypothesize that the formation of phyB photobodies and the associated sequestration of signaling molecules allows for the formation of cell-type specific memory about light conditions. To address this hypothesis, we first developed a live imaging setup of phyB photobodies which shows that they do not follow classic liquid-liquid phase separation dynamics, but instead have a restriction on their size, intensity and minimum number. Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) then showed that photobodies between cell types have different levels of mobilities and diffusivities, suggesting that they are more stable in darkness or high red light, versus low red light. These differences in phyB photobody stability between cell types were also confirmed through whole-mount confocal imaging and single-nucleus transcriptomics in the same light-perturbation series. Through sci-Seq single nucleus spatial transcriptomics of the cotyledon in this light perturbation series, we identify a photobody-associated transcriptional cluster of nuclei that regulates photosynthesis, circadian rhythm, and RNA processing; the phyB photobody likely promotes its own stability by regulating TZP expression. The correlation between photobodies and transcriptional regulation shows how phyB condensates can provide cell-type specific light responses and exhibit signaling memory in changing environmental conditions.
affiliations: Light Signaling and Cell Biology, Centre for Organismal Studies, Heidelberg University, Im Neuenheimer Feld 230, 69120, Heidelberg, Germany (corresponding author)

papers.title: Genomes of Solenogastres Shed Light on Ancestral Molluscan Biomineralization Genes
papers.abstract: Aplacophora (Solenogastres + Caudofoveata) is a group of worm-like molluscs that lack a shell and instead are covered with aragonitic spines and scales called sclerites. Sclerites are also found along the girdle in chitons (Polyplacophora) and are a synapomorphy for Aculifera (Aplacophora + Polyplacophora), which is the sister taxon of all other shell-bearing molluscs (Conchifera). However, whether the same genetic mechanism underlies the process of biomineralization in aculiferans and conchiferans is unknown. To investigate evolution of genes involved in biomineralization across Mollusca, we re-sequenced the genomes of two species of Solenogastres, Epimenia babai and Neomenia megatrapezata , producing near-chromosome-level assemblies through PacBio HiFi and Hi-C scaffolding. Using a combination of orthology inference and similarity searches against a known SMP database we identified 1,244 putative SMP orthogroups across Mollusca, 292 of which were present in at least one solenogaster genome. SMPs undergoing significant expansion/contraction at key nodes were further investigated. Of these, 15 were found in at least one solenogaster genome and included families containing chitin-binding, von Willebrand factor A, and C-type lectin domains. Across Mollusca, Solenogastres showed the highest number of significant losses in all gene families, including the SMPs investigated. Targeted searches for structural, silk-like proteins in Aculifera show further reductions in Solenogastres (16-17) compared to caudofoveates (29) and chitons (46-80). Altogether, our results support a conserved but reduced biomineralization toolkit underlying sclerite formation in Solenogastres and identify candidate genes for further proteomic and functional study.
affiliations: The University of Alabama (corresponding author)

papers.title: MaaD-TAD: an all-atom model of the duplicated PRAMEF/HNRNPCL chromatin domain built from sequence homology
papers.abstract: In the nucleus, the placement of genes in the 3D fold of DNA affects how they function. Models of this fold use two kinds of data: contact maps constructed from Hi-C, and nucleosome maps showing where DNA is wound around nucleosomes. Over evolution, sections of the genome were copied, creating near-identical regions. Reads from these regions cannot be assigned to one copy and are discarded, leaving "void regions" in both maps. We tested MaaD-TAD, a pipeline that models topologically associating domains (TADs) at the atomic level, on the PRAMEF/HNRNPCL locus on human chromosome 1. This challenging locus spans 652 kb, with only 15% of its nucleosome positions known and most contact data missing. To test our hypothesis that copies with similar sequence lie close in space, i.e. homology as a surrogate for proximity, we constructed a map of sequence homology in place of Hi-C and used CSynth to fold it into a 3D path. We then lengthened the path to fit a chromatin fibre, and refined the model by adding cohesin complexes, which stabilize chromatin structure. Cohesin is a ring-shaped protein complex through which a loop of chromatin is threaded; the loop is commonly anchored by CTCF proteins bound on either leg. Using known databases, we placed CTCF sites in our model and joined three to their copies with cohesin rings; in each pair the sites face each other, as loop anchors do. The final model holds 3,359 nucleosomes and about 55 million atoms. Micro-C, an advanced, higher-resolution form of Hi-C, provided data on two other duplicated regions that support our hypothesis: matching copies touched 1.2 to 1.9 times more often than expected. Our approach provides a novel method to reconstruct DNA regions with absent contact data and, to our knowledge, the first all-atom model of a complete TAD.
affiliations: University of Alberta (corresponding author)

papers.title: Leave-One-Out-Cross-Validation Based Machine Learning Algorithms for Efficient, Scalable, and Robust Prediction of Artemisinin Resistance in Plasmodium falciparum Kelch13 mutants.
papers.abstract: Emerging Plasmodium falciparum resistance to frontline artemisinin (ART) derivatives threatens global malaria control efforts. Current protocols assigning ART-sensitive (ART-S) or -resistant (ART-R) phenotypes to parasite strains with Kelch13 (K13) mutations remain time-intensive for real-time surveillance. Ring-survival assay (RSA), an ex vivo gold standard mandates laboratory-adaptation under culture conditions and frequently does not replicate clinical ART-responsiveness, thereby limiting its utility for rapidly triaging newly emerging K13 variants. In contrast, advent of artificial intelligence (AI)-derived models hold potential to screen >100 K13 variants within hours, enabling rapid near-real-time prediction of ART-S/R. Here, we engineered a panel of forty representative K13 variants by computing their relative deviations from wild-type K13 across ten physicochemical and structural descriptors, yielding a compact feature set which captures mutation-induced perturbations in folding, stability, and solvent exposure. These can be further utilized to train and validate AI classifier to predict resistance.
affiliations: Jawaharlal Nehru University (corresponding author)

papers.title: COTree: A Statistical Framework for Deciphering Cell-Resolved Multi-Omics Trajectories
papers.abstract: Recent advances in whole-cell modeling enable the computational tracking of the temporal evolution of thousands of molecular species across genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic layers. These models provide a complementary perspective for studying cellular dynamics, offering continuous, system-wide observations that are difficult to obtain from experimental technologies, which are often destructive and yield only static measurements from limited modalities. While whole-cell models generate multi-omic simulation trajectories with high temporal resolution, analyzing and interpreting such complex data remains a major challenge that limits their potential to elucidate cellular dynamics. To address this challenge, we propose COTree, a statistical framework that learns integrated multi-omic representations and constructs a trajectory principal tree to summarize cellular progression patterns. COTree enables a broad range of downstream analyses, including cell classification, fate prediction, developmental time detection, and driver species identification, that provide new insights into how cells develop and differentiate. To demonstrate its practical utility, we apply COTree to a multi-omic trajectory dataset generated from the whole-cell model of JCVI-Syn3A, revealing cell types, characterizing long-term cellular dynamics, and identifying key driver species associated with cell death and replication.
affiliations: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (corresponding author)

papers.title: How AlphaFold 3 helps with multiscale drug discovery
papers.abstract: AlphaFold 3 (AF3) predicts protein ligand complexes, but the utility of its confidence scores for drug discovery remains unclear. We benchmarked AF3 interaction scores against BANDOCK+, an experimentally informed approach, using approved drugs and human protein libraries. AF3 ipTM achieved slightly higher observed aggregate disease ranking scores in a matched 1,103 protein comparison, with performance varying among individual indications. BANDOCK+ enabled substantially broader protein coverage using a computationally less demanding approach, including a 20,158 protein reference library. These findings highlight the potential of AF3 confidence scores for computational drug discovery and the tradeoffs between predictive performance and scalability.
affiliations: University at Buffalo (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cell cycle progression and stalked cell morphogenesis in Caulobacter crescentus are regulated independently by the flagellum
papers.abstract: Bacteria colonize surfaces and form biofilms to survive in stressful environmental conditions. Many bacteria use an appendage called the flagellum to sense surface contact, and responding to these mechanical cues triggers rapid physiological changes to promote downstream attachment. Bacteria are known to secrete adhesins and alter their motility behavior to facilitate surface colonization, but these changes alone are insufficient to explain the breadth of adaptations observed in surface-attached cells. Disrupting flagellar assembly in the bacterium Caulobacter crescentus constitutively activates the surface sensing pathway, and this gain-of-function phenotype was previously used to identify a suite of flagellar signaling suppressor (fss) genes that promotes surface adhesion downstream of the flagellum. We show herein that a subset of fss genes also regulates the C. crescentus developmental program. Live-cell microscopy analysis of fss mutants identified independent sub-pathways that target stalked cell morphogenesis and cell cycle progression. We identify the predicted chemotaxis genes fssD and fssE as novel regulators of stalked cell morphogenesis and show that these genes act to stimulate the diguanylate cyclase PleD in flagellar assembly mutants. A separate pathway that includes the stator protein MotB and the recently characterized dNTPase FssC regulates entry into S phase downstream of the flagellum. We show that motB regulates cell cycle progression specifically in response to surface cues, and that stator-dependent cell cycle control occurs independently of c-di-GMP and CtrA. This work clarifies the downstream targets of the surface sensing network and establishes a comprehensive model for how surface sensing influences the C. crescentus developmental program.
affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cholinergic modulation engages a CHRM1-IL-17 neuroimmune axis to promote diabetic wound repair
papers.abstract: Chronic non-healing wounds are a major complication of diabetes, where persistent inflammation fails to transition into effective tissue repair (1-3). Here we identify cholinergic modulation as a mechanism that promotes productive inflammation and diabetic wound healing. Using a healing-associated fibroblast signature derived from single-cell profiling of human diabetic foot ulcers (3), we identified the acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibitor metrifonate as a candidate inducer of reparative wound programs. Topical delivery accelerated healing in diabetic mice and increased acetylcholine availability within the wound. Complementary receptor pharmacology identified muscarinic acetylcholine receptor 1 (CHRM1) as the principal receptor mediating the reparative response. Transcriptomic and cellular analyses revealed early induction of IL-17-associated inflammatory programs and enrichment of CHRM1NK1.1 innate lymphocytes. Depletion of NK1.1 cells or neutralization of IL-17A abolished the pro-healing effect, whereas spatial transcriptomics revealed treatment-associated organization of NK cells within vascular niches. Localized treatment further promoted repair in diabetic porcine wounds and human skin models. Together, these findings identify a CHRM1-IL-17 neuroimmune axis linking cholinergic modulation to diabetic wound repair and establish local AChE inhibition as a potential therapeutic strategy for chronic wounds.
affiliations: Joslin-Beth Israel Deaconess Foot Center and The Rongxiang Xu, MD, Center for Regenerative Therapeutics, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical S (corresponding author)

papers.title: Deep phenomics of African green monkey and Baboon PBMCs using a 30-marker spectral flow cytometry panel
papers.abstract: Vaccines are the best way to prevent and combat diseases. Non-human primate (NHP) models have proven to be the gold standard model for studying the efficacy of certain vaccine candidates prior to human trials. Cell-mediated immunity serves as a surrogate marker for predicting vaccine efficacy. Despite the availability of deep-immunophenotyping panels for T cells in the peripheral blood of humans, their application to NHPs, particularly African Green Monkeys (AGMs) and baboons, remains limited. Notably, AGMs are valuable for HIV and COVID-19 research, while baboons are utilized for pertussis research as a natural infection model and vaccine trial. To overcome such limitation, using spectral flow cytometry, we developed a 30-parameter panel to profile major immune cell subsets (B cells, NK cells, DCs, monocytes) either in AGM or baboon PBMCs. We also profiled T cells, memory phenotypes, functional cytokines by tracking established Th1 markers IFN{gamma}, TNF and IL-2; Th2 markers IL-4/5/13 and the Th17 marker, IL-17, activation-induced markers (AIMs) and FoxP3+ Tregs in both AGM and baboon PBMCs in steady state as well as in mitogen stimulated conditions. For AIMs, CD69, CD134 (OX40) and CD137 (4-1BB) are included and validated in both NHP species. This panel holds potential for exploratory analysis of the impact of these functional cytokines, AIMs, or Tregs on host immunity following infection or vaccination. The panels high level of customization empowers researchers to tailor it to their specific research needs.
affiliations: 1Precision Vaccines Program, Boston Children's Hospital, Boston, MA, USA, 2Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: 41% of Gram-negative bacteria encode a Type Six Secretion System
papers.abstract: The type six secretion system (T6SS) is a highly studied, versatile bacterial nanoweapon that is important in bacterial pathogenesis and evolution. Despite extensive study, its prevalence remains poorly quantified. Analyzing 35,467 representative genomes, we find that approximately 41% of genomes in the average well-sampled Gram-negative genus (more than 30 sampled genomes) encode a T6SS. Further, we show that the distribution of the T6SS is patchy at all taxonomic levels. The uneven distribution we found is consistent with context-dependent selection, repeated evolutionary loss, or greater evolutionary lability. Our dataset provides a foundation for studying the drivers of T6SS distribution, and our pipeline enables similar surveys of other secretion systems, gene clusters, and multi-protein complexes across bacteria.
affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Reversible decrease in swimming motility accompanies emergent β-lactam antibiotic resistance in Escherichia coli
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) threatens global health, food security, and development; however, the evolutionary and molecular pathways that drive AMR remain poorly understood, limiting our ability to advance diagnostics and rapidly detect newly emerging resistance. In this report, we employed laboratory evolution of an environmental Escherichia coli strain (NIST 0056) under B-lactam antibiotic pressure (ampicillin and cephalexin) to specifically investigate the relationship between resistance genotype and motility phenotype. Within 10 passages, populations evolved varying levels of B-lactam resistance (including high-level resistance > 32 ug/mL) and showed consistent, dose-dependent reductions in swimming motility. Whole-population genome sequencing revealed large deletions in marR, SNPs in efflux pump gene acrB and fumarate reductase gene frdD, and mutations with evidence of amplification in the chromosomal class C B-lactamase gene ampC, collectively linking these efflux-mediated, B-lactam resistance mechanisms to loss of motility. Notably, motility reductions were more pronounced in individual clones than in the mixed populations (p < 0.005, Mann-Whitney; two-tailed test). Following removal of antibiotic pressure, motility was restored and AMR-associated mutations decreased in frequency, suggesting fitness costs associated with resistance. In aggregate, our results demonstrate that reduced swimming motility accompanies specific efflux-driven, B-lactam resistance mechanisms. Further work will investigate if the behavior is generalizable across flagellated Enterobacteriaceae. Because these rapid changes are amenable to high-throughput measurement, swimming motility may offer a tractable physiological metric for AMR detection in environmental surveillance.
affiliations: NIST (corresponding author)

papers.title: Network inference at single-cell resolution reveals morphoregulatory divergence and multilayered buffering in limb evolution
papers.abstract: How changes in conserved developmental genetic programs contribute to morphological evolution remains poorly understood, particularly in non-conventional model species. Here, we combine single-cell transcriptomic and chromatin-accessibility profiling with cross-species label transfer and gene regulatory network inference to compare mouse and pig limb development. Our analyses identify broadly conserved cellular organization but discrete divergence in HOX-, FGF- and SHH-regulated programs. FGFR inhibition in mouse limb buds phenocopies the distal expansion of pig GREM1 expression, while altered SHH responses and anterior-posterior polarity converge on the PTCH1 regulatory landscape. Its functional dissection reveals degeneration of a limb regulatory module in artiodactyls, conservation of an additional distal enhancer, and extensive redundancy among cis-regulatory inputs. Allele-specific analyses further show that reduced Ptch1 dosage is buffered by transcriptional compensation. Together, these findings reveal how cis-regulatory and pathway-level robustness can accommodate distributed regulatory change while preserving developmental function, providing a mechanistic framework for the evolution of artiodactyl limb morphology.
affiliations: Centro Andaluz de Biologia del Desarrollo (CABD-CSIC), Sevilla, Spain (corresponding author)

papers.title: Developmentally-regulated splice remodeling shapes functional CACNA1C channel diversity during human neurodevelopment
papers.abstract: CACNA1C encodes the pore-forming subunit of the CaV1.2 L-type voltage-gated calcium channel, a major regulator of neuronal calcium signaling and one of the strongest genetic risk loci for bipolar disorder and other psychiatric disorders. Although extensive alternative splicing of CACNA1C has been described in the adult human brain, how alternative splicing of CACNA1C is regulated during early human neurodevelopment remains largely unknown. Here, we used long-read RNA sequencing to characterize full-length CACNA1C transcripts during differentiation of human induced pluripotent stem cells, from healthy controls and patients with bipolar disorder homozygous for either the A or G allele at rs1006737, into cortical glutamatergic neurons. We identified 60 putative isoforms, including ten annotated transcripts and 23 previously reported in adult human brain. We also demonstrate that CACNA1C undergoes developmentally-regulated remodeling of isoform composition during neuronal differentiation. This remodeling was characterized by an exon-switching program involving mutually exclusive exon pairs and alternative splice site usage, including prominent developmental transitions between exon pairs 8/8a, 21/22, and 31/32. Neither rs1006737 genotype, diagnosis, sex nor age significantly affected splicing profiles. The developmental splice trajectories were recapitulated in dorsal forebrain organoids, showing that CACNA1C splice remodeling is conserved across independent human neural differentiation models. Electrophysiological characterization of the two most abundant neuronal isoforms found that exon 31/32 switching alters channel inactivation properties. Together, our findings demonstrate that developmentally-regulated alternative splicing of CACNA1C transcripts contributes to the functional diversity of CaV1.2 channels expressed during human neurodevelopment.
affiliations: University of Gothenburg (corresponding author)

papers.title: Embryonic integrin signaling establishes a program of differential cell elongation in a growing proprioceptive organ
papers.abstract: The ChO is a proprioceptive sensory organ that undergoes extensive morphological remodeling during larval growth. A key feature of this process is the dramatic elongation of cap cells, while adjacent ligament cells remain short. How these contrasting growth behaviors are established and coordinated is largely unknown. Using targeted RNAi screens of extracellular matrix (ECM) components, ECM receptors, and their intracellular effectors, we identified distinct molecular mechanisms controlling ChO architecture. We found that basement membrane components, including collagens and laminins, are required to maintain the characteristic straight morphology of cap cells, whereas Thrombospondin and Tiggrin contribute to the stability of cellular attachments. Unexpectedly, we discovered that Thrombospondin and an PS2{beta}PS integrin signaling module, comprising Talin and the ILK-PINCH-Parvin complex, regulate the relative lengths of cap and ligament cells. Cell-type-specific knockdown demonstrated that this pathway acts within ligament cells to restrict their elongation. Disruption of integrin signaling causes ligament cells to elongate dramatically at the expense of cap cell extension, effectively reversing their normal growth behaviors. Importantly, this function is distinct from the role of integrin-associated proteins in maintaining cellular attachments. Temporal manipulation of integrin expression revealed that the short morphology of ligament cells is established during a critical developmental time window during embryogenesis, before the organ becomes functional. Restoring integrin expression after hatching fails to rescue the phenotype, indicating that embryonic integrin signaling establishes a persistent developmental state. Together, these findings reveal that ligament cell elongation is actively restricted by an embryonically established integrin-dependent mechanism, providing the structural basis for subsequent cap cell elongation and organ maturation.
affiliations: Department of Genetics and Developmental Biology, The Ruth and Bruce Rappaport Faculty of Medicine and Research Institute, Technion-Israel Institute of Technolo (corresponding author)

papers.title: Receptor-guided engineering of oncolytic vaccinia creates a synthetic support niche for off-the-shelf NK cell therapy
papers.abstract: Combining adoptive cell therapy with oncolytic viruses offers a means to provide localized support within solid tumors, yet viral chassis and therapeutic payloads are often selected independently of the biological state of the manufactured cell product. Here, we establish an engineering framework that uses the phenotypic and functional features of an adoptive cell product as design inputs for a complementary oncolytic niche. Using off-the-shelf expanded, frozen, and thawed (EFT) natural killer (NK) cells as a model system, we identified manufacturing-associated reductions in chemokine responsiveness, dependence on extrinsic cytokine support, and loss of sustained function at limiting effector-to-target ratios. In a head-to-head evaluation under human NK-cell antiviral pressure, oncolytic vaccinia virus (VV) retained replication and spread, whereas HSV-1 was rapidly restricted, establishing VV as a compatible viral chassis. Mapping endogenous receptor expression and applying sequential functional screening under increasingly limiting effector densities then prioritized a five-factor program comprising CXCL11, IL-15, IL-27, IL-2, and IL-1{beta} that supported NK-cell migration, survival, cytotoxicity, and metabolic fitness at effector-to-target ratios as low as 1:10. Consolidating these signals into a single viral chassis increased antitumor activity but revealed a systemic inflammatory liability associated with constitutive IL-1{beta} expression. We therefore placed the IL-2/IL-1{beta} module under chemically inducible control, retaining in vivo antitumor activity while limiting systemic toxicity. Together, these findings establish a framework in which the post-manufacturing state of an adoptive cell product guides viral chassis selection, payload prioritization, and programmable control of a complementary oncolytic support niche.
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania (corresponding author)

papers.title: Tissue-like Viscoelasticity Drives Muscle Stem Cell Expansion Through Mechanical Memory Formation
papers.abstract: Mechanical cues are potent regulators of stem cell fate, with even transient exposure to substrates with varied elastic stiffness driving persistent changes in cell fate. Such elastic mechanical memory contributes to the loss of regenerative potential in skeletal muscle stem cells (MuSCs) when cultured on rigid substrates, hampering the translation of myogenic cell replacement therapies. Beyond elastic mechanical properties, cells also respond to time-dependent, viscoelastic mechanical properties, such as stress relaxation. However, whether tissue-like viscoelasticity can impart a mechanical memory that directs stem cell fate remains an open question. Accordingly, dual-network hydrogel biomaterials with decoupled control of stiffness, stress relaxation, and adhesive ligand presentation were engineered to recapitulate the viscoelastic mechanical properties of native muscle. Muscle-like viscoelastic substrates promote in vitro MuSC activation and accelerate stem cell expansion, matching in vivo activation timescales. Mechanistically, physiological viscoelasticity promotes focal adhesion stabilization and enhances Rac-Akt signaling, establishing a viscoelastic mechanical memory that supports progenitor expansion and persistent maintenance of a stem-like phenotype. These findings identify matrix viscoelasticity as a potent and persistent regulator of MuSC fate and provide a framework for engineering biomaterials that preserve MuSC stemness and expansion ex vivo.
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania (corresponding author)

papers.title: PRISM: probabilistic cell-type resolution with integrated spatial modelling for simultaneous ambient RNA decontamination and doublet correction in spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics count matrices are confounded by ambient RNA contamination and cell-segmentation doublets, two artifacts that co-occur but are rarely modelled jointly. We present PRISM, an Expectation-Maximization framework that simultaneously (i) assigns each cell a probabilistic cell-type identity, (ii) detects doublets via log-likelihood ratio testing of two-component mixtures, and (iii) estimates a per-cell contamination fraction anchored to a spatially resolved ambient profile. In an in silico benchmark of 40,800 simulated cells, PRISM recovers with Pearson r=1.000 across all contamination levels (0.05 to 0.50) and UMI depths (500 to 5,000), with zero doublet false positives and 100% singlet accuracy. Applied to a Visium HD mouse cerebellum dataset (four samples, 125,289 cells, 17 reference types) from a metachromatic leukodystrophy (MLD) model, PRISM identifies a median =0.60, flags 67.4% doublets (driven by the densely packed cerebellar granule layer), eliminates spurious myelin signal from microglia (0.82% to 0.00%), and doubles oligodendrocyte myelin purity (2.8% to 5.6%). PRISM runs on commodity CPUs in under 15 minutes and returns decontaminated integer count matrices for every measured gene.
affiliations: CNR-ITB (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Three-View System for CRISPR-Cas12a crRNA Activity Ranking: When to Ensemble, When Context Matters More
papers.abstract: CRISPR-Cas12a assays require effective crRNA selection, but experimentally screening all possible candidates is costly. We developed TriCasRank, a ranking model that combines sequence features with EasyDesign reference mapping and activity summaries from related training records. Historical summaries were calculated within each training fold to avoid information leakage. In five-fold target-grouped cross-validation using out-of-fold predictions, TriCasRank improved the Spearman correlation from 0.741 for the sequence-only ensemble to 0.821 (paired difference, 0.080; 95% target-group bootstrap interval, 0.072 to 0.090). However, its performance was comparable to that of a strong sequence-plus-mapping XGBoost model (SCC, 0.822; paired difference, -0.001; 95% interval, -0.007 to 0.005). Separate perturbation analyses supported the predictive value of mapping and historical features, although their effect sizes were not directly comparable because they were evaluated using different model configurations. Prediction errors remained larger at the extremes of the activity distribution. Performance also became less stable when template identities were separated between training and evaluation. TriCasRank may therefore be useful for ranking candidates represented within the EasyDesign-derived domain, but evaluation on an independent experimental cohort is still needed.
affiliations: University of Washington (corresponding author)

papers.title: Integrated genotyping, annotation and epigenetic characterization of transposable elements with GraffiTE
papers.abstract: Genotyping, annotating and characterizing TE variation leaped forward with long-read sequencing (LRS) and de novo assembly. LRS techniques also reveal CpG methylation, which enables measuring the impact of TEs on epigenomes and sheds light on the role of TEs as regulatory sequences. Yet, TE genotyping tools discard the valuable allele-specific epigenetic information. We introduce GraffiTE v1.1, the first Nextflow pipeline that genotypes SVs, annotates polymorphic mobile elements (MEI), and maps epigenetic data to TEs using pangenome graphs in one command. GraffiTE v1.1 is designed to map any epigenetic information that is based on LRS stencils, including Fiber-seq. We demonstrate the capabilities of GraffiTE v1.1 by analyzing genomes and methylomes obtained from 20 Quebec residents of French-Canadian descent. In these genomes, TE annotation yields 4,908 Alu, 704 LINE1, 112 SVA and 21 HERVK (HML-2) distinct polymorphic mobile elements (MEIs). We also identify 10 fixed HERVK insertions that vary between solo LTR and provirus, or in proviral copy number. We determine that these MEIs contribute 144,748 additional CpGs not present in the reference. From this, we identify 480 Alus, 67 LINE1s, 12 SVAs and 2 HERVKs in hypomethylated states. We note that Alus and SVAs are more methylated than other LINE1 and HERVK. Lastly, MEIs dating reported a mean of age 1.08 Mya (median: 640 kya) and beta regression identified a moderate demethylating effect of age on MEIs (effect: -0.069 log-odds per log10 years, P < 6.08 x 10-19). Our results show that the methylation level of a LINE1 MEI is expected to decrease from 86.4% to 80.8% in the first Mya. In conclusion, GraffiTE v1.1 genotypes SVs, annotates MEI, and characterizes their epigenetic state at the scale of populations by leveraging the full potential of LRS. While we showcase its application in human data, the pipeline can be deployed in any model for which a TE library is available.
affiliations: Children's Mercy Hospital in Kansas City (corresponding author)

papers.title: FACT frees Ubp10 from nucleosome sequestration after rapid H2B deubiquitination
papers.abstract: Chromatin-modifying enzymes must engage their substrate, act on it and release it, but which step limits their turnover is unclear. Using three-color single-molecule fluorescence, we directly visualized the yeast deubiquitinase Ubp10 removing ubiquitin from H2B on individual nucleosomes. Ubp10 cleaved the mark within seconds of binding, without detectable DNA unwrapping, yet it did not let go: ~80% of nucleosomes remained bound after 45 minutes, and unmodified nucleosomes formed similarly long-lived complexes. Ubp10 turnover is therefore limited by release rather than catalysis. The histone chaperone FACT relieved this bottleneck by accelerating Ubp10-nucleosome dissociation. In living yeast, nuclear depletion of the FACT subunit Spt16 increased the slowly diffusing, chromatin-bound fraction of nucleoplasmic Ubp10. These findings identify FACT-dependent release as a likely mechanism for recycling Ubp10 on chromatin. More broadly, a nucleosome can sequester the enzyme acting on it, making enzyme release a step at which chromatin modification can be controlled.
affiliations: Boston Children's Hospital (corresponding author)

papers.title: Microenvironmental Fingerprint of Maturing Tau Condensates from Spectral and Lifetime Phasor Analysis of a Solvatochromic Dye
papers.abstract: Solvatochromic dyes respond to changes in their local environment through variations in both spectral properties and fluorescence lifetime. These responses arise from the excited-state behavior of the probe, but the sensitivity of each response to a given environment can differ. In this work, we developed a multimodal phasor-based framework for two-photon spectral and fluorescence lifetime imaging analysis. To validate the framework, we imaged the solvatochromic dye ACDAN in water, glycerol, and ethanol. ACDAN showed clear spectral differences among the three solvents, whereas its fluorescence lifetime separated water from both organic solvents but not glycerol from ethanol, indicating that the two observables respond differently to the same environmental change. We then applied ACDAN to a well-described model system, the maturation of liquid-liquid phase-separated condensates of the microtubule-binding, neurodegeneration-related protein Tau into later-stage assemblies. Across Tau samples incubated for 1, 4, and 48 h, a progressive decrease in the ACDAN spectral phasor angle {theta} and increase in its phase-derived lifetime {tau}P suggested increasingly restricted dipolar relaxation in the probe environment. Differences among condensates were apparent by 4 h, whereas pronounced spatial heterogeneity within assemblies was observed at 48 h. Lastly, we evaluated the multimodal framework on Tau assemblies labeled with the fluorogenic probe Thioflavin T. As expected, this dye predominantly sensed its environment through its fluorescence lifetime, with comparatively limited spectral changes, whereas ACDAN reported microenvironmental changes in both coordinates. Together, this framework combines spectral and lifetime descriptors to characterize changes in the fluorescence response across Tau assembly maturation while retaining their spatial distribution.
affiliations: Hasselt University (corresponding author)

papers.title: EGF and EREG regulate early oncoprotein-mediated tissue transformation in intestinal organoids.
papers.abstract: Somatic mutations, coupled with abnormal extracellular signaling cues, promote tumor development. The abundance and affinity of EGF-family ligands for EGFR influence tissue development and play a central role in organoid culture by differentially regulating the balance between crypt proliferation and villus differentiation in mouse small intestinal organoids (mSIOs). To test how medium ligand composition affects early oncogenic transformation, we generated a Ptprg KO organoid line by CRISPR/Cas9 and two previously described organoid lines harboring synthetic bio-orthogonal expression systems for KRASG12V and {beta}-Ctn4A, activated by the membrane-diffusible ligands TMP or TMP-Cl. Measurements of crypt and villus region area showed that acute oncogenic activity did not alter organoid growth in media containing 50 ng/mL EGF; however, organoids grown without EGF consistently showed differential growth of the crypt region. Furthermore, EREG and sub-saturating EGF (0.5-5 ng/mL) treatments differentially affected crypt/villus development in each organoid line. Finally, we measured organoid morphology and found that crypt domain spatial distribution is independent of crypt area and requires EGF or EREG, highlighting the role of both proliferation and crypt organization in oncogenic tissue transformation.
affiliations: Max Planck Institute of Molecular Physiology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Targeted Deletions Uncover Previously Uncharacterised C1-fixing Cluster Genes as Essential for Autotrophy in Clostridium autoethanogenum
papers.abstract: Recycling carbon oxides from industrial off-gases and gasified organic waste using gas fermentation offers a sustainable route for biomanufacturing of fuels and chemicals. Acetogens are attractive biocatalysts here and fix CO and CO2 via the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway (WLP). However, the incomplete functional annotation of the associated C1-fixing gene cluster limits rational engineering of acetogen cell factories. Here, we investigated five highly conserved but previously uncharacterised C1-fixing cluster genes to quantify their contributions to the growth of the model-acetogen Clostridium autoethanogenum using targeted CRISPR/Cas9-mediated single-gene deletions, physiological characterisation, comparative computational structural analyses, CRISPRi, and functional genomics. Importantly, we identified acsV, lpdA, cooC, and cooC2 as essential for autotrophy but not heterotrophy, whereas deletion of gcvH reduced autotrophic growth and shifted carbon flux from acetate towards 2,3-butanediol. Amino acid supplementation experiments and computational analyses indicate that lpdA and gcvH do not primarily function in glycine or serine biosynthesis but instead fulfil specialised roles in WLP-associated C1 and redox metabolism. Furthermore, genetic and physiological analyses showed that the two CooC-family ATPases, CooC and CooC2, have non-redundant roles in growth, with only cooC2 deletion impairing heterotrophy. Acetate supplementation tests revealed that {Delta}acsV cells retained metabolic activity despite abolished autotrophy, and computational analyses suggest a likely role for acsV in ATP-dependent corrinoid activation. Surprisingly, CRISPRi-mediated repression of acsV was translationally buffered, resulting in altered carbon partitioning without impairing autotrophy. Together, our findings provide insights into the physiological importance of the C1-fixing cluster genes in acetogens and support their metabolic engineering as gas-fermenting cell factories.
affiliations: Institute of Bioengineering, University of Tartu, Tartu, Estonia (corresponding author)

papers.title: Intracellular bio-synthesizing Gold Nanoparticles using bacterial systems and their applications in photothermal therapy (A green approach)
papers.abstract: Background: Conventional cancer therapies are heavily constrained by systemic toxicity, off-target side effects, and poor deep-tissue penetration due to the highly heterogeneous tumor microenvironment (TME). Although gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) possess exceptional localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) properties ideal for photothermal therapy (PTT), their clinical translation is bottlenecked by inconsistent passive accumulation and chemical toxicity arising from conventional synthetic surfactants. Objective: This study developed a sustainable, biocompatible bio-hybrid platform utilizing the probiotic Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN) as an autonomous, tumor-homing living carrier integrated with AuNPs synthesized via an eco-friendly intracellular green chemistry approach. Methods: EcN cultures were prepared in Luria-Bertani (LB) medium and subsequently exposed to a 1 mM chloroauric acid (HAuCl4) metallic precursor. A facile, room-temperature green synthesis protocol was established by utilizing ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) as a non-toxic co-reductant to drive a seed-mediated crystallization onto intra-bacterial metallic seeds. The bio-hybrid system (EcN::AuNPs) was characterized via visual inspection, UV-Vis spectroscopy, and in vitro PTT assays under continuous-wave near-infrared (NIR) laser irradiation. Results: Visual confirmation showed an irreversible color shift from pale yellow to a deep dark-brownish hue, serving as a direct diagnostic indicator of successful Au3+ to Au0 reduction. UV-Vis spectroscopic analysis revealed a distinct, broadened surface plasmon resonance (SPR) band centered at 560nm, indicating the formation of stabilized, isotropic gold nanostructures (30-60nm) subjected to near-field electromagnetic coupling within the complex intracellular compartments (periplasm and cytoplasm). Biocompatibility assays demonstrated a significant collapse in cell viability from 10^8CFU/mL down to 10^3CFU/mL, driven by a combination of trivalent gold heavy-metal toxicity, mechanical disruption of the peptidoglycan wall from spatial confinement, and severe metabolic/oxidative stress. Nevertheless, the remaining surviving population maintained required active chemotactic capabilities, while the lysed bacterial matrix provided a natural protein capping layer that prevented nanoparticle aggregation. Under 5 minutes of continuous NIR laser irradiation, the EcN::AuNPs platform exhibited exceptional concentration-dependent hyperthermia kinetics, triggering a drastic thermal escalation from 20 C to an absolute peak of 75.4 C, vastly outperforming all baseline control groups (pure EcN, bare HAuCl4, and standalone ascorbic acid). Conclusion: The engineered EcN::AuNPs bio-hybrid platform represents a highly efficient and biosafe "bacteriobot" paradigm. By shifting the SPR footprint and leveraging the native bacterial cell envelope for colloidal stability, this system achieves an optimal equilibrium between active biological tumor targeting and rapid, localized photothermal ablation, offering a promising alternative for targeted oncological interventions.
