papers.title: Mucin promotes pneumococcal colonization via autolysis suppression and tryptophan-mediated immune modulation
papers.abstract: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a leading human respiratory pathogen, yet its success depends not on disease but on its ability to persist as an asymptomatic colonizer of the nasopharynx. The nasopharyngeal mucosa is lined with mucus, whose heavily O-glycosylated mucin proteins are the most abundant macromolecules in the pneumococcal natural niche. While mucus is canonically viewed as a host defense barrier, we found that mucin actively reprograms pneumococcal physiology to promote colonization through two distinct mechanisms. First, mucin suppresses pneumococcal autolysis by specifically inhibiting the enzymatic activity of the major autolysin LytA, prolonging bacterial survival and restricting release of the cholesterol-dependent cytotoxin pneumolysin, thereby reducing host cell damage. Second, mucin induces de novo biosynthesis and extracellular release of tryptophan, an essential amino acid that humans cannot synthesize and that serves as a substrate for host immunomodulatory pathways. Tryptophan biosynthesis was critical for pneumococcal survival against macrophage killing, and its disruption abolished both colonization and invasive disease. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that tryptophan biosynthesis enables the pneumococcus to survive a bactericidal macrophage state while preventing macrophage transition to proliferative tissue repair. Together, these findings reveal that mucin is not merely a barrier but an active signal that reprograms the pneumococcus toward a persistent, host-tolerant state, identifying a distinctive repertoire of colonization mechanisms that allow a virulent respiratory pathogen to sustain long-term asymptomatic carriage in its human reservoir.
affiliations: St Jude Children's Research Hospital (corresponding author)

papers.title: SeekNSee: A Rule-Based Framework for Prioritizing Proteotypic Peptides
papers.abstract: Selecting peptides candidates for target proteomics requires integrating a multicriteria problem, particularly when users lack prior experimental data, programming expertise, or stable access to external repositories. We development SeekNSee, a locally executed R/Shiny application designed to improve the reproducibility and auditability of peptide-candidate screening through enzyme-aware in silico digestion, configurable and traceable rule-level decision tracking. Starting from a user provided reference proteome and target sequences, SeekNSee generates peptides-candidates using nine digestion configurations and evaluates them with 12 rules configured as ignore, apply, or block. Numerical score and retained/blocking status are stored independently, and every candidate-rule outcome is preserved in a rule-level trace. Computational validation confirmed the specified behavior in controlled cases through 198 passing automated assertions, complemented by successful operational and processing tests on Windows and Ubuntu. Proteome-wide application covered all 20,416 reviewed human proteins, generating 733,864 peptide-candidate and 581,026 unique peptides sequences while preserving data integrity, decision traceability, and candidate-specific context. DIA, DDA, and deep-fractionated proteomics benchmarking showed strong associations between SeekNSee scores categories, peptide observation, and multiple analytical measurements. Together, these results support that SeekNSee provides a transparent and traceable screening layer for generating peptide-candidates for subsequent assay and experimental validation.
affiliations: Brazilian Center of Research in Energy and Materials (corresponding author)

papers.title: Rapid generation of marsupial induced pluripotent stem cells suitable for use in next-generation conservation
papers.abstract: Marsupials account for a disproportionate share of recent and impending mammalian extinctions, that has prompted investment in the development of "next generation" conservation biotechnologies. These include the generation of genetically selected/modified individuals for improved population fitness. Given the inherent limitations of working with threatened species, a flexible vehicle to develop these technologies is through the generation and editing of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). However, it is deemed necessary to derive transgene-free iPSCs for conservation target species, which can be highly time consuming and expensive. This study describes the generation of iPSCs from the marsupial fat-tailed dunnart (diPSCs) that serves as a model species for next generation conservation initiatives. These diPSCs exhibit features of totipotency when cells are maintained with exogenous reprogramming factors for long periods, until differentiation potential is required. Neonatal dunnart fibroblasts were reprogrammed using doxycycline-inducible Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, Lin28 and Myc, and the resulting iPSC lines were characterised at the transcriptomic, epigenetic and functional level (trilineage differentiation, embryoid body formation and mouse blastocyst injection assays). Dunnart iPSCs exhibited robust transcriptional and epigenetic activation of core pluripotency factors (POU5F1, POU5F3, SALL4) as well as factors associated with the naive and primed states of eutherian pluripotency (TBX3, KLF2, TFCP2L1, SOX11, DNMT3A). Dunnart iPSCs readily differentiated in trilineage and embryoid body formation assays, where they expressed markers of all three germ lineages. When injected into 8-cell mouse blastocysts, dunnart iPSCs integrated into both the inner cell mass and trophoblast, reflecting a capacity to contribute to embryonic and extra embryonic lineages during early development. Further, we show that diPSCs can maintain their potential in the presence of exogenous pluripotency factors, until required for differentiation. This robust iPSC generation and maintenance approach is a valuable avenue for the rapid application of next-generation conservation technologies in threatened species.

papers.title: Dynamic regulation of single-cell contractile heterogeneity in the human trabecular meshwork
papers.abstract: Altered trabecular meshwork (TM) mechanics contribute to increased aqueous humor outflow resistance and elevated intraocular pressure in glaucoma, yet how contractility is regulated across individual TM cells remains poorly understood. Using a high-throughput single-cell contractility assay, we quantified time-resolved contractile behavior in primary human TM cells under defined extracellular matrix (ECM) compositions, substrate stiffnesses, and pharmacologic perturbations, and related functional mechanical behavior to intracellular protein abundance. Single-cell analyses revealed that TM contractility is not a uniform population property but a context-dependent contractile state shaped by both extracellular and intracellular regulation. ECM composition established distinct contractile programs, with collagen IV promoting rapid convergence toward a highly contractile state, collagen I supporting a slower but similar response, and fibronectin maintaining a persistently heterogeneous low-contractility state. In contrast, the intracellular perturbation dexamethasone (DEX) did not uniformly increase contractility but selectively prolonged contractile activity within the most mechanically active cells, thereby sustaining highly contractile states. This response was progressively constrained as ECM stiffness increased and was absent on pathologically stiff substrates, demonstrating that extracellular mechanical context conditions glucocorticoid responsiveness. Conversely, ROCK inhibition overrode both basal and DEX-induced contractile programs, collapsing the heterogeneous population into a uniformly low-contractility state. Finally, intracellular protein abundance poorly predicted functional mechanical behavior, with weak pooled associations reflecting divergent donor-specific relationships rather than consistent molecular-mechanical coupling. Together, these findings show that TM contractility emerges from integrating intrinsic cellular state and the extracellular mechanical environment rather than from either alone. More broadly, they identify single-cell contractile state as a functional dimension of TM cell identity that cannot be inferred from static molecular marker abundance or population-averaged mechanical measurements.
affiliations: UCLA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Stathmin-2 regulates microtubule dynamics and axonal resilience in human motor neurons
papers.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is characterized by the selective degeneration of motor neurons, yet the mechanisms that either induce neurodegeneration or confer neuronal resilience remain poorly understood. Loss of the microtubule-associated protein Stathmin-2 (STMN2) is a downstream consequence of TDP-43 pathology present in nearly all cases of ALS and has emerged as a central feature of disease. However, the mechanisms by which STMN2 maintains homeostasis in motor neurons remain incompletely defined. Here, we investigated the role of STMN2 in regulating cytoskeletal organization and axonal function. Using TIRF microscopy, we quantified STMN2-dependent changes in microtubule growth and catastrophe at single-microtubule resolution. In human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived motor neurons, STMN2 depletion increased baseline rates of microtubule polymerization. However, STMN2 depletion impaired recovery of axonal microtubules following transient nocodazole-induced depolymerization, indicating that STMN2 is required for efficient cytoskeletal remodeling after stress. Consistent with these findings, STMN2-depleted neurons exhibited impaired microtubule recovery following acute depolymerization and reduced axonal recoil after optically induced local microtubule severing. Finally, STMN2 depletion disrupted the formation of neuromuscular junction-like contacts in human motor neuron-myocyte co-cultures, linking impaired cytoskeletal homeostasis to loss of distal neuronal connectivity. Together, these findings identify STMN2 as a key regulator of cytoskeletal resilience that coordinates microtubule remodeling, mitochondrial transport, and maintenance of neuromuscular junctions. We propose that impaired resilience of the axonal cytoskeleton represents a critical point of vulnerability in motor neurons in patients with ALS, establishing cytoskeletal resilience as a potential therapeutic target downstream of TDP-43 pathology.
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania Perelman School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: BCAS3 regulates WIPI2b via a direct interaction in the ATG16L1-binding cleft
papers.abstract: De novo formation of the phagophore membrane is a fundamental step in autophagy and relies on recruitment of the E3-like ligase complex via an interaction between ATG16L1 and phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PtdIns3P)-effector protein, WIPI2b. Although WIPI2b can directly bind membranes, how its membrane association is regulated is still not fully understood. Here, we describe BCAS3 as a novel direct interactor of WIPI2b and demonstrate that a peptide of BCAS3 binds in the ATG16L1-binding cleft of WIPI2b with low micromolar affinity. We show that BCAS3 and its partner PHAF1 induce recruitment of WIPI2b to membranes via the interaction of BCAS3 with PtdIns3P. This not only challenges the current paradigm, whereby ATG16L1 is the only confirmed binder of WIPI2b in this region, but also offers a mechanism through which WIPI2b membrane association might be regulated.
affiliations: The Francis Crick Institute (corresponding author)

papers.title: Agile manufacturing of PDMS microfluidic devices for cell culture without a clean room
papers.abstract: Microfluidic devices control fluid flow and the cellular microenvironment, and their fabrication usually relies on photolithography in a clean room. For devices with features of hundreds of micrometers to millimeters, this route is slow and costly, especially during prototyping, when the design changes after each test. Here, we describe and benchmark a workflow to fabricate polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) devices from laser-cut master molds, with equipment accessible to most biology laboratories. We cut three inexpensive materials, poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA), polystyrene and polyvinyl chloride (PVC) tape, over a grid of laser power and speed and measured each cut by scanning electron microscopy. Cut depth and width increased line-arly with the laser energy delivered per unit length, which gives a simple rule to choose the settings for each material. We then bonded the PDMS replicas to glass without a plasma cleaner, by stopping curing early, once the replica could be demolded, and completing it in contact with the glass. Without any surface treatment, these devices held up to about 400 mbar; activating the glass with a handheld corona device raised this to about 900 mbar, enough for perfusion. The master material set the surface of the device: PMMA gave smooth replicas, whereas PVC tape gave rough walls. A three-channel device molded on PMMA held two cell-laden gels in place with phase guides and supported the co-culture of cancer cells and fibroblasts under perfusion. Further analysis of flow laminarity and different mixer designs confirmed the robustness of this method. This workflow takes a digital design to a working de-vice within a day and lets biology laboratories adapt microfluidic devices to their experiments without the need of a clean room.
affiliations: EPFL (corresponding author)

papers.title: BioMeme: biological response memory for virtual cells
papers.abstract: Virtual cells predict responses to unmeasured perturbations, but neural models absorb measurements into weights, require retraining and cannot cite supporting experiments. Here we introduce biological response memory, replacing a learned state-to-response layer with a memory of measured experiments. BioMeme predicts next-dose responses in a new cell type from measured lower-dose states, recalling similarly responding compounds in that cell and the same compound in a reference cell line. Each prediction is an exact weighted sum of named measurements, and memory updates with one linear solve. In all nine preregistered comparisons across three screens, memory predicted response direction better than the learners it replaced. In U2OS, BioMeme outperformed input-matched ridge, adapted chemCPA and a neural layer in memory's place, and matched a full-panel network reading reference responses directly (error within 3.4%). Transfer was compound-specific, lowering error by 21.2% against at most 1.8% for wrong compounds, and replicated in reserved MCF7 data. With 20 references, fitting took seconds on one CPU thread, at least 420 times faster than neural tuning and fitting. Adding its prediction to one measured well cut that well's error by 27-31%. Biological response memory establishes a design principle for virtual cells any laboratory can update, inspect and run.
affiliations: School of Electronics and Computer Science, University of Southampton, Southampton, SO17 1BJ, UK (corresponding author)

papers.title: Dietary fibre combinations modulate gut microbiome composition and metabolic responses in zebrafish, with lasting effects on intestinal barrier gene expression
papers.abstract: Food sources provide a complex mixture of dietary fibres, not a single type. Consuming a diverse range of these dietary fibre-containing foods is associated with health benefits. However, how the effects of combining dietary fibres translate across different biological levels remains poorly characterised. This study uses an integrated microbiome-metabolome analytical approach that combines 16S rRNA gene sequencing with metabolomic profiling of the intestine, brain and liver. Specifically, we examined the combined effects of apple pectin (AP) and cellulose (C) within the same diet, compared with their isolated effects, in adult female and male zebrafish (Danio rerio). Notably, the combined apple pectin and cellulose diet (APC) produced a microbiome composition that could not be predicted by simply adding the changes observed with each dietary fibre individually, indicating a significant non-additive interaction between the two dietary components, specifically a less-than-additive response in gut microbiome composition. The resulting community composition under the combined diet also more closely resembled that induced by apple pectin. We found that predicted microbial functional capabilities did not translate directly into quantified intestinal and brain short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) concentrations, nor did intestinal SCFA levels directly mirror those observed in the brain. Moreover, we used targeted qPCR gene expression analysis to assess responses to a subsequent saponin challenge after dietary fibre cessation, revealing a potentially protective effect on the intestinal barrier. Collectively, we show that dietary fibres within the same diet interact to shape the gut microbiome and do not act in isolation, leading to non-linear health ramifications for the host that may persist even after active consumption ends.
affiliations: School of Biological Sciences, University of East Anglia, Norwich Research Park, NR4 7TJ, Norwich, UK (corresponding author)

papers.title: Mapping the reactive cysteine landscape of the NOD-like receptor pyrin domain-containing 3 protein
papers.abstract: NOD-like receptor pyring-containing protein 3 (NLRP3) is a cytosolic pattern recognition receptor that drives assembly of an oligomeric inflammasome complex to stimulate pro-inflammatory cytokine production and pyroptotic cell death. Extensive research has shown that NLRP3 activation is dependent on intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS). Despite this, the precise targets of ROS in this process remain undefined. In this study, a combination of chemoproteomics, in vitro biochemical assays and molecular dynamics simulations were used to characterize reactive Cys and how they may impact NLRP3 conformation and activity status. Affinity-captured NLRP3 was subjected to reverse-thiol trapping to reveal a pool of reactive Cys residues that were identified in subsequent chemoproteomic analyses. C150, C196, and C884 were consistently detected with both in vitro and in cellulo experiments. Several NLRP3 mutants were generated; C150A and C196A (NACHT domain) as well as C933A and C941A (LRR domain) reduced IL-1b output in a reconstituted inflammasome assay. Molecular simulation of Cys sulfenylation in the LRR suggests structural alterations that reposition the trLRR loop to destabilize the inactive NLRP3 structure. Structural modelling provided insights for how Cys oxidation of the LRR may impact on NLRP3 structure. Collectively, the results establish a mechanistic understanding for how ROS may promote NLRP3 inflammasome activation.
affiliations: University of Calgary (corresponding author)

papers.title: Decoupling Quantification and Identification for Label-Free Top-Down Proteomics Improves Proteome Coverage
papers.abstract: Quantifying proteoforms is essential for understanding biological processes. The most widely used quantification approach in top-down proteomics (TDP) is label-free quantification (LFQ), where quantification and identification compete for acquisition time. We identified missing values, insufficient fragmentation, and undersampling of low-abundance proteoforms as major factors limiting conventional TDP-LFQ workflows. Our proposed workflow decouples quantification and identification through MS1-only quantification followed by targeted data-dependent MS2 identification. The MS1-only acquisition more than doubled the number of mass features quantified reliably and improved quantification precision. Focusing targeted MS2 acquisition on significantly differentially abundant features enables optimization of MS2 parameters and increases identification coverage by 50%. The workflow was validated across different chromatographic conditions, MS acquisition setups, and sample preparation strategies. In Escherichia coli grown on glucose or acetate, the increased depth enabled by this workflow revealed biological insights inaccessible to a previously published bottom-up proteomics dataset. Overall, decoupling quantification and identification improves quantitative depth and proteoform coverage in TDP-LFQ and provides a flexible strategy for high-sensitivity and high-throughput proteoform quantification.
affiliations: Christian-Albrechts-Universität zu Kiel (corresponding author)

papers.title: Generative design of de novo AAV vectors with unique serological profiles
papers.abstract: More than 5000 monogenic diseases are potentially curable by replacing a single defective gene with one that functions normally. Currently, the only clinically approved vector able to effectively deliver a therapeutic gene to a target tissue is Adeno-Associated Viruses (AAVs). However, despite decades of work, only a handful of gene replacement therapies have been approved, and many patients remain ineligible for even those. A major barrier to broad adoption of AAV therapies is pre-existing immunity to AAVs, mediated by neutralizing antibodies (nAbs). It is potentially possible to change exposed capsid surfaces in AAV capsids to avoid nAb recognition. However, traditional techniques such as rational design and directed evolution only allow modest changes. AAV function becomes compromised long before full nAb avoidance is achieved. Recent advances in protein design by generative modelling provide a new way to overcome this problem by learning AAV design constraints from natural sequences. We built a variational autoencoder that could learn these sequence constraints and generate functional AAV capsid proteins de novo. More than 255 designs were synthesized and tested in vitro in two design sets, with one set dedicated to exploring uncertain regions of the sequence space. Between the two campaigns, seven designs transduced human cells with >50% efficiency, of which four avoided nAb neutralization (NT50 < 1:50) in all human sera that were reactive to AAV. In one of these designs, sequence identity to the nearest natural AAV sequence was 18% divergent. Given the radical sequence diversity and its unique serological profile, this new capsid design would represent the first ever AAV serotype designed de novo.
affiliations: University of Toronto (corresponding author)

papers.title: ERV-derived dsRNAs induce stress granules that drive neural crest fate to initiate melanoma
papers.abstract: Melanoma arises when melanocytes are oncogenically reprogrammed into neural crest-like cells, but what initiates this switch is unknown. Here we show that endogenous retrovirus (ERV)-derived double stranded RNAs (dsRNAs) induce stress granules (SGs) that drive this fate change. In zebrafish, melanoma progresses through a stage-specific ERV switch: zferv marks precursor cells before crestin activates in tumor cells. Both elements generate dsRNA that triggers eif2ak2-dependent SGs within precursor lesions and through transformation. SGs are tumorigenic as G3BP1 overexpression accelerates melanoma onset, whereas mosaic, melanocyte-specific g3bp1/2 knockout delays it. Small molecule-mediated inhibition of G3BP1/2 eliminates precursor lesions and reduces tumor burden. Similarly, blocking dsRNA sensing prevents SG formation and lowers melanoma incidence. Human nevi and melanomas show analogous, stage-specific ERV programs and SG assembly. In human melanoma cells, SGs sequester and translationally repress SOX10-regulating mRNAs, including the tumor suppressor KMT2D. Mosaic knockout of kmt2d in vivo enhances SOX10-driven neural crest reactivation. Thus, an ERV-SG axis establishes an oncogenic translatome that enables melanoma fate, with diagnostic and therapeutic potential.
affiliations: Boston Children's Hospital (corresponding author)

papers.title: DIALECT: DNA-Programmable Synthetic Cells Communicate with Mammalian Cells through Synthetic Receptors
papers.abstract: Synthetic cells can regulate mammalian signalling through the controlled release of diffusible protein ligands, but coupling programmable synthetic-cell senders to orthogonal, engineered mammalian receptors remains challenging. Here we present DIALECT (DNA-Instructed Assembly of Ligands for Engineered Cellular Transduction), a platform in which proteinosome-based synthetic cells translate sequence-defined DNA inputs into coiled-coil signalling ligand outputs for engineered mammalian receptors. DNA-ligand conjugates are localized within semipermeable proteinosomes through DNA hybridization and released by toehold-mediated DNA strand displacement (TMSD). The released ligands diffuse to neighbouring mammalian cells and activate cognate CC-GEMS receptors, inducing JAK/STAT3 signalling and reporter activation, with a higher response in cognate than non-cognate receiver cells under activation conditions. We further implement distributed Boolean AND logic using two independently programmed proteinosome populations that respond to distinct DNA inputs and release complementary ligand components. Simultaneous addition of both inputs produces substantially higher reporter activity than the respective single-input conditions, consistent with extracellular assembly of an active receptor agonist. DIALECT thus establishes a modular interface linking DNA-based molecular computation in synthetic cells to orthogonal signalling pathways in mammalian cells, providing a foundation for hybrid artificial-biological communication networks.
affiliations: Eindhoven University of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Freshwater Microbiomes Shape Viral Inactivation in Continuous Cultures
papers.abstract: In freshwater environments, bacteria are known to enhance the removal and inactivation of human viruses. Rates of inactivation differ across freshwater ecosystems, though the influence of community diversity and composition on this process remain poorly understood. Here, we used dilution-to-extinction to generate 64 distinct freshwater communities from three lakes and three aquifers. After establishing freshwater communities in chemostat cultures, each community was challenged with two viruses, coxsackievirus B5 and human adenovirus 2. Both viruses were inactivated more rapidly in lake-derived than in groundwater-derived communities, and adenovirus was inactivated faster than coxsackievirus in both freshwater types. Community-level parameters (e.g., cell numbers, richness) were not significant predictors of viral inactivation. Instead, differential abundance analyses identified bacterial OTUs associated with inactivation: Acidovorax sp. were associated across sources and Brevundimonas sp., Sphingopyxis sp., and Hydrogenophaga sp. showed source-specific associations. Together, these findings provide new insights into the ecological drivers of viral stability and suggest that viral inactivation may depend more strongly on specific microbial taxa and their environmental context than on overall community diversity. Identifying these associations improves our understanding of the factors governing viral stability in freshwater environments.
affiliations: Laboratory of Environmental Virology, School of Architecture, Civil and Environmental Engineering (ENAC), Ecole Polytechnique Federale de Lausanne (EPFL), Lausa (corresponding author)

papers.title: Structural conservation of the gabapentinoid binding site in human and Caenorhabditis elegans α2δ subunits: a docking and molecular dynamics perspective
papers.abstract: Pain is a global health burden requiring effective therapeutic strategies. Gabapentin (GBP) and pregabalin (PGB), used for neuropathic pain, act primarily through alpha2delta subunits of voltage-gated calcium channels. Caenorhabditis elegans expresses UNC-36, an ortholog of mammalian alpha2delta proteins involved in calcium-channel function and nocifensive behavior. However, whether UNC-36 retains the features essential for gabapentinoid recognition remains unclear. We compared human alpha2delta-1 and UNC-36 using sequence and structural analyses, docking, one 500-ns molecular dynamics trajectory per complex, distance-based contact profiling, principal component and free-energy landscape analyses, and MM/GBSA calculations. The modeled proteins showed C-alpha correspondence within a selected 13-residue pocket core (RMSD 0.53 Angstrom), whereas the complete 14-residue mapping yielded 9.07 Angstrom. All four trajectories showed recurrent ligand-protein proximity contacts with residue-level patterns. Aromatic-residue contacts accounted for a larger fraction of contact records in human trajectories, whereas basic-residue proximity was more frequent in UNC-36 trajectories, including recurrent Arg501 and Arg503 contacts. Human alpha2delta-1/PGB showed the lowest ligand RMSD, while alpha2delta-1/GBP showed greater positional variation. In UNC-36, PGB deviated more from its initial pose than GBP. The first two principal components accounted for more conformational variance in UNC-36 complexes than in human complexes. MM/GBSA estimates, without an explicit conformational-entropy contribution, were more negative for PGB than GBP in human trajectories and for GBP than PGB in UNC-36 trajectories. These simulations suggest that selected pocket-core correspondence coexists with differences in modeled contacts, sampled motions, and estimates. They provide hypotheses for investigating gabapentinoid recognition by UNC-36 and its pharmacological relevance.
affiliations: Universite de Montreal (corresponding author)

papers.title: A nuclear targeting approach enables efficient transgenesis in the milkweed bug Oncopeltus fasciatus
papers.abstract: Insects show extreme diversity and have long intrigued biologists. Although gene editing and transgenesis should enable the use of almost any insect species for biological research, species-specific challenges remain and conditions must be optimized carefully. Here, using the milkweed bug Oncopeltus fasciatus, we first generate a useful eye- and body-color mutant strain by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing. Using this strain, we develop an efficient piggyBac-mediated transgenesis system with a nuclear targeting approach. Incorporating 1x and 3x nuclear localization signals into piggyBac mRNA substantially enhances overall transformation efficiency in O. fasciatus. Taking advantage of the mutant strain and the efficient transgenesis system, we integrated multiple expression cassettes ranging from 1.8 to 7.2 kb, including attP strains for phiC31-mediated integration and histone-labelled strains for live imaging. We further show that the Q system, a binary expression system, is functional in this species, paving the way for sophisticated genetic manipulations. Together, our results expand the genetic toolkit of O. fasciatus as a comparative model insect and provide a practical framework for developing efficient transgenesis in other non-traditional model organisms.
affiliations: Harvard University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Tandem clustering of toxin genes exceeds gene-family-size expectations in four venomous bilaterians
papers.abstract: Toxin genes of venomous animals often lie in tandem arrays, which are commonly read as a signature of venom-specific evolution. However, large gene families of any function also cluster, so how much of this architecture is specific to toxins remains unclear. In this study, we compared toxin clustering in five venomous genomes with random genes and with size-matched non-toxin families. It is anchored on a new chromosome-level genome of the centipede Scolopendra mutilans, whose venom-gland proteome (12 individuals) detected 163 of 188 curated toxins and resolved 141 to single loci. Against random genes, the odds of a toxin gene having another toxin gene within 100 kb were 14-31 times higher in four bilaterians (centipede, snake, spider and scorpion). Against size-matched non-toxin families, the odds ratio fell to about 2-6 but remained above 1 under three gene-family definitions and, under the primary definition, for windows of 25-200 kb, after matching on within-family sequence similarity and, in the snake, with published venom-gene annotations. In the sea anemone, evidence for an excess was insufficient. The excess was spread across many toxin families and was carried mainly by adjacent homologous copies. Duplication topology and expression did not distinguish toxin from control tandem families, and in a congener toxin arrays were recovered less often and copy-number comparisons were uncertain. Thus, a random-gene baseline overstates the exceptionality of toxin clustering, but toxin families keep more homologous copies in local arrays than equally sized families; whether such arrays form more often or persist longer remains open.
affiliations: Key Laboratory of Ethnic Medical Resources Research and Southeast Asian International Cooperation in Yunnan Province, School of Tea and Coffee, Pu'er University (corresponding author)

papers.title: From junk to deleterious: Natural subtelomeric repeat amplifications impact fitness and cellular phenotypes in yeast
papers.abstract: Eukaryotic genomes exhibit astounding levels of complexity. Much of this complexity resides in repetitive DNA thought to evolve neutrally, meaning that its impact on fitness is so small that natural selection cannot act efficiently to favor or purge it. Yet, repetitive DNA greatly facilitates the generation of structural variants (SVs), which fuel evolution with both adaptive and deleterious variation. How SVs involving initially neutral repetitive DNA can bring new evolutionarily meaningful impacts is not well understood. This is in part because finding and interpreting molecular signatures of these transitions using comparative genomics over long evolutionary timescales is challenging. Here, we document one such transition over a microevolutionary timescale using budding yeast population genomics. We characterize multiple massive amplifications of the Y' element, a highly polymorphic and dispensable subtelomeric tandem repeat. We uncover extreme structural diversity in Y' tandem amplifications among near-isogenic strains, and show that these amplifications bring a significant fitness cost. We further link Y' amplifications with transcriptome rewiring, heightened DNA replication stress sensitivity and DNA damage response activation. Together, our results support a model by which massive subtelomeric tandem amplification pushed a repetitive DNA family outside of effective neutrality to become deleterious.
affiliations: University of Colorado Anschutz Medical School (corresponding author)

papers.title: SoluProtMut: Siamese Deep Learning for Predicting Solubility Effects of Protein Mutations with Experimental Validation
papers.abstract: Protein solubility is an attractive engineering target because it is a critical property influencing the scalability of protein production and the success of therapeutic proteins in biomedical applications. However, predicting in silico solubility changes upon mutation is challenging due to data heterogeneity and protein bias. Here, we explore how different sources of solubility data can be used for machine learning and present SoluProtMut, a Siamese deep geometric neural network trained to predict the impact of mutations on protein solubility. Our final model was trained exclusively on deep mutational scanning data derived from recombinant protein expression assays in bacterial and yeast systems. We compare our model with five established solubility prediction methods. On an independent set of 44 proteins, the model achieves the highest informedness among the methods compared, with the largest margin for multipoint mutations (a ternary informedness of 26.5%, 8.8 percentage points above the next-best method). Our findings also reaffirm that the scarcity of solubility data continues to hamper progress in this field. To address this limitation, we experimentally quantified solubility changes for 277 single-point and multipoint mutants of haloalkane dehalogenase. Complemented by recent deep-mutational-scanning data on myoglobin, we employed both datasets for external validation. We identify protein-level generalization, rather than model capacity or training-set size, as the main limiting factor in the domain. Integrating high-throughput assays with deep learning nonetheless offers a route to improving the accuracy and scope of solubility prediction.
affiliations: RECETOX, Masaryk University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Decoding the BRCA2 reversion principles underlying PARP inhibitor resistance
papers.abstract: Reversion mutations that restore BRCA2 function represent a major mechanism of resistance to poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) in BRCA2-mutant cancers. Predicting these events could inform treatment strategies, identify patients at increased risk of acquiring PARPi resistance, and improve interpretation of secondary variants. Here, we use an isogenic cell system and CRISPR editing to define the principles governing BRCA2 reversion. We show that local sequence context shapes the spectrum of reading-frame restoration events, whereas domain architecture determines which of these events are selected as PARPi-resistant reversions. We characterize two routes of BRCA2 restoration that operate both within and across exons: DNA-level reading-frame restoration and transcript-level rescue via alternative splicing. Lastly, we identify distinct exon 11 restoration mechanisms, including large genomic deletions and recurrent splice isoforms that can bypass the loss of the canonical splice donor. These findings provide a basis for defining a predictive code for BRCA2 reversions that confer PARPi resistance.

papers.title: Choline kinase A is required for alkylating agent resistance via lipid droplet formation
papers.abstract: Tolerance of DNA damage promotes cellular fitness, particularly in cancer cells under chemotherapeutic pressure. However, the biology and regulation of DNA damage responses remain incompletely understood. Using an unbiased genetic screen, we found that choline kinase A (CHKA) is required for alkylating resistance in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL). CHKA is best-known as a cytoplasmic enzyme that catalyzes the first step in phosphatidylcholine biosynthesis, but alkylating agent resistance was mediated by a nuclear function of CHKA. We found that CHKA positively regulates transcription of the DNA repair factor RAD51 via formation of lipid droplets. Restoring lipid droplet formation or RAD51 expression was sufficient to confer alkylating agent resistance despite CHKA inactivation. Our findings link lipid droplet formation to transcriptional control of the DNA damage response, providing a mechanism through which cellular lipid metabolism can control the maintenance of genome integrity.

papers.title: An atlas of human histological diversity
papers.abstract: Descriptions of tissues by histopathologists rest on verbal statements limited by quantitative inaccuracies and personal cognitive biases. Here we propose an unsupervised computational framework that transposes to histology the concepts and methods of RNA-seq gene expression analysis, setting histology on an unbiased quantitative ground. Leveraging this framework and the GTEx dataset, we built an atlas surveying the histological diversity of 40 organs from 946 non-diseased individuals and documenting 11,125,747 associations between 2,560 morphemes - the histological analogs of genes in our framework - and 9 layers of patho-clinical and multi-omic molecular data, providing a rich context to interpret histology. In contrast with the ideally healthy normal specimens depicted in histology textbooks, the atlas reveals the influence of age, sex, genetics and sub-clinical pathologies on tissue structures. For example, we report that female eccrine sweat glands are surrounded by more adipocytes than their male counterparts, and that distinct calcification-associated aorta morphemes are driven by either smoking or genetic polymorphisms. Cross-organ analyses also delineate the systemic histological impact of diabetes and other conditions and establish the power of blood gene expression to predict disease-related morphemes. The atlas is released as an interactive web resource aimed at researchers.

The transcriptional regulator IκBζ is essential for ILC2 effector functions
papers.abstract: Group 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2) are the sentinels that ensure tissue homeostasis and engage in the immune response to helminths by secreting type 2 cytokines. Here we show that IκBζ, an atypical member of the IκB family, controls basal IL-5 production by ILC2s and governs their effector program during helminth infection and asthma. Peripheral ILC2s express IκBζ at steady state, and its expression is further induced upon stimulation with IL-33 or IL-25 in an NF-κB- and STAT3/5-dependent manner. Upon activation, IκBζ refines chromatin accessibility at regulatory elements of effector cytokine loci, thereby licensing transcription. Due to reduced type 2 cytokine secretion and impaired proliferative capacity of ILC2s, mice with IκBζ-deficient ILC2s show delayed clearance of the hookworm Nippostrongylus brasiliensis and reduced papain-induced airway inflammation. Taken together, our study highlights the central role of IκBζ in orchestrating the ILC2 effector program in different tissues in health and disease. Group 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2) are important for the anti-helminth immune response. Here the authors show that the effector program of ILC2s depends on transcriptional regulation of the alarmins IL-25 and IL-33 by IκBζ, leading to efficient hookworm clearance in a mouse model.

papers.title: Evidence and measures of the digital usage divide from 40 million Windows devices
papers.abstract: Digital infrastructure is crucial for economic opportunities, social inclusion, and civic participation, but benefits remain unevenly distributed. Existing measures, such as computer ownership and broadband adoption, do not capture the depth and variety of digital use. We develop measures using Microsoft telemetry collected during operating system updates from 40 million Windows devices in U.S. households. These measures provide greater coverage and granularity than existing commercial or government surveys. Device representations at the ZIP-code level reveal substantial variation in usage, including an urban-rural divide and disparities within narrowly defined Metropolitan Statistical Areas. Income and education correlate with these differences. These effects are large and suggest that digital usage gaps extend beyond the local availability of essential IT infrastructure. The findings call for interventions that complement infrastructure access with support for technology use and skills development. The resulting indices are publicly available to support future research on digital inequality. Using usage data from 40 million Windows devices, this paper develops measures of digital engagement in the USA, revealing digital inequalities that are not captured by traditional measures of internet access alone.

papers.title: Cancer-associated fibroblasts as architects of tumor immune geography and lymphoid organization
papers.abstract: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) shape how immune cells are organized within tumors and either support or hinder the formation of immune niches associated with clinical outcomes and treatment response known as tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs). Some CAF states support immune-cell recruitment and TLS establishment, whereas others create dense, fibrotic environments that restrict immune organization. Importantly, the presence of TLSs does not by itself indicate antitumor immunity. Their function depends on surrounding CAFs, extracellular matrix, and blood and lymphatic vessels. In this Review, we argue that the TLS-CAF axis is a key determinant of antitumor immunity, highlighting a potential therapeutic opportunity for selective stromal reprogramming. Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are a heterogeneous population of stromal cells that participate in the formation of tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs). Here, the authors review the current knowledge on how CAF subsets shape the organization and function of immune cells within TLS and discuss the clinical implications of these CAF-TLS interactions.

papers.title: SimPoly: Simulation of polymers with machine learning force fields derived from first principles
papers.abstract: Polymers are a versatile class of materials with widespread industrial applications. Advanced computational tools could revolutionize their design, but the complex, multi-scale nature of polymers poses significant modeling challenges. Classical force fields often lack the accuracy and transferability that polymers demand, while quantum-chemical methods are prohibitively expensive for the large systems and long timescales involved. Here we develop a fast, scalable machine learning force field and show that, trained on quantum-chemical calculations alone, without any experimental data, it predicts measured bulk properties across a broad range of polymers. It reproduces polymer densities as accurately as, or better than, established classical force fields and captures the glass transition signature in the density-temperature curve, enabling the prediction of glass transition temperatures. To accelerate progress in this domain, we release a benchmark of experimental bulk properties for 130 polymers and an accompanying quantum-chemical dataset, laying the foundation for a fully in silico design pipeline for next-generation polymeric materials. The authors develop a machine learning force field trained only on quantum-chemical data that can reproduce measured key polymer properties such as densities and glass transition temperatures.

papers.title: Calpain-mediated TBP cleavage disturbs neuronal AMOT-YAP1 signalling
papers.abstract: The transcription factor TATA-box-binding protein (TBP) plays a crucial role in neurons, as highlighted by its involvement in spinocerebellar ataxia type 17 (SCA17), where pathological polyglutamine expansions disrupt its function. While the molecular pathomechanisms remain unclear, our previous study showed that calcium-activated calpains cleave TBP in SCA17 cell and animal models. Here, we pinpoint a major calpain cleavage site after residue T106, C-terminal to TBP’s polyglutamine tract. The resulting polyglutamine-containing N-terminal fragments mislocalise to the cytoplasm and exhibit increased aggregation. Both the N-terminal and the nuclear-localised C-terminal fragments contribute to calpain overactivation. SCA17 cell line-based multi-omics analyses revealed that TBP fragments alter pathways linked to neuronal function and neurodegeneration, identifying AMOT as a key player. Further analyses in SCA17 cell lines, patient-derived fibroblasts and induced neurons as well as in rat and zebrafish models confirmed AMOT’s pivotal role in neurons, regulated by TBP and mediated via YAP1-dependent signalling. These findings offer further insights into TBP’s neuronal function and suggest broader implications of AMOT for neurodegenerative and neurodevelopmental disorders. TBP fragments activate calpains and disrupt AMOT-YAP1 signalling, revealing a pathway involved in normal neural development and implicated in spinocerebellar ataxia type 17.

papers.title: Hydration water drives elastin’s entropic elasticity
papers.abstract: Elastin endows arteries, skin and lungs with elasticity, yet the molecular origin of its entropic recoil remains debated. Using multi-microsecond all-atom simulations of a representative elastomeric region of human tropoelastin, the monomeric precursor of elastin, we quantify protein conformational entropy, hydration-water entropy, and protein- and water-mediated interaction enthalpies during stretching. Protein conformational entropy decreases modestly overall, with heterogeneous local entropic responses governed by secondary structure and sequence context. In contrast, hydration water provides the dominant unfavorable entropic contribution because stretching recruits many water molecules from bulk into a persistently low-entropy first hydration layer. Stretching also disrupts favorable intra-protein interactions while strengthening protein–water interactions, producing opposing enthalpic contributions that largely compensate the entropic penalty. Together, these results support a hydration-coupled thermodynamic mechanism in which water is the dominant entropic contributor to elastin recoil within a strongly compensating enthalpy–entropy balance. Elastin endows biological tissues with their remarkable elasticity, yet the molecular basis of its recoil has long remained unresolved. By simulating a representative elastomeric region of monomeric tropoelastin, and quantifying both protein conformational entropy and hydrationwater entropy, the authors provide an atomistic comparison of their respective contributions to elasticity. Their analysis reveals that hydration water is the dominant entropic driver of elastin recoil, acting within a finely balanced thermodynamic framework that governs stretch-induced molecular responses.

papers.title: Two functionally distinct amyloid-β intermediates link aggregation pathways to pathology in Alzheimer’s disease
papers.abstract: Neurotoxic intermediates formed during amyloid-β (Aβ) aggregation are thought to drive Alzheimer’s disease, yet their rarity and transient nature have obscured their identity and formation pathways in the human brain. Here, we combine super-resolution microscopy and single-molecule functional imaging with kinetic modelling to classify Aβ intermediates according to their membrane-disrupting activity and connect their damaging effects to the aggregation pathways that generate them. Applying this framework to recombinant Aβ42, an Alzheimer’s knock-in mouse model and human Alzheimer’s brain tissue, we find two functionally distinct intermediate populations present across all systems. They form through separate aggregation routes and differ in their neurotoxicity, abundance and susceptibility to inhibition. Both damage neurons and glia, but only one converts into plaques. Suppressing these intermediates pharmacologically in mice reduces plaque burden, attenuates astrogliosis and improves cognition. Our findings connect model systems with human pathology and identify intermediate formation pathways as actionable therapeutic targets across protein-misfolding disorders. Authors combine super-resolution microscopy and single-molecule functional imaging with kinetic modelling to classify Aβ intermediates according to their membrane-disrupting activity and connect their damaging effects to the aggregation pathways that generate them, connecting model systems with human pathology.

papers.title: Archival and palaeoenvironmental documentation of extreme climate events reveals generational amnesia in collective memory
papers.abstract: Collective memory shapes how societies respond to extreme climate events, yet long-term evidence on how the collective memory of such events becomes perceptually biased over time is lacking. Here, we utilise four centuries (1470–1900) of climatic archives from northern China, along with tree–ring–based hydroclimate reconstructions, which are validated against instrumental observations of Wet/Dry Index (1901–2000) to fill the gap. We find that historical records reveal systematic, non-random mismatches, where severity assessments are often biased toward recent experience rather than absolute climatic anomalies. Correlations between historical and natural records increase when the natural series is re-standardised using 20–40-year sliding windows, reflecting a generational offset. A heuristic agent-based model reproduces this pattern, suggesting that generational amnesia is sufficient to explain the offsets in perception of environmental change. We argue that historical archives carry a generational imprint of perceptual bias, in which the severity of climate extremes is judged against recent lived experience rather than long-term climate variability. This has implications for bias-aware corrections for risk assessment, adaptation, and paleoclimate reconstruction. Collective memory shapes how societies respond to climate extremes, but its long-term biases are hard to observe. Here, the authors show that historical severity assessments of droughts and floods in northern China over 430 years are biased toward recent experience, consistent with an agent-based model of generational amnesia.

Repeated loss of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet’s Amundsen Sea sector during late Pleistocene interglacials
papers.abstract: Sea-level reconstructions and numerical models suggest that the vulnerable West Antarctic Ice Sheet underwent major mass losses during the late Pleistocene, raising global sea level by several metres. However, direct evidence from ice-sheet proximal records for such retreat has remained inconclusive. Here we investigate variations in clay mineral assemblages and past ocean temperatures archived in West Antarctic continental margin sediments during the last 800,000 years. Our results demonstrate that the supply of glacigenic detritus sourced from the main outlet glaciers in the Amundsen Sea sector of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet ceased almost entirely during all previous warm periods, documenting the loss of their drainage basins. Concomitant seawater warming, revealed by a microfossil proxy, is attributed to intensified deep-water advection towards Antarctica’s Pacific margin, which is corroborated by the clay mineralogical evidence. Our findings show that ocean forcing can drive major deglaciation of West Antarctica and related global sea-level rise. The mineralogical composition of the fine-grained fraction of Antarctic continental margin sediments reveals major retreat of glaciers draining the Amundsen Sea sector of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet during each warm period of the last 800,000 years.

papers.title: Single-cell machine learning uncovers genetically anchored, cell-type specific programs of Alzheimer’s disease
papers.abstract: Univariate differential expression analysis dominates single-cell transcriptomic studies of Alzheimer’s disease, yet marginal testing alone cannot resolve multivariate disease-associated structure or distinguish clinical from neuropathological signatures. Here we introduce TriSCOPE, a framework integrating multivariate predictive modeling, donor-aware differential expression, and pseudotime inference, applied to six Alzheimer’s disease snRNA-seq datasets comprising ~4.2 million nuclei from 627 donors. Across six major brain cell types and 41 subclusters, we identify cell-type-specific predictively expressed genes that are largely non-overlapping with differentially expressed genes, revealing disease-relevant signals invisible to univariate approaches. Conditional GWAS–eQTL colocalization anchors a subset of these predictively expressed genes to inherited Alzheimer’s disease risk loci, including 27 genetically supported gene–cell type pairs (among them ARL17B, JAZF1) with no significant differential expression. Integration across all three analytical branches nominates high-confidence convergent programs including astrocytic stress markers (such as GFAP, MT2A), neuronal signaling genes (like RASGEF1B, LINGO1, NRG1), and microglial and oligodendrocyte regulators (including SYTL3, SPP1, APOD). Comparison of clinical and neuropathological models reveals cell-type-specific divergence between cognitive and pathological Alzheimer’s disease signatures. Key predictively expressed genes including ARL17B, LINGO1, and APOE replicate across independent cohorts, with cross-cohort generalizability confirmed across all three analytical branches of TriSCOPE. Univariate analyses alone cannot resolve multivariate disease-associated structure. Here, the authors develop TriSCOPE, a machine learning approach that identifies gene programs specific to individual brain cell types in Alzheimer’s disease.

papers.title: Correlative nanoscale chemical imaging reveals delocalized Faradaic processes at isolated MXene flakes
papers.abstract: Two-dimensional transition metal carbides and nitrides (MXenes) combine an electrochemically active surface with high conductivity and hydrophilicity, which makes them a unique class of materials for electrochemical applications. While the pseudocapacitive behaviour of MXenes in acidic environments is relatively well understood on macroscale electrodes, intrinsic electrochemical phenomena occurring on single MXene flakes remain unclear. Here, we use scanning X-ray microscopy (SXM) to correlate the electronic structure of Ti3C2Tx MXene flakes at the nanoscale with local electrochemical reactions triggered at the sub-flake level by scanning electrochemical cell microscopy (SECCM). For several proton-coupled electron transfer reactions, including electrochemical oxidation and the hydrogen evolution reaction, we demonstrate a delocalization of the reactions well beyond the MXene flake area in contact with the droplet cell. Furthermore, we show evidence of hydrogen storage on monolayer MXene flakes. This work highlights fundamental insights into the role of interfacial water on surface redox reactions. The authors employ a nanoscale chemical imaging technique to image local electrochemical reactions triggered on single MXene flakes. For several electrochemical reactions, a delocalization of the reactions well beyond the MXene flake area in contact with the droplet cell is demonstrated.

papers.title: LLM ensemble PREVIA predicts future PTSD risk from emergency department trauma narratives with expert-level accuracy
papers.abstract: Post-traumatic stress disorder affects numerous trauma survivors following emergency department discharge, making this encounter vital for early risk stratification. Yet emergency clinicians face severe time constraints, making existing screening tools impractical. We introduce PREVIA, a clinically-informed large language model ensemble, that predicts post-traumatic stress disorder risk from unstructured patient trauma narratives, collected in response to a routine-care question asked in the emergency department, by extracting early post-traumatic stress symptoms, peri-traumatic symptoms, risk, and protective factors. Within an ongoing longitudinal study, we included N = 145 patients across two New York City level-1 trauma centers within 24 hours of trauma and assessed post-traumatic stress disorder 1-month post-trauma. In this work, PREVIA accurately forecasts post-traumatic stress disorder (AUROC = 78.49% ± 5.75%, sensitivity=95.4% ± 3.99%, precision=46.76% ± 8.66%), performs comparably to an emergency clinician specialized in post-traumatic stress disorder on 30 randomly selected patients (PREVIA: AUROC = 84.39%, sensitivity=100.00%, precision=50.00%; clinician: AUROC = 83.86%, sensitivity=88.89%, precision=50.00%), and generates interpretable explanations without additional clinical burden. These initial findings support PREVIA’s potential as a scalable emergency department screener for timely, targeted interventions, and warrant validation in larger, independent cohorts. PTSD screening is rarely feasible in busy emergency departments. Here, the authors show that a scalable AI ensemble can predict 1-month PTSD risk from a single routine-care question, a first step toward low-burden implementation at point of care.

papers.title: Crystal records of erupted vs. trapped magma in volcanic arcs
papers.abstract: Arc andesites are hybrids generated by mixing of mafic and silicic magmas. The silicic endmember can contribute to crustal growth or trigger explosive eruptions, yet remains difficult to constrain due to limited representation in the erupted record. Here, we show that textural, elemental and isotopic records preserved in plagioclase can distinguish between trapped and erupted crystal mush, thus constraining conditions of magma storage vs. eruption in arc systems. We define the plagioclase eruptibility field, a narrow and recurrent anorthite range (An~61) that represents erupted melt across Central Andes volcanoes upon mafic recharge. The recycled plagioclase cargo is dominantly An~43, recording prolonged crystallisation and assimilation within silicic mushes. This pattern repeats in continental and composite arcs globally, indicating strong eruptive filtering of arc magmas and widespread occurrence of dormant felsic and mafic mushes that, in most cases, contribute to crustal growth; yet exceptionally, felsic mushes can rapidly remobilise to generate super-eruptions. Arc andesites are hybrids generated by mixing of mafic and silicic magmas. Here, the authors show that textural, elemental and isotopic records preserved in plagioclase can distinguish between trapped and erupted crystal mush, thus constraining conditions of magma storage vs. eruption in arc systems.

papers.title: Nanometer-resolution imaging of living bacteria across species and cellular orientations
papers.abstract: The bacterial cell envelope is a complex superstructure that is an important target and a major barrier for antibiotics. To date, highest-resolution images of native cell envelopes have been obtained by atomic force microscopy (AFM), but its use is limited by challenges in bacterial immobilization. We establish glutaraldehyde-functionalized glass surfaces for reversible covalent attachment, enabling robust adhesion across species and cellular orientations while preserving cell viability and growth. This approach allowed imaging of Escherichia coli both expressing O-antigen and fully lacking lipopolysaccharide (LPS) oligosaccharides, revealing that AFM contrast depends on LPS complexity and confirming previously observed outer membrane domains as LPS-enriched islands. It also enabled imaging of Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii outer membranes, which lack the characteristic protein trimers observed in model E. coli. Finally, we discovered growth-phase dependent alterations in E. coli pole morphology, where trimer networks typical of exponential-phase cells were unresolved and morphological defects appeared. The use of atomic force microscopy for high-resolution imaging of the surface of live bacterial cells is limited by challenges in cell immobilization. Here, Scheeder et al. present an improved immobilization method that allows imaging of diverse bacteria, including imaging of bacterial cell poles.

Electrode-associated growth reveals structure of OmcZ-type cytochrome nanowires in anaerobic methanotrophic archaea
papers.abstract: Anaerobic methanotrophic (ANME) archaea are key regulators of methane emissions in anoxic environments, yet their physiology remains poorly understood due to the lack of axenic cultures. Here, we show that cultivation on poised electrodes yields near-axenic cultures (95.8% relative abundance) of a freshwater ANME, for which we propose the name ‘Candidatus Methanoperedens vercellensis’. We identified key physiological properties of ‘Ca. M. vercellensis’: doubling times of 4.6 days at 30 °C, menaquinone as respiratory electron carrier, the inability to oxidize ethane, and preferential reduction of iron oxides over nitrate after cultivation on electrodes. A 3.3 Å cryo-electron microscopy structure of filaments displayed on the archaeal surface revealed polymerized OmcZ-type cytochrome nanowires, which are homologous to OmcZ nanowires essential for long-range (>10 μm) extracellular electron transfer (EET) in Geobacter sulfurreducens. The archaeal OmcZ-type nanowires include dense, collinear stacking of protected hemesakin to bacterial OmcZ nanowires, but with post-translational modification, thus yielding morphology distinct from bacterial OmcZ nanowires. Notably, in contrast to bacterial OmcZ, archaeal OmcZ-type nanowires do not form interconnected networks, and hemes are less solvent-exposed, which can protect them from the environment. Surprisingly, these archaea assemble OmcZ into nanowires even in the apparent absence of prolyl isomerase involved in folding bacterial OmcZ. This work establishes a model system for molecular understanding of nanowire-mediated EET in archaea. Anaerobic methanotrophic archaea are key regulators of methane emissions in anoxic environments. Here, the authors report near-axenic cultivation of these microorganisms on electrodes, describing key physiological traits and presence of OmcZ-type cytochrome nanowires likely involved in extracellular electron transfer.

papers.title: Absolute quantification and profiling of cellular tRNAs by nanopore sequencing and a deep learning classifier
papers.abstract: Transfer RNAs (tRNAs) link mRNA codons to amino acids during translation. Their abundance and modification states are dynamically regulated and influence translation efficiency, mRNA stability, and proteostasis. Accurate profiling of tRNAs is essential, but deep sequencing suffers from modification-induced biases during cDNA synthesis, while nanopore direct RNA sequencing (DRS) still faces challenges in accurate tRNA profiling. Here, we develop an end-to-end deep learning model, termed nano tRNA classifier, that directly uses nanopore-DRS ionic current signals to classify tRNAs without basecalling. The model achieves 98.2% classification accuracy with high read retention across all Escherichia coli tRNA species. Using an equimolar mixture of native tRNAs as a ground-truth reference, we correct read-count bias, enabling absolute quantification and profiling under diverse culture conditions. We further develop binary classifiers that detect specific tRNA modifications at the single-molecule level with high accuracy. This nanopore-based platform integrates accurate tRNA classification, absolute quantification, and single-molecule modification detection. Here the authors develop a nanopore-based method using deep learning to classify cellular tRNAs, quantify their absolute abundance, and detect chemical modifications at the single molecule level.

papers.abstract: A barrier to precision medicine for ulcerative colitis (UC) is the inability to predict and mechanistically explain treatment responses. Using patient-reported outcomes (PROs) from a phase 3b comparative trial of 768 participants, we identified four distinct patient response-trajectory groups for vedolizumab (anti-integrin) and adalimumab (antitumor necrosis factor). Validation in a second phase 3 trial of 576 participants linked PRO-defined vedolizumab trajectories to long-term disease complications. Bulk, single cell, and spatial transcriptomics and proteomics identified vascular inflammation as associated with vedolizumab nonresponse through interactions between SPP1+ macrophages and endothelial cells. In two separate real-world cohorts of 4,981 and 3,854 patients with UC, concomitant use of renin–angiotensin system inhibitors (modulators of vascular inflammation) was associated with reduced long-term complications for vedolizumab but not anticytokine therapies. These findings define a response-trajectory-based taxonomy that requires prospective validation for clinical utility and applications for selecting vedolizumab combination therapy in UC. An analysis of patient-reported trajectories of response to vedolizumab in ulcerative colitis defines disease endotypes and identifies vascular inflammation as a potential resistance mechanism.

Deciphering the gene-centric spatial dynamics across tissue and time with GeneSPOT
papers.abstract: Spatial omics technologies provide unprecedented opportunities to investigate how molecular programs are organized within tissues. However, existing analytical frameworks primarily focus on identifying cellular states and characterizing differentially expressed molecular features across these states. The relational spatial organization of molecular features and its dynamics across biological contexts therefore remain largely unexplored. Here we present Gene SPatial Optimal Transport (GeneSPOT), a gene-centric computational framework for characterizing the spatial relationships among genes and quantifying their reorganization across biological conditions. Although gene-centric in design, GeneSPOT generalizes to other molecular features. Across diverse applications, GeneSPOT resolved tissue structures, integrated paired and unpaired spatial multi-omics data, unveiled the spatial convergence of gene programs during embryonic development and identified aging-associated spatial reorganization among genes whose expression did not change significantly with age. GeneSPOT thus complements conventional cell-centric analysis, providing a framework for deciphering how spatial relationships among molecular features are reorganized across biological conditions and over time. GeneSPOT is a framework that enables gene-centric exploration of spatial transcriptomic data.

Mechanosensitive YAP–RUNX1 signaling drives TH1 cell dysfunction and tumor immunosuppression
papers.abstract: Tissue stiffening is a predominant malignant physical alteration in cancer progression, yet its effect on specific immune subsets within the tumor microenvironment is not well defined. Here we show that elevated tissue stiffness subverts tumor-infiltrating type 1 helper T (TH1) cells to drive immunosuppression in pancreatic cancer. Mechanistically, stiffness triggers integrin-mediated mechanotransduction to activate YAP, which translocates to the nucleus and cooperates with RUNX1 to transcriptionally upregulate a set of dysfunction-associated genes. These reprogrammed TH1 cells acquire a distinct dysfunction-associated secretory phenotype, which in turn drives M2-like polarization of macrophages and amplifies local immunosuppression. Notably, inhibiting YAP expression or disrupting YAP–RUNX1 interaction reverses the dysfunctional state of TH1 cells and restores antitumor immunity. These findings delineate a mechano–immunological mechanism by which tumor stiffness subverts TH1 cell functions, indicating a possible therapeutic avenue to alleviate immunosuppression and potentiate immunotherapy efficacy in stiff tumors. Solid tumor stiffness can limit the ability of immune cells to enter and kill tumor cells. Here the authors show that this stiffness activates YAP signaling in type 1 helper T cells, making them dysfunctional and thereby leading to a more immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment.

papers.title: A multi-tissue atlas of genetic regulatory effects in sheep
papers.abstract: Characterizing how genetic variants influence genome function and complex traits in livestock is essential for the development of sustainable precision agriculture and comparative genomics. Here, as part of the Farm Animal Genotype-Tissue Expression (FarmGTEx) project, we present the pilot phase of the SheepGTEx resource by analyzing 6,761 RNA sequencing samples from 51 primary tissues in a multibreed sheep cohort. We identify millions of regulatory variants associated with 7 types of molecular phenotypes and fine-map 322,468 primary and 114,017 nonprimary effects, revealing extensive regulatory allelic heterogeneity. We systematically characterize the pleiotropic effects of these variants on molecular phenotypes; assess their context-specific regulation across tissues, breeds, sexes and developmental stages; and explore their evolutionary constraints across mammals. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of SheepGTEx by identifying regulatory mechanisms underpinning 34 complex traits, population divergence between European and Asian breeds and adaptive evolution in sheep over the past 10 millennia. This study presents SheepGTEx, a comprehensive multi-tissue atlas of genetic regulatory variants derived from 6,761 samples across 51 tissues, providing insights into complex traits, population selection and domestication history in sheep.

papers.title: Full-length RNA sequencing profiles intracellular and extracellular RNAs in euploid and aneuploid human embryos
papers.abstract: Cell-free RNA (cfRNA) in human embryo culture medium may provide molecular information about preimplantation development, but its origin and regulation remain unclear. Here we show, using full-length total RNA sequencing of individual human blastocysts and matched spent media, that extracellular cfRNA profiles differ according to embryonic chromosomal status. Euploid embryos showed relatively stable intracellular and extracellular transcriptomic programmes, whereas aneuploid embryos displayed disrupted transcriptional states with stress-associated signatures, including nonsense-mediated decay and TP53-mediated apoptosis. Analyses of stable non-differentially expressed genes and long non-coding RNA–mRNA co-expression modules linked cfRNA signatures to RNA processing, RNA export, vesicle trafficking, autophagy and RNA degradation pathways. Mouse perturbation experiments further supported a connection between autophagy–lysosome–vesicle pathway activity and embryo-derived cfRNA signatures. These data establish a transcriptomic resource for studying intracellular and extracellular RNA states in human embryos and support cfRNA as a biologically informative readout of embryonic state. Sugimoto, Mariya et al. use full-length total RNA sequencing on human euploid and aneuploid blastocysts and their matched spent medium. They propose that cell-free RNA release is a process involving vesicle trafficking and autophagy.

Structure of chlorophyll synthase in complex with the LHC-like protein HliD
papers.abstract: Chlorophyll synthase (ChlG) is a transmembrane enzyme that attaches the tetraprenyl tail to chlorophyllide to produce chlorophyll a, the key pigment of oxygenic photosynthesis. In the cyanobacterium Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803, ChlG forms a complex with the light-harvesting complex (LHC)-like high-light-inducible protein (Hlip) HliD. Here, to understand the catalytic mechanism of ChlG and the role of HliD, we used cryogenic electron microscopy to determine the structure of a ChlG2HliD2 complex in substrate-free and geranylgeranyl-pyrophosphate-bound states and AlphaFold to model binding of chlorophyllide at the active site of ChlG. In combination with site-directed mutagenesis and molecular dynamics simulations, our structural data allow us to propose the mechanisms of substrate specificity and catalysis by ChlG. Our structures also reveal how a central HliD homodimer binds two ChlG monomers, as well as the arrangement of the four chlorophyll and two carotenoid pigments bound by the Hlips, and shed light on the evolution of eukaryotic LHC antennae. The molecular mechanisms underlying chlorophyll a biosynthesis, photoprotection and transfer to photosystems are unclear. Now, cryogenic electron microscopy structures of cyanobacterial chlorophyll synthase bound to the light-harvesting complex (LHC)-like high-light-inducible protein HliD, chlorophyll and carotenoid molecules shed light on these mechanisms and the evolution of eukaryotic LHCs.

Programming supramolecular polymer network topology via homochiral self-sorting
papers.abstract: While stereochemistry has a strong influence on polymer structure and assembly, its use as a design handle to regulate polymer network topology remains unexplored. Here we demonstrate that homochiral self-sorting can be harnessed to suppress primary loops in end-linked polymer networks. We synthesized linear polymers terminated with heterochiral bi-2-naphthol-based ligands that cross-link via palladium(II)-mediated Pd2L4 metal–organic cage (MOC) assembly. This design exploits a thermodynamic preference for homochiral MOCs, enforcing a bias against intramolecular cyclization. Compared with networks formed from homochiral polymers, which can form primary loops through MOC formation, networks formed from heterochiral polymers exhibit lower primary loop densities and enhanced mechanical properties. The presence of sacrificial loops at low concentrations also enables topology editing by adding functionalized free ligands with minimal impact on network integrity. This work establishes chiral self-sorting as a versatile approach to controlling polymer topology and provides a generalizable strategy for designing robust and functional polymer networks. Stereochemistry greatly influences polymer structure and assembly, yet its use in controlling polymer network topology remains underexplored. Now, homochiral self-sorting is used to suppress primary-loop formation in end-linked polymer networks, offering a strategy for controlling network topology.

papers.title: Conditional biologics in cancer immunotherapy: mechanisms, applications and clinical progress
papers.abstract: Immunotherapy has transformed cancer treatment, enabling durable responses and long-term survival in many patients. However, widespread use remains limited by refractory indications, immune-related toxicities and acquired resistance. Complications such as cytokine release syndrome, immune-related adverse events, infusion-related reactions and on-target, off-tumour toxicities have emerged as specific safety concerns. Approaches that can direct immunotherapy to the tumour microenvironment (TME), such as intratumoural administration, have only partially mitigated these risks and present additional logistical and technical barriers. Conditional biologics, in which proteins are engineered to become active in response to tumour-associated signals or in the TME, enable the uncoupling of efficacy from toxicity. By enhancing tumour accumulation, targeting activity to a particular cell type and minimizing off-target effects, conditional activation offers a potential strategy to expand the therapeutic window of cancer therapeutics. This Review provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms, applications, challenges and future directions of this approach, while assessing completed and ongoing clinical trials. Conditional biologics (CBs) — protein therapeutics engineered to selectively activate within the tumour microenvironment — have the potential to increase the potency and limit the off-target adverse effects of cancer immunotherapies. This Review describes the design principles and activation mechanisms of CBs, assesses those being investigated in the clinic, and addresses ongoing challenges and future directions for the field.
