In yeast, Gcn2 is the sole eIF2 alpha kinase that inhibits translation initiation in response to diverse stresses. We show that PB formation depends strongly on Gcn2 during amino acid starvation but only partially during oxidative stress. Constitutively active Gcn2 also induces PB formation in unstressed cells. Surprisingly, PBs are still constitutively formed in a gcn3 mutant strain that is insensitive to eIF2 alpha phosphorylation suggesting that Gcn2 also promotes PB formation independently of eIF2 alpha phosphorylation. Analysis of several putative Gcn2-substrates involved in RNA metabolism identified several proteins required for Gcn2-mediated PB formation. Among these, Smu2, which was not previously implicated in PB formation, localises to PBs and is required for stress-induced coalescence of mRNA granules into PBs. Together, our findings indicate that Gcn2 promotes PB formation via two complementary routes: eIF2 alpha phosphorylation, which generates untranslated mRNAs, and Smu2-dependent maturation of mRNA granules into PBs.
affiliations: University of Manchester (corresponding author)

papers.title: A PTN-Rich MSC Subtype Promotes Cartilage Repair in End-Stage Knee Osteoarthritis
papers.abstract: Mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) therapy for end-stage knee osteoarthritis (KOA) shows inconsistent efficacy, and whether MSCs retain cartilage repair capacity in the inflammatory joint remains unclear. Using single-cell RNA sequencing of human Kellgren-Lawrence grade (G ) and (G ) KOA joint tissues and exogenous MSCs, we found that pleiotrophin (PTN) signalling shifts from MSC-chondrocyte crosstalk to chondrocyte-dominated autocrine signalling, with PTN exhaustion and elevated cluster of differentiation 74 (CD74) in G cartilage. We therefore identified and sorted a PTN-rich CD74-low placenta-derived MSC subtype and evaluated it in a murine KOA model and in co-culture with patient-derived chondrocytes. This subtype enhanced cartilage repair, upregulated SOX9, and suppressed MMP13, CD74, IL-6, and IL-1{beta}, potentially through CD74 suppression and reduced NF-{kappa}B signaling. These findings provide a basis for functionally defined, stage-matched cell therapy tailored to the pathological microenvironment of end-stage KOA.
affiliations: Shandong First Medical University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Junction-level imaging and modeling of transient leaks in epithelia predicts a dynamic tight junction strand network
papers.abstract: Epithelial tight junctions restrict paracellular permeability, but how small solutes leak through the barrier is not fully understood, because permeability is usually measured globally. Here, we combined fast zinc-based barrier imaging (ZnUMBA) with computational modelling of the dynamic tight junction strand network to study transient leaks at single bicellular junctions in MDCK II cells. Leaks were short-lived, with a median duration of 17 s in wild-type cells, and occurred in all cell lines studied, including ZO-1 knockout, ZO-2 knockout, and ZO-1-overexpressing cells. In ZO-2 knockout and ZO-1-overexpressing cells, leaks lasted longer without changes in their frequency or transepithelial electrical resistance (TER). ZO-1 knockout increased the junctional ZnUMBA signal and reduced TER and the number of detected leaks. Simulations showed that stochastic breaking and sealing of tight junction strands is sufficient to explain the observed leak frequencies and durations, and that a single pair of strand break formation and sealing rates reproduces both junction-level leaks and global permeability. Whereas leak frequency mainly reflects the ratio of these rates, leak duration provides independent information on strand sealing that global measurements cannot resolve. Modulating myosin II activity had little effect on leaks, whereas actin depolymerization compromised the barrier. Together, these results link junction-level leaks of ions and small solutes to tight junction strand dynamics.
affiliations: Biosciences Unit, Faculty of Medicine and Health Technology, Tampere University, Tampere, Finland (corresponding author)

papers.title: Anisotropic regulation of lateral surface tension directs invagination in C. elegans gastrulation
papers.abstract: Epithelial invagination is commonly attributed to actomyosin-driven apical constriction, but how the direction of tissue deformation is determined remains unclear. Here, we show that gastrulation in Caenorhabditis elegans involves anisotropic invagination, with preferential anterior-posterior convergence of neighboring cells. Laser ablation revealed no detectable directional bias in apical cortical recoil, suggesting that anisotropy in apical cortical tension is unlikely to be the primary determinant of the observed directional deformation. Instead, HMR-1/E-cadherin exhibited anisotropic accumulation preferentially at specific lateral cell-cell interfaces, where its enrichment is associated with junctional geometry consistent with reduced interfacial surface tension. Three-dimensional mechanical simulations showed that selectively reducing tension at these interfaces reproduces the observed anisotropic deformation and markedly enhances invagination, whereas uniform tension reduction does not. These findings reveal that spatially patterned lateral surface tension cooperates with apical constriction to control the direction and extent of invagination, uncovering a mechanical role for cell adhesion beyond force transmission.
affiliations: National Institute of Genetics (corresponding author)

papers.title: Host control and regulation of human anellovirus persistence
papers.abstract: Anelloviruses are the most abundant and diverse eukaryotic viruses known to infect humans and can persist throughout our lifetimes. Despite their ubiquity, the host factors governing their physiologic distribution and abundance remain poorly understood. Here, we construct a viral pangenome of 2,023 strains to quantify anellovirus DNA in >1.1 million participants spanning three genetic biobanks. Genome-wide association studies identify 121 loci linked to viral persistence, predominantly via immune regulation by NF-kB signaling. Further, we associate variable anellovirus detection with conditions characterized by immune dysfunction, including lymphoid malignancies. By screening 3.2 petabases of human single-cell sequencing data, we identify myeloid progenitors in the bone marrow as a prominent site of anellovirus transcription in vivo. Finally, Perturb-seq of anellovirus proteins reveals that anellovirus ORF2, particularly from Alphatorquevirus, attenuates TNF-a-induced NF-kB signaling, connecting host genetic variation, cellular context, and viral immunomodulation to characterize the persistence of the eukaryotic human virome's most abundant component.
affiliations: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: A genomic prediction framework for growth traits in black soldier fly (Hermetia illucens) breeding programmes
papers.abstract: Background Genomic prediction has been applied in livestock, plant and aquaculture species to accelerate genetic gain. However, its application and potential still remain unexplored in farmed black soldier fly (BSF), an emerging globally important insect production species. Due to the diversity of BSF feed sources, selection strategies need to be evaluated across various feedstocks and production environments to aid in building genomic selection into BSF breeding programmes. In this study, 2,083 BSF larvae from the base population were reared on three diets (SYK: Soy-okara, BSG: brewers' spent grain and FVW: fruit and vegetable waste), and 536 from the F7 population were reared on a chicken starter feed diet. Larvae were phenotyped for four growth traits (LBW, larval body weight; LL, larval length; LW, larval width; LSA, larval surface area) and genotyped across 4,680 SNPs. Genomic prediction was evaluated using seven methods under additive (A) and additive-dominance (AD) models, considering across- and within-diet effects, genotype by diet (G x D) interactions, differences amongst reference and test generations, and SNP densities. Results Performance varied across all scenarios, with LBW showing higher predictive ability (PA) among the growth traits. Accounting for dominance generally improved PA. Multivariate models accounting for G x D performed similarly to, or marginally better than, within-diet predictions. Cross-diet prediction was more variable and generally lower than within-diet prediction, showing reduced transferability across untested nutritional environments. Reducing the SNP density from 4,680 to 3,000 SNPs maintained comparable PA; however, PA decreased below 3,000 SNPs. Across multiple generations, predictive performance declined, resulting from reduced genetic connectivity and possible genotype-by-environment (G x E) interactions between the reference and testing populations. Conclusions Overall, these results provide an application-based framework for genomic prediction in BSF in semi- or commercial production settings. Results also highlight the importance of the genetic model, representative reference populations, and appropriate marker densities for genomic selection.
affiliations: James Cook University, Australia (corresponding author)

papers.title: Interventional breath analysis reveals oral microbial conversion of 1,2-Propanediol into Propanal and 1-Propanol
papers.abstract: Background: Orally exhaled breath contains volatile organic compounds (VOCs) that may reflect local microbial metabolism as well as systemic processes. Consequently, the breath sampling route can influence VOC profiles and complicate biomarker interpretation. Previous studies have shown that 1-propanol is substantially enriched in orally compared with nasally exhaled breath. Objective: To determine whether a controlled oral challenge with 1,2-propanediol (1,2-PD) induces sampling route-dependent changes in breath 1-propanol concentrations. Methods: Ten healthy volunteers received 0.1 mL 1,2-PD diluted in approximately 50 mL water. The solution was used as an oral rinse for approximately 30 s and then expectorated. Matched oral and nasal end-tidal breath samples were collected before administration, immediately afterwards, and at 15-min intervals. Propanal, 1-propanol, acetol, acetone, and isoprene were analysed using gas chromatograph-ion mobility spectrometer (GC-IMS). Results: Oral 1,2-PD exposure produced a rapid and transient increase in exhaled propanal and 1-propanol signals, with the largest responses immediately after administration and at the second post-intervention measurement. In contrast, nasal signals remained comparatively stable. Acetone and isoprene showed no consistent intervention-related changes, regardless of the sampling route. No reproducible increase in acetol was detected, although interpretation was limited by analytical interference. Conclusion: A controlled oral 1,2-PD challenge elicited a route-specific propanal and 1-propanol response, consistent with local microbial metabolism of 1,2-PD within the oral cavity. Both fucose and 1,2-PD have been previously reported in human saliva, including elevated concentrations in selected disease-associated contexts. Bacteria can degrade salivary mucin glycans, releasing sugars including fucose. Together, these observations motivate investigation of a proposed pathway linking mucin-derived fucose to 1,2-PD and subsequent propanal and 1-propanol formation in the human oral cavity.
affiliations: University of Innsbruck (corresponding author)

papers.title: Bacterial major vault protein homologs form divergent vault structures
papers.abstract: Vaults are large, enigmatic macromolecular protein complexes composed of symmetrically arranged major vault protein (MVP) subunits with a wide variety of proposed functions. While MVP is conserved in most eukaryotes, its prevalence in other domains of life has not been well studied. Furthermore, whether bacterial MVP homologs assemble into vaults remains unknown. Here, we identify and examine a subset of bacterial MVP homologs and report cryoEM structures of an intact vault from Corallococcus praedator and a half-vault from a Deltaproteobacteria bacterium. Both bacterial vault complexes exhibit architectures unlike any other previously characterized vault with barrel/cap symmetries of D35/C13 and C48/C16, respectively. These data demonstrate that bacterial MVP homologs can assemble into vault structures and highlight the structural diversity of vaults across domains of life.
affiliations: Regeneron Pharmaceuticals (corresponding author)

papers.title: Positive cooperativity enhances coupling of a second G protein to a GPCR dimer
papers.abstract: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are cell surface integral membrane proteins that transduce environmental, hormonal and neurotransmitter molecular signals into intracellular responses. Here we studied a class D1 fungal receptor, Ste2, an obligate dimer that couples two G proteins per dimer and show that coupling of the second G protein has an 18-fold higher affinity than coupling of the first. The molecular mechanism uncovered suggests that coupling of the first G protein to one protomer stabilizes the adjacent protomer in an active conformation with a pre-formed G protein coupling site, thus increasing the affinity for coupling of the second G protein. Protomer-based stabilization of an adjacent protomer in a unique conformational state within a dimer may represent a general mechanism by which oligomerization alters GPCR pharmacology.
affiliations: MRC LMB Cambridge, UK (corresponding author)

papers.title: PP271, a novel bacteriophage primase-polymerase, enables Primer-Free DNA Amplification
papers.abstract: Primases are essential enzymes that initiate DNA replication by synthesizing de novo primers for replicative DNA polymerases, which ensure accurate genome duplication owing to their high specificity, fidelity, and processivity. PrimPols have emerged as versatile DNA-initiating enzymes that are widely distributed across diverse replication systems, from bacteriophages to humans. In this work, a novel PrimPol enzyme, PP271, encoded by bacteriophage vB-EfaS-271, was characterized. PP271 belongs to the archaeal-eukaryotic primase (AEP) superfamily and contains the conserved catalytic core, together with a C-terminal PriCT domain. Enzymatic analysis demonstrated that PP271 functions as a bona fide PrimPol, i.e. a DNA primase capable of synthetizing short DNA primers. PP271 priming activity is strongly stimulated by ADP, which serves as the preferred initiating nucleotide. Additionally, PP271 exhibits relaxed specificity for selecting the priming site, compared to other PrimPols with more restricted template preferences. TruePrime amplification technology combines the Thermus thermophilus PrimPol and the highly processive Phi29 DNA polymerase to achieve primer-free DNA amplification. While highly efficient, further improvements in amplification yield, fidelity and product complexity remain possible. Here, we show that DNA primers synthesized by PP271 are efficiently extended by Phi29 DNA polymerase, enabling their coordinated action. Moreover, the short primers generated by PP271 are expected to minimize the contribution of primase-derived errors to the final amplification product while allowing efficient DNA synthesis across a broader range of sequence contexts. Altogether, these findings identify PP271 as a promising alternative for improving primase-dependent DNA amplification.
affiliations: Centro de Biologia Molecular Severo Ochoa (corresponding author)

papers.title: S. pombe Mto1:Mto2 stabilizes γ-tubulin positions within the γ-TuRC
papers.abstract: Microtubules are present in all eukaryotes and are nucleated by multiprotein {gamma}-tubulin ring complexes ({gamma}-TuRCs), ring-shaped structures that contain several copies of the {gamma}-tubulin small complex ({gamma}-TuSC). {gamma}-TuRCs nucleate microtubules via a template-based mechanism in which the positions of {gamma}-tubulins in the {gamma}-TuSCs match the position of {gamma}-tubulin dimers in the microtubule lattice. Although {gamma}-TuSC proteins are highly conserved, other components of the {gamma}-TuRC can vary in different organisms, as can their relative importance. Here, we characterize two different simplified {gamma}-TuRCs from fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, using recombinant purified proteins and negative stain electron microscopy. We show that a nucleation-incompetent {gamma}-TuRC that contains only {gamma}-TuSC proteins plus the microprotein Mzt1 ({gamma}-TuSC:Mzt1) can form rings as efficiently as a large, nucleation-competent complex (MGM) that additionally contains the proteins Mto1 and Mto2. We find that the position of {gamma}-tubulins in {gamma}-TuSC:Mzt1 are less well defined than in MGM. Comparative modelling using our electron microscopy and crosslinking mass spectrometry data, together with structures of {gamma}-TuRCs from other organisms, suggests that Mto1 and Mto2 form a multimeric outer mantle surrounding the {gamma}-TuSC:Mzt1 {gamma}-TuRC. This mantle may stabilize positions of {gamma}-tubulins within MGM, explaining the microtubule-nucleating ability of MGM and highlighting the diversity of non-{gamma}-TuSC proteins in modulating {gamma}-TuRC structure and function.
affiliations: The University of Edinburgh (corresponding author)

papers.title: Multimodal imaging links molecular identity with nanoscale-resolved 3D cell morphology in opossum cortical cultures
papers.abstract: In the mammalian central nervous system (CNS), the ability to regenerate after injury drops sharply in the first weeks after birth, but how this change is reflected in cell morphology and organization is still not fully understood. Here we cultivated cortical cell cultures from the gray short-tailed opossum (Monodelphis domestica) and compared cells derived from early postnatal pups (postnatal day 3-6, "Pyoung") with those from older pups (postnatal day 16-18, "Pold"), which differ in their capacity to regenerate after injury. For each culture, we assessed marker-defined cellular composition using fluorescently labeled markers for neurons, glia, and immature/progenitor cells, and characterized their nanoscale-resolved three-dimensional morphology using label-free scanning ion conductance microscopy (SICM). Pyoung cultures exhibited active change in shape over time, contained a higher proportion of immature SOX2 cells, and grew more neurites (TUJ1) into the lesion site after injury. Moreover, Pold cultures showed more stable soma size (e.g., thickness, area, volume), a larger astroglial (SOX9) population early in culture, and a glia-dominated lesion response. These early astroglia included more immature or reactive (vimentin) astrocytes. SICM further revealed cellular bridges across the lesion, ridges left in the substrate by the injury, and aligned neurite outgrowth. Across all measurements, changes in molecular markers were associated with corresponding changes in cell morphology. This multimodal combination of fluorescence labeling and SICM therefore relates marker-defined cellular composition to physical organization across micro- and nanoscale features during and after postnatal in vitro development.
affiliations: Ecole Polytechnique Federal de Lausanne (corresponding author)

papers.title: Mitochondrial transplantation redirects rather than suppresses the inflammatory response in primary human monocytes
papers.abstract: Circulating monocytes are recruited into inflamed tissue, where local cues determine whether the macrophages they become drive inflammation or resolve it. Because that decision occurs after cells leave the blood, the circulating stage offers a window to alter monocyte programming, and monocyte inflammatory function is closely coupled to mitochondrial metabolism. Here we transplanted freshly isolated, respiration-competent mitochondria from HEK293T cells into primary human CD14 monocytes and characterized the resulting mitochondria-transplanted monocytes (MTM) across surface phenotype, respiration, and inflammatory function. Isolated mitochondria were intact and respiration-competent, with a respiratory control ratio of 8.7 and a coupling efficiency of 78.9 %. Monocytes internalized them in proportion to the dose supplied; within 3 h, 88% of viable cells were positive for labeled mitochondria, with no loss of viability detected; isolated mitochondria did not activate NF-{kappa}B or IRF reporters in THP1-Dual cells. Transplantation reduced the frequency of the pro-inflammatory intermediate subset, increased CD14 by 2.11-fold and HLA-DR by 1.31-fold, and decreased CD163. MTM showed reduced ATP-linked respiration with maximal capacity preserved, and a trend toward a higher maximal-to-basal respiration ratio. Following stimulation with LPS, MTM released markedly less TNF- (0.06-fold) and CXCL10/IP-10 (0.25-fold) and, in most donors, more IL-10 (3.33-fold), while the remaining analytes were largely unchanged. Mitochondrial transplantation therefore shifts primary human monocytes toward a phenotype with selectively reduced inflammatory mediator release and increased IL-10 in most donors. It identifies circulating monocytes as a tractable target for mitochondria-based modulation of inflammation.
affiliations: Massachusetts General Hospital (corresponding author)

papers.title: An Accessible and Scalable Pipette-Driven Microfluidic Platform for Lipid Nanoparticle Formulation
papers.abstract: Advances in lipid nanoparticle (LNP) technology have increased the need for accessible and scalable methods that accelerate low-volume formulation screening. Here, we describe a disposable microfluidic mixer actuated by a positive-displacement pipette equipped with dual-chamber pipette tip, providing volumetric control at a fixed flow rate ratio without external microfluidic pumps. Computational fluid dynamics analysis predicted shorter micromixing times in the high-shear spiral channel than in the low-shear design. Across three benchmark lipid formulations, the high-shear mixer reproducibly generated smaller LNPs with higher mRNA encapsulation efficiency than the low-shear mixer or manual pipetting. Orthogonal characterization further revealed higher particle concentrations, structural features consistent with compact particles, more uniform mRNA loading, and a lower empty-particle fraction. LNPs prepared using the selected high-shear mixer mediated functional mRNA delivery in 2D cell cultures, a 3D human liver tissue model, and mice. Integration with a liquid-handling robot enabled automated screening of formulation parameters. Dimensionless mixing-time analysis guided enlargement of the mixer geometry for a separate production system, which produced 75 mL preparations at 150 mL/min with particle size and mRNA encapsulation efficiency comparable to those obtained with the small-scale mixer. This platform provides an accessible, automation-compatible approach to LNP formulation screening and a route to larger-scale production.
affiliations: Sartorius Stedim North America Inc. (corresponding author)

papers.title: Citrate-Based Hydrogels Promote Closure of Infected Diabetic Wounds
papers.abstract: Diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) are a significant threat to the quality of life for individuals with diabetes, affecting approximately 1.6 million patients in the US, as of 2023. When these wounds do not heal and become chronic wounds, they can become infected and increase the risk of digit and/or lower limb amputation. Therefore, there is a critical need for therapies that promote wound closure in the presence and absence of infection. We have previously reported the potential benefits of the thermoresponsive citrate-based macromolecule poly(polyethylene glycol citrate-co-N-isopropylacrylamide) (PPCN) in diabetic rodent and swine models of non-infected full thickness dermal wounds. In this study, we compared four PPCN formulations (PPCN, PPCN-CMOF, A5G81-PPCN, and A5G81-PPCN-CMOF), which are functionalized with the laminin-derived cell adhesion peptide A5G81 and/or contain entrapped copper metal-organic framework nanoparticles (CMOF) designed to release Cu2+ slowly, in diabetic mice with wounds infected with S. aureus. In infected wounds, all four formulations significantly improved cumulative closure relative to saline (adjusted p = 0.002-0.021). In non-infected wounds, only PPCN-CMOF significantly improved cumulative closure relative to saline (p = 0.046), although all four formulations reached [≥]95% closure earlier than saline (adjusted p = 0.009-0.045). In vitro, the CMOF-containing formulations produced the highest bacterial killing (90% for A5G81-PPCN-CMOF and 84% for PPCN-CMOF), whereas A5G81-PPCN and PPCN reduced bacterial colonies by 76% and 59%. PPCN modification with A5G81 and/or CMOF increased endothelial mesh formation in vitro. In vivo, PPCN-based formulations increased granulation tissue thickness and, depending on formulation and infection status, vascular marker expression. These results suggest that PPCN and PPCN formulations containing CMOF and/or A5G81 are a potentially viable technology that can be added to the wound care toolbox to accelerate healing of diabetic foot ulcers in the presence of infection. These findings support further investigation of PPCN as an instructive pro-regenerative biomaterial in a preclinical large animal model.
affiliations: Northwestern University (corresponding author)

papers.title: TideCluster: clustering and classification of tandem repeats for comparative and pangenomic analysis
papers.abstract: Satellite DNA, composed of tandem arrays of relatively short repeated units, is a ubiquitous component of plant and animal genomes. Despite its biological importance, systematic investigation of satellite DNA remains challenging, in part because integrated bioinformatic tools for structured comparative analyses across individual arrays, chromosomes, and genomes are lacking. Here, we present TideCluster, a reference-independent pipeline that converts fragmented tandem repeat detections into genome-wide, interpretable repeat family catalogs. Starting from a genome assembly, TideCluster consolidates detected regions into arrays, clusters arrays by sequence similarity, reconstructs representative monomer consensus sequences, estimates locus-specific periodicity, identifies higher-order repeats, and generates GFF3 annotations. In addition to predefined visualizations, including the chromosomal distributions of satellite repeat families, TideCluster produces information-rich outputs that can be adapted for user-specific downstream analyses. We demonstrate its capabilities using the well-characterized genome of Arabidopsis thaliana and a set of Solanum species with highly diverse satellite repeat complements that vary markedly in abundance and have monomer lengths ranging from a few base pairs to more than 20 kb.
affiliations: Biology Centre, Czech Academy of Sciences, Ceske Budejovice, Czech Republic (corresponding author)

papers.title: HERACLES for fast and accurate likelihood-based reconstruction of massive lineages
papers.abstract: CRISPR-based lineage recording technologies can trace the ancestry of hundreds of thousands of cells, yet reconstructing accurate phylogenies at this scale remains computationally challenging. Likelihood-based methods employ explicit evolutionary models of CRISPR editing that improve tree accuracy but require computationally expensive searches over tree topologies, whereas distance-based alternatives scale efficiently but rely on distances that may not faithfully represent the editing process, introducing biases whose magnitude and direction are unknown. Here, we introduce HERACLES, which optimizes cell coordinates in hyperbolic space under a quartet-based composite likelihood of CRISPR editing. By recovering local branching structures directly from embedded distances, HERACLES guides continuous optimization with an explicit evolutionary model without repeatedly constructing and evaluating complete phylogenies. Across simulated benchmarks, HERACLES improves reconstruction accuracy over existing methods and scales to lineages containing 150,000 cells in about four hours on a single GPU. On experimental KP-tracer and PEtracer datasets, HERACLES reconstructs phylogenies consistent with independent anatomical annotations and temporal lineage markers. Its flexible likelihood framework also accommodates different recording mechanisms: incorporating sequential editing improves reconstruction of simulated DNA Typewriter lineages. Together, these results establish continuous optimization of local evolutionary relationships as a scalable and flexible approach to probabilistic lineage reconstruction.
affiliations: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: GeneEmbedLLM: Harnessing Large Language Models for Gene Functional Embedding and Association Prediction
papers.abstract: Effective and high-quality gene function representations are crucial for bioinformatics tasks. While biological knowledge about genes is inherently textual, encompassing functional descriptions and pathway annotations, current methods often rely on single-source, non-textual data, failing to capture the rich semantic information in multi-source gene annotations. In this paper, we propose GeneEmbedLLM, a Large Language Model (LLM)-powered framework for generating universal, semantically-aware gene embeddings. The proposed approach advances the gene representation learning through multi-source structured text integration from five authoritative databases and attribute-aware attention based on Longformer architecture and contrastive learning. Experimental results on diverse downstream tasks, ranging from molecular interactions and phenotypic dependencies to epigenetic regulation, confirm the validity and effectiveness of our proposed approach, where competitive performance is achieved across all evaluated benchmarks. We further validate the quality of the generated embeddings through comprehensive analyses, including embedding visualizations, intra-pathway similarity assessments, ablation study, and parameter analysis.
affiliations: Guangzhou National Laboratory (corresponding author)

papers.title: LinearKnot: linear-time ensemble analysis of RNA density-2 pseudoknots under hierarchical folding
papers.abstract: Motivation: A pseudoknot is an arrangement of crossing base pairs. Pseudoknots complicate structure prediction and calculations over possible structures (an ensemble). CParty sums structure weights for hierarchical pseudoknots that keep a supplied pseudoknot-free structure (scaffold). Its time is cubic in sequence length. Results: LinearKnot approximates CParty with beam pruning. It combines at most two partial structures in each step and keeps the highest-ranked candidates. At fixed beam width, hairpin length limit, and scaffold search limit, partition functions, minimum-free-energy (MFE) predictions, and representative {gamma}-centroid structures from base-pairing probabilities take linear time in sequence length. Loop profiles give probabilities for pairing and six unpaired loop types, including gaps between crossing stems (PseudoLoop). Window accessibility is the probability that a window is unpaired. For each RNA, we compared each base's distributions over pairing partners (including the unpaired state) and structural contexts with exact probabilities and averaged their total variation (TV) distances over bases unpaired in the scaffold. At width 200, the 90th percentiles of these RNA averages among 300-399-base RNAs were 0.0015 for pairing and 0.0017 for contexts. At width 100, LinearKnot completed partition functions for all 107 real RNAs through 29 kilobases. Under our settings, CParty completed RNAs up to about 1 kilobase and was faster on them. For the RNAcentral long non-coding RNA URS00023A4DB9 (29,106 nt), partition-function, pairing-probability, and MFE calculations at width 100 took about 7 minutes and 3.22 GiB. We compared free energy and pairing probabilities before and after each increase in beam width and local limits. These changes generally became smaller at larger widths. At width 200, the calculations for URS00023A4DB9 took about 20 minutes and 5.68 GiB. In rat telomerase RNA, a four-base window next to a pseudoknot was mostly unpaired as part of a PseudoLoop. A pseudoknot-free calculation with the same scaffold gave lower accessibility and placed the window mainly in a hairpin when unpaired. Availability and implementation: LinearKnot provides the linearknot command at https://github.com/TakumiOtagaki/LinearKnot. Experiment scripts and data are at https://github.com/TakumiOtagaki/LinearKnotExperiments.
affiliations: Institute of Science Tokyo (corresponding author)

papers.title: RabbitCD-HIT: Distributed High-Sensitivity Greedy Incremental Clustering for Billion-Scale Protein Sequences in Hours
papers.abstract: We present RabbitCD-HIT, a scalable distributed high-sensitivity greedy incremental clustering tool for ultra-large protein sequence datasets. It fully exploits cluster resources to enable efficient billion-scale clustering. RabbitCD-HIT clustered the March 10, 2026 NCBI nr snapshot (1.02 billion sequences; 487 GB FASTA) at 90\% identity within 5 hours on 64 nodes; the resulting representatives and cluster assignments are released as a public database resource. On a 256-core server, RabbitCD-HIT achieved a 2.1$\times$--6.6$\times$ speedup over CD-HIT with identical results under matched settings. Our approach addresses performance bottlenecks of traditional greedy incremental algorithms and provides an effective solution for large-scale protein sequence clustering.
affiliations: Shandong University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Extracting and Updating Compact Colored k-mer Indexes
papers.abstract: Colored k-mer indexes record, for every k-mer of a collection of genomes, the genomes or species that contain it, and underpin pseudoalignment and sequence search against large collections. Construction of such an index is expensive, yet the collection it represents is rarely final: genomes are retracted or found to be contaminated, users need an index of a single species or clade, and new genomes keep arriving. Rebuilding the index after every such change requires the original sequences and repeats the costly construction. We show that colored indexes based on the spectral Burrows-Wheeler transform (SBWT) can instead be updated efficiently in batches, without the original sequences, and with a result equivalent to the index built from scratch. Given an SBWT and any subset of its k-mers, we first extract the SBWT of this subset directly from the input, in one linear pass and without building a new index. Removing genomes, intersection and difference all reduce to this operation. We then carry the colors through every operation, by finding from the inputs alone where the color sets of the result change, so that removing or extracting genomes, as well as the union, intersection and difference of two colored indexes, each directly yield a complete colored index. In our experiments, editing paid off for large results: removing a genome from an index of 3,682 E. coli genomes took 54 seconds instead of 13 minutes for a rebuild, and adding one took about a minute. On AllTheBacteria, with 192 billion k-mers and 12,733 species, extracting M. tuberculosis, with 180,094 genomes, took less than four hours, and set operations then traced contamination of its color, some of which the next release of AllTheBacteria still contains. Our work turns large colored k-mer indexes from static snapshots of a collection into resources that can be maintained as the collection evolves. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/LoreDepuydt/colored-sbwt-setops.
affiliations: University of Lille (corresponding author)

papers.title: π-SPECFormer: A Mass Spectrometry-based Foundation Model for Decoding the Dark Proteome
papers.abstract: In mass-spectrometry-based proteomics, a substantial proportion of acquired spectra remain unidentified, concealing a vast reservoir of biological variations commonly termed the "dark proteome", potentially obscuring sequence mutations, non-canonical peptides and post-translational modifications. Existing deep-learning methods largely rely on supervised training with peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs), limiting their ability to learn from the much larger pool of unannotated spectra. Here we introduce {pi}-SPECFormer, a mass-spectrometry foundation model pre-trained on 291 million spectra through a two-stage framework that combines self-supervised and PSMs-guided representation learning. {pi}-SPECFormer transfers effectively to de novo peptide sequencing, spectrum clustering and modification detection, consistently outperforming task-specific baselines. When applied to proteomic profiles from 103 individuals with lung adenocarcinoma, the model identified nine high-confidence mutated peptides, including six that were absent from the reference databases. {pi}-SPECFormer thus enables unbiased decoding of molecular complexity beyond the boundaries of the canonical proteome.
affiliations: National Center for Protein Sciences (Beijing) (corresponding author)

papers.title: BEHAV3D-Explorer enables natural language-assisted profiling of 3D cellular dynamics
papers.abstract: Obtaining quantitative measurements from live 3D microscopy remains difficult to implement across research settings, particularly without profound image-analysis expertise. We present BEHAV3D-Explorer, an interactive, user-friendly platform that uses natural-language guidance to help users select analysis strategies, tune parameters and configure workflows. BEHAV3D-Explorer enables time-resolved behavioral classification and integrates it with morphological, interaction and functional analyses, thereby connecting dynamic readouts to yield interpretable results across imaging applications.
affiliations: Institute for Biomedical Research Sols-Morreale (IIBM), Spanish National Research Council (CSIC)-Universidad Autonoma de Madrid, Madrid, Spain (corresponding author)

papers.title: Nutrient Availability as a Driver of Transcriptome Reprogramming in Osteosarcoma
papers.abstract: Background: Gene expression in mammalian cells is intricately regulated by environmental and metabolic cues. Among these, nutrient availability represents a key feature of the tumor microenvironment and has recently emerged as a potent modulator of oncogenic signaling networks. In this study, we employed a cell-line model of osteosarcoma, a rare but highly aggressive bone malignancy affecting both humans and dogs. We demonstrate that altering the concentration of a single nutrient can profoundly reprogram gene expression in osteosarcoma cells, revealing a previously underexplored phenomenon: nutrient-dependent gene regulation. This finding highlights potential opportunities for therapeutic intervention and underscores the broader implications of metabolic regulation for personalized medicine and nutrition. Methods/Results: We performed bulk RNA sequencing of an established osteosarcoma cell line cultured under varying concentrations of two key nutrients, glucose and glutamine. Differential gene expression analysis revealed a pronounced nutrient-dependent transcriptional response. The identified genes were functionally associated with pathways involved in cancer, development, nervous system regulation, metabolism, cellular signaling, and immune responses. We identified seven distinct expression patterns, one of which exhibited a striking correlation with cell growth rate and resembled a FOS-like transcriptional signature. Notably, the proto-oncogene FOS was among the identified genes and displayed a strong growth-rate-dependent expression pattern. Conclusion/Impact: Our findings demonstrate that modulation of nutrient availability profoundly reshapes the gene expression landscape of osteosarcoma cells, revealing nutrient-responsive targets with potential therapeutic relevance. This work expands our understanding of metabolic regulation in cancer and suggests that nutrient-based interventions may provide a controllable means of influencing tumor progression. Beyond oncology, such approaches may also have broader implications for developmental biology, autoimmune disorders, and nervous system function. More broadly, this study highlights the potential of metabolic interventions as a strategy for targeted modulation of gene expression programs.
affiliations: GenSiLab Inc. (corresponding author)

papers.title: Integrating Microbial Ecology and Sustainability: Linking Agricultural Waste Gas Streams to Microbial Community Shifts in a Photobioreactor
papers.abstract: Photobioreactors (PBRs) coupled to animal housing offer potential for mitigating gaseous emissions such as CO2 and NH3 while simultaneously producing biomass. Here, we present a time-resolved characterization of microbial community dynamics, with a focus on the genetic potential for carbon and nitrogen metabolism. Using a cone-shaped, helical PBR cultivating Arthrospira platensis (Spirulina) and supplied with exhaust air from a chicken house, we characterized microbial communities over continuous exhaust-air exposure and periodic biomass harvesting. Microbiome and gene-centric profiling revealed temporal variation in community composition and in the representation of genes associated with carbon and nitrogen metabolism. Cycle-based dissolved inorganic nitrogen balances showed that the decrease in dissolved inorganic nitrogen was only partially recovered in harvested biomass, while ammonia-oxidizing microorganisms were associated with structured, low-light niches. These observations indicate ammonia-oxidizing potential but do not establish a quantitatively relevant nitrification flux. Structured carrier matrices provided attached-growth niches harboring microbial populations underrepresented in the circulating suspension, while pre-colonized carriers facilitated biomass development during re-inoculation. Overall, our results show that coupling PBRs to agricultural exhaust streams can support biomass production while sustaining spatially structured microbial communities with taxonomic and functional potential. These findings may inform their further development for emission mitigation and circular biomass production.
affiliations: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: SAMP1/TMEM201 protects alveolar type 2 cells from DNA damage-associated senescence and restrains pulmonary fibrosis
papers.abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a progressive interstitial lung disease in which repetitive injury to the alveolar epithelium and senescence of alveolar type 2 (AT2) cells drive persistent myofibroblast activation and extracellular matrix deposition. Inner nuclear membrane (INM) proteins organise nuclear architecture and participate in the DNA damage response, but whether they influence epithelial senescence and fibrogenesis is unknown. Here we identify SAMP1/TMEM201, an INM protein that binds lamin A/C, emerin and LINC-complex components, as a compartment-selective protector of AT2 cells. In the bleomycin model of pulmonary fibrosis, SAMP1 was reduced in AT2 cells but unchanged in lung fibroblasts. AT2 cell-specific deletion of Samp1 (Sftpc-Cre^ERT2^; Samp1^flox/flox^) aggravated fibrosis at day 21, with higher Ashcroft scores and increased pulmonary Tnfa and Acta2 expression, whereas intratracheal delivery of AAV6-CAG-Samp1 before bleomycin attenuated both histological fibrosis and these transcriptional responses. In primary AT2 cells analysed immediately after isolation without in vitro stimulation, SAMP1 loss was accompanied by reduced 53BP1 protein, comparable gammaH2AX levels, and upregulation of the senescence-associated and profibrotic markers p16^INK4a^ and PAI-1. These findings define a SAMP1-AT2 senescence axis that constrains pulmonary fibrogenesis and suggest that preserving INM-dependent genome surveillance in the alveolar epithelium may offer an epithelium-directed therapeutic strategy for IPF. Because DNA damage signalling was assessed only under baseline conditions, the data establish an association with altered DNA damage signalling rather than a definitive defect in lesion repair.
affiliations: National Center for Disease Prevention and Health Promotion, Italian National Institute of Health (corresponding author)

papers.title: Genome-scale modelling and stable isotope tracing reveal dynamic metabolic reprogramming in a human cardiac hypertrophy model
papers.abstract: Pathological cardiac hypertrophy is associated with metabolic remodelling; however the temporal dynamics of this remodelling remain poorly defined in human cardiomyocyte systems. Here, we combined transcriptomic profiling, genome-scale metabolic modelling and stable isotope-resolved metabolomics (SIRM) to map the metabolic consequences of endothelin-1 (ET-1) stimulation in human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs). Integration of RNA sequencing data obtained after 8 and 48 hours of ET-1 treatment with the Human2.0 genome-scale metabolic model predicted time-dependent remodelling, characterised by progressive increases in glycolytic flux, enhanced glucose carbon entry into the TCA cycle, and a decrease in fatty acid {beta}-oxidation. Computational flux predictions were independently confirmed by extracellular flux analysis and 13C-substrate tracing, with concordance between modelled and measured fluxes. Extracellular flux analysis showed increased glycolytic capacity and mitochondrial respiration after 48 hours, with greater sensitivity to inhibition of mitochondrial pyruvate transport. Glucose tracing revealed increased 13C enrichment of glycolytic, pentose phosphate pathway, serine-glycine and TCA cycle metabolites, consistent with altered glucose-derived carbon allocation. Increased m+3 labelling of selected TCA-related metabolites was compatible with pyruvate anaplerosis, although pathway-specific fluxes were not resolved. In three-dimensional engineered heart tissue (EHTs) treated with ET-1 for 7 days, increased hypertrophic marker expression was accompanied by a blunted inotropic response, and metabolomics showed similar changes in metabolite abundance and glucose-derived labelling to 2D cultures. These findings support hiPSC-CMs and EHTs as complementary platforms for studying early metabolic remodelling in pathological cardiac hypertrophy and provide an integrated framework linking model predictions to functional and isotope-tracing measurements.
affiliations: King's College London (corresponding author)

papers.title: A largely shared genetic architecture underlies Saccharomyces cerevisiae persistence across different mouse host genotypes
papers.abstract: The extent to which interactions between microbial and host genotypes shape opportunistic pathogen persistence within hosts is an important open question. To assess the contribution of these interactions to persistence, we used Saccharomyces cerevisiae , a genetically tractable model for studying opportunistic fungal persistence in mammalian hosts. A pooled panel of barcoded haploid segregants from a cross between a laboratory strain and a clinical isolate, together with both parents, was introduced intravenously into seven genetically diverse mouse strains. We measured the relative persistence of segregants in mouse brains and livers using barcode sequencing. Persistence showed transgressive segregation in both organs. On average across the two organs, yeast genotype explained 45.2% of the variance in segregant persistence, whereas yeast genotype-by-host genotype interactions explained only 2.9%. Linkage mapping showed that loci detected in more host genotypes generally explained more phenotypic variance than those detected in fewer host genotypes. At some loci, genetic variation correlated with increased yeast persistence across multiple organs (general loci) while at others increased persistence in one organ came at the cost of decreased persistence in another (antagonistic loci). General loci contributed disproportionately to brain persistence, whereas liver persistence reflected contributions from both classes. The clinical parent showed greater persistence than the laboratory parent in every host-organ combination, and the additive effects of detected loci predicted the direction of this advantage. Overall, this work shows that in this system, relative microbial persistence is polygenic, with a strong additive component and only a very small contribution from microbial genotype-by-host genotype interactions.
affiliations: University of Southern California (corresponding author)

papers.title: Genomic signatures of long-term selection in the Langhill dairy herd: the power of a five-decade experiment for sustainable dairy cattle breeding
papers.abstract: Background Selective breeding has transformed dairy cattle productivity, but the genomic consequences of long-term directional selection - what it costs in diversity and where in the genome it acts - are hard to quantify because contemporaneous control populations are rare. The Langhill experiment, established in 1973, is one of the world's longest-running dairy cattle selection trials with a designed control line kept under common management. We used this resource population to ask what five decades of bull selection have cost in genetic diversity, where in the genome selection has acted, and whether complementary scans converge on the loci under selection. Results We genotyped archived blood samples from 1,126 cows of two genetic lines: a Select line sired by bulls in the top decile of UK genetic merit for milk fat-plus-protein yield, and a Control line sired by bulls of average merit. The Select line showed the expected gains in every yield trait. Inbreeding accumulated at the same annual rate in both lines, and effective population size, estimated from that rate, was approximately 33. Linkage disequilibrium was higher in the Select line at every marker distance from 2 to 300 kb. Autozygosity was 24.7% higher in the Select line than in the Control line (0.078 versus 0.063), a difference robust across four calling parameter sets and two independent callers. The excess was confined to runs of homozygosity longer than 2 Mb; shorter runs did not differ between lines, confirming a shared founder base and placing all divergence after the lines were split. It did not arise from a numerically narrower sire pool: the Select line used more sires (79 versus 72), each with fewer daughters, yet its cows were three times more related to one another. Twenty-eight regions across thirteen chromosomes showed strong differentiation; intersecting five scans identified a four-method signal on chromosome 21 spanning the SERPINA gene cluster and sixteen three-method regions, including chromosome 3, with haplotype and diversity statistics agreeing on the line carrying the signal in fourteen of seventeen. Autozygosity itself did not localise to any region. Conclusions Selection left two genomic footprints: diffuse, recent inbreeding accumulated through the narrow ancestry of the elite sire pool, and localised differentiation at specific loci. Runs of homozygosity index only the first process; the second is captured by frequency- and haplotype-based differentiation scans. Because the cost of inbreeding is incurred through ancestry rather than the number of bulls used, mating schemes that constrain the rate of co-ancestry would be preferable to simply managing the number of sires selected and used.
affiliations: Scotland's Rural College; (corresponding author)

papers.title: Genome assembly and characterization of two Brazilian soybean cultivars contrasting for stink bug resistance
papers.abstract: Brazil's tropical soybean germplasm still has few genomic resources: only one assembly of a Brazilian cultivar is available at NCBI. Here we describe chromosome-level de novo assemblies of two contrasting cultivars: IAC-100, described as resistant to phytophagous stink bugs, and CD-215, susceptible. We sequenced high molecular weight DNA using 10x Genomics linked reads, assembled the reads with Supernova, anchored the assembly to the Williams 82 reference with RaGOO and corrected structural errors with REAPR. The assemblies span 1.057 and 1.061 Gb, with scaffold N50 values of 53.6 and 54.2 Mb (48.0 and 47.7 Mb excluding gaps), and recover more than 97% of conserved plant genes assessed by BUSCO. Homology-based projection of the reference protein-coding genes generated 46,774 and 46,620 gene models. Comparing the proteomes of the two cultivars, we identified 2,002 divergent isoforms in 1,427 loci, classified by sequence divergence, length variation, combined divergence and non-conserved homology. These data expand the genomic resources for tropical soybean germplasm, still underrepresented in public databases, and for studies of insect resistance.
