papers.title: Rapid environmental DNA detection with isothermal amplification methods: a comparison with the real-time quantitative PCR in the natterjack toad (Epidalea calamita).
papers.abstract: Species detection relying on environmental DNA (eDNA) traditionally relies on Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR). This amplification technique takes in general a minimum of one hour and requires in most cases access to specialized laboratories and equipment. Isothermal amplification techniques, originating from clinical research, are emerging as rapid and field-deployable alternative methods. Yet, whether their sensitivity, specificity, and cost/time-efficiency are comparable to the traditional real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR) remains to be assessed. In this work, we compare the performance of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) and recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) with qPCR to detect the natterjack toad (Epidalea calamita) from aquatic filtrations. This objective was achieved in three steps. First, we developed LAMP and RPA primers specific to the target species based on its mitochondrial genome. Second, we amplified DNA extracts from E. calamita and from tissues of closely related species using real-time fluorescence detection with LAMP, RPA, and qPCR commercially available protocols to evaluate and compare the sensitivity and specificity of the three methods. Finally, we validated all protocols on eDNA extracts recovered from water samples from ponds surveyed by field scientists. We show that RPA had a sensitivity equivalent to that of the qPCR, while LAMP sensitivity was ten times lower. All our assays amplified the species DNA in eDNA samples where the species was observed by field scientists. Through this work, we thus propose a robust methodology for implementing isothermal amplification assays for eDNA applications and show that RPA is a good alternative to qPCR for detecting conservation-priority species (i.e. protected or invasive species) when time and lab facilities are constrained.
affiliations: Argaly, Montmelian, France and Centre de Recherche sur la Biodiversite et l'Environnement (CRBE), UMR 5300 CNRS, IRD, INP, UT, Toulouse, France (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Continuum Fibre Network Model for the Anisotropic and Compressible Mechanics of Human Skin
papers.abstract: We present a Continuum Fibre Network (CFN) formulation for modelling anisotropy, strain stiffening and volume change in fibrous soft tissues. The model combines a three-dimensional fibre orientation distribution, a bilinear tensile fibre law and a separate phenomenological volumetric potential. We calibrated the model using published uniaxial tensile and volume-change data for excised human skin from separate studies. Changes in cross-sectional area affected the tensile stress estimates for models that predicted volume change. Simulations of indentation, shear and biaxial tension illustrate predictions of the calibrated formulation under additional loading conditions. The CFN formulation included a weak isotropic neo-Hookean ground matrix with a prescribed shear modulus of 0.1 MPa.
affiliations: Biomechanics Research Centre (BMEC), School of Engineering, Institute for Health Discovery and Innovation, College of Science and Engineering, University of Gal (corresponding author)

papers.title: Bioinformatic pipeline for functional inference of Rickettsia akari hypothetical proteins reveals virulence-associated and effector candidates
papers.abstract: Background Rickettsia akari, the causative agent of rickettsialpox, is an obligate intracellular pathogen with a highly reduced genome encoding numerous hypothetical proteins (HPs) of unknown function. Many of these HPs are expressed during host-cell infection, yet their roles in bacterial physiology and potential contribution to virulence remain unclear. Methodology/Principal Findings We performed an integrative in silico characterization of 54 R. akari HPs previously identified by mass spectrometry in purified bacterial cells. Using a benchmarked computational workflow, we predicted their physicochemical properties, subcellular localization, putative secretion signals, protein folds, potential interaction partners, and evolutionary conservation. Most HPs were predicted to be thermostable. The majority of HPs were predicted to be cytoplasmic (37.00%) or membrane-associated (29.63%). Predicted features associated with the type IV secretion system were more frequent than those associated with type I secretion. Network and structural analyses identified candidate HPs with features consistent with potential roles in outer membrane assembly, host-cell interaction, and immune modulation, including predicted peptidyl-prolyl cis/trans isomerases, oxidoreductases, methyltransferases, and putative E3 ubiquitin ligases. Several HPs were predicted to be antigenic and showed conservation across multiple rickettsial genomes. Molecular docking and normal mode analysis supported the plausibility of selected predicted protein-protein and protein-ligand interactions. Evolutionary analyses indicated predominant purifying selection among the analyzed HPs. A8GP20 showed elevated sequence divergence and warrants further investigation as a potential effector candidate. Conclusions/Significance Our findings prioritize A8GPG8, A8GP63, A8GNV4, A8GMM8, A8GM41, A8GMJ7, A8GMI5, A8GP20, A8GN23, A8GMB4, A8GM08, and A8GM39 as promising candidates for experimental validation of their predicted functions and potential roles in R. akari biology and pathogenicity. This work provides an integrative and reproducible bioinformatic framework to guide functional discovery in R. akari and related neglected intracellular pathogens, and identifies candidate proteins for future studies of rickettsial pathogenesis, antigen discovery, and therapeutic target development.
affiliations: Biomedical Research Center Slovak Academy of Sciences (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cisplatin-triggered sensory dysfunction in NER-defective C. elegans involves GABAergic and cholinergic signaling
papers.abstract: Cisplatin (CisPt) is a widely used anticancer drug that causes neurotoxicity as a dose-limiting adverse effect. DNA damage contributes to CisPt-induced neurotoxicity, yet the molecular mechanisms involved remain unclear. Here, we aim to identify pathophysiological mechanisms contributing to DNA damage-driven development of sensory neuronal dysfunction using the 3R-compliant model organism Caenorhabditis elegans. To this end, we employed the nucleotide excision repair (NER)-deficient ercc-1 mutant, which shows enhanced CisPt-induced sensory dysfunction as monitored by the chemotaxis assay, to elucidate drug-induced alterations in neurotransmission and transcriptome. We found that CisPt reduces gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) levels in the nematode and that GABA supplementation rescues ercc-1 mutants from CisPt-evoked sensory neurotoxicity, pointing to a neuroprotective function of GABA in the context of our study. Moreover, CisPt impairs the morphological integrity of GABAergic neurons particularly in ercc-1 mutants, which again is rescued by GABA substitution. Conversely, the cholinergic agonist carbachol impairs sensory function and exacerbates the neurotoxic effects of CisPt in ercc-1 mutants, indicating detrimental effects resulting from cholinergic excitation. Transcriptome analysis revealed that CisPt treatment stimulates a broard transcriptional response, including pathways involved in the regulation of neuronal communication, including acetylcholine-mediated neurotransmission, with pronounced effects occurring in the absence of ERCC-1. Based on these finding we suggest impaired GABAergic signaling and the loss of neuronal integrity GABAergic neurons as well as excessive cholinergic excitation as key mechanisms linking CisPt-induced DNA damage in NER defective nematodes to sensory dysfunction. Hence, targeting the balance between GABAergic inhibition and cholinergic excitation is suggested to counteract sensory neurotoxicity triggered by CisPt.
affiliations: Heinrich-Heine-University Duesseldorf, Medical Faculty, Institute of Toxicology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Photomechanical engineering of immunogenic whole-cell vaccines by laser-induced vapor nanobubbles for bladder cancer prophylaxis
papers.abstract: Whole-cell cancer vaccines can provide broad tumor-antigen repertoires, but their efficacy depends on manufacturing methods that inactivate tumor cells while preserving immunogenic danger signals. Here we show that laser-induced vapor nanobubbles (VNB) generated from dextran-coated iron oxide nanoparticles provide a drug-free photomechanical route to engineer immunogenic whole-cell vaccines against bladder cancer. Using MB49 murine urothelial carcinoma cells, we established VNB conditions that induced rapid tumor-cell killing together with calreticulin exposure and extracellular ATP and HMGB1 release. Rapid cell killing and calreticulin exposure were also reproduced in the molecularly distinct UPPL1541 bladder cancer model, supporting the generalizability of the early photomechanical response across bladder cancer cell lines. Vaccination with VNB-killed MB49 cells reduced tumor incidence and growth after subcutaneous challenge and enhanced splenocyte-mediated antitumor activity against MB49 cells. In an orthotopic bladder cancer model, vaccination prevented MRI-detectable tumor formation and was associated with marked early bladder enrichment of CD8 T cells and inflammatory monocytes. A single administration of the VNB-generated vaccine preparation showed no evident local or systemic toxicity during seven days of follow-up. These findings provide proof of concept for an externally triggered, drug-free manufacturing approach in which short laser irradiation induces rapid photomechanical killing of tumor cells on demand, generating immunogenic whole-tumor-cell vaccine preparations for further evaluation in therapeutic, post-resection and tumor-derived settings.
affiliations: Institute for Advanced Chemistry of Catalonia (IQAC-CSIC) (corresponding author)

papers.title: Circulating CD4 regulatory T cells are broadly preserved in Parkinson's disease despite altered HELIOS expression
papers.abstract: Background Regulatory T cells (Tregs) are an important component of adaptive immune regulation and have been implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD), with previous studies suggesting altered Treg proportions, phenotype and, in some cases, function. However, existing studies have been limited by variable phenotyping approaches and a lack of detailed functional assessment. Given the growing interest in Tregs as potential therapies in PD, better understanding of their phenotype and function in the disease is important. Methods Circulating FOXP3+ Tregs were characterised in individuals with PD and age-matched healthy controls (HC) using a 24-colour spectral flow cytometry panel. Treg suppressive function was assessed by their ability to inhibit proliferation and cytokine production by polyclonally stimulated autologous T effector cells in vitro. Treg lineage stability was assessed by analysis of FOXP3 TSDR demethylation. Results The proportions and phenotypic characteristics of circulating CD4 Tregs were broadly similar between individuals with PD and HCs, as were Treg suppressive function and FOXP3 TSDR demethylation. However, naive CD4 Tregs from individuals with PD showed reduced HELIOS expression, with a similar but non-significant trend in FOXP3 expression. Reduced HELIOS expression was also observed in the CD8 naive Treg compartment. Conclusions Major quantitative or functional abnormalities in circulating Tregs do not appear to be a dominant feature PD. However, reduced HELIOS expression in naive Tregs suggests more subtle phenotypic alterations that warrant further investigation. The broadly preserved suppressive function is reassuring for therapeutic approaches aimed at increasing Treg numbers, although it will be important to establish that expanded Tregs retain a stable phenotype and suppressive function in inflammatory and tissue environments.
affiliations: University of Cambridge (corresponding author)

papers.title: Environmental Frass Remodels the Larval Gut Microbiome to Enable Black Soldier Fly (Hermetia illucens) Bioconversion of Livestock Manure
papers.abstract: Black Soldier Fly larvae (BSFL) consume nearly any organic material and show promise for the remediation of agricultural waste, including livestock manure. BSFL feeding generates frass, a mixture of unconsumed substrate, larval feces, and microorganisms. We identified a wild population of BSFL (Yuba strain) thriving on rabbit manure, a challenging substrate due to its high lignocellulose content. We investigated if frass extract from this source was necessary and sufficient to support bioconversion of manure and if such effects are altered by captive husbandry. Larvae supplemented with domestic frass failed to grow on rabbit manure but grew well when supplemented with wild-sourced frass. Microbiome analysis revealed that wild-sourced frass contributes a cohort of lignocellulose-degrading microorganisms to the BSFL gut, particularly Rummeliibacillus bacteria and Scedosporium fungi. These growth-promoting effects extended to cattle manure. Following initial seeding with wild-sourced frass, lab-cultured frass ultimately failed to support growth on rabbit manure and the gut microbiome shifted toward bacteria commonly found in domestic BSFL. This study reveals that frass extract derived from environmental sources can improve the bioconversion ability of BSFL and that beneficial microbes are lost during captive-rearing.
affiliations: University of California Merced (corresponding author)

papers.title: Polyphosphate metabolism genes are associated with hydroxyapatite biomineralization capacity in a novel hydrogenotrophic methanogen Methanobacterium AMB_03
papers.abstract: Methanogenic archaea play crucial roles in sedimentary phosphorus cycling, but their capacity for phosphate biomineralization remains poorly understood. Here we demonstrate that Methanobacterium AMB_03, isolated from a serpentinizing environment, mediates extracellular precipitation of carbonate-substituted hydroxyapatite (HAp) under phosphate-enriched conditions. Comparative genomic analysis of AMB_03 versus non-mineralizing strains (Methanobacterium oryzae, Methanoculleus bourgensis MAB1) shows that AMB_03 encodes polyphosphate kinase 1 (ppk1), enabling polyphosphate synthesis from ATP. In contrast, M. oryzae and MAB1 completely lack ppk1, preventing polyphosphate accumulation. Phylogenomic analysis of 320 Methanobacteriota genomes further shows that complete polyP cycling capacity is present in only ~25% of representatives, placing AMB_03 among a minority of methanogens with this capability. Experimental cultivation across phosphate gradients (0-6 mM) showed HAp early-onset precipitation was preferential at [≥]3 mM. Precipitation was eventually observed at all phosphate concentrations (except P0) by 49 weeks and was associated with extracellular polymeric substance production and localized pH increases of up to 8.08. Raman spectroscopy confirmed carbonate-substituted HAp, with characteristic peaks at 960.5 cm-1 (PO43-) and 1070-1072 cm-1 (CO32-). These findings identify a strong genomic association between polyphosphate metabolism genes and biomineralization capacity, suggesting that methanogens with complete polyP cycling systems may create localized phosphate-rich environments that promote authigenic mineral formation in sedimentary systems.
affiliations: Department of Earth Sciences, Uppsala University, Sweden (corresponding author)

papers.title: Structural and functional examination of Neisseria gonorrhoeae TfpC reveals a dynamic two-domain architecture required for type IV pilus function
papers.abstract: The Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Gc) Type IV pilus (T4p) is a critical apparatus for colonization and virulence. This molecular machine resides at the host-pathogen interface and mediates adherence to host cells, twitching motility, natural transformation, and resistance to oxidative agents. Previously, we identified a DUF4124 family, T4p component, TfpC. TfpC is required for full T4p elaboration, and deleting the tfpC gene reduced natural transformation competence and resulted in an under-piliated colony morphology. Our earlier models suggested TfpC is composed of an N-terminal transmembrane helix and a proline-rich disordered region followed by a C-terminal coiled-coil. Here, we used targeted structural and genetic approaches to define TfpC's molecular structure. Our new data show that TfpC's N-terminal domain forms a novel, dynamic three-stranded {beta}-sheet structure. These data indicate that the flexible disordered region acts as a linker between the N- and C-terminal domains. Functionally, we illustrate TfpC requires an acidic face within the C-terminal coiled-coil domain to mediate pilus biogenesis and function. This study characterizes a unique protein fold and family and defines the contributions of TfpC's domains to its function.
affiliations: King's College London (corresponding author)

papers.title: Seasonal H1N1 influenza A virus preferentially infects a pre-existing ciliogenesis-primed secretory cell state
papers.abstract: Influenza A viruses (IAV) infect secretory and ciliated cells of the human airway epithelium , but whether all cells within one cell type are equally susceptible to infection remains unresolved. Here, single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of primary human bronchial epithelial cultures from three donors identified preferential infection of a transcriptionally distinct subpopulation of secretory cells by seasonal H1N1 IAV A/Hawaii/70/2019 . Genes upregulated in this subpopulation showed enrichment for cilium-related gene ontology terms. In an ex post facto approach, this enrichment persisted after excluding genes differentially expressed between infected and mock-treated samples, including those identified in secretory cell-specific comparisons. Single-cell analysis further revealed no significant increase in ciliogenesis scores in infected secretory cells compared to mock infected cells at 6 hours post-infection , arguing against infection-induced activation of the canonical ciliogenesis programme during the initial viral replication cycle . Collectively, these results support preferential infection of ciliogenesis-primed secretory cells and refine IAV tropism beyond cell type to encompass epithelial differentiation state.
affiliations: Universität Zürich (corresponding author)

papers.title: MmuPV1 and HPV E6 Elevate Nuclear Accumulation of IKK? to Impair NF-κB Signaling to Promote Persistent Infection
papers.abstract: The mouse papillomavirus (MmuPV1) E6 oncoprotein is essential for persistent infection and cancer development. Previous studies identified amino acid R130 of MmuPV1 E6 as critical for its interaction with the tumor suppressor MAML1. Mutation of this residue (R130A) disrupts MAML1 binding and prevents disease development in mice. In this study, we demonstrate that MmuPV1 E6 also disrupts NF-{kappa}B signaling through interactions with proteins in the I{kappa}B kinase (IKK) complex. Specifically, the MmuPV1 E6R130A mutant is defective in binding IKK complex proteins and fails to impair NF-{kappa}B signaling in mouse keratinocytes, suggesting that these interactions are necessary for E6-mediated disruption of this pathway. Furthermore, MmuPV1 E6 expression is associated with increased nuclear localization of IKK?, whereas cells expressing the E6R130A mutant exhibit no such increase. These findings suggest that E6-mediated nuclear localization of IKK? depends on its interaction with IKK complex proteins. Importantly, we demonstrate that the human papillomavirus HPV16 E6 oncoprotein similarly impairs NF-{kappa}B signaling and increases nuclear IKK? localization in human keratinocytes, suggesting a shared mechanism between mouse and human papillomaviruses. Additionally, analysis of previously published RNA sequencing data reveals that MmuPV1 E6 induces several transcriptional changes associated with increased nuclear IKK?. Together, these findings demonstrate that both MmuPV1 and HPV16 E6 disrupt NF-{kappa}B signaling in association with increased nuclear IKK? localization. This study provides the first evidence of an E6 oncoprotein interacting with and changing subcellular localization of IKK? to disrupt cellular homeostasis.
affiliations: Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: SPARK: Systematic Profiling of Antibiotic-Phage Response Kinetics
papers.abstract: Phage therapy is, in practice, combination therapy: phage are almost always added to an ongoing antibiotic regimen, yet the combination is rarely designed to have a specific interaction pattern. Interactions can be antagonistic, additive or synergistic and cannot be inferred from either agent alone. Here we introduce SPARK, a method which quantifies phage antibiotic interaction from growth curves as the integrated deviation of observed growth from the growth expected under Bliss independence. We profiled 42 combinations spanning the ESKAPE pathogens and Escherichia coli with twelve antibiotics. We show that i) synergy and antagonism are resolvable within a single high-throughput assay, with the interaction determined by the phage antibiotic bacteria pairing; ii) 21 clinical Staphylococcus aureus isolates differ among themselves as widely as the seven species do; and, iii) interactions change between a few hours and two days, several reversing direction. Overall, SPARK needs only a plate reader and the analysis is performed with a specific openly available web tool.
affiliations: Uppsala University (corresponding author)

papers.title: The role of Plasmodium falciparum acyl-coenzyme A synthetase 10 in fatty acid acquisition and lipid synthesis
papers.abstract: During the asexual blood stage, malaria parasites synthesize large quantities of lipids to support their rapid proliferation. Exogenous fatty acids obtained from host plasma are activated for lipid synthesis by parasite acyl-coenzyme A synthetases (ACSs). Of the twelve Plasmodium falciparum ACS homologs, ACS10 has emerged as a key blood-stage enzyme. Here, we sought to define the role of ACS10 in fatty acid acquisition and lipid synthesis during asexual development. To accomplish this, we have employed fatty acid alkyne probes of parasite lipid synthesis together with selective depletion of ACS10 in a conditional knockdown parasite line. This approach revealed that ACS10 is required for efficient incorporation of 16- to 20-carbon unsaturated fatty acid alkynes and a 20-carbon, saturated fatty acid alkyne into the major parasite phospholipids and neutral lipids. In contrast, shorter saturated fatty acid alkynes were either unaffected by ACS10 depletion or were hyper-incorporated into parasite lipids. ACS10 knockdown elicited a profound deformation of the food vacuole, which was likely caused by an imbalance of saturated and unsaturated fatty acids in parasite lipids. To promote the discovery and characterization of ACS inhibitors, we have established a fatty acid alkyne-based approach for identifying compounds that target ACS10 as their primary mode of action.
affiliations: Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Quantitative trait loci mapping identifies genetic loci modifying MafAS64F-mediated dysglycemia
papers.abstract: Increasing evidence has shown the role of genetic background on the penetrance of monogenic diabetes. A missense mutation of the pancreatic {beta}-cell-enriched transcription factor MafA co-segregates with diabetes (MafA-MODY) and non-syndromic insulinomatosis. We recently investigated the effects of genetic background on MafAS64F-driven dysglycemia in genetically diverse mice harboring this mutation. Here we leveraged the effects of genetic background on phenotypic penetrance to map quantitative trait loci (QTL) potentially modifying glycemia in response to this variant. We investigated MafaS64F/+ mice from an F2 intercross of the C57BL/6J and SJL/J genetic backgrounds through oral glucose tolerance testing at 4, 5, 6, and 8 weeks of age to evaluate glucose tolerance and glycemic trajectory. All F2 mice were genetically monitored for single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) between the C57BL/6J and SJL/J backgrounds, allowing us to identify modifying loci on 6 chromosomes (2, 126 Mbp; 3, 59 Mbp and 103 Mbp; 7, 47 Mbp; 11 45 Mbp; 13, 4 Mbp; and 16, 85-97 Mbp), containing 172 candidate genes. For example, known MODY genes Abcc8 (Sur1) and Kcnj11 (Kir6.2) are within the QTL region on chromosome 7 and contain polymorphisms between backgrounds that may impart combinatorial effects on the phenotypic penetrance of MafAS64F-mediated dysglycemia
affiliations: Vanderbilt University Medical Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Overlapping enhancer activity robustly regulates rax expression during ocular development in zebrafish
papers.abstract: Vertebrate eye development relies on the tightly regulated yet highly dynamic spatiotemporal expression of eye field transcription factors that coordinate developmental programs required for the formation of a functional eye. The gene rax is among the earliest expressed eye field transcription factors and is specifically associated with ocular-fated tissue. It encodes a transcription factor that is essential for optic vesicle evagination, the precursor to the optic cup and retina. Although the developmental functions of rax are well characterized, the cis-regulatory elements that control its expression remain poorly understood. Using zebrafish (Danio rerio), I identified five novel ocular enhancers and demonstrate that they drive similar spatiotemporal expression patterns as rax at three key stages of eye development. Furthermore, I performed an in-depth characterization of two enhancers and demonstrate that they exhibit substantial transcript-level overlap with endogenous rax expression during development. Additionally, through the generation of enhancer deletion lines, I further demonstrate that the gene regulatory network (GRN) controlling rax expression is largely robust to individual and combinatorial enhancer perturbations. However, perturbation of this regulatory network can result in rax-associated ocular abnormalities, including microphthalmia and anophthalmia. Together, these findings highlight the importance of studying developmental ocular enhancers to better understand the functions of noncoding genomic regions and provide insight into potential causes of unexplained congenital eye disease.
affiliations: University of Pittsburgh (corresponding author)

papers.title: Pseudo-observations of longevity improve detection of resilience-associated genes in the Radiation Late Effects Cohort of rhesus macaques.
papers.abstract: Non-human primates are an ideal model for interrogating the genetic basis of human lifespan and resilience due to their long lifespan compared to other model organisms, development of similar age-related chronic conditions, and genetic similarity. However, like humans, statistical methods for modeling survival suffer from the challenges of dealing with non-proportionality of hazards, large numbers of living individuals that must be censored, and loss-to-follow-up over studies that may last a decade or more. Here we overcome these challenges through the use of pseudo-observations of Restricted Mean Survival Time as a measure of resilience to the acute challenge of radiation exposure and chronic challenges of aging and a Western-style diet in rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) from the Wake Forest Non-Human Primate Radiation Late Effects Cohort. Our whole-exome analysis used Genome-wide Efficient Mixed Model Association (GEMMA) to identify variants associated with longevity, and a subsequent Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) highlighted the cadherin and integrin signaling pathways as central to this resilience. As dysregulation of cell adhesion and extracellular matrix signaling is central to the development of fibrosis, we tested the functional relevance of these signals using a targeted Combined Annotation Dependent Depletion (CADD) score-weighted Sequence Kernel Association Test-Optimal (SKAT-O) analysis of GSEA leading-edge genes from both the cadherin and integrin pathways. This linked variant burden in PCDHGA5, PCDHGA3, PCDHGB2, PCDHA11, and PSENEN to the severity of myocardial fibrosis, and in IBSP, PDGFD, and LAMC2 to the severity of pulmonary fibrosis observed at necropsy. Critically, we note that the genetic variants are not caused by the radiation but rather create an underlying risk for disease that is then exacerbated by the acute and persistent stressors challenging these animals' intrinsic resilience. The success of this method in identifying biologically relevant genetic variants underlying survival in animals undergoing a strong challenge to their resilience highlights not only the role of genes predisposing animals to fibrosis in lifespan, but the overall utility of pseudo-observations in overcoming the limitations of survival analyses in humans and other long-lived species.
affiliations: Wake Forest University School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Chromosome-level genome assembly of Greenland scurvy-grass (Cochlearia groenlandica) reveals extensive centromeric satellite arrays
papers.abstract: We present a chromosome-level, haplotype-resolved genome assembly from Greenland scurvy-grass (Cochlearia groenlandica). The assembly comprises two pseudo-haplotypes of 322 Mb and 295 Mb, with 89.7% and 95.6% respectively, each scaffolded into 7 chromosomes. Assembly completeness is high (BUSCO 97.8% in each haplotype), with 34,213 and 29,684 annotated protein-coding genes for haplotypes one and two, respectively. The chromosomes contain extensive centromeric satellite arrays that cover up to half of some chromosomes. Their precise functional boundaries remain undetermined.
affiliations: Department of Biosciences, University of Oslo (corresponding author)

papers.title: Mutation and Recombination Rates in Free-Ranging Polar Bears
papers.abstract: Mutation rate () and recombination rate (r) are fundamental population-genetic parameters, yet demographic and conservation inference in polar bears (Ursus maritimus) has relied on values borrowed from humans and other mammals. Known values vary by an order of magnitude across mammals, and inaccuracies in these estimates propagate into downstream analyses, such as inferences of demographic history. To address this, we used high-coverage whole-genome resequencing of eight parent-offspring trios from the Western Hudson Bay subpopulation of polar bears. We identified 329 de novo mutations and estimated a pedigree-based germline mutation rate of 1.22 x 10?? per site per generation, which is within the mammalian range and close to values previously assumed for this species. Trio-based phasing yielded 522 crossovers across 16 meioses (32.6 per meiosis), and a pedigree-inferred recombination rate of 1.50 cM/Mb. From 44 unrelated individuals sampled from the same subpopulation, we inferred a demography-aware recombination map with a length-weighted genome-wide recombination rate of 3.03 cM/Mb (median 1.28 cM/Mb). We also identified 8,515 recombination hotspot regions covering 2.10% of the genome, accounting for 43.8% of total map length, a 20.9-fold concentration. Crossovers overlapped LD-defined hotspots 5.06-fold more often than expected by chance (p < 0.001). Nucleotide diversity was low and positively rank-correlated with recombination rate, consistent with linked selection. Genomic features explained only ~3% of recombination rate variation, with GC content and SINE abundance the only significant predictors. These species-specific parameters provide an empirical foundation for future demographic reconstruction and population projection in this vulnerable, ice-obligate species.
affiliations: Trent University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Segment-dependent phylogenetic resolution reveals geographic and host sampling gaps in Oropouche virus genomes
papers.abstract: Background. Oropouche virus (OROV) has been reported in areas beyond its historical Amazonian range since 2023, accompanied by rapid growth in publicly available genomic data. However, the extent to which these data provide reliable phylogenetic and epidemiological resolution, and whether that resolution differs among genome segments, has not been systematically examined. Methods. Nucleotide sequences annotated under Orthobunyavirus oropoucheense were retrieved from NCBI Virus (accessed 13 May 2025) and filtered to retain records at least 70% of the reference length for each segment, yielding 898 S, 831 M, and 832 L sequences. Segments were aligned independently with MAFFT, and maximum-likelihood phylogenies were inferred with IQ-TREE using ModelFinder and ultrafast bootstrap approximation. Trees were annotated with collection date, country, and host in iTOL. Results. Phylogenetic resolution differed among segments. Contemporary Brazilian sequences formed a largely unresolved region in the S segment tree, whereas the M and L trees resolved recent clusters to differing degrees. Resolution did not track segment length: the M tree resolved contemporary structure more strongly than the longer L tree, and total tree length was approximately 3.5 times greater in the M tree despite near-identical taxon sampling. Sequences collected before 2010 were recovered in supported clusters in all three segment trees, although their configuration differed by segment. These sequences were also predominantly non-Brazilian and non-human, preventing collection date, geographic origin, and host from being separated as explanations for the observed clustering. The species-level query also retained three reassortant viruses, which may influence segment-specific topologies; sequences annotated to the United States were Iquitos virus rather than OROV. Two Italian sequences clustered with Cuban sequences across all three trees, concordant with published travel histories. Conclusions. Publicly available sequences contain phylogenetic structure that differs among the S, M, and L segment trees, but interpretation is constrained by uneven temporal, geographic, and host sampling and by the inclusion of reassortant species in a species-level dataset. The concentration of sequences from Brazil and human hosts, together with limited representation of non-human hosts, restricts inference about OROV diversity and ecology. Broader and more balanced genomic surveillance would improve the ability to resolve OROV evolutionary and transmission patterns.
affiliations: Ross University School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Transcriptome profiling reveals gene regulatory network governing seed size in Brassica napus
papers.abstract: Seed size is a critical trait influencing yield and quality in oilseed crops such as Brassica napus. Despite their economic importance, the genetic and molecular mechanisms regulating seed size remain unclear, particularly in polyploid species, such as B. napus. To deepen our understanding of seed size regulation, we performed a comprehensive transcriptomic analysis across four developmental stages (heart, torpedo, green, and mature) and three distinct seed organs: the seed coat, embryo, and endosperm. Differential expression analysis between B. napus var. Zhongshuang (ZS11) and B. napus cv. Ragged Jack (RJ) was performed to uncover regulatory networks involved in seed size control. Our results uncovered dynamic gene regulatory networks (GRNs) and pinpointed key regulators, including well-established factors like ABI5 and BRI1, as well as novel candidate genes such as KNAT5, ARF11, SUS2, UGT72B1, UGT89A2, and SBT1.7. The present research provides an understanding of the regulatory networks governing seed size in B. napus. These findings not only enhance our knowledge of seed biology but also offer valuable resources for future breeding strategies aimed at optimizing seed size and yield in polyploid oilseed crops.
affiliations: Rothamsted Research (corresponding author)

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Personalised Gene Expression Prediction Improves Cell-Type-Specific Association Testing
papers.abstract: Linking genetic variation to disease requires accurate prediction of its effects on gene expression in relevant cell types. Sequence-to-function models offer a way to predict these effects and, with training on personal genomes, have begun to capture inter-individual expression differences. However, effect sign accuracy remains limited, and predictive uncertainty is unquantified. Here we introduce ATTICUS, which combines personalised sequence representations with uncertainty-aware expression prediction. ATTICUS transfers regulatory information learned in bulk expression pretraining to cell-type-specific expression prediction without requiring genotypes paired with single-cell expression data. Across blood and brain cell types in OneK1K and ROSMAP, ATTICUS approximately doubles expression prediction correlations relative to scPrediXcan and substantially improves sign accuracy. Moreover, ATTICUS enables uncertainty-aware transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS). Applied to systemic lupus erythematosus and Alzheimer's disease, ATTICUS identifies more associations, with greater cell-type specificity and stronger directional concordance, and reduced statistical inflation. Together, our results demonstrate that personalised training makes predictions more directionally consistent, and uncertainty propagation improves the calibration of TWAS and the prioritisation of disease genes. ATTICUS provides a framework for both, enabling the use of single-cell expression datasets without matched genotypes to inform uncertainty-aware TWAS, expanding their use in prioritising disease-associated genes and cell types.
affiliations: ETH Zurich (corresponding author)

papers.title: Integrating bacterial genomics and host transcriptomics links Burkholderia pseudomallei variation to melioidosis mortality and neutrophil responses
papers.abstract: Bacterial genetic variation contributes to the outcome of infection, but its relationship with host immune responses is rarely investigated in the same patients, limiting the biological interpretation of pathogen-associated disease severity. Here, we integrated pathogen genomics, clinical outcomes and host transcriptomics to investigate host-pathogen interactions in melioidosis, a frequently fatal infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei. We analysed prospective clinical data from 2,142 patients, whole-genome sequences from 2,101 infecting isolates and 646 paired host blood transcriptomes across five cohorts collected between 2012 and 2023. Infections were typically dominated by a single strain, with limited within-host diversification, supporting the use of an infecting isolate genome to investigate pathogen-associated clinical outcomes. Bacterial genome-wide association studies identified one locus associated with binary mortality at genome-wide significance. Incorporating patient age, sex, body mass index and Charlson Comorbidity Index increased this to four, while modelling time to death as a continuous phenotype identified seven loci. Integration with paired host transcriptomes linked mortality-associated bacterial genetic variation to imputed signatures of increased immature neutrophils and reduced neutrophil degranulation. An intergenic region upstream of the polyketide synthesis locus BPSS1006-BPSS1011 was additionally associated with downregulation of host genes involved in myeloid-cell signalling and cell proliferation pathways. These findings connect naturally occurring B. pseudomallei genomic variation associated with mortality to distinct host immune signatures, providing insight into pathogen-host interactions underlying severe melioidosis and a framework for investigating the contribution of pathogen genetic diversity to clinical outcomes.
affiliations: Mahidol-Oxford Tropical Medicine Research Unit, Faculty of Tropical Medicine, Mahidol University, Bangkok, Thailand (corresponding author)

papers.title: Synergy-informed bilevel optimization reveals joint-specific benefits for realistic exoskeleton torque prediction
papers.abstract: Simulation-driven optimization can guide exoskeleton control design, but its utility is limited by the accuracy with which muscle coordination is predicted. Strict effort-minimization formulations predict non-physiological muscle shutdown under high exoskeleton assistance, leading to peak assistive torques that exceed values reported in human-in-the-loop experiments. We evaluated the accuracy of synergy-informed simulations at predicting assistance across four single-joint exoskeleton configurations: ankle plantarflexion, knee extension, hip flexion, and hip abduction. We implemented a bilevel optimization to predict a parameterized assistive torque that minimizes metabolic cost, with assisted muscle dynamics estimated via either effort-minimization simulations (minimizing muscle effort only) or synergy-informed simulations (minimizing muscle effort constrained to a synergy structure). We used experimental data from five unimpaired adults walking at their preferred speed and compared results descriptively between the two formulations within each subject. Assistance based on effort-minimization simulations shut down agonist muscle activations and overestimated peak assistive torque compared with experimental values. In contrast, constraining muscle controls to a synergy structure prevented non-physiological muscle shutdown and yielded assistive torques closer to those measured in human-in-the-loop experiments. This benefit was not observed equally across all assisted degrees of freedom or subjects, emerging only where no single synergy could be suppressed to unload the assisted muscles. Synergy weights can therefore be interpreted as joint-specific predictors of when simulations can reliably inform wearable robot design.

papers.title: Rapid generation of antibody conformational ensembles using machine learning
papers.abstract: We introduce Cadense, a generative framework for antibody ensemble prediction that produces diverse Fv structures from sequence, informed by conformational dynamics. While a valuable resource, static structure prediction provides only a single snapshot of dynamic proteins, whose motions influence their binding and other properties. This is particularly relevant for antibodies, an important class of molecules for drug discovery, where flexible complementarity determining region (CDR) loops are difficult to model with static approaches. Cadense addresses this gap by generating ensembles that match conformational and biophysical property distributions from molecular dynamics (MD), while reducing the computational burden from days of simulation to seconds of generation. We show Cadense ensembles can recover both apo and holo conformations of the same antibody and serve as effective input to physics-based docking, capturing the conformational flexibility important to properly model antibody antigen interactions. Together, these results establish Cadense as a useful tool for antibody conformational ensemble generation with the promise to enable faster, dynamics-aware antibody design.
affiliations: Genentech (corresponding author)

papers.title: PEEK: integrated primer design for silent-mutation and restriction-site engineering, validated in silico and by whole-plasmid sequencing
papers.abstract: Motivation: Silent introduction of restriction sites, direct site insertion, and verification of the result are routine operations in molecular cloning, yet they are typically distributed across separate tools built on inconsistent thermodynamics. Primer design is itself mature and heavily validated; the gap is not accuracy in principle but integration, together with the absence of any explicit account of why one synonymous edit should be preferred over another. Because melting temperature (Tm) gates which primers a tool will accept, any unified tool must first be shown to compute Tm correctly against an external standard, and then shown to produce the edits it proposes. Results: PEEK, a web-based toolkit, unifies silent-mutation discovery, restriction-site insertion, and amplification and screening primer design built on a single thermodynamic model of primer melting temperature (Tm). PEEK's silent-mutation engine identifies the smallest set of synonymous changes required to form a restriction site at a specific position, and ranks the options by codon usage, local mRNA folding, and edit size. Predicted melting temperatures closely matched those of the NEB Q5 Tm Calculator across 17 primers of varying length and GC content (Pearson R^2 = 0.9995, mean absolute error 1.32 C) without any fitted correction, and annealing-temperature (Ta) recommendations exactly matched NEB's rules. In independent trials, a total of 15 silent-mutation designs were translationally silent and contained the intended restriction site. Experimental validation was performed by installing a KpnI site into a 9.9 kb lentiviral CAR plasmid using both a silent-mutation primer and an insertion primer. Whole-plasmid sequencing confirmed that each primer introduced exactly the designed changes, with no off-target differences across the construct and no change to the encoded protein. Availability and implementation: PEEK runs at https://peekbiology.com and requires no registration. Source code, documentation, and test data are available at https://github.com/nkura-arch/PEEK-Protein-Engineering Efficiency-Kit. Implemented in Python 3.11 with Flask, Biopython, and ViennaRNA. Contact: nathan.singh@wustl.edu
affiliations: Washington University School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Contrasting within-donor gene covariation identifies disease-associated cells and genes in case-control single-cell studies
papers.abstract: In case-control single-cell studies, disease often affects only a subset of cells of a given type within each patient. Comparing all cells from patients with all cells from control donors therefore dilutes disease signals, while donor variation and recorded or unrecorded batch effects can be confounded with disease status. We present IDC (Identification of Disease-associated Cells), which uses this cellular heterogeneity as signal. A mixture of affected and unaffected cells creates coordinated variation among disease-associated genes within each patient, whereas shifts shared by all cells of a donor leave this within-donor covariance unchanged. IDC therefore contrasts within-donor gene-gene covariance between patients and controls to learn disease-associated expression programs without batch labels, then applies positive-unlabeled learning to score each cell's disease-like state and estimate each donor's disease burden. IDC also computes, in closed form, gene contribution scores and leave-gene-out cell scores that exclude each tested gene, enabling within-donor differential expression testing and cross-donor meta-analysis without retraining. In simulations, IDC identified affected cells and estimated donor burden more accurately than deep generative and label-refinement methods, remained robust to strong unrecorded batch effects, and detected differentially expressed genes more sensitively than case-control pseudobulk methods while controlling false discoveries. In human pancreatic islets and prefrontal cortex, disease burden in held-out donors separated type 2 diabetes (T2D) from non-diabetic donors in beta cells, and late-stage Alzheimer's disease (AD) from non-AD donors in astrocytes and inhibitory neurons, while placing prediabetic and early-AD donors at intermediate levels. Genes with the highest IDC contribution scores were more strongly enriched for the KEGG T2D and AD pathways than case-control pseudobulk rankings, and within-donor testing revealed coordinated metabolic, cell-adhesion and synaptic changes along the inferred disease axis.
affiliations: Center for Computational Biology and Bioinformatics, Department of Medical and Molecular Genetics, Indiana University School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Unveiling immune targets via TriStageHLA: high-throughput screening of peptide presentation, peptide-HLA binding, and immunogenicity
papers.abstract: High-throughput screening of HLA class I epitopes underpins neoantigen vaccine design, T cell therapies, and pathogen immune monitoring, yet proteome-scale prioritization remains challenging under severe class imbalance. We present TriStageHLA, a compact three-stage framework that decomposes epitope discovery into peptide-only screening (PRE), allele-specific binding/presentation prediction (BIND), and immunogenicity prediction (IM). PRE performs early pruning via a LoRA-adapted ESM-2 classifier; BIND integrates quantitative binding affinity and eluted ligand data with a dual-branch architecture combining global cross-attention and local motif extraction; IM is fine-tuned on curated human T-cell assay data with a decoupled LoRA head. Trained on IEDB-derived datasets with per-allele balancing and allele-discordant supervision, TriStageHLA-BIND achieves AUROC of 96.2% and AUPRC of 95.2% on combined BA/EL evaluation, while TriStageHLA-IM reaches AUROC of 81.4\% and AUPRC of 73.8\% on held-out immunogenicity data, improving over the strongest immunogenicity baselines ImmuneApp (70.7% / 63.6%) and BigMHC-IM (60.1% / 51.5%). With substantially fewer trainable parameters than prior models, TriStageHLA enables efficient, calibrated epitope prioritization across binding, presentation, and immunogenicity. Code and pretrained weights are available at https://github.com/SkywalkerLuke/TriStageHLA.
affiliations: City University of Hong Kong (corresponding author)

papers.title: AOPTK: Open-Source Software for AI-Assisted Toxicological Literature Analysis
papers.abstract: Motivation: Toxicologists today face a challenge: although vast amounts of data describing how chemicals affect human health are available across scientific publications and regulatory reports, much of this information remains underutilized because extracting and interpreting evidence across thousands of studies is impractical to perform manually. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly in large language models (LLMs), provide new opportunities to automate toxicological literature analysis. Results: Herein, we present the Adverse Outcome Pathway Toolkit (AOPTK), an open-source Python package for AI-enhanced analysis of toxicological and biomedical literature. AOPTK supports (i) automated literature retrieval from databases such as PubMed Central and Europe PMC, (ii) direct processing of full-text articles in PDF format, and (iii) LLM-assisted analysis tools to identify chemicals and extract their relationships to biological effects under user-defined conditions. We demonstrate its utilities through a case-study identifying potential non-genotoxic carcinogens based on their ability to inhibit gap junction intercellular communication (GJIC). The LLM-enhanced analysis achieves 81% agreement with an expert-curated inhibitor list and 95% accuracy in predicting inhibition versus no inhibition when analysing the same subset of 86 publications. Automated retrieval and analysis of 1 124 publications from PubMed Central further demonstrated the feasibility of applying AOPTK to large-scale literature analyses. Availability: The package is developed open source on GitHub, disseminated through PyPI and Bioconda and releases are archived on Zenodo. Individual tools are available in the Galaxy platform for accessible data analysis with user-friendly, findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR) and end-to-end workflows provided via WorkflowHub. The tools are available on usegalaxy.eu and usegalaxy.cz and are developed open source on GitHub.
affiliations: RECETOX, Faculty of Science, Masaryk University, Kotlarska 2, 611 37 Brno, Czech Republic (corresponding author)

papers.title: scHiR learns joint cellular representations from paired single-cell transcriptome and 3D genome data
papers.abstract: Simultaneously sequenced scRNA-seq and scHi-C technologies provide matched measurements of gene expression and three-dimensional (3D) genome organization within individual cells, offering complementary insights into cellular state. However, integrative analysis remains challenging due to the heterogeneous structures and characteristics of these modalities. To realize the full potential of such data, we need effective computational methods to learn joint cellular representations. Here, we present scHiR, a framework based on a hyperspherical variational autoencoder (S-VAE) for learning co-embeddings from paired gene-expression profiles and chromatin contact maps. The framework facilitate downstream analyses such as cell clustering, fine-grained cell-state characterization, and developmental trajectory inference, while modality-specific decoders enable the signal recovery of input profiles. We evaluated scHiR across six paired datasets generated by HiRES, GAGE-seq, and LiMCA. scHiR captured cell-type-specific information and achieved improved clustering performance compared with representative single-omics methods. It was also capable of resolving fine-grained subclusters and revealed discordant and distinct cellular profiles. In developmental biological datasets, scHiR preserved trajectory-related structure and improved pseudotime in agreement with known developmental progression. Finally, scHiR generated reconstructed transcriptomic and chromatin contact profiles with reduced noise, enhanced cell-type-related signals, and improved recovery of held-out chromatin contacts. These results demonstrate that scHiR provides an effective method for learning joint cellular representations from paired scRNA-seq and scHi-C data.
affiliations: Central South University (corresponding author)

papers.title: PyTorch Frustratometer: An Ultra-fast, Parallelized Tool for Proteome-Scale Local Energetic Frustration Analysis
papers.abstract: Most natural protein sequences fold into well-defined three-dimensional structural ensembles, satisfying interactions that have been shaped over evolutionary timescales. The principle of minimal frustration states that most native interactions are energetically more favorable than alternative non-native ones, resulting in a funnel-shaped folding energy landscape. The FrustratometeR tool measures how the energetics of a residue or contact compares to decoys with different amino acid identities or configurations. Contacts are classified as minimally frustrated when these are more stable than random alternatives, highly frustrated when less stable, or neutral when energetically indistinguishable from them. Clusters of highly frustrated interactions are often evolutionarily conserved and are typically associated with functional regions. Therefore, identifying and quantifying local frustration can provide insights into both protein stability and function. Here we present a PyTorch reimplementation of FrustratometeR that accelerates conventional frustration calculations by 70-13,000x on a single GPU, depending on chosen frustration mode and protein size, with substantially larger gains for exhaustive mutational scanning, enabling proteome-scale local frustration analysis. We benchmark against the original algorithm on the CATH v4.4 S40 dataset and show near-identical results across all three frustration modes and mutational scanning. Source code is freely available at https://github.com/ParraLab-ESBG/pytorch-frustratometer.
affiliations: Evolutionary Systems Biophysics Group, Life Sciences Department, Barcelona Supercomputing Center, Barcelona, Spain (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Deformulating Multi-Attribute SEC Method for Simultaneous Quantification of Total RNA, Conjugated Antibody, and Free Antibody in Targeted Lipid Nanoparticles
papers.abstract: Targeted lipid nanoparticles (tLNPs) hold promise for improving cell- and tissue-selective delivery of therapeutic payloads but introduce analytical challenges associated with characterizing both encapsulated cargo and surface-associated targeting ligands within the same formulation. Conventional nucleic acid and protein assays can be affected by nanoparticle scattering, matrix interference, or a limited ability to distinguish conjugated antibody from free antibody. Here, we report an online deformulating size-exclusion high-performance liquid chromatography (SE-HPLC) method that enables simultaneous quantification of total RNA, conjugated antibody, and free antibody from 5 L of tLNP sample. Following injection, exposure to a mobile phase containing sodium dodecyl sulfate and isopropanol disrupts the nanoparticles, enabling chromatographic separation of RNA, conjugated antibody, and free (unconjugated) antibody while minimizing sample handling prior to analysis. RNA was quantified by UV260 detection, whereas antibody was quantified by UV280 or intrinsic fluorescence detection to maximize sensitivity. The method demonstrated linear response over the evaluated concentration ranges, spike recoveries of 88-122%, and precision below 5% relative standard deviation. Application to purified tLNP formulations demonstrated simultaneous assessment of total RNA and conjugated antibody content, while confirming the absence of detectable free antibody following purification. Together, these results establish online deformulating SE-HPLC as a practical multi-attribute analytical method for characterization of tLNPs, enabling concurrent assessment of total RNA concentration, conjugated antibody concentration, and free antibody concentration using standard HPLC instrumentation.
affiliations: ModeX Therapeutics (corresponding author)

papers.title: Engineering Nanobody Conformational Switches
papers.abstract: Conformational signaling is widely used in biology, but remains difficult to engineer into proteins. Here, we explore ligand-induced folding of nanobodies as a general strategy to generate conformational receptors for a broad range of target ligands. More specifically, we have generated partially unfolded nanobody variants that fold exclusively upon binding to their target ligand. To do so, we have introduced destabilizing mutations in the framework region, carefully tuning their stability while preserving molecular recognition. Given the high conservation of the framework across different nanobodies, this approach is broadly applicable to many other target ligands, which has enabled us to engineer conformational switches for three different important biomarkers and drugs: the pregnancy hormone chorionic gonadotropin, the cytokine tumor necrosis factor alpha, and the chemotherapy and immunosuppressant drug methotrexate. Another useful property of conformational signaling is that it can directly gate signal transduction, which we have leveraged to build an optical sensor for the quantitative detection of the pregnancy hormone in urine. Finally, conformational signaling introduces new mechanisms for the allosteric modulation of binding, which we have explored to control the affinity and dynamic range of the sensor. Our work thus establishes a rational strategy for engineering conformational signaling receptors with customizable properties and generalizable for many different target ligands.
affiliations: CIC bioGUNE (corresponding author)

papers.title: sPLA2 inhibitor-loaded nanoparticles mitigate spontaneous osteoarthritis in guinea pigs
papers.abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a prevalent degenerative joint disease lacking effective disease-modifying therapies. Secreted phospholipase A2 (sPLA2), a key upstream regulator of inflammatory lipid mediators, has been implicated in OA pathogenesis, but its therapeutic potential in age-related OA remains unclear. Here, we evaluated the role of sPLA2 and the efficacy of nanoparticle-mediated sPLA2 inhibition in a spontaneous OA model using female Dunkin-Hartley (DH) guinea pigs. We first characterized OA progression and observed age-dependent increases in cartilage degeneration, synovitis, oxidative stress, and sPLA2 expression and enzymatic activity. We then developed sPLA2 inhibitor (thioetheramide-PC)-loaded nanoparticles (sPLA2i-NPs) and demonstrated their superior ability, compared to free inhibitor, to prevent IL-1{beta}-induced cartilage degeneration in guinea pig cartilage explants. In vivo, intra-articular administration of sPLA2i-NPs from 3 months of age significantly attenuated cartilage destruction, synovial inflammation, and osteophyte formation in 7- and 10-month-old guinea pigs. These structural improvements were accompanied by normalization of anabolic and catabolic gene expression and a marked reduction in synovial fluid sPLA2 activity. Importantly, longitudinal gait analysis revealed that sPLA2i-NP treatment preserved limb loading, propulsion, and locomotor performance, demonstrating functional recovery. No systemic toxicity was observed following long-term treatment. Collectively, our findings identify sPLA2 as a key driver of spontaneous OA and establish nanoparticle-mediated sPLA2 inhibition as a promising disease-modifying strategy for age-related OA.
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania (corresponding author)

papers.title: Choice of annotation data significantly impacts automated reconstruction of genome-scale metabolic networks
papers.abstract: Genome-scale metabolic models are valuable tools for studying metabolism in many applications, such as metabolic engineering or understanding human disease. However, curated models are available for only a limited number of organisms, and generating high-quality models for additional organisms remains a challenge. To help address this challenge, several software tools have been developed that can produce draft models in an automated fashion, but the quality of these draft models lags behind manually curated ones. Thus, there is still a need to improve these tools. Previous work has focused primarily on developing better methods for each step in the reconstruction process, such as gene annotation and gap-filling. Here, we focus on the data that underlies these methods, such as known connections between protein sequence and function. We find that changing the source of reconstruction data has a substantial impact on the contents and predictions of generated models. In fact, the source of data can have a bigger impact than the choice of reconstruction method. Additionally, we show that the reconstruction process is sensitive to the accuracy of gene annotations in the reconstruction data. Finally, we demonstrate the importance of having functional annotation data from an organism that is closely related to the one for which a model is being built. These observations highlight the importance of reconstruction data and identify principles that should be considered when selecting data for reconstruction tools.
affiliations: University of Virginia (corresponding author)

papers.title: Calibrating developmental dynamics from single-cell atlases: lineage paths outrun least-action routes
papers.abstract: Single-cell atlases infer developmental dynamics from destructive snapshots, yet how far realized lineage paths depart from such inferred dynamics has never been measured with controls. We introduce LADD (Least-Action Developmental Dynamics), a measurement framework that learns a stochastic developmental vector field from time-series single-cell RNA-seq and computes minimum-action and minimum-time paths, together with a three-layer calibration protocol that separates genuine path deviation from the generic cost of centroid measurement, and we compare its forecasting component with optimal-transport and flow-matching methods. In the lineage-resolved Caenorhabditis elegans atlas, the raw action ratio of observed lineage-centroid trajectories to optimal paths is 3.79, yet forward-simulated ensembles of the learned model itself score 2.07, leaving a genuine excess of about two-fold. In zebrafish (Danio rerio), the observed ratio sits entirely at the model's floor. Three mechanisms that could explain the residual deviation (detours, flow-opposition, and fate-map complexity) are each excluded; what remains is speed, with lineages moving 30-43% faster along the learned flow. We report validity boundaries for temporal resolution, cross-species comparison, and energetic interpretation, delimiting where action-based trajectory comparisons are meaningful.
affiliations: Jinan University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Low-fidelity simulator selection for multi-fidelity inference of epithelial vertex models
papers.abstract: Vertex models link cell division, neighbour exchange, and intercellular forces to epithelial tissue form through parameters such as junctional line tension and perimeter contractility. Bayesian inference of these parameters from data quantifies their uncertainty, but for stochastic models of proliferating tissues it requires many costly simulations. Multi-fidelity simulation-based inference reduces this cost by training on many runs of a cheaper, less accurate ('low-fidelity') simulator before refining with a few full ('high-fidelity') runs. Low-fidelity versions can be constructed in several ways, for example by stopping simulations early, coarsening the timestep, or averaging fewer replicates, but it is unclear which to choose before committing to costly training. To address this, we introduce PRISM (Paired Ranking Index for Simulator Matching), a screen that compares each candidate with the full simulator on paired runs, scoring agreement in cell-packing statistics against cost. For a vertex model of a proliferating tissue, PRISM flags stopping early as unreliable before training; once trained, this choice can produce confidently wrong parameter estimates. By contrast, a coarser timestep, within the range tested, is cheap and accurate; while fewer replicates are accurate but too costly. Using a screened low-fidelity simulator, multi-fidelity inference outperforms approximate Bayesian computation and neural-network inference trained on full simulations alone, at matched cost and with well-calibrated uncertainty. The same pattern recurs for a second vertex model fitted to published Drosophila pupal-wing imaging data, although there stopping halfway proves safe. Together, our findings suggest that which approximations are safe depends on the model, and that screening them before training makes multi-fidelity inference of tissue mechanics practical.
affiliations: University of Sheffield (corresponding author)

papers.title: Structural evolution of Fcα/μR-mediated antibody recognition
papers.abstract: The Fc alpha-mu receptor (Fc/R) is an ancient Fc-receptor sharing common ancestry with the polymeric Ig receptor (pIgR) and binding polymeric IgM and IgA ligands. In several vertebrate lineages, including birds, Fc/R may serve as the sole IgM and IgA Fc receptor; yet its evolution and ligand-recognition mechanisms across vertebrates remain poorly understood. Here, we identify FCAMR expression in duck (Anas platyrhynchos, ap) lymphoid tissues and demonstrate that recombinantly expressed apFc/R ectodomain binds apIgM and apIgA ligands. apFc/R affinity was ~10-fold higher for apIgM versus apIgA and ~10-fold higher than mouse (mm) Fc/R. Cryo-EM structures of apFc/R in complex with pentameric apIgM (3.27 [A]) and tetrameric apIgA (3.57 [A]) showed three Ig-like domains (D1-D3) bound asymmetrically with 1:1 stoichiometry. Comparisons to avian pIgR, which contains four Ig-like domains (D1-D4), revealed overlapping contacts between apFc/R-D1 and pIgR-D1. apFc/R D2-D3 engaged sites similar to pIgR D3-D4, yet formed distinct contact networks. Parallel analysis of a mmFc/R-mmIgM structure (4.13 [A]) revealed mmFc/R's single Ig-domain bound analogous to apFc/R-D1 and to mammalian pIgR-D1, whereas downstream ectodomain regions were not observed. Collectively, the data elucidate PIGR-family mechanisms across vertebrates, providing a foundation for delineating common and divergent functions.
affiliations: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (corresponding author)

papers.title: Thienothiazolocarboxamides: rapidly cidal agents causing catastrophic thiol collapse in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
papers.abstract: Thienothiazolocarboxamides (TTCs) were discovered as a hit in a whole cell screen for new antituberculosis agents. These molecules were rapidly cidal under both replicating and non-replicating conditions and killed Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) in macrophages. The heterobicyclic core of this scaffold was essential for activity and resistance to these agents was mediated by loss of EthA, a flavin containing monooxygenase also responsible for the bioactivation of ethionamide. EthA-mediated activation of TTCs in whole cells was found to produce mycothiol adducts and RNAseq profiles revealed a mechanism of action identical to the fungal mycotoxins patulin and nidulalin A. EthA oxidizes the sulfur of the thiazole ring to create a relatively stable sulfenic acid that reacts with cellular thiols. This unique, replication-independent, mechanism suggests the possibility that these molecules may contribute significantly to shortening the duration of tuberculosis chemotherapy.
affiliations: Tuberculosis Research Section, LCID, NIAID, NIH (corresponding author)

papers.title: RCDome: A Multi-Database Human Gene Atlas of Regulated Cell Death
papers.abstract: Introduction: Regulated cell death (RCD) governs tissue homeostasis, development, and disease, and is executed or regulated by specific genes. Yet for the researcher asking which genes execute or regulate a given RCD form, the answer is rarely simple: gene lists for the same form rarely agree across databases, many associations carry no traceable source, and most have never been systematically checked against primary literature. We built RCDome to answer the most basic question a researcher can ask: where did this gene-RCD association come from, and what is the evidence? Methods: RCDome is a multi-database human gene atlas built through a staged architecture integrating multi-source compilation, literature validation and evidence recovery, mechanistic classification, human-governed ontological adjudication, and web deployment. Five complementary evidence channels (PubMed Boolean search, curated databases, AI-assisted screening, manual curation, and Elicit systematic review) were integrated from 20 public databases into a unified matrix. Sixty-two original name strings were canonicalized into 53 RCD-related entities with curator-adjudicated operational definitions and ontological levels. Gene-RCD associations were systematically evaluated through an independent DeepSeek two-call LLM validation, Europe PMC full-text recovery and deep evidence extraction, an independent Consensus literature-search channel, and GPT-4o arbitration of disagreements. Source-grounding controls rejected extracted evidence not found verbatim in the source document, while the governance contract was enforced as executable code. Results: The compendium holds 22,473 association rows spanning 9,265 unique HGNC-validated genes (21,568 unique gene-RCD pairs). Evidence-first adjudication resolved 5,138 pairs (23.8%) as mechanistically involved; across the 4,775 role-resolved pairs, 225 (4.7%) are executors, 4,455 (93.3%) are regulators, and 95 are markers, revealing a small death-executing core embedded in a vast regulatory network. Under a separate seven-class mechanistic criterion applied to all 22,473 rows, only 3,063 (13.6%) were mechanistically confirmed and 286 (1.3%) were database-only with no verifiable paper trail. Conclusion: RCDome makes the RCD evidence landscape measurable and traceable, showing that AI-assisted curation can be verifiable, human-governed, and explicit about uncertainty. It is delivered as a Shiny web application that lets any researcher query the atlas and inspect the evidence behind each association. Availability: RCDome is freely available at https://rcdome.org/ (source code and data at https://github.com/BioCancerInformatics/RCDome).
affiliations: Universidade Estadual do Norte Fluminense Darcy Ribeiro (corresponding author)

papers.title: Circadian Clock Coordination of the Notch-to-Wnt Signaling Switch Promotes Regenerative Myogenesis
papers.abstract: Regenerative deficits of muscle stem cells (MuSCs) contribute to progressive muscle loss in muscular dystrophy. Successful regenerative repair requires a Notch to Wnt switch to allow MuSC expansion and myogenic differentiation, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Leveraging complementary genetic and pharmacological approaches, here we identify the circadian clock as a key regulator of the Notch to Wnt signaling transition to promote regeneration with therapeutic potential for dystrophic disease. Circadian clock activity marks cycling myogenic progenitors during muscle regeneration, and clock induction occurs in concert with Notch activation. We identify that key components of the Notch pathway are direct transcriptional targets of the clock that were induced by clock activation. Mechanistically, clock coordination of Notch and Wnt signaling promoted MuSC proliferative expansion while facilitating myogenic progression during regeneration. Importantly, this clock-regulated mechanism was preserved in dystrophin-deficient mouse and human myoblasts, and clock-activating compounds enhanced regenerative myogenesis in dystrophic muscle. Collectively, our findings uncover a circadian clock-controlled mechanism that orchestrates regenerative signaling transition with potential for therapeutic targeting to restore regenerative capacity in dystrophic disease.
affiliations: Beckman Research Institute of City of Hope (corresponding author)

papers.title: Regulation of sociality and neuronal development by the translation initiation factor eIF4H1 in Drosophila
papers.abstract: Most animal species exhibit some level of sociality. However, whether sociality-related traits evolved independently, or are instead derived from common core mechanisms, remains controversial. Nevertheless, an emerging theoretical framework stipulates that key aspects of how animals interact with their social environments may be regulated by a phylogenetically conserved genetic toolkit. Therefore, we hypothesized that mutations that lead to social deficits in specific human disorders may implicate genes that play conserved roles in the regulation of core social traits across Animalia. Specifically, here we focus on genes associated with Williams syndrome (WS), a rare human multi-system disorder characterized in part by hypersocial cognitive traits. WS is caused by a hemizygous chromosomal microdeletion of 25-28 protein-coding genes. Consequently, it has been hypothesized that haploinsufficiency in at least one of these genes plays an important role in the development and/or function of social neural circuits in humans. Because the Drosophila genome encodes orthologs of 17 of the 28 genes deleted in WS, we reasoned that at least some of them may serve a conserved role in the regulation of social traits across flies and humans, as predicted by the genetic toolkit framework. Using a neuron-specific RNAi knockdown screen, we identified eIF4H1, an ortholog of a highly conserved subunit of the eukaryotic translation initiation complex eIF4F, as a candidate gene for neuronal regulation of sociality in the fly. We show that eIF4H1 expression is predominantly neuronal in the adult fly brain, and that its action plays a differential role in the organization of specific dopaminergic neuron subtypes that are associated with sociality and cognitive functions. These results indicate that eIF4H1 may serve a conserved function in regulating the development of the neuronal circuits that regulate social behaviors, thus supporting the idea of a conserved sociality genetic toolkit.
affiliations: Washington University in St. Louis (corresponding author)

papers.title: Systematic promoter perturbation reveals limitations of AlphaGenome gene expression predictions
papers.abstract: Sequence-to-function (S2F) models promise to facilitate the interpretation of noncoding variants by predicting their effects on gene regulation directly from genomic sequence. However, whether these models recapitulate fundamental principles of transcriptional biology remains unclear. Here, we tested whether AlphaGenome recognizes the expected consequences of promoter disruption on predicted gene expression. We systematically perturbed annotated promoter elements in silico for 2,111 promoter-gene pairs using dinucleotide shuffling, GC-adjusted random base substitution, and N-masking. We then compared AlphaGenome-predicted CAGE and RNA-sequencing signals across 20 tissues for reference and promoter-disrupted sequences. While CAGE and RNA-sequencing predictions were strongly correlated for reference sequences, promoter disruption markedly reduced predicted CAGE activity, with N masking producing reductions of approximately three orders of magnitude. By contrast, the predicted RNA-sequencing signals were substantially less affected, resulting in an uncoupling of two molecular readouts of gene expression. Exon-level analyses showed that AlphaGenome predicted reduced RNA-sequencing signal when exonic sequences are within the disrupted region, but frequently failed to propagate this effect to downstream exons. This divergence between the CAGE and RNA-sequencing readouts was apparent from the second exon onward and was more pronounced in longer genes. Although alternative transcription initiation and shared downstream exons may explain individual cases, it is unlikely to account for the systematic discordance between CAGE and RNA-sequencing predictions. These findings indicate that AlphaGenome can recognize the local loss of promoter activity without consistently capturing its consequences across the corresponding transcript. More broadly, our results show that predictions from individual S2F output tracks do not necessarily reflect a coherent model of transcription. Systematic biological benchmarking and experimental validation therefore remain essential before such predictions can be used to prioritize or classify noncoding variants in research or diagnostic settings.
