papers.title: Hemodynamic effects of semaglutide in individuals with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and obesity: a placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial
papers.abstract: The glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist semaglutide improves symptoms in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) through unclear mechanisms. Here, in this double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, we randomly assigned 81 patients (47 women) with HFpEF and obesity to semaglutide (2.4 mg weekly) or placebo for 52 weeks. The primary outcome was the change in invasively measured pulmonary artery wedge pressure (PAWP), a direct measure of cardiac congestion, during low-intensity exercise. Additional mechanistic outcomes included other hemodynamic measures and hemodynamic HFpEF remission (defined as normal PAWP under conditions of both rest and exercise at 52 weeks). At baseline, PAWP was 17.5 ± 4.3 mmHg at rest and 31.7 ± 5.2 mmHg during exercise. After 52 weeks, the mean change in PAWP during exercise was −9.8 (95% confidence interval (CI): −11.3 to −8.2) mmHg with semaglutide and +0.9 (95% CI: −1.3 to 3.0) mmHg with placebo (estimated difference, −10.6 mmHg; 95% CI: −13.3 to −8.0; P < 0.0001). As compared to placebo, semaglutide also decreased resting PAWP (estimated difference, −7.1 mmHg; 95% CI: −9.8 to −4.4; P < 0.0001), and semaglutide-treated patients were more likely to experience hemodynamic remission (53.7% versus 7.4%, odds ratio = 14.1, 95% CI: 3.0−134.6, P < 0.001). The results from this trial indicate that, in patients with HFpEF and obesity, treatment with semaglutide reduced left heart filling pressures during exercise and at rest and was associated with hemodynamic HFpEF remission in over half of treated patients. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05371496 . As presented at the 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Sessions, in a placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial, semaglutide significantly improved pulmonary artery wedge pressure and other hemodynamic parameters during low-intensity exercise in individuals with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and obesity.

papers.title: Effects of semaglutide on cardiac structure and function in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and obesity: a pre-specified cardiac magnetic resonance substudy of the CAMEO-SEMA trial
papers.abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists improve symptoms in patients with obesity and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). We recently demonstrated that semaglutide reduces exertional pulmonary artery wedge pressure (PAWP) in obesity-related HFpEF, but potential effects of semaglutide on cardiac structure and function that may underlie these hemodynamic improvements remain unclear. In this prespecified cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) substudy of the randomized CAMEO-SEMA trial, 49 participants (33 semaglutide, 16 placebo, 28 female) underwent CMR at baseline and 52 weeks, within 1 day of invasive exercise hemodynamic assessment. The prespecified primary CMR endpoint was change in left atrial (LA) reservoir strain; other prespecified CMR endpoints included LV filling dynamics, which were assessed by early filling rate indexed to end-diastolic volume (eFR/EDV). Compared with placebo, semaglutide improved LA reservoir strain (+5.7% [95% CI, +0.3 to +9.7]; P=0.037) and eFR/EDV (+0.64 s−1 [95% CI, +0.42 to +1.00]; P<0.0001). Improvements in LA reservoir strain and LV filling dynamics were associated with reductions in exercise PAWP (r=−0.46, P<0.001 and r=−0.65, P<0.0001, respectively). With respect to other prespecified CMR endpoints, semaglutide reduced LV mass, restored more physiologic LV geometry, and improved right ventricular function and biventricular myocardial mechanics. The results of this CMR substudy indicate that in patients with obesity-related HFpEF, semaglutide improves LA function and LV diastolic filling dynamics, identifying improvements in myocardial function that may contribute to semaglutide’s improvement of hemodynamics. ClinicalTrials.gov number: NCT05371496. As presented at the 2026 AHA Scientific Sessions, a cardiac magnetic resonance substudy of the CAMEO-SEMA trial showed that semaglutide significantly improved cardiac structure and function, including left atrial reservoir strain and left ventricular filling dynamics, in individuals with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and obesity.

papers.title: Melting and resistivity of iron at Earth core conditions using pulsed Joule heating
papers.abstract: The melting temperature and electrical resistivity of iron at high pressure are essential for understanding Earth’s core. Here we use a new high-pressure method – microsecond pulsed Joule heating in diamond anvil cells – to identify melting and measure resistivity of solid and liquid iron. More than 300 reproducible melting measurements indicate a surprisingly shallow melting curve, reaching 6 K/GPa and 4160 ± 80 K at 200 GPa. Extrapolating in pressure and iron alloy composition, and combining with our 76 μ Ω cm measurement of liquid iron’s resistivity, we infer a relatively cold core-mantle boundary (3430 K) with a low adiabatic outer core heat flow (9.8 TW). This suggests thermal convection alone could have powered the geodynamo prior to inner core formation and that today’s lowermost mantle is fully solid.

papers.title: Three-dimensional mapping of human lung fibrosis identifies spatial coupling between tissue microarchitecture and maladaptive repair states
papers.abstract: Human lung fibrosis progressively destroys three-dimensional tissue architecture, yet how the structural microenvironment shapes cellular states remains unclear. Integrating 3D X-ray histology with spatial omics, we generate a volumetric multimodal atlas of human lung fibrosis that enables direct interrogation of relationships between tissue microarchitecture and spatial molecular programmes. We identify collapse of the alveolar-capillary unit - the coupled loss of alveolar type 1 epithelial cells, capillary endothelial cells, and basement membrane integrity - as a structural transition associated with early fibrogenesis. Surrounding transitional zones exhibit aberrant epithelial differentiation and proteolytic matrix remodelling, with epithelium shifting toward bronchiolised, airway-like states. Stromal activation converges on spatially restricted fibrogenic cores, sites of maximal collagen maturation and matrix stabilisation that function as signalling hubs within surrounding perifocal and vascular microenvironments. Molecular signatures of atlas-defined tissue states were associated with lung function and mortality across independent patient cohorts. Together, these data support a model in which fibrosis emerges as a spatial tissue-state process, with alveolar-capillary collapse redirecting repair towards mechanically stabilised niches that reinforce pathological remodelling.

papers.title: Proliferation and mutation as humoral immune response
papers.abstract: The affinity maturation process, through which antibodies acquire relatively high affinity for an invading pathogen, involves complex mechanisms whose relative importance is not yet fully understood. This study proposes an analytical model of this process, to investigate the main factors governing proliferation and mutation and assess their respective roles. The model suggests that the immune system should not be expected to follow a single, rigid evolutionary pattern, as a wide range of proliferation and mutation strategies can yield nearly optimal outcomes. Keywords: Antibody, antigen, affinity, B-cell, mutation, proliferation

papers.title: StableProt: Structure-Aware Deep Learning for Protein Thermostability (Tm) and Environmental Adaptation (OGT) Prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting protein melting temperature (Tm) and organismal optimal growth temperature (OGT) is essential for enzyme engineering, biocatalyst design, and metagenomic bioprospecting, yet computational prediction faces several fundamental bottlenecks: sequence-only representations miss tertiary packing; dual-task coupling induces destructive gradient conflict; natural database skew (>87% mesophiles) drives mesophilic collapse; and existing tools produce uncalibrated point predictions. To address these challenges, we present StableProt, a structure-aware framework that couples amino acid sequences with Foldseek 3Di structural tokens via a frozen SaProt backbone to capture 3D contacts. Disjoint heads condition thermodynamic stability on ecological context without gradient conflict, while targeted 14% mesophilic subsampling expands thermophile representation to eliminate mesophilic collapse. Calibrated ensemble modeling reduces calibration error to 1.92%, providing dependable 95% confidence intervals. Evaluating models across 10{degrees}C temperature intervals reveals severe baseline collapse at thermal extremes, whereas StableProt maintains robust accuracy across regimes. On ProThermDB and zero-shot FireProtDB, StableProt achieves state-of-the-art probabilistic accuracy (CRPS = 4.52{degrees}C and 8.71{degrees}C) while recovering 92.0% of hyperthermophiles ([≥]80{degrees}C), and in prospective validation, its calibrated intervals capture both enzyme stability (75.3% coverage) and host environmental growth temperatures (78.1% coverage). StableProt is freely accessible as an interactive web server at https://stableprot.dixitlab.org/.

papers.title: Daily briefing: Ancient cave art found hiding in plain sight
Phosphorylation-driven targeted protein degradation of oncogenic β-catenin
papers.abstract: Therapeutic strategies to inhibit the Wnt signaling pathway for cancer treatment have, so far, failed to advance to the clinic. Induced-proximity drugs are revolutionizing our ability to tackle targets previously considered undruggable. Here, we use an unbiased genome-scale approach to identify induced-proximity protein candidates that inhibit the central Wnt signaling effector β-catenin in colorectal cancer cells. While the identification of several E3 ubiquitin ligases validates our approach, we uncover that inducing proximity to members of the Casein kinase I (CSNK1) family leads to β-catenin degradation and inhibits the growth of colorectal cancer cells harboring Wnt pathway mutations. We show that β-catenin degradation induced by CSNK1 proximity is kinase activity- and proteasome-dependent. We propose that the formation of a neo-degron, through kinase recruitment, can expand induced-proximity drug targeting strategies. Wolf et al. used proteome-scale induced-proximity screens for inhibitors of the oncogene β-catenin in colorectal cancer and discovered induced kinase-dependent degradation as an expansion of the Targeted Protein Degradation concept.

papers.title: Transposable element polymorphisms underlie epigenetic variation and phenotypic diversification during foxtail millet domestication
papers.abstract: Transposable elements (TEs) generate genomic variation, yet how TE polymorphisms reshape the epigenetic landscape and contribute to phenotypic diversification during domestication remains unclear. Here, we show that TE-associated genetic variants drive heritable epigenetic changes underlying key domestication traits in foxtail millet (Setaria italica), one of the oldest cereal crops domesticated in China. By analyzing DNA methylomes from 60 wild and domesticated accessions, we identify 76,815 differentially methylated regions associated with extensive polymorphic TE insertions. Epigenomic variation enables the identification of a TE inventory associated with seed shattering, branching, and growth habits. Functional analyses reveal that two DNA/PIF-Harbinger element insertions in the 5′ UTR of the pleiotropic gene SiGW3 modulate its expression and affect plant architecture, panicle morphology, and grain size. Our findings demonstrate that naturally occurring TE polymorphisms generate heritable epigenetic variation and contribute to phenotypic evolution during crop domestication, with implications for crop improvement. Foxtail millet is one of the oldest domesticated crops with climate-resilient trait and balanced nutrients. Here, the authors analyze methylome over a set of 60 foxtail millet accessions and reveal transposable element polymorphisms underlying epigenetic variation and phenotypic diversification during domestication.

papers.title: Coupling electrolyte mechanical reinforcement and interfacial stress relaxation for near-ambient sulfide all-solid-state lithium metal batteries
papers.abstract: All-solid-state lithium metal batteries offer the promise of higher energy density and improved safety compared with conventional lithium-ion batteries; however, their practical operation at room temperature and low stack pressures ( ~ 0.1 MPa) remains challenging due to lithium dendrite formation and stress-induced interfacial degradation. Herein, we demonstrate near-ambient operation ( ≤ 0.3 MPa, room temperature) of all-solid-state lithium metal batteries through a combined electrolyte–current collector design. A self-polymerizable thioctic acid-modified composite solid electrolyte suppresses internal lithium metal creep with high stress tolerance, while a porous carbon matrix current collector provides localized stress relaxation and accommodates lithium deposition within internal voids. As a result, stable long-term cycling is achieved under near-ambient conditions even at a high areal loading of 2.4 mAh cm−2 using a LiNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2 positive electrode operated at 0.1 C. These findings highlight the importance of controlling lithium deformation and stress relaxation for the development of practical all-solid-state lithium metal batteries. All-solid-state lithium metal batteries can suffer from dendrite growth and interfacial stress at low pressures. Here, authors couple a self-polymerizable composite sulfide electrolyte with a porous carbon current collector, enabling stable near-ambient condition cycling at high areal loading.

papers.title: Selective depolymerization of poly(ethylene terephthalate) for economical closed-loop recycling of mixed textiles
papers.abstract: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is the second largest source of plastic wastes. An ideal solution is to chemically convert PET back into its monomers. Although many strategies have been reported, their extension towards PET-containing waste textiles is economically prohibitive. This is because chemical depolymerization can degrade multiple components in mixed textiles, yielding complex mixtures that are cost-prohibitive to separate and purify. Here, we report highly efficient processes that overcome this bottleneck. We find that, for thermally treated mixed textiles, the depolymerization of PET via methanolysis can be achieved in a rapid yet highly selective manner under mild conditions. This greatly simplifies the chemical recycling process, yielding high-purity DMT monomer ( ≥ 99.92%) at a yield of 91%. Techno-economic analysis shows that our strategy is economically competitive, suggesting a feasible closed-loop option for this indispensable commodity polymer. Recovering polymerization-grade monomers from waste textiles remains challenging. Here the authors report that the depolymerization of PET from thermally treated mixed textiles via methanolysis can be achieved in a rapid yet highly selective manner under mild conditions.

papers.title: Fully Integrated Deep-Ocean Flexible Temperature–Depth Sensor with Neural Network Compensation
papers.abstract: Earth’s deep ocean shapes global heat transport, carbon cycling and abyssal circulation, yet large regions remain undersampled. While conventional instruments provide precise single point measurements, their rigidity and weight limit deployment on emerging platforms that could extend observational reach. Here, we introduce the fully integrated, flexible temperature–depth sensor deployable on curved and mobile surfaces for deep-sea measurements. The compact, lightweight, stress-adaptive low-power electronics (average quiescent current: 24.63 µA) unit operates as a co-designed cyber–physical platform, where the porous laser-induced graphene–polydimethylsiloxane composite sensing element achieves a broad measurement range over 0–10 MPa hydrostatic pressure, while temperature–pressure compensation through a dual-hidden-layer neural network combined with polynomial fitting yields a depth error of ≤±0.91% full scale and temperature accuracy of ≤±0.29 °C. Deep-sea trials to 4812.2 m show structural integrity under ~50 MPa hydrostatic pressure, demonstrating durability in extreme environments and enabling sensing on platforms inaccessible to conventional instruments. Marine pressure monitoring helps reveal ocean dynamics and assess human impacts. This work reports a self-contained low-power flexible marine temperature depth (FMTD) sensor featuring wide range, high precision and restrained temperature drift.

papers.title: Ultra-high precision speckle spectrometer enabling radio-frequency scale resolution of atomic spectra
papers.abstract: Laser speckle, the granular intensity pattern arising from random optical interference, provides a high-dimensional encoding of spectral information that can be exploited for precision metrology. Speckle-based spectrometers have advanced rapidly owing to their compact footprint, mechanical robustness and alignment agnostic nature, yet their spectral resolution has remained limited to the picometre scale. In this work, we break this limit by employing an integrating sphere as a multiply scattering cavity with access to a high range of path lengths to enhance spectral sensitivity. At 780 nm, the resulting device achieves a resolution of 6 fm, corresponding to a resolving power of 1.3 × 108, representing an approximately 80-fold improvement over previous implementations. This ultra-high resolution enables clear discrimination of laser sidebands generated by an electro-optical modulator, with extracted sideband powers agreeing with expected values to within 1%. It further permits a direct speckle-based measurement of the hyperfine structure of the D2 transition in 85Rb, with transmission spectra differing by no more than 3.7% from independent wavemeter-referenced measurements. These results establish speckle as a platform for ultra-high precision spectroscopy, radio-frequency spectrometry, and microwave photonics. A speckle spectrometer based on an integrating sphere achieved a resolution of 3 MHz and a resolving power of 1.3 × 108. This enables precise measurements of laser sidebands and the atomic spectrum of rubidium in a simple optical system.

papers.title: Fractional quantum Hall states and oscillatory Landau charge squeezing in Bernal tetralayer graphene
papers.abstract: The precise layer-number control in graphene provides valuable opportunities to explore the physics from the two-dimensional limit to the bulk crystalline regime. As the thickness increases, a fundamental question is how this increased dimensionality influences the integer and fractional quantum Hall states. Here, we perform magnetotransport measurements on high-quality Bernal tetralayer graphene and uncover a variety of fractional quantum Hall states at filling factors with both odd-denominator and even ones (ν − 1/2 = 3, 5, 7, 8, 10), which may be non-Abelian states. Moreover, the fractional quantum Hall states exhibit a sawtooth pattern when an out-of-plane displacement field D is tuned. Theoretical calculations reveal that these patterns arise from oscillatory Landau charge squeezing effect caused by subtle competitions between Landau levels with vastly disparate spatial distributions. Our results establish Bernal tetralayer graphene as a promising platform, where the layer degree of freedom provides distinctive tunability to explore rich correlated phenomena. Fractional quantum Hall states have been observed in monolayer, bilayer and trilayer graphene. Here, the authors observe in Bernal tetralayer graphene fractional quantum Hall states at filling factors with both even- and odd-denominators as well as an oscillatory Landau charge squeezing effect.

papers.title: Nanofluid wetting of Cu enables thin lithium negative electrodes for high-energy and long-cycling lithium metal batteries
papers.abstract: Exploiting thin Li foils ≤ 20 μm is required for high-energy-density and long-cycling-lifespan battery, but is severely hindered by the poor processability of Li, as well as its inhomogeneous plating behaviors and resulting low Coulombic efficiency. Herein, an approach balancing Li supply and consumption is fulfilled by designing thin molten-salt-derived, nanocomposite Li@LiX metal negative electrodes. Benefitting from the formation of nanofluid due to the spontaneous reaction of inorganic nanoparticles in molten Li, the bonding states at both Li surface and Li|Cu interface are effectively regulated, displaying an enhanced wetting behaviour of Li on Cu. This approach enables the fabrication of an 800-nm-thick Li-based negative electrode foil as well as the formation of an inorganic-rich interphase upon cycling, which suppresses Li consumption by reducing corrosion susceptibility. As a result, practical pouch cells composed of 10-μm-thick Li@lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (LiFSI) and LiFePO4 offer stable cycling over 250 cycles, while those composed of 20-μm-thick Li@LiFSI and LiNi0.92Co0.03Mn0.05O2 with an areal capacity of 4.6 mAh cm−2 achieve 100 cycles, yielding specific energy of 498 Wh kg−1 and energy density of 1,142 Wh L−1, indicating that this design strategy is applicable to lithium metal batteries. Lithium metal batteries face trade-offs between energy density and cycling life owing to lithium processability and plating challenges. Here, authors develop a nanofluid-wetting method to fabricate thin Li foils down to 800 nm, which enables anode-lean pouch cells with 498 Wh kg–1 / 1,142 Wh L–1 and stable cycling over 250 cycles.

papers.title: Proteolytic dissection of eIF4G reveals that closed-loop mRNP formation is dispensable for bulk translation in mammalian cells
papers.abstract: Johnston et al. use auxin-inducible degrons to remove both eIF4E-binding-capable eIF4G paralogs, or both major PABP paralogs, within hours. Closed-loop mRNP formation is dispensable for bulk translation, and PABP primarily protects mRNAs from decay rather than promoting initiation. The closed-loop mRNP may be coopted by enteroviruses to inhibit translation.

papers.title: ROP GTPases are required for YUC transcription and auxin-mediated root hair growth in Arabidopsis
papers.abstract: Li et al. show that ROP2/4/6 GTPases are important for regulation of auxin biosynthesis gene (YUC) expression in root hair growth. Suppression of rop2/4/6 phenotypes in root hair growth and YUC2/8 expression by phosphomimetic Pol II CTD suggests that ROP2/4/6 modulates the Pol II CTD code in YUC transcriptional control.

papers.title: Sequential pathways preserve kinetochore integrity in meiosis
papers.abstract: Kinetochores connect chromosomes to spindle microtubules, but how their integrity is maintained as they are remodelled during meiosis remains poorly understood. Here, we identify three distinct pathways linking centromeric chromatin to the outer kinetochore in budding yeast, mediated by the Ctf19 complex (Ctf19cCCAN), Mif2CENP-C and binding of Okp1CENP-Q-Ame1CENP-U to the Cse4CENP-A essential N-terminal domain (END). Although partially redundant during mitosis, all three connections are required during meiosis, with distinct temporal requirements. The assembled Ctf19cCCAN and Mif2CENP-C-dependent pathways maintain kinetochore integrity from meiotic entry, while Cse4CENP-A-Okp1CENP-Q-Ame1CENP-U binding becomes critical during prophase and the meiotic divisions. We further show that Ipl1Aurora B maintains kinetochore integrity independently of Ctf19cCCAN and provide evidence for an outer kinetochore-associated Ipl1Aurora B pool. Strikingly, Cse4CENP-A phosphomimetic mutations that restore kinetochore integrity upon Ipl1Aurora B depletion instead exacerbate defects in cells lacking Ctf19cCCAN. Our findings suggest that phosphorylation of the Cse4CENP-A N-terminal domain (NTD) by Ipl1Aurora B may regulate the use of alternative centromere-kinetochore connections to adapt to the changing requirements of meiosis.
affiliations: University of Edinburgh (corresponding author)

papers.title: SPACE-Tag Enables High-Throughput Spatial Chromatin Profiling With CUT&Tag
papers.abstract: Spatial epigenomics maps chromatin states within intact tissues, yet current methods remain limited by accessibility and scale. We developed SPACE-Tag, a spatial CUT&Tag framework that converts epigenetic marks-associated DNA into polyadenylated RNA through T7 based linear amplification, enabling direct integration with standard spatial transcriptomic workflows. Applied to the mouse brain, SPACETag resolved activating and repressive chromatin landscapes, recovered region-specific gene regulatory programs across anatomical domains, and showed strong correlation with existing bulk and single cell reference data. We generated an integrated multimodal atlas of the aging mouse brain, profiling five histone modifications and the transcriptome in parallel across the adult lifespan to establish the largest spatial multimodal dataset to date. This analysis uncovered sharp regional divergence with aging in the brain: fiber tracts showed widespread transcriptional downregulation, often without nearby chromatin state transitions, whereas the isocortex showed coordinated chromatin transcriptome changes, including an H3K4me1 peak module that increased with age, was enriched at super-enhancers and linked to upregulation of neuronal plasticity regulators. These findings highlight the power of multimodal and high throughput spatial genomics in uncovering the divergent regulatory logic that governs tissue-specific vulnerability and resilience in the aging brain.
affiliations: Columbia Unviersity (corresponding author)

papers.title: The MarR-family regulator TilR links biosynthesis of enterotoxin tilimycin with physiologic adaptation in Klebsiella oxytoca
papers.abstract: Members of the Klebsiella oxytoca species complex (KoSC) are ubiquitous gut colonizers that produce the DNA-damaging enterotoxin tilimycin (TM) as part of their virulence-related program. A MarR-like transcriptional regulator, herein designated TilR, controls expression of the divergently transcribed aroX- and NRPS-operons responsible for TM production. Deletion of tilR resulted in pronounced induction of both operons, elevated toxin production, and increased cytotoxicity - establishing TilR as the key repressor of TM biosynthesis. TilR is encoded downstream of the NRPS operon and binds a 20 bp motif within the aroX-NRPS intergenic region, spatially separated from the predicted promoters driving toxin gene expression. Analysis of global transcriptome profiles revealed that TilR, the most highly expressed of the seven MarRs in KoSC, links toxin biosynthesis to a broader transcriptional network involved in nutrient acquisition, stress adaptation, and central metabolism. In addition, TM production coincided with induction of multiple virulence-associated genes involved in adhesion, biofilm formation, and iron acquisition. Phylogenetic and structural analyses revealed that TilR is distinct from canonical MarRs and absent from members of the closely related, competing Klebsiella pneumoniae species complex (KpSC). These findings identify TilR as an evolutionarily specialized global regulator that coordinates TM biosynthesis with broader metabolic, stress-adaptive, and virulence-associated transcriptional responses.

papers.title: Citrobacter rodentium infection disrupts colonic mucus barrier function via ablation of intercrypt goblet cells
papers.abstract: The colonic mucus barrier, composed of distinct layers maintained by specialized goblet cell (GC) subtypes, forms the first line of defense against enteric pathogens. However, the individual contributions of inner (IML) and fecal (FML) mucus layers to barrier integrity, and how these layers and the GC responses are dynamically modulated during infection remain incompletely understood. Using Citrobacter rodentium infection in mice, we show that early colonization disrupts the inner mucus layer, increases mucus penetrability and drives alterations in faecal mucus layer thickness. Spatial imaging revealed progressive crypt infiltration and concurrent accumulation of pathogen clusters within the FML. Transcriptomic and functional analyses identified Spdef-dependent intercrypt goblet cells (icGCs) as essential for sustaining IML integrity and limiting epithelial access. Spdef-deficient mice exhibited delayed clearance and enhanced crypt invasion, highlighting the protective role of icGCs. Infection selectively depleted icGCs, collapsing the intercrypt mucus and creating permissive niches for colonization. Mechanistically, C. rodentium leveraged its type III secretion system, specifically the EspF effector to reprogram GC transcriptional responses, inducing metabolic stress and promoting apoptotic signatures in GCs specifically. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized virulence strategy in which EspF-driven GC remodeling compromises intercrypt mucus defenses, potentially facilitating pathogen persistence and transmission.

papers.title: Microbially conjugated bile acids differentially affect the lifecycle and pathogenesis of Clostridioides difficile
papers.abstract: Clostridioides difficile is a Gram-positive bacterium that causes C. difficile infection (CDI). In healthy adults, it has been proposed that the gut microbiota provides colonization resistance against C. difficile by competition through nutrient limitation and antagonism through secondary bile acid metabolism, the latter of which is mediated by the deconjugation of host-derived bile acids with bacterial bile salt hydrolases (BSH). Recently, BSHs have also shown an ability to reconjugate non-canonical (i.e., not glycine or taurine) amino acids to sterol cores, resulting in novel microbially conjugated bile acids (MCBAs). MCBAs have been associated with the resolution of recurrent CDI, though the mechanism underlying these effects are not well understood. To address this gap, we synthesized 36 MCBAs with nine amino acids (cysteine, isoleucine, leucine, phenylalanine, proline, serine, tryptophan, tyrosine, and valine) conjugated to the primary and secondary bile acids found in the human gut (CA, DCA, CDCA, and LCA) and tested their impact on various stages of C. difficiles lifecycle including bacterial outgrowth, membrane integrity, sporulation, and toxin activity. We show that BSH-mediated amidation of bile acid sterol cores can either increase or decrease inhibitory effects on C. difficile in an amino acid-dependent manner. For example, serine MCBAs enhanced C. difficiles ability to grow in otherwise inhibitory bile acid concentrations, increased spore production, and elevated toxin activity. Tryptophan MCBAs increased inhibition. By demonstrating these variable effects, our work clarifies the molecular determinants of MCBA activity and highlights specific MCBAs as promising targets for the development of C. difficile microbial-based therapeutics.

papers.title: Frequency-Dependent Structural Responses of Amyloid-β Fibrils to Terahertz Pulses: A Nonequilibrium Molecular Dynamics Study
papers.abstract: The abnormal aggregation of amyloid proteins into fibrils is closely associated with several neurodegenerative diseases, highlighting the importance of developing effective strategies to modulate fibril structural stability. Here, we employed nonequilibrium molecular dynamics(NEMD) simulations to examine the effects of intense terahertz-to-mid-infrared pulses on three amyloid fibrils (2LMP, 2MXU, and 5OQV), focusing on the combined effects of pulse frequency and electric-field strength. Frequency scans from 0.5 to 60 THz in 0.5 THz steps revealed frequency-dependent losses of {beta}-sheet content, with several common response patterns in these fibrils. Comparisons at 2, 23, 33, and 50 THz showed that pulse-induced changes in secondary structure differed from those in high-temperature controls. Hydrogen-bond analysis showed that total hydrogen-bond counts could partially recover even as interchain hydrogen bonds continued to decrease, with distinct responses among representative chain pairs. We therefore propose a two-threshold electric-field framework for fibril disruption: Eth1 describes the onset of structural perturbation, whereas Eth2 indicates persistent structural loss after the pulse. This framework offers a testable approach for characterizing amyloid structural responses to external fields, although the underlying energy-coupling mechanisms, quantitative thresholds, and long-term recovery require further validation. These findings may provide a theoretical basis for exploring external-field-based strategies to modulate protein aggregation.

papers.title: Magnetic organelle gene clusters enable bacterial growth and ATP homeostasis under oxidizing conditions
papers.abstract: Biological organisms can produce magnetic nanoparticles made of magnetite to detect the Earth's magnetic field for orientation. The evolutionary mechanisms that led to the acquisition of this capacity remain unknown. The most ancient organisms known to perform magnetic orientation are magnetotactic bacteria. Under tight genetic control, they produce chains of magnetite nanoparticles in dedicated organelles to allow efficient navigation in aquatic environments containing molecular oxygen. Yet, these bacteria have been proposed to emerge before molecular oxygen became abundant on Earth, at a time when this navigation system could not have served its current function. Here, we show that gene clusters responsible of magnetite formation and organization enable resistance against hydrogen peroxide, a toxic oxygen-derived compound that was produced during the early stages of Earth's oxygenation when iron oxidation consumed molecular oxygen. Characterization of the nanoparticle's oxidation state supported the involvement of magnetite in resistance to hydrogen peroxide-induced oxidative stress. These findings are compatible with an early emergence of magnetotactic bacteria, before natural waters became oxygenated. We propose a conceptual framework to explain the origin of magnetic orientation in bacteria, and offer tools to identify the initiation of Earth's oxygenation in a time-resolved manner.

papers.title: Identification and characterization of new P. aeruginosa phages using a surface receptor platform
papers.abstract: Bacteriophages are of increasing interest for their potential use as alternatives to antibiotics for treating drug-resistant infections. Phage steering, specifically receptor-based steering, involves use of phages that bias the development of resistance in bacteria towards phenotypes such as reduced fitness. Phage therapy typically involves administering cocktails of phages with different targets to reduce the likelihood of resistance emerging. To ensure effective steering and cocktail design, there is a need to identify the receptors used by phages of interest, and to isolate phages that use diverse receptors. Here we describe a SURFAce Receptor (SURFAR) platform consisting of a set of defined Pseudomonas aeruginosa strains and mutants for rapid characterization of phage receptors. This platform can also be used to enrich for and isolate diverse phages from environmental samples, yielding novel phage genomes from wastewater. Using the SURFAR platform, two new phages were isolated and characterized: Dalewood, which targets both flagella and the conserved LPS outer core, and Bowman, a biofilm targeting phage capable of supressing growth of a subset of carbapenem-resistant clinical isolates. This tool helps to standardize the laborious but important task of phage receptor characterization, with the goal of expanding the known repertoire of P. aeruginosa phage receptors and phages.
affiliations: McMaster University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cryo-EM structures of an Acinetobacter baumannii podovirus reveal a canonical capsid maturation
papers.abstract: Phages that hunting multidrug resistant bacteria represent a promising approach in precision medicine nowadays, including these infecting Acinetobacter baumannii. To data, a large number of A. baumannii phages has been isolated, however, complete structural information remains not adequately released. Previously, we reported a podovirus, AbP20, that infects A. baumannii with potent efficacy in mouse model. In the present work, we further report the high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of AbP20 and its procapsid. The near-atomic resolution reveals that AbP20 is composed of five distinct structural subunits, i.e., capsid, portal, nozzle, fiber, and adaptor. We then characterized the assembly mechanisms of molecular interactions within capsid and portal-tail complex. By co-expressing the scaffold protein and the capsid protein of AbP20, we constructed the self-assembled DNA-free procapsid of AbP20. A near-atomic resolution reconstruction reveals it a double-layered concentric spherical architecture with a nearly 1:1 ratio of these two proteins. Comparison between the mature and apo-form of the capsid of AbP20 uncovers a canonical model of conformational switch from procapsid to capsid. Altogether, the present work reports the first whole atom structure of a podovirus infecting A. baumannii, providing a reference for structure-based phage engineering and editing.

papers.title: Fatty Acid Synthase Binds Cellular mRNAs and its Depletion Reduces Translational Efficiency
papers.abstract: Metabolic enzymes with non-canonical RNA binding activity have drawn a growing interest, due to their implications for basic biology and disease. Here we present the first endogenous RNA interactome of fatty acid synthase (FASN), an emerging oncological and virological target. Utilizing crosslinking-based approaches, we characterize the direct RNA association of FASN in two human cell lines, identifying over 6000 binding sites across over 3500 protein-coding genes, with a striking preference for the 5' UTR. We provide a functional cross-screen on the effects of FASN depletion on cellular translation. This integration with ribosome profiling indicated a preferential reduction in the translational efficiencies of FASN-associated mRNAs - an effect shown to be dependent on binding location and site number. Associated transcripts were enriched for morphogenic and cell division-related functions, as well as palmitoylated proteins. This correlative work primes further investigation of FASN as a regulator of translation of its target mRNAs.

papers.title: spearfish: ultrafast Δ-mapping of long reads to redundant transcriptomes
papers.abstract: In a transcriptome, isoforms share most of their sequence, and gene families add further near-copies. Yet most long-read mappers treat each isoform as a separate target and repeat seeding, chaining and alignment for each. We introduce spearfish, a long-read mapper built for this redundancy. Its delta mapping ({Delta}-mapping) computes each target's alignment-score difference from the best candidate. It skips sequence that all candidates share, which cannot change the difference, and aligns where they differ once per distinct sequence rather than once per target. Seeds come from locally consistent parsing (LCP), so every isoform that contains an exon receives the same seeds in its interior. Collapsing them gives a core graph, a de Bruijn-like graph whose size is bounded by the distinct exonic sequence plus a small term per splice junction, independent of the number of isoforms. Over this graph, spearfish computes the exact colinear chaining score of every candidate transcript, sharing dynamic-programming state among transcripts via a procedure which we prove is equivalent to chaining on each transcript separately. Across RNA-seq experiments, using 32 threads, spearfish maps reads 26-83x faster than minimap2 in at most a seventh of the memory, and 2.6-11.3x faster than lr-kallisto's pseudoalignment. On simulated reads it ranks the true transcript first more often than minimap2 on HiFi reads and within 0.5 percentage points of it on ONT reads at 95% accuracy. When using spearfish's {Delta}-mapping with oarfish for abundance estimation, the abundance estimates match or improve on those that make use of minimap2's alignments on both simulated reads (especially when they are untrimmed) and on seven SG-NEx runs with spike-ins, and quantification is 3.0-8.8x faster than lr-kallisto in going from reads to abundances.

papers.title: Homeostatic fibroblast niche collapse in clinically uninvolved skin marks a pre-fibrotic stage of systemic sclerosis
papers.abstract: Systemic sclerosis, or scleroderma, is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by vasculopathy, immune dysregulation, and progressive fibrosis of the skin and internal organs. Heterogeneous clinical presentation and polygenic risk complicate our understanding of disease mechanisms and the path to effective therapy. Single-cell analyses have revealed substantial transcriptional diversity in skin, but disease-associated reprogramming remains poorly defined. To address this, we performed high-resolution spatial transcriptomic profiling of paired clinically uninvolved and clinically affected scleroderma donor skin alongside healthy controls. We identified a continuum of cellular, molecular, and spatial changes to the stroma that were already evident in clinically uninvolved tissue yet remained distinct from the broader and more advanced changes in paired fibrotic biopsies. Uninvolved skin was comparable to healthy tissue by clinical and histopathological assessment, but distinguishable by the numerical reduction, transcriptional reprogramming, and spatial isolation of LGR5+SCARA5+PI16+ progenitor fibroblasts. In parallel, the dermal vascular smooth muscle compartment shifted from a contractile to a synthetic, activated state, suggesting reprogramming that begins before overt fibrosis. Cell neighborhood analysis revealed that progenitor fibroblasts occupy dense stromal niches in healthy skin that collapse in clinically uninvolved tissue, replaced by isolated, disease-associated fibroblast populations. These data indicate that clinically uninvolved skin occupies an intermediate stage along the pathologic continuum of scleroderma, establishing a framework for strategies to allow early diagnosis and preserve homeostatic fibroblast niches before irreversible tissue remodeling and fibrotic commitment.

papers.title: pLM-bVAE: protein language model-enhanced binary representation improves quantum annealing-based protein sequence design
papers.abstract: Quantum annealing (QA) has been explored as an approach for protein design in vast combinatorial sequence spaces. Applying QA to protein sequence design requires amino acid sequences to be encoded as binary vectors, and optimized vectors to be decoded back into amino acid sequences. Thus, both the quality of binary encoding and sequence reconstruction accuracy are important for effective QA-based optimization. Binary variational autoencoder (bVAE) has been used to map protein sequences to binary representations in QA-based protein sequence design. However, bVAE was originally developed for natural language modeling, and its suitability for proteins has not been systematically evaluated. Here, we present pLM-bVAE, which incorporates protein representations derived from a pretrained protein language model (pLM) into the original bVAE model. In computational experiments on three public protein variant datasets, pLM-bVAE showed higher sequence reconstruction accuracy and binary encoding performance than bVAE. Moreover, we incorporated pLM-bVAE into a QA-based protein sequence design framework. Across all three datasets, pLM-bVAE generated more high-scoring sequences with greater sequence dissimilarity from the training and validation data than bVAE. Our results demonstrate that pLM-bVAE provides an effective binary representation for improving QA-based protein sequence design. Availability The source code used in this manuscript is available at https://github.com/hueda8/pLM-bVAE.

papers.title: Joint protein-DNA language modeling enables prediction and engineering of DNA recognition specificity
papers.abstract: Protein-DNA recognition specificity underlies transcriptional regulation, DNA replication, chromatin remodeling and genome editing. Protein-DNA recognition depends on both interacting sequences, yet language models that learn this cross-molecular dependence explicitly during pretraining remain limited. Here, we developed the Protein-DNA Language Models (PDLMs), interaction-aware language models that jointly represent protein and DNA sequences. PDLMs were built by continued pretraining from ESM2 with masked language modeling on paired protein-DNA sequences. A shared encoder places amino acids and nucleotides in the same molecular context, enabling conditional sequence scoring and transferable pair representations. We further introduced a domain-aware masking strategy that increased masking probability within DNA-binding domains to strengthen learning of interaction-relevant regions. Across downstream tasks, PDLMs improved protein-DNA pair classification relative to independent-encoder baselines and supported prediction of mutation-associated binding changes. Zero-shot scoring recovered known changes in DNA-recognition specificity and prioritized variants with higher editing activity. Learned representations also supported cross-study prediction of base editor activity. After fine-tuning on transcription factor binding data, PDLMs predicted DNA motifs directly from protein sequences. Together, PDLMs provide a framework for interaction-aware biomolecular language modeling, with potential applications in protein engineering and genome editing.

papers.title: Mapping Future Energy Journeys Through Modeling the Global Transport of Synthetic Energy Carriers
papers.abstract: Synthetic energy carriers can connect renewable-energy-rich potential production regions with distant demand centers, but the emergence of trade depends on total supply costs. Here, we develop a spatially resolved heuristic combining hydrogen production costs with ports, pipelines, and shipping routes, as well as syntheses, cracking, and reformation processes, to identify key import corridors. Across 10,883 production locations and seven different scenarios, we find that export regions connected to the importer through retrofit-ready pipelines remain competitive despite only moderate renewable potentials. Meanwhile, for remote exporters competitiveness depends on port availability and coastal access through pipeline networks. Gaseous hydrogen dominates short pipeline routes, and ammonia is preferred for maritime trade, whereas methanol and methane emerge in long multimodal chains. Additional results show that low-cost heat availability is required for the competitiveness of liquid organic hydrogen carriers, while accounting for market values of conventional counterparts boosts ammonia and methanol trade. This study maps cost-efficient global supply routes for renewable hydrogen and related fuels. It shows that infrastructure is as important as low hydrogen production costs, because pipelines, ports and coastal access enable affordable imports.

papers.title: CO2 responsive nanoscopic and macroscopic materials directed by peptides
papers.abstract: Stimuli such as pH, light, and electromagnetic fields have enabled precise control over nanoscale interactions, yet gases remain relatively unexplored as regulators of material behavior despite their central roles in biology, energy, and climate. Here, we introduce carbon dioxide (CO2) as a dynamic and reversible stimulus for controlling nanoscale and macroscale matter using sequence-specific peptide design. Peptide-functionalized nanoparticles exhibit pronounced and tunable responses to CO2 across orders of magnitude changes in gas flow rate, with sensitivity governed by site- and sequence-specific changes in peptide structure. The aggregation sequence-dependence is described by six design principles while quantitative modeling show that aggregation rate scales with flow rate rather than cumulative CO2 dose. This gas-controlled response translates from colloidal nanoparticles to cm-scale biocompatible hydrogels that reversibly and colorimetrically respond to CO2. Leveraging this responsiveness, we further demonstrate spatial patterning of a hydrogel through a gas-permeable mask using CO2 as a lithographic stimulus. Consequently, this work establishes gas-mediated control as a general and scalable strategy for programming responsive materials across length scales. Stimuli responsive assemblies can offer precise control over behaviour, but use of gases for this control is rare. Here, the authors report the use of carbon dioxide for tuneable nanoparticle response, directed by changes in peptide structure.

papers.title: Propofol induces sustained suppression of alcohol drinking via habenular activation in mice
papers.abstract: Targeting the lateral habenula (LHb), a key brain region regulating alcohol consumption, presents a promising framework for reducing drinking. LHb neurons exhibit high sensitivity and responsiveness to the intravenous anesthetic propofol. However, whether and how propofol-activated habenular neurons regulate alcohol drinking remains unknown. Here, we show that a single dose of propofol rapidly and persistently reduces alcohol consumption in mice for approximately six days. This effect is mediated by sustained hyperactivity of the habenular ensemble activated by propofol. Furthermore, this ensemble is enriched in 5-HT2C receptors, and we identify the V209 site as the specific binding site through which propofol induces ensemble activation. Disrupting this binding abolishes both the propofol-induced activation of the habenular ensemble and the subsequent reduction in alcohol drinking. Our findings pinpoint a locus of 5-HT2C receptor action within the LHb through which propofol suppresses alcohol consumption, offering a mechanistic framework for understanding alcohol drinking behavior. The lateral habenula is known to regulate alcohol drinking behaviors in mice. Here, the authors show that a single dose of propofol reduces voluntary alcohol drinking in mice via hyperactivity of neurons in the lateral habenula, and through propofol interaction with the 5-HT2C receptor.

papers.title: Antagonistic second-messenger signalling coordinates Pseudomonas aeruginosa surface colonization and virulence
papers.abstract: Efficient colonisation of host tissue surfaces is a prerequisite for bacterial infection. In the human pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa, the second messengers cAMP and c-di-GMP regulate surface behaviours and virulence, but how these pathways are coordinated during tissue infection has remained unclear. Here we demonstrate that cAMP and c-di-GMP establish mutually exclusive signalling states at the single-cell level, generating distinct subpopulations of motile and surface-attached cells through pathway-specific control of type IV pili (T4P). Initial surface contact triggers an increase in c-di-GMP, activating FimW and driving stable attachment via bipolar T4P formation. This state is progressively replaced by cAMP, which inactivates FimW-dependent attachment and induces FimX-mediated T4P polarisation, surface motility and virulence activation. The resulting signalling transition enforces coexisting subpopulations, with attached cells gradually displaced by spreading cells. Using a human airway tissue model, we show that both T4P-mediated adhesion and twitching motility are required for invasion and tissue damage. Based on this, we propose that reciprocal cAMP–c-di-GMP signalling coordinates complementary T4P functions to optimise P. aeruginosa surface colonisation and infection. Second messengers cAMP and c-di-GMP regulate surface behaviours and virulence in Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Here, the authors show how the bacteria switch between attachment and surface movement by coordinating the two signalling systems, allowing distinct bacterial populations to work together to colonise and damage human airway tissue.

papers.title: Soft robotic and computational models of left atrial hemodynamics in sinus rhythm and atrial fibrillation
papers.abstract: Atrial fibrillation poses significant challenges because the complex geometry of the left atrial appendage complicates personalized interventions for stroke prevention. Current reliance on animals and cadavers raises reproducibility concerns, necessitating the development of high fidelity, physiologically relevant tools. To address this, we develop a multimodal framework including a soft robotic benchtop simulator and a lumped parameter computational model to replicate left atrial function. The system integrates patient-specific geometries with soft robotic actuators to reproduce realistic wall motion and hemodynamics. Complementary lumped parameter model provides mechanistic insights, quantifying systemic hemodynamic changes during disease and interventions. The models effectively replicate the clinical markers of atrial dysfunction and arrhythmia disorders, and their accuracy is demonstrated through validation against human imaging and porcine models. We show that this scalable, versatile experimental and computational framework advances cardiovascular biomechanics, enabling device development, clinical research and training, and personalized atrial fibrillation treatment to improve patient outcomes. A soft robotic and computational framework replicates left atrial hemodynamics. Validated with human and porcine data, the platform enables personalized preclinical testing of left atrial appendage occlusion devices for atrial fibrillation.

papers.title: Genome-wide CRISPR screening in Spodoptera frugiperda reveals the determinants of insecticide activation and sensitivity
papers.abstract: Insecticide resistance poses a growing threat to global human health and food security. Addressing this challenge requires a comprehensive understanding of the molecular determinants that govern insecticide action and insect sensitivity. However, identifying and functionally validating the specific genes - among the tens of thousands present in a typical insect genome - that contribute to insecticide mode of action and resistance remains a major challenge. Here, we present a genome-wide CRISPR knockout screening system in a cell line derived from Spodoptera frugiperda, a highly damaging insect pest, and demonstrate its utility for dissecting the molecular basis of insecticide activity and resistance. We construct a library of 90,759 single guide RNAs (sgRNAs) targeting 14,434 genes and conduct a three-round screen under successively increasing concentrations of the insecticide pyridalyl. This enriches for the cytochrome P450 gene CYP333B4. Subsequent P450 inhibitor assays, gene knockout in S. frugiperda, and ectopic expression in Drosophila melanogaster confirm that members of the CYP333B subfamily are key mediators of pyridalyl activation and serve as potential resistance targets. Collectively, our findings establish a versatile and scalable platform for genome-wide interrogation of insecticide mode of action and resistance, while uncovering the long-elusive determinants of pyridalyl activity and sensitivity in insects. New tools to investigate the molecular determinants of insect sensitivity to insecticides are needed. Here, a new genome-wide CRISPR-based screening platform is established and used to identify genes involved in activating the insecticide pyridalyl.

papers.title: WASH orchestrates phagosomal maturation and bacterial killing in neutrophils through syntaxin 19-mediated lysosomal fusion
papers.abstract: Neutrophil phagocytosis is crucial for combating infections, yet the actin-mediated regulation of vesicular trafficking during late phagosomal maturation remains obscure. Using neutrophils lacking the actin nucleation regulator Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome Protein and Scar Homolog (WASH), we identify a mechanism linking actin remodeling, lysosomal fusion, and bacterial killing. Although WASH is dispensable for particle internalization, WASH deficiency impairs lysosome-phagosome fusion and intracellular bacterial killing. Lysosomes from WASH-deficient neutrophils show decreased association with actin comets and impaired dynamics. Rac1 activation rescues lysosomal trafficking but not phagosomal maturation. Mass spectrometry of phagolysosomes and TR-FRET identify atypical syntaxin 19 (STX19) as a WASH binding partner, and WASH recruits STX19 to phagosomes. Reconstituting WASH in primary neutrophils rescues phagocytosis, STX19 interference impairs phagosomal maturation, while STX19 overexpression enhances it. WASH is thus a central mediator of phagosomal maturation through STX19-mediated membrane fusion and actin-driven lysosomal dynamics, revealing how dysregulated trafficking contributes to immunodeficiency. How actin regulates late phagosomal maturation and microbial killing in neutrophils remains unclear. The authors here show that WASH drives actin-dependent lysosomal dynamics and STX19 recruitment to phagosomes, enabling lysosome fusion and bacterial killing.

papers.title: Insular motor and error encoding supports self-correcting intracranial brain-computer interface
papers.abstract: Error recognition is fundamental to adaptive behavior, enabling rapid compensatory action when outcomes deviate from expectations. Central to this function are neural circuits for performance monitoring, encoding cognitive signals that could support more reliable neural interfaces. Here, we recorded intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) in epilepsy patients to enable a motor brain-computer interface (BCI) while sampling error-related activity across a distributed network. Our work reveals high-frequency population dynamics emerging in the anterior insula and propagating to the prefrontal cortex as the interface fails to follow the user’s intention. We identify spatially organized insular responses to error processing and movement feedback, highlighting it as a heterogeneous hub linking action and outcome. Frontoinsular recording sites were found to preferentially encode error-related activity, while centroparietal responses were intermixed with compensatory motor signals, making the former a compelling target for real-time error correction. Together, our findings demonstrate a human intracranial BCI harnessing insular brain activity, integrating cognitive processes directly into device control. Weger and colleagues demonstrate a brain-computer interface harnessing insular activity to detect errors and enable real-time correction, while characterizing the spatio-temporal progression of error signals from insular to prefrontal cortices.

papers.title: Topological Josephson trijunctions as a Majorana source and path
papers.abstract: Majorana bound states (MBSs) are zero-energy localized states in topological superconductors, obeying non-Abelian braiding statistics. Manipulation of mobile MBSs, encompassing their on-demand generation, propagation, and fusion, is essential for braiding MBSs and operating topological qubits. We show that the manipulation is enabled by a trijunction formed on a topological insulator in a perpendicular magnetic field, where three Josephson junctions meet. While the superconducting phases at the trijunction center evolve to cross a boundary between topological and non-topological phase domains, the trijunction offers two distinct dynamics, source/sink and path, depending on the phase boundaries. At a source/sink boundary, two MBSs are pairwise generated at the center, and one of them is ejected to a Josephson junction. The reverse, pair annihilation by collision of two MBSs, can also happen. At a path boundary, an MBS moves from a Josephson junction to the trijunction center or vice versa, without involving other MBSs. Exploiting the two dynamics, fusion and braiding of MBSs can be operated in a trijunction network. We illustrate this with a double trijunction setup, where non-Abelian state evolutions associated with MBSs can be manipulated without dynamical control of the setup and detected by Josephson emission spectroscopy. Manipulating Majorana bound states is a key requirement for topological quantum computation. Here, the authors propose a topological insulator Josephson trijunction in a magnetic field that enables the generation, transport, and fusion of Majorana bound states through static control of superconducting phases.

papers.title: Retrospective single cell lineage tracing with highly mutable homopolymers
papers.abstract: Retrospective reconstruction of cell lineages from somatic mutations holds substantial promise for understanding development, tissue homeostasis, and disease. Yet, current approaches are often constrained by low marker density, technical noise, and incomplete molecular readouts that limit the resolution and accuracy of inferred lineages. Here, we present RETrace2, a single-cell dual-omic method for simultaneous lineage tracing and cell-type identification. By identifying and targeting highly mutable homopolymers, which we show are approximately twice as informative as conventional microsatellite repeats, combined with technical improvements to increase marker coverage and reduce experimental errors of reading and amplifying homopolymers, RETrace2 can trace lineage continuously at an estimated resolution of fewer than five cell divisions in microsatellite-unstable organisms. Simultaneously, sparse methylation profiles are obtained from the same cells for cell-type identification. We validate the method using in vitro ground-truth models and demonstrate its utility in vivo by reconstructing multi-organ lineage trees from the brain, kidney and liver of Msh2-deficient mice. Cell lineage reconstruction can reveal developmental histories, but current methods are limited by marker density and accuracy. Here, the authors develop RETrace2, a dual‑omic single‑cell approach that combines highly mutable homopolymer markers with methylation profiling to enable high‑resolution lineage tracing and cell‑type identification.

papers.title: The FERONIA receptor kinase is required for high-humidity responses in Arabidopsis
papers.abstract: Opachaloemphan and Hilleary et al. show that the receptor kinase FERONIA is required for Arabidopsis high-humidity responses. FERONIA modulates early transcriptional reprogramming and petiole-localized Ca2+ waves that precede hyponastic leaf movement, identifying FERONIA as a critical receptor kinase linking humidity perception to rapid transcriptomic, calcium, and growth phenotypes.

papers.title: Biotechnology has outgrown the organism
papers.abstract: Synthetic biology increasingly produces hybrid constructs that blur the boundaries of organism-based biosafety regulation. We propose using the term ‘biological entity’, defined by its capacity to interact meaningfully with biological systems or to facilitate biological processes, as an initial screening category before regulatory classification, enabling more coherent and proportionate oversight.

papers.title: FMRP safeguards long mRNA expression by opposing repressive RNP states
papers.abstract: Fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein (FMRP) is widely viewed as a translational repressor, yet its loss paradoxically compromises expression of exceptionally long, dosage-sensitive neurodevelopmental mRNAs. First shown in Drosophila oocytes, this selective loss extends to mouse cortex and hippocampus, but its mechanism remains unknown. Here, we uncover a protective function for FMRP: shielding long mRNAs from repression by Me31B/DDX6, a conserved RNA helicase that organizes repressive RNP complexes. In Drosophila oocytes, FMRP loss redirects target mRNAs into Me31B-marked P-bodies. Transcriptome-wide binding maps reveal extensive FMRP-Me31B co-occupancy, preferentially concentrated on long coding sequences whose translation depends on FMRP. Strikingly, disrupting Me31B-dependent repression preferentially enhances translation of FMRP targets in FMRP-deficient oocytes. We identify Rin/G3BP, Caprin, and Lig/UBAP2L as FMRP-associated cofactors supporting expression of distinct targets. Together, our findings challenge the prevailing view of FMRP as a translational repressor, revealing instead a mechanism that safeguards vulnerable neurodevelopmental mRNAs from inappropriate cytoplasmic silencing.

papers.title: Open-source benchmarking of dairy and dairy-free products
papers.abstract: Dairy-free products offer opportunities to reduce the environmental impact of food. However, they must reproduce the diverse sensory and functional properties of conventional dairy, from foam stabilization in a latte to acid-gel structure in yogurt and melt--stretch behavior in mozzarella. Yet, large-scale, open-source sensory benchmarks across dairy product categories remain scarce. Here we show that the sensory gap between dairy and dairy-free products varies substantially across ten categories: barista milk, butter, cheddar, cream cheese, creamer, ice cream, fluid milk, mozzarella, sour cream, and Greek-style yogurt. We analyze the NECTAR Taste of the Industry 2026 dataset, which includes 1,437 respondents, 3,220 overall-liking ratings, and 79,027 recorded survey responses, including 35,762 product-linked responses. Leading dairy-free beverages, barista milk ($+0.17$), fluid milk ($+0.02$), and creamer ($-0.06$), closely approach their dairy benchmarks in overall liking on a seven-point scale. In contrast, mozzarella shows the largest deficit ($-1.46$), followed by Greek-style yogurt ($-0.68$) and butter ($-0.54$). All three deficits remain statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Across categories, descriptive penalty analysis identifies off-flavor (1.85 points), stale or cardboard notes (1.81 points), and artificial or chemical notes (1.80 points) as the sensory attributes associated with the largest reductions in overall liking. Together, these results establish the first open sensory benchmark for dairy and dairy-free products, identify beverage categories that approach conventional dairy in overall liking, and reveal the sensory attributes and product categories with the greatest opportunities for future innovation.

papers.title: CryoSHIELDs: tunable amphipathic peptide additives for cryo-EM
papers.abstract: While cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) has transformed structural biology, sample preparation remains a major determinant of success. Specifically, the air-water interface (AWI) can damage complexes, impose preferred orientation, and reduce particle density. Here, we introduce cryoSHIELDs, a library of peptide additives designed to modulate the AWI and improve cryo-EM grid preparation. Across 24 diverse protein systems, cryoSHIELDs improved particle distribution, angular sampling, complex integrity, and, in selected cases, map quality and resolution. CryoSHIELDs enabled structure determination of the OSMR{beta}-Vixarelimab complex, the multi-subunit CCAN kinetochore complex without chemical cross-linking, and membrane proteins including ABCC6 and the -opioid receptor-Gi complex, the latter resolved at 2.3 A using tenfold lower protein concentration without compromising map quality. CryoSHIELDs provide a simple, tunable, and broadly applicable platform for more reliable cryo-EM in discovery biology and structure-based drug development.

papers.title: The methionine cycle sustains the mesenchymal phenotype of tumor cells and drives PDA progression
papers.abstract: Mesenchymal traits are associated with poor prognosis in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDA), but direct targeting of mesenchymal tumor cells remains a challenge. Metabolic profiling of tumor cells isolated from murine PDA and liver metastases (LM) revealed that LM rely more on the methionine cycle than does primary PDA. This metabolic shift was specifically associated with increased activation of the methionine cycle in mesenchymal tumor cells compared to differentiated tumor cells. We show that the targeting of the key enzyme of the methionine cycle S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase (SAHH) in mesenchymal cells lowers the levels of homocysteine (Hcy) and glutathione, resulting in reduced antioxidant capacity, deregulated intracellular calcium homeostasis, and ultimately loss of mesenchymal markers. Together, these events decrease cell proliferation and invasion, blunting the tumorigenic and metastatic potential of SAHH-deficient cells, eventually impeding tumor growth and progression of the metastatic disease. Clinically, the high expression of SAHH in patients with mesenchymal PDA is correlated with poor survival, positioning SAHH as a potential therapeutic target to impede the pro-metastatic, mesenchymal phenotype of PDA.

papers.title: Hierarchical organization in sparse gene regulatory networks shapes structural coherence and emergent regulatory coordination
papers.abstract: A fundamental challenge in systems biology is understanding how regulatory coordination is maintained within extremely sparse gene regulatory networks (GRNs). While traditional unsigned network metrics can quantify the overall magnitude of influence a specific node or edge exerts over the network, they cannot predict the functional direction and consistency of these regulatory changes. To address this gap, we introduce the coherence matrix. This topology-based framework for signed, directed GRNs computes a strictly bounded, interpretable measure of directional regulatory coordination between gene pairs. Using synthetic network ensembles, we demonstrate that architectures with low intrinsic structural coherence suffer severe density-driven scaling penalties. Such structures cannot scale without requiring biologically unrealistic edge densities. Applying this framework to six whole-organism GRNs reveals how biological topologies overcome these limitations. Whole-organism GRNs exhibit lower overall coherence and more fragmented structures than expected, avoiding rigid global co-regulation to maximize regulatory degrees of freedom. Furthermore, these systems resolve the scaling penalties of complex, low-coherence architectures by restricting dense regulatory crosstalk to a compact intermediate core. Modeling synthetic hierarchical networks confirms that this architecture, a compact core within a globally feed-forward scaffold, neutralizes scaling penalties by minimizing nodes requiring dense connectivity. This allows GRNs to efficiently route decisions despite extreme sparsity. Finally, validation with transcriptomic data confirms that coherence matrix accurately predicts empirical co-regulation directionality. By moving beyond unsigned connectivity, the structural coherence framework provides a quantitative tool to map how the intrinsic behavior of localized interactions scales into macroscopic, system-wide coordination.

papers.title: Proteome-wide discovery of novel diagnostic antigens for coccidioidomycosis
papers.abstract: Coccidioidomycosis, commonly called Valley Fever (VF), caused by Coccidioides spp., is an understudied fungal disease that accounts for a substantial fraction of pneumonias in endemic areas. Diagnosis remains challenging because the mainstay of diagnosis is serology, and current assays have modest sensitivity in early infection. Discovery of new antigens could improve serologic detection early in disease. Here, we use PepSeq, a DNA-programmable serology platform, to represent the complete proteome of Coccidioides within a library of 244,000 DNA-barcoded peptides. By profiling antibody reactivity at the protein and epitope levels in VF patients, naturally infected pigtail macaques, and healthy controls, we identify numerous previously-unrecognized antigens and epitopes, including some shared between humans and macaque responses. When translated into a pooled peptide ELISA, we show that a subset of identified antigens can discriminate VF cases from controls in an independent cohort with high accuracy (AUC = 0.91). These findings establish high-dimensional peptide serology as a scalable approach for fungal antigen discovery and identify new targets for improved VF diagnosis.

papers.title: Near real-time data on the human neutralizing antibody landscape to influenza virus in summer of 2026 shows antigenic advance of H3N2 subclade K region D mutants and H1N1 D.3.1.1 Sa mutants
papers.abstract: Human seasonal influenza evolves rapidly, necessitating twice yearly decisions about whether to update the strains in the vaccine. To help inform this decision, we have been using high-throughput sequencing-based neutralization assays to make twice yearly measurements of how recent human sera neutralize current human H3N2 and H1N1 strains. Here we provide the third installment in this series of measurements by reporting 52,268 titers representing neutralization of 148 viral strains by 355 human sera collected between April and August of 2026. Our measurements show that new H3N2 subclade K strains with mutations in antigenic region D and new H1N1 subclade D.3.1.1 strains with mutations in antigenic region Sa (such as G155E) have reduced neutralization by human sera, with notable heterogeneity in the impact of some of these mutations across sera from different individuals. This paper is accompanied by an interactive summary (https://jbloomlab.github.io/flu-seqneut-2026/summary.html) that enables detailed exploration of the results, and all titer data are publicly available for further analysis to aid vaccine antigen selection and studies of viral evolution.

papers.title: Integrated omics analysis reveals reorganization of nitrogen and lipid metabolism in a toluene-degrading bacterium in the gas phase
papers.abstract: Gas-phase bioprocesses, in which microbial cells are immobilized on solid carriers exposed to the gas phase, enable efficient conversion of poorly water-soluble compounds for biodegradation and bioproduction. However, operation without a surrounding bulk aqueous medium can constrain the replenishment of water and nonvolatile nutrients. The metabolic mechanisms that sustain cellular activity in these low-water environments remain largely unknown. Here, we elucidated the metabolic alterations in the highly adhesive bacterium Acinetobacter sp. Tol 5 degrading toluene in the gas and aqueous phases. Polyurethane carriers bearing cells from independent cultures were assigned to the gas phase or to two aqueous media, nitrogen-depleted basal salt medium and phosphate-buffered saline, so that the conditions differed only in phase and nutrient availability. In cells actively degrading toluene, integrated metabolomics, lipidomics, and transcriptomics (97 metabolites, 108 lipids, and 3,899 genes) revealed a metabolic state specific to the gas phase. Under gas-phase conditions, amino acid and nucleotide degradation was enhanced while the intracellular glutamate pool was maintained at a high level, and citrulline specifically accumulated. Membrane lipids were remodeled, and the storage lipid triacylglycerol was consumed, suggesting that it serves as an endogenous carbon and energy source and may also contribute to metabolic water production under nutrient- and water-limited gas-phase conditions. These findings highlight nitrogen metabolism and lipid mobilization as features of gas-phase adaptation, providing a rational basis for designing robust gas-phase bioprocesses and selecting suitable microbial chassis.
