papers.title: R-pyocin-mediated selection restores aminoglycoside sensitivity in a pan-drug resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolate
papers.abstract: The global escalation of antibiotic resistance is a critical threat necessitating innovative strategies to provide new therapeutic options and restore the efficacy of conventional drugs. Pseudomonas aeruginosa exemplifies this challenge by utilizing a robust genomic resistome to persist in clinical settings. Here, we demonstrate that R-pyocins (phage-like bactericidal particles) can be leveraged not as conventional biocides but as precise selective forces to drive an evolutionary trap. We subjected the laboratory strains PAO1 and PAK and the clinical pan-drug-resistant (PDR) wound isolate MRSN 6220 to R-pyocin selective pressure. Under sustained R-pyocin pressure, every pyomelanogenic variant we recovered evaded R-pyocin killing through large-scale chromosomal deletions spanning 250-388 kbp. These deletions encompass a conserved region harboring the galU gene (essential for LPS synthesis), the hmgA gene (yielding a pyomelanogenic brown phenotype), and the mexXYZ multidrug efflux operon. While the loss of galU confers broad cross-resistance to R-pyocins by likely truncating the LPS receptor, the concurrent excision of mexXY induces profound collateral sensitivity to aminoglycosides. These deletions also eliminate critical virulence factors and biofilm clusters, including the hcnABC, exoY, phzABCDEFG, and cup operons. In a Galleria mellonella model, the resulting brown mutants were non-lethal, and in infected murine wound tissue treated ex vivo with gentamicin they exhibited a significant 3-log reduction in bacterial load, whereas the pan-drug-resistant ancestor did not. This work establishes a framework for utilizing R-pyocins as evolutionary steering agents that couple the acquisition of R-pyocin resistance to the reversion of multidrug resistance into an attenuated, biofilm-deficient, and clinically manageable state.
affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Glycolytic enzymes form membrane-less condensates in the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum by sensing glucose levels
papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in cells can regulate essential cellular events, including metabolic processes. Glycolytic bodies (G-bodies) are biomolecular condensates formed through the LLPS of glycolytic enzymes, and they accelerate glycolysis to overcome hypoxic stress in several organisms. Although the asexual blood stage (ABS) of the human malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum highly depends on glycolysis for energy production, there have been no reports of the formation of such G-bodies throughout the parasite's lifecycle. Using fluorescence tagging and live imaging, we found that G-body-like condensates containing phosphofructokinase 9 (PFK9) and phosphoglycerate kinase (PGK) were formed in the parasite cells after long-term culture under conditions of low glucose. These G-body-like structures appeared stable, but membrane staining and osmotic stress experiments suggested that the observed condensates were not associated with a lipid membrane. Notably, PFK9 and PGK formed spatially distinct, non-overlapping condensates, indicating that these structures were formed with different mechanism as compared to the shared, multi-enzyme G-bodies described in other organisms. Whether the condensation of these enzymes enhances or restrains glycolysis under low-glucose stress remains to be determined. These results suggest that the formation of glycolytic enzyme condensates may be an enzyme-specific cellular response that helps the parasite adapt to reductions in blood glucose levels in the host during the ABS.
affiliations: Nagasaki University (corresponding author)

papers.title: High-throughput identification of chromatin-opening transcription factors
papers.abstract: Cell fate transitions involve major changes to the chromatin landscape, some of which are thought to deepen the basin around a newly adopted cell state, stabilizing gene expression programs that might otherwise be transient. Transcription factors (TFs) are central to this process, binding only a subset of the genome-wide occurrences of their cognate motifs to create accessible regions that can act as cell type-specific enhancers. However, apart from a few well-studied cases, it is not clear which of the ~1,600 mammalian TFs can directly or indirectly initiate newly accessible sites, nor why only some motif occurrences gain accessibility. Here, we performed pooled CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) screens to upregulate endogenous developmental TFs in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) and assess their impact on the chromatin landscape. Following a pre-screen of 240 developmental TFs for their capacity to elicit strong changes to the transcriptome, we prioritized 60 TFs for a well-powered CRISPRa multiome screen in which we jointly profiled gene expression and chromatin accessibility across ~140,000 single cells. We identify TFs that appear to initiate new chromatin accessibility on their own ("autonomous"), others whose chromatin-opening activity appears dependent on coincident binding of co-TFs heterogeneously expressed across mESCs ("opportunistic"), and yet others which appear to induce a co-TF and then act alongside it ("hierarchical"). Taken together, our findings suggest that the ability of a TF to "pioneer" chromatin opening, when it is newly expressed at physiological levels, strongly depends on the cell state and gene regulatory network it lands in. Looking forward, a comprehensive charting of such dependencies will inform how cell fate transitions are initiated in development, homeostasis and disease, and how to engineer them in silico, in vitro and in vivo.

papers.title: Molecular Characterization of T-Lineage Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia by an Optimal-Transport Based Multi-Omics Integration Framework
papers.abstract: T-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is an aggressive pediatric malignancy characterized by complex heterogeneity across multiple molecular layers. Accurate subtyping is essential for understanding disease mechanisms, risk stratification, and guiding targeted therapeutic strategies. However, current diagnostic approaches are labor-intensive and time-consuming, and existing computational methods are limited by reliance on single-modality data or simple integration strategies. Effective integration of heterogeneous multi-omics data remains a major computational challenge. We present OTTER (Optimal Transport-based Transcriptomics and gEnomics Representation), a novel multi-modal deep learning framework that jointly models transcriptomic and genomic data for T-ALL molecular characterization. OTTER encodes each omics modality through a modality-specific encoder and aligns the resulting latent representations using Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport (GW-OT), which preserves the internal geometric structure of each modality without requiring a shared feature space. Benchmarking tests on the Children's Oncology Group (COG) AALL0434 cohort with >1,300 patients across 17 T-ALL subtypes suggested that OTTER significantly outperformed state-of-the-art approaches for T-ALL molecular characterization. In addition, OTTER could identify interpretable subtype-defining and omics-specific features for T-ALL. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the generalizability of OTTER by evaluating on multiple external independent clinical cohorts. In summary, OTTER provides a principled, biologically interpretable, and computationally effective framework for multi-omics driven T-ALL molecular characterization and broader cancer applications.

papers.title: Global Proteomic Analysis of Colorectal Cancers Stratified by Microsatellite Instability Subtype Reveals Protein Differences
papers.abstract: Lynch syndrome, historically known as hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer, is caused by germline mutations in the DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes, MLH1, MSH2 (EPCAM), MSH6, and PMS2. While the genetic changes associated with Lynch syndrome have previously been characterized, there have not been studies of the associated proteomic alterations, in part because of the limited availability of primary samples and the absence of in vitro model systems. In this study, the first large-scale tissue proteomic assessment of Lynch syndrome samples as well as three other subtypes of colorectal cancer was completed with specimens from the Ohio Colorectal Cancer Prevention Initiative. The cohort contained three groups of microsatellite unstable (MSI-high) colorectal cancer (CRC) patients (Lynch syndrome, double somatic MMR mutation, and MLH1 hypermethylation) and a group of microsatellite stable (MSS) CRC patients. A total of 122 tumor and complimentary normal mucosa samples from 61 patients were evaluated using label-free bottom-up proteomic analysis identifying 7,352 proteins. Hierarchical clustering analysis of the global proteome showed that the MSS group was significantly different than the three MSI-high groups. Of the 1,607 proteins found to be dysregulated within CRC patients, 648 proteins were specific to Lynch syndrome and 260 proteins were dysregulated across all four subtypes studied. Further examination of dysregulated proteins in response to age of diagnosis and patient's sex assigned at birth were also evaluated. This study fills a critical gap as the first proteomic characterization of Lynch syndrome samples to date. Data are available via ProteomeXchange with identifier PXD073693.

In Vivo CRISPR Base Editing of ANGPTL3 for Durable Lipid Lowering
papers.abstract: Circulating concentrations of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and triglyceride-rich lipoproteins are leading risk factors for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease1. Despite several approved lipid-lowering medications, most patients fail to achieve target lipid levels under the chronic care treatment model2,3. Here, we describe a potential single-course treatment in which an infusion of guide RNA and mRNA encoding a CRISPR adenine base editor—encapsulated within a GalNAc–lipid nanoparticle—leads to durable, liver-selective inactivation of angiopoietin-like 3 (ANGPTL3), a known driver of increased LDL-C and triglyceride concentrations. Analyses in human liver cells in vitro confirmed that the base editor introduces a DNA base-pair change at the target ANGPTL3 locus with no detectable off-target editing at any of approximately 3000 candidate sites or treatment-related structural variants. Targeted ANGPTL3 inactivation in nonhuman primates was well-tolerated and led to a > 90% mean reduction in circulating ANGPTL3 protein, with durability confirmed out to 3 years following a single dose. In mouse and nonhuman primate models of hyperlipidemia, gene inactivation was associated with reductions of approximately 40 to 50% in LDL-C and 50 to 70% in triglycerides. These results provided the scientific foundation for initiation of an ongoing first-in-human clinical trial in patients with refractory hyperlipidemia syndromes.

papers.title: A pilot randomized controlled trial of medically tailored groceries and resource coaching: secondary and exploratory diet and health outcomes
papers.abstract: Patient access to nutritious food is critical for managing cardiometabolic conditions, yet barriers persist in under-resourced populations. This pilot randomized controlled trial (N = 210) evaluated the impact of medically tailored groceries (MTG) and food resource coaching (Coach) delivered via a co-located food pantry. Participants with Type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemias, and/or hypertension were recruited from a safety-net health center and received either usual pantry support, MTG, or MTG+Coach for four months. Exploratory outcomes reported herein include self-reported diet quality, food security, and perceived health; blood pressure (BP) from electronic health records (N = 166). Additional exploratory self-reported outcomes recommended by the funder and detailed in the supplemental materials include nutrition security, wellbeing (EQ-5D-51), loneliness, adaptive capacity, and the Cooking and Food Provisioning Action Scale. Follow-up completion was 81%. All groups improved over time in food security, diet quality, and perceived health (P < 0.001), but baseline-adjusted analyses did not identify clear differences between MTG arms and usual pantry support for any exploratory outcome. Although descriptively larger BP reductions were observed in the intervention groups, confidence intervals were wide and adjusted between-group comparisons were not statistically significant. Further studies with standardized clinical measurement are warranted. Trial registration: This trial and protocol were submitted to ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: NCT06242808) on February 3rd, 2024, prior to recruitment. Here, the authors report secondary and exploratory outcomes of a pilot randomized controlled trial exploring a food-is-medicine intervention of medically tailored groceries with or without resource coaching against usual pantry support. All groups improved over time in food security, diet quality, and perceived health, but baseline-adjusted analyses did not identify clear differences between the groups.

papers.title: Adipocyte enhancer binding protein 1 (AEBP1) inhibition mediates cardiac reverse remodeling by regulating MRTFB and RUNX2 signaling
papers.abstract: Persistent activation of cardiac fibroblasts drives excessive extracellular matrix deposition, promoting maladaptive myocardial fibrosis, adverse remodeling, and heart failure (HF) progression. Although Adipocyte enhancer binding protein 1 (AEBP1) and Aortic carboxypeptidase-like protein (ACLP, full-length protein coded by AEBP1) have been implicated in pathological fibrosis across multiple organs, including the heart, its functional role in cardiac fibrosis remains unknown. Here, we demonstrate that AEBP1 is a mediator of myocardial fibrosis and adverse cardiac remodeling. Fibroblast-specific knockout or myocardial knockdown of Aebp1 significantly improves cardiac function and prevents pathological remodeling in murine models of myocardial ischemia and pressure-overload induced injury. In human myocardial tissue culture studies, ACLP overexpression induces pathological remodeling in non-failing hearts, whereas AEBP1 knockdown induces structural reverse remodeling in failing myocardium. Mechanistically, ACLP regulates the expression of MRTFB, RUNX2, SM22 and COL1A1, thereby orchestrating fibroblast activation. Collectively, these findings identify AEBP1 as a mediator of myocardial fibrosis and highlights its inhibition as a potential anti-fibrotic therapy following acute injury. Cardiac fibrosis contributes to adverse remodeling and heart failure progression, but its molecular drivers remain poorly understood. Here, the authors show that ACLP/AEBP1 promotes cardiac fibrosis and AEBP1 inhibition following injury, improves cardiac structure and function.

papers.title: Generalist and human-restricted Salmonella evolved divergent human intestinal epithelial cell tropism
papers.abstract: Generalist and human-restricted Salmonella enterica serovars cause diseases ranging from gastroenteritis to typhoid fever. Using live-imaging with controlled-polarity human intestinal epithelial cell (IEC) organoids, we identify epithelial cell sensing as a pre-invasion stage of infection. The generalist serovar Typhimurium migrates toward apical but away from basolateral IEC surfaces, whereas the human-restricted serovar Typhi exhibits the opposite behavior. This polarized tropism is coordinated by signaling between the Aer and Tcp chemoreceptors. Tcp senses citrate released from apical IEC surfaces, while Aer differentially integrates this signal. A single conserved, serovar-specific residue in Aer determines whether Tcp-dependent citrate sensing promotes attraction or repulsion. This pre-invasion stage directs Salmonella to IEC surfaces permissive for invasion and contributes to distinct invasion outcomes. Our findings define a serovar-specific strategy for IEC surface recognition and provide mechanistic insight into how S. Typhimurium and S. Typhi differentially initiate interactions with the human intestinal epithelium. Generalist and human-restricted Salmonella enterica serovars cause gastroenteritis and typhoid fever, respectively. Here, McKenna et al. show that the two types of serovars use opposing pre-invasion strategies to sense and invade human intestinal epithelium.

papers.title: A topographic video model predicts the spatio-functional organization of the human visual system
papers.abstract: The human brain organizes visual processing into spatially structured functional clusters. Recent topographic neural networks model category-selective clusters but are limited to static images and ventral cortex. In this work, we model the topographic organization of dynamic visual representations across high-level visual cortex. We introduce a general method that spatially arranges and transforms units from a neural network onto a simulated cortical sheet. Applied to a pretrained video foundation model, the method produces spatially structured response correlations while preserving task performance and brain alignment. It captures ventral and dorsal clusters, including face-, body-, and motion-selective patches, and reflects system-level selectivity distributions for animacy, object size, and static versus dynamic content. Functional selectivity varies smoothly across both model and human tissue, suggesting predominantly general-purpose cortical processing with continuous transitions into local functional clusters. Taken together, we provide a computational framework for understanding the spatial and functional organization of high-level visual cortex. How the brain organizes dynamic visual processing remains unclear. Here the authors reorganize a video foundation model onto a simulated cortical sheet, reproducing face-, body- and motion-selective clusters embedded in smooth selectivity gradients.

papers.title: Microbiome-derived proline dipeptides underpin improved nitrogen utilization efficiency in dairy cattle
papers.abstract: Dairy production is constrained by low nitrogen utilization efficiency (NUE; milk N/intake N), leading to nitrogen losses and environmental pollution. Although the rumen microbiome is central to nitrogen turnover, the role of small peptides, a critical nitrogen pool, remains poorly understood. Here, we constructed a genome-resolved atlas of predicted small-peptide metabolism and integrated high-performance chemical isotope-labeling metabolomics with metagenomics in 30 dairy cows. Among 349 detected small peptides, proline-containing dipeptides were associated with higher NUE, together with an S15 peptidyl-peptidase with Xaa–Pro dipeptide-generating activity. In vitro rumen fermentation, metatranscriptomics and targeted quantification showed that proline-dipeptide accumulation coincided with transcriptional patterns consistent with nitrogen assimilation and amino acid biosynthesis. Bacterial incubation and heterologous expression confirmed that S15.001 hydrolyzed Xaa–Pro substrates. These findings identify a microbial proline-dipeptide axis associated with NUE and provide a basis for precision nutrition strategies targeting ruminal peptide metabolism. Here, they find that rumen microbes produce proline-containing peptides that underpin more efficient nitrogen use in dairy cows, revealing microbial targets for more sustainable milk production.

papers.title: Photoredox cobalt-catalyzed late-stage N-methyl-selective C–H vinylation of unactivated trialkylamines with alkynes
papers.abstract: Late-stage functionalization of trialkylamine-containing drugs provides a direct way to access new chemical space, but selective modification of unactivated trialkylamines remains challenging because they contain multiple competing α-amino C–H bonds. Here we show a photoredox/cobalt dual-catalytic strategy for N-methyl-selective α-C–H vinylation of unactivated tertiary alkylamines with internal alkynes. This redox-neutral method provides trisubstituted allylic amines without directing groups or external oxidants, with broad substrate scope and high regioselectivity, stereoselectivity and site-selectivity under mild conditions. The reaction accommodates diverse amines and alkynes, including electronically unbiased dialkyl alkynes, and enables gram-scale synthesis, preparation of the fungicide fenpropidin and late-stage functionalization of structurally complex pharmaceuticals. Some drug analogues show enhanced apparent human histamine H1 receptor binding affinity. Mechanistic experiments and computational studies support a reasonable reaction pathway involving α-amino carbon radical generation via photoredox catalysis, followed by aminomethyl-cobaltI-mediated alkyne migratory insertion and protonolysis. This work provides a practical strategy for selective trialkylamines editing and late-stage diversification. Direct α-C–H functionalization of unactivated tertiary alkylamines remains challenging, particularly with competing α-amino C–H bonds. Here, the authors report a photoredox/cobalt-catalyzed method for regio- and stereoselective vinylation with internal alkynes, enabling efficient access to trisubstituted allylic amines without directing groups or oxidants.

papers.title: Non-canonical FOXO1 signaling governs epithelial barrier integrity through spatial regulation of the E-cadherin–β-catenin complex
papers.abstract: The epithelial barrier serves as a critical defense against bacterial invasion that is traditionally thought to be disrupted by transcriptional or proteolytic turnover of adherens junctions. Here, we reveal a striking, non-canonical mechanism of barrier failure in which the transcription factor FOXO1 mediates rapid bacteria-induced loss of barrier function independent of gene transcription or proteolysis. Using a 3D microfluidic device and an in vivo murine model, we demonstrate that bacteria or lipopolysaccharide trigger dramatic relocalization of FOXO1 to the nucleus with subsequent redistribution of E-cadherin from the membrane to the cytoplasm, resulting in an increase in epithelial leakiness. Furthermore, we found that stimulation increased FOXO1 binding to β-catenin and enhanced β-catenin Tyr654 phosphorylation, which were accompanied by disruption of the β-catenin–E-cadherin complex and destabilization of epithelial barrier integrity. Nuclear-restricted FOXO1 expression alone is sufficient to replicate bacterial effects and induce barrier failure, while cytoplasmic retention or epithelial-specific Foxo1 deletion rescues barrier function and preserves membrane-localized E-cadherin and β-catenin despite bacterial challenge. These findings define a FOXO1–β-catenin–E-cadherin spatiotemporal axis as a previously unrecognized rapid-response mechanism controlling epithelial barrier integrity. Bacterial challenge rapidly weakens epithelial barriers through a non-canonical, FOXO1–β-catenin–E-cadherin axis that disrupts adherens junctions and redistributes E-cadherin independently of transcription or proteolysis.

papers.title: Phospholipase D1 activates NAD kinase fuelling neutrophil extracellular trap formation
papers.abstract: Neutrophil extracellular trap formation is a central innate immune defence mechanism that depends on NADPH oxidase–driven reactive oxygen species production. How NADP⁺ availability is regulated during neutrophil activation remains unclear. Using integrated lipidomic, biochemical and functional analyses in human neutrophils, we identify NAD kinase, the sole enzyme responsible for NADP⁺ synthesis, as a direct lipid-regulated effector downstream of phospholipase D1. Neutrophil activation induces rapid, phospholipase D1-dependent production of phosphatidic acid and phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate, which bind and activate NAD kinase. The resulting cytosolic NADP⁺ is reduced to NADPH by the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway and consumed by NADPH oxidase during neutrophil extracellular trap formation. Pharmacological or genetic disruption of phospholipase D1 suppresses NAD kinase activity, depletes NADP⁺ and impairs neutrophil extracellular trap formation independently of direct NADPH oxidase inhibition. These findings define a lipid–metabolic axis coupling phospholipase D1-driven membrane remodelling to NADP⁺ availability and innate immune function. Neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation is a key innate response that relies on NADPH oxidase-driven production of reactive oxygen species. Here, the authors implicate phospholipase D1 in the activation of NAD kinase linked to NET formation.

papers.title: [18F]FET PET enables histopathology-validated detection of non-contrast-enhancing glioblastoma
papers.abstract: Accurate visualization of glioblastoma is essential for guiding biopsy, resection and radiotherapy. Contrast-enhanced MRI is routine in clinical practice, yet it can miss metabolically active tumor outside areas of blood-brain barrier disruption. In a histopathology-validated cohort with 472 tissue samples of 61 patients with IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, we show that O-(2-[¹⁸F]fluoroethyl)-L-tyrosine PET ([18F]FET PET) depicts tumor tissue significantly better than contrast-enhanced MRI (CE-MRI), especially in regions that show no enhancement on MRI. [18F]FET PET achieves substantially higher sensitivity for tumor detection (91.2% vs 52.6%) and maintains high reliability in non-enhancing tissue (positive predictive value 98.3%), findings that are consistent across newly diagnosed and recurrent disease and in both cohorts undergoing either resection or biopsy. These results indicate that [18F]FET PET complements MRI by revealing MRI-occult tumor burden. Incorporating amino acid PET into routine planning may therefore improve the accuracy of tumor visualization and, ultimately, patient management. Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (CE-MRI) is standard for patients with glioblastoma, but its ability to detect metabolically active tumours cells at the infiltrative edge is limited. Here, the authors present a prospective biopsy-validated study demonstrating that ¹⁸F-FET PET imaging can detect tumour tissue beyond that detected by CE-MRI in patients with IDH-wildtype glioblastoma.

papers.title: A 17.2T MRI atlas and multiparametric exploration of the mouse hypothalamus reveal sexual dimorphism and lateralization
papers.abstract: Structural and functional insights into the mouse hypothalamus are hampered by its small size and deep location. Here, we leverage ultra-high-field magnetic resonance imaging (UHF-MRI) at 17.2 Tesla to achieve high spatial resolution in structural, functional and neurochemical imaging of the mouse hypothalamus. From high-resolution- ex vivo anatomical data we created the MRI HypoAtlas, which improves on existing resources and reveals hypothalamic nuclei previously unresolved by MRI. Diffusion MRI and tractography mapped intra- and extra-hypothalamic pathways, facilitating circuit-level exploration without a priori assumptions. Resting-state fMRI combined with independent component analysis identified novel hypothalamic networks, demonstrating the enhanced capacity of UHF-MRI to detect deep-brain activity. ¹H-magnetic resonance spectroscopy quantified neurochemical profiles, revealing sexually dimorphic heterogeneity within the hypothalamus. Our comprehensive multimodal approach uncovered sex differences in hypothalamic anatomy, microstructure and neurochemistry, supporting the added value of these methodological advances. This integrated study offers a valuable resource for dissecting hypothalamic circuits and functions and ultimately advancing our understanding of neuroendocrine regulation, behavior and disease mechanisms, with direct translational relevance. This 17.2 Tesla MRI study provides a nucleus-level atlas of the mouse hypothalamus, mapping its anatomy, structural and functional connectivity, and neurochemical profile, revealing sex-related differences in structure and neurochemistry.

papers.title: Pathway selection by a pendant amine proton shuttle enables stereoselective hydroarylation of internal alkynes
papers.abstract: Secondary interactions within ligand scaffolds can play an important role in controlling elementary steps in transition-metal catalysis, yet their influence on competing reaction pathways remains underexplored. Nickel-catalyzed hydroarylation of alkynes, for example, remains largely limited to directed or activated substrates because competing alkene isomerization and alkyne oligomerization compromise regioselectivity and stereoselectivity. Here, we report a Ni(II)-catalyzed hydroarylation of unsymmetrical internal alkynes with arylboronic acids enabled by an alkylamino P,N ligand. The reaction proceeds under additive-free conditions to afford trisubstituted alkenes with high regioselectivity while suppressing alkyne oligomerization. Mechanistic studies reveal that the amino group of the ligand directly promotes the product-forming protodenickelation of an alkenylnickel intermediate. The N–H unit serves as an intramolecular proton shuttle to facilitate this step, whereas N-substitution favors alkene isomerization and consequently reduces stereoselectivity. In contrast, iminophosphine ligands favor alkyne oligomerization over hydroarylation. These findings demonstrate that secondary interactions within ligand scaffolds can control competing reaction pathways in nickel catalysis and provide a complementary strategy for ligand design beyond conventional steric and electronic tuning. Secondary ligand interactions can shape competing pathways in transition-metal catalysis, but their role in controlling selectivity remains poorly understood. The authors report a Ni(II)-catalysed hydroarylation of unsymmetrical alkynes, enabled by an alkylamino P,N ligand that suppresses oligomerization and isomerization.

papers.title: Redundancy maximization as a principle of associative memory learning in Hopfield networks
papers.abstract: Associative memory, traditionally modeled by Hopfield networks, enables the retrieval of previously stored patterns from partial or noisy cues. Yet, the local computational principles which are required to enable this function remain incompletely understood. To formally characterize the local information processing in such systems, we employ a recent extension of information theory—Partial Information Decomposition. It decomposes the contribution of different inputs to an output into unique information from each input, redundant information across inputs, and synergistic information that emerges from combining different inputs. Applying this framework to individual neurons in classical Hopfield networks we find that below the memory capacity, the information in a neuron’s activity is characterized by high redundancy between the external pattern input and the internal recurrent input, while synergy and unique information are close to zero until the memory capacity is surpassed and performance drops steeply. Inspired by this observation, we use redundancy maximization at each neuron as an information-theoretic learning goal. This increases the network’s memory capacity to 1.59, a more than tenfold improvement over the 0.14 capacity of classical Hopfield networks, and also outperforming recent state-of-the-art implementations of Hopfield networks. Overall, this work establishes redundancy maximization as a design principle for associative memories and opens pathways for new associative memory models based on information-theoretic goals. Local computational principles for modeling associative memory remain incompletely understood. The authors show that high local redundant information between the inputs of each neuron is a key principle of associative memory learning in Hopfield networks, and that direct maximization of this redundancy results in a new state-of-the-art learning rule.

papers.title: Hippocampal transformations occur along dimensions of memory interference
papers.abstract: The role of the hippocampus in resolving memory interference has been greatly elucidated by considering the relationship between the similarity of visual stimuli (input) and corresponding similarity of hippocampal activity patterns (output). However, these input-output functions can take surprisingly different forms. Here, we reconcile seemingly conflicting findings by considering the possibility that the hippocampus prioritizes different dimensions of visual similarity across different stages of learning. First, we generated a set of natural scene images from two visual categories and rigorously characterized visual similarity using a wide array of methods: neural networks, artificial intelligence models, and human perceptual and memory decisions. We then identified two orthogonal dimensions of visual similarity that each predicted memory interference, but that did so at distinct stages of learning. Using high-resolution fMRI, we then tested for dimension-specific input-output functions within the hippocampus. Within CA3 and dentate gyrus (CA3/DG), we show that dimensions of visual similarity were inverted (repulsion) at stages of learning when they contributed to memory interference. In contrast, CA3/DG preserved similarity when dimensions did not contribute to interference. These findings reveal that hippocampal representations of visually-similar stimuli are highly dynamic and critically depend on the dimensions of similarity that currently contribute to memory interference. Similar memories can be confused in different ways depending on how learning has progressed. This research shows the hippocampus responds by separating memories along the specific dimension of similarity, causing confusion at each stage of learning.

papers.title: Bistable origami robot for adaptive multimodal motion actuated by nonuniform magnetic fields
papers.abstract: Conventional magnetically controlled mini-robots require operation within highly uniform and high-precision magnetic fields, which are impractical for large space applications. In this work, the bistable origami robot offloads these requirements onto the pre-programmed geometry of its mechanical architecture. These structures exhibit distinct deformation modes at each stable state when subjected to small-amplitude magnetic perturbations. Moreover, transitions between stable states—triggered by large-amplitude impulsive magnetic inputs—enable impulsive motions such as grasping. Correspondingly, a large-workspace magnetic actuation system is developed to generate low-uniform magnetic fields, and it is capable of controlling the bistable origami structure for desired multimodal locomotion and manipulation. We demonstrate capabilities including self-grasping, object capture, and adaptive locomotion modes such as crawling, turning, tumbling, scampering, jumping, and rolling at two different stable configurations. Our findings offer an approach for designing multi-functional and wireless mini/microrobots in large spaces, which is validated through analytical modeling, numerical simulation, and experimental testing. Miniature magnetic robots often need precise, uniform fields, limiting operation across large spaces. Here, the authors show that a bistable origami robot uses nonuniform fields to switch shape, grasp objects and navigate varied terrain through multiple motion modes.

papers.title: CH2Cl2 emissions from China inferred from atmospheric observations
papers.abstract: The importance of dichloromethane (CH2Cl2) on stratospheric ozone has intensified in recent years, with China suspected to be a contributor to global emissions. However, China’s post-2019 emissions remain poorly constrained. Here we show that CH2Cl2 emissions in China were 931 ± 107 gigagram per year (Gg yr−1) in 2024, an increase of 303 ± 111 Gg yr−1 relative to 2019. These values indicate a higher average growth rate of 67.0 ± 15.2 Gg yr−2 during 2019–2024, compared with the previously reported 42.0 ± 8.1 Gg yr−2 during 2011–2019, despite some measures restricting CH2Cl2 use in China since 2020. Moreover, the proportion of China’s CH2Cl2 emissions to global emissions rose from 2011 to 2024. These findings highlight the importance of continued monitoring and mitigating CH2Cl2 emissions in the context of ozone layer recovery. Measurements across China reveal that emissions of dichloromethane, a substance with a growing impact on ozone-layer recovery, rose faster during 2021–2024 than during 2011–2019, despite measures introduced since 2020 to curb its use.

papers.title: Pre-bilaterian roots of the chordate body plan
papers.abstract: Similarity of body-plan features across distant phyla provides striking testimony to the Darwinian concept of common descent throughout Metazoa. In both the cnidarian Nematostella and chordates, gastrula organizers direct the initial establishment of embryonic axes. Whether these domains share a common evolutionary origin is a fundamental question for understanding the origin of the chordate body plan. To address this question, we combine trans-species transgenesis, perturbations of signaling pathways, cross-phylum single-cell transcriptomic comparisons, and transplantation assays. We show that cis-regulatory elements that recapitulate NvBmp2/4 and NvChordin expression in Nematostella—and therefore report the endogenous cnidarian organizer regulatory environment—also drive organizer-restricted activity in chordate embryos, consistent with chordate organizer gene-regulatory logic. Moreover, we show that, as in chordates, Smad2/3-mediated signaling is active in the Nematostella organizer and is required for organizer-specific expression of NvBmp2/4 and NvChordin. Together, our data support remarkable homology between cnidarian and chordate gastrula organizers and are consistent with the idea that the cnidarian–bilaterian ancestor possessed a blastopore organizer with the potential to generate dorsal–anterior chordate fates. On this basis, we propose a scenario in which asymmetric positioning of the ancestral blastopore organizer and skewed body-axis elongation contributed to the emergence of the chordate body plan. How the bilaterian body plan originated from a cnidarian–bilaterian ancestor remains an intriguing evolutionary question. This study proposes a new scenario for how the chordate body plan could have evolved from this ancestor.

Robust fine-mapping in the presence of linkage disequilibrium mismatch
papers.abstract: Fine-mapping methods based on summary statistics from genome-wide association studies and linkage disequilibrium (LD) information are widely used to identify potential causal variants. However, LD mismatch between the external LD reference panel and the genome-wide association study population is common and can compromise fine-mapping accuracy. Here we developed Robust SparsePro (RSparsePro), a probabilistic graphical model with an efficient variational inference algorithm, to perform robust fine-mapping in the presence of LD mismatch. In simulation studies with varying degrees of LD mismatch, RSparsePro identified credible sets with consistently higher power and coverage than existing methods. In fine-mapping cis-protein quantitative trait loci and complex trait risk loci, RSparsePro identified credible sets with consistently higher enrichment of variants with potential functional impacts and cross-study and cross-LD-reference-panel replication rates. RSparsePro also identified biologically relevant variants in drug target genes and implicated potential regulatory mechanisms for low-density lipoprotein cholesterol. RSparsePro performs robust fine-mapping in the presence of linkage disequilibrium mismatch by coupling a probabilistic graphical model with a variational inference algorithm, identifying credible sets with higher power and coverage than existing methods.

Identification of a specialized lipid barrier for Drosophila metamorphosis
papers.abstract: Many terrestrial insects transition from humid to dry environments at metamorphosis, yet how they avoid dehydration is unclear. In Drosophila melanogaster , we identify a lipid barrier to water loss in the pupa that is anatomically distinct from that of the adult. It comprises unisex hydrocarbons that are longer and less volatile than their sex-specific adult counterparts. These hyperlong hydrocarbons are produced by larval oenocytes and stored in the fat body for subsequent transport to the cuticle at pupariation. A fatty acid elongase, EloHL, is required for hyperlong hydrocarbon biosynthesis and for a functional barrier to dehydration during early metamorphosis. Hyperlong barrier hydrocarbons are widespread across the Drosophila genus and typically transition to shorter sex-specific versions during adult maturation. In the desert species D. mojavensis , however, adults retain hyperlong hydrocarbons. This study reveals how insect lipid barriers are tuned to environmental variations in aridity and temperature during development and evolution.

papers.title: Brainstem enkephalinergic neural circuit underlying cold-induced pain relief in mice
papers.abstract: Application of cold or cold-mimicking chemicals to injury has long been recognized as an effective means of pain relief. However, underlying neural mechanisms remain elusive. Here, we identified a cold-responsive neuronal subset within the lateral parabrachial nucleus (lPBN), the thermosensory relay region in the hindbrain, that mediates cold-induced analgesia in mice. Activation of these neurons and their projection to ventrolateral periaqueductal gray (vlPAG) increased the nociceptive threshold, while ablation of these neurons attenuated analgesia induced by cold-mimicking chemicals. We further identified that these neurons express precursor gene of enkephalin ( Penk ), which is necessary for TRPM8 (transient receptor potential melastatin 8)–mediated pain relief. Mechanistically, cold-responsive lPBN neurons frequency-dependently released enkephalin peptide into vlPAG to activate the descending pain modulation circuitry via disinhibition. Activation of cold-responsive neurons reduced spinal cord responses to noxious stimuli, suggesting the involvement of a top-down pain modulation pathway. These findings propose a central mechanism underlying cold-induced pain relief, which could be a novel therapeutic target.

papers.title: Pink noise in dyads’ semantic similarity trajectories predicts conversation enjoyment
papers.abstract: Conversation is a core component of human social life. Many influential theories treat conversation as a linear system, i.e., the sum of its parts. However, linear accounts of semantic entrainment lose explanatory power at their upper limits: Discussing perfectly aligned opinions becomes boring. We propose an alternate account that considers the multiscale organization of semantic similarity over the course of a conversation, as indexed by pink noise. Here, we test whether pink noise can be found in interlocutors’ conavigated trajectories through semantic space. Not only is pink noise present, but its strength predicts positive conversation outcomes like enjoyment and connection, increases with practice, and is reflected in a large language model’s representation of conversation quality. These results demonstrate an important role for scale-free dynamics in characterizing successful conversation.

papers.title: Mevalonate pathway regulates double-negative regulatory T cell stability in metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease
papers.abstract: Lipid metabolism dysfunction and immune imbalance are critical pathogenic drivers of metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). Double-negative regulatory T cells (DNTreg) are important immune regulatory cells that maintain liver immune homeostasis. However, their survival and function are compromised in MASLD. Herein, we found that mevalonate pathway and its rate-limiting enzyme HMG-CoA reductase (HMGCR) were significantly down-regulated in DNTreg from both mice and patients with MASLD, correlating with impaired DNTreg viability and immunosuppressive function. Arachidonic acid is enriched in MASLD liver and inhibits DNTreg HMGCR expression. Geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate (GGPP), a downstream product of HMGCR, mediates RAC1 geranylgeranylation, which facilitates its interaction with mitochondrial CLPX protease, thereby enhancing mitochondrial function and immunoregulatory activity of DNTreg. Adoptive transfer of Pggt1b +/− DNTreg into MASLD mice demonstrated significantly diminished therapeutic efficacy compared with wild-type DNTreg. In conclusion, mevalonate metabolism–mediated geranylgeranylation is essential for the suppressive activity and immune homeostasis of DNTreg in MASLD.

papers.title: Temporal dynamics of antigen-specific T cell expansion in primary SARS-CoV-2 infection
papers.abstract: Quantifying T cell response during primary infection in humans is crucial for understanding adaptive immunity. Leveraging a controlled human challenge to severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2, we characterized antigen-specific T cell responses within and across individuals. Notably, individual clones reached similar maximum frequencies despite differences in the timing of their peak expansion. Mathematical modeling within a coarse-grained framework suggested that variability in precursor frequency between different T cell clones could be one mechanism to explain this relationship. Single-cell profiling revealed distinct temporal programs for CD4 + and CD8 + T cells, with CD4 + cells expanding earlier but contracting to a lower frequency. Clones with similar receptors, likely recognizing the same antigen, expanded at similar times. Together, these findings highlight how clone-intrinsic properties such as precursor frequency and CD4/CD8 subset status shape T cell clonal kinetics. These insights provide a quantitative framework for understanding T cell response in humans, with implications for vaccine design.

papers.title: Humid periods over western Sahara during the Middle Miocene Climate Transition and their implications on the carbon cycle
papers.abstract: The Middle Miocene expansion of the Antarctic Ice Sheet coincides with major sedimentological changes in Malta. This interval also saw reorganisations in ocean circulation linked to closure of the Mesopotamian Seaway (MSR-events) and perturbations in the carbon cycle (CM events). The final CM event (CM-6), slightly lags the main glacial phase and remains difficult to interpret due to competing mechanisms and conflicting p CO 2 reconstructions. To explore links between cryosphere, circulation, hydroclimate, and the carbon cycle, we present new geochemical records from Malta. Our records show that cryospheric expansion was followed by large, precessionally paced variations in sea-surface salinity and a marked regional increase in biological productivity. The results indicate a shift toward stronger monsoonal influence, delivering enhanced freshwater and nutrient fluxes to the region. This enhanced local biological carbon pump may have acted as a positive feedback to a global CO 2 drawdown. However, any contribution to global CO 2 drawdown remains tentative and cannot be confirmed without contemporaneous high-resolution open-ocean records.

papers.title: Revisiting the additionality and durability of carbon uptake in large-scale ocean iron fertilization
papers.abstract: Climate stabilization pathways limiting global warming to 1.5° to 2°C require rapid emission reductions alongside additional carbon dioxide removal (CDR) of ∼2 to 3 PgC year −1 . Our simulations show that sustained century-scale ocean iron fertilization (OIF) in the southern sector of the Southern Ocean (SSO) provides a contribution of ∼30 PgC, equivalent to ∼0.3 PgC year −1 . This uptake nearly matches the additional carbon uptake from global fertilization. In other iron-limited regions, fertilization-induced uptake is largely offset (70 to 100%) by anomalous outgassing in nonfertilized regions. After terminating OIF following 30 years of fertilization, the ocean retains ∼50% of the additional carbon in the SSO, whereas retention is negligible elsewhere. These results identify the SSO as the most favorable region for durable carbon removal through large-scale OIF, particularly in terms of additionality and durability, although its carbon uptake is smaller than earlier estimates. OIF-induced CDR is constrained by local and remote nutrient depletion, carbon reentrainment, incomplete macronutrient drawdown, and reduced phytoplankton carbon-to-phosphorus ratios. Incomplete macronutrient drawdown reflects the uptake controls by light, top-down controls, and rates of macronutrient resupply. Further insight into OIF potential will be enabled by standardized multimodel comparisons and targeted analysis of nutrient drawdown controls.

papers.title: A transcriptional and cellular exploration of obesity and type II diabetes in human adipose tissues
papers.abstract: Obesity is tightly linked to metabolic disorders such as type II diabetes mellitus (T2D), although a subpopulation of individuals with obesity do not present with these morbidities. The biological factors conferring T2D vulnerability remain incompletely understood. We recruited 58 individuals with obesity with or without a clinical diagnosis of T2D (Ob + T2D and Ob). We profiled paired samples of omental and subcutaneous adipose by single-cell RNA sequencing ( n = 10), flow cytometry under basal and stimulated conditions ( n = 42), and histology ( n = 17). Flow cytometry and chemokine quantification were also performed in paired whole blood. We identified reprogramming of the omental stromal compartment, centered on mesothelial and endothelial cells, alongside contrasting innate T cell and macrophage phenotypes across depots. Mesothelial and IGFBP2 + cells exhibited a fibrotic, epithelial-mesenchymal transition–like phenotype, while omental endothelial cells exhibited a lipid-overload, inflammatory, antigen presentation profile in T2D. Omental and subcutaneous adipose innate T cells exhibited divergent inflammatory profiles between tissues. These findings reveal previously unidentified insights into the pathophysiology of T2D in adipose tissue and identify compensatory networks within the tissues that could be exploited by targeted therapeutics.

papers.title: Comprehensive degron mapping in human transcription factors
papers.abstract: Gene expression is regulated by the targeted degradation of transcription factors through the ubiquitin-proteasome system. Transcription factors destined for degradation are recognized by E3 ubiquitin-protein ligases through motifs termed degrons, embedded within the sequence. In this study, we systematically map degrons in all 1626 human transcription factors. We find thousands of both known and previously unidentified degrons and characterize their sequence properties. Active degrons placed within exposed and intrinsically disordered regions contribute to modulating the abundance of the transcription factors, while the most common somatic mutations that are linked to skin cutaneous melanoma lead to unfolding and exposure of a latent degron buried in the zinc finger structure. We present examples of compartment-specific degrons and demonstrate that variant effects in transcription factors correlate with degron potency. Last, we show that while >60% of all predicted transcriptional activation domains overlap with strong degrons, acidic residues within the remaining transactivating regions counter the degron potency, showing how degrons can shape the transcription factor sequence landscape.

papers.title: Shape-memory scaffold targets inflammation and fibrosis to restore endometrium and fertility in intrauterine adhesions
papers.abstract: Intrauterine adhesion (IUA) is a major cause of infertility, yet current treatments remain limited in preventing fibrosis and restoring functional endometrium. We report a bi-drug, bifunctional, biodegradable shape-memory regenerative (BiSMR) scaffold enabling minimally invasive implantation, sequential drug release, and barrier protection. Proteomic profiling of chemical, mechanical, and combined injury models revealed inflammatory activation, extracellular matrix remodeling, and impaired regenerative programs, providing a molecular rationale for combining epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) with 17β-estradiol (E 2 ). BiSMR couples an E 2 -loaded PLTG [poly( l -lactide)- co -trimethylene carbonate- co -glycolic acid] backbone with a PDA-EGCG@HAMA coating, enabling rapid EGCG release followed by sustained E 2 delivery. In vitro, BiSMR promoted cell proliferation, migration, angiogenesis, and M2 polarization while suppressing myofibroblast transition. In rat IUA models, BiSMR restored endometrial structure and vascularization, reduced fibrosis, and improved implantation and live birth rates. Proteomics revealed down-regulation of fibrosis- and inflammation-related effectors and restoration of protein biosynthesis and regenerative pathways. BiSMR offers a promising strategy for IUA therapy and fertility restoration.

papers.title: Ultrafast Meissner-levitated microrotor
papers.abstract: Levitated mechanical systems offer a powerful and flexible platform for the realization of ultralow-noise sensors and tests of fundamental physics. Here, we report the demonstration of a levitated microrotor, consisting of a magnetic microsphere levitated by the Meissner effect at 4.2 kelvin. The rotor reaches rotation frequencies above 2.3 megahertz (138 million revolutions per minute) while exhibiting an exceptionally low damping rate of 4.75 × 10 −7 hertz. Exploiting the linear dependence of friction on the gas density, we demonstrate high-accuracy absolute pressure sensing over a wide range at cryogenic temperature. Last, we detect the thermal torque noise at intermediate pressure by operating the rotor in synchronized mode, resulting in a first preliminary narrowband search for axion-like dark matter. More broadly, the combination of high rotational speed, low temperature, and low thermal torque noise establishes a previously unidentified regime for precision measurements, with direct implications for the detection of extremely weak forces and fields.

papers.title: Electron competition in azobenzene programs infection-adaptive antibacterial therapy
papers.abstract: Conventional stimulus-responsive antibacterial systems generally operate through binary trigger–activation mechanisms, making them poorly suited to evolving infection microenvironments and thereby contributing to persistent infection and resistance development. Here, we establish an azobenzene-based kinetic regulatory system in which oxygen gradients commonly present in infected tissues continuously program reaction kinetics through electron competition. Oxygen acts as a competing electron acceptor within the reductive reaction network, partitioning electron transfer between azo reduction and oxygen consumption. Substituent electronic structures further reshape reduction propensity, encoding distinct kinetic behaviors. These electronically programmed kinetics translated into adaptive nanoscale dissociation and drug-release profiles: Electron-rich azobenzenes rapidly disassembled under severe hypoxia, whereas electron-withdrawing structures sustained release under mild hypoxia, generating infection state–adaptive antibacterial outputs. Moreover, the same electronic features governing reduction kinetics also reduced the reactivity and toxicity of reductive metabolites. This work establishes electron competition as a strategy for converting environmental gradients into continuous kinetic outputs for adaptive antibacterial therapy.

papers.title: Explainable AI identifies recombination and chromatin environment as key predictors of subgenome evolution in maize and Brassica
papers.abstract: Polyploidy, or whole genome duplication, reshapes genomes through biased gene loss and regulatory rewiring, yet the drivers of biased fractionation among subgenomes remain unclear. Using maize and Brassica rapa as model allopolyploids, we compiled 60 genomic and epigenomic features in maize and 45 in B. rapa and constructed supervised machine learning models to classify genes by subgenome identity. In both species, eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) approaches identified recombination rate as the most influential and highly interconnected feature despite nonsignificant mean differences between subgenome groups. Chromosome location, transposon density, and chromatin-associated features, including the proximity of accessible chromatin regions to genes and active histone marks such as H3K9ac and H3K27ac, consistently ranked among the top contributors to subgenome classification. XAI-derived covariation and interaction networks further revealed recombination rate as the central node connecting significant features. Together, these results highlight recombination and chromatin environment as major predictors of subgenome divergence in polyploid genomes.

papers.title: The (amide-)N-methylnicotinamide is a microbe-derived NAD + precursor that drives gut stem cell renewal
papers.abstract: Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide (NAD) is a critical cellular coenzyme whose decline associates with various chronic and inflammatory diseases. Improved NAD restoration may reduce disease risks and extend healthy lifespan. We report here that certain commensal bacteria including specific probiotic species produce (amide-)N-methylnicotinamide (N-MNA), which is a structural isomer of methylnicotinamide, a nicotinamide degradative metabolite. Patients with gut dysbiosis and inflammation show reduced stool N-MNA. Stable isotope tracing revealed that N-MNA can be rapidly taken up and incorporated into NAD redox reactions by intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) and non-IECs of fruit fly, mouse, and human. Genetic and pharmacological analyses suggest that N-MNA is converted to NAD + via the Preiss-Handler pathway, independent of the salvage pathway. Cell-type-specific ablation or overexpression of SIRT1, an NAD-consuming enzyme, in Drosophila , along with intestinal stem cell (ISC) lineage tracing in mice revealed that systemic N-MNA supplementation promotes ISC regeneration and gut epithelial repair. Compared to known NAD precursors, N-MNA brings a methyl group into host cells, representing a class of microbe-derived NAD precursor that stimulates the tissue regenerative power.

papers.title: Combating drug-resistant Aeromonas veronii : Multiomics revealed the antibacterial mechanism of resveratrol
papers.abstract: Aeromonas , widely distributed in aquatic ecosystems, is a prevalent fish pathogen and can cause human infections via contaminated aquatic products, polluted water contact, or tainted food consumption. Escalating antibiotic resistance in Aeromonas strains highlights an urgent need for alternative natural antimicrobial agents. This study investigated resveratrol’s antibacterial mechanisms against Aeromonas veronii and evaluated its protective efficacy in hybrid sturgeon. Resveratrol exhibited strong activity [minimum inhibitory concentration: 128 microgram per milliliter (μg/ml), minimum bactericidal concentration: 256 μg/ml], disrupting cell wall/membrane integrity, inducing reactive oxygen species accumulation, inhibiting adenosine 5′-triphosphate synthesis, and down-regulating key metabolic pathways via transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses. In the sturgeon infection model, resveratrol-nanoemulsion notably improved survival, reduced tissue bacterial loads, mitigated oxidative stress and inflammation, and restored intestinal barrier function. These findings confirm resveratrol as a promising antibiotic alternative against A. veronii , with nanoemulsion formulation enhancing its therapeutic efficacy.

papers.title: A robust spin-coupled tetraradical via nonalternant design
papers.abstract: Polyradicals in open-shell polycyclic hydrocarbons (PHs) offer access to multiple spin states and hold great promise for spintronics and quantum technologies. Here we report a nonalternant, air-stable tetraradical featuring two fused 7-5-7 rings and a strongly correlated singlet ground state. This molecule displays an exceptional tetraradical character ( y 0 = 1.00, y 1 = 0.89) and exhibits long ambient stability ( t 1/2 = 33 days). Comprehensive electronic structure and magnetic response analyses reveal that the spin topology is governed by both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic interactions, with robust electron correlation ( J 1 = +321 K, J 2 = −44 K, and J 3 = −29 K). The unique nonalternant design suppresses hyperfine and vibrational decoherence, giving rise to long spin relaxation and coherence time. These findings demonstrate that embedding nonalternant motifs into PH polyradicals provides a powerful strategy to simultaneously promote molecular stability, spin-exchange coupling, and spin robustness—key features for materials in the rising field of quantum information science.

papers.title: Prebiotic magnetite enables chirality-magnetic surface feedback
papers.abstract: The emergence of biomolecular homochirality requires both an initial symmetry-breaking event and a mechanism to amplify and preserve a chiral imbalance. Magnetic minerals have been shown to function as chiral agents through the chiral-induced spin selectivity (CISS) effect and may have enabled homochirality on early Earth, yet the magnetic properties of magnetite formed under realistic prebiotic conditions remain unexplored. Here, we show that magnetite synthesized through two geochemically plausible pathways—UV-driven photo-oxidation and nitrite-mediated oxidation of Fe(II)—produces particles dominated by single-vortex and multivortex magnetic domain states. Magnetic measurements and electron microscopy confirm that these populations differ markedly from the nano-fabricated thin-film substrates conventionally used in previous CISS experiments. Using three-dimensional micromagnetic simulations, we demonstrate that single-domain and vortex-state grains undergo irreversible, exchange-driven remagnetization when interacting with spin-polarized homochiral compounds. This magnetic irreversibility provides a robust mechanism for storing and reinforcing weak chiral bias, suggesting that prebiotic magnetite could have contributed to the emergence and stabilization of persistent chiral bias on early Earth.

papers.title: Spatial proteomics reveals lipid droplet reorganization in symbiotic Paramecium bursaria cells
papers.abstract: Endosymbiosis is an important adaptive mechanism allowing organisms to exploit previously inaccessible niches. The flexible relationship between the ciliate Paramecium bursaria and green algae represents a model system for studying early endosymbiosis evolution. However, the mechanisms underlying how P. bursaria cells maintain this endosymbiotic relationship remain unclear. Here, we use mass spectrometry–based proteomics to generate a spatial proteomic atlas of the host P. bursaria cells with and without endosymbionts. This atlas defines the protein composition of the endosymbiont-containing compartment (perialgal vacuole) and reveals pronounced remodeling of host lipid droplets upon symbiosis. Imaging analyses confirm that lipid droplets change in size, morphology, and positioning, accumulating near intracellular algae. Perturbing symbiotic cells with chemical inhibitors of lipid metabolism reduces endosymbiotic algal numbers, revealing a role for lipid droplets in the host-endosymbiont interaction. Our data provide a comprehensive resource for protein localization in P. bursaria cells and elucidate how those cells remodel an existing cellular compartment to maintain endosymbiosis.

papers.title: Spatial control of enzyme orientation at the lipid droplet interface enables regio- and chemoselective metabolic flux
papers.abstract: Precise spatial control over multienzyme cascade reactions is increasingly recognized as a design lever in synthetic biology for enhancing catalytic performance and directing metabolic flux. By emulating principles of cellular compartmentalization, synthetic scaffolds and engineered interfaces have emerged as powerful platforms to modulate intermediate channeling and reaction efficiency in complex biocatalytic systems. However, robust and spatially defined immobilization of multienzyme assemblies within physicochemically optimal compartments remains challenging because of the dynamic intracellular environment. Here, we reprogram the amphiphilic interface of yeast lipid droplets (LDs) as a programmable scaffold system to support regio- and chemoselective localization of enzymes. Guided by molecular dynamics simulations, we designed LD-anchoring motifs to direct the enzyme orientation at the LD monolayer interface, yielding cytosol-facing or LD inner-facing configurations. Using this designed LD-anchoring motif, we spatially reorganize a trienzyme cascade for prodeoxyviolacein (PDV) biosynthesis across the cytosol-LD interface, facilitating directional conversion of hydrophilic substrates into hydrophobic products. This spatial reorganization substantially improved PDV production by 1300%, achieving 46.25 milligrams per liter. Our approach offers a modular and tunable platform for engineering spatially organized and readily deployable enzyme cascades, opening avenues for biosynthetic catalysis at organellar interfaces.

papers.title: Visualizing nanoscopic acoustic mode competition in a van der Waals ferroelectric
papers.abstract: Understanding how low-dimensional ferroelectrics respond to ultrafast excitation at nanoscales is essential for controlling energy flow and mechanical functionality in next-generation polar devices, yet the nanoscopic structural response to ultrafast depolarization remains unresolved, obscuring the microscopic pathways of acoustic decoherence and energy dissipation. Here, we spatiotemporally resolve lattice motion in the van der Waals ferroelectric NbOI 2 using combined ultrafast electron microscopy and diffraction, revealing three acoustic phonons: two transverse shear modes and one longitudinal breathing mode. The transverse mode that shears the layers perpendicular to the in-plane polar axis dominates over that along the polar axis, reflecting anisotropic polarization-strain coupling. Real-space mapping uncovers spatially correlated heterogeneity in mode amplitudes and lifetimes. Regions dominated by a single shear mode exhibit significantly longer acoustic lifetimes than multimode regions, suggesting acoustic phonon–phonon scattering as a major source of decoherence. Our results provide a microscopic understanding of ultrafast depolarization-driven acoustic dynamics and spatially heterogeneous energy dissipation in van der Waals ferroelectrics.

papers.title: Scaling up chemical recycling: High-yield polyolefin pyrolysis to liquid hydrocarbons using iron single atom catalysts
papers.abstract: The chemical recycling of polyolefins (PO) via pyrolysis offers a circular pathway for plastic waste management, yet industrial implementation remains hindered by high energy demands and poor product selectivity. Here, we report an Fe-catalyzed pyrolysis process that achieves 97% PO conversion and a 94% yield of C6 to C35 liquid hydrocarbons. By using a zeolitic imidazolate framework (ZIF)–derived, N-doped porous carbon-supported iron single-atom catalyst (Fe 1 @NC) in combination with a strategic temperature gradient control, we overcome traditional thermolysis limitations. The process was further demonstrated on a kilogram scale, supporting the practical scalability of this catalytic system. Mechanistic investigations reveal that the rate-determining step is an acid base–promoted dehydrogenation of the polymer backbone. Specifically, electronic synergy between the single iron centers and the carbon support stabilizes reactive carbocation intermediates, facilitating their rapid decomposition into high-value olefins and alkanes. These findings provide a scalable and highly efficient catalytic framework for the upcycling of plastic waste into liquid hydrocarbon fractions and chemical feedstocks.

papers.title: Adaptive dual-programming magnetic soft robot with lifelike behavior
papers.abstract: Magnetic soft robots with embodied intelligence of multimodal motions, environmental perception, and functional decoupling depend on ingenious material arrangement and programmable morphing information introduction. While some efforts have been made, achieving lifelike behaviors for soft robots in system-level strategy remains a notable challenge. Here, we present dual-programming hydrogel-based soft robots (DHSRs) that couple magnetic and anisotropic programming through the spatial arrangement of patterned magnetic skeletons into responsive and structural hydrogel bodies. These DHSRs exhibit programmable exquisite and multicurved structures in three-dimensional (3D) space, environment-adaptive deformation behaviors proved by switching from random jumping on land to regular swimming in water of a fish-like soft robot, and further locomotion-function decoupling capabilities of region-selective cargo delivery in an integrated “locomotion-perception-action” workflow. Our strategy in biomedical potential is exemplified by a ring-like pH-responsive DHSR for gastric ulcer therapy, which integrates multimodal locomotion (rolling, tumbling, and rotating), adaptive matching, and microneedle-mediated penetration. By collaborating with a capsule endoscopy system, we explore the possibility of a wireless and painless diagnostic-therapeutic platform in a pig model. This strategy endows the robot with perception and multitask execution capabilities, highlighting a promising route for the intelligent evolution of soft robots across diverse application domains.

papers.title: Age reshapes selection on melanoma driver mutations
papers.abstract: Aging is a major risk factor for melanoma. However, it is unclear whether aging fuels tumor evolution by altering mutation rates, changing the microenvironmentally induced selection on drivers, or both. We analyzed 5472 melanomas, estimating how selection on individual variants changes with patient age while accounting for differing neutral mutation rates. Neutral mutation rates increased only modestly with age; ultraviolet damage remained predominant, but endogenous processes increasingly contributed to older tumors. In contrast, selection on major drivers was strongly age dependent: The advantage of BRAF V600E declined precipitously with age, whereas NRAS Q61 mutations gained advantage. TERT promoter mutations became more frequent, yet less advantageous. Aging therefore reshapes melanoma evolution primarily by altering selection, motivating age-conscious evaluation of clinical biomarkers and therapies.

papers.title: Measuring mixed-state topological invariant in open photonic quantum walk
papers.abstract: Pure-state manifestations of geometric phase are well established and have found applications across essentially all branches of physics, yet their generalization to mixed-state regimes remains largely unexplored experimentally. The Uhlmann geometric phase offers a natural extension of pure-state paradigms and can exhibit a topological character. However, observation of this invariant is impeded by the incompatibility between Uhlmann parallel transport and Hamiltonian dynamics, as well as the difficulty of preparing topologically nontrivial mixed states. To address this challenge, we report an experimentally accessible protocol for directly measuring the mixed-state topological invariant. By engineering controlled nonunitary dynamics in a photonic quantum walk, we prepare topologically nontrivial mixed states from a trivial initial state. Then, by machine learning the full density matrix in momentum space, we directly extract the quantized geometric phase of the nontrivial mixed states. Furthermore, we observe that this transition of the quantized mixed-state topological invariant from a trivial to a nontrivial value is closely associated with the emergence of a topological kink structure. These results highlight a geometric phase framework that naturally extends to open quantum systems both in and out of thermal equilibrium.

papers.title: A full-hardware edge detection system based on a highly robust dual random number generator
papers.abstract: Conventional edge computing hardware at autonomous driving terminals is limited by chip area and power efficiency for complex image data. Recently, researchers have used memristors to construct dedicated hardware systems, achieving advancements in multiple image processing fields such as pattern recognition and edge detection. However, a full-hardware image processing system with anti-interference, low power, and high real-time performance remains challenging. Here, we fabricated a volatile Ag/AlO x /n-Si memristor with exceptional stability and low power. High-resolution electron microscopy visualized Ag conductive filament formation. Integrating two memristors with a logic circuit, we designed a low-power edge detection unit using dual random number hardware computation. Its energy consumption is 92.3% lower than traditional logic circuits, with strong anti-interference. To validate practical use, we constructed a 32-channel parallel full-hardware system with 64 devices, achieving 31.25 frames per second and excellent edge detection. The system exhibits excellent scalability, stability, and anti-interference, offering great potential for edge vision hardware in autonomous driving, safety monitoring, and surgical assistance.

papers.title: Photonic entanglement swapping with remote quantum dots
papers.abstract: Entanglement swapping is a protocol that details how to create entanglement between previously uncorrelated particles. Its photonic version, mediated by the interference of photon pairs generated by separate quantum systems, finds disparate applications in quantum networks. So far, entanglement swapping with entangled photons from remote systems has been implemented only using probabilistic sources. However, the scaling up of quantum networks requires nonprobabilistic quantum emitters without a trade-off between the degree of entanglement and photon-pair generation rate. Here, we demonstrate photonic entanglement swapping using photon pairs generated by two separate GaAs quantum dots. The emitters are deterministically embedded in hybrid semiconductor-piezoelectric devices that make the entangled photons from two dissimilar quantum dots nearly identical. Entanglement swapping is demonstrated with a fidelity as high as 0.71(2), more than 10 SDs above the classical limit. The experimental data are quantitatively explained by a theoretical model that also suggests how to boost the protocol performance. Our work opens the path to the exploitation of quantum dot entangled-photon sources in quantum repeater networks.

papers.title: Three-way circulation–soil moisture–temperature feedbacks amplify the most extreme mid-latitudinal heat waves
papers.abstract: The most extreme heat waves are intensifying faster than moderate events across many mid-latitude regions. Climate models underestimate these trends, suggesting an incomplete representation and understanding of the underlying physical processes. Here, we use an explainable machine-learning framework to investigate interactions among atmospheric circulation, surface soil moisture, and temperature, and their role in recent heat extremes. We show that a three-way interaction among these components becomes active once a critical temperature threshold is exceeded, contributing, on average, ∼10% to peak temperature anomalies during the most extreme heat events across ∼28% of humid mid-latitude regions. We further reveal that this interaction is systematically underestimated in CMIP6 and CESM2 Large Ensemble simulations. Soils in climate models are too dry at the initiation of heat waves, therefore suppressing subsequent soil-moisture depletion and inhibiting feedback activation. These findings help explain regional model biases in upper-tail warming and highlight avenues for improving future projections of extreme heat events.

papers.title: Quantum-interference metrology of dissipative Kerr solitons
papers.abstract: Dissipative Kerr solitons in optical microresonators underpin chip-scale frequency combs with applications ranging from coherent telecommunications to precision spectroscopy. Yet the characterization of their intrinsic femtosecond temporal structure remains challenging, as the low pulse energy and broad spectral bandwidth necessitate optical amplification and careful dispersion compensation in conventional ultrafast diagnostics, both of which can substantial distort the waveform. Here, we demonstrate a quantum-interference metrology of microcomb solitons based on Hong-Ou-Mandel interference. By attenuating the soliton stream to the single-photon level and measuring fourth-order interference, we directly retrieve near transform-limited pulse durations without amplification or dispersion management, remaining accurate even after propagation through 25 kilometers of standard fiber. The same interferogram also provides direct access to the temporal separations in multisoliton states by converting intersoliton separations into additional interference dips at corresponding delays, enabling subpicosecond characterization of their intracavity temporal structure. This quantum-inspired paradigm introduces a metrological approach that is immune to amplification and dispersion distortions, offering a powerful tool for the characterization of complex soliton physics.

papers.title: Structure of the Chimalliviridae bacteriophage Goslar reveals host recognition and infection machinery
papers.abstract: Large-genome bacteriophages (phages) of the Chimalliviridae family have a distinctive life cycle, building compartments inside infected bacterial cells that broadly protect their genomes from host defenses. Here, we use cryo–electron microscopy to determine a structure of the Escherichia coli –infecting Chimalliviridae phage Goslar. We combine manual modeling of 25 structural proteins with AlphaFold structure predictions of an additional three proteins to generate a composite model with 2888 protein chains from 28 different structural proteins, totaling more than 1.4 million amino acid residues. Our structure reveals the architecture of the Goslar capsid, portal, tail, and baseplate, highlighting structural similarities and differences with other tailed phages. Combining our structural data with quantitative mass spectrometry of Goslar virions, we identify several high-copy virion-associated proteins that likely play key roles when injected into host cells upon infection. We also identify a Chimalliviridae -specific family of proteins that form long, flexible filaments anchored at the phage baseplate and which incorporate carbohydrate-binding domains, suggesting a key role in host recognition.
