papers.title: Reciprocal control of genome instability and RNA processing in cancer: Mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities
papers.abstract: Genomic instability and dysregulated RNA processing are each recognized as core hallmarks of cancer, but accumulating evidence indicates that they are mechanistically intertwined rather than independent features. Chromosomal instability, mismatch-repair deficiency, and homologous recombination deficiency can reshape RNA splicing, 3′ end formation, and RNA surveillance through changes in gene dosage, DNA damage signaling, and alterations in regulatory elements. Conversely, aberrant splicing, polyadenylation, and RNA modifications can impair DNA repair, perturb mitotic control, and promote replication stress, thereby reinforcing genomic instability. This bidirectional circuit drives clinically relevant phenotypes, including therapeutic resistance, immune modulation, and emergent vulnerabilities that are not captured by DNA-centric biomarkers alone. Here, we present a unified framework for the genome instability–RNA processing axis and its direct clinical implications for cancer diagnosis, treatment stratification, and therapeutic exploitation, highlighting the most actionable mechanistic interfaces and discussing how integrated DNA-RNA biomarkers and rational combination strategies could extend precision oncology beyond static genomic lesions.

papers.title: High-impulse and reactant-regenerative combustion-based micro actuators
papers.abstract: The use of combustibles in micro-actuator technologies enables powerful impulsive actuation capabilities comparable to those of natural organisms. However, the exogenous dependence of fuel limits the development of combustion-based actuators. We present a closed-cycle reactant regeneration strategy wherein the bidirectional interconversion between hydrogen and water achieves real-time fuel replenishment for reactant-regenerative electrolysis and combustion reactions. Based on this, we develop a 1.5-centimeter actuator that generates forces above 20 newtons and operates continuously for >7200 cycles without refueling (a two orders-of-magnitude improvement over existing combustion-based actuators). Experiments confirm its strength and cross-environment versatility for removing obstacles, jetting, and striking via underwater cavitation. These features enable the actuator to be integrated into small robotic platforms, allowing them to reconfigure local surroundings in an active manner.

papers.title: Dual-acting compounds that deliver an acidifying domain via zanamivir to the virus surface are potent influenza inhibitors
papers.abstract: While contemporary antiviral development primarily strives to produce “lock and key” inhibitors, we present here a different approach to drug design that uses compounds devised to alter the microenvironment of the virion surface, making it incompatible with virus entry. We illustrate this strategy with inhibitors of influenza virus and show that compounds designed to produce a proton-rich mantle above the virion surface affect the ability of the viral hemagglutinin to interact with cellular receptors and gain entry to the cell. The compounds show exceptional antiviral activity both in vitro and in vivo and protect against influenza illness in ferrets and in mice after a single dose, either therapeutically or prophylactically.

papers.title: Strigolactone receptor D14 integrates phosphate and strigolactone signaling by interacting with and stabilizing PHR1
papers.abstract: Strigolactone (SL) and low phosphate (LP) signaling coordinately regulate shoot and root architecture and plant adaptation. While LP signaling is generally considered upstream of SL biosynthesis, their interaction is more complex. For instance, exogenous SL exerts opposite effects on lateral root formation under low versus high phosphorus. Here, we show that under LP, SL-induced anthocyanin accumulation requires PHR1, demonstrating that PHR1 functions downstream of SL signaling. We uncovered an SL-dependent physical interaction between PHR1 and the SL receptor DWARF14 (D14). This interaction promotes PHR1 dimerization, stabilizes PHR1 by inhibiting its ubiquitination-mediated degradation, and enhances its transcriptional activation activity. The D14-PHR1 complex directly binds and up-regulates the SL biosynthesis gene MAX3 and anthocyanin biosynthesis genes, thereby inhibiting branching and hypocotyl elongation and promoting anthocyanin accumulation. These findings indicate that PHR1 mediates the coordination of SL and LP signaling, potentially explaining SL’s opposing effects on lateral root formation under different phosphorus conditions. In the phr1 mutant, exogenous SL inhibited lateral roots under both LP and Pi-sufficient conditions, confirming that the promoting role of SL under LP requires PHR1. PHR1 also interacted with D14 to activate LBDs and HB23 , regulating lateral root formation. Collectively, LP signaling coordinates with SL signaling via two parallel pathways: regulating SL biosynthesis to align SL functions with LP requirements and enhancing PHR1 activity through PHR1-D14 interaction to amplify LP signaling outputs.

papers.title: MYC primes a paralog synthetic lethality involving the mitochondrial translocase subunits TIMM17A and TIMM17B and N-Acetylaspartate
papers.abstract: To identify the genes and pathways required for the survival of MYC -amplified cancers, we engineered an isogenic cell system in which transformation is driven by oncogenic MYC . Using a genome-scale CRISPR-Cas9 library, we identified the mitochondrial membrane translocase TIMM17A as uniquely essential for the survival of MYC-transformed cells. This dependency arises from MYC-driven suppression of TIMM17B , the paralog of TIMM17A . TIMM17A/B is an essential component of the TIM23 mitochondrial protein import complex, and the MYC-induced suppression of TIMM17B creates a strong dependency on TIMM17A . N-acetylaspartate supplementation rescued TIMM17A dependency in MYC -amplified cell lines, highlighting the unique and crucial role of this metabolite in the cell fitness of MYC -amplified cancers. These observations identify a paralog dependency required for the survival of a subset of MYC-driven cancers.

papers.title: Y chromosome instability in the early mouse embryo
papers.abstract: The Y chromosome lacks canonical centromeric repeats necessary for high-fidelity chromosome segregation. In adult tissues, this causes Y loss and predisposes to disease. However, its impact on embryogenesis is unknown. Here, we identify the first mouse embryonic mitoses as a window during which the Y centromere is unusually weak. This vulnerability impairs kinetochore strength and the Y becomes preferentially trapped at the spindle pole, resulting in missegregation. To study the impact of Y loss, we generate an aggregation model to track specific aneuploidies in mosaic embryos. Loss of the Y slows down cell division and compromises embryo size. Our findings reveal a developmental window during which the Y is especially vulnerable to loss, with implications for male sex determination and the origin of Turner syndrome (XO).

papers.title: CD8 + T cells induce RIPK1-regulated brain endothelial cell death in cerebral malaria
papers.abstract: Cerebral malaria (CM) is a potentially lethal complication of Plasmodium falciparum infection characterized by blood-brain barrier disruption and brain hemorrhage. Although immune-mediated endothelial damage is central to CM pathology, the mechanisms linking cytotoxic immune responses to endothelial injury remain unclear. Here, we show that CD8 + T cells induce receptor-interacting serine/threonine-protein kinase 1 (RIPK1)–regulated cell death of brain endothelial cells in mouse CM, while RIPK1 phosphorylation is increased in brain endothelial cells in human CM. Using magnetic resonance imaging, three-dimensional tissue-cleared brain imaging, cross-species pathology, endothelial translatomics, immunocerebrovascular interactomics, and genetic association testing, we identify a CD8 + T cell–dependent, RIPK1-centered mouse endothelial cell death program. Combined RIPK1 and caspase inhibition protected cross-presenting endothelial cells from CD8 + T cell–mediated death in vitro. In vivo, brain endothelial-specific genetic inactivation or systemic pharmacological inhibition of RIPK1 kinase activity prolonged survival in mouse CM without altering parasitemia. These findings support RIPK1 inhibition as a promising therapeutic strategy to counter CD8 + T cell–induced endothelial death in CM.

papers.title: Molecular engineering of noncoordinating backbones in Zr-MOFs for ultrasensitive piezofluorochromism-based high pressure sensing
papers.abstract: Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) are promising pressure-responsive luminescent materials, but precise control of their emission under pressure remains a substantial challenge. Here, we engineered the piezofluorochromic response of zirconium-based MOFs by tuning the polarity of the emissive moieties through noncoordinating phenyl substituents. Four isostructural UiO-67 derivatives were synthesized. The most polar ligand, in UiO-67-PA, yields ultrasensitive piezofluorochromism with a bathochromic shift of 190 nanometers per gigapascal below 0.36 gigapascals. This sensitivity arises from two cooperative effects: enhanced conjugation through pressure-driven rotation of the aromatic rings and amplified orbital overlap resulting from polarity-induced electronic redistribution. This work broadens the strategies for modulating MOF luminescence and highlights their potential for pressure sensing.

papers.title: A single–amino acid difference between rodent and human Andes virus affects viral glycoprotein trafficking
papers.abstract: Andes virus (ANDV) causes hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), with rare outbreaks involving person-to-person transmission. A human ANDV isolate from one such outbreak and a rodent isolate from the same region differ in lethality in Syrian golden hamsters. Genomic analysis revealed 25 nonsynonymous substitutions, including one leading to a T641I change in the human ANDV glycoprotein precursor near its cleavage site. Although the isolates differed in growth kinetics, strand-specific RT-qPCR did not support major differences in viral RNA synthesis, whereas virion release was delayed in the case of the human isolate. In human cell expression systems, a single I641T substitution in the human ANDV glycoprotein resulted in decreased Golgi retention and faster release of virion-like particles relative to wild-type glycoprotein. Since ANDV egress takes place at the Golgi, the T641I change present in the human ANDV isolate may represent a human adaptive mutation influencing glycoprotein trafficking and virus particle release.

The structural basis of IL-36R proinflammatory signaling mediated by IL-36γ and IL-37
papers.abstract: The interleukin-36 receptor (IL-36R) drives proinflammatory signaling and is therapeutically targeted by spesolimab in acute skin inflammation. Beyond its three canonical agonists (IL-36α, IL-36β, and IL-36γ), IL-36R was recently proposed to be activated by IL-37. Together with antagonism by IL-36R antagonist (IL-36RA) and IL-38, this creates a complex structure-function landscape that remains poorly understood. Here, we report the cryo–electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of human IL-36γ bound to IL-36R and the shared co-receptor IL-1R accessory protein (IL-1RAcP). IL-36γ engages IL-36R with low affinity, enabling high-affinity IL-1RAcP recruitment. IL-37 exhibits the opposite binding signature, binding IL-36R with high affinity but IL-1RAcP weakly. Functional comparison of IL-36R engagement by IL-36γ and IL-37 confirmed their common proinflammatory signature, with IL-36γ exhibiting markedly higher potency, consistent with its more stable signaling complex. Structural comparison of cytokine-bound versus antibody-antagonized IL-36R revealed that spesolimab acts as an allosteric antagonist. This study therefore provides a structural and mechanistic blueprint for IL-36R activation by distinct cytokines.

papers.title: Programming immunity in situ: A new frontier of in vivo cell engineering
papers.abstract: In vivo cell engineering enables the direct programming of immune cells inside patients. Instead of isolating, modifying, and reinfusing cells, therapeutic instructions are delivered directly to selected immune cells through lipid nanoparticles or viral vectors. This approach could facilitate rapid and scalable deployment of varied immune cell therapies across disease contexts. Early clinical studies in oncology and autoimmunity demonstrate increasing technical and clinical feasibility. The next challenge lies in enhancing precision to ensure that vectors reach the target cell type and tissue, deliver the appropriate payload, and produce desired transient or durable activity. Progress in targeting ligands, vector design, biodistribution control, and genome editing is beginning to address these barriers. Ensuring safety against immunogenicity, inflammatory toxicity, off-target editing, and uncontrolled persistence remains a central priority. By mastering these constraints, in vivo engineering could turn endogenous immune cells into therapeutic agents generated directly in the body, expanding cell therapy to diseases refractory to current modalities.

Nuclear TRiC states captured in situ
papers.abstract: Xing et al. visualize the duty cycle of nuclear TRiC using cryo-electron tomography and identify TRiC interactors in the nucleus. These findings indicate that TRiC may act on misfolded proteins in the nucleus.

papers.title: PARP1 hyperactivation uncouples transcription from protein expression through nuclear RNA retention
papers.abstract: Ortega et al. show that PARP1 hyperactivation suppresses translation by promoting nuclear RNA retention. APE1-dependent cleavage of abasic sites triggers PARP1 hyperactivation, increasing nuclear PAR, which competes with RNA for binding to RNA-binding proteins. This disrupts RNA splicing and export, limiting expression of DNA damage-induced stress-response proteins.

papers.title: Identification and regulation of an ACC1-associated lipogenic metabolon in liver
papers.abstract: Zhu et al. identify a nutrient-responsive ACC1-centered metabolon that organizes lipid-synthesis enzymes near lipid droplets and associates with intracellular trafficking proteins. ACC1-associated interactions increase in steatotic, insulin-resistant livers, revealing a potential target for modulating hepatic lipid production in MASLD.

papers.title: Self-amplifying RNA vaccines encoding chimeric and mosaic hemagglutinins confer immunity against phylogenetically diverse influenza A viruses
papers.abstract: Seasonal influenza vaccines require annual reformulation and offer limited protection. Abbad et al. show that self-amplifying mRNA vaccines encoding chimeric and mosaic hemagglutinins elicit broadly protective antibodies against diverse influenza A virus strains, acting largely through Fc-mediated effector functions rather than neutralization, while remaining effective at very low doses.

papers.title: Chronotherapy leveraging dietary context overcomes circadian rhythm influence on cancer cell response to PPAR antagonists
papers.abstract: Bruno et al. demonstrate that feeding-fasting cycles, rather than tumor-intrinsic clocks, govern colorectal cancer sensitivity to PPAR antagonists. These findings highlight how dietary timing can maximize anticancer efficacy of metabolic drugs while minimizing toxicity for healthy tissues.

papers.title: Succinate promotes multiple myeloma cell proliferation through TCA cycle oxidation
papers.abstract: Multiple myeloma develops in the bone marrow, which exhibits altered metabolic features, including elevated succinate abundance. Gudgeon et al. interrogate implications of this, observing myeloma cells take up and oxidize environmental succinate, which increases mitochondrial respiration and drives proliferation. Consistently, elevated mitochondrial succinate transporter expression associates with accelerated myeloma progression.

papers.title: TNF- and IL-1-induced inflammation are enhanced through cooperative interactions between Nrf2 and NF-κB
papers.abstract: How reactive oxygen enhances inflammation is poorly understood. Here, Costigan et al. show that the redox-responsive transcription factor, Nrf2, can act as an enhancer of TNF- and IL-1- initiated inflammation through cooperative interactions with p65 RelA at NFkB-regulated promoters.

papers.title: A pangene family atlas of cereals uncovers hidden intraspecific and interspecific diversity
papers.abstract: This work presents a pangene-family atlas of four major cereals that captures gene diversity beyond individual reference genomes. Across four major cereals, pangene families capture highly dynamic composition and copy number, providing a broader view of gene-family diversity and evolution in crop pangenomes.

papers.title: Terminus est: Repurposing public RNA-seq data to map 3′ transcript termini in bacteria
A genome-wide CRISPR screening identifies targets that drive tolerogenic dendritic cells
papers.abstract: Li et al. performed a genome-wide CRISPR screen in primary dendritic cells and established CD86 as a phenotypic marker associated with tolerogenic dendritic cell (TolDC) function. They characterize molecular regulators of TolDC function and describe a UBE2L6-ISG15-USP18 pathway associated with dendritic cell-mediated tolerance.

papers.title: Cell-type specific and nanoscale control of hippocampal presynaptic homeostatic plasticity
papers.abstract: Using a combination of patch clamp electrophysiology and 3D transmission electron microscopy, Chipman et al. provide evidence for target specific control of presynaptic homeostatic plasticity (PHP) in adult mouse hippocampus area CA1. Even synapses contained within multi-spine boutons, separated by hundreds of nanometers, can differentially express PHP.

papers.title: Neural interface instructs layer 4-appropriate circuit reconstruction with engrafted human brain organoids and improves visually guided behavior
papers.abstract: Li and colleagues show that targeted neuromodulation guided by endogenous narrowband gamma rhythms instructs human brain organoid grafts to acquire layer 4-appropriate molecular and functional properties in the injured mouse visual cortex, enabling bidirectional host connectivity, direction-selective responses, and improved visually guided behavior.

papers.title: Phase-separated SOX5 drives human cranial neural crest fate commitment
papers.abstract: How transcription factors drive human cranial neural crest fate is poorly understood. Huang et al. combine an hPSC model with a TFome CRISPR screen to identify SOX5 as a fate switch. SOX5 forms phase-separated condensates that organize active chromatin through KU80 to promote neural crest commitment.

papers.title: Propionate, a short-chain fatty acid, is associated with disease activity in pediatric-onset multiple sclerosis
authors: the US Network of Pediatric MS Centers
papers.abstract: In young individuals shortly after multiple sclerosis onset, Schoeps et al. show that higher plasma and stool propionate levels are consistently associated with lower clinical and imaging disease activity. These findings suggest that a gut microbiome-derived short-chain fatty acid modulates early inflammatory activity and supports clinical testing of targeted supplementation.

papers.title: Unimodal imaging foundation models and vision-language models in MRI: A systematic review of emerging methods and clinical applications
papers.abstract: Tordjman et al. review 35 studies on MRI foundation and vision-language models, highlighting their diverse applications in diagnosis, segmentation, automated reporting, and outcome prediction. The authors identify methodological heterogeneity and a scarcity of paired image-text datasets as the primary barriers to widespread clinical translation.

papers.title: Effects of dietary carbohydrate-to-fat ratio on the gut microbiome following weight loss
papers.abstract: Kohli et al. conduct an ancillary gut microbiome-focused study within a controlled feeding trial, where participants undergo calorie restriction and weight loss, followed by randomization to diets varying in carbohydrate-to-fat ratio. While weight loss results in major changes in the microbiome, the carbohydrate-to-fat ratio is not associated with microbiome differences.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal dynamic evolution of the tumor microenvironment during neoadjuvant immunotherapy for bladder cancer
papers.abstract: Hu et al. map phenotypic evolution of the bladder cancer microenvironment during neoadjuvant immunotherapy. Treatment drives divergent tumor cell fates, establishes an immunotherapy-induced tumor-myeloid barrier, promotes terminal T cell exhaustion, and induces a senescent iCAF phenotype. SERPINH1 emerges as a potential therapeutic target for acquired resistance.

papers.title: Senescent T cells within the tumor microenvironment are a potent driver for tumor growth, stemness, and chemotherapy resistance
papers.abstract: Zhang et al. identify that senescent T (Tsen) cells accumulate within tumors and drive tumor growth, metastasis, stemness, and chemotherapy resistance. Mechanistically, lipid-enriched Tsen SASPs reprogram tumor lipid metabolism and activate STAT1/STAT3 signaling. Targeting Tsen cells or their metabolic crosstalk with tumor cells suppresses tumor progression and enhances therapeutic efficacy.

papers.title: Origins and heterogeneity of colorectal cancer
papers.abstract: The undulating topography of the intestinal epithelium creates regionalized homeostatic niches at the base of each crypt, with each niche supporting neutrally evolving oligoclonal stem cell populations. At the crypt base, the fate of stem cell progeny is tightly regulated by intercompartmental polarized morphogenetic gradients, which converge to instruct continuous, but controlled, epithelial-cell turnover. To initiate tumorigenesis, a neoplastic clone must defy or escape such morphogenetic constraints either by outcompeting neighbouring stem cells or by establishing an ectopic stem cell population de novo. The position of the cell-of-origin within the crypt thus determines the oncogenic mechanisms required to subvert local homeostatic control. In turn, this defines the route of carcinogenesis and underpins the pervasive heterogeneity of colorectal cancers. Here, we explore the relationship between the position of the cell-of-origin on the vertical crypt axis and the cell plasticity mechanisms co-opted and corrupted to escape homeostatic control. We consider how this influences clonal dynamics at the pre-cancer stage and initiates distinct carcinogenesis pathways engendering morphologically discrete precursor lesions. Finally, we discuss how such lesions progress to molecularly heterogeneous subtypes with distinct clinicopathological features and therapeutic outcomes, and how phenotypic, rather than just genotypic, heterogeneity promotes tumour-cell adaptation, therapeutic resistance and metastasis. This Review by Sphyris et al. discusses how the cell-of-origin determines the route of colorectal carcinogenesis and how phenotypic plasticity and heterogeneity shape tumour evolution, disease recurrence, metastatic competence and response to therapy.

papers.title: Decision quality in biopharma portfolio renewal
Regulatory lessons from FDA review of approved AAV gene therapies
The immune code of metal-dependent cell death
papers.abstract: Metal-dependent cell death can provoke, suppress, or evade immune recognition. We propose that these divergent outcomes reflect two interacting sources of information: signals generated by dying cells and changes in metal availability and localization that shape their perception. Their integration, rather than the death pathway alone, may determine immunogenicity.

papers.title: Creation of genomic chimeras via megabase scale genome expansion
papers.abstract: An organism's physiology is controlled by its genomic content. Building genomic chimeras would enable melding of the diverse functions and properties of life. However, prior arts in genome synthesis are limited to reconstituting pre-existing functions within a singular genome rather than combining diverse genomic functions across multiple distinct genomes. Existing methods are also prohibitively expensive, labor intensive, and time consuming, and thus fundamentally not scalable for creating large synthetic chimeric genomes. To address all these limitations, we invented Additive Conjugative-CAST Engineering (ACE) combining conjugation with CRISPR-associated transposition (CAST) to deliver and integrate up to half a genome per step from a donor cell into a precisely defined position in the recipient's genome. We have demonstrated ACE's capability to integrate at least a 2-megabase donor genomic segment in a single step and at least 3 megabase in two consecutive steps. Importantly, we confirmed ACE's generality through the creation of multiple genomic chimeras across species, genus, and at least order barriers. With ACE, we further demonstrate such chimeric organisms, or what we call genome expanded organisms (GEOs), can be stably forged from at least three starting bacterial strains, and can be stably maintained to express all their acquired genomic parts in a single chimera. ACE offers a new paradigm of creating artificial lifeforms to combine desired properties and potentially create novel functions beyond the constraints of nature. ACE also offers a unique perspective to probe unexplored plasticity in genome architecture and expression patterns of novel, massively expanded genomes.
affiliations: California Institute of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: TACO: An open, interpretable model for microsecond-scale TCR specificity prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting antigen-induced T-cell activation from T-cell receptor (TCR) and peptide sequence remains difficult for TCRs and peptides not represented in training data. We present TACO (T-Cell Activation from Chemistry and Orientation), an open statistical model for predicting TCR specificity against HLA-A*02:01-presented peptides. TACO takes as input the peptide sequence and six TCR CDR loop sequences. Learning from binary activation labels, TACO selects a single canonical orientation of the CDR loops over the peptide and learns five amino-acid contact-potential matrices as well as two peptide-exposure profiles.The orientation is fixed and does not require experimentally determined or predicted structures. We evaluate TACO on held-out peptides separated by Levenshtein distance at least four from all training and validation peptides, limiting near-neighbor shortcut learning. TACO achieves AUROC 0.67 on a large held-out activation dataset and 0.68 on IMMREP25 HLA-A*02:01, exceeding the open structure-based models evaluated here and matching the reported AlphaFold3-TCRdock result. The model has 2,019 fitted parameters, retains most within-peptide ranking signal with TCR$\beta$ sequence alone, and reaches 406,000 TCR--peptide predictions per second on CPU. This throughput enables computational evaluation of large TCR-peptide search spaces. We show its potential use for prioritizing candidate target peptides from large peptide libraries, reducing the search space for downstream experimental investigation. TACO fitted parameters also expose candidate physicochemical patterns that can be inspected directly. We release TACO's parameters and complete training, evaluation, and inference code.
affiliations: Adaptive Biotechnologies Corp (corresponding author)

papers.title: CauloBrowser 2.0: an AI powered update
papers.abstract: CauloBrowser is a systems-biology database for Caulobacter crescentus that organizes the largest repository of experimental data for this model bacterium. The original CauloBrowser provided a web interface for accessing these data, but the growing number of experimental datasets and advances in AI chatbots motivated an updated resource. We developed CauloBrowser 2.0 (CauloBrowser.org) as an open-source application that broadens access to RNA-seq, microarray, ribosome profiling, Tn-seq, ChIP-seq, and genome annotation data. The CauloChat AI interface allows users to query these datasets in natural language, generate visualizations, and achieve complex biological insights. While the database is hosted freely on the web, users may also download the database and run it locally, reducing dependence on the web-hosted service and allowing laboratories to use compatible unpublished datasets. Altogether, CauloBrowser 2.0 provides a significant update for exploring diverse systems biology data in C. crescentus.
affiliations: Indiana University Bloomington (corresponding author)

papers.title: Integrative identification of Tetratostichococcus sp. CCAH0201 (Trebouxiophyceae, Chlorophyta) from Rhizophora leaves in the Can Gio Mangrove Forest, Vietnam
papers.abstract: A microalgal strain from Rhizophora leaves in the Can Gio Mangrove Forest, Vietnam, was examined by light microscopy and three molecular markers. Thirty-six cells from 22 micrographs measured 6.68-12.74 by 3.49-4.79 micrometres. Homologous phylogenetic windows comprised 550 nucleotides for SSU rDNA, 711 for ITS and 1,170 for rbcL. CCAH0201, P1 and Tetratostichococcus jenerensis SAG 2138 shared the SSU 3-prime sequence, whereas ITS and rbcL placed CCAH0201 with P1 (SH-aLRT/UFBoot 87/94 and 96.9/99). CCAH0201 differed from P1 at 22/711 ITS and 4/1,170 rbcL sites. Structure-guided ITS2 comparison identified one strict CBC, one two-sided change from a wobble pair and three hemi-CBCs relative to P1. CCAH0201 is thus identified as Tetratostichococcus sp. in a lineage close to P1.
affiliations: Ho Chi Minh City University of Industry and Trade (HUIT), (corresponding author)

papers.title: The enemy of my enemy: A bacterial antagonist rescues Chlamydomonas by inactivating a toxin from a rival
papers.abstract: Microbial interactions are shaped by multiple community members, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated a tripartite interaction between the microalga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii and two Pseudomonas bacteria that coexist in the same soil habitat. In pairwise cultures, all three interactions are amensalistic (-like): Pseudomonas protegens Pf-5 antagonizes both C. reinhardtii and Pseudomonas fluorescens HKI0770 without benefit, while P. fluorescens inhibits C. reinhardtii without profiting from the alga. However, in a tripartite culture, P. fluorescens protects C. reinhardtii from P. protegens and promotes algal recovery. This protection is not stopped when the used carbon source, acetate, is supplemented. The P. fluorescens rescue effect is associated with reduced levels of the polyyne toxin protegencin produced by P. protegens. Protegencin levels, detected by Raman microspectroscopy, are decreased by application of spent medium or protein extracts from P. fluorescens, while heat- and protease-treatment abolish this activity. A heat-sensitive, proteinaceous factor, likely an enzyme(s), appears to contribute to protegencin inactivation. Our results show that P. fluorescens rescues C. reinhardtii by inactivating protegencin, despite being inhibited by P. protegens. These findings demonstrate the importance of investigating higher-order effects, since additional community members can transform pairwise antagonistic interactions into conditional protection through toxin inactivation.
affiliations: Matthias Schleiden Institute of Genetics, Bioinformatics and Molecular Botany, Friedrich Schiller University Jena, 07743 Jena, Germany and Cluster of Excellence (corresponding author)

papers.title: Charting the Structure and Functional Landscape of the SF3B1 Intrinsically Disordered Region
papers.abstract: Despite its essential role in pre-mRNA splicing, the structure and functional significance of the intrinsically disordered N-terminal domain (NTD) of SF3B1, a core component of the SF3b spliceosome complex, remain poorly understood. Here, we combine nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS), biochemistry, bioinformatics approaches, with molecular dynamics simulations to characterize the conformational landscape of the SF3B1-NTD and its phosphorylation-dependent remodelling. Specifically, we focus on the 186-341 region (186-341SF3B1), which contains at least four regulatory phosphorylation sites. We reveal that 186-341SF3B1 is highly dynamic, lacking a stable secondary structure, and that phosphorylation of T211, T235, T313, and T328 induces a shift toward more compact states driven by the formation of intramolecular interactions. Additionally, we unveil that 186-341SF3B1 interacts with RNA primarily via the arginine residues flaking one of the conserved tryptophan-centred motifs present within SF3B1-NTD. These interactions are transient and heterogeneous, reflecting a nonspecific yet sequence-dependent recognition mechanism. Collectively, this study provides a comprehensive description of the conformational landscape and functional features of the SF3B1-NTD, and expands the portfolio of its possible interactors, thus broadening our understanding of how intrinsic disorder, post-translational modifications, and sequence-encoded motifs cooperate to regulate pre-mRNA splicing.
affiliations: CNR-IOM (corresponding author)

papers.title: Rapid, accurate, and memory-frugal sub-gene-level quantification of probe-based, multiplexed single-cell data
papers.abstract: Probe-based, multiplexed single-cell assays enable accurate transcriptome profiling while processing multiple samples in parallel. Their predefined probe sequences and additional sample barcodes introduce computational requirements that differ from those of poly(A)-based assays, for which many existing single-cell quantification tools were developed. We extend simpleaf to enable efficient demultiplexing and quantification of probe-based single-cell libraries. A new, cache-friendly dictionary specializes lookup to small probe references, while a shared thread budget balances parallel decompression and mapping. We extend RAD and downstream tools with reusable sample-scoped correction plans and external-memory collation of hierarchically barcoded data, retaining probe identities through quantification to enable rapid mapping and quantification with a small working memory budget. Across five 10x Genomics Flex datasets comprising 44 samples, simpleaf had the shortest runtime and lowest peak memory use of the three tools on every library, while producing gene-expression estimates, cell clusters, and marker genes concordant with cyto and Cell Ranger. Compared with cyto, simpleaf was on average 2 times faster and used approximately one-thirteenth as much memory. simpleaf also exports probe-level quantification results, allowing a range of analyses at sub-gene resolution. Here, we show that individual probe counts reveal expression changes obscured by gene-level aggregation, identify the transcript groups contributing to gene-level changes, and provide insight into splicing dynamics across cell types. These results demonstrate the computational and biological value of retaining probe-level information in multiplexed singlecell analysis.
affiliations: University of Maryland (corresponding author)

papers.title: Inferring gene regulatory networks from single-cell perturbation data by optimizing causal reach of latent mediator dynamics
papers.abstract: Resolving the causal structure of gene regulatory networks is central to understanding cellular regulation. Pooled CRISPR screens with single-cell RNA readouts measure the transcriptional consequences of many interventions in parallel, providing a powerful resource for causal discovery. Combinatorial designs that perturb multiple regulators per cell increase throughput and can reveal responses that single-gene perturbations do not. However, inferring causal gene networks from these experiments remains challenging because gene regulatory interactions are nonlinear, dynamic, and often involve feedback. Thus, attributing the combined effect of several perturbations to individual regulators remains difficult. Additionally, transcriptional regulation is ultimately carried out by proteins, while single-cell perturbation datasets generally measure only RNA levels. Existing methods often simplify regulatory dynamics or rely on assumptions that conflict with gene regulation, such as acyclicity. Moreover, current evaluation practices usually rely on expression prediction error, which is readily computable in real datasets, but does not necessarily reflect graph quality. A complementary metric is needed to assess inferred regulatory connections using observed perturbation responses in real data. To address these challenges, we present CausalODE, a differentiable framework for learning causal graphs from single-cell perturbation data. Our approach incorporates three central insights to improve upon previous methods. First, genes that are differentially expressed when a gene is perturbed should be downstream of the target gene in the regulatory network; we quantify this property with a metric we term causal reach. Second, causal interactions involve transient cellular responses in RNA transcription, splicing, and degradation. Third, gene regulatory interactions are mediated by proteins, whose levels are not directly measured in single-cell RNA-seq experiments. Building on these insights, CausalODE learns a graph that optimizes the causal reach metric, captures transient cellular responses to perturbation, and explicitly models the latent dynamics of protein levels. Together, these components allow nonlinear responses, feedback loops, and time-lagged regulation. Across simulated Perturb-seq datasets with different sparsities and graph structures, CausalODE improves AUPRC and precision among top-ranked edges compared with baselines and competing methods, while achieving competitive AUROC. We introduce a metric to evaluate the causal reach of inferred graphs on real data by measuring how well the graphs explain differentially expressed genes in single-cell perturbation experiments. Using this metric, CausalODE outperforms the strongest competing method or baseline by approximately 60% on the CaRPool-seq knockdown dataset and 80% on the Norman et al. activation dataset. Its top-ranked edges generally show greater enrichment for high-confidence evidence from cell-type-matched ChIP-seq, CollecTRI, and regulatory STRING than those of other methods. The inferred graphs also distinguish non-additive from approximately additive genetic interactions in held-out perturbation pairs. Finally, ablation analyses show that optimizing causal reach improves performance on held-out perturbations, and the learned latent regulator activities track simulated protein dynamics, with median temporal correlations ranging from 0.79 to 0.99.
affiliations: University of Michigan (corresponding author)

papers.title: Murine Toll-like receptor 8 is a functional sensor of nucleic acid fragments
papers.abstract: Toll-like receptors 7 and 8 (TLR7 and TLR8) detect nucleic acid degradation products to initiate innate immune responses, although their ligand-sensing functions differ between species. Whereas human TLR8 is a well-established nucleic acid sensor, murine TLR8 (mTLR8) has long been considered unable to detect nucleic acids. Here, we show that mTLR8 is an active receptor that responds to the synthetic agonist TL8-506 and the endogenous cyclic nucleotide 2',3'-cGMP, with signalling potentiated by cooperative binding of nucleic acid fragments at the secondary ligand-binding site. Using Tlr7-deficient mice expressing mTlr8 under control of the Tlr7 promoter, we demonstrate that mTLR8 partially restores TLR7-dependent tonic transcriptional programs in splenocytes, indicating responsiveness to physiological ligands in vivo. Comparison with a chimeric human-mouse TLR8 knock-in model expressing human TLR8 from the endogenous murine Tlr7 locus demonstrated that the mTLR8 ectodomain is intrinsically less sensitive, consistent with sequence divergence in the LRR11-12 region that links agonist recognition to antagonist regulation. Collectively, these findings establish mTLR8 as a functional nucleic acid sensor specialized for combinatorial detection of nucleic acid degradation products, extending the murine endosomal nucleic acid-sensing repertoire beyond TLR3, TLR7, TLR9, and TLR13.
affiliations: Neuroscience Research Center, Charite - Universitaetsmedizin Berlin, corporate member of Freie Universitaet Berlin, Humboldt-Universitaet zu Berlin, and Berlin (corresponding author)

papers.title: 2'-O-Methylated ncRNA condensates form a recombination center for IgH synapsis
papers.abstract: How fibrillarin (FBL), an RNA 2'-O-methyltransferase, regulates antibody diversification remains unclear. This study demonstrated that FBL promotes switch (S)-S DNA synapsis at the IgH locus during class switch recombination (CSR), without affecting DNA cleavage. Both RNA-binding and catalytic activities of FBL were essential for CSR. Moreover, MED19 supported DNA cleavage and synapsis by regulating snoRNAs that guide 2'-O-methylation. Mechanistically, FBL methylated -germline transcripts (-GLTs), cis-acting noncoding RNAs forming nuclear condensates harboring machinery for RNA processing, RNP remodeling, and chromatin dynamics. FBL-mediated 2'-O-methylation governed condensate protein composition. FBL suppression aberrantly enriched nucleolar proteins, including WDR74. Crucially, low WDR74 expression in B cells promoted - and -GLT condensate fusion, thereby enhancing S-S synapsis, CSR, and IgH/c-Myc translocation, potentially contributing to poor myeloma prognosis. Altogether, our findings revealed that RNA 2'-O-methylation dictates GLT condensate composition and fusion dynamics to establish a recombination center, driving genomic DNA synapsis in B cells.
affiliations: Department of Immunology and Genomic Medicine, Center for Cancer Immunotherapy and Immunobiology, Graduate School of Medicine, Kyoto University (corresponding author)

papers.title: RadMultiBench: A Reproducible Dual-Task Benchmark Exposing the Limits of Pre-Trained Vision-Language Models Across Thoracic and Breast Imaging
papers.abstract: We present RadMultiBench, a multimodal benchmark of 6,148 medical images paired with expert radiological impressions across five categories--Breast Cancer, Lung Benign, Lung Malignant, Pneumonia, and Tuberculosis--targeting two core clinical tasks: automated report generation and disease classification. To enable reliable, repeatable experimentation, we provide a reproducible pipeline for data ingestion, de-identification, split management, and standardized reporting of text and classification metrics, facilitating dataset versioning and continuous benchmark testing. We compare three architectures: (1) a classical CNN-RNN with Bahdanau attention (ResNet-LSTM), (2) a general-domain vision-language (V-L) prefix-projection model (CLIP-GPT), and (3) a domain-specific V-L prefix-projection model (BioViL-T). Results reveal a sharp performance divide: the ResNet-LSTM attains near-perfect classification (99.5% accuracy) and is the only model to generate coherent reports (BLEU-4 = 0.021), whereas both prefix-projection models catastrophically fail generation (BLEU-4 [≤] 0.0001); moreover, the domain-specific BioViL-T also fails classification (11.5% accuracy). From a data-engineering angle, the pipeline is productionizable with lineage, feature registries, and continuous integration to guard against silent regressions when updating models or data; from a data-science angle, the benchmark provides baselines and analyses that foreground feature alignment and architectural suitability as first-order concerns, inviting ablations on multimodal objectives, retrieval-augmented encoders, and uncertainty-aware decoding. Overall, RadMultiBench highlights that state-of-the-art status in general V-L domains does not translate automatically to high-stakes clinical tasks, and it furnishes the tooling and evidence base needed to develop robust, clinically viable multimodal systems.
affiliations: North South University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Organised streaming of cerebrospinal fluid in the human third ventricle
papers.abstract: Quasi-periodic pressure pulses associated with cardiac and respiratory activity generate reciprocating cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) motion in the human ventricles. Regular waves dominated by the cardiac cycle are overlaid with cycles of low-frequency respiratory waves, the latter to become stronger in forced breathing or even dominated by large successive flushes in NREM sleep. The present study investigates how such waves contribute to residual streaming within the human ventricles. Transient CFD simulations were performed in the third ventricle at varying parameters of frequency, stroke volume and wave-form asymmetry. Increasing the aqueduct peak Reynolds-number, either by small stroke volume and high frequency or large stroke volume at low frequency, transfers the flow from a reversible flow pattern to the formation of clear preferential pathways, alternating between the in- and outflow cycle. The resulting permanent streaming flux across the aqueduct relative to the mean oscillatory flow-rate, i.e. the dimensionless streaming ratio SR follows a rational saturation relation, SR [~] ReAq,peak/(C + ReAq,peak), demonstrating that increasing the peak aqueduct Reynolds number yields diminishing returns and bounds the relative contribution of residual inter-ventricular streaming. These findings demonstrate differences in hydrodynamic organisation in the third ventricle and highlight the importance of this organisation for intraventricular fluid exchange.
affiliations: City University London (corresponding author)

papers.title: Expanding Therapeutic Target Space from Genes to Disease-Relevant Molecular Forms with Agent3Diso
papers.abstract: Therapeutic targets are commonly defined at the gene or canonical protein level, yet therapeutic effects are ultimately exerted through specific molecular states operating in specific biological contexts. Alternative splicing generates diverse RNA and translated protein forms whose functional consequences, disease relevance, and therapeutic vulnerabilities can differ substantially within the same gene. Resolving these disease-relevant molecular forms creates opportunities for selective intervention across complementary RNA- and protein-directed modalities, but requires reasoning across tightly coupled molecular layers, heterogeneous evidence, explicit biological constraints, and modality-specific therapeutic requirements. Here, we present Agent3Diso, a hybrid deterministic--agent multimodal framework for molecular-form-resolved therapeutic discovery. Agent3Diso establishes cross-layer molecular coherence from transcript identity and translation to structure, function, and disease context; enforces explicit molecular and therapeutic constraints through deterministic computation; and applies specialized agentic reasoning to evidence synthesis, mechanistic interpretation, conflict resolution, hypothesis critique, and experimental design. The framework evaluates therapeutic opportunities across multiple intervention modalities and translates prioritized disease-relevant molecular states into traceable hypotheses linking molecular identity, therapeutic rationale, modality, concrete intervention, uncertainty, and experimental validation. By integrating molecular resolution with constraint-aware and modality-conditioned agentic reasoning, Agent3Diso provides a framework for extending therapeutic discovery beyond gene-level targets toward disease-relevant molecular forms.
affiliations: The Chinese University Of Hong Kong (corresponding author)

papers.title: PIKfyve inhibition induces LRRK2 activation through phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate and CASM
papers.abstract: LRRK2 is a Parkinson's disease (PD)-associated kinase that phosphorylates Rab GTPases. Hyperactivation of LRRK2, which is thought to cause PD, occurs on stressed endolysosomal membranes via CASM (conjugation of ATG8 to single membranes) and Rab, whereas the involvement of specific membrane lipids remained unclear. Here, we found that the inhibition of PIKfyve that metabolizes phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI3P) induces hyperactivation of LRRK2, and that additional inhibition of the class III phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) that generates PI3P suppressed LRRK2 hyperactivation. Cellular PI3P levels were indeed elevated when LRRK2 was activated. CASM-induced activation of LRRK2, but not CASM itself, was suppressed by PI3K inhibitors, whereas inhibition of CASM or Rab12/Rab29 suppressed LRRK2 activation induced by PIKfyve inhibitors. LRRK2 and phospho-Rab10 were co-localized with PI3P on LAMP1-positive enlarged vacuoles, and LRRK2 directly bound PI3P in vitro via its N-terminal positively charged amino acids. Together, we propose an updated mechanism of LRRK2 hyperactivation that simultaneously requires CASM, Rab and PI3P-rich membranes.
affiliations: The University of Tokyo (corresponding author)

papers.title: Intravital microscopy and statistical image analysis of early engraftment of haematopoietic stem cells reveal dynamic and evolving cellular behaviours linked to progressive differentiation.
papers.abstract: Haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) have long been used in the clinic for bone marrow transplantation applications, critical for the survival of an increasingly wide range of patients with haematological, oncological and immunological pathologies. Despite this, little is known about the mechanisms through which relatively few stem cells are able to regenerate the entire haematopoietic tissue of transplant recipients. To gain insights on this biological process, we used intravital microscopy of calvarium bone marrow, collecting tissue-wide images and a total of 850 hours of tracks of engrafting haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells from 24 hours to 8 days following injection in lethally irradiated recipients. Analysis of the data revealed that regenerating HSCs and their immediate progeny are highly dynamic, migrating through the parenchyma at both the microscopic and near-macroscopic scales, i.e. within and in-and-out of fields of view. HSC-derived cell clusters, expanded locally between day 2 and day 4 post-transplant, leading to patches of densely populated bone marrow by day 8. Single cell level analysis highlighted increasingly heterogenous cellular behaviours over time. Track clustering based on migration and niche interaction parameters combined with post-tracking whole mount immunostaining revealed that persistence in the vicinity of nestin-GFP perivascular cells and relatively slow movement correlated with stemness, while more heterogeneous niche interactions coupled with slowest or faster migration correlated with differentiation, validated through flow cytometry analysis and functional studies. The findings presented here shed light on the fundamental principles driving haematopoietic regeneration in transplantation settings.
affiliations: Imperial College London (corresponding author)

papers.title: Preferential Isoform Usage and Isoform Switching in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Patients with Distinct Autoantibody Profile
papers.abstract: RNA sequencing has advanced our understanding of molecular heterogeneity in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), yet most studies have focused on differential gene expression (DGE), which overlooks transcript-level complexity. Alternative splicing and polyadenylation generate multiple isoforms from a single gene, and their dysregulation may contribute to autoimmune pathogenesis, including through the production of non-canonical isoforms with potential autoantigenic properties. To explore this underexamined dimension, we analysed differential isoform usage (DIU) and major isoform switching (MIS) across SLE subgroups stratified by autoantibody profile: anti-dsDNA+, anti-ENA+ and anti-dsDNA+ENA+. Subgroup-specific DIU and MIS events were enriched in RNA-binding and transcription-related functions. In the anti-dsDNA+ subgroup, the T-cell receptor adaptor GRAP2 showed isoform switching accompanied by expansion of a non-coding retained-intron transcript. In the anti-ENA+ subgroup, IGHM switched from the membrane-bound to the secretory form, consistent with an antibody-secreting cell signature; NACA, a reported IgE autoantigen, showed isoform switching; and BRI3, linked to TNF--induced cell death, switched toward its protein-coding transcript. In the anti-dsDNA+ENA+ subgroup, TNFAIP2, a TNF--induced gene, showed isoform redistribution with loss of a uORF-containing transcript. These findings highlight isoform regulation as a distinct, subgroup-specific and functionally relevant layer of transcriptomic dysregulation in SLE.
affiliations: Department of Molecular and Human Genetics, Institute of Science, Banaras Hindu University, Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh, India (corresponding author)

papers.title: Metabolites cross the membrane, the transcriptome does not follow: co-localization is required for the cyanobacterial response to a yeast partner
papers.abstract: Interactions between phototrophs and heterotrophs are usually explained by cross-feeding, yet whether that exchange alone accounts for the phototroph's response has rarely been tested. We grew the sucrose-secreting cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus with the yeast Rhodotorula toruloides as a synthetic community, either in mixed co-culture or in membrane-separated co-culture (0.22 m pore size), each with a matched axenic control. Metabolite exchange occurred in both configurations: sucrose reached the yeast and was consumed, and yeast-derived metabolites reached the cyanobacterium. The yeast reached a higher final density behind the membrane, whereas the cyanobacterium gained about 9% over its axenic control only in mixed co-culture. Yet the cyanobacterial transcriptome responded only with co-localization: expression of 51 genes changed consistently across time points (day-averaged q < 0.05), against one gene behind the membrane, and the number of differentially expressed genes rose from 20 on day 4 to 91 and 127 on days 6 and 8. Nine regulatory programs (iModulons), mainly nitrogen and photosynthesis, responded in mixed co-culture and none behind the membrane. Reactor configuration alone changed 40 genes in axenic culture. These results suggest that co-localization, in addition to metabolite exchange, was required for the heterotrophic partner to trigger a response in the phototroph. Co-culture studies that infer interactions from shared metabolites may miss effects that depend on spatial structure. Importance Partnerships between light-powered microbes and the heterotrophs living alongside them move large amounts of carbon in oceans and soils, and are now built on purpose to turn carbon dioxide into fuels and chemicals. Such partnerships are usually described by the chemicals the partners trade, so we asked whether those chemicals are enough. The cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus and the yeast Rhodotorula toruloides were grown together in one vessel, or in two chambers divided by a membrane that molecules cross but cells cannot. The yeast fed on cyanobacterial sugar in both, yet the cyanobacterium changed its gene activity only when the two shared a space. Partners in nature are usually clustered rather than evenly mixed, so closeness may contribute as much as the chemicals themselves. Keeping partners apart in engineered cultures can still deliver carbon to the heterotroph, but may not deliver the benefits of partnership to the phototroph.
affiliations: Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (corresponding author)

papers.title: Tools for genetic mapping and gene identification in Caenorhabditis briggsae
papers.abstract: The nematode Caenorhabditis briggsae serves as an important companion species for Caenorhabditis elegans for comparative studies. Because C. briggsae exhibits androdioecious reproduction and ease of laboratory culture similar to C. elegans, it has long been used for genetic studies in cross-species comparisons of mutant phenotypes to uncover the evolution of gene function. Here, we provide an updated toolkit for C. briggsae genetic experiments, leveraging the resource of recently improved C. briggsae genome sequence assemblies with variant mapping tools and gene identification methods. We identify and validate a set of indel variants between CGC2 (AF16) and two divergent strains, HK104 and VX34. We then use these variants to genetically map 10 previously isolated mutations and identify the impacted genes using high-throughput sequencing. We combine these new genes with others curated from the literature into an updated map with 73 genes, providing an enriched resource for C. briggsae genetic studies.
affiliations: Ohio State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: TestNet-PA: Sampling-Zero-Aware Inference of Microbial Presence-Absence Networks
papers.abstract: Microbial presence-absence networks, also referred to as co-occurrence networks, characterize patterns of coexistence and incompatibility among taxa. However, sequencing-based presence--absence analysis can be compromised by pervasive 'sampling zeros' in microbiome data, causing widely used methods such as Fisher's exact test to identify spurious co-occurrence dependence. To our knowledge, no existing method is designed to account for sampling zeros in this setting. We introduce TestNet-PA, a method for testing pairwise microbial co-occurrence dependence. TestNet-PA models each observed zero as arising from a mixture of 'structural' and 'sampling' zeros, with the mixing probabilities governed by library size and relative abundance. Because the relative abundance underlying an observed zero is unobserved, we impute it by borrowing information from other samples. We then construct a quasi-likelihood and develop an EM algorithm to infer dependence between the underlying true presence--absence statuses. Extensive simulations based on real gut, vaginal, and oral microbiome data templates showed that TestNet-PA consistently controlled the FDR while maintaining good sensitivity. By contrast, Fisher's exact test generally yielded inflated FDR. Analyses of the three real microbiome datasets further illustrated how accounting for sampling zeros can affect the inferred co-occurrence networks.
affiliations: Department of Biostatistics, School of Public Health, Peking University, Beijing, 100191, China (corresponding author)

papers.title: Generative Models for Novel Enzymatic Reactions: How Far Do They Go?
papers.abstract: Enzyme function prediction is a long-standing problem in biology, and deep learning methods have recently become popular to improve performance on this task. While most of these models focus on classifying enzymes or mapping them to known reactions, predicting unknown biochemical reactions remains underexplored. Here we thoroughly examine an approach that generates reactions absent from the training data from the enzyme alone. Existing methods such as BLASTp or CLIPZyme cannot, by design, output reactions that are absent from their training data or were not supplied at inference. The closest prior model, RxnPred, reports high fingerprint-similarity scores on held-out enzymes, a less stringent criterion than exact recovery, but fails to recover the correct answer on unseen reactions. We present a structure-conditioned generative model that outputs a complete reaction, reactants and products, and evaluate it on EnzymeMap_x, a reaction-disjoint benchmark in which no test reaction appears in training, under exact, stereo-respecting scoring. On this benchmark, within 400 sampled candidates, the model generates the complete, correct reaction for 25.0% of the subset of test enzyme--reaction pairs whose reaction is a new combination of metabolites seen in training. Surprisingly, it also correctly generates a few reactions composed of metabolites it has not seen in training (1.6%), though their embeddings are present in the vocabulary. With a lower budget, re-ranking places the correct reaction first for 5.6% of pairs and in the top ten for 12.4%, when the reaction is assumed not to be already known (0.2% and 8.1% without that assumption) along with confidence scores. Assessed more leniently, the model produces at least one correct reaction known for the enzyme (usually memorised from training) for 71.2% of test pairs. Going further, without any retraining, a sequence-only model given the reactants as well as the enzyme produces the correct product set for 9.5% of pairs within five candidates, without re-ranking. We also present head-to-head comparisons on these tasks with BLASTp, DIAMOND, RxnPred and Horizyn. Structure conditioning improves fingerprint similarity on homology-stratified splits, but a matched sequence-only ablation at the best configuration finds no measurable effect on exact recovery. Data coverage and chemical initialisation of the vocabulary seem to matter more than encoder geometry.
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology Madras, Chennai, India (corresponding author)

papers.title: Integrative Multiomics Analysis of the Angiogenesis-EMT Interface in Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma
papers.abstract: Angiogenesis and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) are key hallmarks that contribute to the progression of oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), but whether the two programs vary simultaneously across tumors and how much of this reflects tumor composition remain unclear. We scored predefined, non-overlapping 20-gene angiogenesis and EMT signatures with a rank-based method in 342 primary oral cavity tumors from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA-OSCC). The two programs were strongly correlated (Spearman rho = 0.809, P = 2.7 x 10^-80), and 2,396 bridge genes were associated with both programs across the transcriptome. The bridge genes were enriched in pathways associated with focal adhesion and extracellular matrix-receptor interaction. In the cellular case, fibroblast and endothelial marker scores were prominent and correlated with the program scores. The coupling was attenuated but remained positive after joint adjustment for tumor purity and stromal and immune scores (partial rho = 0.406) and with an epithelial-restricted EMT score (rho = 0.710). Further correlation was performed with a partial EMT (pEMT), which shows a significant positive correlation (rho = 0.59) and an inverse correlation with tumor purity (rho = -0.70). 146 final gene candidates were found using multi-omic evidence and candidate-level testing on the external cohort GSE30784; after adjusting for inferred cell fractions, 101 of these candidates supported the dual program. For thorough characterization, three candidates with an emphasis on OSMR, MICAL2, and LHFPL2 were chosen. Additional CPTAC data were used to confirm protein-level support, which was strongest for MICAL2. No significant connection was seen between the Interface score and overall survival (hazard ratio per 1-SD increase, 0.92; 95% CI, 0.78-1.08). These results describe a coordinated angiogenesis-EMT transcriptional state in OSCC that is attenuated but retained after accounting for tumor composition, and nominate candidate genes for experimental study.
affiliations: University of Florida (corresponding author)

papers.title: Hub labeling makes exact distance calculation practical for large human pangenome graphs
papers.abstract: Pangenome graphs are now a standard reference representation, and tools built on them depend on fast minimum-distance queries between graph positions, for example, when clustering seed matches during read alignment. The baseline distance index, previously used by the vg toolkit, answers such queries based on a decomposition of the graph into nested subgraphs called "snarls". Within each snarl, the index uses a dense all-pairs distance matrix. Because such a matrix is quadratic in a snarl's number of children, the large, complex snarls that often occur in many pangenome graphs dominate the overall index size. This means whole-genome graphs can be impractical to index. To mitigate this, the baseline distance index does not fully index the largest snarls, and thus cannot itself answer certain queries involving them. We replace the dense matrix with a hub labeling for snarls above a size limit. Because hub labeling and associated methods are defined for directed graphs, we introduce a directed representation of a snarl's bidirected internal "net graph", whose shortest path lengths are the net graph's minimum walk lengths. Hub labels are built using pruned landmark labeling, ordered by a contraction hierarchy. On four human chromosome pangenomes, our hub-labeling-based distance index indexes every snarl in 0.9 GB to 3.0 GB at a snarl limit of 500, an estimated 28x to 119x less space than dense distance matrices would need for those snarls with more than 500 children, and supports the 3-18.6% of node-to-node queries that the previous index cannot answer by itself. On the queries both indexes can answer, query time distributions broadly overlap. We explore the snarl limit parameter space and are able to build indexes under 50 GB for four human whole-genome pangenomes in under 6 hours, where we estimate dense matrices could have required multiple terabytes.
affiliations: University of California, Santa Cruz (corresponding author)

papers.title: Label-free flow operators and stability operators from single-cell time courses: what local dynamical operators can and cannot identify
papers.abstract: Local Jacobians of single-cell dynamics are used to locate unstable cells along trajectories, but what they identify from measured data has rarely been tested against independent truth. We present scJDO2, which separates two per-cell operators by the time information they require: a score operator, the Hessian of a score-matched log density, available from any snapshot; and a flow operator, the Jacobian of a drift fitted to a measured velocity, here estimated label-free from a sampled time course by entropic optimal transport. Both are summarized in a shared operator space of magnitude-free descriptors, with the invariance of each stated, and evaluated with pre-registered tests. On synthetic data calibrated to six real datasets, the flow operator from the time course alone separated fate-bifurcation cells from committed cells on held-out seeds (AUC 0.89-1.00) with a-priori settings; tuning on development seeds overfit. On LARRY lineage-traced hematopoiesis, its fitted drift predicted the clonal displacement of barcoded cells beyond population movement (Spearman 0.56, permutation p < 0.001; 0.50 after removing the mean shift) and a held-out sampling day better than mean-displacement and no-movement baselines (energy distance 0.69, 95 % CI 0.66-0.73, vs 0.87 and 0.88); lineage thus validates the velocity, not {lambda}. Mini-batch transport reproduced dense transport (velocity cosine 0.9998) and scaled to all 130,887 cells (transport 5 min and 2.5 GB; drift fit and Jacobians 21 min and 1.3 GB). On an independent simulator it detected two of three bifurcations and two of three cycles and never reported instability on linear trajectories. Several readings failed. Neither operator recovers the values of the true Jacobian; the flow operators leading eigenvalue ranks branching cells empirically. The flow operator depends on the transport metric and inverts on Factor Analysis. Operator archetypes isolated bifurcation cells but did not outperform expression clustering and were unstable across fit seeds. The score operator did not predict CRISPRi knockdown responses or sister-cell fate coherence. A confirmatory test of transition timing could not be constructed, and diffusion is not identifiable at typical sampling intervals. The released software reports these diagnostics.
affiliations: Brigham Young University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Multimodal cellular context enables molecular phenotyping from single-molecule trajectories
papers.abstract: Single-molecule tracking (SMT) provides direct measurements of molecular dynamics in living cells, but motion alone rarely specifies the underlying biological process, without accounting for the cellular environment in which that motion occurs. Here, we present MIST (Multimodal Interpretation of Single-molecule Trajectories), a framework that brings the paradigm of image-based profiling to single molecules by integrating trajectory dynamics, emitter properties and cellular context into a common, reusable phenotype space. Using a reference panel of nine proteins in live Escherichia coli, we show that multimodal context more than doubled protein-specific information relative to trajectory features alone, a gap that learned trajectory representations did not close. MIST allowed de novo identification of shared transcription-translation phenotype at the nucleoid periphery. A fixed reference space detected effects of previously uncharacterized MukB ATPase mutations without retraining. MIST provides an interpretable and extensible framework for comparing proteins, mutants and conditions within a common space of molecular phenotypes.
affiliations: Aalto University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Quantum Entanglement as a Physical Determinant of Genomic Instability in TP53
papers.abstract: Abstract Mutations in the TP53 tumor suppressor gene are among the most frequent alterations in human cancers, but whether quantum mechanical effects such as DNA entanglement, influence mutation patterns remain unexplored. Here, we applied a coupled quantum harmonic oscillator model to compute von Neumann Entropy (VNE), a proxy for quantum entanglement, across the TP53 sequence. We found that known mutational hot spots exhibited significantly elevated VNE compared to non-hot spot regions, suggesting that local quantum coupling may reflect structural instability or altered repair accessibility. CpG sites, traditionally linked to methylation-driven mutability, did not exhibit elevated VNE, indicating that quantum properties captured by our closed model are distinct from classical biochemical mechanisms. While these computational results raise the possibility that quantum effects could contribute to genomic instability in TP53, we caution that the analysis is limited by the small number of validated hot spots (n=6) and lacks biological validation. our findings are exploratory and should be interpreted carefully. If confirmed in a larger, multi-gene studies with biophysical measurements, a quantum informed framework could open new avenues for predicting mutation hot spots and understanding cancer mutagenesis. We advocate for interdisciplinary efforts bridging quantum physics and oncology to explore these possibilities further.
affiliations: University of South Florida (corresponding author)

papers.title: Hypoxia-inducible factor 2-alpha promotes fitness of cytokine-activated human natural killer cells
papers.abstract: Natural Killer (NK) cells are innate effector cells with potent antiviral, antitumor, and immunoregulatory functions that are relevant for the treatment of human diseases. There is a pressing need to better understand the mechanisms governing cellular fitness and functional persistence of NK cells to generate therapeutics regimens of sufficient durability to achieve meaningful clinical benefit. Given the central role of interleukin-2 (IL-2) and IL-15 in the survival and proliferation of NK cells, we sought to identify transcription factors induced by these cytokines that are essential for maintaining the fitness of human NK cells from healthy human blood donors. Culture in IL-2 or IL-15 increased protein expression of hypoxia inducible factor 2 alpha (HIF-2, encoded by EPAS1) but not HIF-1 in NK cells. Unexpectedly, induction of HIF-2 was not dependent on limited oxygen availability. CRISPR targeting of EPAS1 or pharmacological inhibition of HIF-2 protein expression markedly compromised the survival of cytokine-activated human NK cells. In contrast, inhibition of canonical HIF-2 transcription factor activity via blocking HIF-2/HIF-1{beta} heterodimer formation had no apparent effects on NK cell viability, function, or metabolism. These results suggest that cytokines, rather than hypoxia, activate an unconventional HIF-1{beta} independent, HIF-2 pathway that helps to maintain NK cells during cellular activation, revealing the potential promise of manipulating HIF-2 to improve the efficacy of adoptive NK cell therapies.
affiliations: Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: LAP-TLR2 Axis Drives Inflammatory Pathology during Listeria monocytogenes Gastroenteritis
papers.abstract: Listeria monocytogenes (Lm) causes acute gastroenteritis that precedes systemic invasive listeriosis, yet the molecular mechanisms coordinating bacterial virulence with host inflammatory responses during the enteric phase remain poorly understood. We show that Lm-associated gastroenteritis is dose-dependent, and a high infectious dose (~1x10^10 CFU/mouse), reflecting epidemic cases, recapitulates hallmark features of gastroenteritis in a mouse model, including early onset, epithelial erosion, and profound inflammatory cell infiltration. We identify Listeria adhesion protein (LAP), rather than classical virulence factors such as internalin A and listeriolysin O, as the primary mediator of enteric pathology, driving epithelial cell death and neutrophil recruitment. Transcriptomic (mRNA-seq) profiling implicates LAP-driven engagement of the TLR2-MyD88 pathway. Using the HEK-Dual hTLR2 (NF-kB) reporter cell line and TLR2 knockout mice, we show that LAP engages TLR2 to activate TNFalpha; NF-kB signaling and compromises the gut epithelial barrier. Disease severity correlates with myeloid hyperactivation and intestinal ion channel dysregulation, as CD11b-; mice exhibit attenuated diarrhea despite elevated bacterial tissue loads. Finally, studies in MLCK knock-out mice confirm that this myeloid-driven pathology requires MLCK-dependent tight junction opening for paracellular neutrophil migration, which works in concert with LAP-TLR2 signaling during Lm-induced gastroenteritis.
affiliations: Purdue University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Contrasting Range and Demographic Histories in two Palearctic Dragonfly Species (Odonata: Anisoptera)
papers.abstract: Climatic suitability is often used to infer historical range changes, yet whether suitable area predicts effective population size remains unexplored. We investigated this relationship in two Palearctic dragonflies with contrasting ecologies: Somatochlora arctica, a widespread peatland specialist, and S. meridionalis, a southern European species associated with shaded streams. We combined demographic reconstructions from individual reference genomes using the pairwise sequentially Markovian coalescent (PSMC), maximum entropy (MaxEnt) species distribution models projected across six paleoclimatic intervals spanning approximately 3.3 million years, and ancestral state reconstructions of peatland specialization. Predicted suitable area was consistently greater for S. arctica, reaching its greatest extent during the Last Glacial Maximum. However, its inferred effective population size was smaller than that of S. meridionalis for most of the last ~275,000 years. Ancestral reconstructions placed the most probable gain of peatland specialization in the S. arctica lineage (Clade I) during the late Miocene, with a median age of 9.4 million years, predating the modeled climatic intervals. These findings indicate a decoupling of climatic suitability and demographic history. Patchy breeding habitat, population structure, and the isolated Scottish origin of the sampled S. arctica may contribute to this mismatch. Combining genomic, ecological, and phylogenetic approaches provides complementary insights into historical biogeography and highlights the limitations of interpreting suitable climate as available breeding habitat or using individual genomes to characterize species-wide demographic histories.
affiliations: University of Illinos Urbana-Champaign (corresponding author)

papers.title: Structural Variant Aware Identity-by-Descent Detection on Pangenome Graphs
papers.abstract: Identity-by-descent (IBD) detection identifies genomic segments inherited from a common ancestor, and supports studies of relatedness, demographic history, and disease mapping. Existing methods primarily use linear genome representations and do not identify structural variants (SVs) shared within IBD segments. Pangenome graphs encode SVs and store each haplotype as a path through the graph. We present GIBD (Graph Identity-by-Descent), which detects IBD segments in the Graph Burrows-Wheeler Transform (GBWT) of a pangenome graph and annotates each detected segment with the SVs it carries. GIBD enumerates the pairwise-maximal exact matches between all pairs of haplotype paths in a single traversal of the GBWT, and visits each shared subpath once. On graphs of bounded degree, the traversal takes time linear in the number of nodes on the haplotype paths and the number of matches it enumerates. On a standard IBD benchmark, the power and accuracy of GIBD are within 0.009 and 0.001 of hap-ibd, a widely used linear method. Compared with impop_k, a pangenome-based IBD method, GIBD detects more 2-4 cM segments and runs in 33 seconds instead of 9.6 hours. In simulations of 1,000 haplotypes built from assemblies of the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium (HPRC), the insertion, deletion, and inversion labels of GIBD have a precision of 1.000, with and without assembly error. In a real four-generation family, GIBD identifies the inherited allele on parent-offspring segments at all 3,235 SVs on chromosome 20 where the parent is heterozygous, and reports no IBD between unrelated members. It also tracks a disease-associated 900-kb inversion at 17q21.31 across three generations and correctly labels all segments that share it. GIBD makes SVs visible in IBD detection from pangenome graphs.
affiliations: University of Florida (corresponding author)

papers.title: A single-cell transcriptomic atlas of paper wasp brains highlights Kenyon cells' role in social behavior
papers.abstract: Social insects provide unique opportunities for studying social interactions, but the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying these behaviors are poorly understood. Here, we performed single-cell sequencing to profile the transcriptomes of 96,310 cells across four phenotypes of Polistes fuscatus paper wasps: foundresses, workers, gynes, and males, to determine how social states and social interactions are encoded in the physiology of the central brain. We characterized the cellular diversity of the Polistes brain and demonstrate that a substantial portion of the brain is composed of diverse populations of Kenyon cell neurons. The composition and gene-expression profiles of these Kenyon cells, as well other neural and non-neural cell populations, vary across sex, caste, and season. We also demonstrate that social interactions, and even the mere observation of a social interaction, induce significant transcriptomic responses, including signatures of neural activation, across populations of Kenyon cell neurons.
