Notably, the transcriptional and activational signatures elicited by observing a social interaction frequently overlapped with those induced by direct social interaction, suggesting that a shared neural program underlies both direct social interactions and social observation.
affiliations: Cornell University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Plumage diversity without differential expression of pigmentation genes in a rapid avian radiation
papers.abstract: Uncovering the molecular basis of reproductive traits is key to understanding species divergence. Capuchino Seedeaters ( Sporophila ), a radiation of genetically similar birds differing mainly in male reproductive plumage color, can be leveraged to study how such traits evolve. Outlier scans identified candidate pigmentation variants primarily in noncoding sequence, implying regulatory changes. However, RNA-seq of growing feather follicles generally did not show differential expression of pigmentation genes among different colors, with only ASIP downregulated in crown feathers. Gene expression patterns instead varied by body region. The largest difference between dimorphic sexes was the upregulation of the carotenoid-degrading gene BCO2 in males, accompanied by lower carotenoid content in male feathers. An improved genome annotation assigned 9.5% of candidate variants into coding and untranslated sequence. This suggests species-diagnostic variants lie within transcribed sequence and could act post-transcriptionally, rather than through transcript abundance, leading to a revised hypothesis for plumage divergence in this radiation.
affiliations: Fuller Evolutionary Biology Program, Cornell Lab of Ornithology, 159 Sapsucker Woods Road, Ithaca, NY 14850, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Generative 3D Spatial Reconstruction of Cellular Organization from Single Cell Expression
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing profiles cellular states at scale but removes their three-dimensional (3D) spatial organization. Reconstructing this organization requires recovering not only individual cell positions but also the physical size, geometry, and neighborhoods of an entire tissue. Existing methods either map cells onto measured spatial references or reconstruct two-dimensional sections independently, leaving the joint reconstruction of a new 3D specimen unresolved. Moreover, predicting the average plausible position of each cell can reduce per-cell error while compressing tissue geometry. We introduce ORBIS, a generative framework that jointly reconstructs whole 3D specimens from single-cell gene expression without requiring a spatial reference at inference. ORBIS learns spatial organization through flow matching in a shared physical coordinate frame, using training views sampled from sparse serial sections, tissue blocks, and whole specimens. At inference, a shared spatial state is iteratively updated through dynamically regrouped windows, enabling the generation of millions of cell positions without independently reconstructing and stitching tissue regions. We evaluate physical size, cell-population shape, per-cell placement, and neighborhood organization separately to distinguish accurate tissue geometry from low per-cell error. Across eight held-out specimens spanning whole mouse brains, thick brain blocks, and Drosophila embryos, ORBIS achieves lower cell-population shape error than all five evaluated baselines on every test and reconstructs specimens containing up to 3.7 million cells. On a single GPU, ORBIS samples million-cell brains in 0.9-2.8 minutes, approximately 38 times faster than the sampler of LUNA-3D, our 3D extension of the state-of-the-art generative spatial reconstruction method LUNA. On two held-out brain tests, sampling reduces size error by 3.3-fold and shape error by 1.8-fold compared with a single-call variant. On an independent dissociated single-cell brain atlas, ORBIS returns on average 37.9% of each region's cells to their dissection region across 23 regions, compared with 28.5% for LUNA-3D.
affiliations: UNIVERSITY OF CENTRAL FLORIDA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Bioprocess Modeling Made Easy With Hybrax
papers.abstract: Hybrid models that embed neural networks in ordinary differential equations are increasingly popular in bioprocess modeling, but they are challenging to set up. Much of the effort goes into the code around the model: wet-lab data must be imported and pre-processed, feeds and sampling must be accounted for in the balance equations, and a training loop with cross-validation must be set up. Researchers usually write this code from scratch for each project. In addition, no widely adopted format for bioprocess data exists, and datasets are mostly published in bespoke spreadsheets or not at all. As a result, models and datasets from the literature are difficult to reproduce, reuse, or compare.We present Hybrax, an open-source Python framework that addresses these problems. It combines a flexible format for bioprocess data with a customizable end-to-end training pipeline for mechanistic and hybrid models. Hybrax derives the transport terms in the process dynamics automatically and provides the utilities needed for training, so that researchers can focus on developing the model itself. It also facilitates model sharing and reproducibility: each training checkpoint contains the model parameters, code, configuration, and training data required to run the model or retrain it from scratch. We demonstrate Hybrax by re-implementing two models from the literature, one trained on real-world E. coli data and one on synthetic HEK293 data, with performance comparable to the original models. Hybrax is available at https://github.com/hybrax/hybrax.
affiliations: University of Vienna (corresponding author)

papers.title: FUSION PORE CLOSURE DETERMINES SUBQUANTAL KISS-AND-RUN SEROTONIN RELEASE FROM FULLY LOADED DENSE-CORE VESICLES
papers.abstract: During kiss-and-run exocytosis, a transient fusion pore opens, releases part of the vesicular quantum, and closes without full fusion. This report investigates two questions: first, whether dense-core vesicles undergoing kiss-and-run contain the same number of molecules as those undergoing full fusion; second, whether subquantal release results from pore closure or vesicle depletion. We analyzed amperometric recordings of extrasynaptic serotonin release from dense-core vesicles in cultured leech Retzius neurons. Full-fusion events released 91,585{+/-}34,428 molecules (n=14), whereas kiss-and-run events released 58,344{+/-}20,759 molecules, 64% of the quantum. We analyzed the biexponential dynamics of the filtered amperometric current using Ohmic equations for cylindrical and toroidal pores. Hydrated flux packing (HFP) independently estimated the minimum peak pore diameter from the number of hydrated serotonin molecules crossing the pore. Kiss-and-run peak diameters were 2.1 to 3.2 nm, corresponding to the passage of 4 to 10 hydrated molecules. The vesicular serotonin content of individual kiss-and-run events was estimated by a frozen pore extrapolation (FPE), in which pores were kept at the peak HFP diameter. FPE yielded 102,650{+/-}10,989 molecules per vesicle (n=15), similar to the quantum obtained by integrating full-fusion events. Therefore, kiss-and-run subquantal release did not reflect a smaller quantum. We then compared the decay of serotonin flux with that estimated through the frozen pore at its peak diameter. In every event, the flux decayed faster, reaching half its peak in 0.59 (0.23 to 0.95) of the time taken by the frozen pore flux. We conclude that subquantal release during kiss-and-run exocytosis is governed by fusion-pore closure rather than vesicle depletion.
affiliations: Universidad Nacional Autonoma de Mexico (corresponding author)

papers.title: Multi-scale biophysical modeling of fungal colony growth
papers.abstract: Fungal colony growth is shaped by the fundamental physical operating principles of hyphal elongation, branching, and anastomosis, which collectively organize into macroscopic foraging networks. While sophisticated 3D models utilizing adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) on high-performance computing architectures can explicitly capture these discrete cellular mechanics, their immense computational cost prevents their integration into predictive ecosystem simulators. Here, building upon the Biological Modeling and interface eXchange (BMX) framework, we combine high-fidelity discrete hyphal mechanics with an analytically tractable, stochastic traveling-wave surrogate (sBARE) to provide multiscale simulations of fungal colonies at a fraction of the computational cost. By leveraging demographic fluctuations at the advancing front, our framework uniquely resolves macroscopic parameter degeneracies, separating the directed forward drift of leading tips from their effective diffusion to capture the macroscopic signature of negative autotropism in 3D networks. Simulations reproduce experimentally observed traveling wave profiles and confirm that interior network density under replete conditions emerges as an invariant self-regulated by fusion. Furthermore, global sensitivity analysis reveals that expansion speed and network density are governed by largely disjoint microscopic parameters. We demonstrate that because the physics of hyphal growth permit networks that are both exceptionally fast and dense, the empirical trade-off between sparse 'explorer' and dense 'exploiter' strategies observed in nature is not a strict mechanical constraint, pointing instead to metabolic limits on local growth rules. Our mathematically tractable approach bridges exascale-level cellular mechanics with macroscopic wave dynamics, enabling the integration of trait-driven advective fluxes and carrying capacities into the spatial transport and reaction network schemes of large-scale biogeochemical models.
affiliations: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (corresponding author)

papers.title: Distributed Network Sensing as an Escape Strategy
papers.abstract: The response of a swarm of ants or birds, living tissue of cells, or a robotic swarm, to spatial signals from the environment as a whole is a fundamental challenge for these decentralized systems. A promising alternative is embodied distributed sensing and decision-making, so that local environmental cues directly shape coordinated reconfiguration, growth, or movement without centralized control. Fluidic networks offer a physical basis for such systems, yet existing implementations are predesigned and limited in their ability to process spatial information across extended systems. Here, we investigate how fluid transport networks enable environmental sensing and adaptive response using the slime mould Physarum polycephalum. By exposing Physarum vein networks to dynamic pH environments, we show that the organism's ability to respond to aversive stimuli is governed by its spatial extent and network connectivity. Above a certain size, organisms with network morphology reliably detect and escape harmful conditions by network reconfiguration, whereas disconnected or spatially confined organisms fail to respond. In environments with competing stimuli, network morphologies enable integration of spatial information and repositioning into favorable regions. We identify local contractions as a physical mechanism that drives fluid redistribution and converts local stimulation into system-level responses. Finally, we generate different morphologies using fluidic and electrochemical control, demonstrating large-scale adaptation to complex environments. These results establish distributed fluidic networks as a framework for integrated sensing and actuation, providing design principles for autonomous soft robotic systems in dynamic environments.
affiliations: Technische Universitat Munchen (corresponding author)

papers.title: Genomic analysis of the Streptococcus anginosus group; taxonomic implications, evolutionary insights and clinical considerations
papers.abstract: Background: The Streptococcus anginosus group (SAG) (S. anginosus, S. intermedius, and S. constellatus) causes serious, potentially life-threatening, invasive infections, often in otherwise healthy individuals. However, the group's diversity is still poorly understood, and with it, the ability to identify prognostic markers of severe disease. Methods: Long-read sequencing produced closed genomes for 29 isolates from 25 patients hospitalised primarily for invasive SAG infections, and 21 isolates from 20 non-hospitalised controls. Genomes were classified with GTDB-Tk and combined with 211 reference genomes. After dereplication, 207 SAG genomes (38 isolate, 169 reference) representing 206 strains were analysed using: GTDB classification, average nucleotide identity, multi-marker and core-genome SNP phylogenies, recombination-aware analyses, mobilome, CAZyme and gapseq metabolic profiling, and lineage-aware genome-wide association testing for invasive phenotype. Results: Agreement between GTDB-Tk and MALDI-TOF taxonomic classifications was low (42.8%), including two S. massiliensis cases mis-identified by MALDI-TOF as SAG. S. anginosus resolved into four taxa (S. anginosus, S. hominis, S. whileyi and S. vaginalis). Phylogenies based on core genome single-nucleotide polymorphisms resolved these species into distinct clades, whereas 16S rRNA gene and multilocus sequence analysis phylogenies did not. The four ex-S. anginosus taxa showed a gradient of genomic cohesion, with S. vaginalis being near-clonal, in contrast to S. anginosus, which shared high levels of sequence ancestry with other neighbouring taxa. Carbohydrate utilisation was strongly lineage-associated, as was propensity for invasive disease. A ~15Kbp glycosaminoglycan utilisation locus was found in the three taxa of highest disease severity propensity (S. intermedius, S. constellatus, S. whileyi) which predicts a direct host glycosaminoglycan feeding mechanism that may contribute to invasive disease. No single functional feature, gene or core-genome SNP was associated with invasiveness however after lineage-adjustment. Combined feature analysis suggests S. vaginalis has undergone a niche restriction and has evolved for a primary existence in the female urogenital tract. Conclusions: Under-reported species may be mis-diagnosed as SAG invasive infections. SAG is more diverse than its current three-species definition, with the conventional S. anginosus species proposed to be classed into a complex of four distinct taxa. Invasive capacity appears to be an emergent system-level property rather than from individual features.
affiliations: Australian Centre for Ecogenomics, University of Queensland, St Lucia, Queensland, Australia (corresponding author)

papers.title: Disparities in avian genomic resources highlight gaps across the Global South
papers.abstract: Avian genomes have proliferated rapidly in recent years while expanding our knowledge of genomic evolution. However, evaluating bird sampling across the tree of life and across their distributions is necessary to assess their contributions to global bird diversity and diversification patterns. We evaluated all available avian genome assemblies across geography, taxonomy, conservation status, and time. The 1,712 species with at least one genome assembly represent only ~15% of recognized avian diversity. Although all orders were represented, 24 bird families (all restricted to the Global South) lacked any genome assembly, and only ~37% (N= 2,397) of recognized genera had genomic representation. Nearly 78% of the most evolutionarily distinct and globally endangered (EDGE) lineages lacked a genome. Genomic resources are concentrated in temperate regions of the Global North, whereas species-rich tropical regions in Africa, South America, and Southeast Asia remain severely underrepresented relative to their diversity. Even after accounting for conservation status, evolutionary distinctiveness, and ecology, Global South species had roughly fourfold lower odds of having a genome than Global North species. Notably, the post-2021 surge in genome sequencing has counter-intuitively widened this gap. Together, our results highlight persistent gaps in genomic resources across the Global South and the need to collectively address these global knowledge gaps via collaborative efforts.
affiliations: Louisiana State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Multi-omics integration reveals candidate genes and molecular mechanisms associated with resistance to sugarcane smut
papers.abstract: Sugarcane smut, caused by the fungus Sporisorium scitamineum (Syd.), is one of the main diseases affecting sugarcane and is capable of causing severe yield losses in susceptible varieties. Given the limitations of classical breeding, mainly due to the genetic complexity of sugarcane cultivars, molecular and omics approaches have gained increasing prominence for studying the genetic basis of traits such as disease resistance. In this context, we investigated sugarcane resistance to smut through the integration of association mapping methods and transcriptomics. A panel of 155 genotypes was genotyped with 33,335 SNP markers and inoculated with S. scitamineum generating three phenotypic variables. These data were jointly analyzed through genome-wide association analyses to identify marker-trait associations. In addition, transcriptomic analyses were performed using publicly available datasets from four studies evaluating sugarcane responses to smut. The integration of these multi-omics data enabled the identification of candidate genes involved in structural reinforcement, immune signaling, redox homeostasis, genome maintenance, and cellular adaptation. These findings provide valuable molecular resources for functional validation and breeding strategies aimed at developing sugarcane cultivars with enhanced smut resistance.
affiliations: Universidade Estadual de Campinas (UNICAMP) (corresponding author)

papers.title: Somatic structural variation discovery on cancer pangenome graphs
papers.abstract: Somatic structural variants (SVs) drive tumorigenesis across most cancers, yet low variant allele frequencies in subclonal populations often necessitate multi-sample sequencing per patient. Existing somatic SV callers rely on whole-genome read alignments against a single linear reference, incurring high computational costs and reference bias. We present JANUS, which discovers somatic SVs directly within a personal pangenome, a colored de Bruijn-like graph of locally consistent parsing (LCP) cores built from matched normal and tumor PacBio HiFi reads. JANUS identifies candidate SV sites traversed exclusively by tumor reads without prior alignment, mapping only short read snippets surrounding each site. Across five tumor-normal pairs in the CASTLE panel, JANUS leads the 18-caller consensus with a mean F1 score of 0.887 (next-best caller: 0.858), widening its lead under low-signal regimes (0.489 versus 0.362 at 5x; 0.683 versus 0.520 at 20% purity). End to end, JANUS analyzes a tumor-normal pair in ~11 minutes on average with 16 threads, which is ~24x faster than read alignment alone on the same machine. In a 20-tumor patient simulation, joint graph calling outperforms independent pairwise runs in speed and accuracy, particularly at low depth. By processing multi-sample cohorts jointly and maintaining sensitivity at low coverage and purity, JANUS provides an efficient, reference-unbiased framework for cancer genomics. JANUS is available at https://github.com/BilkentCompGen/janus.
affiliations: Bilkent University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Development of a Pan-Proteome Multi-Epitope Vaccine Candidate Against Nipah Virus Using Reverse Vaccinology and Immunoinformatics Approaches
papers.abstract: Nipah virus (NiV) is a high-consequence zoonotic pathogen for which no licensed human vaccine is currently available. This study applied a consensus-guided pan-proteome immunoinformatics framework to design and prioritize a multi-epitope vaccine candidate using sequence information from all nine NiV proteins. A total of 901 NiV protein sequences were retrieved, of which 842 passed quality filtering and were processed through clustering, multiple-sequence alignment, and protein-specific consensus generation. Consensus-derived fragments were screened for cytotoxic T-lymphocyte, helper T-lymphocyte, and B-cell epitopes, followed by multi-criterion filtering based on antigenicity, allergenicity, toxicity, conservancy, class-specific immune-response properties, and human-proteome similarity. Ten epitope-selection strategies were combined with two adjuvant candidates and three construct architectures to generate 60 vaccine constructs. Shortlisted candidates were subsequently evaluated for physicochemical properties, HLA population coverage, structural characteristics, conformational B-cell epitopes, TLR3 docking, molecular dynamics, immune-response simulation, and expression-oriented optimization. VC033_V6_BD_L03 construct was prioritized as the lead candidate and showed combined predicted population coverage of 99.78% worldwide and 99.96% in South Asia. Docking against human TLR3 structure 1ZIW yielded a ClusPro score of -1624.8. During a 100-ns molecular-dynamics simulation, the complex underwent early conformational reorganization followed by lower late-phase structural variation and persistent interchain hydrogen bonding. MM/GBSA analysis yielded a mean interaction-energy estimate of -20.52, 15.42 kcal/mol. C-ImmSim predicted coordinated humoral and cellular responses, while codon optimization generated a 1,539-bp expression sequence compatible with virtual cloning into pET-28a(+). These analyses prioritize VC033_V6_BD_L03 as a consensus-derived, pan-proteome NiV multi-epitope vaccine candidate for experimental evaluation of expression, immunogenicity, safety, and protective efficacy.
affiliations: Department of Microbiology, Jagannath University, Dhaka (corresponding author)

papers.title: Deducing splicing events from transcript sets with splicelogic
papers.abstract: Long-read RNA sequencing captures a greater proportion of full-length transcripts, enabling more accurate isoform identification, discovery of novel isoforms, and more precise differential transcript usage analysis. However, comparing transcripts, whether between conditions or between sets such as novel and annotated isoforms, yields complex isoform changes that are hard to manipulate, summarize, and visualize. This is compounded by vertical integration of some tools, where downstream analysis depends on the specific output of a particular upstream tool. To address this gap, we have developed splicelogic, an R/Bioconductor package that makes transcript-set comparisons biologically interpretable by turning them into discrete splicing events, such as exon skipping, alternative splice sites, intron retention, and alternative transcription start and end sites. We designed splicelogic to integrate easily with existing RNA-seq workflows and tools. The splicelogic functions are modular, readable, and extensible, making it easy for users to adapt core logic to their own custom scientific questions or novel splicing definitions. By obtaining interpretable splicing events from transcript changes, splicelogic enables downstream analyses, including annotation of RNA-binding protein recognition sites, alongside summary statistics and visualization. The splicelogic package is publicly available and distributed through Bioconductor.
affiliations: UNC-Chapel Hill (corresponding author)

papers.title: Coarse-graining genome-scale metabolic models for dynamic, multi-scale simulations of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in gel environments
papers.abstract: Microbial communities are shaped by coupled interactions between microenvironment conditions and the intracellular adaptations that emerge in response external metabolic cues. For pathogenic microbes such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa, these interactions can rapidly generate heterogeneous sub-populations that exhibit adaptations for sustaining host infection and resisting antibiotic treatment. Technological strides in -omics data collection, combined with robust computational tools like genome-scale metabolic models (GEM) for predicting cellular metabolism, have yielded promising multi-scale depictions of microbial population development in simulated spatial environments. These multi-scale model simulations help establish and evaluate mechanistic contexts for how infection-enhancing behaviors might emerge in the population or be influenced by variable perturbations in the biological system. However, the number and rigorous tuning of parameters influencing the connections between intracellular-extracellular events pose barriers when shaping simulations to different in vitro systems of interest. In this work, we present a genome-scale, metabolism-informed continuum model (GEM-CM), a computational framework for coupling a reaction-diffusion model to a surrogate GEM representation that generates metabolic rate predictions informed by flux balance analysis outputs. A key feature of GEM-CM is its application of random forest regression, or ensembles, to coarse-grain the interface connecting the GEM and reaction-diffusion models down to a small set of input metabolites methodically chosen through the random forests evaluation of feature importance. To demonstrate GEM-CMs utility, we evaluated simulation predictions against P. aeruginosa PA14 populations radially propagating in low weight percentage agar gels. In addition to biomass growth, we simulated PA14 populations producing the cytotoxic secondary metabolite pyocyanin (PCN). GEM-CM could capture PA14 growth dynamics in agar gels when ensembles were provided with three carbon source inputs describing the simulated growth media. Bacterial motility parameters and the random forest ensemble allowed GEM-CM simulations to accurately predict spatial biomass distributions for PA14 populations over time and probe their PCN production dynamics. Ensembles also demonstrated robust performance for single gene knockout conditions with GEM-CM simulation accurately capturing the partial or total biomass and PCN inhibition observed in transposon mutant screenings. When evaluating transposon mutant population development, the GEM-CM framework additionally suggested that metH may be a promising target to inhibit the spatial propagation of PA14. This works proof-of-concept applications illustrated GEM-CM utility as an early stage multi-scale modeling tool for interrogating in vitro metabolic behavior in microbial populations.
affiliations: University of Virginia (corresponding author)

papers.title: A novel KIR3DL2-directed CAR T-cell therapy for cutaneous and systemic T-cell lymphomas
papers.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has transformed the treatment of B-cell malignancies and multiple myeloma, but its extension to T-cell lymphomas (TCLs) has been constrained by the paucity of antigens that can be safely targeted. While targeting pan-T antigens broadens the therapeutic reach across various TCLs, it carries a substantial risk of immunosuppression and infection. Here, we report killer cell immunoglobulin-like receptor, three Ig domains and long cytoplasmic tail 2 (KIR3DL2/CD158k) as a viable target for CAR T-cell therapy against a wide range of TCLs. Using single-cell RNA-seq data analysis and flow cytometric phenotyping, we observed that KIR3DL2 expression is restricted to a subset of mature NK cells and a minor fraction of CD8 T cells, with negligible expression in other healthy adult tissues. Among TCLs, KIR3DL2 expression was noted in various subtypes of cutaneous and systemic TCLs. Anti-KIR3DL2 CAR constructs (3DL2CARs) efficiently and selectively redirected T cells against antigen-positive cell lines but not isogenic KIR3DL2-negative counterparts, with antigen-specific signaling, cytotoxicity, proliferation, and cytokine production. Importantly, 3DL2CART cells produced sustained tumor regression and prolonged survival in two distinct cell line-derived xenograft models of cutaneous TCL and in one patient-derived xenograft model of hepatosplenic TCL. 3DL2CART cells exhibited minimal off-target activity against bystander immune cells and showed no appreciable fratricide. To mitigate the risk of tumor cell contamination in autologous CAR T-cell products, we established a two-tiered strategy that integrates immunomagnetic depletion of KIR3DL2-positive tumor cells with in vivo activation of a safety switch if inadvertently transduced malignant cells contribute to immune escape. Together, our results establish the preclinical efficacy and safety of 3DL2CART-cell therapy and support its clinical translation. This approach may offer a targeted alternative to pan-T-cell-directed CAR T-cell strategies for patients with relapsed/refractory cutaneous and systemic TCLs, addressing a critical unmet clinical need.
affiliations: The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Galectin-9 drives thrombo-inflammatory circuits initiating venous thrombosis
papers.abstract: Background: Venous thromboembolism is increasingly recognized as a thrombo-inflammatory disease, yet the pathways linking inflammation to venous thrombus initiation remain incompletely defined. Galectin-9 (Gal-9), a {beta}-galactoside-binding lectin elevated in inflammatory disorders, has no defined role in venous thrombosis. Methods: Using plasma from patients with deep vein thrombosis (DVT), Gal-9-deficient mice, an inferior vena cava stenosis model, intravital microscopy, microfluidics, and ex vivo platelet and neutrophil assays, we assessed the functional contribution of Gal-9 to venous thrombosis. Results: Plasma Gal-9 was elevated in DVT patients, correlated with D-dimer at presentation, and declined over 3-month follow-up. Gal-9 deletion did not alter hemostasis but markedly impaired thrombus initiation, with reduced platelet and neutrophil recruitment to the vessel wall and reduced intra-thrombus neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation. TNF-/IFN-{gamma}-stimulated endothelial cells upregulated Gal-9 and promoted platelet adhesion and fibrin(ogen) deposition, which Gal-9 neutralization partially reversed. Under venous shear, immobilized recombinant Gal-9 potentiated platelet activation and thrombus formation, particularly alongside collagen, whereas Gal-9 inhibition suppressed these responses. Gal-9-activated platelets promoted NETosis and shifted thrombus composition toward a NET-rich inflammatory phenotype. Conclusions: Gal-9 is a previously unrecognized driver of venous thrombo-inflammation, linking vascular inflammation to platelet activation, NET formation, and thrombosis. Genetic deletion attenuated these responses in vivo, and antibody-mediated Gal-9 neutralization suppressed platelet activation and thrombus formation in vitro, identifying the Gal-9 glycan-binding pathway as a therapeutic target that disrupts thrombosis without impairing hemostasis.
affiliations: University of Birmingham (corresponding author)

papers.title: Establishing an ex vivo platform for molecular profiling of skin structural cells using frozen human skin biopsies
papers.abstract: Skin structural cells, including keratinocytes, melanocytes, endothelial cells, and fibroblasts, play critical roles in the development of chronic inflammatory skin disease. Inflammatory stimuli induce transcriptional reprogramming and epigenetic changes in skin structural cells, which contribute to disease pathogenesis. Although two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) skin culture models have been widely used to investigate inflammatory responses in skin structural cells, ex vivo systems that maintain skin structure and cellular composition remain limited. To address this gap, we explored using frozen skin biopsies as an experimental platform to study the responses of skin structural cells to inflammatory stimuli. Using a simple air-liquid interface culture method on permeable Transwell inserts, we showed that viable skin structural cells that retain cell-type-specific transcriptional profiles can be recovered from frozen skin biopsies after prolonged in vitro culture. Stimulation with IFN-{gamma} induced robust transcriptional and chromatin accessibility changes that were largely resolved after stimulus removal, with transcriptional responses to secondary stimulation comparable to the primary stimulation. Treatment of cultured skin biopsies with histone-modifying enzyme inhibitors effectively altered global histone modification levels, but did not substantially affect the transcriptional resolution of IFN-{gamma}-induced responses. Collectively, these findings establish cryopreserved human skin biopsies as a scalable ex vivo platform that enables mechanistic studies of inflammatory responses of multiple populations of skin structural cells.
affiliations: Benaroya Research Institute (corresponding author)

papers.title: Onsite fixation preserves phosphoprotein profile in human whole blood
papers.abstract: Phospho-flow cytometry is increasingly used as a pharmacodynamic readout of kinase-pathway activity, including in JAK inhibitor trials. Phosphoprotein states are intrinsically labile ex vivo and are further altered by conventional workflows, which typically involve PBMC isolation, cryopreservation, and transit times of hours to days before measurement. Here, we fix whole blood at collection and quantify six phosphoproteins by mass cytometry, benchmarked against matched cryopreserved PBMCs. Unlike PBMCs, whole blood retained neutrophils, ~75-80% of which were pSTAT3-positive at baseline. Basal pSTAT3 was also markedly higher in whole blood monocytes (~41% positive vs. ~9% in PBMCs), whereas T, B, and NK cells differed by less than 1 percentage point. Stimulation produced subset-specific phosphorylation patterns that were retained after 6 weeks of storage. Because fixation does not require centrifugation and retains neutrophils, samples can be fixed at collection sites without on-site processing laboratories and analyzed centrally in batches.
affiliations: Teiko (corresponding author)

papers.title: Decoding the molecular cues regulating the transition of Influenza virus polymerase from transcriptase to replicase.
papers.abstract: Influenza virus polymerase (FluPol) dynamically transitions between distinct conformational states to coordinate viral gene transcription and genome replication. While vRNP-associated monomeric FluPol supports transcription, ANP32-dependent asymmetric and ANP32-independent symmetric polymerase dimers mediate genome and antigenome (vRNA/cRNA) replication. How FluPol coordinates these distinct functional states to maintain the transcription-replication balance remains poorly understood. Here, we identify and characterize interdomain interactions within PB2 that govern the stability of the replication-competent conformation of FluPol. Specifically, a highly conserved salt bridge between PB2 Mid-E282 and NLS-K752 stabilizes the replicase conformation, while the charge state of residue 627 (E or K) dictates ANP32 engagement, together coordinating polymerase dimerization and replication activity. Strikingly, bat influenza A viruses H17N10 and H18N11 harbor unconventional serine substitutions at both positions, compromising polymerase dimerization, ANP32 interaction, and vRNA/cRNA replication. Remarkably, introducing these bat-signature substitutions (E282S/K627S) into human H1N1 polymerase results in phosphorylation at both positions in human cells. These findings suggest that phosphorylation can partially compensate for the loss of negative charge at these residues, revealing a phosphomimetic adaptation mechanism that modulates polymerase conformational dynamics and function. Collectively, our study reveals how a conserved interdomain interaction within PB2 regulates conformational transitions and transcription-replication balance of FluPol, which might have been driven by phosphomimetic adaptations during the course of a diverse range of influenza virus evolution.
affiliations: Department of Bioscience and Biotechnology, Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Kharagpur, India, West Bengal, India (corresponding author)

papers.title: Asymmetric division and polar growth define a non-canonical cell cycle in Bradyrhizobium.
papers.abstract: Bradyrhizobia are widely used as plant growth promoters in agriculture, yet their cell biology remains poorly understood. Here, we described for the first time, nucleoid segregation dynamics and the cell cycle of Bradyrhizobium at the cellular level. We show that highly asymmetric polar growth generates a short daughter cell and a longer mother cell at each division. Nucleoid compaction and positioning change across growth phases, culminating in a highly compacted, asymmetrically positioned nucleoid in stationary phase. ParB presents a subpolar localization, at the nucleoid periphery. Despite this pronounced cellular asymmetry and the presence of a single large chromosome, chromosome conformation capture reveals a global chromosome organization similar to that of bacteria undergoing conventional binary fission Together, these findings uncover a distinctive cell cycle program in Bradyrhizobium. showing that such extreme asymmetry in growth and division, significantly different from closely related characterized -Proteobacteriota, is compatible with conserved principles of chromosome organization.
affiliations: Laboratorio de Genomica Experimental Bacteriana, Instituto de Investigaciones Biotecnologicas (IIB), Escuela de Bio y Nanotecnologias (EByN), Universidad Nacion (corresponding author)

papers.title: SARDINE unlocks EWAS summary statistics for large-scale epigenetic biomarker analysis
papers.abstract: Epigenetic clocks are increasingly used to study biological aging, yet their interpretation and utility remain uncertain. Meanwhile, the growing wealth of epigenome-wide association study (EWAS) summary statistics remains largely untapped for evaluating these biomarkers. Here, we introduce SARDINE, a statistical framework that estimates epigenetic clock-phenotype associations using EWAS summary statistics, clock weights, and reference methylation covariance, without individual-level data. SARDINE accurately reproduced individual-level association estimates across 38 epigenetic biomarkers and four phenotypes in 15,677 individuals. Applying SARDINE to diverse EWAS datasets revealed substantial heterogeneity in biomarker associations with aging, diseases, and lifestyle factors. By transforming CpG-level EWAS results into interpretable biomarker-level associations, SARDINE unlocks a largely underutilized data resource and establishes a scalable paradigm for systematic biomarker evaluation and discovery in aging research.
affiliations: Department of Biostatistics and Medical Informatics, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Isoform diversity as a complementary dimension of gene expression
papers.abstract: Most human genes produce multiple mRNA isoforms through alternative splicing and alternative transcription start and end sites. Isoforms of the same gene can differ in function, and their relative abundance varies between tissues and conditions. However, gene expression analysis is often restricted to the gene level, masking its diversification into mRNA and protein isoforms with potentially distinct functionality. Here we show, using an adaptation of Shannon evenness applied to 4,814 GTEx samples from 25 tissues, that isoform diversity constitutes a distinct dimension of gene expression, complementary to gene-level abundance and whole transcriptome diversity. Isoform diversity separated tissues based on non-differentially expressed genes and changed with age in a gene- and tissue-specific manner, most strongly in the brain and often without changes in overall gene expression levels. During neuronal differentiation, it increased most notably in RNA processing and splicing genes. Our results suggest that isoform diversity represents an independent dimension of gene expression and may help explain functional differences between tissues and cell states that are not captured by analyzing expression levels alone.
affiliations: University of Haifa (corresponding author)

papers.title: Hierarchical Temporal Transformer for Cancer Grade Prediction and Cross-Cancer Transfer Learning from Pathology Reports
papers.abstract: Background: Language models for cancer reports usually read one document at a time and are tested on tumour types seen in training. Continuous-time sequence models address the first gap, but whether they use visit timing, not just order, is seldom tested. Methods: We developed the Hierarchical Temporal Transformer (HTT), which encodes reports with adapted BiomedBERT and reads the sequence with a cancer-type-conditioned temporal transformer. We evaluated it against best-possible AUROC ceilings on two synthetic benchmarks, one with the label stated in the text and one recoverable only from tumour sizes and visit intervals (ten seeds). Diagnostics led to an interval-aware time code (HTT-IA). On 4,786 TCGA pathology reports in 14 types, three types were withheld, and a text-only HTT was compared with a survival model. Results: On the phrase benchmark HTT reached AUROC 0.931 +/- 0.012 against 0.913 +/- 0.007 for a last-report baseline (+0.018, 95% CI -0.009 to +0.050); dates cannot raise the ceiling there. On the growth benchmark the initial time code scored 0.790, equal to a no-time model (0.787), whereas HTT-IA reached 0.843 (+0.053, 0.026 to 0.082) against ceilings of 0.894 without and 0.979 with dates. On unseen tumour types HTT reached 0.925 +/- 0.007, equal to in-distribution performance and to a single-report baseline. Text-only macro C-index was 0.592 (CALM 0.626-0.652). Conclusion: Cross-type transfer is carried by the pre-trained encoder. Visit timing is used only when the data make it identifiable and the time code is on a clinical scale. Ceilings, order-only ablations and re-dating probes are inexpensive checks for such models.
affiliations: Duke University (corresponding author)

papers.title: scCircaSim: A Circadian Simulator for Single-Cell and Spatial Transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Motivation: Simulated single-cell and spatial transcriptomic datasets that capture circadian dynamics while providing known ground truth remain scarce, limiting systematic evaluation of circadian analysis methods. Results: We developed scCircaSim to generate circadian single-cell and spatial transcriptomic data from a single-time-point reference. The framework combines phase progression with reference-derived network propagation of anchor gene rhythms and incorporates neighborhood effects for spatial simulation. Outputs retain reference heterogeneity and provide known cell or spot phases, rhythmicity labels, and gene-level mesor, amplitude, and phase values. Validation showed retention of reference structure and recovery of specified temporal patterns. Benchmarks of four cell phase inference methods and three rhythmic gene analysis methods revealed differences in phase accuracy, rhythmicity detection, and parameter recovery. scCircaSim supports reproducible method evaluation and preliminary experimental planning. Availability and Implementation: scCircaSim is implemented in R and available at https://github.com/Liwei-DynamicsLab/scCircaSim.
affiliations: Department of Cardiac Ultrasound, The Affiliated Hospital of Qingdao University, Qingdao, China (corresponding author)

papers.title: Toward space-optimal approximate colored indexes at scale
papers.abstract: Searching current petabase-scale sequence repositories requires indexes that combine compact storage with high query throughput. Although exact colored indexes retain complete sequence information, their construction and storage costs can become substantial for highly diverse collections. Indexes based on approximate membership query (AMQ) filters offer a compact alternative with fast construction and queries. Being hash-based, these indexes support different seeding schemes without structural changes, while sampling can reduce storage requirements, construction time and query time by an order of magnitude. Within the AMQ framework, querying many independent filters causes scattered memory accesses, reducing throughput. This motivates interleaved filters, which address this weakness by storing filter slots contiguously by position, enabling cache-friendly access and simultaneous membership queries. However, existing implementations face a trade-off between guaranteed construction and space-efficiency. Here, we introduce a new indexing framework based on interleaved ZOR filters, fingerprint-based structures with guaranteed construction that require only approximately 1% more space than the theoretical minimum for AMQ. To exploit redundancy between genomes, we introduce a color-preserving merging mechanism that extends fingerprints with membership bits, allowing multiple genomes to share a filter while retaining their individual identities. Together with a lightweight, sketch-based layout planner, this mechanism yields a compact index structure that accommodates collections with widely varying genome sizes and degrees of similarity. Our third contribution extends the AMQ framework beyond contiguous -mers through a low-density minimizer scheme alongside efficient implementations of sensitive seeds, including gapped -mers and randstrobes. We implement these methods in Zindex, a parallel, SIMD-accelerated Rust index that scales to millions of genomes while supporting diverse seeding and sampling schemes. Zindex indexes the latest RefSeq release of 564,401 assembled genomes in under 22 hours, producing a 289.5 GB index. It further scales to all 2,763,297 genomes of AllTheBacteria, producing a 406.3 GB index in four days with a peak memory footprint of 43.8 GB. Availability. Zindex is available at https://github.com/Malfoy/Zindex
affiliations: Univ. Lille, CNRS, Centrale Lille, UMR 9189 CRIStAL, F-59000 Lille, France (corresponding author)

papers.title: MOCHI enables systematic identification of candidate independent intronic transcriptional signals from short-read RNA-seq data
papers.abstract: Standard short-read RNA-seq analysis pipelines quantify expression over annotated exons and disregard signals mapped to introns, thereby missing independently transcribed intronic RNAs. Existing strategies depend on annotation, biologically crude whole-intron quantification, or subjective, low-throughput manual genome-browser inspection. We present MOCHI (Mapping of Cryptic Hidden Intronic Transcripts), a framework that couples reference-independent, k-mer-based signal discovery with reference-guided genomic interpretation and a custom multi-step filtering module to systematically curate potential independent intronic transcription units from strand-specific short-read RNA-seq data. On two simulated datasets, MOCHI recovered annotated sense-intronic long non-coding RNAs removed from the reference and distinguished them from intronic signal confounders. Across paired ribosomal RNA-depleted and poly(A)-selected libraries from ten cancer cell lines, MOCHI curated candidates whose host introns are strongly enriched for a transcription-initiation signal. Candidate expression is largely uncoupled from host-gene exons, and their genomic features resemble those of annotated long non-coding RNAs. In ten matched cohorts from The Cancer Genome Atlas, candidates were detected in tumor samples, and a subset was associated with overall survival after adjustment for age and host-gene expression. Consequently, MOCHI extends the transcriptomic landscape that can be mined from existing short-read RNA-seq data and provides a curated resource of candidate intronic transcripts for downstream analyses.
affiliations: Izmir Institute of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: LeadWeaver: Topology-Aware Masked-Lead Modeling for Robust 12-Lead ECG Diagnosis
papers.abstract: Clinical electrocardiography is organized as a structured set of correlated leads, yet most neural ECG classifiers assume that all twelve leads are present, correctly ordered, and acquired under the same device conditions at training and deployment. We propose LeadWeaver, a topology-aware ECG representation model designed for diagnosis under missing, corrupted, or device-shifted leads. LeadWeaver represents each lead as a temporal token stream, couples leads through a fixed-plus-learned physiological lead graph, and performs masked-lead latent completion rather than waveform synthesis. A reliability router estimates which observed leads should dominate each diagnostic decision, while a consistency objective aligns complete-lead and incomplete-lead predictions. We evaluate the model on PTB-XL and CPSC-style settings using complete-input diagnosis, arbitrary missing-lead subsets, lead corruption, cross-dataset transfer, calibration, and selective prediction. The central hypothesis is that robust ECG diagnosis requires explicitly modeling both inter-lead topology and uncertainty about unavailable evidence, rather than treating missing channels as zero-valued inputs.
affiliations: German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence (DFKI) (corresponding author)

papers.title: Lysenin Induced Membrane Curvature on Erythrocytes and Nanoporous Mica Free Standing Membranes
papers.abstract: Beta porin toxins are virulence factors that oligomerize in host cell membranes, forming beta-barrel pores that permeabilize target cells, leading to osmotic imbalance, cell lysis, and immune evasion. Despite extensive research on beta-pore-forming toxins (PFTs), significant gaps remain in understanding their role as actors of large-scale supramolecular membrane remodeling. While beta-PFTs are traditionally viewed as passive cylindrical conduits, their biological efficacy is fundamentally tied to an evolved ability to structurally alter the host cell membrane. In this study, we combine erythrocytes, model membranes and a novel engineered nanopores on mica substrates. We overcome the limitation of traditional mica substrates and demonstrate that lysenin pores do not merely permeabilize the membrane; they curve it into rigid, dome-like supramolecular structures. Moreover, to gain biophysical insight beyond the standard membrane models which do not directly consider the membrane insertions, we propose a hybrid model combining the biophysical models and the architectural models of pendentive domes, where the intrinsic wedge-shaped geometry of the monomers is considered. Experimental mechanical assessment of the lysenins domes shows a non-linear mechanical of stiffness with respect the radius of curvature as predicted by our hybrid model. Collectively, our work suggests that the beta-PFTs induce membrane curvature by the assembly of wedges. Beyond their pore-forming function, this membrane-bending activity may represent an additional mechanism by which beta-PFTs interfere with host-cell membrane repair.
affiliations: Aix Marseille Universite INSERM DyNaMo U1325 (corresponding author)

papers.title: Elevated precontractile calcium set point is sustained by limited PMCA1 export in dystrophic muscle
papers.abstract: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is caused by loss of dystrophin and marked by elevated muscle calcium, usually attributed to contraction-induced membrane damage. Whether calcium rises before muscle can contract, and what sustains it, is unresolved. In Caenorhabditis elegans embryos and patient-derived human myoblasts, dystrophic muscle carries an elevated resting calcium set point before contraction is possible. Embryonic calcium is elevated 400 minutes after fertilization, before movement is detectable or the neuromuscular junction forms. Silencing the plasma membrane calcium pump gene mca-1 raises calcium in wild-type but not dystrophic animals, whereas silencing its paralogue raises it in both: the limitation is specific to that export route. Dystrophic human myoblasts have less pump; pump inhibition or silencing increases calcium preferentially in healthy cells, and raising pump expression lowers calcium most in dystrophic cells. Constrained calcium export is an early, continuing determinant of the dystrophic set point.
affiliations: Illinois State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Aging, HIV Status, and Sex Differentially Influence Antiretroviral Therapy Disposition Pathways in Rectosigmoid Tissue and Peripheral Blood Mononuclear Cells
papers.abstract: People living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) are increasingly surviving into older age due to the effectiveness of antiretroviral (ARV) therapy (ART), creating a growing population in whom age-related changes may influence treatment outcomes. Although aging is known to affect drug disposition, the molecular mechanisms by which aging alters ARV pharmacology remain incompletely understood, particularly within tissue compartments, including the rectosigmoid region of the colon, that serve as sites of HIV transmission and persistence. To address this knowledge gap, we used proteomics by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) to evaluate the impact of age and HIV status on proteins and pathways relevant to ARV disposition in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) and rectosigmoid colon tissue obtained from young (18-50) HIV-seronegative adults, older (65-80) HIV-seronegative adults, and older virally suppressed people living with HIV. We found that aging and HIV infection differentially influenced proteins predominantly within nucleos(t)ide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) pathways, in rectosigmoid tissue and PBMC. HIV-associated effects to the proteome were more prominent in PBMC, whereas aging produced broader alterations in ARV disposition-related proteins in rectosigmoid tissue, including proteins involved in drug transport, intracellular drug activation, dephosphorylation, and nucleotide homeostasis. Several age-associated changes were further influenced by biologic sex, suggesting that aging may not affect ARV disposition uniformly across populations. To place these findings within a broader context, pathway analyses were performed that identified extensive tissue-specific remodeling associated with aging and HIV infection involving drug disposition, immune regulation, cellular metabolism, and disease-related pathways. Notably, aging was associated with alterations in pathways relevant to nucleotide metabolism and gastrointestinal tissue function, suggesting that processes beyond traditional drug transport and metabolism pathways may contribute to variability in ARV disposition with advancing age. Together, these findings identify aging as an important modifier of pathways that regulate ARV disposition within compartments relevant to HIV transmission and persistence. While the clinical consequences of our findings are unknown, these data provide a mechanistic foundation for future studies investigating whether age-associated changes influence the effectiveness of ART and HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis in older adults.
affiliations: Emory University School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Microglial AhR Drives Sex-Biased Amyloid Pathology
papers.abstract: Microglia integrate local and systemic signals that can modify their response to amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}), but the molecular pathways connecting these signals to Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR), a sensor of microbiota- and host-derived metabolites, as a microglial regulator of amyloid pathology. Sustained administration of the AhR agonist indoxyl-3-sulfate (I3S) exacerbated cortical A{beta} deposition and plaque-associated neuritic damage in APPNL-F mice. Conversely, constitutive AhR deficiency reduced amyloid burden, promoted plaque compaction, and preserved behavioural performance, whereas inducible deletion of AhR in microglia was sufficient to reduce plaque accumulation. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that AhR loss reprogrammed microglia toward phagolysosomal and A{beta}-recognition states and enhanced microglial A{beta} uptake, with markedly stronger effects in females. APPNL-F mice also exhibited sex-dependent remodelling of the gut microbiota and tryptophan-derived metabolites. Circulating indole-3-aldehyde (IAld) robustly activated AhR and was associated with cortical amyloid pathology. AhR-activating bioactivity was increased in mouse serum, cortex and faecal extracts and was higher in serum from the COGNIBIO12 analytical subcohort than in independently recruited cognitively unimpaired H2H participants. Among amyloid-positive patients, higher serum AhR bioactivity was associated with lower CSF A{beta}42 concentrations. Together, these findings identify microglial AhR as a metabolically responsive regulator linking systemic ligand availability, biological sex, and microglial control of amyloid pathology.
affiliations: Centro Nacional de Investigaciones Cardiovasculares Carlos III, Madrid, Spain; Unidad de Investigacion Neurovascular, Depto. Farmacologia y Toxicologia, Faculta (corresponding author)

papers.title: Starve, stress, and mate: Activation of the CCAAT-Binding complex overrides sterility of mating-type heterozygous Candida albicans
papers.abstract: Sexual reproduction in the human fungal pathogen Candida albicans is typically restricted by a strict genetic lock: the a1-2 repressor present in standard mating-type heterozygous (MTLa/) diploid strains, which actively represses mating competency. While severe environmental pressures are known to influence fungal development, the molecular mechanisms that allow cells to override this genetic sterility block remain poorly understood. Here, we identify the highly conserved CCAAT-binding complex (CBC) as the critical developmental hub that integrates environmental stress to unlock mating in heterozygous diploids. By combining proteomic mapping (ChIP-SICAP) and transcriptomics (RNA-Seq) to define the regulatory network of the core CBC subunit Hap5, we demonstrate that CBC hyperactivation completely overrides the a1-2 repressor. This activation triggers a robust white-to-opaque phenotypic switch and initiates a mating-competence program in MTLa/ strains genetically locked in a sterile state. Crucially, this developmental transition is antagonized by the iron-regulatory partner Hap43, but is strictly dependent on physical interaction at the chromatin level with Cap1, the master regulator of the oxidative stress response. Our findings reveal that the CBC and Cap1 couple metabolic starvation (glucose and iron limitation) and oxidative stress to a core reproductive program, providing a mechanistic basis for how C. albicans bypasses genetic constraints on sexual reproduction to generate genetic diversity under hostile host conditions.
affiliations: Institut Pasteur (corresponding author)

papers.title: Analysis of reproductive traits associated with lipoprotein(a) deficiency in participants from the Pakistan Genome Resource
papers.abstract: Aims. Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a genetically determined, independent risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, driving development of LPA-targeting therapies that markedly lower circulating Lp(a). Because LPA?the gene encoding apolipoprotein(a)?is absent in most model organisms, preclinical studies have limited value for assessing effects such as reproductive safety. Therefore, naturally occurring human LPA ?knockouts? were analyzed to evaluate reproductive outcomes of on-target Lp(a) lowering. Methods and Results. Individuals carrying high-confidence LPA loss-of-function (LoF) variants which reduce Lp(a) in a gene-dosage?dependent manner within the Pakistan Genome Resource were identified. LoF variants showed no depletion of homozygotes relative to Hardy?Weinberg expectations. LPA LoF associations with fertility-related traits (ever having a child and number of children) under additive and recessive models were assessed using regenie-based burden testing, including sex-stratified analyses, and no significant associations were observed. A recall-by-genotype study of female LoF homozygotes alongside heterozygous and non-carrier family member controls was performed, surveying reproductive histories and offspring outcomes. Across 107 pregnancies and 87 children in 19 homozygous LoF women, rates of miscarriage, maternal complications (including preeclampsia, hypertension, and gestational diabetes), delivery complications, neonatal intensive care admission, birth defects, and child health problems were comparable across genotypes with no statistically significant genotype?outcome associations. Conclusions. These genetic and by-genotype analyses indicate that complete lifelong LPA deficiency due to high-confidence LPA loss-of-function variants is not associated with overt adverse maternal fertility, pregnancy or child health outcomes. These findings offer human genetic reassurance regarding reproductive and developmental safety in the context of sustained Lp(a)-lowering, with implications for long-term therapies targeting Lp(a).
affiliations: Novartis (corresponding author)

papers.title: How mutation rate evolves: Gene expression shapes genome-wide mutation rates in Drosophila melanogaster and Caenorhabditis elegans
papers.abstract: Mutation rates vary across the genome, linked to biochemical properties of local DNA sequences. However, mutation rate variation also associates with functional genomic features, raising the possibility that intragenomic mutation rate variation is shaped by adaptive evolution. In particular, recent studies in the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana suggested that highly conserved genes under strong purifying selection also have reduced de novo mutation rates, suggesting that natural selection may have acted to reduce mutation rate specifically at important genes. However, whether this is true for wider taxa, including animals, remains unknown. Here we repurposed published mutation accumulation datasets from Drosophila melanogaster and Caenorhabditis elegans to investigate the determinants of de novo single nucleotide variant (DNV) rates genome-wide under minimal selection. Loci under stronger purifying selection accumulated fewer mutations, including intronic and synonymous mutations. Various sequence-specific (i.e. GC content) and regulatory features (e.g. chromatin modifications) were strongly correlated with mutation rate, but gene expression best explained the depletion of mutations within strongly conserved loci, even after accounting for correlations amongst variables. Using excision repair (XR)-sequencing data we determined that higher levels of transcription- coupled repair (TCR) were associated with reduced mutation rates, strongly suggesting that TCR lowers mutation rate of highly conserved genes. Furthermore, by comparing orthologs between C. elegans and its close relative Pristionchus pacificus, we found that altered gene expression across evolutionary time correlated with altered mutation rate. These findings support a model whereby developmental transcription modulates local mutation rates through TCR. A corollary is that adaptive mutation bias may emerge indirectly, downstream of gene regulation evolution, providing a mechanistic framework that reconciles non-random local mutation rate variation with established evolutionary theory.
affiliations: University of Oxford (corresponding author)

papers.title: Measuring American black bear genetic load in fixed structural variants and runs of homozygosity
papers.abstract: Populations living in geographically isolated regions are expected to have reduced gene flow, increased genetic drift, and elevated levels of inbreeding, influencing both genetic load and possibly the distribution of structural variants. The American black bear (Ursus americanus) is widely found across Ontario, Canada, where populations inhabit diverse landscapes ranging from relatively intact contiguous forested landscapes to isolated regions such as the Saugeen Peninsula. Here, we investigated the population genomic history across five Ontario black bear populations using a combination of short-read (SR) and long-read (LR) sequencing data. We compared population genetic metrics including nucleotide diversity ({pi}), Tajimas D, runs of homozygosity (ROH), and genome-wide structural variants (SVs) to assess population health and identify signatures of isolation. Our results showed that the isolated Saugeen Peninsula population is genetically distinct and exhibited reduced nucleotide diversity, greater ROH and SV abundance compared with mainland populations. The population also showed elevated genetic load in all genomic features, suggesting increased exposure of deleterious variation that are expressed in ROH and population specific SVs. We further discuss the integration of ROH, SVs and genetic load in conservation assessments.
affiliations: Trent University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Genome-wide Analysis of the VQ Gene Family and Expression Profiling in Sorghum bicolor
papers.abstract: Soil salinization severely restricts agricultural productivity, making the stress-tolerant sorghum an ideal model for studying crop adaptation. VQ motif-containing proteins are plant-specific transcriptional co-regulators vital for stress responses, yet their roles in sorghum remain underexplored. Here, we identified 35 VQ genes in sorghum, classifying them into seven subfamilies. Evolutionary analysis indicated that the family's expansion was primarily driven by segmental duplication. Notably, synteny analysis revealed a lack of collinearity between sorghum and Arabidopsis VQ genes, suggesting significant functional divergence during monocot evolution. Expression profiling showed distinct patterns among VQ members, with SbVQ34, SbVQ39 adn SbVQ40 significantly upregulated under salt stress. Furthermore, protein-protein interaction analysis highlighted SbVQ39 as a potential key regulator in sorghum salt tolerance. This study provides novel insights into sorghum's salinity tolerance mechanisms and establishes a foundation for utilizing VQ genes in breeding salt-tolerant crops.
