papers.title: Somatic Structural Variant Discovery from Tumor Specific Strings Computed Against a Draft Composite Germline Reference
papers.abstract: Somatic structural variants (SVs) are among the most clinically relevant genomic alterations in cancer. However, their accurate detection remains challenging due to complex genomic rearrangements, repetitive genomic regions, difficulties in distinguishing somatic variants from germline variation and sequencing artifacts, and limited sequencing support for low-frequency events. Existing mapping-based somatic SV callers are susceptible to alignment ambiguities in repetitive regions and near complex SV breakpoints, while approaches relying on comparisons of independently generated tumor and normal variant callsets may propagate errors from both callsets. Building on the concept of specific strings, previously applied to germline SV discovery, we introduce VESPA-SS, a novel approach for detecting somatic SVs from paired tumor-normal long-read whole-genome sequencing data. VESPA-SS directly extracts somatic SV signals using specific strings computed from tumor reads against a Draft Composite Germline Reference, without requiring initial read mapping or a high-quality germline assembly. These signals are subsequently clustered and refined through consensus sequence generation and alignment-based procedures to identify somatic SVs. Evaluation on real PacBio HiFi datasets demonstrates that VESPA-SS outperforms state-of-the-art somatic SV callers, achieving F1 scores exceeding 0.92 and 0.90 on the well-characterized HG008 and COLO829 cancer cell lines, respectively, compared with the highest F1 scores of 0.86 and 0.85 achieved by the evaluated methods. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of specific string based signal extraction for accurate somatic SV discovery and establish a new computational paradigm for identifying complex genomic alterations in cancer. VESPA-SS is freely available at https://github.com/dcmonti/VESPA.
affiliations: University of Milano-Bicocca (corresponding author)

papers.title: Recording proteome dynamics in the late-stage embryo at hour-timescale, spatial, and single-cell resolution with MEMBRYO
papers.abstract: Cell fate during development is directed by new gene expression states that replace prior ones. When and where a protein is first translated, and how long it will remain in the cell, dictate the timing and extent of a gene's phenotypic effect. Accessing protein synthesis and turnover information in the rapidly developing embryo remains a major challenge. Here we present MEMBRYO: a method for continuous stable isotope labeling (SILAC) of newly synthesized proteins throughout the live embryo at the hour-timescales of developmental phenotypes. We extend embryo culture into the late stages of organogenesis, thereby accessing the proteome of neurogenesis in the forebrain ex utero. Variations in protein synthesis and turnover activity lead to expression patterns that diverge from the corresponding transcripts, impacting molecular pathways and key milestones of cortical neuron differentiation. The high labeling depth enabled both spatial and single-cell SILAC proteomics analysis of cortical cells, revealing distinct layers of post-transcriptional gene expression regulation in progenitors and neurons. By continuous metabolic labeling in the live embryo, MEMBRYO tracks the past, present, and future of the developmental proteome.
affiliations: Max Planck Institute for Molecular Genetics (corresponding author)

papers.title: Interrogating contrastive learning embeddings for structure-based virtual screening: a case study on DrugCLIP
papers.abstract: Virtual screening has become central to early-stage drug discovery, and structure-based approaches have recently been reframed as a retrieval problem through contrastive learning methods such as DrugCLIP, which project protein pockets and ligands into a shared embedding space. However, what these abstract representations encode and how they relate to conventional notions of structural and chemical similarity remain unclear. Here we present a systematic dissection of DrugCLIP's latent space. We show that its pocket embeddings, despite not being explicitly trained for this task, achieve state-of-the-art performance in pocket similarity search while running over 10,000 times faster than existing structural descriptors. We further demonstrate that this embedding space is structurally coherent and robust to conformational variation. Ligand embeddings, by contrast, capture a pocket-aware notion of chemical similarity that extends beyond conventional fingerprint-based measures. Using a rigorous de-leakage benchmark, we show that DrugCLIP generalises beyond its fine-tuning set, retrieving the crystallographic ligand within the top 1% of a library of 48,999 compounds for 56.5% of 223 pockets with low protein sequence identity (SI [≤] 30%) and limited ligand chemical similarity (TS [≤] 0.7) to the fine-tuning set. Nevertheless, performance declines under increasingly realistic screening conditions, primarily due to differences in sidechain orientation across apo, holo and AlphaFold-predicted structures, and mismatches in pocket residue composition when using predicted pockets. These findings delineate the practical limits of DrugCLIP's applicability, highlight accurate pocket identification and representation as key factors for improving performance, and provide a transferable framework for interpreting the latent spaces of related contrastive pocket-ligand models. Together, these results offer insight to guide the refinement of existing methods and the development of future contrastive screening approaches.
affiliations: University College London (corresponding author)

papers.title: A fine-tuned genomic language model captures nucleotide-level information overlooked by missense variant impact predictors
papers.abstract: Established missense variant impact predictors primarily capture protein-level consequences, yet missense-annotated variants can also act through nucleotide sequence context. We developed GLM-Missense by systematically optimizing the fine-tuning of a genomic language model for missense variant impact prediction. GLM-Missense contributed the most complementary information to seven established predictors on held-out ClinVar variants and independent RAD51D saturation genome editing data. The complementary signal partly reflects splicing disruption, including disrupted exonic splicing regulatory elements largely missed by SpliceAI, and possibly codon-level effects on mRNA stability. These findings suggest fine-tuned genomic language models capture nucleotide-level information overlooked by current missense variant impact predictors.
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley (corresponding author)

papers.title: Genome-resolved metatranscriptomic analysis of arsenic demethylation and detoxification in a methanogenic rice paddy soil
papers.abstract: Microbial methylation and demethylation of arsenic in rice paddy soils influence the speciation and toxicity of arsenic in rice, with implications for human health and rice yields. Here, we combine genome-resolved metatranscriptomics with arsenic speciation analysis in methanogenic paddy soil incubations to elucidate microbial pathways regulating As demethylation, with emphasis on: (i) evaluating links between methyltransferase gene transcription by methylotrophic methanogens and arsenic demethylation; and (ii) assessing how toxicity-induced microbial responses regulate As demethylation and the resulting distribution of As species. Experiments with dimethylarsinic (DMAs) and 2-bromoethanesulfonate as a methanogenesis inhibitor confirm an important role of methanogens in anaerobic arsenic demethylation. Amendment of the methylotrophic substrate trimethylamine accelerated arsenic demethylation and induced an association between arsenic demethylation rates and the transcription of diverse methylotrophic methyltransferases. Six Methanosarcina metagenome assembled genomes dominated methyltransferase transcription and concurrently transcribed genes involved in multiple (methyl)arsenic oxidation and efflux pathways, illustrating a link between putative demethylation and arsenic detoxification at the genome level. Paddy soil incubations also demonstrated toxicity-driven feedbacks between DMAs concentrations and demethylation rates, wherein higher DMAs concentrations inhibited methanogenesis and decreased pseudo first-order demethylation rate constants. These findings provide new insights into links between methylotrophic methanogenesis and arsenic demethylation in anaerobic conditions, with implications for biogeochemical control of arsenic speciation in rice paddy soils.
affiliations: Cornell University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Deaminase-based RNA recording enables high throughput mutational profiling of protein-RNA interactions
papers.abstract: Protein-RNA interactions regulate RNA metabolism and are frequently dysregulated in disease. Scalable methods are needed to connect RNA and protein sequence requirements across biochemical and cellular settings. Here, we use the engineered TadA8.20 deaminase to record protein-RNA recognition as nucleotide edits read by DNA sequencing. Using the {lambda}N-boxB complex, we establish a common recording readout for three complementary comparisons. Pooled mutational scanning on both the RNA and protein sides recovers key boxB nucleotides and {lambda}N residues involved in recognition. Comparison of boxB libraries in vitro and in human cells reveals conserved sequence requirements for protein-RNA recognition. Direct fusion and split recruitment of deaminase through nanobody and protein A/G fusions preserve similar patterns of sequence discrimination. Together, these results establish RNA recording as a scalable approach to map sequence determinants of protein-RNA recognition across molecular and cellular contexts.
affiliations: Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: MintCNA: A Unified Framework for Integrative Copy Number Profiling with Single-Cell Multi-Omics Data
papers.abstract: Chromosomal copy number alterations (CNAs) are key drivers of tumor evolution, disease progression and therapeutic resistance, and their identification is critical for delineating tumor clonal structure. However, accurately detecting CNAs from single-cell data remains challenging as most existing CNA callers still analyze a single omics layer and are susceptible to assay-specific noise. Recently, single-cell multi-omics techniques have enabled joint sequencing of multiple molecular layers (e.g., genomics and transcriptomics) simultaneously in the same cells, yet computational methods that fully exploit such complementary multi-omics data for CNA analysis remain limited. Here, we present MintCNA, a unified framework for CNA detection from paired single-cell multi-omics data. MintCNA integrates deep-learning based denoising with a missingness-adjusted multivariate change-point detection procedure to enhance CNA profiling across omics layers. In simulations, MintCNA outperformed existing single-cell CNA callers across all evaluated scenarios. MintCNA showed the highest correlation with bulk whole-genome sequencing in a colorectal cancer dataset and revealed progressive loss of chromosome 17 during metastasis. In an IDH-mutant glioma cohort, MintCNA generalized to paired single-cell ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data and identified copy number subclones corresponding to distinct malignant cell states. MintCNA provides an advanced multi-omics integrative single-cell CNA analysis tool for better delineating the mechanisms underlying disease progression and tumor evolution.
affiliations: Department of Biostatistics, College of Public Health and Health Professions and College of Medicine, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL, 32603, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Polar Marine Microbial Communities as Reservoirs of Polyester Degrading Enzymes
papers.abstract: Background: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is one of the most widely used plastics and a major contributor to marine pollution. While the diversity of PET hydrolases (PETases), which degrade PET into mono(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (MHET), terephthalate (TPA) and ethylene glycol, has been documented in temperate and tropical waters, their potential presence in polar oceans remains unascertained. Results: Here, we systematically screened polar and non-polar marine metagenomes using Hidden Markov models (HMM) generated using experimentally validated PETases. We identified >680 putative PETase-like sequences, with Antarctic and Arctic candidates enriched in high-fidelity motifs associated with PETase-like activity. Phylogenetic and structural analyses defined a high-confidence PETase-like clade comprising both Type I and Type II enzymes, differing in thermostability-related features and PET-binding motifs. Experimental assays confirmed polyesterase activity in 5/9 candidates from this clade, including polar-derived variants active at 14-25{degrees}C. Downstream enzymes for PET consumption were also widespread, detecting 209 putative MHET hydrolases and 442 TPA-catabolyzing enzymes. Further, we reconstructed 112 metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) carrying at least one enzyme of the PET degradation pathway, 89 of them carrying a PETase-like gene. Notably, 15 MAGs encoded multiple PETase-like enzymes, nine of them from polar datasets, and one polar MAG harbored a complete PETase-MHETase-TPA pathway, suggesting the genomic potential for a fully integrated degradation potential in cold-adapted taxa. Conclusions: Together, these results demonstrate that polar oceans act as previously overlooked reservoirs of taxonomically and functionally diverse plastic-degrading enzymes. The enrichment of PETase-like enzymes and downstream pathways in polar microbial communities expands the global biogeography of plastic biodegradation and highlights cold-active enzymes as promising candidates for developing low-temperature plastic bioremediation strategies.
affiliations: Universidad Mayor (corresponding author)

papers.title: Long-Term Neurovascular Dysfunction and Altered Placenta-Derived EV miRNA Profiles in a Rat Model with Preeclamptic Features
papers.abstract: Objective: Preeclampsia increases long-term cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, and cognitive risk but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. We examined cerebrovascular function, cognitive performance, and placenta-derived extracellular-vesicle (PD-EV) microRNA profiles in a transgenic rat model with preeclamptic features (TGA-PE) at 2 months after delivery (2M). Methods: Middle cerebral artery (MCA) hemodynamics were assessed by transcranial Doppler (TCD), and cerebral oxygenation was measured by photoacoustic imaging (PAI) in TGA-PE and Sprague-Dawley control rats. Blood pressure was measured using a tail-cuff method. Touchscreen-based cognitive tasks evaluated learning and reward-directed responding, while histological assessment evaluated MCA structure. MicroRNA sequencing was performed on circulating PD-EV, and miRNA target networks were analyzed using KEGG-based NEST-Scoring (Node, Edge, System, Topology). Validation of miR-363-3p was performed in PD-EV, plasma, non-PD-EV, and human brain endothelial cells (HBEC-5i). Results: TGA-PE rats were hypertensive and exhibited lower MCA resistance and pulsatility indexes with unchanged blood flow velocities. Cognitive testing revealed impaired associative learning and reduced motivation to respond on a progressive-ratio schedule. Temporal brain oxygen saturation was higher in TGA-PE rats with unchanged total hemoglobin, lower brain HIF-2, and unchanged VEGF levels. MCA elastin content was reduced in TGA-PE rats without changes in total collagen. PD-EV sequencing identified 29 differentially expressed miRNAs, including reduced miR-363-3p in non-placental EVs and plasma at 2M. Inhibition of miR-363-3p in human cerebral endothelial cell line HBEC-5i upregulated NOX4, p21, and {beta}-galactosidase levels. NEST-Scoring highlighted pathways involving MAPK, Ras, TNF, focal adhesion, cytoskeletal regulation, and cellular senescence. Conclusions: The exposure to experimental preeclampsia resulted in altered MCA flow resistance, cerebral oxygenation, vascular structure and behavioral performance. Although direct mechanistic studies are needed to establish the role of miRNA363-3p in neurovascular health, the increased endothelial oxidative stress and senescence-associated markers in HBEC-5i cells in response to miRNA363-3p inhibition suggest a potential protective role for miRNA363-3p. A novel NEST-Scoring analysis also identified potential pathways for future mechanistic investigations. Overall, the TGA-PE model provides a useful experimental system for investigating candidate mechanisms that may contribute to long-term maternal neurovascular changes following hypertensive pregnancy and sequelae of preeclamptic pathophysiology.
affiliations: Wake Forest University School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: MAXWELL: Calibrating the probabilistic outputs of protein language models to the mutation-induced stability change landscape
papers.abstract: Designing mutations that enhance protein stability is a central goal in protein engineering. However, experimentally screening large numbers of candidate mutations is costly and time-consuming, creating a strong need for computational methods that can identify potentially stabilizing mutations. Among these approaches, protein language models are particularly promising because they learn context-dependent amino acid preferences from large-scale sequence and structure datasets. Nevertheless, most existing stability prediction methods use these models primarily as feature extractors and do not fully exploit the amino acid probability distributions they encode. Here, we introduce MAXWELL (Matrix-wise Landscape Learning), a novel post-training method that calibrates the probabilistic outputs learned by protein language models during pretraining to generate mutational landscapes that quantify the effects of individual amino acid substitutions on protein stability. When applied to ProteinMPNN, MAXWELL yields a state-of-the-art predictor of the effects of protein mutations on stability, outperforming ThermoMPNN and other representative methods on a curated benchmark of experimentally measured stability changes. We next applied MAXWELL to the design of ten single-point mutations in the DhaA dehalogenase, seven of which (70%) increased thermal stability. Among them, G171W showed the largest improvement, with a measured {Delta}T of 4.91 . These experimental results establish MAXWELL as a novel post-training strategy for protein language models and a practical framework for designing stabilizing mutations.
affiliations: School of Physics and Astronomy & Institute of Natural Sciences, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai 200240, China; Zhangjiang Institute for Advanced Study, (corresponding author)

papers.title: Stochasticity in Metabolism: Oxidative Stress Response Phenotypes As Emergent Consequences of Network Topology
papers.abstract: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are ubiquitous yet elusive due to their reactivity and short half-lives, making simulation essential for mechanistic insight. Traditional ROS modeling has been confined to small ODE frameworks limited by kinetic-parameter scarcity. Here, we recast ROS dynamics as a flux-balance analysis (FBA) optimization problem using COBRA and CPLEX, augmenting the Escherichia coli iJO1366 genome-scale model with 84 spontaneous oxidation, 14 redox, and 9 detoxification reactions, targeting three ROS species: hydroxyl radicals, superoxide, and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). We also formalize five fundamental rules of oxidation biology in the form of mixed-integer linear constraints, allowing us to dynamically incorporate reaction rate constants and let complex behavior emerge from first principles. Among these phenomena is the bimodal killing pattern under H2O2 stress, first announced over 40 years ago and never computationally recapitulated until now. We observe it by stochastically sampling our models with GapSplit, simulating bet-hedging and partitioning solutions into growers, persisters, and non-survivors. In our simulations, this killing effect arises solely from the metabolic network topology during random exploration of alternative metabolic configurations. The conservation of steady state creates a stochastic bias for detoxification when central carbon metabolism reaches its metabolic capacity to deal with ROS, causing the famous survival recovery phase. The recovery phase is thus part of Mode 1 metabolism, characterized by spare detoxification capacity and fulfilled by the Ahp reaction in E. coli. Mode 2 has no spare detoxification. We anticipate this to be an overlooked universal principle.
affiliations: Albert Einstein College of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Small RNA-mediated genomic silencing promotes telomere stability in the absence of telomerase in C. elegans
papers.abstract: We previously found that small RNAs with perfect homology to (TTAGGC)n telomere repeats are very rare. Here we use long read sequencing to reveal that most N2 wild type C. elegans strains have few telomere mutations at 5 prime ends of telomeres, where the telomeric lncRNA TERRA is transcribed. Therefore, telomere mutations cannot explain the absence of perfect small RNAs to (TTAGGC)n telomere repeats. We show that the heterochromatin mark H3K9me2 is enriched at C. elegans sub-telomeres and that the HP1 protein HPL-2 that binds H3K9me2 promotes telomere stability in the absence of telomerase. Small RNA silencing can promote H3K9 methylation, and telomere stability in the absence of telomerase requires germ granule proteins MUT-7 and MUT-14 that promote small RNA biogenesis and also WAGO-1 and HRDE-1 Argonaute proteins that bind subtelomeric small RNAs. Loss of telomerase induced biogenesis of small RNAs from the subtelomeric 5 prime end of the telomeric lncRNA TERRA but not from telomere repeats of TERRA. Loss of both telomerase and small RNA-mediated genome silencing induced TERRA expression, telomere damage and accelerated sterility. We propose that small RNA-mediated heterochromatin formation and telomerase function redundantly to repress a form of telomeric DNA damage that is coupled to TERRA expression and subtelomeric small RNA biogenesis. However, telomere repeats of TERRA strongly resisted RNA-dependent RNA polymerase activity in telomerase mutants, revealing an exceptional quality of telomere repeat RNA.
affiliations: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (corresponding author)

papers.title: Microfluidic sieve and detector for rapid ultrasensitive assays with single-molecule sensitivity
papers.abstract: The advent of ultrasensitive assays enabled many new research and clinical applications, but the time-to-result is hours and has not significantly improved over time, limiting their potential. We introduce the microfluidic sieve and detector (MFSD) that can sieve 200 microlitres in just one minute, and quantify captured analytes in four minutes, down to zeptomolar (10^-19M) concentration. The MFSD comprises half a million 8-m-diameter pores that bind analytes upon Brownian motion-induced wall collision. Conventional ensemble models and a stochastic Brownian agent dynamics introduced here reveal rapid, predictable and tuneable analyte capture under flow. Digital sandwich assays are completed by sequentially flowing the sample and reagents, partitioning the pores, and digitally revealing single trapped analytes by enzymatic amplification. The MFSD tests are specific and reproducible, exhibit a large dynamic range, and are simple, tuneable and versatile, enabling measurement of different proteins including influenza A nucleoprotein in clinical samples, and even nucleic acids while being both faster and more sensitive than PCR. As such, the MFSD could open a new chapter for analysis and diagnostics.
affiliations: McGill University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Scalable high-density tactile arenas for measuring ground-contact forces in freely moving animals
papers.abstract: Understanding how animals physically interact with their environment is fundamental to studying movement, sensorimotor control, and neurological function. Yet most behavioral measurement systems primarily capture movement and posture, while direct measurements of contact forces often require specialized instrumentation or involve trade-offs among spatial coverage, resolution, and acquisition speed. Here, we introduce a scalable tactile sensing platform that transforms the surface beneath freely moving animals into a high-resolution contact-imaging instrument. By combining modular sensor arrays with adaptive compressive tactile sampling, the platform provides 16,384 tactile sensing elements at 2-mm pitch across a 512 x 128-mm runway, with nominal 1 kHz acquisition. Rather than exhaustively scanning the entire array, the system concentrates measurements around active contacts, enabling high-speed sensing across an extended behavioral surface. Synchronized overhead video and a camera-assisted analysis pipeline enable paw-resolved measurements of contact loading, stance dynamics, footprint morphology, interlimb weight redistribution, and center-of-pressure trajectories. In a longitudinal rat model of sciatic nerve injury, the platform detected reduced loading of the injured hindlimb and increased loading of the contralateral limb, including changes that conventional gait timing measures underestimated. The modular architecture, together with openly available hardware designs, software and data, provides an accessible framework for studying the mechanical interactions underlying freely moving behavior, with potential applications across neuroscience, injury, and motor recovery research.
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Metastable Dimeric Intermediate Drives Native-like Spidroin Fibrillogenesis, while Dehydration Promotes Cross-β Transition
papers.abstract: The exceptional mechanical properties of spider dragline silk originate from hierarchical spidroin self-assembly, yet mimicking this process to generate native-like structures remains challenging. Here, we report a metastable dimeric intermediate as an essential molecular factor for fibrillogenesis. Small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) and atomic force microscopy (AFM) revealed a compact core stabilized by solvent-excluded "dry interfaces" surrounded by extended random coil regions. Within the core, a subset of the polyalanine blocks is held by side-chain packing rather than by main-chain {beta}-sheets; the majority remain exposed in the surrounding coil regions. Upon lowering the denaturant concentration, these exposed polyalanine segments pair with their counterparts at a fibril end, forming intermolecular {beta}-sheets that act as linkers and drive the stepwise end-to-end polymerization of the dimeric particles. In solution, the resulting fibrils exhibit an ordered {beta}-structure in which the polypeptide chains run parallel to the fibril axis, in contrast to amyloid-like cross-{beta}, in which the strands lie perpendicular to it; this matches key features of native silk nanofibril architecture. However, X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis demonstrates that these native-like nanofibrils undergo an effectively irreversible transition toward amyloid-like cross-{beta} structures upon drying. Native-like fibrils are thus achievable by self-assembly, but structural control is lost during the final dehydration step. Accordingly, we propose a general principle for decoupling self-assembly from dehydration: native-like nanofibrils are formed first, then dried under conditions that restrict molecular-chain mobility (for example, mechanical constraint or immobilization on a surface), which we expect to suppress thermodynamic relaxation into cross-{beta} structures.
affiliations: Division of Materials Science, Graduate School of Science and Technology, Nara Institute of Science and Technology, 8916-5, Takayama, Ikoma, Nara 630-0192, Japa (corresponding author)

papers.title: From exact gradients to exact standard errors: third- and fourth-order sensitivities for the Laplacian population likelihood family
papers.abstract: Asymptotic standard errors for the parameters of a nonlinear mixed effects model fitted by Laplacian estimation, first-order conditional estimation (FOCE), or FOCE with interaction (FOCEI) require the observed (Fisher) information, the negative second derivative of the population objective at the optimum. The gradient of this objective can be computed exactly from sensitivity equations, but the observed information is still formed by finite differencing, which is less accurate, step-size dependent, and requires empirical Bayes reoptimization. These perturbed individual optimization problems can fail even after a successful fit. Our objectives are to (1) extend the exact-gradient sensitivity framework by one differentiation and give the observed information of the Laplacian population likelihood family in closed form and (2) illustrate covariance calculation without further empirical Bayes optimization in a case example. Writing the objective as a data term plus the log-determinant of the inner Hessian, the population Hessian splits so that the data term reuses second-order sensitivities, whereas the log determinant term requires third-order sensitivities for FOCE/FOCEI and fourth-order sensitivities for the full Laplacian method. We illustrate this on a two-compartment oral model with first-order absorption fitted to simulated data. The analytic covariance involves no differencing step and uses the fitted empirical Bayes estimates without reoptimization, avoiding this source of covariance-step failure. Implemented for FOCE/FOCEI in the open-source R package nlmixr2, the construction provides exact, reproducible standard errors for the approximate likelihood, limited by numerical solution accuracy and conditioning. This supports more dependable confidence intervals, identifiability assessment, and uncertainty propagation.
affiliations: Division of Systems Pharmacology and Pharmacy, Leiden Academic Centre for Drug Research, Leiden University, Leiden, The Netherlands (corresponding author)

papers.title: Non-canonical peptidoglycan cross-linking is essential for Mycobacterium tuberculosis acid resistance
papers.abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis withstands acidic conditions to survive and replicate within macrophages. To define the genetic determinants of this adaptation, we performed a transposon screen in a lipid-rich, acidic medium that mimics the host environment and supports robust M. tuberculosis growth. This screen identified ldtB, encoding an L,D transpeptidase, as essential for growth and survival under acid stress. Loss of LdtB decreased 3-3 peptidoglycan cross-linking, disrupted cell wall architecture, and impaired intrabacterial pH homeostasis, resulting in increased susceptibility to cell wall-active antibiotics. Notably, M. tuberculosis lacking LdtB displayed heightened sensitivity to meropenem within macrophages, suggesting that targeting this enzyme could potentiate beta-lactam efficacy during infection. These findings establish LdtB as a key mediator linking peptidoglycan homeostasis to acid stress resistance and underscores the importance of in vitro culture models that recapitulate the host microenvironment for uncovering new in vivo active therapeutic targets.
affiliations: Weill Cornell Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Do plasmid-dependent phages enable the survival of costly plasmids?
papers.abstract: Plasmids store auxiliary genes that address environmental challenges such as antibiotics. In the short term, plasmid loss can be advantageous to hosts if plasmid benefits are temporary but costs are permanent. However, this loss can proceed to plasmid extinction, with access to plasmid-derived benefits permanently lost. We consider a worst-case scenario: a plasmid that yields benefits only infrequently, imposes heavy costs that cannot be alleviated, and whose host population faces a competitor that cannot acquire the costly plasmid. Thus, horizontal transmission of this plasmid is detrimental to the host population when the plasmid does not provide benefits. Using population models, we demonstrate that -- counterintuitively -- plasmid-dependent phages can enable high-cost plasmid survival. Phage predation pins the plasmid at low abundance, effectively neutralizing the plasmid cost at the population level and boosting persistence time. When the costly plasmid becomes beneficial, it spreads and survives by vertical transmission until benefits subside.
affiliations: Princeton University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Evolutionary tuning of rhodopsin-mediated light protection
papers.abstract: Visual sensitivity introduces the inherent risk of blinding photodamage. Rhodopsin directly mediates this vulnerability, as activation drives excessive signaling via the Meta-II (MII) state, which subsequently releases the toxic, desensitizing agonist all-trans retinal (atRAL). In dim-light specialists, slow atRAL release is assumed to reflect extended MII signaling; however, this model ignores that arrestin quenches signaling in milliseconds and that apparent release reflects reversible atRAL rebinding. Here we reveal that extended post-bleach lifetimes, including an atRAL-driven shift toward non-signaling Meta-III (MIII), evolved independently of intrinsic G-protein signaling to dually protect retinal cells against photochemical toxicity and shield neighboring receptors from agonist noise. Dim-light specialists whose rod-dense retinas experience daytime solar flux, such as megabats, possess an extremely cytoprotective rhodopsin that retains nearly 60% of atRAL at equilibrium by partitioning into MIII, validating long-standing predictions that MIII buffers retinoid toxicity while explaining why bat rhodopsin signals more weakly than faster-releasing human or bovine orthologs. To definitively uncouple sequestration from intrinsic signaling, we engineered an active-state-locked, signaling-null rhodopsin that achieves 100% atRAL sequestration and confers extreme cytoprotection in retinal cells. Mimicking partial bleaches with heterogeneous active and inactive receptor populations, co-incubation reveals that this signaling-null sink acts in trans to boost wild-type rhodopsin regeneration and signaling by shielding neighboring dark-state receptors from agonist interference. Lastly, while consensus human rhodopsin is non-protective, alleles restoring cytoprotective sequestration emerged in high-irradiance geographies, conferring a 38% reduced risk of blindness in modern populations. Our findings redefine rhodopsin as a tunable light buffer shaping adaptation and human disease.
affiliations: Vanderbilt University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Fully integrated SNV, fusion, and isoform analysis of cancer drivers with FLAIR3 for improved functional interpretation
papers.abstract: Background: Although the impact of genomic variants and changes in transcriptome regulation are often studied in isolation, their interaction is critical to understanding oncogenesis. We developed FLAIR3, which performs a comprehensive and integrated analysis of single nucleotide variants (SNVs), indels, gene fusions, and alternative splicing using long-read RNA sequencing (lrRNA-seq) and predicts their combined impact on amino acid sequence. Results: By applying FLAIR3 to lrRNA-seq datasets from osteosarcoma and lung adenocarcinoma, we demonstrated that long-read technology captures the full-length molecules required to phase variants with specific isoforms. In the osteosarcoma samples, FLAIR3 identified alternative splicing of gene fusions in known driver genes, including TP53. In the lung adenocarcinoma samples, FLAIR3 revealed isoform-biased expression of oncogenic SNVs, including BRAF, CDKN2A, and TP53. Conclusions: FLAIR3 provides a robust method for resolving the complex interplay between variants and transcript isoforms, offering deeper insights into the molecular drivers of cancer.

papers.title: RoDPAA: A Robust Dissimilarity-Based Principal Angle Analysis Framework for Multi-View Microbiome Data Integration
papers.abstract: Multiview microbiome studies profile the same participants across body sites or molecular layers, but integration is hampered by sparse, compositional data, modest sample sizes and methods that recognize only exact sharing. We present RoDPAA (Robust Dissimilarity-based Principal Angle Analysis), a framework that represents each view through any data-appropriate dissimilarity, such as Bray--Curtis, without log-ratio transformation or likelihood assumptions. RoDPAA aligns view-specific signal subspaces through principal angles, captures complete and partial sharing, and tests by permutation how many components are shared, using only eigendecomposition and little tuning. In Gaussian simulations, RoDPAA matched JIVE and MOFA given true ranks, ran faster and alone recovered the shared dimension in every replicate. In two inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) cohorts with sparse, zero-inflated data, Bray--Curtis-based RoDPAA recovered shared structure that was stable to prevalence filtering, whereas log-ratio-based alternatives were not. Its leading microbiome--metabolome factors, learned without disease labels, were the only ones associated with IBD.

papers.title: Molecular diffusion and binding kinetics are sufficient to explain condensate-like nuclear clustering
papers.abstract: Many key transcriptional regulators form clusters in cell nuclei that are proposed to promote transcription by concentrating reactants. These clusters exhibit emergent biophysical properties consistent with biomolecular condensates such as high local densities, spherical morphologies, fusion, and rapid molecular exchange kinetics. Whether these properties are specific hallmarks of condensation or can arise from simpler mechanisms is unclear. Here we developed SPARK (Simulation of Protein Accumulation from Reaction Kinetics), a computational framework parameterized by genomic, and molecular diffusion and binding kinetics data, to simulate the spatial distributions of chromatin-binding proteins as they would appear under an optical microscope. These simulations recapitulate key reported features of Brd4, Nanog, Sox2, and Bicoid clusters, without including any higher-order protein-protein interactions or phase separation. We demonstrate that commonly used signatures of condensates instead emerge directly from molecular scale binding and diffusion kinetics. Through systematic variation of nuclear concentrations and enhancer binding-site composition, we show that distinct combinations of molecular kinetics can result in similar spatial distributions of transcription factors. These analyses establish that imaging-based features of protein clusters cannot uniquely define the underlying physical mechanism of their formation. We therefore conclude that condensation is not required to drive transcription factor occupancy and that protein-protein interactions off chromatin are not required to explain cluster formation. Our results instead imply that mechanisms other than clustering are sufficient for target-search acceleration and robust occupancy. SPARK thus provides a quantitative null model for identifying which molecular mechanisms are necessary to explain experimental observations of nuclear protein clustering.

papers.title: Material context and TGF-β blockade timing determine matrix retained after withdrawal in patient-derived GelMA-bioprinted keratoconus stroma
papers.abstract: Stromal repair requires newly formed matrix to persist while the contractile response to TGF-{beta} is controlled. We developed patient-derived bioprinted gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA) stroma to connect material-dependent cell responses with matrix retention after timed receptor blockade. In constructs from six keratoconus (KC) and six normal donors, KC cells retained disease-associated transcription while secreting procollagen I and lumican at normal-donor levels per unit DNA. Comparisons with two-dimensional culture and matched cast GelMA showed that the three-dimensional environment increased matrix induction and lowered resting contractile expression. Printing added a stromal identity response that persisted as retained lumican. Delayed blockade after a TGF-{beta}1 pulse preserved matrix transcription and late secretion. Eleven days after withdrawal, this finite course left more native collagen and lower contractile-gene expression than vehicle in 9/12 donors. Across the tested blockade regimens, at least one regimen achieved both outcomes at the final endpoint in 11/12 donors, including every KC donor. Culture format changed the preferred regimen. Choosing finite blockade by retained collagen instead of secretion changed the schedule in half the donors; the selected arms contained 22.2% more collagen. Retained collagen and contractile expression therefore provide joint endpoints for designing when TGF-{beta}-pathway courses, including losartan and TGF-{beta}3 treatment for keratoconic and scarred corneas, should start and stop.

papers.title: Systematic comparison of gliflozins identifies a selective anti-calcifying effect of canagliflozin beyond canonical SGLT2 inhibition
papers.abstract: Background: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) provide important cardiorenal benefits in chronic kidney disease (CKD), but their effects on vascular calcification remain conflicting. Whether potential anti-calcifying effects are shared across gliflozins or involve mechanisms beyond canonical SGLT2 inhibition is unknown. Methods: We systematically compared canagliflozin, dapagliflozin and empagliflozin in a high-phosphate diet-induced mouse model of vascular calcification and complementary ex vivo and in vitro models, including rodent and human vascular tissues and vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs). Aortic transcriptional response was investigated by RNA sequencing. VSMC calcification, proliferation, migration, viability, glucose uptake and bioenergetics were investigated using complementary cellular assays, including OsteoSense staining, Annexin V/propidium iodide staining, radiolabeled 2-deoxyglucose uptake and Seahorse ATP rate analysis. SGLT2/1 expression was examined by RT-qPCR, Western blotting and immunofluorescence. We also evaluated sotagliflozin, a dual SGLT1/2 inhibitor, and mizagliflozin, a selective SGLT1 inhibitor. Results: Among the three gliflozins, only canagliflozin significantly reduced aortic calcification in vivo. Its anti-calcifying effect was also observed in rodent aortic rings, human vascular explants, cultured VSMCs and aortic rings from diabetic db/db mice. Aortic RNA-seq revealed that canagliflozin partially reversed HPD-induced transcriptional alterations, including changes in pro-calcific signaling and cellular metabolism, while some endothelial and inflammatory responses were shared among gliflozins. In mouse VSMCs, canagliflozin reduced calcification across all tested concentrations, dose-dependently decreased osteogenic marker expression, and reduced proliferation and migration. Increased apoptotic and damaged cell fractions were observed at higher concentrations, but not at lower concentrations. Canagliflozin also reduced glucose uptake and mitochondrial ATP production, without significantly affecting glycolytic ATP production. Neither dapagliflozin nor empagliflozin reproduced these cellular and metabolic effects at any of the concentrations tested. SGLT2 and SGLT1 expression was low or undetectable in vascular tissues and cells, and neither sotagliflozin nor mizagliflozin reproduced the anti-calcifying effect of canagliflozin in vivo or in vitro. Conclusions: Canagliflozin exhibits a selective anti-calcifying profile among the gliflozins tested, associated with changes in VSMC responses and cellular metabolism. These findings suggest that its vascular protective effects may involve mechanisms beyond canonical SGLT2 inhibition.

papers.title: Receptor-proximal phosphoform organization precedes β2 integrin activation
papers.abstract: Receptor signaling is often framed as protein recruitment after stimulation, but whether receptor-proximal environments are organized in composition and phosphorylation state beforehand remains unclear. We used CD18-APEX2 proximity labeling and a spatial membrane reference to quantify proteins and phosphosites near leukocyte {beta}2 integrins. At rest, receptors, adaptors and Rap GTPases were preferentially represented relative to several catalytic classes. Parent-protein correction revealed spatial phosphoform organization, with 32% of 4,564 phosphosites deviating significantly from the distribution center and 56% of proteins with multiple quantified sites showing divergence beyond measurement error. Sustained activation altered 31% of phosphosites while 95.9% of proteins remained equivalent within {+/-}0.5 log2 and spatial phosphoform organization largely persisted. Most phosphorylation responses were shared across both labeling environments, whereas receptor-preferential changes were dominated by phosphosites. These findings suggest that receptor signaling can regulate pre-existing molecular states without extensive protein redistribution.

papers.title: Language-guided domain adaptation improves protein sequence representations for antimicrobial resistance analysis
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR), particularly antibiotic resistance in bacterial pathogens, complicates infectious disease management. Because bacterial resistance is often mediated by protein functions, including antibiotic inactivation and efflux, protein sequence analysis provides a molecular basis for digital AMR surveillance and therapeutic intervention. We developed BacLLM, a language guided protein representation framework that integrates annotation-derived functional knowledge into protein language model representations for AMR analysis in WHO priority bacterial pathogens. Through sequence enhancement, semantic enrichment of UniProt annotations, and cross modal contrastive learning, BacLLM transfers LLM encoded annotation priors into the sequence encoder. Compared with baselines, BacLLM provided more informative representations for resistance-gene identification and mechanism prediction, captured resistance associated mutational signals at single-residue resolution, and preserved taxonomic relationships not reflected by phenotype based clinical groupings. Moreover, BacLLM recovered resistance associated functional organization within a TolC-centered protein association network, prioritizing proteins with low sequence identity to TolC but predicted structural similarity to TolC. Extending from AMR characterization to therapeutic prioritization, BacLLM also improved strain-level phage host matching for phage therapy candidate prioritization. Together, these findings establish BacLLM as a protein representation framework supporting AMR surveillance, functional characterization, and therapeutic candidate prioritization.

papers.title: Hybrid RY-mers increase aDNA alignment sensitivity
papers.abstract: One of the key steps in ancient DNA data analysis is the accurate identification of endogenous short reads that originate from the ancient genome. Currently, this step is performed using general-purpose sequence aligners, such as BWA-aln, with parameter settings optimized for sensitivity. This approach results in increased runtime, even relative to standard DNA alignment workflows, and is not sufficient for aligning samples that are highly divergent from a reference database. We introduce hybrid RY-mers, a seed construct designed to incorporate aDNA-specific sequence damage. We adapt hybrid RY-mers to the existing concept of multi-context seeds and implement them in the read aligner strobealign. On simulated genomic and metagenomic datasets, we show that hybrid RY-mers result in higher mapping accuracy, while also reducing runtime by 4-6 times compared to the state-of-the-art aDNA alignment method BWA-aln. Furthermore, substituting aDNA aligner MALT in the metagenomic tool-suite aMeta with our new alignment approach demonstrated that aMeta gave a faster and less memory consuming detection of ancient taxa present in the samples.

Resolving phonons in superconductor Bi2Sr2CaCu2O8+δ at sub-unit-cell resolution
papers.abstract: The role of phonons in cuprates remains controversial, with their complex lattice structure complicating the investigation. Here, we identify phonon modes originating from charge reservoir and superconducting layers of Bi2Sr2CaCu2O8+δ using sub-unit-cell resolved electron energy loss spectroscopy in a scanning transmission electron microscope. We reveal several phonon modes exhibiting layer-specific localization: ~78 meV in-plane modes localized in the CuO2 planes, ~42 meV hybrid (in-plane and out-of-plane) modes in the CuO2 planes, and ~38 meV hybrid modes in the BiO layers. We also observe a periodic modulation of phonon frequencies induced by the superstructure, spatially correlating with the superconducting gap variation. Our findings offer new insights into the lattice dynamics in cuprates, fostering deeper exploration of the microscopic linkage between structural modulation, electronic inhomogeneity, and electron-phonon coupling. The role of phonons in cuprate superconductivity remains debated, partly because their layered structures host complex lattice dynamics. Here, sub-unit-cell spectroscopy resolves layer-localized phonons in Bi-2212 and reveals a spatial correlation between superstructure-driven phonon frequency modulations and superconducting gap variations.

papers.title: Agentic AI needs a science of interaction
Full-sunlight-driven photocatalytic recovery of critical metals from spent lithium-ion batteries via organic acid leaching
papers.abstract: The rapidly increasing deployment of secondary batteries has intensified pressures on resource security and waste management, exposing fundamental limitations of current battery recycling technologies that require intensive use of energy and chemicals. To enable sustainable battery waste management, systems must improve economic and environmental feasibility at the process level while retaining versatility toward diverse cathode chemistries. Here, we report a sunlight-driven photocatalytic leaching framework that enables robust recovery of critical metals from diverse commercial cathode materials. The process couples mild organic acids with a reusable photocatalyst to orchestrate a twofold leaching mechanism driven by sunlight, in which hydrogen peroxide is generated in situ across the solar spectrum and further activated by UV components to enhance metal extraction without external oxidizing agents. Importantly, the system maintains consistent performance over multiple operation cycles, supporting process robustness and scalability. Beyond its technical performance, techno-economic and life cycle analyses demonstrate clear advantages over conventional recycling methods, including lower energy inputs and reduced greenhouse gas emissions. This work establishes a versatile, profitable, and environmentally benign approach to battery recycling, offering a scalable pathway toward a sustainable circular economy. Researchers developed a light-driven method using organic acids to recover critical metals from used lithium-ion batteries, offering a more sustainable route for battery recycling powered by natural sunlight.

papers.title: Rescue treatment for medium vessel occlusion by intra-arterial tenecteplase: the RESCUE-TNK randomized clinical trial
papers.abstract: In patients with acute ischemic stroke caused by medium vessel occlusion (MeVO), intra-arterial tenecteplase may offer a targeted strategy to improve recanalization; we hypothesized that intra-arterial tenecteplase would increase successful reperfusion compared with standard care with a comparable safety profile. This phase 2, prospective, randomised, open-label, blinded-endpoint, multicentre study aims to assess the efficacy and safety of intra-arterial tenecteplase for patients with acute ischemic stroke caused by MeVO. Patients with MeVO were randomly (1:1) assigned to receive intra-arterial tenecteplase or standard care. The primary outcome was successful reperfusion of medium vessel occlusion. A total of 80 patients were randomized to either the tenecteplase group (n = 41) or control group (n = 39). Successful reperfusion reached 61.0% (25/41) in the tenecteplase group versus 28.2% (11/39) in the control group (unadjusted odds ratio 3.98, 95% CI 1.56-10.16; P = 0.004). Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage within 24 h was similar between the tenecteplase and control groups. This work suggests that intra-arterial tenecteplase significantly increased the probability of successful reperfusion compared with standard care, with a comparable safety profile in this stroke population. (Funded by Shenyang Science Tech Project and hospital-initiated grants; ClinicalTrials.gov registration: NCT05657470) Medium-vessel occlusion accounts for a substantial proportion of acute ischemic stroke cases, yet optimal reperfusion treatment strategies remain unclear for patients ineligible for mechanical endovascular thrombectomy. Here, the authors show that intra-arterial tenecteplase significantly increases reperfusion rates for medium-vessel occlusion with acceptable safety, although statistically-significant improvements in 90-day functional outcomes were not detected in this phase-2 randomized trial.

papers.title: Estimating the resilience of non-stationary systems
papers.abstract: A wide body of work has applied the concept of critical slowing down to estimate the stability of different Earth system components. Most of them – such as global vegetation – are inherently non-stationary, for example due to strong seasonal forcing that complicates the estimation of their resilience to external perturbations. Here, we introduce a method to account for non-stationarity in estimating the resilience of diverse synthetic and real-world systems via a regression-based formulation of the Langevin equation. Our method does not require extensive data pre-processing, is robust to gaps in the data record, and does not require regular time sampling. We further show that our method can incorporate time-varying data uncertainties, derive uncertainty bounds for stability estimates, and can be natively extended to examine spatial systems. Our method is a drop-in replacement for widely-used autocorrelation-based resilience estimates, and can be applied across diverse Earth system components. The authors introduce a method applicable to diverse Earth system components that directly estimates recovery rates and robust uncertainty estimates and can accommodate data with uneven sampling, seasonality, and time-varying uncertainties.

papers.title: Intra-arterial tenecteplase for acute basilar artery occlusion with sufficient recanalization after thrombectomy: the INSIST-IT randomized clinical trial
papers.abstract: The clinical effect of adjunctive intra-arterial tenecteplase after successful recanalization in acute basilar artery occlusion (BAO) remains uncertain. In this prospective, randomized, adaptive-enrichment, open label, blinded-end point, multi-center trial, patients with BAO within 24 h of estimated symptom onset who achieved successful reperfusion after endovascular treatment (EVT) were randomized (1:1) to intra-arterial tenecteplase (n = 75) or control (only received standard medical therapy, n = 69). The primary efficacy outcome was independent ambulation (modified Rankin Scale 0–3) at 90 days; the primary safety outcome was symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH). The trial was stopped early due to safety concerns and lack of efficacy per Data Safety and Monitoring Committee recommendation. Among 144 randomized patients, 143 (99.3%) completed follow-up. At 90 days, independent ambulation was achieved in 40.0% of the tenecteplase group versus 50.0% in the control group (OR 0.67; 95% CI 0.34–1.29; P = 0.23). sICH occurred in 6.2% versus 4.8% (OR 1.31; 95% CI 0.28–6.89; P = 0.73). All-cause mortality at 90 days was 41.3% versus 26.5% (OR 1.96; 95% CI 0.97–4.03; P = 0.063). In this prematurely terminated trial, adjunctive intra-arterial tenecteplase did not improve functional outcomes in patients with BAO. Acute basilar artery occlusion (BAO) is a life-threatening cause of stroke, and whether intra-arterial tenecteplase after successful recanalization leads to improved outcomes is unclear. This randomized trial by Chen and colleagues was stopped early for safety concerns and shows that adjunctive intra-arterial tenecteplase does not improve functional outcomes in acute BAO.

papers.title: Intra-arterial tenecteplase during thrombectomy for acute ischemic stroke: the BRETIS-TNK2 trial
papers.abstract: Intra-arterial tenecteplase during endovascular treatment (EVT) may increase first-pass recanalization and dissolve microcirculatory thrombi, but its efficacy and safety are uncertain. We hypothesised that this strategy would improve functional outcomes versus EVT alone. This phase 3, randomised, adaptive-enrichment, open-label, blinded-endpoint multicentre study aims to evaluate whether intra‑arterial tenecteplase improves clinical outcomes for patients with acute ischemic stroke. Patients with large‑vessel occlusion eligible for EVT within 24 hours of symptom onset were randomly assigned (1:1) to the tenecteplase group receiving intra‑arterial tenecteplase during EVT or the control group receiving EVT alone. The primary endpoint was favorable functional outcome. Of 380 randomised patients (192 in the tenecteplase group and 188 in the control group), primary outcome data were available for 190 and 186 patients, respectively. Favorable 90-day functional outcomes (modified Rankin Scale 0–2) occurred in 40.0% of the tenecteplase group versus 46.8% of the control group (unadjusted odds ratio 0.76, [95% CI 0.50–1.14], P = 0.19). This work suggests intra-arterial tenecteplase during thrombectomy did not improve 90-day functional outcomes in this population. (Funded by National Science and Technology Major Project and hospital-initiated grants; ClinicalTrials.gov registration: NCT05657444) It is unclear whether adjunct intra-arterial Tenecteplase during thrombectomy improves clinical outcomes in patients with acute large vessel occlusion. Here, the authors show that adjunct intra-arterial tenecteplase during thrombectomy does not improve 90-day functional outcomes in this population.

papers.title: Continuous directed evolution using engineered human B cell lines
papers.abstract: The B cells of the human immune system have evolved somatic hypermutation (SHM) mechanisms that introduce mutations at the immunoglobulin genomic loci at a significantly higher frequency than the rest of the genome thereby allowing them to evolve antibody sequences without compromising fitness due to genome-wide mutations. Inspired by these observations, here we develop a continuous directed evolution platform in human B cell lines (CODE-HB) that repurposes the SHM mechanisms to a stable, non-immunoglobulin genomic locus of the human B cell lines to continuously evolve cytosolic and surface displayed proteins with a broad mutational spectrum comprising of substitutions, deletions and insertions. Using our human B cell surface display platform and CODE-HB, we evolve neutralizing antibodies targeting avian influenza and escape variants of influenza. Given the modularity and simplicity of CODE-HB, we anticipate that this platform can be used for rapidly evolving biotechnologically relevant biomolecules directly in human cells. This study describes the development of a continuous directed evolution platform in human B cell lines (CODE-HB) that repurposes the somatic hypermutation (SHM) mechanisms to evolve cytoplasmic reporter proteins as well as therapeutically relevant antibodies.

papers.title: Fe(III) hydrolysis-driven Fe(III)/Fe(IV) redox couple for iron sludge-free Fenton-like oxidation
papers.abstract: Conventional Fe(II/III) cyclically mediated Fenton processes exhibit strict acid pH-dependence and excessive iron sludge output due to sluggish Fe(III) reduction. Here, we leverage the intrinsic hydrolysis of Fe(III) to strategically modulate its hydroxyl coordination, achieving efficient contaminant degradation through peroxymonosulfate (PMS) activation. Theoretical and experimental results show that hydroxyl coordination accelerates electron transport from Fe(III) to PMS, lowering the energy barrier for simultaneously generating Fe(IV) and sulfate radical. Moreover, Fe(IV) further oxidizes contaminants with Fe(III) regeneration, promoting sustained and complete PMS decomposition via Fe(III/IV) redox couple. Based on this mechanism, a Fe(III)-cycled Fenton-like process operating under neutral conditions was developed for the effective treatment of actual wastewater without iron sludge output. Techno-economic analysis and life cycle assessment confirm its enhanced economic viability and environmental sustainability compared to the conventional Fenton process. This work provides an iron sludge-free and acid pH-independent Fenton-like oxidation strategy for water decontamination. This study reveals that Fe(III) hydrolysis can establish the Fe(III)/Fe(IV) redox couple to activate peroxymonosulfate under neutral conditions. This enables an iron sludge-free and acid pH-independent Fenton-like process for water decontamination.

papers.title: Addressing the 1000-h/1000-nit stability challenge in perovskite LEDs
papers.abstract: Perovskite light-emitting diodes (PeLEDs) offer exceptional colour purity and efficiency for next-generation display applications. Despite the recent advances in device stability, achieving long-term stable PeLEDs under display-relevant conditions remains a critical challenge. The actual device half-life (T50) experimentally measured for visible PeLEDs were in most cases limited to below 1000 h for any given brightness, in contrast to the much longer extrapolated lifetimes reported. Here, we demonstrate stable green PeLEDs with a T50 lifetime of 1350 h at an initial luminance of 1000 cd m−2 (nits), a maximum energy-conversion efficiency of 28.0%, and a peak external quantum efficiency of 24.5%. The exceptional performance is enabled by the insertion of a fluorinated self-assembled monolayer between the metal oxide and polymeric hole-transport layers. This molecular interlayer leads to Ohmic-like characteristics for charge injection, lowering the operating voltage at ~1000 nits to sub-bandgap levels (~2.1 V) where ion migration is suppressed. The accumulated photon output of our PeLEDs over the course of their T50 lifespan is found to sharply increase as the driving voltage drops to sub-bandgap values, highlighting the critical role of employing low-voltage device architectures in reaching the 1350-h/1000-nit stability milestone. Finally, a flexible active-matrix PeLED display prototype is developed, showing the potential of the devices for wearable optoelectronics. Perovskite light-emitting diodes offer vivid, efficient displays, but long-term stability at practical brightness remains difficult. Yuan et al. add a fluorinated molecular layer to lower voltage, extending device life and enabling a stable flexible perovskite display.

Decoherence resilience of the non-Hermitian skin effect
papers.abstract: Decoherence and dissipation, arising from interactions with the environment, can exert a dual influence on transport in physical systems, suppressing coherent propagation while inducing diffusion and mitigating localization in disordered systems. Non-Hermitian physics offers a distinct scenario, where structured dissipation induces directional bulk-to-boundary transport, known as the non-Hermitian skin effect. Whether such transport can persist, be enhanced, or hindered under decoherence remains a largely open question. Here we experimentally address this question using photonic quantum walks with two tunable prototypical decoherence channels, dephasing and amplitude damping. Under dephasing, the non-Hermitian skin effect survives up to the fully incoherent regime and is observed to even be enhanced by dephasing, yielding drift velocities that exceed those of coherent dynamics. By contrast, amplitude damping shows a pronounced order dependence: applied before the non-Hermitian loss operator, it suppresses and ultimately eliminates the non-Hermitian skin effect in the fully incoherent limit; applied afterward, the non-Hermitian skin effect persists and can be enhanced at sufficiently large loss strengths. Our work bridges quantum and classical non-Hermitian dynamics, demonstrates the resilience of the non-Hermitian skin effect to decoherence, and opens avenues for harnessing decoherence to enhance directional transport in noisy, nonequilibrium systems. Decoherence, often viewed as detrimental to coherent transport, can instead enhance the non-Hermitian skin effect, which persists into the fully incoherent regime. Its effect can be tuned by the type and implementation of decoherence.

Cas12a-based combinatorial knockout screens define the genetic architecture of the DNA damage response
papers.abstract: To elucidate the genetic architecture of the DNA damage response (DDR) network, we conduct unbiased genetic interaction screens using Cas12a. We disrupt 233 DDR genes frequently mutated in cancer and other genetic diseases, either individually or in pairwise combinations, enabling us to assess the phenotypic effects induced by the loss of DDR gene pairs under unperturbed cell growth conditions. We identify high-confidence positive and negative gene–gene interactions, along with connections between previously unlinked DDR pathways. Among the identified genetic interactions, we uncover synthetic lethal interactions between genes encoding the translesion polymerase REV1–Pol ζ complex and the MCM8–MCM9–HROB DNA helicase complex, between Fanconi anemia genes and various mitotic DNA repair genes, as well as between genes encoding the DNA translocase SMARCAL1 and components of the FANCM complex, suggesting opportunities for targeted treatments in tumors carrying mutations in these genes. Collectively, our genetic map of the DDR network identifies synthetic lethal and buffering interactions with therapeutic potential. A genetic interaction map of the DNA damage response (DDR) identifies functional relationships among DDR genes and pathways.

papers.title: A gait foundation model for prediction of multisystem health phenotypes from 3D skeletal motion
papers.abstract: Gait is increasingly recognized as a vital sign, yet current approaches treat it as a symptom of specific pathologies rather than a systemic biomarker. Here we developed a gait foundation model for three-dimensional skeletal motion, which was recorded via a single-depth camera during 5 motor tasks, from 3,328 deeply phenotyped adults. Our purpose was to capture the full pattern of a person’s movement and use it to predict health phenotypes such as grip strength and sleep quality across 18 body systems. Gait is conventionally described by engineered features (for example, calculated measurements such as cadence and stride length), which may fail to capture the fine detail of how a person moves. Our model instead translates movement into learned embeddings: sets of numbers that describe how all body joints move together over time. Learned embeddings outperformed engineered features for prediction of age (Pearsonʼs r = 0.69), body mass index (r = 0.91) and visceral adipose tissue area (r = 0.83), and embeddings significantly predicted 1,887 of 3,210 tested phenotypes. Relative to a baseline model using age, body mass index, visceral adipose tissue and height alone, gait embeddings improved prediction in all 18 systems in males and 17 of 18 in females, as well as prediction of clinical diagnoses and medication use. Anatomical ablation analyses revealed that leg dynamics dominated metabolic and frailty predictions, and torso dynamics encoded sleep and lifestyle phenotypes. These findings establish gait as an independent, multisystem biosignal, motivating integration of gait analysis into routine clinical assessment as a scalable, passive vital sign. A gait foundation model, developed using three-dimensional skeletal motion data from 3,328 adults, predicts a wide array of clinical characteristics and diagnoses, including cardiometabolic, mental health and frailty phenotypes.

papers.title: Efficient and accurate mixed model association tool for single-cell eQTL analysis
papers.abstract: Genetic effects on gene expression often vary across cell types, motivating expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) mapping in single-cell RNA sequencing data. Existing approaches generally aggregate expression across cells, use Gaussian models poorly suited to read counts or do not scale. Here we show that SAIGE-QTL, a Poisson mixed model that directly models single-cell read counts, enables calibrated and computationally scalable eQTL mapping while accounting for donor-level and cell-level covariates and unequal numbers of cells per donor. In simulations and three single-cell datasets, SAIGE-QTL improved statistical efficiency and discovery of genes with significant eQTLs (eGenes) relative to pseudobulk methods and produced results consistent with existing single-cell models at substantially lower computational cost. In 1.2 million immune cells, SAIGE-QTL identified 48.8% more eGenes than pseudobulk analysis. SAIGE-QTL further enabled genome-wide trans-eQTL mapping and rare variant set-based testing, identifying rare variant associations independent of common eQTL signals. SAIGE-QTL therefore expands single-cell eQTL discovery across common, rare and trans-acting genetic variation. SAIGE-QTL is a framework for eQTL mapping that directly models single-cell read counts using a Poisson mixed model, achieving improved statistical efficiency and power and enabling rare variant set-based testing in the single-cell eQTL setting.

papers.title: Author Correction: The formation of migrasomes is initiated by the assembly of sphingomyelin synthase 2 foci at the leading edge of migrating cells
Membrane flexibility matters
Oligomeric plasticity in ion channels as an unexplored structure–function mechanism
Autoantibodies tip the balance towards preterm birth
From tissue adaptation to disease-associated eosinophil states
papers.abstract: Eosinophils are highly adaptable immune cells whose phenotype and function are shaped by developmental, spatial, temporal, and inflammatory cues. Beyond their classical roles in type 2 immunity, eosinophils participate in chronic inflammation, fibrosis, metabolic disease, infection, and cancer. Here, we review how disease-associated eosinophil states emerge through perturbation of four interconnected determinants: eosinophil development, local tissue environment, tissue residency time, and inflammatory context. We discuss how disease can alter eosinophil development before tissue entry and reshape eosinophil adaptation within tissues, and how these processes may influence therapeutic responses. Together, these observations provide a framework for understanding disease-associated eosinophil diversity and for considering therapeutic strategies that preserve beneficial tissue-associated functions.

papers.title: Editing dual-function susceptibility genes for multistress-resilient crops
papers.abstract: Climate change increasingly exposes crops to simultaneous abiotic stresses, including drought, salinity, and heat, alongside disease, yet crop improvement often treats these threats as separate objectives. We argue that suitable susceptibility (S) genes should be considered as potential dual-function targets in crop biotechnology and breeding. Inactivating S genes can improve disease resistance and abiotic stress tolerance; we term genes with experimental support for both benefits as dual-function S genes. We propose to prioritise these genes and their orthologs in many crops and to screen candidates in both directions by testing S genes for abiotic stress benefits and testing negative abiotic stress regulators for disease resistance. With CRISPR technologies and regulatory frameworks maturing, such editing could support the development of climate-ready crops.

papers.title: PREMISE: A Quality-Aware Probabilistic Framework for High-Resolution Source Assignment in Metagenomic Sequencing
papers.abstract: Metagenomic applications, from influenza A virus (IAV) subtype tracking to bacterial strain resolution, frequently require sub-species resolution.However, traditional $k$-mer-based methods fragment reads into short $k$-mers and discard per-base quality scores.By omitting both intra-read linkage and error information, these methods confound closely related genomic variants, thereby impeding real-time pathogen surveillance and containment.We introduce \premise (Pathogen Resolution via Expectation-Maximization In Sequencing Experiments), a probabilistic, alignment-based framework implemented in Rust for high-resolution source assignment against near-complete reference databases.\premise aligns whole reads using a bidirectional run-length FM-index and quantifies reference abundances with a quality-aware Expectation-Maximization algorithm mapped over a taxonomy.This framework applies an optional sparsity penalty to resolve ambiguous assignments, which is particularly important when sparse samples are mapped against reference databases rich in highly homologous candidate references.On ten dense CAMI II strain-madness samples, \premise achieves the highest species-level read classification F1 score ($0.992$) among eight evaluated methods, with no false-positive or missed species.At the strain level, \premise maps reads to their source genome with top precision ($0.80$ vs. at most $0.64$ for competing methods), achieves 100\% recall, and estimates abundances as accurately as the best competing tool.These results demonstrate \premise's ability to provide rigorous, uncertainty-aware source resolution across both dense and sparse metagenomes, accurately resolving targets ranging from viral subtypes to bacterial strains.\\textbf{Availability:} \url{https://github.com/sriram98v/premise} under an MIT license.\\textbf{Contact:} \href{sriramv@iastate.edu}{sriramv@iastate.edu}\\
