papers.title: Mathematical model of phenotypic plasticity predicts interconversion is a drug target for neuroblastoma.
papers.abstract: Neuroblastoma is a paediatric cancer arising from the sympathetic nervous system as neural crest cells, made up of noradrenergic (NOR/ADRN/N), mesenchymal like (MES/S), and intermediate (I-type/I) cell types. These cells can interconvert between types, contributing to treatment resistance and relapse. We developed a mathematical model to investigate how interconversion patterns affect the efficacy of phenotype-specific inhibitors. We used three ordinary differential equations to describe the dynamics of the three populations, including logistic growth, interconversion, and drug-induced death. Of the 64 possible interconversion patterns, five reduced the target population: two for N cells and three for S cells. N targeting patterns were more effective with higher interconversion rates, while mesenchymal targeting patterns were more effective with lower interconversion rates. Stability analysis revealed that natural tumour growth was always unstable, but during treatment, N-suppressing patterns combined with an S inhibitor gave the most consistently stable origin. Testing multi-stage and cyclic treatment schedules revealed that N-suppressing patterns with an S inhibitor, followed by an S-suppressing pattern with an N inhibitor, achieved more reliable remission. Three of the five patterns of interest correspond to reported biological plausibility, and known compounds exist to induce most of the required transitions, supporting the clinical relevance of these strategies for improving neuroblastoma treatment outcomes.
affiliations: University of Hull (corresponding author)

papers.title: A three-factor model can explain symmetry breaking and the n-1 rule during X-chromosome inactivation
papers.abstract: X-chromosome inactivation (XCI) is a mammalian gene regulatory process that via chromosome-scale transcriptional silencing, leaves active a single X chromosome per diploid genome complement. The mechanisms that enable cells to select the appropriate number of X chromosomes to inactivate while leaving others active remain unclear. We demonstrate that all known chromosomal counting scenarios during XCI can be accounted for by a three-factor mathematical model that includes (1) Xist, the long noncoding RNA (lncRNA) responsible for gene silencing during XCI in eutherians, (2) an X-linked transcriptional activator of Xist, and (3) the autosomally-encoded SPEN, an Xist RNA-binding protein that is essential for gene silencing during XCI. In our model, symmetry between active X chromosomes is broken by stochastic differences in the number of Xist molecules that associate with the X chromosomes at the onset of XCI. Subsequently, integrated positive and negative feedback loops amplify then propagate superstoichiometric assemblies of SPEN complexed with Xist on the inactive chromosome(s), and select for levels of X-linked activator that enable only one X chromosome per diploid genome complement to remain active. Thus, asymmetric propagation of the SPEN-Xist ribonucleoprotein complex may play an essential role in symmetry breaking and chromosomal counting during XCI, independently of or in concert with cis-acting networks of DNA regulatory elements. Our results also have conceptual implications for gene regulatory circuits on autosomes.
affiliations: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (corresponding author)

papers.title: γδ T cell-derived IL-17A aggravates experimental epidermolysis bullosa acquisita in response to IL-1β
papers.abstract: Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (EBA) is a mucocutaneous autoimmune blistering disorder mediated by autoantibodies against type VII collagen and subsequent splitting of the dermal-epidermal junction. Interleukin (IL)-17A promotes the production of chemokines and cytokines involved in neutrophil recruitment and activation, suggesting that IL-17A may contribute to EBA pathogenesis. We aimed to clarify the role of IL-17A in experimental EBA. Using an antibody transfer-induced EBA mouse model, we demonstrate that IL-17A promotes disease development, as pharmacological blockade of IL-17A with a neutralizing antibody ameliorated skin lesions. Gamma-delta ({gamma}{delta}) T cells were identified as the predominant cellular source of IL-17A, supported by the attenuated disease phenotype observed in {gamma}{delta}TCR-deficient mice. In addition, CD4+ T cells and neutrophils contributed to IL-17A production in experimental EBA. Mechanistically, IL-1-beta, rather than IL-23, was identified as a critical mediator of IL-17A production by {gamma}{delta} T cells in vitro, consistent with our in vivo findings. Whereas EBA severity was not reduced in IL-23p19-deficient mice, disease was markedly attenuated in IL-1R-deficient animals. Together, our study provides the first evidence that {gamma}{delta} T cell-derived IL-17A plays a pivotal role in experimental EBA and identifies a previously unrecognized IL-1{beta}/{gamma}{delta} T cell/IL-17A axis that expands current understanding of EBA immunopathogenesis.

papers.title: Cell-scale confinement reorders bacterial speed rankings
papers.abstract: Which bacterium swims fastest depends on where the race is run. Speeds are usually measured in open liquid, yet many bacteria live in pores, mucus and host passages no wider than a cell. Using a microfluidic device with eight channel widths (0.80-3.00 m) in one field of view, we tracked unlabeled cells of eight species spanning five motility systems. Chamber height, a polymer additive and channel width each reordered the ranking. Vibrio alginolyticus, the fastest in open liquid, slowed to ~4 m/s in 1.25-m channels, whereas Campylobacter jejuni and Bacillus subtilis kept 33-46 m/s. Open liquid speed did not predict robustness to confinement. In two unrelated lineages, host symbionts that pass through narrow passages during colonization, Caballeronia insecticola and Vibrio fischeri, outran their non-symbiotic relatives in the channels, and crossed them with flagella wrapped around the cell body at nearly the speed of unwrapped cells. Where space is tight, the ability to keep moving, not top speed, sets the ranking.

papers.title: Dual regulation of chemical stress-induced DDI2/3 expression by a transcription factor Fzf1 and nucleosome in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
papers.abstract: DDI2 and DDI3 (DDI2/3) are duplicated genes in Saccharomyces cerevisiae that exhibit strong induction by a transcription factor Fzf1 in response to chemical treatments like cyanamide (CY) and methyl methanesulfonate (MMS). Although, like DDI2/3, SSU1, YHB1 and YNR064C also contain an Fzf1-binding consensus sequence CS2 and are coordinately regulated by Fzf1, these genes are only modestly induced by CY and MMS. To identify additional cis-acting elements in the DDI2/3 promoter, we made DDI2/3 promoter deletions in a reporter system and identified upstream repressing sequences (URS) spanning 480 nucleotides. To test a hypothesis that the chromatin structure constitutes the URS, we utilized a yeast strain capable of histone H3/H4 depletion by shifting carbon sources. Following histone depletion, DDI2/3 were strongly induced in an Fzf1 dependent manner, while YHB1 was repressed. Interestingly, under histone depletion conditions, CY or MMS treatment further increased expression of all Fzf1-regulated genes to comparable levels in an Fzf1 dependent manner. A genome-wide MNase-seq analysis showed that CY treatment reduced the nucleosome occupancy at the mapped DDI2/3 URS region in wild-type cells, but not in in fzf1{Delta} cells. These findings collectively indicate that Fzf1 plays dual roles in regulating the DDI2/3 response to CY. Firstly, it binds CS2 and serves as a transcription activator. Secondly, it is required for the chromatin remodeling at URS. This two-tier regulation at the DDI2/3 promoter helps to explain why DDI2/3 achieve much higher fold induction by CY and MMS than other Fzf1-regulated genes, suggesting Fzf1 to be a candidate pioneer transcription factor.

papers.title: ER stress-associated IRE1α signalling links impaired QPRT-dependent NAD⁺ biosynthesis to reduced oocyte competence
papers.abstract: Oocyte quality is closely linked to metabolic and organelle homeostasis, but the mechanisms underlying naturally occurring differences in oocyte quality remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify a link between endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, impaired NAD biosynthesis and poor oocyte quality. Poor-grade goat oocytes exhibited profound NAD depletion, accompanied by quinolinic acid accumulation and reduced expression of quinolinate phosphoribosyltransferase (QPRT), suggesting a bottleneck in de novo NAD biosynthesis. Restoring QPRT expression or bypassing this metabolic step improved meiotic maturation. Further analyses revealed altered ER stress signalling, increased IRE1-associated activity and reduced QPRT RNA stability. Recombinant IRE1 processed QPRT RNA in vitro, suggesting a possible link between IRE1 activity and QPRT transcript regulation. Supplementation with nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) restored NAD levels and improved several features of poor-quality oocytes, including calcium homeostasis, oxidative stress and mitochondrial membrane potential. NMN treatment also improved early embryonic development, with its beneficial effects involving SIRT6 activity and changes in DNA methylation-associated fluorescence. Importantly, NMN supplementation improved meiotic maturation in poor-grade bovine and porcine oocytes, indicating that this metabolic intervention may have broader relevance across mammals. Analysis of published human oocyte proteomic data further revealed age-associated changes in ER proteostasis and NAD-related proteins. Together, our findings identify ER stress-associated disruption of QPRT-dependent NAD biosynthesis as a potential contributor to poor oocyte quality and suggest that restoring NAD metabolism may offer a strategy to improve the functional properties of compromised oocytes.
affiliations: National Institute of Animal Biotechnology (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Dynamic Stem Cell State Links Environmental Cues to Skeletal and Regenerative Fates
papers.abstract: Stem cells faithfully generate tissue architecture during development, yet how their identity and regenerative output are reshaped as anatomical niches mature and environmental signals change with aging and injury remains poorly understood. Rare skeletal stem cells (SSCs) across diverse skeletal sites are defined by combinations of cell-surface markers, precluding their genetic interrogation in vivo. Here, using spatially informed single cell transcriptomics, we identify Pannexin-3 (Panx3) to mark a dynamic functional state within bona fide SSCs and establish Panx3-CreERT2 mice for its longitudinal interrogation. Panx3 SSCs exhibit long-term clonal persistence, self-renewal and multipotency, whereas Panx3- SSCs can acquire this state. Successive SSC cohorts engage the Panx3 state during skeletal development, osteoanabolic stimulation expands pre-existing Panx3 SSC clones and injury induces it locally in previously unlabeled progenitors. Thus, anatomically distinct progenitors can converge on a common stem cell state in response to different environmental inputs. Three-dimensional reconstruction of chondrogenic niches further identifies signals that redirect Panx3-lineage cells towards stable cartilage, enabling durable regeneration in aged and osteoarthritic joints and with human SSCs. These findings establish anatomical origin, stem cell state and lineage fate as separable dimensions of stem cell identity and provide genetic access for interrogating and directing endogenous SSC function.
affiliations: UC Davis (corresponding author)

papers.title: Proteome-wide profiling reveals compartment-specific RNA buffering of protein aggregation during stress
papers.abstract: Cellular adaptation to stress requires extensive remodeling of RNA metabolism. The rewiring of the RNA-protein interaction landscape and the assembly of biomolecular condensates are central to this response, yet the global stress-induced reorganization of macromolecular RNA-protein assemblies remains incompletely characterized. Here, we apply R-DeeP, a density gradient approach coupled to quantitative mass spectrometry, to profile the RNA-dependent sedimentation behaviour of the Saccha-romyces cerevisiae proteome during heat and salt stress. We demonstrate that stress triggers a profound, stress-specific reorganization of the RNA interactome. Many proteins undergo pronounced, selective shifts into high-molecular weight fractions, indicative of aggregation. RNase treatment markedly exacerbates this aggregation, consistent with the model that RNA acts as a general chaperone that keeps proteins with intrinsically disordered regions soluble. Strikingly, our data demonstrate that this protection is compartmentalised. Nuclear proteins are partially shielded from stress-induced aggregation. This protection coincides with the nuclear accumulation of RNA caused by a block of RNA export during stress, and RNase treatment abolishes this protection. Nuclear RNA retention may therefore act as a buffer that actively increases the local chaperoning capacity of the nucleus. In contrast, cytoplasmic proteins, including translation factors and ribonucleoprotein granule components, exhibit increased aggregation under stress. Fluorescence microscopy confirmed that increased biochemical aggregation in density gradients reflects changes in assembly state in vivo. For many stress-induced aggregators, these changes are visible as spatial reorganisation in stressed cells, such as the formation of foci. Our findings suggest that cells use subcellular RNA distribution to tune the condensation and/or aggregation threshold of proteins in a compartment-specific manner.

papers.title: Mutually Repressive Transcription Factors Drive Intestinal Maturation for Weaning
papers.abstract: In mammals, rapid neonatal growth depends on specialized intestinal enterocytes that absorb nutrients from milk. These cells exhibit distinct functions, morphologies, and gene expression programs that support neonatal nutrition before transitioning to an adult state at weaning. However, the transcriptional mechanisms that establish neonatal enterocyte identity and coordinate their maturation remain poorly understood. Here we show that the transcription factors BLIMP1 and CASZ1 form a central switch in the timing of enterocyte maturation. While BLIMP1 marks and promotes neonatal enterocytes, CASZ1 is expressed in adult enterocytes and is required for the proper timing of their emergence. Genetic analysis indicates that these neonatal and adult factors are mutually repressive, forming a genetic switch underlying weaning. This regulatory mechanism also controls glucocorticoid-induced maturation, a process relevant to both normal weaning and the clinical use of corticosteroids to promote epithelial maturation in preterm infants. We show that corticosteroids act directly on the intestinal epithelium and require CASZ1 to induce maturation. Together, these findings reveal a transcriptional mechanism that coordinates intestinal epithelial identity with the changing nutritional demands of early life and mediates the response to maturation-promoting hormones.
affiliations: Duke University Medical Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Measuring satellite arrays of the human Y chromosome from sequencing reads
papers.abstract: Human Y chromosome satellites vary widely but remain difficult to measure in large cohorts. In response, we developed Yruler, which uses pangenome assemblies to measure satellite lengths, composition and Y dosage from sequencing reads without alignment. Analyses reveal centromere-length differences between related lineages, extend observations of short non-centromeric arrays across a lineage, and show unequal component variability and composition changes with heterochromatin length within lineages. Yruler brings satellite variation into population-scale phenotype studies.
affiliations: Translational Genomics Research Institute (corresponding author)

papers.title: Epigenome-informed Polymer Modeling Reveals Chromosome Folding Landscapes across Distinct Genetic and Epigenetic Contexts
papers.abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) genome organization is critical for gene regulation, enabling long-range interactions between genes and distal regulatory elements. Genomic structural variations and epigenetic differences can perturb this organization, contributing to phenotypic variation and tissue-specific gene regulation. Prior studies have assessed the impact of these genetic and epigenetic changes on 3D genome folding, primarily using population-averaged features such as topologically associating domains and loops. However, growing evidence from single-cell and live-imaging studies indicates that chromosomes are highly dynamic and exist as heterogeneous ensembles of conformations. Here, we applied an epigenetic-state-informed polymer modeling framework to generate chromosomal conformational ensembles directly from cell- and tissue-specific epigenomic data. The resulting ensembles reproduced experimental Hi-C maps across cell lines and tissue types. Comparison of these conformational ensembles revealed that, although polymer dynamics were conserved across cell lines, their folding landscapes diverged. These differences arose primarily from cell-line-specific chromatin-state interaction networks and were concentrated in rare, long-lived contacts. Furthermore, modeling a TAD-boundary-disrupting deletion without re-optimizing the model parameters indicated a shift in the chromatin conformational ensemble from predominantly insulated to predominantly fused states. The modeled deletion also selectively strengthened active chromatin contacts and differentially disrupted enhancer contacts involving neighboring genes. Finally, comparison of two tissue types from the same donor revealed epigenetically driven rewiring of chromatin-state interaction networks. These findings establish chromosomal conformational ensembles as a sensitive readout of genome reorganization across distinct genetic and epigenetic contexts.
affiliations: University of Toronto (corresponding author)

papers.title: Sexing carnivores from faecal metagenomes: calibrating Rx for stone marten and red fox
papers.abstract: Knowing the sex of the animal that deposited a scat adds value to non-invasive monitoring, but read-ratio sexing methods were developed for human ancient DNA. We examined their use in shotgun metagenomes of seven stone marten (Martes foina) and red fox (Vulpes vulpes) scats. Human DNA, present in every library, was removed by competitive mapping against the host assembly and the human reference. Applying the Skoglund Ry metric to the marten samples yielded 0 to 25 Y-mapping reads per sample and failed to identify either of the two animals that Rx places firmly in the male range, so we adopted the X-to-autosome ratio Rx of Mittnik et al. instead, reimplemented as an open-source, species-agnostic Python tool. To test whether its human-derived thresholds transfer, we simulated female and male genomes of both species and drew 200 replicate subsamples at each of fourteen depths from 1,000 to 100,000 mapped reads. Nine of 11,200 replicates were assigned to the wrong sex, all of them below 2,000 mapped reads; above that depth the only failure was non-assignment, in under 5% of replicates above 7,500 reads and under 1% above 15,000. Applied to the scats, Rx identified four females and two males; one sample with 596 host-assigned reads was left unassigned. With competitive removal of human reads, Rx and its original thresholds are usable in these carnivores.

papers.title: A Minimal Synthetic Cleavage Module Enables Selective Degradation of Pathogenic r(CUG) Repeats in Cells
papers.abstract: Although direct RNA degradation offers an alternative to occupancy-driven activity, it has relied on complex natural product-derived cleavage modules such as bleomycin. Here, we show that a compact synthetic Fe(II)-coordinating warhead can be programmed for selective RNA degradation in cells. Coupling this cleavage module to a small molecule that recognizes expanded r(CUG) repeats that cause myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) afforded selective degradation of the pathogenic RNA while sparing wild type and transcripts harboring short r(CUG) repeats. In DM1 patient-derived myoblasts, degradation of mutant repeat RNA reduced DM1-associated pathology including formation of nuclear foci, sequestration of MBNL1, and alternative pre-mRNA splicing defects, without inducing DNA damage. These studies establish that minimal synthetic cleavage modules can replace complex natural product warheads to enable selective degradation of disease-causing RNAs in cells.
affiliations: Scripps Florida (corresponding author)

papers.title: The structures of two intermediates en route to DNA repair within a (6-4) photolyase
papers.abstract: Pyrimidine (6-4) pyrimidone photoproducts (6-4PPs) are mutagenic DNA lesions produced when UV light crosslinks two adjacent pyrimidine bases. These lesions must be repaired to maintain genome integrity, a function executed by the (6-4) photolyase enzymes. This repair chemistry is complex, involving the transfer of a hydroxyl group from one base to another, accompanied or followed by cleavage of an interbase bond. It remains unclear how the enzyme orchestrates this reaction. Typically, models invoke a stepwise process in which an oxetane intermediate is transiently populated, but despite over thirty years of investigation, such an intermediate has never been definitively observed. Conducting dose-controlled X-ray crystallography on the (6-4) photolyase from Vibrio cholerae, we observed the transformation of 6-4PP into an oxetane species. Furthermore, we identified a previously unanticipated hemi-cleaved intermediate. The progressive transformation of 6-4PP into oxetane, hemi-cleaved, and fully repaired species requires a reexamination of the existing models of DNA repair by (6-4) photolyases.
affiliations: Deutsches Elektronen Synchrotron (corresponding author)

papers.title: RNA-targeted aminopyridine compounds provide a new antifungal strategy
papers.abstract: While RNA is an emerging therapeutic target class, progress is limited by a shortage of well-defined targets in which ligand binding is coupled to measurable function. The group I intron, a self-splicing ribozyme essential in fungal mitochondria but absent from humans, offers both a tractable platform for exploring first principles of small molecule-RNA targeting and a selective antifungal target. We recalibrated an intron-splicing assay to approximate cellular conditions and performed an extensive, cryo-EM-guided structure-activity relationship campaign against the Candida albicans mtLSU intron. Ligands containing a flexible diamine outperformed conformationally constrained analogues, suggesting a general principle for engaging dynamic RNA surfaces and yielding lead aminopyridine 56 (IC 21.6 nM). Compound 56 synergizes with amphotericin B against C. albicans, suggesting a path for combination therapies. RT-qPCR confirmed direct target engagement in cells. This work establishes the fungal group I intron as a viable, mechanistically distinct antifungal target and a model platform for RNA-targeted discovery.
affiliations: Yale University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Active site electrostatic effects modulate DBO inhibitor potency against OXA-48 variants
papers.abstract: The OXA-48 class D {beta}-lactamase and its variants are clinically concerning through their carbapenemase and cephalosporinase activity. Effective inhibitors are therefore urgently needed. Diazabicyclooctanes (DBOs) are newly introduced non {beta}-lactam based inhibitors, but their potency is affected by mutations, with the more recently developed nacubactam consistently less potent than avibactam, the first DBO, towards OXA-48 variants. This difference is most pronounced for OXA-48 compared to its variants OXA-163 and -405, which contain mutations in the {beta}5-{beta}6 loop and preferentially hydrolyse cephalosporins over carbapenems. Here we use multiscale simulations to uncover the origin of these differences after determining that the second step of DBO acylation is rate-limiting. Using QM/MM MD simulations we show that nacubactam exhibits a consistently higher energy barrier than avibactam for covalent inhibition of OXA-48-like enzymes, a difference attributable to DBO-specific changes in the active site electric field. Simulations of non-covalent complexes further indicate that weaker binding, due to electrostatic repulsion between the positively charged nacubactam tail and Arg214 in the {beta}5-{beta}6 loop, partially explains the lower potency of nacubactam towards OXA-48, compared to OXA-163 and -405. Combining computational predictions of covalent reaction rates and non-covalent binding affinities accurately reproduces the relative order of experimental IC50 values, and predicts potency towards OXA-517, a recently discovered OXA-48 variant capable of hydrolysing many antibiotics. This work provides mechanistic insight into the inhibition of class D {beta}-lactamases and reveals the origins of differential DBO potency towards OXA-48 variants, highlighting how subtle differences between enzymes modulate inhibitory effects.
affiliations: University of Bristol (corresponding author)

papers.title: Endothelial protein C receptor is an entry receptor for Langya virus
papers.abstract: Langya virus (LayV) was recently discovered in infected individuals with febrile illness and classified as a Parahenipavirus, a group of poorly understood pathogens. LayV is distantly related to Nipah henipavirus which causes recurring outbreaks with case fatality rates reaching up to 90%. No vaccines or therapeutics are approved for use in humans for any parahenipavirus or henipavirus despite their broad geographic distribution and pandemic potential. Here, we discovered that human endothelial protein C receptor (EPCR) is an entry receptor for LayV and that the tetrameric LayV attachment glycoprotein (G) binds EPCR avidly. We reveal the molecular basis of LayV G recognition of the EPCR receptor and provide a blueprint of the determinants of receptor ortholog usage. We found that human and shrew EPCR orthologs promote cell entry of LayV and of the closely related Mojiang pseudoviruses. These results along with the detection of several Parahenipaviruses in shrews set these pathogens apart from Henipaviruses, which use Pteropid fruit bats as reservoir hosts. Our data support future surveillance efforts, by enabling prediction of EPCR utilization among newly discovered Parahenipaviruses, and the development and evaluation of countermeasures targeting this emerging group of human pathogens.
affiliations: University of Washington (corresponding author)

papers.title: MitoDecode: quantitative phenotypic decoding of mitochondrial stress states from fluorescence images
papers.abstract: The quantitative measurement of mitochondrial stress from fluorescence images of cells remains a challenging task. Existing methods rely on mitochondrial segmentation, manually predefined features, and discrete phenotype severity classes, which are prone to error and bias. Here, we present MitoDecode, a deep learning network that automatically assesses type and severity of mitochondrial stress from fluorescence microscopy images. MitoDecode eliminates the need for mitochondrial segmentation, is parameter-free, and operates across both diffraction-limited and super-resolution optical imaging modalities. It assigns a phenotypic probability profile for each individual cell, indicating both type and severity of phenotypic stress. The readout thus enables comparisons between different stressors and provides clues for underlying mechanisms. Furthermore, the method captures phenotypic shifts continuously across treatment doses, revealing subtle variations that would otherwise be missed. We demonstrate MitoDecode's adaptability across diverse cell types, imaging modalities, and stress conditions, and show that it can reliably detect mitochondrial phenotypes, even when stressors target non-mitochondrial pathways. We validate the reliability of the model with biochemical assays, showcase its utility for phenotypic stress profiling of drug treatments, and envisage its application for early-stage disease detection, drug discovery, and mechanistic lead generation.
affiliations: University of Cambridge (corresponding author)

papers.title: Extensional Flow Microfluidics Reveal Size-Dependent Core-Shell Mechanical Heterogeneity in Pancreatic Tumor Spheroids
papers.abstract: Understanding the mechanical behavior of cancer cell aggregates is important for investigating metastatic potential and developing effective therapeutics. Tumor cell clusters are major contributors to metastasis and can undergo extreme deformation to migrate through capillaries smaller than the cluster size, suggesting complex multicellular mechanics. Despite their clinical significance, the mechanics of multicellular spheroids remain underexplored. In this study, the mechanical behavior of spheroids formed from the pancreatic cancer cell line PANC-1 was investigated using a cross-slot microfluidic device. Suspended spheroids from two size ranges were stretched in non-contact extensional flow (small spheroids mostly 40 < D0 < 75 m, large spheroids mostly 90 < D0 < 145 m). Digital image correlation analyses of intra-spheroid strains revealed strong deformation differences for small and large spheroids while analyses based on 2D projected contours of the spheroid shape did not show trends. Smaller spheroids deformed relatively homogeneously and exhibited significant overall stretching. In contrast, larger spheroids displayed heterogeneous deformation characterized by a stiff central core and a deformable outer shell. To investigate the origin of these mechanical differences, cellular morphology and the expression of stiffness-associated proteins, including vimentin and E-cadherin, were assessed from confocal microscopy. Larger spheroids display significantly lower nuclear sphericity than small spheroids, indicating more cellular packing with increasing spheroid size. Additionally, vimentin expression was concentrated in the outer shell of large spheroids, whereas small spheroids exhibit vimentin expression throughout the aggregate. Thus individual cell morphology and cytoskeletal networks seemed to contribute to the core-shell biomechanical behavior of the large spheroids and lack thereof for small spheroids. Taken together, this study suggests that as spheroids grow, they transition from an irregular and disorganized cluster at low cell numbers to a coordinated and hierarchical structure at sufficient cell numbers that corresponds to diameters {gtrsim} 100 m.
affiliations: University of Massachusetts Boston (corresponding author)

papers.title: Preserving Nanotherapy-Induced Allogeneic Murine Islet Graft Tolerance During Distal Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus Skin Infection
papers.abstract: Eliminating lifelong immunosuppression can make islet transplantation a durable alternative to insulin therapy for type 1 diabetes. As short-course tolerogenic regimens are developed to replace lifelong immunosuppression, it is critical to test their robustness against perturbations such as hospital-acquired infections, which transplant recipients routinely encounter. Herein, we investigated whether rapamycin-loaded polymersomes (rPS), a subcutaneous nanotherapy that induces long-term murine islet allograft survival, can preserve host defenses in a Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) skin infection, and whether the resulting immune response from this distal infection relative to graft location erodes rPS-induced tolerance. rPS maintained neutrophil antibacterial activity despite inhibiting oxidative mechanisms in vitro, and rPS-treated mice demonstrated normal recovery following MRSA challenge. However, MRSA skin infection caused a decline of ~43% in recipient survival for rPS-treated mice, despite surviving recipients retaining glucose-stimulated insulin responsiveness. This erosion of allograft acceptance coincided with a burst of IL-6 within 24h of the infection followed by elevated TNF-[a] and neutrophilia at 13 days post-infection. Combining rPS with a single dose of methylprednisolone reduced IL-6 and TNF- without altering neutrophilia, nearly doubling survival among infected recipients to 80%. Our findings demonstrate that partial dampening of inflammatory insults can restore superior islet allograft acceptance following perioperative infection.
affiliations: Northwestern University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Learning Strand-Equivariant Tokenizations of DNA with MirrorDNA
papers.abstract: DNA has two strands, and for most regulatory label prediction tasks a sequence and its reverse complement should get same answer. Yet DNA language models are tokenized, trained and tested on one strand at a time. We show that this makes them inconsistent. BPE and $k$-mer tokenizers split 92--100\% of transcription-factor motifs differently on the two strands, and NT-v2, DNABERT-2 and HyenaDNA change 25-31\% of their predictions when the test sequences are reverse-complemented. We introduce {\model}, a compact DNA language model with a learned tokenizer that guarantees mirror-symmetric token boundaries across reverse-complement sequences, regardless of its learned parameters. We prove that this symmetry holds through the whole model. As a result, the same model can give identical answers on both strands when the label does not depend on the strand, and can still tell the strands apart when it does, which no strand-blind model can learn. Counting only predictions that are correct on both strands, \model\ more than doubles the MCC of NT-v2, DNABERT-2 and HyenaDNA. With 2.3M parameters, it is more accurate than the Caduceus models trained on the same data, and not significantly different from NT-v2 (98M parameters) on Genomic Benchmarks or from DNABERT-2 (117M) on the Nucleotide Transformer tasks. It also stays accurate on inputs sixteen times longer than those it was trained on. The same model trained with reverse-complement augmentation instead still changes about one prediction in ten with the strand, unless its outputs are averaged over both strands. Without any annotation, the tokenizer learns to keep the splice-donor signal \texttt{AGGT} in a single token. Code: https://github.com/NIRJHOR-DATTA/MirrorDNA.
affiliations: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology, Dhaka, Bangladesh (corresponding author)

papers.title: Automahout: an autonomous image analysis system for cell tracking
papers.abstract: Cell tracking in time-lapse images is complex image analysis that involves detection, linking and proofreading, often requiring the algorithm to be tuned for every new dataset. We present Automahout, an autonomous agent for the Mastodon/ELEPHANT platform that carries out these operations. It looks at the data and tries existing models; where none fits, it annotates reference cells, trains a detector from those sparse annotations, reviews its output against them and feeds the corrections back until its own stopping criteria are met. It then links, checks the lineage and moves on. On three public datasets, a 2D fluorescence culture, a 2D phase-contrast culture and a 3D embryo, it produced lineages without human input and reached TRA scores of 0.95-0.96.
affiliations: Laboratory for Developmental Dynamics, RIKEN Center for Biosystems Dynamics Research (corresponding author)

papers.title: scDisentangle: sequential disentanglement for single-cell perturbation response prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting the transcriptional response of single cells to perturbation is a central goal of single-cell modeling, with broad application to analysis and experimental design. Existing methods often fail to beat simple baselines and offer little insight into how biological variation is organized. We present scDisentangle, a model that decomposes single-cell expression into observed attributes and a sequence of residual components, generating counterfactuals that preserve source cell identity. scDisentangle outperformed current models and naive baselines on cytokine stimulation, liver infection, and unseen combinatorial genetic perturbations, on which accuracy was largely independent of how closely a response resembled the average perturbation effect. In an immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated myocarditis cohort, cell-resolved counterfactuals predicted donor-specific intracardiac CD8+ T cell states from peripheral blood. In a castration-regeneration prostate atlas, predictions recapitulated luminal dynamics and progenitor-marker kinetics upon androgen add-back. scDisentangle's coarse-to-fine latent structure aligned with hematopoietic lineage organization, with early levels capturing a less differentiated core progressively refined into cell-type-specific programs.
affiliations: University Mohammed VI Polytechnic (corresponding author)

papers.title: RPFace: From biased structural benchmarks to generalizable RNA-protein interface prediction
papers.abstract: Modeling protein-RNA complexes with co-folding and docking methods is routine, yet these methods are evaluated on benchmarks whose composition mirrors the deposited structures on which they were trained or tuned, leaving open whether their reported performance reflects true generalization. Here, we focus the evaluation on the region that carries the biological signal: the binding interface. For the first time, we construct and release a fair benchmark that stratifies protein-RNA data into distinct structural and experimental groups, providing a more stringent test of generalization than aggregate averages. On this benchmark, we find that accuracy of detecting the binding site using co-folding methods is concentrated in ribosomal complexes and varies systematically with factors such as experimental modality. For docking methods, it is reliable only when the input conformations are already close to the bound state, and it is inconsistent across RNA classes. Both families of methods fail to transfer to in vivo CLIP experiments. To address this gap, we introduce RPFace, to the best of our knowledge the first model that jointly predicts the binding preference of every protein residue and every RNA nucleotide directly from sequence, requiring no experimental structure, template, or multiple sequence alignment. RPFace combines an ensemble of predicted secondary structures with a multi-modal embedding-enrichment scheme that fuses representations from RNA foundation models and structure prediction models. Unlike existing approaches, it is a very small and fast model that delivers stable performance across structural and experimental conditions, is robust to conformational change, and generalizes to in vivo datasets without extensive pretraining. As a result, RPFace matches the state-of-the-art methods on protein interfaces with no evolutionary information, and outperforms them on RNA interfaces, with the largest gains in zero-shot settings despite using only sequence information. The model, code, and data are available at Github.
affiliations: Bilkent University (corresponding author)

papers.title: LinearRaccess: linear-time approximation of RNA accessibility without base-pair span limits
papers.abstract: Motivation: RNA accessibility is the probability that every nucleotide in a contiguous interval is simultaneously unpaired; it is widely used to predict binding sites for RNA-binding proteins and other RNA-RNA interactions, often in the form of the opening energy, an equivalent measure on a logarithmic scale. Existing tools restrict the maximum base-pair span, discarding long-range base pairs that matter biologically. Others sample structures, introducing statistical variance, or compute accessibility exactly without a span limit, at cubic time cost. No existing method computes the accessibility of windows longer than one nucleotide deterministically in linear time while preserving long-range base pairs. We present LinearRaccess, which computes accessibility directly in linear time via beam-pruned inside-outside dynamic programming with a difference-array aggregation step, without restricting base-pair span. Results: For a sequence of length N and a fixed beam width b, LinearRaccess runs in O(N) time and O(Nb) memory. Against exact accessibility on 12,872 bpRNA-1m(90) sequences of 100-1,000 nt, its median opening-energy error is below 0.001 kcal/mol (0.14 kcal/mol for 700-1,000 nt), and it distinguishes windows of very small accessibility, including 35-nt windows, below the resolution of sampling-based estimates. LinearRaccess analyzes the full 29,903-nt SARS-CoV-2 genome in 419 seconds. Conclusion: LinearRaccess is the first method to compute the accessibility of windows longer than one nucleotide deterministically (without sampling) in linear time without restricting base-pair span. Availability: https://github.com/TakumiOtagaki/LinearRaccess, archived at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23598502).
affiliations: Institute of Science Tokyo (corresponding author)

papers.title: Quantitative live imaging reveals region-dependent medulloblastoma disseminationin the zebrafish brain
papers.abstract: Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant pediatric brain tumor, and relapse is frequently driven by dissemination within the central nervous system. Yet the early dynamics of tumor spread remain difficult to resolve in vivo. Here, we orthotopically transplanted human medulloblastoma cells into larval zebrafish and followed individual xenografts by longitudinal high-resolution confocal imaging. ONS-76 showed particularly robust dissemination, with hindbrain tumors spreading into the developing cerebellum in 81.5% of larvae, more than fourfold the frequency observed for forebrain or midbrain tumors. Disseminating cells extended along brain-surface and leptomeningeal-like regions and frequently associated with cerebral vasculature. Quantitative analysis of tumor area, perimeter, compactness, convex hull area, and fractal dimension captured changes in growth and spatial complexity over time. Dasatinib reduced tumor expansion and dissemination-related features in a concentration-dependent manner, while higher doses revealed host toxicity. These findings establish a powerful in vivo model for resolving medulloblastoma dissemination and therapeutic response.
affiliations: University of Zurich (corresponding author)

papers.title: Midlife nonlinearities across scale in Biondi body amyloid formation in the human choroid plexus
papers.abstract: Human choroid plexus epithelial cells (CPECs), which produce cerebrospinal fluid and form the blood-cerebrospinal fluid barrier, accumulate discrete intracellular amyloid inclusions called Biondi bodies (BBs). Using systematic manual and machine learning approaches on the choroid plexus glomus, we determined the percentages of CPECs containing thioflavin S-stained BBs as well as BB load and spatial distributions in whole slide images from 77 cases across the human lifespan. On average, BB prevalence was near zero until age 40, rose steeply in the 5th and 6th decades, and exceeded 50% after age 70. As prevalence plateaued, BB load continued to rise with age. Accelerated BB accumulation was seen in two cases of diabetic ketoacidosis, including a 16-year-old, while an 85-year-old with the relatively rare APOE2/E2 genotype had fewer BBs than expected. BB prevalence in the choroid plexus glomus was not associated with Alzheimer's disease, but was lower in females than males. Notably, spatial clustering of BBs was universal across cases while nearest-neighbor analyses suggested cell-to-cell, prion-like BB spread that can account for the nonlinearities seen at tissue and population scales. The abrupt, nonlinear BB accumulation during midlife coincides with or precedes other common aging-associated neuropathologies of the human brain, consistent with broad BB and choroid plexus contributions to brain aging and disease.
affiliations: Department of Pathology & Laboratory Medicine, University of California Irvine, Irvine, CA, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: stem.MAP: Identification of cell-type-specific protein complexes in mammalian embryonic stem cells.
papers.abstract: Protein complexes carry out critical functions during development. Mapping cell-type-specific protein complexes in early embryogenesis is essential for uncovering the molecular mechanisms of embryonic development. We unfortunately currently lack a catalog of protein complexes specific for embryogenesis including embryonic stem cells. Here we develop a proteomics-based machine learning workflow to predict protein complexes present in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESC). Our method integrates data from a cell-type agnostic protein complex resource with co-fractionation mass spectrometry (CF-MS) experiments on mESC. Our resource, stem.MAP, identifies 3,986 complexes encompassing ~133,000 unique interactions, and 8,616 proteins. stem.MAP captures variant complexes critical for stem cell function including the PRC2, BAF and NuRD complexes. stem.MAP also discriminates mutually exclusive interactions specific to embryonic stem cells (e.g. Eif4ebp2 - Eif4e). Finally we observe 1,388 high confidence stem.MAP interactions found only in mESC CF-MS data, many with support from AlphaFold modeling and a gastruloid coregulation network. We make stem.MAP protein complexes available through our web resource: stem.proteincomplexes.org. We anticipate stem.MAP will be beneficial to the study of early development and we expect our proteomics-based machine learning workflow to be applicable to the creation of any context-specific protein interaction network.
affiliations: University of Illinois at Chicago (corresponding author)

papers.title: A reporter mouse model to map RIG-I expression and function in vivo
papers.abstract: The cytosolic RNA sensor RIG-I is a critical component of the innate immune response to RNA viruses, yet few tools exist to track RIG-I in vivo. Herein, we report the development of a RIG-I reporter mouse, termed RIG-ImScar, that enables fluorescence imaging and tractable immunoprecipitation of RIG-I in vivo. These mice revealed enrichment of RIG-I expression in circulatory, lymphoid, and mucosal tissues and broad expression across immune cell types. RIG-I itself is upregulated in response to IFN. To distinguish RIG-I sentinel cells, which are programmed to express RIG-I at steady state, from IFN-responder cells, we crossed RIG-ImScar mice with Mx1GFP mice. Blocking IFNAR with a monoclonal antibody showed that basal RIG-I expression in immune cells was largely independent of type I IFN signaling, although Ly6Chi monocytes required IFNAR for RIG-I expression. To probe functional responses in vivo, we intranasally administered a RIG-I-specific agonist, SLR14. Mapping RIG-I expression across the lung identified alveolar macrophages as a critical RIG-I sensor cell population, and depletion of alveolar macrophages, but not neutrophils, slightly impaired lung IFN responses. Together, these findings support the use of the RIG-ImScar model to probe RIG-I dynamics in vivo and predict functional sensor cell populations across tissues.
affiliations: Yale University School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: The biochemical composition of coronavirus Nucleocapsid proteins drives the bicistronic properties of their sub-genomic mRNAs
papers.abstract: The nucleocapsid (N) gene of coronaviruses (CoVs) encodes a structural RNA-binding protein required for viral assembly. In SARS- and MERS-CoV viruses, reading frame 2 of N contains an overlapping open reading frame (ORF) encoding an innate immune antagonist accessory protein. However, the extent of this dual coding capacity across the CoV family, and the genetic features driving overlapping ORF formation, remain unexamined. Here, we developed an in-silico tool (ORFan) to screen structural gene sub-genomic mRNA sequences from 152 species of coronavirus for the presence of overlapping accessory gene candidates. We found that frame 2 of the N gene in Alpha-, Beta- and Delta-CoVs frequently contains a potential accessory ORF (AcORF), conserved at the subgenus level, unlike the spike, envelope and membrane genes. We also show that CoV nucleotide biases in conjunction with codon biases integral to N protein function drive the relatively high abundances of start codons in frame two and stop codons in frame three, explaining the tendency towards frame 2 AcORFs. We further suggest that viral nucleotide biases and the codon composition required for RNA-binding function facilitate overlapping ORF formation in other virus families
affiliations: University of Edinburgh (corresponding author)

papers.title: The mycotoxin zearalenone couples secondary metabolism to N-acetylglucosamine catabolism
papers.abstract: Fungal secondary metabolites are often viewed as terminal products of specialized metabolism, yet how their production influences the physiology of the producing organism remains poorly understood. Here, we show that zearalenone (ZEA) production is functionally coupled to N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) catabolism in Fusarium graminearum. Transcriptome profiling of a ZEB2-overexpressing strain revealed enrichment of GlcNAc metabolic functions, and exogenous ZEA induced key catabolic genes independently of Zeb2. Among pathway components, NAG, encoding GlcNAc-6-phosphate deacetylase, was critical for GlcNAc utilization, and its loss caused severe GlcNAc-dependent growth inhibition. Genetic impairment of NAG was poorly tolerated under elevated ZEA pathway activity. Conversely, NAG overexpression increased tolerance to exogenous ZEA and alleviated the growth defect associated with ZEB2 overexpression. Together, these findings reveal a functional connection between secondary metabolite production and primary nutrient metabolism and suggest that ZEA-associated metabolic remodeling contributes to the fitness of the producing fungus.
affiliations: Seoul National University (corresponding author)

papers.title: The long noncoding RNA FOSIL shapes the dynamics of FOS induction
papers.abstract: Immediate-early genes require rapid, transient, and precisely tuned transcriptional activation in response to extracellular signals, yet how this kinetic precision is achieved remains poorly understood. We characterize FOSIL (LINC01220), an inducible lncRNA locus downstream of FOS. Depleting FOSIL RNA delays heregulin (HRG)-induced FOS mRNA and protein accumulation and prolongs the response, indicating that FOSIL sharpens both the onset and the shutoff of the induction wave. Capture Micro-C maps show that FOSIL depletion weakens the chromatin boundary between FOS and FOSIL and increases local compaction across the pre-assembled FOS-FOSIL neighborhood during serum starvation, demonstrating that basal FOSIL production maintains a locally insulated, poised conformation prior to signal arrival. Upon HRG stimulation, FOSIL depletion blunts the rapid movement of the locus toward nuclear speckles, diminishes early speckle-proximal FOS transcription, and extends late firing at speckle-distant alleles. At single transcription active sites, nascent FOSIL activity correlates with closer speckle proximity and higher FOS output, and activating the endogenous FOSIL promoter by CRISPRa, but not supplying FOSIL RNA in trans, enhances both speckle association and FOS induction. Together, these findings support a mechanism where endogenous FOSIL activity coordinates pre-stimulus chromatin folding with dynamic nuclear speckle positioning to fine-tune the onset, amplitude, and resolution of immediate-early gene expression.
affiliations: Weizmann Institute of Science (corresponding author)

papers.title: PARP1-mediated PARylation of SPRTN restrains its DNA-protein crosslink repair activity
papers.abstract: SPRTN is a DNA-dependent metalloprotease that resolves DNA-protein crosslinks, but how its activity is restrained on chromatin remains unclear. Here we show that SPRTN is PARylated in a PARP1- and HPF1-dependent manner. Mass spectrometry datasets identify seven modified residues in the C-terminal region, and substituting them (SPRTN-PARless) strongly reduces PARylation. The Nudix homology domain is required for SPRTN to interact with PARP1 and for efficient PARylation. SPRTN-PARless accumulates faster and to higher levels at laser-induced DNA damage than wild-type SPRTN. PARylation reduces single-stranded DNA binding of both cell-derived and purified SPRTN, and PARG treatment reverses this effect for cell-derived protein. SPRTN-PARless shows increased autocleavage and accelerates clearance of camptotheci-induced TOP1 cleavage complexes. These findings suggest that PARylation acts as negative feedback on SPRTN after its PAR-dependent recruitment, restraining its DNA engagement and proteolytic activity.
affiliations: The University of Texas at Austin (corresponding author)

papers.title: RhoGEF Solo regulates cell density-dependent keratin remodeling and desmosome maturation
papers.abstract: Desmosomes (DSMs) are specialized cell-cell adhesion structures that anchor keratin intermediate filaments and play a crucial role in maintaining the mechanical integrity of epithelial tissues. Keratin filaments associate with DSMs in two characteristic patterns: radial spokes extending from DSMs into the cytoplasmic keratin network and circumferential rims connecting neighboring DSMs. Solo is a Rho-guanine nucleotide exchange factor (RhoGEF) involved in cellular responses to mechanical stress and keratin network reorganization. Here, we investigated the role of Solo in regulating keratin-DSM interactions in response to cell density. The number of radial keratin spokes at cell-cell adhesion sites was markedly reduced at high cell density, concomitant with increased Solo localization at these sites. Conversely, Solo knockout (KO) increased the number of radial keratin spokes. Expression of wild-type Solo, but not a GEF-inactive Solo mutant, rescued the increase in radial keratin spokes in confluent Solo-KO cells, indicating that Solo RhoGEF activity is required for this regulation. Inhibition of actin polymerization or ROCK activity also suppressed the reduction in radial spoke density. Furthermore, expansion microscopy and electron microscopy revealed that DSMs in Solo-KO cells remained small and immature even under confluent conditions. Solo was also partially required for the localization of plakoglobin (PG), a core DSM protein, whereas PG-KO markedly increased the number of radial keratin spokes. These findings suggest that increased cell density promotes DSM maturation accompanied by a reduction in radial keratin spokes, and Solo contributes to both processes, potentially through facilitating PG localization at DSMs and regulating Rho-ROCK-dependent actin cytoskeletal remodeling.
affiliations: Tohoku University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Endothelial Cell Specific Thioredoxin 1-Dependent Signaling in Oxygen-1 Induced Retinopathy
papers.abstract: Purpose: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is a leading cause of childhood blindness, characterized byoxidative stress and dysregulated angiogenesis in preterm infants with immature antioxidant systems.This study aimed to investigate the specific role of endothelial cell-specific thioredoxin 1 (TXN1), a crucial oxidoreductase, in oxygen-induced retinopathy, hypothesizing that the absence of endothelial TXN1 directly impairs angiogenesis and exacerbates hyperoxia-induced injury. Methods: We generated tamoxifen-inducible, endothelial cell-specific Txn1 knockout mice (Txn1-iECKO) and utilized the oxygen-induced retinopathy (OIR) model, exposing litters to 85% oxygen from postnatal day 7 (P7) to P12. Retinal vascular morphology during vaso-obliteration and neovascularization phases, endothelial cell proliferation, and apoptotic cell death were assessed. Furthermore, human retinal microvascular endothelial cells (HRMECs) with TXN1 knockdown were subjected to hyperoxic conditions, followed by comprehensive gene expression profiling using RT2 Profiler PCR arrays and Ingenuity Pathway Analysis. Results: Deletion of endothelial Txn1 significantly enhanced vascular regression during the hyperoxic vaso-obliteration phase at P12 and markedly exacerbated pathological neovascularization at P17. Txn1-deficient retinas exhibited significantly impaired endothelial cell proliferation during the vaso-obliteration phase, while apoptotic cell death remained unchanged. Transcriptomic analysis of TXN1-deficient HRMECs under hyperoxia revealed an enhanced activation of NRF2-mediated oxidative stress response pathways. Conclusions: These findings identify endothelial TXN1 as an essential and oxygen-dependent regulator of vascular development in ischemic retinopathy, primarily influencing endothelial proliferation and redox signaling. This suggests TXN1's crucial protective role and highlights its therapeutic potential to mitigate ROP progression by modulating endothelial cell responses to oxidative stress.
affiliations: University of Oklahoma Harold Hamm Health Campus (corresponding author)

papers.title: Prenatal THC exposure alters metabolic gene expression and KEAP1 regulation in the mouse placental labyrinth
papers.abstract: Introduction: Prenatal cannabinoid exposure may influence fetal development through changes in placental biology, yet its effects on metabolic gene regulation remain poorly understood. We examined the effects of {Delta}9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and cannabidiol (CBD) on the mouse placental labyrinth zone. Methods: Pregnant C57BL/6JRj mice received THC (5 mg/kg), CBD (5 mg/kg), or vehicle daily by intraperitoneal injection from gestational day 5 to 17.5. Targeted NanoString profiling and pathway analysis were combined with RT-qPCR and protein measurements. Results: THC exposure reduced glutaminase (Gls), Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (Keap1), and FMS-like tyrosine kinase 3 (Flt3) expression (false discovery rate = 0.0904 for each). Pathway analysis identified transcriptional changes in the nine-gene arginine-metabolism set (false discovery rate = 0.0527). No genes or pathways met the significance criteria following CBD exposure. RT-qPCR confirmed lower Keap1 expression with sexes pooled and identified lower Gls and Flt3 expression in male samples. KEAP1 protein abundance increased despite lower Keap1 mRNA, while nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 localization and heme oxygenase 1 (Hmox1) expression showed no significant differences. Discussion: These findings identify amino acid metabolic gene expression and KEAP1 regulation as complementary components of the placental response to prenatal THC exposure, connecting transcriptional changes with protein regulation within the placental exchange region.
affiliations: Translational Neuropsychiatry Unit, Department of Clinical Medicine, Aarhus University, Palle Juul-Jensens Boulevard 11, A601, 8200 Aarhus N, Denmark; Nanopsych (corresponding author)

papers.title: Functional Data Clustering of Filopodia Dynamics
authors: De Silva, S. H. D. S.
papers.abstract: Notch signaling plays a significant role in tissue patterning. During patterning of the fruit fly dorsal thorax peripheral nervous system, basal filopodia extend the spatial range of cell-cell communication, yet it is still unclear how Notch is activated in long range signaling via filopodia interaction. Filopodia undergo dynamic length changes during their lifetime, which could supply the mechanical pulling force required for notch activation. However, their dynamics are often characterized using individual scalar values such as maximum length and extension rate which could obscure more intricate dynamics. Our hypothesis is that signaling filopodia exhibit distinct and recurrent temporal patterns which can be identified by a consideration of their complete lifetime trajectories. Our work analyzes 60 filopodia trajectories at the basal surface of the fly dorsal thorax during patterning. Length profiles were smoothed using cubic B-splines and clustered by first reducing them to their dominant functional principal component followed by the application of various clustering algorithms. We found that 94.29% of the overall trajectory variation is explained by the first four functional principal components which account for variations in maximal length, extension and retraction rate, duration of stationary phase and length fluctuation frequency. Five recurrent temporal profiles (dynamic extension modes) with varying trajectory shapes and physical attributes, were identified using trimmed K-means. These findings demonstrate that whereas the major source of structural variation in filopodia profiles remains the length, extension rate and retraction rate, nontrivial combinations of these create distinct dynamic modes of extension which provide new insight into their length profiles. Our work thus offers a quantitative framework for future research connecting filopodia dynamic extension modes to productive Notch activation.
affiliations: Clarkson University (corresponding author)

papers.title: High piRNA abundance is a hallmark of evolutionarily persistent piRNA-producing loci.
papers.abstract: PIWI-interacting RNAs (piRNAs) silence transposons in the germline, and the loci that produce them diverge rapidly between species. Yet, some loci retain both their genomic location and their piRNA production across large evolutionary distances, and the basis for this conservation is unclear. To identify the features that distinguish these persistent loci, we compared piRNA production at orthologous loci in three closely related mouse species, contrasting loci that produce piRNAs in all three species with those that do so in only one. Transposon content and UTR features, often linked to piRNA production, did not distinguish the two groups. Transcription extending beyond gene ends (readthrough) was more frequent at conserved loci, but did not explain conservation once the amount of piRNAs produced was taken into account. Instead, we found that the conserved loci are those that produce the most piRNAs. The same association holds true in human and two other primate species. We speculate that most piRNAs expressed in testis are tolerated molecular noise, and that only the highly expressed minority are likely to be functional.
affiliations: Josep Carreras Leukemia Research Institute (IJC), Ctra de Can Ruti, Camí de les Escoles s/n, Badalona, Barcelona 08916, Spain. (corresponding author)

papers.title: Application of metagenomic sequencing to improve sessile serrated lesion detection using the faecal immunochemical test
papers.abstract: Most population colorectal cancer (CRC) screening programs use the faecal immunochemical test (FIT), which quantifies occult haemoglobin in faeces and has proven to be effective in detecting and reducing CRC incidence and mortality. Sessile serrated lesions (SSLs) account for up to 30% of sporadic CRC, yet FIT has low sensitivity to detect them. Faecal microbial biomarkers may improve their detection, but FIT samples have not previously been used to study the SSL microbiome. We asked whether FIT samples preserve the faecal microbiome as accurately as fresh collection, and whether they can reveal a microbial signature of SSL. We first reanalysed a published dataset of paired FIT and fresh faecal samples from the same participants. Donor identity explained 63.5% of compositional variance compared with 16.7% for collection method, indicating that FIT preserves the donor-specific signature on which biomarker discovery depends. We then generated shotgun metagenomes from FIT samples of 24 adults scheduled for diagnostic colonoscopy, twelve with at least one clinically significant SSL and twelve with no neoplasia (NN) and compared each group with a published fresh faeces cohort matched on colonoscopy outcome. Collection method explained 6.3% to 7.6% of variance, and no individual species was significantly differentially abundant between methods. Between SSL and NN FIT samples, community structure did not significantly differ, and conservative differential abundance analysis returned no results. More permissive count-based models suggested a depletion of fermentative commensals in SSL. Functionally, SSL samples encoded significantly fewer KEGG orthologs and less polyamine biosynthesis capacity, while orthologs carried by several Bifidobacterium species were more abundant. Many depleted functions reflected Enterobacteriaceae gene content concentrated in a few control samples. No single feature was diagnostic on its own. A multi-feature signature, confirmed in larger cohorts and applied to samples that screening programs already collect, may increase the detection rate of SSLs.
affiliations: Flinders Health and Medical Research Institute, College of Medicine and Public Health, Flinders University, Adelaide, SA, Australia (corresponding author)

papers.title: Learning interpretable compositional features associated with continuous covariates
papers.abstract: Compositional variation as a function of continuous covariates, such as time, presents challenges for learning interpretable features and accounting for their construction in subsequent inference. Motivated by temporal change in isoform usage in genomics, we introduce IsoVita, a statistical framework integrating covariate-informed balance learning designed for compositional data with complementary tests for abrupt and gradual compositional variation. IsoVita estimates a dominant covariate-dependent direction in the log-ratio coordinates and approximates it as a log ratio of their geometric mean proportions between two learned component groups, linking statistical evidence to explicit component membership. Change point and spline tests evaluate this interpretable feature, while a selection-aware permutation procedure repeats feature construction and testing under each permutation. In transcript-level simulations, IsoVita maintained low empirical false discovery proportions with power to detect differences and change point accuracy improving as temporal signals strengthened. However, the performance depended on trajectory shape and study design. Applications to two human brain bulk RNA-sequencing datasets identified widespread temporal variation in isoform composition while retaining transcript-level interpretability. IsoVita integrates interpretable compositional feature learning with inference along continuous covariates, with potential applications beyond transcriptomics. IsoVita is available as a PyPI package (https://pypi.org/project/isovita).
