papers.title: Plate design confounds donor variation and model evaluation in single-cell perturbation screens
papers.abstract: Single-cell screens of immune cells from many donors are used to study why individuals respond differently and to benchmark response models. Each donor-perturbation combination typically occupies one well, controls are grouped, and donors share one layout, so technical effects can look biological. Using a 90-cytokine screen, two compound screens, four cohorts and simulations, we show that well effects explain most replicate-control variation in abundant cell types, controls carry a shared offset, and identical control wells differ by hundreds of differentially expressed genes at a standard threshold, about as many as two receptor-negative proteins do. Negative controls, design-aware estimators and perturbation-specific evaluation change the interpretation of four recent analyses. A deep-learning model that scores below a perturbation-agnostic predictor under standard evaluation outperforms a simple baseline on perturbation-specific differences in two of three cell types (significantly in one with stricter controls), but predicts less well the component shared with inert wells.
affiliations: Wright State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: U-statistics-based Pairwise Discordance Regression for Joint Mean-Variability Inference in Longitudinal Studies with Missing Data
papers.abstract: Longitudinal studies are central to scientific inquiry across disciplines; yet, statistical analyses have predominantly focused on mean trajectories while treating variability as a secondary or nuisance component. Increasing evidence suggests that temporal variability and heterogeneity themselves encode critical scientific information, particularly in studies with repeated measurements, heterogeneous populations, or rich covariate structures. The classical mixed-effects and location-scale model family represents variability through latent variable components but relies on strong parametric assumptions and often requires numerical approximation or computationally intensive estimation. Here we introduce the semiparametric pairwise discordance regression, a unified framework for longitudinal data that directly models pairwise contrasts to simultaneously characterize mean trajectories, between-subject heterogeneity, and within-subject temporal variability. By targeting pairwise discordances rather than latent variance components, the proposed approach enables robust inference without specifying full parametric distributions for latent components or error terms, provided the specified conditional moment restrictions hold. Pair-level covariate encodings further accommodate flexible covariate structures and allow variability parameters to be interpreted through pairwise contrasts or dissimilarities. Estimation and inference are carried out via (weighted) U-statistic-based generalized estimating equations (UGEE) with a valid sandwich variance estimator, and we extend the fitting procedure to accommodate missing-at-random dropout. We establish the asymptotic distributions of the resulting estimators under mild regularity conditions. Simulation studies demonstrate reliable finite-sample performance in the settings considered, including non-Gaussian errors and misspecified working correlation structures, whereas likelihood-based parametric fits can be sensitive to distributional assumptions or numerically unstable. An application to longitudinal blood pressure during pregnancy illustrates the framework on real data.
affiliations: Vanderbilt University Medical Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Temperature-dependent Fano resonance in Microtubules and Tubulin investigated with Spontaneous Raman Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Microtubules are self-assembled biological hollow nanotubes composed by protein tubulin. They are essential for many biological functions, including cell motility, cell division, and act as intracellular track for organelle transport. In turn, through dynamic assembly and disassembly, they form spindle fibers for chromosome segregation during mitosis and meiosis. In this paper, we have measured the Raman spectra of microtubules and their constituent protein tubulin in dry powder form for a range of temperatures, from nitrogen liquid T=77 K up to room and physiological temperature T=310 K, to determine if molecular bond vibrations present potential Fano resonance asymmetry. We have found nontrivial persistence of Fano resonances, q<5, at room and physiological temperatures for some specific vibrational modes.
affiliations: Italian National Research Council, Institute of Bophysics (corresponding author)

papers.title: Highly conserved talin isoforms encode distinct mechanical responses and ligand-binding capabilities
papers.abstract: Talin is a central mechanosensitive adaptor that links integrins to the actin cytoskeleton and converts mechanical force into biochemical signals. Vertebrates express two highly homologous talin isoforms, talin-1 and talin-2, yet the molecular basis for their nonredundant functions remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate how isoform-specific sequence differences alter the mechanical response and ligand-binding capabilities of the talin rod. Using single-molecule force spectroscopy and biochemical binding assays, we show that talin-2 preserves the overall mechanical architecture of talin-1 but exhibits distinct mechanical responses in key rod regions. Talin-2 R7-R9 exhibits a previously unobserved three-domain cooperative unfolding pathway, while an alternative sequential pathway reveals early unfolding of R9 at substantially lower force than in talin-1. Strikingly, talin-2 R4-R6 has acquired two additional mechanically regulated interactions: a previously unrecognized vinculin-binding site in R5 and an A-kinase anchoring protein (AKAP) region within R5-R6 that recruits protein kinase A (PKA). Together with the conserved R9 AKAP site, this establishes two spatially separated, mechanically regulated PKA-anchoring regions within the talin-2 scaffold. These findings establish that isoform-specific sequence divergence not only reshapes the mechanical response of the talin scaffold but also expands its repertoire of force-regulated interactions, providing a mechanism for the assembly of different structural and signaling complexes in an isoform-dependent manner.
affiliations: Mechanobiology Institute, Department of Physics, National University of Singapore (corresponding author)

papers.title: Amyloid stability and condensate material properties independently govern the hnRNPA2 condensate to fibril transition
papers.abstract: hnRNPA2 is a component of cellular membraneless organelles many of which contain RNA and RNA-binding proteins (RBPs). RBPs frequently contain low-complexity domains (LCDs) that can also assemble into amyloid fibrils. Fibrils isolated from patients with frontotemporal lobar degeneration contain ordered segments of these LCDs and disease-associated mutations can enhance the homotypic interactions that promote aggregation. Although previous studies have largely examined the condensate-to-fibril transition by altering condensate stability, how amyloid structure governs this process remains poorly understood. Here, we show that the hnRNPA2 LCD forms a reproducible fibril fold and by combining structure-guided thermodynamic profiling, peptide design, mutagenesis and in vitro characterization under conditions with (two-phase) and without (one-phase) condensates, we define the molecular determinants of its assembly. We identify an aromatic triad within the fibril core that controls fibril formation kinetics and thermodynamic stability. Mutational analysis further reveals that condensate stability and fibril stability are largely independent. Finally, microrheology linked reduced condensate viscosity to faster fibril formation, supporting a role for condensate material properties in regulating aggregation kinetics. Together, these findings support a model in which the condensate-to-fibril transition is governed by the interplay between a disordered ''fuzzy coat'' and a fibril-forming aromatic triad within hnRNPA2. This work provides a structural framework for understanding how condensates can transition into amyloid assemblies.
affiliations: University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: hAM-pe soluble extract increases human keratinocyte HaCaT cell-line mobility in scratch assays
papers.abstract: We have studied the impact of human amniotic membrane (hAM-pe) on wound closing speed in a scratch assay of human keratinocytes (HaCaT). Though not without limitations, scratch assays are useful for studying collective cellular displacement as a model of wound healing. We show that the treatment is effective in decreasing the average time that the cells need to completely close the wound, in agreement with previous \emph{in vivo} experiments. We developed an automated segmentation software, and verified that a linear fit, though not completely describing the wound edge dynamics, is a robust method for comparing treatments and control measurements. By tracking the individual motion of a subset of cells, we found that individual treatment does not cause an increase in individual speed enough to explain the effect of the treatment at the collective (wound edge) level. Instead, the mean squared displacement and numerical simulations of a simple model of interacting active Brownian particles support the view that the main effect of the treatment at the individual level is to increase the persistence of cellular motion.
affiliations: Instituto de Fisica de Liquidos y Sistemas Biologicos (IFLySiB-UNLP-CONICET) (corresponding author)

papers.title: Arrest-associated transcriptional programmes outweigh apoptosis-associated programmes in treatment-naive pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
papers.abstract: Background: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is driven by mutant KRAS, and RAS inhibitors now extend survival in previously treated metastatic disease. Whether treatment shrinks a tumour or only halts its growth depends partly on whether cancer cells die or stop dividing, yet how untreated PDAC cells are balanced between these programmes is unknown. Aims: We aimed to characterise the balance between apoptosis-associated and arrest-associated transcriptional programmes in treatment-naive PDAC and to examine their relationships with tumour subtype, TGM2 expression, tissue organisation, survival and drug sensitivity. Methods and results: We scored 52,999 malignant cells from 18 untreated patients in the Hwang atlas using a transcriptional contrast between genes associated with apoptosis and genes associated with resistance to apoptosis or cell-cycle arrest. In every patient the contrast was shifted toward the arrest-associated side: using equality between the two sides as the dividing threshold, 86.3% of cells with an informative score fell on that side, although the proportion depends on the threshold chosen. The shift recurred in the independent Steele atlas (median 71.6% per sample, range 37.1% to 90.8%). In the discovery cohort, tumours with higher basal-like scores had fewer arrest-side cells, and TGM2 expression was modestly higher on the arrest-associated side in both cohorts. The contrast did not track cell-line drug sensitivity or survival in bulk tumours. Conclusion: Untreated PDAC cells show a reproducible transcriptional bias toward anti-apoptotic and cell-cycle-arrest programmes. Whether this bias predicts cellular responses to treatment remains to be tested.
affiliations: University of Oxford (corresponding author)

papers.title: Organism-dependent ecotoxicological effects of transition metal-containing layered double hydroxides
papers.abstract: Due to low environmental stability of certain molecule classes, such as phytohormones and RNA interference, layered double hydroxides (LDHs) have been investigated as nanocarriers capable of protecting and transporting molecules of interest in natural systems. Herein, the ecotoxicological effects of LDH nanoparticles composed by different transition metals (Al-Ni, Al-Co, and Al-Cu) were evaluated in maize (Zea mays), tomato (Lycopersicum esculentum), and the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, two important crops and one soil organism found in agricultural systems. Plants were exposed to the nanoparticles through foliar spraying (5, 50, and 500 ug/mL), and physiological parameters were evaluated. In C. elegans, lethality, locomotion, larval development, and body length were analyzed. The nanoparticles exhibited high colloidal stability and characteristic lamellar morphology. The results demonstrated low phytotoxicity for all formulations, without significant changes in photochemical activity, effective quantum yield of photosystem II (psi-PSII), stomatal conductance (gs), and chlorophyll index (Chl a+b; ICF) in plants. In contrast, C. elegans exhibited greater sensitivity, showing reduced motility, developmental delay, and decreased body length, although mortality remained below 12% under all evaluated conditions. Toxicity was dependent on the metallic composition, following the order Al-Cu > Al-Ni > Al-Co. Collectively, the results indicate that LDHs exhibit high compatibility with those two crops but may cause sublethal effects in soil organisms. These findings highlight the importance of multispecies ecotoxicological assessments for the safe development of nanocarriers intended for agricultural applications.
affiliations: Universidade Estadual de Campinas - UNICAMP (corresponding author)

papers.title: A mammalian fibroblast zoo reveals barriers to cross-species virus replication and differential regulation of antiviral immunity
papers.abstract: Virus zoonosis represents a continual threat to humans. Viruses emerge in humans directly or indirectly through interactions with mammals. However, our understanding of virus-host susceptibility across the diversity of mammals is limited and experimental model systems are restricted to a very small set of model organisms. Mammals are highly diverse and different habitats, lifestyles, diets, and exposures to different pathogens have driven substantial genetic diversity. We generated a library of primary fibroblasts across 86 mammalian species and used these cells to build an atlas of virus-host susceptibility across a panel of arboviruses that infect diverse mammals including humans. Perturbing the innate immune system revealed some virus-host pairs where restriction is controlled by the immune system and others where there is an incompatibility with host factors. Transcriptomic profiling of the library in response to virus sensing mimicked by poly(I:C) or antiviral signaling with type I interferon reveals a core set of conserved genes that respond as well as substantial species- and order-specific responses. Together these data provide a comparative atlas of innate immune responses across mammals and offer a window into how these systems have evolved across animals.
affiliations: University of Minnesota (corresponding author)

papers.title: Monounsaturated fatty acid depletion is a metabolic pattern of pathogenesis surveilled to activate p38 MAPK innate immunity
papers.abstract: Pathogen infection profoundly remodels host metabolism. Whether hosts sense specific pathogen-induced metabolic changes to identify microbial infection is not known. Here, we find that depletion the monounsaturated fatty acid oleate is a metabolic pattern of pathogenesis, specifically surveilled by the nematode C. elegans to identify active infection with a bacterial pathogen. We previously demonstrated that the enzymatic TIR (Toll/interleukin-1 receptor/resistance)-domain containing protein, TIR-1/SARM1, the key upstream activator of p38 MAPK PMK-1 immunity, is a guard protein in an effector-triggered immune response, positioned specifically on the surface of lysosome-related organelles to sense the toxic effects of bacterial infection. Here, we show that acute loss of oleate in intestinal cells during bacterial infection causes lysosome-related organelles to collapse, which induces the aggregation and activation of TIR-1/SARM1. Further, we find that oleate deficiency is a host vulnerability that concomitantly activates the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) KGB-1 nutrient sensing pathway, an adaptive response that promotes expression of TIR-1/SARM1 on lysosome-related organelles and is required for survival during infection. These data establish a mechanistic connection between fatty acid nutrition and innate immune regulation, and reveal that specific changes in host metabolism are surveilled to identify pathogen attack.
affiliations: University of Massachusetts Medical School (corresponding author)

papers.title: UVC Irradiation Induces Time-Dependent Proteomic Remodeling in Geodermatophilus obscurus G20
papers.abstract: Geodermatophilus obscurus G20 is a multi-resistant extremophile observed to survive significant dosages of ultraviolet (UV) radiation. Despite previous work having measured G. obscurus G20s proteome in relation to its genome sequence, its proteomic response to stressors has yet to be explored. This study utilizes bottom-up proteomics with data independent acquisition to derive comprehensive proteomic measurements in both healthy and two UV-stressed conditions induced through 254 nm UV radiation administered at a median lethal dose. The first, an acute response treatment group, was recovered and flash-frozen immediately after UV radiation. The second, a recovery response treatment group, was allowed to incubate for 1 hour following UV radiation. Gene enrichment analysis revealed an increase in NADH dehydrogenase activity among both stressed treatment groups, however the recovery response treatment group experienced additional changes including reduced peptidoglycan synthesis and increased translational activity. Results suggest that the repair process undergone by G. obscurus G20 persists well after initial UV exposure and is likely to be inducing noteworthy energetic demands to facilitate UV induced genomic repair. Proteomic analyses revealed patterns that advance our mechanistic and temporal understanding of the G. obscurus metabolic response to UV irradiation.
affiliations: University of Wyoming (corresponding author)

papers.title: Genomic signatures distinguish isolates of Salmonella Typhimurium from humans and livestock
papers.abstract: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium is a major cause of human salmonellosis and livestock represent an important reservoir for human infection through the food chain. However, it remains unclear whether isolates recovered from human disease reflect the broader livestock population or constitute a subset of livestock-associated isolates characterized by specific genetic features. Here, we analysed 1,398 S. Typhimurium genomes from human, poultry, bovine and swine isolates to evaluate whether isolates associated with human disease can be distinguished from those circulating in livestock and to identify the genetic features underlying this discrimination. Whole-genome multilocus sequence typing profiles were converted into a gene presence/absence matrix and analysed using four machine-learning algorithms, which showed high and consistent discriminatory performance. Model performance was influenced by the phylogenetic structure of the population and by the variable distribution of human- and livestock-associated isolates across lineages of sequence type (ST) 19, the most prevalent S. Typhimurium ST. Nevertheless, within ST19, 97 genes were significantly enriched and 36 were significantly depleted in human-associated genomes relative to genomes from each of the three livestock sources. Human-enriched genes included 14 genes required for biosynthesis of the lipopolysaccharide core, the O-antigen, the T1 antigen, and six virulence factors. These genes were consistently absent from livestock-associated genomes across ST19 lineages. Conversely, human-depleted genes included the galactitol utilisation cluster and five virulence genes, which are predominantly absent in specific ST19 lineages. Overall, our findings support the existence of host-associated genomic signatures that distinguish isolates associated with human disease from those sampled from the livestock reservoir.
affiliations: Center for Genomic Epidemiology, Research and Education Department, Istituto Zooprofilattico Sperimentale della Lombardia e dell'Emilia-Romagna, 43126 Parma, It (corresponding author)

papers.title: Visual surfaceomics reveals the substrate-scavenging cell surface of Asgard archaea
papers.abstract: The emergence of eukaryotes from Asgard archaeal ancestors likely required a specialized cell envelope that enabled sustained physical and metabolic interactions with proto-mitochondrial symbionts. While the protrusion-rich cell architecture of Asgard archaea may enable such interactions, the molecular composition of their cell surface and its role in establishing cell-cell contacts remains unknown. Here, we developed a "visual surfaceomics" approach, integrating subtomogram averaging, predictive structural modeling, transcriptomics, proteomics, and expansion microscopy to identify surface proteins in situ. We show that Asgard cell bodies and protrusions lack an archaea-typical paracrystalline S-layer and are instead decorated by two main classes of surface proteins: subtilisin-like serine proteases (SubSs) and oligopeptide-binding proteins (OppAs). SubSs were detected as membrane-anchored dimers and were sparsely distributed across the surface. OppAs showed near-total membrane coverage but lacked any rigid, higher order assembly. Thermal shift assays and single particle cryo-EM showed that OppA binds oligopeptides in vitro. Comparative genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics suggest that this peptidophilic surface architecture is conserved across Asgard archaeal phyla. Finally, we discovered that the cell surface was remodeled at cell-cell contact sites. Altogether, our integrative approach revealed a metabolically specialized and structurally flexible cell surface that couples extracellular protein degradation with peptide capture and uptake, while potentially contributing to establishing and maintaining the symbiotic interactions of Asgard archaea.
affiliations: Department of Biology, Institute of Molecular Biology & Biophysics, Eidgenossische Technische Hochschule Zurich, Otto-Stern-Weg 5, 8093 Zurich, Switzerland (corresponding author)

papers.title: Evaluating non-oxidative glycolysis using 13C metabolic flux analysis
papers.abstract: Non-oxidative glycolysis (NOG) converts glucose to acetyl-CoA without emitting CO2 during Escherichia coli bioproduction. Although 13C-metabolic flux analysis (13C-MFA) has the potential to evaluate NOG flux distribution in vivo, the precision of these estimates depends on the labeling patterns of glucose tracers. Because E. coli has multiple native glycolysis pathways, selecting the optimal glucose tracer is important for precise estimates. This study used simulations to evaluate the performance of 18 commercially available glucose tracers in precisely predicting NOG flux. We artificially generated flux distributions of central metabolic pathways, including three types of NOG pathways, and obtained 13C labeling patterns of amino acids metabolized from each glucose tracer. Using these data, we then calculated 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for NOG pathway fluxes. Comparing the sum of CI widths from three NOG fluxes showed that estimation with [1,3-13C]-glucose yielded the narrowest CIs. Several tracers, including [2,3-13C]glucose, were capable of determining fluxes with high precision, but [1-13C]glucose was not one of them, despite often being used for estimating glycolytic fluxes. We then experimentally evaluated [2,3-13C]- and [1-13C]glucose as tracers in E. coli strains with and without the expression of phosphoketolase, which is required for NOG pathways to function. The results suggested that [1-13C]glucose could not detect NOG fluxes, whereas [2,3-13C]glucose estimated the fluxes of all three NOG pathways with narrow CIs.
affiliations: The University of Osaka (corresponding author)

papers.title: Metatranscriptomic Profiling of Viral Diversity in Aquatic Environments with a Focus on Microalgal Viruses
papers.abstract: Freshwater microeukaryotes contribute to aquatic productivity, yet the RNA viruses associated with these communities remain incompletely characterized compared with their marine counterparts. Here, we used metatranscriptomics to profile viral diversity across five Finnish freshwater sites (one river and four lakes) and one coastal marine sample from Hiroshima Bay in the Seto Inland Sea, Japan. We recovered 399 viral operational taxonomic units (vOTUs), of which 285 (71.4%) represented RNA viruses distributed across five viral phyla and putatively associated with fungal, plant or algal, metazoan and bacterial hosts. DNA viruses formed a smaller component of the dataset, including bacteriophage-like vOTUs with transcripts encoding replication, structural, packaging, and lysis proteins. Two vOTUs, which were detected in the Vantaanjoki river sample, were putatively classified within the family Marnaviridae, which comprises RNA viruses that infect protists in marine and freshwater environments. Both vOTUs encoded conserved replication and picornavirus-like capsid domains, and one represented a near-complete dicistronic genome. RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) -based phylogeny placed these vOTUs in a strongly supported lineage outside the currently recognized genera within the family Marnaviridae, supporting their provisional assignment to the candidate genus Vandarnavirus proposed here within Marnaviridae. Whole-genome comparisons using the IMG/VR v4 database revealed genetic similarities between the vOTUs representing the candidate Vandarnavirus genus and picorna-like virus sequences from freshwater, wetland, saltmarsh, and estuarine metatranscriptomes. These findings expand the known ecological range of marnavirus-like RNA viruses and identify freshwater habitats as under-sampled reservoirs of microalgae-associated viral sequences.
affiliations: university of helsinki (corresponding author)

papers.title: Stoichiometric Encoding of Amplification Kinetics Enables High-Level Multiplexing in Single-Channel TaqMan Real-Time PCR
papers.abstract: Multiplexing in TaqMan real-time PCR (qPCR) is limited to four-six targets per reaction by fluorophore spectral overlap. Amplification curve analysis (ACA) can discriminate several targets within one fluorescence channel from amplification curves (AC) kinetic features, but has been confined mainly to digital qPCR (dqPCR) and is sensitive to domain shifts between instruments and specimen types. Here, we co-design biochemical encoding of target-specific information into ACs and their computational decoding to achieve single-channel 8-plex TaqMan qPCR on a standard thermocycler. Using asymmetric PCR, we show that forward primer, reverse primer and probe concentrations act as a programmable encoding mechanism, generating a 27-condition design space of reproducible non-canonical ACs, conserved from digital to bulk qPCR. Applying this stoichiometric encoding to an 8-plex central nervous system pathogens panel increased inter-target separability, raising the mean silhouette score from 0.329 to 0.711. To decode ACs without labelled target-domain bulk qPCR data, we pretrained a transformer encoder by self-supervised learning on more than 170,000 unlabelled dqPCR curves and aligned source and target domains using conditional domain adversarial training. On contrived clinical specimens, the framework classified a canonical 7-plex respiratory virus panel with 83.6% accuracy (versus 67.7% for a supervised baseline) and the encoded 8-plex panel with 89.8% accuracy. Furthermore, stoichiometric encoding enabled resolution of double- and triple-target co-amplification events with 98.7% accuracy in controlled dqPCR experiments. This approach expands the information capacity of existing qPCR instrumentation without new hardware, fluorophores or oligonucleotides, offering a low-cost route to syndromic molecular diagnostics.
affiliations: Imperial College London; Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust (corresponding author)

papers.title: Global repression of mesenchymal genes in epithelial cells by the histone demethylase LSD1
papers.abstract: Epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) is an essential process in development, tissue repair, and tumour metastasis, and is triggered by SNAI, ZEB and TWIST transcription factors, that recruit lysine-specific demethylase 1 (LSD1) to repress epithelial genes such as E-cadherin. In mesenchymal cells, LSD1 inhibition restores E-cadherin expression and reduces migration and invasion, consistent with LSD1 inhibition reverting EMT, and offering a therapeutic modality for EMT-associated disease. Recent data, however, suggest context-dependent roles for LSD1, as its inhibition in epithelial cells increases mesenchymal marker expression, potentially promoting EMT. To investigate this discrepancy, we mapped genome-wide binding of LSD1 in HCT116 epithelial cells and used rapid degron-mediated ablation of endogenous LSD1 to measure changes in nascent and steady-state transcription and chromatin accessibility. In epithelial cells, LSD1 binds constitutively-accessible, primed mesenchymal promoters. These are rapidly derepressed after LSD1 ablation, with activation of SNAI2 and ZEB1, which repress epithelial hallmarks such as E-cadherin. Re-introduction of LSD1 downregulates SNAI2 and ZEB1 but, surprisingly, further represses E-cadherin, indicating sustained loss of epithelial characteristics. Collectively, our results show that LSD1 maintains epithelial identity by repressing mesenchymal genes, questioning the therapeutic utility of LSD1 inhibition for EMT control.
affiliations: Institute for Structural and Chemical Biology and Division of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of Leicester, Leicester, LE1 7RH (corresponding author)

papers.title: Stepwise assembly and mechanical stability of nsP3 Helical Scaffolds in Chikungunya Virus
papers.abstract: Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) is a positive-sense, single-stranded RNA virus that replicates its genome through a viral replication complex (RC) essential for successful infection. The RC consists of four non-structural proteins: nsP1, nsP2, nsP3, and nsP4. In this study, we focused on nsP3, which comprises three distinct domains: the alphavirus unique domain (AUD), the long and intrinsically disordered hypervariable domain (HVD), and the enzymatic macrodomain (MD). Notably, nsP3 assembles into helicoidal macrostructures, termed helical scaffolds (HSs), which are components of the CHIKV replication complex and are involved in the formation of macromolecular traps in the cytoplasm of the infected cell called Alphagranules (AGs). HSs form tubular helical scaffolds assembled through the AUD, with the MD and HVD flexibly deployed to the scaffold exterior. Despite their functional importance, the mechanisms governing HS formation remain poorly understood. Using High-Speed Atomic Force Microscopy (HS-AFM) and Electron Microscopy (EM) we achieved new findings on the structure, mechanics and assembly of these macrostructures. Our results show the nsP3 monomers follow intermediate steps before completing the assembly into full helical scaffolds, with each nsP3 domain contributing differently to this process. The macrodomain (MD) provides mechanical stability, yet it fractures under tens of piconewtons of force. This rigidity acts as a mechanical regulator that constrains the position of the HVD, which in turn mediates interactions with host factors and neighboring HSs. Through this interplay, nsP3 achieves both structural cohesion and functional adaptability, promoting the higher-order organization of HSs into honeycomb-like networks.
affiliations: Aix-Marseille Universite NSERM DyNaMo U1325 (corresponding author)

papers.title: Optogenetic induction of TAD boundary pairing promotes gene activity
papers.abstract: The genome folds inside the nucleus into distinct structures across multiple levels of organization. Topologically associating domains (TADs) are a ubiquitous architectural feature of genomes delineated by boundaries enriched in the CTCF protein and the cohesin complex. TADs are dynamic structures as their boundaries undergo continuous, short-lived pairing events. Whether the structural integrity of TADs contributes to regulation of the genes within the TAD is unclear. To directly test the structure-function relationship of TADs, we have developed OptoTet, an optogenetic tool to rapidly and directly manipulate chromatin contacts in a controlled fashion using light without the need for mutation or protein depletion. Using the TADs containing the ERRFI1 or MYC gene as model systems, we show that OptoTet promotes TAD boundary looping. When applied to probing the structure-function relationship of TADs, light-induced pairing of TAD boundaries promoted transcriptional activity of ERRFI1 as indicated by increased gene bursting. In contrast, bursting of MYC was insensitive to boundary pairing. Enhanced TAD boundary pairing also partially rescued the effect of depletion of cohesin components on ERRF1 but not on MYC. Our results suggest that TADs boundary pairing dynamics can contribute to gene regulation in a gene-specific manner.
affiliations: National Cancer Institute, NIH (corresponding author)

papers.title: Persistent and recyclable myosin II minifilaments drive cortical contractility in the early C. elegans embryo
papers.abstract: Non-muscle myosin II is a key regulator of cell and tissue morphogenesis, yet the cortical dynamics of myosin minifilaments in vivo remain poorly understood. Here, we combine SIM-TIRF and single-molecule TIRF microscopy to characterize the structure and dynamics of myosin minifilaments in an early developing embryo. High-temporal-resolution SIM-TIRF imaging revealed diverse minifilament behaviors, including partition-like events, long-range alignment of multiple minifilaments into collective structures we called proto-stress fibers, partial unbinding, and sequential unbinding and rebinding to the cortex. Photoconversion experiments showed that minifilaments persist as intact units after cortical unbinding, diffuse through the cytoplasm, and can be recycled over long distances rather than disassembling upon detachment. Despite these dynamic behaviors, minifilaments are predominantly stationary when bound to actin. Numerical simulations demonstrated that this static behavior is essential to sustain cortical stress within a continuously remodeling actin network. Using myosin motor-domain mutants, we further investigated the contribution of motor activity to these behaviors. Together, our results reveal that myosin minifilaments can persist as stable units while cycling between the cortex and cytoplasm, and that their predominantly static behavior when bound to actin enables sustained force generation in a continuously renewing cortical network. These findings provide new insights into myosin organization, recycling, and force generation during early embryonic development.
affiliations: Institute for Biology Paris-Seine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Multicellular Perturb-seq Reveals Lineage-Specific Transcriptional Control During Human Cardiac Organoid Development
papers.abstract: Heart development requires the coordinated differentiation of multiple cell lineages, including cardiomyocytes (CMs) and endothelial cells (ECs). Transcription factors (TFs) orchestrate lineage specification, morphogenesis, and maturation, yet how cardiac and vascular TFs shape multicellular organization and their interactions remain poorly understood. Many TFs exhibit pleiotropic and stage-dependent effects across cardiac lineages, particularly in cardiac progenitor cells, suggesting the presence of shared regulatory networks that synchronize cardiac and vascular programs during development and in response to stress. Human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) differentiated cardiac organoid provides a physiologically relevant 3D model to study these multicellular interactions, enabling simultaneous differentiation of ECs and CMs within a human genetic context. When combined with CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) based Perturb-seq, this system allows systematic, high-throughput dissection of TF-driven regulatory programs at single-cell resolution. In this study, we investigated how cardiac and vascular TFs coordinate lineage commitment and the cross-lineage signaling in human cardiovascular differentiation.
affiliations: Medical College of Wisconsin (corresponding author)

papers.title: A multipotent mouse distal airway secretory cell population that contributes to both airway and alveolar regeneration
papers.abstract: The distal airway is a spatially distinct compartment whose contribution to lung repair remains poorly defined. We have identified an epithelial cell population enriched in the most distal airways of the mouse lung, that is not present in the alveolar epithelium. Using lineage tracing tools based on Cldn10 expression which marks these cells, we show that the Cldn10+ lineage in homeostatic conditions marks distal airway secretory cells in a highly specific manner, with only a small contribution to multi-ciliated cells and no contribution towards the basal stem cell lineage. Remarkably, these Cldn10+ distal secretory cells proliferate and display a high degree of multi-potency across the lung epithelial axis after injury, generating basal cells, multi-ciliated cells, and alveolar epithelium. In severely remodeled regions after injury, we show that Cldn10 lineage-labeled cells migrate from the airways and differentiate into alveolar epithelial cells. These findings establish the Cldn10 lineage that defines a distal airway secretory facultative progenitor with both intrapulmonary airway and alveolar potential, providing a genetic system for studying distal lung repair.
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania (corresponding author)

papers.title: Regenerative epithelial spike cells instruct immune niche homeostasis in zebrafish fin epidermis
papers.abstract: Epithelia comprise diverse specialized epithelial cells that interact with immune cells, yet how these interactions sustain immune cell pools remain poorly understood. Here, we integrated single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis with transgenic assays in zebrafish and discovered a previously unrecognized epithelial population marked by advillin (avil). We identified epithelial cells exhibiting unique morphology and localization, characterized by an apical spike projecting outward from the body - which we term spike cells. These cells exhibit features reminiscent of mammalian tuft cells. Notably, avil+ spike cells exhibit close spatial association with a subset of mpeg1+ immune cells. Following fin amputation, spike cells are replenished de novo from precursors and undergo dynamic changes in density, morphology, and orientation, and their regeneration depends on Alk signaling. Moreover, spike cells dynamically interact with mpeg1+ immune cells to maintain the immune cell population. Together, our findings identify a unique epithelial population in zebrafish fins and define their roles in maintaining immune cell niche dynamics.
affiliations: Department of Cell and Regenerative Biology, School of Medicine and Public Health, University of Wisconsin - Madison, Madison, WI, 53705, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: SOPSim: A cell vertex-based application for simulating sensory bristle patterning with dynamic filopodia
papers.abstract: Repeating patterns, such as the bristles on the thorax of fruit flies developed from sensory organ precursor (SOP) cells, play important roles in the lives of flies as they are connected to the central nervous system and help detect environmental cues and threats. Notch signaling is known to regulate the formation of these patterns. Primarily, Notch signaling involves local communication between neighboring cells in direct contact (apical or junctional interaction). However, this short-range interaction alone cannot fully explain the complex biological patterns observed. Further studies have revealed long-range communication between cells through actin-based protrusions known as filopodia. The precise understanding of how the dynamics of filopodia, such as protrusion and retraction, lead to Notch-Delta activation remains unclear, which limits our ability to fully comprehend the mechanisms underlying cell fate decisions and the emergence of spatially organized patterns during tissue development and regeneration. In this study, we extend the modeling framework for Notch signaling by incorporating a filopodia dynamics model driven by myosin-mediated contraction. We address existing gaps by defining criteria under which any given pair of filopodia will physically intersect. We also introduce the local sensory area (LSA), a metric for quantifying local SOP spacing, and use experimental data to calibrate a Notch threshold that distinguishes SOP from epithelial cells. Through numerical simulations, we confirm that long-range communication via filopodia is essential for reproducing the refined patterns observed in vivo. Additionally, we explore how filopodia length, lifetime, and orientation influence the spatial organization of SOP cells. To this end, a Python library has been developed which allows users to perform simulations of Notch Delta signaling via a (1) Graphical User Interface/website, local to the user's computer, (2) via commands in the command line interface, or (3) by calling the simulation using a function via a Python API. This library allows users without computational expertise to easily specify a small number of input parameters and generate simulations of the model.
affiliations: Clarkson University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Deep transcriptomic analysis of molecular mediators of complex traits in heterogeneous stock (HS) rats
papers.abstract: Rats are a powerful model organism for genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of physiological and behavioral traits. Heterogeneous Stock (HS) rats, which were created by intercrossing 8 inbred rat strains, are heavily used for this purpose because of their genetic diversity and accumulated recombinations due to over 100 generations of outbreeding, which improves mapping precision. However, functional genomics resources for post-GWAS interpretation of genomic findings have been limited. We processed 3,160 RNA-seq samples, 1,932 of which were previously unpublished, from 13 tissues as part of RatGTEx. We used Pantry to quantify six modalities of transcriptome regulation (expression, isoform ratio, intron excision ratio, alternative transcription start site (TSS), alternative poly(A), and RNA stability) in each sample, which allowed us to identify 144,876 independent quantitative trait loci (QTL) for 22,599 genes. We performed a transcriptome-wide association study (TWAS) with 19,796 unique genes across tissues and transcriptional modalities and 308 traits collected from 14 studies using FUSION, which identified 7,473 significant gene-trait associations. This work presents a significant expansion of the RatGTEx resource in terms of samples, modes of transcriptome regulation, and genetic analyses. Our findings provide molecular evidence for the involvement of specific genes in mediating GWAS signals through a range of transcriptome regulatory mechanisms. These gene-to-phenotype relationships can be easily applied to genetic analyses in humans and other species. Further experiments can use this evidence to confirm these molecular mediators and target them for the treatment of behavioral and physiological traits and disorders. To facilitate use of these results, we have updated results on RatGTEx.org and provided a new interactive TWAS web portal (twas.ratgtex.org).
affiliations: University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Genomic and Epigenomic Relationships Capture Different Patterns of Genotype-by-Environment Interaction in Grapevine Clones
papers.abstract: Genotype-by-environment interaction (GEI) challenges selection in clonally propagated perennial crops by reducing the consistency of clone performance across years. In perennial crops, both genetic and epigenetic variation are likely to contribute to complex trait variation among clones. However, the extent to which each molecular source contribute to GEI remains poorly understood. Here, we used UMR-seq, an assay that recovers SNPs and unmethylated-region (UMR; DNA methylation) profiles from a single library, to generate paired genomic and epigenomic profiles for 206 Riesling (Vitis vinifera L.) clones phenotyped for yield and juice quality traits across nine growing seasons. We then partitioned the contribution of each omic layer to clonal variation and GEI, and examined the genomic distribution of their effects. In models without explicit GEI, environmental and residual effects were the largest source of phenotypic variance and the clonal main effect was modest. Genomic relationships accounted for most of the clonal variance in four of five traits, and adding an epigenomic relationship matrix (ERM) to the genomic relationship matrix (GRM) had little effect. In contrast, when GEI effects were modelled using factor-analytic covariance structures, the epigenomic layer captured a substantial proportion of GEI variance and exceeded the genomic contribution in four of five traits. The two omic layers differed not only in the amount of GEI captured, but also in the pattern of clone re-ranking across years. When back-solved effects were aggregated into genomic windows, the largest genomic and epigenomic effects tended to fall in different regions, with overlap no greater than expected by chance. Together, these results show that genomic and epigenomic relationships capture complementary components of year-to-year variation in clone performance, with the epigenomic contribution expressed primarily through GEI. These findings provide a basis for investigating the molecular drivers of GEI and for testing whether genomic and epigenomic information can inform selection for stable clonal performance across variable environments.
affiliations: Department of Plant Breeding, Hochschule Geisenheim University, Geisenheim, Germany (corresponding author)

papers.title: Long-read DNA sequencing reveals global hypomethylation and focal hypermethylation in SDHx-deficient pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma
papers.abstract: Pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas (PPGL) are highly heritable neuroendocrine tumors of the autonomic ganglia. Genomic DNA in most cancer cells is hypomethylated. However, DNA in PPGLs secondary to mutations in succinate dehydrogenase complex (SDHx) genes is reportedly hypermethylated due to succinate-mediated inhibition of DNA demethylases. We used nanopore long-read sequencing to characterize the methylome of tumor and white blood cell DNA from SDHx and non-SDHx PPGL patients, alongside normal adrenal medulla. We find that both SDHx and non-SDHx PPGLs are globally hypomethylated, particularly at centromeres. In normal adrenal medulla, CpG islands marked by H3K4 methylation are hypomethylated, whereas CpG islands lacking H3K4 methylation are hypermethylated. In SDHx-related PPGL, some H3K4me-marked CpG islands are hypermethylated, but most are not. We propose that DNA methylation in SDHx-related PPGL reflects the global hypomethylation generally observed in tumors, partly offset by succinate-mediated inhibition of TET DNA demethylases. Opposing effects of succinate may alter the balance between DNA methylation (indirect inhibition of the DNMT3A/B DNA methylases via inhibition of H3K4me demethylases) and DNA demethylation (inhibition of TET DNA demethylases) at active CpG islands.
affiliations: NIH (corresponding author)

papers.title: Genomic characterization and evolutionary path of human satellite 1B in primates highlight a dynamic relationship with transposable elements
papers.abstract: Human Satellite 1B (HSat1B) remains one of the least characterized classical human satellite DNAs, despite its massive abundance on the human Y chromosome. Its tripartite ~2.5 kb monomer - comprising an AluY fragment, a GC-rich unit (here named H1B) and an AT-rich block - points to an evolutionary origin tightly linked to transposable elements (TEs). Here, we present the first comprehensive comparative genomic, phylogenetic and transcriptional characterization of HSat1B across 10 primate species using Telomere-to-Telomere (T2T) and chromosome-scale long-read assemblies, combined with DNA-FISH, RNA-FISH and long-read transcriptomic analyses. We demonstrate that while canonical tandem HSat1B arrays are restricted to Homininae (human, chimpanzee, bonobo and gorilla), the core H1B unit and its structural variants (H1Bsv1 and H1Bsv2) occur across all 10 primate genomes, including strepsirrhines (lemur). This indicates that the H1B sequence predates the assembly of the composite HSat1B monomer by at least 60 million years. H1B variants consistently map within TE-rich genomic contexts, supporting a stepwise, TE-mediated model of satellite diversification and mobilization. Within Homininae, humans exhibit a dramatic lineage-specific expansion driven by Yq12 amplification (~14.2 Mb; 92% of total genomic content), whereas non-human great apes carry smaller, highly polymorphic autosomal and Y-linked arrays. Finally, we show that H1B-containing sequences are transcriptionally active in human and gorilla nuclei via RNA-FISH and characterize heterogeneous H1B/Alu chimeric non-coding transcripts in the human male germline. Collectively, our findings uncover the birth and Homininae-specific expansion of a composite satellite DNA seeded by an ancient primate sequence module and sculpted by transposable elements.
affiliations: CytoGenomics Lab-UTAD/RISE-Health (corresponding author)

papers.title: Transcriptome reallocation during infection reshapes synonymous codon demand in Botrytis cinerea
papers.abstract: While genomic codon usage is fixed within an individual isolate, the synonymous codons represented in its RNA pool can change when transcription shifts among genes. We tested whether this transcript-level phenotype accompanies infection by reanalyzing 39 libraries from three public Botrytis cinerea RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) time series in S. lycopersicum, Arabidopsis thaliana, and Physcomitrium patens. Gene counts were corrected for coding length, combined with fixed gene-specific codon inventories, and analyzed as centered log ratios within synonymous amino-acid families. Sampling time accounted for 95-98% of fungal codon-demand variation in each series. The association persisted after effective-length correction, unique-only competitive mapping, host-homology exclusion, depth equalization, protein-family weighting, and removal of translation-associated genes. Change vectors over the interpolated, time-aligned 16-24-h interval were positively aligned among studies, whereas later trajectories diverged. Matched reassignments of complete expression trajectories showed more full-series organization than expected in S. lycopersicum and Arabidopsis, but not in P. patens. Codon-preference-weighted abundance and expression breadth also changed through infection, although their directions were not universal. Across systems, large non-translation contributors repeatedly carried ATP-synthase/respiratory and extracellular annotations, although their timing and companion functions differed. Infection-associated transcriptional reallocation therefore repeatedly restructures the synonymous composition of the inferred fungal transcript pool. This establishes a dynamic allocation phenotype and a basis for testing consequences for RNA stability and translation during host-pathogen interactions.
affiliations: Louisiana State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Global Data Fitting Enables Kinetic Dissection of Cullin-RING Ligase-Catalyzed Ubiquitylation: From Substrate Priming to Poly-ubiquitin Chain Formation
papers.abstract: The discovery and characterization of the ubiquitin system was founded on classical enzymology approaches that established fundamental principles of protein ubiquitylation. Cullin-RING ligases (CRLs) represent the largest class of human ubiquitin ligases, yet detailed enzymology of these multi-subunit assemblies has lagged behind other systems such as nucleic acid polymerases. Here, we employed pre-steady state kinetics and global data fitting using KinTek Explorer to systematically investigate the kinetic parameters controlling CRL-dependent ubiquitin transfer. Using a well-characterized in vitro reconstituted system exploring CUL2-dependent CRLs, we modeled substrate priming, showing that the system is highly amenable to global fitting of kinetic data. The results show that product dissociation from the CRL is significantly slower than substrate dissociation, explaining previously reported slow steady-state ubiquitylation rates. Extending this framework to poly-ubiquitin chain formation revealed catalytic efficiencies 15-42-fold greater than substrate priming. Comparative analysis of CUL1-dependent and CUL2-dependent systems showed remarkably similar kinetic parameters, including the Km of ubiquitin-carrying enzyme for CRLs, despite differences in substrate receptor and enzyme architecture. We further examined drug-induced neo-substrate ubiquitylation using the pomalidomide-CRBN-SALL4 system, revealing atypical kinetics characterized by rapid ubiquitin transfer paired with an elevated Km, ultimately yielding catalytic efficiencies comparable to natural substrates. The findings establish pre-steady state kinetics and global data fitting as powerful enzymological tools for dissecting CRL-dependent ubiquitylation across different CRL families and substrate contexts, with important implications for understanding both physiological ubiquitylation and therapeutic targeted protein degradation strategies.
affiliations: University of Nevada, Las Vegas (corresponding author)

papers.title: Commensal Engineered Living Materials for Sustained Secretome Delivery and Wound Healing
papers.abstract: Using living cells as dynamic biological factories offers immense potential for the continuous, localized production of therapeutic proteins within compromised tissues. This strategy is particularly compelling for treating chronic non-healing wounds, which lack therapeutics that are able to function effectively in the inflammatory microenvironment. Commensal bacteria have been shown to promote healing in these hostile microenvironments, yet applying live microbes directly onto compromised tissue is clinically unfeasible due off-target safety risks and engraftment challenges. Herein, we establish a well-defined commensal Engineered Living Material (cELM) that allows encapsulation, retention, function, and delivery of native beneficial bacteria for localized production and release of a pro-healing secretome over weeks. We specifically encapsulated a pro-healing human wound bacterial isolate, Alcaligenes faecalis, using biocompatible, click-reactive hydrogel building blocks (thiol- or vinyl-sulfone-functionalized multi-arm poly(ethylene glycol)) and systematically varied the density of the polymer network and of the encapsulated bacteria to establish design rules for creating pro-healing cELMs. Physical confinement in the hydrogel network ensured bacterial biocontainment, while the hydrogel mesh size still permitted diffusion of the therapeutic secretome. Notably, controlling encapsulation density revealed an inverse relationship wherein lower cell densities yielded significantly enhanced per-cell metabolic activity and provided sustained production of pro-healing secreted factors. In a murine diabetic wound model, these A. faecalis cELMs shielded the encapsulated bacteria from host clearance, maintained biocontainment, accelerated re-epithelialization, and improved wound bed maturity. Together, these findings establish design principles for cELMs that couple bacterial biocontainment with sustained secretome delivery, providing a promising platform for localized treatment of chronic wounds.
affiliations: University of Delaware (corresponding author)

papers.title: From Fill to Freeze: Redesigning homeRNA to Enable Robust Sampling and Scalable Downstream Processing Workflows for Remote Blood Transcriptomics
papers.abstract: In-person research can introduce barriers to participation, including proximity to a study site and scheduling constraints. Our lab developed the homeRNA platform to address these barriers, enabling remote blood collection and RNA stabilization for transcriptomic research. To increase the applicability of homeRNA for large-scale studies, a redesigned version was developed with modifications to 1) improve usability for both participants and downstream processing laboratories, 2) allow for high-throughput manufacturing, and 3) extend the shelf life of the stabilizer tube. In this work, we systematically tested this design against anticipated stresses that can occur throughout a remote study (e.g., high temperature exposure during shipment) to identify and characterize its limitations. We found that the homeRNA device can be prepared and stored at room temperature at least three months in advance of sampling with continued shelf life analysis underway. We also found that the homeRNA platform produces RNA of sufficient quality for downstream transcriptomic analysis under standard shipping durations (i.e., 2 days in transit) and ambient-to-high temperature conditions (i.e., 25-40 {degrees}C) and that RNA quality is unaffected by variable blood volumes collected by participants (mean RIN=7.8 in blood volumes 0.25-1 mL). Lastly, we also found that samples can be stored in typical cold storage temperatures and even up to standard room temperature for at least 4 weeks (mean RIN=8.1 after 4 weeks of storage at -80 to 20 {degrees}C). This work validates that the new homeRNA platform is robust to many of the expected stresses that samples can experience during remote studies.
affiliations: University of Washington (corresponding author)

papers.title: scCont: Interpretable Contrastive Learning for Functional Characterization of Cellular State Transitions
papers.abstract: Timecourse single-cell RNA (scRNA) datasets have become indispensable biological tools for studying and uncovering the underlying regulatory processes driving continuous cell-state transitions such as the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition. However, these highly fluid, non-linear gene program dynamics remain difficult to disentangle. While deep neural network models can effectively map complex topologies, they are biological black boxes, lacking the gene-level interpretability required by experimental practitioners. Here, we introduce scCont, a fully unsupervised contrastive learning framework for extracting interpretable functional transition units from scRNA-seq data. Rather than relying on explicit temporal labels or clustering priors, scCont uses an unsupervised k-nearest neighbors approach to project local transcriptomic neighborhoods into a low-dimensional embedding. During post-training analysis, scCont employs Shapley network attribution to determine gene-latent relationships, mapping latent dimensions directly into functional gene programs. We quantitatively and qualitatively validate this representation by demonstrating that scCont captures biologically interpretable dynamics more effectively than baseline methods such as LDVAE. Evaluated across 13 diverse EMT timecourse datasets and four simulated datasets, scCont exposes interpretable functional dynamics and effectively maps context-dependent functional groups, helping to bridge the gap between deep learning representation and translational biological utility. scCont is an open source software available on GitHub (https://github.com/nramani611/scCont).
affiliations: Boston University (corresponding author)

papers.title: QUANTA: A quantum annealing framework for species tree estimation using weighted quartet amalgamation
papers.abstract: Reconstructing species trees from genome-scale data is challenging due to pervasive gene tree discordance. Maximizing quartet consistency is a widely used approach for species tree inference from multi-locus data. Quartet amalgamation approaches, such as Quartet Fiduccia-Mattheyse (QFM) and Quartet MaxCut (QMC) families, have emerged as highly accurate quartet-based species tree inference techniques, but their reliance on computationally expensive classical bipartitioning heuristics, such as Fiduccia-Mattheyses (FM) and MaxCut, limits their scalability. Here, we introduce QUANTA, a quantum annealing-based quartet amalgamation method that, to our knowledge, represents the first quantum formulation of quartet-based approaches and the first species tree estimation method for multi-locus data that runs on real quantum hardware. At the core of QUANTA is a novel, general formulation of weighted quartet bipartitioning as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem that enables quantum annealing to replace the classical bipartitioning strategies underlying the QFM and QMC families of methods. We prove that our formulation uses the minimum possible number of qubits to represent bipartitions and that its energy function correctly orders satisfied, deferred, and violated quartets for any positive penalty weights. We implemented QUANTA on real D-Wave quantum annealing hardware, and evaluated it on a wide range of simulated and biological datasets. QUANTA achieves accuracy comparable to the state-of-the-art methods, including ASTRAL and wQFM, under challenging evolutionary conditions. We also reanalyzed several biological datasets, including the avian phylogenomic dataset comprising 14,446 genes across 48 genomes, on which QUANTA reconstructed a species tree with a higher quartet score than wQFM. Remarkably, despite running on current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware, QUANTA's bipartition technique achieved 4100x speedup over the FM bipartitioning technique in wQFM on bipartition containing 90-200 taxa, while maintaining comparable tree accuracy. By establishing a theoretically grounded, hardware-independent quantum optimization framework for weighted quartet amalgamation, QUANTA opens a new direction for quantum-assisted phylogenomics and provides a foundation for increasingly scalable and accurate species tree estimation as quantum computing hardware advances. QUANTA is publicly available at https://github.com/QuitttCat/QUANTA-Phylogenomics.
affiliations: Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Theoretical prediction of assembly contiguity
papers.abstract: Theoretical methods for predicting the performance of assembly algorithms have the potential to guide experimental design on a scale that simulations cannot. A fundamental question of experimental design is how deep to sequence in order to obtain an assembly with long-enough contigs. More precisely, given a certain read length and coverage, what is the expected contig length that an assembler would produce on a given genome? The foundational work of Lander and Waterman tackled this question, but their method is not applicable to modern high-throughput sequencing. In this paper, we derive what we call a Z-value, which is a formula that takes as input the read length, coverage, and basic properties of the genome, and returns a prediction of the mean contig length produced by a simple single-k assembler on error-free data. We show on a benchmark of 14 genomes that the Z-value is highly accurate, with a mean absolute prediction error of less than 2 percent. We further show how this formula can be used to determine the best choice of k for the assembler and how to choose a coverage level that gives contig lengths within a desired fraction of the optimal. Finally, we show how the Z-value can also predict the performance of a more complicated assembler like Velvet and how it can be used to guide the choice between instruments when there is a tradeoff between coverage and read length and the budget is limited.
affiliations: The Pennsylvania State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Virtual dynamics of spatiotemporal single-cell interactions
papers.abstract: Building virtual cells and tissues requires reconstructing how interacting cell populations evolve in space and time, yet spatial omics experiments provide only sparse snapshots of this process. Here, we introduce CytoBridge, a computational method that reconstructs continuous virtual cell dynamics from discrete spatial transcriptomic data. Starting from a joint transcriptomic-spatial space, CytoBridge learns stochastic trajectories of cell states, positions, and population sizes through an unbalanced mean-field Schrodinger bridge formulation that explicitly incorporates cell-cell interaction as a dynamical driver. A time-varying interaction graph built from spatial proximity and ligand-receptor priors allows the velocity to be decomposed into an interaction component estimated from observed neighborhoods and ligand-receptor features, and an intrinsic-context component that captures intrinsic regulatory processes and unmeasured contextual influences. Applied to five datasets across three spatial transcriptomics platforms and spanning development, regeneration, and neurodegeneration, CytoBridge accurately generates tissue dynamics at unmeasured time points, follows ligand-receptor signaling through measured and unmeasured stages, and supports hypothesis-generating in silico perturbation. CytoBridge provides a general method for turning heterogeneous spatiotemporal transcriptomic measurements into continuously evolving virtual tissues.
affiliations: Peking University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Contrastive Learning Improves Generalization on M2OR Olfactory Binding Dataset
papers.abstract: Olfaction-based biosensors stand to have profound impacts in fields such as medical diagnostics, national security, and drug discovery. A promising mode of vapor phase biodetection mimics volatile organic compound-olfactory receptor (VOC-OR) interactions with target-specific protein or peptide probes; however, lack of experimental coverage remains a core bottleneck. Current computational approaches aim to improve prediction of VOC-OR binding to reduce experimental burden, and current machine learning approaches fail to demonstrate a level of generalization that addresses current engineering challenges. Here, using the Molecular to Olfactory Dataset (M2OR) and Insect Olfactory Binding Protein Database (iOBPdb) datasets, data partitioning methods and their performance are evaluated on a neural network and contrastive learning framework on such VOC-OR binding datasets, varying: model training, architecture, and structure of the input data distribution. It was found that holding out certain chemical or proteomic motifs from the training data diminished model performance with a two layer neural network model. The model was able to generalize to state of the art performance (0.88 AUCROC) on every data split by applying a contrastive learning objective defined by shared molecular constituents and a stochastic sampler. This suggests the contrastive objective provides a strong inductive bias for neural networks to predict novel VOC-OR pairs. These findings highlight that model performance on pairwise biological interaction datasets can be inflated through identity leakage from constituent overlap, and emphasize the need for more robust evaluation protocols. Furthermore, we show contrastive regularization mitigates dataset degeneracy through enforcement of compatibility in the models latent geometry that may extend to other binder target-datasets where identity leakage confounds evaluation.
affiliations: University of Washington (corresponding author)

papers.title: QRAFT: Scaling coalescent-based species tree inference to one million taxa
papers.abstract: Species tree inference from multi-locus data under the multispecies coalescent has not kept pace with phylogenomic datasets that now span hundreds of thousands of species. We present QRAFT, a statistically consistent method for estimating species trees by maximizing quartet support on phylogenomic datasets at unprecedented scales. For n taxa and k gene trees, QRAFT achieves near-linear running time of O(kn log^2 n) when its recursion is balanced, which is within a polylogarithmic factor of the O(kn) time required simply to read the input. It also achieves asymptotically optimal O(kn) memory, so its memory requirements grow only linearly with the input size. QRAFT infers a million-taxon species tree from 1,000 genes in just three hours using only 298 GB of RAM, 64 CPU threads, and no GPUs. We estimate that the same analysis with ASTRAL-MP, a scalable parallel implementation of the widely used method ASTRAL, would take about 36 years (>100,000 times longer) and require prohibitive amounts of memory, far beyond practical computational limits. QRAFT maintains accuracy comparable to, and in many cases better than, leading species tree estimation methods. Notably, QRAFT reconstructed a microbial tree of life comprising 199,330 genomes in just a few hours using modest CPU resources. Thus, QRAFT brings highly accurate statistically consistent coalescent-based species tree inference to the unprecedented million-taxon regime and enables phylogenomic analyses towards the scale of the tree of life. QRAFT is publicly available at https://github.com/risenfromashes/qraft.
affiliations: Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Towards a foundation model for raw nanopore signal through discrete tokenization
papers.abstract: Nanopore sequencing reads nucleic acids as changes in ionic current that carry information beyond the base sequence. Self-supervised pretrained models have advanced genomic sequence modeling and single-cell analysis, but remain underexplored for raw nanopore signals, which are continuous and lack a native token vocabulary. Here we present Brieno, an approach combining reconstruction-based tokenization through residual vector quantization with a Transformer for contextual representation learning. We pretrain the Transformer using masked-token prediction on raw nanopore signals from 118 million reads. With frozen or fine-tuned features, the model identifies species without requiring reference genomes. It complements Dorado by accurately classifying reads left unclassified in native-barcode demultiplexing, approaches Dorado's basecalling performance across six genomes, and exceeds Dorado's specialized 5-methylcytosine model as well as a dedicated 6-methyladenine caller. Brieno also supports accurate CpG methylation detection with limited labeled data. Across tasks, pretrained contextual representations improve downstream performance over non-pretrained baselines and generalize across sequencing runs. Together, these findings support self-supervised pretraining as a basis for transferable representations of raw nanopore signals.
affiliations: University of Helsinki (corresponding author)

papers.title: DisCell: Separating Spillover from Niche Response in Spatial Transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics at single-cell resolution measures every cell in its place in the tissue, but diffusion and segmentation errors also add transcripts of neighboring cells to a cell's counts. This spillover makes a cell resemble its neighbors, and a response to the niche makes cells in the same niche resemble each other. Both tie a cell's expression to its surroundings. The count data alone cannot tell the two apart. Findings from single-cell transcriptomes, such as a gene program that is higher in one niche than in another or signaling genes that change depending on the neighborhood, may therefore be artifacts of spillover. Current models describe a cell by its intrinsic state together with either its niche response or spillover, but none models all three. We present DisCell, the first method that models all three components jointly and measures how robust each finding is to spillover. DisCell is a generative model that describes single-cell gene expression profiles in terms of two latent variables, an intrinsic state and a response to the niche, and adds spillover from its neighbors as a separate term. DisCell fits the model at increasing levels of spillover and recomputes each finding on the spillover-free expression to see how much spillover it withstands. DisCell also estimates the most spillover a section can contain, and a finding that holds even at that amount is not explained by spillover. In simulated tissue, DisCell recovers each cell's intrinsic state and response and tells findings created by spillover apart from genuine responses. On five sections of ovarian and lung tissue, the intrinsic state keeps more of each cell's own properties, measured by its cell-cycle phase, than any competing method that holds as little of its neighborhood. Within each cell type, the model partitions the variation of each gene into intrinsic state, niche response and spillover. Using DisCell, we rank findings about niches by their robustness to spillover and confirm that a previously reported finding withstands spillover, that esophageal cancer cells in niches infiltrated by immune or stromal cells express more of an epithelial-mesenchymal transition program. DisCell also predicts what the gene expression of a cell type would be in another niche, with its spillover part separated, at lower error on most tasks than the competing method built for this purpose. Training the model takes under ten minutes on one consumer GPU for sections of up to 400,000 cells.
affiliations: KTH royal institute of technology stockholm, SciLifeLab (corresponding author)

papers.title: Growing a Root from Its Genome : Emergent Tissue Layers and Zones in a GPU-Native Simulation of the Arabidopsis Root Tip
papers.abstract: Models of the Arabidopsis root tip usually take its cell identities as given. Here we grow a root tip from a single genome. In a two-dimensional median section, every cell reads the same network of 62 genes (26 core genes from an earlier, unpublished model of callus and 36 added for the root) and starts with the same expression; the only spatial cues are the polarity of auxin transport, auxin from the shoot and the free surface. Identities and zones are never given to the simulation; they are read from gene expression. Cells are polygons of a shared mesh, relaxed towards mechanical equilibrium under turgor at every step. In 48 simulated hours, a tip-shaped template grows into a root of 3 000-4 500 cells with epidermis, cortex, endodermis, pericycle and stele in order along most of its length, SHORT-ROOT and SCARECROW in the endodermis, an auxin maximum, a quiescent centre and a cap at its tip, and meristem, elongation and mature zones. A WOX5 gate built from published interactions and one hypothesis keeps a quiescent centre to 48 h in 17 of 20 simulated roots that were not used for tuning (85%; Wilson 95% interval 64-95%; criteria fixed before the run), against 9 of 20 roots used for tuning, before the gate. The niche is not maintained beyond 48 h: grown on to 73 h, only 6 of these 20 roots still have a quiescent centre (30%; 15-52%). All pre-registered criteria hold in only 1 of 20 roots, because the quiescent centre is too wide at 0 h; without that count, 12 of 20. The meristem is too long, and cortical cells made after the start of growth elongate only three- to four-fold instead of eightto thirty-fold, a limit set in large part by the numerical growth scheme. Mutants are a major weakness: several look like their published phenotype, but an exploratory re-run of a mutant benchmark fixed in advance for our first model passes one of nine predictions. Nor does the root regenerate: cut near its tip, it re-forms an auxin maximum and a columella but no quiescent centre. On a first, simpler model and without any polarity cue, a mass of identical cells still sorts into concentric layers and, when PIN carriers follow the auxin flux, concentrates auxin into a few foci, but forms no stem-cell niche: the genome lacks a lateral inhibition between foci. We state the limitations and the next stages.

papers.title: Predicting Transcriptional Responses to Unseen Compounds through Context Modeling and Multi-View Transfer
papers.abstract: Predicting drug-induced transcriptional responses could support in silico screening of new compounds, yet existing models barely use the compound: on a drug-blind L1000 benchmark, removing the drug input from seven published models changes accuracy by at most 0.012 Pearson correlation. They capture shared cellular and experimental variation while overlooking the compound-specific signals that distinguish drug effects. We present UnDetect, a framework that separates contextual variation from compound effects to predict responses to transcriptionally unprofiled compounds. UnDetect integrates chemical structure, annotated targets, mechanisms of action and Cell Painting morphology into a normalized multi-view kernel that accommodates incomplete compound information, and transfers residual responses within and across profiled cell lines, so that pharmacological and phenotypic relationships inform predictions beyond chemical similarity. On a drug-blind benchmark, where the paired control reveals the assay plate, UnDetect is the only model to beat a network that ignores the compound, in every fold; on a within-plate score that is zero for any compound-blind prediction, it reaches 0.117 against 0.092 for the strongest published model. On DeepCE's benchmark it reaches 0.602 Pearson correlation against the reported 0.491. Transfer across cell lines improves 28 of 28 LINCS L1000 and, at the two higher doses, 47 and 49 of 50 Tahoe-100M cell-line evaluations. These results show that separating context from compound effects and integrating complementary compound information improves transcriptional prediction and extends the utility of perturbation atlases for virtual screening.
