papers.title: Single-cell atlas uncovers layer 4 heterogeneity and functional gradients in rhesus macaque visual cortex
papers.abstract: Non-human primates like rhesus macaques are pivotal models for decoding human visual cortex physiology and disorders. However, there is a lack of high-resolution transcriptomic atlases comparing distinct areas of the visual cortex in macaque. Here, we developed BrainSPACE, an innovative pipeline for rapid and precise brain tissue banking, to sample visual cortex areas: V1, V2, V4, MT, and TEO. We applied single-nucleus RNA-sequencing (snRNA-seq) to unravel neuronal diversity in BrainSPACE-banked V1 and V4 areas ( ~ 100,000 nuclei). We uncovered conserved GABAergic neuron profiles but stark area-specific diversity in principal neurons, featuring seven unique layer 4 subtypes in V1 and one in V4. Complementary smFISH validated transcriptional gradients across these areas, aligning with ventral and dorsal stream hierarchies. Gene ontology analyses highlighted plasticity-related pathways in unique layer 4 subtypes, with genes like NTNG1 and NLGN1 linked to neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism and schizophrenia. Our insights bridge molecular architecture to visual processing, offering an interactive atlas for community use. By revealing how layer 4 heterogeneity drives hierarchical specialization, our work advances primate brain mapping and informs therapeutic strategies for vision-related pathologies. Macaques are pivotal models for decoding human visual processing, but there is a lack of area-specific data on their visual cortex. Here, authors show area-specific diversity in principal neurons along the visual processing hierarchy.

papers.title: Engineering phosphorescence and pH-responsive fluorescence of molecular luminophores and elastomers
papers.abstract: Organic ultralong room-temperature phosphorescence (RTP) enables time-gated optical readout by separating long-lived triplet emission from short-lived autofluorescence. However, coupling RTP with biochemical responsiveness at both the molecular and materials levels remains a fundamental challenge due to the lack of a luminophore-intrinsic design principle for linking chemical responsiveness to triplet-state photophysics and the conflict between rigid, shielded microenvironments and deformable polymer matrices. Here we present an ArKMK design paradigm that electronically couples an aromatic ketone to a pH-responsive α-methyleneketone within a carbonyl-rich framework, yielding homophthalic anhydride (HA) and homophthalimides as a family of luminophores that integrate pH responsiveness with RTP. To preserve long-lived emission in elastomeric matrices, we further develop a two-pots-in-one (TPiO) strategy that separately preforms hydrophilic and hydrophobic segments and then co-reacts them to generate phase-separated microenvironments in biodegradable polyesters. The resulting materials reconcile mechanical compliance with triplet-state stabilization, while covalently integrating ArKMK luminophores through the same esterification chemistry. These biodegradable polyesters enable time-gated subcutaneous imaging, gastrointestinal tracking and wound-status reporting through coupled RTP and pH-indicating fluorescence. This work establishes a molecular-to-polymer framework for integrating pH responsiveness with long-lived triplet emission in soft, biodegradable materials. Combining organic room temperature phosphorescence with biochemical responses is desirable, but challenging. Here, the authors report the development of a design combining an aromatic ketone and a methylene ketone to give materials with room temperature phosphorescence and pH-responsive fluorescence.

papers.title: Distributed range adaptation in human parietal encoding of numbers
papers.abstract: The brain’s representations are encoded in the collective activity of neural populations whose non-monotonic tuning properties define the population code. Adaptive behavior calls for flexible retuning of this code as stimulus statistics change across contexts. Yet how such adaptation occurs is unknown. Using fMRI during a numerosity-estimation task with variable number ranges, we show that number representations in human parietal cortex dynamically recalibrate to context, enabling context-sensitive behavioral accuracy. The tuning properties of neural populations collectively shift and rescale with the range. This distributed range adaptation achieves efficient coding in real time: neural precision scales with the range and predicts corresponding changes in behavioral precision. Individuals with stronger neural adaptation show larger behavioral adjustments. These findings extend static sensory efficient coding to adaptive representations of abstract magnitudes. Such flexible population tuning may constitute a canonical mechanism of encoding networks that enables the brain to sustain precise, adaptive behavior. Using fMRI, the authors show that numerosity-sensitive neural populations in human parietal cortex shift and rescale their tuning to match the range of numbers encountered. This neural flexibility supports behavioral adaptability.

papers.title: Disrupting the semantic network shifts activity to domain-general brain regions
papers.abstract: Semantic processing relies on flexible interactions between specialized lexico-semantic regions and domain-general control networks, particularly under challenging conditions. Using transcranial magnetic stimulation interleaved with functional magnetic resonance imaging, we investigated acute network adaptation when the left posterior middle temporal gyrus—a core lexico-semantic region—was perturbed during lexico-semantic decisions in 25 healthy participants. High-intensity transcranial magnetic stimulation over the posterior middle temporal gyrus induced task-specific activity increases across semantic control and lexical retrieval areas, as well as remote domain-general regions. Critically, increased local activity at the stimulation site correlated with slower reaction times, whereas greater upregulation in domain-general frontal regions was associated with less disrupted semantic performance. These findings indicate that acute semantic disruption triggers immediate, flexible recruitment of domain-general control areas consistent with the maintenance of task performance, highlighting the brain’s capacity to dynamically adapt to interference. Our findings contribute to the current understanding of putative compensatory network-level mechanisms supporting lexico-semantic cognition. Disrupting a key language region prompts increased activity in widespread brain regions. Stronger engagement of frontal control regions helps preserve cognitive performance, revealing the brain’s capacity to adapt to interference in real time.

papers.title: Conveyor-mode electron shuttling through a T-junction in Si/SiGe
papers.abstract: Conveyor-mode shuttling in gated Si/SiGe devices enables adiabatic transfer of single electrons, electron patterns and spin qubits confined in quantum dots across several microns with a scalable number of signal lines. To realize their full potential, linear shuttle lanes must connect into a two-dimensional grid with controllable routing. We introduce a T-junction device linking two independently driven shuttle lanes. Electron routing across the junction requires no extra control lines beyond the four channels per conveyor belt. We measure an inter-lane charge transfer fidelity of $$F={100.0000000}_{-9\times 1{0}^{-7}}^{+0}\,\%$$ at an instantaneous electron velocity of 270 mm s−1. The filling of 54 quantum dots is controlled by simple atomic pulses, allowing us to swap electron patterns, laying the groundwork for a native spin-qubit SWAP gate. This T-junction establishes a path towards scalable, two-dimensional quantum computing architectures with flexible spin qubit routing for quantum error correction. Conveyor-mode electron shuttling offers a scalable route to connecting spin qubits, but extension to two-dimensional architectures requires reliable routing between shuttle lanes. Here, the authors demonstrate a silicon T-junction enabling near-unity fidelity transfer of single electrons between conveyor mode channels.

papers.title: Energy-guided combinatorial co-optimization of antibody affinity and stability
papers.abstract: Affinity maturation is an essential process in antibody engineering. Although powerful, it is iterative, time-consuming, and can result in trade-offs, where affinity is gained at the cost of important properties, such as specificity and stability. We present a scalable strategy, called LAffAb, that starts from a crystallographic structure of the antibody-antigen complex and introduces combinations of mutations to the antibody to optimize the energy of the complex. A combinatorial library comprising 7000 variants with up to nine mutations results in gains of up to 30-fold in affinity while co-optimizing stability. Surprisingly, the library does not converge on a single solution, instead favoring diverse variants with a high mutational load. Small-scale screening of 10 designs against a potential drug target improves affinity by an order-of-magnitude while maintaining high developability. We also apply LAffAb to improve the developability of a therapeutic antibody while maintaining affinity. We envision that LAffAb can be used to design stable, specific, and high-affinity binders and to improve our understanding of sequence, structure, and function relationships in antibodies. Here, Tennenhouse et al. develop LAffAb, a structure-based method for designing CDR mutations to improve affinity and developability. By filtering mutations predicted to disrupt stability and foldability, LAffAb enables accurate, one-shot design.

papers.title: Mannitol-stimulated Copeptin for diagnosing Arginine Vasopressin Deficiency: a randomized controlled proof of concept and a single-arm pilot study
papers.abstract: Differentiating arginine vasopressin (AVP) deficiency from primary polydipsia is challenging. The most accurate test, hypertonic saline–stimulated copeptin, requires intensive monitoring. Intravenous mannitol stimulates AVP release and may provide a simpler alternative. In a randomized double-blind crossover trial, 22 healthy adults received mannitol and placebo in random order, of whom 21 were included in the primary analysis. In a pilot study, 10 patients with AVP deficiency and 10 with primary polydipsia received mannitol. The primary outcome was copeptin after mannitol infusion. Mannitol resulted in a 2.29-fold higher copeptin at 90 minutes (+6.4 pmol/L (95% CI: +5.2, +7.7; p <0.001)) than after placebo at mean baseline copeptin levels in healthy adults. In patients, copeptin after 30 minutes was 11.7 pmol/L (95% CI: 6.5, 17.0) higher in primary polydipsia than in AVP deficiency. Mannitol infusion shows promise as a new diagnostic approach. Larger confirmatory studies are required to validate both the optimal diagnostic cut-off and patient safety. Trial Registration number: NCT06542198. Distinguishing arginine vasopressin deficiency from primary polydipsia can be difficult and current tests are challenging. Here, the authors show that mannitol-stimulated copeptin may offer a simple, rapid, safe and accurate diagnostic alternative.

papers.title: Non-van der Waals superlattices reconcile the strength and conductivity of MXene films
papers.abstract: Conventional strategies for assembling macroscopic MXene films require excessive binders, such as polymer chains or cellulose, to bridge adjacent nanosheets, which undermine intrinsic functionalities and reduce MXenes to mere conductive fillers. Here, we present a strategy that leverages the intrinsic structural evolution of MXenes to achieve non-van der Waals superlattice roll-ups, simultaneously enhancing interlayer stress transfer and establishing efficient conductive pathways, thereby overcoming the traditional trade-off between mechanical and electrical performance in MXene films. The resulting scalable high-performance MXene films exhibit remarkable tensile strength (598 MPa) and electrical conductivity (13682 S/cm), while also demonstrating excellent electromagnetic interference shielding. However, a systematic understanding on the reinforcement mechanisms across multiple scales is lacking which limits the rational design of high-performance MXene films. To address this, we systematically elucidate the complex reinforcement mechanisms across multiple scales, from crack deflection at the microscopic level, to dynamic slip and energy dissipation at the nanoscale, and local charge rearrangement through molecular interactions. This work establishes a multiscale blueprint for mechanical enhancement spanning microscopic, nanoscopic, and molecular regimes, representing a significant advance in the development of high-performance films. This study develops non-van der Waals superlattice roll-ups to enhance MXene films, overcoming the strength-conductivity trade-off and revealing multiscale reinforcement mechanisms for advanced multifunctional materials

papers.title: Silicon photonics provides a unified solution for all-distance optical communications
papers.abstract: Optical links underpin global communications from chip-to-chip interconnects to transoceanic fibre networks. Conventional architectures remain distance-dependent: long-haul systems rely on coherent transmission for high spectral efficiency and capacity, while short-reach links favour intensity modulation due to hardware complexity and power constraints. This divide impedes scalability for AI-driven intra-data-centre traffic and low-latency, flexible cloud-to-edge connectivity. Here we demonstrate a unified silicon photonic coherent solution for all-distance optical communications. By employing an ultralow-loss silicon nitride external cavity, we achieve 70 mW of direct laser output with a sub-kHz linewidth and 13.7% wall-plug efficiency. Paired with silicon photonic transceivers, this platform enables short-distance transmission without optical amplification across 256 wavelength channels, corresponding to an aggregate data rate of 81.92 Tb/s, as well as transmission exceeding 4400 km. It also supports wavelength switching and transmission re-establishment at tens-of-microseconds timescales. These results indicate the potential to simplify optical interfaces and enable flexible wavelength-routed connectivity. The authors demonstrate a silicon-photonic coherent platform using a high-power tunable laser and silicon-photonic transceivers, enabling broadband unamplified short-reach transmission, links beyond 4400 km and rapid wavelength switching.

papers.title: Coordination-directed synthesis of two-dimensional metal-organic covalent organic frameworks
papers.abstract: Metal-organic covalent organic frameworks (MOCOFs) combine the advantages of covalent and metal-organic frameworks, but research remains sparse due to characterization difficulties, leaving unclear whether their formation is covalent- or coordination-directed. To date, only a few three-dimensional MOCOFs have been reported, while two-dimensional (2D) MOCOFs remain unexplored. Here, we strategically synthesize two single-crystal 2D MOCOFs with high porosity, denoted as PUMC-1 and PUMC-2. Leveraging three-dimensional electron diffraction, we are able to elucidate their formation process in detail. First, one-dimensional coordination polymers (1D CPs) are constructed from two sub-building units: tetrakis(4-aminophenyl) porphyrin and cobalt(II) trans-A₂B₂ porphyrin. Second, 1D CPs with covalent extension sites are used to construct two distinct 2D MOCOF conformations via covalent self-assembly under different conditions. Notably, the same 2D MOCOFs can also be directly obtained via one-pot synthesis with the same monomers, providing experimental evidence for a coordination-directed covalent assembly mechanism. This work not only expands the dimensionality of MOCOFs but also opens new avenues in reticular chemistry. Metal-organic covalent organic frameworks (MOCOFs) combine the advantages of covalent and metal-organic frameworks, but two-dimensional (2D) MOCOFs remain unexplored. Here, the authors synthesize two 2D MOCOFs with high porosity and elucidate their formation process in detail.

papers.title: Chemokine and opioid peptide scavenging through constitutive and ligand-induced release of ACKR3-bearing extracellular vesicles
papers.abstract: Atypical chemokine receptors (ACKRs) are non-signaling GPCRs that regulate ligand availability, with ACKR3 functioning as a dual scavenger of chemokines and opioid peptides. Here, we demonstrate that following ligand stimulation, besides the canonical internalization, ACKR3 is released on extracellular vesicles (EVs). ACKR3 was also found on EVs released under basal conditions, although to a lesser extent. These observations were confirmed across multiple cellular contexts, including endogenous systems. Mechanistically, basal and ligand-induced EV release are independent of GRKs and β-arrestin but each relies on different trafficking routes and C-terminal determinants. Ligand-induced EV release is associated with plasma membrane localization and receptor recycling pathways. In contrast, basal EV release is governed by intracellular sorting processes and influenced by receptor ubiquitination and RAMP3. Functionally, EV-associated ACKR3 retains high-affinity ligand binding, enabling sequestration of CXCL12 and opioid peptides and thereby attenuating their signaling through CXCR4 and MOR. We also show that the release on EVs, in particular under basal conditions, is observed for other receptors such as KOR, CXCR4 and several ACKRs. Collectively, these findings establish EVs as regulators in chemokine and opioid systems and as a distinct dimension of ACKR3 and more broadly GPCR biology. Ligand scavenging by ACKR3 is known to rely on intracellular uptake. Here, authors show that ACKR3 is also released on extracellular vesicles as a functional sequestrator of chemokines and opioid peptides, revealing another dimension of regulation.

papers.title: Two distinct α2β1 integrin glycan interactions mediate cell entry of a picornavirus
papers.abstract: Equine rhinitis A virus (ERAV), a picornavirus closely related to foot-and-mouth disease virus, causes respiratory infections in horses. We performed a HEK293T CRISPRi screen and identified integrin α2β1 as a protein receptor for ERAV. Using knock-out cells and pretreating cells with an antibody or soluble receptor, we confirmed the importance of this integrin for infection of multiple cell types, including equine fibroblasts. Cryo-EM and glycoproteomics analyses revealed that ERAV binds integrin α2β1 in its closed conformation by attaching to the β-propeller of the α2 chain, independent of divalent cations, as well as to a high-mannose glycan on α2 N112 and a sialylated glycan on β1 N269. Using glycan knockout and knock-in cells and by reconstituting integrin α2β1-depleted cells with mutant receptors, we demonstrated the importance of these glycans for virus entry. Our results identify a hitherto unseen combination of protein and glycan interactions between a virus and its receptor. Equine rhinitis A virus (ERAV) causes respiratory infections in horses, yet its receptor for binding remained elusive. Using a combination of virological, genetic, structural, and glycoproteomic approaches, Owino et al. show that ERAV utilizes integrin α2β1 as a receptor in a cation-independent manner.

papers.title: Effective enzyme engineering through modeling kinetic parameter changes upon mutations with geometric deep learning
papers.abstract: Quantifying enzyme kinetic parameter changes upon mutations is essential for accelerating enzyme evolution. Current methods focus on predicting absolute values of kinetic parameters (turnover numbers kcat and Michaelis constants Km), yet they fail to accurately capture mutation effects. To our knowledge, no method directly models mutation effects (Δkcat and ΔKm) due to the scarcity of such training data. Moreover, these methods haven’t fully exploited protein structural geometry. Here, we establish a high-quality enzyme mutation effect dataset by pairing wild-type and mutant kinetic parameters measured under identical experimental conditions via a semi-automatic procedure combining language model-assisted parsing and manual verification. Leveraging this dataset, we develop DeltaCata, a Siamese geometric graph neural network to directly predict the changes in kinetic parameters induced by residue substitutions. DeltaCata demonstrates substantial performance improvements over existing methods, especially for enzymes unseen in the training sets. Its utility is further validated through in silico beneficial mutation screening experiments using deep mutational scanning datasets. Finally, we apply DeltaCata to engineer the methyltransferase sGmOMT2, achieving up to a 7.0-fold improvement in catalytic efficiency for in vitro icaritin synthesis. These results suggest the high potential of DeltaCata for industrial enzyme engineering. Predicting how mutations affect enzyme catalytic efficiency remains challenging. Here the authors build a benchmark dataset and develop DeltaCata, a geometric deep learning model that predicts changes in enzyme kinetics and guides enzyme engineering.

papers.title: Opposing microbiome-mediated axes link modifiable lifestyles to health and chronic diseases
papers.abstract: Analyses disentangling the role of the gut microbiome in linking lifestyle factors to health outcomes remain limited. Here, using fecal shotgun metagenomics from 6,803 adults in the Japanese 4D cohort, we identified two opposing microbiome-mediated axes linking lifestyle to health and 15 diseases. A health-associated axis enriched in microbial metabolism of dietary components was linked to plant-based, soy and dairy intake. In contrast, a disease-associated axis, enriched in oral-derived bacteria and pathobionts, was linked to refined carbohydrates and sedentary behavior. Starter culture microorganisms used to ferment foods did not show statistically significant mediation of the observed health effects. Alcohol was associated with both health- and disease-oriented mediation patterns involving microbial host-glycan utilization. Microbiome-defined health- and disease-oriented mediator axes were supported by fecal short-chain fatty acids and plasma cytokines from >1,700 individuals, revealing butyrate-associated anti-inflammatory and pro-inflammatory host profiles, respectively. Microbiome-based prediction (MADE) scores captured lifestyle–microbiome–disease mediation patterns and distinguished individual diseases across 13 independent external cohorts from the United States, China, Sweden, Russia and Australia. We identify the gut microbiome as a key mediator linking lifestyle to health and disease, providing a framework for microbiome-based assessment to guide lifestyle interventions for health promotion and disease prevention. Fecal shotgun metagenomics from 6,803 adults in the Japanese 4D cohort and microbiome-based prediction scores validated across 13 independent and geographically diverse cohorts revealed two opposing microbiome-mediated axes linking lifestyle to health and 15 diseases.

papers.title: Integration and annotation of spatial multi-omic data with DIRAC
papers.abstract: Spatial multi-omic technologies measure multiple molecular layers within intact tissues. Two central challenges are vertical integration, which combines different molecular modalities, and horizontal integration, which aligns cell types across studies. Here we show domain invariant representation through adaptive calibration (DIRAC), a geometric deep learning model that unifies these tasks in a generalized domain adaptation framework. DIRAC learns task-discriminative features that are insensitive to domain shifts caused by batch effects, omic modalities or study sites, enabling a shared embedding space and automated cell-type annotation through label transfer from reference datasets. Across sequencing-based and imaging-based datasets, DIRAC identified a new microvascular proliferation domain in glioblastoma, corrected cortical-layer annotations in severe Alzheimer’s disease, resolved subtle structures in mouse embryos and remained robust to missing data and unseen cell types. We generated mouse spleen and thymus Stereo-CITE-seq data and used DIRAC to reveal thymic T cell migration and splenic immune cell interactions. DIRAC is fast and scales to millions of cells. DIRAC is a geometric deep learning model that enables both vertical and horizontal integration and annotation of spatial multi-omic data.

papers.title: Automated identification of individual birds by song enables multi-year recapture from passive acoustic monitoring data
papers.abstract: Autonomous sensors and machine learning are transforming ecology by enabling large-scale observation of organisms and ecosystems. However, camera traps, audio recorders and other sensors currently produce species-level detections. Tracking individuals continues to require invasive, high-effort capture–mark–recapture. Here we introduce an automated, general approach that identifies individual animals in passive acoustic recordings based on individually distinctive vocalizations. We train a convolutional neural network to extract salient features from audio recordings using a location-prediction task, then apply dimensionality reduction and clustering on features to achieve song-based individual identification. We identify individuals not included in the training data with 96% accuracy. We apply this approach to track 405 male ovenbirds (Seiurus aurocapilla) from 126 locations across 4 years, then model abundance and apparent survival. We provide open-source code to facilitate applications of our approach to other species. Performing automated individual identification on passive acoustic datasets will support the study of population trajectories and inform proactive ecosystem management to prevent biodiversity loss. A machine learning-based method distinguishes individual ovenbirds in the wild by their distinct vocalizations, collected by passive acoustic recording.

papers.title: Unlocking spatial diversity of circular RNAs with abcFISH
abcFISH enables multiplexed, single-molecule visualization of circular RNA spatial heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Understanding the subcellular localization of RNAs is critical for their functions, but visualizing circular RNAs (circRNAs) has been hindered by their sequence overlap with linear counterparts. Here we developed amplicon-based circRNA fluorescence in situ hybridization (abcFISH), which uses an optimized rolling-circle amplification strategy targeting back-splicing junction sites for robust, high specificity, single-molecule circRNA imaging. abcFISH enables quantitative, multiplexed imaging in cells and tissues, allowing us to reveal alternative circularization patterns from the single locus, uncover cell-type-specific circRNA expression linked to combinatorial effects of RNA-binding proteins, map distinct spatial distribution patterns of circRNAs in neurons and brain tissues, and show functional colocalization of circRNA Cdr1as and long noncoding RNA Cyrano. We further applied abcFISH to validate therapeutic double-stranded circRNA aptamers, simultaneously visualizing AAV-delivered double-stranded circRNA aptamers and the resulting reduction in astrocyte infiltration around transduced cells. Collectively, abcFISH provides a robust, user-friendly toolkit for deciphering circRNA localization and function in vivo. abcFISH is an imaging method for multiplexed, single‑molecule circular RNA detection in cells and in vivo, revealing single-cell expression heterogeneity and direct therapeutic efficacy of circular aptamers.

papers.title: Germinal centers as evolutionary islands
Multiscale multimodal integration of spatial omics through a deep generative model with CORAL
papers.abstract: Spatial omics enable the in situ characterization of tissue architecture by measuring molecular modalities. However, integrating these datasets remains challenging due to differences in spatial resolution, cross-modal alignment and molecular coverage. Here we show that Cross-scale spatial Omics Registration and Analysis via graph Learning (CORAL), a probabilistic deep generative model, leverages graph attention to integrate diverse spatial transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic and epigenomic data across spatial scales. CORAL jointly models high-resolution datasets with limited molecular coverage and low-resolution genome-wide datasets, generating unified representations with broad molecular coverage and high spatial resolution. Across synthetic and experimental datasets from diverse tissues and platforms, CORAL accurately identifies spatial domains, predicts high-resolution molecular profiles, detects spatially variable genes and infers cell–cell interactions. Applied to spatial transcriptomic and proteomic data from hepatocellular carcinoma patients before and after immunotherapy, CORAL identified organized immune-cell subsets and signaling pathways associated with therapeutic resistance. These results demonstrate CORAL’s broad applicability for resolving tissue organization and clinically relevant multicellular interactions. Cross-scale spatial Omics Registration and Analysis via graph Learning is a deep generative model that integrates multiscale spatial multi-omics data using graph-attention aggregation mechanisms, enabling a comprehensive spatial analysis.

papers.title: An information-theoretic framework for inferring T cell dynamics from single-cell RNA and T cell receptor sequencing
papers.abstract: Single-cell T cell receptor (TCR) repertoire sequencing enables simultaneous profiling of gene expression and TCR sequences, providing a coregistered measure of T cell phenotypic diversity and clonal dynamics. However, principled probabilistic frameworks for joint modeling of clonotype and phenotype have remained limited. Here we introduce TCRi, a hierarchical Bayesian information-theoretic framework that infers the joint probability distribution between genetic clonotype and transcriptional phenotype from paired single-cell transcriptomic and TCR sequencing data. TCRi treats phenotype assignment as a probabilistic inference problem: a variational autoencoder embeds single-cell expression into a structured latent space, and a hierarchical Bayesian model learns clonotype-specific phenotype distributions through principled information-sharing across clonotypes, patients and covariates. From these distributions, TCRi computes information-theoretic quantities: clonotypic entropy, phenotypic entropy, phenotypic flux and mutual information between clonotype and phenotype. When TCRi was applied to four real-world datasets comprising 167,118 CD8 T cells from patients with cancer treated with anti-PD-(L)1 immune checkpoint blockade, mutual information emerged as a robust discriminator of therapeutic response. T cells provide a unique setting for quantification of the relationship between genotype and phenotype. The authors introduce TCRi, an information-theoretic framework for this, and find mutual information to be a robust determinant of immunotherapeutic response.

papers.title: AI-guided cancer survival prediction could spare some children high-dose brain radiation
Tau monomers and fibrils escape microglial clearance via distinct cellular mechanisms
papers.abstract: Tauopathies, such as Alzheimer’s disease, are neurodegenerative disorders characterized by the accumulation and propagation of toxic extracellular forms of the microtubule-associated protein tau across brain regions. Microglia, the resident macrophages of the brain, are known for clearing and degrading toxic proteins. However, emerging evidence suggests that microglia also enhance tau spreading. To dissect the molecular mechanisms underlying microglial responses to extracellular tau, we use high-resolution imaging and biochemical approaches to assess the trafficking dynamics of different extracellular tau species in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived microglia. Here we find that tau monomers are internalized by microglia via cell-surface LRP1 receptors but fail to reach terminally degradative lysosomes; instead, they are persistently recycled back to the extracellular space. In contrast, tau fibrils are not internalized and primarily adhere to the cell surface through an HSPG-dependent mechanism, triggering TLR4-mediated microglial activation and the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Heparin or anti-tau treatments dampen tau fibril-mediated microglial activation. In addition, disease-associated variants of the Alzheimer’s disease-related protein APOE reduce microglia–tau interactions, further reducing tau uptake. Together, these findings demonstrate that microglia fail to efficiently clear extracellular tau monomers and fibrils through mechanistically distinct cellular processes, emphasizing the need for tailored therapeutic strategies to enhance extracellular tau clearance in neurodegenerative diseases. Kulkarni et al. show distinct fates of monomeric versus fibrillar tau in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived microglia. Monomeric tau is internalized but does not reach degradative lysosomes; fibrillar tau adheres to the cell surface and triggers microglial activation.

papers.title: Positional replication fork instability drives PARP inhibitor cytotoxicity
papers.abstract: Although poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) show promise for treating homologous recombination-deficient cancers, the observed PARPi hypersensitivity in additional genetic contexts expands their potential use in precision oncology. Yet, the DNA lesions driving PARPi-induced cytotoxicity remain poorly defined. Here we uncover distinct replication-fork lesions in specific genomic regions as key determinants of PARPi cytotoxicity. Using CRISPR screens, we identify that loss of replication-coupled cohesin acetyltransferase ESCO2 confers PARPi hypersensitivity independently of homologous recombination deficiency. Quantitative single-molecule imaging reveals that ESCO2 loss promotes accumulation of G-quadruplex (G4) DNA structures at a subset of replication-associated sites, associated with PARP1 activation and engagement of fork protection factor TIMELESS to mitigate G4-induced stress. Notably, these G4 lesions localize to fragile pericentromeric regions and engage the G4 helicase DDX11. PARP inhibition disrupts this protective G4-processing response by preventing PARP1-dependent engagement of TIMELESS and DDX11, leading to G4 accumulation, DNA damage and chromosomal instability. Together, our findings define the G4–PARP1–TIMELESS–DDX11 axis as a critical safeguard of replication fork stability at hard-to-replicate loci and reveal ESCO2 as a therapeutic target for promoting synthetic lethality in PARPi-treated cancers. Through CRISPR screens and single-molecule imaging, Gupta et al. show that loss of the cohesion acetyltransferase ESCO2 leads to increased G-quadruplex formation at specific regions and drives PARP activation and PARPi hypersensitivity.

papers.title: Basophils boost early antitumor immunity by restraining Treg cells
Spatiotemporal control of CAR-T cell TNF release via tumor-targeted irradiation
papers.abstract: Adoptive chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapies have limited efficacy in solid tumors because of poor infiltration and impaired effector function, whereas radiotherapy is constrained by radioresistance and metastatic spread. Here we show that integrating the spatial precision of ionizing radiation with the biological specificity of CAR-T cells enables localized delivery of the inflammatory cytokine tumor necrosis factor (TNF). We identified radiation-responsive genes in tumor-infiltrating T cells and engineered synthetic radioinducible promoters to drive TNF expression. Human CAR-T cells carrying this construct (riTNF CAR-T cells) secreted high levels of TNF upon irradiation, independently of antigen engagement. In human xenograft and murine tumor models, the combination of riTNF CAR-T cells and local irradiation produced greater tumor regression than either treatment alone or standard CAR-T cells with irradiation. This response was associated with high intratumoral, but not systemic, TNF levels, increased tumor necrosis and apoptosis, vascular disruption and greater CAR-T cell infiltration. These findings establish a platform for spatially and temporally controlled cytokine delivery from engineered CAR-T cells. Masoumi et al. engineered CAR-T cells with a radiation-inducible promoter controlling the expression and local release of the cytokine TNF upon tumor irradiation.

papers.title: IDO1 methylation by EZH2 confers resistance to its targeted therapy in colorectal cancer through tryptophan-kynurenine metabolic rewiring
papers.abstract: Using a genome-wide CRISPR knockout screen and metabolomics, Tang et al. demonstrate that EZH2 blockade remodels tryptophan-kynurenine metabolism by upregulating IDO1. These results identify IDO1 as a non-histone substrate of EZH2 and validate that targeting tryptophan metabolism represents a viable strategy to overcome EZH2 inhibitor resistance.

papers.title: ApoE-dependent lipid handling by median eminence microglia supports myelin remodeling and metabolic function
papers.abstract: McGrath et al. identify an ApoE-dependent lipid-handling program that enables hypothalamic median eminence microglia to adapt to dietary stress and support myelin remodeling. Human APOE4 compromises this response, while LXR activation reprograms microglial lipid handling and improves metabolic function.

papers.title: A bivalent chromatin reader-WOX5 module maintains root stem cell niche in Arabidopsis
papers.abstract: Zhang, Qian, and Zhong show that the bivalent chromatin reader EBS controls root stem cell maintenance in Arabidopsis through a chromatin-based positive autoregulatory circuit, revealing a framework for epigenetic control of stem cell fate.

papers.title: Theta-based organization of information in the frontal cortex
papers.abstract: Broschard et al. find that theta rhythms in the monkey frontal cortex function like a “master clock.” These rhythms coordinate spiking activity and higher-frequency rhythms to signal behavioral choices as well as errors.

papers.title: Mechanisms and consequences of nucleosome remodeling by mammalian SWI/SNF complexes
papers.abstract: Mammalian SWI/SNF complexes, also known as BRG1/BRM-associated factor (BAF) complexes, are ATP-dependent chromatin remodelers that mobilize nucleosomes to regulate chromatin accessibility and the transcriptional programs that establish cell identity and responses to environmental stimuli. In this Review, we discuss recent insights into the structural organization and modular assembly of BAF complexes, examine how they are recruited to chromatin by transcription factors, noncoding RNAs and histone modifications and describe their roles in transcription, from RNA polymerase II pausing and R-loop homeostasis to enhancer activation and phase separation. Throughout, we emphasize unifying principles that operate across physiological and pathological contexts. This Review discusses recent insights into the structure and assembly of mammalian SWI/SNF chromatin remodelers, their recruitment to chromatin and their roles in transcription.

papers.title: Aptamers enable a distinct mode of conformational DNA recognition
papers.abstract: Watson–Crick base-pairing defines the classical paradigm of nucleic-acid interactions, but growing research reveals noncanonical modes beyond this framework. Here we uncover a mode of interactions by which two DNA strands associate through a ligand-induced conformational rearrangement. Upon binding a small molecule, a structure-switching primary aptamer folds into a conformation that exposes a previously inaccessible docking interface. An independently evolved secondary aptamer recognizes this interface primarily through noncanonical interactions rather than sequence complementarity, reporting the ligand-bound state of the primary aptamer. This interaction is conformation-sensitive: single base-pair changes in the primary aptamer modulate secondary aptamer recognition. Across four chemically distinct small-molecule targets—serotonin, dopamine, testosterone and deoxycorticosterone 21-glucoside—secondary aptamers were identified for three, and the serotonin system was translated into surface-based sandwich assays. These results demonstrate that a ligand-induced conformational state, rather than sequence complementarity or the chemical identity of the ligand, can serve as the epitope for nucleic-acid recognition, expanding the molecular features that DNA can be evolved to detect. Aptamers have generally been understood as nucleic acids that recognize a specific ligand. Now it has been shown that secondary aptamers can recognize the ligand-bound conformation of a primary aptamer, enabling recognition of molecules that lack multiple binding sites for sandwich assays. This mechanism can be integrated into lateral flow assays for targets, including serotonin.

papers.title: A binuclear copper enzyme platform for enantioconvergent radical (pseudo)halogenation
papers.abstract: Despite their intriguing native metalloenzymology, naturally occurring copper enzymes remain underexploited for new-to-nature biocatalytic reactions. Here we report the systematic investigation and reprogramming of natural copper enzymes to catalyse unnatural free-radical (pseudo)halogenation reactions with high enantioselectivity. Evaluation of Cu enzymes in the decarboxylative azidation of redox-active esters revealed activity across multiple copper enzyme families, with type III binuclear copper enzymes, particularly Bacillus megaterium tyrosinase (BmTyr), exhibiting superior activity and enantioselectivity towards both stabilized and unstabilized alkyl radicals after further engineering. The strong halide binding affinity of the binuclear copper system also enabled challenging enantioconvergent bromination, chlorination and isothiocyanation reactions that remained inaccessible to repurposed non-haem iron enzymes. Electron paramagnetic resonance and ultraviolet–visible spectroscopic analyses confirmed the coupled binuclear nature of wild-type and engineered bacterial tyrosinases and provided insight into the origin of their enhanced activity. Collectively, this study establishes binuclear copper enzymes as a powerful platform for new-to-nature stereoselective radical reactions, expanding the scope of metalloenzyme catalysis beyond mononuclear systems. Binuclear metalloenzymes remain underexplored for new-to-nature biocatalytic reactions. Now binuclear copper enzymes, particularly a Bacillus megaterium tyrosinase, are used as a catalytic platform for stereoselective radical azidation, bromination, chlorination and isothiocyanation reactions, expanding metalloenzyme catalysis beyond mononuclear systems.

papers.title: Degraders take on GPCRs
Sonochemistry
papers.abstract: Sonochemistry converts acoustic energy into chemical reactivity through acoustic cavitation in liquids. The nucleation, oscillation, growth and collapse of gas–vapour bubbles generate transient hot spots, interfacial reaction zones, shock waves, microstreaming and radical species. This Primer presents the physical basis, experimental implementation and quantitative analysis of sonochemistry by acoustic cavitation. Key aspects include reactor architecture, electrical drive systems, ultrasound transducers, reaction vessels, batch and continuous-flow operation, and the role of frequency, acoustic pressure, gas atmosphere, temperature, solvent properties and geometry. Methods for characterizing cavitation activity and chemical output are discussed, including calorimetry, sonoluminescence imaging and spectroscopy, passive acoustic detection, high-speed imaging, electron paramagnetic resonance spin trapping, and radical dosimetry. Modelling approaches linking ultrasound propagation, bubble dynamics, heat and mass transfer, and chemical kinetics to reactor-scale performance are also considered. Applications in synthesis, catalysis, environmental remediation and materials processing highlight opportunities, whereas standardization, energy efficiency, scale-up and predictive reactor design remain central challenges. This Primer explores the dynamics of acoustic cavitation bubbles, focusing on how the energy released during their collapse can be harnessed to drive chemical reactions. Applications, reactor design and practical recommendations for accurately assessing cavitation in chemistry are provided, offering a comprehensive guide for researchers in sonochemistry.

papers.abstract: Recent Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency initiatives for live biotherapeutic products, fecal microbiota transplantation, and phage therapy medicinal products illustrate a dialog-driven regulatory approach for microbiome-based medicines. We compare this strategy with evolving Food and Drug Administration and European Medicines Agency frameworks and identify priorities for future regulatory development and international alignment.

papers.title: Identifying and targeting the Mg-Fe-PmrAB regulatory circuit reverses phosphate starvation-driven polymyxin tolerance in Enterobacteriaceae
papers.abstract: Phosphate (Pi) scarcity, a pervasive stressor prevalent in bacterial infections and dysbiotic host environments, potently alters antimicrobial susceptibility against cationic antibiotics like polymyxins across diverse bacterial taxa. While established Pi depletion-induced antimicrobial tolerance mechanisms often involve membrane phospholipid remodelling, Enterobacteriaceae largely lack these pathways, leaving the mechanism underlying their adaptation to Pi scarcity unresolved. Here, we reveal that Pi limitation robustly induces polymyxin tolerance in Enterobacteriaceae through 4-amino-4-deoxy-L-arabinose (L-Ara4N) modification of the Gram-negative outer membrane component lipid A, reflecting a distinct adaptive strategy. This modification is driven by strong arn operon induction, mediated by the PmrAB two-component system. We discover that Pi depletion triggers cellular Mg2+ release, prompting compensatory Fe3+ mobilization to the cell envelope that directly activates PmrAB. Crucially, this metal-dependent signaling axis offers a directly targetable mechanism for reversing polymyxin tolerance, a significant deviation from the less accessible, PhoBR-regulated phospholipid remodelling strategies in other bacteria. We demonstrate that Mg2+ supplementation or Fe3+ chelation effectively suppresses PmrAB activation and restores polymyxin susceptibility, thereby establishing a novel, metal-centric paradigm for understanding and pharmacological intervention in stress-induced antimicrobial tolerance.

papers.title: Scalable methylome-transcriptome profiling resolves clonal organization in human hematopoiesis
papers.abstract: Understanding human tissue maintenance and remodeling requires linking clonal ancestry to molecular state, yet scalable joint measurement remains challenging. Here, we introduce Droplet-MT and an integrated computational workflow for joint transcriptome and methylome profiling at ~10,000 cells per library. Methylation epimutations enable mutation-independent clonal reconstruction from high-coverage methylomes, while reference-based label transfer assigns cells to established clones at ~0.2% CpG coverage, reducing sequencing cost. Clone-aggregated somatic variants provide genetic annotation without additional single-cell genotyping. Across ~21,000 paired profiles from healthy blood and longitudinal acute myeloid leukemia, we resolved small and expanded clones with heterogeneous lineage output. In leukemia, the framework distinguished changes in malignant clonal abundance, state remodeling within persistent clones, and recovery of healthy polyclonal hematopoiesis. Malignant monocytes remained transcriptionally and epigenetically distinct from healthy and recovery-associated cells despite treatment-associated remodeling. Droplet-MT enables scalable analysis of human tissues by linking clonal organization with molecular state and retrospective genetic annotation.

papers.title: Amide I kurtosis maps cardiac amyloid in human tissue by ultrabroadband multiplex coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (CARS) microscopy
papers.abstract: Cardiac amyloidosis is caused by deposits of misfolded proteins in the heart and can lead to heart failure. Histological confirmation typically involves staining tissue sections with Congo red and examining them under polarized light for apple-green birefringence; however, achieving an interpretable, label-free, and observer-independent assessment remains challenging. Here we show that Pearson kurtosis of channel intensities within the amide I window provides an interpretable, fitting-free contrast for cardiac amyloid in unstained human cardiac tissue sections imaged by ultrabroadband multiplex coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (CARS). In two participants, high-kurtosis regions corresponded with Congo red-positive tissue in adjacent stained sections (descriptive spatial AUCs, 0.79 and 0.73). Across 15 fields from nine participants, including one of these two, kurtosis values did not overlap between severe-deposition and amyloid-negative tissue. Among the descriptors examined, kurtosis showed the largest standardized participant-level separation. Exploratory multivariate curve resolution yielded a deposit-associated component with aromatic-residue features shared with reagent transthyretin. Second harmonic generation (SHG), acquired simultaneously with CARS, showed a broadly inverse spatial pattern relative to kurtosis, providing complementary architectural contrast. These findings support a label-free approach to detecting cardiac amyloid deposits that combines broadband CARS-derived amide I kurtosis with SHG.

papers.title: Gene regulatory architecture in antibiotic resistance is optimized for specific dynamic regimens
papers.abstract: Cellular responses to antibiotics face a fundamental trade-off: resistance must be deployed quickly enough to prevent the accumulation of drug inside the cell, but expression of resistance genes is costly in the absence of the drug. Therefore, antibiotic responses are typically regulated, controlling not only whether resistance is expressed, but also when, how strongly, and for how long. These regulatory strategies are implemented through the strength and arrangement of promoters and operators. However, it is still not clear how the dynamics of drug exposure select for specific regulatory strategies. Here, we develop a dynamical model of a typical antibiotic response, where a transcriptional repressor senses the drug and regulates expression of a resistance protein, coupled to the effects of the drug on cell growth and gene expression. We define a cost function that weighs the different burdens imposed on the cell over the course of the response, and perform in silico optimization of the regulatory parameters under different selective pressures for three architectures of increasing complexity: constitutive expression of resistance, repression by a constitutively expressed repressor, and repression by a self-regulated repressor. We find that strong drug exposures favor constitutive expression of resistance, high costs of basal expression favor repression by a constitutive repressor, and self-regulation of the repressor is favored only when the response must provide protection while also restraining overexpression of resistance. Stochastic simulations further show that self-regulation of the repressor protects cells against fluctuations in repressor levels, which cause unnecessary induction of resistance before exposure and failed induction after exposure. This framework links the dynamics of the environment to the evolution of gene regulation, providing a basis to predict which regulatory strategies are expected to arise under specific selective pressures.

papers.title: Identification of T-Cell specific signature miRNAs and target pathways in Psoriasis
papers.abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic skin disease characterized by keratinocyte hyperproliferation, involving T cells as the major players in the manifestation of lesional and systemic inflammation. With the extensive exploration of keratinocyte dysfunctionality, T cell centric deregulation has gained much focus with limited molecular understanding in the context of disease etiology. miRNAs, the molecular switches known to drive disease manifestation via altering keratinocyte biology, have not been much studied in the context of T cell alterations. This study aims to explore T cell-associated miRNAs and their target signaling networks to understand their role in modulating psoriasis specific T cell changes. miRNAs with altered expression in psoriatic T cells were identified through a comprehensive analysis of the available literature and datasets. The relevant miRNAs were used for prediction and enrichment of cognate targets and mapping of associated pathways involved in different modalities of T cell functionality. The study identified 14 miRNAs dysregulated in psoriatic T cells along with 256 downstream targets involved in 15 distinct T cell associated signaling pathways. 5/14 miRNAs identified were further validated with a significant increase in their expression in enriched CD3+T cells from blood of psoriatic patients versus healthy subjects. The psoriatic T cell specific miRNA driven signaling cascades identified were modelled to propose yet unexplored molecular basis of dysregulated T cell activation, proliferation, survival, and subset differentiation associated with the disease. The new findings delineate candidate miRNA target signaling components that need to be validated in T cell disease etiology. Importantly, the key miRNAs/targets can be employed towards psoriasis-specific diagnostics and therapeutic interventions.

papers.title: Clonally Convergent Tph/Tfh-like CD4+ T Cells are Shared Across Recovery and Recurrence in Experimental Periodontitis
papers.abstract: Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disease of the tooth-supporting structures (periodontium) that requires life-long maintenance to prevent progression. Using a sensitized model of recurrent periodontitis in mice (SeRPD), in which regulatory breakdown was induced by temporary Treg depletion concurrent with disease, we mapped the gingival T cell imprint across each disease phase. Transient regulatory breakdown left a durable mucosal imprint after clinical recovery, characterized by enrichment of local and regional CD4 T cells. Paired single-cell RNA and TCR sequencing of gingival immune cells identified a convergent clonotype expanded from recovery into recurrence that carried a Tfh/Tph-like transcriptional identity. An analogous CD4 T cell population was detected in human periodontitis lesions by single-cell transcriptomics. Together, these findings support a paradigm in which clinical recovery does not ensure a local T cell repertoire reset; instead, a reservoir of antigen-experienced, tissue-adapted CD4 T cells persist in the mucosa and participate in recurrence.

papers.title: Temperature alters Culex tarsalis West Nile virus vector competence, tissue bottlenecks, and transcriptional responses
papers.abstract: West Nile virus is an arbovirus transmitted by Culex mosquitoes. Temperature is frequently the strongest abiotic factor impacting transmission in many virus-vector pairings, including WNV and Culex. However, it is unknown how temperature impacts WNV population bottlenecks and transcriptional responses to infection in Culex tarsalis. We found that elevated temperatures led to increased likelihood of transmission of rare virus variants due to increased vector competence and less stringent tissue barriers. Analysis of Cx. tarsalis transcriptional responses confirmed that WNV infection had minimal impacts on transcriptional activity. Temperature, however, induced significant changes to mosquito gene expression, whereas canonical immune gene expression minimally changed in response to infection. Thus, temperature impacts bottlenecks in the Culex-WNV system independent of known antiviral pathways, possibly by altering virus replication dynamics. While temperature had a dramatic impact on bottleneck stringency, this is likely independent of antiviral pathways and instead some other change to mosquito biology. Together, these results shed light on the relationships between temperature, virus evolutionary dynamics and antiviral immunity.

papers.title: RNA Polymerase Backtracking Promotes Type III-A CRISPR DNA Targeting
papers.abstract: Type III CRISPR-Cas systems provide transcription-dependent immunity against mobile genetic elements, yet the mechanism underlying their DNA targeting remains unclear. Although the type III effector Cas10-Csm functions as a single-stranded DNase in vitro, type III systems eliminate double-stranded DNA targets in vivo, suggesting that transcription generates critical DNA substrates. Here, we show that conserved RNA polymerase anti-backtracking factors, such as GreA, selectively inhibit DNA-targeting of type III immunity. GreA overexpression abolishes protection against both phages and conjugative plasmids, whereas mutations that disrupt GreA anti-backtracking activity eliminate this effect. In contrast, immunity mediated by the type II CRISPR-Cas system or the auxiliary type III RNase Csm6 remain unaffected, demonstrating that GreA specifically suppresses Cas10-dependent DNA interference. These findings identify RNA polymerase backtracking as a key determinant of Cas10-Csm activity and support a model in which arrested transcription complexes generate substrates for DNA degradation, opening up new anti-CRISPR strategies against type III.

papers.title: Phage lysates are reservoirs of biologically active quorum sensing signals
papers.abstract: Bacteriophage lysates are widely used to study phage-bacterial interactions and are typically applied after filtration without further purification. As a result, host-derived metabolites produced during phage propagation are transferred alongside phage particles, yet the biological consequences of this carryover remain largely unexplored. Here, we show that the Pseudomonas aeruginosa quorum sensing signal PQS persists in a bioactive state in phage lysates for at least one year. In contrast, the quorum sensing molecules 3OC12-HSL and C4-HSL are rapidly degraded. We demonstrate that PQS stability is caused by its association with outer membrane vesicles, which protect the signal from degradation. PQS from phage lysates induces production of the virulence factor pyocyanin and increases mortality in a Galleria mellonella model of P. aeruginosa infection. Importantly, PQS carryover does not explain previous reports of phage mediated activation of the PQS system, as this response also occurs in PQS free phage lysates, establishing phage lysate-mediated signal transfer and phage-induced signaling as distinct mechanisms. Because hydrophobic signaling molecules are associated with outer membrane vesicles in diverse Gram-negative bacteria, including Vibrio harveyi (CAI-1) and Paracoccus (C16-HSL), our findings suggest that phage lysates may serve as reservoirs and overlooked vectors of host-derived communication signals in a broad range of phage-host systems. Our results reveal a previously overlooked layer of phage-host interactions in which biologically active bacterial signals persist beyond phage lysate preparation and influence recipient-cell behavior independently of phage infection.

papers.title: Pneumocystis phosphoglucomutase links glucose-phosphate metabolism to β-1,3-glucan synthesis and cell-wall integrity
papers.abstract: The fungal cell wall is a dynamic, carbohydrate-rich structure whose composition is closely coordinated with cellular metabolism. Phosphoglucomutase (PGM) interconverts glucose-1-phosphate and glucose-6-phosphate, linking carbon metabolism with UDP-glucose-dependent cell-wall biosynthesis. We previously identified functional Pgm2 homologs from Pneumocystis jirovecii and Pneumocystis murina. Here, using a Saccharomyces cerevisiae pgm2{Delta} complementation model, we examined the relationship between Pgm2 activity, {beta}-1,3-glucan, and cell-wall integrity. Pgm2 deficiency reduced {beta}-1,3-glucan content and altered zymolyase sensitivity without major changes in cell-wall thickness. Bulk RNA sequencing revealed that the pgm2{Delta} mutant exhibited coordinated metabolic and cell-wall transcriptional responses, including increased SLT2/MPK1, RLM1, FKS2/GSC2, GFA1, CHS1, CRH1, SED1, and CWP1 expression and decreased FKS1, GAS1, GAS3, and CHS2 expression. Expression of either Pjpgm2 or Pmpgm2 broadly shifted these responses toward wild-type levels. Selected transcriptional changes were further evaluated by qRT-PCR, which supported the major stress and cell-wall responses identified by RNA sequencing. FKS2/GSC2 showed the same directional pattern, although differences were not statistically significant by qRT-PCR. Despite this compensatory response, Pgm2-deficient cells were markedly more susceptible to sublethal caspofungin, whereas either Pneumocystis Pgm2 homolog restored tolerance toward wild-type levels. These findings link Pgm2-dependent glucose-phosphate metabolism with {beta}-1,3-glucan levels and cell-wall function. Given the importance of {beta}-1,3-glucan to the Pneumocystis cyst wall and its limited cell-wall biosynthetic pathways, these findings further support Pgm2 as an important component of Pneumocystis cell-wall biology and a potential antifungal target.
affiliations: Mayo Clinic (corresponding author)

papers.title: Optimal compositions of potent sliced-siRNA with DNA bases substitution and insights of Ago2 slicing actions
papers.abstract: We have previously characterized the nucleotide compositions of single-stranded ago2-sliced small interfering RNAs (sliced-siRNA, sliRNA), a novel type of potent RNAi trigger designed based on the biogenesis mechanism of miRNA-451. sliRNAs have on par antisense mediated silencing activity but about 1000-fold reduced passenger strand activity compared to siRNA. In the current study, to further characterize sliRNAs to facilitate their in vivo application, we have investigated the effects of substituting RNA nucleotides (nts) in sliRNA with DNA nts (sliDRNAs), which will allow us to study the potential effects on their processing, maturation, and silencing activity from individual or multiple nts at different positions. Our results showed sliDRNAs have distinguished composition from siRNA with DNA nts (siDRNA), indicated that, in addition to their different biogenesis mechanisms, these two types of RNAi triggers may also have adopted additional different silencing mechanisms. Our results also revealed some mechanism related to how Ago2 executes its slicer activity and the effects on sliRNA potency by trimming and tailing during sliRNA maturation. These results have paved the way for using other chemically modified nts in sliRNAs that may enhance their in vivo stability and transportability to facilitate their in vivo applications.
affiliations: Beckman Research Institute of the City of Hope (corresponding author)

papers.title: Insulin stimulation induces dynamic interaction between 14-3-3 and the C-terminal tail domain of Kinesin-2 subunit KIF3B in vitro
papers.abstract: Heterotrimeric kinesin[ndash]2 mediates diverse intracellular transport processes, yet the mechanisms governing its cargo specificity and regulation remain poorly understood. In this study, we report the regulation of interaction between the kinesin[ndash]2 subunit KIF3B and a candidate adaptor protein, 14[ndash]3[ndash]3[epsilon];. Using splitAPEX2 proximity labelling and fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) assays in HEK293T cells, we demonstrate that 14[ndash]3[ndash]3[epsilon]; interacts with KIF3B within discrete subcellular compartments. This interaction is significantly enhanced upon insulin stimulation, indicating regulation by signalling pathways. Time resolved FLIM analysis further reveals that the site of interaction is dynamic, suggesting spatial and temporal control of motora[ndash]daptor association. Finally, the interactions are mapped to two serine residues in the C[ndash]terminal tail region of KIF3B that are highly conserved across species. Together, these findings uncover a conditional and reversible interaction between KIF3B and 14[ndash]3[ndash]3[epsilon], providing insight into how kinesin[ndash]2 may achieve context specific cargo engagement and transport within cells.
affiliations: Tata Institute of Fundamental Research- Mumbai, Birla Institute of Technology and Sciences, Pilani (BITS-Pilani), Hyderabad (corresponding author)

papers.title: N-terminal cysteine independent effects of oxidative stress on the stability of RGS4 and 5
papers.abstract: Oxidative post-translational modifications on the sulfhydryl group of cysteines can occur spontaneously or enzymatically. The enzymatic dioxygenation of N-terminal cysteines has emerged as a new oxygen sensing paradigm, catalysed by 2-aminoethanethiol dioxygenase (ADO) in mammals. Conflicting evidence has been reported in recent years on whether this reaction can occur spontaneously in the absence of ADO. Here we sought to address whether cellular oxidative stress can interfere with ADO-catalysed N-terminal cysteine dioxygenation. Using a system to produce titratable intracellular levels of H2O2, we demonstrate that the stability of RGS4 and 5 is not affected by physiological levels of oxidative stress, whether ADO is present or not. However, cytotoxic levels of oxidative stress induced by tert-butyl hydroperoxide did induce a substantial increase in RGS4/5 protein stability that occurred independently of the Cys N-degron pathway. This effect of tBHP was abolished by Fe2+ chelation, lysosomal pH perturbation, and lipid peroxide scavenging. We conclude that N-terminal cysteine dependent proteolysis of RGS4/5 is not sensitive to physiological oxidative stress, but these proteins can be stabilised during the process of oxidative stress-induced cell death through an N-terminal cysteine independent mechanism.
affiliations: University of Oxford (corresponding author)

papers.title: Variation in the embryonic cell lineages of Caenorhabditis elegans natural populations
papers.abstract: Developmental variation has often been appreciated as a major phenotypic substrate of evolutionary innovation in multicellular organisms. Although quantification of developmental variation in isogenic populations has a long history, it has been difficult to accomplish across natural populations until recently. Given its invariant cell lineage, Caenorhabditis elegans represents an ideal model system for studying how natural diversity in development is expressed at the resolution of single cells, cell lineages, and the whole embryo. Using embGAN, a deep-learning pipeline that enables label-free lineage tracing without the bottleneck and potential confounding effects of generating transgenic strains, we reconstructed the early embryonic lineage of 78 embryos spanning eight genetic backgrounds, including six wild strains, and quantified cell-cycle timing with a lineage-aligned graph metric that separates global rescaling of developmental rate from localized changes in lineage structure. We found that cell-cycle timing differs reproducibly among genotypes, with between-strain variation consistently exceeding within-strain variation. The magnitude of this variation was itself genotype-specific and not correlated with levels of genetic divergence. Unlike the global shifts in the tempo of development that dominate divergence between species, these differences are predominantly in lineage patterning, changing the timing of specific divisions, and they align to cell fate. Thus, the invariant lineage of C. elegans is built on a structured, genotype-specific landscape of developmental variation, a potential source of trait variation from which drift in developmental systems can emerge.
affiliations: UCLA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Short-read whole-genome sequencing identifies the Tg(Tal1-cre/ERT)42-056Jrg transgene insertion site on mouse chromosome 4
papers.abstract: Tg(Tal1-cre/ERT)42-056Jrg, also known as HSC-Scl-CreERT, is a well-used transgenic allele that enables genetic manipulation in mouse hematopoietic cells. Using short-read whole-genome sequencing, we identified the transgene insertion site on chromosome 4 approximately 6 kb upstream of Echdc2.
affiliations: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Epigenetic reprogramming by promoter hypomethylation is linked to aberrant gene expression and transcriptomic plasticity in colorectal cancer
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) has high phenotypic plasticity, but regulatory mechanisms of aberrant cell states are not well described. We investigated DNA methylation-based regulation of cancer cell-intrinsic transcriptomic heterogeneity in 1,183 multiregional primary tumor samples, liver metastases and tumor organoids. Most genes with strong methylation-transcriptomic association reflected canonical promoter hypermethylation and expression repression related to the CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP). However, promoter hypomethylation and overexpression of APOLD1 and ELF5 identified two largely non-overlapping subgroups of canonical CIMP-negative CRCs enriched with stem-like and transit-amplifying cell states. APOLD1 tumors were further highly proliferative while ELF5 tumors were slow-cycling and associated with good survival in early-stage disease. Target genes showed patient-specific expression changes in matched primary-metastasis samples, and ELF5 aberrant metastases showed ex vivo sensitivity to putative targeting of stem cells by PI3K/mTOR inhibition, fetal de-differentiation and transition into non-canonical intestinal states. This implicates focal promoter hypomethylation in phenotypic plasticity in CRC metastasis.
affiliations: Oslo University Hospital (corresponding author)

papers.title: Structural basis for inefficient G protein coupling by Frizzled receptors
papers.abstract: Frizzleds (FZDs) are class F G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) that primarily signal through Dishevelled (DVL) to initiate Wnt signalling, with evidence for context-specific coupling to heterotrimeric G proteins. Every FZD-G protein structure to date has been determined without an agonist, implying that agonist binding is not required for stable complex formation in vitro and directly contradicting the difficulty of demonstrating G protein coupling in cells. All these structures contain unassigned density between the receptor and the heterotrimeric G protein. From structures generated by single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) of FZD7-Gs and FZD5-Gq, we identify this density as the detergent lauryl maltose neopentyl glycol (LMNG), which bridges the receptor and G protein to stabilise a weak, shallow interface. Absence of LMNG - in biochemical preparations and molecular dynamics simulations - destabilises the complex, showing that constitutive FZD-G protein engagement is intrinsically weak. The weak G protein coupling is governed by a conserved intracellular interface that when mutated differentially influences DVL and G protein signalling. Our findings show that LMNG has masked the instability of purified FZD-G protein complexes and provide the structural basis of FZDs as inherently weak G protein activators that are predisposed to DVL signalling.
affiliations: WEHI (corresponding author)

papers.title: Jade1S SUMOylates tau and targets oligomers for degradation
papers.abstract: The accumulation of insoluble tau aggregates is a pathological hallmark of tauopathies, including Alzheimer's disease. While molecular chaperones and clearance pathways regulate tau homeostasis, the mechanisms governing tau oligomerization and degradation remain incompletely defined. Recent genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have linked the JADE1 locus to tauopathy, and the PHD zinc finger protein Jade1S has been identified in complexes with tau in post-mortem brain tissue, prompting investigation into their biochemical relationship. Here, we characterize the reciprocal interactions between Jade1S and 0N4R tau stability and turnover. Covalent labeling mass spectrometry and co-immunoprecipitation mappings reveal that Jade1S binds wild-type 0N4R tau through redundant sites within its N-terminal and plant homeodomain (PHD) zinc finger domains. In vitro assays demonstrate that Jade1S functions as a SUMO E3 ligase, utilizing its PHD domains to mediate tau SUMOylation. Cell-based cycloheximide chase assays reveal a reciprocal stabilization dynamic: tau co-expression extends the overall physiological half-life of Jade1S from less than an hour to ~17 hours, arresting its turnover specifically within sarkosyl-insoluble fractions. Conversely, Jade1S selectively accelerates the degradation of sarkosyl-insoluble tau without altering the turnover of the soluble monomeric pool over chased time. Mechanistically, Jade1S redirects the clearance of SUMO2/3-modified tau oligomers away from basal autophagic-lysosomal pathways and toward proteasome-dependent degradation. Furthermore, Jade1S exhibits intrinsic molecular chaperone activity, inhibiting arachidonic acid-induced tau oligomerization in vitro. Together, these data characterize Jade1S as a dual-function SUMO ligase and chaperone that regulates tau stability, prevents oligomer assembly, and promotes the targeted proteasomal clearance of aggregated tau.
affiliations: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai (corresponding author)

papers.title: Multi-objective domain adaptation for pan-cancer transfer of pharmacogenomic drug response to patient tumours
papers.abstract: Large-scale pharmacogenomic screens provide rich drug-sensitivity measurements in cancer cell lines, but transferring these measurements to patient tumours remains limited by biological heterogeneity and cross-domain distribution shift. Existing machine learning approaches, including adversarial autoencoder and domain adaptation, address this gap by learning shared latent representations between preclinical models and patient samples. However, alignment without explicit biological constraints can produce unreliable representations when cancer lineage structure and clinically relevant patient heterogeneity are not preserved. Here, we introduce MODAE+, a pan-cancer multi-objective deep learning domain adaptation framework that jointly balances domain alignment, deconfounding, drug-response prediction, survival prediction, and cancer-lineage classification across 9,696 TCGA tumours, 1,293 CCLE cancer cell lines, and CTRP sensitivity profiles for 544 compounds in 738 matched cell lines. This multi-objective design improved cross-domain alignment while preserving cancer-lineage organization and patient heterogeneity. For drugs shared between the pharmacogenomic screen and TCGA treatment records, MODAE+ predicted sensitivity was significantly associated with overall survival among patients who received each drug in 46.3% of evaluated cancer-drug pairs by log-rank testing and 41.5% by multivariable Cox analysis. Biological validation across four curated drug-gene resources identified significant expression differences exceeding 1.5-fold for 34.9-64.4% of drugs in pan-cancer analyses, based on the lowest-p-value annotated gene per drug. Drug-class-specific patterns involved intended molecular targets for targeted therapies and predominantly transport, metabolism, detoxification and resistance-related genes for classical chemotherapies. As an additional validation, we derived pretreatment responder-nonresponder gene-expression signatures from 13 external breast cancer datasets and evaluated their concordance with MODAE+ predictions across 69 signature-drug comparisons in TCGA patients treated with paclitaxel or doxorubicin. Consensus signature scores showed Spearman correlations of 0.791 with predicted paclitaxel sensitivity and 0.724 with predicted doxorubicin sensitivity, averaging 0.758 across the two drugs. Together, these complementary analyses provide supporting evidence for the clinical relevance and biological consistency of MODAE+ predictions, suggesting their potential to identify drug-sensitive tumour subgroups and generate hypotheses about mechanisms of drug resistance.
affiliations: University of Eastern Finland (corresponding author)

papers.title: TRACE: a framework for traceable biomedical resource construction demonstrated through single-cell glaucoma data
papers.abstract: The growing availability of public omics datasets presents opportunities for biomedical research, yet constructing research question-driven resources from distributed studies remains challenging due to heterogeneous data, incomplete metadata and limited documentation of curation decisions. Here, we present TRACE (Traceable Resource Assembly and Curation Ecosystem), a general framework that links systematic knowledge discovery, data curation and resource delivery while preserving provenance throughout resource construction. We demonstrate TRACE through TRACE-scGlaucoma, a curated single-cell transcriptomics resource for glaucoma and optic nerve biology. Systematic screening identified 57 eligible studies, of which 42 provided accessible datasets comprising approximately 3.3 million cells. The resource provides harmonised metadata, standardised cell-type annotations and reusable expression objects while retaining original study information and curation provenance. We demonstrate its analytical utility through cellular enrichment of glaucoma GWAS-associated genes, comparing candidate drug-repurposing signals across distinct biological contexts and assessment of cell-type annotation reliability. TRACE provides a systematic and traceable approach to transforming fragmented public datasets into reusable biomedical resources, supporting reproducible analyses and future extensions across disease areas and data modalities.
affiliations: The University of Sydney (corresponding author)

papers.title: OncoSpot enables benchmarking of cancer spatial transcriptomics methods across tumor evolutionary modes
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) is increasingly used to map clonal architecture within tumors, yet methods for analyzing cancer ST data are difficult to evaluate because real tumors lack ground truth for copy-number alterations (CNAs), subclonal identity, and malignant cell fraction. Existing ST simulators model normal tissue and do not represent tumor evolution, CNA-driven expression, or the spatial organization of malignant subclones. We present OncoSpot, a cancer-aware simulator of Visium-like spot-based ST data. OncoSpot combines a spatial evolutionary scaffold from DEMON, CNAs generated along the resulting clonal phylogeny with CNAsim, cancer-type-specific malignant transcriptional programs, and spatially clustered nonmalignant cell types, and aggregates cells into spots with known malignant fraction, subclone, and copy-number profiles. We demonstrate OncoSpot on high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma, colorectal cancer, and hepatocellular carcinoma, which represent three distinct modes of tumor evolution.
