Simulated subclones were spatially clustered and showed stronger phylogeny-space concordance than those generated by scCube under matched subclone populations. Benchmarking CopyKAT, CancerFinder, Clonalscope, and RCTD revealed cancer-dependent performance: Clonalscope recovered copy-number signals more accurately in ovarian and colorectal cancer, whereas CopyKAT performed better in hepatocellular carcinoma, reflecting both the assumptions of each method and the copy-number landscapes of the three cancers. OncoSpot's ground truth also exposed a failure mode in Clonalscope's malignant spot identification, in which tumor and normal labels were inverted, and allowed us to trace its cause. These method-dependent behaviors would be difficult to detect in real data. OncoSpot provides a framework for benchmarking CNA inference, subclone detection, malignant spot identification, and normal spot deconvolution, and its modular design and guidelines allow extension to additional cancer types. OncoSpot is freely available at https://github.com/compbio-mallory/OncoSpot.
affiliations: Florida State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: PartiDesign: A structure-sequence co-design paradigm for practical all-to-all biomolecules design
papers.abstract: Engineering interactions among biomolecules offers a route to creating new biological functions. Although unified models have advanced biomolecular structure prediction and design, efficient and controllable generation across molecular modalities remains challenging. A key challenge is to couple three-dimensional structure generation with sequence or chemical-identity design across chemically diverse systems. Here, we introduce PartiDesign, a unified structure-sequence co-design model that extends the partially latent framework of La-Proteina to proteins, nucleic acids and small molecules. PartiDesign jointly generates molecular structures and their corresponding sequences or chemical identities, while providing fine-grained control over secondary structure, chemical bonding and amino acid preferences. Across diverse benchmarks for the de novo design of proteins, nucleic acids and small molecules against specified targets, PartiDesign achieved the highest estimated successful-design throughput among the evaluated methods on most benchmarks under the adopted compute-budget protocols. Its configurable constraints further support cyclic peptide and antibody design, allowing generation to be tailored to specific structural and chemical requirements. PartiDesign was developed using 128 Huawei Ascend 910B accelerators, each with 64 GB of memory. The source code is available at https://github.com/MegaGatlingPea/PartiDesign-official, and a freely accessible web server at https://cadd.zju.edu.cn/partidesign/ enables users to generate binding partners without programming expertise. Together, these capabilities provide a versatile and accessible framework for all-to-all biomolecular design, with applications in molecular engineering and drug discovery.
affiliations: School of Pharmacy, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou 310058, China (corresponding author)

papers.title: FoldAbS: Repurposing the Protein Folding Model as a Foundation Encoder for Antibody Screening
papers.abstract: Therapeutic antibody screening requires prioritizing antibody candidates across specificity, affinity, and developability. Current pipelines typically silo these objectives and underuse structural information that governs antibody-antigen recognition. To address these inefficacies, we introduce FoldAbS, a unified supervised screening framework that reconceptualizes protein folding models as frozen foundation encoders, exploiting their internal representations to capture rich sequence, geometric, and interaction dynamics well beyond basic structure prediction. By coupling the folding model with lightweight, task-specific heads, FoldAbS seamlessly evaluates all three therapeutic criteria within a single architecture. Instantiating this framework with the open-source Protenix model (FoldAbS-Px) yields consistent improvements over baseline approaches, achieving significant performance gains of up to 13.1%, 9.2%, and 6.2% in specificity, affinity, and developability, respectively. Collectively, these results reposition protein folding models from structure predictors and confidence scorers into reusable foundation encoders for comprehensive and supervised antibody screening. Our code is available at https://github.com/nohandsomewujun/FoldAbS.
affiliations: Tencent (corresponding author)

papers.title: RPI-Zero: Zero-shot RNA-Protein Interaction Prediction
papers.abstract: In vivo protein-RNA interactions are mapped almost exclusively by CLIP-seq, which profiles one protein in one cell type per experiment and needs a specific antibody; only about 10% of the roughly 2,000 human RNA-binding proteins have been assayed, and the Protein Data Bank holds around 5,000 protein-RNA complexes, a quarter of them ribosomes. Sequence-based prediction could extend coverage to unprofiled, newly discovered, or designed molecules, but existing predictors are not built for that case. One family trains a separate model per protein and cannot move beyond proteins with CLIP data; the other scores pairs but targets a single RNA class. Most are evaluated with random splits and randomly paired negatives that leave near-identical sequences on both sides of the split, and many require structure or read only short windows, discarding the context around a binding site. Their accuracy falls sharply when whole molecules are held out. We address this with two contributions. First, a strict benchmark of 2.1 million examples built from 11.6 million peaks of CLIP experiments targeting 209 proteins, taken from four public databases, in which each RNA is a spliced transcript with nucleotide-level labels, and sequence-similarity clusters are assigned whole to training, validation, and test sets, giving separate slices for unseen RNAs, unseen proteins, and unseen pairs. Negatives are matched to positives in length and in the number of other proteins binding the transcript, removing the shortcut by which a model predicts binding from how popular a transcript is without reading the protein. Second, RPI-Zero, a sequence-only model that reads any full-length protein and RNA jointly in up to 4,096 tokens, so the RNA representation is conditioned on the protein, and describes every protein as a mixture of shared motif prototypes, placing unseen proteins in the same terms as training ones. One model covers all proteins and RNA classes, uses no structure, and needs no interaction data for a new molecule. Compared with five state-of-the-art methods, it achieves the highest score in eight different metrics on unseen RNAs, unseen proteins, and unseen pairs. The model and data are available at https://github.com/ciceklab/RPI-Zero and https://zenodo.org/records/23748141, respectively.
affiliations: Bilkent University (corresponding author)

papers.title: mRNArchitect: sequence design of mRNA medicines
papers.abstract: Sequence design is a critical first step in the development of mRNA medicines. The primary sequence can be optimised to improve translation, stability and immunogenicity. Here, we present mRNArchitect, a software toolkit for the design and optimisation of primary mRNA sequences according to codon usage, secondary structure and manufacturability. mRNArchitect supports multiple optimisation strategies tailored for short or long expression profiles, and different clinical applications, including vaccines, cell and gene therapies. mRNArchitect is complemented by a catalogue of validated RNA elements, including UTRs, microRNA binding sites, and regulatory elements, that provide programmable, cell-type-specific control of mRNA expression. We experimentally validate mRNArchitect designs, demonstrating improvements in expression, stability, and immunogenicity, across multiple cell types and tissues compared to current design methods. mRNArchitect is provided as an experimentally validated, software package for the design and optimisation of mRNA medicines, available at: https://basefacility.org.au/software/.
affiliations: The University of Queensland (corresponding author)

papers.title: The binding landscape of Ras/effector interactions provides insights on Ras switching and oncogenesis
papers.abstract: Protein-protein interactions (PPIs) regulate essential cellular processes, yet the evolutionary principles that shape their specificity, adaptability, and dysregulation in disease remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the evolution of a signaling PPI between the small GTPase Ras and its effector Nore1A, a tumor suppressor involved in Ras-mediated signaling. Ras acts as a molecular switch, engaging effectors in its GTP-bound active state and releasing them after GTP hydrolysis, whereas oncogenic mutations such as G12D lock Ras in the active state, promoting aberrant signaling in cancer. Using yeast surface display, deep mutational scanning, and data normalization, we systematically mapped the Ras/Nore1A binding landscape under different physiological and oncogenic states. We generated and screened $\sim$33,000 Nore1A single and double mutants against RasWT and RasG12D in both GTP- and GDP-bound states. Our data revealed that most Nore1A mutations produce small-to-moderate decrease in Ras affinity, while a small number of substitutions enhance affinity. Unexpectedly, GTP hydrolysis causes minimal remodeling of the interaction landscape. Conversely, the oncogenic RasG12D mutation reshapes the binding landscape, revealing many Nore1A variants with enhanced and selective affinity for mutant Ras. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of Nore1A-Ras variant complexes suggest that the non-optimality of the Nore1A/RasG12D binding landscape arises, in part, from the greater intrinsic flexibility of RasG12D and the pronounced reduction in flexibility induced by affinity-enhancing Nore1A mutations. These findings demonstrate that disease-associated mutations can create new evolutionary trajectories in signaling PPIs by changing interaction dynamics and provide a framework for engineering selective protein-based inhibitors targeting oncogenic Ras variants.
affiliations: Hebrew University of Jerusalem (corresponding author)

papers.title: AnDi-J: diffusion analysis of single-particle tracking data in Fiji
papers.abstract: Characterizing how particles diffuse is key to understanding biology across scales, yet extracting the underlying physical properties typically requires specialized tools rarely accessible to biology labs. Here we introduce AnDi-J, a Fiji plugin combining classical estimators with state-of-the-art machine learning for single-trajectory analysis and segmentation, requiring minimal knowledge of stochastic processes. It extracts diffusion coefficients and anomalous exponents, classifies trajectories into diffusion models, and segments heterogeneous trajectories into diffusive states, through powerful, easy-to-use visualization tools. See more at https://github.com/gorkamunoz/andi-j .
affiliations: University of Innsbruck (corresponding author)

papers.title: BCL10 Gain-of-Function Impairs Germinal Center Participation by Naive B Cells and Cooperates with BCL6 to Drive Extrafollicular Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma
papers.abstract: BCL10 gain-of-function (GoF) mutations occur in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) cases of the BN2/C1 molecular subgroup. These alterations activate CARD11-BCL10-MALT1 (CBM) signaling and drive resistance to multiple drug classes, but their role in disease pathogenesis is incompletely understood. In particular, interactions between BCL10 GoF and additional DLBCL oncogenes are undefined. Here, we show BCL10 GoF in naive B cells blocks their participation in germinal center (GC) reactions and permits transformation to DLBCL with a non-GC B-cell phenotype. Most clinical cases with BCL10 GoF also carry translocation of the BCL6 proto-oncogene, and we show that co-activation of these two lesions together promotes pronounced oncogenic synergy. Detailed single-cell analyses of underlying premalignant B-cell populations revealed expansion of extrafollicular memory B cells whose gene-expression program remains prominent in resulting lymphomas in both the mouse and corresponding human tumors. We therefore define a novel role for BCL10 activating mutations in enabling BCL6 lymphomagenesis.
affiliations: University of Miami Miller School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Targeting CDK12 condensates at nuclear speckles with rationally designed cyclin K molecular glue degraders
papers.abstract: Transcriptional machinery often operates in the configuration of biomolecular condensates, presenting emerging opportunities to develop therapies targeting transcriptionally addicted malignancies. In this study, we discovered that cyclin-dependent kinase 12 (CDK12), a key regulator of transcription elongation, formed dynamic liquid-like droplets at nuclear speckles, a process enhanced by high CDK12 expression and CDK12 inhibitor exposure. Notably, CDK12 condensation limited sensitivity to kinase inhibition, potentially through enhanced cyclin K recruitment and local enrichment of CDK12-cyclin K complexes. To disrupt these assemblies, we rationally designed HQY1428, a potent modular cyclin K molecular glue degrader that coupled CDK12-binding and DDB1-engaging moieties. Structural and biochemical analyses showed that HQY1428 promoted CDK12-DDB1 association and rapid cyclin K degradation, accompanied by CDK12 depletion and loss of CDK12 condensates. Functionally, HQY1428 treatment perturbed oncogenic transcription and suppressed ovarian cancer growth in vitro and in vivo. Given the frequent genomic co-amplification of CDK12 and ERBB2 across diverse human cancers, we showed that combining HQY1428 with HER2 inhibitors provided synergistic therapeutic benefits. Collectively, our findings establish CDK12 condensation at nuclear speckles as an exploitable vulnerability and support targeting CDK12 condensates with cyclin K molecular glue degraders.
affiliations: Interdisciplinary Research Center on Biology and Chemistry, Shanghai Institute of Organic Chemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shanghai, China (corresponding author)

papers.title: Gut Roseburia hominis-derived 10-hydroxystearic acid alleviates metabolic disorder by restoring hepatic fatty acid metabolism
papers.abstract: Metabolic disorders and health-promoting dietary interventions represent complementary contexts of metabolic impairment and improvement, providing an opportunity to identify gut microbial taxa associated with both disease status and dietary response. Here, we integrated five independent human cohorts spanning metabolic disorders and dietary interventions and identified Roseburia hominis as a gut microbial taxon that consistently decreased in metabolic disorders and increased after dietary interventions. Beyond species abundance, strain-level genetic variation in R. hominis provided additional information for distinguishing metabolic disorder status and stratifying cardiometabolic severity. Integration of phenotype-associated variants with circulating metabolomics prioritized ohyA, encoding an oleate hydratase, as a candidate functional determinant linking R. hominis genetic variation to host metabolic heterogeneity. An ohyA-based genetic burden score was associated with adverse cardiometabolic traits and changed longitudinally during dietary intervention, while circulating metabolites statistically accounted for part of the associations between ohyA variants and host phenotypes. Functional experiments demonstrated that R. hominis OhyA protein converts oleic acid to 10-hydroxystearic acid (10-HSA), whereas an OhyA carrying five prioritized missense substitutions showed markedly impaired enzymatic activity. In high-fat diet-fed mice, 10-HSA attenuated body-weight gain, improved glucose homeostasis and insulin sensitivity, and reduced dyslipidemia and hepatic steatosis. Multi-omics profiling revealed limited remodeling of the gut microbiota but pronounced hepatic transcriptional and metabolic responses, characterized by activation of PPAR-associated lipid-metabolic pathways, altered fatty-acid oxidation and desaturation, and remodeling of hepatic lipid composition. Together, these findings establish a diet-responsive R. hominis-OhyA-10-HSA axis linking microbial variation to host metabolic dysfunction and show that 10-HSA can improve metabolic health in mice.
affiliations: Nanyang Technological University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Physiological mapping and prediction reveal stress-responsive translation initiation landscapes
papers.abstract: Translation initiation defines the protein output of the transcriptome, but its physiological dynamics in cells and tissues remain incompletely characterized. Here we develop TISCA2, an inhibitor-free method that captures eIF5B-associated initiating ribosomes to map translation initiation sites genome-wide. By directly identifying start sites rather than inferring translation from elongating-ribosome periodicity, TISCA2 improves the detection of short and overlapping translons. Translation of a subset of TISCA2-identified translons is supported by N-terminal proteomics and HLA-I immunopeptidomics. The arsenite-induced integrated stress response broadly redistributes start-site usage, reducing upstream initiation in favor of downstream initiation. TISCA2 further reveals tissue-specific initiation landscapes in vivo, with increased detection of downstream candidate start sites in the testis. Finally, we develop IncepTIS, a sequence-based deep learning model that predicts position-resolved and condition-dependent initiation landscapes. IncepTIS-guided optimization generates de novo mRNA 5' leaders with stress-responsive initiation patterns. Together, TISCA2 and IncepTIS provide an experimental and computational framework for mapping, predicting and engineering translation initiation in mammalian cells and tissues.
affiliations: Division of Biological Science, Graduate School of Science, Nagoya University, Nagoya 464-8602 Japan.; Research Institute of Environmental Medicine, Nagoya Univ (corresponding author)

papers.title: Diversification of budding yeast polarization dynamics after compensatory experimental evolution
papers.abstract: Essential cellular processes evolve under strong selection, yet protein networks underlying conserved functions can vary substantially. To what extent evolution constrains the intracellular dynamics of proteins performing essential functions is currently largely unknown. Here, we characterize budding yeast polarization phenotypes along a previously established evolutionary recovery trajectory, compensating for the loss of near-essential polarity gene BEM1. Through quantitative live cell imaging, we show that loss of BEM1 weakens and destabilizes polarization. Surprisingly, in recovered evolved lineages, protein dynamics change significantly compared to the ancestor: most notably, presence of main regulator Cdc42-GTP is strongly decreased, while polarisome member Spa2 localizes more slowly into mobile foci. Although separate phenotypic characteristics are only weakly constrained, we find evidence of effective protein-independent localization modes, revealing signs of convergence along the evolutionary trajectory. Together, our results show that evolution can restore global cellular function without conserving microscopic organization, instead giving rise to novel molecular phenotypes.
affiliations: Delft University of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Platycodin D2 Targets Vimentin to Suppress Fibroblast-Myofibroblast Transition: A Novel Therapeutic Strategy Against Pulmonary Fibrosis
papers.abstract: Background Pulmonary fibrosis is a progressive lung disease characterized by excessive extracellular matrix deposition and irreversible decline in lung function with limited effective therapeutic targets. Vimentin, a type III intermediate filament protein, plays a critical role in fibroblast activation and fibrogenesis, representing a promising drug target. Methods Novel vimentin ligands were screened via virtual screening. SPR assay verified compound-vimentin binding affinity. CETSA and CD spectroscopy analyzed protein structural changes after compound binding. In vitro FMT model and in vivo bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis model were used to assess antifibrotic effects, and mutagenesis assays identified key binding amino acid residues. Results Platycodin D2 (PD2) from Platycodon grandiflorus was identified as a novel high-affinity vimentin ligand (Kd = 392.8 nM). PD2 binds vimentin directly, alters its secondary structure and induces insoluble aggregation. It effectively inhibits TGF-{beta}1-induced FMT in vitro and mitigates bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis in vivo, reducing collagen deposition and improving animal survival. Critically, mutagenesis validation confirmed that key residues (Glu138 in chain A, Glu132 and Glu143 in chain B, as well as Glu50 and Arg54 in chain C) are essential for this interaction. Conclusions Our findings establish PD2 as a novel pharmacological inducer of aberrant vimentin aggregation, presenting a distinct target-driven strategy for antifibrotic drug development.
affiliations: School of Basic Medical Sciences, Cheeloo College of Medicine, Shandong University, Jinan, China (corresponding author)

papers.title: Compartment-Resolved Matrisome Shifts During Postnatal Tendon Maturation in Mice
papers.abstract: Tendons acquire their load-bearing capacity during the first month of postnatal growth, driven by the extensive remodeling of the extracellular matrix (ECM). While the role of specific individual components to this process have been well characterized, a comprehensive assessment of how the tendon matrisome changes during this critical window is lacking. This, in part, is due to the challenges associated with solubilization of mature ECM, which is underrepresented by conventical proteomic approaches. To address this, we performed compartment-resolved proteomics on murine Achilles and plantaris tendons at postnatal days 0 (P0), P14, and P28. Sequential extraction methods leveraged a CHAPS-soluble fraction, capturing cellular and soluble matrisome proteins, from the insoluble mature ECM fraction, solubilized by guanidine hydrochloride and hydroxylamine hydrochloride and separately analyzed by label-free quantitative LC-MS/MS. Analysis shows that the two compartments followed distinct trajectories during maturation. The insoluble matrix was dominated by collagenous proteins, which increased from 95% to over 99% of the identified signal intensity, and its composition was largely established by P14. Within the soluble matrisome compartment, collagens increased from 50% to over 60% by P14, accompanied by dynamic regulation of proteins implicated in collagen processing (P4HA1, PCOLCE), crosslinking (LOX, LOXL2), and regulators of collagen fibril assembly and growth (DCN, BGN, FMOD, THBS3, THBS4). Beyond these established regulators, we observed dynamic regulation of less-characterized fibril-associated proteoglycans (KERA, OGN, CHAD), matricellular (COMP, POSTN, MATN2), and angiogenic regulatorily proteins (SERPINF1, ECM1). Together, this work establishes a comprehensive protein-level reference for postnatal tendon maturating, provides new insights into the molecular regulation of functional tendon development.
affiliations: Massachusetts General Hospital (corresponding author)

papers.title: NanoPAMDA enables rapid PAM characterization of metagenome-derived Cas9 effectors
papers.abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 orthologs remain functionally underexplored despite the rapidly growing scale of publicly available metagenomic sequencing data. Here, we applied a multi-stage computational discovery pipeline to two independent sources of metagenomic sequence data, a multi-biome collection of 660,185 metagenome-assembled genomes spanning 17 public catalogs, and raw sequencing reads from human microbiome studies assembled de novo, to identify novel Cas9 orthologs. Candidates were filtered for guide RNA architectural plausibility, sequence novelty, conservation of catalytic residues, and structural integrity, yielding 14 candidates spanning both data sources for experimental characterization. To determine PAM preference at scale, we developed a cost-effective Nanopore long-read-based adaptation of the high-throughput PAM determination assay (NanoPAMDA), enabling rapid, time-resolved, kinetic PAM profiling across many candidates in parallel. One Cas9 effector, E10, showed PAM-specific activity in vitro and was catalytically active in E. coli. Together, these findings demonstrate a scalable, long-read sequencing-based framework for discovering and biochemically characterizing novel Cas9 orthologs from metagenomic data.
affiliations: Department of Molecular Biology and Genetics, Faculty of Science, Bogazici University (corresponding author)

papers.title: RNA-triggered Cas12a2 antibacterial activity and resistance plasmid degradation
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) necessitates programmable antibacterial strategies with novel mechanisms. Here, we evaluated an inducible intracellular CRISPR/Cas12a2 system in engineered Escherichia coli targeting a chloramphenicol-resistance (Chl) transcript. Cas12a2 activation significantly delayed bacterial growth and reduced recoverable colony-forming units (CFU) by 3-log10 in vitro, and reduced bacterial burdens in a mouse skin wound model. Transcriptomic profiling revealed upregulation of recA, a key mediator of the SOS response. We therefore designed a Chl-recA dual-targeting construct, which produced a greater growth delay than either single-targeting counterpart. The optimized dual-targeting system led to an approximately 4-log10 reduction in bacterial burden in vivo. Furthermore, exploratory qPCR of culture supernatants suggested a treatment-associated decrease in amplifiable plasmid DNA. Overall, this study provides proof-of-concept for resistance-transcript-guided Cas12a2 antibacterial activity and highlights the potential of co-targeting stress-associated transcripts to enhance programmable antimicrobials.
affiliations: China Pharmaceutical University (corresponding author)

papers.title: 1D model simulations suggest biofilms can suppress cathodic H2 bubble formation
papers.abstract: Microbial electrosynthesis (MES) electrochemically generates H2 for the reduction of CO2 into acetate by acetogens. So far, the importance of a biofilm on the cathode of such systems remains under debate. Here, we investigated the role of cathodic biofilms through computational modelling. We developed MES-BIOFILM, a comprehensive one-dimensional model to simulate steady-state H2 and CO2 concentration gradients within cathodic biofilms, while accounting for the limited solubility of H2. The effects of key biofilm properties, including thickness, cell density and H2 consumption rate were analysed. Overall, our simulations indicate that cathodic biofilms play an important role in (1) minimizing H2 loss from the system through H2 consumption within the biofilm; and (2) suppressing H2 bubble formation by maintaining the H2 concentrations at the cathode surface below saturation. Our model predicts that the current density at which H2 bubbles begin to form can be increased by 5.5-fold relative to a bare electrode when biofilms exhibit a high cell density and high H2 consumption rate. This effect requires biofilms of at least 50 m thickness, whereas CO2 diffusion limitations arise above 200 m. These findings highlight the critical role of biofilms to increase MES performance, while requiring further experimental validation.
affiliations: Biological and Chemical Engineering, Aarhus University, Denmark (corresponding author)

papers.title: Benchmarking Statistical Methods for Differential Composition Analysis in Population-Scale Single-Cell Data
papers.abstract: Population-scale single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data capture cellular composition across cohorts ranging from several dozen to thousands of individuals, enabling the detection of cell-type composition differences between conditions. These differences reveal cellular shifts in disease pathogenesis and suggest potential targets for therapeutic intervention. However, differential composition analysis in scRNA-seq data is challenged by the unique features of cell count data, such as compositionality, prevalence of zeros, overdispersion, and confounding by technical and biological covariates. While this analysis is routinely performed, no study has yet systematically evaluated existing methods. Here, we benchmarked 12 methods for differential composition analysis using three population-scale scRNA-seq datasets with diverse and representative characteristics. Analyses of real data revealed low agreement across methods, while permutations and simulations based on the real data demonstrated excessive false discoveries for most methods. Overall, LOCOM emerged as the top-performing method that controls the false discovery rate while maintaining good statistical power, followed by ANCOM-BC and linear regression with centered-log-ratio transformation. Integrating evidence from real-data analyses and data-informed permutation and simulation experiments, we provide practical guidance tailored to common real-world challenges in differential composition analysis.
affiliations: Department of Biostatistics and Bioinformatics, Emory University, Atlanta, GA, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: A comparative transcriptomic framework across kidney organoid, assembloid, and transplantation models
papers.abstract: Human kidney organoids recapitulate key aspects of renal development and have emerged as valuable platforms for disease modeling, nephrotoxicity screening, and therapeutic development. The field now includes a wide range of emerging protocols with distinct cellular compositions and maturation states, which complicates systematic comparison and model selection. Here, we integrated single-cell and single-nucleus transcriptomes from 11 studies spanning kidney organoid and assembloids, both in vitro and following transplantation, benchmarked against fetal and adult kidney references. Transcriptional maturation toward adult identity is compartment specific and does not correlate with protocol complexity. Assembloid protocols show the most adult-like podocyte and distal nephron signatures, transplantation is associated with enhanced tubular oxidative metabolic features, only protocols incorporating ureteric progenitors reliably generate collecting-duct lineages, and no protocol achieves mature adult proximal tubule identity. Annotating against either fetal or adult kidney reference alone leads to misassignment, because early fetal nephron epithelium transcriptionally resembles injury-dedifferentiated adult proximal tubule cells. Assembloid and transplantation models share elevated mechanosensing pathway expression independently of vascularization. Together, these findings provide a framework for kidney organoid model selection.
affiliations: University of Hawaii at Manoa (corresponding author)

papers.title: Improving phosphoproteomic kinase activity inference by contextual refinement of Kinase Library relationships
papers.abstract: Kinase activity inference from phosphoproteomic data relies on kinase-specific substrate sets defined by kinase-substrate relationship (KSR) priors. Kinase Library (KL) expands candidate substrate coverage using experimentally derived kinase specificity profiles, but its predictions reflect sequence compatibility rather than established intracellular regulation. We benchmarked KL-expanded KSR priors using 222 perturbation phosphoproteomic samples covering 396 annotated activation or inhibition events across 78 kinases. Broad KL expansion increased the number of scoreable kinases from 108 to 391, but reduced perturbed-kinase discrimination, directional accuracy and ranking performance. Higher error rates occurred among kinases with limited curated substrate support, while broad expansion also increased redundancy among inferred activity profiles. To improve the reliability of motif-derived relationships, we constrained KL-derived KSRs using predicted protein co-localization and protein-association evidence. Protein-association filtering consistently improved inference performance, reduced activity redundancy and provided a more favorable accuracy-coverage balance than co-localization filtering. The selected protein-association-filtered prior retained activity estimates for 308 kinases with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) above 0.75 and extended inference to 200 kinases not scoreable using curated KSRs, which were significantly enriched for dark kinases. These newly scoreable kinases showed structured activity patterns across perturbation contexts and interpretable signaling associations. Our results show that protein-association evidence can refine motif-derived KSR priors while preserving broad kinome coverage, providing a practical framework for more reliable phosphoproteomic kinase activity inference.
affiliations: Tongji University (corresponding author)

papers.title: memVar: an integrated resource for interpreting human membrane protein variation in molecular and disease contexts
papers.abstract: Interpreting membrane protein variation requires connecting clinical evidence to the membrane environments and molecular interactions that govern protein functions. Here, we introduce memVar (https://memvar.sunnylab.org), an integrated database of 10,906,688unique single-nucleotide variants from ClinVar, COSMIC, and gnomAD across 7,732 human membrane-associated proteins. memVar reconciles genomic, transcript, and protein coordinates to link variants with membrane topology, bilayer depth, lipid contacts, functional sites, partner-specific interaction interfaces, and variant-effect predictions, alongside disease, tissue-expression and regulatory annotations. Coordinated sequence, structure and variant views retain source provenance and distinguish clinical assertions, experimental observations, and computational predictions. Our analysis reveals that pathogenic/likely pathogenic missense substitutions are enriched in transmembrane segments and predicted protein-protein interaction sites relative to benign/likely benign substitutions, with pooled odds ratios of 2.47 and 6.67, respectively. IntAct-derived interaction loss or decrease was experimentally recorded for 57.9% of pathogenic/likely pathogenic substitutions versus 7.4% of benign/likely benign substitutions. CFTR examples contextualize the established G551D gating defect and prioritize W202R, a variant of uncertain significance, for tests of protein maturation, surface abundance and channel activity. By connecting variant records to specific molecular questions, memVar potentially supports mechanism-oriented investigation and prioritization of functional experiments.
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) (corresponding author)

papers.title: Lipidic α-synuclein fibrils catalyze the formation of pathological mature fibrils
papers.abstract: The aggregation of -synuclein into amyloid fibrils is a hallmark of a collection of neurodegenerative diseases termed synucleinopathies, including Parkinson's disease (PD). Interactions between -synuclein and lipid membranes modulate -synuclein aggregation and can produce protofibril structures consisting of both protein and lipid, termed lipidic fibrils. These lipidic fibrils can mature into mature fibrils, which resemble ex vivo fibrils extracted from Lewy bodies found in post-mortem brain samples of PD patients. Here, through the combination of experiments and kinetic theory, we study the influence of lipids and lipidic fibrils on the formation of mature fibrils. We find that lipidic fibrils catalyze mature fibril formation via a heterogeneous primary nucleation mechanism, which lowers the activation energy barrier of mature fibril formation relative to lipid-independent primary nucleation. The final stage of the reaction is governed by mature fibril elongation becoming limited by the rate at which protein monomers dissociate from the metastable lipidic fibrils, confirming that fibrils form in order of stability following Ostwald's Rule of Stages. This mechanism is validated using the small molecule inhibitor ambroxol, which selectively suppresses the formation of lipidic fibrils and in this manner shifts the aggregation kinetics to the slow, lipid-independent pathway. Taken together, these findings reveal that lipidic fibrils act as on-pathway intermediates and accelerate the aggregation of mature fibrils, which could provide a quantitative framework to design novel therapeutic strategies to inhibit pathological -synuclein aggregation.
affiliations: ETH Zurich (corresponding author)

papers.title: Robust T and B cell activation is associated with rapid clearance of infectious SARS-CoV-2
papers.abstract: The immunologic correlates of rapid clearance of SARS-CoV-2 shedding are not well understood, partly due to challenges of collecting samples early after infection and the fact that most studies do not measure infectious virus. Here, we performed mass cytometry profiling of peripheral blood cells collected from people 4-6 days after onset of symptoms from acute SARS-CoV-2 infection who underwent daily nasopharyngeal testing for SARS-CoV-2 culture positivity. We identified broad and coordinated activation of innate and adaptive immune cells in unvaccinated individuals with primary infection. Faster clearance of infectious virus shedding was associated with robust adaptive immune cell activation and proliferation, namely among cytotoxic CD8+, CD4+, and {gamma}{delta} T cells and plasmablasts. In contrast, vaccinated individuals who rapidly cleared breakthrough infection showed minimal cellular immune activation. Our findings identify early immune correlates of rapid clearance of infectious SARS-CoV-2 shedding that may inform future prevention and therapeutic approaches to reduce disease burden and transmission.
affiliations: University of California, San Francisco (corresponding author)

papers.title: Live attenuated YFV-17D vaccine induces robust B and T cell immunity in vaccine-draining lymph nodes
papers.abstract: The yellow fever virus-17D (YFV-17D) vaccine is widely regarded as one of the most effective vaccines in existence, with protection linked to robust elicitation of neutralising antibodies1. The features of the germinal centre (GC) reaction driving this durable and potent antibody responses remain unclear. Here we examined immune dynamics in blood and lymph nodes (LNs) after primary YFV-17D immunisation in humans. Using fine needle biopsy (FNB), we identified robust T and B lymphocyte responses within draining LNs, underpinning maturation of antibodies targeting the viral envelope (E). Early antibody responses were largely IgM, with gradual accumulation of E-specific memory B cells and anti-viral IgG in the subsequent months. Monoclonal antibodies derived from GC B cells had specificity for E, with diversification in the LN capable of driving increases in binding and neutralising potency. While circulating vaccine-specific CD4+ T cells peaked two weeks post-vaccination, clonally related GC and IL-10+ T follicular helper populations progressively accumulated in the LN. Comparison of FNB transcriptional datasets following YFV-17D, SARS-CoV-2 mRNA/LNP, and seasonal influenza vaccination identified a conserved GC program involving similar B and T lymphocyte subpopulations. Collectively, we find that while YFV-17D induces robust GC activity, this trait is shared with other vaccine platforms and the notably durable protection against infection may reflect an incapacity of the virus to escape host immunity.
affiliations: University of Melbourne (corresponding author)

papers.title: Long-read shotgun metagenomics identifies distinct urogenital microbial community states associated with functional potential and urinary tract infection during pregnancy
papers.abstract: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are among the most common bacterial infections during pregnancy and are associated with adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes. Although previous studies used enhanced culture, 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and/or short-read shotgun metagenomic sequencing to characterize the urogenital microbiome of adult females, few have assessed the urogenital microbiome during pregnancy and thus this microbiome remains poorly understood. Here, we applied Oxford Nanopore long-read shotgun metagenomic sequencing to characterize urogenital microbial composition, functional potential, metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), and the urogenital virome of pregnant females. Taxonomic profiling identified three distinct microbial community states predominated by Lactobacillus crispatus, Gardnerella species, and L. iners. The Gardnerella-predominated community was associated with a higher frequency of UTI during pregnancy. Functional profiles strongly reflected these community states, demonstrating that taxonomic differences were accompanied by distinct functional potential. Genome-resolved analysis recovered 415 MAGs, including 29 high-quality genomes, revealing substantial genomic diversity among urogenital microbes. Viral sequences, predominantly bacteriophages, also were detected in most samples, highlighting an additional component of the pregnancy-associated urogenital microbiome. These findings demonstrate that pregnant females possess distinct urogenital microbial community states and show that they differ not only in taxonomic composition but also in their functional potential.
affiliations: Loyola University Chicago Stritch School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: The Pseudomonas protegens PBL3 secretome exerts antimicrobial activity against Burkholderia glumae by disrupting cell envelope homeostasis and impairing bacterial replication
papers.abstract: The effectiveness of antimicrobials used to manage bacterial infections is increasingly threatened by the emergence of antimicrobial resistance. Many conventional antimicrobials act on a single defined target that pathogens can circumvent through target modification or pathway adaptation. In contrast, antimicrobials that disrupt multiple cellular processes may impose greater fitness costs and reduce the likelihood of resistance development, making their discovery a priority for pharmaceutical and agricultural applications. We previously demonstrated that the environmental bacterium Pseudomonas protegens PBL3 secretes a complex mixture of molecules (secretome) with antimicrobial activity against several plants and human pathogens. However, the mechanism underlying this activity remained unknown. Here, we used the plant pathogen Burkholderia glumae to investigate the mode of action of the P. protegens PBL3 secretome. We showed that the P. protegens PLB3 secretome causes extensive cell envelope damage that results in cell death and interferes with bacterial multiplication. Transcriptomic analysis further revealed broad disruption of processes associated with cell-envelope biogenesis and homeostasis and bacterial replication. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the P. protegens PBL3 secretome acts as a multi-target antimicrobial that could be harnessed in the development of therapeutics to control bacterial infections of agricultural and medical importance.
affiliations: University of Nebraska-Lincoln (corresponding author)

papers.title: Phenotypic and Molecular Characterization of Potentially New Shigella boydii Serotype in Bangladesh
papers.abstract: Objective: Shigella is a major cause of bacillary dysentery among children under 5 years of age, especially in low- and middle-income countries. At Dhaka hospital of icddr,b, every year around 3% of Shigella isolates from patients with diarrhea are identified as Shigella-like organisms (SLOs). These isolates do not react with any of the existing and provisional Shigella antisera. The major aims of the present study were to characterize a unique cluster of SLOs using phenotypic and genotypic methods. Methods: A cluster of 6 SLOs was characterized using biochemical tests, serotyping, antimicrobial susceptibility, and virulence assay by using the Sereny test, PCR and compared their pulsed-field gel electrophoresis (PFGE) patterns with known serotypes of Shigella spp. Antisera against the isolate were raised in a rabbit model to determine cross-reactivity with known serotypes. Results: All six SLOs were mannitol fermenting, have invasive properties, positive for ipaH and Shigella enterotoxin 2 gene along with possession of virulence plasmid of ~ 140 MDa. All isolates were resistant to ampicillin, tetracycline, sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim, but were sensitive to mecillinam, nalidixic acid, and ciprofloxacin. Plasmid and PFGE profiles showed that the genomic patterns of these isolates were identical but were different from all other S. boydii serotypes. Antiserum prepared against one of the isolates agglutinated with all isolates but did not cross-react with other Shigella and E. coli reference strains. Conclusion: This unique cluster of isolates might belong to a new provisional serovar of S. boydii and further analysis is required to incorporate it into the stereotypic scheme of Shigella.
affiliations: Primeasia University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Ferroptosis of selective progenitor cell types during embryogenesis ensures proper organ morphogenesis
papers.abstract: Ferroptosis, a form of non-apoptotic cell death, is induced by lipid peroxidation resulting from an intracellular accumulation of labile iron (1). While apoptosis is involved in embryonic development (2), the role of ferroptosis in embryogenesis is unknown. Here, we report that the ferroptosis process occurs in the embryonic lung and kidney at mid- and late-gestation. In these tissues, pro-ferroptotic cells include subpopulations of the Sox9+ distal lung epithelial cells and the Flk1+ vascular progenitors in the kidney glomeruli. Lipidomic analysis reveals mixed lipid peroxidation as the driver for ferroptosis. The role of ferroptosis in the morphogenesis of these organs was confirmed by triple positivity of TfR1, 4-HNE and TUNEL, mitochondrial defects, cell membrane breakage, dead cell remnants, single-cell RNA-sequencing of a ferroptosis gene signature. Genetic manipulation of Gpx4, an endogenous inhibitor of ferroptosis. Further, genetic knockout or transgenic overexpression of Gpx4 affects lung and kidney development and results in cystic lungs and kidneys. Notably, conditional deletion Gpx4 results in hypoplasia of the lung epithelia and of the renal glomeruli, while transgenic overexpression of Gpx4 resulted in atelectasis with collapsed lung alveoli and hypertrophic glomeruli. Together, these findings show that ferroptosis regulates lung and kidney morphogenesis by acting in key progenitor cell populations during gestation. Supplementation of iron or polyunsaturated fatty acid during pregnancy has implications for organogenesis.
affiliations: University of Maryland School of medicine, Baltimore (corresponding author)

papers.title: Light-dependent conversion of body color change pattern during zebrafish development
papers.abstract: Zebrafish (Danio rerio) shows body color change in response to light: when light comes, it whitens body color. Our previous study has shown that larval zebrafish as early as 5 days post-fertilization (dpf) have this capacity fully developed whereas 2-dpf larvae exhibit light-induced darkening in sharp contrast (Shiraki et al. 2010). Here, we discovered that the conversion in body color change pattern between 2 dpf and 5 dpf is light-dependent: larvae reared in darkness exhibited light-induced darkening of body color, reminiscent of 2-dpf larvae. We also found that a 14-h light exposure on 3 or 4 dpf is sufficient to trigger this conversion, and that the conversion by light on 4 dpf still occurred after ablation of most exorh-expressing pineal photoreceptor cells. The dark-reared larvae had significantly lower transcription levels of pmch and pmchl, which encode melanin-concentrating hormone precursors, than the LD-reared larvae. However, the levels in larvae that had undergone the conversion (3-L and 4-L) were not significantly different from those in dark-reared larvae, indicating that the reduced pmch/pmchl expression alone does not account for the conversion. In conclusion, light exposure in rearing is indispensable for the maturation of body color change ability in larval zebrafish through a regulatory mechanism independent of exorh-expressing pineal photoreceptors.
affiliations: University of Tokyo (corresponding author)

papers.title: Transportability of mouse gene knockout models to human complex phenotypes
papers.abstract: Mouse gene knockout studies are a valuable resource for understanding human gene function and the mechanisms underlying disease. However, translating insights to humans requires causal similarities between mouse and human phenotypes. A mouse model is transportable if gene perturbations that impact the mouse phenotype also affect (in orthologous genes) the corresponding human phenotype of interest, with consistent directionality. To assess the transportability of mouse models to human complex traits we combined laboratory mouse gene perturbation data from the high-throughput International Mouse Phenotyping Consortium with predicted loss-of-function data from the UK Biobank within the Gene Perturbation Analysis for Transportability (GPAT) framework. Applying GPAT to 30 matched mouse-human phenotype pairs, we found evidence of transportability for 12 mouse phenotypes including biochemical (e.g. total cholesterol), cellular (e.g. lymphocyte counts) and anthropometric (e.g. length/height) phenotypes. In contrast, there was limited evidence for others such as fat mass and body mass index in the context of the murine experimental conditions. We also found some evidence of transportability of mouse glucose measurements to diabetes mellitus in humans. Genome-wide perturbation effects on matched phenotypes were on average positively correlated between mice and humans (meta-analysis GPAT P = 2.3x10-27). However, the degree of correlation was generally modest and heterogeneous across phenotypes with some gene perturbations strongly associated in both species in opposite directions. Our framework illustrates how perturbation data can be used to quantitatively validate experimental models for understanding human disease aetiology and highlights the need for a range of orthogonal model systems, which may include challenges and perturbations to the mouse knockouts, to interrogate the mechanistic basis of human genetic associations.
affiliations: GSK (corresponding author)

papers.title: Translating chemical reactions into enzyme sequences enables formate dehydrogenase engineering
papers.abstract: Enzyme engineering has broad applications across chemistry and biotechnology but remains costly and susceptible to low success rates. Generative artificial intelligence can substantially expand the sequence space accessible to enzyme engineering; however, directing generation towards enzymes that catalyse a user-defined chemical reaction remains challenging. Inspired by machine translation, we formulate enzyme generation as translation between two molecular languages: chemical reactions and amino acid sequences. Here, we introduce REXzyme, a translation model that generates enzymes conditioned on user-defined reactions. First, we evaluate its designs using multiple in silico metrics and characterize the strengths and limitations of its generalisation capacity. Then, we steer REXzyme towards the generation of enhanced formate dehydrogenases for their reverse natural reaction, i.e., the reduction of carbon dioxide. All 20 generated enzymes were expressed and purified as soluble proteins and exhibited CO2-reduction activity, with the most active design reaching 2.5-fold the specific activity of the reference enzyme. Notably, all substitutions in the designed variants were performed on distal positions outside the catalytic site. Our results show that reaction-to-sequence translation provides a route for efficiently engineering enhanced biocatalysts.
affiliations: Centre for Genomic Regulation (corresponding author)

papers.title: Quantitative Spatial Analysis of Matrix Remodelling in Wounds Using Digital Pathology and Fractal Analysis
papers.abstract: Wound healing involves spatially heterogeneous changes in matrix composition and organisation that can be difficult to capture using qualitative histological assessment alone. We developed a reproducible digital pathology workflow to quantify matrix features in cutaneous wound sections, compare them with unwounded skin, and derive an exploratory Histological Wound Index (HWI). Four normal-skin and six wound sections were analysed using QuPath, ImageJ/FracLac and Python. Approximately 500 x 500 micrometer regions of interest (ROI) were assigned to normal skin, wound centre, proximal edge or distant edge. Collagen, mucin and necrotic tissue coverage were quantified using image classifiers and analysed with linear mixed-effects models. Collagen architecture was assessed from collagen-selective binary masks using fractal dimension and lacunarity. Collagen coverage, fractal dimension, mucin coverage, necrosis and lacunarity were z-standardised and integrated into the HWI. Unwounded skin showed high collagen coverage and fractal dimension, with low lacunarity, mucin and necrosis. In contrast, wound-centre tissue showed low collagen coverage and fractal dimension together with higher mucin and necrosis. Distant-edge regions retained comparatively normal-like characteristics, whereas proximal-edge regions showed intermediate values. HWI was highest in normal skin and lowest in the wound centre. A descriptive matched-ROI comparison of two wound sections reproduced this regional ordering when all component measures were derived from identical ROI boundaries. This workflow provides a reproducible framework for quantifying regional ECM features and collagen-mask architecture in wound histology. The HWI is an exploratory histological summary requiring validation in larger longitudinal datasets.
affiliations: The University of Manchester, FBMH, School of Biological Sciences (corresponding author)

papers.title: Reconstruction of Cellular Trajectories with Biologically Interpretable States
papers.abstract: Elucidating the trajectories of cellular evolution provides biologists with deeper insights into biological systems and disease progression, ultimately facilitating more informed discovery of mechanisms and therapeutic design. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is widely used to study cellular evolution. However, it faces two primary limitations. First, because the process destroys cells during gene-expression measurement, it is impossible to track the gene-expression profile of the same cell throughout the entire trajectory. Second, because scRNA-seq captures cells at discrete time points, it provides only static snapshots rather than continuous trajectories, limiting its ability to resolve the full dynamics of cellular transitions. Consequently, various computational approaches have been developed to address these challenges. However, existing models fail to capture the hidden state of each cell, which is essential for reconstructing gene expression at unobserved time points. As the gene expression profiles depend on the cell state, and may vary according to time, we propose a Latent Cell-State Model, where we approximate cell state transition as a Markov chain and obtain the gene expression of each cell at unobserved timepoints depending on the cell state, time, and a latent variable that represents the high-dimensional gene expression profile of a cell. Our model is able to infer biologically meaningful cell states and generate high-quality gene expression profiles at unobserved timepoints, showing potential for accurate trajectory reconstruction.
affiliations: The University of Manchester (corresponding author)

papers.title: Growth-driven mechanical buckling as a mechanism of age-related tortuosity in human cerebral arteries
papers.abstract: Human cerebral arteries become increasingly, sometimes abnormally, winding with age, but the mechanical basis of this change remains incompletely understood. To examine how arterial bends form and what sets their spacing, we modeled a cerebral artery as a slender elastic vessel supported by surrounding tissue. The distance between its ends remains constant, and the vessel can bend only in a plane tangent to the brain surface. As its natural length increases, axial compression builds until the vessel buckles. Bending partly relieves the compression, and the resulting waves grow in amplitude as elongation continues. Arterial bending stiffness and tissue support determine the wavelength, which is much larger than and proportional to vessel diameter, with comparatively weak dependence on other parameters. Numerical simulations captured a pre-buckling phase, rapid amplification of waves, and slow post-buckling growth during continued elongation. We evaluated these predictions using three-dimensional centerlines of cerebral arteries reconstructed from magnetic resonance angiography in healthy adults. Older age was associated with greater arterial length and excess-length ratio. For arterial waves oriented mostly parallel to the brain surface, wavelength increased with vessel diameter. Both this relationship and the observed wavelength-to-diameter ratio were consistent with model predictions. However, wave amplitude was not significantly associated with age. Overall, the modeling and imaging results support growth-driven buckling and post-buckling deformation under spatial constraint as a plausible mechanical explanation for age-related cerebral arterial tortuosity. This framework links vascular aging to growth-driven instability and pattern formation, with potential applications to diseased arteries beyond the brain.
affiliations: Department of Neurosurgery, Graduate School of Medical Sciences, Kyushu University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Response to azacitidine and the TIM-3 inhibitor, sabatolimab, in MDS and CMML is associated with distinct immune and antigen-presentation states
papers.abstract: Targeting the immune checkpoint TIM-3 is of interest in myeloid neoplasms, yet the hematopoietic and immune changes associated with anti-TIM-3 therapy remain poorly characterized. We used single-cell RNA sequencing to profile bone marrow (BM) and peripheral blood from patients with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML) treated with the hypomethylating agent azacitidine combined with sabatolimab, a monoclonal antibody targeting TIM-3, and integrated Human Cell Atlas reference datasets for comparison. CITE-seq profiling showed that TIM-3 was predominantly expressed on dendritic cells and NK cells, with variable expression across other populations, including CD34 cells and CD8 T cells. At baseline, we identified a population of CD34 myeloid-biased progenitors specific to MDS/CMML samples ("HSPC-like") characterized by inflammatory gene expression programs and features of impaired differentiation. In MDS, elevated baseline HLA class II expression across hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs), HSPC-like cells, and multiple myeloid populations was associated with response. Consistent with this finding, trajectory analysis suggested that nonresponders bypassed HLA class II-high states during myeloid differentiation. In MDS, the presence of distinct CD8 T-cell populations and increased interferon-response programs in CD8 T and NK cells at baseline was also associated with response. In both MDS and CMML, treatment among responders was associated with contraction of BM CD8 and CD4 T-cell populations characterized by type I interferon-responsive and inflammatory programs, including IFIT1, IFIT2, and TNF, along with expansion of a distinct GZMH/IFITM1-expressing cytotoxic CD8 T-cell population. Together, these findings identify baseline antigen-presentation and immune-response programs associated with therapeutic response and reveal coordinated remodeling of myeloid and lymphoid compartments during azacitidine/sabatolimab treatment in MDS and CMML.
affiliations: Center for Immunology and Inflammatory Diseases, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA; Krantz Family Center for Cancer Research, Massachusetts General Hos (corresponding author)

papers.title: Failed allogeneic corneal lenticules show fibrosis and identity loss without dominant T cell rejection
papers.abstract: Failed allogeneic corneal stromal lenticules develop progressive opacity, but the state of the implanted tissue is unknown. Here we show that six explants from three patients occupy a fibrotic integration-failure state with scar-matrix production and loss of corneal identity without a dominant T cell rejection program. Scar-matrix, transparency and corneal-identity programs separated every patient from eight unimplanted donor controls, the last defined by independent human single-cell references. Calibrated immune programs and repertoire reconstruction distinguished the explants from canonical adaptive rejection. Exchange reduced interface reflectivity initially, followed by recurrent opacity in two patients and corneal steepening with declining uncorrected acuity in the third. In non-scarring rabbit repair, identity moved toward the uninjured state as backscatter returned toward normal despite increasing similarity to the explant-derived expression signature. Within one culture experiment, marked scar suppression accompanied opposite identity responses. Tacrolimus and rapamycin likewise suppressed canonical rejection while moving identity in opposite directions. Resveratrol combined reduced scar-associated programs and increased identity with improved graft appearance in the source study. These findings establish classic-rejection activity and tissue integration as separable axes and direct treatment of failed lenticules from escalating immunosuppression toward control of stromal remodeling and preservation of corneal identity.
affiliations: Department of Ophthalmology, Peking Union Medical College Hospital, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences and Peking Union Medical College (corresponding author)

papers.title: Orsay virus infection is associated with reduced locomotion and alters cue-dependent food choice in Caenorhabditis elegans
papers.abstract: Behavioral responses are an important component of host defense; however, most evidence in Caenorhabditis elegans comes from bacterial pathogens. Here, we tested whether infection with Orsay virus (OrV) alters host dispersal and food choice and whether these responses involve the RNA-processing factor EOL-1. When measuring distance travelled over a certain period of time in control and infected wild-type animals, we observed that OrV infection was associated with lower locomotion. Moreover, when presenting infected and control animals with food choices, we observed that infected animals preferred OrV infected food sources only when the alternative was a pure food source, preferring a non-inoculated food source when both control and viral food sources contained a C. elegans filtrate. Moreover, loss of EOL-1 altered baseline locomotion and attenuated the infection-associated reduction detected in the earlier motility assay, while also modifying the food choice response, suggesting that eol-1 contributes to the motility and behavioral changes induced by OrV infection. Collectively, these results support an overall association between OrV infection and reduced host dispersal, whereas its effect on food choice depends on the sensory context. These findings extend infection-associated behavioral responses to a natural viral pathogen and identify eol-1 as a modulator of their expression.
affiliations: I2SysBio-CSIC (corresponding author)

papers.title: Bayesian phylogenetic inference accounting for recombination in whole bacterial genomes
papers.abstract: Recombination is a major evolutionary force in bacteria, and ignoring it distorts phylogenies and can invalidate downstream analyses such as dating. We present ClonalFrame2, a new software for Bayesian phylogenetic inference from whole bacterial genomes that accounts for recombination. It replaces both ClonalFrame and ClonalFrameML while using the same evolutionary model, in which both mutation and recombination events occur on the branches of the clonal genealogy. The locations of recombination events are integrated out of the likelihood using a hidden Markov model, so the algorithm targets only the clonal genealogy and three recombination parameters. Ancestral sequences are recomputed whenever the tree changes and are used to propose efficient topology updates. We validated the method by analysing data-free datasets, which recovered the prior, and by comparing the approximated likelihood with the exact one on simulated data. Across 100 simulated datasets of 100 genomes each, the recombination parameters were accurately recovered, and trees inferred while accounting for recombination were many times more accurate than when ignoring it. In Staphylococcus aureus ST239, we showed that accounting for recombination gave a stronger temporal signal and a more robust dated phylogeny. In Neisseria gonorrhoeae, we identified interesting patterns of clustered recombination events happening repeatedly across the branches of the tree.
affiliations: University of Warwick (corresponding author)

papers.title: Wild wood mouse gut microbiota are influenced by captivity and cross-fostering
papers.abstract: Background Wild and laboratory animals harbour profoundly different gut microbiota, but how microbiomes shift between these states, and the relative roles of captivity, microbial history, and host identity in shaping that shift, remain unclear. Here, we developed a unique wood mouse (Apodemus sylvaticus) system comprising free-living mice (Wild:As), a wild-derived colony maintained in captivity for over a decade (Wild-like:As), and a second colony that we generated from the Wild-like:As mice by caesarean rederivation and cross-fostering to laboratory Mus musculus (Lab-like:As). We compared these three Apodemus cohorts with conventional laboratory Mus musculus (Lab:Mm) to ask how microbial diversity, community composition, and functional potential vary across a spectrum of wild-to-laboratory conditions. Results We found that alpha diversity varied substantially among cohorts but showed no consistent wild-to-laboratory trend: Shannon diversity was higher in Lab:Mm and Lab-like:As than in Wild:As and Wild-like:As mice, whereas phylogenetic diversity was similarly high in both the Wild:As and Lab:Mm groups. Community composition more closely reflected cohort histories. Despite over a decade in captivity, Wild-like:As mice remained most similar to Wild:As conspecifics, whereas Lab-like:As mice shifted strongly away from Wild-like:As and toward, but remained distinct from, Lab:Mm mice. The clearest wild-to-laboratory pattern emerged in microbiome consistency: core ASVs (present in [≥]90% of individuals) increased from 9 in Wild:As to 46 in Wild-like:As, 72 in Lab-like:As, and 138 in Lab:Mm mice. Predicted functional potential revealed a further distinction between taxonomic and functional patterns: Wild:As and Wild-like:As microbiomes did not differ significantly, whereas Lab-like:As shifted toward the Lab:Mm state despite remaining taxonomically distinct. Conclusions Together, these results show that laboratory-associated microbiomes do not emerge through simple loss of wild microbial diversity, but through broader reorganisation of community composition, consistency, and predicted functional potential reflecting microbial history and host context. The persistent Wild-like and Lab-like microbiome states within Apodemus provide a powerful experimental system for future timely work testing how microbiome history influences host physiology, resilience, and responses to environmental challenges.
affiliations: University of Edinburgh (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Staphylococcus phage recombination cassette that enables recombineering across distant bacteria
papers.abstract: Modifying bacterial genomes with phage recombinases, a process termed recombineering, has enabled precise genome editing, but its reach is limited by host specificity: each new organism generally requires its own recombinase to be identified and optimized. Using known phage recombination genes as synteny anchors, we mined Staphylococcus genomes and recovered a diverse collection of phage recombination cassettes, spanning the RAD52-like annealase superfamily (Sak, Erf) and the RAD51/RecA-like Sak4 family. Functional testing of representatives in S. aureus identified several highly efficient systems that support recombineering. We engineered the most efficient of these into a single-plasmid tool that yields markerless editing in S. aureus in four days. Notably, where other recombineering systems rely on host-specific factors for nuclease evasion and ssDNA loading, this cassette encodes both activities itself: a predicted broad-spectrum nuclease inhibitor and a dedicated single-stranded DNA-binding protein. We therefore tested the cassette across phylogenetically distant hosts, and observed recombination in Streptococcus pyogenes, Enterococcus faecium, Francisella novicida, and Escherichia coli. These results identify a self-sufficient class of phage recombination systems and provide a portable tool for
affiliations: University of Rochester (corresponding author)

papers.title: Second-site capsule-locus mutations, not Ade efflux disruption, determine phage susceptibility across an Acinetobacter baumannii transposon mutant panel
papers.abstract: Resistance-Nodulation-Division (RND) efflux pumps have been implicated in phage adsorption in several Gram-negative bacteria, suggesting that AdeABC, AdeFGH and AdeIJK, the three characterised RND efflux systems of multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, could play a similar role. We tested this hypothesis using five phages (Equilibrator, Taro, AT01, BB02, and AC03) and a panel of 13 A. baumannii strains, including nine AB5075 transposon mutants affecting AdeABC, AdeFGH, or AdeIJK. Host-range testing, efficiency-of-plating assays, capsule-associated density measurements, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and whole-genome sequencing were performed to assess the relationship between genotype and phage infection. Overall, the data did not support a role for the Ade components as receptors. Phages Equilibrator, Taro and AT01 formed plaques on every strain, and the restricted host ranges of BB02 and AC03 did not correspond to disruption of a particular efflux system. Sequencing instead identified second-site mutations in the KL25 capsule locus in six of the ten AB5075 strains. These included a 1,998-bp deletion affecting wzc, substitutions in mnaA and mnaB, an ISAba13 insertion in a putative glycosyltransferase and a subpopulation-associated frameshift in wzx. AC03 formed plaques on all six strains with capsule-locus changes but on none of the five strains without them. Capsule dependence differed among the other phages: relative to the parental AB5075, infection by these phages, Equilibrator, Taro and BB02, was restricted on the capsule-deficient wzc::T26 strain, whereas AT01 efficiency was only slightly reduced. Insertion-site mapping also distinguished a near-terminal adeK insertion that retained the parental antimicrobial phenotype from an early adeK insertion associated with loss of AdeIJK function. Together, these findings identify capsule-locus variation as the strongest correlation with phage susceptibility in this panel and demonstrate the importance of verifying mutant genomes before assigning phenotypes to their annotated insertions.
affiliations: Flinders University (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Urinary Metabolomic Signature Associated with Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth in Children with Short Bowel Syndrome
papers.abstract: Direct sampling of the small intestinal microbiome is challenging. Urinary metabolites may offer a noninvasive approach to studying microbial functional activity. We used clinically available gas chromatography/mass spectrometry to profile urinary organic acids in 94 children with short bowel syndrome, comparing those with clinically defined small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO; n=21) with those without SIBO (n=73). SIBO-associated metabolites included microbial fermentation products, dietary derivatives, and host metabolic intermediates. Metabolites enriched in SIBO mapped to aromatic amino acid metabolism, including tryptophan and tyrosine pathways, consistent with altered microbial fermentation. Many associations persisted after adjustment for intestinal anatomy, age, antibiotic exposure, and nutritional composition. These findings identified a urinary metabolic profile associated with clinically defined SIBO in children with short bowel syndrome and support further evaluation of urinary metabolomics as a noninvasive approach to studying small intestinal microbial function.
affiliations: UTSW (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cytomegalovirus Infection in Human Cortical Organoids Induces Unique Developmental and Viral Substates
papers.abstract: Human Cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is a ubiquitous {beta}-herpesvirus with exposure resulting in a life-long infection. Severe HCMV disease can occur in conditions of insufficient immunity, and this includes congenital infection. Infection of the developing brain can cause severe birth defects including microcephaly and sensorineural hearing loss. Also, increasing evidence suggests the contribution of HCMV infection in adult CNS diseases. Studying HCMV replication and its impact on CNS is restricted by host tropism and anatomy. In these studies, we define the impact of infection on healthy iPSC-derived cortical organoids using single cell RNA sequencing. We uncovered 16 cell type clusters in uninfected tissues using the Human Neural Organoid Cell Atlas. Following infection by HCMV expressing GFP, several clusters were altered in both GFP-positive and GFP-negative populations, including the likely transition of the Glutamatergic/GABAergic Neuron cluster into a CMV-Infected Cell cluster. Expressions of viral genes varied between cells and cell types, requiring us to introduce a TC (temporal class) indexing score to account for varying stages of infection. This analysis in conjunction with machine learning approaches revealed cells that are likely producing de novo HCMV along with several viral sub-states. Several viral sub-states had significant enrichments of genes involved in epithelial-to-mesenchymal (EMT) transition, including expression of EpCAM. We independently verified HCMV-induction of EpCAM protein expression in cortical organoids and glutamatergic neurons. In summary, our studies reveal unique features of HCMV infection of cortical organoid tissues, including varying viral sub-states and tropisms, and introduced new approaches to analyze these multi-dimensional complex data sets.
affiliations: The Medical College of Wisconsin (corresponding author)

papers.title: Metformin lowers HMGA1a and RBM3 protein in breast cancer cells, and its effect on ESR1 splicing depends on cell density and exposure time
papers.abstract: The ESR1 gene produces ER46, an N-terminally truncated isoform generated by skipping of exon 1, which is reduced in tamoxifen-resistant breast cancer cells. We have reported that metformin moves the ratio of full-length ER to ER46 in opposite directions in MCF-7 cells and their tamoxifen-resistant subline TAMR1, and that metformin reduces TAMR1 xenograft growth (Harada et al., Am J Pharm Health Res 2022;10(11)). That report leaves two questions open: whether the effect is dosedependent and stable across culture conditions, and what splicing factor might carry it. Here we report the experiments that bear on both. Across a full dose range from 0.25 to 5 mM at high seeding density, metformin produced no consistent change in the full-length share of ESR1 transcript in either line: densitometry of the gel gave 42%, 43%, 42%, 43%, 45% and 48% in MCF-7 cells and 55%, 44%, 52%, 47%, 68% and 43% in TAMR1 cells. The reported shift therefore depends on the seeding density used, and the comparison that produced it is not reproduced at high density. At low density the MCF-7 response persisted to 48 h (52%, 62% and 68% at 0, 2.5 and 5 mM). Metformin lowered HMGA1a protein in MCF-7 cells and showed the same tendency in TAMR1 cells, at both seeding densities, and lowered RBM3 protein in TAMR1 cells at 24 and 48 h. HMGA1a is the factor we previously showed to generate ER46 by trapping U1 snRNP at an upstream pseudo-5' splice site, so a fall in HMGA1a predicts less ER46, the opposite of what was seen in TAMR1 cells at low density. The fall in RBM3, the protein through which metformin alters splicing in myotonic dystrophy, is the more plausible candidate. RT-PCR of the xenograft tumours from the earlier study detected full-length ESR1 transcript in the untreated and tamoxifen-plus-metformin groups but not in the singleagent groups, with amplification failing in several lanes; these panels do not separate the treatments. Taken together, the direction of the metformin effect on ESR1 splicing is conditional on culture density and does not survive a dose-response test at high density, and HMGA1a is unlikely to be the factor that carries it.
affiliations: Faculty of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Fukuoka University, (corresponding author)

papers.title: Hijacking Cellular S-Acylation with Molecular Assemblies Rewires Oncogenic Signaling
papers.abstract: KRAS-mutant cancers are generally treated by suppressing oncogenic signaling. Here, we investigated whether endogenous lipidation machinery could instead be used to spatially perturb that signaling. The thioester-bearing peptide precursor Stb-DPhe-DPhe-SAc (1) potently reduced PANC-1 cell viability and formed a palmitoylated product in treated cells. Synthetic palmitoylated 1 displayed increased assembly propensity, while fluorescent analogue 2 accumulated at the Golgi in a 2-bromopalmitate-sensitive manner. Compound 1 increased plasma-membrane-associated KRAS staining and ERK/AKT phosphorylation and induced pronounced LC3B and p62 remodeling. Inhibition of palmitoylation suppressed Golgi accumulation, attenuated the LC3B response, and rescued cell viability. These findings support a model in which cellular S-acylation drives organelle-localized molecular assembly that perturbs KRAS localization, oncogenic signaling, and associated stress responses. This work identifies endogenous lipidation machinery as a synthetic handle for spatial control of cancer signaling.
affiliations: Brandeis University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Human lymphatic organoids reconstruct convergent developmental routes to functional lymphatic vessels
