papers.abstract: The lymphatic vasculature maintains fluid balance, regulates immune surveillance, and supports tissue repair, yet how human lymphatic vessels arise and acquire specialized functions remains poorly understood. Here, guided by single-cell and spatial analyses of human embryos, we found that both lateral plate and paraxial mesoderm converge on venous endothelial intermediates with cardinal vein-like characteristics prior to lymphatic specification. Informed by these developmental trajectories, we generated three-dimensional lymphatic organoids from human pluripotent stem cells through two distinct mesodermal routes. The organoids formed capillary-like vascular networks with emerging button-like junctions and distinct endothelial and stromal programs. The lymphatic organoids were transcriptionally benchmarked to human fetal lymphatic endothelium. The organoids supported immune-cell interactions and antigen accumulation and, following transplantation, exhibited interstitial tracer uptake and transport. These findings establish a platform for investigating how distinct developmental origins shape human lymphatic specification, vascular organization, and function, with applications to lymphatic disease modeling and tissue repair.
affiliations: UCLA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Mapping the regulatory wiring of endothelial cell differentiation reveals a critical role for Hippo mechanosignaling
papers.abstract: At each step of development, stem cells encounter a branching decision to differentiate into one type of cell or another. This decision is executed through the action of competing gene programs that specify different cellular identities. Consequently, creating a comprehensive map of the gene programs that drive each branching step of human cell differentiation remains a long-sought goal of developmental and stem cell biology. Here, we introduce a framework combining genome-wide CRISPR screens, single-cell readouts, and gene program inference to systematically discover and characterize regulators of cell differentiation. This framework includes a method for CRISPR perturbations paired with single-cell RNA-seq called circular capture Perturb-seq (CC-Perturb-seq), which improves gRNA detection from split-pool combinatorial indexing protocols and enables perturbing many candidate regulators to map their effects on gene programs. We applied this framework to map how human pluripotent stem cells differentiate into arterial endothelial cells (ECs), and identified 174 regulators that promote or inhibit EC differentiation. By tracking gene programs across three stages of differentiation, we resolved when and how regulators divert cells toward alternative fates. This map revealed an unexpected requirement for the Hippo mechanosignaling pathway in EC specification. During lateral mesoderm differentiation, Hippo mechanosignaling was required to activate ETV2, the master transcriptional regulator of endothelial identity. Inhibiting Hippo blocked ETV2 even in the presence of VEGF and diverted progenitors to a mesenchymal fate in vitro. Likewise, Hippo signaling was required for maximal etv2 expression in developing zebrafish embryos. Conversely, pharmacologically activating the Hippo pathway increased the purity of both arterial and venous EC differentiation in vitro. Our framework thus identifies novel regulators of endothelial cell differentiation, improves stem-cell differentiation protocols via manipulation of mechanosignaling, and provides a generalizable platform for mapping the regulatory wiring of human development.
affiliations: Stanford University (corresponding author)

papers.title: WheatPanRef: a unified linear pan-reference genome for wheat genomics
papers.abstract: Linear reference genomes provide coordinates for read mapping, variant discovery and multi-omics data integration, yet assembly-specific coordinate systems limit data reuse, particularly in the large, repetitive and polyploid wheat genome. Here, we present WheatPanRef, a scalable linear pan-reference and coordinate framework that integrates wheat sequence diversity within a stable coordinate system. We reconciled independent Chinese Spring assemblies by resolving structural and sequences discrepancies to constructed a 14.50-Gb consensus sequences CS-NP. Using CS-NP as backbone, we incorporated 4.37 Gb of non-redundant non-CS sequences from 37 diverse wheat accessions, generating WheatPanRef (18.87 Gb). WheatPanRef improves read-alignment performance and captures putative wild-relative introgressions and sequences absent or unanchored in conventional references. Bidirectional coordinate-translation system enables accurate projection between WheatPanRef and individual assemblies without remapping, facilitating genomic resource integration and reuse. WheatPanRef provides a common sequence and coordinate foundation for population-scale wheat genomics, with potential utility for genomic resource integration in other complex crops.
affiliations: State Key Laboratory of High-Efficiency Production of Wheat-Maize Double Cropping, China Agricultural University, Beijing, China (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Binuclear Cluster Supports Functional Asymmetry in Dark-Operative Protochlorophyllide Reductase
papers.abstract: Many photosynthetic bacteria rely on the nitrogenase-like dark-operative protochlorophyllide oxidoreductase (DPOR) to sustain (bacterio)chlorophyll synthesis in the dark. DPOR couples ATP hydrolysis to electron transfer from a reducing component (L-protein) to a catalytic component (NB-protein) that reduces protochlorophyllide. NB-protein is an 2{beta}2 heterotetramer, and each heterodimeric half contains an active site and a [Fe4S4] cluster. Although the two halves are identical, they react sequentially rather than in parallel. How the two halves communicate has remained unknown. Here we show, using Cu K-edge x-ray absorption spectroscopy and cryo-EM, that the NB-protein tetramer interface holds a binuclear, sulfur-bridged [Cu2S2] cluster. Each Cu is reduced and three-coordinate, with short Cu-S and Cu-Cu distances (2.26 and 2.62 Å). Mutagenesis excludes the nearest cysteine as the bridging ligand, supporting inorganic sulfide as the most likely sulfur donor. To our knowledge, this is the first sulfide-bridged dicopper cluster identified in a protein. The cluster is conserved in three purple non-sulfur bacteria and connects the BchB C-terminal helices that contact opposing active sites. Loss of Cu abolishes DPOR activity and asymmetric L-protein binding without disturbing overall fold. We propose that the cluster relays substrate-binding information between active sites, suggesting a metal-mediated mechanism for cooperativity in nitrogenase-like enzymes.
affiliations: SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory (corresponding author)

papers.title: Unlocking Targeted Underwater Delivery of Coral Probiotics
papers.abstract: The rapid global decline of coral reefs has intensified the need for innovative conservation strategies, including microbial therapies to enhance coral health and resilience. A major limitation, however, is the lack of effective delivery systems for administering Beneficial Microorganisms for Corals (BMCs). In this study, we present natural, biodegradable systems for the underwater delivery of probiotic bacteria to corals. Three customized alginate-based delivery formats (beads, hydrogels, and filaments) were developed and loaded with the probiotic Pseudoalteromonas peptidolytica. The materials were loaded with the bacterium at an average concentration of 10^(4) CFU/g of dry polymer and engineered to sink underwater while keeping their structural integrity over time. In vitro assays showed controlled release kinetics, with encapsulated probiotics remaining viable and capable of replication. In vivo experiments compared syringe-based inoculation with the application of alginate beads, hydrogels, and filaments to corals. Microbiome analyses performed before and after inoculation confirmed successful probiotic colonization following deployment of the alginate-based delivery systems. Relative abundance of the probiotic genus Pseudoalteromonas increased markedly in treated corals, reaching 11.5 % after 48 h with alginate beads, 12.7 % after 48 h with hydrogels, and 12.6 % after 24 h with filaments. Furthermore, the degradation mechanisms of the three delivery systems were investigated. As the first biomaterial-based underwater delivery systems specifically engineered for coral probiotics, these alginate-based materials provide a promising foundation for advancing microbial therapies in both controlled aquaria and natural reef environments.
affiliations: University Milano-Bicocca (corresponding author)

papers.title: MorphoProt: RNA-Conditioned Integration of Multiscale Histology for Spatial Protein Inference
papers.abstract: Spatially resolved protein abundance reveals cellular states and tissue organization that RNA expression cannot fully capture, yet direct spatial protein profiling remains costly and limited in coverage. Histology images routinely accompany spatial transcriptomics and offer complementary morphological information for protein inference. Here, we introduce MorphoProt, a multimodal framework that jointly predicts spatial protein abundance from RNA expression, multiscale histology and tissue neighborhoods. MorphoProt uses RNA-guided cross-attention over five histological fields of view, so that the morphological context read for each spot is conditioned on its molecular state. The fused representation is refined by gated aggregation of RNA-derived information from physical and transcriptomic neighborhoods before joint protein prediction. On held-out sections of human tonsil, mouse spleen and human liver, MorphoProt achieves mean proteinwise Spearman correlations of 0.652, 0.604 and 0.372, outperforming matched RNA-only and graph-based baselines and the histology-based HIPI and multimodal SPRINT baselines in all three tissues. Combining fields of view, rather than any single one, carries the histology gain: in spleen and liver, the multiscale model outperforms every single-field model, and its learned scale preference separates white-pulp from red-pulp compartments. Predicted proteins preserve protein-defined tissue domains and their marker identity, and recover pathologist-annotated germinal centers as accurately as measured proteins.
affiliations: Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen), Shenzhen, China (corresponding author)

papers.title: FeatureMAP enables network-guided interpretation of untargeted metabolomics
papers.abstract: Untargeted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) metabolomics generates thousands of features, but incomplete metabolite annotation and reliance on predefined pathways limit their biological interpretation. Here we present FeatureMAP, an LC-MS feature-centric computational framework that integrates multi-evidence metabolite annotation, network-guided refinement, metabolic module discovery, and structured large language model-based functional interpretation. Across ten public datasets, FeatureMAP improved MS1-based metabolite candidate prioritization while reducing annotation redundancy. In semi-synthetic benchmarks, FeatureMAP recovered coordinated metabolic perturbations, achieving 92% recovery of a simulated perturbation, and distinguished concurrent metabolic processes. Controlled benchmarks further evaluated functional interpretation under competing metabolite-level signals. Based on FeatureMAP, we additionally developed PhenoMAP, a phenotype-aware knowledge graph comprising 12,929 dysregulated metabolic modules from 501 human metabolomics studies spanning 326 phenotypes. Module-level comparisons revealed reproducible metabolic similarities across independent studies and biologically supported relationships among phenotypes. Application to Alzheimer's disease cerebrospinal fluid and cellular datasets identified convergent membrane-lipid alterations and implicated galactose-linked glycosphingolipid remodeling. Together, FeatureMAP and PhenoMAP enable network-grounded interpretation of incompletely annotated LC-MS metabolomics data and systematic investigation of metabolic dysregulation across biological conditions.
affiliations: Nanyang Technological University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Earl Grey ParTEA: scalable, consistent transposable element annotation from pangenomes to deep phylogenetic scopes
papers.abstract: Transposable elements (TEs) are major drivers of genomic diversity, yet understanding their mobility and functional impact requires their accurate description in genomes. TE annotation is still typically performed genome-by-genome. TEs are often shared between some members of the same or closely related species. Hence, TE annotation with a library from a single reference misses families absent from that assembly, whereas building independent per-genome libraries fails to consistently surface shared TEs, hindering comparison. Here, we present Earl Grey ParTEA, a fully automated Snakemake pipeline extending the functionality of Earl Grey for comparative TE annotation across genome panels. ParTEA builds a single non-redundant TE library from all input genomes, resolves chimeric consensus sequences, and uses this shared library to annotate every genome, enabling direct comparison of TE family diversity, abundance, shared and private content, and activity landscapes. Optional modules provide TE library saturation analysis, BUSCO-based assembly quality control, and phylogenetic ordering of outputs. We applied ParTEA to sets of genomes spanning evolutionary scales: ten Arabidopsis thaliana accessions, ten Drosophila species, and ten species spanning the fungal kingdom. The Drosophila TE library expanded from 343 to 1,852 curated families including a previously missed rolling circle element with over 6,000 copies in D. miranda. The proportion of TE families shared across all genomes was highest within A. thaliana (97.3%), 37.7% across Drosophila species and only 0.5% across the set of fungi. ParTEA is available through Bioconda and represents a computationally efficient reproducible framework for comparative TE analysis in the era of large-scale genome analyses.
affiliations: Swedish Museum of Natural History (corresponding author)

papers.title: A protein language model for domain, functional site, and variant effect prediction
papers.abstract: Protein sequence databases are growing far faster than experimentally curated annotations, limiting functional interpretation of newly identified proteins and coding variants. We developed PALM, a protein annotation language model that jointly predicts domain and functional-site occurrence, while preserving overlapping and nested annotations through a soft-target objective. PALM integrates ESM2 with low-rank adaptation (LoRA), learned layer aggregation, and a bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) encoder. PALM was trained on ~15 million InterPro-annotated UniRef50 sequences spanning 17,951 domain and 1,383 site classes. Across 2.3 million held-out proteins, PALM achieved domain- and site-occurrence F1 scores of 0.941 and 0.877, respectively, and retained substantial performance in proteins with <20% sequence identity to the training and validation data. PALM also substantially outperformed ESM3 annotation baseline. Without training on variant-pathogenicity labels, PALM embedding disruption distinguished 151,823 ClinVar missense variants more accurately than ESM2 embedding disruption (AUROC 0.835 versus 0.710), and combining PALM embedding disruption with the ESM2 likelihood-ratio signal reached an AUROC of 0.877. The same combined zero-shot score outperformed AlphaMissense on a benchmark dataset on 128,161 missense variants, that were derived from literature but not present in ClinVar database. At the protein level, PALM embeddings showed stronger CATH-Gene3D superfamily organization than frozen ESM2 and ESM3 embeddings, and improved prediction of experimental activation and repression effects when combined with ESM2. In a downstream case study, we demonstrated the ability to use PALM-derived embedding as proxy of deep mutational scanning (DMS), showcasing the broad application of PALM. Together, PALM converts curated residue-level knowledge into transferable and mechanistically interpretable representations that connect protein sequence, function, and variant consequence.
affiliations: Children's Hospital of Philadelphia (corresponding author)

papers.title: TIGRdisco: a tool for the discovery of TIGR arrays and TIGR-associated Tas proteins from nucleotide sequences
papers.abstract: Tandem Interspaced Guide RNA (TIGR)-TIGR-associated protein (Tas) systems mediate DNA targeting through a hypercompact Tas effector, guided by dual spacers within a tigRNA that is processed from TIGR arrays. TIGR-Tas loci are composed of a Tas coding sequence associated with TIGR arrays of short units in either dual-repeat or stem-loop architecture. Unlike CRISPR (Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats) arrays that comprise units of direct repeats interspersed with unique spacers, units within the two distinct TIGR architectures only conform through extremely short box motifs, complicating detection. Here, we present TIGRdisco, an integrated tool capable of discovering both the Tas protein and its associated TIGR arrays directly from unannotated nucleotide sequences. TIGRdisco implements independent engines to detect the two array architectures through a motif-agnostic approach. We benchmarked TIGRdisco against a reference dataset of TIGR-Tas loci, recovering more than 80% of array units within its search window. Furthermore, TIGRdisco recovered arrays for loci within entire clades of Tas where associated arrays were unannotated in the reference. We found that these arrays largely contain non-canonical box motifs or unit lengths. Lastly, as a case study, we utilized TIGRdisco and successfully uncovered TIGR-Tas loci across metagenomic and genomic datasets.
affiliations: School of Agriculture, Food and Wine, Adelaide University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Neural Crest-Derived Endocardial Cells Required for Heart Valve Development
papers.abstract: Abnormalities in cardiac valves, which maintain unidirectional blood flow through the heart, affect 2-3% of people worldwide and are the most common form of structural heart disease (1).Yet the cell types that make up the valve, and how they communicate to direct development and homeostasis, remain poorly understood. Here, we identify a rare, essential population of highly secretory valve endocardial cells in mouse and human that derive from migrating neural crest cells. Ablation of these cells in mice caused perinatal lethality with thickened leaflets, stenosis, and regurgitation, mirroring human valve disease. This subset of endocardial cells uniquely expresses the secreted signaling protein parathyroid hormone-like hormone (Pthlh). Global disruption of Pthlh caused valve stenosis and lethality and neural crest-specific deletion produced similar valve disease, with impaired maturation of valvular interstitial cells and disrupted bone morphogenetic protein signaling. These findings identify a previously unrecognized cell type and signaling pathway essential for valve morphogenesis, with implications for the pathogenesis and treatment of human valve defects.
affiliations: Gladstone Institutes (corresponding author)

papers.title: The Test Used to Choose Between Pesticide Survival Models Tracks Lesion Persistence, Not Hazard Structure
papers.abstract: Aquatic pesticide risk assessment predicts survival with toxicokinetic-toxicodynamic models that offer two hazard structures, cumulative or peak-based, which disagree about which exposure patterns are dangerous; for imidacloprid, published choices differ across eight species. The choice is made from one observation: deaths after transfer to clean water are taken to refute the peak-based structure. That inference holds only if damage is falling, which is not measured in these tests but taken from a fitted model. The observation responds to the compound and design, not the hazard structure. Across thirty-two Gammarus pulex treatments the post-exposure death rate places anticholinesterases above uncouplers, in the order of lesion persistence. For diazinon, one series returns opposite verdicts over its sixteen-day window and its first four days. For imidacloprid in Daphnia magna, one damage stage favours the cumulative structure by 78 likelihood units and two stages the peak-based one by 7. Four conditions make a design informative; thirteen of thirty-six treatments in a thirteen-compound archive meet them. Spreading a fixed exposure over longer intervals raises mortality in one of five species, which no repair law reproduces with the kinetics of the models. For neonicotinoids, predictions for such patterns are unvalidated, not conservative.
affiliations: Research Institute of Environmental Health and Safety, EH R&C Co. (corresponding author)

papers.title: Pervasive chromothripsis drives pleural mesothelioma to impact gene function and patient survival
papers.abstract: Pleural mesothelioma (PM) is a tumour type showing high structural complexity but the full spectrum of variants present and their impacts are poorly understood. We comprehensively describe the mutational landscape of mesothelioma, exploiting a large (N=443) cohort profiling the tumour genome and transcriptome in parallel. We find that the majority of candidate driver variants are mediated by copy number alterations (CNAs) and discover high frequencies of complex rearrangements across most tumours, dominated by chromothripsis (74% of tumours) and chromoplexy (59%). Chromothripsis contributes to significant CNA hotspots to delete known PM tumour suppressor genes such as CDKN2A, NF2 and BAP1, thought to be among the earliest events in PM development; and the presence of chromothripsis is associated with significantly worse patient survival. We also discover multi-faceted crosstalk between the mitochondrial and nuclear genomes during PM evolution, involving alterations to both genomes, and mitochondrial expression changes associated with subtypes and chromothripsis.

papers.title: Hazard Structure and Repair Kinetics: A 2x2 Classification that Resolves the Stochastic-Death / Individual-Tolerance Dilemma
papers.abstract: The two variants of GUTS (General Unified Threshold model of Survival), stochastic death and individual tolerance, disagree about no-effect concentrations under time-variable exposure, and no standard test separates them. Each variant fixes two independent choices, which form a 2x2 classification: whether the hazard accumulates while damage exceeds a threshold (cumulative) or is set by the highest damage reached (peak-based), and whether repair is proportional or saturating. Calibration fit cannot choose: each structure fits by adjusting its own damage recovery, the cumulative one faster in twelve of fourteen compounds. For two identical pulses separated by complete recovery, the cumulative hazard predicts equal survival through both whatever the parameters, so a carry-over ratio (second-to-first survival) above one excludes it; in Gammarus pulex fourteen of fifteen ratios are at or above one, seven significantly. The peak-based hazard predicts the maximum of the ratio, approached as intervals lengthen in five of six compounds. For organophosphates, whose recovery outlasts the published pulse intervals, the one test on measured damage favours the peak-based hazard: diazinon-exposed Daphnia magna stopped being immobilised once acetylcholinesterase, still inhibited, began to recover. The peak-based hazard is the appropriate default for toxicokinetic-toxicodynamic risk assessment of narcotics and uncouplers, and provisionally of organophosphates.

Observation of prethermal dynamical phase transitions and resonant melting
papers.abstract: The dynamics of isolated quantum systems following a sudden quench has a central role in many areas of material science, high-energy physics and quantum chemistry1–4. Such far-from-equilibrium quantum dynamics—which features complex phenomena with implications for thermalization, non-equilibrium phase transitions and Floquet phase engineering5–8—is challenging to study numerically, in particular, in high-dimensional systems9,10. Here we use a programmable neutral-atom quantum simulator11 to systematically explore quench dynamics in spin models with up to 180 qubits. By initializing the system in a product state and performing quenches across a broad parameter space, we discover several stable, qualitatively distinct dynamical regimes. We trace their robustness to Floquet-like prethermal steady states8 that are stabilized over exponentially long emergent timescales by strong dynamical constraints. We further observe sharp peaks in the dynamical response that are quantitatively explained by the structured melting of prethermalization through resonances. In two dimensions, we uncover a prethermally driven, first-order dynamical phase transition linked to the proliferation of Néel-order defects6,12, and probe it quantitatively using a generalized Clausius–Clapeyron test. Together, these results establish a programmable route to high-energy prethermal phase structure: long-lived dynamical phases, their resonant breakdown and a first-order dynamical phase transition that is not inherited from the equilibrium phase boundaries. A programmable neutral-atom quantum simulator is used to explore quench dynamics in spin models with up to 180 qubits, revealing prethermal dynamical phase transitions and resonant melting.

papers.title: Synergy in viral–bacterial co-infection expedites algal bloom demise
papers.abstract: Algal bloom demise, often caused by viruses, is a major driver of carbon cycling in the surface ocean1,2. However, although blooms collapse synchronously, fewer than 30% of algal cells are actively infected by viruses3, indicating the involvement of additional mortality agents. Here we quantified tripartite interactions within a synthetic community composed of the abundant coccolithophore Gephyrocapsa huxleyi, bacteria and viruses isolated during a bloom. We found that bacteria significantly enhanced virus-induced algal mortality in G. huxleyi as well as in three other globally widespread microalgae. We quantified this interaction using two new metrics: the synergy index, which measures viral–bacterial interaction strength, and the benefit index, which assesses changes in bacterial fitness. We identified Alteromonas bacteria as drivers of viral–bacterial co-infection, with consistently high synergy index and benefit index. We found that during algal blooms, Alteromonas displayed high chemoattraction towards infected cell extracts, accumulated in aggregates derived from bloom demise, and increased in abundance during oceanic bloom collapse. Viral–bacterial synergy represents a previously unrecognized mortality agent that controls bloom termination, modulating the balance between the carbon-recycling viral shunt and the carbon-exporting viral shuttle pathways, which influence global carbon cycling4–6. Viral–bacterial synergy accelerates algal bloom collapse by enhancing virus-induced mortality, driven by Alteromonas chemoattraction and co-infection, revealing a previously unrecognized mortality agent that influences oceanic carbon cycling .

papers.title: Aggression experience and observation drive shared behavioural and neural changes
papers.abstract: The ability to observe the social behaviour of others and use observed information to bias future action is a fundamental building block of social cognition1–3. Aggression observation activates hypothalamic neurons relevant for aggression control4,5, but whether observation and experience engage common circuit mechanisms that promote a new shared behavioural policy is unclear. Here we develop a strategy to perform large-scale cell-type-specific recordings across subcortical networks for social behaviour generation and learning. We record longitudinally while animals train through direct aggression experience or observation, then probe shared differences in behaviour and neural activity in a novel aggression context. After training, we detect unique signatures of a shared adaptive behavioural strategy that is absent in animals without training. During aggression observation, observed behaviour recruits widespread activation across subcortical networks for behavioural generation and mimics activity evoked by experienced behaviour, and shared neural changes persist into the novel aggression context. Multiregion modelling reveals shared changes to a core aggression network across both experience and observation, including a widespread reduction in inhibition, which we find is necessary for adaptive behavioural change. Together, this demonstrates that experience-like activity during aggression observation can recruit a shared inhibitory plasticity mechanism that biases behaviour toward adaptive proactive behavioural strategies. Aggression experience and observation recruit a brain-wide network of excitatory, inhibitory and valence signals, and changes to this activation pattern predict a shared adaptive behaviour-control policy in a new aggression context.

papers.title: Twist-angle-dependent quantum phase diagrams in moiré bilayer MoTe2
papers.abstract: Two-dimensional semiconducting moiré superlattices provide a highly tunable platform for investigating strongly correlated and topological quantum phases1–5. As a prototypical example, twisted bilayer MoTe2 (tMoTe2) has been shown to host fractional topological phases at zero magnetic field6–20. However, their evolution with twist angle and competition with other correlated quantum states remain largely unexplored. Here we report a systematic transport study of twist-angle-dependent phase diagrams in tMoTe2 across a range of 3.79°–5.76°, revealing an evolution from valley-polarized, fractional topological states to valley-degenerate correlated states and superconductivity. At relatively small twist angles, partially filled Chern bands of tMoTe2 host fractional quantum anomalous Hall states following the Jain sequence, together with signatures of an anomalous composite Fermi liquid at moiré hole filling factor νh = 1/2. Increasing twist angle progressively suppresses fractional topological phases and reconstructs the half-filled Chern band into symmetry-breaking integer Chern insulating states. At νh = 1, we observe a transition from robust integer quantum anomalous Hall insulators at small angles to displacement-field-tuned, topologically trivial correlated insulators at larger angles. At twist angles above approximately 5.6°, superconductivity emerges adjacent to the νh = 1 correlated insulator, with a phase diagram closely resembling that recently reported in twisted bilayer WSe2 (refs. 21–24). Our results indicate a unified twist-angle-driven phase evolution linking fractional topology, symmetry breaking, magnetic order and superconductivity, providing new insight into the emergent quantum phenomena in moiré systems. Twist-angle-dependent studies of moiré bilayer MoTe2 reveal a transition from fractional topological states to correlated insulators and superconductivity, linking topology, symmetry breaking and magnetism in moiré quantum materials.

papers.title: Comprehensive mapping of essential-gene interactions in M. tuberculosis
papers.abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the causative agent of tuberculosis, remains the world’s deadliest pathogen1. Despite intensive study, many of its genes remain uncharacterized, which limits the insight that can be gained into tuberculosis biology and constrains drug development. Genetic interaction (GI) mapping is a powerful strategy to define functional relationships between genes by quantifying how the phenotypic effects of combined perturbations deviate from expectations based on single-gene perturbations2,3. Here we develop a dual-sgRNA CRISPR-interference platform that enables high-throughput GI mapping in mycobacteria. We address key technical challenges in library construction and data interpretation by incorporating unique barcodes for each sgRNA pair and implementing a robust statistical pipeline for GI detection. Focusing on essential genes, we generate comprehensive GI maps in the model mycobacterium Mycobacterium smegmatis and the pathogen M. tuberculosis. These maps recapitulate known biology, uncover thousands of previously unrecognized interactions and identify functional connections between essential genes and drug targets. By generating AlphaFold3-based protein–protein interaction predictions4 for all gene pairs in our GI maps, we show that a subset of GIs is likely to reflect underlying physical associations. Validation of selected GIs confirms both novel biological relationships and opportunities for synergistic targeting. Overall, this work establishes a generalizable framework for dual-gene perturbation and defines the architecture of essential-gene networks in mycobacteria, advancing both our understanding of tuberculosis biology and the rational design of combination therapies. A high-throughput CRISPR-interference platform allows the mapping of interactions between essential genes in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, revealing many previously unknown genetic interactions and providing insight into gene function and drug–target relationships that could enable the development of new therapies for tuberculosis.

papers.title: In vivo CAR-T double knockout screen maps synergistic antitumour gene pairs
papers.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has transformed the treatment of haematological malignancies, but its efficacy remains limited by multiple negative regulatory mechanisms intrinsic to T cells1–4. Here we perform a high-throughput in vivo CAR-T double-knockout (DKO) CRISPR screen, and identify multiple DKO gene pairs that are both effective and synergistic. The top pair, NR4A1–SOCS3 DKO, has multiple favourable immunological features. Whole-transcriptome profiling and in vivo single-cell RNA sequencing reveal that NR4A1–SOCS3 DKO specifically upregulates metabolic pathways in CAR-T cells, which show significantly higher metabolic fitness and mitochondrial activity. NR4A1–SOCS3 DKO CAR-T cells and T cells exhibit exceptionally potent antitumour efficacy and long-term tumour control across different tumour models without compromising safety features. NR4A1–SOCS3 DKO outperforms several benchmark single-gene and dual-gene modifications in T cells and CAR-T cells5–9. These data demonstrate high-throughput in vivo CAR-T DKO screening for rapid discovery of combination targets, and establish NR4A1–SOCS3 as a promising pair of intracellular checkpoints to engineer high-performance CAR-T therapies against cancer. Using high-throughput in vivo CAR-T double knockout screening, synergistic gene combinations to improve CAR-T cell therapy are revealed.

papers.title: Cancer-selective gene circuits via intrinsic ribosomal frameshifting
papers.abstract: Ribosomal frameshifting, an uncommon translational recoding event, is best known for its regulatory roles in viral gene expression1,2, whereas its physiological relevance in mammals remains poorly understood. Here we show that specific codon pairs trigger efficient −1 frameshifting preferentially in cancer cells. Mechanistically, this recoding arises from ribosomal pausing associated with tRNA and amino acid availability, and is amplified by impaired ribosome quality control and sustained phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6. We found that this codon-pair-specific frameshifting represents an intrinsic state of translational dysregulation, which is prevalent across cancer cells and reshapes protein synthesis. Taking advantage of this frameshifting-permissive state in cancer cells, we engineered a frameshifting-activated synthetic therapeutic circuit (FAST) that conditionally expresses the pyroptotic effector gasdermin D. FAST is activated across diverse cancer cell types, inducing potent and selective pyroptosis, while sparing normal tissues from detectable toxicity. As a proof of concept, systemic AAV9-mediated delivery of FAST in mouse models of colorectal and pancreatic cancer elicited pronounced tumour regression, robust immune activation and synergistic effects with immune checkpoint blockade. Collectively, these findings reveal codon-pair-dependent ribosomal frameshifting as a feature of translational dysregulation in cancer cells and establish translation-coupled gene circuits as a strategy for cancer-selective therapy. Codon-pair-dependent ribosomal frameshifting is a feature of translational dysregulation in cancer cells.

papers.title: An AI-native experimental laboratory for autonomous biomolecular operations
papers.abstract: Developing artificial intelligence (AI)-native experimental laboratories for autonomous scientific exploration with minimal human intervention represents a long-standing goal. Although autonomous experimental systems are emerging1–4, especially in chemical and materials science, they remain largely confined to domains with singular objectives, well-defined workflows and simple instrumentation. This limitation may reflect an ‘add-on’ architecture that uses AI as a task-specific tool rather than providing it with a global understanding of experiments, especially under engineering-oriented circumstances. Here we present AutoDNA, an AI-native autonomous biomolecular engineering laboratory targeting multi-objective experiments across diverse instruments. Through the co-design of models, experiments and instruments, AutoDNA realizes the co-evolution of AI and the automation system within an end-to-end multi-user framework. The system autonomously orchestrates over 20 types of instruments across more than 11,000 steps to execute core nucleic acid operations including synthesis, transcription, amplification and sequencing, while human intervention is limited to hardware maintenance tasks, such as reagent and labware replenishment. Across four representative applications, AutoDNA matched expert-optimized enzymatic DNA synthesis yields, accelerated concurrent protocol execution by 3.2-fold, completed an end-to-end DNA data storage cycle with exact recovery of the original digital content, and identified and validated a clinically detected KRAS G13D mutation. AutoDNA establishes a blueprint towards science-as-a-service, accelerating biological discovery and advancing various applications in synthetic biology and information storage. AutoDNA is an artificial intelligence (AI)-native autonomous biomolecular engineering laboratory targeting multi-objective experiments across diverse instruments, realizing the co-evolution of AI and the automation system within an end-to-end multi-user framework.

papers.title: The neural basis of flavour–nutrient learning
papers.abstract: Animals learn about the external world in part through interoceptive signals1,2. For example, the nutrient content of food is first estimated in the mouth, in the form of flavour, and then it is measured again through slower signals from the gut. How these signals from the mouth and gut are integrated to drive learning is unclear. Here we identify a dopamine (DA) pathway that enables learning about the nutrient content of food. We show that DA neurons in the ventral tegmental area are necessary for associating nutrients with flavours, and that post-ingestive nutrients trigger DA release selectively in a small region of the anterior basolateral amygdala (BLA) but not in canonical DA targets in striatum. This nutrient-triggered DA release occurs preferentially in the left BLA in mice, and this same structure is preferentially activated by post-ingestive nutrients in humans. We identify the gut sensors that are responsible for nutrient-triggered DA release; show that they activate BLA-projecting DA neurons defined by expression of cholecystokinin; and demonstrate that stimulation of DA axon terminals in the anterior BLA drives flavour–nutrient learning but not other aspects of feeding behaviour. Two-photon imaging of neurons in the left anterior BLA reveals that they integrate gustatory and post-ingestive cues, and silencing these neurons prevents flavour–nutrient learning. These findings establish a neural basis for how animals learn about the nutrient content of their food. A dopamine pathway to the basolateral amygdala is necessary for associating nutrients with flavours.

papers.title: Hard X-ray attosecond metrology
papers.abstract: Sub-ångström spatial resolution combined with attosecond temporal resolution enables direct observation of electron motion in matter1. Attosecond hard X-ray pulses generated at X-ray free-electron laser sources provide the requisite spatiotemporal sensitivity, yet their application has been limited by the absence of precise pulse metrology and control. Here, building on a broadband X-ray split-delay line, we establish metrology of attosecond hard X-ray pulses. Field-correlation measurements provide the first time-domain characterization of the pulse coherence time and demonstrate attosecond synchronization between the generated pulse pairs. By exploiting non-sequential two-photon absorption as a nonlinear probe, intensity autocorrelation quantifies the average pulse duration directly in the time domain to be 170 as. The demonstrated experimental tools and techniques enable systematic attosecond time-resolved experiments, including X-ray pump–X-ray probe spectroscopy and diffraction, and open a pathway to probing electronic phenomena with unprecedented spatial-temporal resolution. Metrology techniques are developed to characterize and control attosecond hard X-ray pulses, directly measuring a 170-attosecond duration and enabling ultrafast studies of electronic dynamics in quantum systems.

papers.title: Transcriptomic convergence and the female protective effect in autism
papers.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is highly heritable, and mutations in hundreds of genes have been implicated as individually rare causes of ASD1–3. Understanding how disruptions to these functionally diverse genes lead to the core features of ASD remains a major challenge4. Moreover, ASD is three- to four-fold more common in male than in female individuals5, and female autistic people tend to carry more autosomal risk alleles for ASD compared with their male counterparts6,7; however, the biological basis of this ‘female protective effect’ (FPE) has remained unknown8,9. Here we show that individual perturbations of 18 ASD genes in human neural progenitor cells converge on shared effects on gene expression, including widespread downregulation of other ASD genes. De novo reconstruction of a gene regulatory network enabled identification of central transcriptional regulators that drive this transcriptomic convergence, including prominent ASD gene CHD8 and candidates including REST. Furthermore, X-linked transcription factor ZFX, which is expressed from both the active and the inactive X chromosomes in female individuals10, emerged as a key activator of many ASD genes: we propose that the higher ZFX expression level observed in the female brain can buffer damaging mutations in diverse ASD genes, contributing to the female protective effect. Together, these results show how key gene regulatory networks can become broadly and similarly dysregulated upon disruption of individual ASD genes and provide molecular insight into the female protective effect in ASD. Gene network analysis shows how mutations in diverse genes associated with autism spectrum disorder can converge to exert shared effects, with X-linked transcription factor ZFX emerging as a key protective factor in the female brain.

papers.title: A spatiotemporal cancer cell trajectory underlies glioblastoma heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Cancer cells show highly heterogeneous and plastic states in glioblastoma, an incurable brain tumour1–5. However, how these malignant states arise and whether they follow defined cellular trajectories across tumours is poorly understood. Here we generated a deep single-cell and spatial multi-omic atlas of human glioblastoma that pairs transcriptomic, epigenomic and genomic profiling of 12 tumours across many regions. We identify that glioblastoma heterogeneity is driven by spatially patterned transitions of cancer cells from developmental-like states towards those defined by a glial injury response and hypoxia. This cellular trajectory regionalizes tumours into distinct tissue microenvironments and manifests in a molecularly conserved manner across tumours as well as genetically distinct tumour subclones. Consistently, using a new deep-learning framework to map cancer cell states jointly with clones in situ, we show that tumour subclones are finely spatially intermixed through glioblastoma tissue microenvironments. We validate this cellular trajectory by using somatic mutation-based hierarchies in vivo and an experimental patient-derived organoid model ex vivo. Finally, we show that this cancer cell trajectory is intimately linked to myeloid heterogeneity and unfolds across regionalized myeloid signalling environments. Our findings define a stereotyped trajectory of cancer cells in glioblastoma and unify glioblastoma tumour heterogeneity into a tractable cellular and tissue framework. A deep single-cell and spatial multi-omic atlas of human glioblastoma is generated, pairing transcriptomic, epigenomic and genomic profiling, and tracing glioblastoma tumour heterogeneity to a stereotyped and spatially patterned trajectory of cancer cells.

papers.title: A conserved flowering-time module underlies double-season cropping
papers.abstract: Adapting crops to intensive cultivation systems under climate change requires varieties that combine yield potential with optimized flowering and maturation1,2. In central and eastern China, barley has long been cultivated in a double-season cropping system, in which early flowering and maturation are critical for escaping presummer terminal heat stress and enabling flexible rotation with summer crops3,4. Here we trace the genomic footprints of 80 years of modern breeding in China using 505 representative cultivars and identify a flowering-time module defined by a single amino acid substitution in PHYTOCHROME C in combination with a winter-type VERNALIZATION 1 haplotype that underpins this adaptation. The derived allele accelerates heading and maturity, and its frequency has risen sharply in modern autumn-sown varieties. Using base editing in barley and wheat, we confirm causality and demonstrate that this flowering-time combination module, PhyC–VRN1, is functionally conserved across Triticeae. Our results identify and experimentally validate a breeding-relevant flowering-time module that has been selected during modern breeding to enable intensive crop rotations, as well as demonstrate how precision genome editing can be used to reconstruct such adaptive modules for climate-resilient crop design. The genomic footprints of 80 years of modern breeding in China are traced using representative cultivars, demonstrating how precision genome editing can be used to reconstruct adaptive modules for climate-resilient crop design.

papers.title: Nectin-4 mediates rubella virus entry in airway and placental cells
papers.abstract: Rubella virus (RuV) causes rubella and, when acquired during pregnancy, congenital rubella syndrome1. Despite its clinical significance, the cellular entry mechanism of RuV remains poorly characterized, owing to limited identification of host receptors2, which hinders pathogenesis research and therapeutic development. Here, using proximity biotin labelling-based proteomics coupled with CRISPR–Cas9 validation, we identify nectin-4 as a functional RuV entry receptor. Ectopic expression of nectin-4 conferred susceptibility to RuV in non-permissive cells, whereas blocking or genetic ablation of nectin-4 reduced infection, results that demonstrate that nectin-4 is a major entry factor. Mechanistically, nectin-4 directly interacts with the RuV envelope glycoprotein heterodimer and facilitates receptor-mediated endocytosis following initial calcium-dependent viral attachment to cellular lipids. In polarized airway epithelial models, nectin-4 mediates basolateral entry of RuV and supports apical progeny release, a finding that provides a molecular mechanism for respiratory transmission. In placental models, nectin-4 is highly expressed on syncytiotrophoblasts and facilitates infection at the maternal–fetal interface, although additional nectin-4-independent pathways contribute to infection of other trophoblast populations. Together, these data establish nectin-4 as a key factor for respiratory transmission and early placental infection of RuV and highlight it as a promising therapeutic target for the prevention of rubella and related diseases. Nectin-4 is identified as a pivotal host entry receptor for respiratory transmission and early placental infection of rubella virus.

papers.title: An open structure-guided RNA foundation model for generalizable prediction
papers.abstract: RNA language models have achieved strong performance across diverse downstream tasks by leveraging large-scale sequence data. However, RNA function is fundamentally shaped by hierarchical structure, making structural information important for pre-training. Existing approaches often depend on noisy annotations or task-specific objectives that can limit generalizability. Here we present structRFM, a structure-guided RNA foundation model trained on 21 million RNA sequence–structure pairs by integrating base-pairing interactions into masked language modelling through a pair-matching operation. We also introduce MUSES, a multi-source ensemble of secondary structures designed to mitigate predictor bias, and a dynamic masking ratio that balances structure-guided and nucleotide-level masking. structRFM learns joint sequence and structure representations as sequence-level, nucleotide-level and pairwise features for broad downstream adaptation. It ranks highly in zero-shot homology classification and establishes new benchmarks for secondary-structure prediction. Its tertiary-structure adaptation, Zfold, consistently improves both three-dimensional predictions and their extracted secondary structures, with performance comparable to AlphaFold31 across CASP15-natural, CASP16 and RNA-Puzzles. structRFM also improves performance on function-prediction tasks and generalizes to newly released RNA families and long non-coding RNAs. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of structure-guided pre-training and highlight multimodal RNA language models for robust structural and functional inference. The complete 21-million-pair dataset, model weights and source code are openly available to support multimodal RNA foundation-model development. structRFM, a structure-guided RNA foundation model pre-trained on 21 million sequence–structure pairs, learns multimodal representations that improve secondary and tertiary structure prediction, functional inference and zero-shot generalization across diverse RNA families.

papers.title: A two-dimensional reticular triaxial molecularly woven fabric
papers.abstract: Inspired by macroscopic weaving techniques1–4, molecular weaving, which interlaces molecular strands into ordered networks, has emerged as a powerful strategy for designing functional materials with emergent properties5,6. However, so far, molecular weaving has relied mainly on linear building blocks and biaxial structures. Higher-order weaving (≥3 axes) of nonlinear building blocks is expected to produce intriguing architectures and bring new and unforeseen functions to the resulting materials; however, their construction and property investigation remain underexplored. Here we report a two-dimensional reticular triaxial woven polymer network constructed by incorporating C3-symmetric macrocycles into the woven structure through dative B–N polymerization. The resulting material not only exhibits unique topological chirality and robust mechanical properties but it also serves as a porous material that permits the separation of representative aromatic/aliphatic compounds. This functional utility highlights how higher-order triaxial woven topologies can provide unique advantages in terms of regulating material properties and introduces an extra topological dimension for the construction of functional materials. A two-dimensional reticular triaxial woven network material is constructed by incorporating C3-symmetric macrocycles into a triangular weave pattern, enabling an extra topological dimension to be used for the construction of functional materials.

papers.title: Microbiome-wide PheWAS links gut microbial SNVs to health and exposures
papers.abstract: Alterations in the microbial composition of the human gut have been associated with a wide range of chronic diseases1,2. Yet species-level composition alone can obscure extensive within-species genetic diversity and functional variation. This has driven a shift towards strain-resolved, genetic-level analysis of the microbiome, leveraging microbial genetic variation to identify disease-relevant genes and pathways3–6. Here we conducted a phenome-wide association study (PheWAS) analysing 12.8 million gut microbial single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) with 244 host health phenotypes and environmental exposures in 10,781 individuals from 6 independent cohorts. We identify 940 independent associations across 69 host factors, including age, sex and cardiovascular and metabolic parameters. Structural analyses identified host-phenotype-associated SNVs in functionally important regions of proteins, findings that inform mechanistic hypotheses about how microbial genetic changes relate to environmental and host physiological factors. For example, we identified an age-associated SNV in Faecalibacterium prausnitzii that affects an amino acid within the protein pocket that binds glutathione. To support future efforts, all study summary statistics are provided in an online catalogue ( https://fulab.web.rug.nl/SNV-MWAS/ ). Together, these results identify new biological connections between the human host and microbial genetic variants at base pair resolution and provide a resource for hypothesis generation that will aid future understanding of the strain-level functionality of the gut microbiota. Gut microbial single-nucleotide variants across 10,781 individuals reveal 940 associations that link strain-level genetic variation to 69 host traits, with structural analyses pinpointing host phenotype-associated variants, providing a base pair-resolution resource for mechanistic hypothesis generation.

papers.title: Towards observing interstitial hydrogen in solution in metal lattices
papers.abstract: Hydrogen-bearing materials are central to low-carbon energy technologies1, but hydrogen itself is difficult to detect and localize at the nanoscale2–6. This hinders the development of advanced materials with better efficiency. Atom probe tomography (APT) can map hydrogen in three dimensions and at high resolution, yet characterization of dilute, mobile, interstitial hydrogen in metals has remained challenging because of low solubility, the ambiguity owing to hydrogen trapping by structural defects, as well as the artefacts introduced during hydrogen introduction4–6. Here we address whether interstitial hydrogen in solution in materials can be distinguished from defect-trapped hydrogen in APT. Using deuterium as a proxy for hydrogen, together with face-centred cubic (FCC) multi-principal-element alloys (MPEAs) containing coherent FCC precipitates, we show that deuterium atoms reproducibly concentrate in hydrogen-affinitive phases in a manner consistent with theoretical predictions. We further resolve differences in deuterium content between phases with distinct local chemistries and crystal structures, consistent with their different calculated hydrogen solution energies. These findings demonstrate that APT can move beyond identifying hydrides and solute-decorated defects to examine hydrogen in solid solution, providing new insights into hydrogen partitioning in structural alloys and informing materials design for hydrogen-related applications. Using deuterium as a proxy for hydrogen, atom probe tomography provides experimental evidence for interstitial hydrogen in solid solution across different FCC phases, consistent with theoretical predictions of hydrogen affinity, revealing hydrogen partitioning in structural alloys.

papers.title: Venousization enables angiogenesis in the absence of VEGFR signalling
papers.abstract: The vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) ligand and its main receptor VEGFR2 are considered to be essential for endothelial differentiation, proliferation, sprouting and survival1. Blood vessels cannot form in growing embryos or tissues when VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling is compromised in all cells2,3. The anti-VEGF antibody, which can block angiogenesis in cancer, wound healing or ischaemic diseases, is among the most widely used antibodies in the clinic. However, vascular resistance to anti-VEGF therapy has been reported4,5. Here we used iFlpMosaics and iSuRe–HadCre to induce and track genetic mosaics of endothelial cells (ECs) lacking VEGFR2 during the entire embryonic and postnatal development. These Vegfr2-knockout (Vegfr2KO) ECs adapted, proliferated normally and competed with wild-type cells over time, eventually forming a substantial portion of the vascular network in most organs. Vegfr2KO ECs could not sprout during the first wave of angiogenesis in most tissues, because this process is highly VEGF-dependent and favours growth and mobilization of wild-type ECs. However, owing to their inability to respond to VEGF, Vegfr2KO ECs became dominant in veins, which represented a long-term and continuous source of ECs for subsequent waves of VEGF-independent angiogenesis. Comparative single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of ECs with acute and long-term loss of VEGFR2 identified both common and organ-specific molecular mechanisms of adaptation and resistance to VEGF signalling loss. These included significant endothelial venousization and upregulation of ligands for VEGFR1 and VEGFR3. VEGFR1 only partially compensated for VEGFR2 loss in capillary ECs, whereas VEGFR3 compensated only in arterial ECs. Loss of the three VEGF receptors did not compromise venous growth. Notably, loss of the master regulator of venous development, NR2F2 (also known as COUP-TFII), significantly compromised expansion of Vegfr2KO ECs. This work has implications for our understanding of the role of VEGF receptors in angiogenesis and demonstrates venousization as a mechanism of adaptation and resistance to VEGF signalling loss during angiogenesis. Longitudinal tracking of endothelial cells shows they can adapt to loss of VEGFR2 and form new functional vessels, challenging conventional views of the essential role of VEGF receptors in angiogenesis and providing insight into resistance to anti-VEGF therapies.

papers.title: Ecological and social cues orchestrate concerted courtship in Drosophila
papers.abstract: Mating decisions are often attributed to the sensory signalling between prospective sexual partners. Yet these interactions are also shaped by the broader environmental context in which they unfold, to appropriately align sexual arousal with reproductive opportunities1–6. Here we show that in Drosophila erecta mating is strictly contingent on the ecological and social environment generated as flies densely aggregate in groups on a food patch. We find that food volatiles directly promote male sexual arousal, triggering individuals to sample and pursue potential mates, giving rise to dynamic interactions across the group. The ensuing visual motion transforms each male’s visual field, which in turn further amplifies his arousal, generating a multisensory feedback loop that coordinately promotes courtship across individuals. D. erecta’s strict dependence on environmental cues appears latent in related species, such as Drosophila melanogaster, where food odour can promote arousal7 but is dispensable for vigorous courtship. Comparative circuit analyses show that species-specific thresholds for sexual arousal reflect variation in how olfactory input modulates conserved nodes controlling courtship drive, rendering food volatiles a strict sensory gate only in D. erecta. Together, our findings highlight how environmental cues not directly tied to sexual signalling can profoundly influence reproductive behaviour and reorganize the social landscape to ensure mating occurs in contexts where reproductive opportunities are abundant. In Drosophila erecta, food odours initiate male sexual arousal, which is subsequently reinforced by the visual motion of other courting flies, creating a multisensory mechanism that synchronizes courtship in groups when conditions are favourable for reproduction.

papers.title: The deep Earth origin of the Great Unconformity
papers.abstract: The Great Unconformity marks a globally extensive erosive surface linked to climatic shifts1 and environmental transitions2 that preceded the Cambrian explosion of life. The processes proposed to explain the formation of the Great Unconformity include glacial erosion during the Snowball Earth1,3,4, rifting and plume activity5–7, sea-level fall8 and mantle-driven dynamic topography6,9–11. However, the dynamics of these processes have not been tested. Here we show that continental-scale uplift and subsidence associated with long-wavelength dynamic topography12 due to mantle convection drove the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity. Our models predict prolonged continental-scale Neoproterozoic uplift and long-term Phanerozoic subsidence for Laurentia, Baltica and North China. This vertical motion scenario is ideal for the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity, which is a first-order surface expression of deep Earth processes. The predicted prolonged continental uplift throughout Cryogenian times would have resulted in marked erosion due to the action of glaciers13. The large area of Laurentia and limited deformation at its margins explain why the Great Unconformity is best preserved and documented there. Our models predict cycles of dynamic topography that are broadly reflected in preserved sediment volume across continents1,14, and open new avenues for understanding the environments of Cambrian animal diversification. Continental-scale uplift and subsidence associated with long-wavelength dynamic topography due to mantle convection drove the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity.

papers.title: Tracing the spread of Celtic languages using ancient genomics
papers.abstract: Celtic languages are today restricted to Europe’s Atlantic fringes but were widely spoken across the continent during the Iron Age1–3. How Celtic achieved this early distribution remains contested4, with alternative archaeological and linguistic models proposing different homelands and dispersal routes. Here we analyse genome-wide data from 4,587 ancient individuals, focusing on Bronze and Iron Age Europe, to test the extent to which these models fit reconstructed demographic histories. We identify three main processes shaping European population structure that are relevant to the Celtic dispersal. First, the arrival of Steppe-related ancestry with Bell Beaker-associated groups after around 4400 bp (calibrated years before present or 1950 ce) across the region in which Celtic and related languages were later spoken. Second, a movement from southwestern Europe into Britain during the Bronze Age (3800–3200 bp), consistent with scenarios in which Celtic formed along the Atlantic façade. Third, a westward expansion of ancestry related to Late Bronze Age Knovíz–Urnfield-associated populations from eastern central Europe (3200–2800 bp), affecting France, the British Isles, northeastern Iberia and Italy and later associated with Iron Age Hallstatt and La Tène contexts5–8. Although all three movements have parallels with proposed models, we argue that the final movement, from eastern central Europe, is most parsimonious for the spread of Celtic. Although human history does not necessarily follow a parsimonious trajectory9 and language shifts need not track genetic change, these results delimit the demographic scenarios that are plausible for the emergence of Celtic in prehistoric Europe. Genome-wide data from 4,587 ancient individuals are analysed, focusing on Bronze and Iron Age Europe, to test the extent to which alternative archaeological and linguistic models for the origin and spread of Celtic fit reconstructed demographic histories.

papers.title: Conjugation-regulated self-assembled molecules for tandem solar cells
papers.abstract: Perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells on rough textured substrates are at present limited by a critical trade-off in self-assembled monolayer (SAM) design because increasing molecular conjugation enhances conductivity but often leads to unfavourable aggregation that impairs conformal coverage1,2. Here we overcome this challenge using a rationally engineered molecular spatial conjugation that incorporates tailored intramolecular distortion to suppress excess π–π stacking without sacrificing charge-transport efficiency. This steric regulation facilitates the formation of a highly ordered, conformal SAM across rough pyramidal textures. By reconciling molecular packing with interfacial coverage, the tailored interface provides optimized energy-level alignment for ultrafast charge extraction, enables improved defect passivation through adaptive conformational adjustment and acts as a robust template for high-quality perovskite film growth. Making use of this interface, the optimized tandem device achieves a notable fill factor (FF) of 85%, yielding a certified stabilized power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 35.1%. Furthermore, the device demonstrates outstanding stability, retaining more than 94% of its initial performance after 1,500 h of ageing under the ISOS-L-1 protocol. Our findings provide a clear molecular engineering route to reconcile conductivity and film uniformity while maximizing the performance of tandem photovoltaics on textured silicon substrates. Rationally engineered molecular spatial conjugation is used for the formation of highly ordered, conformal self-assembled molecules, enabling the fabrication of high-performance perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells.

papers.title: Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit
papers.abstract: Exoplanet imaging is the main method for detailed characterization of planets orbiting beyond 1 au (ref. 1) but it requires suppressing the bright glare of the star to see the faint planet light. As well as sophisticated instrumentation2,3, effective image processing is necessary for starlight suppression, which continues to be a substantial limitation4. Standard algorithms use reference images for starlight modelling and thus they are limited by inevitable telescope instabilities that change from reference to science observation5,6. Addressing this challenge will increase the number of planets amenable to direct imaging and will be a notable step towards imaging exo-Earths with future observatories7. Here we present a new physics-based method for starlight subtraction. Our method combines a multistep optimization with a flexible physical model to produce a starlight model, allowing modelling and compensation of instrument instabilities. We use automatic differentiation (autodiff)8 to optimize millions of model parameters. We demonstrate our method on observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) Near-InfraRed Camera (NIRCam)9–11 coronagraph instrument. We achieve sensitivity 2–15 times superior to standard techniques, including the first detection of 51 Eridani b (ref. 12) at 4.3 μm. This is the first time, to our knowledge, that such an approach has demonstrated substantially improved sensitivity on real, on-sky coronagraphic imaging. Our framework can be extended to other current and future ground-based and space-based observatories, including the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO), potentially relaxing the unprecedented stability requirements needed to make these a success. A new physics-based method combining the use of automatic differentiation to optimize millions of model parameters with a flexible physical model is described for starlight subtraction from real, on-sky coronagraphic images to greatly improve sensitivity.

papers.title: Multimodal X-ray imaging reveals hierarchical fibre mechanics
papers.abstract: Fibrous materials, ranging from connective tissues1–4 to engineered composites5–8, are vital to many biological and man-made systems, optimized to withstand complex in operando or in vivo loading. The load-bearing capacity of intervertebral discs (IVDs) of the spine depends on a hierarchical extracellular matrix, where plywood-like lamellae of collagen fibres in the annulus fibrosus contain nanometre-scale fibrils built from staggered triple-helical monomers4,9,10. How intact IVDs couple fibril-scale mechanics to fibre-scale organization under load remains unresolved. Here we introduce TomoSAXS, a full-field 3D small-angle X-ray scattering tomography that maps fibril-to-fibre mechanics across an intact tissue. We show that intrafibrillar molecular pre-strain (D-period stagger) is lamellar textured and tightly correlated with microscale fibre strain. Pre-strain is inversely related to fibril strain and its variability, consistent with load-sharing through molecular unwinding. Radial strain bridges and high-curvature zones at the annulus fibrosus–nucleus pulposus interfaces emerge as critical regulators of local mechanics. These findings reveal concerted fibril–fibre interactions that sustain mechanical equilibrium in the IVD, preserving elasticity and shape. More broadly, TomoSAXS establishes a platform to visualize nanoscale-to-microscale matrix mechanics across biological and synthetic fibrous materials, with applications in ageing and disease, therapeutic evaluation and the design of bio-based and bio-inspired materials. The X-ray visualization platform TomoSAXS, demonstrated here on intervertebral spinal discs, can visualize nanoscale to macroscale mechanics in intact biological organs and fibrous materials.

papers.title: Carbon radical generation by irreversible metal-to-ligand charge transfer
papers.abstract: Metal-to-ligand charge transfer (MLCT) is a fundamental photoinduced process that underpins a broad range of energy- or electron-transfer events1,2. In the absence of productive substrate engagement, the MLCT excited state typically relaxes to the ground state via photophysical deactivation, reflecting its largely reversible character3,4. Here we report a class of isolable copper–heteroaryl sulfone complexes that, upon visible light irradiation, undergo an irreversible MLCT-driven fragmentation through C–S bond cleavage within the coordinated sulfone ligand, generating carbon-centered radicals. Spectroscopic and computational studies support the formation of MLCT-derived excited states and a low-barrier pathway for C–S bond cleavage. This reactivity is largely independent of the reduction potentials of the corresponding free sulfones, enabling the generation of fluoroalkyl and non-fluorinated tertiary, secondary, and primary (even methyl) alkyl radicals. We demonstrate the utility of this platform in copper-catalyzed C–H fluoroalkylation of arenes and terminal alkynes. Leveraging these MLCT-generated trifluoromethyl radicals to initiate halogen-atom transfer (XAT) from perfluorocyclobutyl iodide (I-FCB), we also achieve radical perfluorocyclobutylation–iodination of alkenes, addressing a longstanding challenge in the incorporation of perfluorocyclobutyl motifs.

papers.title: Accelerating commercialization and deployment of indoor photovoltaics
papers.abstract: The growing reliance on distributed electronics, such as Internet of Things (IoT) nodes, smart-home devices and portable consumer products, has intensified demand for indoor energy-harvesting technologies that reduce battery replacement and servicing. Consequently, indoor photovoltaics (PVs) have advanced rapidly; however, translating state-of-the-art cells into deployable products requires design principles that reflect real indoor conditions. Here recent progress in perovskite (bulk and quantum dot), organic, amorphous-silicon, III–V and dye-sensitized PVs is examined to identify bottlenecks that arise under low-light conditions and during scale-up. This Review highlights how low-light operation favours wide-bandgap absorbers and reduced non-radiative voltage losses while reshaping module design: lower series-resistance (RS) penalties permit wider subcells and fewer interconnections, increasing geometric fill factor, whereas shunt and leakage pathways consume more of the weak photocurrent. Measurement practices for credible cross-technology benchmarking are discussed, emphasizing the transparent reporting of spectra, illuminance/irradiance, stabilization and uncertainty. Finally, the relationship between device performance and manufacturability and product integration is considered, including power-management requirements and chemical/regulatory constraints (for example, restricted substances and end-of-life handling). These guidelines provide a practical framework for evaluating indoor PVs on the basis of delivered and retained power and for accelerating the transition from laboratory-scale demonstrations to reliable, visually adaptable products for the built environment. Recent progress in photovoltaics has been investigated to translate state-of-the-art cells in the laboratory into deployable products suited to real indoor conditions, focusing on wide-bandgap absorbers, reduced non-radiative voltage losses and reshaping module design.

papers.title: AI agents run this automated biology lab that sequences DNA and more
Decoding the regulatory programs governing glioblastoma plasticity
papers.abstract: Glioblastoma is incurable and resistant to therapy despite genomic stability under treatment1–8, suggesting that non-genetic cellular plasticity is a central driver of progression. Whether such plasticity reflects stochastic state switching or is governed by predictable gene regulation has remained unclear9–13. Here we introduce scDORI (single-cell deep multi-omic regulatory inference)—a deep-learning framework that infers enhancer-driven gene-regulatory networks at single-cell resolution—and apply it to single-nucleus multiome profiles of more than one million cells from primary glioblastomas. Integrating computational inference with systematic perturbation screens across patient-derived models, we show that a structured regulatory program with an asymmetric interplay of activators and repressors governs cellular plasticity in glioblastoma. The resulting transition landscape is hierarchical and predictable, but permits cross-lineage trajectories that are absent from normal neurodevelopment. Within this landscape, low-plasticity states such as the neuronal-like state are not stable differentiation end points but actively maintained configurations, stabilized by a network of safeguard repressors that silence alternative fates. We identify MYT1L as the dominant member of this network, and show that it binds to and represses master regulators of every alternative state to consolidate neuronal-like identity. MYT1L restricted plasticity even under standard-of-care therapy and suppressed tumour growth and invasion in vivo. Conversely, loss of MYT1L reactivated plasticity and accelerated malignant features, indicating that low-plasticity identity requires continuous repression. These findings reframe malignant cell state stability as a balance between activation and continuous repression, and nominate safeguard repressors as candidate therapeutic targets that are distinct from differentiation-inducing activators, with potential relevance across cancers in which phenotypic switching drives therapy resistance. Multi-omic analyses of cells from patients with glioblastoma (GB) provide insight into the role of non-genetic cellular plasticity in disease progression, showing that state stability in GB cells is controlled by a network of interacting activators and repressors.

A sublattice polarimeter to probe the quantum geometry of synthetic photonic lattices
papers.abstract: Measuring the electronic structure of crystalline materials is key in advancing our understanding of their physical properties. While techniques such as angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy have provided unprecedented insights into electronic orbitals of natural crystals, an equivalent tool to characterize photonic lattices is still lacking. Here, we introduce a sublattice polarimeter that enables full reconstruction of the Bloch wavefunctions in bipartite photonic lattices. Using a spatial light modulator to apply controlled phase shifts and attenuations to each sublattice, we extract the amplitude and phase of the crystal orbitals across the Brillouin zone, including close to band degeneracies. This allows experimentally accessing the Bloch Hamiltonian, thereby determining the quantum geometric tensor and the band Chern numbers. Beyond bipartite lattices, the method can be generalized to address multiple internal degrees of freedom, opening routes to experimentally probe complex topological structures such as trigonal warping, Chern insulators and Euler curvature in multiband settings. The authors introduce a sublattice polarimeter to measure the Bloch wavefunctions in bipartite photonic lattices. Using their method, they experimentally access the quantum metric, Berry curvature and band Chern numbers.

papers.title: Agentic intelligent data engine for scientific large language models
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping scientific discovery across diverse fields. Yet scientific AI remains constrained by data curation, which demands substantial manual effort and deep domain expertise, creating major cost and scalability barriers. Here we present the Agentic Intelligent Data Engine (AIDE), a multi-agent framework that automates data curation for scientific AI. AIDE collects, selects, and organizes data in three stages, providing an end-to-end pipeline that turns a data request into training-ready datasets. We benchmarked AIDE on 14 tasks across biomedical and chemical domains. Scientific AI models built with AIDE-curated datasets matched or outperformed those built with manually curated data, and AIDE’s fully automated preparation delivered significant gains in efficiency and data utilization without compromising quality. These findings provide consistent evidence of AIDE’s applicability across scientific domains and usage paradigms and demonstrate its potential to accelerate scientific AI development and democratize access to scientific AI. Here, authors develop AIDE, a multiagent framework that automates scientific data curation, and demonstrate across biomedical and chemical tasks that its automatically curated datasets can match or outperform manually curated data while improving efficiency.
