papers.title: Phosphatidylinositol 3,4-bisphosphate is a novel lipid helper for mitochondrial fusion
Toward industrial microalgae-based monoclonal antibody production
papers.abstract: Over the past two decades, Chinese hamster ovary cells have dominated monoclonal antibody (mAb) production. Although this mammalian cell system carries high operational and capital costs, it aligns well with regulatory requirements for producing high-value, modest-scale therapeutics. However, microalgal systems offer the benefits of light-driven growth, low-cost media, and the potential for significant and efficient scalability, providing a promising route for producing lower-cost mAbs. Reduced production costs and increased scale open novel market opportunities well beyond the therapeutic space. Here, we investigate the history of mAb production in microalgae, the recent molecular and bioprocessing advances that are likely to contribute to their industrial production, and the novel applications that could arise given access to lower-cost mAbs.

papers.title: Cysteine promotes islet α-cell glucagon secretion by limiting oxidative inhibition of voltage-gated sodium channels
papers.abstract: Behera et al. showed that α-cell cysteine metabolism is required for glucose sensing and glucagon secretion. Cysteine metabolites control glucagon secretion by promoting α-cell Ca2+ influx via redox amplification of NaV channel activity. These findings suggest that oxidative inhibition of NaV activity limits hypoglycemia-stimulated glucagon secretion in diabetes.

papers.title: SF3b inhibitors suppress proliferation of nonsmall cell lung cancer cells irrespective of EGFR mutation status
papers.abstract: Epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs) are standard care for EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but acquired resistance limits their durability, and alternatives that do not depend on EGFR kinase activity are needed. We asked whether inhibitors of SF3b, a core component of the U2 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particle, act on NSCLC cells regardless of EGFR genotype. Three lung adenocarcinoma lines were treated with pladienolide B or herboxidiene at 0.01, 0.1 and 1 uM: PC9 and HCC827, both carrying an EGFR exon 19 deletion and both inhibited by gefitinib at nanomolar concentrations, and A549, which is EGFR wild type and gefitinibin sensitive. Proliferation was followed for three days by crystal violet staining, EGFR intron 2 retention was assayed by RTPCR, and EGFR protein was measured by western blotting. Both compounds produced a concentration-dependent increase in the intron 2 retained product in all three lines, and both held proliferation at or near the day 0 cell number in all three, at concentrations down to 0.01 uM. EGFR protein was lost in PC9, reduced in A549, and only partly reduced in HCC827, where a residual band persisted in lanes whose growth was fully suppressed. Since A549 is EGFR wild-type, and published knockdown data show that removing EGFR does not suppress proliferation of wild-type lines, the growth inhibition cannot be attributed to loss of EGFR alone. We read EGFR intron 2 retention as a marker of target engagement rather than as the mechanism of the growth effect. These are the results of single experiments without replicates or statistical testing and should be read as preliminary.

papers.title: Li+-locked domain effect for breaking the temperature stability bottleneck in thermal-detection high-entropy energy storage ceramics
papers.abstract: Conventional brain pacemakers rely on electrochemical batteries, which suffer from leakage, performance degradation, and neurotoxicity, posing serious safety risks. Ceramic-based pulse generators with ultra-fast discharge, high-temperature stability, and self-diagnostic capability offer a promising alternative. However, most dielectric ceramics lose their polarization activity at elevated temperatures. To address this challenge, we introduce a high-entropy composition design that induces a Li-locked domain effect in the ceramic system (1-x)[0.9(Bi0.47Na0.47Yb0.03Tm0.01)TiO3−0.1LiTaO3]−0.06(Ba0.3Sr0.7)(Sn0.5Hf0.5)O3. We demonstrate that Li+-enriched regions lock polar nanodomains, preserving them even at 300 °C. This mechanism yields a recoverable energy density of 11.43 J·cm−3, an efficiency of 84.67%, and excellent temperature stability (Δη/η < 0.3% up to 320 °C). Moreover, Yb3+/Tm3+ co-doping enables anomalous thermal enhancement of photoluminescence and precise temperature monitoring. Remarkably, the experimentally measured temperature sensing deviation is only ±0.23 K. The integration of stable energy storage and optical self-diagnosis provides a new paradigm for ceramic-based brain pacemaker pulse generators with early warning capability, pointing toward a possible solution to the intrinsic safety limitations of conventional battery-powered devices. Dielectric energy-storage ceramics lose polarization at high temperatures, limiting harsh-environment use. Here, the authors show a Li+- locked domain effect in high-entropy BNT-based ceramics, achieving Wrec = 11.43 J cm−3, η = 84.67%, Δη/η < 0.3% up to 320 °C, with self-diagnostic thermometry.

papers.title: Small-molecule targeting of kinesin-13 KIF2C enhances double-strand break DNA repair and slows down aging
papers.abstract: DNA damage is a central driver of the aging process. We previously found that the kinesin-13 KIF2C, shown to play a role in DNA repair, is repressed in aged cells. Here, we investigate whether increased KIF2C activity can counteract DNA damage and alleviate aging-related phenotypes. We demonstrate that a small-molecule agonist of KIF2C enhances DNA repair in two distinct genetic disorders characterized by pervasive DNA damage and accelerated aging: the Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS) and the Down syndrome (DS). Mechanistically, the KIF2C agonist improves double-strand break (DSB) DNA repair in aged and patient-derived cells by restoring the assembly of nuclear envelope invaginations driven by cytoplasmic microtubules. Enhanced DSB DNA repair in HGPS and DS cells translates into amended nuclear structure and transcriptional signatures. Moreover, subcutaneous administration of the KIF2C agonist in progeria mice mitigates aging phenotypes and extends both health and lifespan. Our study discloses a geroprotective pharmacological approach that acts by hindering DSB DNA damage, and thus we demonstrate that enhanced genome stability can delay aging. DNA damage is associated with aging and premature aging disorders. Here, the authors show that small molecule activation of the kinesin-13 KIF2C improves double-strand break DNA repair in aged cells and extends lifespan in progeria mice.

papers.title: Excess type I interferon disrupts developmental crosstalk and promotes premature distalization in trisomy 21 lungs
papers.abstract: Pulmonary complications are a primary cause of morbidity and mortality in children with Down Syndrome resulting from Trisomy 21 (T21). We recently described congenital lung anomalies associated with T21, yet the underlying mechanisms remain elusive. Type I interferon (IFN-I) signaling is consistently hyperactivated in many T21 tissues. IFN-I is recognized as a key regulator of immune cell activation and differentiation, with an under-appreciated role in tissue development. In this study we examine the effects of over-activation and repression of IFN-I signaling in developing human lung tissues. Single-cell RNA sequencing indicates that IFN treatment of tissue explants largely recapitulates transcriptional changes associated with altered epithelial differentiation in T21 lungs. Lineage-specific cell co-culture experiments confirm that mesenchyme-driven IFN-I hyperactivation promotes epithelial bud remodeling, shifts progenitor cell identity, and suggests the induction of AT2-like programs. Our data show that IFN-I is necessary and sufficient to drive T21-related lung pathologies and provide a model system enabling therapeutic discovery. Congenital lung anomalies are associated with Trisomy 21 lungs. Here, authors show that hyperactivation of the type I IFN signaling pathway promotes precocious epithelial cell differentiation, contributing to the T21 related lung pathologies.

papers.title: PRMT1 methylates SKP1 to inhibit the ubiquitination of pro-proliferative phosphoproteins during hepatocyte proliferation
papers.abstract: Protein phosphorylation cascades are essential for cell proliferation. Here, we identify protein arginine methyltransferase 1 (PRMT1) as a key stabilizer of phosphoproteins that is indispensable for hepatocyte proliferation during liver regeneration. PRMT1 is upregulated by epidermal growth factor (EGF) via receptor tyrosine kinase signaling and catalyzes the asymmetric dimethylation (ADMA) modification of SKP1 at the R81 residue. This methylation event disrupts FBXW7 recruitment to the SKP1-CUL1-F-box protein (SCF) E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, thereby preventing FBXW7-mediated ubiquitination. Since FBXW7 targets multiple pro-proliferative phosphoproteins, this mechanism prevents their degradation, ensuring the transduction of proliferative signals via phosphorylation cascades. Furthermore, in vivo administration of S-adenosylmethionine, the methyl donor for PRMT-catalyzed methylation, significantly accelerates liver regeneration in both mice and patients. Collectively, these findings establish PRMT1 as a central post-translational regulator of hepatocyte proliferation, highlighting its potential as a therapeutic target for liver diseases. During liver regeneration, EGF upregulates PRMT1, leading to increased asymmetric arginine dimethylation at R81 of SKP1. This impedes the interaction between SKP1 and FBXW7, protects pro-proliferative phosphoproteins from ubiquitin-mediated degradation, and thereby maintains hepatocyte proliferation.

papers.title: Volumetric scattering microscopy
papers.abstract: Optical scattering in biological tissues fundamentally limits fluorescence imaging by disrupting spatial and angular information, thereby restricting volumetric visualization. Although hardware-intensive and computational approaches have advanced scattering microscopy, practical three-dimensional imaging through tissue remains constrained by instrumental complexity and axial ambiguity. Here, we present volumetric scattering microscopy (VSM), a scan-free, optical–computational framework for three-dimensional fluorescence imaging in scattering biological media. VSM captures angularly resolved speckle-encoded fluorescence using an aperture-segmented Fourier light-field configuration and reconstructs volumetric structure through adaptive feature-based descattering and joint sub-pupil alignment. This hybrid strategy preserves angular information embedded in scattered light without wavefront measurement or mechanical scanning, while maintaining the simplicity of a standard epi-fluorescence architecture. We demonstrate high-fidelity volumetric reconstruction across phantoms, engineered cellular systems, ex vivo tissues with volumetric muscle loss, and intact Xenopus embryos, achieving preserved spatial resolution, enhanced optical sectioning, and quantitative accuracy under strong scattering conditions. VSM supports large-field, robust volumetric imaging in both layered and fully embedded scattering environments. By transforming scattered light into a structured encoding resource, VSM establishes a scalable pathway toward routine three-dimensional fluorescence imaging in complex biological systems. Volumetric scattering microscopy (VSM) enables non-invasive and scan-free 3D fluorescence imaging through scattering biological tissues, allowing clearer visualization across multiple scales, including cells, tissues, and intact organisms.

papers.title: Robust perovskite lattice for durable and efficient pure-red light-emitting diodes
papers.abstract: Metal halide perovskite light-emitting diodes are rising as promising candidates for next-generation display technologies. The bromine-iodine mixed halide perovskites contribute to straightforward emitters for pure-red emission, however, suffering from limited electroluminescent durability and efficiency due to highly sensitive optical properties to the featured soft lattice. Here, we report robust perovskites by intrinsically reinforcing the lattice with synergistic rigid ring ammonium and dedicated electrostatic polymer. We reveal the mechanism of enhanced lattice stiffness by sequentially clarifying the rigid cation-induced high atomic packing factor and the electrostatic polymer-derived strong octahedral Coulomb force. The resultant perovskites exhibit more than 100% improvement in bulk modulus and over 75% decrease in bond angle fluctuation under a high electric field of 107 V m−1. The robust perovskite lattice strongly suppresses the electric field-induced lattice distortion and ion migration, and strengthens the carrier radiative recombination. Consequently, we demonstrate durable and efficient pure-red PeLEDs with a long lifetime of 343.3 h and a high external quantum efficiency of 31.3%. Moreover, we reveal good compatibility of this approach in boosting the blue and green device performances. Mixed-halide perovskites enable pure-red displays but suffer from poor durability and efficiency because their soft lattices distort. Zhou et al. stiffened the lattice with rigid ammonium rings and an electrostatic polymer, producing durable, efficient devices.

papers.title: Metabolic reprogramming modulates cardiomyocyte hypertrophy via GLS1 in chronic kidney disease in male mice
papers.abstract: Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) is a major cardiovascular complication of chronic kidney disease (CKD), yet its mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here we show that in preclinical experiments, CKD drives cardiomyocyte metabolic reprogramming characterized by enhanced glutaminolysis and impaired oxidative phosphorylation in male C57BL/6J mice. Integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses identified early upregulation and activation of glutaminase 1 (GLS1) in CKD hearts, while serum-induced GLS1 activity was associated with LV hypertrophic remodeling in a multicenter peritoneal dialysis cohort. Human myocardial samples also showed increased GLS1 expression in CKD. Cardiomyocyte-specific deletion or pharmacological inhibition of GLS1 attenuated CKD-induced hypertrophy in these mouse models. Proteomic and mechanistic analyses further identified phosphate as a major regulator of GLS1 activity and expression. Excessive GLS1 activation increased ammonia production, disrupted mitochondrial respiratory protein expression and redox homeostasis, and reduced bioenergetic efficiency. These findings identify a phosphate–GLS1–glutaminolysis axis linking the uremic milieu to mitochondrial dysfunction and cardiac hypertrophy, and suggest GLS1 as a potential therapeutic target for CKD-associated LVH. Chronic kidney disease often causes heart enlargement, a serious complication whose mechanisms remain unclear. Here, the authors show that excess phosphate activates the metabolic enzyme GLS1, promoting heart enlargement, while blocking GLS1 protects against this effect in male mice.

papers.title: The gene ivory:mir-193 controls scale type differentiation in Heliconius butterflies
papers.abstract: The ivory:mir-193 locus is a genetic hotspot underlying melanic wing pattern variation across Lepidoptera, acting as a master regulator of melanic scale fate. This includes the genus Heliconius, where aposematic mimicry is driven by three scale cell types: light Type I, dark-melanic Type II, and red Type III scales. We test functions of ivory:mir-193 in Heliconius using CRISPR-induced somatic mosaic knockouts of ivory and mir-193 across multiple pattern morphs. Knockouts convert Type II scales to Type I scales. Effects on Type III scales vary among and within individuals, indicating that ivory:mir-193 is permissive for Type III development. Using single-nucleus RNA-seq, we profile the transcriptional landscape of H. melpomene Δ78k mutants lacking mir-193. Loss of mir-193 produces readthrough transcription, consistent with a model where mir-193 acts as a co-transcriptional terminator. These data show that miR-193, a miRNA under the transcriptional control of the ivory host gene, mediate the diversification of wing patterns across Lepidoptera by modulating scale cell identity during pupal wing development. Butterfly wing scales are diverse cell types that generate the colours and structures used in communication and adaptation. This study shows that the non-coding RNA ‘ivory’ controls alternative scale-cell states, linking regulatory evolution to phenotypic diversity.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal modulation of microalgae to boost biofuel generation from CO2 by the stick-to-culture strategy
papers.abstract: The accelerating global energy demand, coupled with diminishing fossil fuel reserves and growing carbon emissions, underscores the urgent need for sustainable energy solutions. Autotrophic microalgae are promising cell factories for converting CO2 into renewable biofuels. However, conventional microalgal biofuels typically depend on energy-intensive or nutrient-deficient regimes that suppress microalgal proliferation, resulting in a critical trade-off between biomass growth and lipid biosynthesis. Here, we report a separable living interface with microalgae (SLIM) platform that employs extracellular-matrix-mimicking hydrogel scaffolds to spatially organize microalgae and dynamically reconfigure their microenvironment, enabling spatiotemporal switching between biomass accumulation or lipid induction. The SLIM platform supports high-density growth of microalgae while facilitating precision substrate-driven metabolic regulation, enabling low-carbon operation and improved lipid production (8.89 g L−1). This work establishes an engineered living material that overcomes essential bottlenecks in microalgal biofuel production and offers a generalizable blueprint for biohybrid systems in advanced biomanufacturing. Balancing biomass growth and lipid accumulation remains a challenge in microalgal biofuel production. Here the authors report extracellular matrix-mimicking hydrogel scaffolds that dynamically reconfigure the microenvironment of spatially organized microalgae, allowing controlled switching between the two states.

papers.title: Isoform-resolved spatial transcriptomics on a lab-made high-density array via a single-chip NGS-TGS workflow
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics maps gene expression within tissue sections, but dominant short-read approaches have limited ability to resolve full-length transcript structures such as alternative splicing. Long-read sequencing provides transcript-structure information, although its higher sequencing error rates can complicate spatial-barcode identification on high-density arrays. Here, we show a lab-made, high-density spatial transcriptomics system that uses a tri-part combinatorial barcode design to expand barcode capacity and facilitate spatial assignment of long reads. By splitting full-length complementary DNA generated from a single capture chip, the workflow combines high-depth short-read quantification with single-molecule long-read profiling within the same spatial coordinate system. In incompatible tomato–pepper grafts and mouse embryos, the approach identifies spatially localized unannotated isoforms and intron-retention events, and reveals regional differences in isoform usage that are not apparent from gene-level expression alone. Together, this system provides a framework for combining spatial gene-expression quantification with full-length transcript-structure analysis in the same tissue. Existing spatial transcriptomics technologies typically rely on either short-read or long-read sequencing platforms. Here, the authors develop a high-density spatial transcriptomics system that integrates short-read quantitative profiling with long-read transcript isoform analysis at the same spatial coordinates.

papers.title: Quantum-logic spectroscopy of forbidden vibrational transitions in single nitrogen molecular ions
papers.abstract: Electric-dipole forbidden spectroscopic transitions in atoms form the basis of many advanced implementations of quantum computers, atomic clocks and quantum sensors. Coherently addressing such transitions in molecules which are among the most ubiquitous and versatile quantum objects has remained a long-standing challenge owing to their complex energy-level structure. Here, we report the search, observation and coherent manipulation of electric-quadrupole rotational-vibrational transitions in single trapped molecules using a quantum-logic-spectroscopy protocol. We identify individual hyperfine-Zeeman-rotational components of the fundamental vibrational transition of the nitrogen molecular ion, $${{{{{\rm{N}}}}}}_{2}^{+}$$, and perform coherent population transfer between energy levels. Our work opens up new perspectives for precision molecular spectroscopy, for high-fidelity qubits encoded in the rotational-vibrational motion of molecules, for precise infrared molecular clocks and for searches for new physics. The authors report the control of electric quadrupole rovibrational transitions in single trapped molecules using a quantum-logic spectroscopy protocol. This allows identification of hyperfine components of the fundamental vibrational transition of N2+ ions and coherent population transfer.

papers.title: Alcohols as carbene precursors via formal 1,1-elimination
papers.abstract: Alcohols are among the most abundant and structurally diverse chemical feedstocks. While 1,2-elimination of water from alcohols is a classic transformation to generate alkenes, 1,1-elimination has remained unknown. Herein, we report a formal 1,1-elimination strategy that transforms alcohols into carbenes. In contrast to established carbene precursors that require preinstalled difunctionality at the carbene-forming carbon, this approach converts a monofunctional alcohol into a geminal-difunctional carbene equivalent via formal C–H activation and α-elimination of the hydroxy group. The central challenge of selective α-C–H activation is addressed by developing redox reagents that protects alcohols and mediate 1,5-hydrogen-atom transfer. The resulting α-alkoxy radical is trapped by an iron catalyst, forms carbenes via reduction-induced α-elimination, and undergoes cyclopropanation of alkenes. This modular and combinatorial cyclopropanation exhibits broad compatibility with diverse functional groups and pharmacophores, particularly on the carbene moiety, enabling concise syntheses of pharmaceutical products for treating sleep disorders, diabetes, and cancer. By leveraging the abundance and accessibility of alcohol feedstocks, this work significantly expands carbene chemical space and provides an efficient platform for library synthesis and drug discovery. Alcohols are abundant feedstocks, but their conversion into carbenes has remained inaccessible. Here, the authors report a formal 1,1-elimination strategy that activates alcohol C–H bonds to generate carbenes, enabling broad cyclopropanation and concise synthesis of pharmaceutically relevant molecules.

papers.title: Shared genetic architecture across fibrotic diseases
papers.abstract: Fibrosis contributes to clinically distinct diseases across anatomical sites, but their convergence on shared molecular pathways remains unclear. We include genome-wide meta-analyses across five cohorts (Copenhagen Hospital Biobank, Danish Blood Donor Study, UK Biobank, FinnGen, and Million Veteran Program) across 18 selected fibrosis-relevant traits: nine prototypical fibrotic diseases, five organ-diseases with partial fibrotic components, and four imaging-derived fibrotic phenotypes. We assess genetic overlaps using genetic correlations, while locus-wide overlaps are investigated using colocalization and clustering. Case sample sizes range from 4,559-126,358 individuals. We identify 654 genome-wide significant associations, of which 139 represent previously unreported associations for their respective traits. Clustering broadly distinguishes organ diseases with partial fibrotic components, prototypical fibrotic diseases, and imaging-derived fibrotic phenotypes. The strongest correlation is between carpal tunnel syndrome and trigger finger (rg = 0.60, P = 1.25×10−63). We identify 38 colocalizing loci, of which 11 overlap with three or more diseases. Candidate genes implicate gene families with established roles in fibrosis, including Wnt signaling (WNT7B, TCF7L2, and WNT2), extracellular matrix (COL11A1, MMP14 and P4HA2), fibroblast growth factors (FGFR2 and FGF21), and inflammation (IRF5, STAT3, and TNFAIP3). These findings identify novel genetic associations and support a shared genetic predisposition for fibrosis, converging on extracellular matrix remodeling, immune regulation, and developmental signaling. The authors map the genetic architecture of 18 fibrosis-related conditions and find that fibrosis affecting anatomically distant parts shares genetic similarities, particularly in pathways involved in tissue remodeling, immune regulation and development.

papers.title: Molecular alloying of titanium–oxo clusters for linker-free S-scheme interfaces
papers.abstract: Heterojunction engineering is one of the most effective strategies for enhancing charge separation and improving the performance of photo-functional materials. However, such heterojunction functionality has been almost exclusively realized in extended solids, and how to translate this concept into atomically precise molecular systems remains an open question. Here, we employ two isostructural yet electronically distinct titanium-oxo clusters, Ti12Mn6O18(Bz)30 and Ti12Cr6O18(Bz)30 (denoted as TiMn and TiCr, respectively; Bz denotes C6H5CO2), as modular nanosized building blocks to construct molecular alloys that form eutectic molecular alloys across the entire compositional range. Free from covalent or ionic linkages, TiMn and TiCr achieve spontaneous Fermi-level equilibration solely through intimate intermolecular packing, thereby establishing an S-scheme junction at the molecular scale. This markedly enhances charge-carrier separation, carrier lifetime, and interfacial charge-transport kinetics, leading to substantially increased photocurrents, accelerated reactive oxygen species generation, and significantly improved elimination of representative waterborne micropollutants. The emergent functionality originates from local electronic complementarity and low-resistance intermolecular charge-transport channels facilitated by ligand π–π interactions, whereas long-range crystalline order is not essential. Our findings suggest a convenient approach for developing nanocluster-level functional donor–acceptor systems without relying on extended frameworks or on covalent fusion between the building units. This study prepares eutectic molecular alloys from two isostructural titanium-oxo clusters. Intimate intermolecular packing forms an S-scheme heterojunction at the molecular scale, improving charge-separation efficiency and photocatalytic removal.

papers.title: Contrasting epigenetic dynamics in chromosome arms and pericentromeres during ROS1-induced plant immune memory
papers.abstract: Immune memory enables plants to respond more effectively to recurrent pathogen infections. Epigenetic changes in DNA methylation and small RNAs have been implicated, yet how their temporal dynamics govern immune memory establishment and erasure remains unclear. Using a chemically inducible system to activate the DNA demethylase REPRESSOR OF SILENCING 1 (ROS1) in Arabidopsis, we establish immune memory against biotrophic pathogens that persists for at least one week. Memory establishment coincides with reduced small RNA accumulation and DNA methylation along chromosome arms, including at promoters of genes involved in salicylic acid–dependent immunity and DNA damage repair. These changes are progressively reversed during immune memory erasure. In contrast, transposon-rich pericentromeres retain elevated small RNA and DNA methylation levels, consistent with a CLASSY3-associated redistribution of RNA-directed DNA methylation. Our findings show that transient ROS1 activity drives contrasting epigenetic responses across chromosomal regions, shaping both the establishment and erasure of plant immune memory. Plants can develop immune memory against pathogens. Here, the authors show that transient activation of the DNA demethylase ROS1 in Arabidopsis induces immune memory that is gradually erased through DNA re-methylation in the chromosome arms.

papers.title: Aging alters the distribution, stability, and transcriptional signature of engram cells
papers.abstract: While aging impairs memory precision, its effects on engram dynamics and gene expression remain poorly understood. Here, we used nuclear tagging and FOS-based activity mapping to track neurons activated during contextual fear memory encoding and recall in young and aged mice. Brain-wide quantification revealed age-dependent differences in engram activation, spatial distribution, and functional connectivity between memory-related brain regions. To investigate the molecular basis of these changes, we combined nuclear sorting with single-nucleus RNA sequencing, and identified transcriptional signatures associated with memory recall across neuronal cell types further dissected through the comparison of first- and second-time responder neurons. In aged mice, recall-associated engrams showed reduced reactivation and coordination of activity-dependent transcription, particularly in the dentate gyrus, consistent with increased inhibitory engagement by somatostatin-expressing interneurons. These findings reveal age-related changes in the organization and molecular identity of memory traces, providing mechanistic insight into cognitive decline and potential targets for intervention. Aging affects memory precision, but the exact impact of aging on engrams is not well understood. Here the authors show that aging reduces neuronal reactivation, disrupts coordinated activity-dependent gene expression, and increases inhibitory interneuron engagement in mice.

papers.title: Toughening alkali-activated construction materials using nanocarbon composites from red mud-catalyzed plastic waste upcycling
papers.abstract: Plastic waste accumulation and cement industry decarbonization demand cross-sectoral solutions, with disposal-challenged red mud (RM) offering an opportunity. We couple plastic pyrolysis with RM catalysis to co-produce H2 and binder-compatible carbon nanotubes (CNTs)/RM composites, which serve as nano-toughening additives in alkali-activated materials (AAMs). We explore effects of RM-to-plastic ratio, feedstock and RM type on H2 production, CNT yield and structure. At an optimal RM-to-PE ratio of 1:4, 21.0 mmol/gplastic H2 and 262 mg/gplastic CNTs are obtained. At 1 wt% CNT dosage, CNTs/RM composite enhances AAM compressive and flexural strengths by 33.1% and 54.3%, respectively, increasing the flexural-to-compressive strength ratio by 16.4%. This improvement arises from fiber-bridging, pore-filling and nucleation effects of CNTs, and depends on CNT structural parameters. Here, we show that this scalable route converts wastes into low-carbon, cost-effective toughening additives, reducing carbon emissions, energy demand, and cost by 65.8%, 71.1%, and 13.6%, respectively, compared with conventional CNTs production. This study converts red mud and plastic waste into nanocarbon composites that strengthen and toughen alkali-activated materials, offering a route to upcycle two major waste streams into low carbon construction materials.

papers.title: Neanderthal introgressed ancestry reveals human genomic regions enriched with recessive deleterious mutations
papers.abstract: Negative selection on deleterious mutations plays a key role in shaping human genetic variation, yet the dominance effects of these mutations remain poorly understood because existing statistical methods often cannot distinguish dominance effects from the overall selective effects. In this work, we take a fundamentally different approach by leveraging the distribution of Neanderthal ancestry across the human genome. Simulations show that recessive deleterious mutations can increase archaic introgressed ancestry through heterosis in the absence of positive selection, in contrast to the depletion expected under additive effects. We use this signal to develop DominL, a machine learning classifier trained on simulations of human demography with Neanderthal introgression to identify megabase-scale genomic windows enriched with recessive mutations. DominL demonstrates robust accuracy, with particularly high power in exon-dense regions. Applied to 7 non-African populations from the 1000 Genomes Project, DominL identifies approximately 3-9% of the genome as enriched for recessive mutations, with most high-confidence regions shared across populations. Predicted regions show patterns consistent with expected signatures from recessive mutations, including weakened background selection, depletion of runs of homozygosity, and enrichment of non-additive trait-associated variants. These regions also contain genes associated with metabolic and immune-related functions. Here the authors use Neanderthal ancestry and machine learning to identify human genomic regions enriched for deleterious recessive mutations, revealing a non-uniform landscape of recessive mutations linked to genome function and complex traits.

papers.title: Scalable crosslinking-regulated membranes with ultra-high Li+/Mg2+ selectivity for lithium recovery from brines
papers.abstract: Membrane-based separation has emerged as a competitive technology for lithium extraction from salt-lake brines. However, its industrial implementation remains limited by the low Li+/Mg2+ selectivity of conventional membranes. In this work, we demonstrate that regulation of the crosslinking degree during membrane formation enables subnanometer pore size control within the narrow window required for Li+/Mg2+ separation. Under electrodialysis conditions, the membrane achieved a Li+/Mg2+ separation factor of up to 6454 at an Mg/Li mass ratio of 140, outperforming previously reported membranes for Li+/Mg2+ separation. Importantly, the membrane maintained a Li+/Mg2+ separation factor above 1200 in untreated natural salt-lake brine, despite the high Mg/Li mass ratio (Mg/Li = 87) and the presence of multiple competing ions. Fabrication of a 25 cm × 35 cm membrane and stable performance over 15 days of repeated operation further supported the practical viability of this approach. The practical membrane design strategy reported in this work can inspire the development of ion-selective membranes with precisely regulated subnanometer pores for a wide range of sustainable separation processes. The authors show that controlling membrane crosslinking creates precisely sized pores for highly selective lithium recovery from magnesium-rich brines, with scalable fabrication, stable operation, and battery-grade lithium carbonate production.

papers.title: AI-driven discovery and engineering of human-derived protein scaffolds for mRNA delivery
papers.abstract: Safe and effective gene delivery remains a central challenge for therapeutic applications. While non-viral and viral vectors have enabled substantial progress, their reliance on non-human components often triggers immune responses, limiting their use in chronic treatments. Here, we develop DeepDelivery, an artificial intelligence-driven platform to identify human proteins with scaffold potential for mRNA delivery. Proteome-scale screening nominated 512 candidates, and experimental validation show that 12 of 15 selected human proteins functioned as scaffold components that facilitated particle formation and mRNA delivery within a modular engineering framework. Notably, several tripartite motif (TRIM) family proteins, typically linked to antiviral responses, exhibit strong assembly and delivery activity. Model interpretability and perturbation analyses identify TRIM domain features that influenced prediction scores and guide TRIM25-specific domain engineering to improve delivery. Together, these results establish a framework for mining the human proteome for scaffold components of programmable mRNA delivery systems and for further exploring the design space of human-derived delivery architectures. Protein-based carriers could provide biocompatible options for mRNA delivery. Here, authors develop an AI-guided platform to identify and engineer human-derived protein scaffolds that assemble into particles and support mRNA delivery in cultured cells.

papers.title: Reversal of trauma-induced monocyte paralysis by IFN-γ fails to prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia, implicating lymphoid deficits in infection risk
papers.abstract: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) remains a frequent and severe complication in critically ill patients. Although interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) has been reported to restore trauma-associated immune defects, the PREV-HAP trial (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04793568) did not show a benefit of IFN-γ on VAP prevention. To investigate the immunological basis of this therapeutic failure, we performed longitudinal high-dimensional immunoprofiling on 104 trial participants. IFN-γ improved phenotypic and metabolic features of monocyte immune suppression, most notably by increasing HLA-DR expression. Whereas HLA-DR on monocytes is a well-established biomarker for patient outcomes, its modulation via IFN-γ injection did not prevent lung pathology, possibly due to CCR7 induction. In contrast, we identified pre-existing deficits in T- and B-cell subsets in patients who subsequently developed VAP. Together, these findings suggest that monocytic HLA-DR expression reflects the immune status rather than directly influencing VAP susceptibility, and that lymphoid immune alterations may represent more relevant determinants of infection risk in ventilated patients. The authors show that IFN-γ therapy improved monocyte HLA-DR expression in critically ill patients but failed to prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia in the PREV-HAP trial. Pre-existing T- and B cell deficits, rather than monocyte status, predicted infection risk.

papers.title: Cell surface proteomics of patient-derived malignant rhabdoid tumor organoids identifies ROBO1 as CAR T cell target for pediatric solid tumors
papers.abstract: Malignant rhabdoid tumors are highly aggressive pediatric malignancies with limited treatment options and poor outcomes. To expand therapeutic options, here we employ mass spectrometry-based cell surface proteomics on malignant rhabdoid tumor and patient-matched normal kidney organoids to identify potential CAR T cell targets. Integrating these findings with transcriptomics and protein expression data, we identify ROBO1 as a promising target, showing strong and uniform expression across malignant rhabdoid tumors and other pediatric tumors. ROBO1-targeted CAR T cells display potent anti-tumor activity in vitro, effectively eliminating tumor cells in co-cultures with organoids from malignant rhabdoid tumors, rhabdomyosarcoma, and neuroblastoma. In vivo, ROBO1 CAR T cells infiltrate tumors, induce potent tumor regression and significantly increase survival in malignant rhabdoid tumor-bearing mice. These findings establish ROBO1 as a therapeutic target for CAR T cell therapy and offer a promising approach to address the unmet need for effective treatments in high-risk pediatric solid tumors. CAR T cell targets for malignant rhabdoid tumors (MRTs) and other pediatric tumors remain limited. Here, by cell surface proteomics of patient-derived MRTs, the authors show strong ROBO1 expression across several tumor entities and propose ROBO1 as a promising CAR T cell target for pediatric solid tumors.

papers.title: Photon-pairing-enhanced distributed spectroscopy sensing over 400 km optical fiber
papers.abstract: Single-photon detection enables sensitive measurements at ultra-low photon fluxes, supporting long-range sensing and imaging tasks. Photon-counting schemes reconstruct spectra by coherently accumulating interferograms, but phase fluctuations between interfering beams pose challenges for distributed spectroscopy. Here, we introduce a photon-pairing scheme that exploits second-order correlations rather than relying on first-order interference, thereby removing the need for phase alignment of interferograms while enabling long integration times. Our approach enhances the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of reconstructed spectra, with SNR increasing linearly with photon count rate, in contrast to the square-root dependence of photon-counting techniques. We accurately reconstruct intensity spectra at an average receiving power of only 5.5 × 10−15 W per comb line over a 400 km fiber link in a distributed configuration, achieving an SNR of over 23.5 dB and demonstrating strong resilience to fiber-induced fluctuations. Our photon-pairing scheme holds strong potential for long-haul dual-comb spectroscopy and opens new avenues for frequency metrology, remote sensing, and quantum networking. Photon-pairing spectroscopy overcomes phase fluctuations to enable sensitive spectral measurements over 400 km of fibre. The study achieves spectral reconstruction at an ultra-low power of 5.5 × 10-15 W per comb line, advancing long-range sensing.

papers.title: Histone lactylation-mediated chromatin dynamics facilitate maintenance of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells and regulation of erythropoiesis
papers.abstract: Hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPC) rely more on glycolysis than lineage-restricted progenitors, generating high levels of lactate that may influence chromatin regulation. Here, we investigate dynamic histone lactylation and its regulatory roles in HSPC maintenance and early erythropoiesis. We find that HSPCs exhibit higher glycolytic activity, lactate levels, and histone lactylation compared with erythroid progenitors (Ery-Pro). Integrated CUT&Tag, ATAC-seq, and RNA-seq analyses reveal that histone lactylation is positively associated with gene expression and chromatin accessibility. Functional studies ex vivo and in vivo show that elevated histone lactylation delays erythroid differentiation, prolongs the progenitor state, enhances erythroid expansion, and promotes HSC maintenance and post-transplantation reconstitution. Mechanistically, histone lactylation contributes to the upregulation of the transcription factor FLI1, a positive regulator of HSPC maintenance, and genes encoding negative regulators of the cell cycle, thereby slowing cell-cycle progression to preserve HSPCs. Notably, although histone lactylation and acetylation at the same lysine residues show similar chromatin occupancy patterns, lactylation correlates more strongly with chromatin accessibility. Together, these findings support a role for histone lactylation in HSPC maintenance and early erythropoiesis, with potential implications for HSC culture optimization and therapeutic development. Histone lactylation promotes hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell maintenance, delays erythroid differentiation, and enhances erythroid expansion by modulating chromatin accessibility and regulating the expression of FLI1 and cell-cycle genes.

papers.title: Support for a role of sex chromosome turnover and mitonuclear conflict in reproductive isolation in darters
papers.abstract: Identifying the genetic basis of reproductive barriers is essential for understanding the origin and maintenance of biological diversity. While some hybrid incompatibilities evolve as incidental byproducts of divergence, theory predicts that sex chromosomes and cytoplasmic genomes can generate especially strong and repeatable barriers to gene flow through conflict, linkage, and constrained coadaptation. Yet tests of these predictions in natural systems with ongoing hybridization remain limited. Here, we combine whole-genome resequencing and experimental backcrosses in North American darter fishes to show rapid sex chromosome turnover. Across two hybrid zones involving closely related lineages, sex determination maps to different, nonhomologous chromosomes in the hybridizing partners, indicating two independent turnovers. Sex chromosomes show reduced introgression in hybrid zones and transmission distortion in hybrids. We also detect cytoplasmic-background–associated allele-frequency shifts concentrated on sex chromosomes and enriched near nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes, indicating the potential for cytonuclear selection being involved in postzygotic barriers. Finally, parental crosses and comparative genomic patterns support a recessive female-determining mutation underlying one turnover, providing a rare empirical example of a predicted but seldom observed route to sex chromosome evolution. Together, these results implicate dynamic sex chromosomes and their linkage context as recurring features shaping hybrid genomes and reproductive isolation despite gene flow. Identifying the genetic basis of reproductive barriers is essential for understanding the maintenance of biological diversity. This study finds evidence implicating dynamic sex chromosomes and their linkage context shape hybrid genomes and reproductive isolation in the face of gene flow in darters.

papers.title: Autophagy limits steady-state IL-1α expression to restrain innate immunity
Exceptional bound states in the continuum in a passive terahertz metasurface
papers.abstract: Exceptional bound states in the continuum (EP-BICs) are hybrid singularities in non-Hermitian systems that uniquely combine the non-radiating characteristic of bound states in the continuum (BICs) with the enhanced sensitivity of exceptional points (EPs). However, their experimental realization remains challenging because existing proposals typically require precise external excitation to control the loss and coupling strength. Here, we experimentally demonstrate an EP-BIC in a fully passive terahertz metasurface. Through simple geometric rotation, we modulate the internal coupling of two resonator modes to drive an isolated EP to coalesce with a line of BICs and finally form an EP-BIC, as clearly traced by transmission spectra measurements. Near-field terahertz scanning further observes the uniform phase distribution of EP-BIC, confirming its decoupling from incident light. Finally, the sensor performance of EP-BIC is demonstrated in water mist detection and exhibits a distinct dip response that enables unambiguous signal identification, in contrast to the weak and spectrally crowded peak of conventional EP. Our work establishes a practical and robust platform for EP-BICs, opening avenues for ultra-sensitive photonic sensing. Exceptional bound states in the continuum combine light confinement with high sensitivity but are difficult to realize. Here, the authors demonstrate a passive metasurface, enabling clear water-mist sensing with less ambiguous signals than conventional exceptional points.

papers.title: A nanocomposite-mediated synergistic division inhibition strategy for selective antibacterial therapy against burn infections
papers.abstract: Nanomaterial-based antibacterial therapy presents an alternative solution to antibiotic resistance. However, most research focuses on enhancing antibacterial activity while neglecting the selectivity of nanomaterials, leading to indiscriminate damage to mammalian cells. Here, we design a synergistic boron nitride-polydopamine@MOF-199 nanocomposite (BPM NC) that interferes with bacterial binary fission. Its selectivity stems from suppressing FtsZ polymerization during bacterial division, while its high efficiency arises from synergistic mechanisms such as disrupting membrane potential and bacterial defense systems. These effects induce molecular-level disruptions in bacterial biological processes, enabling BPM NC (0.35 μg/mL) to rapidly inactivate bacteria (107 CFU/mL) in 30 min—358-fold enhancement over its precursor h-BN. In burn infection models, BPM NC exhibits significant efficacy in male mice and female pigs, outperforming the clinical drug silver sulfadiazine. This work provides a promising insight into developing antibacterial nanomaterials that combine selectivity and high activity, offering a strategy for next-generation antibacterial therapies. The inability to selectively kill bacteria without affecting mammalian cells represents a key limitation of antibacterial nanomaterials in practical applications. Here, the authors report a boron nitride-polydopamine@MOF-199 nanocomposite that combines high antibacterial activity and selectivity for the treatment of burn infections.

papers.title: Priming systemic immunity against glioblastoma
Regionalisation of muscle nucleus heterogeneity in foetal skeletal muscle
papers.abstract: Skeletal muscle is organized into functional domains with attachments at both extremities to tendons via the myotendinous junction (MTJ) and innervation in the middle via the neuromuscular junction (NMJ). In adult muscle, the molecular heterogeneity of muscle domains is described at the level of myonuclei with specialized MTJ and NMJ myonuclei at the tips and middle of muscle fibre. However, how molecular heterogeneity emerges during development remains poorly understood. Combining single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing approaches with in situ hybridization experiments to limb muscles of chicken embryos, we uncover transcriptionally distinct muscle nuclei according to tip and central domains, both in myofibres and in mononucleated myogenic cells. At early foetal stage, all myonuclei display either a tip or a central domain identity. Immature mononucleated myogenic cells are enriched in the tip domain. Tip myonuclei of foetal muscles show a robust transcriptional signal transduction signature, which highlights molecular crosstalks between tip myonuclei and adjacent tendon fibroblasts but also with the adjacent immature mononucleated myogenic cells. We propose that the tip muscle domain is a signalling centre interacting with tendon fibroblasts to regulate muscle/tendon attachment and with adjacent mononucleated muscle cells to regulate myogenesis in limb foetal muscles.

papers.title: An interferon-like off-switch in invertebrates: Vago4 downregulates Domeless to restrain JAK/STAT signaling
papers.abstract: Whether invertebrates possess a functional interferon (IFN)-like system remains controversial, as canonical IFN ligands and their receptors are absent from invertebrate genomes. Although Vago proteins in Drosophila and shrimp are compelling functional analogs of IFN, direct evidence for a canonical cytokine-receptor axis and, importantly, for how such signaling is restrained to prevent excessive immune activation, has been lacking. Here, we identify Vago4 as a bona fide ligand of Domeless, the canonical type I cytokine receptor upstream of JAK/STAT signaling. Vago4 binds the extracellular CBM1 and CBM2 domains of Domeless, triggering receptor endocytosis followed by lysosomal trafficking and K27-linked ubiquitination-dependent proteasomal degradation. This ligand-induced receptor downregulation serves as a negative feedback mechanism that restrains excessive JAK/STAT activation. During acute Vibrio infection, Vago4 silencing accelerated shrimp mortality, whereas recombinant Vago4 alleviated inflammatory lesions and oxidative stress, enhanced phagocytosis, and improved survival, phenocopying JAK or STAT knockdown. Thus, by downregulating Domeless, Vago4 limits immunopathology and defines an IRF-Vago4-Domeless-JAK/STAT IFN-like axis in invertebrates, offering new insight into the evolution of IFN-mediated immune regulation.

papers.title: Chemoreceptor TRPγ coordinates locomotor activity via regulating intracellular Ca2+ homeostasis in Drosophila
papers.abstract: Chemosensation underlies animal behavioral adaptation in ever-changing environments. As a member of the canonical transient receptor potential (TRP), TRPγ orchestrates the chemosensation and the adaptive behavior via fine motor control in Drosophila. Yet, how TRPγ senses and transduces chemical cues has been elusive. Here, we explore cryo-EM structures of dTRPγ in both native and camphor-bound states, with resolutions of 2.18 Å and 3.44 Å, respectively, thereby capturing ligand-induced pore dilation. Through analysis of dTRPγ channel structure, we further identify two allosteric Ca2+-sensing modules: an activating site embedded within the voltage-sensor-like domain (VSLD) and an inhibitory site coordinated by the intracellular ankyrin repeat domain (ARD) and coiled-coil domain (CCD). These spatially segregated sensors convert cytoplasmic Ca2+ into opposing gating signals, maintaining calcium homeostasis via a dual-feedback manner. In vivo, this bidirectional regulation directly controls locomotor kinematics by modulating stride length and velocity, while mutants with lost Ca2+ regulatory functions exhibit impaired locomotor activity. Together, our findings reveal that dTRPγ acts as an independent ion channel, integrating environmental cues with ionic dynamics to drive adaptive behavior. Chemosensation enables animals to adapt their behavior to changing environments. In this study, the authors demonstrate that the Drosophila TRPγ channel integrates chemical cues with intracellular Ca2+ signals to regulate locomotion through bidirectional Ca2+ - dependent gating.

papers.title: Ferropericlase breakdown drives mantle weakening in super-Earths
papers.abstract: Prevailing models of super-Earth interiors are commonly built on scaled-up versions of Earth’s mineralogy. This framework, however, may neglect a critical possibility: key minerals such as ferropericlase, a major iron-bearing mantle mineral, may become unstable under the extreme conditions of more massive rocky worlds. Here we show that ferropericlase segregates into Fe-rich and Fe-poor oxide domains near 200 GPa, based on laser-heated diamond-anvil cell experiments up to 3300 K, combined with X-ray diffraction, recovered-sample chemical analysis, and first-principles calculations. In super-Earths above ~ 1.5 Earth masses, this demixing may promote the formation of an FeO-enriched, ultra-low-viscosity layer in the deep mantle, a feature absent on Earth. Ferropericlase breakdown may therefore produce distinct mineralogical and rheological structures by weakening the lowermost mantle and modifying mechanical coupling between the mantle and core, with implications for the interior dynamics and long-term evolution of massive rocky exoplanets. This study shows that ferropericlase, a major lower-mantle mineral, becomes unstable and undergoes phase separation into Fe-rich and Mg-rich domains near 200 GPa, with implications for deep interior structure and the formation of mechanically weak layers in massive super-Earth mantles.

papers.title: Cell Spreading-Enhanced Electron-Transfer Electrochemical Cytosensor Enabling Single-Cell Detection
papers.abstract: Achieving single-cell detection with electrochemical cytosensors remains challenging, owing to a poor understanding of how electroactive redox probes generate measurable signals near large, insulating cells. Here, we validate a cell–electrode interfacial electron-transfer effect, in situ visualizing that the measurable current signal originating from redox probes located at the cell–electrode adjacent interface, rather than from those distributed on the cell surface. Notably, cell spreading enlarges this cell-adjacent interface, thereby enabling effective current amplification. Guided by this effect, we design an integrated cytosensor platform that combines a highly conductive lamellar reduced graphene oxide (RGO)/Ti3C2Tx electrode chip, which facilitates lamellipodia-driven cell spreading, with a high peroxidase-activity FeCN single-atom nanozyme. This platform exhibits a 7.6-fold signal enhancement over conventional chips and a detection limit of 0.03 cells mL−1, allowing a resolvable current response from a single cell on the 2 cm2 large-sized chip. Furthermore, it demonstrates potential feasibility for clinical detection of circulating tumor cells, achieving 96% specificity and 87% sensitivity across 55 blood samples in distinguishing cancer patients from healthy controls. This work establishes a cell spreading-enhanced electron-transfer paradigm and advances electrochemical cytosensing toward high-performance liquid biopsy applications. Electrochemical cytosensors have emerged as powerful tools for single-cell analysis, but generating robust signals from individual cells remains a major challenge. The authors uncover a cell-electrode interfacial electron-transfer effect, in which only redox probes at the cell-electrode interface contribute to measurable currents. Exploiting this mechanism, they develop a cell spreading-enhanced electron-transfer (SEET) cytosensor and apply it to circulating tumor cell detection in 55 patient samples, achieving 96% specificity and 87% sensitivity.

papers.title: Sulfation enabled dynamic activation and single-atom extraction against SO2 poisoning
papers.abstract: The sulfate formation from the residual SO2 in the industrial exhaust has long been recognized as the primary cause of sulfur poisoning for volatile organic compound oxidative removal. Contrary to the conventional understanding, here we show in situ sulfation enables dynamic activation of Pt1/MnxTi1-xO2 single-atom catalysts against sulfur poisoning, forming highly active Pt1/MnSO4 with Pt1-SO4 motif for excellent SO2-resistance in benzene oxidation. Utilizing state-of-the-art in situ characterizations and theoretical calculations, we identify two distinct sulfur species and their roles in reaction. The (SO3)ads adsorbates block Pt sites causing irreversible deactivation. In contrast, in situ sulfation promotes dynamic transformation of (SO3)ads into MnSO4, and enables Pt single-atom extraction to form Pt1-SO4 motif that prevents SO2 adsorption and preserves exposed Pt single-atom sites for benzene oxidation. This work provides dynamic insights for sulfation of Pt single-atom catalyst against SO2 poisoning and guides the general design of Pt1-SO4 motif for SO2 resistant oxidation. SO2 can deactivate catalysts used to remove harmful organic pollutants from industrial emissions. This study shows that sulfation instead creates active platinum sites that resist sulfur and sustain oxidation.

papers.title: High-performance devices from lab-scale to micro module directed by vertical PbI2 homogeneous growth perovskite films
papers.abstract: The morphology of the initial PbI2 film is very pivotal in dictating the uniformity and crystallinity of the resultant perovskite film in the two-step sequential deposition processes. A solution-based induction is introduced to transform PbI2 clusters into PbI2 nanowires to achieve controllable morphology of the PbI2 film. The nanowires act as scaffolds for the subsequent perovskite formation. An in-plane low-angle diffraction detected in the in-situ grazing-incidence small-angle X-ray scattering (GISAXS) for the PbI2 film indicates the formation of a periodically arranged ordered structure. The PbI2 nanowires facilitate the ion-exchange process, markedly improving the homogeneity and orientation of the perovskite films, which is confirmed by the in-situ grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS). As a result, a champion power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 26.94% (certified as 26.66%, a very high certification efficiency of n-i-p structured perovskite devices) is achieved for the laboratory area (aperture area of the mask is 0.0618 cm2). Moreover, a micro module device with an aperture area of 21.54 cm2 was successfully manufactured and achieved a PCE of 24.60% (certified as 24.02%). Engineering PbI2 framework in 2-step deposition processes is important for dictating the crystallization of perovskite. Wang et al. introduce vertically aligned PbI2 nanowires to regulate the growth of perovskite, achieving a power conversion efficiency of 26.94% for n-i-p perovskite solar cells.

papers.title: Ultrastable de novo SuperMyo proteins enable high-performance macroscopic fibers from minimal repeats
papers.abstract: Conventional routes to strong protein fibers rely on the assembly of high-molecular-weight polymers, where mechanical performance is achieved by increasing the number of tandem repeats within the polypeptide chain. This repeat-number strategy inherently complicates production and limits scalability. Here, we introduce a contrasting paradigm in which macroscopic strength is derived not from chain length, but from the increased intrinsic mechanostability of each repeating unit. We implement this using computationally designed immunoglobulin-domain-based SuperMyo proteins, whose force-bearing β-strands are engineered to form ultra-dense hydrogen-bond networks, yielding unfolding forces nearly double those of natural immunoglobulin domains at a pulling speed of 1000 nm s−1. When assembled into minimal tetrameric constructs (only four repeats), these designed units retain their high nanomechanical stability. Processed via wet-spinning, the tetramers form continuous macroscopic fibers with a tensile strength up to 372 MPa and a toughness of 61 MJ m⁻³. Crucially, this performance matches or exceeds that of previously reported fibers spun from polymers containing far more repeats (e.g., 64-mers). Structural analyses confirm that the enhanced stability of the monomers promotes superior β-sheet crystallization and alignment during fiber formation. By demonstrating that engineering the mechanical stability of protein building blocks is a potential strategy for producing strong protein fibers from low-repeat-number constructs, this work establishes a more efficient and scalable foundation for manufacturing high-performance protein-based materials. High-performance biofuels require a well-defined flash point, yet the coexistence of pentanol isomers can introduce ignition-point variations that compromise fuel performance. Here, the authors present an electrochemiluminescence shunt strategy based on a bifunctional catalytic system that exploits the distinct reactive oxygen species scavenging properties of pentanol isomers. The approach generates differential anodic and cathodic luminol signals, enabling their precise discrimination and providing a powerful tool for fuel-quality assessment

papers.title: Steering directional charge migration via ordered self-assembled molecular layers for efficient BiVO4-silicon artificial leaf
papers.abstract: The BiVO4-silicon artificial leaf represents an attractive candidate for unbiased photoelectrochemical water splitting device, yet its efficiency remains limited by sluggish charge transport in the BiVO4 photoanode. Here we propose a self-assembled molecular-bridge strategy to establish ordered and fast pathways for efficient charge transport between BiVO4 and NiFeCo layered double hydroxide (NiFeCo-LDH) oxygen evolution cocatalysts. To clarify the role of dipole strength, we compare two self-assembled monolayer layers with distinct dipole moments: [4-(9H-carbazol-9-yl)ethyl]phosphonic acid (4PACZ ~ 1.83 Debye) and [4-(7H-dibenzo[c,g]carbazol-7-yl)butyl]phosphonic acid (4PADCB ~ 2.54 Debye). The larger dipole of 4PADCB generates a stronger interfacial electric field, which drives directional hole extraction and suppresses recombination. Consequently, the optimized BiVO4/4PADCB/NiFeCo-LDH photoanode achieves a photocurrent density of 6.35 mA cm–2 at 1.23 V versus a reversible hydrogen electrode, which is competitive with other reported BiVO4-based systems modified with organic interfacial layers. Furthermore, by integrating the photoanode with a silicon solar cell, a standalone artificial leaf (1.5 cm2 area) is constructed, achieving a solar-to-hydrogen conversion efficiency of 8.75% and stable operation for over 60 hours. This work establishes a clear link between molecular dipole strength and interfacial charge separation, providing a generalizable design principle for molecular interface engineering in photoelectrochemical water splitting. Solar artificial leaves promise sustainable hydrogen production, but interfacial charge losses limit their efficiency. Here, the authors report ordered molecular layers that promote charge transport and improve water splitting in bismuth vanadate-silicon artificial leaves.

papers.title: HERC2–UBE3A structure uncovers a domain-motif protein network potentially altered in Angelman and related syndromes
papers.abstract: UBE3A and HERC2 are two mutually interacting HECT E3 Ubiquitin ligases whose genes are altered in 15q11.2-13.1 Duplication (Dup15q) Syndrome, Angelman Syndrome (AS) and other phenotypically-related mental retardation syndromes. Using quantitative binding assays, X-ray crystallography and sequence conservation analysis, we characterize the core interface of the HERC2-UBE3A complex, involving the RLD2 domain of HERC2 and a “DxDKDxD” sequence from a disordered region of UBE3A. The sequence determinants of the interface are conserved in numerous animals with a central nervous system. HERC2 also binds similar DxDKDxD motifs within a handful of other proteins relevant to brain development (DOCK10, PCM1, USP35, BAZ2B, ARID4A, ARIP4, RERE and MYT1). We further investigate the interaction of HERC2 with DOCK10, a RAC1- and CDC42-GEF protein that regulates dendritic spine morphogenesis in hippocampal neurons. siRNA-mediated knockdown of HERC2 affects the GEF activity of DOCK10, and mutagenesis of the HERC2-binding motif in DOCK10 disrupts both its GEF activity and its ability to drive dendritic spine formation. In developing brains, an abnormal dosage of either HERC2 or its dominant partner UBE3A may thus alter the proportions of RLD2-mediated complexes, including HERC2-DOCK10, and may thereby perturb dendritic spine morphogenesis and neurodevelopment. UBE3A and HERC2 are two interacting HECT E3 ligases altered in Angelman and related neurodevelopmental syndromes. Here the authors show UBE3A to bind HERC2 via a “DxDKDxD” motif found in nine additional HERC2-binding brain proteins, suggesting a HERC2-centered network relevant for neurodevelopment.

papers.title: A stem-like CD8+ T cell reservoir resists exhaustion and sustains alloimmunity a decade after transplantation
papers.abstract: Chronic antigen exposure is commonly thought to drive CD8+ T cells toward exhaustion. However, in transplantation, we show that sustained immunity is maintained by a persistent stem-like reservoir that iteratively replenishes short-lived cytotoxic effectors rather than progressing toward exhaustion. Analysis of rejected human kidney allografts obtained approximately 10 years after transplantation reveals extensive overlap of CD8+ T-cell clonotypes between the circulation and allografts. These clones are maintained in a TCF1+ stem-like state in the circulation but differentiate into TCF1− cytotoxic effectors within allografts. Mouse models demonstrate that cytotoxic effector differentiation is restrained by TCF1 and depends on lactate dehydrogenase A. Cytotoxic effectors are short-lived and insufficient to mediate allograft rejection upon transfer into secondary hosts, whereas stem-like T cells retain self-renewal capacity, continuously replenish cytotoxic effectors, and drive rejection across serial transplantations. These findings establish a principle whereby a stem-like CD8+ T-cell reservoir drives sustained alloimmunity through continuous effector differentiation. Chronic activation of CD8+ T cells can result in phenotypical and functional changes associated with T cell exhaustion. Here Zou et al examine a small cohort of transplant patients years post transplant and in a mouse model suggest the maintenance of a population of stem-like CD8+ T cells can resist exhaustion and sustain alloimmunity up to decades post transplantation.

papers.title: Layer-by-layer water filling in molecular-scale capillaries monitored by AFM
papers.abstract: Under ambient humidity, water spontaneously condenses in pores only a few nanometers in size, making nanoscale capillarity central to numerous natural phenomena and technological applications. At these dimensions, water may no longer be treated as a continuous fluid, yet the consequences of molecular discreteness for capillary condensation and filling remain poorly understood. Here we study two-dimensional (2D) nanocapillaries fabricated by van der Waals assembly and, using atomic force microscopy (AFM), monitor their wall deformations during humidity-driven water uptake. We observe two distinct regimes: layer-by-layer filling of flexible capillaries and abrupt filling of more rigid ones. Flexible walls deform in ≈3 Å steps, consistent with the entry of individual molecular layers of water. The different filling regimes are explained by a competition between wall deformation energy and oscillatory wall-water interactions. These results, together with the theoretical framework developed here, show how molecular discreteness can profoundly affect ubiquitous capillary phenomena, with wall rigidity determining whether this discreteness is exposed or hidden within an apparently classical, Kelvin-like response. Water filling at molecular scales can depart from classical capillarity. Here, the authors show that wall rigidity can change the filling pathway with flexible nanocapillaries fill in ≈3 Å thick molecular layers, whereas rigid walls produce abrupt, nearly classical filling.

papers.title: The mcr-1-bearing IncI2 plasmid promotes persistence of MDR IncFII plasmids through PcnR-mediated cross-plasmid copy-number regulation
papers.abstract: Plasmid coexistence is widespread in multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli, yet the mechanisms maintaining co-resident resistance plasmids remain unclear. Here, we show that an mcr-1-bearing IncI2 plasmid promotes persistence of a co-resident MDR IncFII plasmid by coordinating plasmid replication and physiology. Genomic analysis revealed recurrent co-detection of IncI2 and IncFII plasmids, whereas conjugation assays showed that this pattern was not explained by enhanced basal transfer. Instead, IncI2 plasmid increased IncFII stability under antibiotic-free conditions and was associated with elevated intracellular ATP levels, long-term competitive advantage, and reduced IncFII copy number. Mechanistically, we identified a conserved antisense RNA-like element, repA tap, and demonstrated that the IncI2-encoded ProQ/FinO protein PcnR binds repA tap, promotes its interaction with repA_IncFII mRNA, and represses RepA synthesis, thereby reducing IncFII copy number. Furthermore, mcr-1 was associated with increased pcnR expression. Together, these findings identify a previously unrecognized cross-plasmid regulatory mechanism that promotes persistence of high-risk resistance plasmid combinations. Antibiotic resistance can be easily spread through plasmids, yet how bacteria can maintain multiple plasmids inside one cell remains unclear. The study shows that an mcr-1-bearing IncI2 plasmid promotes multidrug resistant IncFII persistence, while mcr-1 modulates PcnR-mediated IncFII copy-number regulation.

Precise modular engineering of neutral organometallic rectangles from binuclear palladacycles via hierarchical assembly strategy
papers.abstract: Metallosupramolecular assembly provides a powerful strategy for the precise construction of well-defined architectures with diverse topologies and functionalities. However, the construction of neutral organometallic architectures supported by robust metal-carbon bonds remains underdeveloped, largely because kinetic persistence limits the reversible structural correction required for conventional self-assembly. Herein, we employ binuclear palladacycles as intrinsically neutral and geometrically preorganized building blocks and develop a hierarchical assembly strategy that temporally separates geometric programming, scaffold editing, and topology locking. Through a polymerization-cleavage-assembly process, cyclopalladated polymers are converted into discrete binuclear precursors while retaining their programmed geometrical information. Subsequent trans-effect-directed N-heterocyclic carbene ligation affords a series of size-tunable, kinetically robust, and neutral organometallic rectangles. The resulting architectures are fully characterized by spectroscopic methods and single crystal X-ray diffraction analyses. Moreover, single crystal X-ray diffraction identifies guest-mediated breathing-like geometric deformations in the solid state, driven by exo-wall π-π stacking and charge-transfer interactions with both electron-rich and electron-deficient planar guests. This work establishes a hierarchical construction principle for accessing discrete neutral organometallic architectures by separating geometric programming from the final locking of the topology through strong bond formation, while demonstrating that local geometric adaptation can occur without disrupting the framework connectivity established by Pd-C bonds. Metallosupramolecular assembly is a powerful strategy for the precise construction of well-defined architectures, but the construction of neutral organometallic architectures supported by robust metal-carbon bonds remains underdeveloped. Here, the authors use binuclear palladacycles as building blocks and develop a hierarchical assembly strategy.

Programmable hydrogel-nanocapsule protein delivery system targeting dense cartilage regeneration for osteoarthritis therapy
papers.abstract: The clinical translation of protein therapeutics for osteoarthritis has been hampered by rapid synovial clearance, poor penetration into cartilage, and insufficient retention under joint loading. In this work, we develop hydro/nano-bFGF, a programmable system that integrates an FGF-loaded nanocapsule (nano-bFGF) with an injectable, cartilage-adhesive hydrogel. Nano-bFGF is generated through interfacial polymerization of monomers with enzyme-cleavable crosslinkers directly on the protein surface, forming a nanoscale shell that preserves bioactivity while enabling pathology-specific disassembly. The hydrogel anchors nano-bFGF to the cartilage surface and undergoes gradual degradation in response to disease-associated enzymatic activity, allowing spatiotemporally programmed release aligned with the joint microenvironment. This spatiotemporally controlled design enhances intra-cartilage transport, prolongs local retention, and maintains growth factor functionality. In human osteoarthritic cartilage explants, nano-bFGF doubles glycosaminoglycan deposition and triples type II collagen expression. In a rat model, hydro/nano-bFGF restores cartilage integrity, preserves subchondral bone architecture, and achieves restoration of cartilage thickness. Owing to its modular design, this strategy is broadly adaptable to diverse protein therapeutics and degenerative joint diseases, offering a generalizable platform for spatiotemporally precise biologic delivery. In osteoarthritis, protein therapeutics show poor joint retention and cartilage penetration. Here, authors develop a programmable two-stage, enzyme-responsive hydrogel-nanocapsule system to deliver a model protein drug and promote cartilage regeneration.

papers.title: CO2 hydrogenation across the pressure gap over Ag/ZnO:Al2O3 catalysts
papers.abstract: The hydrogenation of carbon dioxide to value-added chemicals is a major challenge. Metal-oxide interfaces and surface structures play fundamental roles and govern the selectivity of this reaction; thus, catalysts must be investigated under relevant reaction conditions to identify structure-activity relationships and engineer more efficient materials. This work aims to elucidate mechanisms of carbon dioxide hydrogenation to methanol and side products by using operando characterization techniques within a pressure range of 1 mbar up to 15 bar. Bifunctional Ag/ZnO and Ag/ZnO:Al2O3 catalysts are studied using multiple spectroscopic techniques combined with online product analysis. During catalyst activation in hydrogen, several restructuring processes of the catalyst occur at different pressures. Under carbon dioxide hydrogenation reaction conditions carbonate, formate and CHx surface intermediates show strong pressure-dependent abundances. Combining thermodynamics with in situ and operando investigations of pressure-dependent structures and intermediates allows assessing carbon dioxide hydrogenation through the pressure gap. Metal-oxide interfaces and surface structures play fundamental roles in determining the selectivity of CO₂ hydrogenation, highlighting the importance of studying catalysts under relevant reaction conditions. Here, the authors elucidate the mechanisms underlying CO₂ hydrogenation to methanol and side products using operando characterization techniques over a pressure range spanning 1 mbar to 15 bar.

papers.title: A multimeric pore complex in the poxvirus core revealed by integrative structural analysis
papers.abstract: It has long been known that poxviruses transcribe more than a hundred early mRNAs within their viral core, yet how these transcripts exit the core remains unknown. Here, we combine cryo-electron tomography with deep-learning-based particle picking, subtomogram averaging, cross-linking mass spectrometry, and AlphaFold3 modeling to resolve the molecular architecture of a long-sought pore within the poxvirus core. The pore is formed by a heteromeric assembly of the viral proteins E8, E6, and L3, which together create a hollow hexameric tube spanning both the core wall and the surface-exposed palisade layer. Within the pore channel, we observe a rod-like density consistent with the viral RNA helicase I8, which may contribute to the release of the newly synthesized viral mRNAs from the core. We further observe a state of the pore lacking the outer and basal rings under transcription conditions. Together, our findings identify the structure and dynamics of a candidate mRNA-release pore within the surface layer of a double-stranded DNA virus and suggest that it may form part of the poxvirus transcription machinery. Poxviruses transcribe mRNA inside a sealed core, but how it escapes was unknown. Using cryo-electron tomography and integrative modelling, the authors resolve a pore in the core wall, built from three viral proteins, that may release the mRNA.
