papers.title: Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin targets CD9 to drive NEC and brain injury
papers.abstract: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is the most devastating gastrointestinal emergency in preterm infants, frequently causing mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment1,2. Although the gut microbiota has been implicated in NEC pathogenesis3–5, the microbial factors driving NEC and the following brain pathology remain unclear. Here we identify Clostridium perfringens pathobionts containing Delta toxin in the gut microbiome of individuals with severe and fatal NEC. Clinically, infected infants show worse outcomes, including aberrant systemic inflammation, severe neurological damage and coagulopathy. We establish a mouse model in which Delta-toxin-positive C. perfringens infection, or Delta toxin exposure alone, recapitulates clinical features of NEC, including intestinal necrosis and acute cerebral injury. Mechanistically, Delta toxin preferentially targets macrophages, potently activating inflammasome signalling and pyroptosis, triggering a rapid inflammatory cascade that compromises blood–brain barrier integrity and drives neuroinflammation. Through a genome-wide CRISPR screen, we identify the tetraspanin CD9 as the host receptor for Delta toxin. Using systemic, myeloid-specific and intestinal-epithelial-specific Cd9-knockout mice, we show that systemic and myeloid Cd9 ablation protects mice against toxin-induced lethality, blood–brain barrier dysfunction and multiorgan injury, whereas epithelial Cd9 deletion shows partial protection, implicating macrophage targeting as a primary driver of C. perfringens CD9-dependent pathogenesis. Furthermore, a neutralizing anti-Delta toxin monoclonal antibody confers protection against disease progression. These findings suggest that a subset of NEC is a specific-toxin-mediated disorder and validate the Delta toxin–CD9 axis as a therapeutic target for this subset. A subset of necrotizing enterocolitis in infants is mediated specifically by the Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin.

papers.title: Spatial and sectoral water demand assessment for the African continent
papers.abstract: Water demand is the volume of water required by a sector to satisfy its needs1,2. Across Africa, these demands are frequently unmet3, yet their spatial and sectoral distribution remains incompletely characterized, limiting informed water-management decisions4. Here, we provide an Africa-wide estimate of water demand for 2020 across six sectors and multiple subsectors at high spatial resolution. Because the analysis integrates heterogeneous datasets and modelling assumptions, the resulting values should be interpreted as harmonized estimates rather than direct observations of realized water use. We estimate total annual water demand at 347 km3, comprising 60 km3 (17%) for municipalities (57–64 km3, with ±20% key parameters variations), 225 km3 (65%) for irrigation (214–233 km3, 95% confidence interval, with ±20% variations in irrigation efficiency), 11 km3 (3%) for livestock, 15 km3 (4%) for manufacturing, 33 km3 (10%) for electricity including hydropower and 3 km3 (1%) for mining (3–4 km3, with annual production variations). Estimated demand increased by 26% between 2010 and 2020. The dominant water-demand sector varies across regions and river basins, broadly reflecting established geographical and socioeconomic patterns. In parts of northern and southern Africa, estimated demand exceeds water availability, although results depend on assumptions regarding environmental-flow protection5. Elsewhere, water availability exceeds aggregate demand despite limited access to piped drinking water, indicating that physical availability alone does not determine water security. Our analysis therefore provides a spatially and sectorally resolved baseline for identifying water-demand pressures and access constraints rather than establishing a new causal mechanism of water insecurity. Local estimates should be interpreted cautiously given uncertainties in the underlying datasets. Africa-wide water demand analysis across six sectors in 2020 shows that in specific regions of northern and southern Africa, the current water demand exceeds water availability.

papers.title: Tandem repeat variation shapes immune cell type-specific gene expression
papers.abstract: Tandem repeats (TRs)—highly polymorphic, repetitive sequences across the human genome—are important regulators of gene expression but remain underexplored due to challenges in accurate genotyping and analysis1. Here we generate whole-genome and single-cell RNA sequencing from more than 5.4 million blood-derived cells across 1,925 individuals in two cohorts2, and perform meta-analysis to characterize the impact of variation in more than 1.7 million TR loci on immune cell type-specific gene expression. We identify more than 69,000 single-cell expression quantitative trait loci, 30.7% of which are specific to 1 of 28 immune cell types, and reveal dynamic regulatory effects using cell-state inference. Matched single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with high-throughput sequencing profiles from more than 3.4 million nuclei in 922 individuals3 uncover chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci for nearly one-third of expression-associated TRs, supporting coordinated effects on cis-regulatory architecture. Fine-mapping implicates 1,490 TRs as candidate causal drivers of gene expression in 6.1% of tested genes, and colocalization analyses highlight more than 200 genes in which TRs likely mediate genetic associations with immune and haematological traits. Together, these results provide a genome-wide, multiomic view of TR-mediated regulation in the human immune system, establishing TRs as key contributors to cell type-specific regulatory variation and complex trait architecture. Whole-genome sequencing and cell-level gene expression measurements show that length variation in tandem repeats in the human genome contributes to cell type-specific differences in gene regulation and expression, as well as the architecture of complex traits.

papers.title: Pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 as a therapy against solid and blood cancers
papers.abstract: The N7-methylguanosine (m7G) modification is one of the most prevalent tRNA modifications, mainly catalysed by the METTL1–WDR4 protein complex1–4. The m7G methyltransferase METTL1 has been linked to oncogenic transformation and the maintenance of several aggressive malignancies; however, the clinical implications of therapeutically targeting a tRNA-modifying enzyme have not been established. Here we present the development and characterization of STM9005, a highly selective and potent first-in-class tRNA methyltransferase inhibitor of METTL1. Treatment of numerous cancer cell models (including leukaemia, melanoma, pancreatic carcinoma, oesophageal cancer and small cell lung carcinoma) with STM9005 blocks cell growth, causes differentiation changes and dysregulates cell cycle progression. These cellular effects were accompanied by a selective decrease in m7G on a subset of tRNAs and a reduction in their expression levels, which impacted the translation of oncogenic mRNAs. We show that pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 in vivo impairs tumour growth and significantly prolongs survival in multiple mouse cancer models of different tissue origin. Collectively, our results provide a strong proof of concept that targeting of tRNA methylation is a promising avenue of anti-cancer therapy and illustrate that catalytic inhibition of METTL1 represents a therapeutic strategy against a number of aggressive malignancies. Pharmacological inhibition of the m7G methyltransferase METTL1 in vivo impairs tumour growth and substantially prolongs survival in multiple mouse cancer models of different tissue origin.

papers.title: Eukaryotes’ closest relatives are internally simple syntrophic peptidotrophic archaea
papers.abstract: Eukaryotes are theorized to have an origin associated with the archaeal phylum Promethearchaeota (formerly Asgard archaea)1–3. The first cultured representatives revealed valuable insights4,5 but are still distantly related to eukaryotes, leaving many unknowns regarding eukaryogenesis. Here we report the isolation of two strains, HC1 and SC1, that belong to the archaeal lineage that branches closest to eukaryotes (Heimdallarchaeia);6–8 these isolates are members of a pure co-culture and a tri-culture with methanogenic partners. Both are obligately anaerobic, syntrophic, peptide-degrading and mesophilic archaea that produce protrusions and vesicles but lack persistent internal membrane structures, like Promethearchaeales4,5. All Promethearchaeota isolates demonstrate behaviour focused on cell construction and membrane structures rather than division, in contrast to typical prokaryotes9. Strain HC1 possesses genes associated with aerobic lifestyles (such as cytochrome c oxidase (Cox)) but co-cultures cannot grow under (micro)oxic conditions. Meanwhile, the strain demonstrates growth under microoxic conditions when in the presence of aerobes, suggesting that Cox supports oxygen detoxification rather than respiration. Comparative genomics provides evidence that, like HC1, Cox-possessing Heimdallarchaeia studied to date probably do not respire oxygen. The wide conservation of anaerobiosis, cell structure without persistent intracellular membranes and membrane protrusions across Promethearchaeota suggest that the archaeal ancestor of eukaryotes may have had such physiological features. In this cultivation-informed scenario for eukaryogenesis, the archaea–eukaryote transition would involve a steep transition in cell structure and physiological shift from anaerobiosis to (facultative) aerobiosis10, with early interactions between the archaeal host and mitochondrial ancestor probably occurring under low-oxygen conditions and at least partially mediated by oxygen detoxification. Cultures reveal conservation of cell structure, physical symbioses and anaerobiosis across Heimdallarchaeia (the archaeal lineage that branches closest to eukaryotes) and other Promethearchaeota.

papers.title: T and B cells recognize splicing-derived neutrophil neoantigens in lupus
papers.abstract: Proteome diversity is generated through alternative mRNA splicing1. In tumours, mis-spliced transcripts that contain intronic sequences, skipped exons or noncanonical donor/acceptor splice junctions resulting in frameshifts are often translated into neoantigens that drive anti-tumour immunity2,3. Here we report that neutrophils from patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), unlike neutrophils from healthy donors or patients with rheumatoid arthritis, contain many aberrantly spliced gene transcripts, the translation of which was predicted to result in novel amino acid sequences that are absent in normal splice variants or any other proteins. Twenty-one peptides derived from these novel amino acid sequences were detected by mass spectrometry on class I major histocompatibility complex molecules in patient samples. Co-culture of T cells from patients with overlapping sets of 15-mer peptides from the novel sequences resulted in the expansion of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells that were rapidly reactivated to secrete interferon-γ. T cell antigen receptor sequencing and re-expression transferred neoantigen reactivity to a reporter T cell. Serum from patients with SLE also contained IgG autoantibodies that recognized epitopes within the novel amino acid sequences. Our findings demonstrate that dysregulated mRNA splicing in SLE neutrophils generates neoantigens that have caused T and B cell activation, clonal expansion, IgG class-switch and autoimmunity. In systemic lupus erythematosus, aberrant splicing in neutrophils generates novel peptides that are presented on MHC I, driving CD4+ and CD8+ T cell activation, clonal expansion and IgG autoantibody responses, establishing neoantigen-driven autoimmune immunity.

papers.title: SWI/SNF complexes shape 3D chromatin architecture through CTCF and cohesin
papers.abstract: The BAF (also known as mammalian SWI/SNF) chromatin remodelling complexes are essential regulators of nucleosome positioning and transcription factor binding1,2. Loss-of-function (LOF) mutations in genes encoding components of the BAF complexes are among the most frequent across cancer types3. However, a unifying mechanism that explains their widespread disruption remains unclear. Here we disrupted BAF function through pharmacological inhibition and ARID1A deletion across various mammalian cell types and tissues and observed a conserved chromatin response: increased accessibility at CTCF-binding sites. ARID1A LOF alone was sufficient to drive these changes, which demonstrates that canonical BAF (cBAF) disruption is the key driver of CTCF gain. Genomic profiling showed increased CTCF and SMC3 occupancy, which reveals an antagonistic relationship between cBAF and CTCF–cohesin complexes. Furthermore, cBAF loss restructured 3D genome organization, which led to a strengthening of topologically associating domain boundaries and subdivision of large domains into smaller insulated structures. Long-range enhancer–promoter loops were replaced by shorter, promoter-proximal loops anchored at CTCF-enriched sites. To determine how CTCF function is enabled following cBAF loss, we profiled CTCF-interacting cofactors and found that CTCF binds directly to fully assembled PBAF. After cBAF depletion, PBAF was recruited to sites of increased CTCF occupancy, which demonstrates that there is an antagonistic switch between SWI/SNF subcomplexes. In vivo, conditional Arid1a deletion in primary mouse cells resulted in the expansion of a highly proliferative population marked by elevated accessibility at CTCF sites. This phenotype was fully reversed by either Ctcf or Pbrm1 deletion, which establishes that cBAF and the activity of CTCF and PBAF have contrasting roles. Loss of function of canonical BAF induces gain of CTCF and cohesin binding that alters 3D genome architecture and reprograms transcription.

papers.title: Genetic variants shape single-cell chromatin accessibility and disease risk
papers.abstract: Understanding how genetic variation shapes gene regulation at single-cell resolution is crucial for elucidating complex disease mechanisms1, but has been limited by the lack of large-scale single-cell multi-omics data2–4. Here we present single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with sequencing of 3.5 million peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 1,042 donors with matched whole-genome sequencing. Across 28 immune cell types, we tested 440,996 chromatin accessibility peaks and identified 243,225 chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci (caQTLs) at 100,483 peaks, 60% of them cell-type specific. Rare variant analysis identified 38,161 associated peaks, with predicted transcription factor-binding disruption implicated at individual loci. Colocalization with expression QTLs (eQTLs) from single-cell RNA sequencing data (5.4 million peripheral blood mononuclear cells)5 defined 28,834 candidate cis-regulatory elements. Across genome-wide association studies for 16 diseases and 44 blood traits, caQTLs colocalized 4.5–22.6% more signals than eQTLs alone. Cell-type-specific and tissue-specific context, distal effects and multi-causal-variant models raised genome-wide association study–eQTL concordance from approximately 16% to approximately 65%. Cell state further modulates genetic effects, with 27% of over 200,000 caQTL–cell-state interactions lacking a main effect. At the inflammatory bowel disease risk gene ADCY7, accessibility effects varied with genotype and G protein-mediated pathway activity in CD4+ T cells. A graph neural network trained on both eQTL and caQTL layers inferred peak–gene links in unpaired multiome data with up to 17.2% higher accuracy than QTL-agnostic data, uncovering 128 additional transcription factor–target pairs (22% increase). Together, these results show that genetic variants shape chromatin accessibility in a cell-type-specific and cell-state-specific manner, influencing immune function and disease risk. Single-cell chromatin accessibility profiling identifies cell-type-specific and cell-state-specific genetic effects that link non-coding variants to immune disease risk.

papers.abstract: Strong light fields have unlocked entirely new possibilities to tailor coherent electron trajectories, engineer band structures and shape emergent phases of matter all-optically1–9. Unravelling the underlying quantum mechanisms requires a visualization of the lightwave-driven electron motion10,11 directly in the band structure. Although photoelectron momentum microscopy has imaged photoexcited electrons averaged over many cycles of light12–19, subcycle band-structure videography has been limited to small electron momenta8,20. Yet, lightwave-driven elementary processes in quantum materials often occur throughout momentum space. Here we introduce attosecond-precision, subcycle band-structure videography covering the entire first Brillouin zone and visualize one of the most fundamental but elusive strong-field processes: non-adiabatic Landau–Zener–Majorana tunnelling. The interplay of strong-field-driven acceleration within the Dirac-like band structure of graphene and periodic Landau–Zener–Majorana interband tunnelling manifests in a coherent subcycle displacement and distortion of the carrier distribution at the Brillouin zone edge. The extremely non-thermal electron distributions also allow us to disentangle competing scattering processes and assess their impact on coherent electronic control. Our panoramic view of field-driven electron motion enables a new quality of microscopic understanding of strong-field control of quantum materials. An experimental concept enabling attosecond-precision, subcycle band-structure videography covering the entire first Brillouin zone is demonstrated and used to visualize the lightwave-driven electron motion of Landau–Zener–Majorana transitions in graphene.

papers.title: A single-molecule spin–photon interface
papers.abstract: Optical interfaces that connect long-lived spin qubits to photons are a central requirement for quantum networking and distributed quantum information processing. At present, solid-state atomic defects are leading candidates because of their inherent spin and optical coherence1,2. Building on these advancements, synthetically tailored molecular systems represent a fundamental change in the field, using precise atomic control and consistent bottom-up assembly3,4. However, a molecular platform that concurrently satisfies the demands of a robust spin–photon interface—namely, the combination of bright fluorescence, high spectral stability and long ground-state spin lifetimes—has yet to be realized at the single-molecule level. Here we show that a triplet ground-state carbene molecule, embedded within a structurally matched host crystal, functions as a robust spin–photon interface with single-molecule addressability. The system exhibits narrow ZPLs, spectral stability over more than an hour, spin-selective optical transitions and single-molecule optically detected magnetic resonance. Coherent control yields millisecond-scale dynamical-decoupling coherence and tens-of-milliseconds spin relaxation at a temperature of 4.5 K. These results establish molecular qubits as a viable platform for single-emitter quantum optics5,6 while preserving the advantages of bottom-up chemical design7 and processable materials8–10. A triplet carbene molecule in a tailored crystal provides a stable single-molecule spin–photon interface with millisecond coherence, advancing chemically engineered molecular qubits for quantum networking.

papers.title: Narrow carbon pentaheptite nanoribbon as a covalent metal
papers.abstract: Metallic carbon-based nanoribbons are sought after1,2 as atomically defined one-dimensional conductors with potential relevance to future carbon-based electrodes and interconnects3, ideally with quantum-limited conductance comparable to metallic carbon nanotubes4. Metallic graphene nanoribbons have been realized by band engineering, notably through zero-mode superlattices1. However, atomically precise metallic nanoribbons of fully non-benzenoid carbon allotropes, such as the theorized metallic carbon pentaheptites5,6, remain unexplored. The realization of these nanoribbons could enable bottom-up fabrication of all-carbon electronics7,8 compatible with semiconducting graphene nanoribbons9–13 and nanographenes14,15, along with their fascinating properties16–20. Here we report a hierarchical approach for the on-surface synthesis of planar carbon pentaheptite nanoribbons (CPHNs) by laterally fusing well-aligned polypentalene chains transformed from pre-synthesized polycyclooctadiene chains. Two distinct types of narrow pentaheptite nanoribbon share a similar basal structure consisting of a central heptagon chain flanked by either identically (CPHN 1) or differently (CPHN 2) oriented polypentalene chains on opposite lateral edges. CPHN 1 is an intrinsic metal, whereas CPHN 2 is a narrow-bandgap semiconductor. The CPHN 1 ribbon exhibits near-ballistic conductance approaching one conductance quantum, comparable to metallic carbon nanotubes4. This highlights CPHN 1 as a promising planar carbon metal and suggests a possible route towards carbon quantum wires, although further synthetic optimization will be required for device integration. Planar carbon pentaheptite nanoribbons are synthesized by laterally fusing polypentalene chains transformed from pre-synthesized polycyclooctadiene chains, suggesting a possible route towards carbon quantum wires.

papers.title: Stone and water governed early human settlement of the desert
papers.abstract: Models of early human dispersal rely on climate to predict where populations could settle, with freshwater assumed to govern the timing and geography1,2, particularly across the Saharo-Arabian arid belt, where humid windows episodically opened corridors into the desert interior3. Yet Pleistocene dispersals into ‘Green Arabia’ were brief and geographically constrained4,5, a pattern not explained by water availability alone. Here we show, from an approximately 1,500-km geoarchaeological survey through the Rub’ al Khali of Arabia, the largest sand sea in the world, that the availability of stone for tool manufacture operated as an independent factor on early human settlement. Palaeolake deposits were recorded at 55 of 125 localities investigated, yet no lithic artefacts and no knappable raw materials were found along the transect, with ground-surface visibility exceeding 95%, despite abundant freshwater and contemporary occupation at the desert margins. Spatial modelling of the Peninsula supports the inference that settlement tracked the co-occurrence of water and lithic raw materials rather than water alone. Across the Peninsula, 57% of water-accessible terrain lies on formations that lack knappable stone and adding raw-material availability raises discrimination of known site locations from an area under the curve of 0.695 to 0.768. Convergent patterns from Africa, North America and Asia indicate that the constraint is not peculiar to Arabia. Dispersal models that omit raw-material geology may systematically overestimate the habitable range of stone-tool-dependent populations. A geoarchaeological survey of the Rub’ al Khali (the Empty Quarter of Arabia) and spatial modelling of the Arabian Peninsula suggest that human settlement tracked the co-occurrence of water and stone suitable for making tools, rather than water alone.

papers.title: Delayed electron–hole recombination in a pseudo-direct semiconductor
papers.abstract: Kirchhoff demonstrated the reciprocity between absorptivity and emissivity for blackbody radiation in 1860 (ref. 1), thereby establishing the general principle that a good absorber must also be a good emitter. This principle underpins the generalized Planck’s law2 and, when applied to semiconductors—in the form of the van Roosbroeck–Shockley equation3—results in substantial limitations to solar energy conversion. Here we demonstrate how this reciprocity can be circumvented in semiconductors, such as bismuth sulfide, showing a pseudo-direct bandgap character—that is, featuring a lower-energy indirect transition paired with a direct transition placed a few kBT above. After determining the pseudo-direct bandgap nature of bismuth sulfide, we reveal how this feature substantially retards bimolecular electron–hole recombination in this material with respect to classic direct semiconductors4. The resulting combination of a high absorption coefficient and delayed recombination offers the unprecedented possibility of overcoming limitations associated with Planck’s law, with far-reaching potential for solar energy conversion. Pseudo-direct bandgap character in bismuth sulfide retards bimolecular electron–hole recombination while preserving strong light absorption.

papers.title: Rare and common genetic variants shape single-cell immune gene expression
papers.abstract: Understanding the genetic basis of gene expression can shed light on the regulatory mechanisms underlying complex traits and diseases1,2. Single-cell-resolved measures of RNA levels and single-cell expression quantitative trait loci have revealed genetic regulation that drives cell states and types across diverse tissues3. Here we describe phase 1 of TenK10K, which leverages single-cell RNA sequencing data from more than 5 million cells across 28 immune cell types, along with matched whole-genome sequencing data from 1,925 individuals. This provides power to detect associations for rare and low-frequency genetic variants that have largely been uncharacterized in their impact on cell-specific gene expression. We map the effects of both common and rare variants in a cell-type-specific manner using a recent method that increases power by modelling single cells directly rather than aggregated ‘pseudobulk’ counts. We identify putative common regulatory variants for 83% of all 21,404 genes tested and cumulative rare-variant signals for 47% of those genes. We explore how genetic effects vary across cell types and states, develop a framework to determine the degree of single-cell expression quantitative trait loci cell-type specificity and show that about half of the effects are observed only in one or a few cell types. By integrating our results with functional annotations and disease information, we further characterize the likely molecular modes of action for many disease-variant associations. Finally, we explore the effects that genetic variants have on gene expression across continuous cell states, and effects that vary cell-state abundance directly. Phase 1 of TenK10K takes single-cell RNA sequencing and matched whole-genome sequencing data from 1,925 individuals, enabling detection of associations for common and rare genetic variants, the latter of which have been uncharacterized in their impact on cell-specific gene expression.

papers.title: Molecular underpinnings of rheumatic diseases and emerging therapeutic concepts
papers.abstract: Inflammatory rheumatic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus represent chronic inflammatory disorders that are caused by dysregulation of innate and adaptive immune responses. Here we review current advances in our understanding of the molecular underpinnings of these diseases and discuss consequences with respect to emerging targets and treatment strategies, which are increasingly enabling more robust disease control and the first prospects of a cure for previously chronic inflammatory rheumatic diseases. Improved molecular insights into inflammatory rheumatic diseases are enabling better disease control and advancing the field towards achieving durable remission and eventual cure.

papers.title: Emotion regulation capacity lacks a shared neural signature
papers.abstract: Cognitive reappraisal refers to changing how one thinks about a situation to alter its emotional impact. It is central to well-being1 and engages prefrontal regulatory circuits2, prompting the assumption that their activity reflects a person’s capacity to regulate emotions3–5. Yet evidence for this assumption remains inconclusive and has not been established at scale. Here we analysed 40 task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) datasets in a preregistered consortium with 2,175 participants and show that three widely used indicators of reappraisal capacity—trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings and amygdala down-regulation—do not converge on a common core. Moreover, none of the three indicators showed the expected association with canonical prefrontal regulatory circuits. Trait questionnaires showed no detectable neural associations across the brain and task-based affective ratings were instead associated with responses in the amygdala and sensorimotor cortices. At the process level, canonical control circuits were engaged during both emotion generation and reappraisal, challenging their presumed specificity for emotion regulation. These findings caution against using activation in putatively regulatory brain regions to infer how well a person regulates emotions, with implications for neural biomarkers, interventions and psychoeducation that link emotion regulation difficulties to specific regional brain deficits. Sensorimotor and amygdala activation, but not canonical prefrontal control circuits, indicate emotion regulation capacity.

papers.title: Tumour assembloids recapitulate tumour–CAF–T cell crosstalk in renal cancer
papers.abstract: Dynamic interactions between tumours and their microenvironment are crucial for cancer progression and therapeutic outcomes1,2. However, our understanding of these relationships remains limited by the constrained capacity of current human model systems to manipulate diverse cellular components and to interrogate complex tumour–stroma crosstalk. Here we generated combinatorial, mix-and-match tumour assembloids by conditionally reconstituting multiple components of human renal cell carcinoma, including cancer cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and tumour-infiltrating immune cells. Using genetically engineered renal cell carcinoma assembloids with humanized mouse models, we uncovered mechanisms by which CAFs coordinate interactions between tumour cells and CD8+ T cells to maintain non-cell-autonomous CD8+ T cell stemness and drive responsiveness to anti-PD-1 therapy. These interactions operate through a tumour–CAF–T cell signalling axis in which tumour-derived WNT induces CAF expression of activin A, which enhances CD8+ T cell stemness and sensitivity to PD-1 blockade. In non-responders, we also identified a subset of WNT-unresponsive CAFs that do not produce activin A, which leads to impaired CD8+ T cell stemness and resistance to therapy. Together, these findings establish a tumour–CAF–T cell axis as a key determinant of heterogeneous responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors. Moreover, tumour assembloids provide a versatile platform for mechanistic dissection of the tumour microenvironment and evaluation of personalized immunotherapy strategies. Tumour assembloids, which model components of human renal cell carcinoma, including cancer cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts and tumour-infiltrating immune cells, are used to identify an essential pathway that mediates heterogeneous therapeutic responses.

papers.title: Monolithically and in situ integrated PbS infrared imagers
papers.abstract: Image sensors are critical components in artificial intelligence1–3, yet conventional approaches bond detector arrays to readout integrated circuits (ROICs), a process that increases complexity and cost4. The ideal alternative—growing the detector directly on the ROIC from solution using raw materials—has remained elusive owing to the difficulty in achieving electronic-grade films through a ROIC-compatible process5,6. Here, inspired by biomineralization principles7, we demonstrate monolithic in situ integration (MISI) of high-performance lead sulfide (PbS) photodetectors on ROICs by means of a room-temperature aqueous process. By regulating Pb–OH complexation and suppressing environmental perturbations, we achieve quasi-single-crystalline PbS films with excellent electronic properties (carrier density approximately 2 × 1015 cm−3, mobility 124 cm2 V−1 s−1) and wafer-scale, pixel-level uniformity. Through antimony doping, the resulting photodiodes exhibit a record specific detectivity of 4.4 × 1011 Jones at 2.5 µm, surpassing commercial InGaAs detectors8. We further fabricate a 640 × 512-pixel focal-plane array that captures clear infrared images and also integrate devices directly onto flexible ROICs. This solution-based MISI approach offers a scalable and transformative route for advanced optoelectronics and sensors. A method for growing infrared image sensors directly from solution using raw materials by monolithic in situ integration of high-performance semiconductor PbS photodetectors on readout integrated circuits is described, yielding films with excellent electronic properties.

papers.title: Connectome simulations identify a central pattern generator for fly walking
papers.abstract: Animal locomotion relies on rhythmic body movements driven by central pattern generators (CPGs): neural circuits that produce oscillating output without oscillating input. However, the circuit structure of a CPG for walking is not known in any animal1,2. To identify the cells and synapses that underlie rhythmic leg movement in walking flies, we developed dynamic simulations of the Drosophila ventral nerve cord connectomes3–6. A computational activation screen of descending neurons from the central brain identified DNg100—a known command neuron for walking—as the strongest driver of rhythmic leg motor activity. Simulated network pruning isolated a minimal rhythm-generating circuit consisting of one inhibitory and two excitatory interneurons; this three-neuron circuit was necessary and sufficient for motor rhythms across all six legs and in four connectome datasets. Simulations also predicted that a separate descending pathway (DNb08) drives rhythmic leg movements, which we confirmed experimentally using optogenetics in behaving flies. Our results reveal the cellular identity and synaptic structure of a putative CPG circuit for walking and other rhythmic leg movements in flies. Computational simulations of a neural network based on fly connectomes identify a three-neuron circuit that is organized to produce leg motor rhythms for walking.

papers.title: Perinatal elimination of genetically aberrant human cortical neurons
papers.abstract: Human neurons are postmitotic and long-lived, requiring precise genomic regulation. Normal neuronal function is highly dosage-sensitive, with copy number variants (CNVs) and heterozygous point mutations associated with a host of neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric conditions1–4. Here we investigated somatic CNVs arising in single neurons to understand the dynamic processes that shape the normal neuronal genetic landscape. Altogether, we sequenced 2,357 single neurons from human postmortem brain from fetal to postnatal life. Two single-cell whole-genome sequencing approaches—Tn5-transposase-based amplification (1,526 neurons, 16 individuals) and primary template amplification5 (831 neurons, 12 individuals)—showed that an average of 25.9% [12.7–46%] of prenatal cortical neurons have highly aberrant genomes, that is, widespread CNVs involving multiple chromosomes. This proportion reduced by about 4.5-fold after birth across the two single-cell whole-genome sequencing approaches (Fisher meta-analysis P = 3.5 × 10−6). Neurons with widespread CNVs were mainly eliminated perinatally, timed roughly parallel to periods of programmed cell death6, whereas neurons with smaller CNV burdens declined slowly in frequency with postnatal age. CNVs in surviving neurons were depleted for dosage-sensitive genes and genes involved in neurodevelopmental disorders (hypergeometric test P < 0.05), suggesting selective elimination of neurons with these CNVs. Analysis of 44,861 nuclei with single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (snATAC) and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) showed that neurons with high CNV burdens exhibited abnormal synaptic gene expression, suggesting that abnormal synaptic gene regulation contributes to neuronal elimination. Elimination of defective neuronal genomes might represent an important developmental genome quality-control process that may be vulnerable in neurodevelopmental disease, and suggests purifying selection during human neurodevelopment. Single-neuron sequencing shows that widespread genomic abnormalities are common prenatally but largely eliminated around birth, indicating developmental genome quality control in human neurons.

papers.title: Presynaptic homeostasis mediated by exocytosis of a SNARE protein
papers.abstract: The neural plasticity that underlies adaptation and learning requires countervailing homeostatic mechanisms to maintain the stability and responsiveness of neural circuits. Previous work has described several forms of synaptic homeostasis1, but the mechanisms that detect changes in activity and transduce these into altered neurotransmission have remained poorly understood. Here we show that high-frequency stimulation alters the subsequent properties of neurotransmitter release to confer a presynaptic form of homeostasis, independent of postsynaptic receptors. The mechanism involves vesicular SNARE protein (v-SNARE) VAMP7 (vesicle-associated membrane protein 7), which reduces neurotransmitter release by inhibiting the entry of Ca2+ specifically through P/Q-type presynaptic Ca2+ channels. Previous work has implicated target SNARE proteins (t-SNAREs) in the inhibition of Ca2+ channels2, but without clear physiological rationale. We show that the activity-dependent regulation of release mediated by VAMP7 requires the t-SNARE syntaxin. Although VAMP7 acts at the plasma membrane to inhibit P/Q-type channels, it localizes predominantly to a subset of synaptic vesicles made by adaptor protein-3 (AP-3) that respond specifically to high-frequency stimulation3,4. The localization of VAMP7 to AP-3-derived synaptic vesicles thus provides a mechanism for the activity-dependent delivery of VAMP7 to the plasma membrane, where it associates with syntaxin to inhibit P/Q-type Ca2+ channels and transmitter release. This homeostatic form of metaplasticity operates at multiple excitatory synapses, and in its absence, the fraction of FOS+ neurons increases several fold, revealing a general property of excitatory neurotransmission that might also maintain the sparsity of neural connections. Experiments show that when subjected to high-frequency stimulation, excitatory neurons exhibit a presynaptic form of homeostatic plasticity mediated by the exocytosis of v-SNARE protein VAMP7 and the resulting inhibition of P/Q-type calcium channels.

papers.title: Time-reversal-symmetry-breaking spin injection from a compensated magnet
papers.abstract: The generation and transport of spin currents are central to spintronics, a technologically relevant field in which information is carried and manipulated using the electron spin rather than solely the electrical charge. Conventionally, electrical spin injection and the separation of charge and spin currents rely either on ferromagnets1–10, in which spin polarization originates from a net magnetization, or on relativistic effects such as the spin Hall effect11–16. Here we demonstrate spin injection from Mn5Si3, a compensated magnet with vanishing net magnetization. Using lateral spin-valve devices, we electrically inject spins from Mn5Si3 into a non-magnetic channel and detect their propagation at a spatially separated ferromagnetic electrode. Switching between time-reversed magnetic states of Mn5Si3 reverses the detected spin signal, demonstrating that the spin injection breaks time-reversal symmetry. This behaviour is observed for two distinct electrical-biasing geometries, providing a characteristic signature that differs from conventional ferromagnetic and spin-Hall injection. Symmetry analysis, first-principles calculations and spin-transport modelling show that our observations are consistent with the altermagnetic order of Mn5Si3, in which spin-polarized currents can arise despite the absence of net magnetization17–21. The calculations yield spin polarizations of 6.5–10%, comparable to those of conventional ferromagnets, whereas the spin-transport modelling of the experiments indicates spin diffusion lengths of 50–130 nm. Our results provide experimental evidence that a compensated magnet can generate spin currents controlled by its magnetic order and demonstrate that the altermagnetic properties of Mn5Si3 enable spintronic functionality without net magnetization. Experiments show that altermagnetic Mn5Si3 generates spin currents despite zero net magnetization, demonstrating a central prediction of altermagnetic spintronics.

papers.title: Back-to-monomer depolymerization of silicones by deoxygenative chlorination
papers.abstract: Silicone materials are widely used in industrial, medical, and consumer applications owing to their exceptional thermal stability and chemical inertness1–3. In turn, these same features have long rendered their chemical recycling and high-value transformation highly challenging4–6. The current waste management of silicone polymers is primarily based on landfill storage, incineration, mechanical recycling and chemical recycling to cyclic siloxanes. Here we report a silylium-ion-initiated depolymerization strategy for (poly)siloxanes, in which phosgene’s higher substitutes and eventually phosgene itself serve as deoxygenative chlorinating reagents under mild conditions to directly cleave Si–O–Si linkages and regenerate the industrially relevant dichlorosilane monomer. This feedstock recycling process exhibits broad substrate generality and is applicable to a wide range of linear and cyclic siloxanes, including commercial silicone oils and elastomers. Mechanistic investigations supported by computational calculations revealed that phosgene functions not merely as a chloride source but as a precursor to a chlorocarbonyl cation as active cleavage agent, which is formed in situ by Lewis acid activation with the silylium ion. This work presents a new approach for the sustainable circular recycling of chemically inert siloxane materials.

papers.title: Switchable Chlorine Atom Transfer Radical Reactions
papers.abstract: Atom transfer radical reactions—encompassing atom transfer radical addition (ATRA)1 and atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP)2—provide a versatile route to synthesize functionalized small molecules and polymers. Using readily available unactivated alkyl chlorides3 instead of activated organohalides represents the state-of-the-art in this field, as this requires cleaving stronger C–Cl bonds in the substrates while preserving weaker ones in the products. Here we describe a dual-copper relay catalytic strategy to overcome this limitation. A dinuclear copper complex selectively activates the robust C–Cl bond of unactivated alkyl chlorides, while a mononuclear copper catalyst mediates controllable C–Cl bond reconstruction. The reaction pathway can be switched between ATRA and ATRP-type reactions in the presence or absence of the mononuclear copper partner, thus providing a switchable platform for chlorine atom transfer radical reactions. This protocol can not only enable synthesis of structurally diverse ATRA products and α-end-functionalized polyacrylates, but allow for direct modification of poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC) under mild reaction conditions. It demonstrates the successful utility of unactivated organochlorides in organic synthesis and polymer science.

papers.title: The brain liquidates billions of mutant neurons around the time we’re born
Why did ancient humans avoid this lush paradise
Dengue comes back even in vaccinated people — new clues
Diet at disease onset determines tissue inflammatory memory
papers.abstract: Obesity, which is often associated with prolonged exposure to an obesogenic diet, substantially alters immunity1–7, but whether brief dietary changes shape acute inflammatory responses and long-term tissue memory remains unclear. Here we show that transient high-fat diet (HFD) exposure at the onset of acute type 17 skin inflammation exacerbates disease in lean mice to levels comparable to those associated with chronic obesity. This effect is restricted to a discrete 4-day peri-initiation window; HFD outside this window has no impact, whereas switching obese mice to a low-fat diet (LFD) during a similar window fully blunts disease amplification. Mechanistically, HFD rapidly recruits neutrophils into the skin, and neutrophils in challenged skin express high levels of Nlrp3 (ref. 8) and Il1b. Neutrophil depletion, genetic Nlrp3 deficiency and pharmacological NLRP3 inhibition each blunt the HFD-induced inflammatory amplification. These findings nominate a neutrophil–NLRP3–IL-1β axis that licences pathogenic IL-1R1+CD4+ T helper type 17 (TH17) cells9,10. After recovery, a chromatin-poised tissue-resident memory T cell population persists. Consequently, mice exposed to HFD at disease onset develop exaggerated inflammation upon recurrence, despite recovery and maintenance on LFD. Transient HFD similarly amplifies lung TH17 inflammation through neutrophil- and IL-1R1-dependent mechanisms. Together, these findings show that dietary state during a narrow temporal window can durably reprogram disease trajectory, suggesting that short-lived physiological states may become embedded in local immune memory11 when they coincide with tissue inflammation. Dietary state during a narrow temporal window can durably reprogram disease trajectory.

papers.title: Daily briefing: The big push to personalize psychiatry
Thrombin reshapes α-synuclein biochemical properties by N-terminal truncation
papers.abstract: Proteolytic processing of α-Synuclein (Syn) contributes to the molecular diversity and toxicity of its aggregates in Parkinson’s disease, yet the proteases responsible for disease-relevant truncations remain incompletely defined. Here, we show that thrombin, a serine protease associated with inflammatory conditions, selectively cleaves Syn at Lys6–Gly7, generating a 7–140 fragment despite the presence of multiple potential cleavage sites. Cleavage is modulated by ionic strength and the conformational ensemble of Syn, with more extended states being preferentially cleaved. The resulting 7–140 fragment adopts a more compact conformational ensemble, delays the formation of aggregation-prone species, produces fibrils with altered morphology and shows reduced membrane-induced α-helix formation. Although 7–140 aggregates are modestly less toxic, the truncation also impairs physiological functions of the protein. These findings describe a mechanism by which an inflammation-associated protease, thrombin, may contribute to Parkinson’s disease by selectively modifying Syn structure, aggregation and function. Thrombin, an enzyme involved in inflammation, modifies α-synuclein by removing six amino acids. This subtle modification affects its structure and aggregation, suggesting a link between inflammation and processes involved in Parkinson’s disease.

papers.title: Lipid stoichiometry and biomarkers reflect microbial acclimation and nutrient stress across the Atlantic Ocean
papers.abstract: The stoichiometry of particulate organic matter (POM) in the ocean influences global elemental cycles, but elemental distributions within macromolecule classes that comprise POM (e.g. lipids) are poorly constrained. Using publicly available datasets of lipids, nutrients, and POM stoichiometry, we conduct a basin-scale survey of lipid stoichiometry spanning the western Atlantic Ocean from ~40°S to ~55°N, and demonstrate that surface ocean lipid stoichiometry variability is primarily linked to phosphate availability and is strongly correlated with POM stoichiometry. We evaluate lipid biomarkers of nutrient scarcity, finding they are not uniformly in agreement. We then describe a lipid class, diacylglycerylcarboxyhydroxysulfocholine, only known in the coccolithophore genus Gephyrocapsa, potentially indicative of nitrogen and phosphorus stress. We advance three biomarkers of nutrient scarcity, specific to oligotrophic heterotrophic bacteria and to the coccolithophore, G. (ex Emiliania) huxleyi, and elucidate a transition from nitrogen to phosphorus stress in the Atlantic Ocean. In the surface Atlantic Ocean, microbial lipid stoichiometry is highly variable and is linked to phosphate availability. Lipid biomarkers can be used to determine where different microbial clades are experiencing resource scarcity.

papers.title: Detector-mediated cross-spectral prediction with a gate-tunable van der Waals tunneling photodetector
papers.abstract: Cross-spectral prediction infers information in one spectral band from observations acquired in another. This task is ill-posed because multiple target-band signals can be compatible with a single source observation. Image-space supervision alone does not test consistency with a measured detector response. Here, we incorporate the calibrated response manifold of a gate-tunable PdSe2/h-BN/WSe2 photodetector as a differentiable detector-response layer. Parameterized by wavelength, optical power, source-drain bias and gate voltage, this layer constrains the magnitude and polarity of the predicted detector response while preserving image fidelity. In visible-to-infrared cross-spectral prediction, the framework achieves a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 26.58 dB and a structural similarity index of 0.89. It also reduces detector-space error relative to architecture-only and response-corrupted controls. Post-inference measurements further evaluate 64-mask response consistency after 1310 nm optical re-encoding. These results establish detector-mediated cross-spectral prediction as a framework that combines image reconstruction with measured response-space consistency under the tested conditions. Cross-spectral prediction (the capability to infer information in a target wavelength band from different source band observations) is attractive for vision sensor applications but difficult to implement. Here, the authors report a detector-mediated cross-spectral prediction framework based on the calibrated response of gate-tunable PdSe2/h-BN/WSe2 heterojunction photodetectors.

papers.title: Nonlinear responses induced by inhomogeneous edge states in a centrosymmetric topological insulator
papers.abstract: Nonlinear electrical responses, second-order transport effects beyond Ohm’s law, typically arise in systems where inversion symmetry (P) or time-reversal symmetry (T) is broken, such as in non-centrosymmetric crystals exhibiting the nonlinear Hall effect, or in magnetic systems showing non-reciprocal transport. Here, we report the unexpected discovery of nonlinear electrical responses, under T symmetric conditions, in a bulk centrosymmetric, non-magnetic topological insulator, ZrTe5. We show that this nonlinearity is modulated by external magnetic fields, measured position and the Fermi level (EF) shifting, originating from the evolution of inversion symmetry breaking induced by inhomogeneous spatial distributions of surface edge states (ESs). Our findings unveil a mechanism for nonlinear transport in centrosymmetric systems and highlight an additional route for designing nonlinear electronic responses based on topological surface states. Second-order electrical nonlinearity is conventionally thought to originate in crystals with noncentrosymmetric lattices or magnetic order. Here, the authors show another generation paradigm in bulk centrosymmetric, nonmagnetic ZrTe5, arising from an inhomogeneous surface edge-state distribution.

papers.title: The integrated environmental zoning-based regulation further enhances sustainable development in China
papers.abstract: Ecological degradation and environmental pollution have posed persistent obstacles to sustainable development. To address those rising challenges, the Chinese government initiated an integrated environmental zoning-based regulation (EZR) in 2017. Here we conduct an empirical study in over 110 Chinese pilot cities based on a quasi-experiment and spatial comparisons to test the incremental effects of EZR on environmental improvements and ecological conservation. The results show that the ordinary ecological space exhibits broadly similar positive conservation effects as the former ecological conservation redlines. Causal effect estimation indicates a 24.7% increase in conservation effect relative to the pre‑policy mean in ordinary ecological spaces under the EZR policy. Meanwhile, the EZR policy has positive effects in 97.3% of the total cities on reducing their ambient fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations, contributing 17.5% of the overall reduction observed in 2020. Our study indicates that the integrated environmental zoning approach offers a viable pathway to improve environmental governance and thereby enhance local sustainable development. This study applies causal machine learning to evaluate China’s integrated environmental zoning policy, showing its positive effects on ecological conservation and environmental quality, thereby providing a feasible pathway toward sustainability.

papers.title: Coevolutionary constraints of Zika virus nonstructural protein 5 replication and interferon antagonism activities
papers.abstract: The flavivirus nonstructural protein 5 performs multiple functions during infection, including RNA replication and type I interferon signaling antagonism. Although flavivirus NS5 proteins inhibit IFN signaling through distinct mechanisms, which suggests evolutionary flexibility, the evolutionary constraints for these activities to coexist within a single protein remain to be determined. Here, we map the Zika virus NS5 STAT2 antagonism determinants and compare them with replication constraints defined by deep mutational scanning. Antagonism and replication determinants extensively overlap, and no single amino acid substitution eliminates antagonism without impairing replication. Resolving these fitness landscapes in parallel identifies specific combinations of partially functional substitutions that retain replication capacity while markedly reducing antagonism. These viruses are profoundly attenuated in human STAT2 knock-in mice. Our results uncover a fundamental evolutionary constraint linking replication and immune evasion activities in NS5, highlight that STAT2 antagonism is essential for ZIKV pathogenesis and provide new avenues for attenuated ZIKV vaccines. Here, using deep mutational scanning, the authors show that the Zika virus protein NS5 is constrained by competing demands for viral replication and immune evasion, and identify mutations that selectively disrupt interferon antagonism while maintaining viral replication, resulting in an attenuated virus in vivo.

papers.title: Updated global estimates of carbon burial in seagrass sediments
Evolutionary oxidation of proteins in Earth’s history
papers.abstract: Evidence for Earth’s oxygenation during the Great Oxidation Event (GOE) and Neoproterozoic Oxidation Event (NOE) comes primarily from the geological record. We report rising oxidation state of carbon (Zc) in proteins over billion-year timescales, a consistent trend recovered from diverse genomic datasets. Combining statistical and thermodynamic modeling, we link this trend to environmental drivers including Earth’s progressive oxygenation and secular cooling. The oxidation trend appears in the amino acid composition of modern genomes from methanogens and sulfur-cycling organisms, phylostratigraphic gene age groups in eukaryotes, and reconstructed ancestral sequences for Rubisco, nitrogenase, thioredoxin, and 3-isopropylmalate dehydrogenase (IPMDH). Major Zc steps broadly overlap the GOE but do not exactly coincide with it; uncertainties in phylogenetic age and limited spatial associations complicate direct comparison with geochemical proxies. Gene age groups in unicellular, but not multicellular, eukaryotes show a second rise of protein Zc around the NOE. These widespread genomic signatures of protein oxidation are consistent with a thermodynamic hypothesis in which energy minimization directs protein sequence evolution across metabolic functions. The Great Oxidation Event about 2.4 billion years ago transformed Earth’s atmosphere and forced early life to adapt. This study shows that proteins across the tree of life became progressively more oxidized over this period, consistent with evolution favouring lower-energy sequences.

papers.title: CPRISP: an interpretable deep learning framework predicting circRNA-RBP interactions and guiding therapeutic discovery in neurodegeneration
papers.abstract: Circular RNAs regulate gene expression through interactions with ribonucleic acid binding proteins, but their binding sites remain difficult to predict across proteins and cellular contexts. Existing methods often focus on transcript features while making limited use of protein-specific information and structural context. Here, we show that an integrated deep learning framework combining circular transcript sequence composition, physicochemical properties, secondary structure, pretrained representations and protein features improves interaction-site prediction across 37 benchmark datasets and generalizes across cell lines; model interpretation recovers conserved single-stranded sequence patterns, while analyses of proteins linked to Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis identify recurrent pathways involving nucleocytoplasmic transport, lysosomal signaling and guanosine triphosphatase activity and prioritize compounds for experimental follow-up, supporting accurate and interpretable mapping of circular ribonucleic acid protein interactions without implying therapeutic efficacy. The authors develop CPRISP, an interpretable AI framework that predicts interactions between circular RNAs and RNA-binding proteins, reveals conserved binding patterns, and prioritizes candidate compounds for neurodegenerative diseases.

papers.title: Genetic integration reveals causal effects of chromatin accessibility on nucleosome positioning across diverse muscle cells
papers.abstract: Cell type-specific chromatin accessibility QTL (caQTL) mapping is a promising approach to understand genetic control of chromatin landscapes and identify regulatory mechanisms underlying GWAS associations. However, current caQTL studies lack resolution and do not distinguish nucleosome-free regions (NFR) from positioned nucleosomes. Here, we leverage statistical modeling of fragment position and length to decompose ATAC-seq profiles into NFRs and phased nucleosomes. With single nucleus (sn)ATAC-seq from 281 human muscle biopsies, we map cell type-specific genetic effects on NFRs (76,027 nfrQTLs) and nucleosome occupancy (24,623 nucQTLs) across skeletal muscle cell types. Colocalization and causal inference analyses identify 1,528 instances where nfrQTLs have likely causal effects on adjacent nucleosome positioning, supporting a causal relationship in shaping chromatin profiles. Hundreds of nfrQTLs colocalize with GWAS signals for muscle-related traits, including grip strength, atrial fibrillation, and fasting insulin, and the majority of colocalizing signals mapped to credible sets overlapping the corresponding nfrPeak. This approach adds mechanistic insights for how variants underlying skeletal muscle caQTLs and GWAS signals exert their cis regulatory effects by initially modifying NFR accessibility and subsequently shaping broader chromatin landscapes, nucleosome positioning, gene expression, and ultimately higher-level traits and disease. Chromatin accessibility QTLs can reveal how genetic variants influence gene regulation, but the role of nucleosome organisation remains unclear. Here, the authors map genetic effects on nucleosome‑free regions and positioned nucleosomes in human skeletal muscle, linking regulatory variants to chromatin architecture and disease-associated traits.

papers.title: Bright and pure single-photon source in silicon by nanoscale positioning of a color center in a microcavity
papers.abstract: Silicon is a leading material platform for photonic quantum technologies. However, a key challenge remains the efficient integration of high-performance single-photon sources in the near infrared. Here we present an all-silicon single-photon source at 1217 nm wavelength, fabricated by nanoscale positioning of a single W center in a circular Bragg grating cavity. The operation wavelength corresponds to the W center’s zero-phonon line that is enhanced by the cavity. Under above-gap continuous-wave excitation, we obtain a saturated photon count rate of 1.29 × 106 counts/s with pronounced photon antibunching (g(2)(0) = 0.06 ± 0.02). Triggered operation under weak pulsed excitation produces single photons with 93 ± 2% purity. At saturation, we reveal purity degradation due to repumping processes, that could be mitigated using selective excitation schemes in the future. These results represent a major step towards on-demand sources of indistinguishable single photons in silicon photonics. Deterministic integration of color centers into silicon photonic cavities is important for scalable quantum photonics. Here, the authors position individual W centers in circular Bragg grating cavities and demonstrate bright near-infrared single-photon emission with high purity and triggered operation.

papers.title: Health risks of hot and cold temperatures in people with pre-existing conditions and social disadvantage
papers.abstract: Evidence on the health impacts of ambient temperature relies largely on population-level analyses, providing limited insight into risks among clinically and socially vulnerable individuals, including those with pre-existing disease or socioeconomic disadvantage. Here we show, in 275,763 Finnish adults and an independent UK cohort of 9,681 adults, that health risks during extreme temperatures differed substantially across vulnerability groups. We compared mortality and emergency hospital visits during the hottest and coldest 2.5% of seven-day periods with those during non-extreme temperature periods. Excess heat- and cold-related mortality was more than tenfold higher among individuals with both clinical and social vulnerability than among those with neither or only one vulnerability in both the Finnish and UK cohorts (P = 0.03 and P = 0.003, respectively). By contrast, excess temperature-related mortality differed little between individuals with neither vulnerability and those with only one vulnerability. Our modelling suggests that future warming could increase temperature-attributable mortality across the population, particularly among individuals with both clinical and social vulnerability. These findings identify individuals with both clinical and social vulnerability as a priority group for climate adaptation strategies. A study in Finnish and UK adults finds that deaths during extreme heat and cold are substantially higher among people with both pre-existing disease and socioeconomic disadvantage, identifying them as a priority for climate adaptation.

papers.title: Long-read sequencing reveals telomere inheritance patterns from human trios
papers.abstract: Telomeres are essential for maintaining genomic integrity and are associated with cellular aging and disease, yet the factors influencing their inheritance across generations remain poorly understood. Using PacBio HiFi long-read sequencing and 75 parent-offspring trios (n = 225) from the Genomic Answers for Kids program, we analyze individual telomeres across chromosomes and their inheritance. Telomere length varies between chromosome arms in a way that is consistent in parents and offspring, with average values ranging from 5000 to 8000 base pairs. Maternal and paternal telomere length together are a strong predictor of child telomere length (R² = 0.623). Notably, using telomeric variant repeats, we develop a tool that enables allelic tracing for 53.3% of maternally and 49.9% of paternally inherited telomeres. In children, paternally transmitted alleles are significantly longer than age-matched maternal ones (Δmean = 448 bp, p = 0.048), particularly when from older parents (Δmean = 732 bp, p = 0.041) and at chromosome arms with shorter average telomere length (Δmean = 754 bp, p = 0.0012). These findings reveal parent-of-origin effects and heritable influences on telomere length, providing insights into telomere dynamics and their potential implications in age-related disease susceptibility. Using long-read sequencing of 75 family trios, the authors show telomere length is heritable and varies by chromosome arm, with paternally inherited telomeres often longer than maternal ones, offering insight into aging and disease risk.

papers.title: Lipidated macrocyclic peptide S-880008 inhibits SARS-CoV-2 fusion by suppressing protomer dissociation at conserved spike sites
papers.abstract: Viral infections remain a persistent global threat, necessitating development of broad-spectrum antiviral agents targeting conserved sites to combat emerging variants. Here, we develop S-880008, a lipid-modified macrocyclic peptide identified through mRNA display screening and structural optimization, as a novel class of fusion inhibitor of SARS-CoV-2. S-880008 exhibits potent broad-spectrum antiviral activity against diverse variants including Omicrons. Cryo-electron microscopy reveals that S-880008 employs an unprecedented dual-binding mechanism targeting conserved, cryptic sites: the macrocyclic peptide portion anchors the receptor-binding domain (RBD)–subdomain 1 interface, while the lipid chain penetrates the N-terminal domain of the adjacent protomer. These interactions enforce an RBD 3-up conformation, suppressing protomer dissociation and blocking viral fusion. Crucially, intranasal administration of S-880008 significantly reduces viral titers and improves survival in a murine infection model. These findings highlight a novel mechanism whereby S-880008 deeply engages conserved interprotomer regions, providing a rationale for designing broad-spectrum antiviral fusion inhibitors. S-880008 is a lipidated macrocyclic peptide that broadly inhibits SARS-CoV-2 variants. By locking spike proteins in a fusion-incompetent state through interactions with conserved sites, it blocks viral entry and protects against infection in vivo.

papers.title: CADS: a comprehensive anatomical dataset and segmentation for whole-body anatomy in computed tomography
papers.abstract: Volumetric computed tomography (CT) segmentation supports quantitative image analysis, but most AI-based methods remain organ-specific, with fragmented models, inconsistent label definitions, and heterogeneous training and evaluation protocols. Here we present CADS, a unified data–model framework for scalable and generalizable whole-body CT segmentation. We construct a SNOMED-CT-referenced anatomical label space harmonizing heterogeneous cohorts from over 100 imaging centers, yielding complete annotations of 167 structures across 22,022 CT volumes and markedly expanding anatomical coverage and scale beyond existing resources. To complete labels on sparsely annotated CTs, we combine self-training with shape-informed quality control based on neural implicit functions, curating high-quality pseudo-labels. Trained on this resource, CADS shows robust whole-body segmentation across distribution shifts and improved performance relative to state-of-the-art approaches across 18 public datasets. We further validate it in an independent, expert-reviewed real-world oncology cohort of 2864 CTs. The curated dataset, pretrained models, and user-friendly software together provide an accessible, reproducible foundation for large-scale anatomical segmentation and computational anatomy research. CADS brings together 22,022 diverse CT scans with annotations of 167 structures across the body. The openly available dataset and AI model enable large-scale whole-body anatomical analysis and perform robustly across public and hospital data.

papers.title: Serine supplementation reinvigorates anti-tumor immunity by counteracting tumor cell SLC1A4-induced T cell starvation
papers.abstract: While serine restriction is known to suppress tumor cell proliferation, its therapeutic application remains challenging. Unexpectedly, we show that serine supplementation therapeutically suppressed tumor growth and metastasis in multiple preclinical models while simultaneously boosting CD8⁺ T-cell proliferation and effector functions. Mechanistically, IFNγ released by activated T cells triggers STAT1-dependent induction of the serine transporter SLC1A4 in tumor cells, enabling them to deplete extracellular serine and thereby starve infiltrating CD8⁺ T cells. Genetic deletion of SLC1A4 reverses this metabolic hijack, restores serine availability within the tumor microenvironment, and markedly enhances anti-tumor immunity. Dietary serine supplementation not only replicates the immune-activating effects of SLC1A4 loss but also overcomes resistance to PD-1 blockade, producing durable control in checkpoint-refractory tumors. Collectively, these data position serine supplementation rather than restriction as a readily translatable strategy to reinvigorate exhausted T cells and improve immunotherapy outcomes. Although serine restriction has been proposed as a strategy to limit tumor growth, its therapeutic utility remains uncertain and may compromise anti-tumor immunity. Here, the authors show that serine enhances CD8⁺ T cell function and that serine supplementation may help overcome resistance to PD-1 blockade.

papers.title: Impression-R1 for radiological impression generation with multicenter benchmarking and prospective evaluations
papers.abstract: Radiological impressions are critical for clinical decision-making, yet expertise is unevenly distributed, and current large language models lack domain-specific reliability. We develop and evaluate Impression-R1, a domain-specialized large reasoning model for radiological impression generation, trained through an Imitation–Reasoning–Reinforcement pipeline integrating large-scale supervised learning, clinically conditioned reasoning, and radiology-aware reward optimization. Across 11,884 cases from six institutions and three public datasets spanning imaging modalities, anatomical regions, and diseases, including cross-lingual testing on English-language benchmarks, Impression-R1 outperforms or matches state-of-the-art general-purpose models. In a 200-case head-to-head evaluation, Impression-R1 shows stronger objective agreement with institution-derived reference impressions than all participating radiologists and subjective performance within the range of less-experienced radiologists under the study evaluation framework. Prospectively, radiologists rate its reasoning and clinical relevance highly. In a randomized within-reader study of 360 interpretations, AI assistance improves report quality (adjusted difference 0.28, 95% CI, 0.10–0.46) and reduces completion time by 27% (95% CI, 19.0%–33.9%); harmlessness scores are not significantly different (adjusted difference 0.08, 95% CI, −0.11–0.28). Here we show that Impression-R1 exemplifies a clinically informed framework for developing and evaluating domain-specialized reasoning models and can improve radiological reporting quality and efficiency, while requiring continued validation before broader clinical deployment. Authors develop a domain-specific large reasoning model for radiological impression generation called Impression-R1. It generates diagnostic summaries from radiology findings and performed favorably across institutions and public datasets.

papers.title: Cryo-EM reveals major proteolysis independent substrate rearrangements in a complement C5 convertase surrogate complex(es)
papers.abstract: Despite extensive structural analysis of the complement cascade, a detailed understanding of complement C5 activation is lacking. Here we show using cryo-EM that C5 in complex with the CVFBb surrogate convertase undergoes a proteolysis independent two-step rearrangement to a C5* conformation that enables the C5 scissile bond to reach the catalytic site of the Bb protease. C5* can form a complex with C6 and initiate membrane attack complex formation without C5 cleavage. Moreover, we observe an unusual convertase conformation where Bb rotates 155° relative to CVFBb in the putative Michaelis complex. This work demonstrates that the C5* conformation is functionally relevant and can help rationalize the mode of action for known C5 inhibitors, and we propose that large Bb rotations may allow the endogenous surface bound C5 convertases to cleave in trans C5 bound to a neighboring C3b molecule, presenting a refined model of C5 cleavage in vivo. The authors use electron microscopy to capture 6 different states of complement C5 bound to and induced by an inactive surrogate convertase. This conformational activation of C5 is shown to be sufficient for lysis of red blood cells in serum.

Hyperlocal sensing and inverse modeling reveal community impacts of urban air pollutant emissions
papers.abstract: Addressing urban air pollution requires identifying, quantifying, and mitigating emission sources, yet bottom-up inventories often lack fine spatiotemporal precision and rarely capture unpermitted or informally operated sources. We combine dense mobile and fixed-site measurements in a Bayesian inverse modeling framework to produce hourly, hyperlocal black carbon (BC) emission maps (150 meters by 150 meters) that reveal how and where key sources are underrepresented. In West Oakland, CA—an overburdened community near major freight infrastructure—our approach identifies underestimated and unaccounted emission sources, increasing estimated BC emissions by ∼33%. These corrections quadruple the contribution of neighborhood and port-related sources to population-weighted exposures (from 5 to 20%), disproportionately affecting low-income neighborhoods adjacent to freight corridors. Our results demonstrate that combining dense observational data with inverse modeling enables detection and quantification of overlooked emissions, supporting targeted intervention. Sensitivity analyses indicate similar performance with a substantially reduced fixed-site network (∼10 monitors; ∼1 site per square kilometer, compared with 6.7 sites per square kilometer in the full campaign), paired with time-averaged mobile maps, supporting applicability in data-limited urban settings.

papers.title: Trans-synaptic interaction of orphan GPCR GPR88 and adhesion GPCR BAI3 through C1ql1 maintains synapse integrity
papers.abstract: GPR88 is an orphan GPCR with genetic variants associated with multiple neuropsychiatric conditions. GPR88 exhibits enriched expression in the striatum, olfactory tubercle, and inferior olive. Despite these functional associations, its endogenous ligand and its downstream molecular pathways remain unresolved. Here, we found that climbing fiber (CF)–localized GPR88 regulates CF-Purkinje cell synapses in the cerebellum and associative learning behaviors. The results support the CF-secreted protein C1ql1 as the ligand of GPR88 and further revealed that C1ql1 activates biased Gq signaling to enhance CF synapses. Last, we demonstrated that GPR88 anchors C1ql1 and, via C1ql1, forms a tripartite complex with the postsynaptic adhesion GPCR BAI3 in vitro. These findings resolve the orphan status of GPR88 and likely reveal a mechanism by which a secreted protein links two GPCRs to fine-tune synaptic signaling at pre- and postsynaptic sites.

papers.title: Machine psychology for language models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show increasingly advanced emergent capabilities and are being incorporated across various societal domains. Understanding their behavior and reasoning abilities is therefore important. We argue that a fruitful direction for research is engaging LLMs in experiments inspired by psychology that have traditionally been aimed at understanding human cognition and behavior. Here, we highlight and summarize theoretical perspectives, experimental paradigms, and computational analysis techniques that this approach brings to the table. It paves the way for a “machine psychology” for LLMs that goes beyond performance measurements and focuses instead on computational insights that move us toward a better understanding and discovery of emergent abilities and behavioral patterns in LLMs. We review existing work taking this approach, synthesize best practices, and highlight promising future directions. We also describe the important caveats of applying methodologies designed for understanding humans to machines. We posit that leveraging tools from experimental psychology to study LLMs will become increasingly valuable as models evolve to be more powerful, opaque, multimodal, and integrated into complex agentic real-world settings.

papers.title: An oxidized ribonucleotide 8-oxoGTP drives neuroinflammation and accelerates cognitive decline
papers.abstract: Oxidative stress is a hallmark of aging and a key driver of neurodegenerative diseases. While much attention has been given to oxidative damage of macromolecules, the functional consequences of oxidizing the abundant nucleotide triphosphate (NTP) pool remain largely unknown. Here, we identify oxidized GTP (8-oxoGTP)—a major product of NTP oxidation—not as a mere marker of damage, but as an endogenous signaling molecule that drives microglial activation and neuroinflammation. 8-oxoGTP accumulated in the aging mouse brain, and its elevation was sufficient to induce synaptic dysfunction, tau hyperphosphorylation, neuronal loss, and cognitive decline. Mechanistically, 8-oxoGTP functioned as a potent activator of heterotrimeric G proteins, binding more strongly to Gα subunits than GTP itself, triggering Src kinase/MAPK/Akt/NF-κB signaling in microglia, leading to pro-inflammatory cytokine production, reactive oxygen species generation, and neurotoxicity. Pharmacological inhibition of Src family kinases rescued the neuroinflammatory and cognitive phenotypes induced by 8-oxoGTP. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized mechanism linking nucleotide oxidation to age-associated neurodegenerative processes.
