papers.title: BAK and BAX form a multiprotein complex to drive mtDNA efflux and caspase-independent cell death
papers.abstract: The apoptotic regulators BAX and BAK, once activated, form homo-oligomers to trigger mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP), activating the apoptosome and caspases. Activation of BAX-BAK without apoptosome activation triggers sustained efflux of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and caspase-independent cell death. However, the molecular basis of mtDNA efflux remains unclear. We purified a macromolecular complex comprising BAK, BAX, activator BH3-only molecules, voltage-dependent anion channels 1 and 2 (VDAC1 and VDAC2), and prohibitins that released mtDNA from mitoplasts. BAX-BAK activation resulted in VDAC closure, mitochondrial calcium influx, and mtDNA efflux. Loss of VDAC1, VDAC2, or prohibitins prevented BAX-BAK activation–induced mtDNA efflux and caspase-independent cell death without affecting MOMP or mitochondrial inner membrane herniation. These findings support differential regulation of cytochrome c and mtDNA efflux by distinct BAX-BAK complexes.

papers.title: Intron retention regulates STAT2 function and associates with immunotherapy response in lung cancer
papers.abstract: Immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibitors has revolutionized cancer therapy and enabled considerable therapeutic advances for treating various diseases, including lung cancer. However, the molecular determinants of variable patient outcomes remain unclear. Using long-read RNA sequencing, we mapped the landscape of alternative RNA splicing in human primary lung adenocarcinomas. We identified more than 149,000 full-length messenger RNA (mRNA) isoforms, more than half of which were unannotated and many that occurred in immune-related genes, particularly within the type I interferon response pathway. We functionally characterized retained introns in the STAT2 gene that produced altered protein isoforms that regulated immune signaling and interferon responses and correlated with patient survival after anti–programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) immunotherapy. These findings position alternative splicing as a regulator of tumor immune responses and reveal intron retention in STAT2 as an interferon regulatory axis that correlates with PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitor response.

papers.title: Late Holocene reexpansion of the Laurentide Ice Sheet
papers.abstract: During interglaciations, the Laurentide Ice Sheet (LIS), which is the largest of the Pleistocene ice sheets, retreats to Arctic Canada, where it achieves a minimum configuration. The reexpansion of the LIS following this minimum marks the start of the next glaciation. Here, we show that the last remaining remnant of the most recent LIS, Barnes Ice Cap (Baffin Island, Canada), achieved its minimum interglacial dimensions after ~3.6 thousand years ago, before reexpanding ~2000 years ago, marking the onset of the next glaciation. The new LIS reached maximum dimensions in ~1960 CE, after which anthropogenic summer warming resulted in a negative mass balance, ice margin recession, and the termination of the next glaciation. The demise of the next glaciation, despite the ongoing decline in summer insolation, illustrates the influence of anomalous greenhouse gas forcing on climate.

papers.title: Ultrarapid decision-making in an avian brain
papers.abstract: Perceptual decision-making is well studied in mammals, but its operation in other vertebrates remains unclear. We show that carrion crows ( Corvus corone ) make deliberate decisions in a classic visual motion discrimination task with unprecedented speed, reporting choices in approximately 235 milliseconds on average, which is roughly twice as fast as has been observed in monkeys or humans and without sacrificing accuracy. Recordings from the pallial endbrain reveal that direction-selective neurons encode the upcoming choice as early as about 70 milliseconds after stimulus onset and about 170 milliseconds before the response, with ramping activity scaling with sensory evidence and converging at response onset. These findings highlight the extraordinary efficiency of avian decision-making circuitry, possibly shaped by evolutionary pressures for rapid visuomotor control.

papers.title: Dynamic functionality–enabled fast and selective transport in nanochannels
papers.abstract: Nanochannels capable of fast and selective mass transport are central to applications in energy, resources, biomedicine, and the environment. However, extreme nanoscale confinement, often coupled with rigid channel environments, imposes substantial frictional and adhesive barriers, causing sluggish transport and constrained selectivity. We identified nanochannel dynamics as a key to addressing these challenges by harnessing the intrinsic mobility (e.g., self-rotation) of confined functionalities to enhance molecular transport. Through a combination of experiments and simulations, we demonstrated that such dynamics reshape transport by promoting kinetic energy transfer and enabling more efficient molecular relays, thereby improving separation performance beyond current benchmarks. Our findings highlight the role of nanochannel dynamics in regulating mass transport under confinement and provide a framework for designing advanced nanochannel systems.

papers.title: Imaging electron-hole asymmetry in the quantum melting of generalized Wigner crystals
papers.abstract: Two-dimensional moiré materials provide a versatile platform to explore phase transitions in strongly correlated systems. Using scanning tunneling microscopy, we imaged the density-driven melting of generalized Wigner crystals (GWCs) and Mott insulators (MIs) in electron-doped, near-60°–twisted molybdenum diselenide bilayers featuring a triangular moiré superlattice. We observed notable electron-hole asymmetry in GWC melting: Hole-doped GWCs yielded interaction-driven disordered states, whereas electron-doped GWCs melted into delocalized liquid-like states. This asymmetry arose from the broken particle-hole symmetry of the moiré superlattice, which produced electron and hole Fermi pockets with different momentum geometries upon GWC condensation. MI states melted without such asymmetry, consistent with the absence of a symmetry-breaking density modulation. This work provides direct visualization of the emergent phases that appear as GWCs undergo quantum melting transitions.

papers.title: Visualizing symmetry-broken Chern insulators and their quantum melting
papers.abstract: In the presence of a magnetic field, electronic states of moiré quantum materials develop a Hofstadter spectrum that provides a distinctive setting for studying the interplay between band topology and strong electron-electron interaction. Using scanning tunneling microscopy, we studied Hofstadter’s states in bilayer graphene aligned with hexagonal boron nitride and directly visualized the formation of interaction-driven symmetry breaking Chern insulators. Our measurements revealed the formation of phases that double, triple, or quadruple the moiré unit cell at fractional filling of the Hofstadter bands as well as states with complex intra–unit cell wave functions. We visualized two distinct quantum phenomena in different Chern states, including quantum melting driven by the appearance and proliferation of topological defects and a quantum transition co-occurring with phase competition and separation.

papers.abstract: The power conversion efficiency (PCE) and stability of flexible perovskite solar modules (PSMs) are less than those of their rigid devices because surface hydroxyls desorption on flexible substrates, which disrupts self-assembled monolayer (SAM) anchoring and perovskite crystallization. We developed a decoupled SAM-perovskite codeposition strategy that accelerates SAM anchoring by reducing the SAM-perovskite interaction and ameliorates perovskite crystallization. The certified PCE with phenethylammonium iodide as the passivation molecule was 20.2% on PSMs with device areas of 750 cm 2 . papers.title: Sequential diagnosis with language models
papers.abstract: We explored the capabilities of frontier language models in sequential diagnosis, a diagnostic paradigm that captures the iterative nature of clinical reasoning. Given a brief clinical presentation, clinicians selectively acquired information to reach a diagnosis, enabling assessment of diagnostic accuracy and workup cost. We developed an interactive benchmark and an artificial intelligence (AI) system that simulates a panel of physicians, continually revising the differential diagnosis and selecting cost-effective tests. Using this benchmark, the system achieved 83.2% accuracy on New England Journal of Medicine clinicopathological conference cases and 80.3% on MIMIC-IV-ED emergency department admissions, outperforming generalist physicians (36.1 and 46.8%, respectively). Although these findings were obtained in a controlled benchmark setting, they highlight the promise of language models for supporting more accurate, lower-cost diagnoses.

The Virtual Biotech: A multi-agent AI framework for therapeutic discovery and development
papers.abstract: Drug development requires evidence integration across biological scales and modalities, but relevant tools are fragmented. We introduce the Virtual Biotech, an organization of artificial intelligence (AI) agents modeled on a drug-development company, with agentic divisions spanning target discovery, safety assessment, modality selection, and clinical development. We demonstrate its utility at three drug-development decision points. First, more than 37,000 agents annotated outcomes from 55,984 trials and found that drugs targeting cell type–specific genes were 48% more likely to reach market with 32% fewer adverse events. Second, it integrated multimodal evidence to propose a therapeutic strategy in lung cancer. Third, it analyzed a terminated ulcerative colitis trial and inferred potential mechanisms of failure. These results demonstrate that human-guided multi-agent systems can conduct transparent, multiscale analyses to inform therapeutic-development decisions.

papers.title: Response to Magkos and Silva: Diet macronutrient content and metabolic function in metabolically unhealthy obesity

As noted by Magkos, a common limitation of diet studies is ensuring compliance with the prescribed diets and studying participants when they are weight stable to avoid the confounding effect of negative energy balance and active weight loss on study outcomes. We addressed both of these issues by providing all meals to participants in conjunction with careful dietary supervision, and by studying participants after weight loss when they had been weight stable for 3–4 weeks.

papers.title: Genetic dissection of rapid proteolysis identifies TXNDC15 as a key factor of ERAD and lipid homeostasis
papers.abstract: ER-associated protein degradation is central to organelle homeostasis, yet many regulatory components remain unknown. Liu et al. exploit the rapid turnover of short-lived proteins to identify TXNDC15 as a noncanonical MARCHF6-dependent ERAD factor that links proteostasis to lipid homeostasis, illustrating how rapid proteolysis can uncover hidden metabolic regulatory circuits.

papers.title: Targeted lactate depletion via gluconeogenesis by engineered hepatocyte-based micronanorobots for radiosensitization and immune activation
papers.abstract: Fan et al. develop CXCR4-engineered hepatocyte cytoplasts integrated with Au-Pt nanorobots to deplete tumor lactate through gluconeogenesis. Lactate depletion suppresses repair-associated lactylation and impairs MRN-mediated DNA repair, while Au-Pt catalysis amplifies radiation-induced damage. This metabolic remodeling simultaneously alleviates immunosuppression and promotes systemic antitumor immunity.

papers.title: Hit the pause button
Cancer theranostics
papers.abstract: Theranostics refers to the inseparable combination of disease diagnosis and therapy, with the former critically guiding the selection, application and outcome of the latter. In oncology, theranostics traditionally encompass radiolabelled peptides for in vivo molecular imaging of receptor expression by cancer cells, followed by radionuclide treatment using the same peptides labelled with β-emitting radioisotopes. Here we provide an overview of the basic principles and current clinical practice of theranostic probes and protocols, and we expand the terminology to include locally and systemically applied nanotheranostics and microtheranostics, as well as imaging-guided surgical interventions. Building on solid progress in target identification, probe design and hardware development, as well as on promising recent results achieved in clinical trials, we foresee a bright and broad future for multiscale theranostics, for the treatment of oncological pathologies and beyond. Theranostics integrates diagnostic imaging with targeted therapy to enhance cancer treatment. In this Review, Sofias et al. discuss recent advances in radiotheranostic strategies, advances in nanotheranostic and microtheranostic platforms, and image-guided therapeutic and surgical interventions in oncology.

papers.title: Molecular functions, cellular responses and pathological implications of the RNA modification N 6 -methyladenosine
papers.abstract: The RNA modification N6-methyladenosine (m6A) precisely regulates eukaryotic gene expression. The deposition of m6A is governed by chromatin environment, transcription and RNA processing. m6A modifications influence chromatin function and RNA splicing, stability, localization and translation, and enable cellular adaptation to environmental changes. Dysregulation of m6A has been implicated in pathological processes, including neurodegenerative diseases and cancer. In this Review, we dissect the m6A machinery by describing how writers and erasers coordinate m6A deposition and reader proteins translate these modifications into diverse functional outcomes. We illustrate how this dynamic regulatory network orchestrates cellular stress responses, metabolic homeostasis and antitumour immunity, and outline the pathological consequences of m6A dysregulation in brain disorders and cancer. Finally, we highlight translational prospects of m6A biology, including the development of specific small-molecule inhibitors and precise editing technologies, and address the remaining challenges for clinical interventions targeting m6A. This Review discusses how the RNA modification N6-methyladenosine (m6A) precisely regulates eukaryotic gene expression and orchestrates cellular stress responses, metabolic homeostasis and immunity. It also explores the pathological consequences of m6A dysregulation in brain disorders and cancer.

papers.title: Sensing a problem here: nucleotide signaling in immunity
papers.abstract: Cyclic nucleotides are shared messengers of antiviral immunity across bacteria and animals, yet the same chemical signal can produce strikingly different cellular outcomes. Recent studies show that bacteria generate the mammalian cyclic GMP–AMP synthase product, 2′-5′,3′-5′-cyclic GMP–AMP, during phage infection and use it to activate membrane-disrupting SMODS-associated and fused to various effector domains-family effectors. Structural work further reveals how ligand binding drives receptor oligomerization, filament formation, and vertical membrane shearing. In parallel, viral proteins that degrade or sequester cyclic nucleotides have exposed new evolutionary pressures on these pathways. We discuss how receptor architecture, supramolecular assembly, and antagonism determine signal meaning and how newly defined defense systems invert conventional signaling logic by sensing the loss rather than the production of an immune nucleotide.

papers.title: Nondestructive quality control across the life cycle of bioprinted products
papers.abstract: Bioprinting is a transformative technology paving the way toward complex tissue-engineered products, yet its translation is constrained by major quality control challenges. Variability in cells, bioinks, bioprinting parameters, and tissue maturation can compromise reproducibility and product consistency. Addressing such variability requires repeated measurements across the multistage, multifactorial bioprinting pipeline that conventional destructive assays cannot provide. In this opinion article, we argue that nondestructive testing (NDT) should become an enabling component of reliable bioprinting. We discuss how complementary NDT modalities could support monitoring, optimization, automation, and scalability in the short term, while validated multimodal strategies could support clinical translation in the long term.

papers.title: Integrated nanocoating and biofilm engineering enhance extracellular electron transfer
papers.abstract: Microbes exchange electrons with electrodes to generate electricity or drive chemical reactions. This study combines conductive cell coatings, cellular recovery, and light-controlled formation of electrode biofilms to improve electron transfer in both directions, providing a strategy for designing more effective interfaces between living cells and electrodes.

Trans-ancestry genome-wide association meta-analysis of gallstone disease
papers.abstract: Gallstone disease is a highly prevalent and costly gastrointestinal disease. Yet, genetic variation in gallstone susceptibility and its implication in metabolic pathways remain to be explored. We report a trans-ancestry genome-wide association meta-analysis of gallstone disease including 100,856 cases and 1,596,602 controls in the UK Biobank, FinnGen, Biobank Japan, and Million Veteran Program. We identified 116 (59 novel) risk loci across meta-analysis and found replication in statistically compelling signals in the All of Us Research Program. A polygenic risk score constructed from trans-ancestry lead variants was positively associated with liver chemistry and alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency and negatively associated with total cholesterol and low-density lipoprotein levels among trans-ancestry and European ancestry groups in the Penn Medicine BioBank. Colocalization of risk loci with 44 traits and with expression quantitative trait loci from eight tissues yielded 321 and 110 significant colocalizations, respectively. These findings broaden our understanding of the genetic architecture of gallstone disease. Gallstone disease is common, but its genetic basis remains incompletely understood. Here, the authors conduct a trans‑ancestry GWAS identifying 116 risk loci, linking gallstone susceptibility to lipid and liver metabolism pathways and expanding understanding of disease biology across diverse populations.

papers.title: A porous solid electrolyte interface enables efficient electroreduction of captured carbon to CO
papers.abstract: Direct electrochemical conversion of captured carbon species offers a route to avoid the energy-intensive steps of thermal CO2 release, compression and transport in conventional carbon capture and utilization. In proton exchange membrane (PEM) reactors, however, the acidic cathode environment promotes hydrogen evolution and limits CO2 regeneration from (bi)carbonate capture media, resulting in low carbon utilization and high energy demand. Here we show a modular PEM–porous solid electrolyte (PSE) reactor for direct conversion of (bi)carbonate to CO. Using a transparent cell with in situ visualization, we reveal that the PSE regulates proton transport, reduces local proton reduction, limits bubble accumulation and facilitates CO2 transport to the cathode. The PEM–PSE reactor achieves a CO Faradaic efficiency of 90% at 200 mA cm−2, a carbon efficiency of 84%, and an energy consumption of ~26.0 GJ t−1 CO. It operates at current densities up to 800 mA cm−2, reaching a CO rate of ~8.0 mmol h−1 cm−2. These results highlight the regulation of proton and gas transport in the electrochemical conversion of captured carbon. Turning captured carbon dioxide into useful chemicals can save energy, but combining capture and conversion is difficult. Here, the authors report a membrane reactor converts bicarbonate solutions directly into carbon monoxide with high carbon efficiency and lower energy use.

papers.title: NHEJ-mediated DNA synapsis and RPA-driven MRX exonuclease balance DNA end resection to control DSB repair
papers.abstract: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) are repaired by Ku-dependent non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) or DNA end resection-dependent homologous recombination (HR). Previously, it was shown that short-range resection by MRX-pSae2 can remove Ku from DSBs and initiate resection, showing flexibility in DSB repair pathway choice. However, which NHEJ intermediates can be disrupted by resection factors remains unknown. Using reconstituted reactions with purified S. cerevisiae proteins, we show here that short-range resection by MRX-pSae2 is not directly inhibited by any of the core NHEJ factors. Instead, we find that MRX-pSae2 is inhibited structurally. DNA synapsis, a dynamic NHEJ intermediate that bridges DSBs, strongly suppresses resection. Non-ligatable ends are refractory to MRX-pSae2 once synapsis formed, and NHEJ assemblies with catalytic mutants of DNA ligase IV that permit synapsis but do not allow ligation likewise inhibit resection. We further demonstrate that removal of Ku from DSBs requires RPA, which interacts with MRX and pSae2 to synergistically stimulate MRX 3′−5′ exonuclease activity, generating free 3′ overhangs. Our data support a model in which DNA synapsis temporarily prevents resection, allowing NHEJ to execute ligation. If ligation fails and synapsis dissociates, MRX-pSae2 and RPA promote resection that removes non-productive NHEJ assemblies and channels DSB repair toward HR. The data help explain the suppression of NHEJ by RPA observed in previous genetic experiments. DSBs are repaired by NHEJ or HR. Using reconstituted reactions with purified yeast proteins, the authors show that DNA end synapsis blocks short-range resection, giving NHEJ time to ligate. Moreover, RPA promotes HR by stimulating the exonuclease of MRXpSae2 and allowing Ku removal from DNA ends.

papers.title: Enhancing bosonic qubit protection by squeezing
papers.abstract: Bosonic qubits implement error correction by harnessing the high-dimensional Hilbert space of a harmonic oscillator to redundantly encode logical quantum information. Squeezing of quantum states — a cornerstone of precision metrology — redistributes uncertainty between conjugate quadratures to enhance sensitivity in one variable at the expense of the other. In bosonic codes, decoherence can be seen as the environment performing an unwanted measurement on a noise-sensitive quadrature, collapsing superpositions and inducing errors. By redistributing uncertainty to that quadrature, squeezing can be leveraged to reduce the environment’s measurement strength, thereby prolonging coherence. Here, we exploit this insight to implement a squeezing deformation of the simplest bosonic code — the cat qubit — extending the bit-flip time with minimal impact on the phase-flip rate. We observe a dramatic reduction in bit-flip errors, achieving a 160-fold improvement over standard cat qubits and bringing multi-cat architectures closer to fault-tolerant quantum computation. In bosonic codes, decoherence can be seen as the environment performing an unwanted measurement on a noise-sensitive quadrature, collapsing superpositions and inducing errors. Here, the authors show how to use squeezing to further protect bosonic codes from noise, extending the bit-flip times of the cat qubit by two orders of magnitude without reducing phase-flip times.

papers.title: Determining depth-resolved spatial distribution of solid–electrolyte interphase using non-destructive angle-resolved X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy for lithium-metal batteries
papers.abstract: The solid electrolyte interphase is a key performance regulator in Li-metal batteries, which are regarded as an important technology for future energy storage. Understanding this crucial interphase through non-destructive analysis is essential to advance the performance and lifespan of Li-metal batteries. We introduce angle-resolved X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy as a non-destructive technique for the depth-profile analysis of the solid electrolyte interphase in Li-metal batteries. Importantly, we show that this characterization technique displays a distinct advantage in preserving the solid electrolyte interphase's integrity compared to traditional sputtering-based depth-profiling. Our findings add to the understanding of compositional differences in the solid electrolyte interphase before the onset of Li electrodeposition and after Li plating. Moreover, we find significant variations in the thickness and distribution of solid electrolyte interphase species across different classes of electrolytes, which strongly influence the solid electrolyte interphase's protective properties and, by extension, Li-metal battery performance. This study benchmarks the application of angle-resolved X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy in revealing detailed, depth-resolved chemical composition of the solid electrolyte interphase in a non-destructive approach. Understanding the solid–electrolyte interphase formed on lithium is vital for improving the lifetime of lithium metal batteries. Here, authors show that angle-resolved X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy can reveal the depth-dependent composition of the interfacial layer without damaging it by ion sputtering.

papers.title: Laser-enhanced quantum sensing boosts sensitivity and dynamic range
papers.abstract: While magnetometers based on nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond have emerged as the most important solid-state quantum sensors, ensembles are typically limited to a few percent optical contrast. Here, we demonstrate a laser threshold magnetometry-based NV system that achieves 100% optical contrast in combination with strong output signals up to 50 mW. By integrating the NV centers into a laser cavity, we show magnetic-field-dependent shifts of the laser threshold, allowing the laser system to be entirely switched off with the NV centers’ magnetic resonance. We determine the photon-shot-noise fundamental sensitivity limit to be < 400 fT/ $$\sqrt{{{\rm{Hz}}}}$$ for all vector components and demonstrate that it improves super-linearly with contrast. This sensitivity is not achieved at the usual cost of smaller linewidth, i.e., maintains good intrinsic dynamic range. This provides a perspective for highly sensitive magnetometry operated outside magnetically-shielded rooms for applications including magnetoencephalography, magnetic navigation, and magnetic anomaly detection. Integrating quantum defects with optical cavities offers a route to enhanced magnetic field sensing. Here, the authors embed nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond within a laser cavity and demonstrate laser threshold magnetometry with 100% optical contrast and photon shot noise sensitivity limit below 400 fT Hz−1/2 while retaining vector sensing capability.

papers.title: Observation of inherent chiral Smith–Purcell effect via symmetry breaking
papers.abstract: The Smith–Purcell effect arises when charged particles move near a periodic structure, emitting radiation. Conventional approaches for generating chiral Smith–Purcell radiation rely on metasurface phase engineering or resonant mode interference, typically producing narrow-band, weakly chiral emission. Here, we introduce a resonance-interference-free mechanism that leverages the properties of the charged particles themselves. Using a non-chiral, non-resonant silicon grating, we demonstrate broadband, tunable Smith–Purcell radiation with high chirality, achieving a record-high degree of polarization of 0.87. This is enabled by converting the transverse spin angular momentum of electron-induced evanescent waves into a longitudinal form, producing opposite chirality at different azimuthal angles. Beam twisting or displacement offers precise control over chirality, paving the way for compact chiral light sources, advanced X-ray imaging, and integrated particle diagnostics platforms. Existing approaches for generating chiral Smith–Purcell radiation remain limited. Here, the authors overcome these limitations by uncovering the inherent chirality of the Smith–Purcell effect using non-chiral, non-resonant silicon gratings. By controlling the electron–grating configuration, this chirality can be selectively manipulated to produce tunable and highly chiral polarized radiation.

papers.title: Reduced-DSP 200G/λ low-voltage slow-light silicon modulator enabled by built-in EO equalizer
papers.abstract: Multi-Tb/s optical interconnects for artificial intelligence data centers necessitate high-speed, energy-efficient, and compact transceivers. However, conventional silicon Mach-Zehnder modulators are fundamentally limited by low modulation efficiency and large physical dimensions that typically extend several millimeters, requiring high-swing drivers and power-intensive digital signal processing to achieve data rates exceeding 100 Gb/s per lane. Here we show a silicon photonic crystal waveguide slow-light modulator that overcomes the bandwidth-efficiency trade-off via a built-in electro-optic equalizer. By monolithically integrating optical delay lines and crossings within segmented slow-light phase shifters, we synthesized an on-chip feedforward response that extends the 3-dB bandwidth. The fabricated modulator with a small device length of 320 µm demonstrated 140-Gb/s on-off keying operation with an energy consumption of 26 fJ/bit using drive voltages compatible with fin field-effect transistor-based complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor technology. Furthermore, four-level pulse amplitude modulation achieved 180 Gb/s without digital signal processing and 200 Gb/s with a low-complexity 11-tap digital equalizer. By reducing reliance on power-dissipating electronics, this strategy provides a potential route toward future dense multi-Tb/s co-packaged optics for energy-constrained switching systems. Silicon photonic modulators are central to future high-capacity optical interconnects but face a trade-off between efficiency and bandwidth. This work addresses that challenge using a slow-light modulator with an integrated EO equalizer, enabling 200 Gb/s operation.

papers.title: Ocean acidification, reduced silicate availability and declines in Ocean productivity
papers.abstract: Understanding rising atmospheric CO2 effects on the chemistry of the world’s ecosystems remains nascent. CO2 dissolved in water forms carbonic acid, thereby lowering pH (ocean acidification [OA]). Diatoms, which generate 40% of ocean primary productivity, depend on dissolved silicon to construct their silica frustules; lower pH reduces silica (SiO2) solubility in seawater. Recent experiments document enhanced silica sedimentation under elevated CO2, implying reduced Si recycling and availability to support diatom production at the ecosystem scale. We tested this hypothesis using long-term data from a productive Pacific coastline undergoing rapid pH decline. Over two decades, as pH declined, dissolved Si:N and water column chlorophyll concurrently declined strongly. Accounting for variation in potential Si transport vectors did not change these relationships. Our results support the OA Si loss hypothesis and indicate that this process is already ongoing in some productive ocean regions, with implications for the carbon cycle, coastal food webs, and human well-being. Long-term CO2-generated declines in ocean pH block recycling of silicon, an essential nutrient for diatom-driven ocean production. Associated reductions in chlorophyll and plankton-feeding fish reveal a novel CO2 impact on marine ecosystem health.

papers.title: Light-powered photosynthetic living actuator
papers.abstract: Highly compliant deformable soft actuators enable the engineering of adaptive life-like systems. Biohybrid living materials expand possibilities for autonomous, self-powered, environmentally responsive systems with easy biological integration. Here, we present a light-driven living soft actuator that integrates the photosynthetic microalga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii with a pH-responsive poly(3-(acrylamido)phenylboronic acid-acrylamide)/polyacrylamide bilayer hydrogel. When exposed to light, through photosynthesis and N-assimilation, the microalgae locally ionize the polymer network, causing the bilayer actuator to bend. In darkness, through respiration, the microalgae locally release CO2 that protonates the polymer chains, reversing the deformation. This algae actuator enables finely controlled and reversible motions, with a large bending amplitude achieved within 18 hours and an initial response time of 10-20 s, which is maintained over 10 cycles of continuous operation. We demonstrate light-controlled grippers, highlighting the potential of algae-powered actuation for sustainable and autonomous soft devices. Deformable actuators can be used for adaptive life-like systems, and biohybrid materials can expand the possibilities for responsive materials. Here the authors integrate microalgae into a pH-responsive hydrogel to achieve a biohybrid photoresponsive actuator.

papers.title: XIST drives X-chromosome inactivation and safeguards female extraembryonic cells in humans
papers.abstract: X-chromosome inactivation (XCI) is essential for extraembryonic tissue growth and embryo development in mice. However, species-specific differences in its timing and regulation have left its role in human development unclear. Here, we show that the in vitro differentiation of naive human pluripotent stem cells to trophoblast stem cells and extraembryonic mesoderm cells is accompanied by XCI. The inactive X chromosome displays an atypical chromatin state, lacking DNA methylation and canonical heterochromatin marks. We demonstrate that extraembryonic differentiation and XCI are temporally linked. Using loss of function approaches, we found that XIST is required for XCI establishment in humans. Furthermore, we show that XCI is needed for the survival of human female extraembryonic cells. Together, these findings link XCI to the formation of human extraembryonic lineages, with important implications for human reproductive biology. X-chromosome inactivation (XCI) silences one of the two X chromosomes in females, but its role in human development is unclear. Here, the authors show that human extraembryonic differentiation triggers XIST-dependent XCI, important for cell survival.

papers.title: Tau isoform mapping across tissues and biofluids reveals a signature distinguishing Alzheimer’s disease from amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
papers.abstract: Blood phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217) accurately detects Alzheimer’s disease (AD) pathology but is also elevated in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), likely reflecting peripheral (big) tau released from muscle. Assays selectively measuring brain-derived (BD-) tau and BD-p-tau217 are therefore needed. We analysed serum BD-tau and p-tau217 in ALS (n = 139), AD (n = 101) and controls (n = 75) using direct immunoassays and after BD-Tau immunoprecipitation (BD-Tau-IP), and tau species in brain (n = 16), spinal cord (n = 11) and muscle (n = 10) by targeted mass spectrometry. With the direct immunoassays, BD-tau and p-tau217 were increased in AD and ALS versus controls. After BD-Tau-IP, BD-tau and BD-p-tau217 were elevated in AD only, improving diagnostic accuracy. Mass spectrometry revealed a central-to-peripheral shift from BD-tau to big tau predominance, with exclusively big p-tau217 detected in muscle. Selective detection of BD-tau species improves the specificity of blood AD biomarkers by reducing peripheral tau confounding. Blood p-tau217 is a leading Alzheimer’s test but is also raised in ALS. Here, the authors show that muscle makes its own form of tau which leaks into the blood, and that detecting brain-derived p-tau217 improves the test’s accuracy.

CauTrigger: deciphering biological system state transitions by hierarchical causal decomposition
papers.abstract: Biological systems exhibit complex hierarchical regulation, with interactions across multiple layers governing transitions between states. Identifying the causal architecture underlying these state transitions remains challenging because confounding can produce spurious associations in observational data. Here we present CauTrigger, a hierarchical deep latent variable model that integrates do-calculus to identify potential causal triggers and predict perturbation outcomes across multiple regulatory layers. By disentangling causal and spurious latent factors, CauTrigger recursively reconstructs the underlying regulatory hierarchy and enables interpretable reasoning from observational data. Across synthetic and real-world datasets with multilayer regulatory structures, CauTrigger outperforms existing methods in identifying causal triggers and forecasting system-level responses. Applied to single-cell multi-omics and gut microbiome datasets, CauTrigger prioritizes candidate causal triggers and uses in silico perturbations to generate testable hypotheses about biological state transitions and inform potential strategies for state navigation. Together, these results establish CauTrigger as a general-purpose framework for causal discovery in complex biological systems. CauTrigger is a hierarchical deep latent variable model that can identify potential causal triggers and predict outcomes of perturbation events.

papers.title: OpenDVP: an experimental and computational framework for community-empowered deep visual proteomics
papers.abstract: Deep visual proteomics (DVP) is an emerging approach for cell-type-specific and spatially resolved proteomics. However, its broad adoption has been constrained by the lack of an open-source end-to-end workflow within a community-driven ecosystem. Here we introduce openDVP, an experimental and computational framework for accessible and scalable DVP. OpenDVP combines open-source image analysis tools (MCMICRO, QuPath and napari) with scverse formats (AnnData and SpatialData) for multiomics integration. It provides two workflows: a fast-track pipeline requiring no image analysis expertise, and an artificial intelligence-powered pipeline incorporating state-of-the-art methods for image preprocessing, segmentation and spatial analysis. We apply openDVP across three archival tissue studies (human placenta, early stage lung cancer and locally relapsed breast cancer), integrating spatial single-cell phenotypes with exploratory proteomic measurements. Finally, we introduce deep proteomic profiling of cellular neighborhoods as a scalable approach for spatial discovery proteomics. OpenDVP enables scalable and high-resolution proteomic profiling of cellular neighborhoods.

papers.title: Tracing causal cascades underlying biological state changes
Serine protease inhibitor A3 is a soluble SIRPα ligand that suppresses inflammation and antitumor immunity
papers.abstract: SIRPα is an inhibitory receptor with the canonical ligand CD47. Here, we show that human serine protease inhibitor A3 (SERPINA3) and its mouse ortholog SERPINA3k function as soluble binders and activators of SIRPα, suppressing SIRPα+ macrophages, neutrophils, dendritic cells and natural killer cells. SERPINA3(k) treatment alleviates lipopolysaccharide-induced pneumonia and ameliorates experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis and rheumatoid arthritis. Although wild-type SERPINA3 provokes inflammation in cardiomyocytes and brain vascular endothelial cells, the SERPINA3D2 mutant, identified through functional domain mapping for SIRPα interaction, abolishes these adverse effects while retaining full inhibitory capacity. Notably, cancer cells secrete large amounts of SERPINA3(k), exceeding CD47 levels. Anti-SERPINA3(k) antibodies, used alone or in combination with blockade of programmed cell death 1 receptor/programmed cell death ligand 1, inhibit tumor growth in multiple preclinical models. This work identifies a potent soluble SIRPα ligand, offering effective therapeutic strategies for inflammatory/autoimmune diseases and a promising target for cancer immunotherapy. Here the authors show that SERPINA3 is a soluble SIRPα ligand with immunosuppressive and therapeutic activity against inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, whereas cancer cells overexpress SERPINA3 and blocking it can be protective.

papers.title: Genome-wide detection of genotype–environment interactions at biobank scale with fastGxE
papers.abstract: Traditional genome-wide association studies have primarily focused on detecting main genotype effects, often overlooking genotype–environment interactions (GxE), which are essential for understanding context-specific genetic effects and refining disease etiology. Here we present fast genotype–environment interaction analysis (fastGxE), a scalable and effective genome-wide GxE method designed to identify genetic variants that interact with environmental factors to influence traits of interest. fastGxE controls for polygenic effects, polygenic interaction effects and noise heterogeneity; it remains robust to the number of environmental factors involved in GxE interactions; and it ensures scalability for genome-wide GxE analysis in large biobank studies, achieving speed improvements of 32.98–126.49 times over existing approaches. We illustrate the benefits of fastGxE through extensive simulations and an in-depth analysis of 32 physical traits and 67 blood biomarkers from the UK Biobank. In real-data applications, fastGxE identifies 7 genomic loci associated with physical traits, including 4 novel ones, and 18 genomic loci associated with blood biomarkers, 12 of which are novel. The new discoveries highlight the dynamic interplay between genetics and the environment, uncovering potentially clinically relevant pathways that could inform personalized interventions and treatment strategies. fastGxE is a powerful and computationally efficient method for genome-wide detection of genotype–environment interactions across multiple environmental factors at biobank scale.

papers.title: Near-complete assembly of wild emmer wheat unveils centromere reorganization during polyploid evolution
papers.abstract: Wild emmer wheat (Triticum turgidum ssp. dicoccoides, BBAA), the wild progenitor of cultivated tetraploid and hexaploid wheats, provides an important reference for investigating centromere reorganization during polyploidization and domestication. Here we generated a near-complete genome assembly of wild emmer wheat, including centromeric regions for all 14 centromeres. Comparative analyses with cultivated tetraploid and hexaploid wheats revealed extensive variation in centromere-associated sequences and centromere-proximal structure, as well as distinct subgenome-associated patterns in the A and B subgenomes. The A subgenome was characterized by positional shifts and sequence turnover of CRW-rich centromere-derived blocks, whereas the B subgenome showed reduced CentT566 satellite abundance accompanied by localized retention or expansion on specific chromosomes. These results provide a high-resolution tetraploid wheat reference and reveal subgenome-associated patterns of centromere remodeling during wheat polyploid evolution. A near-complete genome assembly of wild emmer wheat with resolved centromeric regions across 14 chromosomes highlights subgenome-associated patterns of centromere remodeling during wheat polyploid evolution.

papers.title: High false sign rates in transcriptome-wide association studies
papers.abstract: Transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) are widely used to identify genes involved in complex traits and to infer the direction of gene effects on traits. However, despite their popularity, it remains unclear how accurately TWAS recover the true direction of a gene’s effect on a trait. Here we estimate the false sign rate of TWAS for plasma proteins, leveraging the expectation that increased gene expression should generally increase protein expression. We then extend this framework to complex traits, where loss-of-function burden tests provide the expected direction of effect. In both analyses, we observe high discordance with expectations, with TWAS showing a false sign rate of 23% for plasma proteins and 33% for complex traits. We propose that much of the sign discordance arises when expression quantitative trait loci in non-trait-relevant tissues tag haplotypes associated with traits in genome-wide association studies via distinct, tightly linked regulatory variants, yielding spurious TWAS associations with the correct genes but with unreliable direction of effect. These findings show that TWAS-based direction-of-effect estimates should be interpreted with caution and raise concerns about the reliability of TWAS more broadly. This study finds that the direction of effect captured by transcriptome-wide association studies is often reversed relative to the true biological mechanism, suggesting that caution is needed when interpreting these studies and using the results for downstream applications.

papers.title: Co-regulation confounds direction of genetic effects in transcriptome-wide association studies
Keratin 9 regulates mechanosensitive YAP1 signalling in palmoplantar epidermis
papers.abstract: The palmoplantar epidermis, in adapting to the exceptional mechanical strain it bears during locomotion, is histologically and molecularly distinct from other skin body sites. The mechanisms specifying and maintaining its unique identity remain incompletely defined. Here we identify the type I keratin 9 (KRT9/K9), a protein uniquely expressed in palmoplantar epidermis, as a key modulator of mechanosensitive YAP1 signalling in response to postnatal mechanical compression. K9 loss-of-function variants driving KRT9-pEDD, a palmoplantar epidermal differentiation disorder, result in aberrant YAP1 subcellular partitioning and elevated levels of the stress-induced keratin 16 (KRT16/K16). Krt9 null mice recapitulate these molecular phenotypes as early as postnatal day 3. We further identify dynamic, YAP1-dependent regulation of Krt16/K16, upstream of and necessary for Krt9/K9 expression, during early postnatal development in situ and in response to mechanical compression of keratinocytes ex vivo, highlighting the role of mechanical stress in epidermal specification. Mechanistically, K9 interacts with the YAP1 binding protein 14-3-3σ and sequesters YAP1 in the cytoplasm, inhibiting its transcriptional activity; these functions are disrupted by KRT9-pEDD-causing variants in K9. Finally, we show that genetic or pharmacological inhibition of YAP1 ameliorates palmoplantar keratoderma in Krt9 null mice. These findings reveal a role for mechanical cues in specification and maintenance of palmoplantar skin and suggest new therapeutic interventions for inherited palmoplantar epidermal differentiation disorders. Steiner et al. propose that keratin 9 (K9) interacts with 14-3-3, sequestering YAP1 in the cytoplasm and inhibiting YAP1 activity. They identify dysregulated YAP in palmoplantar keratinization diseases, with K9 as a downstream regulator of YAP.

papers.title: Chemogenetic activation of mitochondria counteracts the Warburg effect in tumor cells
papers.abstract: Upregulation of glycolysis and downregulation of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, termed as the Warburg effect, is characteristic of tumor cells. Restriction of pyruvate flux into the mitochondrial matrix is one of the major mechanisms underlying this phenomenon. Warburg metabolism is beneficial for rapidly proliferating cells; however, the metabolic consequences of activation of mitochondrial respiration in such cells remain unclear. Here we created a chemogenetic instrument, Grubraw, that generates pyruvate from ᴅ-alanine directly in the mitochondrial matrix, bypassing restricted pyruvate influx. In cancer cells, Grubraw-produced mitochondrial pyruvate increased oxidative metabolism. Chemogenetic activation of mitochondria slowed the growth rate of human melanoma xenografts. Moreover, activation of cancer cell mitochondria suppressed the transcription of genes that control cell-cycle progression, cell proliferation and DNA replication. Surprisingly, we found that cancer cells with Warburg metabolism control carbon flux by disposing of excess mitochondrial pyruvate produced by Grubraw and exporting it out of the cell. The chemogenetic tool Grubraw activates mitochondria by generating pyruvate in the mitochondrial matrix. This triggers a genetic switch that slows down tumor cell proliferation. Tumor cells counteract this by exporting excess pyruvate outward.

papers.title: Putting the Warburg effect in reverse
Structural remodeling and activation of the hdeAB and proVWX operons in response to pH and salt stress
papers.abstract: How bacteria reorganize their chromosomes to adapt to environmental stress remains poorly understood. This study shows that acid stress reshapes H-NS-dependent chromosome organization in Escherichia coli, while its partner StpA contributes differently across genes, revealing how bacterial chromosome organization links environmental sensing to transcriptional adaptation.

papers.title: Programmed DNA breaks drive chromatin reconfiguration and facilitate transcriptional potentiation at neuronal early response genes
papers.abstract: Heady et al. report that artificially generating DSBs within ERG promoters can recapitulate chromosome contacts observed at these sites upon neuronal stimulation. Recurrently forming such DSBs amplifies ERG inducibility while pruning cis chromosomal interactions at ERG promoters, indicating how activity-induced DSBs facilitate the transcription of associated genes.

papers.title: ALKBH8 promotes acute myeloid leukemia progression by coupling codon-dependent translation elongation to mRNA stability
papers.abstract: Li et al. demonstrate that the RNA methyltransferase ALKBH8 promotes AML progression by enhancing translation elongation and stabilizing adenine-ending transcripts, such as BRCA1. Targeting ALKBH8 suppresses leukemic growth and sensitizes AML cells to PARP inhibitors, revealing a potential codon-specific therapeutic strategy for patients with AML.

papers.title: RIF1 coordinates the stepwise post-replicative H3K9me3 recovery
papers.abstract: Chen et al. demonstrate that after DNA replication-driven dilution, the reconstitution of H3K9me3 pre-replication levels requires RIF1 at multiple steps; (1) during mitotic exit, bringing PP1α back to heterochromatin, facilitating re-loading of Suv39h1/HP1α; (2) throughout G1/early S phase, counteracting early Aurora B activity on H3S10, perhaps enabling stable Suv39h1/HP1α chromatin association.

papers.title: Agentic AI systems for scientific discovery
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are emerging in scientific research as systems that can transform the accumulated decisions of scientists into traceable workflows. In fact, modern scientific practice depends on continual coordination of knowledge dispersed across literature, data, theory and experiment, which, however, is often made through manual, case-by-case judgement. This Primer introduces agentic AI systems as a general method to structure this process through natural language interfaces, serving as a computational brain in the laboratory. Central to this framework are practical workflows for in-depth literature search and knowledge mining, orchestration of physics-based simulations, and integration with automated experimental platforms. We begin by describing the foundations of AI agents, including task decomposition, memory, tool use and communication between agents, and by distinguishing single-agent and multi-agent designs, as well as fully autonomous and human-in-the-loop configurations. Equally important are the means by which these systems are evaluated, documented and reported reproducibly. Finally, we examine major bottlenecks, including hallucination, tool misuse, limited interpretability and safety risks, and outline a future in which coordinated networks of agents, instruments and researchers transform scientific discovery from isolated tasks into continuous adaptive experimentation. Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems enhance scientific workflows by structuring knowledge coordination through natural language interfaces. In this Primer, Feng et al. examine the challenges and opportunities involved in integrating AI agents in the laboratory.

The proteome of Middle Pleistocene Xujiayao and common Denisovan morphology
papers.abstract: The taxonomy and phylogeny of late Middle Pleistocene hominins in East Asia remain highly debated1. Xujiayao, a key representative assemblage with many fossils and a clear stratigraphy dating to around 199–138 thousand years ago, has been extensively studied, but its evolutionary position remains uncertain. Here, to clarify this, we analysed Xujiayao material through both palaeoproteomic analysis and morphological comparisons with other East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo. Proteomic analysis of two specimens identified 18 endogenous proteins, and the Denisova-specific COL1A2-996 R>K mutation strongly supported their affiliation with the Denisovan lineage. Extended analysis identifies a set of shared morphological traits between Denisovan fossils (Xujiayao and Harbin) and other East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo (such as Jinniushan, Dali and Hualongdong), indicating that they all belong to the Denisovan lineage. This analysis provides a comprehensive view of Denisovan features, showing both traits reminiscent of Homo erectus (such as a thick cranial vault) and those characteristic of modern humans (for example, a strongly arched temporal squama). They also share features with late Neanderthals, such as the structure of the temporal labyrinth and the presence of a suprainiac fossa. Notably, Denisovans are distinctive, with a low cranial profile with near-parallel lateral walls, a massive supraorbital torus, a flat zygomaxillary region and weak prognathism. Denisovans from the Xujiayao and other East Asian sites are morphologically distinctive, with a low cranial profile with near-parallel lateral walls, a massive supraorbital torus, a flat zygomaxillary region and weak prognathism.

papers.title: Persistent neuronal stress signalling underlies Angelman syndrome phenotypes
papers.abstract: Angelman syndrome is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder caused by the loss of UBE3A, a gene that encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase1,2. The mechanisms that underlie Angelman syndrome are not well understood, and in particular, the link between UBE3A substrates and disease phenotypes remains uncertain3. Here, using gain- and loss-of-function mutations in UBE3A4,5 along with unbiased proteomics, we show that asparagine synthetase (ASNS) is a target of UBE3A. We find that ASNS protein abundance is increased in the brains of Ube3a-null mice and in human neurons6. Genetic correction of ASNS overabundance rescues microcephaly and many behavioural deficits. Detailed molecular analyses show that ASNS overabundance activates stress signalling and causes a global reduction in neuronal protein synthesis. Our results suggest that loss of UBE3A traps neurons in a state of persistent stress and stunts neuronal growth during developmentally sensitive periods. Moreover, our results indicate that targeting ASNS and the stress response could hold therapeutic potential in Angelman syndrome. Genetic and proteomic analyses in human neurons and mouse models of Angelman syndrome (AS) show that loss of the ubiquitin ligase UBE3A leads to an overabundance of asparagine synthetase, and that this is linked with many AS phenotypes.

papers.title: Functional architecture of the human insula
papers.abstract: The insular cortex has a central role in pain1,2, interoception3,4 and feelings5,6, yet its functional architecture and causal electrophysiological relationships among its subregions remain poorly understood. Here we combine intracranial electrical stimulation and task-based electroencephalography recordings with connectivity mapping within a cytoarchitectonic atlas of the human insula7–10 in 87 participants implanted with intracranial electrodes, and identify a quadripartite functional architecture comprising four distinct regions: (1) a dorsal–posterior region encoding somatotopically organized nociceptive/thermoceptive and somatosensory signals; (2) a ventral–posterior region with access to somatic information across multiple body parts; (3) a mid-anterior region associated with visceral sensations and anxiety states; and (4) an anterior–polar region, largely silent to direct stimulation, yet showing robust activation during salience detection and change of action mode. Critically, this anterior region, with its strong connections with the prefrontal cortex, including the anterior cingulate cortex, exerts strong and direct influence over other insular regions, while receiving less-strong indirect inputs from them, revealing an electrophysiological pathway for cognitive modulation of pain and bodily perception. Together, these findings define a functional architecture of the human insula that links cytoarchitecture to directed and asymmetric electrophysiological interactions, with mechanistic implications for cognitive modulation of pain and interoceptive experience. A functional architecture of the human insula links cytoarchitecture to directed and asymmetric electrophysiological interactions, with mechanistic implications for cognitive modulation of pain and interoceptive experience.

papers.title: Additive manufacturing of ultralong and architected single crystals
papers.abstract: Single-crystal materials are indispensable for high-performance applications, yet their deployment remains constrained by conventional manufacturing techniques that depend on strict quasi-steady thermal conditions1. This requirement fundamentally conflicts with the intense cyclic thermal fluctuations inherent to additive manufacturing2, historically preventing the 3D printing of large or architected single crystals. Here we present a free-form additive manufacturing approach that resolves this contradiction by using delicately controlled alternating and pulsed heat inputs to govern and direct single-crystal growth. Using this method, we demonstrate the fabrication of metre-tall, centimetre-diameter single-crystal Ti-6Al-4V alongside, to our knowledge, the first single-crystal lattice structures containing complex zigzag ligaments, effectively eliminating theoretical size constraints for single-crystal components. The resulting bulk single-crystal Ti-6Al-4V exhibits an order-of-magnitude increase in creep resistance over standard grain-size scaling predictions, driven by the synergistic elimination of grain boundaries and an additive manufacturing-induced hierarchical α/β-architecture that regulates dislocation density, mobility and void evolution. Furthermore, we demonstrate the broad applicability of this technique by printing single crystals of hard-to-process refractory metals, including W, Mo, Nb and MoNb alloys. Our work introduces a large-scale method for single-crystal additive manufacturing, expanding the accessible materials library and enabling high-performance, complex geometries previously unattainable by classical methods. A free-form additive manufacturing method that uses alternating and pulsed heat inputs is described for fabricating metre-tall, centimetre-diameter single crystals of Ti-6Al-4V, as well as hard-to-process refractory metals, including W, Mo, Nb and MoNb alloys.

papers.title: An environmentally regulated dichotomy in cell lineages of the root
papers.abstract: Plant development is highly plastic, with growth and architecture continuously shaped by environmental conditions. Roots, for instance, adjust their development to local water, nutrient and soil conditions. Despite this plasticity, individual root cell types are generally viewed as largely homogeneous populations that progress along a single developmental trajectory1. Here we show that rather than progressing along a single developmental trajectory, most Arabidopsis root cell lineage trajectories exhibit a stereotyped bifid topology, as revealed by single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcript mapping. One branch is characterized by a transcriptional program that is shared across multiple cell types and enriched for genes associated with environmental responses, including abscisic acid (ABA) signalling. This state occurs reproducibly in a subset of cells across multiple cell types, independent of developmental lineage, thereby revealing an additional layer of root cell identity. It is conserved across Arabidopsis ecotypes and persists despite major perturbations in developmental identity. Moreover, it is reduced in ABA-deficient and ABA-insensitive mutants and becomes more prevalent under water-deficit conditions. Together, these findings reveal an additional layer of root cell identity that is superimposed on developmental lineage and its prevalence is modulated by environmental conditions. These results uncover a previously unrecognized source of environment-associated transcriptional heterogeneity shared across root cell types. An environment-regulated state is identified across multiple cell types at the root tip, revealing a shared dichotomy between cells with and without this state.

papers.title: Structural basis for protocadherin-1 recognition by New World hantaviruses
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are rodent-borne pathogens that cause severe human disease for which no approved therapeutics are available. New World hantaviruses, including Andes virus (ANDV), use the cell-surface receptor protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) to enter host cells1. However, the structural basis of this interaction remains unclear. Here we describe the structure of PCDH1 bound to the ANDV spike at near-atomic resolution. PCDH1 asymmetrically engages a deep central pocket formed by four Gn protomers in the spike, explaining why only intact viral particles or soluble tetramers recognize it. Mutagenesis identified three Gn loops that shape the receptor-binding site and afford the transfer of PCDH1 binding from New World to Old World glycoproteins. Structural and functional analyses of four neutralizing antibodies revealed that they block receptor binding through two distinct mechanisms—occluding access to the PCDH1-binding site or sterically preventing receptor engagement. Together, these findings define the structural determinants of hantavirus–receptor recognition, reveal how a virus can mask its receptor-binding site by recessing it in a surface depression and how antibodies can counter this strategy, and provide a framework for the design of antiviral therapeutics targeting the hantavirus spike. The structure of PCDH1 bound to the ANDV spike defines the structural determinants of hantavirus–receptor recognition.

papers.title: Multimodal precision diagnostics in clinical xenotransplantation
papers.abstract: Recent breakthroughs in pig-to-human xenotransplantation have successfully prevented hyperacute rejection of kidney, heart, liver and lung xenografts, marking a milestone long considered a critical barrier. However, these major advances also brought new challenges into focus, as immune-mediated graft injuries including antibody-mediated rejection, T cell-mediated rejection and innate immune activation have been observed in most xenotransplantation procedures to date. Detection and management of these injuries remain a critical bottleneck, as conventional histopathology and standard clinical monitoring lack the sensitivity required to identify subclinical injury early enough to guide timely intervention. This diagnostic gap underscores an urgent need for the development of advanced, multimodal precision diagnostic frameworks to enhance immune surveillance, which will be essential for standardizing clinical protocols and enabling pathogenesis-driven therapeutic intervention. This approach will inform both immunosuppressive regimens and future gene editing strategies aimed at engineering rejection-resistant porcine organs, ultimately prolonging graft survival. Broad adoption of such an integrative strategy will be essential to transition xenotransplantation from an experimental intervention into a safe, scalable and patient-centred clinical therapy. In this Review, we synthesize recent progress in xenotransplantation and position multimodal precision diagnostics as a pivotal strategy to address the remaining immunological and clinical barriers to widespread clinical implementation. Now that hyperacute rejection of pig xenografts can be reliably prevented, subtler immune-mediated graft injuries have emerged that conventional diagnostics often miss; a multimodal precision diagnostic framework is proposed to detect these injuries earlier, guide personalized immunosuppression and inform future gene editing strategies.

papers.title: Octupole-driven spin torque switching of antiferromagnetic tunnel junctions
papers.abstract: Magnetic tunnel junctions based on ferromagnets are canonical devices in spintronics, with wide-ranging applications in data storage, computing and sensing. They simultaneously exhibit mechanisms for electrical detection and control of magnetic order through the tunnelling magnetoresistance (TMR)1–5 and spin-transfer torque6–9 effects, respectively. It was long assumed that neither of these effects could be sizeable in all-antiferromagnetic tunnel junctions (AATJs), considering that they have no net magnetization. However, it was recently shown that AATJs based on chiral antiferromagnets do exhibit TMR due to their non-relativistic momentum-dependent spin polarization and cluster magnetic octupole moment, which are manifestations of their spin–split band structure10–13. However, the reciprocal effect, that is, the antiferromagnetic counterpart of spin–transfer torque, has been assumed non-existent due to the total electric current being spin-neutral. Here we report nanoscale AATJs that display this reciprocal effect, which we term octupole-driven spin-transfer torque (OTT). We demonstrate current-induced OTT switching of PtMn3|MgO|PtMn3 AATJs, with a TMR value of 363% at room temperature and switching current densities of the order of 10 MA cm–2. Our theoretical modelling explains the origin of OTT in terms of the imbalance between intra- and inter-sublattice spin currents across the AATJ, and, equivalently, in terms of the non-zero net cluster octupole polarization of each PtMn3 layer. This work establishes a new materials platform for antiferromagnetic spintronics and provides a pathway towards deeply scaled magnetic memory and room-temperature terahertz technologies. All-antiferromagnetic tunnel junctions can display both a large TMR and a reciprocal switching effect, octupole-driven spin-transfer torque, enabling nanoscale magnetic memory and potentially room-temperature terahertz spintronic devices.

papers.title: CD51 delineates functionally distinct astrocyte subtypes in neural circuits
papers.abstract: Astrocytes perform a diverse range of tasks that facilitate brain physiology, raising the possibility that these diverse astrocytic roles are enabled by functionally distinct subtypes1,2. Recent studies identified molecular diversity among astrocytes3; however, whether this molecular heterogeneity reflects specialized astrocyte subpopulations with distinct functions remains unclear. Here, on the basis of previous molecular and functional studies4, we generated a CD51-FLP mouse line that enables direct comparison of the functional properties between CD51+ and CD51− astrocyte subpopulations in neural circuits in vivo. We show that CD51+ and CD51− astrocytes have unique morphological, physiological and developmental properties in both the cortex and hippocampus. Functional studies demonstrate that CD51+ astrocytes selectively promote synapse formation in the developing cortex and circuit plasticity in the hippocampus. Mechanistically, we found that CD51+ astrocytes function through glypican 6 to promote synapse formation in the cortex, while CD51 itself drives circuit plasticity in the hippocampus. Applying these findings to brain injury, we found that CD51+ astrocytes promote functional recovery after stroke through enhanced synaptic remodelling. Taken together, our studies identify specialized astrocyte subpopulations that exhibit distinct functional properties in the developing, mature and injured brain. CD51+ astrocytes promote synapse formation in the developing cortex, circuit plasticity in the hippocampus and circuit remodelling after stroke.

papers.title: Amazon carbon emissions driven by human actions amplified by droughts
papers.abstract: The Amazon carbon sink is weakening as deforestation1–5, rising tree mortality6–8 and climate change disrupt the climatic conditions that sustain a humid tropical forest9–11. Forest loss reduces precipitation, increases temperatures and lengthens the dry season, driving higher carbon emissions1–4,11,12. Climate stress is stronger in more deforested regions, rendering forests progressively more flammable1,9,13. Large-scale climate events, such as El Niño, further amplify regional climate impacts9,14–17. Here we present an analysis of 15 years of Amazonian carbon fluxes derived from atmospheric CO2 measurements. We determine a carbon balance of 0.32 ± 0.08 PgC yr−1, with fires acting as the dominant source (0.40 ± 0.07 PgC yr−1) and forest uptake becoming increasingly unable to offset emissions. Furthermore, we investigate key drivers of the carbon emissions of Amazonia and identify three distinct year groups. Group 1 (2011–2014, 2017 and 2018) represents the role of the Amazon in the global carbon balance (0.11 ± 0.08 PgC yr−1) during wetter years with low human activity, such as deforestation, biomass burning and degradation. Group 2 (2019–2022) represents Amazon carbon emissions (0.43 ± 0.13 PgC yr−1) from human activities (mainly deforestation and degradation) during years with low climatic stress. Group 3 (2010, 2015, 2016, 2023 and 2024) has the highest carbon emissions (0.49 ± 0.07 PgC yr−1) and comprises warm and dry years (high climate stress), such as El Niño and the warming of the Tropical North Atlantic Ocean, associated with biomass burning. Fifteen years of atmospheric CO2 measurements show that the Amazon carbon sink is weakening, with fires, deforestation and climate stress driving increasingly high carbon emissions.

papers.title: WEE1 opposes APC/CCDH1 activity to promote S phase entry
papers.abstract: WEE1 phosphorylates and inhibits the activity of cyclin-dependent kinases to prevent mitotic entry and establish a G2 DNA damage checkpoint1–3. Consequently, WEE1 inhibitors have been developed to be synthetically lethal in TP53-mutated tumours that become reliant on this WEE1-mediated checkpoint, and such inhibitors are undergoing clinical trials. However, WEE1 inhibitors also have efficacy in TP53-wild-type tumours, and many trials have been terminated owing to high levels of toxic side effects, suggesting that WEE1 has unknown functions. Here we show that WEE1 promotes cell cycle re-entry from quiescence (G0) by opposing the activity of the E3 ubiquitin ligase, anaphase-promoting complex–cyclosome bound to CDH1 (APC/CCDH1). WEE1 phosphorylates CDH1 (FZR1) at key residues that mediate the interaction between CDH1 and APC/C. Cells with loss of function of WEE1 during G0/G1 have delayed S phase entry, impaired G1/S transition, abnormal S phase accumulation of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p21Cip1/Kip1 and a p21-dependent G2 arrest. Reduced expression of APC/CCDH1 or p21 renders cells more sensitive to acute WEE1 inhibition, and both pathways are downregulated in cells with acquired WEE1 inhibitor resistance. These results reveal a mechanism of cell cycle control that has implications for how WEE1 inhibitors should be used in the clinic. Experimental and modelling data indicate that WEE1 promotes re-entry of quiescent cells into the cell cycle, potentially explaining the toxic side effects of WEE1 inhibitors in cancer therapies.

papers.title: Touch-sensing digital pixel fibre enables interactive garment GUI
papers.abstract: Wearable computing promises to transform human interaction with information, yet conventional graphical user interfaces (GUIs) rely on planar, rigid displays incompatible with textiles, which are composed of one-dimensional fibres. Despite recent progress1,2 in flexible and fibre-based displays, bridging this fundamental dimensional mismatch remains challenging because existing approaches do not naturally provide the digitally addressable, high-throughput, information-rich interfaces required for interactive GUIs. Here we present a digital pixel fibre integrating addressable pixels, a common propagation-axis interconnection for scalable in-fibre circuitry and a coaxial sensing layer for fibre-level touch localization. Microelectronic components and a touch-gated resistive path system form a linear circuit that acts as both an interactive display backbone and a computational bus, while peripheral multimodal fibre sensors and actuators enable physiological, inertial, optical, and acoustic input and output. We integrate these fibres into the forearm portion of a garment sleeve to realize a GUI with a 96 × 54-pixel display, 30-frame-per-second refresh rate and 8-bit colour depth. It supports dynamic graphics, integrated audio–video playback, wireless data exchange and interactive computing functions, while maintaining the flexibility, washability, breathability and mechanical robustness of everyday textiles. By merging display, sensing and computation within a single fibre, this work establishes a scalable platform for intrinsically interactive textiles, opening pathways toward garments that operate as fully integrated computational systems. Multifunctional digital fibres integrate display, touch sensing, computation and multimodal input–output, enabling flexible, washable garments with interactive graphical interfaces and wireless multimedia capabilities.

papers.title: Enzyme-embedded polyesters for accelerated biodegradation in the deep sea
papers.abstract: The accumulation of persistent plastics in the ocean is causing wide-ranging environmental problems1–3. Some commercially available compostable plastics4–7, developed to address these issues, degrade efficiently under industrial composting conditions; however, their degradation in marine environments, particularly in the deep sea, remains limited8–10. Here we demonstrate that thermally embedding enzymes into compostable polyesters (poly(butylene succinate) (PBS), poly(butylene succinate-co-adipate) (PBSA), poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) and poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT)) significantly accelerates their degradation in both coastal and deep-sea environments from water depths of 2–6 m to 5,503 m. Enzyme-embedded polyesters achieved near-complete degradation at a deep-sea depth of 757 m within 5 months. Furthermore, moderate biodegradation of enzyme-embedded polyesters was observed under extreme conditions on deep-sea floors of 5,503 m. In coastal seawater, films embedded with trace amounts (0.1 wt%) of enzyme underwent rapid degradation. The mechanical properties of enzyme-embedded polyesters were similar to those of enzyme-free polyesters. Chemical analysis confirmed the formation of low-molecular-mass degradation products and biochemical oxygen demand measurements supported the mineralization of the enzyme-embedded polyesters. The enzyme-embedding strategy enables enhanced marine degradation of compostable polyesters and represents a potential solution to marine plastic pollution. Near-complete deep-sea degradation of enzyme-embedded compostable polyesters shows that thermal enzyme embedding greatly accelerates breakdown across marine environments while preserving material performance, offering a promising strategy to mitigate persistent ocean plastic pollution.

papers.title: Zeolite-catalysed olefin carbonylation based on tuning spatial confinement
papers.abstract: Carbonylation is an important process used to produce aldehydes, carboxylic acids and esters1–5 that is usually catalysed by homogeneous metal complexes with ligands and iodide promoters6–12. Koch has reported that protons of mineral acids can also catalyse carbonylation13. Previous studies have demonstrated that Brønsted acidic zeolites can act as a heterogeneous, Koch-type catalyst for carbonylation of alcohols and olefins, but the products in this case are limited to tertiary carboxylic acids14–18. Here we show that targeted use of spatial confinement in a zeolite together with a high CO/olefin ratio can help break this limitation. We report that, with FER zeolite and a CO/olefin ratio of 360, olefin carbonylation can produce primary and secondary carboxylic acids as the main products; ethylene carbonylation to propanoic acid (PA) is achieved with 80% selectivity over 100 h and propylene carbonylation to isobutyric acid (IBA) is achieved with 95% selectivity over 750 h. The propylene and ethylene carbonylation selectivities decrease to 61% and 57%, respectively, as the CO/olefin ratio decreases to 24 and 90, respectively. Experiments in combination with theoretical calculations suggest that T2-O5 in eight-membered ring (8-MR) cavities of FER zeolite are the primary active sites for ethylene carbonylation and T3-O1 in ten-membered rings (10-MRs) are the primary active sites for propylene carbonylation. Our findings open new directions for olefin carbonylation and provide critical insights into the prerequisites for developing new zeolite-based carbonylation processes. The use of zeolites with an appropriate pore structure combined with a high CO/olefin ratio is shown to catalyse olefin carbonylation and produce primary and secondary carboxylic acids as the main products.
