papers.title: IL-2-producing TFH cells sustain Treg cell homeostasis and immune tolerance in the gut
papers.abstract: Follicular helper T (TFH) cells are well known for their role in supporting B cell responses. Here, we identify a critical B cell-independent function for TFH cells in sustaining regulatory T (Treg) cells within gut-associated lymphoid tissues (GALT). We demonstrate that TFH cells produce interleukin-2 (IL-2) at the T cell–B cell border and within interfollicular regions and that this localized IL-2 is required to maintain GALT Treg cell homeostasis and restrain the expansion of pathogenic effector T cells. Mice selectively lacking IL-2-producing TFH cells develop colitis and fatal multiorgan inflammation, driven by impaired GALT Treg cell responses and uncontrolled effector T cell activation. Broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment alleviates both intestinal and extraintestinal pathology, indicating that loss of tolerance to commensal-derived antigens is a key driver of disease. Together, these findings define a spatially restricted TFH cell-derived IL-2 niche critical for GALT Treg cell stability and uncover an unexpected immunoregulatory role for TFH cells in maintaining gastrointestinal tolerance beyond B cell help. Ballesteros-Tato and colleagues identify a spatially restricted follicular helper T cell-dependent interleukin-2 niche critical for regulatory T cell stability in gut-associated lymphoid tissues.

papers.title: Genome-wide analyses identify 60 loci associated with liver triglyceride content
papers.abstract: We performed a large-scale genome-wide association study meta-analysis of magnetic resonance imaging-derived liver triglyceride content across 71,488 European-ancestry participants from the UK Biobank, approximately doubling the sample size of previous genome-wide association studies1. We identified 60 independent loci, including 31 not previously reported, and estimated the single nucleotide polymorphism-based heritability of liver triglyceride content at 25%. Integrative fine-mapping and gene-prioritization analyses nominated candidate effector genes for 48 loci. Of the 31 newly identified variants, 14 were validated in meta-analyses of clinically diagnosed metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (42,163 cases and 1,646,254 controls). People in the highest versus lowest decile of a polygenic risk score for liver triglyceride content had 2.71-fold higher odds of cirrhosis and 7.47-fold higher odds of hepatocellular carcinoma. Plasma proteins associated with the liver triglyceride polygenic risk score were enriched for metabolic remodeling and inflammatory pathways, with liver-enriched protein signatures increasing and visceral adipose signatures decreasing with higher genetic risk. Together, these findings refine the genetic architecture of liver triglyceride content, linking polygenic susceptibility to downstream metabolic and inflammatory pathways and providing insights into the genetic basis of steatotic liver disease. Genome-wide association analyses of liver triglyceride content in 71,488 UK Biobank participants identify 60 independent loci and yield polygenic scores correlated with higher risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.

papers.title: Leveraging genomic deep learning models for the prediction of noncoding variant effects
papers.abstract: Characterizing noncoding variant function remains an important challenge in human genetics. Genomic deep learning models have emerged as a promising approach to enable in silico prediction of variant effects. These models include supervised sequence-to-activity models, which predict molecular phenotypes such as genome-wide chromatin states or gene expression levels directly from DNA sequence, and self-supervised genomic language models. Here we review progress in leveraging these models for noncoding variant effect prediction. We describe practical considerations for making such predictions and categorize the types of ground-truth data used to evaluate variant effect predictions, providing insight into the settings in which current models are most useful. Our Review highlights key considerations for practitioners and opportunities for improvement in model development and evaluation. This Review outlines progress in leveraging genomic deep learning models for the prediction of noncoding variant effects in humans, highlighting key considerations for practitioners, current performance trends and opportunities for improvement.

papers.title: The rise of reducing reagent-resistant TfR1 dimer marks ferroptosis
papers.abstract: Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent type of cell death caused by excessive membrane lipid peroxidation. It remains a challenge to detect ferroptotic cells, especially in in vivo settings, hindering translational studies. Here we discover that a reducing reagent-resistant (3R) dimer of the transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1) is a highly specific indicator for lipid peroxidation. The 3R dimer is elevated in cells when ferroptosis is induced, either by pharmacological agents or by genetic perturbations. Furthermore, the 3R dimer can be used to detect disease-associated ferroptosis in tissue and in extracellular vesicles isolated from mouse or patient plasma. Given the near-ubiquitous expression of TfR1, we posit that the 3R dimer may function as a ferroptosis marker with widespread potential utility for basic and translational studies. He et al. report the upregulation of a reducing reagent-resistant form of the transferrin receptor 1 dimer during lipid peroxidation and demonstrate its utility in detecting ferroptosis in tissue lysates and extracellular vesicles from mice and humans.

papers.title: Molecular control of bacterial immunity
papers.abstract: Phage infection places strong selective pressure on bacteria to mount a rapid immune response to ensure survival. Although recent studies have uncovered a wide diversity of bacterial immune systems, how these systems function under the tight time constraints of phage infection remains poorly understood. Here we summarize structural, biochemical and genetic insights into bacterial immunity, focusing on steps that link infection sensing to activation and effector function. We highlight how conformational change, protein assembly and spatial organization shape immune activation, and how phages employ counter-defense strategies that disrupt these processes. In this Review, the authors summarize structural, biochemical and genetic insights into bacterial immunity, focusing on steps that link infection sensing to activation and effector function.

papers.title: Architecture of the Norrin signaling complex and structure-guided surrogate design
papers.abstract: Norrin binds Frizzled 4 (FZD4), tetraspanin 12 (TSPAN12) and low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 5 (LRP5) to regulate angiogenesis and the integrity of the blood–brain barrier and inner blood–retina barrier (BRB). Aberrant Norrin signal causes retinopathies, BRB defects and deafness. Therapeutic mimetics of Norrin are currently in clinical trials for eye diseases. To characterize the mechanism of Norrin signal biogenesis, we determined the structure of a Norrin–FZD4–TSPAN12–LRP5 signaling complex using a de novo designed FZD4 binder as a ‘protein glue’. Our structure shows that two curved Norrin homodimers bridge two FZD4–TSPAN12 heterodimers. LRP5LA3 simultaneously interacts with TSPAN12 and two Norrin homodimers, positioning the cytosolic FZD4 and LRP5 tails for signal activation. On the basis of our findings, we designed FZD4CRD–LRP5LA3 bispecific binders that act as Norrin surrogates. Our signaling assays showed that oligomerization of the Norrin surrogate enhances signaling potency. Thus, this work reveals how the Norrin signal is generated and may assist in the development of Norrin/Wnt mimetics. Hu, Li et al. uncover how Norrin assembles Frizzled 4, tetraspanin 12 and low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 5 into a signaling complex and use this structural insight to design potent Norrin surrogates, providing a framework for developing therapies for retinal vascular diseases.

papers.title: Cooling water to near freezing breaks the activity–stability trade-off of water oxidation electrocatalysis
papers.abstract: Temperature is a fundamental parameter in reaction kinetics, typically accelerating rates according to the Arrhenius law. In catalytic systems, however, competing pathways often respond differently to temperature, allowing the selective promotion of desired reactions while suppressing undesired ones through temperature modulation. Here we show that regulating the temperature near the freezing point of water can resolve the activity–stability trade-off in the oxygen evolution reaction on manganese dioxide. Although lowering the temperature decreases water oxidation rates, catalyst degradation through permanganate formation is suppressed more effectively, extending catalyst lifetime. Counterintuitively, further cooling below 0 °C accelerates permanganate formation, yielding an optimum temperature near 0 °C that balances activity and stability. This anti-Arrhenius behaviour, arising from electrolyte supercooling, is a rare example of anomalous temperature-dependent electrocatalysis under subzero conditions. Our findings highlight temperature regulation as a viable strategy for enhancing catalytic lifetime, with implications for electrochemical systems operating in wintertime and in polar and extraterrestrial environments. Temperature can influence competing catalytic pathways differently, but its role in balancing electrocatalytic activity and stability remains underexplored. Now it has been shown that cooling water to near freezing selectively suppresses manganese dioxide dissolution, extending water oxidation lifetime and revealing anomalous subzero kinetics.

Universal platform for rapid green surface functionalization of diverse porous membranes for sustainable water treatment
papers.abstract: Surface engineering is pivotal for tailoring membranes to complex water treatment processes, yet conventional strategies often involve multiple steps, toxic reagents, structural alteration, or specialized equipment. Here, we report a rapid, green, and universal surface modification strategy using Fenton-catalyzed hydrogel coating. Within minutes, an ultrathin cross-linked polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) network forms on porous membranes with diverse chemistries, pore sizes, and surface properties without altering their original pore architecture or porosity. The robust coating resists acid, alkali, heat, ultrasonication, and repeated folding. It enhances hydrophilicity, underwater superoleophobicity, and antifouling performance against oil-in-water emulsions, humic acid, and bovine serum albumin. The PVP network also enables uniform and stable deposition of carbon nanotubes, graphitic carbon nitride, MXene nanosheets, and titanium dioxide nanoparticles. The resulting composite membranes exhibit excellent long-term desalination performance. This simple, scalable, and eco-friendly platform provides a versatile route to advanced functional membranes for sustainable water treatment and resource recovery. Surface engineering is pivotal for designing water treatment membranes, though often requires unfavorable reagents and complex, time consuming procedures. Here, the authors develop a rapid and green surface-engineering strategy based on a modified polyvinylpyrrolidone network for water treatment membranes.

Mathematical modeling and experiments reveal that promiscuous SMAD heterocomplex formation redirects BMP-associated mediators toward TGF-β transcriptional targets, providing a computational mechanism for integrating conflicting signals and controlling cell fate.

papers.title: Small-molecule modulation of VDAC enhances glucose-stimulated insulin secretion by promoting ATP flux
papers.abstract: Enhancing insulin secretion is a major therapeutic strategy for diabetes. Matsunaga et al. identify DPEU, a small molecule that promotes mitochondrial ATP export through VDACs to enhance glucose-stimulated insulin secretion. Their findings establish VDAC-mediated ATP flux as a therapeutic mechanism for potentiating insulin secretion.

papers.title: Gut-derived glucagon-like peptides attenuate T cell-induced intestinal injury
papers.abstract: Koehler et al. demonstrate distinct physiological roles for GLP-1R and GLP-2R signaling in protecting the intestine from αCD3-induced enteropathy. Conversely, GLP-1R/GLP-2R agonists, administered separately or together, attenuate the heightened intestinal damage induced by T cell activation in mice with selective loss of intestinal proglucagon gene expression.

papers.title: The next click in antibody drug conjugate development
CD47 fuels intestinal fibrosis by inducing fibroblast phagocytic evasion and represents a therapeutic target
papers.abstract: CD47 marks a pathogenic fibroblast state in intestinal fibrosis, creating a phagocytic-evasion niche with macrophages via IL-1β crosstalk. Blocking this checkpoint restores macrophage clearance of fibroblasts and attenuates fibrosis, establishing CD47-SIRPα as a therapeutic target for Crohn’s disease complications.

papers.title: 20 years of iPSCs: From cellular reprogramming to clinical translation
From genome editing to chromosome engineering in plants
papers.abstract: Engineering large genomic segments is rapidly expanding the scope of plant genome manipulation from individual genes to chromosome-scale redesign. Recent advances in double-strand break-, prime-editing-, recombinase-, and transposase-based technologies now enable programmable deletion, insertion, replacement, duplication, inversion, and translocation of DNA fragments ranging from kilobases to megabases. In this review, we summarize the major strategies for large-fragment genome engineering in plants, compare their strengths and limitations, and discuss their applications in both fundamental plant biology and crop breeding. We further highlight that the integration of artificial intelligence is catalyzing the rapid optimization of large-fragment genome engineering. The ongoing transition from genome editing to chromosome engineering promises to revolutionize crop breeding and plant synthetic biology, ultimately enabling rational design of plant genomes.

papers.title: Modular in vivo engineering of the reductive methylaspartate cycles for synthetic CO2 fixation
papers.abstract: Rainaldi et al. design and computationally analyze four synthetic carbon-fixation cycles, two of which have higher theoretical biomass yield than existing alternatives. Using growth-coupled selection in Escherichia coli, they validate different modules, achieve CO2-dependent growth via the fastest known carboxylase, and establish a fourth pathway for acetate assimilation.

papers.title: Data storage with amino acid sequences
papers.abstract: Amino acid sequences in peptides and proteins can be used to store data with the advantages of high capacity and stability, offering a solution for storing ever-increasing amounts of data. Compared with peptides, proteins have longer sequences and can be produced at a much lower cost, enabling more efficient data storage and allowing specific functions to be incorporated using established protein techniques. Although data storage using peptides and proteins has been demonstrated, challenges related to cost, throughput, error rates, data density, and scalability remain to be addressed. Emerging technologies to overcome these challenges are under active development, and their successful commercialization could drive a paradigm shift, enabling high-density and very long-term data storage.

papers.title: Europe and the rest of the world must come up with an answer to US science strategy
Bundle water safeguards into critical-mineral licences
Nobel-prizewinning breakthroughs can emerge from neglected organisms
Conservation planning should follow animal clocks
Nepal’s disaster is an urgent wake-up call
Will this sleep-disorder drug be the next big blockbuster?
Direct observation of the Lindhard continuum using resonant inelastic X-ray scattering
papers.abstract: Understanding the excitations of quantum materials is essential for unraveling how their microscopic constituents interact. Among these, particle-hole excitations form a particularly important class, as they govern fundamental processes such as screening, dissipation, and transport. In metals, the continuum of electron-hole excitations is described by the Lindhard function. Although central to the theory of Fermi liquids, the corresponding Lindhard continuum has remained experimentally elusive. Here we report its direct observation in the weakly correlated metal MgB2 using ultra-soft resonant inelastic X-ray scattering. We resolve a linearly dispersing excitation with velocity comparable to the Fermi velocity and find quantitative agreement with simulations of the non-interacting charge susceptibility. A detailed analysis and decomposition of the simulations reveal the intra-band origin of this low-energy excitation, confirming it as the Lindhard continuum. Our results establish ultra-soft resonant inelastic X-ray scattering as a momentum-resolved probe of the fermiology in metals. In metals, the continuum of electron-hole excitations is described by the Lindhard function. Here, the authors directly observe the corresponding Lindhard continuum in the weakly correlated metal MgB2 using ultra-soft resonant inelastic X-ray scattering.

papers.title: Three-photon population imaging of subcortical brain regions
papers.abstract: Monitoring large-scale neuronal activity in deep brain circuits is crucial for understanding the principles of brain function. However, existing large-scale cellular-resolution imaging techniques are limited in imaging depth and cannot monitor activity in areas deeper than the cortex in the intact brain. To address this challenge, we developed a Large Imaging Field of view Three-photon (LIFT) microscope with a FOV of > 3 mm2. LIFT combines high-numerical-aperture optimized sampling, using a custom scanning module, with deep learning-based denoising, to enable population imaging in subcortical brain regions of mice and deep cortical regions of rats. We demonstrate calcium imaging in the intact mouse brain from more than 1500 cells across CA1, the surrounding white matter, and adjacent deep layers of the cortex, and show population imaging with high SNR at a depth of 1.2 mm in the rat cortex. The LIFT microscope offers versatility in imaging scale and rate and was built entirely from off-the-shelf components. Imaging large cell populations below the cortex in the intact brain is key for understanding brain function. LIFT, a multiscale three-photon microscope, tracks activity in over 1,500 cells across the hippocampus and adjacent regions in behaving mice.

papers.title: A prefrontal–bed nucleus pathway controls aversive memory specificity independently of glucocorticoids
papers.abstract: Adaptive memory requires balancing generalization to avoid similar threats with discrimination to recognize safety. The prevailing view is that stress-induced increases in glucocorticoids underlie the enhancement of memory consolidation, strengthening memories and promoting their generalization—referred to here as the standard model. However, circuits that drive memory consolidation often also regulate glucocorticoid release, confounding whether their effects on memory are circuit-driven or hormonally mediated. Here we identify a prefrontal pathway that controls memory specificity independently of glucocorticoids. Using optogenetic manipulations in male rats, we found that post-training inhibition of the rostral prelimbic cortex (rPL) to anteroventral bed nuclei of the stria terminalis (avBST) pathway promoted contextual generalization in an inhibitory avoidance discrimination task without affecting memory strength. Although this manipulation further elevated corticosterone, it produced generalization even in adrenalectomized rats, demonstrating glucocorticoid independence. Conversely, post-training pathway excitation enhanced contextual discrimination. Recordings of calcium signals revealed context-specific engagement of both avBST and avBST-projecting rPL neurons during memory retrieval, with greater responses in the neutral than the aversive context. These findings reveal glucocorticoid-independent circuit control of memory specificity, setting boundary conditions on the standard model and demonstrating mechanistic heterogeneity that may inform stress-related disorders where memory generalization is a core feature. Overgeneralizing aversive memories to safe contexts is a feature of stress-related disorders. Here, authors show that a prefrontal–bed nucleus pathway controls the specificity of aversive memories independently of glucocorticoids.

papers.title: Strong field spectroscopy of many-body interactions in solids
papers.abstract: High-order harmonic generation (HHG) in solids offers a promising route to compact ultrafast sources of quantum light, but its efficiency and coherence are limited by ultrafast dephasing of laser-driven electron–hole polarization. Although widely described by a phenomenological coherence time, the microscopic origin of this dephasing has remained unresolved. Here, we combine wavelength-dependent HHG measurements in monolayer and bulk semiconductors with ab initio many-body calculations of electron–phonon scattering and strong-field simulations. We show that the measured wavelength scaling of the HHG yield is quantitatively reproduced only when semiconductor Bloch equations incorporate momentum-dependent dephasing derived from first principles scattering rates. The calculations reveal that strong-field-driven carriers rapidly enter regions of the Brillouin zone with enhanced electron–phonon scattering, giving rise to effective few-femtosecond dephasing. Our results establish a microscopic foundation for dephasing in solid-state HHG and provide a framework for engineering coherence in strongly driven solids for quantum photonic applications. Despite numerous studies on solid-state high-harmonic generation (HHG), there is a lack of microscopic understanding of decoherence effects. Here, the authors study experimentally and by real-time ab-initio simulations the wavelength dependence of HHG in monolayer films, promoting momentum-resolved electron-phonon scattering as the dominant many-body interaction causing ultrafast decoherence.

papers.title: Balancing the Performance Trade-off of Polymer Blends with Heterogeneously Dispersed Nanodomains via Reactive Processing
papers.abstract: Polymer blends are ubiquitous though there are persistent material-property trade-offs, due to the limitation of structural design. Here we report a reactive processing strategy that creates heterogeneously dispersed nano-domains (hDNs) of rubbery ethylene-acrylic ester-glycidyl methacrylate terpolymer (EGMA) in polyoxymethylene (POM) matrix. Pre-reactive blending of EGMA with poly (L-lactide) (PLLA) and subsequent melt processing with POM result in formation of the unique morphology, where PLLA serving as the leveraging forces for opposing uniform distribution via chemical bonds and macro-phase separation by physical associations. The resulting materials exhibited optimized mechanical performance impossible to be acquired with conventional counterparts. This work identifies herein innovates how reactive processing can regulate phase morphology while balancing the trade-off among toughness, ductility, strength and stiffness in multicomponent polymer blends, representing a paradigm shift in narrowing gap between structure and tailor-made property towards pilot plant scale. Polymer blends are ubiquitous though there are persistent material-property trade-offs, due to structural design. Here the authors design multicomponent polymers optimizing the material properties.

papers.title: Nutrient stress-driven ACSS1 controls metabolic flexibility and bone formation
papers.abstract: Metabolic dysregulation under nutrient stress disrupts bone homeostasis. Although acetate metabolism is linked to diabetes and alcoholism, its role in the skeletal complications of these conditions remains unknown. Here we identify acetyl-CoA synthetase 1 (ACSS1) as a key stress responder that mediates mitonuclear communication in bone marrow skeletal stem cells. ACSS1-driven rewiring of acetate metabolism impairs cellular metabolic flexibility, mitochondrial function, and osteogenesis. Mechanistically, nutrient excess from glucose, alcohol or acetate upregulates ACSS1 via a mitochondrial ROS activated integrated stress response-CEBPB pathway. Maladaptive ACSS1 accumulation enforces excessive acetyl-CoA production from either exogenous or glucose/ethanol-derived endogenous acetate, promoting mitochondrial protein hyperacetylation specifically inactivating ME2 via lysine 94 acetylation. This ACSS1-triggered ME2 inactivation disturbs the malate-aspartate shuttle, leading to a self-perpetuating cycle of redox imbalance and oxidative stress that exacerbates mitochondrial dysfunction and osteogenic impairment. Importantly, genetic deletion of Acss1 or AAV-delivered non-acetylatable ME2 mutant in osteoprogenitor cells restores mitochondrial resilience, osteogenic capacity, and bone formation, protecting against osteoporosis or osteonecrosis in male mouse models of type 2 diabetes and chronic alcohol consumption. These results unveil an essential role for ACSS1 in controlling metabolic flexibility and osteogenesis, identifying ACSS1 as a potential therapeutic target for metabolic stress-related bone disorders. ACSS1 mediates maladaptive mitonuclear communication under nutrient stress, impairing metabolic flexibility and osteogenesis. Targeting ACSS1 preserves bone integrity in diabetic and alcoholic mice by sustaining bone formation.

papers.title: Production of abundant defective viral genomes by an insect-specific alphavirus revealed by nanopore sequencing
papers.abstract: Defective viral genomes (DVGs) shape virus-host interactions and evolution, yet remain poorly characterized in insect-specific viruses. Using Nanopore direct RNA sequencing (DRS), we profile full-length RNA species of Eilat virus (EILV), a mosquito-restricted alphavirus. We found that EILV produces abundant deletion-type DVGs far exceeding those seen in related arboviruses under identical conditions. These DVGs retain intact terminal sequences with conserved junction motifs. A modified DRS approach reveals widespread premature termination during EILV genomic RNA synthesis, linking DVG formation to reduced replicase processivity. Notably, a subset of DVGs is selectively replicated and packaged, accumulating over serial passages and interfering with parental virus replication. Our findings uncover an intrinsic, high DVG-generating capacity in EILV, linking low-processivity RNA synthesis with increased genomic plasticity. This suggests that elevated DVG production may be an adaptive mechanism, providing important insights into alphavirus evolution and replication fidelity in insect-specific RNA viruses. Using Nanopore direct RNA sequencing, authors show Eilat virus has abundant deletion-type defective viral genomes; delineating it from other arthropod-borne alphaviruses. This is likely driven by low replicase processivity and premature termination.

papers.title: Terahertz emission by X-ray difference-frequency generation
papers.abstract: Nonlinear interactions between X-rays and matter represent a new frontier in ultrafast science. However, X-ray difference-frequency generation (DFG)—a fundamental second-order nonlinear optical process—has not been experimentally observed until now. Here, we report the first observation of terahertz emission induced by hard X-ray free-electron laser (XFEL) pulses in solids, providing evidence for X-ray DFG. Using 10-fs, 10-keV XFEL pulses incident on ZnTe, we detected terahertz emission arising from wave mixing between different spectral components within the XFEL bandwidth. The emitted terahertz waves originate from second-order nonlinear polarization evolving on a femtosecond timescale. The polarization and angular dependences of the terahertz emission confirm that X-ray DFG is mediated not only by DFG without spatial inversion symmetry but also by DFG with spatial inversion symmetry. Quantitative analysis yields a DFG susceptibility ratio of the former to the latter of 58±4%, and the generation efficiency for 10 keV excitation is approximately 1% of that for near-infrared 1.55 eV excitation in the 100-μm-thick ZnTe crystal, while the intrinsic response normalized by interaction length is comparable. These results establish XFEL-induced terahertz emission as a general platform for probing second-order X-ray nonlinearities and ultrafast polarization dynamics in solids. The authors show that hard X-ray free-electron laser (XFEL) pulses generate terahertz emission in ZnTe through X-ray difference-frequency generation (DFG). The findings establish a route to probing second-order X-ray nonlinearity and ultrafast polarization dynamics in solids.

papers.title: Comprehensive spectroscopic analysis of energy inversion of the lowest singlet and triplet excited states in the heptazine HzTFEX2
papers.abstract: Detailed photophysical measurements of the non-symmetric heptazine, HzTFEX2, previously reported as having inverted S1-T1 levels, show complex behaviour, highly dependent on environment, concentration and aggregation. Here we show that, single crystals of HzTFEX2 show anti-Kasha S0←S2 and excimer emission. Solution state absorption shows a hypsochromic shift of the π-π* S0→S1, linearly dependent on solvent polarizability. In most environments, emission is dominated by excimer species, only in toluene and frozen 2-MeTHF do monomeric properties dominate. In frozen solutions, aggregation phenomena are solvent dependent. Given such complexity, time-dependent emission spectra are crowded, making it difficult to resolve monomeric phosphorescence. However, by exciting S0→S2 at 77 K, we observe a consistent phosphorescence signal at 425 nm, 110 ± 20 meV above the S0←S1 emission, whereas exciting S0→S1 does not give phosphorescence or delayed fluorescence (DF). We conclude that coupling between S2 and S1 is very weak, S2-TN intersystem crossing is effective, whereas S1↔T1 intersystem crossing is thermally activated, fulfilling the conditions required for the observation of inverted phosphorescence. At room temperature, no long-lived DF is observed because exothermic T1→S1 ISC becomes allowed, such that in an OLED, high efficiency can be achieved. Through a comprehensive photophysical investigation, the conditions enabling the observation of phosphorescence from a substituted heptazine, HzTFEX2, have been elucidated so that the inversion of its singlet and triplet states is shown experimentally.

papers.title: The Emirati pangenome featuring a diploid chromosome-level reference
papers.abstract: Reference genomes are essential for identifying and representing human genomic variation, yet single-genome sequences fail to capture population-specific diversity. We present the Emirati pangenome comprising a trio-based, diploid chromosome-level assembly from deep, multi-platform sequencing data and 57 additional high-quality HiFi sequencing-based chromosome-scale assemblies, 27 of which are trio-based. Haplotypes demonstrate high contiguity (median N50 of 151.9 Mb) and good base accuracy (median QV score of 59.31). Of all assembled chromosomes, 31.8% are telomere-to-telomere (T2T) scaffolds (chromosome-spanning sequences flanked by telomeric repeats at both ends), and 64.3% achieved chromosome-level continuity (single scaffolds spanning an entire chromosome but retaining one or more sequence gaps or lacking a telomeric signature at one or both ends). These assemblies form the foundation of the population-specific pangenome graph of the Emirati Reference Genome Project (ERGP), which captures genomic variation comparable to the globally diverse HPRC reference graph, while covering regionally enriched variation. Applying the ERGP pangenome to short‑read genotyping of an independent Emirati cohort revealed structural variant sites in linkage disequilibrium with phenotype‑associated GWAS variants, demonstrating the value of population-graph-based variant inference. The ERGP reference complements human pangenomes and provides a critical foundation for population-specific genomics and precision medicine in the United Arab Emirates. Here the authors present a chromosome-level Emirati pangenome, capturing population-specific genetic diversity and improving the detection of genomic variants. The resource will support more accurate genetic research and precision medicine in the United Arab Emirates.

papers.title: G-quadruplex structures affect the immune response to bacterial infection in mouse macrophages
papers.abstract: Macrophages orchestrate immunity via transcriptional reprogramming, largely controlled by the master regulator NF-κB. However, mechanisms of promoter selection remain enigmatic. Here, we reveal that DNA secondary structures called G-quadruplexes (G4s) modulate the macrophage transcriptome during inflammation. By investigating the G4 ligand pyridostatin (PDS) in lipopolysaccharide-stimulated macrophages, we establish that G4 stabilization significantly decreases the inflammatory response without affecting mitochondrial metabolism or pathogen clearance. Instead, NF-κB-dependent transcription of activation markers and proinflammatory cytokines is selectively repressed. Using chromatin accessibility profiling, NF-κB ChIP, and in silico predictions, we demonstrate that G4 stabilization sterically hinders NF-κB promoter occupancy. Furthermore, PDS stabilizes transient, transcription-induced G4s, prematurely shutting down transcription and reverting local chromatin to a dormant state. Thus, G4 formation represents a potential strategy to modulate dysregulated macrophage activation. G-quadruplexes (G4) are dynamic nucleic acid structures regulating various cellular functions. Here, the authors show that G4 formation sterically inhibits NF-κB-driven activation of pro-inflammatory genes, such as Il1b, acting as structural checkpoint to limit macrophage inflammatory responses.

papers.title: Anterior cingulate input tunes striatal dynamics for context-dependent social preference in a mouse model of autism
papers.abstract: Social preference in autism spectrum disorder varies across contexts, but the underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear. Here we show that Shank3 knockout (KO) mice, an autism mouse model, exhibit reduced preference for social over nonsocial stimuli while retaining a preference for females over males. Calcium imaging reveals context-dependent differences between KO and wild-type (WT) mice in the organization of neuronal population dynamics in the dorsomedial striatum (DMS), corresponding to their behavioural preferences. Functional imaging and molecular analyses reveal reduced functional connectivity between the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and DMS and molecular alterations more pronounced in the striatal matrix. ACC inhibition eliminates genotype-dependent differences in DMS dynamics. Inhibiting the ACC–DMS pathway impairs social preference, whereas its activation in KO mice shifts DMS dynamics towards WT patterns and improves social preference. These findings identify a cortical pathway that shapes striatal population dynamics and context-dependent social preference in an autism mouse model. The mechanisms underlying social behavioural deficits in mouse models of autism are not fully understood. Here the authors link neural embedding geometry to context-dependent social deficits in the Shank3 knockout mouse.

papers.title: Terahertz field-induced giant symmetry modulations in a van der Waals antiferromagnet
papers.abstract: Strong-field terahertz (THz) excitations enable dynamic control over electronic, lattice and symmetry degrees of freedom in quantum materials. Here, we uncover pronounced terahertz-induced symmetry modulations and coherent phonon dynamics in the van der Waals antiferromagnet MnPS3, in which inversion symmetry is broken by its antiferromagnetic spin configuration. Our time-resolved second harmonic generation measurements reveal long-lived giant oscillations in the antiferromagnetic phase, with amplitudes comparable to the equilibrium signal, driven by phonons involving percent-level atomic displacements relative to the equilibrium bond lengths. The temporal evolution of the rotational anisotropy patterns indicates a dynamic breaking of mirror symmetry, modulated by two vibrational modes at 1.7 THz and 4.5 THz, with the former corresponding to a hidden mode not observed in equilibrium spectroscopy. These effects arise in part from a field-induced charge rearrangement mechanism that lowers the local crystal symmetry and couples to the phonon modes. We uncover a long-lived field-driven response with a complex THz polarization dependence, consistent with a metastable state of reduced symmetry. Through comparison with simulations, we interpret this response in terms of a potential antiferromagnetic-to-ferrimagnetic transition. Our results establish an effective field-tunable pathway for driving excitations otherwise weak in equilibrium. Strong terahertz excitation can be used to drive the collective phases of materials. Here, Haque et al use time-resolved second harmonic generation measurements to track the evolution of the antiferromagnetic state of MnPS3 when subjected to strong terahertz light.

papers.title: Fatty acids in the tumor microenvironment reprogram neutrophils to induce adenosine-mediated immunosuppression in mice
papers.abstract: As solid tumors progress, the tumor microenvironment becomes increasingly immunosuppressive, impairing cytotoxic T-cell activity and limiting the efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade. However, the mechanistic drivers of this immunosuppression remain poorly understood. Here, we identify a tumor-derived lipid–neutrophil–adenosine axis as a critical regulator of immune suppression in advanced colorectal cancer (CRC). We show that fatty acids enriched in tumor interstitial fluid reprogram neutrophils toward an immunosuppressive phenotype through PPARα activation, upregulation of CD39 and CD73, and adenosine generation, ultimately leading to T-cell suppression. AB928, a dual A2aR/A2bR adenosine receptor antagonist currently in clinical trials, restores T-cell proliferation, effector function, and tumor-killing capacity in vitro and in vivo. Importantly, AB928 synergizes with anti-PD-1 therapy to enhance survival in an immunotherapy-resistant autochthonous model of metastatic CRC. Thus, our findings define a metabolic immune evasion mechanism in the microenvironment and provide a rationale for targeting neutrophil-derived adenosine signaling to improve immunotherapy responses in CRC. Lipid accumulation in solid tumors supports tumor progression by promoting immune evasion. Yet the molecular basis of this lipid-mediated immunosuppression remains unclear. Here, using murine models of advanced colorectal cancer, the authors uncover a metabolic-immune axis whereby tumor-derived fatty acids activate neutrophil PPARα, resulting in adenosine generation and T cell suppression. Importantly, treatment with a dual adenosine receptor antagonist restores T cell-mediated antitumor immunity and synergizes with anti-PD-1 therapy to enhance animal survival.

papers.title: Divergent anaerobic fates of biodegradable plastics in landfill leachate
papers.abstract: Biodegradable plastics (BPs) are increasingly promoted as sustainable alternatives to conventional polymers, yet their fate in landfills remains poorly understood. Here, we evaluated the anaerobic biodegradability of three BPs, polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB), poly(lactic acid) (PLA), and poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT), in landfill leachate under mesophilic conditions by quantifying carbon conversion to biogas. The BPs exhibited sharply contrasting degradation trajectories: PHB mineralized completely within 17 d, whereas PLA underwent substantial mineralization over 320 d (83.6%), extending beyond the well-established expectation of limited mesophilic degradation. In contrast, PBAT remained largely recalcitrant. Multi-omics analyses linked PHB and PLA depolymerization to the biofilm–polymer interface, with depolymerase transcription tracking their distinct degradation phases. Putative depolymerase homologs were widespread across recovered bacterial genomes, yet only a subset showed transcriptional support. This active fraction included multiple under-characterized lineages outside the taxonomic range of experimentally validated degrader genomes, revealing a marked disconnect between genomic potential and realized activity. Our findings show that anaerobic biodegradation outcomes in landfill leachate cannot be inferred from biodegradability labels or genomic potential alone, but emerge from polymer-specific depolymerization constraints and depolymerase transcription enriched at the biofilm–polymer interface. How different biodegradable plastics break down within landfills, particularly landfill leachate, remain unclear. Here, they evaluated the anaerobic biodegradability of three BPs, polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB), poly(lactic acid) (PLA), and poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT), using a combination of genome-resolved multi-omics.

papers.title: Oncogenic signalling and host immunocompetency govern senescent cell clearance and systemic inflammation in a mouse model of oncogene-induced senescence
papers.abstract: Senescence is a stress-induced program defined by permanent cell-cycle arrest and a pro-inflammatory senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Defective clearance of senescent cells promotes inflammation, tissue dysfunction, and ageing, yet determinants of their elimination remain poorly understood. Here, we model oncogene-induced senescence in the hematopoietic system by transplanting BrafV600E- or BrafΔN-expressing hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells into recipients with distinct immune backgrounds. BrafV600E induces a stronger senescence program and more aggressive disease than BrafΔN. Survival depends on oncogene-expressing cell burden and host immunity: immunocompetent, lower-burden mice clear oncogene-expressing cells and survive long-term, whereas higher-burden mice show checkpoint upregulation, T-cell exhaustion, and early death. NSG, Rag1KO, and lymphocyte-depleted hosts fail to clear these cells, developing sustained inflammation and bone marrow failure. Rapamycin administration attenuates senescence-associated features and improves survival. These findings identify oncogenic intensity and adaptive immune competence as coupled determinants of senescent-cell fate, with implications for chronic inflammation and senescence-targeted therapies. Defective clearance of senescent cells contributes to chronic systemic inflammation and tissue damage. Here, the authors adopt a mouse model of oncogene-induced senescence and report that oncogenic signal strength and the adaptive immune response govern senescent cell clearance, ultimately influencing animal survival

papers.title: Large-scale proteomic characterization reveals clinically relevant subtypes of early-stage papillary thyroid cancer for prognostic prediction
papers.abstract: Papillary thyroid cancer (PTC) has a rising incidence. The majority are diagnosed at an early stage, albeit with a minority exhibiting aggressive tendencies. Given its generally indolent nature, controversy persists regarding the management of early-stage PTCs, particularly surgical intervention and long-term surveillance strategies. Here, we conduct a large-scale proteomic characterization of early-stage PTC based on tumor samples from 797 patients. Proteomic profiling unveils clinically relevant modules and identifies six subtypes, capturing the spectrum of heterogeneity from indolent to progressive disease states. Notably, subtypes associated with higher progression risk display enhanced signatures of ribogenesis and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Furthermore, integrating machine learning with protein co-expression network analysis, we identify predictive markers of PTC progression risk such as GPX3 and TMSB4X. Integration of clinical and proteomic data provides a valuable resource for a deeper understanding of early-stage PTC biology and may inform personalized management strategies for patients with indolent or progressive disease. Papillary thyroid cancer (PTC) is often slow growing, but a subset of tumors can be aggressive. Here, the authors profile tumors from 797 PTC patients to define six molecular subtypes, identify protein markers linked to low- and high-risk disease, and develop a proteomic classification framework that may improve risk stratification and treatment decisions.

papers.title: Peripheral glia drive the initiation of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma
papers.abstract: Although tumor innervation is known to promote cancer progression, underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood and have mostly been linked to axonal signaling. Here, we identify peripheral glia as critical drivers of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC), the second most common skin cancer in humans. Tumor-associated glial cells (TAGs) resemble embryonic Schwann cell lineage stages, are abundant in the stroma of premalignant lesions and established murine and human cSCC, and are essential for tumor formation. TAG activation in premalignant lesions is triggered by UV-induced anti-inflammatory macrophages, which in turn are polarized by TAGs into pro-tumorigenic FcεRIα⁺ macrophages, key components of the cSCC microenvironment. Consequently, TAG depletion reduces FcεRIα⁺ macrophages, cancer-associated fibroblasts, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition in keratinocytes, thereby impairing cSCC initiation by disrupting intercellular communication required for tumor development. As most solid tumors are innervated and harbor peripheral glia, our findings reveal TAGs as regulators of tumor initiation with potential relevance beyond skin cancer. Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma develops within a complex tissue environment, but the factors that initiate tumor formation are not fully understood. Here, the authors identify tumor-associated peripheral glial cells as drivers of tumor initiation, showing that they promote pro-tumor macrophage activation and stromal changes required for early cancer development.

papers.title: Human hemoglobin protects the parasite cytoskeleton during Plasmodium falciparum gametocyte development
papers.abstract: Transmission of Plasmodium falciparum requires the differentiation of asexual parasites into male and female gametocytes, which undergo extensive cytoskeletal remodeling, assembling a non-canonical subpellicular microtubule (SPMT) network. Using single-particle cryo-electron microscopy, we determined structures of SPMTs isolated from developing gametocytes. Unexpectedly, we identified human hemoglobin as a prominent microtubule-associated factor that binds to P. falciparum SPMTs in a dimeric form rather than the canonical tetramer. Pharmacological perturbation of microtubules and hemoglobin isoform switching experiments demonstrate that this hemoglobin-SPMT association is essential for proper SPMT organization and gametocyte maturation. Together, these findings reveal a strategy by which P. falciparum repurposes a host metabolic protein to stabilize its cytoskeleton, highlight the intimate co-evolution between parasite and host, and suggest avenues to block malaria transmission. Wang et al. apply single particle cryo-EM to developing gametocytes of Plasmodium falciparum, and identify human hemoglobin as a prominent factor that binds to P. falciparum subpellicular microtubule (SPMT) network.

papers.title: Epithelial NF-κB shapes protective Treg cell responses to restrain intestinal inflammation
papers.abstract: Inflammation resolution depends on coordinated communication between tissue compartments, yet how the intestinal epithelium shapes its immune microenvironment remains poorly understood. Here, using colonic biopsies from patients with ulcerative colitis (UC) and mouse models enabling tissue-wide visualization of NF-κB activity, we combine single-cell RNA sequencing and secretome analysis to define epithelial communication during colitis. We show that, paradoxically, the NF-κB-driven pro-inflammatory secretome of intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) is essential for recovery and prevents unrestrained inflammation. Mechanistically, epithelial NF-κB promotes CCL22-dependent regulatory T cell (Treg cell) recruitment and promotes a tolerogenic, pro-repair cell state, accompanied by induction of the lipid-metabolism-associated GDPD3 and CCR4. In UC, epithelial NF-κB is not uniformly activated but instead induces a selective pro-inflammatory transcriptional program while repressing targets regulating T cell recruitment. Thus, we identify dynamic epithelial–immune communication and demonstrate a protective IEC NF-κB–Treg cell axis important for resolution of intestinal inflammation. Inflammation and recovery from ulcerative colitis (UC) involves various immune cells and mediators. Here the authors examine the function of NFκB using patient samples and reporter mice to show that NFκB promotes T regulatory cell recruitment through CCL22 and a propensity towards repair.

papers.title: Identification and genetic characterization of megabase-scale plasmids of Enterobacteriaceae
papers.abstract: Humans and animals are ubiquitously colonized by Enterobacteriaceae, including both commensals and clinically significant pathogens. Here, we report 21 complete Enterobacteriaceae megaplasmid genomes of up to 1.58 Mbp in length spanning two major clades that are highly divergent from previously described plasmids. Of these, three were reconstructed from isolates of Escherichia coli and Shigella flexneri; others were potentially hosted by species of Citrobacter and Enterobacter. Related megabase-scale plasmids were detected in at least 400 infant and adult gut, and other microbiomes. Diverse Enterobacteriaceae hosts, conjugation machinery, and DNA modification patterns suggest that these elements are self-transmissible, with a broad host range. The plasmids encode multi-drug efflux systems and potential secreted effectors. Up to 208 tRNAs are encoded and include sequence variants that may counter tRNA-centric defense mechanisms. Overall, the vast plasmid coding capacity may broaden host range, increase competitiveness, control invasion by other elements, and counter programmed cell death. Here, the authors report the identification and characterization of large, up to 1.58 million base-pair-long plasmids in gut microbiomes worldwide, showing that while most genes remain uncharacterized, these plasmids are linked to E. coli and Shigella isolates and can greatly expand host function.

papers.title: High-risk antimicrobial resistance genomic traits in multidrug-resistant Salmonella across China’s food chain: projections to 2050
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is rising globally, yet factors shaping its genomic evolution remain poorly understood. We investigated how socioeconomic, climate, and health factors are associated with AMR spread in multi-drug resistant (MDR) Salmonella enterica across China’s food chain, mapped hotspots and forecasted genomic trait prevalence to 2050. We analysed 2,536 MDR genomes from 15 provinces over 16 years, covering patients, food and non-food workers, meat, livestock, and environmental sources. A machine learning framework integrated genomic surveillance with risk assessment to identify high-risk AMR traits (clinically relevant, MDR, mobile). Regression models linked trait prevalence to socioeconomic, climate, health, and antimicrobial consumption data, informing projections to 2050. Eighty-four high-risk traits, including carbapenem, colistin, and β-lactam resistance, are projected to rise, with antibiotic use, population growth, healthcare spending, and urbanisation. Projections were trait-specific: blaCTX-M-64 and blaTEM-1 may increase up to 20%, while blaCTX-M-65 and blaCTX-M-14 remain below 5%. A mechanistic shift in fluoroquinolone resistance is projected: mutation-based resistance (gyrA 87) declines while plasmid-mediated genes (qnrB17, qnrS1) rise. Food workers emerged as a potential reservoir, showing higher trait prevalence than food sources, uniquely carrying last-resort antibiotic-resistance genes (blaTEM-30, blaNDM-5, blaCTX-M-64). Integrating genomic with socioeconomic surveillance could shift AMR interventions from reactive to preventive. A study of 2,536 MDR Salmonella genomes across China’s food chain forecasts resistance to 2050. Antibiotic use and population growth associate with rising carbapenem and colistin resistance, with food workers an overlooked last-resort ARG reservoir.

papers.title: Type I IFN promotes ILC2-to-ILC1 plasticity in pre-clinical radiation-induced lung injury
papers.abstract: Radiation-induced lung injury (RILI) is a common dose-limiting toxicity after radiotherapy for lung cancer, but the immunological mechanisms contributing to RILI pathogenesis remain poorly understood. Here we analyze a RILI mouse model using high-dose, restricted-field irradiation to the left lung. Flow cytometry and cytokine profiling analysis of innate lymphoid cells (ILC) reveals a radiation-induced shift from lung-resident type 2 ILCs (ILC2) toward pro-inflammatory type 1 ILCs (ILC1). Single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis of mouse lung ILC populations after radiation suggests that type I interferon (IFN) promotes radiation-induced ILC2-to-ILC1 plasticity. In vitro, IFN-β stimulation of mouse ILC2s leads to increased expression of the ILC1 markers T-bet and IFN-γ, while IFN-β stimulation of human peripheral blood mononuclear cells increases the ILC1-to-ILC2 ratio. In vivo, inhibition of type I IFN signaling attenuates lung damage after irradiation in our RILI model. Thus, our findings indicate that radiation-induced type I IFN induces ILC2-to-ILC1 plasticity to contribute to RILI pathogenesis, and suggest that targeting type I IFN signaling may be a therapeutic strategy to mitigate radiation-induced lung injury. Radiotherapy for lung cancer often induces radiation-induced lung injury (RILI). Here, the authors analyze innate lymphoid cells (ILC) in a RILI mouse model, finding that radiation-induced type I interferon directs ILC2-to-ILC1 plasticity, and inhibition of type I interferon signaling reduces ILC plasticity and RILI.

papers.title: Exploring healthy aging through preclinical Alzheimer disease in the Knight Alzheimer Research Imaging dataset
papers.abstract: Alzheimer disease (AD) remains a significant global public health challenge, requiring robust multimodal datasets to elucidate its prolonged preclinical phase, improve early detection, advance understanding of disease trajectories, and guide intervention strategies. Here we present the Knight Alzheimer Research Imaging (KARI) dataset, established by the Washington University Knight ADRC to address this critical need. We detail comprehensive multimodal neuroimaging from 1,645 participants (aged 42-97) across 6,217 acquisitions. Spanning the AD spectrum from healthy aging to symptomatic disease, the cohort undergoes extensive longitudinal imaging using structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) alongside positron emission tomography (PET) tracers for amyloid and tau pathology. This is complemented by rich clinical, cognitive, genetic, and biomarker data. In addition to raw imaging, the dataset provides quality-controlled processed outputs, including anatomical segmentations and biomarker quantification. By making this data accessible to researchers, the Knight ADRC aims to accelerate discoveries in pathophysiology, biomarker identification, and therapeutic development. The KARI dataset maps healthy aging through preclinical Alzheimer disease across >6,000 scans from 1,645 adults. Demonstrating its utility, imaging biomarkers scale with clinical severity, providing a resource to accelerate future Alzheimer research.

papers.title: Genetic code expansion enables plant-directed control of bacterial activity
papers.abstract: Microorganisms have the potential to deliver growth-promoting benefits to plants and crops; however, to be useful in a field setting, their gene expression should be programmable and restricted to specific plant hosts and conditions. Here, using O-methyl-L-tyrosine (OMY) as a model compound, we establish noncanonical amino acids (ncAAs) as a tool for plant-based control of associated microbial activity. We use genetic code expansion to engineer OMY-dependent control of protein synthesis in the soil bacterium Bacillus subtilis. Engineered B. subtilis strains express an orthogonal aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase and tRNA pair that, upon provision of OMY, results in suppression of in-frame amber stop codons in target transcripts. We engineer Arabidopsis, tomato and poplar to biosynthesize OMY, showing that plant-derived OMY can stimulate gene expression in both model and wild soil bacteria. This demonstrates that inducible and tissue-specific expression of a single biosynthetic enzyme by the plant enables on-demand control over microbial activity, establishing ncAAs as a tool for programming plant–microorganism partnerships. The noncanonical amino acid O-methyl-L-tyrosine is used as a tool to control microbial protein synthesis across diverse plants.

papers.title: Engineered human Argonaute 2 for targeted C-to-U RNA base editing
papers.abstract: Tools for manipulating RNA that rely on nonhuman proteins, such as ISC-based and Cas-based scaffolds, can lead to unintended and little-understood effects on human cells and present challenges in therapeutic translation. Replacing them with human proteins engineered for expanded, programmable functions could bypass the limitations of these foreign proteins. Here we demonstrate that human Argonaute 2 (AGO2) can be repurposed as a modular RNA targeting domain. AGO2 fused to a C-to-U deaminase enables AGO-led targeted editing of RNA (ALTER). Using guide RNAs that remodel target RNA structure for selective editing and reduced nuclease activity, we show that ALTER achieves, on average, 1.9-fold higher C-to-U editing on mRNA targets in HEK293T cells compared with Cas13 editors CURE and RESCUE. Transcriptome-wide RNA-seq revealed similar or lower levels of off-target editing compared to the same Cas13-based editors. Machine learning models predict that far fewer immunogenic peptides will result from ALTER and we show that ALTER is amenable to a validated workflow for artificial intelligence-directed deimmunization. Human Argonaute is repurposed for RNA editing.

papers.title: A systems perspective on monoallelic inborn errors of immunity
papers.abstract: The genetic architecture of inborn errors of immunity continues to grow in complexity, exposing the limitations of variant-centric concepts that have long shaped the field. While complete loss-of-function genotypes have been instrumental in defining essential gene functions in human immunity and inflammation, they have also entrenched binary interpretations of causality that fail to account for pleiotropy, variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance—especially in monoallelic disease. Monoallelic variants often perturb signaling rather than abolishing it. The integration of these perturbations into molecular and cellular systems, and eventually immune circuits, governs phenotypic expression. Here, we revisit and extend classic concepts of genetic dominance and genetic pleiotropy and suggest that these are not sole properties of alleles but emerge from the complex and dynamic behavior of molecular, cellular and immune systems to buffer genetic variance. Monoallelic variants introduce qualitative and quantitative perturbations that act as inputs to biological systems. Their dynamic integration across molecular, cellular and immune systems governs genetic dominance and expression of immune phenotypes.

papers.title: Imputation of fluid intelligence to increase power for gene discovery
Multiancestry conditional and joint analysis applied to GWAS summary statistics
papers.abstract: Conditional and joint (COJO) analysis of genome-wide association study (GWAS) data is a standard post-GWAS analysis for identifying statistically independent associations. Although GWAS meta-analyses are increasingly conducted across multiple ancestry groups, the optimal strategy for multiancestry COJO analysis remains unclear. Here we introduce Manc-COJO, a method for multiancestry COJO analysis. Simulations and real-data analyses show that Manc-COJO improves detection of independent association signals while reducing false positives compared with single-ancestry COJO implemented in genome-wide complex trait analysis (GCTA) and its ad-hoc multiancestry adaptations. We also introduce Manc-COJO:FIX, a follow-up algorithm to identify ancestry-specific independent associations. The C++ implementation of Manc-COJO is over 120-fold faster than GCTA-COJO and supports linkage disequilibrium references derived from either individual-level genotype data or pre-computed matrices, facilitating analyses when data sharing is limited. This study introduces Manc-COJO, a method for detecting independent genetic associations by integrating data from multiple ancestries, reducing false positives and enabling fast, flexible analyses across diverse populations.

papers.title: The landscape of gene loss and missense variation across the mammalian tree informs on gene essentiality
papers.abstract: Patterns of gene and sequence preservation across species provide insight into gene essentiality under natural selection. Here we developed two interspecies constraint metrics across 462 mammalian species: Gene Identity Score of Mammalian Orthologs (GISMO), which quantifies gene loss weighted by evolutionary distance to humans, and GISMO-mis, which measures missense constraint using the ratio of missense to synonymous variation across mammals. Both metrics are strongly correlated with human loss of function, missense and dosage constraint derived from large-scale sequencing studies, yet are largely independent of coding sequence length. GISMO and GISMO-mis identify essential genes missed by existing human-only metrics, particularly short genes. Genes in the most constrained deciles are enriched for rare variant associations in disorders linked to reduced fecundity, including schizophrenia, autism and neurodevelopmental disorders, and show strong enrichment for common variant heritability. These deciles also exhibit reduced copy number variation, consistent with dosage sensitivity. In addition, GISMO improves prioritization of recessive disease genes and captures signatures of homozygous selection across the mammalian tree. Taken together, GISMO and GISMO-mis leverage deep mammalian evolution to provide complementary, length-robust measures of gene essentiality that strengthen disease–gene prioritization and illuminate the selective forces shaping human biology. GISMO and GISMO-mis are new metrics of evolutionary constraint developed across 462 mammalian species. These metrics provide complementary measures of gene essentiality and improve prioritization of human disease genes.

papers.title: Spatial multi-omic atlas profiles early organogenesis of a Carnegie stage 12 human embryo
papers.abstract: Organogenesis marks one of the most dynamic periods of early human embryonic development. Although the morphological features of this period have been described, the underlying transcriptional and metabolic landscapes remain poorly understood owing to the lack of an integrated spatial strategy. We present spatial transcriptomic and metabolomic maps of a Carnegie stage 12 (CS12) human embryo, co-registered with embryonic anatomy to generate a unified spatial multi-omic framework. Unsupervised clustering of the spatial transcriptomic data identified 17 cell populations covering the major organ primordia. Notably, we observed spatially separable hepatocyte- and cholangiocyte-lineage primed transcriptional programmes within the liver primordium, and detected cardiac outflow tract and sinoatrial node progenitors at CS12. Furthermore, integration of gene and metabolite abundance highlighted regional associations between transcription factors and metabolic pathways underpinning lineage specification. Our work presents a spatially resolved multi-omic atlas of a human embryo at the onset of organogenesis. Wang et al. map a Carnegie stage 12 human embryo with spatial transcriptomics and metabolomics.

papers.title: Mechanism of M18BP1-mediated activation of condensin II for mitotic DNA compaction
papers.abstract: DNA compaction by human condensin II is crucial for the correct organization of mitotic chromosomes. Mitotic activation of condensin II is a multilayered process, controlled mainly by the opposing activity of the MCPH1 and M18BP1 proteins, acting as an interphase inhibitor and a mitotic activator, respectively. Mitotic phosphorylation favors M18BP1 binding to condensin II, resulting in effective and timely chromosome compaction. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying condensin II activation in driving DNA compaction remain uncharacterized. Here, combining cryo-electron microscopy with single-molecule imaging, we unravel the mechanism of condensin II activation by M18BP1 and elucidate their role in DNA compaction. The specific interaction with phosphorylated M18BP1 induces conformational changes in the condensin II complex, relieving an autoinhibitory conformation and allowing stable DNA binding and DNA compaction. Beyond the activity of isolated condensin II complexes on DNA, we observe the emergence of multimeric species that withstand the forces applied by optical tweezers, suggesting that condensin II multimerization might contribute to the mechanical reinforcement of mitotic chromosomes. Here, the authors show that phosphorylated M18BP1 activates condensin II by relieving an autoinhibitory interface, enabling stable DNA binding and compaction. Additionally, the M18BP1–condensin II complex forms clusters that might mechanically reinforce mitotic chromosomes.

Small variant calling in the era of long-read sequencing
papers.abstract: Long-read sequencing enables accurate analysis of complex and repetitive genomic regions but has distinct error profiles compared to short-read sequencing. Consequently, the tools for calling small variants — the predominant source of human genetic diversity — have shifted towards deep learning-based methods. This transition has reshaped variant calling across biological contexts, including germline, de novo, somatic and mosaic variants, and sequencing modalities for capturing both DNA and RNA at different resolutions. These deep learning frameworks are being developed in combination with alignment-based, assembly-based and pangenome-based strategies for small variant detection. In this Review, we chart the trajectory towards complete telomere-to-telomere profiling of small variants and consider the computational innovations needed to benchmark newly accessible repetitive regions and complex variants. Long-read sequencing is expanding the scope of small-variant detection, enabling analysis of genomic regions that were previously difficult to interrogate. In this Review, the authors examine approaches for long-read small-variant calling across sequencing platforms and applications, highlighting advances in deep learning, assembly-based and pangenome-based methods, benchmarking strategies and future challenges.

papers.title: Cortex-wide imaging in naturally behaving mice with 1-gram wireless mesoscopes
papers.abstract: Revealing how distributed cortical circuits coordinate behavior in freely moving animals remains a central challenge in systems neuroscience, constrained by limited fields of view, low throughput, and the tethering required by current miniaturized microscopes1-4. Here, we present Airscope, a wireless mesoscope delivering 4 μm lateral resolution across a 6 mm field of view at 12.5 Hz, weighing 1.0 gram. An aspheric-lens design achieves a 2.84× shorter total track length than previous miniaturized microscopes1,2,5,6 while matching the neuron yield of benchtop one-photon mesoscopes; a tailored wireless link supports cable-free calcium imaging from >8,500 neurons per animal (25‑fold increase). Paired with a zero-shot behavior analyzer, Airscope enables cortical imaging across rich behavioral conditions, including room-scale enriched arenas, swimming assays, and multi-organ implantation, with concurrent recording from multiple animals. Using Airscope, we demonstrate versatile applications of untethered cortical imaging across diverse behavioral paradigms. We identify cortical activity patterns across multiple dorsal regions that correlate with behavioral signatures of social dominance, and show dorsal-cortical population activity prospectively decodes competition outcomes across paired animals. We observe reward-location-associated cortical activity patterns during maze exploration, and characterize Granger-causal influence from spinal cord to cortex during fear conditioning, enabled by simultaneous brain-spinal recordings. By uniting large-scale, cellular-resolution recording with unconstrained behavior, Airscope makes naturalistic, multi-animal cortical recording experimentally practical, and provides a broadly accessible technology for systems neuroscience.

A plasma-based tau staging system integrating p-tau217 and eMTBR-tau243 closely aligned with PET-based tau staging and predicted longitudinal cognitive trajectories. These findings support plasma eMTBR-tau243 as a prototypical T2 biomarker and highlight the potential of plasma-based tau staging for prognosis and therapeutic decision-making in AD. This study shows complementary roles of plasma p-tau217 and eMTBRtau243 across Alzheimer’s disease, supporting their use for blood-based assessment of tau pathology, biological staging and prognosis.

papers.title: Crystallization-mediated twisting of supramolecular nanoribbons from plant-derived triterpenes
papers.abstract: Controlling crystallization can tailor crystal properties, yet directing the supramolecular organization of small bio-based molecules remains challenging because of their configurational diversity and chemical complexity. Here, we direct the self-assembly of birch-bark-derived betulin (BT), a nonionic triterpene, into twisted supramolecular nanoribbons (BT_S). By interrupting classical nanolayer restacking and coupling interfacial dynamics with amphiphilic balance, surfactant- and salt-mediated antisolvent crystallization perturbs growth symmetry and biases directional molecular packing. The resulting twisted nanoribbons exhibit defined dimensions (width ~200 nm, thickness ~50 nm and ∼3.6 μm pitch) and aligned BT nanolayers with ~1.3 nm interlayer spacing. Polarization-resolved optical coherence tomography reveals depth-resolved mesoscale polarization anisotropy and links ribbon topology to effective refractive index and linear and circular birefringence. Molecular dynamics simulations support cooperative twisting driven by hydrophobic interactions and London dispersion forces. This crystallization-mediated strategy enables multiscale periodicity and tunable optical anisotropy, expanding opportunities for sustainable soft photonic and optoelectronic materials derived from biomolecules. Controlling the crystallization conditions allows to tailor the properties of crystals, but achieving directed supramolecular organization of small bio-based molecules remains challenging. Here the authors demonstrate direct supramolecular twisting and hierarchical organization in a triterpene system by directing the self-assembly of betulin into nanoribbons.

papers.title: Towards scalable DNA data storage with DNA-SaM codec system
papers.abstract: The exponential growth of global data volume is driving an urgent need for novel storage medium. Deoxyribonucleic Acid (DNA), nature’s genetic repository, presents a transformative solution with data storage density and lifespan orders of magnitude higher than conventional media. However, scaling DNA storage has been hindered by the complexity of codec algorithms, the generation of biochemically problematic sequences, and the absence of robust architecture for large-scale data. We present DNA-SaM, a system integrating highly efficient encoding, stringent biochemical constraint checks, and a storage unit distribution paradigm facilitated by a two-tiered indexing architecture. DNA-SaM demonstrates linear encoding time complexity and substantially reduced encoding time compared with representative approaches by in silico analysis. Critically, it proactively excludes sequences such as homopolymer runs, tandem repeats, and potential promoter motifs that could interfere with downstream biochemical processes, showing improved compatibility with in vitro and in vivo applications. It is further validated by practical data storage both in vitro and in vivo with a 100% success rate. On the basis of its encoding scheme and sequence design space, DNA-SaM could theoretically store data exceeding 270 petabytes (PB), marking an advancement in the scalability of DNA-based data storage. Scaling DNA storage is limited by complex codecs, biochemically problematic sequences, and insufficient architecture for large-scale data. Here, the authors present DNA-SaM, integrating efficient encoding, biochemical checks, and a storage unit distribution with a two-tiered indexing architecture.

papers.title: A genetic platform to deconvolve efficacy and toxicity reveals the on-target effects of CDK11 inhibition in vivo
papers.abstract: The cyclin-dependent kinase CDK11 is an understudied kinase that has been the subject of conflicting reports regarding its function in cancer. Here, we combine genetic and pharmacological approaches to demonstrate that CDK11 is a critical regulator of cancer cell survival that is required for RNA splicing and the expression of homologous recombination genes. Inhibition of CDK11 disrupts genome stability, promotes the retention of intronic sequences in mature mRNAs, and induces synthetic lethality with PARP inhibitors. Through integrative analysis of functional genomics datasets, we identify heterozygous deletions of chromosome 1p36 - which encompasses CDK11 and its activating cyclin CCNL2 - as a recurrent and predictive biomarker of sensitivity to CDK11 inhibition. To assess the therapeutic potential of CDK11, we establish a genetically-engineered mouse model that allows us to differentiate between the on-target and off-target effects of CDK11 inhibitors in vivo. Using this platform, we demonstrate that MEL-495R, an orally bioavailable CDK11 inhibitor, induces widespread on-target toxicity, revealing a narrow therapeutic index. Experiments with a chemically distinct CDK11 inhibitor similarly reveal minimal anti-cancer activity at tolerable doses. Together, these findings define CDK11 as a core cancer dependency, uncover a chromosomal deletion that sensitizes tumors to CDK11 inhibition, demonstrate that on-target toxicity limits the efficacy of CDK11-targeting therapies, and provide a generalizable strategy for deconvolving drug efficacy and toxicity in vivo for novel oncology targets. CDK11 encodes a poorly-characterized cyclin-dependent kinase. Here, the authors demonstrate that CDK11 is essential for cancer proliferation, but the function(s) of CDK11 in normal tissue limits the efficacy of CDK11 inhibition as a therapeutic strategy.

papers.title: Transforming electrified railway into mechanical energy storage for electricity system decarbonization
papers.abstract: Decarbonizing electricity requires vast energy storage capacity worldwide, but constructing dedicated storage assets creates substantial capital, material and embodied carbon burdens. Electrified railways already exchange energy with electricity systems through traction and regenerative braking, but their inherent potential as mechanical energy storage remains unexploited. Here we show that modulation of train operations can transform electrified railways into Electrified Rail-Based Energy Storage. By analyzing 326,034 inter-stop train operations, we estimate its global potential at 190 gigawatts in 2025 and 315–579 gigawatts by 2050. Capacity expansion models for China, Europe and India indicate that it can reduce investment in conventional storage by 11.9–20.0%, corresponding to an extrapolated global value of US$14.9–35.1 billion annually. Without increasing total system cost, electricity systems with this flexible resource could further reduce operational CO2 emissions by 94.3–258.9 million tonnes per year. Electrified railways can therefore complement conventional storage technologies for electricity system decarbonization. Coordinating train operations can transform electrified railways into mechanical energy storage for electricity system decarbonization, reducing the need for newly built storage while lowering system costs and carbon emissions.

papers.title: dITP shifts the assembly equilibrium of Kongming to activate NAD+ hydrolysis
papers.abstract: The Kongming (Kom) system, consisting of KomA, KomB, and KomC, protects bacteria from phage infection. KomA collaborates with a phage enzyme to generate deoxyinosine 5′-triphosphate (dITP), which activates the KomBC complex to hydrolyze NAD⁺ and trigger cell death. Recent studies propose that dITP activates KomBC through a simple conformational change. Our findings instead reveal a more dynamic mechanism. Without dITP, KomBC complexes exist in equilibrium between tightly packed oligomers and loosely packed filaments, both inactive. Tight packing accumulates unfavorable electrostatic interactions without positioning catalytic residues for NAD⁺ hydrolysis, whereas loose packing relieves these interactions but leaves catalytic residues misaligned. dITP binding at KomB stabilizes tightly packed KomC cores in the filament while aligning catalytic residues. Therefore, a small-molecule signal activates signaling by shifting the assembly equilibrium of higher-order protein complexes toward a catalytically competent state. Nucleotide signals activate bacterial immune defenses against phages. Here, authors show that dITP activates the Kongming system by shifting protein assemblies toward a catalytically active state
