papers.title: De novo design of cysteine proteases
papers.abstract: Despite advances in de novo enzyme design, success has been largely limited to low-energy-barrier model reactions. Amide bonds such as those linking amino acids along the peptide backbone are stable for hundreds of years in neutral aqueous solution because of the high energy barrier to hydrolysis1. Here we describe the de novo design of enzymes that use an activated cysteine nucleophile to hydrolyse the polypeptide backbone in a sequence-dependent manner, with a success rate of 13/69 = 19% and rate enhancements over the background reaction (kcat/kuncat) of up to 3 × 107. The designed proteases have folds that are very different from proteases in nature (TM score < 0.50), and six crystal structures are very close to the design models (Cα root mean squared deviation of <1.2 Å), highlighting the capacity for generalization and the accuracy of the design methodology. Experimental and computational analyses suggest that the remaining gap in activity to the most active native cysteine proteases arises from imperfections in active-site preorganization and substrate positioning. The designed proteases efficiently cleave their targets in mammalian cells, opening the door to a wide range of synthetic biology applications. De novo-designed enzymes use an activated cysteine nucleophile to hydrolyse polypeptide backbones in a sequence-dependent manner.

papers.title: Sexual dimorphism in epidermal stem cell dynamics
papers.abstract: The epidermis is a stratified epithelium comprising proliferative basal cells and differentiated suprabasal cells that are continuously renewed throughout life. Conflicting theories have been proposed regarding the heterogeneity of the basal cell layer, with some studies proposing that all proliferative cells have self-renewal potential during homeostasis1–5. Meanwhile, others posit a model in which stem cell differentiation occurs through an intermediate transit-amplifying-like progenitor state with strictly limited proliferative potential6–10. Here, to determine the heterogeneity and pattern of cell fate, we performed intravital time-lapse imaging to track the fate of lineage-labelled cells in the skin interfollicular epidermis. Results from quantitative analyses of clonal dynamics support a two-compartment model of epidermal homeostasis, whereby basal cells are organized in a stem cell–transit-amplifying cell hierarchy. Critical to these conclusions was the discovery of sexual dimorphism in epidermal fate, with female mice showing a highly synchronized pattern of cell division, differentiation and delamination that contributes to accelerated wound healing. Single-cell RNA sequencing, transcriptional profiling and clonal analyses of castrated mice revealed that male sex hormones promote stem cell differentiation and delamination. In summary, our study provides insight into the functional identity of the stem cell population and identifies sex-specific differences in the regulation of epidermal stem cells and transit-amplifying cell fate. Long-term live imaging of adult mouse ear skin reveals sex-specific differences in the clonal dynamics of epidermal stem cells and transit-amplifying cells during homeostasis.

papers.title: Jurassic flightless bird reveals early ecological diversity of avialans
papers.abstract: The origin and early diversification of birds remain highly debated in vertebrate evolution. Although estimates of the evolutionary timescales suggest a Jurassic period radiation1,2, a profound scarcity of fossils from this period has hampered how the distinctive bird bauplan was assembled3–5. Selection for powered flight has been viewed as the primary driver of early avialan skeletal modifications3,6,7, attesting to the independent occurrences of aerodynamic features among paravian lineages8. Here we report on the discovery of a Late Jurassic avialan, Yuezhuornis yangyuanensis, gen. et sp. nov., from the Zhenghe Fauna of southeastern China9. As one of the earliest diverging avialans, Y. yangyuanensis exhibits a striking mosaic of features, combining a mixture of avialan- and troodontid-like cranial characters, paired with derived postcranial traits and a deinonychosaur-like hyperextensible second pedal digit. Phylogenetically informed analyses show that Y. yangyuanensis possesses markedly short forelimbs—a condition present widely among non-avialan theropods. These findings provide strong evidence for a terrestrial, flightless lifestyle of Y. yangyuanensis. Our study demonstrates that evolution works intensively as exemplified by the occurrence of several, divergent ecological pathways being exploited in the initial diversification of birds. A fossil bird from the Upper Jurassic Zhenghe Fauna of southeastern China contemporary with Archaeopteryx and that clearly could not fly sheds new light on the ecological diversification of early-diverging avialans.

papers.title: Computational design of metalloproteases
papers.abstract: De novo design of enzymes that cleave amide bonds represents a major challenge1,2. Here we use RFdiffusion methods3,4 to de novo design proteins with water-activating zinc-based active sites adjacent to a peptide substrate binding pocket. Of 135 designs tested, 36% catalyse cleavage of their cognate peptide substrates at the targeted scissile bond. The best design accelerates peptide-bond hydrolysis by more than 108-fold relative to the uncatalysed reaction; four substitutions increase this acceleration to more than 1010-fold by improving active-site preorganization5. We use this approach to design metalloproteases that selectively cleave the human disease-associated proteins TDP-43, amyloid-β and serum amyloid A, with rate enhancements of up to 109-fold. We further design caged cytokines and receptor antagonists that are selectively activated by the designed proteases, enabling bioorthogonal control of cell state. Thus, de novo design can yield highly active, programmable proteases with applications in therapeutics, biotechnology and bioremediation. RFdiffusion methods are used to de novo design proteins with water-activating zinc-based active sites adjacent to a peptide substrate binding pocket, yielding highly active, programmable proteases with potential applications in therapeutics, biotechnology and bioremediation.

papers.title: Rh3+ stabilized in KRh@MFI catalyses regioselective hydroformylation
papers.abstract: Hydroformylation has been a cornerstone of industrial organometallic catalysis, with regioselectivity being a critical aspect in this process1,2. Present industrial systems use homogeneous Rh-based catalysts with expensive and toxic phosphine-containing ligands, underscoring the need to develop alternative heterogeneous catalysts that could compete with the actual homogeneous ones3. In this direction, atomically dispersed Rh catalysts have been proposed as promising candidates for hydroformylation4,5. However, achieving high regioselectivity at high conversion is still a big challenge. Here subnanometre Rh2O3 clusters are confined inside the channels of the MFI zeolite, which under reaction conditions disrupt into isolated Rh3+ and Rh+ species. Density functional theory (DFT) investigations combined with spectroscopic and catalytic studies demonstrate that Rh3+-mediated hydroformylation is energetically plausibly similar to Rh+, with Rh3+ being intrinsically more selective for hydroformylation and less selective for double-bond isomerization than Rh+. In the coexistence of both Rh3+ and Rh+ species, we demonstrate the possibility to selectively inhibit Rh+ sites through the addition of N-containing molecules such as N-methylpyrrolidine (MP) or 1-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP), which preferentially coordinate to Rh+ inside MFI zeolite channel, thereby suppressing its isomerization function while leaving Rh3+ sites catalytically accessible. This strategy results in a notable enhancement of regioselectivity, with a state-of-the-art reported highest linear to branched aldehydes (l/b) ratio of 817 with 96% undecanal selectivity at 99.8% 1-decene conversion, using NMP as additive. DFT investigations combined with spectroscopic and catalytic studies of disrupted subnanometric Rh2O3 clusters show that Rh+ centres in a zeolite-based catalyst are blocked with N-containing molecules, whereas Rh3+ sites are stabilized, allowing hydroformylation reactions with enhanced regioselectivity and efficiency.

papers.title: Engineered TYK2 dependence enables myeloid-selective IL-10 receptor agonism
papers.abstract: Interleukin-10 (IL-10) is a central anti-inflammatory cytokine that suppresses immune responses in myeloid cells but can also activate T cells, limiting its therapeutic use in chronic inflammatory diseases owing to narrow efficacy windows and dose-limiting toxicities1–5. Here we show that myeloid and T cells differ in their dependence on JAK-family kinase pairing for IL-10 signalling and function. We took advantage of this differential kinase dependence to engineer a tetravalent nanobody-based myeloid-selective IL-10 receptor agonist (msIL-10R agonist) that fully recapitulates IL-10’s potent suppression of monocytes, macrophages and dendritic cells while avoiding stimulation of T cells. Cryo-electron microscopy structural analysis reveals a distinct receptor cross-linking geometry of the msIL-10R agonist compared with native IL-10 family cytokines. This tetravalent architecture renders signalling strictly TYK2-dependent and highly sensitive to IL-10Rα and IL-10Rβ receptor abundance, thereby conferring selective activity in myeloid cells. This msIL-10R agonist reduces inflammation in humanized mouse models of lipopolysaccharide challenge, delayed-type hypersensitivity and colitis. A humanized version exhibits IgG-like pharmacokinetics, sustained receptor occupancy and durable myeloid suppression up to 30 days without T cell activation or haematological toxicities in non-human primates. These findings establish a geometry-based strategy for achieving cell-type-selective cytokine signalling and identify the msIL-10R agonist as a therapeutic candidate for myeloid-driven inflammatory diseases, including inflammatory bowel diseases. A tetravalent nanobody-based myeloid-selective IL-10 receptor agonist recapitulates IL-10’s potent suppression of monocytes, macrophages and dendritic cells while avoiding stimulation of T cells.

papers.title: Elp1 is required for myeloid differentiation and brain repopulation
papers.abstract: Haematopoietic stem and progenitor cell (HSPC) transplantation-mediated replacement of microglia—the reconstitution of the central nervous system microglial niche with donor-derived myeloid cells—represents a promising strategy for brain cell therapies1–7. However, the cell-intrinsic molecular regulators of HSPC-derived myeloid lineage commitment in the brain have remained largely uncharacterized. This is partially because the scarcity of primary HSPCs has rendered large-scale genetic interrogation intractable. Here we explored whether ex vivo expansion of primary cultured HSPCs (cHSPCs) enables unbiased genetic interrogation of haematopoietic differentiation. We established that cHSPCs can be genetically manipulated and readily differentiate into myeloid cells and repopulate microglia niches of the brain after transplantation. Moreover, primary neonatal astrocytes contained strong signals to induce myeloid specification of cHSPCs in vitro. To identify genes that regulate glia-induced myeloid differentiation, we successfully screened around 20,000 individual genetic perturbations and characterized genes involved in the regulation of cell signalling, cell cycle, mitochondrial function and protein translation. Among these genes was elongator acetyltransferase complex subunit 1 (Elp1), which suppressed the unfolded protein response during myeloid specification and was essential for the generation but not maintenance of myeloid cells. Our work establishes a platform to investigate the molecular mechanisms of brain myeloid biology. Primary cultured haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells are used to analyse the molecular mechanisms of brain myeloid differentiation, and this platform enabled the identification of elongation factor ELP1 as an important regulator of this process.

papers.title: Early tetrapod neck mobility modelled using an extant analogue
papers.abstract: Tetrapods arose from lobe-finned fishes with a notochord-dominated axial column1–3. During this transition, the skull became separated from the shoulder girdle4–6, giving rise to a neck region. This head–shoulder separation has generated hypotheses suggesting that neck mobility increased during the origin of tetrapods, facilitating the ecological transition towards more terrestrial habitats4,5,7–9. However, incompletely co-ossified vertebral components10 have posed a challenge to modelling the mobility of these early tetrapod necks. Here we used material tests on the similarly configured axial columns of sturgeon to predict the capacities of the tetrapod neck region for lateral flexion, extension and rotation across the tetrapod stem. Our model indicates that the soft tissue-dominated axial column was surprisingly rigid, despite lacking co-ossified vertebral components. We estimate that most stem tetrapods could move their heads less than 6° laterally and less than 3° dorsally but could not rotate them. Notably, mobility did not shift in conjunction with the head–shoulder separation that occurred between the origin of tristichopterids (represented by Eusthenopteron) and that of more crownward stem tetrapods. Therefore, mobility in the tetrapod neck did not serve as a functional driver of head–shoulder separation. Instead, forelimb-driven locomotion, implicated in early tetrapods11–14, provides a better functional explanation for the head–shoulder separation. Biomechanical analysis of several early tetrapods using sturgeon as an analogue revealed that early tetrapods had limited neck mobility despite separation of the head and shoulders.

papers.title: Educational intervention can rewire village social networks
papers.abstract: Social networks shape behaviour, affect information dissemination and undergird collective action. And they can be exploited in the design of interventions in these domains1–7. Although social networks obey fundamental principles, such as the degree distribution8,9, they can nevertheless evolve as ties form and break. Here, through a randomized controlled trial involving a total of 8,331 people in 110 remote Honduran villages, we evaluate the secondary effects of a 22-month public-health intervention1 on pre-existing social-network structure. We used a design in which a varying fraction of village households received the intervention, and villages in which no one received the intervention were used as the primary reference group. In ‘low-dosage’ villages (in which 5–30% of households received the intervention), people who received the intervention tended to sever ties with untreated individuals to whom they previously went for health advice. Conversely, in high-dosage villages (50–100%), treated individuals increased their ties. These average changes are explained mainly by tie dynamics; that is, treated–treated pairs persist and form new links, whereas treated–untreated ties dissolve. A mediation analysis indicates that absorption of health information increases the likelihood of tie formation and persistence. The rewiring patterns generally lasted for three years after the intervention ceased. Moreover, although the intervention delivered health information, it reshaped friendship and financial ties, not just health-advice connections. In aggregate, the introduction of a new information regime acted as a kind of social institution, rewiring individuals’ connections even though the overall degree distribution of village-wide networks remained relatively stable. A randomized controlled trial involving a health-education intervention in rural villages in Honduras shows that the intervention changed social network connections, including not only health-related connections but also friendships and financial ties.

papers.title: Structural basis of ligand recognition and gating in mosquito IRs
papers.abstract: Ionotropic receptors (IRs) are essential for insect olfaction, enabling the detection of carboxylic acids, amines, moisture, and temperature cues that mediate critical behaviors, including mosquito host-seeking 1,2. However, the structural mechanisms underlying ligand specificity and channel activation in these receptors remain unclear. Here, we report cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures and functional validation of the IR8a-IR75k complex from the malaria mosquito Anopheles stephensi, a carboxylic acid detector, captured in four states: the ligand-free full-length closed form (apo state), the ligand induced full-length open state, and the nonanoic acid (NA)- and octanoic acid (OA)-bound extracellular domains. These structures reveal a dynamic ligand-binding pocket in IR75k, in which specificity is determined by alkyl chain length and carboxylate geometry. Ligand binding triggers closure of IR75k’s bilobed ligand binding domain (LBD), and this conformational change propagates through conserved mechanical linkers to the transmembrane domain (TMD), functioning as a molecular lever that dilates the pore via outward displacement of transmembrane helices. This gating mechanism was further corroborated by molecular dynamics simulations and electrophysiology. These insights provide an atomic resolution view of IR mediated host detection in mosquitoes and establish a foundation for the rational design of next generation mosquito control strategies targeting host-seeking behavior.

papers.title: Catalytic transfer of carbon atoms enables spirofusion of C–C σ-bonds
papers.abstract: Spirocyclic frameworks, polycyclic structures in which two rings share a single carbon atom, constitute key structural motifs across diverse areas, including optoelectronic and hole-transporting materials1–3, ligand design for coordination complexes4–6, and numerous natural products7. In a spiro skeleton, the two molecular units adopt an orthogonal arrangement, generating a rigid three-dimensional (3D) architecture. Introducing a single carbon atom to join two components to form the spiro centre therefore represents a direct strategy for constructing such frameworks. Previous carbon-atom-transfer approaches have largely relied on π-bond reactivity, whereas controlled insertion of a carbon atom into C–C σ-bonds remains challenging8–11. Here we report a rhodium-catalysed spiro-carbon-atom insertion reaction that converts biphenylene substrates into spirocyclic structures through sequential C–C bond activation. Using N-isocyanoiminophosphorane (PINC)12–14 as an atomic carbon equivalent, the reaction forms four new C–C bonds at a spiro centre. The transformation enables both homo- and cross-spirofusion of biphenylenes and can be extended to reactions combining σ- and π-bond activation. These results establish a catalytic strategy for constructing structurally complex spirocyclic frameworks through C–C σ-bond activation, with a single carbon atom serving as a central linchpin.

papers.abstract: Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex is a key regulator of metabolism, controlling flux from glycolysis into the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. PDH is often dysregulated in metabolic diseases and cancer. We discover here that in addition to its well characterized regulation by phosphorylation, PDH activity is also regulated via inhibitory oxidation of three cysteines of the DLAT subunit - Cys488, Cys586 and Cys618. Oxidation of these cysteines increases under oxidative stress, and is highly prevalent in mouse and human tissues. This mechanism enables cells to efficiently fight oxidative stress. Under oxidative stress, cells execute a metabolic shift, blocking glycolytic flux into the TCA cycle to shunt glycolytic carbons toward the pentose phosphate pathway. This generates NADPH which cells use to detoxify H2O2 and to reduce oxidized cysteines. We find that DLAT oxidation is required for cells to mount an effective antioxidant response. Mutations preventing DLAT oxidation render PDH resistant to oxidative inhibition, impair NADPH generation, reduce peroxide detoxification, and sensitize cells to oxidative damage and death. DLAT oxidation also drives a Warburg-like metabolic phenotype of increased glucose uptake, elevated lactate secretion, and reduced TCA cycle activity. Thus DLAT oxidation is a redox-sensing mechanism that regulates PDH activity and central carbon metabolism. Garcia-Cortizo et al. discover that the metabolic enzyme Pyruvate Dehydrogenase (PDH), which acts as a gatekeeper for metabolic flux from glycolysis into the TCA cycle, is inhibited by oxidation on three cysteines of the PDH subunit DLAT.

papers.title: Multiplexed live imaging deciphers nuclear force-driven chromatin dynamics and embryo development
papers.abstract: Mechanical forces transmitted to the nucleus regulate chromatin organization and gene expression to guide cell fate transitions. However, how the forces dynamically reshape the genome in living systems remains unclear. Here, inspired by the visualization of perinuclear chromatin detachment under low tension, we develop a genetically encoded fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET)-based nuclear tension sensor (NuTS) that directly quantifies forces transmitted into the nucleus through LINC complex proteins SUN1/2 and their effect on chromatin reorganization. NuTS enables high spatiotemporal mapping of forces across the nuclear envelope. Combined imaging of NuTS and lamina-associated domains (LADs) reveals that force fluctuations are coupled to LADs repositioning, and that a force of approximately 6 pN on SUN2 is required to maintain perinuclear chromatin anchoring. A drop below this threshold triggers lamin A phosphorylation at Ser22, which precedes and drives perinuclear chromatin dissociation and LAD reorganization by about 10 min. LINC-complex force transmission critically regulates cell migration and is essential for embryonic notochord development in vitro and in vivo. Our study establishes a mechanochemical framework linking nuclear forces to chromatin organization and function. Here, they develop a nuclear tension sensor (NuTS) to quantify SUN2 force for perinuclear chromatin anchoring at ~6 pN. They further demonstrate that LINC-complex force transmission is critical for cell migration and zebrafish notochord development.

papers.title: Signatures of bi-altermagnetism revealed by sublattice-specific circular dichroism in resonant inelastic X-ray scattering
papers.abstract: An altermagnet is a recently identified class of magnets that exhibit a zero net magnetic moment but break symmetry under the combined operations of parity and time reversal. It typically consists of two magnetic sites of opposite spins related by rotation within the unit cell. Here, we use circular dichroism (CD) in resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) to reveal symmetry signatures of a distinct form of altermagnetism, namely bi-altermagnetism, in the correlated insulator Fe2Mo3O8, which comprises two altermagnetic sublattices: one with alternating quasi-octahedral Fe environments and the other with alternating tetrahedral Fe environments. We experimentally revealed the emergence of CD in an achiral, zero-magnetization system, thereby probing mirror-symmetry breaking associated with altermagnetic order. Notably, the CD appeared at sublattice-specific excitations of the octahedral and tetrahedral sites, indicating symmetry breaking in both altermagnetic sublattices. Calculations based on a model with the bi-altermagnetic order along the c axis successfully reproduce the observed CD. Our findings support the realization of bi-altermagnetism in Fe2Mo3O8, and showcase the use of RIXS-CD as a probe of magnetic sublattices in systems with zero net magnetization. The standard definition of altermagnetism is of two magnetic sites of opposite spin related by rotation within the unit of a material. Here, using resonant inelastic X-ray scattering, Channagowdra et al. unveil a ’bi-altermagnetic’ state in Fe2Mo3O8, where the two inequivalent Fe sites each form an opposite-spin sublattice pair that independently satisfies the conventional criteria for altermagnetism.

papers.title: Shifting balance between habitat and climate in boreal biodiversity patterns across space, time and taxa
papers.abstract: Climate and habitat are key drivers of biodiversity patterns. However, how they independently and jointly affect species distribution across space, time, and taxa remains poorly understood. Here, we evaluate the relative importance of habitat and climate variables underpinning occurrence and abundance patterns of 503 terrestrial animal species over 20 years and a ~ 1100 km latitudinal gradient in Finland. Habitat composition is the main explanatory variable of biodiversity patterns, with varying importance and uncertainty across taxa, regions, and years, and with effects being partially correlated for many species. Specifically, habitat dominate in importance for butterflies, birds, and small mammals, while both habitat and climate explain the patterns of large mammals and moths. Additionally, patterns between biogeographical regions and years are mainly explained by climate, while habitat explains most variation within regions and years. Further differences emerge among functional groups, as body size, pace of life and specialization modulate the relative importance of habitat and climate. Our findings emphasize that land use is a major force in shaping terrestrial biodiversity, while highlighting its tight connection with climate. Considering functional, spatial, and temporal contexts is thus essential for building effective conservation strategies for biodiversity under global change. Climate and habitat jointly shape species distributions and biodiversity. The authors show that habitat is the main driver of boreal terrestrial biodiversity, while the relative roles of climate and habitat vary by region, year and species traits.

papers.title: On predictability of slip, rupture geometry, and speed of the 2025 M7.8 Mandalay, Myanmar, earthquake
papers.abstract: The 2025 M7.8 Mandalay earthquake ruptured ~480 km of the Sagaing Fault, producing one of the longest strike-slip events documented and impacting a vulnerable region. Here we combine remote sensing observations and numerical modeling to show that the subsurface fault geometry and slip distribution could be anticipated from pre-event observations. Along-strike variations in coseismic and interseismic deformation reveal a helix-shaped fault geometry. The average coseismic slip equals or exceeds the interseismic slip deficit, consistent with a minimally slip-predictable model. We generate an ensemble of 3D dynamic rupture models, constrained by the best-fit static slip model, then discriminate among them using independent space-geodetic, seismic, and near-field video observations. The preferred scenario begins bilaterally, then transitions to unilateral southward supershear propagation at depth, while shallow rupture remains subshear. These dynamics are shaped by localized stress heterogeneity and low fracture energy, characteristic of a structurally mature fault zone. Our approach can inform rupture scenarios in understudied regions. In this study, the authors combine geodetic, seismic and dynamic rupture models to examine key features of the 2025 Mandalay earthquake and assess to what extent pre-event data can be used to forecast characteristics of large damaging earthquakes.

papers.title: Small viruses reveal bidirectional evolution between HK97-fold viruses and encapsulins via procapsids
papers.abstract: The HK97-fold is an ancient, conserved protein structure that assembles protein shells, forming the capsids of Duplodnaviria viruses and prokaryotic biochemical compartments called encapsulsins. It has been proposed that encapsulins evolved from HK97-fold viruses. But the higher complexity of viral capsids represents a biophysical paradox in the evolution of HK97-fold protein shells. To resolve this problem, we hypothesize the existence of simpler HK97-fold viral capsids associated with smaller genomes than those of known HK97-fold viruses. Such small viral genomes are searched in environmental metagenomes across public databases, including IMG/M and MGnify. Using hidden Markov models and protein language models, we identify and characterize small viral genomes encoding HK97-fold proteins that exhibit molecular similarities to encapsulins yet lack portal and tail genes. The phylogenetic analyses of HK97-fold proteins reveal independent mixed groups of viruses and encapsulins, and structural analyses identify similarities between encapsulins and procapsids, the immature state of viral capsids. The observations support a bidirectional evolution between encapsulins and HK97-fold viruses enabled by the viral procapsid state. Using biophysical and genomic arguments, we introduce an evolutionary model of HK97-fold protein shells, predicting that they emerged as lower-symmetry biochemical compartments and that HK97-fold viral capsids may retain biochemical functions. In this study, mining environmental metagenomics data, the authors show that small HK97-fold-encoding viral genomes bridge Duplodnaviria viral capsids and cellular protein shells, revealing bidirectional evolution in which viral procapsids enable the transitions between viral and metabolic compartments.

papers.title: Vacancy-mediated ultrafast oxide-ion conduction in excess-oxygen Sillén oxybromides
papers.abstract: Solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) require electrolytes with high oxide-ion conductivity at low temperatures (200–400 °C) to reduce costs. Here, we report that Bi1.9Te0.1LaO4.05Br exhibits oxide-ion conductivity of 0.01 S cm⁻¹ at 233 °C within the “Norby gap” in dry atmospheres. This performance exceeds that of leading proton conductors, such as BaZr0.8Y0.2O2.9 and BaZr0.4Ce0.4Y0.1Yb0.1O2.9, as well as representative oxide-ion conductors, including yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ), LaGaO3-based phases (LSGM), and Bi2V0.7Sb0.3O5.5. Bi1.9Te0.1LaO4.05Br also exhibits negligible chemical expansion and high chemical stability under oxidizing, reducing, and CO2-containing atmospheres. The high conductivity is associated with a layered Sillén structure composed of Bi-containing triple fluorite-like slabs and Br layers, together with oxygen vacancies that enable vacancy-mediated oxide-ion migration. Despite the presence of excess oxide ions, oxide-ion transport predominantly occurs via a vacancy mechanism, as revealed by ab initio molecular dynamics simulations, static density functional theory calculations, and neutron diffraction analyses. These findings establish a design principle for high-performance oxide-ion conductors based on vacancy-mediated oxide-ion transport in excess-oxygen Bi-containing Sillén oxyhalides. The authors report Sillén oxybromides that enables fast oxide-ion transport at low temperatures. The study reveals that oxygen vacancies, rather than excess interstitial oxygen, mediate ion migration, providing a design strategy for high oxide-ion conductors.

papers.title: EphrinA4/EphA4 controls blood pressure via arterial sympathetic innervation in male mice
papers.abstract: The autonomic sympathetic nervous system innervates peripheral resistance arteries, thereby controlling arterial diameter and modulating blood supply to organs and arterial tone. Despite its fundamental role in blood flow regulation and cardiovascular adaptation to challenging situations, how sympathetic arterial innervation develops remains poorly understood. We here show that sympathetic arterial innervation is regulated by the axonal guidance molecule EphrinA4 in arterial Smooth Muscle Cells (SMCs), which repels sympathetic axons via the EphA4 receptor. Using the EphA4flox-THCRE mouse, we specifically inactivated EphA4 in sympathetic axons, inducing a loss of repulsion and increased sympathetic innervation of peripheral arteries throughout life. Functional consequences included a significant increase in arterial tone, including resistivity and vasoconstriction, associated with elevated systemic arterial blood pressure at rest and a marked increase during acute stress. These findings identify a pathway that negatively regulates sympathetic arterial innervation and could contribute to elevated systemic blood pressure in male mice. The sympathetic nervous system regulates blood pressure, but how arterial sympathetic innervation is established remains unclear. Here, the authors show that EphrinA4/EphA4 signalling limits sympathetic arterial innervation, thereby controlling vascular resistance and systemic blood pressure.

papers.title: Mapping cell-type-specific spatial gene programs uncovers tissue architecture and microenvironment organization
papers.abstract: The complex organization of tissues is shaped by the spatial arrangement of diverse cell types executing specialized gene programs. Cell-type-specific spatial gene programs (SGPs) are transcriptional modules that capture spatial expression co-variation within cell types. However, identifying these SGPs remains challenging in spatial transcriptomics. Here we present MacSGP, a scalable framework that integrates deep graph neural networks with probabilistic modeling to identify cell-type-specific SGPs through low-rank structures while accounting for cell type mixtures. Through comprehensive simulations and real data analyses spanning diverse tissues and technologies, we demonstrate that MacSGP effectively distinguishes cell-type-specific SGPs from cell-type marker gene expression patterns while uncovering tissue architecture and cellular microenvironments. In a mouse brain dataset, we identify replicable SGPs reflecting subregional neuronal specializations, with these genes significantly enriched for heritabilities associated with brain-related phenotypes. Across colorectal cancer datasets from various platforms, MacSGP identifies consistent SGPs that define distinct cellular niches within the tumor microenvironment. MacSGP identifies cell-type-specific spatial gene programs, capturing coordinated gene activity that varies across locations within cell types. This study dissects gene programs that reveal patterns of tissue organisation and cellular environments within brain and tumour contexts.

papers.title: Effects of time-restricted eating and supervised exercise on intrahepatic fat and cardiometabolic health in adults with obesity: the TEMPUS randomized controlled trial
papers.abstract: Lifestyle interventions targeting intrahepatic fat remain limited. We investigated whether 8-hour time-restricted eating (TRE), supervised exercise, or their combination reduced intrahepatic fat fraction (IHFF) more than usual care (UC; Mediterranean diet and physical activity education) and each other. This investigator-initiated, parallel-group randomized controlled trial was conducted in Granada, Spain. Participants were recruited from May 2023 to April 2024, and the trial was completed on 5 September 2025. Primary outcome assessors and statisticians were blinded to group allocation, whereas intervention personnel were not. All 187 randomized adults with obesity (50% women) were included in the primary intention-to-treat analysis: UC (n = 48), TRE (n = 46), Exercise (n = 47), and TRE+Exercise (n = 46). The primary outcome was change in IHFF measured by magnetic resonance imaging after 12 weeks. IHFF change did not differ with TRE (−0.4%; 95% CI, −2.0 to 1.2; P = 0.93), Exercise (−0.8%; −2.4 to 0.8; P = 0.54), or TRE+Exercise (−1.1%; −2.7 to 0.5; P = 0.28) compared with UC, nor among intervention groups. These findings do not support greater short-term IHFF reductions with TRE, exercise, or their combination than with UC or between intervention groups. Trial registration: NCT05897073. Time-restricted eating and structured exercise training have both been reported to reduce hepatic steatosis and improve cardiometabolic profile. Here the authors report a randomized controlled trial showing that in adults with obesity, time-restricted eating, supervised exercise, or their combination did not reduce intrahepatic fat more than usual care that consisted of Mediterranean diet and physical activity education.

papers.title: Observation of dark magnons in a van der Waals antiferromagnet/ferromagnet interface
papers.abstract: Magnons, the quanta of spin waves, offer a promising platform for low-power information processing owing to their charge-free propagation. Dark magnon modes, which are intrinsically decoupled from electromagnetic fields, exhibit high robustness against environmental perturbations and enable stealth-like propagation, making them highly attractive for magnonic applications. However, the excitation and detection of dark magnons in antiferromagnets remain highly challenging. Here, we report the direct observation of a magnon dark mode in a van der Waals antiferromagnet CrSBr interfaced with a ferromagnetic insulator YIG. In CrSBr, the canted (spin-flop) phase is nearly bypassed and the spin-flip phase has two magnon branches, one of which, the dark mode, has nearly zero net dynamic magnetization. We demonstrate that the interfacial exchange interaction enables the experimental detection of the magnon dark mode, while its presence is confirmed by the observation of coherent magnon-magnon coupling between YIG and CrSBr magnons. Micromagnetic simulations and a theoretical model reveal that the dark mode in CrSBr at the heterostructure interface hybridizes with YIG magnons via interfacial exchange interaction. Our results provide a new route for detecting dark magnon modes in antiferromagnets and open up opportunities for stealth-like magnon transport and hybrid magnonic devices based on van der Waals heterostructures. Dark magnons refer to magnons that are decoupled from electromagnetic fields, making them robust against external perturbations. This feature also makes dark magnons challenging to detect, but here, Yu, Wang, Hu, He, and coauthors succeed in directly observing the dark magnon mode in the van der Waals antiferromagnet CrSBr, by interfacing a thin flake of CrSBr with ferrimagnetic YIG.

papers.title: Lesion penetration predicts tuberculosis treatment shortening through a validated translational tool to de-risk development
papers.abstract: Anti-tuberculosis (TB) drugs must reach the disease site to be effective, but complex TB pathology limits drug distribution and efficacy, as bacteria in the necrotic center of lung cavities are difficult to access and kill. Our study generates the most comprehensive database of site-of-disease distribution for 24 drugs and drug candidates in a rabbit model of cavitary TB. We validate a lung lesion penetration model with clinical data and develop an integrated approach that combines microenvironment-specific pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics. Next, we simulate site-of-disease coverage of shortened regimens tested in major Phase 3 trials over the past decade, allowing direct comparisons with trial outcomes. We propose that regimens including at least two drugs achieving bactericidal concentrations in pulmonary cavities are more likely to meet primary clinical endpoints in patients with cavitary disease. Our translational platform constitutes a validated tool to support drug evaluation, smart regimen design, and de-risking of late-stage trials. In this study authors showcase a rabbit-to-human translational model that predicts anti-tuberculosis drug distribution in patient lesions and effectively discerns Phase 3 regimen outcomes, helping to design more robust strategies for regimen prioritization.

papers.title: A single-nucleus multiome map of the human cerebellum with Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias
papers.abstract: Although cerebellum is neuropathologically affected in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and AD-related dementia (ADRD), the cell type-specific genomic and epigenomic changes remain poorly understood. Here, we present single-nucleus multiome (RNA-seq and ATAC-seq) analysis of 103,861 nuclei isolated from both the cerebellum and frontal cortex of diseased individuals and cognitively healthy controls. We identify 431,834 significant peak-to-gene linkages across cell subtypes, revealing cis-regulatory elements linked to cell type-specific and disease-associated transcriptomic and regulatory network changes. Differential trajectory analysis pinpoints disease-associated genes in cerebellar granule cells, such as STMN1 and CLU. Integrating epigenomic, genetic, and three-dimensional genome data, we pinpoint two likely causal variants linked to SEZ6L2 in Purkinje cells and KANSL1 in granule cells. Through CRISPR interference in patient-derived cerebellar organoids, we show that silencing the variant-containing regulatory elements suppresses SEZ6L2 and KANSL1 expression, which perturbs neurodegeneration-associated gene programs. This cell type-specific regulatory landscape provides genomic and epigenomic insights into the pathological role of the cerebellum in AD/ADRD. Alzheimer’s disease affects multiple brain regions, but cerebellar cell type‑specific changes are poorly understood. Here, the authors use single‑nucleus multiomics to map disease‑associated regulatory alterations in cerebellar cell types and identify functional risk variants linked to neurodegeneration.

papers.title: A South Atlantic atmospheric river dipole as a key precursor of Amazon wildfires
papers.abstract: Wildfires in the Amazon have far-reaching climatic and ecological impacts, yet their predictability remains limited. Here we identify a large-scale atmospheric precursor of August–September Amazon wildfires: a June–July dipole mode of South Atlantic atmospheric rivers (ARs), characterized by suppressed AR activity in the north and enhanced activity in the south. This dipole is strongly linked to interannual variability in Amazon wildfire activity through land–atmosphere feedbacks associated with reduced precipitation and humidity, enhanced surface warming and solar radiation, and increased vegetation stress. We estimate that wildfire-related forest loss associated with this AR dipole mode accounts for approximately 26% of the observed interannual variability in total forest loss. Adding the South Atlantic AR dipole to predictors based on May–June sea surface temperature anomalies and June–July wildfire activity yields substantial predictive skill for August–September burned area (R² = 0.67). Climate model projections further indicate a future intensification of the South Atlantic AR dipole mode, implying increased wildfire-driven ecological degradation in the Amazon under continued warming. This study identifies a South Atlantic atmospheric river dipole as an early warning signal for Amazon wildfires, linking shifts in moisture transport to hotter, drier conditions and increased fire activity in the region.

papers.title: Whole-genome sequencing reveals inter-household networks of gut-colonising ESBL-producing Escherichia coli in two rural Malawian districts
papers.abstract: Infection with extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing Escherichia coli (ESBL-Ec) is a global health concern that disproportionately affects sub-Saharan Africa. Gut mucosal colonisation is thought to precede invasive infection. Understanding ESBL-Ec colonisation and transmission across communities is therefore essential. Here, we investigate the genomic epidemiology and spatial structure of 159 gut-colonising ESBL-Ec isolates from the faeces of 211 people in two rural Malawian villages using longitudinal sampling (2023–24), whole-genome sequencing and household mapping. Colonisation prevalence rose from 34.1% (95% CI: 27.8–41.0) to 54.2% (95% CI: 46.0–62.3) over one year. Isolates belonged to 33 sequence types (STs), most commonly ST38 and ST131, harbouring 46 distinct antimicrobial resistance gene types. Fifteen strains were identified in ≥3 households that were typically separated by short geographic distances ( < 400 m). Of 190 pairwise comparisons between same-strain isolates from different households sampled concurrently within villages, 88.9% differed by ≤10 single nucleotide polymorphisms, consistent with multi-household involvement in community transmission networks. Lineage-specific ST38 and ST131 network analyses linked rural isolates to urban Malawian isolates collected within the last decade. Our findings provide a transferable framework for inferring ESBL-Ec flow in community settings and highlight the need for One Health surveillance and improved sanitation infrastructure to limit transmission. The study examined the genomic epidemiology and spatial structure of antibiotic-resistant Escherichia coli in two villages in rural Malawi. Genomic analysis reveals sharing of almost identical isolates between people from nearby households.

papers.title: Universal crystallization kinetics of solution-processed semiconductors
papers.abstract: Heterogeneous crystallization kinetics critically govern the morphology and performance of solution-processed semiconductors, yet morphology control is often achieved through trial-and-error optimization. Quantitative understanding of crystallization is essential for precise morphology control but is limited by the simultaneous occurrence of heterogeneous nucleation and crystal growth. Here, a time-defined induced nucleation strategy has been developed to initiate crystallization at specific stages of solution processing. Systematic variation of nucleation timing reveals three distinct morphological regimes, whose emergence is explained by the concentration-dependent critical cluster radius in bulk, interfacial, and cusp environments. On this basis, a quantitative, dimensionless model is developed for heterogeneous crystallization kinetics across diverse processing conditions. The model demonstrates universality across perovskite and organic semiconductors. In situ studies reveal identical growth kinetics for induced and spontaneous nuclei, validating its generality. The resulting morphology control enables tuning of crystallinity and charge transport in solution-processed transistors. The work establishes a universal, experimentally validated model of heterogeneous nucleation and diffusion-controlled crystallization, predicting domain growth across diverse solution-processed semiconductors for efficient charge transport.

Interpretable and scalable spatial gene set activity analysis with GESSO uncovers functional tissue architecture
papers.abstract: Spatially resolved transcriptomics (SRT) measures gene expression within tissues. Existing methods that summarize the activity of functionally related genes often ignore relationships between neighboring locations and offer limited statistical testing, gene-level interpretation, or scalability. Here we present GESSO, a method that incorporates spatial information to estimate gene set activity within tissues, quantify how strongly each gene contributes to the resulting activity scores, and perform location-specific statistical tests for elevated pathway activity. In simulations and analyses of 13 datasets from five SRT platforms, GESSO better recovers known spatial patterns, provides well-calibrated statistical tests and interpretable gene-level contributions, and scales more efficiently than existing methods. Applications across tumor, embryonic, and lymphoid tissues reveal localized biological programs, including epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition at tumor-stroma interfaces, developmental signaling gradients, and coordinated immune pathways within germinal centers. Therefore, GESSO enables interpretable and scalable spatial mapping of gene set activity across diverse SRT technologies and biological settings. Spatial transcriptomics measures gene activity while preserving tissue structure. Here, the authors present GESSO, a scalable method that uses spatial information to quantify pathway activity and detect localized biological programs.

Rapid Renin Angiotensin Aldosterone System inhibitor optimisation in patients with chronic kidney disease and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction using potassium binder: a randomised, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial
papers.abstract: Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone inhibitors (RAASi) improve outcomes in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), but their use is often limited by hyperkalaemia in chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients. This double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised trial evaluated whether sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC) enables RAASi up-titration in HFrEF patients with CKD stages 3–5 and serum potassium of 5.0–5.5 mmol/L over 14 weeks. The primary binary outcome was defined as achieving the target dose of RAAS inhibition therapy without reaching hyperkalaemia (serum potassium ≥5.6 mmol/L) over 14 weeks or otherwise. Participants (n = 112) were randomised 1:1 to receive sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC) or placebo. The per-protocol (PP) analyses included 43 out of 53 (81%) in the SZC arm and 53 out of 59 participants (90%) in the placebo arm; the intention-to-treat (ITT) analyses included all 112. At the end of the trial, 24 of 43 participants (56%) in the SZC group achieved the target RAASi dose without developing hyperkalaemia compared with 15 of 53 patients (28%) in the placebo group (PP analysis, p = 0.006, ITT analysis, p = 0.007,). Participants in the SZC group were 3 times more likely to reach the target dose without reaching potassium 5.6 mmol/L (OR = 3.16; 95% CI 1.35–7.39; p = 0.008) than in the placebo group (ITT analysis). No significant differences in adverse events between the two groups were observed. SZC appears to safely support rapid RAASi optimisation in HFrEF patients with CKD. This trial was funded by AstraZeneca via Externally Sponsored Scientific Research grant ESR-19-20174. Trial Registration: Clinicaltrials.gov NCT05004363 and EudraCT number 2020-002946-18. In this randomized controlled trial, authors show that sodium zirconium cyclosilicate helped people with heart failure and chronic kidney disease reach recommended doses of key heart failure medicines, while reducing episodes of high blood potassium without added safety concerns.

papers.title: Replacing anaerobic fermentation with reverse β-oxidation enables growth-coupled evolution for enhanced fatty-alcohol production
papers.abstract: Engineering robust fermentation hosts remains a barrier to scalable biomanufacturing. In this work we replace canonical mixed-acid fermentation in Escherichia coli with a redox‑balanced reverse β‑oxidation (rBOX) pathway that produces medium‑chain fatty alcohols and is bioenergetically equivalent to ethanol fermentation. This synthetic fermentation restores anaerobic growth, tightly coupling fitness to product formation and enabling adaptive laboratory evolution that selects for mutations increasing rBOX flux. Evolved strains increase maximum productivity fourfold (110 ± 0.15 mg/L/hr) and titer more than threefold up to 4.0 ± 0.28 g/L compared to the unevolved strain. Proteomic analyses of evolved strains indicate differential expression of enzymes at key metabolic nodes and activation of latent genes with functions overlapping those of rBOX enzymes. These results establish redox-balanced growth coupling as a powerful tool for strain improvement and demonstrate rBOX as a practical synthetic fermentation pathway. Engineering robust fermentation hosts remains a barrier to scalable biomanufacturing. Here the authors link E. coli growth to fatty-alcohol production via the reverse β‑oxidation pathway, enabling self-improvement of alcohol production through bacterial evolution.

papers.title: High-performance p-type two-dimensional transistors enabled by weak disorder engineering
papers.abstract: High-performance field effect transistors (FETs) demand efficient charge doping alongside superior charge transport, which has proven challenging for p-type two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors. Conventional substitutional impurity doping often induces severe lattice damage and deep-level acceptor states within 2D semiconductors, severely deteriorating carrier transport. Here, we demonstrate weak disorder engineering (WD)—a mild two-step procedure involving sulfur vacancy creation and subsequent oxygen passivation—to simultaneously achieve efficient hole doping and exceptional hole transport in 2D semiconductors (e.g., MoS2 and WS2, collectively denoted as MS2). First-principles calculations reveal that oxygen-passivated sulfur vacancies suppress deep trap states while preserving near-valence-edge occupied states (NVOS), rationalizing the simultaneous hole doping and high hole mobility. Photoelectron spectroscopy indicates the Fermi level (EF) of WD-MS2 is shifted by ~ 240 meV toward the valence band. Structural and Raman characterizations show that the mild process preserves the lattice integrity of 2D semiconductors and introduces compressive strain. Owing to NVOS‑induced efficient hole doping, suppressed deep‑trap states, preserved lattice integrity, and engineered compressive strain, the p‑type 2D WD‑MS2 FETs deliver high hole mobilities, high on/off ratios, and large current densities. Furthermore, high‑gain, low‑power 2D Complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) inverters are constructed by integrating p‑type WD-WS2 FETs. Stable p-type doping of 2D semiconductors remains an important challenge towards the development of complementary 2D electronics. Here, the authors report a procedure involving sulphur vacancy creation and subsequent oxygen passivation to realize high-performance 2D MoS2 and WS2 p-type transistors.

papers.title: Evaluating the effects of population mobility on transmission during the COVID-19 pandemic
papers.abstract: Changes to community mobility during the COVID-19 pandemic, together with unprecedented availability of surveillance and mobility data, provide a unique opportunity to quantify the effect of mobility on respiratory infection transmission. We present a renewal model that incorporates epidemiological mechanisms influencing SARS-CoV-2 transmission along with a non-mechanistic scaling process. We compare models with and without mobility using epidemic data from 122 countries and quantify the influence of mobility through reductions in non-mechanistic scaling. In several countries, this non-mechanistic process closely tracks mobility trends and varies substantially less when mobility is incorporated. This is especially evident in Western Europe and North America, but not in several countries of West Africa and the Arabian Peninsula. Google and Facebook data produce similar findings, and parks is frequently assigned the lowest weight in the multi-location Google analysis. Mobility trends are strongly aligned with short-term transmission dynamics in many high-income settings, although between-country heterogeneity remains. Here the authors analyse mobility and COVID-19 data from 122 countries to examine how changes in movement affected virus transmission. They find that mobility data improved estimates of SARS-CoV-2 spread, particularly in Western Europe and North America.

papers.title: Surface carbonation governs olivine reactivity for rapid CO2 mineralization
papers.abstract: Ultramafic rocks are a global resource with vast potential for permanent CO2 mineralization. However, the origin of the striking reactivity difference between Ca- and Mg-bearing olivine remains poorly understood. Here we show that this difference arises not merely from the type of cation, but more fundamentally from how these cations modulate the oxygen reactivity. Nonbridging oxygens serve as the oxygen source for CO2 surface reactions, which in Ca-olivine reduce the Ca2+ dissolution barrier by 60% and accelerate ion release by six orders of magnitude. The calculated apparent dissolution rate constants reproduce the experimentally observed complete conversion of Ca-olivine within hours under 1 atm CO2. This multiscale framework reveals how surface reactions govern silicate carbonation and provides a predictive basis for modeling and engineering large-scale CO2 mineralization in both synthetic materials and basaltic reservoirs. The authors explain the role of reactivity contrast between Ca2+ and Mg2+ in olivine group silicates for CO2 removal and show that surface reactions with CO2 accelerate mineral dissolution, helping elucidate rapid, permanent carbon storage in rocks.

papers.title: Fever enhances host bacterial defence while limiting mitochondrial damage
papers.abstract: Infection triggers the fever response, but the response’s effect on antimicrobial peptide (AMP) function remains unknown. We discovered that human AMP LL-37 antibacterial activity is temperature-dependent and were curious as to why. Its temperature dependence is not an accident, as AMPs from other animals with different body temperatures have distinct temperature sensitivities. We find that AMP temperature sensitivities are tuned to animals’ body temperatures, and that for animals able to raise their body temperature, this is used to increase the AMP’s antibacterial efficacy. This effect reflects a balance between optimizing antibacterial killing while minimizing mitochondrial damage. In contrast, cold-blooded animals that are unable to raise their body temperature use a different strategy to avoid mitochondrial damage. Together, this study suggests that fever is beneficial for antimicrobial defense by raising AMP activity towards bacteria while reducing mitochondrial damage when pathogens are absent. Animals’ antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are evolutionarily tuned for their body temperatures, but vertebrates’ fever boosts their AMPs' killing ability. We show this reflects a trade-off to avoid mitochondrial damage.

papers.title: The claustrum contributes to working memory maintenance in mice
papers.abstract: Working memory (WM) enables the temporary maintenance and manipulation of sensory information to guide behavior, yet the neural circuits supporting this process remain incompletely defined. The claustrum is a highly interconnected brain structure positioned to integrate distributed cortical activity, but its contribution to WM has remained unclear. Here, we combined microendoscopic calcium imaging, chemogenetic and optogenetic manipulations in mice performing sensory-guided WM tasks to examine the role of the claustrum in WM. Claustrum neurons exhibited cue-evoked activity that persisted across delay periods and evolved dynamically over time, with population states retaining information about cue identity on single trials. Reducing claustrum excitability during encoding, delay maintenance, or target comparison similarly impaired WM performance across sensory modalities, without affecting sensory processing, motor output, arousal or inhibitory control. Together, these findings reveal an important causal contribution of the claustrum to WM maintenance. Neural mechanisms underlying working memory are not fully understood. Here authors show that in mice, the claustrum helps keep memories alive: its neurons sustain information during working memory, while disrupting claustrum activity impairs memory across sensory modalities.

papers.title: 11 million days of longitudinal Fitbit data reveal novel future health insights
papers.abstract: Wearable devices offer a scalable, objective measurement of physical activity, but most studies reduce these data to a single metric over 7-days. Here, we compare wearable-derived phenotyping approaches to understand their impact on activity-disease associations, analyzing 11 million days of Fitbit data from 29,303 All of Us Research Program participants. We derive four daily activity metrics (step count, peak 1-min cadence, peak 30-min cadence, and heart rate per step) across five time-windows (1-day, 1-week, 1-month, 6-months, 1-year), then run phenome-wide analyses across > 700 incident and >1,400 prevalent disease outcomes. Though all phenotypes are highly correlated, longer measurement windows yield stronger, more stable associations: 1-year step count was associated with 389 prevalent and 61 incident outcomes (versus 271 and 33 for 1-day step count) after Bonferroni-correction, including novel links to chronic pain syndrome and SARS-CoV-2. Differences between prevalent and incident associations suggest that activity metrics may act as both early markers of disease and risk factors. These findings highlight how large-scale, longitudinal wearable data can advance understanding of health and disease. Researchers linked four Fitbit-derived activity measures, from step count to cadence, to over 400 diseases in 29,303 adults, revealing new associations with conditions including chronic pain and autoimmune disorders.

papers.title: Fatty acid metabolism controls plasma membrane cholesterol accessibility via ATGL-dependent phospholipid remodeling
papers.abstract: Accessible cholesterol, the pool of membrane cholesterol with high chemical activity, regulates vital processes including vertebrate development and pathogen evasion. The mechanisms that govern plasma membrane (PM) cholesterol accessibility are incompletely understood. Using a genome-wide screen we find that acetyl-CoA carboxylase alpha (ACC1) loss causes a ~10-fold increase in PM accessible cholesterol in cells and a male mouse model. We demonstrate that reduced fatty acyl-CoA levels, achieved by targeting metabolic enzymes including ACC1, fatty acid synthase (FASN) or acyl-CoA synthetases long chain (ACSL1, 3 and 4), results in the activation of adipose triacylglycerol lipase (ATGL). ATGL activation elevates polyunsaturated diacylglycerols even in triacylglycerol-deficient backgrounds, suggesting that ATGL acts independently of triacylglycerol hydrolysis. These diacylglycerol species are utilized to generate polyunsaturated phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine, which raises PM fluidity and cholesterol accessibility. Conversely, ATGL inhibition rigidifies the PM, reducing PM accessible cholesterol. Increased PM fluidity impairs cholesterol transport, triggering SREBP2 activation. This study reveals a surprising link between fatty acid metabolism and cholesterol homeostasis, demonstrating how ATGL-dependent lipid remodeling tunes membrane fluidity to regulate intracellular cholesterol signaling. Accessible cholesterol levels in the plasma membrane are governed by complex regulatory processes. Here Wijesinghe et al. discover that fatty acid starvation activates ATGL to boost the production of polyunsaturated phospholipids which in turn increase the chemical activity of cholesterol and activates cholesterol biosynthesis.

papers.title: Origami-inspired folded-interlocked nanofiber aerogels for thermal insulation
papers.abstract: Nanofiber aerogels (NFAs) are promising thermal insulation materials for extreme environments; however, simultaneously achieving mechanical robustness, resilience, and low thermal conductivity remains a long-standing challenge in layered NFAs, where interlaminar instability often compromises structural reliability. Here we present an origami-inspired structural engineering strategy to construct folded-interlocked nanofiber aerogels. A folded-interlocked origami skeleton, integrated with a tailored interlaminar structure, introduces geometric confinement and fiber-mediated interlaminar toughening. As a result, the aerogels exhibit high compressive strength (548.02 kPa at 80% strain) and a near-zero Poisson’s ratio. Importantly, the robust interlaminar network enhances resistance to delamination, allowing the aerogels to sustain tensile deformation up to approximately 40% strain before interlaminar failure. Meanwhile, interlaminar-guided heat-flow redistribution yields a low axial thermal conductivity of 0.035 W m−1 K−1 and pronounced anisotropic thermal insulation. This work provides an architectural strategy for designing folded-interlocked NFAs for thermal protection in aerospace and other harsh environments. Chen et al. report origami-inspired folded-interlocked nanofiber aerogels that combine mechanical resilience with low axial thermal conductivity through geometric confinement and an interlaminar fibrous network.

papers.title: Global expansion of compound drought–heatwave risk
papers.abstract: The increasing frequency of compound drought and heatwave (CDHW) events poses a growing threat to water security, agriculture, and ecosystems. However, the evolution, expansion, and spatial reorganization of CDHW hotspots across global land regions remain largely unexplored. Here we track more than 2500 CDHW events using a three-dimensional connected-component (CC3D) labeling approach and show that CDHWs, often treated as spatially stationary extremes, exhibit systematic displacement over time. Larger and longer-lasting events tend to travel farther and faster, expanding the spatial footprint of compound heat and moisture stress. Most contiguous events persist for 6–12 days, displace by up to ~500 km, and reach peak daily spatial extents of 2–5 × 10⁵ km². Migration is strongest in the Northern Hemisphere mid-latitudes and is predominantly eastward. We identify emerging hotspots of increasing CDHW migration potential across the European Plains, western North America, the Amazon, the West African Sahel, Central Asia, and northern Australia. These shifts are linked to evolving large-scale atmospheric circulation and are reinforced by downstream drying through reduced moisture transport and strengthened land–atmosphere coupling. Increasing CDHW migration potential over agricultural landscapes may expand exposure to compound heat and moisture stress, particularly in grazing-dependent regions vulnerable to pastureland-to-scrubland transitions. This study shows that compound drought-heatwave events exhibit systematic displacement over time, with larger and longer-lasting events tending to travel farther and faster, especially in the Northern Hemisphere mid-latitudes, with a dominant eastward direction.

papers.title: A swing-type solid-state host–guest system enabling spontaneous adsorption–desorption cycling
papers.abstract: Macrocycle-based solid-state adsorbents offer molecularly precise platforms for the selective capture of volatile organic molecules. However, regeneration of these materials commonly relies on thermal or solvent stimulation, limiting energy efficiency and the recovery of adsorbed molecules. Developing solid-state adsorption systems that enable reversible guest release under mild conditions remains challenging, particularly for structurally similar volatile molecules. Here we show a swing-type solid-state host–guest system based on a fluorinated pillar[5]arene that enables reversible adsorption–desorption cycling of volatile methylpyridines at ambient temperature without heat or solvent stimulation. Competitive binding of nonvolatile electron-deficient acceptors drives the transformation of volatile guest inclusion phases into charge-transfer phases, releasing the volatile guests and producing a visible chromic response. Re-exposure to excess volatile vapor reverses the phase transformation, with the direction and extent of switching influenced by the relative stability of the competing host–guest assemblies and further modulated by guest size and lattice accessibility. These findings highlight an appropriate degree of thermodynamic proximity between competing solid-state complexes as an important design consideration for reversible guest exchange. More broadly, this strategy provides a route to adaptive macrocycle-based adsorbents for low-energy, visually traceable adsorption–desorption processes. Solid-state host–guest complexes derived from macrocycles provide a direct pathway from molecular recognition to adaptive functional materials, but desorption typically requires thermal activation. Here, the authors report a solid-state host–guest system with a swing-type adsorption–desorption cycle without heat or solvent stimulation.

papers.title: Evolutionary remodeling of the ventral retina enables aerial vision in the four-eyed fish Anableps anableps
papers.abstract: The emergence of evolutionary novelties remains a central challenge in biology, particularly for complex organs such as the vertebrate eye. Here, we use the four-eyed fish Anableps anableps to investigate adaptation to simultaneous aerial and aquatic vision. Single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomics reveal that the ventral retina, which processes aerial light, is developmentally expanded and exhibits region-specific opsin expression. Ventral PR1 cones express opn1mw2 rather than the longer-wavelength-sensitive opn1lw paralogs expressed dorsally. Machine-learning predictions indicate that Opn1mw2 is red-shifted relative to Opn1mw1 but remains blue-shifted relative to dorsal Opn1lw pigments. Dorsal-ventral patterning markers further reveal an overrepresentation of ventral retinal identities. Comparative spatial profiling of developing and adult Anableps and killifish indicates dorsal displacement of the retinal boundary, producing a proportionally larger ventral domain. Thus, Anableps evolved aerial vision through developmental expansion of the ventral retina and regional reconfiguration of opsin expression within conserved cone subtypes. Using single-nucleus RNA-sequencing and spatial transcriptomics, researchers showed the four-eyed fish Anableps evolved aerial vision through developmental expansion of its ventral retina and regional opsin gene tuning.

papers.title: Genome-reduced Aridivitia evolved predation to thrive in Earth’s oligotrophic depths
papers.abstract: Deep soils represent one of Earth’s largest yet most enigmatic microbial habitats, where survival strategies under extreme oligotrophy remain poorly understood. Here, we report the Aridivitia group, a globally distributed bacterial lineage enriched in oligotrophic soils and thriving down to 22 m depth across sites in the United States and China. Despite its genome reduction (average size ~2.9 Mb), Aridivitia exhibits high metabolic flexibility in utilizing diverse carbon and energy sources. Cellular, genomic, and metatranscriptomic evidence, including small cell and genome sizes, host-associated metabolism, and the active expression of attachment- and attack-associated surface structures such as Tad pili and pore-forming toxins, indicate a predatory lifestyle in Aridivitia. Ancestral genome reconstruction reveals that Aridivitia originated as free-living mixotrophs, but subsequently lost the ability to fix carbon as they evolved a predatory lifestyle. Collectively, Aridivitia exemplifies a unique evolutionary strategy that reconciles genome reduction with functional versatility, expanding our understanding of microbial adaptation and evolution at the energetic limits of life. This study reveals that the uncultivated bacterial group Aridivitia thrives in oligotrophic deep soils, with reduced genomes, metabolic flexibility, and an evolutionary transition from free-living mixotrophy to predation.

LoL-align: sensitive and fast probabilistic protein structure alignment
papers.abstract: The ubiquitous availability of protein structures permits replacing sequence alignment with more accurate and sensitive structure alignment algorithms. LoL-align maximizes a local log-odds score for proteins to be homologous, given their intra-protein Cα − Cα distances. Here we show that LoL-align is markedly more sensitive in detecting remote homologs than TM-align and Dali on single- and multidomain benchmarks and achieves better alignment quality at 5–20 × their speed. LoL-align is fully integrated into Foldseek. LoL-align is a probabilistic, distance-based protein structure alignment algorithm that iteratively optimizes a local log-odds score, achieving higher sensitivity for remote homologs and better alignment quality than available methods.

papers.title: MassNet: billion-scale AI-ready mass spectral corpus empowering scalable deep learning in proteomics
papers.abstract: Here we present MassNet, inspired by large-scale data corpora of text and images; MassNet is an artificial intelligence (AI)-ready data corpus for mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics. The corpus contains 1.5 billion tandem MS spectra from high-quality data-dependent acquisition (DDA) MS data across 35 species. Approximately 1.7 million peptide precursors are from human samples. We further present an AI-ready DDA data format called Mass Spectrometry DDA Tensor (MSDT) for compact and standardized storage, curation and reuse of data from multiple sources, which can be optionally converted to a Lightning Memory-Mapped Database for accelerated input/output in deep learning. On the basis of MassNet, we develop XuanjiNovo, a nonautoregressive transformer model that leverages a curriculum learning strategy for de novo peptide sequencing. XuanjiNovo achieves 38.35–143.57% improvement over state-of-the-art methods on human Astral data. MassNet also supports additional downstream tasks, including retention time prediction and PSM rescoring. MassNet represents a foundational MS-based proteomics data resource, marking a critical milestone for AI proteomics research. This Article presents MassNet, a large-scale AI-ready corpus of 1.5 billion MS/MS spectra spanning 35 species, paired with a standardized storage format called Mass Spectrometry DDA Tensor (MSDT). Built on this resource, XuanjiNovo is a nonautoregressive transformer for de novo peptide sequencing that substantially outperforms previous methods.

Compartment-specific PPARδ activity controls the outcome of cancer–immune cell competition and immunotherapy efficacy
papers.abstract: Most patients with solid tumors fail to sustain antitumor immunity, in part because immune cells cannot outcompete cancer cells inside the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Here, we show the lipid-sensing transcription factor PPARδ is a compartment-specific determinant of cancer–immune fitness balance and immunotherapy efficacy. Activating PPARδ in cancer cells promotes their growth and impairs antitumor immunity, whereas activating it in immune cells drives tumor suppression and overrides tumor-promoting effects of cancer-intrinsic activation. Mechanistically, PPARδ enhances CD8+ T cell fitness against cancer through effector-associated chromatin remodeling and Cpt1a-mediated fatty acid oxidation. Therapeutically, PPARδ-activated CD8+ T cells sensitize immunotherapy-resistant microsatellite stable metastatic colorectal cancer to checkpoint blockade in mice, and pharmacological or genetic PPARδ activation enhances human chimeric antigen receptor T cell function. These findings identify compartment-specific PPARδ activity as a targetable driver of immune cell fitness that can be harnessed to improve outcomes in immunotherapy-resistant tumors. Cancer cells and immune cells compete for metabolic fitness within the tumor microenvironment. Here the authors show that PPARδ is instrumental in this battle and that activating it in immune cells can boost immunotherapy in resistant mouse tumors and improve human chimeric antigen receptor T cells.

papers.title: Evidence for maternal autoantibodies in the pathogenesis of preterm birth
papers.abstract: Preterm birth is associated with breakdown of maternal–fetal tolerance and remains the leading cause of global mortality in young children. However, the role of self-reactive antibodies has been limited to a handful of pathogenic allo- and autoantibodies linked to pregnancy complications. Here we identify a shared autoreactive signature of pregnancy in pregnant sera (n = 2,719) relative to never-pregnant controls (n = 130), using proteome-wide autoantibody profiling. Across eight human pregnancy cohorts, we define autoreactivities associated with preterm birth by comparing preterm (n = 688) and term (n = 1,505) pregnancies. Within the signature, antibodies to IL1 receptor antagonist (IL1RA) induce resorption, inflammation and vascular malperfusion in pregnant mice. IL1RA localizes to placental endothelial adherens junctions, suggesting a role in vascular integrity. These findings identify a term pregnancy humoral immune program and shared changes preceding preterm delivery, including anti-IL1RA, which may have direct pathogenic consequences. Preterm labor is linked to breakdown of maternal–fetal tolerance. Rackaityte et al. report that some pregnant mothers harbor maternal autoantibodies, including those against IL-1 receptor antagonist, that may contribute to preterm delivery.

SpatialZoomer: multi-scale feature analysis of spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Single-cell resolution spatial transcriptomics provides a great opportunity to explore the complex cellular contents in different tissues. Here we introduce SpatialZoomer, a spectral graph-based method that applies a set of low-pass filters to efficiently extract spatial molecular features from spatial transcriptomics data at multiple resolutions or scales, including the single cell scale, the niche scale with dozens of closely interacting cells and the domain scale with spatially organized cell contents. The corresponding critical scales can be automatically identified by partitioning a cross-scale similarity map. Results show that SpatialZoomer can identify disease-progression signals at specific scales in Alzheimer’s disease and spatial context-dependent cell subtypes in tumour microenvironment. The extracted multi-scale features also uncovered spatially heterogeneous niches in cancer. SpatialZoomer achieves comparable or superior performance to existing methods for single-scale tasks, and it also has the advantages of high computational efficiency and low hardware requirements. SpatialZoomer is a spectral graph-based method for analysing spatial transcriptomics data across scales, from single cells to spatially organized domains. The demonstrations highlight the power of studying heterogeneous diseased tissues across scales.

papers.title: From pandemic response to a global scientific network via Tissue Talks
Mitochondrial carbonic anhydrase–VB inhibition rescues brain endothelial stress and memory in Alzheimer’s disease models
papers.abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a devastating neurodegenerative disorder with no effective cure, characterized by the cerebral parenchymal and vascular accumulation of aggregated amyloid-β (Aβ) and hyperphosphorylated tau. Cerebrovascular and mitochondria dysfunction are early causal events in the progression of AD. Previous studies support that inhibiting carbonic anhydrases (CAs) may prevent mitochondrial and cerebrovascular dysfunction in AD models. Here, we selectively target the mitochondrial CA isoform CA-VB by pharmacological and genetic manipulation in human cerebral microvascular endothelial cells (hCMEC), and we confirm the protective effects of the CA-V inhibitor in AD mice. CA-V inhibition and CA-VB KO prevent Aβ induced mitochondria-mediated endothelial apoptosis, loss of barrier resistance, and hCMEC inflammatory activation. Strikingly, CA-V inhibition also mitigates caspase activation and endothelial cell activation in the brains of 3xTg AD mice, resulting in preserved memory function. Our results demonstrate that selective CA-V inhibition is an effective and promising strategy against AD-mediated cerebrovascular pathology, neuroinflammation and cognitive impairment.
